## Volume front matter

### Series title page

*The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of All the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers Who Flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reprint of All the Monuments of Catholic Tradition That Have Survived from the First Twelve Centuries of the Church, According to the Most Accurate Editions, Carefully Corrected by Comparison with One Another and with Several Manuscripts; Continuously Enriched with Dissertations, Commentaries, and Variant Readings; Expanded by All Works Discovered after the Extensive Editions Published during the Last Three Centuries Had Been Completed; Furnished with Particular Analytical Indexes following each individual volume or author of any importance; Adorned with Chapters Properly Arranged within the Text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margins of the individual pages and indicating the subject matter below; Enlarged with works that are doubtful or apocryphal, and with others possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; Enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any of the Fathers has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Holy Scripture, from which it may readily be discovered which Fathers commented on the texts of the individual books of Scripture and in which passages of their works they did so.*

*The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others when the following matters are taken into consideration: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library brings together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.*

## Second Series

In this series appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.

Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

The *Patrologia* has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition costs 1,200 francs; the Greek-Latin edition 1,800 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# In the year of the Lord 868. Ratramnus, monk of Corbie

[Col. 0009]

## Historical notice concerning Ratramnus

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina medii et infimae aetatis*, volume II.)

[Col. 0009A] Bertramus in the editions of Sigebert of Gembloux, chapter 95, and in Trithemius, chapter 274, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and book II, chapter 48, *On Illustrious Benedictines*, and elsewhere; also in the earliest editions of the book *On the Lord’s Supper*, Bertramus. But he should more correctly be called Ratramnus, by which name he appears in the Cellotian Anonymous; in Flodoard, III.15; in Hincmar, *On Predestination*, chapter 5, volume I, page 26, and *Against Gotteschalcus*, pages 413, 438, 450; in Lupus of Ferrières, letter 79; in the Anonymous of Melk, chapter 46; and in the manuscripts of Sigebert at Gembloux and Val-Dieu, as well as in the manuscripts of the books that he himself composed and in other editions.

It is agreed, on the testimony of Hincmar, that he was a monk of Corbie belonging to the Benedictine order. He is suspected to have been a Gaul by nationality, and there is no doubt that he served as provost of the monastery of Orbais in the diocese of Soissons in Gaul. Ordered by Charles the Bald—king of Gaul from the year 840, and emperor from 25 December 875 to 6 October 877—to state his views concerning the Blood and Body of Christ, he wrote that celebrated [Col. 0009B] booklet *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, in which, long before Berengar, he clearly refutes the opinion of Paschasius Radbertus and the doctrine of transubstantiation.

[Note: [Col. 0009C] An old anonymous writer *On the Eucharist*, edited with notes by Louis Cellot, S.J., in 1655; Mabillon, *Benedictine Age IV*, part II, preface, page 45, no. 83, and page 80 of the *German Journey*; Colomesius, *Works*, page 668 and following, where he also discusses other manuscripts.]

He adds to his arguments testimonies of the doctors of the Latin Church drawn from Holy Scripture and sound reason:

[Note: [Col. 0009C] For this reason John Lampadius entitled Ratramnus’s work *The Agreement of the Church concerning the Words of the Holy Supper*.]

Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Isidore, and Fulgentius, as well as the words customarily spoken during the celebration of the Holy Supper from the Sacramentary of Gregory the Great.

Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0009C] Jacobus Basnage, *Dogmatic Ecclesiastical History*, which he published in French, XVI.7, volume II, page 933; and the chancellor of Tübingen, Dr. Christoph Matthaeus Pfaff, *On the Holy Eucharist against Louis Roger*, page 27 and following.] admits that he found the name Ratramnus at the beginning and end of the book in a manuscript from Lobbes dating from the year 800. It also appears in another no less ancient manuscript from Salem, and, before the work was published in 1532, John Fisher, bishop of Rochester, praised Ratramnus in the preface to his books *On the Truth of the Body and Blood of Christ against Oecolampadius*, Cologne, 1527, among Catholic writers on that subject.

It first appeared at Cologne in 1532, octavo, from the press of John Prael, under the title: *Of Bertram the Priest, to the Emperor Charles the Great*, and with a preface by Leo Judae, the translator. [Note: [Col. 0009C] Abraham Ruchat, volume IV of the *History of the Reformation of Switzerland*.] It was published in German at Zurich in the same year, 1532. Thereafter it was published again in Latin at Geneva in 1541, octavo; in *Microbretus* in 1550; and in the first edition of the *Orthodoxographi* in 1555. It appeared together with Paschasius Radbertus at Cologne in 1551, octavo; in the minor works of William Feugercius at Leiden in 1579, octavo; in the *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, edited by Simon Goulart, Geneva, 1608, folio; and with notes by John Lampadius, Bremen, 1614, octavo.

Passing over other editions noted by Hendreich on page 543, after French translations in 1550, 1558, 1560, 1619, and 1653, it was also published in Latin and French, translated by Peter Allix, Paris, 1672, quarto; and from the French translation of Jacob Boileau, with preface and notes, Paris, 1686, duodecimo.

[Note: [Col. 0009C] Du Pin, volume XIX of the *Ecclesiastical Library*, page 68; *Acta Eruditorum*, 1687, page 43; *New Republic of Letters*, page 125.]

It was also published in Latin with defenses against John Hardouin—who had assigned Ratramnus to the heretics—in 1712, duodecimo.

[Note: [Col. 0010C] In the *Dissertation on the Sacrament of the Altar*, pages 165, 193.]

[Note: [Col. 0010C] *Journal des Savants*, 1712, page 646.]

Likewise, after Dutch translations at Rotterdam in 1610 and Utrecht in 1620, and English translations,

[Note: [Col. 0010C] Cave testifies that several English editions exist; he writes learnedly about this author under the year 840. Among other things, he notes that Aelfric repeated much of Ratramnus word for word in his Easter homily, as Hopkins also demonstrated plainly.]

and together with the English translation of the most distinguished William Hopkins, canon of Worcester, London, 1686, duodecimo, and 1688, octavo,

[Note: [Col. 0010C] Anthony Wood, *Athenae Oxonienses*, volume III, page 1074.]

with learned dissertations on Ratramnus and his teaching directed against Boileau and other teachers of the Roman Church. From this English edition, with those dissertations also translated into French, came the booklet of Ratramnus in Latin and French, Amsterdam, 1717, octavo.

Although John Scotus also wrote, at the command of the same Charles the Bald, a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* expressing the same opinion, a book greatly approved by Berengar—who is listed among the saints in certain martyrologies on 10 November—it is nevertheless more probable that the book was lost when Berengar, having been forced to condemn it at the Council of Vercelli in 1050, was forced to burn it at the Council of Rome in 1059, rather than that, contrary to the evidence of so many manuscripts, contrary to the differing styles of writing found in Scotus’s works, and contrary to the other arguments put forward by learned men, the book we possess should be taken away from this Ratramnus and attributed to Scotus.

[Note: [Col. 0010C] For example, by Peter de Marca, *Letter to D’Achery*, before volume II of the *Spicilegium*, and in the new edition, volume III, page 852; by Anselm Paris in a dissertation against Allix, chapter 5, volume IV of *The Perpetuity of the Faith*, part II, page 198 and following; by John Hardouin, etc. I omit the scarcely credible conjectures of those who invent another author, whether much earlier, such as Prosper, or two hundred years later, such as Berengar himself or one of his followers.]

The Roman, Tridentine, Spanish,

[Col. 0011A] Quiroga’s,

and Belgian indexes count it among prohibited writings; the Belgian index, however, judges that it should be assisted by a translation. See Usher, *On the Succession of the Churches*, page 48 and following, and Daille, *On the Use of the Fathers*, page 111 and following.

Thus Laurentius Latinius, in volume I of the *Sacred and Profane Library*, page 110, testifies that he had read Ratramnus’s book placed after Paschasius’s book on the same subject:

“Having forgotten that it was marked in the Index under the name of heresy, after recognizing my error I threw away the booklet, and arranged for myself to be absolved by the most reverend cardinal of Worms, the chief penitentiary.”

Ratramnus also wrote for the same Charles the Bald two books *On Predestination*, in which he agrees with Gotteschalcus and was attacked by Hincmar and others. Gilbert Manguin published them among the writers of the ninth century who wrote on Predestination and Grace, Paris, 1650, quarto; from this they were reprinted in volume XV of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, page 442. Compare the *History of Gotteschalcus* by Usher and Cellot.

“Against the Errors of the Greeks Who Defame the Roman Church,” four books addressed to Nicholas I, Roman pontiff, principally directed against the letters of Photius; in the first three books he treats in full of the procession of the Holy Spirit. D’Achery published them in volume II of the *Spicilegium* (volume I of the new edition, page 63).

“On the Birth of the Virgin, or on the Nativity of Christ,” which occurred in the ordinary and natural manner, without the Virgin’s womb being closed. Paschasius Radbertus opposed two booklets on the birth of the Virgin in defense of the contrary position.

[Col. 0012A] Ratramnus’s words in the preface refer to Paschasius: “I beg your Reverence not to disdain to respond to the suggestion of our smallness.” On that controversy, see Blessed Ittigius, *On the Libraries of the Fathers*, page 169, and the authors cited by Mabillon, *Benedictine Age IV*, part II, preface, chapter 3, and volume II of the *Benedictine Annals* under the year 844, page 652 and following, as well as Natalis Alexander, *Ninth and Tenth Centuries*, part II, dissertation 13.

A letter to Rimbert the priest *On the Cynocephali*, arguing that they should not be counted among the descendants of Adam. It was published from a manuscript of the Paulina Library at Leipzig by the learned Gabriel Dumont in a dissertation *On the Cynocephali*, inserted in volume VI of the *Critical History of the Literary Republic of Masson*, published in French at Amsterdam in 1714, duodecimo, pages 188–196.

A book *On the Soul*, arguing that there is not one soul common to all human beings, as Marianus Scotus had asserted on the basis of a passage from Augustine’s *On the Quantity of the Soul*. This book, which Mabillon possessed and intended to publish, also exists in manuscript in various libraries of England.

[Col. 0012B] From Hincmar’s book *On the One and Not Threefold Deity*, volume I of his works, pages 413 and 438, it is clear that Ratramnus defended, together with Gotteschalcus, and confirmed with the words of Hilary and Augustine, the wording of the ancient hymn: “We beseech you, Triune and One Deity.” Hincmar preferred instead: “You, Supreme Deity.” The book in which Ratramnus did this has not come down to us.

[Col. 0011]

# Two books of Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, on the predestination of God, addressed to King Charles the Bald

(Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum, volume XV.)

## Testimonies of ancient authors concerning these books of Ratramnus

[Col. 0011C] Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, *On Predestination*, addressed to King Charles, chapter 5:

“Ratramnus, nevertheless, a monk of the monastery of Corbie, presented two booklets that you had given us to examine, composed with the intention of showing that, just as the elect are predestined by God to life, so also the reprobate are predestined by God to death.”

Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 95:

“Bertramus wrote a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, and, addressed to Charles, a book *On Predestination*.”

John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

“Bertramus, priest and monk, very well versed in the divine Scriptures [Col. 0012C] and exceptionally learned in books of secular disciplines, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, no less notable in life than in doctrine, wrote many excellent minor works, of which only a few have come to my knowledge. To Charles the king, brother of the emperor Lothair, he wrote a commendable work:

*On Predestination*, book I;

*On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, book I.

He flourished in the time of the emperor Lothair, in the year 830.”

The same Trithemius, in the *Hirsau Chronicle*:

“Bertramus, a monk most learned in every branch of literature, wrote to King Charles on Predestination. Likewise, he wrote *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, along with many other works that have not come to the knowledge of our reading.”

# Author’s preface

[Col. 0013]

[Col. 0013A] To the glorious and most excellent prince Charles: Ratramnus.

Since courage and wisdom illuminate royal majesty—courage, namely, by which it conquers its adversaries, and wisdom, by which it orders the entire body of the commonwealth—these two qualities raise your magnificence still more splendidly: you seek out the secrets of heavenly wisdom and burn with love of religion.

These qualities make you comparable to the princes of former times, who subdued the necks of their enemies by the power of their virtues and, through the radiance of wisdom and the honor of religion, became friends of God. I mean David and Solomon, Hezekiah and Josiah. Just as they devoted themselves to being occupied with the mysteries of divine wisdom, so their fame is immortal and shines adorned with the rewards of eternal blessedness.

Having become their imitators, you order the condition of your commonwealth with admirable prudence, subdue the strength of your enemies with powerful courage, investigate the wisdom of heavenly mysteries with an ineffable love of religion, and labor with every vigilance to ensure that the state of the Catholic faith remains inviolate.

This devotion and these marks of virtue are present in you not as foreign qualities acquired through the study of labor, but as though they were natural. For your father and grandfather, the Augusti of glorious memory, shone forth so greatly in the arms of virtue, the splendor of wisdom, and the elevation of religion that, through the magnificence of their virtues, they both showed the kings who preceded them to be incomparable and left examples of imitation to those who came after them.

From them you derive the origin of your blood, and from both parents you possess both virtue and religion.

[Col. 0013C] But if we wish to examine more deeply the lineage of your nobility, we see that the branches of your ancestry have always adorned the glory of secular power with the honor of religion. Hence it is evident that you possess distinction not only through royal dignity but also through devotion to religion inherited from a holy stock.

Because of your love for this religion, your Majesty has deigned to join yourself to my humility, so that I might send you, concerning a question recently raised but long ago settled by the holy Fathers, chapters collected from their books, by which it might become clearer to you how they judged the matter.

Since you investigate everything carefully and arrange everything diligently, you proceed in this question also—whose depth causes many people to become confused—with great diligence and moderation, so that, learning the judgments of the saints concerning it, you may deliberate what your prudence ought afterward to do.

I, however, desiring to obey your greatness, have endeavored to gather from the judgments of Catholic teachers those things which, because of their brevity, will not burden you amid your occupations, and which, because of the fullness of their judgments, will not conceal the truth of the matter.

And because the mystery of this question—that is, of predestination—is extremely profound, I have decided first to present testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning the divine disposition, and afterward to proceed to an account of predestination. Thus, once it has been proved that everything occurring in the world is governed by the secrets of divine administration, an easier path of understanding may open toward the manifestation of predestination.

In this work, just as I desire to carry out the command of your greatness, so I ask your clemency to be both examiner and judge of what I say. If anything has been said well, may it be confirmed by your judgment; but if anything has appeared otherwise to you, may it be refuted by you. And, because of the clemency of your piety, may your judgment of correction not be concealed from me, nor may what I have brought forward come before the gaze of many unless your wisdom has approved [Col. 0014C] that it has been rightly stated.

Do not attribute to rash presumption the fact that I dare to ask these things of you, but to humility and modesty, which not only fear public examination on account of errors but also hesitate to have even well-spoken words made public.

# Book One: On the divine disposition

[Col. 0013]

[Col. 0013C] But now let us come to the subject at hand. No one who believes rightly in God doubts that his presence contains heaven and earth and that the world is governed by divine providence. Just as nothing is hidden from his wisdom, so his disposition directs and governs everything.

For just as no creature is hidden from his sight, so he knows the actions and thoughts of human beings, because, according to the authority of Holy Scripture:

“There is no creature invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes; and he who knows all things disposes all things” (Heb. 4).

Hence the Book of Wisdom says:

“For in his hand are both we and our words, and all wisdom, and the knowledge of works, and discipline. For he himself gave me true knowledge of the things that exist, so that I might know the arrangement of the world, the power of the elements, the beginning and the end and the middle of times, the changes of the turning points, the conclusions of times, the alterations of customs, and the divisions of times; the course of the year and the arrangements of the stars, the force of winds and the thoughts of human beings, the differences of plants and the powers of roots. Whatever things are hidden and unforeseen, I learned; for the craftsman of all things taught me wisdom” (Wis. 7).

It is clear that these words are not spoken concerning any mortal person, but only concerning the mediator between God and human beings. Insofar as he is the power and wisdom of God the Father, and insofar as he became human, he received knowledge and understanding of all things.

For, according to the testimony of the Gospel, as one who exists full of grace and truth, just as, by becoming human, he was bounded by a body, so, because the Word became flesh, he knew all things whatsoever that are hidden and unforeseen. He sees all things and comprehends all intelligible spirits; and just as he knows all things with the Father, so he disposes all things with him.

Concerning this Wisdom, the same book subsequently says:

“But because of her purity she reaches everywhere” (ibid.);

and again:

“She reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8).

Therefore, since he knows all things and encloses, contains, and disposes all things, the past, present, and future are by no means hidden from him, just as he said above, because he gave human beings the ability to know “the beginning, the middle, and the end of times.”

If a human being has obtained this through God’s gift, how much more does the one who grants these things know them? Therefore, because he knows the past, the present, and the future, he administers and disposes them. And he who knows “the thoughts of human beings” certainly disposes them—not only the good thoughts but also the evil.

Although the perverse thoughts of human beings do not come from God, they nevertheless do not escape his thought or transgress the disposition of his will. Thus he is both the author and arranger of good thoughts, but only the arranger, not the author, of evil thoughts, because “he reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly.”

Therefore, just as he knows these things, so he also knew the number of the elect and of the reprobate. And just as he is the arranger of all things, so also is he their arranger. He knows and disposes not only the deeds they perform in the present life but also their ends.

As for how he deals with each person, he does not conceive it through a new plan or a new thought. Rather, in eternity, all the dispositions of his plan were established concerning how these things would occur through the succession of times, because, as the Apostle says, “with God there is no change or shadow caused by turning.”

For just as he is eternal, so he knows all things eternally; and just as he comprehends all things, so, by the light of his knowledge, he beholds at a single glance whatever exists, whatever has existed, and whatever will exist.

And just as nothing is new with him, so, in his eternal disposition, it is immovably fixed how the order of creatures will unfold through the succession of times. In this disposition of eternity he knew the end of the elect and the end of the reprobate, and what was to be done with each was immutably determined by an eternal plan.

This disposition of the eternal plan is the predestination of God’s works. Through this predestination he disposes the elect for the kingdom and the reprobate for punishments.

From this disposition of God, Blessed Augustine speaks in the book *On Free Choice* (chapter 20), demonstrating that God inclines the wills of all people—not only the good but also the wicked—wherever he wishes, and that they serve his disposition. He says:

> Divine Scripture, if examined carefully, shows that not only the good wills of human beings—which he himself makes out of evil wills, and, once made good by him, directs toward good deeds and eternal life—but also those wills that preserve the creature of the world are so subject to God’s power that he causes them to be inclined wherever and whenever he wishes: either toward benefits to be bestowed upon some, or toward punishments to be inflicted upon others, as he himself judges—indeed, by a most hidden judgment [Col. 0016B], but without any doubt a most just one.
>
> For we find that some sins are also punishments for other sins, as are those who, the Apostle says, are “vessels of wrath, perfected for destruction” (Rom. IX, 22); such was the hardening of Pharaoh, of which it is said that it occurred “to show God’s power in him” (Exod. VII, 3); and such was the flight of the Israelites from the face of their enemies in the city of Ai (Josh. VII, 4–5). Fear had been produced in their minds so that they would flee; and this happened so that sin might be punished in the manner in which it ought to be punished. Hence the Lord said to Joshua: “The children of Israel will not be able to stand before the face of their enemies” (ibid., 12).
>
> What does “they will not be able to stand” mean? Why did they not stand by free choice, but flee with their wills thrown into confusion by fear, unless it is because [Col. 0016C] God rules human wills and, in anger, turns those whom he wishes into fear? Did not the enemies of the Israelites fight of their own will against the people of God, whom Joshua was leading? And yet Scripture says that “it was done by the Lord, who strengthened their hearts so that they would go out to battle against Israel, in order that they might be destroyed” (Josh. XII, 20).
>
> Did not the wicked man, the son of Gemini, curse King David of his own will? And yet what does David say, full of true and profound wisdom? What does he say to the one who wished to strike the man who was cursing? “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah?” he said. “Leave him, so that he may curse, because the Lord has told him to curse David; and who will say to him, ‘Why have you done this?’” (II Sam. XVI, 10).
>
> Then divine Scripture, commending the king’s full statement by repeating it as though from another [Col. 0016D] beginning, says: “And David said to Abishai and to all his servants: ‘Behold, my son, who came forth from my womb, seeks my life; how much more now the son of Gemini. Leave him, so that he may curse, because the Lord has told him to do so, that the Lord may see my humiliation and repay me with good for his cursing on this day’” (ibid., 11–12).
>
> Who among the wise can understand how the Lord told this man to curse David? For God did not say this by commanding him, in which case obedience would have been praised; rather, he inclined his will—which was evil through its own fault—toward this sin by his just and hidden judgment. Therefore it is said, “The Lord told him.” For if he had obeyed God’s command, he would have deserved praise [Col. 0017A] rather than punishment, as we later learn that he was punished for this sin [variant: “for this sin” / “for this offense”].
>
> Nor is the reason hidden why the Lord told him in this manner to curse David—that is, why he cast or permitted his evil heart to fall into this sin: “that the Lord may see my humiliation,” he says, “and repay me with good for his cursing on this day.” Behold how God is shown to use even the hearts of the wicked for the praise and assistance of the good.
>
> Thus he used Judas, who betrayed Christ; thus he used the Jews, who crucified Christ. And how many benefits he thereby provided for peoples who would come to believe! He also uses the devil himself, who is exceedingly wicked, in a supremely good way, to exercise and test the faith and devotion of the good—not for himself, who knows all things before they happen, but for us, for whom it was necessary that he deal with us in this manner [Col. 0017B].
>
> Did not Absalom choose, of his own will, the counsel that harmed him? And yet he did so because the Lord had heard his father praying that this should happen. Therefore Scripture says: “The Lord commanded that the good counsel of Ahithophel be frustrated, so that the Lord might bring all evils upon Absalom” (II Sam. XVII, 14). It called it “good counsel” because for the time being it benefited his cause: it favored him against his father, against whom he had rebelled, so that he might overthrow him—unless the Lord had frustrated the counsel that Ahithophel had given, by acting in Absalom’s heart so that he rejected that counsel and chose another that was not advantageous to him (ibid., 21).
>
> Who would not tremble before these divine judgments, by which God acts even in the hearts of wicked people whatever he wishes [Col. 0017C], while nevertheless repaying them according to their merits? Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, rejected the beneficial counsel of the elders, who had advised him not to deal harshly with the people, and instead accepted the words of his contemporaries, answering threateningly those to whom he ought to have spoken gently (III Kings XII, 6ff.). Why did he do this, if not by his own will? Yet as a result the ten tribes of Israel withdrew from him and established Jeroboam as king for themselves, so that the will of the angry God might be fulfilled—something he had also foretold would happen. For what does Scripture say? “The king did not listen to the people, because the change was from the Lord, so that he might establish his word which he had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat” (ibid., 15 [printed as 159]). Thus that event occurred through the human will, and yet the “change” was “from the Lord.”
>
> Read the Books [Col. 0017D] of Chronicles, and you will find written in the Second Book: “And the Lord stirred up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines and the Arabs who were neighbors of the Ethiopians; and they went up into the land of Judah, devastated it, and seized all the substance that was found in the king’s house” (II Chron. XXI, 16–17). Here God is shown to stir up enemies to lay waste to lands that he judges deserving of such punishment.
>
> Yet did the Philistines and Arabs come to devastate the land of Judah without their own will? Or did they come by their own will in such a way that it is falsely written that the Lord “stirred up their spirit” to do this? No: both are true. They came by their own will, and yet the Lord stirred up their spirit. This can also be expressed as follows: the Lord stirred up their spirit, and yet they came by their own will.
>
> The Almighty acts in human hearts, even in the movement of their wills, so that through them he may do what he himself wishes to do through them—he who cannot possibly will anything unjust [Col. 0018A]. What is the meaning of the words spoken by the man of God to King Amaziah: “Let not the army of Israel go with you, for the Lord is not with Israel and all the children of Ephraim. But if you think that you will prevail through them, God will put you to flight before your enemies, for power belongs to God, both to help and to put to flight” (II Chron. XXV, 7–8)?
>
> How does God’s power help some in battle by giving them confidence, while sending fear upon others and putting them to flight, unless it is because he “who has done whatever he wished in heaven and on earth” (Ps. CXXXIV, 6) also works in human hearts [Col. 0018B]?
>
> We read what Joash, king of Israel, said when he sent a messenger to King Amaziah, who wished to fight him. After some intervening words he said: “Now remain in your house. Why provoke evil against yourself, so that you and Judah with you may fall?” (IV Kings XIV, 9–10). Then Scripture added: “Amaziah did not listen, because it was from God that he should be handed over to evil” [variant: “into his hands”] (II Chron. XV, 19–20), because they had sought the gods of Edom. Behold: God, wishing to punish the sin of idolatry, worked this in the heart of one against whom he was justly angry, so that he would not listen to a salutary warning but, despising it, would go to war and fall there with his army.
>
> Through the prophet Ezekiel God says: “And if a prophet is deceived and speaks, I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet; and I will stretch out my hand [Col. 0018C] against him and destroy him from the midst of my people Israel” (Ezek. XIV, 9).
>
> In the Book of Esther it is written that a woman of the people of Israel, living in the land of captivity, had become the wife of the foreign king Ahasuerus. Thus in her book it is written (chapter III, IV) that, when she was compelled to intervene for her people, whom the king had ordered to be killed wherever they were in his kingdom, she prayed to the Lord. Great necessity forced her to dare to enter to him contrary to the king’s command and contrary to her customary order of conduct. And observe what Scripture says:
>
> “He looked upon her like a bull in the assault of his indignation; and the queen was afraid, and her color changed through faintness, and she bowed herself upon the head of her maidservant who went before her. And God changed his indignation and transferred [Col. 0018D] it into gentleness” (Esther V, according to the Septuagint).
>
> It is also written in Solomon’s Proverbs: “As the rush of water, so is the king’s heart in the hand of God; wherever he wishes, he will incline it” (Prov. XXI, 1). And in Psalm 104 it is written concerning the Egyptians what God did to them: “And he turned their heart so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants” (Ps. CIV, 25).
>
> In the apostolic writings also, see what is written in the Apostle Paul’s Letter to the Romans: “Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their heart, to impurity.” A little later: “For this reason God handed them over to dishonorable passions.” And shortly afterward: “Since they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate [Col. 0019A] mind, to do what is improper” (Rom. I, 24, 26, 28).
>
> And in the Second Letter to the Thessalonians he says concerning certain people: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth, so that they might be saved, therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie and that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” (II Thess. II, 10–11).
>
> By these and similar testimonies of the divine utterances—which it would be too long to recall in their entirety—it is sufficiently clear, as I believe, that God works in human hearts to incline their wills wherever he wishes: either toward good, according to his mercy, or toward evil, according to their merits, by his judgment—sometimes manifest, sometimes hidden, but always just.
>
> This must be fixed and immovable [Col. 0019B] in your hearts: “There is no iniquity with God” (Rom. IX, 14). Therefore, when you read in the writings of truth that people are deceived by God, or that their hearts are dulled or hardened, do not doubt that their evil merits preceded this, so that they might justly suffer these things. Otherwise you may fall under Solomon’s proverb: “The foolishness of a man perverts his ways, but in his heart he blames God” (Prov. XIX, 3, according to the Septuagint).

From these words of Blessed Augustine we are most clearly taught that human thoughts and actions obey the divine disposition, although people themselves do not wish this, and their intention does not wish to obey its will and command.

Concerning this divine disposition, Blessed Gregory speaks in Book XXIX of the *Moralia* (final chapter) as follows:

> To know the order of heaven is to see the hidden predestinations [Col. 0019C] of heavenly dispositions; but to set its reason upon the earth is to disclose before human hearts the causes of such secrets. To set the reason of heaven upon the earth is either, by reflection, to examine the mysteries of heavenly judgments, or, by speaking, to make them known. Yet no one placed in this life can do this.
>
> To proceed from small matters to greater ones: who can understand what the reason of these secrets may be, when often a just man returns from judgment not only without having been vindicated but even punished, while his wicked adversary departs not only unpunished but victorious? Who can understand why one person lives while plotting the deaths of his neighbors, while another dies who would have benefited the lives of many? One person reaches the summit of power, though he strives only to harm; another desires only to defend the harmed [Col. 0019D], and yet lies oppressed himself.
>
> One person longs for leisure but becomes entangled in countless affairs; another desires to be involved in affairs but is compelled to remain at leisure. One person, beginning badly, is drawn on toward worse things until the end of his life; another, beginning well, advances through the passage of time toward an increase of merits.
>
> Conversely, one person who lives badly is preserved for a long time so that he may be corrected; another who appears to live well remains in this life until he breaks forth into perversity. One person born in the error of unbelief dies in that error; another born in the uprightness of the Catholic faith is brought to completion in that same uprightness.
>
> Conversely again, another born from a Catholic mother’s womb is swallowed, near the end of life, by the abyss of error [Col. 0020A]; while another completes his life in Catholic devotion, though born in unbelief and having imbibed the poison of error with his mother’s milk.
>
> One person both wishes and is able to pursue the height of a good life; another neither wishes nor is able; another wishes but is unable; another is able but unwilling.
>
> Who, then, can examine these heavenly secrets of judgment? Who can understand the balanced scales of hidden equity? No one ascends to know the recesses of these secret judgments.
>
> Let it therefore be said to human beings that they should recognize their ignorance; let them recognize that they do not know, so that they may fear; let them fear, so that they may be humbled; let them be humbled, so that they may not presume upon themselves; let them not presume upon themselves, so that they may seek the help of their Creator. And let the one who, trusting in himself, has died live again by desiring the help of his Author.
>
> Let the just man therefore hear—knowing what concerns himself [Col. 0020B], but still not knowing what lies above him: “Do you know the order of heaven, and can you set out its reason upon the earth?” (Job XXXVIII, 33). That is: Do you comprehend the hidden orders of heavenly judgments, or are you capable of disclosing them to human ears?
>
> Blessed Job is therefore questioned concerning the investigation of incomprehensible judgments, as though it were plainly said to him: You ought to endure all that you suffer with all the greater patience because, ignorant of the heavenly secrets, you do not know why you suffer these things.

Speaking of this hidden dispensation of secret judgments (chapter 29), Gregory shows that the Jewish people were rejected and the Gentile people received, saying:

> “The waters are hardened into the likeness of a stone” (Job XXXVIII, 30).

I remember having taught several times that waters signify peoples [Col. 0020C]. In the stone, however, Gentile peoples are sometimes designated because of their very hardness. They worshiped stones, and concerning them it was said through the Prophet: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. XIII, 8).

Therefore John, seeing the Jews exalt themselves on account of the nobility of their ancestry and foreseeing the Gentiles passing by the kinship of faith into the offspring of Abraham, said: “Do not wish to say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. III, 9), calling the Gentiles stones because of the hardness of their unbelief.

Since Judea first believed in God while all the Gentiles remained obstinate in their unbelief, but afterward the hearts of the Gentiles were softened toward faith and the unbelief of the Jews was hardened [Col. 0020D], it was rightly said: “The waters are hardened into the likeness of a stone.” It is as though he said: Those tender and penetrable hearts of the Jews are turned into the insensibility of the Gentiles.

For when the merciful God drew the Gentiles, he rejected Judea in anger. It happened that, just as previously the Gentiles had been hardened against receiving the faith, so afterward, when the Gentiles had been received into the faith, the people of Judea grew hard through the numbness of unbelief.

Hence the Apostle Paul says to those same Gentiles: “Just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief, so they also have not believed because of your mercy, so that they too may obtain mercy. For God has enclosed all in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all [Col. 0021A]” (Rom. XI, 30–32).

Reflecting carefully upon this statement—first concerning the calling of the Jews and the rejection of the Gentiles, and afterward concerning the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews—and considering that he could not comprehend God’s hidden judgments, he continued with an exclamation: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and how unsearchable his ways!” (ibid., 33).

Therefore here also, when the Lord was speaking of the unbelief of the Jews, saying, “The waters are hardened into the likeness of a stone,” to show that his judgments concerning their rejection were hidden, he suitably added: “And the surface of the abyss is congealed” (Job XXXVIII, 30), because, under a kind of veil cast over it by our ignorance, the incomprehensibility of divine judgment cannot in any way be penetrated by the eye of the human [Col. 0021B] mind.

For it is written: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV, 7). Let no one therefore seek to investigate why one person is rejected while another is chosen, or why, when one is chosen, another is rejected; for the surface of the abyss is congealed and, as Paul testifies, “his judgments are unsearchable and his ways unsearchable.”

Again, in the same book (chapter 9), while treating the same disposition, he discusses the statement of blessed Job in which the Lord says to him: “Tell me, if you know all things: in what way does light dwell, and where is the place of darkness?” (Job XXXVIII, 18–19).

> It is as though he said to him: If you suppose that you possess complete knowledge, say in whose heart the innocence that is now absent may come, or in whose heart the wickedness that is now present may persist.
>
> “In what [Col. 0021C] way does light dwell?” That is, whose mind will be filled when justice comes.
>
> “And where is the place of darkness?” That is, in whom will blind iniquity persist.
>
> “So that you may lead each thing to its boundaries.” That is, so that you may judge whether the person who is now seen to be wicked will end his life in wickedness, or whether the person who is seen to be just will conclude the extremity of his life in the perfection of justice.
>
> “And understand the paths of his house.” That is, consider and discern either to whom a persevering good action will grant an eternal dwelling in the kingdom, or whom an evil action, binding him until his end, will condemn to eternal punishment. “House” is used for dwelling, and “path” for action. The path therefore leads to the house, because action draws one toward one’s dwelling.
>
> But who among human beings can examine these matters [Col. 0021D]? Who can hear them, at least, without fear? For we see many each day who shine with the light of justice and yet, toward their end, are darkened by the gloom of wickedness. And we see many wrapped in the darkness of sins who, near the end of their lives, are suddenly restored free to the light of justice.
>
> We also know many who have once found the way of justice and held to it undefiled until death, while we have observed very many who have continually accumulated the crimes they once began until their end.
>
> Who, amid the clouds of these hidden judgments, can send the ray of his mind so as to discern by some consideration who will persist in evil, who will persevere in good, who will be converted from the lowest things to the highest, or who will turn back from the highest to the lowest?
>
> These things lie hidden [Col. 0022A] from human understanding, and nothing concerning anyone’s end is known, because the abyss of divine judgments cannot in any way be penetrated by the eye of the human mind.
>
> We have seen that the Gentile people, once turned away from God, were flooded with the light of justice, while Judea, once beloved, was blinded by the night of unbelief. We also know that the thief passed from the gallows to the kingdom, while Judas fell from the glory of apostleship into Tartarus.
>
> Again, because lots sometimes do not change once they have begun, we know of another thief who reached punishment, and we know that the apostles received the kingdom they had desired.
>
> Who, then, can examine in what way light dwells and where the place of darkness is, so as to lead each thing to its boundaries and understand the paths of its house?
>
> I see Paul called from the fury of persecution [Col. 0022B] to the grace of apostleship (Acts IX, 1), and yet he fears amid these hidden judgments to such an extent that he fears being rejected even after he has been called. For he says: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (I Cor. IX, 27).
>
> And again: “I do not consider myself to have comprehended it; but forgetting what lies behind and stretching myself toward what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus. I pursue, however, if I may comprehend that for which I have also been comprehended” (Phil. III, 13–14).
>
> And certainly it had already been said of him by the voice of the Lord: “He is a vessel of election for me” (Acts IX, 15); yet, still chastising his body, he fears lest he be rejected. Woe to us wretched people, who have not yet heard any word of God concerning our election [Col. 0022C], and already, as though secure, grow numb in idleness.

What, then, does Saint Gregory teach us through these hidden recesses of secret judgments, except that each person’s action and end are ordered by divine governance, while clouds of error confuse human minds so that they cannot know either concerning themselves or concerning others what is taking place in the secret judgments? Nevertheless, they must know that everything is carried out by heavenly dispensation and that the actions of each person are brought to the end that heavenly wisdom has judged appropriate.

Again, in Book XXX (chapter 5), taking testimony from Psalm 41—“I will enter into the place of the tabernacle, admirable even unto the house of God, amid the voice of exultation and the sound of one feasting”—he says:

> Therefore, since he had heard within the voice of exultation and confession and the sound [Col. 0022D] of a feasting city, what else awakened him except the harmony of heaven? Yet this harmony is asleep to the reprobate, because it is in no way made known to their hearts through the voice of compunction.
>
> They do not strive to contemplate that desirable multitude of the citizens above; they do not behold, with any ray of ardor, the feasts of that inner solemnity; they are not lifted up by any wing of inward contemplation. For they serve visible things alone, and therefore hear nothing of heavenly sweetness within, because, as we said above, the deafening tumult of worldly cares presses upon them in the ear of their hearts.

Since, therefore, by the hidden dispensation of judgment what is opened to some is closed to others, what is disclosed to some is concealed from others, it is rightly said [Col. 0023A]:

> “Who will recount the narration of the heavens, and who will make the harmony of heaven sleep?” (Job XXXVIII, 37).

That this voice of exultation and confession resounds in the hearts of some but is hidden from others manifests the working of a hidden dispensation of judgment, showing that all things are governed by heavenly dispositions.

Again, in the same book (chapter 6):

> “When the dust was poured upon the earth and the clods were joined together.”

It is as though he said: When, at the beginning [variant: “then for the first time”], through manifest calling and distinction, I opened spiritual secrets to some—not without mercy—and closed them to others—not without justice; when I rejected some and united others within the Church in the harmony of charity.

Here too he teaches that the rejection of some and the reception of others are the dispensation of divine judgment.

Again, in Book XXXII, speaking under the person of Behemoth [Col. 0023B] concerning the adversary of humanity, he teaches that the adversary’s savagery is restrained by divine governance, so that it may not harm more than the heavenly disposition permits. He says:

> “He who made him has restrained his sword” (Job XL, 14).

The sword of this Behemoth is the very malice by which he seeks to harm. But his sword is drawn back by him by whom he was made good according to nature, because his malice is restrained by divine dispensation, so that he is not permitted to strike human minds as much as he desires.

Thus, although our enemy has great power, he strikes with less force than he possesses; the piety of the Creator binds back his sword, so that, withdrawn, it lies hidden within his conscience, and his malice does not extend itself into the deaths of human beings beyond what is justly ordained from above.

That he prevails forcefully over many things belongs to him from the beginning [Col. 0023C] of his great creation; but that he is conquered by some means that his sword is drawn back by his Author.

For this Behemoth, because he “is the beginning of the ways of God,” when he received permission to tempt the holy man, moved nations, carried off flocks, brought down fire from heaven, raised up winds by disturbing the air, shook the house and brought it down, killed the feasting children, exercised the mind of the wife in the deceit of wicked persuasion, and pierced the flesh of her husband with inflicted wounds. But his sword is drawn back by the Creator when it is said: “Preserve his life” (Job II, 6).

The Gospel bears witness to how weak he is when his sword is drawn back: he could neither remain in the possessed man nor presume, without being commanded, to invade the brute animals again, saying: “If you cast us out, send us in [Col. 0023D]to the herd of swine” (Matt. VIII, 31). The sword of his malice is shown to be so withdrawn that, if power to exercise his malice is not granted him, he is unable even to range among swine.

When, therefore, could he dare of his own accord to harm human beings made in the image of God, when it is clear that, without being commanded, he does not even presume to touch swine?

Again, in Book XXXIII (chapter 13), he shows how [Col. 0024A] the wickedness of the ancient enemy in no way deviates from or conflicts with divine judgment when he treats the statement concerning him: “Will he make a covenant with you, and will you receive him as an everlasting servant?” (Job XL, 23). The words “as I do” are understood.

But it must be observed very carefully that this Leviathan makes a covenant with the Lord so that he may be held by him as an everlasting servant. In a covenant between opposing parties, the will of each side is fulfilled, so that each may reach its desire and conclude its quarrels with the desired outcome.

The ancient enemy, therefore, inflamed by the torch of his malice, is opposed to the sincerity of divine innocence; yet even in his opposition he does not depart from God’s judgment. He always desires to tempt righteous people maliciously, but the Lord permits this either mercifully or justly.

This very permission to tempt is called a covenant: in it the desire of the tempter is carried out, and yet through it, in a marvelous manner, the will of the just disposer is fulfilled.

For the Lord often subjects his elect to the tempter so that they may be instructed. After the gates of paradise and after the secrets of the third heaven, lest Paul be exalted by the greatness of his revelations, an angel of Satan was given to him (II [Col. 0024B] Cor. XII, 7).

But, as we have said, through this very temptation it is arranged that those who might have perished through exaltation may be saved from destruction through humility. Thus, by the hidden order of dispensation, from the very place where the devil’s iniquity is permitted to rage, the goodness of God is piously brought to completion.

And it is rightly said that, by this covenant which he is said to make with the Lord, he is received as a servant, because he obeys the commands of heavenly grace precisely where he exercises the anger of his most wicked will.

He is therefore a servant by covenant: while he is permitted to fulfill his own will, he is bound by the will of the heavenly counsel, so that he tempts God’s elect willingly but, in tempting them, tests them without knowing that he is doing so.

What, then, are we taught by this statement except that, while the temptations of the ancient enemy hasten to harm the saints, the very means by which the cunning enemy seeks to injure them are, by the ordering of heavenly grace, made to multiply their merits? Thus, by the secret order of providential dispensation, the devil is permitted to rage, and yet, through the power granted to him, while the faithful are tested, God’s goodness is commended; and he serves unwillingly by the very means through which he maliciously strives to oppress God’s servants. For the power of the enemy has no effect except insofar as the heavenly power permits it. Hence the enemy’s will is wicked; but while it serves the disposition of the heavenly Judge, it is shown to be just.

Likewise, in Book XII, chapter 2:

[Col. 0024C]

“Nothing that happens to human beings in this world occurs without the hidden counsel of almighty God. For God, foreknowing all things that would follow, decreed before the ages how they should be ordered throughout the ages. It has already been determined for each person both how far the prosperity of this world shall follow him and how far adversity shall strike him, lest either excessive prosperity raise up his chosen ones or excessive adversity crush them. It has also been determined how long each person shall live temporally within this mortal life.

[Col. 0024D]

“For although almighty God added fifteen years to King Hezekiah’s life (2 Kings 20:1), when he permitted him to die, he then foreknew that he would die. Here a question arises: how can the prophet say to him, ‘Set your house in order, for you shall die and shall not live,’ when, after the sentence of death had been pronounced upon him, life was immediately extended in response to his tears? Through the prophet, the Lord declared the time at which he deserved to die; but through the generosity of his mercy, he postponed his death until that time which he himself had foreknown before the ages. The prophet, therefore, was not false, since he made known the time of death at which that man deserved to die; nor were the Lord’s decrees overturned, since it had likewise been fixed before the ages that the years of his life would be increased through God’s generosity. The span of life that was unexpectedly added outwardly had been fixed inwardly without any increase in God’s foreknowledge.

[Col. 0025A]

“Rightly, therefore, it is said: ‘You have appointed his boundaries, which cannot be passed.’ This can also be understood spiritually, because sometimes we strive to advance in virtues and receive certain gifts, while, repelled from others, we lie in the depths. No one attains as many virtues as he desires, because almighty God, discerning the inner person, sets a limit to spiritual progress, so that a person may not exalt himself in those things which he is able to attain, on account of the fact that he strives to attain what he cannot.

[Col. 0025B]

“Hence that distinguished preacher, who had been caught up to the third heaven and had entered the secrets of paradise, was nevertheless unable to remain tranquil and free from temptation after the revelation (2 Cor. 12:1). But because almighty God establishes boundaries for a person that cannot be passed, he both raised Paul up to know sublime things and brought him back again to endure lowly ones. Thus, while he beheld the limits proper to him and strove to attain security but could not, he was prevented from going outside himself through presumption and compelled by humility always to return within his own boundaries.”

By these words, blessed Gregory shows not only that divine providence governs what human beings suffer according to the body, but also that there is a measure of divine ordering in spiritual progress, so that everything done either according to the body or according to the soul is shown never to exceed the limits established by divine governance.

[Col. 0025C]

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 52:

“The days appointed for each person by God’s inward foreknowledge can neither be increased nor diminished, unless it happens that they are foreknown in such a way that they are longer together with the best works or shorter together with the worst. Thus Hezekiah earned an increase of days through the outpouring of his tears (2 Kings 20:6); and concerning the perverse it is written: ‘Death confronts the undisciplined’ (Prov. 29:1).

[Col. 0025D]

“But often the wicked person, although long periods of life have not been predestined for him in the hidden foreknowledge of God, nevertheless, because he desires to live according to the flesh, sets before himself in his mind a long span of days. Since he cannot reach the time he expects, he perishes as though before his days have been completed. By teaching here that the days of human life are fixed by divine predestination, Gregory shows that the actions of human life serve the divine dispensation.

“Likewise, in Book XVI, chapter 10, while treating the statement made concerning the wicked, ‘They were taken away before their time, and a river overturned their foundations’ (Job 22:16), he continues:

[Col. 0026A]

“‘Since the time of life has undoubtedly been fixed for us by divine foreknowledge, it must be carefully asked why it now says that the wicked are removed from the present age before their own time. For almighty God often changes a sentence, but never his plan. Each person, therefore, is removed from this life at the time which, by divine power, was foreknown before the ages.

“‘Yet it must be understood that almighty God, who creates and orders us, assigns the limit of each person’s life according to his merits: so that one wicked person may live briefly, lest he harm many who are acting well; or that this good person may remain longer in this life, so that he may be a helper to many in good works; or, again, that a wicked person may be allowed to remain longer in life, so that he may increase his evil deeds, through whose temptation the righteous, once purified, may live more truly; or that a good person may be removed sooner, lest, if he lived here for a long time, wickedness corrupt his innocence.

[Col. 0026B]

“‘Nevertheless, it must be understood that God’s goodness is shown in granting sinners a period for repentance. But because they turn the time granted to them not toward the fruit of repentance but toward the practice of iniquity, they lose what they could have deserved from divine mercy.

“‘Although almighty God foreknows the time of each person’s death at which his life will end, no one could die at any other time than the one at which he dies. For if fifteen years are said to have been added to Hezekiah’s life, the time of his life certainly increased from the point at which he deserved to die. Divine providence had foreknown at that time the moment at which it would later remove him from the present life.

“‘Since this is so, what does it mean when it says, “The wicked were taken away before their time”? Nothing other than that all who love the present life promise themselves longer spans of that same life. But when death comes upon them and removes them from the present life, it cuts short the spans of their lives which they had been accustomed to extend in their thoughts as though they would last longer.’

[Col. 0026C]

“Likewise, in the same book, chapters 37 and 38, while treating the statement of blessed Job, ‘No one can turn back his thought’ (Job 23:13), he adds:

“‘For just as he is unchangeable in nature, so also is he unchangeable in will. No one turns back his thought, because no one can prevail against his hidden judgments. For although there have been some who seemed, through their prayers, to have turned back his thought, his inward thought was such that they were able to turn back his sentence by praying, and they received from him what they were to do before him.

“‘Let him therefore say, “No one can turn back his thought,” because judgments once fixed can in no way be changed. Hence it is written: “He issued a command, and it shall not pass away” (Ps. 148:6); and again: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Luke 21:33); and again: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are my ways your ways” (Isa. 55:8).

[Col. 0026D]

“‘When, therefore, the sentence appears to be changed outwardly, the inward plan is not changed, because whatever is done outwardly in a changeable manner is established inwardly and unchangeably concerning each matter.

“‘It follows: “And his soul did whatever he wished.” Although God is outside all bodies and within all minds, that very power of his by which he penetrates and orders all things is called his soul. Nothing resists his will—not even those things which appear to be done against his will—because he sometimes permits even what he does not command to be done, so that through it what he commands may be fulfilled more certainly. The perverse will of the apostate angels is wicked; nevertheless, it is ordered so wondrously that even their snares serve the benefit of the good, whom they purify while tempting them.

[Col. 0027A]

“‘Thus his soul did whatever he wished: he fulfills his will even through that by which he seemed to be resisted.’”

In all these statements of blessed Gregory, the hidden ordering of the inward mystery is wonderfully intimated: whatever appears to be done in time concerning the elect remains fixed with God by the counsel of his eternity. Not only are the holy actions which the elect receive through his gift directed by the governance of divine providence, but also the temptations of the adversary by which the elect are tested, so that the enemy’s snares can do nothing against the saints except what the sentence of the Ruler has decreed.

[Col. 0027B]

And although wicked thoughts and unjust temptations, whether of human beings or of demons, may wish to do many things against the will of God, his will is nevertheless always fulfilled through them. For although perverse wills arise from the wickedness of rational creatures that have apostatized from God, their actions nevertheless serve the heavenly ordering. As blessed Gregory says: “His soul did whatever he wished, because he fulfills his will through that by which it is thought that his will is resisted.”

That this is so true, the same holy Gregory confirms by saying that whatever holy men deserve to obtain through prayer was already present in the predestination of the Divinity, so that they might receive it by praying. They can obtain from God through prayers nothing other than what, by the counsel of the Divinity, was predestined to be obtained. Thus he says in his *Dialogues*, chapter 8:

[Col. 0027C]

“Certainly, the saints cannot obtain what has not been predestined; but the things which holy men bring about by praying have been predestined in such a way that they are obtained through prayers. For even the predestination of the everlasting kingdom has been arranged by almighty God in such a way that the elect reach it through labor, in order that by asking they may deserve to receive what almighty God arranged before the ages to give them.”

Concerning this dispensation of divine works, Prosper likewise speaks in Book I, chapter 15, of *The Call of All Nations*:

[Col. 0027D]

“For many things belong to the dispensation of divine works whose effects alone are shown to us, while their causes remain hidden, so that although what is done is evident, why it is done is not evident. The matter is brought into the open, while its rationale is withdrawn into concealment, so that in the same matter presumption concerning what cannot be searched out may be restrained and falsehood concerning what is manifest may be refuted.

“For if I cannot discern why one person is created Greek and another barbarian; why one is born in wealth and another in poverty; why one is elevated by the strength and beauty of a tall body while another is disfigured by the contracted weakness of crippled limbs; why one, born among Catholics, is nourished in the cradle of truth while another, descended from heretics, drinks the poison of error together with his mother’s milk; and, finally, if I cannot judge a thousand other differences—in the appearance of bodies, the qualities of souls, the conditions of times, and the customs of regions—am I therefore ignorant that God is the creator and governor of all these things?

[Col. 0028A]

“He certainly created both the bodies and the spirits of individual human beings in such a way that, apart from the voluntary diversity which would follow from each person’s own choice, he varied them from the very beginning of their creation with a manifold diversity.

“Many opinions of empty talkers would disturb us and pull us in different directions—people who have presumptuously attempted to pronounce unsuitable judgments about things unknowable—and would attribute these original inequalities to fates, which are nothing, and to the stars, unless we held with the certainty of knowledge that God the Creator forms each vessel from the original elements as he wills, and that he regulates the single nature of souls and the single nature of bodies according to measures pleasing to himself.

[Col. 0028B]

“These works of God would not have been withheld from human understanding if they ought to have become known; and it would have been made clear why each thing happens in this way, unless it were sufficient to know that it happens in this way.

“The Lord says to Moses: ‘Who gave a mouth to human beings, and who made them mute and deaf, seeing and blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?’ (Exod. 4:11). And through Isaiah: ‘Is it not I who have made her fruitful and barren? says God’ (Isa. 66:9). In the book of Ecclesiasticus it is written: ‘Good and evil, life and death, poverty and honor are from God’ (Ecclus. 11:14). And Job says: ‘The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, although he has placed everything in their hands’ (Job 12:6).

“And the same man, discussing the prosperity and decline of all human affairs and referring every change to the judgments of God, says: ‘With him are wisdom and strength; he possesses counsel and understanding. If he destroys, no one can build; if he shuts a person in, no one can open; if he holds back the waters, everything will dry up; if he releases them, they will overturn the earth. With him are strength and wisdom; he knows both the deceiver and the one deceived. He brings counselors to a foolish end and judges to bewilderment. He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a rope’ (ibid., 13–18).

[Col. 0028C]

“‘He leads priests away without honor and overthrows nobles; changing the speech of the truthful and taking away the teaching of the elders; pouring contempt upon princes and raising up those who had been oppressed; he reveals deep things from darkness and brings the shadow of death into the light; he multiplies nations and will destroy them, and will restore them, once overthrown, to wholeness; he changes the heart of the rulers of the earth and deceives them, so that they walk in vain through a trackless way; they will grope as in darkness and not in light, and he will make them wander as though drunk’ (ibid., 19–25).

[Col. 0028D]

“And again, declaring that the will of God cannot be rendered void, the same man says: ‘For he alone exists, and no one can turn back his thought; and his soul does whatever he wills.’”

Likewise, Bishop Salvian, at the beginning of Book III of *The Government of God*, asserts in the following words that everything which happens in the world is governed by God’s care, direction, and judgment:

“Thus it is asked: if everything that exists in this world is carried on by God’s care, direction, and judgment, why is the condition of the barbarians far better than ours? Why, even among us, is the lot of the good harsher than that of the wicked? Why do the upright lie prostrate while the wicked grow strong? Why does everything yield most of all to unjust powers?

[Col. 0029A]

“I could indeed answer rationally and with sufficient firmness: ‘I do not know.’ For I am ignorant of the hidden counsel of the Divinity. For the proof of this case, the heavenly oracle is enough for me: God declares that, as we have shown in the preceding books, he sees everything, governs everything, and judges everything. If you wish to know what must be held, you have the sacred writings. It is a complete explanation to hold what you have read.

“But as for the reason why God does these things of which we speak, do not demand that I explain it. I am a human being; I do not understand. I do not dare to investigate the secrets of God, and for that reason I am also afraid even to attempt it, because it is itself a kind of sacrilegious rashness if you desire to know more than you are permitted to know.

[Col. 0029B]

“Let it be enough for you that God testifies that everything is carried on and ordered by him. Why do you ask me why one person is greater and another lesser; why one is wretched and another blessed; why one is strong and another weak? I do not understand the reason for which God does these things, but for a full explanation it is more than enough that I demonstrate that these things are done by God.

“For just as God is greater than all human reason, so what I know to be done by God ought to be greater for me than reason. There is therefore no need in this matter to hear anything new; let God’s authority suffice for all explanations.

“Nor is it permissible to say of things carried on by the divine will that one is just and another unjust. Whatever you see and are convinced is done by God, you must necessarily acknowledge to be more than just.

[Col. 0029C]

“Nothing, therefore, can be said more plainly and forcefully concerning God’s governance and judgment. Nor is it necessary for me to prove by arguments what is established by the very fact that it is spoken by God.

“Thus, when we read that God says he continually observes the whole earth, we prove by that very fact that he observes it, because he says that he observes it. When we read that he governs everything he has made, we approve by that very fact that he governs it, because he testifies that he governs it. When we read that he orders everything by present judgment, it is evident by that very fact that he judges, because he confirms that he judges.

“All other things—that is, human statements—require arguments and witnesses; but God’s word itself is its own witness, because whatever incorruptible truth speaks must be the incorruptible testimony of truth.”

[Col. 0029D]

Thus, on the basis of the many statements of Catholic teachers, we believe it to be established that the world, and everything that is done in the world, is governed by divine dispensation, weighed on the scales of God’s judgments, and ordered according to the counsel of his will.

If this is so—or rather, because it is so—who can deny that the end of both the elect and the reprobate is known by God, and that what is to be done with each of them is already determined by divine examination? For just as he knows the works of each person, that is, of the elect and the reprobate, so he is not ignorant of their number. Therefore, the one who observes the actions of each person, who sees the end of all, and who knows what he will repay to each, already has determined with himself what he will do with them: who will be granted the glory of the kingdom at the end, and who will be struck by the punishment of torments.

To make these matters clearer, it seemed appropriate to add some statements concerning the predestination of the saints—statements sufficient for brevity, which commend divine grace and do not conceal the counsel of predestination.

[Col. 0030A]

That faith is a gift of God, and that none of the predestined perishes, blessed Augustine confirms in his exposition of the Gospel of John, Tractate 72:

“‘The faith of the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly is counted for righteousness’ (Rom. 4:5). In this work let us do the works of Christ, because believing in Christ itself is also the work of Christ. He accomplishes this in us, certainly not without us.

“Listen, then, and understand: ‘The works that I do, he also shall do’ (John 14:12). First I do them; afterward he shall do them, because I make him do them. What works are these, except that he may be made righteous from being ungodly?

[Col. 0030B]

“And he shall do greater works than these. Greater than which, I ask? Does the one who works out his own salvation with fear and trembling—which Christ works in him, but not without him—do works greater than all the works of Christ? (Phil. 2:12.)

“I should certainly say that this is greater than heaven and earth and all that is seen in heaven and on earth. For heaven and earth will pass away, but the salvation and justification of the predestined—that is, of those whom he foreknows—will remain. In the former there are only the works of God; in the latter there is also the image of God.”

Likewise, that the works of the saints are a gift of God, the same teacher confirms in the same book, Tractate 81:

[Col. 0030C]

“‘Just as a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me’ (John 15:4). A great commendation of grace, my brothers: it instructs the hearts of the humble and closes the mouths of the proud.

“Let those who ‘being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, have not submitted themselves to the righteousness of God’ (Rom. 10:3) answer him here, if they dare. Let those who please themselves and do not think God necessary for the performance of good works answer him here.

“Do not people corrupt in mind and reprobate concerning the faith resist this truth when they answer and speak wickedness, saying: ‘From God we have the fact that we are human beings; from ourselves, however, we have the fact that we are righteous’?

“What are you saying? Why do you deceive yourselves? You are not defenders but precipitators of free will, falling from the heights of pride through the emptiness of presumption into the depths of submersion.

[Col. 0030D]

“Your voice, surely, is that a human being makes righteousness from himself. This is the height of your pride. But the truth contradicts you: ‘A branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine’ (John 15:4).

“Go on now over precipices, and, having nowhere to fasten yourselves, be tossed about by windy verbosity. These are the emptinesses of your presumption. But see what follows you, and, if you have any sense, shudder.

“For whoever thinks that he bears fruit from himself is not in the vine; whoever is not in the vine is not in Christ; whoever is not in Christ is not a Christian. These are the depths of your submersion.

“Consider again and again what the Truth adds and says: ‘I am the vine,’ he says, ‘you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing’ (ibid., 5).

[Col. 0031A]

“Lest anyone suppose that a branch can bear even a small amount of fruit from itself, after saying, ‘He bears much fruit,’ he did not say, ‘Because without me you can do a little,’ but ‘you can do nothing.’

“Whether little or much, therefore, it cannot be done without him without whom nothing can be done. If, then, nothing good can be done without the grace of God, every good work must be referred to the grace of God.”

Likewise, that we do not choose Christ, but Christ first chooses us, and that when we were evil he made us good from being evil, the aforementioned teacher instructs us in the same book, Tractate 86:

“‘You did not choose me,’ he says, ‘but I chose you’ (John 15:16).”

[Col. 0031B]

“This is that ineffable grace. For what were we when we had not yet chosen Christ, and therefore did not love him? For whoever has not chosen him, how does he love him? Was what is sung in the psalm already present in us: ‘I have chosen to be despised in the house of my Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners’ (Ps. 83:11)? Certainly not.

“What, then, were we except wicked and lost? For we had not yet believed in him, so that he might choose us. If he chose us when we already believed, he chose those who had already been chosen. Why, then, would he say, ‘You did not choose me,’ unless it were because ‘his mercy came before us’ (Ps. 18:11)?

[Col. 0031C]

“Here the empty reasoning of those who defend foreknowledge against the grace of God is certainly set aside. They say that we were chosen before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4) because God foreknew that we would become good, not because he himself would make us good.

“But the one who says, ‘You did not choose me,’ does not say this. For if he had chosen us because he foreknew that we would become good, he would likewise have foreknown that we would first choose him. We could not otherwise become good—unless perhaps the person who does not choose the good is to be called good.

“What, then, does he choose in those who are not good? They were not chosen because they were good, since they would not have been good unless they had been chosen: ‘Otherwise grace is no longer grace’ (Rom. 11:6), if we insist that merits preceded it.

“This election is grace, of which the Apostle says: ‘So also at the present time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace’ (Rom. 11:5–6). Hence he adds: ‘But if by grace, then not by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.’

[Col. 0031D]

“Listen, ungrateful one, listen: ‘You did not choose me, but I chose you’ (John 15:16). You cannot say, ‘I was chosen because I already believed.’ For if you believed in him, you had already chosen him. But listen: ‘You did not choose me.’

“You cannot say, ‘Before I believed, I was already doing good works; therefore I was chosen.’ For what good work exists before faith, when the Apostle says: ‘Whatever is not from faith is sin’ (Rom. 14:23)?

“What, then, are we to say when we hear, ‘You did not choose me,’ except that we were evil and were chosen so that, through the grace of the one choosing us, we might become good? It would not be grace if merits had preceded; but it is grace.
