“Therefore, grace does not find merits; it creates them. And see, beloved, how he does not choose the good, but makes good those whom he chooses.

[Col. 0032A]

“‘I chose you,’ he says, ‘and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain’ (John 15:16). Is this not the fruit of which he had already said, ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (ibid., 5)?

“He chose and appointed us, therefore, so that we might go and bear fruit. We had no fruit from which he chose us. ‘That you may go,’ he says, ‘and bear fruit.’ We go in order to bear fruit, and he himself is the way by which we go, in which he appointed us so that we might go.

“Accordingly, his mercy comes before us in everything. If in everything, then certainly not only in our actions, but also so that we may have faith and, through his mercy preceding us, attain the will to do good. We cannot even think of what is good, will it, or believe, except through his preceding mercy, because God’s mercy comes before us in everything.”

Likewise, that from the condemned world a world is chosen which is saved, the same teacher establishes in the same book, Tractate 87:

[Col. 0032B]

“‘If you were of the world,’ he says, ‘the world would love what was its own’ (John 15:19).”

He says this, certainly, to the whole Church, which he often also calls by the name “world,” as in the passage: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). Likewise: “The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17). And in his letter John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins, not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world” (1 John 2:1–2).

[Col. 0032C]

“The whole world, therefore, is the Church, and the whole world hates the Church. The world, then, hates the world: the enemy hates the reconciled, the condemned hates the saved, the defiled hates the cleansed. But this world, which God reconciles to himself in Christ, which is saved through Christ, and to which every sin is forgiven through Christ, has been chosen from the hostile, condemned, defiled world.

“For from that mass which entirely perished in Adam there are made ‘vessels of mercy,’ in which is the world belonging to reconciliation. This is the world hated by the world belonging to ‘the vessels of wrath, which have been perfected for destruction’ (Rom. 9:22–23).

“Finally, after saying, ‘If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own,’ he immediately added: ‘But because you are not of the world, and I chose you from the world, therefore the world hates you.’

[Col. 0032D]

“They themselves, therefore, belonged to the source from which they were chosen so that they might no longer belong to it. This did not happen through their merits, since no good works of theirs had preceded it, nor through nature, which had been entirely corrupted at its root by free will, but through a gratuitous gift—that is, true grace.

“For the one who chose the world from the world made what he chose; he did not find it, because ‘a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. But if by grace,’ he says, ‘then not by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace’ (Rom. 11:5–6).

“Here it is shown both that those who are not saved are left in the mass of perdition and that those who are saved are freed from that same mass of perdition, not by their own merit but by the grace of Christ. For if merit is considered, those who are saved were such as those who are judged unworthy of salvation. All were ‘children of wrath’; but those who are saved are made from children of wrath into children of grace.”

Likewise, in the same book, Tractate 104, when he was discussing what the Son said to the Father, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son” (John 17:1), the following is inserted:

[Col. 0033A]

“Therefore, by saying, ‘Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son,’ he shows that every period of time, and what he would do or permit to be done at each time, had been ordered by the one who is not subject to time. For the things that were destined to occur in the successive periods of time have efficient causes in the wisdom of God, in which there are no times.

“By these words we are taught that whatever we see happening at different times, or whatever is certainly to happen, has in God’s predestination the causes for why it happens; and that everything occurs according to the ordering of the one who governs times.

“Hence, in what follows, he also says in the same tractate:

[Col. 0033B]

“‘For the one who predestined all future things by certain and unchangeable causes has already done what he will do. For it was also said of him through the prophet: “He who made the things that shall be” (Isa. 45:11).’

“If, then, God has already done in predestination everything that he will do, he has surely already given in predestination the kingdom to those to whom he will grant it; and those whom he will judge for punishment, he has already judged in predestination.”

Moreover, that the elect are predestined and called according to God’s purpose, the same doctor speaks in his book *On Grace and Correction* (chapters 6 and 7) as follows:

> What, then, is the meaning of what we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and received the word of the Lord; and as many as had been ordained to eternal life believed” (Acts 13:48)? Who worked them for eternal life, except the one who made them vessels of mercy? He also “chose them in his Son before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4), through the election of grace. “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” [Col. 0033C] (Romans 11:6). For they were not called in such a way that they were not also elect; therefore it was said: “Many are called, but few are elect” (Matthew 20:16). But since they were called according to the purpose, they were certainly also elect through election, as has been said, by grace and not by their preceding merits, because grace is their entire merit. Of such people the Apostle says: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose; for those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8:28–30). No one of these perishes, [Col. 0033D] because all are elect. They are elect, moreover, because they are called according to the purpose—not their own purpose, but God’s.

Likewise, that none of the elect who are predestined can perish, and concerning Judas—that he was chosen to the honor of the apostolate by judgment, or for the shedding of Christ’s blood—the aforementioned doctor, while treating in the same book (chapter 7) the Apostle’s passage in which he says, “Those whom he predestined, he also called,” added the following:

> He wishes those to be understood whom he “called according to the purpose,” lest it be thought that among them some were called but not elect, because of that saying of the Lord: “Many are called, but few are elect” (Matthew 20:16). For all who are elect are without doubt also called; but not all who are called are consequently elect. [Col. 0034A] Those, therefore, are elect, as has often been said, who are called according to the purpose, and who are also predestined and foreknown. If any one of these perishes, God is deceived; but none of them perishes, because God is not deceived. If any one of these perishes, God is overcome by human fault; but none of them perishes, because God is overcome by nothing. For they are elect to reign with Christ, not in the manner in which Judas was chosen for the work suited to him. He was chosen by the one who knows how to make good use even of evil things, so that through his damnable work the venerable work for which Christ himself had come might be accomplished. Therefore, when we hear, “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:71), we must understand that they were chosen through mercy, while he was chosen through judgment: they to obtain his kingdom, and he to shed his blood. [Col. 0034B]

In this statement he also displays a twofold election: namely, that some are chosen who will not remain in works of righteousness, of whom it is said, “Many are called”; while others are chosen in such a way that they remain, of whom the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined, he also called” (Romans 8:29). None of the latter can perish. He also calls Judas chosen, but not for the kingdom; rather, he was chosen for the honor of the apostolate. When he says that Judas was chosen to shed Christ’s blood, he speaks on account of that hidden order of predestination by which he disposes the actions of all—both good and evil—through a hidden judgment. For although good works and good thoughts come from God alone, while evil thoughts arise from the desire of rational creatures, [Col. 0034C] and evil works likewise from evil desire, they are nevertheless governed according to the order of divine disposition. For in this commonwealth, which is the whole world, almighty God is both ruler and disposer, and everything that occurs serves his disposition. Indeed, although many things appear to occur contrary to his will, from the very point at which they seem to resist his will they also serve his disposition.

Likewise, that those who perish are not among the elect, we are taught in the same book (chapter 7) as follows:

> Their faith, he says, which works through love, certainly either does not fail at all, or, if there are some whose faith fails, it is restored before this life ends; and, once the intervening iniquity has been erased, they are counted among those who persevere to the end. But those who will not persevere, [Col. 0034D] and who will fall away from the Christian faith and manner of life so that the end of this life finds them in that condition, are undoubtedly not to be counted among their number even at the time when they live well and devoutly. For they were not separated from that mass of perdition by God’s foreknowledge and predestination; therefore they were not called according to the purpose, and consequently they were not elect. Rather, they were among those who are called of whom it was said (Matthew 20:16): “Many are called,” and not among those of whom it was said, “but few are elect.” Yet who would deny that they are elect when they believe, are baptized, and live according to God? They are plainly called elect by those who do not know what they will become, but not by the one who knows that they do not possess the perseverance that leads the elect to blessed life, and who knows that they stand in such a way that he has foreseen they will fall (ibid., chapter 8). [Col. 0035A]

If I am asked here why God did not give them perseverance, when he gave them the love by which they would live as Christians, I answer that I do not know. I do not say this arrogantly, but recognizing my own measure; I hear the Apostle saying: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20). And: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33). Therefore, insofar as he deigns to reveal his judgments to us, let us give thanks; but insofar as he hides them, let us not murmur against his counsel.

Here too, explaining a twofold election, he says that some are chosen in such a way that they remain, while others are chosen for a time but will not persevere to the end. [Col. 0035B] Why some are chosen in one way and others in another is unknown to us, and therefore it is not for us to investigate.

Likewise, that God gives perseverance to the children of unbelievers and does not give it to the children of unbelievers, and that God’s judgments are inscrutable, the same doctor shows in the same book (chapter 8), saying:

> It is indeed astonishing—greatly astonishing—that God does not give perseverance to some of his own children whom he has regenerated in Christ, to whom he has given faith, hope, and love, while he forgives such great crimes to the children of others and, by the grace bestowed, makes them his children. Who would not marvel at this? Who would not be utterly astonished? Yet this also is no less astonishing, and nevertheless true and so manifest that not even the enemies of God’s grace can find a way to deny it: that he takes away from his kingdom, to which he sends their parents, certain children of his friends—that is, of regenerated [Col. 0035C] and good faithful people—who die here as infants without baptism, although, if he had willed, he could have provided them the grace of this washing, since everything is in his power; while he causes certain children of his enemies to come into the hands of Christians and, through this washing, brings them into the kingdom from which their parents are excluded. Yet neither the evil merit of the former infants nor the good merit of the latter derives from their own will. Certainly, because these judgments of God are just and profound, they can neither be censured nor penetrated. Among them is also the matter of perseverance, about which we are now disputing in our uncertainty. Therefore, concerning both matters, let us exclaim: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments!” (Romans 11:33.) [Col. 0035D]

Likewise, that those who perish were not among the number of children, in the same book (chapter 9):

> When the children of God say concerning those who did not have perseverance, “They went out from us, but they were not of us,” and add, “For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19), what else are they saying except that they were not children even when they were in the profession and name of children?

Likewise, that the predestined, although not yet reborn, are nevertheless already children of God and cannot perish, in the same book:

> Therefore, whoever in God’s most provident disposition has been foreknown, predestined, called, justified, and glorified is already a child of God—not only if not yet reborn, but even if not yet born—and cannot possibly perish. [Col. 0036A] Such people will come to Christ, because they come in the manner he himself says: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). And shortly afterward: “This is the will,” he says, “of him who sent me, the Father: that I should lose nothing of everything that he has given me” (ibid., 39). Therefore perseverance in good is also given by him. For it is not given except to those who will not perish, since those who do not persevere will perish. For such people, who love God, “all things work together for good”—so entirely all things that, even if some of them stray and go off course, he makes this very thing contribute to their good, because they return humbler and more instructed. For on the very path of righteousness they learn that they ought to rejoice with trembling, not arrogating to themselves confidence in their perseverance as though it came from their own virtue. [Col. 0036B]

Likewise, that those who fall in such a way that they perish were not among the number of the predestined, in the same book (chapter 12), while he was treating the saying of the Apostle John: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that one should pray for it” (1 John 5:16), blessed Augustine adds these words:

> Since the sin is not expressly identified, many different things may be understood by it. I, however, take it to be the sin of abandoning, unto death, the faith that works through love. Those who no longer serve this sin are free not by their original condition, as that man was, but have been freed by the grace of God through the second Adam; and through this liberation they possess free will by which they serve God, not by which they are taken captive by the devil. For “having been freed from sin, they became slaves of righteousness” (Romans 6:18), in which they will stand to the end, perseverance being granted them by the one who “foreknew and predestined them, and called and justified them according to the purpose,” because what he promised concerning them he has already made future things into accomplished realities. Abraham believed the one who promised, “and it was reckoned to him as righteousness”; for he gave “glory to God, being fully convinced,” as it is written, “that he was able also to do what he had promised” (Romans 4:3, 20–21). [Col. 0036C]

He himself, therefore, makes those people good so that they may do good. For he did not promise them to Abraham because he foreknew that they would become good by themselves. If that were so, what he promised would belong not to him but to them. But Abraham did not believe in that way; rather, “he was not weakened in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that he was able to do what he had promised.” He did not say, “He is able [Col. 0036D] to promise what he foreknew,” or “He is able to reveal what he foretold,” or “He is able to foreknow what he promised.” He himself, therefore, makes those people persevere in good who made them good; but those who fall and perish were not among the predestined.

Although, therefore, the Apostle was speaking of all regenerated people who live devoutly when he said, “Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls,” he immediately turned his attention to the predestined and said: “And he will stand.” And lest they arrogate this to themselves, he added: “For God is able to make them stand” (Romans 14:4). He therefore gives perseverance who is able to establish those who stand, so that they may stand with the utmost perseverance, or to restore those who have fallen: “For the Lord raises up those who are bowed down” (Psalm 145:8). [Col. 0037A]

Likewise, that the number of the predestined is fixed, in the same book, while he was speaking of those who received perseverance from God so that they could not perish, he said the following:

> I am speaking of those who have been predestined to the kingdom of God, whose number is so fixed that no one is added to them and no one is taken away from them—not of those who, after he had proclaimed and spoken, “were multiplied beyond number” (Psalm 39:6). They can be called called, but not elect, because they were not called according to the purpose.

Likewise, that everyone who hears from the Father comes to Christ, the aforementioned doctor speaks in his book *On Predestination* (chapter 8) as follows:

> “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” (John 6:45). What does “everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” mean [Col. 0037B] except that no one hears from the Father and learns without coming to me? For if “everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes,” then certainly everyone who does not come has not heard from the Father and has not learned; for if he had heard and learned, he would come. No one has heard and learned without coming. But, as the Truth says, “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes.”

Likewise, shortly afterward, that divine grace is rejected by no hard heart:

> We see many coming to the Son, because we see many believing in Christ; but where and how they have heard and learned this from the Father, we do not see. This grace is exceedingly hidden, but who would doubt that it is grace? This grace, therefore, which is secretly bestowed upon human hearts by divine generosity, is rejected by no hard heart; for it is bestowed precisely so that the hardness of the heart may first be removed. When the Father is heard inwardly and teaches a person to come to the Son, he “takes away the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh,” as he promised through the prophet (Ezekiel 11:19). Thus he makes “children of promise and vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory.” [Col. 0037C]

Why, then, does he not teach everyone to come to Christ? Is it not because he teaches all whom he teaches through mercy, while those whom he does not teach he does not teach through judgment, since “he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills” (Romans 9:18): he has mercy by granting what is good, and hardens by repaying what is deserved?

Likewise, that those whom the Father wills to teach come to Christ, in the same book (chapter 8):

> The Apostle disclosed why he does not teach everyone, to the extent that he judged it should be disclosed: “Because, wishing to show his wrath and to make known his power, he endured with much patience the vessels of wrath, which have been made ready for destruction, and in order to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Romans 9:22–23). Hence “the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Corinthians 1:18). God teaches all these people to come to Christ; for he wills all these “to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). For if he had wished to teach those for whom “the word of the cross is folly” to come to Christ, they too would undoubtedly come. The one who says, “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” (John 6:45), neither deceives nor is deceived. Far be it, then, that anyone who has heard and learned from the Father should not come. [Col. 0038A]

“Why, then,” they ask, “does he not teach everyone?” If we say that those whom he does not teach do not wish to learn, we will be answered: Where, then, is what is said to him, “O God, when you turn, you will revive us” (Psalm 84:7)? Or if God does not make willing people out of unwilling ones, why does the Church, according to the Lord’s command (Matthew 5:44), pray for its persecutors?

Likewise, that faith, both begun and perfected, is the gift of God, and that it is not for us to investigate why it is given to some and not to others, in the same book (chapter 9):

> Let no one who does not wish to contradict the clearest sacred writings doubt that this gift is given to some and not given to others. The fact that it is not given to everyone should not trouble the faithful person who believes that “all have been brought into condemnation” from one origin, in a condemnation unquestionably just—so that there would be no just reproach against God even if no one were delivered from it. Hence it is clear that great is the grace by which many are delivered, and that those who are not delivered recognize what was owed to them, so that “whoever boasts” may boast “in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31), and not in his own merits, which he sees to be equal to those of the condemned. [Col. 0038B]

Why he delivers this person rather than that one—“his judgments are unsearchable and his ways inscrutable” (Romans 11:33). It is better for us to hear or say here, “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20), than to dare to say, as though we knew it, what the one who could not will anything unjust nevertheless wished to remain hidden.

Likewise, an argument concerning infants, against those who reject grace, in the same book (chapter 12):

> [Col. 0038C] This entire argument by which we defend the truth that the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord truly is grace—that is, that it is not given according to our merits—although it is asserted with the clearest testimonies of the divine utterances, nevertheless encounters considerable difficulty among those who think that they are restrained from every pursuit of piety unless they assign something to themselves which they give first, so that it may be repaid to them. This difficulty arises when dealing with adults who already exercise the judgment of the will; but when one comes to infants, and to the Mediator himself between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, every defense of human merits preceding God’s grace collapses. For he too, although he is human, was made the liberator of human beings without any preceding good merits of his own.

Likewise, why some are granted removal from this life [Col. 0038D] while they are righteous, whereas others are retained in it until they fall, a judgment of God that no one can comprehend, in the same book (chapter 14):

> Of this life it is written in the book of Job: “Is not human life a trial upon the earth?” (Job 7:1). But why are some granted to be taken away from the dangers of this life while they are righteous, whereas others, though righteous, are kept in these same dangers through a longer life until they fall from righteousness? “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Romans 11:34). Nevertheless, from this it may also be understood that those righteous people who preserve good and devout conduct until the maturity of old age and the final day of this life ought to glory not in their own merits but in the Lord. For the one who snatched away the righteous through the brevity of life, “lest wickedness should change his understanding” [Col. 0039A] (Wisdom 4:11), himself preserves the righteous through however long a life, “lest wickedness should change his understanding.” Why he kept this person here, destined to fall, whom he could have taken away before he fell, is entirely most just—but “his judgments are unsearchable.”

Concerning grace and predestination, one example of the Savior is sufficient. Of him it is written in the same book (chapter 15):

> The Savior himself, the Mediator himself between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is also the most splendid light of predestination and grace. In order that he might be this, what preceding merits of his own, whether of works or of faith, did the human nature that is in him acquire? Please answer: How did that man merit this: that, assumed by the Word co-eternal with the Father into the unity of person, he should be the only-begotten Son of God? What good, whatever its kind, preceded him? What did he do? What did he believe? What preceded him, so that he might attain this ineffable excellence? Did not that man himself, through the action and assumption of the Word, begin to be the only Son of God from the moment he began to exist? Did not that woman, full of grace, conceive the only Son of God? Was not the only Son of God born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, not through the desire of the flesh but through God’s singular gift? Was it to be feared that, as age advanced, that man might sin by free choice? Or was free will not in him, and was it not all the more present in him because he could not serve sin? [Col. 0039B]

All these things, singularly wondrous, and whatever other things can most truly be said to belong specifically to him, human nature—that is, our nature—received in him in a unique manner, without any preceding merits of its own. Let this man answer God, if he dares, and say: “Why not me also?” And if he hears, “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” let him not be restrained even then, but increase his shamelessness and say: “How do I hear, ‘Who are you, O man?’ when I am what I hear named, namely, a human being, as is he of whom I am speaking? Why should I not be what he is?” But, someone may say, that man possesses grace of such a kind and such greatness. Why is grace different where nature is common? Certainly, “there is no partiality with God” (Colossians 3:25). Who, I ask—not a Christian, but a madman—would say these things?

Let the very fountain of grace therefore appear to us in our Head, from which he continually pours everything upon all his members according to each one’s measure. Through that grace any human being becomes a Christian from the beginning of his faith, through which grace that man became Christ from the beginning of his existence. This person too is reborn of the very Spirit of whom that man was born; by the same Spirit through whom that man had no sin, the forgiveness of sins is effected in us. [Col. 0039D] [Col. 0039C]

God certainly foreknew that he would do these things. This, then, is the predestination of the saints, which shone forth most clearly in the Holy One of holy ones. Who among those who rightly understand the words of Truth can deny it? For we have also learned that the Lord of glory himself, insofar as he was made human, was made the Son of God by predestination. The Apostle to the Gentiles cries out at the beginning of his Epistles: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification by the resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:1–4). [Col. 0040A]

Jesus was therefore predestined so that, although according to the flesh he was to be David’s son, he would nevertheless be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, because he was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. This is that singular and ineffable assumption of human nature by God the Word, so that the Son of God and the son of man might truly and properly be called both Son of God and son of man: son of man because of the man assumed, and Son of God because of the one who assumed him, the only-begotten God—lest the belief be in a quaternity rather than a Trinity. [Col. 0040B]

This exaltation of human nature, so great, so lofty, and so supreme, was predestined by God, so that it could not be raised higher; just as the divinity itself, for our sake, had nowhere to lower itself more humbly than in the human nature it assumed, with the weakness of the flesh, “even to death on a cross.” Therefore, just as that one was predestined to be our Head, so we, the many, have been predestined to be his members. Let human merits be silent here, for they perished through Adam; and let “the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord,” the only Son of God and the one Lord, reign—the grace that reigns.

Whoever finds in our Head the preceding merits of that singular generation should seek in us, his members, the preceding merits of multiplied regeneration. For that generation was not repaid to Christ but bestowed upon him, so that, free from every obligation of sin, he might be born of the Spirit and [Col. 0040C] the Virgin. Likewise, that we might be “reborn of water and the Spirit” was not repaid to us for any merit but bestowed freely. And if faith led us to the washing of regeneration, we should not therefore think that we first gave something so that this saving regeneration might be repaid to us. For the one who made us believe in Christ is the one who made Christ for us, in whom we believe. He brings about in human beings both the beginning and the perfection of faith in Jesus, just as he made the man Jesus “the pioneer and perfecter of faith.” Thus he is called, as you know, in the Epistle to the Hebrews (Hebrews 12:2). For God calls many predestined people his children, so that he may make them members of his one predestined Son.

Likewise, below (chapter 16, toward the end):

> Those who belong to this calling “are all taught by God” [Col. 0040D] (Isaiah 54:13), and none of them can say, “I believed in order to be called in this way.” For God’s mercy went before that person, because he was called in such a way that he would believe. For “all who are taught by God” come to the Son, because they have heard and learned from the Father through the Son, who most clearly says: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” (John 6:45, 39). None of these perishes, “because he does not lose anything of all that the Father has given him.” Therefore, whoever belongs to that number absolutely does not perish; and those who perished did not belong to it. Hence it was said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19). [Col. 0041A]

Let us therefore understand the calling by which people are made elect: not those who are chosen because they believed, but those who are chosen so that they may believe. The Lord himself makes this sufficiently clear when he says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). For if they were elect because they had believed, they themselves had first chosen him by believing in him, so that they might merit to be chosen. But he entirely removes this notion when he says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.” They certainly chose him when they believed in him; therefore he says, “You did not choose me, but I chose you,” for no other reason than that they did not choose him so that he might choose them. Rather, he chose them so that they might choose him, because his mercy went before them according to grace, not according to debt. [Col. 0041B]

He chose them from the world when he was living here in the flesh [variant: “in the flesh”], but they had already been chosen in him before the foundation of the world. This is the immovable truth of predestination and grace.

For, as can be understood from what we have briefly collected from the books of blessed Augustine, all the righteous deeds, words, and thoughts of the saints by which they are worthy to receive the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom are not possessed by them from themselves; they have received them through the grace of the heavenly gift. And although human free will exists, it is weak and powerless for the work of righteousness unless it is made strong and firm through God’s grace. God’s grace not only follows us, enabling us to perform the good that we know; it also goes before us in all things, producing in us the will by which we desire to do good so that we may be able to do it, and granting the faith by which we not only believe in God but also obtain from God whatever we ask. That is, it gives us both the beginning and the fullness of faith. Moreover, through grace bestowing the ability to act, we receive the ability to perform all righteous works. [Col. 0042A]

These matters are sufficiently clear from the foregoing statements, and they are also plainly evident from the sayings of the holy Fathers, whose testimonies we have omitted here for the sake of brevity.

The testimonies concerning the predestination of the saints that have now been set forth speak so unambiguously that they teach that the number of all the predestined is fixed and that none of them can perish. [Col. 0042B] Since this is so, we must now consider whether the wicked are predestined to punishment. But this can easily be inferred from the predestination of the saints: for if their predestination is certain and none of the elect can perish, it follows that the predestination of the reprobate is also undoubtedly fixed. For God’s disposition, which established the number of the saints in such a way that none of them could perish, did not fail to determine something also concerning the reprobate. What the sayings of the saints teach concerning this will be shown in the following book.

[Note: [Col. 0041B] At the end of the first book, the editor of the Lyon edition of the *Library of the Fathers* inserts the following: “I, Arn. Raymundi, public notary, having seen the original manuscript in the monastery of Lobbes and having compared it at length with my own copy, testify that the present copy agrees word for word with that original. This 4 February of the year 1648.”]

# PREFACE OF THE SECOND BOOK TO KING CHARLES

[Col. 0041]

[Col. 0041C] In the preceding book, religious king, selecting the sayings of the saints with as much brevity as I could, I explained, according to the capacity of our understanding, that everything is governed by divine dispensations. And although the wills of the wicked are evil and their actions perverse, they can in no way escape the judgments of the divine dispensations; rather, in the very way by which they oppose God, they serve his will.

From this also, as we believe, it became clear that heavenly wisdom governs not only what exists but also what is to come, and brings each thing to its proper end. It governs and directs not only the good but also the wicked, according to what it eternally arranged, ordered, and determined before the ages. And just as there is no new thought in God, so there is no new plan; what is to happen to each individual has been arranged and immutably determined in his eternal wisdom. [Col. 0041D]

We also showed that the predestination of the saints is governed by divine grace, and that the number of the elect can neither be diminished nor made uncertain. Rather, just as they were chosen before the ages, so their election will remain unshaken. We demonstrated all these things not in our own words but through the sayings of the saints. [Col. 0042C]

It remains now, according to what your magnificence has deigned to command us, that we collect examples from the sayings of the saints concerning the predestination of the wicked; and there we shall likewise speak about the predestination of the saints. Once these matters have been explained by us, we shall briefly attempt to show how, although God has predestined the wicked to punishment, he is nevertheless not the author of evil, nor is the destruction of the impious his will: “He wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4).

We ask, moreover, that your majestic highness, if you find anything in our writings that displeases you, correct it mercifully, and do not disdain to inform us of what must be corrected. Or, if an accuser should arise against them, let us be granted an opportunity for defense, so that we may either yield to one who reproves us justly or [Col. 0042D] uphold what has been said truly, and may always deserve to find your piety favorably disposed toward our humility.

# BOOK TWO: ON THE PREDESTINATION OF GOD

[Col. 0043]

[Col. 0043A] Before we speak of the predestination of the wicked, let us learn from the statements of blessed Augustine what predestination is. For Augustine says in his book *On Predestination* [Note: Rather, the author of the *Hypognosticon*, Book VI, chapter 2]: “Predestination is so called from sending ahead (or, alternatively, foreseeing), anticipating, or preordaining something future.” By these words he shows that predestination is a sending ahead and a preordination, or anticipation, and that although the terms differ, their meaning does not. Fulgentius likewise says in his book *On Predestination* (Fulgentius, *To Monimus, On the Twofold Predestination*, Book I, chapter 20): “For there is no other predestination of God than the eternal preparation of his future works.” Here too he has called preparation predestination. Therefore, whether we find “preparation” or “predestination” used in the statements of the saints, we are taught that one and the same thing is signified.

And concerning predestination the venerable doctor Augustine says in his *Exposition of the Gospel of John* (Tractate XIV):

> “He who comes from heaven is above all; and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies; and no one accepts his testimony.” If no one does, why did he come? It is therefore “no one” among a certain group. There is a certain people prepared for the wrath of God, to be condemned with the devil: no one among these accepted Christ’s testimony. For if absolutely no one did, there would be no human being. What then is the meaning of what follows? “He who accepts his testimony has certified that God is true.” Certainly, then, it is not “no one,” if you yourself say: “He who accepts his testimony has certified that God is true.” John, perhaps questioned, would answer and say: “I know what I said—‘no one.’ For there is a certain people born for the wrath of God and foreknown for this purpose. God knows who will believe and who will not believe; God knows who will persevere in what they have believed and who will fall away. And all who are destined for eternal life are numbered before God; he already knows that distinct people. And if he himself knows it, and has given the prophets knowledge of it through his Spirit, he also gave it to John.”

Since it has already been shown above, by many testimonies, that there is a predestination of the saints, and since it is now said that there is a certain people prepared for the wrath of God and to be condemned with the devil—and since preparation is predestination, as was made clear above—it is shown that there is a twofold predestination: namely, of those who are numbered before God and belong to eternal life, and of those who are prepared for the wrath of God and are to be condemned with the devil.

[Item in the same work (Tractate XLVIII):]

> “But you do not believe, because you are not among my sheep” (John 10:26). You have already learned above what the sheep are: be sheep. They are sheep by believing; they are sheep by following the shepherd; they are sheep by not despising the Redeemer; they are sheep by entering through the door; they are sheep by going out and finding pasture; they are sheep by enjoying eternal life. How, then, did he say to these people, “You are not among my sheep”? Because he saw that they were predestined to everlasting destruction, not purchased for eternal life by the price of his blood.

Further below:

> “I will give them eternal life,” that is, to my sheep, “and they shall never perish.” Understand this as though he had said to them: “You will perish forever, because you are not among my sheep.” “No one will snatch them from my hand.” Listen more attentively: “What my Father has given me is greater than all.” What can the wolf do? What can the thief and robber do? They destroy only those predestined to destruction. But as for those sheep of whom the Apostle says, “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19), and, “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined; and those whom he predestined he also called; and those whom he called he also justified; and those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:29–30): from these sheep neither the wolf snatches, nor the thief takes away, nor the robber kills. He is secure concerning their number, since he knows what he has given for them. This is what he says: “No one will snatch them from my hand”; and again to the Father: “What my Father has given me is greater than all” (John 10:28–29).

Here too, and above, when he says that those who are not among Christ’s sheep have been prepared for destruction, he shows that there is a twofold predestination: the saints have been predestined to life, and those who will persevere in their sins to destruction.

[Item in the same work (Tractate XLV):]

> If they were faithful Catholics, they were sheep; if they were sheep, how could they hear the voice of a stranger, when the Lord says, “The sheep did not hear them” (John 10:8)? You have heard, brothers, the profundity of the question. I therefore say: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19); he knows those who were foreknown and predestined. For it is said of them: “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified. If God is for us, who can be against us?” Add also: “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also, together with him, grant us all things?” (Romans 8:29–32.) But to whom does “us” refer? To the foreknown, predestined, justified, and glorified. Of these it follows: “Who will bring any accusation against God’s elect?” (ibid., 33.) “The Lord therefore knows those who are his”; they are the sheep.

> Sometimes they themselves do not know it, but the shepherd knows them, according to this predestination, according to this foreknowledge of God, according to the election of the sheep before the foundation of the world. For the Apostle also says this: “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). According to this foreknowledge and predestination of God, how many sheep are outside and how many wolves inside, and how many sheep inside and wolves outside! What do I mean by “how many sheep are outside”? How many now live wantonly but will become chaste; how many blaspheme Christ but will believe in Christ; how many get drunk but will become sober; how many seize the property of others but will give away their own. Yet for the present they hear a stranger’s voice and follow strangers.

> Likewise, how many inside praise him but will blaspheme; are chaste but will commit fornication; are sober but will later bury themselves in wine; stand but will fall—they are not sheep. For we are speaking of the predestined; we are speaking of those of whom “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19). Yet, so long as they think rightly, they themselves hear Christ’s voice. Behold, these hear, while those do not hear; yet according to predestination these are not sheep and those are sheep.

> The question still remains, and for the moment it seems to me that it can be resolved in this way. There is a voice—indeed, there is a voice of the shepherd—in which the sheep do not hear strangers, and in which those who are not sheep do not hear Christ. What voice is this? “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22). One who belongs to him does not disregard this voice; a stranger does not hear it. For the stranger too preaches to him that he should persevere with him to the end, and by not persevering with God he does not hear this voice. He comes to Christ and hears various words, all those words, all of them true and sound; among them is also this voice: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved.” Whoever hears this is a sheep.

> But someone—I do not know who—was hearing it and became foolish, grew cold, and heard a stranger’s voice. If he is predestined, he has gone astray for a time but has not perished forever. He returns, so that he may hear what he neglected and do what he heard. For if he belongs to those who are predestined, God foreknew both his error and his future conversion. If he has wandered, he returns, so that he may hear that voice of the shepherd and follow him who says: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

> A good voice, brothers, a true voice; it is the shepherd’s voice: “The voice of salvation in the tents of the righteous” (Psalm 117:15). It is easy to hear Christ; it is easy to praise the Gospel; it is easy to applaud a disputant. To persevere to the end—this is the voice of the sheep who hear the shepherd. Temptation comes: persevere to the end. To what end will you persevere? Until you have completed the journey. For as long as you do not hear Christ, your adversary is on this journey, that is, in this mortal life. But what does he say? “Make peace with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way” (Matthew 5:25). You heard, believed, and made peace. If you were opposed, make peace. If it has been granted to you to make peace, do not quarrel any longer. You do not know when the journey will end, but he knows.

> If you are a sheep, and if you persevere to the end, you will be saved. Accordingly, those who belong to him do not disregard this voice, while strangers do not hear it.

Here too, when he says that according to predestination these are not sheep and those are sheep, he shows that there is a twofold predestination.

[Item in the same work (Tractate XLII):]

> As for what follows—“Therefore you do not hear, because you are not from God” (John 8:47)—it was said to those who were not merely morally corrupt through sin, for that evil was common to all, but who were also foreknown not to believe with the faith by which alone they could be freed from the bondage of sins. Therefore he foreknew that those to whom he spoke such words would remain in what they had from the devil—that is, they would die in their sins and impiety, in which they were like him—and would not come to regeneration, through which they would become children of God, that is, born from God, by whom they had been created as human beings. According to this predestination the Lord spoke, not because he had found anyone who, according to regeneration, was already from God, or who, according to nature, was no longer from God.

Here too, when he says that the Lord spoke according to predestination, so that some would be from God and others not from God, he shows a twofold predestination.

[Item in the same work (Tractate CX), when he was speaking about the faithful and unbelieving world, he says:]

> What is all this except the world? Not the hostile world, certainly, but the faithful world. For behold, he who had said, “I do not pray for the world” (John 17:9), prays for the world that it may believe, since there is a world of which it is written, “that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Corinthians 11:32). He does not pray for that world, for he does not ignore to what destiny it has been predestined. And there is a world of which it is written, “The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17). Hence the Apostle also says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

When he says that he does not ignore to what destiny the world for which he does not pray has been predestined, he plainly demonstrates the predestination of the reprobate. And because there is a predestination of the elect and of the reprobate, predestination is shown to be twofold.

[Item in the same work (ibid.):]

> As long as we believe what we do not see, we are not yet perfected in the way we shall be when we have been deemed worthy to see what we believe. It is therefore entirely appropriate to say there, “that the world may believe,” and here, “that the world may know.” Yet both there and here the words are, “because you sent me” (John 17:21), so that we may know how much belongs to the invincible love of the Father and the Son: that we now believe what, by believing, we seek to know.

> If he had said, “that they may know that you sent me,” it would have had the same force as what he says, “that the world may know.” For they are the world—not the world that remains hostile, such as the world predestined to condemnation, but the world made from hostile into friendly, for which “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19). Therefore I said, “I in them, and you in me,” as though he were saying: “I in them” to whom you sent me, and “you in me,” reconciling the world to yourself through me. Hence he also adds: “And you loved them as you loved me” (ibid., 23). For the Father loves us in the Son, because “in him he chose us before the foundation of the world.”

Here too, by speaking of the world predestined to condemnation, he shows that predestination is twofold.

[Item in the same work (Tractate XI):]

> How, then, shall we not be with Christ where he is, when we shall be with him in the Father in whom he is? Nor has the Apostle kept silent about this for us, although we do not yet possess the reality but nevertheless hold the hope. For he says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:1–3).

> Behold, for the present, through faith and hope, our life is where Christ is; it is with him, because it is with Christ in God. Behold, it is as though what he prayed might happen had already happened, when he said: “I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). But now it is through faith; when will it be through sight? “When Christ,” he says, “your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:4). Then we shall appear as we shall be, because then it will become evident that we did not vainly believe and hope for this before we had become what we shall be.

> And when the Son had said to the Father, “that they may see my glory, which you have given me,” he immediately added, “because you loved me before the foundation of the world.” In him he loved us before the foundation of the world, and then predestined what would occur at the end of the world. “Righteous Father,” he says, “the world did not know you,” because you are righteous; therefore it did not know you. That world, predestined to condemnation, did not know you deservedly; but the world that he reconciled through Christ came to know you not by merit but by grace. For what is it to know him except eternal life? He certainly did not give this to the condemned world; he gave it to the reconciled world. Therefore “the world did not know you” because you are righteous: you assigned to it, according to its merits, that it should not know. And therefore the reconciled world knew you because you are merciful, and you came to its aid, not according to its merit, but by grace, so that it might know you.

Here too, by speaking of the world predestined to condemnation, he shows that predestination is twofold, since the examples given above sufficiently and abundantly demonstrate the predestination of those who are saved.

[Item in the *Enchiridion* (chapter 100):]

> These are “the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Psalm 110:2), and sought out with such wisdom that, when the angelic and human creature had sinned—that is, had done not what he, but what it itself, had willed—he nevertheless fulfilled through that same creature’s will, by which what the Creator did not will had occurred, what he himself willed. He made good use even of evil things, as supremely good, for the condemnation of those whom he justly predestined to punishment and for the salvation of those whom he graciously predestined to grace.

[Item in Book IV of *On the Nature and Origin of the Soul*, addressed to Vincentius Victor (Book IV, chapter 11):]

> Far be it from me, wishing to dispel this, to say what you yourself have said: that the soul deserved, through the flesh, to be defiled and to become sinful, although before sin it had no act by which it could rightly be said to have deserved this; and that original sins are forgiven even without baptism; and that the kingdom of heaven is also granted at the end to those who have not been baptized. These and similar poisons of the faith—if I were not afraid to say so—I perhaps would not be afraid to make some determination concerning this matter.

> How much better, then, not to discuss the soul separately and affirm what I do not know, but simply to hold what I see the Apostle most clearly teaching (Romans 5:18): “All human beings who are born from Adam go into condemnation from one man,” unless they are reborn in Christ in the manner he ordained that they be reborn before they die bodily—those whom the most merciful giver of grace predestined to eternal life. He is also the most just distributor of punishment for those whom he predestined to eternal death.

In these two testimonies venerable Augustine most clearly demonstrates a twofold predestination.

[Item in Book II of *On the Baptism of Infants*:]

> In order that what was hidden may become known, and what was not pleasing may become sweet, there is the grace of God by which he assists human wills. The reason why they are not assisted is likewise found in those wills themselves, not in God—whether they have been predestined to condemnation because of the iniquity of pride, or whether they are sons of mercy, to be judged and instructed against that same pride.

> Hence Jeremiah, after saying, “I know, Lord, that a person’s way is not in himself, nor is it in a man to walk and direct his steps,” immediately adds: “Correct me, Lord; nevertheless, in judgment, and not in your anger” (Jeremiah 10:23–24). It is as though he were saying: “I know that it belongs to my correction that I am less assisted by you, so that my steps may be perfectly directed. Nevertheless, do not deal with me in the anger by which you have determined to condemn the wicked, but in the judgment by which you teach your own not to be proud.” Hence it is said elsewhere: “Your judgments were helping me” (Psalm 118:175).

> Therefore do not attribute the cause of any human fault to God. For pride is the cause of all human vices.

By this statement the venerable Augustine shows that the wicked are predestined to condemnation because of the iniquity of pride, but not to sin, since sin is not from God. God is not the author of evil, whereas the requital of punishment is from God. For it is just that one who refused to submit to God through humility should, because of pride, be struck by heavenly vengeance.

Accordingly, God’s predestination is to the punishment that the wicked will undergo if they persevere in iniquity, but not to sin; for God is not the author of evil, nor does iniquity please God. God is the predestiner of the things he performs, namely, either the good things he will repay to the saints or the punishments he will inflict when punishing the wicked. But just as he is not the author of evil, so he is not its predestiner. Sin is not from God but from the devil. Therefore he is the predestiner of his own works, which he regards mercifully or punishes justly; but of things he does not perform, just as he is the avenger, so he is not the predestiner.

[Item in Book XV of *The City of God*:]

> I think that we have now dealt sufficiently with the great and difficult questions concerning the beginning or end of the world, the soul, and the human race itself. We have divided the human race into two kinds: one consisting of those who live according to human beings, the other of those who live according to God. We also call these, mystically, two cities—that is, two societies of human beings—one of which is predestined to reign eternally with God, the other to undergo eternal punishment with the devil.

[Item in the final book of *The City of God*, when speaking about the good things that God bestows upon the wicked, he says:]

> What, then, will he give to those whom he predestined to life, who gave these things even to those whom he predestined to death?

[Item in the exposition of the ninth Psalm, taking a testimony from the Gospel:]

> “But he who does not believe,” he says, “has already been judged” (John 3:18)—that is, by this hidden judgment he has already been prepared for that manifest judgment.

Further below:

> He does not confess the Lord with his whole heart if he doubts in any respect concerning his providence. But now he sees, through the hidden wisdom of God, how great is the invisible reward of the one who says, “We rejoice in tribulations” (Romans 5:3), and how all the afflictions inflicted bodily either exercise those who have been converted to God, or admonish them to be converted, or justly prepare the hardened for final condemnation. Thus everything is referred to the governance of divine providence, although fools think that such things happen by chance, randomly, and without any divine administration.

In all these testimonies the wicked are shown to be predestined to punishment, but not predestined to sin, since God is the predestiner of what he will do, whereas he does not predestine what he has not done and will not do. Because he will judge the world and condemn the impious with just punishment for their iniquities, he has predestined the guilty to punishment and predestined punishment for them. But he has not predestined them to sin, because God is not the author of iniquity. For just as righteousness and every good work are from God, so iniquity and every evil work are from the devil.

Hence holy Augustine, likewise intimating this very point, says somewhat above:

> Therefore the cause of no human fault is to be referred to God; for pride is the cause of all human vices.

And when Cassiodorus says that sinners are rejected in predestination, meaning those who are to be condemned at the judgment, he shows that they are to be condemned because of iniquity, which has not been predestined by God. The sinners themselves, however, have been predestined to condemnation, because it is just that punishment be inflicted upon those who refused to obey the commands of righteousness.

[Item in the book *On the Perfection of Righteousness* (chapter 13):]

> “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of human beings, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God” (Psalm 13). This good thing, therefore, which is to seek God, “there was no one who did it; there was not even one” (ibid.), but this was among the human race that had been predestined to destruction. For upon these the foreknowledge of God looked and pronounced sentence.

Since in this statement blessed Augustine says that the wicked are predestined to destruction, lest we understand this “destruction” as sin, we should understand it as the vengeance for sin that is to be repaid to sinners. Blessed Fulgentius demonstrates this sufficiently clearly in his book addressed to his disciple Monimus (Book I, chapter 6). In that book he also teaches that the wicked are predestined to punishment, and by an entirely sound argument makes clear that God predestines no one to iniquity. I have wished to extract a few passages from that book and insert them into this work. He says:

> That the wicked perish before Gehenna is not the work of God but of human beings; but that they will perish in Gehenna is the work of God’s justice, for no iniquity of the sinner pleases him. “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6). And John says: “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin is iniquity” (1 John 3:4). God says through the prophet: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4). Concerning the Son of God, John says: “We know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and there is no sin in him” (1 John 3:5).

> Therefore, just as there is no sin in him, so sin is not from him. What is not from him is certainly not his work. And what is never in his work was never in his predestination. The wicked, therefore, have not been predestined to that by which they act wickedly, being drawn away and enticed by desire, but to that which they unwillingly suffer justly.

> For by the name “predestination” no coercive necessity of a human will is expressed, but the merciful and just eternal disposition of a future divine work is proclaimed. The Church sings to God “mercy and judgment” (Psalm 100:1). His work in a human being is this: by the hidden counsel of his will, though not an unjust one, either to bestow gratuitous mercy upon the wretched or to repay due justice to the unjust.

> Indeed, either in mercy he grants the debtor what he could justly demand if he wished, or in justice he demands with interest what is his, and repays an unjust debtor what is owed according to his iniquities. Thus he either anticipates one who is wholly unworthy of mercy, or finds another worthy in this way.

> For he himself freely gives grace to one unworthy, so that the ungodly person, justified, may be enlightened by the gift of a good will and by the capacity for good cooperation. Thus, with mercy preceding, he begins to will what is good; and with mercy following, he is able to do the good that he wills.

> In predestining both, God also prepared them in that unchangeable will in which he so disposed the future renewal of the human being that the person’s will could not fail to be new in the new work.

[Chapter 8.]

> He also gives grace to one who is worthy, in return for the reward of eternal recompense. Thus, whether, being righteous, he mercifully justifies the ungodly—for the Apostle says of him, “so that he might himself be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26)—or whether, being merciful, he justly glorifies the righteous, because “those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8:30), the operation of grace is the same: it both makes a person’s good merit begin toward righteousness and brings it to completion toward glory.

> First, it begins a good will in the human being; then it assists that same will once begun, so that the will is good by divine gift and, by divine assistance, is able to overcome evil desire. When God subsequently perfects it, the will becomes such that it cannot possess evil desire. Thus in the present life, by the help of grace, it does not yield to weakness; in the future, by the benefit of grace, it will not have weakness. Now it is continually restored by healing assistance; then it will enjoy the eternal fullness of health.

> God has always possessed these things in predestination, and through grace he accomplishes them just as he predestined them. The recognition of this predestination is therefore intimated when Scripture says: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint). It is called “prepared” for no other reason than that it is foretold as going to be given. By the one who prepares it through eternal goodness, it is given through undeserved grace.

In this statement he distinguishes by a convincing argument what God predestines and what he does not predestine, demonstrating that sin is not in God’s predestination, but the punishment of sin. On the other hand, he acknowledges that the blessed merits of the saints and their recompense are both within God’s predestination, because both are from God. The saints possess no good except from God, and the recompense for the good works performed by the elect is from God. Therefore both have been predestined by God.

[Item below (chapter 12):]

> For this reason there is no falsehood in God’s promises: nothing is difficult for the Almighty to accomplish, and therefore the effect of his will is never absent, because the will itself is found to be power. Whatever he wills, he can do; however much he wills, so much he can do. Therefore it is fittingly said of him alone: “He has done whatever he has willed” (Psalms 113 and 135). Again: “Power is yours whenever you will” (Wisdom 12:18).

[Chapter 13.]

> For this reason we said that the power of the will is as great as the will itself is powerful: since in him, to whom the ability to act is always subject whenever he wills, willing is nothing other than being able.

Since God is compelled by no necessity to permit anything unwillingly, no obstacle of adversity prevents him from doing what he has promised either less than he wishes or later than he wishes. Therefore he was able, as he wished, to predestine some to glory and others to punishment. But those whom he predestined to glory he predestined to righteousness; those whom he predestined to punishment he did not predestine to guilt.

Further below:

> In the saints, therefore, God crowns the righteousness that he himself freely bestowed upon them, freely preserved, and freely perfected. But the wicked he condemned for the impiety or injustice that he himself did not create in them. In the former he glorifies his own works; in the latter he condemns works that are not his.

> God therefore predestined what he himself was going to do or what he was going to bestow. But he in no way predestined what he himself was not going to do, whether through grace or through justice.

[Item in the same work (chapter 23):]

> It is fitting for the faithful to believe and confess that the good and just God did indeed foreknow sinful human beings, since nothing future could be hidden from him—for things would not even be future if they had not been present in his foreknowledge—but that he did not predestine any human being to sin. For if God predestined a human being to some sin, he would not punish that human being for sins.

> By God’s predestination, either the merciful remission of sins or the just punishment of sins has been prepared. God therefore could never have predestined a human being to that which he himself had determined to prohibit by commandment, to cleanse by mercy, and to punish by justice.

> Therefore God predestined the wicked whom he foreknew would end this life in sin to be punished with unending punishment. Just as human foreknowledge of iniquity is not to be blamed in them, so the predestination of the most just vengeance is to be praised, so that it might be recognized that God did not predestine a human being to any kind of sin when he predestined that person to be punished for the merit of sin.

[Chapter 24.]

> God therefore foreknew all human works, whether good or evil, since nothing could be hidden from him. But he predestined only the good works that he foreknew he would perform in the children of grace. As for the future evil works of those whom he did not predestine to the kingdom but to destruction, he foreknew them through his most powerful divinity and ordered them through his provident goodness.

> Since he foreknew that he himself would not perform those evil works, and that neither would a human being insofar as that person had humbly adhered to him, he showed us even more clearly the invincible power of his foreknowledge: he did not permit the predestination of his justice to be ineffectual even in the case of evil things.

> Therefore, wishing to show what he foreknew would be repaid and what would be bestowed, God predestined to punishment those whom he foreknew would depart from him through the vice of an evil will. He predestined to the kingdom those whom he foreknew would return to him with the aid of prevenient mercy and would remain in him with the aid of subsequent mercy.

> In the latter he preserves mercy; in the former he maintains justice. To the latter he piously gives what he promised; to the former he justly repays what he likewise foretold.

> God did not, however, promise everything that he foretold, although he foretold everything that he promised. Likewise, he did not predestine everything that he foreknew, although he foreknew everything that was predestined. For he foreknew the good and evil wills of human beings, but he predestined only the good, not the evil.

> And although it was not in his predestination that he should give malice to the human will, it was nevertheless in his predestination what he would repay for the malice of the human will. For, as the Psalmist testifies, “The Lord is merciful and just” (Psalm 114:5). He predestined the righteous to glory and the wicked to punishment.

> To those who were to be justified and glorified, therefore, he both foretold and promised the work of his mercy that had been predestined. But to the wicked he merely foretold the work of his justice that had been predestined; he did not promise it.

[Item in the same work (chapter 26):]

> In the saints, therefore, the Lord will bring to completion what he freely gave so that they might be good. What he foreknew he would give, he predestined in the eternal disposition of his goodness. For this is God’s predestination: the eternal disposition of God’s future work.

> But in the wicked he will punish what he did not give so that they might be evil. He did not predestine them to any iniquity, because he was not going to give them the will to act wickedly. And because the persevering iniquity of an evil will ought not to remain unpunished, he predestined such people to destruction, because he prepared for such people the punishment of just retribution.

> The Lord himself taught this openly in his discourse, by showing that he had prepared not only the kingdom in which the good would rejoice, but also the eternal fire in which the wicked would be tormented. For he will say to the good: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). But to the wicked he will say: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41).

> Behold to what God predestined the iniquitous and impious: namely, to just punishment, not to any unjust work; to penalty, not to guilt; to punishment, not to transgression; to the destruction that the anger of the just Judge has repaid to sinners—not to the destruction by which the iniquity of sinners provoked God’s anger against itself.

> The preaching of the blessed Apostle makes this clear. He calls those wicked people whom God will condemn eternally “vessels of wrath,” not “vessels of guilt.” For he says: “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Romans 9:22–23).

In this final sentence it should be noted that, taking his testimony from the Gospel, he says that the wicked are predestined to eternal fire, because at the judgment the Lord will say—not only to the good, that they may receive the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world, but also to the wicked: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” For from this he proves that the unjust and ungodly have been predestined by the Lord to punishment, since he will say to them [Col. 0053C]: “Go into the eternal fire.”

Hence [Note: [Col. 0053D] On Hincmar and similar writers.] those who wish to say that punishment was predestined for the unjust, but that the unjust were not predestined to punishment, should consider how they understand the words of this author: for the one for whom punishment is prepared is plainly himself prepared for punishment.

Again, in the same work (chapter 26):

> God would never inflict destruction upon the vessels of wrath if the human being were not found to possess sin voluntarily. For God would not justly impose wrath upon a sinful human being if the human being had fallen into guilt through God’s predestination. But because the human being had the cause of his iniquity from his own will, blessed Paul therefore asserts that God “endured with great patience the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction” (Rom. IX, 21). Thus this wrath inflicted destruction upon such vessels because it found in them the merit of voluntary iniquity [Col. 0053D]. But how would the just Lord have brought wrath upon a servant of sin if that servant had sinned through the Lord’s predestination? God therefore fitted these vessels for that in which he predestined them—that is, for destruction: specifically, the destruction which Paul declares will suddenly overtake the wicked, saying: “For when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (I Thess. V, 3). But if God predestined such people to sin, the Apostle would not have preferred to call them “vessels of wrath,” but vessels of guilt; nor would such vessels be said to have been fitted for destruction, but for sin. They are now called “vessels of wrath” so that it may be shown that, in such people, [Col. 0054A] what proceeds from God’s predestination is not what they have wickedly committed, but what has been justly repaid to them (chapter 27).

Destruction is rightly repaid by God to the wicked, although it is a bad destruction for those who are now justly abandoned and will afterward be justly tormented. In such people God begins his judgment by abandonment and completes it by torment. For even at the present time, when God abandons the wicked as they depart from him, he does not work in them what displeases him; rather, through them he works what pleases him, and afterward he will repay them what they deserve from his justice. They will receive their due, not because God made good use of their evil works, but because they themselves made evil use of God’s good works.

[Col. 0054B] Thus God fitted such people for the destruction of punishment, which the just Judge decreed for the sinner by a just predestination—not for sin, which the human being began not through divine predestination but through his own will, by wickedly desiring it, and completed by wicked action. For “desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is complete, gives birth [variant: *generat*, “generates”] to death” (James I, 15).

The wicked, therefore, were not predestined to the first death of the soul; they were predestined to the second, namely, “to the lake of fire and sulfur,” of which blessed John says: “And the devil who deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur” (Apoc. XX, 9); and elsewhere: “And Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire” (ibid., 15). This second death is “the lake of fire”; and whoever was not found written in the book of life “was thrown into the lake of fire.” Again he says: “But for the cowardly and unbelieving, the defiled, murderers, fornicators, [Col. 0054C] sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion is in the lake burning with fire and sulfur, which is the second death” (Apoc. XXI, 8). He calls that the second death which follows from the judge’s sentence, not the death which preceded it in the sinner’s evil desire.

Throughout, this teacher dogmatically maintains that the wicked have been preordained to a life of punishment for their iniquities, but have not been preordained to sin, since iniquity does not please God, and he is not the predestiner of those whose author he is not. But since he knew that the human being would sin and remain in sins, he predestined him to the punishments which he would justly suffer. This predestination did not compel him to sin, or, in any event, necessarily to punishment. [Col. 0054D] For, as he himself testifies, “the one who knows all things” knows also the deeds of each individual and knows the ends of each individual; and from what he saw and knew in them, from that also he predestined what he would do with each.

For just as God’s foreknowledge compels no one to sin—although he certainly foreknew the sins of each person before the eternal ages—so also his predestination compels no one to punishment, even though someone may be predestined to punishment before he is born, if he is going to remain in iniquity. From the fact that he foreknew what each person would do, he also predestined, by the eternity of his counsel, what he would do with each.

[Col. 0055A] Cassiodorus likewise, in his exposition of Psalm 108, when he was treating the verse that says, “Let his descendants be for destruction; in one generation let his name be blotted out,” added the following:

> He calls the same offspring whom above he called orphans. And because some people are accustomed to extend the lineage of sinners far into the future, he also cuts off from them the very hope of prosperity, so that their wicked minds might not console themselves with any good; or rather, that one generation should be understood as referring to the time when we are born in sins. Therefore he asks that they may not reach the second birth—that is, regeneration. Yet they have been rejected in predestination, so that they may perish in the first filth of their sins and not escape the snare of death through the benefit of a second birth.
