[Col. 0055B] These and similar statements are made about those who will be condemned at the Lord’s judgment. Here he called “rejected through predestination” those whom he declares will be sent into eternal condemnation at the judgment. For God saw that the wicked would persevere in evil, and therefore, in his eternal foreknowledge, predestined punishment for such people.

Nevertheless, they are not compelled to punishment because they are judged on the basis of having been predestined; rather, they are recognized as predestined to punishment because they were foreknown as sinners. For just as no one can impute to God the fact that he sins, so neither can anyone impute to him the fact that he is to be punished for sins. He sins by transgressing through his own will, but he is to be punished by the just judgment of the one who judges.

[Col. 0055C] And just as the cause of sin does not descend from God’s foreknowledge—for no one sins because God foreknew that he would sin, but because he obeys his own desire rather than God’s command forbidding sin—so no one goes to punishment merely because this had previously existed in God’s predestination. Rather, because he was foreknown as one who would remain in sins and end his present life without the fruit of repentance, he was appointed to punishment.

Just as the cause of sin is desire, by which one obeys the will of the flesh more than the divine command, so the cause of appointment to punishment is the perpetration of sin and afterward the failure to offer any worthy satisfaction for sin.

[Col. 0055D] For this reason holy Isidore, bishop of Seville, distinguished for the merits of his life and the light of his wisdom, following the teaching of the Catholic masters, teaches in the second book of the *Sentences* (chapter 6), by the testimony both of sense and of words, that there is a twofold predestination, saying:

> Predestination is twofold: either that of the elect to rest, or that of the reprobate to death. Both are governed by divine judgment, so that he always causes the elect to follow what is heavenly and inward, while, by abandoning the reprobate, he always permits them to take pleasure in what is lowly and outward. Just as a human being does not know the boundary between light and darkness, or what the end of either may be, so he does not fully know who, before his end, will be overtaken by the light of justice, or who will remain darkened by the darkness of sins until his end, or who, after falling into darkness, will turn and rise again to the light. All these things are open to God but hidden from the human being. Although the conduct of the righteous in this life may be worthy of approval, it is nevertheless uncertain to human beings to what end they have been predestined; all things are reserved for the future examination.
>
> [Col. 0056A] Wonderful is the arrangement of the heavenly distribution, by which here the righteous person is made more righteous, and the wicked person more filthy. The wicked person is sometimes converted to good, and the good person sometimes turns back to evil. One wishes to be good and is unable; another wishes to be evil and is not permitted to perish; the ability to be good is given to the one who wishes it; another neither wishes it nor is it granted to him to be good. One is born in error and dies in it; another perseveres to the end in the good with which he began. This one stands only until he falls; that one, after living long in evil, is saved at the end, turns after being regarded with favor, and is converted. The righteous person wishes to be useful in good but cannot prevail; the wicked person wishes to do harm and succeeds. This one wishes to be free for God but is hindered by the world; that one wishes to become entangled in business but does not accomplish it. The wicked rules over the good; the good is condemned in place of the wicked; the wicked is honored in place of the righteous. Amid such great obscurity, the human being cannot scrutinize [Col. 0056B] the divine arrangement or discern the hidden order of predestination.

By these words he demonstrates with complete clarity not only that, by the order of divine predestination, the number of the elect is destined to be crowned with reward and the multitude of the reprobate to be sentenced to punishment at the judgment, but also that the life of both orders—that is, of the elect as well as the reprobate—passes through the times of this changing world according to a particular course and path. Just as it does not depart from the law of heavenly governance, so he teaches that it has been predestined by the secret of the heavenly arrangement.

Speaking of the end of both groups, namely the elect and the reprobate, he says:

> Predestination is twofold: either that of the elect to rest, or that of the reprobate to death.

He shows how this predestination operates in individuals in the following sentence:

> Both are governed by divine judgment, so that he always causes the elect to follow what is heavenly and inward, while, by abandoning the reprobate, he always permits them to take pleasure in what is lowly and outward.

[Col. 0056C] For he teaches that the order of predestination is apportioned through the discrimination of heavenly judgment, and that it kindles those who are elect with the flame of divine love, always causing them to desire and follow the inward—that is, spiritual things—and the heavenly—that is, celestial things. But, through a just judgment that is nevertheless hidden from mortals, he permits the reprobate, by failing to illumine them with desire for the heavenly homeland and by abandoning them as exiles from love of the invisible good, to love not inward but outward things, not heavenly but lowly things—that is, not spiritual but bodily things, not celestial but earthly goods.

[Col. 0056D] No one can love or attain the good of truth unless instructed by the light of truth, as Truth itself testifies: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John VI, 44); and elsewhere: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. XI, 27). To be drawn to Christ means nothing other than to believe in him and, by believing, to follow him. Likewise, for the Father to be revealed through the Son means nothing other than to see the Father with the eyes of faith and to honor him through the service of love.

But who is drawn by the Father to Christ, and to whom the Son reveals the Father, is determined not by human judgment but by divine judgment. In this mortal life, however, no one knows who is drawn to Christ in such a way, or to whom the Son reveals the Father, that he may be among the number of the elect.

[Col. 0057A] For this reason blessed Isidore continues, saying:

> Just as a human being does not know the boundary between light and darkness, or what the end of either may be, so he does not fully know who, before his end, will be overtaken by the light of justice, or who will remain darkened by the darkness of sins until his end, or who, after falling into darkness, will turn and rise again to the light.

A human being does not know the limit of light and of darkness because he does not know in whom the light of justice will persevere until the end of life, as until the end of day; nor does he know in whom the darkness of iniquity, like the shadows of night, will have to remain perpetually. Who belongs to the number of the elect and who is counted among the lot of the reprobate is manifest to God, but entirely hidden from human knowledge.

The sentence of this author makes this clear when he says:

> All these things are open to God [Col. 0057B] but hidden from the human being.

Then, further emphasizing the secret of divine predestination, he adds:

> Although the conduct of the righteous in this life may be worthy of approval, it is nevertheless uncertain to human beings to what end they have been predestined; all things are reserved for the future examination.

Even if the righteous appear to strive along a life-course worthy of approval, what is determined concerning their end by the secret of the divine arrangement is manifest only to that wisdom from whose vast knowledge nothing can be hidden. But the human being, suffering the darkness of this mortality, is not illumined by an abyss of such depth; rather, everything is enveloped in the deepest darkness of night until the light of the coming judgment reveals toward what end the deeds of each person have labored.

[Col. 0057C] Then the life of the saints, which appears to proceed along a worthy course amid the changes of this world, will be revealed: whether what they appeared to do as good they performed out of love for the world or out of love for the heavenly homeland. Yet he says that, by the examination of divine predestination, it has been arranged what end each person will receive—that is, who will obtain the blessedness of the heavenly homeland and who will undergo the misery of everlasting suffering.

Thus, in a second place, he discloses the secret of the twofold predestination when he says:

> Although the saints conduct themselves worthily in this life, it is nevertheless uncertain to what end they have been predestined.

By saying that it is uncertain to what end they have been predestined, he shows that not all people strive toward one single end of completion. [Col. 0057D] Rather, some will attain, as the end of their labor, the eternal reward of recompense, while others will receive the torments of perpetual condemnation. Which people belong to which end cannot be discerned in this darkness of mortality by any manifestation of truth; yet this teacher testifies that it has been predestined by the examination of the heavenly dispensation.

The Lord also appears to agree with this sentence when he speaks to Job, saying:

> “Tell me, if you know all things: by what way is the light spread, and what is the place of darkness, so that you may lead each thing to its boundaries?” (Job XXXVIII, 18–20).

[Col. 0058A] By the name “light” he designates the life of the saints, and by the term “darkness” the reprobate, because it is perfectly clear to God, to whom all things are manifest, whom the light of heavenly grace will illumine until the end of life, and whom the darkness of unbelief will not leave before death’s departure.

He rightly says: “By what way is the light spread, and what is the place of darkness?” For the light of divine visitation does not flood the hearts of the elect in one way but in many, glorifying some by one gift and others by another. It converts some from the womb of their mother, others from the time of childhood, others from the fervor of youth, and still others in the course of old age, from the darkness of sins to the light of justice.

Since, therefore, the heavenly Judge magnifies the elect by different gifts of grace and calls them to the way of truth at different ages, it is rightly said: “By what way is the light spread?” That is, by what way—by what order of the heavenly arrangement—is the light of heavenly grace, illuminating the minds of the elect, distributed? Human weakness cannot comprehend this, but the secrets of heavenly judgment know it.

[Col. 0058B] Likewise, “what is the place of darkness”—that is, in whose hearts the shadows either of unbelief or of perverse action must remain dark until the end—is not open to human knowledge, but is known to divine wisdom.

From this it is also added: “So that you may lead each thing to its boundaries.” Each thing is led to its own boundary when what end awaits each person according to the merit of his works is assigned to him: one is adorned with the glory of his studies for the contest of good conduct, while another is restrained by the punishment of his labors for the intention of evil deeds. Thus each receives the end of his course which he sought by the purpose of his struggle.

[Col. 0058C] Accordingly, the one who sought the recompense of the heavenly homeland through zeal for his labor receives as a gift what he desired in the contest. But the one who desired earthly things instead of heavenly, transient things instead of lasting things, will find not the reward of eternal blessedness, which he did not desire, but the punishment of everlasting condemnation, for which he labored.

For although he reaches it unwillingly, and although the one who acts wickedly does not desire punishment at the end but glory, nevertheless, since he will not receive the rewards of eternal life, for which he did not labor, he will receive the eternal punishments of condemnation. For whoever becomes deprived of everlasting good becomes possessed of perpetual evil.

Who, then, will receive one or the other of these things, he alone knows “who leads each thing to its boundaries.” For he alone knows the boundaries of each individual who has known the intention of every heart and is not ignorant of the purpose in which each person will persevere.

[Col. 0058D] And he “leads each one to his own boundaries,” because he will assign to each person the end of recompense toward which the intention of his mind directed his action.

Thus it is proved true that Saint Isidore says:

> Although the conduct of the righteous in this life may be worthy of approval, it is nevertheless uncertain to human beings to what end they have been predestined; all things are reserved for the future examination.

Then, adding what follows, he says:

> Wonderful is the arrangement of the heavenly distribution, by which here the righteous person is made more righteous and the wicked person more filthy.

[Col. 0059A] Above, he discussed the end of each person as arranged by heavenly predestination. Now he begins to teach that the life of both the elect and the reprobate is directed, according to the order of the divine arrangement, throughout the course of this temporal life. He has predestined, by the eternal counsel of his providence, the manner in which the Creator orders the actions of individuals in this life.

For although human actions are new because they are temporal, the plan of the divine arrangement is not new, because it is eternal. He says:

> Wonderful, therefore, is the arrangement of the heavenly distribution, by which here the righteous person is made more righteous and the wicked person more filthy.

Thus it is written in the Apocalypse: “Let the righteous person still be made righteous, and let the one who is filthy still become filthy” (Apoc. XXII, 11).

The wicked person is sometimes converted to good, and the good person sometimes turns back to evil. The Apostle also says: “Therefore he has mercy on whomever he wishes, and he hardens whomever he wishes” (Rom. IX, 18).

[Col. 0059B]

> One wishes to be good and is unable; another wishes to be evil and is not permitted to perish.

Holy Scripture also says: “Consider the works of the Lord, for no one can correct the one whom he has despised” (Eccles. VII, 14).

> It is given to the one who wishes to be good; another neither wishes it nor is it granted to him to be good.

The Apostle likewise says: “Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. IX, 21).

> One is born in error and dies in it; another perseveres to the end in the good with which he began.

And it is sung of Wisdom: “You open, and no one shuts” (Apoc. III, 7).

> This one stands only until he falls; that one, after living long in evil, is saved at the end, turns after being regarded with favor, and is converted.

[Col. 0059C] And the Lord says through Moses: “I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I save, and there is no one who can rescue from my hand” (Deut. XXXII, 39).

> The righteous wishes to be useful in good but cannot prevail; the wicked wishes to do harm and succeeds. This one wishes to be free for God but is hindered by the world; that one wishes to become entangled in business but does not accomplish it. The wicked rules over the good; the good is condemned in place of the wicked; the wicked is honored in place of the righteous.

Ecclesiastes also says:

> “There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, as though proceeding by error from the presence of the ruler: a fool placed in a position of great dignity, while the rich sit below; I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking like servants upon the earth” (Eccles. X, 5–7).

Again:

> “I have seen under the sun, in the place of judgment, wickedness, and in the place of justice, iniquity” (Eccles. III, 16).

[Col. 0059D] The prophecy of Hannah likewise says:

> “The Lord kills and makes alive; he leads down to the underworld and brings back. The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and exalts” (I Reg. II, 6).

Since no Catholic ought to doubt that all these things are accomplished by divine judgment, the reason why they occur is known to God alone. Nevertheless, it cannot be anything other than just, since it comes from him whose arrangement cannot be unjust.

And because it cannot be comprehended by human knowledge, blessed Isidore rightly concludes the end of this sentence by saying:

> Amid such great obscurity, the human being cannot scrutinize the divine arrangement or discern the hidden order of predestination.

[Col. 0060A] Behold, the teacher just mentioned has clearly taught us that the ends both of the elect and of the reprobate have been predestined by God. He has taught not only their ends, but also that the order of divine predestination determines who will persevere to the end in the good with which he began, who will not abandon the evil he began until the end of life, who will be converted from evil to good, and who will at some time turn back from good to evil.

He also testifies that the course of human life is contained within the governance of divine law, as we see the pages of the sacred Scriptures bear witness to his statements.

Since these things are so, I do not know with what confidence we could deny that predestination is twofold. If anyone rejects the sentence of this author, let him consider how he contradicts Holy Scripture, whose testimonies we know to condemn the meaning of this teacher.

Unless, perhaps, someone should say that the world is not ruled by God. But since no Catholic presumes to deny this, it is clear that by the divine arrangement [Col. 0060B] not only present things but also past and future things are governed.

Since this is so, none of the faithful doubts that nothing mutable or variable occurs in God. Once this is believed with complete certainty, it follows that we should understand that there is in God neither a new counsel, nor a new arrangement, nor a new order.

Therefore, everything that God judges, arranges, or orders in his creature throughout the changing courses of time was always judged, arranged, and ordered in the eternity of his counsel in the same way in which it is judged, arranged, and ordered by him in time.

The end both of the wicked and of the good pertains to the divine arrangement, and the course of human life in no way escapes the judgment of the divine arrangement. Both, therefore, have been predestined by the counsel of the everlasting arrangement [Col. 0060C].

Since the end of the elect and of the reprobate is not the same but distinct, and since their courses of life are likewise distinct, it follows that the order of divine predestination by which the end of the good and of the wicked is separated is not one and the same but different.

We are taught this by the sentence of that teacher, who says: “Predestination is twofold,” and so forth.

We have therefore been sufficiently instructed by the authority of Catholic teachers that predestination is twofold. But lest these arguments perhaps seem insufficient to anyone, let us add something also from the books of this same author, so that those who wish to know may be satisfied and those unwilling to yield may be overcome by the abundance of testimonies.

In the book of the *Differences*, while distinguishing the infusion of divine grace from the freedom of the human will, he says (Isidore, book II, [Col. 0060D] *Differences* XXXII, 115–119, 122):

> The difference between the infusion of divine grace and the will of human free choice is this: free choice is the will of a free power, which can spontaneously desire either good or evil. Grace, however, is the free gift of divine mercy, through which we obtain both the beginning of a good will and the fulfillment of a good work.
>
> A human being is preceded by divine grace so that he may be good; human free choice does not precede God’s grace, but God’s grace itself precedes the unwilling human being so that he may also will what is good. For, weighed down by the flesh, the human being is disposed to be ready for sin and slow to repent. He has within himself the means by which he may fall, but he has no means by which he may rise unless the grace of the Creator extends a hand to the one lying prostrate so that he may be raised.
>
> [Col. 0061A] Finally, through God’s grace free choice is restored to the human being, which the first human being had lost. For the first human being possessed free choice to begin the good, although that good was to be perfected with God’s help. But we receive from God’s grace both the beginning and the perfection of free choice, because we have from him both the ability to begin and to perfect the good—from him by whom the gift of grace was given and free choice was restored in us.
>
> The good that we do is therefore God’s, because of preceding and subsequent grace; but it is ours because of the will of free choice that follows. For if it is not God’s, why do we give thanks to him? And if it is not ours, why do we expect the recompense of good works?
>
> [Col. 0061B] Accordingly, insofar as we are preceded by God’s grace, the work is God’s; but insofar as we follow the preceding grace in doing good, it is ours. No one precedes the Lord’s grace by merits, so as to be able to hold him as a debtor. Yet, in a wondrous manner, the equitable Creator chose some beforehand by predestining them, while by a just judgment he abandoned others in their evil ways.
>
> Hence it is entirely true that the gift of grace is not obtained from human virtue or from the merit of free choice, but is bestowed solely through the goodness of divine compassion. Some are saved by the gift of his most gracious preceding mercy, having been made “vessels of mercy”; others, however, rejected and predestined to punishment, are condemned, having been made “vessels of wrath.”
>
> [Col. 0061C] This is gathered from the example of Esau and Jacob before they were born. Although they came from one conception and birth and were bound by the same bond of original sin, the gratuitous grace of divine goodness, preceding and showing mercy, drew one of them to itself; while the other, regarded with hatred through a certain severity of justice, was left in the mass of perdition and condemned.
>
> Thus the same Lord speaks through the prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I; Rom. IX).
>
> It follows, therefore, that grace is not bestowed on the basis of preceding merits, but solely by divine calling. No one is saved or condemned, chosen or rejected except according to the purpose of the predestining God, who is just toward the rejected and merciful toward the elect: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10).
>
> Every gift of grace, however, is not given in its entirety to everyone; rather, separate gifts are distributed to individuals, so that, like the members of a body, they may each have their own functions, and one may supply to another what the other does not have [variant: *indigeat altero*, “may need another”] [Col. 0061D]. Thus all things become common when they become mutually necessary members of one another.

I have wished to set down the text of the entire chapter, lest anyone accuse us if we should have wished to excerpt one part and omit another, as though we were corrupting the authors’ opinions and twisting them into the sequence of our own invention.

Desiring to avoid the charge of such an accusation, we have preferred to record above the statements of the authors—namely, Augustine and the others—at greater length and with almost excessive fullness, choosing rather to appear guilty of excessive verbosity than to incur the charge of violating their statements.

[Col. 0062A] If anyone nevertheless wishes to examine more carefully the words and meaning of this passage, he may perhaps judge that we have included nothing superfluous in it for the purpose of the present discussion. For it commends what we ought to attribute to human free choice and what to divine grace; it also shows that the gift of that same grace is bestowed not because of human merit but through the kindness of the heavenly gift, and that it is arranged by the equity of divine governance to whom it is granted and to whom it is denied.

Thus, while commending the cause by which either the elect are justified or the reprobate are abandoned, he teaches that the order of predestination is diverse, not simple. But in order that what we have said may be made clear, let us briefly examine the chapter of the entire text.

Source preparation: Supplied local source; translated as part of this section.

“Between,” he says, “the infusion of divine grace and the will of human free choice there is this distinction. Free choice is a will possessing free power, which of its own accord and spontaneously [Col. 0062B] can desire either good or evil; grace, however, is the gratuitous gift of divine mercy, through which we merit both the beginning of a good will and the accomplishment of a good work.”

By saying this, he intimates that it belongs to free choice to direct the intention of one’s own will either toward choosing good or toward rejecting evil; but that one obtains both the beginning of a good will and the accomplishment of a righteous action not by one’s own powers, but through the gift of heavenly grace.

For that we cannot have the beginning of a good will except by the grace of the heavenly Giver is attested by the Apostle, who says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). If, then, we have nothing except what has been granted to us from above, and if we cannot attain even the smallest measure of a good will by the powers of human free choice unless something from the fountain of the divine gift has flowed into us [Col. 0062C], we are instructed by the mouth of Truth itself that we cannot accomplish anything good without divine grace, as it says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Moreover, that we are anticipated by divine grace both in willing what is good and in acting rightly, blessed Isidore attests in the following passage, saying: “Indeed, divine grace anticipates a person so that he may be good; human free choice does not precede the grace of God, but the grace of God itself anticipates a person who is unwilling, so that he may also will what is good.” For while he was evil, and was committing the will of his free choice to evil, divine clemency mercifully looked upon him; and, by inspiring the beginning of a good will, it turned his desire for wickedness toward the love of goodness, so that the one who had been evil through loving and doing evil might become good through loving and doing good [Col. 0062D].

Commending this grace of anticipation, Scripture says: “Who has given to him first, and he shall be repaid? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:35–36).

There is also attached the reason that renders human powers weak for doing good unless they have been strengthened by the help of the divine gift. He therefore says: “For, under the weight of the flesh, a person is so driven that he is inclined to sin and slow to repent. He has within himself the source of his fall, but he has no means of rising unless the grace of the Creator extends a hand to the one lying prostrate, so that he may be raised up.”

What, then, is the weight of the flesh except the corruption of sin? He incurred this corruption when, after tasting the forbidden tree, his eyes were opened and he saw the squalor of his nakedness [Col. 0063A]. That opening of the eyes, finally, was the emergence of the desire for carnal passions; and he was then struck with astonishment at finding himself naked, because he was ashamed to see himself stripped of the garment of the virtues. No longer remaining in the warmth of heavenly love, but falling into the desire of carnal concupiscence, he heard the address of the divine visitation in the breeze after midday.

By this weight of sin—namely, the desire for carnal passions—a person is driven to be inclined to sin but slow to repent. For from the moment when he opened the eyes of his heart to the pleasure of sin, he kept them closed to the love of righteousness; and after he lost the garment of virtue, he received the nakedness of weakness.

Therefore, since through the blindness of his heart he cannot see what is good, and through the weakness of his infirmity he cannot perform what is right [Col. 0063B], it is plainly established, in accordance with the judgment of this holy man, that “our mortality has within itself the source of its fall, but has no means of rising.” And rightly is a person said to possess in himself what belongs to weakness, since he received from himself both the loss caused by blindness and the poverty of weakness when, through proud disobedience, he lost the protection of the heavenly light by which he had obtained the light of wisdom and the power of salvation. He is no longer able by his own powers to attain what he lost through the merits of his guilt, unless the grace of the Creator, by the hand of his mercy, removes the blindness of his heart and grants him soundness of virtue, so that the light of righteousness may shine upon him and he may be able, through the steps of virtue, to adhere to the righteousness that he sees.

That the original human being possessed the powers of free choice before the fall of transgression, he indicates when he adds: [Col. 0063C] “Finally, through the grace of God free choice is restored to a person, which the first human being had lost. For he had free choice to begin what was good, although it was to be perfected with God’s help; but we receive from God’s grace both the beginning and the perfection of free choice, because we have from him both the beginning and the completion of what is good—from him by whom the gift of grace has been given and free choice has been restored in us.”

We are therefore taught that, before receiving divine grace, we lie far below the condition of the first human being. He had been created in such a way that, by the power of free choice, he could both will and perform the good of righteousness; we, however, lack both capacities. For neither to will nor to do what is good lies within our power unless it has been granted through the generosity of the divine gift [Col. 0063D].

We therefore remain in the same condition into which he fell after the transgression. Just as, before he sinned, both the beginning and the completion of good were open to him through the capacity of free choice, so after the guilt of his offense it remained impossible for him either to begin or to complete what was good. For he was burdened by the guilt of his own weakness into falling, because he had refused to preserve the state of righteousness before incurring guilt.

We too, propagated from that root of descent, acquired a condition of weakness together with the contagion of sin, so that we cannot begin what is good through the desire of a good will, nor carry it out through the service of holy devotion. Therefore, in order that the powers of free choice—which we lost in our first parent [Col. 0064A]—might be restored to us, so that we might be made capable of both beginning and completing what is good, the grace of the divine gift is restored to us. By God’s grace we are now able to begin and complete what is good, whereas previously the weakness of our infirmity rendered us ineffective for these things. Thus we are subsequently taught that the good we do belongs both to us and to the divine gift.

He therefore says: “The good that we do belongs to God, because of his prevenient and subsequent grace; but it belongs to us because of the obedience of free choice [or, according to another reading, ‘will’]. For if it does not belong to God, why do we give thanks to him? And if it does not belong to us, why do we await a reward for good works?”

It is therefore clear that the good performed by the saints must not be attributed to divine grace in such a way that the capacity of free choice is removed, nor attributed to free choice in such a way that we reject the gift of divine grace [Col. 0064B]. The first position removes the merit of human labor; the second denies the gift of grace. Both are plainly blasphemous and contrary to Catholic doctrine.

Accordingly, so that we may both confess the gift of divine grace and not deny the reward of human merit, let us say, in accordance with the teaching of this doctor, that the good we do belongs both to God and to us: to God because of his prevenient and subsequent grace, and to us because of the obedience of free choice.

Therefore, as the same doctor says: “Insofar as we are anticipated by grace, it belongs to God; but insofar as we follow the prevenient grace in doing good, it belongs to us. No one, however, precedes the grace of God by merits, so as to be able to hold him as though he were a debtor.”

If no one precedes the Lord’s grace, and no one can in any good work hold him as a debtor [Col. 0064C], it follows that every good work and every righteous will are bestowed upon a person through the prevenient grace of God. If these are granted by God’s grace, it is clear that all are evil before they are corrected by the gift of grace. But if all are evil before they are made good from evil by prevenient grace, no one is good except the one whom grace makes good.

And if no one is good except the one whom grace makes good, then grace precedes a person so that he may be good; but in order that a person may become not good, he is abandoned by that same grace. To whom the gift of grace is granted and from whom it is concealed is weighed in the judgment of him whose gift it is.

Hence he continues: “But in a wondrous manner the Creator is equitable toward all: by predestining, he chose some beforehand, while others he justly leaves in their wicked ways.” [Col. 0064D]

This, then, is the twofold predestination, balanced according to the distinction of the heavenly judgment: the gift of grace is divinely bestowed upon those whom the heavenly Author, by the counsel of his eternity, ordained for this purpose; but the gift of this grace is concealed from those whom the disposition of the heavenly Judge determined to leave in their wickedness.

For since each person—as the preceding passages testify—is converted from evil to good not by his own merit but by divine grace, only the one whom the heavenly judgment determined should be anticipated is anticipated by grace. The one who has been excluded from this grace is abandoned because the heavenly Judge determined that he should not be anticipated.

Hence he adds: “Therefore it is most true that the gift of grace is bestowed not from human strength or from the merit of free choice, but from the kindness of divine goodness alone [Col. 0065A].”

For since it is clear that the entire human race was condemned in the root of its origin, just as we are all born from one parent, so all of us have been sentenced to death in one human being. Those who are freed from that sentence are freed by the goodness of divine mercy; those who are not freed from it are left under the sentence by which they were condemned.

Those who are not freed have no grounds for complaining about the punishment of their condemnation, because what is justly deserved is returned to them. Those who are freed, however, have reason to give thanks to their Deliverer, since the same punishment would have held them as well had the goodness of divine mercy not come to their aid.

Thus, to whom the gift of grace is granted and to whom it is not granted is weighed according to the judgment of the divine disposition. Accordingly, it appears that there is a twofold ordinance of predestination [Col. 0065B], since one order consists of those who are freed through grace, and the other of those who are abandoned under the sentence of their condemnation.

He continues: “For some are saved by the aid of his most gracious prevenient mercy, having been made ‘vessels of mercy’; but others, reprobate and predestined to punishment, are condemned, having been made ‘vessels of wrath.’”

Those who are saved are saved by the gift of grace; those who remain alienated from salvation were not among the number predestined to salvation. The former, through the favor of the divine gift, have been made “vessels of mercy”; the latter, through the sentence of just condemnation, have been made “vessels of wrath.”

Both, therefore, are predestined: those who are made worthy of salvation have, according to the purpose of predestination, been made “vessels of mercy”; and those who are rendered unworthy of salvation have likewise [Col. 0065C], according to the purpose of predestination, been made “vessels of wrath.”

For just as the divine judgment determined whom it would justify by the gift of its grace, so it also determined whom it would leave empty of this gift of grace.

Commending this twofold purpose of predestination, this doctor continued concerning the salvation of the elect: “For some are saved by the aid of his most gracious prevenient mercy, having been made ‘vessels of mercy.’” Here is the purpose of one predestination, concerning which the Apostle says: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined” (Rom. 8:29).

But concerning the condemnation of the reprobate, Doctor Isidore says: “But others, reprobate and predestined to punishment, are condemned, having been made ‘vessels of wrath,’” thereby showing another purpose of predestination [Col. 0065D].

Thus, by the teaching of this doctor, we plainly recognize a twofold predestination. Confirming it also by the example of two twins, he added: “This is inferred from Esau and Jacob, who, although not yet born, were brought forth from one conception and one birth and were bound by an equal bond of original sin, yet one of them was drawn to himself by the prevenient goodness of divine mercy through gratuitous grace, while the other, regarded with hatred by a certain severity of justice, was condemned by being left in the mass of perdition. Thus also the Lord speaks through the prophet, saying: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.’”

The Catholic doctor therefore shows that both brothers were bound by the same law of birth and by the same condition of sin; that one of them was saved by the gift of heavenly grace [Col. 0066A], while the other was left in the mass of perdition by the severity of justice; that one was loved by God, while the other was cast far away from the grace of love.

Yet neither of them had done anything by which the one deserved to be loved or the other to be hated. Rather, in the case of both, the judgment of the divine disposition displayed different lots of merit, so that it chose Jacob and rejected Esau.

What we are taught by divine authority that God did with the two twins, we must by no means doubt that he also does, according to his divine disposition, with the whole body of the human race. For he did not restrict the governance of his dispensation, by which he rules the entire world, to the narrow limits of two human beings. Instead, heavenly wisdom wished to teach us through a few examples what we ought to understand concerning all [Col. 0066B].

Hence the heavenly oracle said to the mother, who was carrying them in her womb and asking about the same children: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall go forth from your womb” (Gen. 25:23). That is, this was a figure or prophecy of two peoples. For those two could not yet be called peoples, but they were called by the name they bore in the mystery. They were called two peoples because they bore the figure of the whole human race, distributed into two lots as into two peoples: one, namely, the elect, represented under Jacob; the other, the reprobate, represented under Esau.

These two peoples are also signified in the pages of Holy Scripture by two cities, namely Jerusalem and Babylon [Col. 0066C].

Thus, just as we see that of the two twins one was loved by the grace of election while the other was hated by the severity of justice, so we must understand that the people of election were saved by divine grace, while the multitude of the reprobate were condemned by the severity of heavenly justice; and that, by the judgment of the divine disposition, it was determined whom grace would save and whom justice would condemn.

Hence blessed Isidore also proceeds: “Therefore it follows that grace is bestowed without any preceding merits, but by the divine calling alone; and that no one is saved or condemned except according to the purpose of the predestining God, who is just in the reprobate and merciful in the elect: ‘All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth’ (Ps. 24:10).” [Col. 0066D]

For if Jacob was indeed justified without any preceding merits, but by the divine calling alone, it follows that all the elect are justified without any preceding merits, but by the divine calling alone, so that what we have received as having been done in one person we may recognize as being done throughout the whole number of the elect.

And when he says that each person is saved or rejected, chosen or rejected, according to the purpose of the predestining God, he plainly teaches the secret of twofold predestination. For God does not save one and condemn another, or choose one and reject another, by a newly conceived decision. Rather, he determined concerning each person through the successive moments of time as he had predestined all things, before all times, in the counsel of his eternity.

As Scripture says of him: “He made the things that shall be” (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint). That is, all things that are done by the Lord through the changing intervals of time [Col. 0067A] have always been made in the predestination of divinity.

The works of God have new beginnings according to the condition of their creation, but according to the Creator’s disposition they have never ceased to exist. Although they began to exist in the form of their substance in time, they nevertheless did not receive their beginning from time as regards eternal wisdom.

And because the election of the good and the rejection of the evil consist in the counsel of the divine disposition, just as all things are made by God before they come into being, so these too, as they are temporally carried out in their effectiveness one by one, have always remained accomplished in the presence of the Lord.

For whoever is to be taken up in time into the grace of election has always remained taken up in the disposition of divine wisdom [Col. 0067B]; and whoever, rejected from this saving grace, belongs to the lot of condemnation has always stood rejected in the judgment of the divine disposition.

Likewise, whoever is to receive the inheritance of eternal blessedness has always possessed it in the secret of divine predestination; and whoever is to receive the punishments of eternal flames has always, in the predestination of the heavenly judgment, been appointed to them.

And just as the counsel of eternity can never be weakened, so the entire number of the elect will be saved, and none of them will be able to perish. Likewise, the whole assembly of the reprobate will be condemned, and no one among them will become a participant in eternal salvation.

This, then, is the arrangement of twofold predestination, which blessed Isidore commends with sufficiently clear and Catholic reasoning [Col. 0067C].

Let no one, however, say that the reprobate were predestined to sin because they were predestined to punishment. For God predestined the things that he would do, not the things for which he would punish. He will indeed execute judgment, returning life to the elect and punishments to the reprobate.

Just as these things are to be carried out in the presentation of his works, so they have already been accomplished in the eternal disposition, since there can be neither a new counsel, nor a new disposition, nor a new plan with God. Nothing happens accidentally to God.

But just as God is not the author of sin, so neither is he its predestiner. For what is evil cannot arise from the one who is the supreme good. And who is unaware that sin is evil? It therefore does not descend from God, who is supremely good. Hence what does not belong to his operation [Col. 0067D] does not belong to his predestination.

That a person is good or evil, however, belongs to the work of God—not insofar as he is evil, for God made him good, but insofar as every creature is the work of God. Therefore, whether a person is good or evil, his condition is ordered by God. What is to happen to each person, whether in the present life or in the future judgment, he holds as determined by the counsel of his predestination.

God therefore predestined a person to what he would do with that person, not to what he would punish in that person.

We think that this has been demonstrated by the opinions of not a few ecclesiastical doctors: the evil were predestined to punishment, but not to sin. Since God foresaw that they would become sinners and persevere in their sins, he predestined—or preordained—them to punishment [Col. 0068A].

This preordination, or predestination, does not, however, constrain or impel them by some necessity toward punishment, although it is necessary that what God has predestined come to pass, what he has ordained cannot be changed, and things cannot occur otherwise than he has ordered them.

Since he knows all things and nothing can be hidden from him, he disposes of everything according to the counsel of his will, by a just judgment hidden from mortals. That each person is appointed to everlasting punishment does not arise from the injustice of the judge, but from the justice of the one who decrees.

For he knows them to be such that he has appointed them to punishment and that they are worthy of being so appointed. They sinned by their own will; and although they knew the way of truth, they refused to follow it. They chose iniquity and followed it [Col. 0068B]. Because they rejected the truth, the punishment they deserved will rightly overtake them.

Since, however, nothing can be hidden from God, who comprehends all things and sees past and future as present, he knows their deeds and has determined the judgment due to their deeds. Yet he does not judge anyone on the basis merely of what has been determined with him, but on the basis of what each person does.

And although, in the hidden judgments of God, the merits or punishments of individuals remain concealed, each person is judged when he is to receive either a reward for good conduct or torment for evil works.

For just as God’s foreknowledge compels no one to sin, so the hiddenness of his secrets—in which he has already predestined whatever he will do—condemns no one and rewards no one [Col. 0068C]. Each person is rewarded or condemned by his own action.

Although the testimonies of the doctors cited above sufficiently teach that no one is predestined to sin, since it nevertheless remains certain that the reprobate are predestined to punishment, we shall endeavor to establish this more clearly. The doctors cited above teach it plainly enough when they say that God predestined no one to sin.

For he predestined those things that he himself would do: that is, he disposed his own works in the counsel of eternity. Of him it is written that he “made the things that shall be” (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint)—that is, the things that God will do throughout the intervals of time have already been made in the counsel of predestination.

But sins, since they are not from God—that is, since they are not the work of God but of a rational creature apostatizing from God—are not in the predestination of God [Col. 0068D].

He is their condemner, not their author; and of what he is not the author, he is not the predestiner.

Moreover, since he is to reward his elect with the glory of immortality and punish the reprobate with eternal punishment, he predestined these things: both the rewards that he is to bestow upon the holy and the punishments that he is to return to the wicked for their evil works.

For the punishments that the reprobate will undergo, although they appear evil to those who are tormented, are nevertheless good because they are just; and everything that is just is good.

[The supplied source ends here.]

Hence blessed Augustine, in chapter 9 of the *Retractations*: “[The punishment of the wicked, which comes from God, is indeed an evil for the wicked, but it belongs among God’s good works; for it is just that the wicked be punished, and certainly everything that is just is good.]”

Therefore the punishments of penalties that the wicked undergo under God’s judgment are works of God and, for that reason, predestined; sins, however, are not to be counted among God’s works. Consequently, they are neither predestined by God, nor do those who sin sin by predestination, but they are drawn away and cast down by their own desire. And although it has been made sufficiently clear through the opinions of the doctors mentioned above that the wicked are predestined to punishment, they are nevertheless not predestined to sin.

To make this clearer, I wish to discuss the matter further. Since, however, some people perhaps, when they hear that the wicked are predestined to punishment, suppose that they are dragged toward it by some necessity and cannot in any way be changed by that necessity, it does not seem inappropriate to us to make the point more explicit: the predestination of the wicked to punishment is indeed to be taught, but they do not reach punishment for that reason—that is, because they are predestined. The cause of their arrival is the fault of the offender, not the necessity imposed by the predestiner.

For just as the wicked, because they are predestined to punishment, are not for that reason predestined to sin—for each person is drawn into sin after being overcome by his own desire—so also those who sin are predestined to punishment because they were foreknown as sinners who would not repent of their sins. This will perhaps become clearer from what follows.

From the teaching of sacred Scripture we know that the one who is now prince of the lost angels was, from the beginning, placed in God’s paradise. He stood among the principalities of the heavenly host, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty, according to what the prophet says of him:

> “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God; every precious stone was your covering” (Ezek. XVIII, 12).

Now, while at the beginning of his creation he remained in paradise as the prophetic passage describes him, did God—who knows all things before they happen—not know that he would fall from this blessedness because of pride? Or did God’s knowledge compel him to fall? Certainly not. But sacred Scripture does not conceal what drove him to his fall; it says:

> “You walked perfect in your ways amid the stones of fire, from the day of your creation, until iniquity was found in you. In the multitude of your commerce your inner parts were filled with iniquity, and you sinned” (ibid., 14).

[Col. 0069D] Behold the source of his fall. He was not created in order that he might fall, nor was he set over the heavenly ranks for the purpose of becoming proud. Nor was he perfect in his ways from the day of his creation so that he might turn toward iniquity and, swollen with pride, rise up against the goodness of his Creator.

Yet the One who knows all things, for whom nothing is past and nothing future, but who beholds everything with a present gaze, knew that he would fall in this way. He did not know it only when he fell, or when his inner parts were filled with iniquity; he knew it before he created him. Nevertheless, God’s knowledge did not compel him to fall; his iniquity did.

The prophetic passage continues:

> “And I cast you out from the mountain of God, and destroyed you, O cherub who protected, from the midst of the stones of fire” (ibid., 16).

The cause of his expulsion and destruction is also added:

> “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty; you destroyed your wisdom in your beauty” (ibid., 17).

That is: “I did not compel you to destruction; you yourself were the cause of your destruction. Because of your pride you swelled up against your Creator, and you lost the wisdom that I had bestowed on you, since through it you were unwilling to be subject to your Creator in holy fear. While considering the glory of your exalted position, because of which you scorned to be subject, you lost that very exalted position. Therefore:

> ‘I cast you to the earth; I gave you over before the faces of kings. By the multitude of your iniquities and by the iniquity of your commerce you polluted your sanctuary. Therefore I will bring forth fire from your midst, and it shall consume you; and I will reduce you to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all who see you. All who saw you among the nations shall be astonished at you. You have become nothing, and you shall not exist forever’” (ibid., 18–19).

Behold the punishment of the proud angel: he was cast from paradise to earth; in place of sanctification he received pollution, in place of beauty ashes, in place of the light of wisdom the fire of burning, so that, reduced to nothing, he might be nothing forever.

For we have heard that, after the transgression of the proud angel, the sentence of vengeance was pronounced. But did the Almighty first consider what punishment He should bring upon the sinning angel only after the angel had sinned? If so, the Apostle’s statement would not be true: “With God there is no change, nor shadow of alteration” (Jas. I, 17). For where a thought arises that was not there before, the mind’s former state is changed. Nor can a mind be transferred from one thing to another without alteration when it is unsettled by changing thoughts. But to think such things of the unchangeable Highest is the height of impiety.

Therefore, since there is no change with God, there is no new thought; and if there is no new thought, there is no new plan; if there is no new plan, there is no new decision; and if there is no new decision, there is no new judgment. God’s judgments appear new when they proceed outward from the hidden disposition of His interior counsel, but in the plan of eternity they are never new. Whatever God newly does through the intervals of time has always been done in the eternity of His divinity.

Therefore, although vengeance followed the guilt of the proud angel after his transgression, that vengeance had always been present in the knowledge of the Godhead. Just as God knew, before he sinned, that he would sin, so also He had always held in the plan of eternity the punishment that He would render to him as a sinner. Yet just as God’s foreknowledge did not compel the devil to transgress, so the predetermination of his punishment did not draw him into his fall. He was created good and became evil through his own fault; and avenging punishment overtook the guilt of his wickedness.

Our first parents likewise lived in paradise, free from the contagion of sin, before their conversation with the serpent. But did God not know, before they sinned, that they would sin? Yet this foreknowledge of God did not compel them to sin. The cause of their sin was the cunning persuasion of the crafty enemy and their transgression of the divine command.

They did not sin because God foreknew that they would sin, but because they neglected to keep the command that had been given to them. The guilt of transgression was followed by an immediate punishment, so that the fault of disobedience might be punished by the sentence of death. Yet God did not first devise the punishment with which He would strike the transgressor at the moment when humanity sinned, nor at the moment when, giving the command of obedience, He simultaneously threatened punishment, saying:

> “On whatever day you eat from it”—that is, from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—“you shall surely die” (Gen. II, 17).

Just as nothing new can occur in God’s knowledge, so nothing new can occur in His judgment. Just as from the beginning He knew that humanity would sin, so from the beginning He knew how He would punish the sinner, because with God there is no new thought, just as there is no new plan; and just as there is no new plan, so there is no new judgment.

With Him there is no change; there is no alteration. His wisdom is uniform and His deliberation everlasting. Therefore, just as before humanity sinned He knew that it would sin, so before He punished it He had decreed the punishment by which it would be punished.

Yet humanity was not punished because God had decreed that it should be punished, but because it sinned. Adam did not transgress because God foreknew that he would sin, but because he listened more to the serpent’s persuasion than to God’s command.

Cain rises against his brother Abel. Blinded by the jealousy of envy, he persecutes the innocent and stains the earth with the blood of fratricide. This crime certainly did not escape God. The murderer is reproved, and the cry of the shed blood refutes his denial. But did God first know Cain as a murderer only when he killed his brother? If this were granted, it would follow that God is ignorant of something and learns it through the passage of time. But God cannot learn what He previously did not know. He knows all things—present, past, and future.

Therefore He was never ignorant of what Cain was going to do against his brother; and if He was never ignorant of it, He always knew it. But because whatever God knows will undoubtedly happen and cannot be averted or changed, did God’s knowledge therefore compel Cain to murder his brother? What impious person would say this?

What drove Cain to commit so great a crime, the Book of Genesis does not conceal. It teaches that the Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings, but did not look upon Cain and his offerings (Gen. IV, 4). From this, the monstrousness of the fratricide gathered fuel for hatred. It was not restrained by divine correction, but was completed in the madness of the fury he had begun, through the murder of his brother.

Cain, therefore, was not compelled to fratricide by God’s foreknowledge, but by the malignity of envy and the madness of fury. He could not bear to see his brother’s glory; he could not endure it, and attempted to extinguish it.

Heavenly vengeance, however, did not leave so savage a crime unpunished. Cain was driven “wandering and fugitive upon the earth,” and the iniquity of the murderer was expiated by the blows of a sevenfold vengeance.

But after the enormity of so great a crime had been committed, did God first deliberate how the impious murderer should be punished? Did the freshness of the offense drive Him into meditation upon a new plan, so that, just as a previously unimagined crime had confused the world, the deliberation of a previously unimagined punishment might disturb God? The prudent mind does not accept this. Just as God foreknew Cain’s future wickedness, so He had determined within Himself how Cain would be punished.

Yet Cain was not punished because God had decreed in His predestination that he should be punished, but because Cain himself had committed the crime for which he was punished. God does not condemn anyone by predestination, just as He does not compel anyone to sin by foreknowledge. Each person sins after being enticed by his own desire, and because he has sinned, he is struck by the vengeance of heavenly judgment.

The world is filled with a multitude of human beings, and as the human race multiplies, the number of vices increases. God sees the wickedness of the human heart falling from day to day into worse evil; the accumulation of iniquity continually rising toward what is worse; and the intention of the human heart at all times descending into the depths of vice, without extending its hand toward any thought or pursuit of good, but rushing headlong toward the whirlpool of wickedness.

Therefore, as Scripture says, “it repented Him that He had made humanity” (Gen. VI, 6). To cleanse the world from so great a plague of evils, He commanded an ark to be built in which a seed might be preserved for the age. He announced a flood upon the world; the entire earth was buried beneath masses of water; the summits of the mountains were covered by the devastation of the abyss; the ocean’s flood spread across the whole world; and whatever had been beneath the heavens was overwhelmed by the sea.

What more need be said? “From reptile to bird, from human being to beast, all” were destroyed. Only Noah with his household was saved through the ark. Once those alone were saved whom the ark’s enclosure had contained, everything living that had been outside was destroyed in a single flood.

The truth of Scripture testifies that this happened. But should we suppose that the profanation of the wicked first became known to God when they themselves sinned? It is written of Him that He “knows all things before they happen” (Dan. XIII, 42), and the Psalmist proclaims: “You understood my thoughts from afar” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 3).

If God not only knows but also understands thoughts from afar, then He unquestionably knows from afar the sequence of human actions before they occur. Therefore He knew beforehand the deeds of those whom He destroyed in the foaming flood, before those deeds had been done. Yet they did not do those things because of His knowledge—by which He knew from afar that they would do exactly what they did—but because of the inventions of their own wickedness, for which they deserved to perish.

For if their deeds and God’s foreknowledge are considered, their deeds did not proceed from God’s foreknowledge. Rather, those deeds were included within the divine knowledge that encompasses everything. They took their cause and origin not from that knowledge, but from the presumption of the human heart. For goodness can flow only from the fountain of goodness, and vice never takes its origin from virtue.

Thus, just as the sins by which they offended God were enclosed within the breadth of divine knowledge, so too the punishment by which they were judged was not conceived in the plan of eternity only after they had sinned. Just as their deeds never escaped God’s knowledge, so the measure of the punishment by which such deeds would be condemned never escaped the predestination of divine judgment.

Just as the knowledge of their crimes was eternal, so the sentence of punishment was defined in the heavenly secrets. And just as the foreknowledge of the truth did not drive them into wickedness, so predestination did not compel them to punishment. The evil of desire drew them into guilt; guilt sent them to punishment.

As God, in the wisdom of His complete knowledge, knows everything, so by the plan of the universe He orders everything. Whatever He will do in time already stands predestined in the plan of eternity. Thus the punishment by which they were then chastised already remained decreed in eternal predestination. They were delivered over to punishment, however, when the enormity of their crimes showed them to be worthy of punishment.

Thus neither foreknowledge compelled them to guilt, nor predestination drew them to punishment.

Let us now bring forward Pentapolis, burning with heavenly flames, and examine both the cause of its destruction and the character of its vengeance. The inhabitants were held by every kind of shameful vice, and there was no crime by which they were not afflicted. They were swollen with pride, bloated by gluttony, corrupted by the foulness of lust, weighed down by the torpor of idleness, hardened by the savagery of inhumanity, and alien to the kindness of hospitality.

The tumult of so many crimes flew above the air, split the clouds, broke into heaven, and rushed up to the throne of the divine majesty. Therefore the Book of Genesis says in the person of the heavenly Judge:

> “The cry of Sodom has come to me. I will descend and see whether they have completed in action the cry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. XVIII, 20–21).

Did the One from whom nothing is hidden, of whom it is written that all things are naked and open before His eyes and that no creature is invisible in His sight (Heb. IV, 13), not know the deeds of the Sodomites? Did He, whose eye observes the good and the evil, not see the actions of a few human beings?

He pretends not to know what He does not wish to see, and prefers to be ignorant of what He desires not to punish. How inclined He is to pardon and how reluctant to vengeance is shown by the fact that, for the sake of ten righteous people, He wished to spare many thousands of sinners (Gen. XVIII, 32).

What more need be said? When He sees everyone rushing together toward evil, and no one in so great a multitude is found who seeks to turn from evil to good, heavenly fire envelops them all, and equal vengeance consumes those equal in crime.

If the deeds of the guilty are considered, what is more just than that such crimes should be punished? If we consider the Judge’s clemency, what is more merciful than His unwillingness to strike such people? Behold: we see the iniquity of the guilty, by their own crime, wearying heaven, breaking into the secret counsel of the heavenly King—and yet the Judge’s mercy delays vengeance and searches for an opportunity to spare.

Let us now turn the eyes of our mind to God’s foreknowledge, and see that God knew the crimes of the Sodomites not only after they had been committed but before they were committed, and that He had arranged the vengeance of punishment in the judgment of His predestination before it overtook them.

The Sodomites, however, serving the desires of the flesh, burst into such crimes that they deserved to be consumed by heavenly fire. The source and origin of so many crimes was therefore the pleasure of the flesh; but the weight of their sins extorted the sentence of vengeance. Their destruction, then, must not be attributed to predestination, nor their sinning to foreknowledge.

Egypt oppressed God’s people under the yoke of domination, afflicted them through the labor of slavery, and struck them by the killing of their children. Moses was sent so that God’s people might be released (Exod. VIII and following). Pharaoh was hardened so that Egypt might be struck by many plagues. Finally, the firstborn of the Egyptians were killed, and Israel was released.

Again, repentance seized the Egyptians, and they pursued Israel after its release, hastening to subject it once more to its former slavery. At last divine wonders were renewed. The Red Sea was divided in the likeness of walls; the sea was suspended on the right and left; the earth was exposed amid the waves; and, with dry feet, the multitude of the Israelite people proceeded through the open channel of the sea.

The pursuing Egyptians were overwhelmed by the whirlpools of the waters; the waves invaded them; the sea swallowed them. A wondrous distinction was made between the pious and the impious: the abyss freed the former and engulfed the latter; it brought the former safely to shore with peaceful steps, while the deep chasm held the latter submerged.

Thus the mercy of the Almighty freed the pious, while the Judge’s severity condemned the impious.

If we examine these things more carefully, we shall see that both the affliction and deliverance of the Israelites, and the cruelty and condemnation of the Egyptians, had long existed in divine foreknowledge; and that it had been predestined how God would deal with both peoples.

God speaks to Abraham:

> “Know with foreknowledge that your offspring will be a stranger in a land not its own; they will subject them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years. Nevertheless, I will judge the nation whom they will serve, and afterward they will depart with great wealth” (Gen. XV).

They had not yet been born; they still existed in Abraham’s loins. Yet already they were foretold as destined for slavery, already promised release, and already Egypt was threatened with judgment.

To Moses also, when God sent him into Egypt, He spoke as follows:

> “You shall enter, you and the elders of Israel, to the king of Egypt, and you shall say to him: ‘The Lord God of the Hebrews has called us. We shall go a three-days’ journey through the wilderness, to sacrifice to the Lord our God.’ But I know that the king of Egypt will not release you except by a mighty hand. For I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all my wonders that I shall perform in its midst, and after this he will release you” (Exod. IX and following).

Are we not plainly taught that the manner in which the Egyptians would be punished had been arranged—that is, predestined? For what else is meant by: “I will strike Egypt with all my wonders that I shall perform in its midst”? It is shown that, in the divine predestination, it had been established by which and how many plagues Egypt would be struck, and when it would release Israel.

What else does He mean by: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart”—and, “Pharaoh’s heart was hardened”—except that Pharaoh would not first be softened so as to release God’s people until Egypt had been struck by all the plagues with which divine judgment had arranged that it should be struck?

Thus, when Egypt had been worn down by nine plagues and Pharaoh’s heart had still not been softened, the Lord said to Moses:

> “I will strike Egypt with one more plague, and then Pharaoh will release you.”

Therefore the number and measure of the plagues by which Egypt was worn down had been predestined within the arrangement of divine judgment. Pharaoh’s hardened heart was then softened when the decreed measure of vengeance had been completed.

Finally, the fact that Pharaoh and his army perished in the Red Sea while Israel crossed unharmed, just as it contains the great mystery of the sacrament, was also accomplished through the secret of divine dispensation: the former were to perish, and the latter to be saved.

Since it is therefore clear that, in God’s foreknowledge, the affliction of the Israelites and the cruelty of the Egyptians had existed, so also the deliverance of the former and the destruction of the latter had always existed in the judgment of predestination.

Yet the cruelty of the Egyptians must not be attributed to divine foreknowledge, just as their condemnation must not be attributed to the hidden secret of predestination. God foreknew what the Egyptians would be—that is, He had always known their cruelty—but He did not make them cruel.

Although the Psalmist testifies concerning them that God “turned their heart”—that is, the heart of the Egyptians—“so that they hated His people and dealt deceitfully with His servants” (Ps. CIV, 25), God did not make them deceitful or inflame them with hatred of wickedness. Rather, since they were such as would rage in hatred and deceive by treachery, He arranged to chastise His people through them, so that the people who had abandoned God amid prosperity might, admonished by the scourges, flee back to Him.

God therefore foreknew the cruelty of the Egyptians but did not create it. They did not become such because they were foreknown to become such. They became evil through their own wickedness, not through God’s foreknowledge. For that reason they were predestined, by the hidden arrangement of judgment, to the punishment by which they were punished.

That the wicked are not condemned through predestination but through their own iniquity is testified by sacred Scripture. It says that God told Abraham concerning the Amorites that his offspring would be strangers in a foreign land for four hundred years, and then added:

> “In the fourth generation they shall return here, for the iniquities of the Amorites have not yet been completed to the present time” (Gen. XV, 16).

These words show that their iniquities would reach the summit of wickedness at the time when Abraham’s offspring deserved to be freed from the yoke of slavery, brought into the land, and the nations of the Amorites destroyed.

Thus it is shown that those nations, which had previously possessed the promised land, were destroyed not because of divine predestination but because of their own wickedness.

Therefore no one is condemned by the decree of divine predestination, although the Judge’s justice has decreed that those who will persevere in sins are to be condemned. Each person is condemned when he is judged deserving of condemnation on account of his sins.

It would be lengthy, and would exceed the limits of brevity, if we wished to traverse the whole sequence of the divine Scriptures and establish from all the events of divine judgment both God’s foreknowledge and His predestination—and that foreknowledge does not compel anyone to sin, nor predestination to punishment.

Perhaps this is unnecessary, since what we have said above may be sufficient, and since the piety of faith, just as it believes that God is ignorant of nothing, likewise does not believe that anyone is driven to sin by His foreknowledge. Although faith confesses that everything is ruled by the judgment of divine disposition, it does not accept that anyone is to be condemned by predestination, even though it does not deny that the wicked are predestined to punishment.

The wicked are predestined to punishment because whatever God is going to do has already been predestined in the arrangement of eternity. He will judge the impious and condemn them to everlasting punishment. Since this is counted among God’s works, it cannot be denied that it has been predestined—unless someone should say that the judgment by which the world will be judged is not a work of God.

Since no believer denies this, it likewise cannot be denied that God has arranged in predestination how He will judge each person. For just as there is no new knowledge in God, so there is no new arrangement. The simple nature of divinity, just as it admits nothing changeable, likewise admits nothing composite.

Therefore knowledge and arrangement are not varied in God, as though God knew at one time and arranged at another. Rather, He knows and arranges simultaneously, although He knows certain things that He does not arrange, such as sins. For those things that He Himself does not do do not belong to His arrangement, although those who sin do not escape the judgment of divine power, and by the very means through which they exercise the wickedness of their perversity, they serve the hidden judgment of God.

Thus in God there is neither knowledge without arrangement nor arrangement without knowledge. Otherwise, if He possessed knowledge without arrangement, so that He knew at one time and arranged at another, God would no longer be of a simple nature, nor would He be unchangeable. For wherever intervals of time succeed one another, mutability is present. There would be an interval of time in God if He did not know and arrange simultaneously—if knowledge came first and arrangement followed afterward.

Since the reasoning of a simple nature does not permit this, it follows that arrangement exists together with God’s knowledge. Therefore, concerning those whom He knows will persevere in evil to the end, He has arranged what He will do with them.

Yet they are not to be punished because this has been arranged for them, but because they will persevere in evil.

Let us now bring forward the Antichrist. No believer doubts that he has been foreknown as one who will become evil and has been predestined by divine judgment to punishment. From him let us learn that God’s foreknowledge does not compel anyone to guilt, nor predestination draw anyone to punishment. What we have said about the head, let us understand also of his body.

For just as Christ is the head of the elect, so the Antichrist is the head of the reprobate. And just as all the saints are Christ’s body, so all the wicked are the body of the Antichrist.

That man of perdition has not yet been born, yet his wickedness is already foreknown by all, and it is not unknown that he has already been predestined to destruction. The Apostle, writing to the Thessalonians, says of him (II Thess. II):

> “Let no one deceive you in any way, for unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or is worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, presenting himself as though he were God.”

A little later he says:

> “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of His mouth and destroy him by the brightness of His coming—him whose coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power, sign, and false wonder, and with every seduction of wickedness for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved. And therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity.”

In these words of the Apostle, the wickedness of the Antichrist is demonstrated, as are his destruction and the destruction not only of him but also of those who will belong to his lot.

When he is called the man of sin and the son of perdition, and when it is announced that his arrogance will be so great that he will exalt himself above everything called God and wish to be worshiped as God, the wickedness of his malignity is plainly described. When the Apostle proclaims that he will be killed and destroyed at the Savior’s coming, he plainly indicates his condemnation.

Again, when he implies that many will believe his false signs and wonders, and declares that they will be judged, he reveals both their sin and their punishment. Therefore, when the Apostle says such things about the Antichrist, does he not show that his iniquity has already been foreknown and that he himself has been predestined to punishment?

He will, after all, be a human being consisting of a rational soul and flesh, deriving his origin from the first parent, and thus sharing the origin of all human beings. By calling him both a human being and the son of perdition, the Apostle indicates what his nature will be.

Although he will be a vessel of the devil, he will nevertheless be what the others are who trace the beginning of their birth to Adam. Thus, just as he does not yet exist because he has not yet been born, so he has not yet done anything good or evil. Yet the Apostle testifies that he has already been predestined to punishment.

But because he has been foreknown as one who will become evil, will he therefore be evil? Or because he is now predestined to punishment, will he therefore be condemned?
