If someone should say that, because he will be the devil’s vessel and Satan will exercise through him the punishment of his wickedness, he is already assigned to condemnation with the devil, this would rightly be said if that human being had been created by the devil or were himself the devil.

But since he will be God’s creature, since he will be born from the same parent from whom all human beings are born, since he will be fashioned and made by God’s hands, and since he will be a human being consisting purely of a rational soul and flesh, why will such power be given to the devil over him that he should be regarded as the devil’s most favored vessel?

Here must we not say with the Apostle:

> “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. IX, 20).

And again:

> “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments and untraceable His ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has first given to Him, and it shall be repaid to him?” (Rom. XI, 33–34).

Although we cannot comprehend the reasons for all His works, we know that He who is the fountain of justice does nothing unjustly.

Let us therefore return to what was said above. Since this man of iniquity has already been foreknown as one who will become evil and is held to have been predestined to punishment, will he be evil because of this foreknowledge, or will he perish because he has been assigned to destruction?

If this were so, his wickedness would not be his fault, and therefore he would not be condemned justly. But far be it from us to say that God is the cause of anyone becoming evil, or that He condemns anyone who does not deserve condemnation, since it is written:

> “All the works of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10).

Therefore whoever is condemned by the Judge of truth is condemned because of his own fault.

The man of iniquity, then, will not be wicked because he was foreknown as one who would become such. Rather, he will become wicked by sinning through his own will. Similarly, the one who has already been predestined to punishment is not handed over to the torments of Gehenna for that reason, but because of the weight of his iniquities, on account of which he is even now predestined to death.

Unless someone should say that he has not been predestined to destruction, despite the Apostle’s statement that “the Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of His mouth and destroy him by the presence of His coming” (II Thess. II, 8).

John also speaks of him in the Apocalypse under the figure of the beast:

> “The beast that you saw was, and is not, and it will ascend from the abyss and go into destruction. And the inhabitants of the earth will marvel, whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world” (Rev. XVII, 8).

Here it should be noted that he signifies not only that the beast goes into destruction, but also those whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world.

From this it is apparent that those who are not among the number of the elect go into destruction. Those who are not written in the book of life are not among the number of the elect; for those who are written there cannot perish. Those who are not written there from the beginning of the world will perish.

If they were not written in the book of life from the beginning of the world, they do not belong to life, and therefore they have been assigned to the punishment of death.

Again, concerning the same beast, in the same book:

> “The beast that was and is not, he himself is the eighth and is of the seven, and he goes into destruction” (ibid., 11).

Under the figure of the beast he designates the Antichrist and indicates that he has been predestined to destruction.

Therefore, although he has been predestined to destruction, he will not perish because he was predestined to it, but because of his wickedness, on account of which he is known to have been predestined to perdition.

Thus, just as he was foreknown as one who would become wicked and predestined to destruction, yet will be neither wicked nor destroyed because of God’s foreknowledge or predestination, but will become evil through his own will and perish because of the multitude of his wicked deeds, so likewise all the reprobate, although foreknown as evil and predestined to punishment, have not become—or will not become—evil because of God’s foreknowledge. Rather, they have acted wickedly through the free judgment of their will.

Nor will they be tortured because they were predestined to punishment, but because they did things for which they deserved to undergo punishment.

The Apostle says of them:

> “Because they did not receive the truth so as to be saved, therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” (II Thess. II).

Is it not clear that all these were foreknown as those who would become evil, and that it is not unknown that they belong to the lot of the condemned? If they belong to the lot of the condemned, have they not been assigned to it? And if they have been assigned to it, have they not also been predestined?

Yet they are not to be condemned because they were predestined, just as they will not become evil because God’s foreknowledge knew that they would become such. They will be condemned because of their own wickedness, not because of God’s predestination.

In the same way, they will become evil because, by the free choice of their own will, they chose to be such—not because of divine foreknowledge.

But if someone should contend that there is foreknowledge of the wicked but not predestination, on the ground that whatever is predestined must necessarily happen, the same must also be thought concerning foreknowledge. Whatever God foreknows will undoubtedly happen, and it will happen in the way it is foreknown. For if it is true, it is foreknowledge; if it is not true, it is not foreknowledge.

Therefore whatever God foreknows will certainly happen, and it will happen as it is foreknown. For whoever He foreknows to be among the number of the elect will undoubtedly be elect; but whoever He foreknows to be among the number [fragment ends].
of the reprobate, he will undoubtedly be reprobate. Therefore, since he already knows both these and those [Col. 0079C], and foresaw them from the beginning of the world, those will be elect whom he foresaw to be elect, and those reprobate whom he likewise foresaw to be reprobate; both the one and the other are known to God. Accordingly, if predestination must be rejected because whatever is predestined is unchangeable, foreknowledge must also be rejected, because whatever is foreknown is unchangeable.

But if foreknowledge indicates God’s omniscient knowledge and does not compel anyone to sin, while predestination signifies the preordination and preparation of divine works and drives no one toward punishments, there is no reason why foreknowledge should be accepted and predestination rejected. For just as it is pious and religious to believe of God that he “knows all things before they come to pass” (Dan. XIII, 42), so it is pious and religious [Col. 0080A] to hold of God that he “has made the things that are to be” (Isa. XLV, 11), and: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. CX, 2). The Psalmist also says: “God has spoken once” (Ps. LXI, 12). And blessed Job says: “God speaks once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time” (Job XXXIII, 14).

Now it is the judgment of the Catholic saints that predestination is the eternal disposition of God’s works. Since, therefore, whatever God is going to do he already has disposed in the eternal counsel of his judgment, it follows that all God’s works are predestined. Accordingly, when it is said of the wicked that they are predestined to punishments, this is what is meant: God has, by the hidden sacrament of his judgments, disposed what he is going to do with them. It is therefore not contrary to the divine dispensation [Col. 0080B] if the wicked are said to be predestined to punishment, since predestination concerns God’s works; among those works of God is the judgment by which the reprobate are to be judged.

We have therefore explained, as best we could, how the predestination by which the wicked are said to be assigned to punishments does not constrain them by any necessity to punishment, but that by such an expression the ordering of divine works is being set forth. And since above we demonstrated the statements of the saints in which the wicked are said to be predestined to punishments, whoever denies the predestination of the wicked contradicts not us, but those whose authority we follow.

Let us not therefore be drawn into guilt because we follow the authority of the saints. For if what they say is Catholic and does not conflict with right faith, then we too should not be judged to depart from the rectitude of the Catholic faith [Col. 0080C] if we say and hold what they said and held. Their teaching fortifies the faith of the Church; and we, who are contained within the bosom of the Church, are instructed by their teaching. We do not presume to hold any view other than what they taught us, to go anywhere except where they lead, or to say anything other than what they say.

With these matters thus stated, we beseech the piety of your greatness that, if these writings have not displeased your wisdom, they may remain in your possession and not be made public until the controversy concerning this question has been carefully examined and sifted by all, and what all ought to hold has been confirmed. But if this little book has displeased you, we earnestly ask that it be corrected through your agency, and that the corrections made be not concealed from us.

[Col. 0081]

# A BOOK BY RATRAMNUS, MONK OF CORBIE, ON THE FACT THAT CHRIST WAS BORN OF A VIRGIN

*(In Acherius, volume I of the Spicilegium, p. 52.)*

## ACHERIUS’S NOTICE

[Col. 0081A] Acherius gives the following notice concerning Ratramnus in his Preface:

“Ratramnus—or, as others call him, Bertramnus—monk and priest of Corbie: I have at last, and not without effort, brought back to Gaul his little work *On the Fact That Christ Was Born of a Virgin*, which for so many centuries had been buried in darkness in England. The occasion was provided by Usserius of Armagh, who, in order to besprinkle Ratramnus with the stain of heresy, whispers that he entirely rejects the transformation of the substance of bread into the body of the Son of God in the sacrament of the Eucharist, in the two books which he wrote about that sacrament. Usserius tries improperly to persuade us of this in his *History of Gottschalk*, chapter II, in these words:

‘Among his little works—that is, Ratramnus’s—which did not come to the notice of Trithemius, there is one on the Nativity of Christ, in which he defends the same doctrine that he teaches in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. Another is on the soul,’ and so forth.

[Col. 0081B] “How far this assertion is from the truth is proved by the work itself, in which there is not even the trace of a word or letter of this error. Indeed, the Magdeburg Centuriators themselves, those champions of the opposing cause, briefly refute Usserius in the ninth century, in the chapter ‘On Doctrine,’ column 212:

‘Bertramnus contains the seeds of transubstantiation, for he uses the terms “change” and “conversion.”’

And in chapter 6, ‘On the Ceremonies and Rites of the Church,’ column 243:

‘Bertramnus shows in his book *On the Body and Blood* that the Lord’s body and blood are placed upon the altar or table and distributed from there to the people,’ and so forth.

[Col. 0082A] “Ratramnus has been learnedly and eloquently defended from every blemish by Sixtus of Siena, in the preface to the *Holy Library*, by Cardinal Peronius, and by President Mauguin. The former, in book II of the *Eucharist*, chapters 1 and 2; the latter, in chapter 37 of his *Historical and Chronological Dissertation*. The works which Ratramnus produced testify that he flourished in the time of Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald.”

Thus far we have copied Acherius. We now warn the reader that Ratramnus and his abbot Ratbert wrote about the Virgin’s childbirth in such a way that neither appears to have read the other’s little work. For if they had read them, it is hardly credible that both would have produced the same testimonies in order to establish each his own opinion, without taking any care to show that those testimonies had been twisted by the opponent into a perverse meaning.

It should also not be omitted that the earlier edition was collated with an ancient manuscript of Dallæus by D. Edmond Martene, who communicated its variant readings to us.

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

[Col. 0081]

[Col. 0081C] If all Christians are reckoned under the one Master, Christ; if all believers glory in the one heavenly Father; if by the covenant of one Spirit we are joined together in the solid bond of one charity, I need not fear that I am separated from your gracious regard, so that I may fashion familiar writings for your religious consideration. For blood relationship is not so great as relationship through the Spirit. Earthly descent is far inferior to divine descent, and the duties of temporal service do not produce as much favor of love as the divine fire generates [Col. 0082C] charity.

Accordingly, let an unfamiliar face, an unknown name, or the absence of any comparison of familiarity cease to matter where, for the joining together of a social bond, so many, such great, and such necessary rights of fellowship come together. Therefore do not reject as a stranger the one whom heavenly condition has made your near brother. Since these things are so, I beg your reverence not to disdain responding to the suggestion of our lowliness.

# CHAPTER I  
## Errors in Germany concerning Christ’s birth. The author gives reasons why Christ ought to have been born like other human beings.

[Col. 0083A]

There is a report—and we have learned it from the not-unworthy account of certain people—that the ancient serpent is spreading the poisons of a new faithlessness through the regions of Germany and is attempting, by I know not what subtle fraud, to overthrow the Catholic faith concerning the Savior’s birth. It teaches that Christ’s infancy, through the virginal gate of the womb, did not have the genuine origin of human birth, but emerged monstrously from the secrecy of the womb by an uncertain route of light into the air; that this was not to be born but to burst forth.

For what did not follow the ways of the womb in being born, but burst through wherever it happened to turn, as through the wall of a house, was not properly born but violently emerged. [Col. 0083B] Thus Christ was neither truly born, nor did Mary truly give birth. Yet the Catholic faith holds that Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary.

The angel sent to her announces this in precise words: “Behold,” he says, “you will conceive in your womb and bear a son” (Luke 1:31). See how clearly he rejected the impious sect. He does not say, “You will conceive a son, and he will emerge from your womb,” but “you will conceive and bear,” referring both actions to Mary, so that, with her virginity inviolate, she might conceive as a woman and give birth as a mother. [Note: [Col. 0083D] “With virginity inviolate.” We have emended thus, since the reading was “so that virginity.”] Otherwise she would become glorious as the mother of divinity through conception, but be dishonored by childbirth.

One action would then seem to belong to her own office, the other to the effect of the one conceived; thus neither would she herself be called an intact mother, nor would the Savior’s birth be complete through his mother.

Even if the angel sent to Mary had spoken in this way, it would not necessarily have compelled the belief that Christ’s birth from his mother was extraordinary. For he who chose to be conceived from a virgin woman could readily be believed to have been born from a virgin woman, since he who chose to arise from the more fragile sex of humanity would in no way have rejected the manner of human birth while preserving virginity’s integrity.

It was plainly inconsistent with the plan of the Godhead that he should choose a womb in a virginal body in which he would be conceived, formed, and carried for nine months, yet reject the path of the womb by which he would proceed from the virginal chamber. Therefore, let those who chatter such things either teach another route by which women who give birth lawfully bring forth their children, apart from the customary path of childbirth, or let them confess that Christ had an exit from the Virgin’s womb of the kind that the law of nature demonstrates, without violating the inviolable modesty of her integrity.

It is reported that, before the young vipers reach the time of birth, they do not await the completion of nature’s maturity but emerge by gnawing through their mother’s sides, bringing about their mother’s death. There is also a common belief that the weasel conceives through its mouth and brings forth its offspring through its ear.

Perhaps, then, whoever denies Christ the way of human birth either grants him a viper’s birth, destructive to the mother’s conception, or one fashioned after the weasel in fabulous tales. Thus he would prefer the Redeemer of humanity, conceived of a Virgin, to assume either a serpentine birth contrary to nature or an animal birth invented by fiction rather than a human one.

In this way, then, anything one wishes may be imagined, and Christ may be blasphemed as having been born from anywhere and by any means one pleases, so that the Word made flesh may not have a virginal birth but a monstrous emergence.

# CHAPTER II  
## The violation of the mother’s integrity is alleged. The answer: Mary remained ever a virgin.

But, I ask, why do you refuse to ascribe to Christ the natural progress through the virginal gate? “For this reason,” you say, “because if he left through the gate of the womb, the Virgin’s integrity was not left inviolate.”

In fact, wherever he emerged, according to your opinion her integrity was consequently violated. For if the Savior’s birth necessarily had to corrupt the way of nature, then necessarily, wherever he emerged—whether through the side, the belly, the loins, or the upper or lower parts of the body—he proceeded without preservation of integrity.

But far be it from Catholic understanding that a birth through which corrupted things were restored should be believed to have corrupted what was intact. [Note: [Col. 0083D] “Were corrupted.” In the printed editions the reading was *corrupted*; in the same chapter, where the former term is subsequently denied, we have added *were*.]

At last understand, foolish presumption, that if the Savior’s birth could take place through any part of a virginal body without damage to integrity, then it could consequently take place through the gate of the womb. But if he was going to violate that gate, then wherever he emerged, he violated it.

The Catholic faith, however, confesses concerning the Virgin, the Savior’s mother, that she was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth. You see that both are believed and both confessed: the mother’s virginity and the infant’s emergence.

For, because of the inviolate chamber of modesty, it proclaims her virgin before childbirth, in childbirth, and after childbirth; and because of the emergence of a true birth, it confesses the true childbirth of the woman who gave birth.

For what is “a virgin before childbirth” except a virgin who has conceived? What is “a virgin in childbirth” except a virgin giving birth? And what is “a virgin after childbirth” except a virgin remaining so after childbirth?

Where, then, is the virgin giving birth, if childbirth is denied? Moreover, childbirth is denied when it is proclaimed that the Virgin did not give birth. But she did not give birth if the birth proceeded otherwise than through the gate of nature. Such an emergence is not the childbirth of a virgin, but merely the particular emergence of the infant himself.

Let this invention of falsehood therefore be silenced, and let the unshaken Catholic faith be held: it confesses that Christ was truly born of his mother; it believes, proclaims, and venerates that the Virgin Mary truly conceived and gave birth, and that after childbirth—that is, after bringing forth her son—she remained a virgin.

# CHAPTER III  
## The author proves that Christ emerged through the womb. The parts of the body are not at all shameful. How the parts of the body become defiled. The Holy Spirit sanctified the blessed Virgin from every contamination. Why certain parts of the body are dishonorable.

[Col. 0085A]

You say that it was shameful for the Son of God to proceed through the womb. This is either shameful by nature or because of sin. But nothing is shameful by nature; the reading of Genesis testifies that every creature is good. What is good is honorable, and what is honorable is not shameful. Therefore every creature, insofar as it has been created, is in no way shameful.

Thus the womb of a woman is not shameful but honorable, since all the parts of creation are honorable. The path of the womb, therefore, was not to be avoided by Christ at his birth as something shameful; rather, it was to be received as the instrument of birth. For just as he did not disdain the womb in which he would be conceived and formed, so he did not reject the womb through which he would emerge after being formed.

But you, questioning the bodily senses, judge those parts of the womb to be indecorous. Do not assent to the truth of things through deceptive bodily senses; seek the judgment of the mind, and you will discover that what appears shameful is beautiful.

Indeed, no part or member of creation is anything but beautiful; it becomes indecent when disordered and illicit movement has defiled it. Before the transgression, Adam and Eve were not ashamed, since they felt no disordered movement in their members. But when they had transgressed, they began to be ashamed.

It was not that the members which we now call shameful because of sin were shameful for that reason; for before they sinned, they were not ashamed of them. When a dishonorable movement came upon the genital members, previously modest but now rendered immodest by sin, shame followed—not because of any shamefulness in the honorable parts of the body, but because of the shameful, irrational movements of passion.

When, through the fire of the Holy Spirit, whether in this frail body or in the future life after the resurrection into incorruptibility, this passible movement has been restored to the most dignified harmony of nature, with weakness driven away, the members of nature will possess nothing that is a cause of confusion, shamefulness, or dishonor.

Meanwhile, however, the law that is in our members, so long as it resists the law of the mind and takes us captive to the law of sin, makes us ashamed and confused. But because of this law of sin ruling in our members, there was no need for the Savior to avoid the path of birth established by the law of nature. For the Holy Spirit, who sanctified from every contamination the Virgin’s womb in which the Son of God was to become incarnate, also purified the womb through which he was to be born.

Unless perhaps it seems credible that he made worthy by divine conception that place which is more inflamed by the heat of lust, and which is troubled by a lesser moderation of flame, yet was unable to cleanse it. For we have learned from the words of Holy Scripture that lust holds sway over women at the navel, beneath which the womb lies.

To you, however, the genital member appears dishonorable not because of the law of sin, [Col. 0086A] but because of the deformity of nature. Why is this? Because in investigating things you consult the sense of the flesh, which no wise person has followed in perceiving the truth. It is no wonder that you are deceived, since you are thoroughly instructed by the author of falsehood.

All those follow him who embrace what is merely probable instead of what is true—that is, corruptible things instead of eternal ones. Rather, withdraw your eyes from temporal things, which Ecclesiastes teaches are not merely vanity but vanity of vanities, and learn the perception of truth from senses that participate in truth.

When you have done this, you will see nothing shameful in natures except disordered movements, which they have acquired not from the wisdom of the Creator but from the fault of sin. Henceforth you will not judge the virginal womb unworthy of the Incarnation of the Word for his birth.

Indeed, you will perceive that nothing is more worthy of the Creator’s humanity than to approve the arrangement of his own workmanship: just as he approved the womb in which he was to be conceived, so he would not disapprove the gate of the womb by abolishing his birth, lest by his emergence in becoming human he reject the path of birth which he had established.

You regard these arguments as impious and are devising something new when you assert that nothing was closed to the Savior at his birth, since nothing created can obstruct the Creator, and whatever exists is open and permeable to him. If this is what you mean, you mean it with excellent judgment. But when you intend to subject the beginning of Christ’s birth to this rule, you are making a very clear assertion concerning power.

As for the properties of the body he assumed and the human nature of his birth, [Col. 0086C] you depart very far from the path of truth. For nothing is closed or impenetrable to the power of Christ’s will. But the humanity he assumed, just as it was gathered within the recesses of the womb, so, as long as it remained there, it did not experience the exterior parts of the belly. But as soon as it left the secret chamber of the virginal bridal room, it existed outside and ceased to be inside.

What did this change of place reveal except that, although according to the property of his divinity he is everywhere, according to the circumscription of his body he existed locally? Therefore what is local, just as it is not always everywhere but moves to another place when it leaves its first place, so also, when it makes a passage, it does not occupy the right and left simultaneously, just as it does not move forward and backward at once, nor upward and downward at the same time.

Certainly, just as the Savior at one time was bodily in the womb and at another time outside it, so, when emerging, although nothing was closed to his will to emerge, he nevertheless followed one route of emergence. He did not leave through every part of the body in which he had been formed.

Choose, then, whatever part of the body you wish for the Savior’s birth. He did not emerge through the entire body, although no part of the body was closed to his will to emerge. Nor did he emerge without location—for that belongs to incorporeal nature and is far removed from corporeal nature.

Choose whichever part you prefer. You reject the womb; assign him the navel. Or, if you prefer, choose some other bodily opening, more honorable in your view. And if the openings provided by nature displease you, [Col. 0087A] tear open [Note: [Col. 0087D] “Tear open the belly.” Acherius noted in the margin that *dissect* might perhaps be read. At the beginning of the following chapter we have added *confesses* from the Dallæus manuscript, before *to conceive*.] the belly, strip the ribs, break the spine, or, as certain exceedingly foolish people rave, open the armpit, and thus proclaim the Savior’s birth from a shadowy and dense mountain.

Will such a gate be judged worthy of the birth of the Lord, one fabricated by the opinion of fools and which the Creator’s wisdom gave to nature for conception—but which is to be argued about? Or shall we follow the opinion of the Brahmans, so that, just as they relate that Būddha, the founder of their sect, emerged through a virgin’s side, we proclaim that Christ did likewise?

Or is the Wisdom of God rather born from the Virgin’s brain, as Minerva from Jupiter’s head, or as Father Liber from the thigh? Thus a Christian would be taught not by the ordinary course of nature or the authority of sacred reading, but by pagan superstition and [Col. 0087B] fabulous inventions.

# CHAPTER IV  
## The author produces testimonies from the Old Testament to persuade us that Christ emerged through the Virgin’s womb.

But now let divine testimonies come forward, and from them let us learn the Savior’s origin, lest we be deceived by empty fables and mocked by false opinions.

The prophet Isaiah, unveiling the mystery of this birth, says: “The Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14).

He confesses that a virgin will conceive, that a virgin will give birth, and that this will be a sign given by the Lord: the virgin will remarkably perform both actions—not that the birth will proceed outside the path of nature.

If that were to happen, it ought to have been announced in this prophetic mystery, just as the virginal conception and childbirth were announced. For such a birth would display no less a mark of divine action, since it would have transferred the path of nature to other limits.

But now, excluding the work of a man and indicating the gift of integrity, he teaches that this is the sign given by the Lord: a virgin will bring forth the Savior. He does not designate for the virgin mother a new path of childbirth outside nature, but dedicates what nature has given to the sublimity of birth, crowned with incorruption.

I do not think it necessary, nor does brevity permit, that examples be drawn from the whole body of Scripture to make it clear that women are permitted to give birth and generate only through the legitimate opening of the womb. Such is the passage: “A woman who has conceived seed and given birth to a male child” [Col. 0087D] (Lev. 12:2).

Likewise: “Sanctify to me every firstborn who opens the womb among the children of Israel” (Exod. 13:1). For if a woman gives birth in any other way than through the womb—that is, the mouth of the uterus—then not every firstborn is sanctified to the Lord.

But since it would be foolish to say this, the Virgin gave birth only through the womb. The force and meaning of the word itself plainly provide an argument for understanding: just as seeing is referred to the eyes, hearing to the ears, smelling to the nose, and tasting to the throat, so giving birth is referred to the womb.

Otherwise, if the meaning of words may be varied at everyone’s pleasure, everything will be confused, and giving birth and conceiving will also be attributed to men. Why should these functions of words not be proclaimed of men, if the Savior’s birth did not follow the way of the womb but emerged wherever it happened to?

You also have, as support for your arrogance, the fabrication of poets, according to which a man both conceived and gave birth. But because you are a Christian and instructed in the language of truth, I do not doubt that you reject this.

Therefore do not pervert the legitimate course of nature, proclaimed in customary words, by a new opinion; instead receive the true and customary interpretation. Whenever you read, hear, or say either that the Virgin gave birth to Christ or that Christ was born of the Virgin, let the path of nature—the gate of the womb—immediately come before your mind.

Then error will not lead you along byways, but true understanding will keep you on the straight path. And so that we may not seem to establish these things by arguments alone, learn from testimonies that what we assert concerning the Savior’s origin is true.

The same prophet Isaiah says: “And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son; and the Lord said to me: ‘Call his name: Hasten to strip the spoils, hurry to plunder’” (Isa. 8:3). [Note: [Col. 0088D] “Observe the childbirth.” The final word has been added from the Dallæus manuscript.]

Observe the Virgin’s childbirth, marked by prophetic ministry. The prophet approached the prophetess because the Holy Spirit came to Mary. She conceived and bore a son, more by the gift of the Holy Spirit than by male seed.

Thus Sarah, barren through infertility and already cold with old age, was a prophetic figure of a virgin mother who would conceive and give birth through the Holy Spirit. Both conception and childbirth therefore took place in the prophetess, so that the future heresy might be condemned—the heresy that would assert that Mary conceived but did not give birth as a woman.

The prophetess does not err in one respect while prefiguring the truth in another; for the Virgin mother of the Savior conceived through the Holy Spirit and, like a woman, gave birth while preserving her modesty.

Likewise elsewhere: “Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45:8).

With truly remarkable brevity the prophetic utterance has set forth the angel’s announcement, the prophecies of the prophets, the Virgin’s conception, and the manner of the birth. The angel indicates Christ’s origin; the prophets are not silent; the Virgin’s womb is opened for offspring; and the enclosure of modesty brings forth the Savior.

Thus in the opening you see the Virgin’s conception, and in the sprouting you understand the birth that preserves modesty. For a shoot preserves its natural channel of birth and is not formed from foreign seed but is the seed of its own parent, in accordance with what Genesis testifies when speaking of trees and plants: “Whose seed,” it says, “is in itself” (Gen. 1:11).

So the Virgin Mary conceived not from male seed but from her own seed, and brought forth her conception through the genital stream. For this reason Aaron’s rod opens into a shoot, bursts into flowers, and, with its leaves spread out, forms almonds, signifying the coagulation of seed, the formation of conception, and the bringing forth of birth.

And just as Aaron’s rod produced, without the aid of earth or the irrigation of moisture, yet along its natural paths, a shoot, flowers, and fruit, so the virgin mother, not from a stream of pleasure or from marital intercourse, nevertheless brought forth through the natural path flesh that was the Word made flesh.

# CHAPTER V  
## Further testimonies.

Jeremiah, likewise foreseeing this sacred childbirth of the Virgin, says: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman will surround a man” (Jer. 31:22).

Discern what he says will be newly created: namely, that what is masculine will be formed in the womb solely from feminine seed, through the ministry of the Holy Spirit. And because, in being born, such a conception would not pass outside the paths of the womb—the course of birth granted to all mortals—he rightly remained silent about that which, apart from inviolate modesty, would introduce nothing new under the law of birth.

Ezekiel likewise says: “And I was turned toward the way of the exterior gate of the sanctuary, which faced east; and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it; and it shall remain closed to the prince. He shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate, and he shall go out by its way’” (Ezek. 44:1–3).

I think this passage resolves the entire knot of the question. For the gate described by the prophet was understood by the Fathers as the Virgin Mary, who is rightly shown as closed because she always remains an untouched virgin, and no man shall pass through her.

Pay close attention to whom passage is denied and through what passage it is denied. It is denied entirely to a man, who could violate her, and that is removed from him which could be corrupted through intercourse.

For no one prohibits entry where the order of nature permits neither a way nor a passage. Therefore, when it says, “No man shall pass through her,” it is not speaking of the side, the brain, or the thigh, since conjugal passage pertains to other parts of the body, to which nature has provided a way and passage for intercourse.

But since the passage of a man is removed from the place through which the Lord God of Israel entered, the following words demonstrate this when they say: “The Lord God of Israel has entered through it.” And to remove every ambiguity, [Col. 0089D] it adds: “He shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate, and he shall go out by its way.”

Let the new heresy no longer doubt the path of the Savior which he followed in being born. Behold, the prophet metaphorically sets before your eyes the woman’s womb, its vestibule, and its way.

“The Lord God of Israel entered,” then, “by the way of the vestibule of this gate,” because through the mystery of the Incarnation he entered the virginal womb. And he went out by the way of this gate because, having assumed humanity, he emerged into the house of the world through the undefiled womb.

Therefore do not invent some unknown kind of emergence of the Son of God from his mother’s womb. May the Holy Spirit teach you the truth—the Spirit who sanctified both the bridal chamber worthy of so great a bridegroom and the gate.

But why do we linger over difficult and mystical passages? Let us come to what is clear, and let us move from the enclosures of houses—that is, from the figures of hidden things—to the breadth of gates, so that we may contemplate in the open air the bridegroom’s footsteps and the bride’s outpourings.

In the law every firstborn was sanctified to the Lord, signifying the one who alone was born holy and without sin. Thus it is written concerning this matter: “Sanctify to me every firstborn who opens the womb in Israel” (Exod. 13:1).

Likewise: “When the Lord brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and your fathers, and gives it to you, you shall separate to the Lord everything that opens the womb” (ibid. 13:11–12).

Likewise: “When Pharaoh was hardened and refused to let us go, the Lord killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt. Therefore sacrifice to the Lord everything that opens the womb of the male sex, and redeem all the firstborn of my sons” (ibid. 13:13–15).

Notice that the firstborn are those who, in being born, first open the womb, so that you may consequently understand that to be born from a woman means to emerge by opening the womb.

In the catalogue of commandments: “You shall give me the firstborn of your sons” (Exod. 22:29). Elsewhere: “Everything that opens the womb of the male sex shall be mine” (Exod. 13:2).

In Leviticus: “If a woman, having received seed, gives birth to a male child,” and so forth (Lev. 12:1). Likewise: “But if she gives birth to a female child” (ibid., v. 5), and so forth. It teaches that women’s generating and giving birth mean nothing other than bringing forth a child through the womb.

In Numbers: “Every firstborn is mine, from the time I struck down the firstborn in the land of Egypt. Sanctify to me whatever is firstborn in Israel” (Num. 3:13).

And earlier: “I took the Levites from the children of Israel in place of the firstborn who opens the womb among the children of Israel” (ibid., v. 12).

And in what follows: “Count the firstborn of the male sex among the children of Israel from one month onward” (ibid., v. 40).

And above: “You shall take the Levites for me in place of the firstborn of the children of Israel” (ibid., v. 41).

And below: “I accepted them in place of the firstborn who open every womb in Israel” (Num. 8:16)—namely, the Levites.

“All the firstborn of the children of Israel are mine.” Elsewhere: “Whatever first bursts forth from the womb of all flesh which they offer to the Lord, whether among human beings or cattle, shall be yours” (Num. 18:15).

Therefore every birth, both of human beings and of animals, emerges through the womb. Consequently, everything born from a woman emerges through the womb.

Let us not, then, allow words to generate an uncertain question for us when, according to their customary use and the usage of Scripture, they provide a definite understanding of their meaning. Just as we speak of walking in relation to the function of the feet, so we speak of giving birth in relation to the service of the womb.

Therefore let uncertainty not confuse what the meaning of clear understanding declares. Just as one does not reach the appointed boundary without direction along the road, so the truth of speech is not disclosed except through the true significance of words.

Therefore, whether we call such an action of women “birth,” “being born,” or by any other name, instructed by the truth of nature, the custom of birth, and the authority of Scripture, let us understand of the things signified nothing other than what the words signify, lest we wander far from the truth while either failing to recognize the signs of truth or attempting to pervert them by a wrong interpretation.

According to the rule given, let us consider what the Gospels say concerning the Savior’s birth.

In Matthew we read as follows:

“The angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: ‘Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife, for what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins. Now all this took place so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Behold, a virgin will have a child in her womb and bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us.” Joseph, rising from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord commanded him; and he did not know her until she bore her firstborn son, and he called his name Jesus’” (Matt. 1:20ff.).

When, therefore, Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah, the Savior’s birth is so often proclaimed and the Virgin’s childbirth so often narrated that virginity is emphatically taught and sexual embrace excluded, but the passage through the womb is not denied.

Indeed, both the evangelist’s words and the prophet’s prophecy show that the Savior’s origin took place through the womb, since a woman does not give birth except through the womb, and an infant does not emerge except through the gate of the uterus.

Luke speaks of this birth as follows:

“The angel entered to Mary and said: ‘Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.’ When she heard this, she was troubled and considered what kind of greeting this was. And the angel said to her: ‘Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus.’”

And below:

“Mary said to the angel: ‘How will this happen, since I do not know a man?’ And the angel answered and said to her: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God’” (Luke 1:28ff.).

If you still do not accept, either from the solemnity of nature or from the example of those being born, what it means to give birth, then at least let the angel sent to Zechariah instruct you from the Gospel itself.

The angel said to him: “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son” (Luke 1:13).

One word promises both births; how could it not signify the same opening of the womb? The order of conception differs, but the law of birth does not, since John was conceived from the seed of a man, while Jesus was conceived from the Holy Spirit.

The former was brought forth through the gate through which a man had passed; the latter was generated through the inviolate chamber of modesty. Yet both are born, because each is received through the gate of the womb.

The evangelist also bears witness to our argument when he says: “Therefore the holy one who will be born from you.” Remember what the Lawgiver commanded concerning the firstborn—that is, those who open the womb—and you will understand that the holy one is called firstborn, and that the firstborn is the one who opens the womb; hence Jesus is both called holy to the Lord and termed firstborn.

And if he is firstborn, then certainly he opened the womb—not in order to violate its closure, but in order to open through it the gate of his birth, just as in Ezekiel the gate is described as closed and yet is said to have been opened to the Lord of Israel—not because it removed the doors of its threshold for his emergence, but because, while remaining closed, it stood open to the one who ruled it.

The same evangelist again says:

“And it happened, while they were there, that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her firstborn son” (Luke 2:6).

And nearly the same is written concerning Elizabeth:

“Elizabeth’s time for giving birth was fulfilled, and she bore a son” (Luke 1:57).

Just as the time for both women to give birth is assigned, so the same word points to the same opening of the womb for both infants who were born.

And thereafter:

“When the days of Mary’s purification according to the law of Moses had been fulfilled, they brought Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: ‘Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord’” (Luke 2:22).

If the words by which Mary is emphatically said to have given birth satisfied you insufficiently, so that you chatter that Jesus proceeded from the Virgin’s chamber by some route other than the womb because the woman’s shameful part had to be veiled by more honorable language, then at last, accepting the evangelist’s words, learn that the mouth of the female belly is indicated not by a transferred expression but by its proper name, and that through it the Savior underwent the passage of birth.

For if Mary’s giving birth meant something other than opening her womb to a male child, then, contrary to the command of the Law, he should not have been presented to the Lord, nor should he have been called holy to the Lord: “For every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (ibid., v. 23).

But now Mary the Virgin both gave birth to him, and the Savior emerged through her womb, and as firstborn he opened it—not in order to violate the integrity of the womb, but in order to empty the palace of the belly. Therefore the mother, although she gave birth without receiving male seed, because a male child truly opened her womb, both fulfills the days of purification according to the Law and brings the sacrifice to the temple to present the child to the Lord.

# CHAPTER VI  
## He establishes his opinion from the Fathers.

[Col. 0092D]

But since we have briefly collected these points from the books of divine authority, by which we were to demonstrate that the Savior was born through the untouched womb of the Virgin, I wish also to strengthen our opinion by the traditions of the ancients, so that by the multitude of witnesses the adversary may be refuted and the faithful more abundantly instructed. I shall nevertheless bring forward passages and only a few of their own testimonies, so that I may preserve the measure of brevity I have proposed. Otherwise, if we wished to gather together into one place what even one of them—not to mention all of them—has said on this subject, we should produce a large body of volumes.

Ambrose, the heavenly trumpet, the exemplar of holiness, the unconquerable bulwark of faith, while treating of the Savior’s human birth [Col. 0093A] (*On Luke*, book XI, chapter 2), spoke as follows:

> “Is God proved by insignificant signs: that angels minister, that magi adore, that martyrs confess? He is poured forth from the womb, yet he flashes forth from heaven; he lies in an earthly lodging, yet he flourishes in heavenly light. A married woman gave birth, but a virgin conceived. A married woman conceived, but a virgin gave birth.”

How subtly he teaches the secret of inviolate modesty! How magnificently he describes the virgin, proclaiming her both married and a mother, yet untouched! He says that Christ was poured forth from the womb, so that you may understand him to have proceeded by the way of nature, and not suppose that he required some foreign route for his birth’s exit, since the natural channel of the womb sent him forth into the light. To make this clearer, he added that a married woman gave birth but a virgin conceived, and that a married woman conceived but a virgin gave birth, so that in the Virgin’s conception and childbirth you may remove the participation of a man. You observe, moreover, that the members appointed by nature for their proper functions are distinguished, so that conception is referred to the matrix and childbirth to the opening. Therefore, believe that by those same members through which a married woman conceives and gives birth, the virgin was both made fruitful and delivered.

Again, in what follows:

> “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.”

> “For the Virgin’s childbirth was promised in the words of the law. And truly he is holy, because he is immaculate. Finally, that he is the one designated by the law is declared by the words repeated in the same manner by the angel: ‘Because what shall be born,’ he says, ‘will be called holy, the Son of God.’ For it was not intercourse with a man that opened the secrets of the virginal womb, but the Holy Spirit poured forth the immaculate seed into the inviolate womb. For the Lord Jesus alone, among all those born of woman, is holy in every respect: he did not experience the contaminations of earthly corruption through the birth of an immaculate child, and he drove them away by his heavenly majesty. For if we follow the literal sense, how is every male holy, when it is clear that many were most wicked? Was Ahab holy? Were the false prophets holy, whom the avenging heavenly fire consumed at Elijah’s prayer? But he is holy through whom the pious prescriptions of the divine law signified the figure [Note: [Col. 0093D] “Through whom the figure.” Radbert copied this same passage; in his text we read “whom in figure.” Before these commendations of Ambrose and Augustine, where we printed “the virgin both made fruitful” from Codex Dall., the earlier edition had “the virgin’s fruitfulness.”] of the mystery. And he alone opened the generative secret of the holy virgin Church for the generation of God’s peoples, with immaculate fruitfulness. He alone, therefore, opened the womb for himself. Nor is this surprising: for he who had said through the prophet, ‘Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and in your mother’s womb I sanctified you [Col. 0093D] (Jer. 1),’—he, therefore, who sanctified another’s womb so that the prophet might be born, is the one who opened his mother’s womb so that he might come forth immaculate.”

(*Saint Ambrose, book II on Luke, chapter 2; Saint Augustine, book II on Original Sin, chapter 40, and book I against Julian, chapter 2.*)

The distinguished orator, in this speech, first explaining the decree of the ancient law, teaches that the holy legal figure signified the mystery of the one true Holy One, who, born of a Virgin at the end of the age, did not experience the contaminations of earthly corruption through the novelty of an immaculate birth, opening the virginal [Col. 0094A] womb by being born in such a way that he nevertheless left it closed by not violating it.

Otherwise, if Scripture did not signify him when it decreed that males should be regarded as holy, the perversity of many males shows that the decree is not true. But the law of the Lord is immaculate, and its testimony faithful. Therefore, one must seek an interpretation capable of being suitably applied to the truth: there the one Holy One is mentioned again, who, conceived without sin and born without fault, opened the generative secret of the holy virgin Church for the generation of God’s peoples, with immaculate fruitfulness.

[ [Note: [Col. 0094D] “By which mystical [saying].” All of this was added from Codex Dall.] By this mystical saying he testifies that the virgin mother’s generative secret, with its immaculate fruitfulness, was opened.]

For he would not have adapted this kind of account to the Church by way of mystery unless he had wished to teach that the opening of the virginal womb had truly occurred. The following words confirm this interpretation, for he says: “He alone, therefore, opened the womb for himself.” What more do you require, when the words used to designate the matter bear witness to what we say? He both says “opened” and says “womb,” so that you may not regard anything as having been said figuratively. Thus the explicit statement confirms what the ancient Scripture once declared: “Every male, namely, that should open the womb, shall be called holy to the Lord.” Hence you learn that it was signified not in modern but in the most ancient times—not only that Jesus would be born of a Virgin, but that he would be born through the womb of untouched modesty.

And so that this birth might be understood as undefiled from what was inviolate, not polluted through a corrupt passage, he teaches this further by the example of the prophet sanctified while still in the womb. [Col. 0094C] He adds:

> “For he who had said to the prophet, ‘Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and in your mother’s womb I sanctified you’; he, therefore, who sanctified another’s womb so that the prophet might be born, is the one who opened his mother’s womb so that he might come forth immaculate.”

Let our words now cease, since we are instructed by the words of so great a teacher concerning what we ought to think about the Savior’s birth. We should not explain what he said, since we can more readily obscure it than make it clearer—unless perhaps someone is so ignorant as not to know that the womb is a woman’s shameful part.

## CHAPTER VII. Testimonies from Augustine and Hilary

Let Augustine now come forward: a river of eloquence, an investigator of secrets, a revealer of hidden things, a defender of the Church, a conqueror of heretics; let him openly declare what he thinks about the Savior’s birth. In a sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, while declaiming on the Virgin’s modesty and the Savior’s wondrous conception, he says:

> “When the birth was announced through the angel, the Word began to be formed; through conception God is gathered into man; the womb sustains him for whom the world had been small; and within the brief space of the virginal body majesty was incarnated for our sake. The fruitful womb is stretched by the agency of the Word; when the nine months were completed, the womb poured forth the heavenly man; the angelic utterance proclaims the Lord born.”

With careful description, and in the briefest possible manner, he has covered both the beginnings of conception, the construction of bodily solidity, and the growth of the body; also the passage of the months during which the infant was formed within the womb’s hidden recesses, then the advance into the air, and the angelic proclamation of God’s birth. Observe, surely, that he speaks both of conception, of being formed, and of being poured forth—that is, of having emerged not by some foreign irruption, but of having been poured forth through the vestibule of the virginal womb.

Again, in another sermon on the same nativity:

> “Our Lord, therefore, was born from flesh, but not from carnal corruption: born as man, but not generated as man. He assumed flesh in such a way as to preserve the honor of his majesty; and thus he separated the purity of his birth from the defilement of human formation. In his birth he indeed fulfilled the complete dispensation of man, but he nevertheless did not abandon the dignity of God.”

You see that the learned man designates both the divinity of the Son of God and the order of human birth. For he says that he was born from flesh—that is, from the Virgin’s members and humanity—indeed according to the law of flesh, but apart from the corruption of flesh. And so that you may observe more clearly what is being said, he adds: “Born as man, but not generated as man.”

See how fully he has disclosed the mystery of Christ’s birth. For he says: “Born as man, but not generated as man.” What does “born as man” mean? It means that he came forth from the virgin’s womb through the womb by which every human being is born. And what does “not generated as man” mean? It means that he was incarnated not from the seed of a man but from the Holy Spirit. If he did not emerge through the opening of the womb, it would not be true that he was born as man. But he was born as man; therefore he was born through the opening of the womb, that is, through the vulva.

Hilary, a man distinguished by every virtue and adornment, renowned in life and in eloquence alike, writes in the second book of *The Faith* [*On the Trinity*, book II, in the middle]:

> “The one only-begotten God grows, inserted into the form of a little human body in the womb of the holy Virgin. He who contains all things, and within whom and through whom all things exist, is brought forth according to the law of human childbirth.”

He teaches that Christ assumed the appearance of a body from the Virgin and within the Virgin, and that, according to the customary manner of human birth, he penetrated the secrets of the virginal [Col. 0095D] womb. With a change of wording, he affirms the same thing as Father Augustine: Augustine testifies that Christ was born as man, while Hilary thunders that he was brought forth according to the law of human childbirth. Thus, while both confess with a voice consonant with the sacred Scriptures that the Savior proceeded from the Virgin, truth is taught and falsehood overthrown.

## CHAPTER VIII. Likewise from Pope Gregory and the Venerable Bede

So that no opportunity for contradiction may be left to the adversary, let Gregory come forward: a mirror of holiness, an eloquence flowing with milk, a rule of morals; let him teach in truthful words the manner of the Lord’s birth. [Col. 0096A] In Homily 26, while resolving the question proposed—namely, that the Lord’s body was real and that he entered to the disciples through closed doors—he confirmed it by the following example:

> “For that body of the Lord entered to the disciples through closed doors which, through its birth, came forth for human eyes from a closed womb.”

It is said that just as the Lord Jesus Christ, after the glory of his resurrection, entered the disciples’ lodging with the reality of his body—not through a wall, nor by a back entrance, but through a door, though one not opened—so, proceeding from his mother’s womb, he came forth not elsewhere but through the womb, though it remained closed.

You might perhaps say that the Lord entered to the disciples through closed doors, but not through the place of the doors; rather, that he penetrated through some other part. First, what relevance to a divine miracle would there be in entering elsewhere through closed doors? Or what worthy point would the evangelist have commended by saying that the Lord entered through a place through which any mortal could have found entry? Or, if nothing could be closed against the entrance of the Almighty, why should the same not be accepted concerning the doorway, so that, though the doors were closed, he might nevertheless have entered to the disciples with the doors opened to his arrival?

But what will you say about the tomb, since the risen body was brought forth into the air not only from a closed tomb but from one that had also been sealed? Will you say that Jesus’ body possessed such subtlety that, being thinner than the winds and more tenuous than air, it could not be confined by the walls of the tomb? Yet although it is impious to think this about the Savior’s body, since after the resurrection he said to the disciples:

> “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have,”

and nature does not allow a body hardened by the solidity of both bones and flesh to be thick while, through the tenuity of subtlety, it is made thin, nevertheless the catholic faith does not attribute the fact that he came forth from the closed tomb or penetrated to the disciples through barred doors to the nature or quality of the body, but to the power of the Godhead and the glory of the resurrection.

Otherwise, it would no longer be a miracle commending the distinction of the Godhead if it were held bound by the laws of nature. Nevertheless, we grant even these claims, although they are impious and contrary to the faith. Will you not confess the same concerning the doors, even though they were closed? Whether you wish it or not, you will be caught in this snare. Therefore he came forth from the closed tomb and entered through barred doors. Thus, however unwillingly and however much you resist, you grant the same to the virginal womb: the offspring of the heavenly Power was neither weaker nor less human in relation to the enclosure of his mother’s womb, so that he might both leave it closed and pass through it, just as he either came forth from the signs sealing his tomb or entered through the doorway of the disciples’ house without opening it in passing.

Bede, priest of the English, a sound member of Christ, offers a judgment on this question not unlike that of those mentioned above. In his Commentary on Luke, while speaking about the Savior’s birth and the Virgin’s childbirth, he says:

> “When Mary is described as having given birth to her firstborn Son, we must not understand this, according to Helvidius, to mean that she also produced other sons—as though someone could not be called firstborn unless he had brothers, just as someone is not usually called only-begotten unless he lacks brothers. For both the testimony of the law and clear reasoning show that all only-begotten children can be called firstborn, but not all firstborn children only-begotten. This means not merely the firstborn after whom others followed, but all those born before whom no one else had proceeded from the womb. Finally, because it is commanded that every male who opens the womb be called holy to the Lord, whether brothers follow or not, what is born first from the womb must by right of the firstborn be consecrated.”

By these words he both defends Mary’s virginity and indicates the Savior’s birth according to the law of human childbirth. For when he is fully described as both firstborn and only-begotten, it is shown that he could have had brothers—something that could by no means be true if Christ had not been born according to the law of human birth. Nor would he then rightly be called either firstborn or only-begotten, because one who was not generated would not be generated; but one who was generated was brought forth according to the law of human birth.

Therefore Christ was not born as man; and even if Mary had given birth to someone besides Christ, Christ could not have been called firstborn, since he would not have been generated but would have been either expelled or brought forth contrary to the laws of nature. But now, instructed by both the authority of the law and the truth of the Gospel, this teacher teaches that Jesus was the firstborn of the holy Virgin, because he was both the first and the only one born from her according to the right of human childbirth: by being born he opened the womb, not in order to violate the modesty of the uterus, but so that he might proceed through the designated and untouched door, from the womb’s secret place to human eyes. And for this reason, because he was born first from the womb, he is consecrated by right of the firstborn.

I do not know what further witnesses it is necessary to gather for the confirmation of this question. So many men, and men of such great authority, can not only suffice for any Catholic, but can crush any heretic both by the weight of their faith and by the light of their wisdom.

## CHAPTER IX. Likewise from Jerome

And lest anyone complain that he lacks some invention of novelty, let us now set forth plainly the Virgin’s very shameful parts by their unadorned name, and place before us the Savior who was generated through them.

Jerome, interpreter of the sacred law, most skilled in every discipline, an unshaken tower of faith, most radiant with the lamp of wisdom, most eloquent in speech, and most learned in the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew languages, in his little book against Helvidius first presents Helvidius’s own statements on this matter and then gives his own judgment, by which he confirms what the heretic had well intimated.

Thus we read:

> “Are not little children fashioned daily by the hands of God in wombs, so that we ought rightly to blush that Mary married after childbirth? But if this seems shameful to them, it remains that we should not believe that God was also born through the Virgin’s genitals. For according to them it is more shameful that God was generated through the Virgin’s shameful parts than that the Virgin married her husband after childbirth.”

[Note: [Col. 0097D] “That we should not believe.” Elsewhere, Acherius says in the margin, “let them believe”; that reading pleases me more. From this passage it is clear that the opinion concerning the Virgin’s childbirth which Ratramnus defends was so common that no one thought of the alternative.]

Thus far the heretic barks with unspeakable wickedness about the Virgin’s marriage after childbirth. But he speaks the complete truth about the generation of the Son of God through a human being, as the following speech of our teacher clearly demonstrates. It is as follows:

> “Add, if you wish, other humiliations of nature: the womb growing large for nine months, nausea, childbirth, blood, swaddling clothes. Let the infant himself be described for you, wrapped in the customary covering of membranes. Let the hard manger, the infant’s cries, circumcision on the eighth day, and the time of purification be brought forward. To prove him unclean, we do not blush and we do not remain silent. The more humble are the things he suffered for me, the more I owe him. And when you have recounted everything, you will bring forward nothing more humiliating than the cross, which we confess, believe, and in which we triumph over our enemies. But just as we do not deny what has been written, so we reject what has not been written: we believe that God was born of a Virgin because we read it; we do not believe that Mary married after childbirth because we do not read it.”

With prudent discrimination, the most learned man removed what the adversary had wickedly introduced and accepted what had been stated in a Catholic manner; he confirmed what was truly said and refuted what had been hurled from a blasphemous mouth. He confessed that God was born through the Virgin’s genitals; he rejected the claim that Mary married after childbirth. He condemned as execrable the use of “genitals” and “shameful parts” as an insult to the sacred birth; but he approved the confession that the Word made flesh emerged through the womb’s secret door.

For this reason he also added other humiliations of nature: the womb growing large for nine months, nausea, childbirth, blood, swaddling clothes, the infant wrapped in the customary covering of membranes, the hard manger, cries, circumcision, the time of purification, and finally the humiliation of the cross. As a Catholic, he embraces, accepts, and venerates all these things. For the more humble the things the Creator suffered for the sake of the elect, the more those who consider the speech of this distinguished teacher ought to owe him, since he enumerates no small number of things which the infant could not have endured if he had not been born according to the law of human childbirth—childbirth, blood, swaddling clothes, the wrapping in membranes, and cries. All these things testify both to the secret place of the Virgin’s genitals and to the law of human birth.

Likewise, learn that the Holy Spirit, who testified to this most holy birth, and the holy and learned men who afterward commended it to the peoples in their words and writings, preferred to indicate it through the circumlocution of more honorable speech rather than, by preserving the literal propriety of plain language, bring forward something that might offend their hearers. For it was fitting that so great a matter be explained not in humble but in lofty words, not in sordid but in honorable expressions, such as:

> “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel, and a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall descend from his root. Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Num. 24:17; Isa. 1 and 45:8).

The Holy Spirit did not lack words by which he could have disclosed the Virgin’s generative organ; rather, he chose to teach a splendid and magnificent matter through splendid and magnificent figures. Nevertheless, he also approached the matter more closely and disclosed it in legitimate and proper terms of decorum. Therefore the prophet says:

> “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14).

And:

> “A child is born to us; a son is given to us.”

And the angel says to Mary:

> “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” (Luke 1:31),

along with many similar passages. In all these expressions Christ’s birth is commended in natural and decorous words.

Nevertheless, Scripture avoids mentioning by its proper name that part of the members through which childbirth emerges, since doing so would be neither honorable nor necessary. Otherwise, when the names of functions and their verbs are used, who does not immediately understand the members by which those functions are performed? We understand seeing through the eyes, hearing through the ears, and walking through the feet. Yet when someone is said to have seen, heard, or walked, the eyes, ears, and feet are not mentioned at the same time except for the sake of distinction or clarification. Nor do we understand the meanings of the verbs in such a way that we fail to perceive the body parts without which such functions cannot be performed.

Therefore, what the heavenly oracle avoided stating because it was superfluous and shameful concerning the act of sacred childbirth, holy men also avoided stating. But what was full of meaning and appropriate modesty, they explained. Nor did they avoid even this in every instance, whether because of future enemies of the truth or to remove an opportunity for doubt. Hence the evangelist Luke says:

> “When the days of Mary’s purification according to the law of Moses had been fulfilled, they brought Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: ‘Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord’” (Luke 2:22).

Nor is it surprising that grave and reverend teachers did not wish to report such things in connection with the insult of the most glorious birth—things which even the common people do not blush to mention concerning the childbirth of any poor woman.

Therefore this distinguished teacher, whose testimony we have cited here, having received from the enemy of the truth a testimony to the truth concerning the divine generation, nevertheless resents the insulting language directed against the Virgin: namely, that by those words, although natural and proper, yet humble and insufficiently modest, he described the Virgin’s childbirth.

## CHAPTER X. The Support of Christian Poets Is Brought Forward

There is no longer anything for you to seek, and nothing remains for you to investigate concerning the sacred birth. For we have now reached the Virgin’s generative organs and passed on to the childbirth woman’s shameful parts, so that what conception, childbirth, generation, birth, and the opening of the womb did not make clear may at last be taught by the shameful parts and instructed by the genitals. If natural and honorable terms have not supplied understanding, let at least shameful and figurative terms do so. For our learned men are such investigators of secrets that they prefer obscure and foreign meanings to clear and proper ones.

Let us now summon the support of the poets, so that every form of eloquence may bear witness to the truth. Prudentius, a man not ignorant of liberal studies, while discussing in the *Apotheosis* the injuries suffered by the life of the world for the freedom of the world, and separating from them inviolable nature—that is, divine nature—and assigning them to passible substance—that is, human nature—says:

[Note: [Col. 0099D] “And assigning them to passible [substance].” The latter word was added from Codex Dall.; following its authority, we deleted the word *Gallicus* after *presbyter*. Below, “by which the Virgin.” This marginal reading pleased us more than that in the text, “because the Virgin,” immediately followed in the margin by “from heavenly dew.”]

> This is what human flesh suffered, which a pregnant woman  
> Brought forth under the ancient law, without the law of a husband.

With an entirely faithful and wise account, he both excluded intercourse and described offspring naturally delivered. He removed the law of the husband and substituted the law of the womb, so that he might show that Christ had conceived from the Holy Spirit while not concealing that he had been born through the womb.

A similar testimony is offered by Fortunatus, a foreign-born priest but a heavenly citizen, poor in possessions yet rich in the wealth of faith. In praise of the Virgin Mary he speaks as follows (*Poems*, book VIII, poem 5, after the beginning):

> But I return to sing the praise by which the Virgin draws us:  
> No woman such as she existed, nor will any such woman come.  
> Him whom the clouds rain down, the righteous one from clear dew,  
> This earth gave as Savior from its own seed.  
>   
> This is the closed gate into which no one entered, nor from which anyone exits,  
> Except the Lord alone, for whom even closed things are open.

This does not conflict with what came before; indeed, it designates the same thing in other words. For in a double period, commending the same judgment, he both proclaims the integrity of virginity and indicates the manner of birth according to human custom; he narrates that the Savior was conceived divinely and sprang from the channel of nature. And, to make more evident what he was saying, he testifies that Mary was the Ezekielian gate through which no male had entrance or exit; the Almighty alone, for whom nothing is closed, passed through it, so that he who had determined to be conceived from a Virgin might be born from her according to the law of human childbirth.

After all these, let Athanasius of Alexandria come forward, who, endowed with virtue, steadfastness in proven faith, instruction in wisdom, and perseverance in confession, single-handedly, so to speak, overturned the numerous multitude of Arian perfidy, and, bearing the banner of true belief as an unconquered defender, restored the wall of the Church and strengthened its position. Let him also stand as a confirmer of our argument and vigorously overthrow the sect of error.

Arguing in his letter to Epictetus against those who taught that the Word and the body he assumed for our redemption were of one substance—whereas the Christian faith holds that two substances, divine and human, are joined in Christ, so that in one person each nature retains its distinction—he says, among other things:

> “Therefore Mary was necessary, so that he might assume a body from her and offer his own body for us. Isaiah, prophesying, showed this when he said: ‘Behold, a virgin.’ Gabriel, moreover, was sent to her—not simply to a virgin, but to a virgin betrothed to a man—so that he might show through her betrothed that Mary was truly human. Scripture also mentions childbirth, and says: ‘She wrapped the child.’ And: ‘Blessed are the breasts that he suckled.’ And a sacrifice was offered, because the one who was born opened the womb. These were all signs of a woman giving birth. And Gabriel most certainly proclaimed this when he said, not merely that he would be born, but ‘what shall be born from you,’ so that it might not appear that a body had been given to him from outside, but ‘from you,’ so that it might clearly be believed that what was born was naturally from her. Nature itself demonstrates this, because it is impossible for a virgin to produce milk, and it is impossible for a body to be nourished with milk and wrapped in swaddling clothes if it was not previously born naturally.”

Constant in orthodox faith, the man whom the Lord had placed as a fortified city, an iron wall, and a bronze pillar for the kings of Judah, its princes, and all the people of the land, could neither think nor speak otherwise about the Virgin’s childbirth than the Church thinks and proclaims—the Church that is a house built upon the most solid rock, the pillar and foundation of truth.

Therefore, when he enumerates several things by which he proves that Christ was incarnate and born from a Virgin, so as also to drive away a new heresy, he says that “the one who was born opened the womb.” And, impressing this doctrine of true confession more and more deeply, he adds below:

> “It would be impossible for a virgin to produce milk, and it would be impossible for a body to be nourished by milk and wrapped in swaddling clothes if it had not previously been born naturally.”

What more do you want, authors or defenders of a new and unheard-of heresy unknown to former ages? Behold Athanasius stands against your battle line, he who once fought against Arian perfidy. In that struggle he defended the divinity of the Word; in this contest he champions his humanity. Then the truth of the birth that is from the Father was contradicted; now the truth of the birth that is from the mother is resisted. Those enemies fought to show that the Son had not been born from the substance of the Father but had been made from nothing; these opponents attack the claim that Christ arose naturally from his mother’s womb and instead maintain that he was received by a prodigious process.

Everywhere Christ is opposed; everywhere the world’s liberation is insulted by accursed tongues. But let the learned champion, who knows how to conquer and does not know how to yield—not trusting in himself, but placing his confidence in the one for whom he fights—come forward and cut down with the sword of truth the troop swollen with pride and supported by vanity.

The opposing party aims its weapon at you and declares: “God was not born through the nature of a woman.” The faithful man opposes the shield of faith and brings forward the sword of God’s word:

> “A sacrifice was offered, because the one who was born opened the womb.”

Why are you astonished at the fiction of falsehood? You have not been pricked by a sword but struck by a most powerful weapon. A sacrifice was offered; you cannot deny it.
