Therefore you are compelled also to confess that the womb was opened. And if he opened the womb, he was born through the blood-bearing nature of a woman.

Ancient serpent, where are you turning your edge? Where are you trying to make your slippery head strike? Are you still attempting to hiss into the wound with your forked mouth: “If he opened the womb, he corrupted it”? But let your pestilential mouth now be stopped by a Danielic barrier, so that the scaly dragon, torn apart limb by limb, may cease to madden the Chaldeans.

> “The prophet Isaiah: ‘Behold, a virgin.’ And Gabriel is sent not merely to a virgin, but to a virgin betrothed to a man.” Then, after the childbirth, after the wrapping of the infant, after the nursing, after the offering, he cries out that “the one who was born opened the womb.” These were all signs of a woman giving birth.

Therefore the virgin gives birth and is not corrupted. God, being born from the virgin mother, opened the womb but did not violate the seal of modesty.

Perhaps you will not be entirely quiet even at this, but will dare again to prepare a broken and mangled hand for blows: “Nothing was closed to God when he was about to be born; as soon as the will to be born arose, his exit immediately flowed forth. He did not endure the delays of childbirth, since his birth came into being without a process.”

The defender of the faith strikes down this slander of perfidy—not by attributing anything to the power of the Godhead, but by bearing witness to the human God’s reality of human birth—so that it may plainly be believed that what was born was naturally from her. Therefore he proclaims that the God-man was born naturally, so that you may understand that he proceeded through the womb of nature according to the law of human childbirth.

Hence he also teaches that the Virgin could not otherwise, according to the law of nature, have produced milk, nourished the body with milk, or consequently wrapped it in swaddling clothes, if it had not first been naturally born.

Therefore, with the adversary defeated on every side, let us hold to the truth in faith, confess it with truthful speech: the Word made flesh was naturally born through the ministry of the womb, according both to the consequences of reason, to the testimonies of the divine Scriptures, and to the authority of learned men, which must not be despised.

It has been shown, I believe, sufficiently and abundantly, that the Lord Savior was born from the Virgin as a human being, and that this birth did not violate her integrity: Mary was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and remained a virgin after childbirth. The one who assumed a body from the virgin, and was formed within the virgin womb, was also naturally born through the virgin dwelling.

If these arguments should not be sufficient for someone, whether because of dullness of understanding or eagerness to contradict, there will be no lack of means to assist both defects—provided they prefer to open their own wound and do not love the ruin of contention. We have played these customary exercises of students; if anyone despises them, our exercises will nevertheless please us.

---

# BOOK OF RATRAMNUS, MONK OF CORBIE, ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD

Vindicated from every invention or suspicion of novelty or Calvinist heresy; written for a friendly, candid, and learned refutation of the dissertation of the Reverend Father Jean Hardouin of the Society of Jesus, *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, in which, abandoning his purpose of defending the letter of Saint John Chrysostom to Caesarius the monk, he accused the author of the said book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* of being the earliest inventor and defender of the Calvinist heresy.

By Jacques Boileau, theologian of Paris.

Paris, 1712.

[Col. 0103]

# HISTORICAL PREFACE

[Col. 0103A] So many learned men and erudite scholars have handled the little work you have before you, excellent reader, written *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* at the command of the emperor Charles the Bald eight hundred years ago, through the nights and days of our own age; and they have laboriously investigated its genuine author. It therefore seems not only inconsiderate but also characteristic of a writer abusing leisure and learning without restraint to pile further additions of any kind upon their labors.

Nevertheless, since I have had no intention whatsoever of reworking what others have already said or reheating badly fashioned material, I persuade myself that learned and wise readers will not regard as unwelcome the undertaking by which I resolved to prepare this new edition with care [Col. 0103B] and fidelity, surrounded by notes and reflections. Through these I would defend the doctrine of the author of this little work from every charge of error and undertake to defend it, as written in Latin from a French discourse, as harmonious with the tenets of the Catholic Church.

Nothing written in the age of Charles the Bald can be found that more deserves to be considered through human reflection and thought. Indeed, no work is more useful or necessary for disentangling and explaining the rough places in history that concern the perpetuity of the Catholic faith regarding the Eucharist, that is, the truth of Christ’s body concealed in the sacred mystery. Yet we must admit that the book *On the Body and Blood of Christ* remained no less hidden in the dark caves of the ninth and tenth centuries—namely, from the time when it first emerged from the egg until the year 1532, when, for the first time, with the midwife’s assistance of the printing press, it was brought into the light.

For nothing can arouse greater wonder in the minds of educated men than that, for two hundred years after the author’s death—specifically, during the period when the heresy of Berengar began to break forth—not a single ecclesiastical writer, whether of the Catholic or the opposing party, mentioned it in defense or refutation of the truth of Christ’s true flesh being present, or of the conversion of bread and wine into body and blood, which the theologians of this age later called transubstantiation.

There is only one solitary anonymous author, whose sermons all learned men acknowledge to be without sense or coherent meaning. His age is inaccessible and has been recorded by no learned man who has placed this writer among the opponents of Saint Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corbie, who refined and developed material on the same subject at almost the same time—or at least at a comparable period—in which this monk belonged to the same abbey of Corbie. Writers of the opposing party, and men of no small standing among the learned, have persuaded themselves that he was the abbot of Orbais in the diocese of Soissons, on the basis of Book III, chapter 28, of Flodoard’s *History of Reims*: David Blondel, *Adversarial Clarifications on the Eucharistic Matter*, chapter 13, p. 427; and Jacobus Usserius, *History of Gottschalk*, chapter 11, p. 268.

In truth, later writers seem to me to have acted splendidly and fortunately concerning this anonymous author, a man of whatever slight literary merit, especially since, by a candid omission, they effaced his name from the annals of merchants. Nor would Father Cellotius, the Jesuit, seem to have dealt more successfully with a writer of this kind if, setting aside so much care, he had left his work in darkness and had not burdened it with so many additions of notes and commentaries or made it public through an excessive use of the printing art in the year of Christ 1555. He ought instead to have followed the judgment and prudence of the most learned Jacobus Sirmond, an enduring ornament of the Society of Jesus, who had judged a work of this sort unworthy of public light, as did Usserius, a writer of the opposing party, who reports that he had examined it in the Cotton Library, chapter 11 of his *On the Succession and State of the Christian Churches*, p. 46, §16.

Nevertheless, the *σφάλματα*—“errors” or “blunders”—of this anonymous book can be perceived and understood neither more happily nor more efficiently than from the original manuscript made public by the Jesuit associate Cellotius, with its dense additions of notes and adversarial material.

Moreover, Sigebert of Gembloux, a monk who was also associated with Saint Vincent’s at Metz, and who lived at the beginning of the twelfth century, as well as Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim at the beginning of the fifteenth century, in their *ὑπομνημονεύματα*—memoranda or commentaries—on ecclesiastical writers, list Ratramnus among the true defenders of the faith and of Catholic doctrine. They describe his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, written at the command of Emperor Charles the Bald, as exposed to no suspicion of heresy, as neither written against Saint Paschasius nor in any respect opposed to the judgment of the Catholic Church.

During the same intervening period, the only person who mentioned this work was the illustrious Johannes Fischer, bishop of Rochester in England, elevated to the dignity of cardinal while imprisoned and beheaded by Henry VIII, king of Great Britain, an unjust and lascivious man, for the Catholic faith and his most resolute defense of the Apostolic See at the age of eighty. In the preface to Book IV of his *Eucharist* against Oecolampadius, in 1526—approximately six years before the work was printed at Cologne in 1532—he brought forth Ratramnus’s little book as a testimony to the Catholic faith concerning the presence of Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist and transubstantiation. He added Paschasius to it without introducing any distinction in doctrine.

But when it was first brought into public light through the labor of the printing press, it experienced an extraordinarily varied and changeable fate, such as perhaps had never befallen any Catholic author. Although it displayed nothing opposed or contrary to Catholic truth—as we do not doubt that you, reader, will easily understand from this work—when it was made public with the zeal, care, and printing presses of the German Protestants, they imagined it to be a work favorable to their superstitions and assemblies. Nearly all learned men—Catholics, I know not through what ancient lethargy lulled to sleep—did not reject the Protestants’ assertions and did not resist their perverse designs. They set aside every examination and *ἀνάκρισις*—investigation or scrutiny—of Ratramnus’s work and treated it as a work stained by heretical depravity and excessively contrived through the malicious deceit of the Protestants, who had falsely imposed upon it the name of a Catholic writer so that they might more easily administer poison while concealing the intoxication.

Nevertheless, the censors appointed by the Council of Trent in 1559 to examine the books that the Fathers rightly judged ought to be prohibited placed this book in the catalogue and relegated it among the corrupt works. Thus, even today it appears in the Index under number 5, under the name Bertram, in these words:

> “The book of Bertram entitled *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*.”

This judgment of the censors was immediately promulgated by Pope Pius IV.

Sixtus of Siena, of the Dominican order, in 1566—approximately the third year after the Council of Trent had been fully celebrated—received the book in the preface to his *Holy Library*, which he dedicated to Pius V, with no more civil or favorable hand. There, after exaggerating with a deadly pen and charity diluted by bitterness the audacious insolence of the Protestants, who attacked the doctrine of the Catholic Church with books lacking authorship and bearing false names, favorable to their superstition, he says that they clothed themselves in the name and armor of the ancient Fathers, among whom they included the aforesaid book of Ratramnus.

> “Thus,” says Sixtus of Siena, “in recent years they have circulated Oecolampadius’s pernicious volume against the sacrament of Christ’s body under the title of Bertram the priest, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, addressed to Charlemagne.”

A short time after Sixtus of Siena, the most illustrious Claudius Espenceus, whom in his age no doctor surpassed in Christian learning or knowledge, was not contaminated by those passions which many designate by the name of zeal and Christian speech. Carried away by the waters of a swift river, he allowed himself to be submerged, and Ratramnus appeared to him among the heretics.

While he was exhausting himself in labor on his books *On the Adoration of the Eucharist*, which the illustrious doctor Gilbert Genebrardus published after his death, he recognized many errors against the faith in this little work of Ratramnus, in Book 11, chapter 19. He had first noted by way of preliminary warning that the author entangled the subject more and involved it in rough places more than he disentangled and explained it. He concluded that the work was spurious and that Ratramnus could not have been either its genuine author or its double—that is, its second or alternative author.

Sanctesius, bishop of Évreux, who in the same century defended the truth against heretics with strong and shining weapons, adopted the same judgment. In his second *Repetition on the Eucharist*, chapter 14, he undertook to maintain that Ratramnus could not have been the author of this book.

Pope Clement VIII most willingly approved the same judgment of the censors appointed by the Council of Trent, utterly rejected the book as heretical, and the cardinals Bellarmine, Quiroga, Sandoval, and Alanus obeyed his decisive judgment.

But the doctors of Louvain, commonly called the Doctors of Douai, in 1571—when Espenceus, suffering the pains of strangury, departed from this life to heaven, and when they were occupied with completing the Index of Prohibited Books in Belgium—judged that this book could be exempted from the law of prohibition if certain corrections were admitted, and that it ought not to be listed among the spurious works, contrary to which it would be unjustly charged even by them.

If anyone should persuade himself that these Belgians wished to investigate the matter and amend certain passages so that, after deleting some words, they might arbitrarily add new ones in place of those removed, he can easily understand that they had no other intention than to amend and correct whatever fair, learned, and prudent men might judge necessary and useful for facilitating the understanding of the author’s text and meaning. For example, they held that in number 47 one should read *invisibiliter*, “invisibly,” and not *visibiliter*, “visibly.” The Protestants considered this correction so appropriate that they willingly admitted it in the Basel editions that followed, in the year 1557.

These doctors never persuaded themselves that meanings contrary and opposed to those intended by the author ought to be assigned and applied to his words. Rather, they judged that meanings suited and adapted to him ought to be given, as the most learned Jesuit Jacobus Gretzerus demonstrated fully and perfectly in Book II of *On the Law and Manner of Prohibiting Bad Books*, chapter 10, against Junius, p. 327, printed at Ingolstadt in 1603.

All this signifies nothing other than that the meaning of the Catholic Church must be attributed to him and defended on his behalf. He does not in fact appear more alien from it, as will easily be understood from the original Latin text of Ratramnus’s book, together with the adversarial materials and defenses that we have recently included in this volume against Father Harduinus, the Jesuit associate. In these materials we defend and vindicate the book attributed to Ratramnus, or to Bertram the priest and monk of the abbey of Corbie, against every invention or suspicion of Lutheran or Calvinist novelty and heresy.

The learned Sorbonist doctor Generardus, archbishop of Aix, who, before penetrating the heart of this matter, had placed Ratramnus among the heretics of the ninth century in his *Chronicle*, nevertheless did not deny him an honorable place among the defenders of transubstantiation in the year 1215. The doctors of Louvain opened this furrow for him in the learned soil of antiquity, and Gregorius of Valencia, Jacobus Gretzerus, Antonius Possevinus—the Jesuits—and Nicolaus Romeus, master general of the Dominicans, deepened it.

And in truth Petrus Alixius, while he remained in France among the ministers of Calvinist superstition, a man beyond all exception, wrongly said in his response to Father Paris, canon regular of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris, p. 7, that this procedure of the doctors of Louvain was entirely superfluous from the time when manuscripts of this author were discovered in places not at all suspect, manuscripts plainly agreeing with the printed copies and corresponding to them. For, on the contrary, it had become clear from the discovery of such manuscripts that this author was neither an opponent of Paschasius nor opposed to him, and that he did not reject the doctrine of the Catholic Church.

I know indeed that Cardinal Perronius, who had considered these manuscripts to agree entirely with the printed copies—as he had learned from a highly authentic and autograph manuscript in the library of the distinguished man Jacobus Gilotus, canon of the Most Sacred Chapel of the Paris Palace and senator of the august Parliament of Paris, his friend, who died in 1618, a manuscript that Isaac Casaubon had also seen and carefully examined, as Usserius reports in chapter 2 of *On the Succession of the Churches*, §18—did not hesitate to regard the author of this book as our Ratramnus. Yet he did not refuse to leave him among the heretics, as a writer of doubtful faith who deliberately concealed his thoughts in obscure and difficult words, while expressing and explaining heretical meanings in formally Catholic language and orthodox style.

But Cardinal Perronius would not have proceeded in this manner if he had applied himself to the matter with a more certain intention and, probing the author’s mind more carefully, had reflected upon it. It would have been easy for so great and eminent a doctor to observe that this author’s mind was in no way inclined to acknowledge in the Eucharist merely a figurative body and blood of Christ, with no truth or true presence whatever. Yet he attributes this position to him on p. 672 of his work *On the Eucharist*, although Ratramnus himself is entirely opposed to that opinion. This will, I do not doubt, be very easy to understand from the autograph text and from the notes and other defenses against Father Harduinus appended to and recently published in this volume.

But because the great man was everywhere called “cardinal,” and because the enormous world resounded with the name of the great Perronius, no doctor among mortals dared reject his judgment, especially in our France. There, French translations made by Protestants between 1558 and 1600, highly favorable in their form and method to Protestant fictions, contributed greatly to persuading nearly all unwary people and those thoughtless through the superficiality of their studies that this writer was opposed to the doctrine of the Catholic Church. They also distorted matters so that people would not approve the *ἀνάκρισις*—the investigation—of the doctors of Louvain, which was as just as it was learned.

This was almost the entire course or singular fate of Ratramnus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* until 1655, when the most learned of the Sorbonic professors, Jacobus Samboevius, undertook the defense of the aforesaid book in a treatise *On the Eucharist*. In that work he resolved its difficulties according to the mind of the theologians of Louvain in the Sorbonne schools in that year, with the approval of many of the city’s auditors and the open applause of countless others.

The most illustrious Petrus de Marca, at that time archbishop of Toulouse, designated by the Most Christian King as archbishop of Paris and confirmed by papal bulls, died without taking possession of the office. At the same time, he attempted by a new method and approach to free this famous ninth-century writer from the snares and difficulties in which his book was entangled. Six years earlier, the distinguished president of the Court of the Mint, Mauguinus, had made public two excellent little works of his on Predestination. In that same year, the theologian Dom Lucas Dacherius, eminent for piety and learning, had published four volumes against the Greeks in Volume II of the *Spicilegium*.

The new method of defending the truth concerning this little book of Ratramnus can be understood from the Latin letter that the reverend bishop de Marca wrote to Dom Lucas Dacherius on the Kalends of January 1657, published in Volume II of the *Spicilegium*, which was itself made public in that same year.

The entire method of resolving the matter of Ratramnus’s book seems to rest on this point: de Marca, having abandoned his earlier judgment—if he truly was the author of the French treatise *On the Eucharist* that his relative, the abbot Fuget, published—held that this treatise *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was not the genuine offspring of the said Ratramnus, but of John Scotus, or Erigena, a contemporary of Ratramnus. He had called its author Pseudo-Ratramnus. The work had immediately afterward been condemned at the Council of Vercelli under Leo IX and burned, or consumed by fire, at the Roman Council under Pope Nicholas II in 1059, where the followers of Berengar attributed it to John Scotus.

Father Paris, a learned canon regular of Saint Augustine and professor of sacred theology at the abbey of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris, defended this conjecture of the Lord de Marca vigorously, insofar as he could, in a dissertation printed at the end of Volume I, prepared and published by the authors of the book *The Perpetuity of the Faith*, against Claude, a minister of Calvinist superstition at the temple of Charenton. He also defended it in a repeated response by the aforementioned learned canon regular to the response of another minister of Charenton, Alixius by name, who had refuted Father Paris’s dissertation.

The aforesaid Father Paris added only this moderation and qualification: it seemed incredible to him that John Scotus had attributed and assigned this little book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* to Ratramnus, or had inscribed it under Ratramnus’s name, since it appeared more suitable to Berengar or to his followers, who lived almost two hundred years after Ratramnus.

Moreover, Father Paris did not condemn this book too eagerly or decisively, nor did he relegate it among the heretics and those justly condemned by following Dom de Marca. Rather, he represented it as entangled and involved in many difficult passages of language, whose meaning and judgment are difficult to grasp. In this he followed the furrows opened by the authors of *The Perpetuity of the Faith*, who had not considered it especially useful or necessary either to defend or to accuse the matters of the book, the person of Ratramnus, or the Catholic faith concerning this unknown monk of the ninth century.

This opinion of the most illustrious Father de Marca, which at first appearance gleams with golden brilliance and pricks the minds of those who possess or have acquired any inclination toward study and learning, could scarcely have found followers of any kind. In truth, unless Father Paris had assisted it with the moderation and qualification noted above, the most famous archbishop of Toulouse and Paris, abandoning his association with the canon regular, would have remained in his opinion like a solitary sparrow on a roof.

I am not violently moved to repeat or tear up what has already been said about the subject at hand. Let curious readers go instead to the booksellers who sell works written about this matter, if such *κριτήρια*—critical questions or standards—attract their minds.

For my part, to prove that such a book cannot in any way be attributed to John Scotus, I believe that the argument must be drawn from the difference, variation, and opposition between Scotus’s and Ratramnus’s style and language, and from the doctrine and judgments of the ancient Fathers and doctors of the Church whom both men cite and praise. These features prove them to be so opposed and different that they cannot be confused or mixed, except by those dullards—or *βαλανοφάγοι*, “acorn-eaters”—who have nowhere read their writings either in detail or as wholes with deliberate attention.

A few years ago, in Oxford, in 1681, the famous treatise of John Scotus, *Περὶ φύσεων μερισμοῦ*—“On the Division of Natures”—was printed at the public press. Its structure, order, and manner of writing are so different from and opposed to Ratramnus’s little book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* that I can scarcely imagine anyone who has not departed from the power of reason to whom any doubt could arise about attributing Ratramnus’s little book to John Scotus. They smell of violets as quickly as onions.

But however false or fictitious all these matters may be, what could be offered in reply to the most learned Father Jean Mabillon, the illustrious monk of the Order of Saint Benedict? From his preface placed at the head of the second century of the *Acts of the Benedictines*, we understand, on p. 45, §83, that he compared the writing or characters of the printed manuscript of Ratramnus’s book with a manuscript that we are making public for a second time in this edition, and that he asserts its age to be eight hundred years—that is, from the reign of Charles the Bald to our own time. He does not refuse to serve as a witness that he saw and read such a manuscript, bound together with two books on Predestination, to which the name of Ratramnus is inscribed equally and *παραλλήλως*, “in parallel.”

Moreover, that most learned monk, skilled in recognizing the age and determining the date of ancient handwritten books—a skill that he acquired through painstaking study for the examination of old papers and ancient codices, as is easily understood from the books he wrote *On Diplomatic Matters*—asserts that this book of Ratramnus *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, belonging to the abbey of Lobbes, was written in characters eight hundred years old.

It is impossible to produce a witness of greater authority. Furthermore, that same monk, whom no learned man suspects of falsehood, testifies in his *German Journey*, printed in Paris at the beginning of Volume IV of the *Analecta* in 1685, that he saw with his own eyes and handled with his own hands, in the monastery of Salem-Weiler of the Cistercian order, founded in the time of Saint Bernard in 1137, a manuscript more than seven hundred years old in which the same works, bound together and bearing the name of Ratramnus, appear in parallel.

Since this is so, what room for doubt can remain that such a little work is undoubtedly Ratramnus’s and cannot in any way be assigned to John Scotus?

Whatever the facts may be, nothing now remains for us to prove except that Ratramnus set forth in this work an orthodox and Catholic meaning, a sound and genuinely Catholic doctrine. Father Mabillon has already established this abundantly in the preface to the *Acts of the Benedictines* cited above, p. 45, §88. We hope that all learned and wise readers will easily understand it from this ninth edition of the Latin autograph text communicated to me by Father Mabillon, and from the notes that you now have before you, learned reader. These notes have recently been written in Latin from the French for the benefit of men of letters from foreign nations—Englishmen, Germans, and Spaniards—staying in the city of Paris. We have also added certain considerable supplements that, perhaps with the exception of Father Harduinus, the Jesuit and learned writer, will displease no one.

But before you turn your mind to the careful reading of this work, it seems to me not only useful but necessary to answer two arguments advanced by a man of the Protestant party who wrote Ratramnus’s treatise *On the Body and Blood of Christ* in French, and wrote it worse than the Latin, which is not especially polished or elegant. He put these arguments forward in his preface or introduction to prove that this little work had in fact been composed at the command of Emperor Charles the Bald to refute the doctrine of the Roman Church concerning the true presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist and transubstantiation—a doctrine that the Catholic Church defends today and that, as we maintain, she has always accepted as requiring defense.

The first argument proceeds as follows. Since this writer of the opposing party, drawing arguments from Book III of Albertinus, the minister of Charenton, *On the Eucharist against Cardinal Perronius*, attempted to prove that the aforesaid Ratramnus could not have written his book against a certain sect of Stercoranists, a sect that never existed in reality and was entirely unknown to the ancient historians who wrote about schisms and the various heresies that arose over time, Ratramnus’s little book must necessarily have been written against defenders of the true presence of Christ’s body and of transubstantiation. Therefore, it was allegedly written solely to refute this doctrine of the Roman Church.

The second argument is drawn from the various modes of expression, explicit images, and Latin phrases of this treatise. The writer persuaded himself that these could not have been written or expressed in French unless they were opposed and contrary to the doctrine of the Roman and Catholic Church, and therefore favorable to the meaning of the Protestants.

These are the objections that we must now answer.

First, we readily admit that no sect of Stercoranists existed in Ratramnus’s time—namely, no association of shameless men who persuaded themselves, contrary to the meaning of the Catholic Church, that the body and flesh of Christ which we receive in the sacrament of the Eucharist were subject to digestion, the grinding of food, and the evacuation of excrement, by which human beings, filled with abundant meals, usually relieve their bowels.

This sort of opinion appears so foolish and contrary to right reason that it must have seemed entirely improbable to all men who had not departed from the power of reason. Moreover, Father Mabillon has defended Heribald, bishop of Auxerre; Amalarius, archdeacon of Trier; Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz; and Florus, deacon of the Church of Lyon, from this fiction so successfully, forcefully, and easily that no room for doubt remains that the name and reputation of such outstanding and excellent men should be removed from such a wicked suspicion.

Nevertheless, even if such a heresy had existed, and had not been recklessly and maliciously imposed—during the heat of controversy—upon Catholic men who thought correctly about religion, whom their opponents strove with all their strength to compel to believe that such a disgraceful and shameful delirium followed from the persuasion or faith they held, namely, that the body of the Lord in the Eucharist could in some manner and by some rational process fall under touch and sight and be subject to the other bodily limitations—then it would still be not merely difficult and arduous, but entirely *ἀδύνατον*, “impossible,” to prove that Ratramnus’s aforesaid little work had been composed with the deliberate intention of refuting this Stercoranism. There is not even a *γρῦ*—not the slightest word—about it in the aforesaid book.

It is plainly improbable that a man of sound sense and reason would have written against a heresy while sincerely and truthfully leaving aside and omitting its exposition, especially when it was so trivial and ridiculous that a simple presentation would have made it collapse and be dispelled before everyone.

It is therefore appropriate and necessary to admit that Ratramnus’s book was written against orthodox theologians. But it does not follow from this that the book was deliberately composed to refute the Catholic teaching concerning the true presence of Christ’s body and blood and transubstantiation.

Indeed, the very same argument that proves that it was not written against the opinion of the Stercoranists—about which nothing is stated in explicit words anywhere in this book—equally demonstrates that it was not written against the doctrine of the real presence, which scholastic theologians call *realitas*, “reality,” and about which the book likewise says nothing. And indeed, how would the author have used words and language signifying reality and transubstantiation in a work whose purpose and authorial intention were to attack and refute such a doctrine?

We do not doubt that this will easily be perceived from the various notes with which we have enlarged this edition. All these points must therefore be taken together to conclude that Ratramnus’s purpose and intention were to attack a third opinion, which differs greatly from the other two.

This is easily understood and openly evident from Ratramnus’s own little book, in which the entire matter of the discussion is reduced to two heads or parts, from which the book is composed.

The first concerns those who persuaded themselves that the whole matter, without any qualification, takes place plainly and openly in the Eucharist, striking the eyes and occurring without figure or veil. According to them, it does not take place under any figure or concealment, but through the naked manifestation of the truth itself.

Here are Ratramnus’s actual words. From them it is easy to understand that he did not write against Saint Paschasius Radbertus, nor against the Catholic Church, which has always held that some figure, inseparable from the true reality of Christ’s present body and blood, is contained in the mystery of the Eucharist.

The second matter that Ratramnus attacks follows necessarily from the first. For if nothing in the Eucharist were figured or veiled, it would follow from this assumption that the whole matter must be subject to the knowledge of the senses. The corollary would then be that the flesh and blood of Christ, which were taken by the mouths of the faithful—or everything perceived by the senses—were Christ’s body, the very body born of the blessed Virgin, crucified for us, and buried.

Here is the substance of the second matter, which the French call the “second point.” Ratramnus attacked it, but it has no connection whatever with the doctrine of the Roman Church. For the Roman Church truly believes that Christ’s body is veiled and that what is concealed beneath species accessible to the senses is the very body born of the blessed Virgin and nailed to the cross. But she has never believed or been persuaded that this outward part accessible to the senses, this veil and these species, are Christ’s body in any other way than by figure or representation, according to the mind of Lanfranc, abbot of Bec and later archbishop of Canterbury. Others likewise defended this position against the followers of Berengar, namely Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, and many others, who can plainly be identified from our notes, eighty-six in number.

From these points it is clearly and plainly established that Ratramnus’s treatise could never have been written against Paschasius. Regarding the first part of the discussion, Paschasius makes it just as plainly evident as Ratramnus that there is some figure in the Eucharist, together with veils or coverings, and that the senses do not discern everything contained in it.

Regarding the second part, it is entirely *ἀδύνατον*, “impossible,” that Ratramnus and Paschasius defended opposing and contrary positions. Paschasius never said that what outwardly appears in the Eucharist and is perceived by the senses is the body of Christ itself, born of the Virgin and nailed to the cross. Rather, he said only that what is veiled, concealed, and hidden beneath the outward species accessible to the senses is that body.

Ratramnus does not appear to deny this; indeed, from the autograph text of his treatise *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* and from our notes, which we shall provide in Latin from the French and include in this volume, he appears firmly to demonstrate and confirm it.

Why, then, is it necessary to let the mind’s brain drip through so many brambles and difficult passages of human self-deception in order to perceive and contemplate Ratramnus’s purpose and intention in the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*? What usefulness can there be in the invention and fiction of the Stercoranist sect for refuting a notion so foolish and inconceivable that it is scarcely credible that such a sect ever existed in the world, a sect of which Ratramnus did not utter even a word?

And, conversely, why must one persuade oneself that Ratramnus intended to attack the reality of Christ’s bodily presence in the Eucharist and transubstantiation itself—matters that he does not consider with even a little thought or reflection, and that are as foreign to the two heads of his discussion as is the disgraceful and shameful opinion of the Stercoranists?

Ratramnus’s book is readily available. Let it be read. From it one will easily understand that in the first part he proves without ambiguity or *λογομαχία*—verbal disputation—that there is a singular and partial figure in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, and that the senses do not perceive or apprehend everything contained in it.

In the second part he proves even more fully that this sacramental and mystical body of Christ—that is, what is outwardly figured and made accessible to the senses—is not the same as what was born of the Virgin and crucified.

This second part of the discussion followed naturally from the first. Therefore, the second refutation must necessarily be naturally connected and joined to the first.

In truth, we must acknowledge that Paschasius explained his meaning somewhat more clearly than Ratramnus. But this fuller treatment of Paschasius arises from nothing other than the fact that his speech is more expansive and more fully developed. Whatever the facts may be, the meaning of both is entirely the same, so that, however one of them is read with attentive care, the reader will always understand that both held the same view.

Indeed, although Paschasius says most clearly that Christ’s true body, born of the Virgin, is in the Eucharist, he never says that what is a figure or veil in that same Eucharist is Christ’s body itself. And although Ratramnus says and clearly declares that what appears outwardly to the senses in the sacrament is not Christ’s body itself, born of the Virgin (no. 57), he nowhere denies that it is the veil, covering, or wrapping of the Lord’s body.

On the contrary, he openly says and repeatedly asserts that what appears outwardly is the sacrament of the Lord’s true flesh (no. 16); that there are two different existences belonging to two different things (no. 30); that bread and wine have been converted into the substance of the body and blood (no. 15); and that it cannot be held without guilt that Christ’s body is not received there (no. 99).

He says that the sacrament has both the name and the reality of Christ’s body (no. 13), and that no greater power is required to make a thing from nothing than to change its nature (no. 53). Whatever words or expressions he may have used, one must never persuade oneself that Christ’s body is not received in the Eucharist (no. 101).

For this reason the Protestants have attempted to vindicate their position by claiming that a different meaning, one other than the meaning Ratramnus intended, must be assigned to his words and language. It remains for us now to examine this matter in our response to the second objection, in order to refute the author of the French translation of Ratramnus made in 1672.

He maintains throughout Ratramnus’s whole and unbroken treatise that Ratramnus means the same by the word “truth” as by the word “reality”—a term which began to come into use in medieval Latinity while scholastic learning was still in its infancy amid the ruins of polished Latin, because this term is especially opposed to figure. From this he concludes that, since throughout this book Ratramnus teaches that Christ’s body is given to us not “in truth” but “in mystery,” he must have intended, in explaining the question proposed in express words, to prove that Christ’s body is not truly and really received in the Eucharist, but only in mystery and figure. This, he says, clearly and plainly expresses and signifies the Calvinist meaning [Col. 0115A]. If he had intended to support this design or view with any firm and vigorous proof, it would have been necessary to leave Ratramnus’s cause barren and to follow, by imitation, all those ecclesiastical writers whom we mentioned above. No room for doubt would then have remained that this monk was the first author and progenitor of the Calvinist heresy. On this assumption, he would be the lone and singular witness to the truth, from whom the other writers—his equals or near equals, indeed all or most—would not have feared to dissent. In any case, the Protestant’s entire proof comes down to this, on page XXXII of his preface, printed at Rouen by Jean Lucas in 1672.

> “The word ‘truth,’” he says in French, “may be opposed to falsehood or to a figure. It occurs in Ratramnus first [Col. 0115B] in the sense that the figurative modes of speech used by Jesus Christ in the Gospel are not lies or falsehoods. But in the second sense, in which the word ‘truth’ resembles and is equivalent to the word ‘reality’—for example, when the Lord says, ‘I am the living bread,’ or ‘the bread of life,’ ‘which came down from heaven’ (John 6:41, 51)—the expressions ‘I am the living bread,’ or ‘the bread of life,’ ‘which came down from heaven,’ are figurative expressions, yet they are true, with a truth opposed and contrary to falsehood and falsity. For it would be impious to say that Christ did not speak the truth; and from these expressions it is easy to understand that Christ intended to signify that he provides our souls with what bread supplies to our bodies as nourishment—namely, spiritual life and nourishment—as he explained elsewhere. Nevertheless, such a figure and mode of expression [Col. 0115C] do not signify REALITIES: for the Lord is not truly, or really, or in actual fact bread, but only by virtue of the mystical relation that he bears to bread. Nor should anyone boldly object to us that the same thing can be both truth and figure, as Paschasius says. For even if this is not impossible in some sense or on some occasion, it is altogether impossible in the question proposed by Ratramnus; from that question we plainly distinguish that the words ‘figure’ and ‘truth’ fight against each other and are therefore incompatible. It is consequently necessary, in this question, to hold firmly and securely that the words TRUTH and TRULY signify nothing properly except REAL and REALLY.”

In this controversy there is no question of Ratramnus using the word “truth” in a different sense, whether by opposition to the word “figure” [Col. 0115D]. Yet it by no means follows that he takes “reality” in the sense in which we assert it of Christ’s present body in the Eucharist. I maintain, rather, that in his writing he uses this word only to signify the complete and perfect disclosure of Christ’s flesh and blood; and that, in his view, this disclosure is incompatible with real presence—namely, with Christ’s own substance and his very human nature. From this it is manifest and clear that, in examining this question—whether Christ’s body and blood exist in the Eucharist—he intended to discuss nothing other than whether in the Eucharist there existed some figure, or whether there was an open disclosure [Col. 0116A] of things as they exist in themselves: that is, whether what is presented to the eyes was in actual fact Christ’s body, subject to sight and taste, or simply the species and appearances of bread and wine.

No one can deny this without recognizing that Ratramnus acknowledged the reality of Christ’s body in the manner in which we understand it to be compatible with a figure, since he repeatedly says that this bread and this chalice—that is, the Eucharist—are named “the body of Christ” and are so in fact (no. 99); that the wine could be changed into his own blood (no. 28); that these species are Christ’s body, not the existences of two different things (no. 16); and that in this mystery one thing has been changed into another (no. 13). He also uses the greatest caution with his readers concerning certain expressions, lest they believe that Christ’s body is not offered to them. For if by the word “truth” [Col. 0116B] he had understood “reality,” nothing could appear further removed from common sense or sound reason than the use made in his mouth of certain forms of expression which, with every distinction removed, signify his faith—or, more precisely, Ratramnus’s belief—that the reality of Christ’s body is compatible with a figure.

But this cannot at all be said concerning the disclosure of Christ’s body. For we cannot pass over or forget that Ratramnus used the words “true,” “truth,” and “truly” forty or forty-two times in opposition to “figure”; and that in thirty-three of those instances he intended to signify the disclosure of the Lord’s body to the senses.

In truth, I do not think that Ratramnus used these [Col. 0116C] words elsewhere to signify the presence of Christ’s true body—that reality which theologians call “reality”—except in nos. 3, 49, 67, 83, and 84. From these passages it is inconceivable that Protestants could extract anything favorable or supportive of their position. For Ratramnus proceeded in such a way as to make Catholic believers observe more distinctly that they do not believe, and do not persuade themselves, that Christ’s body is what is disclosed externally outside the mystery; rather, we believe that it is truly present there, apprehended and known by the spirit, but actually hidden beneath the image presented to our eyes and senses.

This is easy to perceive from no. 77, where these words are read explicitly:

> “What appears externally, therefore, is not the thing itself, but the image of the thing; whereas what is perceived and understood by the mind is the truth of the thing.”

And in [Col. 0116D] no. 84:

> “And this mode is in figure and image, so that the truth—the thing itself—may be perceived.”

Whatever the facts may be, when an author’s book lies in the hands of learned and educated men and a question of fact is raised concerning it, the book itself must be consulted above all, so that its meaning may be understood, just as if its author were still alive. Let us suppose, then, that Ratramnus had come back to life, and ask him what he understood by the word “truth,” and what he intended to signify by it in opposition to the word “figure.” He would answer us clearly that it means a demonstration or disclosure of a thing not veiled by any shadows or hidden beneath figures. We would not refuse to believe so clear an answer, entangled in no evasions [Col. 0117A], nor would we doubt that by the word “truth” he understood the disclosure and declaration of the thing itself, with a distinction and difference admitted—if, moreover, he asserted that the thing itself was hidden and veiled beneath a figure, as he truly asserts and affirms concerning Christ’s body in the Eucharist.

But what room for doubt remains that Ratramnus spoke and wrote in precisely this way and opened his mind in no. 8 of his book *On the Body and Blood of Christ*? After explaining the nature of a figure, he speaks as follows:

> “Truth, however, is the manifest demonstration of a thing veiled by many images of shadows.”

He does not introduce his argument by saying that he has undertaken to examine and discuss whether Christ’s body is present or truly exists [Col. 0117B] in the Eucharist. He has no doubt about this; nor, according to Ratramnus (no. 15), can the contrary or opposing view be stated or entertained without guilt. Rather, he openly and thoroughly examines whether Christ’s body is presented to the bodily eyes and perceived by them, or whether it is in no way disclosed, but remains veiled and hidden (no. 5):

> “Whether, without any veiling of the mystery, the outward appearance should behold with the eyes of the body what the sight of the mind contemplates inwardly, so that everything that takes place may shine in the light of manifestation.”

This is the true state of the question, and this is the point at issue in Ratramnus’s discussion of the Eucharist. And although there can be no doubt that the thing itself—or “reality,” as it is called—is sometimes opposed to and set against a figure, this does not always happen, as is clear from the agreement of the writer of the opposing, Calvinist preface that we are discussing [Col. 0117C]. Without any doubt, Ratramnus understood by the word “truth” a disclosure—or, to use his own words, a manifestation or manifest demonstration—since he himself says that the opinion or belief that Christ’s body in the Eucharist is visibly seen and manifestly perceived by the eyes had been adopted and defended by most orthodox theologians. These theologians readily and willingly assented to the faith or persuasion of the Catholic Church and to the common belief in the body of Christ’s truly existing presence and in transubstantiation, more than two hundred years after the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* had been published at the command of Charles the Bald [Col. 0117D].

I do not doubt, excellent reader, that you will perceive this fully from the addition of the notes in which we mentioned Abbot Abbaud and Walter, the distinguished prior of the Abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris. Moreover, it would be pointless, in order to evade and weaken the force of this reply, to argue—as the author of the French preface written in 1672 does on pages 33 and 34—and to insist with all one’s strength that the word and expression “manifestation of truth” signify the very thing which they call “reality,” and therefore that Ratramnus, by denying the manifestation of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, denied reality itself and sincerely rejected the orthodox faith or persuasion. To prove this would be altogether as difficult as it would be ἀδύνατον—that is, impossible.

[Col. 0118A] Indeed, the writer of the opposing or Calvinist position reduces all his efforts to two arguments, in order to show that disclosure or manifestation signifies reality itself, or the true presence of Christ’s true body. It is neither difficult nor arduous for men who apply their will and devote themselves to this task and study to recognize the weakening and rejection of these arguments.

First, they do not hesitate to object that, if Ratramnus did not understand “manifestation” to mean reality, his adversaries must have persuaded themselves that Christ’s body had come within the range of their eyes, under whatever form or appearance of human flesh. Otherwise, they say, it could not be called “manifestation”; and according to the natural meaning of the word [Col. 0118B], it could not properly apply to men with eyes who knew accurately that nothing could be presented to their eyes and sight except ἐπιφάνειαι and παραστάσεις—the appearances and presentations of bread and wine, namely whiteness, roundness, and extension.

But it is necessary that Ratramnus’s adversaries could conceive such a thing or that it should have entered their minds. For I strongly and vigorously maintain that they persuaded themselves that the sight of their eyes was struck by the body and blood of Jesus Christ as affected by the qualities of bread and wine. The most learned Cardinal Perronius adopted this opinion and undertook to defend it: either Christ’s body was surrounded by the same surface as the pre-existing bread and wine, from which an evident consequence followed—namely, that Christ’s body had to affect our senses in the same manner as bread and wine had previously affected them, [Col. 0118C] as the Cartesian philosophers explain; or God himself sculpted or inscribed upon our senses the same images that bread and wine would have impressed, if their transformation had not taken place, as the most learned Father Magnan of the Order of Minims explains.

This is clearly and evidently established by the words of Abbot Abbaud, who wrote after Ratramnus and adopted this position, which he explains and disentangles at length, as will be plainly and clearly evident from our notes:

> “I had thought of replying to those who say that the body itself is not broken, but that something is done to its whiteness and roundness. But, on reconsidering the matter, I judged it absurd to dispute, in the Gospel of Christ, about whiteness and roundness; so, removing such things from ears eager for them, I left them to dialecticians—or at least to children [Col. 0118D]. Especially since anyone can easily see that whiteness or roundness cannot be separated from the body itself which is white or round, so that, while it remains unbroken, they can be broken separately in themselves.”

Walter, prior of Saint-Victor, proceeded in the same way. In both writers the word “truth” likewise served to signify disclosure, or manifest demonstration, or the sensory perception of Christ’s body under the qualities of bread and wine—not, however, his actually existing presence, or what writers of a later age call “reality.”

Let us now undertake to discuss the second part of the arguments. It appears in fact to be broader and more extensive than the first [Col. 0119A], but it must be refuted for a complete understanding of Ratramnus’s book. Four passages in this author give rise to the argument from which the French translator of the opposing position attempts to maintain that, by the word “manifestation,” or “manifest demonstration,” Ratramnus intended to signify reality. But from these four passages it seems to me easier to prove precisely the opposite—namely, the disclosure or manifestation of Christ’s body presented to the senses.

The first passage is taken by Ratramnus from the prayers or Collects of the Roman, Milanese, and Sens Churches [Note: [Col. 0119D] *Book of the Sacraments of the Roman Church*, book II, on the octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul.—The Ambrosian and Sens Missals.]:

> “Receiving the pledge of eternal life, we humbly implore that what we touch in the image of the sacrament we may receive through manifest participation.”

From this it is clearer than daylight that the Church asks God for a clear and open disclosure of Christ’s body, just as it truly exists in eternal glory, while in time she possesses it beneath the paropsidion or veil of the sacrament. This plainly demonstrates that some figure exists in the sacrament, and that what is hidden in it is not disclosed so as to shine forth in manifest light—precisely contrary to what Ratramnus’s adversaries intended, since they admitted or recognized no figure in the mystery, but maintained that everything came within the range of the eyes and was presented to the senses.

The words quoted from the second prayer mean no more than this:

> “That what we now possess under an appearance, we may receive in the truth of the things.”

[Note: [Col. 0120D] *Sacramentary of Saint Gregory*.]

For the word “truth” signifies nothing other than manifestation and manifest demonstration. These are the very words of Ratramnus and of others who adopted the position that he opposed. [Col. 0119C] Moreover, it is easy to understand that the Latin Church borrowed and transferred these prayers into Greek from a passage of Saint Dionysius, chapter 3 of *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, page 286:

> Ἀλλὰ ὦ θειοτάτη καὶ ἱερὰ τελετή, τὰ περικείμενά σοι συμβολικῶς ἀμφιέσματα τῶν αἰνιγμάτων ἀποκαλυψάμενη τηλαυγῶς ἡμῖν ἀναδείχθητι, καὶ τὰς νοερὰς ἡμῶν ὄψεις ἐνιαίου καὶ ἀπερικαλύπτου φωτὸς ἀποπλήρωσον.

> “But, O most divine and sacred rite, having unveiled the symbolic garments of riddles that surround you, reveal yourself clearly to us, and fill our intellectual eyes with undivided and unveiled light.”

Whoever were to draw from these words of Saint Dionysius an argument against the real presence of Christ’s body—which they call “reality”—would be employing a perverse and intemperate form of reasoning. For since the supplicant’s adoration is directed toward the sacrament, the phrase Θειοτάτη καὶ ἱερὰ τελετή, “most divine and sacred rite,” plainly presupposes or implies that Christ’s body is present in it. To him alone could an act or rite of supplication for divine assistance and of adoration in spirit and truth be directed, since, as faith teaches, he is present through the intimate union of the human nature with the person of the Word [Col. 0119D].

The second point follows immediately from the first. For after admitting these terms or words—pledge, image, or figure—Ratramnus says that they signify the thing of which they are signs but do not show it manifestly. From this the word “show” clearly indicates or signifies that figure and image are set against the showing and disclosure of a hidden and concealed thing.

For if the matter were not so, Ratramnus would necessarily appear to be speaking with the mind of a madman and a twisted brain [Col. 0120A]. He would have no dispute or controversy with theologians concerning the presence of Christ’s body, which they had received or defended; rather, his concern would be the disclosure or manifest demonstration of the true body, hidden in the Eucharist, with every veil removed and every figure set aside. For they had persuaded themselves and held in their minds that it was absurd and unnecessary to break the whiteness or roundness of the bread, but that it was instead necessary for Christ’s body to be white and round and broken, in the way in which a white and round thing is understood to be broken. This is understood from the treatise of Abbot Abbaud and from others who did not reject his opinion, but rather religiously supported it.

The third argument arises from no. 85, after the second prayer, where he opposes “manifestation” or “truth”—not “reality”—to the words “species” and “appearance,” as he does throughout the treatise [Col. 0120B]. But there can be no room for a reply at this point. For it cannot be denied that he understood by it the knowledge of Christ’s body through manifest demonstration, not its existence or true presence. The entire difference that he recognizes between Christ’s body veiled and hidden in the Eucharist and the same body shining forth and disclosed in the glory of the saints consists, he says, in this: the glorious body is known as already glorified through the resurrection. It would have been enough to say that it already exists glorified through the resurrection. The word “exists” had by Ratramnus’s time come into use to signify that Christ’s body not only bears this name in the Eucharist, but is and exists in it. Let us add also that this bread and chalice, which are named and exist as Christ’s body and blood (nos. 99 and 16).

The fourth passage is taken from no. 97, where, repeating the difference between Christ’s body in the sacrament and the same body in glory, he says that in glory it is not hidden under figures, but disclosed through manifest demonstration and known in glory:

> “Nor is there in it any figure, but the manifestation of the thing itself is perceived.”

This agrees with what he had said earlier (no. 89): that after the resurrection the body is presented to the senses, palpable and visible even after the resurrection. This is what the Protestant interpreter defends when he says that in Latin it ought to be written in French as *un CORPS RÉEL*, “a REAL BODY.” But this is to trifle with the credulity of readers and intemperately to mock human minds [Col. 0120D].

Many other matters remain in Ratramnus’s usage, concerning which it is necessary to forestall and anticipate preconceived opinions. One such matter is the word “species.” Certain notes may be consulted concerning it; from them it can be understood that the word signifies appearance, not the substance or nature of things, in accordance with the mind of philosophers who, although they use the name “substance,” do not always mean nature by it, but rather the qualities and properties by which nature is affected.

Certain other words also remain to be guarded against—namely, “inwardly,” “outwardly,” and [Col. 0121A] “corporally”—to which the mind must be applied with care. But in truth, if Ratramnus did not use them to designate Christ’s mystical and figurative body, and therefore something opposed to reality or to the true presence of the true body, as we defend in this study, they cannot pose a difficulty that cannot easily and conveniently be dissolved and resolved, as will be clear from this historical preface and from the notes whose additions we have judged should enrich the text of Ratramnus in this edition.

We must now respond to the three careful reflections, or deliberate considerations, of the author of the preface attached to the French translation of Ratramnus’s treatise, published in 1672.

The first of these considerations consists in the claim [Col. 0121B] that neither Paschasius nor Ratramnus makes any mention in his treatise of the adoration of the Eucharist. They ought not to have omitted it, they say, since the doctrine of reality, or of the truly existing presence of Christ’s body, naturally follows from Eucharistic adoration. This doctrine, Protestants and the Jesuit Hardouin imagine, Paschasius wanted to confirm and Ratramnus to refute.

But the interpreter of the opposing side of this book of Ratramnus was gravely mistaken in this matter. Since these two writers do not oppose one another, nor did they in fact fight or contend against each other, but rather remained in the same faith and persuasion concerning Christ’s body in the Eucharist, an argument drawn from adoration could not have been useful to either of them in defending his case. It would have been especially superfluous in the case of Ratramnus, since no one had raised it against him.

Meanwhile, it appears the height of rashness and inconsideration to maintain that, [Col. 0121C] in the ninth century, when Ratramnus and Paschasius lived, the Christian world had not yet adored the sacrament of the Eucharist—that is, the flesh and blood of Christ hidden in the mystery. We have established this truth with arguments as invincible as they are powerful and brilliant, in chapter 16 of Book I *On the Adoration of the Eucharist*, printed in Paris in 1685, drawing on the Second Council of Nicaea, the confession of faith of Alcuin, and the Council of Chalon. We believe that no room for doubt remains, whether concerning the ninth century or the centuries preceding it.

[Col. 0121D] I especially do not doubt that everyone will understand this from the conclusion of this preface to the new and accurate edition of Ratramnus’s aforementioned book *On the Body and Blood of Christ*: how false it is to say that these two writers made no mention of the adoration of the Eucharist, since on the contrary it is abundantly clear that they accepted it as a practice received by the whole Latin Church.

The second consideration does not surpass the first. It consists in the claim that Ratramnus always calls “faithful” those who properly receive Christ’s body administered to them in the Church, or who believe it to be true.

From this, two consequences are naturally drawn. First, it is said that in Ratramnus’s time unbelieving and wicked people did not receive Christ’s true body [Col. 0122A], and that the Church likewise did not believe that it was received by good or bad persons with the mouth of the body, but only with the mouth of the soul—which does not differ from faith.

But it is more than sufficiently clear that Ratramnus was speaking in accordance with Saint Augustine and had persuaded himself that Christ’s body is spirit and life only for those who receive it with faith, although it does not cease to be spirit and life in itself when it is received by unbelievers, the faithless, or those lacking faith. But how can Christ’s body be understood to be spirit and life in itself for unbelievers who receive it unworthily unless it is truly and really—that is, in actual fact and in truth—existing and present, and is received by the mouths of unbelievers? They do not receive it only through the spiritual impulse of faith and charity, as people say, but corporally, or with the mouth of the body [Col. 0122B], entirely apart from and without the benefit or effect of the soul.

Here are the explicit words of Saint Augustine that Ratramnus transmitted, excerpted from his exposition of the Gospel of Saint John:

> “What does ‘they are spirit and life’ mean? They are to be understood spiritually. Have you understood spiritually? They are spirit and life. Have you understood carnally? Even so, they are spirit and life—but they are not so for you.”

From this it is plainly evident that our author had no other meaning in mind when he calls those “faithful” who believe, and never otherwise, those who receive Christ’s body, than that those who receive it as faithful and believers receive it with spirit, life, and nourishment for the soul, with fruit and effect.

Therefore he never said that faith makes Christ’s body what we receive with the mouth and properly partake of in the sacred [Col. 0122C] Eucharist. On the contrary, he says that this body is the object of faith, that it is placed or established there by the powerful working of the Holy Spirit, and that it becomes nourishment for our soul, supplying it with the substance of eternal life. As Ratramnus says in no. 54:

> “It has therefore been changed inwardly by the powerful working of the Holy Spirit: faith beholds it, it nourishes the soul, and it supplies the substance of eternal life.”

Anastasius Sinaita, bishop of Antioch, who died in the year 599, appears plainly to have followed Saint Augustine’s opinion. In Book XII of his *Anagogical Meditations on the Hexaemeron*, whose Greek text, in the author’s own hand, was first printed at London and translated into Latin by the distinguished and learned Dacier in 1682, he says that these words of the Gospel of Saint John [Col. 0122D], chapter 6, verse 57—

> “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him”

—are not to be understood of visible flesh and blood presented to the senses. For Judas and Simon Magus, who received Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist from the bread and chalice, did not remain in Christ Jesus, nor did Christ remain in them; that is, they received the communion administered to them without its fruit.

He says in Greek:

> Λέγει γὰρ ἀκολούθως ὁ Θεὸς Λόγος· Ὁ τρώγων μου τὴν σάρκα, καὶ πίνων μου τὸ αἷμα, ἐν ἐμοὶ μένει, καὶ ἐγὼ ἐν αὐτῷ· οὐ περὶ τῆς ὁρωμένης σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος λέγει. Μετέλαβε γὰρ καὶ Ἰούδας καὶ Σίμων ὁ Μάγος τοῦ σώματος καὶ τοῦ αἵματος τῆς Εὐχαριστίας, τοῦ ἄρτου καὶ τοῦ ποτηρίου, ἀλλ’ οὐ κατῴκησεν, οὐδὲ μεμένηκεν ἐν αὐτοῖς ὁ Χριστός, οὐδὲ αὐτοὶ ἐν αὐτῷ.

> “For the Word of God says accordingly: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.’ He is not speaking of visible flesh and blood. For both Judas and Simon Magus partook of the body and blood of the Eucharist, of the bread and the cup; but Christ did not dwell or remain in them, nor did they remain [Col. 0123A] in him.”

Who could doubt that this is Anastasius’s genuine meaning, and that he held the belief that wicked persons who receive communion unworthily receive the true flesh and true blood of Christ with the mouth? For on an earlier page of the same book he distinguishes and differentiates those who receive unworthily from those who receive worthily in this respect: the worthy recipients will not die eternally, whereas the others—whether wicked, impious, stained by crimes, or earthly—will receive only Christ’s earthly flesh and blood:

> Οἱ δὲ γεί̈νοι καὶ τὰ γεί̈να φρονοῦντες, τῆς γεί̈νης μὲν, καὶ μόνης σαρκὸς τοῦ Χριστοῦ μεταλαμβάνουσιν τολμηρῶς καὶ ἀναξίως.

> “But those who are earthly and think earthly thoughts partake boldly and unworthily of Christ’s earthly flesh alone.”

Some men who are neither inexperienced nor thoughtless may perhaps consider this [Col. 0123B] digression of ours concerning the Greek-Latin edition of the aforementioned twelfth book of Anastasius’s *Meditations* somewhat untimely. It was produced by Protestants in 1682 on the authority of the manuscript in the library of the celebrated senior minister of Charenton, Jean Daillé, which they believe had been transferred to the library of the illustrious minister of the kingdom, Colbert, who was a diligent and curious investigator of ancient books.

But I cannot pass over in respectful silence the translator, a distinguished man worthy of the highest commendation among all investigators of antiquity for his literary achievements in Greek and Latin. I do not know for what reason he departed from the integrity of the Greek text. This must be understood from the words οὐ περὶ τῆς ὁρωμένης σαρκὸς [Col. 0123C] καὶ αἵματος λέγει, which he renders in Latin as:

> “He does not proceed concerning the present flesh and blood.”

This would lead us to understand that Anastasius did not consider or believe that Christ, in the explicit words of the Gospel of Saint John—

> “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him”

—intended to refer to the true presence of Christ’s true body in the Eucharist. But Anastasius’s meaning is that Saint John, in that passage, did not direct his attention to or contemplate visible flesh and blood presented to the senses, although it was truly or really present. There can be no doubt that this is the sincere doctrine of the Catholic Church.

No faithful translator would render these words of Saint John Chrysostom from Homily 73 on chapter 14 of Saint John, verse 7—

> Τοὺς μὲν γὰρ ὁρωμένους δυνάμεθα καὶ ὁρᾶν καὶ ἀγνοεῖν

[Col. 0123D] —as follows:

> “For those who are present we can both see and ignore,”

when the proper sense is:

> “Those whom we see we can see and ignore.”

All Greek dictionaries, manuscripts, and lexica bear witness to this, as do all learned men and all those acquainted with the first elements of the Greek language. They know that the verb ὁράομαι means “I am seen” or “I am visible,” and never “I am present”; ὅρασις means “vision” or “prophecy”; and ἀόρατος means “invisible,” not “absent.”

Those whose Greek learning is far inferior to Dacier’s, in his critical observations on Longinus, *On the Sublime*, the Odes of Horace, and Festus, know this:

> “Sweet-tongued teachers give little cakes,
>
> wishing us to learn the first elements.”

[Col. 0124A] No room for doubt remains that the distinguished and honorable Dacier willingly and freely acknowledged what is true and evident, especially since he sincerely and faithfully renounced the spell of Calvinist superstition.

Let us now proceed to the third consideration and meditation of the interpreter of Ratramnus. Since this concerns the various names given to the Eucharist at different times by inhabitants of different regions and areas of the Christian world, nothing consistent or compatible with sound reason can be deduced from it against the doctrine of the Roman Church. Moreover, it would provide abundant material for an entire book if we undertook to investigate the origin of these names and to show—as would easily be possible—that they were imposed upon the Eucharist by men who had no doubt concerning the presence or reality of Christ’s true body in the Eucharist.

But it is not useful to linger over this matter. We therefore believe that we cannot bring this preface, or history, of Ratramnus’s book to a better conclusion than by setting out three further considerations or meditations concerning this little work of Ratramnus, to which we are confident that the Protestants will have no answer.

First, we consider it false that Ratramnus intended to attack the faith or belief in the true presence of Christ’s true body. At the very least, we do not doubt that he regarded as faithful—and by no means excluded from the assembly of the Church—those who defended this truth.

This is plainly and clearly understood from the explicit words of the second article of Ratramnus’s book:

> “For while some of the faithful say that the body and blood of Christ, which are celebrated daily in the Church, are made not under a figure or under a veil, but through the bare manifestation of the truth itself, others testify that these things are contained under the figure of a mystery, and so forth.”

These words should immediately and decisively establish in our faith and understanding what will be abundantly clear from our notes: the controversy that gave rise to Ratramnus’s little work existed in the ninth-century Church among men who defended the Catholic faith, and it could not have concerned the reality and truth of Christ’s body in the Eucharist. For the faithful could not have defended or attacked this system equally on both sides; nor could they have done so without distinguishing and discriminating between the positions, unless they stood in the middle as uncertain persons [Col. 0124D].

Furthermore, it would be useless and superfluous to say that Ratramnus regarded the division or rupture that might arise in the Church from a diversity of opinions as a highly complicated schism. For it is exceedingly clear that, in that passage, Ratramnus was merely heightening his language in accordance with his customary and ordinary manner of expression.

Thus, in the book he wrote *On the Nativity of Christ*, chapter 10, he treats as a kind of sudden new heresy the opinion, previously unimagined in earlier centuries, of those who had persuaded themselves that the sacred body of Our Lord Jesus Christ had burst forth from the most holy womb of the blessed Virgin by a new kind of miracle, different from that by which other women conceive and give birth to their human beings and children [Col. 0125A]. This opinion is plainly that of Pope Gregory the Great, the first of that name, and of several Fathers and theologians of the Catholic Church. It is utterly incredible and improbable that Ratramnus considered it heretical, since he says that he introduced it as a playful exercise to refresh and cheer the mind:

> “We played with these matters in the customary manner of students. If anyone should despise them, our exercises nevertheless pleased us.”

Our second reflection or consideration concerning Ratramnus consists in this: if he wrote against what they call “reality,” or against the presence of Christ’s true body, or against Paschasius, the book about which we have explained and recounted so much in this historical preface, it seems most incredible and inconceivable that he would deliberately have omitted to respond—or at least to say something—about the celebrated miracle reported by Paschasius in chapter 14 of his treatise *On the Body of Christ*, concerning the appearance of Christ’s sacred body in the Eucharist.

Since everyone believed this miracle at that time and it was reported by trustworthy authorities, to omit it in a case so directly relevant would have been the strongest possible argument for firmly confirming reality [Col. 0125B]. Let the defenders of Calvinist doctrine therefore see and examine how they can extricate themselves from these miracles when they are brought against them, and how they can deny and disparage them. In this way they will understand for themselves how convenient and necessary it would have been for Ratramnus to employ such devices if he had adopted the position that they themselves defend.

Meanwhile, I immediately know that David Blondel, the celebrated minister of Calvinist superstition, attempted to vindicate this chapter 14 of Paschasius by claiming that it did not belong to Paschasius [Col. 0125C] and had been rashly attributed to him [Note: [Col. 0125C] Blondel, *Éclaircissement sur l’Eucharistie*, p. 434]. But since he produced no ancient manuscript in which this chapter was absent, nor any printed edition lacking it, writers of every opposing party have vehemently rejected his opinion. Moreover, nothing prevents anyone from examining a manuscript of this treatise by Paschasius in the Royal Library at Paris, of approximately the same period, under the name of Saint Paschasius, abbot of Corbie, in which this wondrous work, complete in every respect, is reported. This manuscript belonged to the illustrious Putean brothers, prefects of the Royal Library, where it remains under the numerical designation 4356. I saw with my own eyes another, somewhat less ancient manuscript [Col. 0126A] that relates not merely one miracle, but many. All these materials, however, are found in the edition which the Reverend Father Jacques Sirmond published at Paris in 1618 with care and fidelity, under the numerical designation 4357.

Our third reflection, moreover, arises from the fact that, if Ratramnus had regarded the persuasion concerning the real presence as something new and recent, it is incredible that he would not have reproached the Greeks with it, against whom this burden had been laid upon him by the Gallican bishops, who at that time were lavishly adoring the Eucharist, as we understand from their Liturgies, with the agreement of the most illustrious Hugo Grotius, p. 88 of his *Votum for Peace*, cited by me in chapter 14 of book I, *On the Adoration of the Eucharist*. At the very least, he would not have defended against them what are merely consequences and necessary implications of the real presence. Yet this is what he does [Col. 0126B] in book IV, chapter 3, of the aforementioned work, p. 120, where, on the authority of Pope Sylvester and from the account of Eusebius of Caesarea, he proves that in the Catholic regions you ought to institute a solemn feast of the Nativity of the Chalice, just as the Lord’s observance is kept on the fifth weekday of every week. For on that day Christ began to institute the celebration of the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood:

> “We ought likewise to keep the Nativity of the Chalice as a solemn day like Sunday, on which the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood received from the Lord himself the beginning of its celebration.”

Who could persuade himself that the sacrifice of the Eucharist was ever called such while faith in, or belief in, the true body of Christ—truly present and existing in it—was set aside or omitted? Paschasius also used the expression “Nativity of the Chalice” [Col. 0126C] at the beginning of chapter 11 of his work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. From this we understand and clearly perceive the veneration and worship with which the faithful honored the sacrament of the Eucharist; and these are plainly and unmistakably shown to follow from the institution of a solemn feast commemorating its origin and institution. Since it was believed that the sacred reality consisted in, and that the true body of Christ—united to the person of the eternal Word—remained present in it, no other worship could be rendered to it than the adoration of *latria*.

To recount any more of the interpreter’s reflections and meditations on Ratramnus’s book, from the standpoint of the opposing party, would now seem superfluous and useless.

[Col. 0125]

# BOOK ON THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD
