Printed from a copy carefully and faithfully transcribed from an eight-hundred-year-old manuscript of the Abbey of Lobbes.

[Col. 0125D]

## I

You have commanded me, glorious prince [Note: [Col. 0125D] “Glorious prince.” Ratramnus used these words in the dedication of the books that he wrote at the command of that same Charles the Bald, *On Predestination*: “To the glorious and most excellent prince, Charles.” Nor did I hesitate to change the word “magnificence” into “majesty,” since, according to the usage of that period, the word “majesty” was commonly used for “magnificence.” This is clear from the preface to those same books of Ratramnus *On Predestination*.], to explain to your magnificence what I think concerning the mystery of the blood and body of Christ. The task is as worthy of your magnificent rule as it is evidently difficult for the powers of our littleness. For what is more worthy of royal care than to think in a Catholic manner about the sacred mysteries of him who deigned to grant you the royal throne, and not to tolerate that your subjects should hold differing opinions concerning the body of Christ, in which the whole substance of Christian redemption is established?

[Col. 0128A]

## II

For while some of the faithful say that the body and blood of Christ, which is daily celebrated in the Church, takes place [Note: [Col. 0127A] “With no figure beneath it,” etc. The question debated in that period was very different from the question disputed today with the Calvinists. At that time the question was not whether the Eucharistic mystery contained the body merely figuratively, but whether there was any figure, or any degree of figure, in this sacrament, or absolutely none. The Catholic Church has always believed and taught that some figure is present, and that together with this figure the true body and true blood of Christ are received. This is clearly understood from the book of Saint Paschasius Ratbertus, abbot of Corbie, written for this very reason at the same time as Ratramnus wrote his own. In the first chapter of Paschasius, p. 1555 [See *Patrologia*, vol. CXX, ed.], in the edition of Father Jacques Sirmond, Jesuit, an outstanding critic whom scholars have never suspected of falsification, letter E:

> “Whatever the Lord wished, he did in heaven and on earth, and because he wished it. Although in the figure of bread and wine, this must be believed to be nothing other than the flesh and blood after consecration.”

These observations will make it perfectly clear, in continuous discourse, that Ratramnus did not adopt an opinion different from Paschasius on this matter; consequently, it is not probable that he wrote against him, as the heretical Protestants persuade themselves and imagine they have proved. On the contrary, it is evident that Paschasius opposed those who thought that everything in the Eucharist was figurative and nothing real, although he by no means denied that some figure was present, as is clear from book XII of his *Exposition on Saint Matthew*.

The other part of the question—whether the bare manifestation of the truth itself takes place—leaves no room for dispute or controversy between Catholic men and Protestants. We do not defend the proposition that the bodily eyes, in this mystery, gaze upon and perceive without veil or covering what the eyes of the soul see within, as Ratramnus explains in section 5, where he clearly sets out the question on which he was being asked, by imperial command, to pronounce:

> “Whether it contains some secret that is revealed only to the eyes of faith, or whether, without any veiling of the mystery, the bodily sight sees externally what the mind’s vision beholds internally.”

In reality, externally we see or perceive with bodily eyes the appearances of bread and wine; but internally, and beneath these appearances, we believe that the body and blood of Christ lie concealed. Nothing is further removed from the mind of the Catholic Church than the false opinion that Christ’s body in the Eucharist is visible and subject to the senses, and that it is broken and crushed by the teeth of the recipient. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that formerly certain Catholic men did not reject this opinion, but defended it. This is made perfectly clear by two especially notable monuments of antiquity.

The first emerges from a treatise by the abbot Abbaud, whose period of life is uncertain—unless, as is sufficiently probable, he lived in the eleventh century. The learned and reverend Father Dom Mabillon, of the Order of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint-Maur, made it publicly available in volume III of his *Old Analecta*, p. 442, under the title *On the Breaking of Christ’s Body*. In it Abbaud accepts this opinion for defense without deceit or trickery:

> “I believe,” he says, “that he made the bread which he received his body by blessing it. Therefore he broke his own body, and from that same body of his, already blessed and broken, he said to the disciples: ‘This is my body.’”

In continuous argument he vigorously extricates himself from the twisted knots and labyrinths of contradictions into which all the defenders of that opinion were striving to hurl themselves headlong. But after defending and vindicating transubstantiation in explicit terms, he draws a corollary from it. From this it is plainly and clearly evident that several theologians of that period persuaded themselves that the accidents remaining after consecration adhered to Christ’s body. Consequently, since whiteness and roundness could not be understood without the breaking of Christ’s body, Christ’s body itself had to be broken and divided; and since this was placed before the eyes and subjected to the other senses, no human being could deny it.

Here are the author’s exact words:

> “Therefore the person who denies that the Lord’s body is broken must be pressed on whether he believes that what we consecrate and break on the altar is Christ’s body. If he grants this, he does not contradict the breaking of the body; if he denies it, let every faithful person judge whether he ought to be judged faithful. Let him see for himself whom he wishes to believe, since he believes neither evangelical authority nor his own eyes.
>
> “But let us, with the disciples, recognize the Lord in the breaking of bread. I had considered answering those who say that the body itself is not broken, but that something is done to its whiteness and roundness. But, reflecting that it is foolish to dispute in Christ’s Gospel about whiteness and roundness, I dismissed such things from ears that should love better subjects and left them to dialecticians—or at least to children. Especially since anyone can easily see that whiteness, or roundness, cannot be separated from the body itself that is white or round, so that these qualities cannot independently be broken apart from the unbroken body.”

The second monument of antiquity is the manuscript of Walter, the great prior of Saint-Victor of Paris, extracted from the library of that abbey. It contains four books against the four Labyrinths of France—a name by which he specifically designates Peter Abelard, Peter Lombard, Peter of Poitiers, and Gilbert Porretanus. The learned Mabillon published a fragment of this manuscript from chapter II of the third book in his notes to Abbaud’s treatise, volume III of his *Old Analecta*, p. 450.

At last he comes to Berengar. For this heretic asserted that everything took place in figure and sacrament, and nothing in reality. But afterward, having been convicted before Pope Nicholas and several bishops, he confessed—and also swore—that after consecration bread and wine were not merely the sacrament, but truly the body and blood of Christ, and that they were handled sensibly by the priests’ hands, not only sacramentally but also in reality, and were broken and worn down by the teeth of the faithful. Behold the Catholic faith.

But this scholastic [Col. 0128D] (Abelard) explains it as follows:

> “It is truly so,” he says, “but only in the sacrament.”
>
> He also says: “It can properly be said that that breaking occurs in a portion, not in the substance of the body, but in the sacramental form of bread, so that there is a true breaking and division there—not in the substance, but in the sacrament, that is, in the species.”
>
> Again: “There is a true breaking and division, which takes place in the bread, that is, in the form of bread.”
>
> Again: “The breaking and those portions which appear to be made are made in the sacrament, that is, in the visible species.”
>
> Therefore Berengar’s words must be distinguished in such a way that “sensibly,” not only sacramentally but also in reality, is said of Christ’s body being handled by the priests’ hands, broken, and worn down by the teeth of the faithful.
>
> “Truly so, but only in the sacrament.” Therefore there is a true wearing-down and division there.

Thus, while by his customary arguments he distinguishes the Catholic faith, which needs no distinction at all, he proves himself another Berengar.

This opinion concerning the breaking of Christ’s body appears to have been very common at the time when Berengar was compelled to sing his first recantation, or *palinode*, [Col. 0129C] at the Roman council in the year of Christ 1059, under Pope Nicholas II. This is clear from the precise words by which he was made to acknowledge that the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ were handled by the hands of the priests, both sensibly and not merely sacramentally but also in reality, and were broken and worn down by the teeth of the faithful.

But if this opinion was common and more widely disseminated in Berengar’s time, it did not first burst forth from the human mind at that moment, since common opinions do not arise instantaneously. Moreover, he [Paschasius] displayed no disagreement with this opinion, but rather great agreement with it, when he stated that in the Eucharist not only the flesh or blood of Christ is converted into our flesh or blood, in book *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, chapter 20. In that same chapter he observes that in his own age there existed monuments and books or manuscripts from which it could be understood that there had been several theologians who had remained in this belief—namely, that the body of Christ received in the Eucharist was subject to digestion and to the processes of excretion.

If these things are so, the beginning of this opinion may be placed in the time of Charles the Bald, when Paschasius composed his treatise and Ratramnus wrote his. From this it is perfectly clear that he wished to break down and refute two opinions, equally and alike opposed to the doctrine of the Catholic Church and to the fantasies of the Calvinist sect. For he strives to prove that there is some figure in the sacrament of Christ’s body, and that Christ’s body, insofar as it is made present in it, is not subject to the senses—against those who maintained that there was no figure at all in it, since Christ’s body was subject to the senses and visible in the Eucharist.]

without any figure or covering, but is carried out by the bare manifestation of the truth itself, while others testify that these things are contained under the figure of a mystery, and that one thing appears to bodily [Col. 0129A] senses while another is seen by faith, a considerable difference between them is evident. And since the Apostle writes to the faithful (1 Corinthians 1:10) that they should all think the same thing and say the same thing, and that there should be no schism among them, those who speak differently about the mystery of Christ’s body and blood are divided by no small schism.

## III

Therefore your royal sublimity, stirred by zeal for the faith, not weighing these matters with indifference, and desiring, according to the Apostle’s command, that all should think and say the same thing, diligently seeks the secret of the truth, so that you may recall to it those who have strayed. Hence you do not disdain to inquire into the truth of this matter even from the lowliest, knowing that the mystery of so great a secret cannot be recognized unless the Divinity reveals it; and that, without respect of persons, it displays the light of its truth through whomever it chooses.

## IV

For our littleness, obedience to your command is as pleasing as it is difficult to dispute about a matter so far removed from human senses and penetrable only through the instruction of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, subject to the command of your greatness, but trusting in the aid of him about whom we are going to speak, I shall attempt, in whatever words I can, to disclose what I think about this matter—not relying on my own ingenuity, but following in the footsteps of the holy Fathers.

## V

Your Excellency asks whether what is received in the Church from the mouths of the faithful—the body and blood of Christ—takes place [Note: [Col. 0129D] “Whether it takes place in mystery or in reality.” Here “reality” signifies something subject to the senses, as Ratramnus explains in the following words:

> “Whether, without any veiling of the mystery, the bodily sight sees externally what the mind’s vision beholds internally.”

We understand the same from the abbot Abbaud, in whom this word has the same meaning and use:

> “But it is one thing when the truth of any matter is sought according to the proper character of the fact; another when the mystical meaning of that same fact is examined allegorically.”

And he continues:

> “Because Christ’s body is truly broken by the priest’s hands.”

This is likewise the meaning of Walter, prior of Saint-Victor, when he observes that Berengar was compelled to confess that the true body and blood of Christ were handled by the priests’ hands both sensibly and not only sacramentally but also in reality, and were broken and worn down by the teeth of the faithful.

The same meaning is found in Paschasius, book XII of his *Exposition on Matthew*:

> “When these mystical sacraments will no longer exist, the truth which is now rightly enacted in mystery will be set forth in reality, clearer than light, and what we now receive in mystery will be manifest to all in fruition.”

It was a sufficiently widespread usage in the Middle Ages to use the word “reality” to signify the proof or demonstration of a matter. The word was regularly used for the testimonies that witnesses summoned into court customarily offered—testimonies by which crimes do not actually consist in themselves, but by which their proofs and firm, invincible arguments are established. This is abundantly clear in the *Customs of the Islands*, title I, articles 19 and 20; and in the liberties of the town of Saint-Desiderius in Campania, in the year 1228; in the council held at Coyaca in Spain in the year 1050, canon 9, as reported by Ducange, *Glossary*, volume III, p. 1283.]

in mystery or in reality. That is, whether it contains some secret revealed only to the eyes of faith, or whether, without any veiling of the mystery, the bodily sight sees externally what the mind’s vision beholds internally, so that everything done may shine clearly in the light of manifestation; and whether it is the very body that was born from Mary, suffered, died, and was buried, and that, rising again and ascending into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father.

## VI

Let us examine the first of these two questions. And, so that we are not held back by the maze of uncertainty, let us define what figure is and what reality is, so that, looking upon something certain, we may know along what path of reasoning we ought to proceed.

## VII

A figure is a certain shadowing under particular veils, displaying what it intends to show. For example, when we wish to speak of the Word, we call him “bread,” as when in the Lord’s Prayer we ask that daily bread be given to us (Luke 11:3); or when Christ speaks in the Gospel, saying, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41); or when he calls himself the vine and his disciples the branches: “I am the true vine, and you are the branches” (John 15:5). All these expressions say one thing and imply another.

## VIII

Reality, however, is the manifest demonstration of a thing, not veiled by shadowy images, but conveyed through pure and open—and, to speak more plainly, natural—significations. Thus it is when Christ is said to have been born of a Virgin, suffered, crucified, died, and was buried. Nothing here is shadowed under covering figures; rather, the truth of the matter is shown by the natural meanings of the words, and here nothing other than what is said may be understood.

But it is not so in the preceding examples. Substantially, Christ is neither bread nor vine, nor are the apostles branches. Therefore, in the latter examples a figure is shown, whereas in the former reality is shown in the narrative—that is, a bare and open signification.

## IX

Now let us return to the matters for whose sake these things have been said—namely, the body and blood of Christ. [Col. 0131C]

[Note: [Col. 0131C] “For if that mystery is carried out with no figure beneath it.” He repeats this so that everyone may recognize clearly that he is acting only against those who persuaded themselves that everything done in the Eucharist was subject to the senses. He presents an axiom highly favorable to his position and especially appropriate to the affairs of the Church: no mystery can exist in which nothing is hidden and concealed. In reality, he does not say that everything must be hidden and secret, as Calvinist Protestants imagine, persuading themselves that nothing exists in the Eucharist except figure and trope. Ratramnus’s meaning therefore does not differ from that of the Church, which acknowledges some figure, as Paschasius himself says in the cited passage and in his Letter to Frudgard. It follows that Paschasius and Ratramnus were not fighting against one another, but rather wrote against entirely different opponents. Ratramnus attacks those who admitted no figure in the Eucharist, while Paschasius attacks those who maintained that everything was figurative. This is clear from his exposition on Matthew, book XII:

> “Hence I am astonished at what certain people now wish to say: that the reality of Christ’s flesh or blood is not present in the thing itself, but that the power of the flesh, and not the flesh, is present in the sacrament; the power of the blood, and not the blood; figure, and not reality.”]

For if that mystery is carried out with no figure beneath it, it is no longer rightly called a mystery. For that cannot be called a mystery in which nothing is hidden, nothing is removed from bodily senses, and nothing is covered by some veil.

But that bread which, through the ministry of the priest, is made Christ’s body displays one thing externally to human senses and proclaims another thing internally to the minds of the faithful. Externally, [Note: [Col. 0131D] “The form of the bread that had existed before is presented.” This proves that after consecration it is no longer bread, but only the form, color, and taste of the bread that had existed; consequently, the bread itself no longer remains, but Christ’s body exists in its place. The author says in the same section:

> “But that bread which through the ministry of the priest is made Christ’s body,”

and below, in section 28:

> “Thus, shortly before he suffered, he was able to convert the substance of bread and the creature of wine into his own body,” etc.;

and in section 30:

> “But truly, through the mystery, bread and wine have been converted into the substance of my body and blood.”

In the sense of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* IV:

> Ταῦτα μαθὼν καὶ πληροφορηθεὶς ὡς ὁ φαινόμενος ἄρτος οὐκ ἄρτος ἐστὶν, εἰ καὶ γεύσει τοῦτο βούλεται, ἀλλὰ τὸ σῶμα Χριστοῦ· καὶ ὁ φαινόμενος οἶνος, οὐκ οἶνος, εἰ καὶ ἡ γεῦσις τοῦτο βούλεται, ἀλλὰ αἵμα Χριστοῦ.

> “Knowing and being fully convinced that the bread which appears is not bread, even though taste would indicate this, but the body of Jesus Christ; and that the wine which appears is not wine, even though taste would indicate this, but the blood of Jesus Christ.”]

externally the form of the bread that had existed before is presented, its color is shown, and its taste is received. But internally something altogether different, much more precious and excellent, is intimated, because what is shown is heavenly and divine—namely, Christ’s body—which is not seen, received, or eaten by the senses of the flesh, but by the contemplation of the faithful soul.

[Col. 0131B]

## X

The wine also, which through priestly consecration is made the sacrament of Christ’s blood, displays one thing on the surface and contains another internally. For what other than the substance of wine is visible on the surface? Taste it: it tastes of wine. Smell it: it smells of wine. Look at it: the color of wine is perceived. But if you consider what is within, it is no longer the liquid of wine; rather, in the minds of believers, it both tastes as the liquid of Christ’s blood when it is tasted, is recognized as such when it is seen, and is proved to be such when it is smelled.

Since no one can deny that these things are so, it is clear that [Note: [Col. 0132C] “That bread and wine exist figuratively as Christ’s body and blood,” etc. He does not say merely that they are the body and blood in a figure, but “figuratively”; and this means nothing other than that they are the veils of Christ’s body. For according to Ratramnus, figure and veil have exactly the same force, as is clear in section II: “with no figure, with no covering.” And in section 5: “without any veiling of the mystery.” In section 8: “Nothing here is shadowed under covering figures.” In section 9: “For if that mystery is carried out with no figure beneath it, it is no longer rightly called a mystery. For a mystery cannot be said to exist in which nothing is hidden, nothing is removed from bodily senses, and nothing is covered by a veil.”]

that bread and wine exist figuratively as Christ’s body and blood. For, according to what appears, neither the appearance of flesh is recognized in that bread nor a stream of blood is displayed in that wine; nevertheless, after the mystical consecration, it is no longer called bread or [Col. 0131C] wine, but the body and blood of Christ.

## XI

For if, according to certain people, nothing here is received figuratively, [Note: [Col. 0132D] “But everything is seen in reality.” That is, everything that is seen and subjected to the eyes is itself reality—meaning that everything present there is truly everything that is there. Such was the opinion of those whom Ratramnus refutes, who persuaded themselves that there was no figure or veil whatsoever in this mystery.]

but everything is seen in reality, faith accomplishes nothing here, since nothing spiritual is taking place; rather, whatever it is, it is received entirely according to the body. And since faith, according to the Apostle, is “the evidence of things not apparent” (Hebrews 11:1)—that is, not of things that are seen, but of substances that are not seen—we shall receive nothing here according to faith, since we judge everything that exists according to the bodily senses. Nothing is more absurd than to receive bread as flesh and call wine blood. Nor will it then be a mystery, since it will contain nothing secret and nothing hidden.

## XII

And how can it now be called Christ’s body [al. “will it be called”], when it is recognized that no change has taken place? For every change is effected either from what is into what is, or from what is not into what is, or from what is into what is not.

But in this sacrament, if it is considered only in the simplicity of reality, and nothing other than what is seen is believed, no change is recognized as having taken place. For it did not pass from what was not into something that is, as happens in things that come into being: since they did not previously exist, they passed from nonbeing into being in order to exist. But here bread and wine existed before they passed into the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood.

Nor did that transition occur which is from being into nonbeing, a transition that exists in things undergoing destruction and decline. For whatever perishes first existed in subsistence; and what did not exist cannot suffer destruction. Here too, therefore, this transition is not recognized as having taken place, [Note: [Col. 0132D] “Because, according to reality, the species of the creature that had existed before is recognized to have remained.” According to Festus and Tully Cicero, the word *species* indicates the nature or idea of a thing; in the Platonic sense, it signifies the appearance or outward form of a thing subjected to and perceived by the senses, according to this author’s style. This is clear in section 10, where he says that no form or appearance of Christ’s flesh and blood is perceived in this mystery:

> “For, according to what appears, neither the appearance of flesh is recognized in that bread, nor a stream of blood is displayed in that wine.”

This manner of speaking is also found in the author of the books *On the Sacraments*, commonly and not undeservedly attributed to Saint Ambrose. Book II, chapter 5:

> “The Holy Spirit descended from heaven in the appearance of a dove, not in the reality of a dove, but in the appearance of a dove.”]

because, according to [Col. 0133A] reality, the species of the creature that had existed before is recognized to have remained.

## XIII

Likewise, the change which occurs from what is into what is, and which is seen in things undergoing a variation of quality—for example, when what was previously black is changed into white—is not recognized as having taken place here either. For nothing here is detected to have been changed by touch, color, or taste. If therefore nothing here has been changed, it is no different from what it was before.

Yet it is different, since bread has become Christ’s body and wine has become his blood. For he himself says:

> “Take and eat: this is my body” (Matthew 26:26).

Likewise, speaking of the cup, he says:

> “Take and drink: this is the blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for you” (Mark 14:24).

[Col. 0133B]

## XIV

Therefore those who wish to accept nothing here figuratively, but maintain that everything consists in the simplicity of reality, must be asked according to what kind of change it took place, so that they are no longer what they were before—namely, bread and wine—but are the body and blood of Christ.

For according to the appearance of the creature and the form of visible things, neither of these two things—that is, bread and wine—has undergone any change. And if [Col. 0134A] they have undergone no change, they are nothing other than what they were before.

## XV

Your sublimity sees, glorious Prince, what the understanding of those who think in this way comes to: they deny what they are believed to affirm, and they are shown to destroy what they believe. For they faithfully confess Christ’s body and blood; and when they do this, they undoubtedly declare that these are no longer what they were before. If they are different from what they were, they have undergone a change.

Since this cannot be denied, let them say according to what they have been changed: for bodily nothing is perceived to have been changed in them. [Note: [Col. 0133C] “Therefore they must necessarily admit,” etc. These words openly demonstrate that this author did not hesitate to affirm that a real change of one thing into another takes place in the Eucharist. Since what is perceived by the senses appears to be bread and wine, while it must be something else, Ratramnus necessarily believed that a real change of bread into Christ’s body and of wine into his blood takes place. Consequently, the Magdeburg Centuriators openly admit that certain seeds of transubstantiation are found in Ratramnus’s book:

> “Ratramnus possesses the seeds of transubstantiation, for he uses the terms ‘change’ and ‘conversion.’”

—Censure IX, *On Doctrine.*]

Therefore they must necessarily admit either that they have been changed in some respect other than bodily, and consequently that they are not what they truly appear to be, but something else which they are perceived not to be according to their proper essence. [Note: [Col. 0133D] “Or, if they refuse to confess this,” etc. These words indicate the close connection our author recognized between transubstantiation and the true presence, or reality, of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, and that neither can actually exist without the other. For one must deny that Christ’s body is in the Eucharist unless one acknowledges that a certain change of one thing into another has occurred—namely, of bread into Christ’s body.

From this it is also easy to understand how necessary it is for the attainment of eternal salvation to believe, or to possess divine faith in, transubstantiation and the real presence. For if they refuse to confess this, they are compelled to deny that it is Christ’s body and blood—something which is impious not only to say, but even to think.]

Or, if they refuse to confess this, they are compelled to deny that it is Christ’s body and blood—which it is impious not only to say, but even to think.

## XVI

But since they confess that it is both the body and the blood of God, and that this could not have occurred except through a change into something better, [Note: [Col. 0133D] This change, then, must have taken place not corporeally but spiritually—that is, the change did not occur in what is perceived by the senses. For this is the genuine meaning of this compiler of the work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. He truly does not think that no change occurred in the actually corporeal substance of bread and wine, or that a change occurred only in what strikes and affects our sight, namely, the appearances, as he observes in these carefully formulated words, in the number immediately preceding the passage which, as Gellius says, follows directly: “For corporeally nothing in them is seen to have been changed,” that is, nothing perceived by the bodily senses is seen to have been changed.] this change, then, must have taken place not corporeally but spiritually, [Note: [Col. 0134C] It is now necessary to say that it took place figuratively. According to Ratramnus’s style, or his manner and method of writing and speaking, the word “figuratively” does not mean that the change into Christ’s body occurred merely in figure; rather, it means that beneath the veils and covering of the bread and wine, beneath which Christ’s body lies concealed, the spiritual body and spiritual blood of Christ exist, as he says in continuous prose: “For beneath the veil of corporeal bread and corporeal wine there exists the spiritual body and spiritual blood of Christ.”

Paschasius used this same manner of speaking in his letter to Frudgardus, in order clearly to signify the true body of Christ: “His body is not corrupted, because it is spiritual, and everything celebrated in this sacrament is wholly spiritual.” This is not at all alien to the statement of Gregory of Nyssa concerning Christ’s baptism, vol. II, p. 802, letter A: “Ὁ ἄρτος παλὶν ἄρτος ἐστὶ τέως κοινὸς· ἀλλ᾽ ὅταν αὐτὸν τὸ μυστήριον ἱερουργήση, σῶμα Χριστοῦ λέγεταί τε καὶ γίνεται.” “Up to this point the bread is ordinary and common bread; but when the mystery consecrates it, it is called the body of Christ and truly becomes so.”

These things also agree very closely with what had been stated a few years before Paschasius at the Second Council of Nicaea, held in the year 787, vol. IV of Binius’s edition of the Councils, 1618, p. 643: “Ὠς πρὸ τοῦ ἀγιασθῆν, ἐκκλήθη ἀντίτυπα· μετὰ δὲ τὸν ἀγιασμὸν σῶμα Κυριοῦ καὶ αἶμα Χριστοῦ λέγονται καί εἰσι, καὶ πιστέυονται.” “Before consecration they are called figures; after consecration they are properly called the body of the Lord and the blood of Christ, and they are such and are believed to be such.”

Ratramnus repeats this form or manner of speaking and writing concerning Christ’s body actually existing in the Eucharist. At no. 99: “Let us add that this bread and cup, which is named and exists as the body and blood of Christ, represents the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion,” and so forth. Since this is so, no room for doubt can remain concerning the concordant and unanimous judgment of Ratramnus and Paschasius regarding the presence of Christ’s body and blood in the mystery of the Eucharist.] for beneath the veil of corporeal bread and corporeal wine there exists the spiritual body and spiritual blood; [Note: [Col. 0135C] Not that there are two existences of things different from one another. If anyone imagines two existences of different things—namely, the appearances of bread and wine and the body of Christ in the Eucharist—he is dreaming. For these appearances and Christ’s spiritual body have one and the same existence, and they are one and the same thing under different aspects: namely, the same thing can be considered and conceived insofar as it is subjected to the senses and insofar as it conceals or veils beneath itself something spiritual that does not come under the eyes. From this it follows clearly that Christ’s body and blood do not exist with the same existence as the bread and wine; consequently, after consecration no bread and wine, or their substance, can remain and continue to exist alongside the present body and blood of Christ.] not that there are two existences of things different from one another—namely, of body and spirit—but one and the same thing: under one aspect it consists as the appearances of bread and wine, while under another it is the body and blood of Christ. For insofar as both are touched corporeally, they are appearances of corporeal creatures; but insofar as they have been made spiritual through power, they are mysteries of the body and blood of Christ.

## XVII

Let us consider the sacred font of baptism, which is rightly called the fountain of life, because it reforms those who descend into it through the renewal of a better life and grants life in righteousness to those who are dead through sin. Does it possess this power merely insofar as it is seen to be the element of water? Yet unless it possessed the power of sanctification, it could in no way wash away the stain of vices; and unless it contained the vigor of life, it could in no way bestow life upon the dead—dead, that is, not in the flesh but in the soul.

If, however, in that font one considers only what bodily perception sees, an unstable element subject to corruption is observed, possessing no power except to wash bodies. But the power of the Holy Spirit came through the priest’s consecration, and it became effective not only for cleansing bodies but also for cleansing souls and removing spiritual filth through spiritual power.

## XVIII

Behold: in one and the same element we see two things that are mutually opposed—that is, something subject to corruption providing incorruption, and something without life contributing life. It is therefore recognized that in this font there exists what bodily sense can touch and which is therefore changeable and corruptible; and again there exists what faith alone perceives and which therefore can neither be corrupted nor suffer the loss of life.

If you ask what washes outwardly, it is an element; but if you consider what cleanses inwardly, it is a life-giving power, a power of sanctification, a power of immortality. Thus, in its proper nature it is corruptible moisture, but in its mystery it is a healing power.

## XIX

Thus, when considered outwardly, Christ’s body and blood are a creature subject to change and corruption. But if you consider the power of the mystery, it is life, granting immortality to those who partake of it. [Note: [Col. 0135D] Therefore what is seen and what is believed are not the same. From this it is evident that the complete distinction between what is seen and what is believed in the mystery does not arise from a different existence, as he said shortly before, but from the different aspect under which the same thing can be conceived and considered.

Hence Ratramnus says: “Thus, when considered outwardly, Christ’s body and blood are a creature subject to change and corruption. But if you consider the power of the mystery, it is life, granting immortality to those who partake of it.”

Yet from these words it is easy to understand that Ratramnus does not properly and in every respect compare the whole Eucharist with baptism at this point, but rather the body and blood of Jesus Christ that are in the Eucharist. As he says shortly afterward, considered with regard to the condition in which they are subjected to the senses, they are vulnerable to corruption; but considered with regard to the power of the Holy Spirit, they are subject to no corruption and bestow life and immortality.

Once these points have been set forth and established, Ratramnus’s meaning is not that, just as the power of sanctification is added to the substance in baptism, so in the Eucharist merely the power of life and sanctification is added to the substance of the bread. For if this were Ratramnus’s meaning, he would not say that Christ’s body and blood exist there, nor that the appearances subjected to the senses, or the corporeal appearances, have no dual existence with the body—as though they were actually different things; nor would he speak, in a single word, of the change of one thing into another; nor would he say that Christ’s body could not be said or thought not to remain there without crime, fault, or sin.

Our Ratramnus’s meaning must therefore be this—and it is expressed in explicit words: “They are compelled to deny the body and blood of Jesus Christ, which it is impious not only to say but even to think.” In relation to these veils and coverings, there is something subject to corruption; but in relation, or with respect, to the power of the Holy Spirit, through whose force they actually exist and subsist in this mystery, they are not subject or exposed to corruption, but communicate life and immortality to our souls.

The same applies to baptism: considered in relation to the water and to what is subject to the senses, it can be corrupted; but considered likewise in relation to the power and holiness conferred upon it by Christ, it becomes a fountain and source of life and immortality.

From all these things nothing can be understood that is not in agreement or harmony with the doctrine of the Catholic Church, or that could in any respect appear favorable to the dreams of the Protestants. It is especially useful to apply these points and transfer them mentally to the comparison which he makes between this body of Christ and the cloud, the Red Sea, the water brought forth from the rock, and the manna falling upon the sands of the desert—nos. 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, and 25.] Therefore what is seen and what is believed are not the same. For insofar as they are seen, they nourish corruptible bodies—the things themselves are corruptible; but insofar as they are believed, they nourish souls destined to live forever—the things themselves are immortal.

## XX

The Apostle also, writing to the Corinthians, says: “Do you not know that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink? For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them. And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:1–4).

We observe that the sea and the cloud prefigured baptism, and that the fathers of the earlier Testament were baptized in them—that is, in the cloud or in the sea. Could the sea, insofar as it appeared to be an element, possess the power of baptism? Or could the cloud, insofar as it displayed the density of thickened air, [add. “the people”] [Col. 0137A] sanctify them? Yet we do not dare to say that the Apostle, speaking in Christ, did not truly say that our fathers were baptized in the cloud and in the sea.

## XXI

And although that baptism did not prefigure the form of Christ’s baptism, which is administered in the Church today, no sane person will dare deny that it was baptism and that our fathers were baptized in it—unless, in madness, he presumes to contradict the Apostle’s words.

Therefore neither the sea nor the clouds provided the cleansing of sanctification according to the fact that they were corporeal; rather, they did so according to the fact that they invisibly contained the sanctification of the Holy Spirit. For in them there was a visible form that appeared to bodily senses—not in an image but in reality—and inwardly a spiritual power shone forth, appearing not to the eyes of the flesh but to the lights of the mind.

## XXII

Similarly, the manna given from heaven to the people and the water flowing from the rock were corporeal, and corporeally they either fed or gave drink to the people. Yet the Apostle calls both that manna and that water spiritual food and spiritual drink. Why is this? Because within those corporeal substances there was the power of the spiritual Word, which fed and gave drink to the minds rather than the bodies of believers (see no. 15).

And although that food or drink foreshadowed the mystery of the future body and blood of Christ, which the Church celebrates, Saint Paul nevertheless affirms that our fathers ate the same spiritual food and drank the same wholly spiritual drink.

## XXIII

Perhaps you ask: “Which same food?” Certainly, the very food that the congregation of believers now eats and drinks in the Church (see no. 25). For it is not permissible to understand it as different, since it is one and the same Christ who fed the people baptized in the desert, in the cloud, and in the sea with his flesh and then gave them drink from his blood, and who now feeds and gives drink to the people of believers in the Church with the bread of his body and the stream of his blood.

## XXIV

Wishing to make this understood, after saying that our fathers ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink, the Apostle added: “For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them. And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4).

He said this so that we might understand that in the desert Christ stood in the spiritual rock and offered the people the stream of his blood—he who later, in our age, displayed the body taken from the Virgin and hung upon the cross for the salvation of believers, and poured forth from it a stream of blood [Note: [Col. 0137C] “By which we might not only be redeemed but also given drink.” Since the blood of Christ by which we are given drink and redeemed is the same, with every distinction removed, it is necessary to accept these points in order to conclude that, since Ratramnus taught and believed that the blood poured out for human beings was not merely figurative but was the true and properly so-called blood of Christ, drawn from the womb of the blessed Virgin and flowing from the veins of the body affixed to the cross, the Eucharistic blood by which we are given drink must have been drawn from the womb of the blessed Virgin and poured forth from the crucified body. With its fullness he ascended into heaven after he had risen again and sat at the right hand of the Father, as Ratramnus himself says at no. 30.] by which we might not only be redeemed but also given drink.

## XXV

It is certainly astonishing, because it is incomprehensible and beyond estimation! He had not yet assumed humanity, had not yet tasted death for the world’s salvation, and had not yet redeemed us with his blood; yet already our fathers in the desert were eating his body and drinking his blood through spiritual food and invisible drink. The Apostle stands as a witness, crying out that our fathers ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink.

We should not investigate the rational explanation of how this could have happened; rather, we must exercise faith that it did happen. [Note: [Col. 0137C] “For he himself,” and so forth. Ratramnus held the transubstantiation defended by the Catholic Church so firmly in mind that he appears plainly to add that it took place in the time of Moses, in the manna and in the water that flowed from the rock struck by the rod. Thus it is very far from being the case that this comparison should be used as an argument to prove that Ratramnus rejected the Catholic Church’s doctrine concerning the change of bread into Christ’s body. On the contrary, the comparison proves that his mind was so occupied by conviction of this transubstantiation that he readily assented to the notion that the manna itself had been changed into the very body of Christ, although Christ had not yet been born.

But since this sort of opinion is highly unusual and extraordinary, although it is expressed here with the greatest clarity, it is by no means believable that our author adopted it. For it is certain, beyond all doubt, that no human being ever persuaded himself or defended the view that the manna poured down from heaven and the water flowing from the rock had been transubstantiated—that is, truly changed—into Christ’s body.

Rather, our author compares one astonishing change with another full of wonder, although the first and more ancient was a figure of the later and a representation, or displayed image and likeness. Thus, when Ratramnus says at no. 23 that the flesh eaten by the congregation of believers in the Church and the drink it consumes are the same, he does not understand or say that they are numerically and specifically the same flesh and drink, with every distinction and difference removed. He means only that the same flesh is truly eaten and the same drink truly offered today, of which an image had formerly been expressed and figured; and that just as this figurative flesh and figurative blood possessed an inward power of infusing grace, or conferring holiness upon human beings, so the true flesh and true blood possess the power of conferring life and immortality.

We understand this to be the true meaning of Ratramnus the compiler from his explicit words at no. 22: “And although that food or drink foreshadowed the mystery of the future body and blood of Christ, which the Church celebrates, Saint Paul nevertheless affirms that our fathers drank the same spiritual food.”

But since the reason why Saint Paul asserts that our fathers ate the same flesh and drank the same drink arises from the fact that the mystery of Christ’s future body and blood had been expressed in the image of the manna and of the water of the desert rock, it clearly follows that this author or compiler could not have persuaded himself that the manna and water were the numerically and specifically identical body and blood that we receive under the new covenant. Nor could he have believed them to be a mere figure and expressed image empty of the thing they introduce and represent. Otherwise the manna would have been a figure of a figure and an image of an image—something that reason has always rightly found intolerable and that, if Ratramnus was in his right mind, was always alien to his meaning. For it would have been enough for him to say that, once these images of the Mosaic age had been set aside, nothing new had occurred in the new law and nothing had been done that had not previously been done in the old.] For he himself, who now in the Church, by almighty power, spiritually changes bread and wine into the flesh of his body and the stream of his own blood, also then invisibly brought about the manna given from heaven as his body and the water poured forth from the rock as his own blood.

## XXVI

Understanding this, David testified in the Holy Spirit: “Man ate the bread of angels,” he said (Ps. 77:25). For it is ridiculous to suppose that corporeal manna, given to the fathers, nourished the heavenly host, or that those who are nourished by the banquets of the divine Word consumed such food.

The Psalmist—or rather, the Holy Spirit speaking through the Psalmist—certainly shows either what our fathers received in that heavenly manna or what the faithful ought to believe in the mystery of Christ’s body. In both cases Christ is indicated: he feeds the souls of believers and is the food of angels. Both of these things occur not through bodily taste or corporeal nourishment, but through the power of the spiritual Word.

## XXVII

And from the evangelist’s account we have learned that our Lord Jesus Christ, before he suffered, took bread, gave thanks, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “This is my body, which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me.” Likewise, after he had supped, he took the cup, saying: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you” (Matt. 26:26–27; Luke 22:19–20).

We see that Christ had not yet suffered, and yet he had already enacted the mystery of his body and blood.

## XXVIII

For we do not suppose that any believer doubts that the bread had been made Christ’s body, since he gives it to his disciples and says: “This is my body, which is given for you.” Nor should anyone doubt that the cup contains Christ’s blood, concerning which he likewise says: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you.”

Therefore, just as shortly before his Passion he was able to change the substance of the bread and the creature of the wine into his own body, which was destined to suffer, and into his blood, which was afterward to be poured out, [Note: [Col. 0139C] “So also in the desert the manna,” and so forth. These statements fully demonstrate that nothing appeared impossible to our compiler Ratramnus in the mystery of transubstantiation, especially since he had persuaded himself that the manna and the water of the desert rock could be changed into Christ’s body before that body existed. Consequently, no obstacle arose from Christ’s coming into this world, in which he instituted this sacrament.

But all these things signify nothing other than that the one in whose power the figurative change of the manna had been placed could also have had the true change of bread into Christ’s body placed within his power, since both are miracles capable of moving the human mind.] so also in the desert he was able to change the manna and the water from the rock into his flesh and blood, even though much later his flesh was to hang upon the cross for us and his blood was to be poured out for our cleansing.

## XXIX

Here too we must consider how his own statement should be understood: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

For he does not say that his flesh, which hung upon the cross, was to be cut into pieces and eaten by the disciples, or that his blood, which he was to pour out for the redemption of the world, was to be given to the disciples as drink. That would be a crime if, as unbelievers then understood the statement, his blood were drunk or his flesh eaten by the disciples.

## XXX

For this reason, in what follows he says to the disciples—who received Christ’s words not unbelievingly but faithfully, although they did not penetrate how those words were to be understood [add.: “were to be”]—“Does this scandalize you? What then if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?” (John 6:62–63). [Note: [Col. 0139D] “With the fullness of my entire body or blood.” From this Protestants who regard our compiler Ratramnus as favorable to them may see that his mind was more distant from the fantasies of those ministers belonging to the assemblies of the superstitious in France, who imagined that Christ’s body, after he had risen—or after the resurrection—was without blood.

Larrocanus of Quevilly in the region of Rouen, *History of the Eucharist*, book II, chapter 6, p. 275; Allixius [*Dissertation on the Blood of Christ’s Body*, Paris, 1680] of Charenton in the region of Paris, after Albertinus [book I *On the Eucharist*, p. 75], Calvin [Gerard Johannes Vossius, *Theological Theses*, p. 188, no. 14], and Osiander [*Confession of Faith against Morlinus*]. Their refutation may readily be read in the *Dissertation on the Blood of Christ’s Body after the Resurrection*, which we published in print at Paris through Gabriel Martin in 1681.

Ratramnus again approaches the same position at no. 88, and mocks those who said that, after he had risen, the Lord possessed a body lighter and subtler than winds and air.—Chapter 8, *On the Nativity of Christ*, found in vol. I of the *Spicilegium* of the distinguished monk Luc d’Achery, p. 336.] As though he were saying: “Therefore do not suppose that my flesh is to be eaten by you corporeally, or my blood drunk by you, distributed or divided into portions, since after the resurrection you will see me ascending into heaven [with the fullness of my entire body and blood]. Then you will understand that it is not, as unbelievers suppose, my flesh that is to be eaten by believers, but that, truly through the mystery, bread and wine changed into the substance of my body and blood are to be received by believers.”

## XXXI

And consequently he says: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is of no benefit whatever” (John 6:64). He says that the flesh is of no benefit in the manner in which unbelievers understood it; otherwise it does give life, as it is received by the faithful through the mystery.

And why is this so? He himself makes it clear when he says: “It is the Spirit who gives life.” Thus, in this mystery of the body and blood, the operation is spiritual, and it grants life; without that operation those mysteries are of no benefit, since they can indeed nourish the body, but they cannot nourish the soul.

## XXXII

At this point the question arises that many people raise when they say [Note: [Col. 0141B] “That these things take place not in figure but in truth.” At the outset of this little work the question proposed at that point is formulated again in a way that is not very conducive to the affairs of the Catholic Church or to its judgment. For the Church has always taught and maintained that some figure is found in the mystery of the Eucharist and has never denied it.

From this it is again useful to observe that this book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was not written against Paschasius. In his own book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, Paschasius readily assents to the opinion admitting some figure in this most holy mystery, especially and at length in chapter 4, letter A: “Since it is a mystery, a sacrament, we cannot deny that it is also a figure”; and below, letter C: “But if we look at it truthfully, it is rightly called both truth and figure.” By these words he refutes and rejects only those who proclaimed that everything in the Eucharist was figurative, as we have already observed above.

Here it is also worth remembering that Ratramnus and Paschasius always understood “figure” to mean the covering and veil that everyone acknowledges to belong to the appearances of bread and wine. Moreover, it must not be forgotten that by “truth” both of these compilers frequently understood that things are effected in the Eucharist according to the action and manner expressed by the force of the words—that is, in a way subjected to the senses and corporeally—as the abbot Abbaudus and the great prior Gualterius of the Abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris, in the time of Berengar, intended to defend. We produced them earlier as witnesses in our annotation on no. 11.

Furthermore, it is beyond dispute that Ratramnus, by the word “truth,” deliberately intended to signify a mode of eating Christ’s body and swallowing his blood that is subjected to the senses. This is perfectly clear from the testimonies and arguments he brings against those who had undertaken to defend the position that Christ’s body had truly been eaten after every figure had been set aside. He clearly demonstrates that these people were opposed to the ancient Fathers.

For all the testimonies he draws from them plainly indicate that Christ’s flesh, brought or offered to the mouths of the faithful, was in no way presented in a mode subjected to the senses—one which I would not hesitate to call the mode of the Capernaumites—even though the adherents of this opinion did not hesitate to maintain that Christ’s entire body remained in heaven, even if it appeared broken and torn apart upon our altars, as we proved earlier in our annotations on no. 11. Moreover, it is thoroughly and forcefully established that Ratramnus defended himself and repudiated the obscene folly of the Stercoranists.] that these things take place not in figure but in truth. By saying this, they are shown to contradict the writings of the holy Fathers.

## XXXIII

Saint Augustine, the pre-eminent doctor of the Church, writes as follows in the third book of *On Christian Doctrine* (chapter 16):

> “Unless you eat,” says the Savior, “the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). It appears to command a crime or outrage. Therefore it is a figure, commanding that we participate in the Lord’s Passion and faithfully lay up in memory [in Saint Augustine: “and sweetly and beneficially lay up in memory”] that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us.

## XXXIV

We see that this doctor says that the mysteries of the body and blood are celebrated by the faithful under a figure: [Col. 0141B] [Note: [Col. 0142C] For he says that taking his flesh and blood carnally is not a matter of religion but of crime. Elsewhere there is a gloss which may appropriately be added here: “carnally,” that is, by grinding with the teeth or tearing apart into pieces. For this is the true sense of these words in their fallen Latin usage, “carnally” and “corporeally”: without any figure, without any covering, in the naked manifestation of the truth itself, as we proved in our earlier annotations.

Moreover, it is fully evident that Ratramnus intended to indicate nothing else at this point. For, explaining his own meaning by applying his will to the matter, he observes that the word “carnally” refers precisely to what those people imagined in their minds from the Gospel narrative who could not grasp the spiritual meaning of Jesus Christ and therefore abandoned his company. Yet it cannot be denied that such people understood Christ’s speech to mean that flesh and blood would be given to them as ordinary food, to be ground by the teeth and torn apart into pieces.] For he says that taking his flesh and blood carnally is not a matter of religion but of crime.

These were the people who, understanding the Lord’s words in the Gospel not spiritually but carnally, withdrew from him and no longer went about with him (John 6:67).

## XXXV

The same writer, in a letter to the bishop Boniface (letter 23, or 8), says among other things:

> “Indeed, we often speak in such a way that, as Easter approaches, we say that tomorrow or the day after tomorrow is the Lord’s Passion, although he suffered so many years ago and that Passion took place only once. Indeed, on Sunday itself we say: ‘Today the Lord has risen,’ although so many years have passed since he rose.
>
> “Why is no one so foolish as to accuse us, when we speak in this way, of having lied? It is because we name these days according to their resemblance to the days on which these events occurred, so that a day is called the very day which is not that day itself but is similar to it through the revolution of time; and it is said that something takes place on that day because of the celebration of the sacrament, although it took place long ago and not on that day.
>
> “Was Christ not sacrificed once in himself? Yet in the sacrament he is sacrificed not only throughout all the solemnities of Easter but every day for the people; and certainly the person who, when asked, answers that he is being sacrificed does not lie. For if sacraments did not possess some likeness to the things whose sacraments they are, they would not be sacraments at all. From this likeness they very often also receive the names of the things themselves.
>
> “Therefore, just as in a certain manner the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body, and the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood, so the sacrament of faith is faith.”

### XXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0142D] We observe what Saint Augustine says: “Sacraments are one thing, and the things of which they are sacraments another.” These words of Saint Augustine are entirely true. Therefore, since the Eucharist itself is the sacrament of Christ’s body, which was fastened to the cross and slaughtered with an outpouring of blood, it is certain that it differs from that body in some respect and is different from it in a certain way—namely, insofar as that body was slaughtered, fastened to the cross, and poured out its blood for us upon the earth. The Eucharist is called the body of Christ who was slaughtered and fastened to the cross, who was dying and suffering, because sacraments take the names of the things of which they are sacraments. And although Christ’s body remains in the Eucharist, it is neither crucified nor slaughtered there, nor is it subjected to the senses while enduring the pains of death—something that happened once, on the day when he surrendered himself to the executioners for the punishment of the cross. This is the true and constant teaching of the Catholic Church, which Ratramnus explains and clarifies especially through the words of Saint Augustine’s letter to Boniface. Whatever the facts may be, while Sixtus of Siena denies it [Bibliotheca sancta, book VI, observation 196], he intends to demonstrate that some figure exists in the Eucharist. These matters require no fuller discussion: the words of Saint Augustine prove most decisively that this was the view of Ratramnus and Paschasius in the ninth century, and that both of them here appealed to Saint Augustine in defense of this truth—Paschasius, specifically, in his treatise *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, p. 623, letters C and D. Therefore, let the diligent reader take the utmost care never to forget, in either treatise or in both, that the Eucharist, insofar as it is a sacrament, is the memorial, express image, likeness, and figure of Christ’s body dying and crucified and shedding his blood for the benefit and salvation of humankind; and that for this reason it has been given the name of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, and is nothing other than Jesus Christ himself, gasping upon the cross and shedding his blood for us. Yet under these conditions he does not truly remain in the Eucharist except in memorial and likeness—just as the day of Easter is called the day of the resurrection, although many years and centuries earlier the Lord Christ rose once on that same or a similar day; and the day of his death and passion is called Friday, which is called Good Friday, although many years earlier he endured the pains of death once [Col. 0144C]. Yet all this does not prevent Christ’s body, now glorified in heaven, from being present in the Eucharist in a spiritual manner, not subject to the senses and not corporally present, as Ratramnus himself acknowledges in several passages of his treatise, especially nos. 28 and 30 cited above, and nos. 16 and 99, in which the learned theologian says that this bread and cup, which are called and are the body and blood of Christ, are so called and exist. From these words we understand that this sacrament not only takes the name of the thing of which it is the sacrament, but is and exists as that very thing. Moreover, from these passages it appears that he deliberately intended to confirm the same truth that he explained in no. 16, where he says of the appearances of bread and wine under which Christ’s body lies hidden that they do not constitute two existences of things different from one another; and in no. 24, where he explicitly teaches that the one who later displayed in our age the body taken from the Virgin and hung upon the cross for the salvation of believers, and from it poured forth a stream of blood, did so not only so that we might be redeemed but also so that we might drink. And in nos. 25 and 28: “For he himself who now, in the Church, by almighty power spiritually transforms bread and wine into the flesh of his body and the stream of his own blood.” This does not differ from the language and expression of Paschasius, whom no person accustomed to letters doubts to have accepted and defended the same faith in his letter to Frudgardus: “And everything celebrated in this sacrament is spiritual, because it is the Spirit who gives life.”]

We observe that Saint Augustine says that sacraments are one thing and the things of which they are sacraments another. The body in which Christ suffered, and his blood which flowed from his side, are things. The mysteries of these things, he says, are the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood, which are celebrated in memory of the Lord’s passion—not only every year throughout the solemnities of Easter, but also every day of the year.

### XXXVII

Although there is one Lord’s body, in which he suffered once, and one blood, which was poured out for the salvation of the world, nevertheless the sacraments have taken the names of those things, so that they are called Christ’s body and blood, because they are so named on account of their likeness to the things they signify. Thus Easter and the Lord’s Resurrection are celebrated every year, although he suffered and rose once in himself, and those days can no longer be recalled because they have passed [Col. 0143B]. Nevertheless, the days on which the memory of the Lord’s passion or resurrection is commemorated are called by the names of those former days, because they bear the likeness of the days on which the Savior suffered once and rose once.

### XXXVIII

For this reason we say: “Today, or tomorrow, or the day after tomorrow is the Lord’s Easter or Resurrection,” although the days on which these events occurred passed many years ago. Likewise, we say that the Lord is sacrificed when the sacraments of his passion are celebrated, although he was sacrificed once for the salvation of the world in himself, as the Apostle says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow in his footsteps” (1 Peter 2:21). This does not mean that he suffers daily in himself what he accomplished once. Rather, he left us an example that is presented daily to believers in the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, so that whoever approaches it may know that he ought to be united with his sufferings, whose image he awaits in the sacred mysteries [Col. 0144A], in accordance with the saying of Wisdom: “You have approached the table of a powerful man; pay close attention to what has been set before you, knowing that you must prepare such things yourself” (Proverbs 23:1). To approach the table of the powerful man is to become a participant in the divine offering; consideration of what has been set before us is understanding the Lord’s body and blood. Whoever participates in them should recognize that he must prepare such things himself, so that he may become an imitator of the one with whom he dies, whose death he confesses not only by believing but also by tasting its memorial.

### XXXIX

Likewise, the blessed Apostle says in the Letter to the Hebrews: “Such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, as the priests do, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people; for he did this once, offering himself—the Lord Jesus Christ” (Hebrews 7:26–27). What he did once he now repeats daily: for he offered himself once for the sins of the people, yet this same offering is celebrated every day by the faithful, but in mystery, so that what the Lord Jesus Christ accomplished by offering himself once may be performed daily in memory of his passion through the celebration of the mysteries.

### XL

Yet it is not falsely said that in those mysteries the Lord is either sacrificed or suffers, since they bear the likeness of that death and passion, of which they are representations. Thus they are called the Lord’s body and the Lord’s blood, because they take the name of the one whose sacrament they are [Col. 0144C].

For this reason the blessed Isidore says in his books of *Etymologies* (book VI, chapter 19):

“Sacrifice is so called as if it were a sacred act, because it is consecrated by mystical prayer in memory of the Lord’s passion, which he endured for us. Therefore, at his command, we call this the body and blood of Christ [Col. 0145A]. For while it is made from the fruits of the earth, it is sanctified and becomes a sacrament through the invisible working of the Spirit of God. The Greeks call the sacrament of this bread and cup *Eucharist*, which is translated into Latin as ‘good grace’; and what is better than the blood and body of Christ? (Bread and wine are compared with the body and blood for this reason: just as the substance of this visible bread and wine nourishes and intoxicates the outer person, so the Word of God, who is the living bread, refreshes the minds of the faithful through participation in himself [Note: [Col. 0145B] These final words, enclosed in parentheses, are not found in Isidore, *Etymologies*; but in book I of *On Offices*, chapter 18, the following words are found: “Because bread strengthens the body, it is therefore called Christ’s body; but because wine produces blood in the flesh, it is therefore referred to Christ’s blood.”].)”

### XLI

This Catholic teacher likewise teaches that the sacred mystery of the Lord’s passion is to be enacted in memory of the Lord’s passion endured for us. By saying this, he shows that the Lord’s passion occurred once, while its memory is represented in the sacred solemn celebrations.

### XLII

Therefore the bread that is offered, although taken from the fruits of the earth, is transformed into Christ’s body when it is sanctified; and likewise the wine, although it has flowed from the vine, becomes Christ’s blood through the sanctification of the divine mystery—not visibly, but, as the present teacher says, through the invisible working of the Spirit of God [another reading: “the Holy Spirit”].

### XLIII

Thus they are called Christ’s blood and body because they are received not according to what appears outwardly, but according to what they have become inwardly through the working of the divine Spirit. And because through invisible power they exist as something far different from what they visibly appear to be, he distinguishes them by saying that bread and wine are compared with the Lord’s body and blood “because, just as the substance of visible bread and wine nourishes and intoxicates the outer person [Col. 0146A], so the Word of God, who is the living bread, refreshes the minds of the faithful through participation in himself.”

### XLIV

By saying this we confess that, in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, whatever is received outwardly is suited to the nourishment of the body [Note: [Col. 0145C] But the Word of God, who is the invisible bread, exists invisibly in that sacrament, and by invisible participation in himself nourishes the minds of the faithful by giving them life.

Ratramnus’s meaning is that the divine Word exists in the sacrament invisibly—that is, in a wondrous, singular manner different from the manner in which, through his immensity, he fills all things. Otherwise the sacrament would differ in no respect from other created things. But the sacrament’s singular mode arises from nothing other than the hypostatic union of the Word with the human body, by which it is true to say, “The Word became flesh.” From this it can be understood that the Word existed in Mary’s womb and on the cross in another manner and mode than by his immensity throughout the universe and in all created things. It follows clearly from these points that, since Christ’s true body truly existed in Mary’s womb and on the cross, no room for doubt can remain that Ratramnus believed that the same body remains in the Eucharist, because of the intimate union it has with the divine Word. In so many passages, especially no. 15, he asserts that it is wrong not only to say but even to think that Christ’s body is not in the Eucharist—that is, to deny it. He repeats in no. 30 that bread and wine have been transformed “into the substance of my body and blood.” He further adds in nos. 30 and 49 that Christ’s body and blood are figures according to visible appearance, but according to invisible substance—that is, through the power of the divine Word—they truly exist as Christ’s body and blood. From these words it is easily understood that the invisible substance of the Eucharist is truly Christ’s own body, and that this spiritual substance is the power of the Word. Accordingly, when Ratramnus says that the Word exists in the sacrament, he must be understood to mean and believe that this occurs by virtue of the union and binding of the Word with the human flesh, veiled and concealed in the same sacrament in a manner not subject to the eyes [Col. 0146B–C].]

But the Word of God, who exists invisibly in that sacrament as invisible bread, invisibly nourishes the minds of the faithful by giving them life through participation in himself.

### XLV

For this reason the same teacher says (*Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 19):

“A sacrament exists in a certain celebration when an event is performed in such a way that it is understood to signify something which must be received in a holy manner [Note: [Col. 0146C] “Which must be received in a holy manner.” And below, in the same passage: “Which must be received invisibly.” The French translator of this book of Ratramnus, in the 1672 edition, intended this participle, *accipiendum*, not to mean “received” but “taken up” and “understood.” Accordingly, he translated into French, less accurately, “which must be received in a holy manner” and “which must be received invisibly” as “which must be taken up in a holy manner and understood spiritually”: *Qu’il faut prendre saintement, et qu’il faut entendre spirituellement*—as if “which must be received in a holy manner” meant “which must be mentally supplied and spiritually contemplated.” Yet it is abundantly clear from these words that the French translator used this method of writing as the author of a different party, so that he might auspiciously and successfully support the error by which he more easily bewitched his followers, whom he wished to persuade that one must supply and understand that everything usually performed in the Eucharist is figurative and imagistic. Ratramnus, on the contrary, following Saint Isidore of Seville, notes that a sacrament is a thing that must be administered and received in a holy—that is, devout—manner, with holy preparation, since one thing is what appears in it and another is what we perceive in a manner subject to the senses.

All this, moreover, agrees very well with what Saint Chrysostom says in Homily 7 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, p. 318: “We call it a sacrament because we contemplate in it something other than what we see, and truly believe things other than those we see. For such is the nature of our sacraments.”

In Greek: “It is called a mystery in another way because we do not see the very things that we see; rather, we see other things and believe other things. For such is the nature of our mysteries.”

The author of the 1672 French translation, when his own error was no longer at issue and he no longer seemed to have any personal interest in the matter, translated *accipientium* (“of those receiving”) as *recipientium* (“of those receiving”), in the continuous sentence at no. 48: “The divine power more secretly dispenses salvation faithfully to those who receive it.”]

By saying this he shows that every sacrament in divine matters contains something secret, and that one thing appears visibly while another must be received invisibly [Col. 0146B].

### XLVI

Then, showing in turn which sacraments are to be celebrated by the faithful, he says (in the same passage):

“Now the sacraments are baptism and chrism, the body and blood. [Isidore adds in the same place: ‘of Christ.’] They are called sacraments for this reason: under the covering of bodily things, divine power more secretly works salvation in those same sacraments. Hence they are called sacraments either from secret powers or from sacred things.”

And in what follows he says (in the same passage):

“In Greek, it is called *mystery*, because it has a secret and hidden arrangement.”

### XLVII

What else are we taught by this than that the Lord’s body and blood are called mysteries because they have a secret and hidden arrangement—that is, that they are one thing in what they indicate outwardly and another in what they invisibly accomplish inwardly [Col. 0147A]?

### XLVIII

For this reason they are also called sacraments, because under the covering of bodily things divine power more secretly and faithfully dispenses salvation to those who receive them.

### XLIX

From all that has been said thus far it has been demonstrated that Christ’s body and blood, which are received by the mouths of the faithful in the Church, are figures according to visible appearance; but according to invisible substance—that is, through the power of the divine Word—they truly exist as Christ’s body and blood. Therefore, according to visible creation, they nourish the body; but according to the power of the more potent substance, they both nourish and sanctify the minds of the faithful [Col. 0147B]. (See nos. 44, 91, and 96.)

### L

We must now examine the subject of the second question and determine whether the very body that was born of Mary, suffered, died, and was buried, and that sits at the right hand of the Father, is the body that is daily received by the mouths of the faithful in the Church through the mystery of the sacraments.

### LI

Let us ask what Saint Ambrose thinks about this. For in the first book of the *Sacraments* (*On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 8), he says:

“Truly it is wonderful that God rained manna upon the fathers, and that they were fed daily with food from heaven; hence it is said: ‘Man ate the bread of angels’ (Psalm 77:25). Yet all those who ate that bread died in the wilderness. But this food that you receive, this living bread that came down from heaven, supplies the substance of eternal life; and whoever eats it will not die forever [Note: [Col. 0147C] “And it is Christ’s body.” That is, “and because it is Christ’s body,” from Saint Ambrose. The translator of the opposing party in 1672 does not reject this translation and explanation, for it reads: “It is the body of Jesus Christ.”]; and it is Christ’s body.”

### LII

Observe how this teacher says that Christ’s body is the food that the faithful receive in the Church. For he says: “This living bread that came down from heaven supplies the substance of eternal life.” Does the bread that is seen, that is received corporally, that is pressed by the teeth, swallowed by the throat, and taken into the receptacle of the belly, supply the substance of eternal life?
