In this manner it nourishes the flesh that is destined to die and supplies no incorruption; nor can it truly be said that whoever eats it will not die forever (John 6:52). For what the body receives is itself corruptible, and it cannot grant the body that it should not die forever, since what is subject to corruption cannot bestow eternity. Therefore, in that bread there is a life that does not appear to bodily eyes but is contemplated by the sight of faith. That bread exists as the living bread that came down from heaven, and of it it is truly said: “Whoever eats it will not die forever”; and it is Christ’s body [Col. 0148B].

### LIII

Likewise, in what follows (in the same work, chapter 9), when speaking of Christ’s almighty power, he says:

“Therefore, if the word of Christ could make from nothing what did not exist, can it not change existing things into what they were not? [Note: [Col. 0147C] “Is it not greater to give new things than to change natures?” Behold Saint Ambrose’s statement, by which he explicitly and in direct terms establishes a change of natures in the Eucharist. In truth, such natures can only be those of bread and wine, which are transferred into Christ’s flesh and blood. For this reason the French translation added the words “that is, the substance of things,” which Saint Ambrose intended to signify in chapter 9 of *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*: “Will Christ’s word not be able to change the appearances of the elements?” Therefore Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz and a contemporary of Ratramnus, could have meant by these words nothing other than the view that expresses, accurately and plainly, reality and transubstantiation. In book VII, chapter 10, of *On Sacred Orders*, which he addressed to Theotmarus, he wrote: “Who would ever believe that bread could be changed into flesh or wine into blood, unless the Savior himself said so—the one who created bread and wine and made all things from nothing? It is easier to make something from something else than to create it from nothing.”] Is it not greater to give new things than to change natures?” [another reading: “For it is not less to give new things.”]

### LIV

Saint Ambrose says that in that mystery a change of Christ’s blood and body has taken place—miraculously, because it is divine, and ineffably, because it is incomprehensible. Let those who wish to receive nothing here according to an inwardly hidden power, but wish to judge everything according to what appears visibly, say in what respect a change has taken place here.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] “For according to the substance of created things,” etc. Since in the preceding section the author established, on Saint Ambrose’s authority, that a change of natures takes place in the Eucharist, it is not credible that in this section, no. 54, he intended to say the opposite. Since in the preceding sections he taught that in the Eucharist the change of one thing into another takes place, and that the appearances of bread and wine and Christ’s body do not have two different existences, it is inconceivable that he held that Christ’s body and the substance of bread remain after consecration in the same manner in which they existed before. Therefore it is necessary to understand something other than what is commonly understood in the philosophical school of Aristotle by the word “substance”—namely, that after consecration bread and wine are things subsisting in themselves, with no change admitted.

For this reason I have decided not to explain “substance” by “substance,” but by words that express what the things themselves present—words that indicate or signify nothing else explicitly than the qualities subject to the senses, or perceptible qualities, of bread and wine, which remain the same after consecration. The most distinguished Calvinist ministers readily admit that the ancient Fathers used the word “substance” to signify the qualities of things, or what is most proper to a thing, and not at all a true and natural substance in the proper sense. This can easily be understood from the response to the *Office of the Sacrament of the Altar*, printed in Paris in 1665, pp. 264 and 432. We understand from the *Journal of Learned Men in Holland* that its compiler was Matthieu Larroquan Quevilly, a minister of Calvinist superstition in the Rouen countryside.

Indeed, in chapter 46 of book III of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, *Life of Constantine*, we read that the soul of Saint Helena was transformed, after she died, into an angelic substance:

“She was thus transformed in soul into incorruptible and angelic being.”

Her soul, therefore, was re-formed into an incorruptible and angelic substance [Col. 0149B].

In Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, p. 887, letter B: “To rise again to the works of the flesh from the leisure of continence is the substance of the sides”—meaning the strength and vigor of the sides. In book II of *On the Apparel of Women*, p. 175, letter B: “We ought indeed to walk in such holiness and with the whole substance of faith”; and in *Exhortation to Chastity*, p. 670, letter C: “Through continence you will trade in the great substance of chastity.”

In Saint Augustine, on Psalm 68, letter B: “Through iniquity humanity fell from the substance in which it was made.”

In Saint Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 81, at the end, on Christ’s resurrection, we find:

“But the appearance is changed when what is mortal becomes immortal and what is corruptible becomes incorruptible, so that this is to change the substance without changing the person.”

All these passages, copied from the ancient Fathers, clearly show that the Fathers, like Ratramnus, used the word “substance” to signify qualities or properties subject to the senses. Thus in Psalm 68: “I am sunk in the deep mire, and there is no substance” [Greek: “And there is no subsistence”]; and in Psalm 139:11: “In misery they shall not subsist” [Greek: “And they shall certainly not subsist.”] These expressions do not signify a lack of substance, but a distinction of qualities and properties subject to the senses. This accords with Ratramnus’s meaning when he says: “Christ’s body received in the Eucharist supplies the substance of eternal life”—that is, grace to those who worthily eat the flesh and drink the blood, discerning the Lord’s body.”]

“For according to the substance of created things, what they were before consecration, that they remain afterward [Col. 0149A]. Bread and wine existed beforehand; [Note: [Col. 0149C] They also appear to remain in the same appearance even after consecration. The compiler of the French translation explains these words paraphrastically as follows: “And the created substances appear to remain in the same appearance after consecration” [Col. 0149D]. The words “created substances” do not occur in the original Latin text.

As for “appearance,” if it is taken, in Ratramnus’s sense, as appearance or likeness—and nowhere as the very nature of bread or wine, as we showed at no. 12—this paraphrase could be defended. But no room for doubt remains that the vernacular translator understood “appearance” to mean the nature and substance of bread, in the Aristotelian sense. Therefore the French translation necessarily appears alien to the author’s meaning.]

“in the same appearance in which they also seem to remain after consecration.” Therefore something has been changed inwardly by the powerful working of the Holy Spirit: something which faith beholds, nourishes the soul, and supplies the substance of eternal life.

### LV

Likewise, in what follows (in the same work), he says:

“Why do you seek the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the Lord Jesus himself was born from a Virgin contrary to nature?”

### LVI

At this point the listener rises [Note: [Col. 0149D] “And says that what is seen is Christ’s body and what is drunk is his blood.” Ratramnus often repeats and tears apart this response of his opponents, so that they may realize that they never reach the point of the question with the acuity of their minds, and that they are not contending, fighting, or crossing swords with those who believe that Christ’s body remains in the Eucharist, but with those who believe that Christ’s true and proper body is subjected to the senses there, crushed and broken there, concealed by no veils or figures, but perceived by their own eyes [Col. 0150B].]

and says that what is seen is Christ’s body and what is drunk is his blood; and that one should not ask how it was made, but hold that it was made in this way. You seem to have a sound opinion. But if you carefully examine the force of the words, [Col. 0149B] [Note: [Col. 0150B] You faithfully believe that it is Christ’s body and blood—that is, with every doubt set aside. For, according to the precise manner of speaking and writing used by theologians, “to believe faithfully” signifies nothing other than believing without doubt and with doubt removed, which is the mode of belief required for all the articles of faith.

Understand that Christ’s body and blood exist in what is seen not according to appearance but according to power. If regard is paid to Ratramnus’s manner of speaking and writing, the word “appearance” undoubtedly signifies an appearance subject to sight. This requires no other proof than the words of Saint Ambrose that Ratramnus cites, in which he asserts that things were brought forth by the power and authority of Jesus Christ and changed into other things: “And he changes what was created into what it had not previously been.”]

you do indeed faithfully believe that it is Christ’s body and blood. But if you perceived that what you believe you do not yet see—for if you saw it, you would say, “I see,” not “I believe that it is Christ’s body and blood”—then you would understand that, since faith beholds the whole of whatever that whole may be, while the eye of the flesh apprehends nothing, Christ’s body and blood exist in what is seen not according to appearance but according to power [Col. 0150A].

Therefore he says (in the same work):

“The order of nature is not to be considered here, but Christ’s power is to be revered. Whatever he wills, however he wills it, and whatever he wills, he creates that which did not exist and changes what was created into what it had not previously been.”

The same author adds (in the same work):

“Certainly it is true flesh, which was crucified and which was buried; [Note: [Col. 0150C] “Therefore it is truly the sacrament of that flesh.” The Calvinist translator of 1672 conjectures from this that, in place of the adverb *vere* (“truly”), the adjectival form *verae* (“of true flesh”) should be read—namely: “It is the sacrament of that true flesh.” This restoration seems to me, in this case, balanced and largely indifferent. But since the ancient manuscripts of Saint Ambrose and Ratramnus do not report the adjective, we have not abandoned the common reading.

Moreover, since Ratramnus understands from the word “sacrament” or “mystery” that it contains something hidden and concealed, in no way subject to human senses, as he says in no. 9, he is not far from Paschasius, who explicitly says in chapter 3 of his treatise *On the Body and Blood of Christ*: “Therefore the mystery or sacrament that God became man is rightly so called; but it is called a mystery because it has within itself a secret and hidden arrangement.”

It is abundantly clear that Ratramnus—or rather Saint Ambrose—understands “sacrament” here as the cloth and figure that conceal Christ’s body within, whether “truly the veil of flesh” or “of true flesh,” as he says in the following section: “He would say that it is the sacrament of that true flesh in which he was crucified.”]

therefore it is truly the sacrament of that flesh.” The Lord Jesus himself cries out: “This is my body.”

### LVII

How carefully and prudently the distinction is made! Of Christ’s flesh, which was crucified and buried—that is, according to which Christ was both crucified [Col. 0150B] and buried—he says: “It is therefore truly Christ’s flesh.” But of the flesh that is received in the sacrament he says: “Therefore it is truly the sacrament of that flesh” [Note: [Col. 0150D] Distinguishing the sacrament of the flesh from the truth of the flesh. Ratramnus is debating whether what is perceived by the senses, broken, and divided into pieces is truly Christ’s flesh. This was what the Catholic men of his age persuaded themselves of, setting aside an examination of reason—that is, of the manner in which the thing could become a mystery in the Eucharist. They likewise denied firmly that a veil, canopy, or any figure could be present in the sacrament.]

distinguishing the sacrament of the flesh from the truth of the flesh: insofar as he would say that, in the truth of the flesh which Christ had taken from the Virgin, he was crucified and buried; but that the mystery now enacted in the Church is the sacrament of that true flesh in which he was crucified. He plainly instructs the faithful that the flesh according to which Christ was crucified and buried is not a mystery but the truth of nature; whereas this flesh, which now contains its likeness in mystery [Col. 0151A], is not flesh in appearance but in sacrament [Note: [Col. 0151C] “Not flesh in appearance but in sacrament.” From Ratramnus’s entire treatise we understand that by “appearance” he emphatically does not mean the truth of nature, or nature itself—which philosophers call *species*, composed from genus and difference—but only an appearance and express image subject to human senses, or sensible accidents, as has already been observed at no. 12.]. For in appearance it is bread, but in sacrament it is Christ’s true body, as the Lord Jesus himself cries out: “This is my body.”

### LVIII

Likewise, in what follows (in the same work):

“What we should eat and what we should drink the Holy Spirit has elsewhere expressed to you through the Prophet, saying: ‘Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him’” (Psalm 33:9 [Vulgate]).

Does that bread, tasted corporally, or that wine, drunk, show how sweet the Lord is? For whatever has taste is corporeal and delights the throat. Is tasting the Lord, then, something corporeal that can be sensed? He therefore invites us to experience the flavor of spiritual tasting and to think nothing corporeal concerning that drink or bread [Note: [Col. 0151C] “But to perceive everything spiritually.” That is, what is offered to us in the mystery of the Eucharist. These words do not mean merely that what we receive—namely Christ’s body—is only figure and spirit. On the contrary, Christ the Lord’s true body is offered and brought to us with his blood in a manner not subject to the senses but spiritual.

Ratramnus’s intention is not to prove that there is only a figure in the sacrament, but that there is some figure and some spiritual reality. Paschasius embraced this position; no learned person will deny that, together with the universal Church, he believed Christ’s true body to lie hidden in the Eucharist, as we showed above. For he did not reject the same form of expression in his letter to Frudgardus: “And everything celebrated in this sacrament is spiritual.”]

but to perceive everything spiritually, because the Lord is Spirit, and blessed is the man who hopes in him.

### LIX

Likewise, immediately afterward (in the same work):

“Christ is in that sacrament because it is Christ’s body; therefore it is not bodily food but spiritual food.”

What could be clearer? What could be more manifest? What could be more divine? For he says: “Christ is in that sacrament.” He does not say: “That bread and that wine are Christ.” If he said this, he would proclaim Christ to be corruptible—God forbid—and subject to mortality; for whatever in that food is either seen or tasted bodily is plainly subject to corruption.

### LX

He adds: “Because it is the body of Christ.” You rise up and say: “Behold, he plainly confesses that that bread and that drink are the body of Christ.” But observe how he continues: “Therefore it is not bodily food, but spiritual.” Do not, then, apply the sense of the flesh; for nothing here is determined according to it.

> **[Note: [Col. 0151D]** It is the body of Christ, but not bodily; and it is the blood of Christ, but not bodily—that is, not subject to the senses, something that can be torn apart piece by piece and crushed by the teeth. We add this explanation, which is most necessary and useful for removing the ambiguity of the word “bodily,” which might appear to some to exclude and abolish any presence whatsoever of the true body of Jesus Christ. But since Ratramnus sincerely acknowledges that the true body of Christ truly exists, or remains, in the Eucharist, and that it is a sacrament of true flesh—namely, the covering by which it is girded and concealed, since there is no mystery where nothing is hidden—it is necessary to understand from this adverb “bodily” the natural and common mode of existence of all bodies, without exception: that is, of things subject to the senses and friable, which can be torn apart piece by piece. Paschasius calls this kind of body of Jesus Christ a spiritual body in his letter to Frudgard; and Ratramnus, in explicit and unequivocal words, says that the Eucharistic body and blood, according to appearance, manifestation, and subjection to the eyes, are figures, but according to their substance, which is not subject to the eyes—namely, through the power of the Word—they are truly the body and blood of Christ. “They are figures,” he says, “according to visible appearance; but according to invisible substance, that is, through the power of the divine Word, they are truly the body and blood of Christ.” What person of sound mind can deny that there, in section 49, the word “truly” means “in reality,” “actually,” and, in the usage of later Latin, **realiter**?]

It is indeed the body of Christ, but not bodily; rather, it is spiritual. It is the blood of Christ, but not bodily; rather, it is spiritual. Nothing here, therefore, is to be apprehended bodily, but spiritually: it is the body of Christ, but not bodily; and it is the blood of Christ, but not bodily.

### LXI

Again, immediately afterward (ibid.):

> “Hence also the Apostle,” he says, “speaking of its type, says: ‘For our fathers ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink’ (1 Cor. 10:3–4). For the body of God is spiritual; the body of Christ is the body of the divine Spirit, because Christ is spirit, as we read in Lamentations: ‘The Spirit before our face is Christ the Lord’ (Lam. 4:20).”

### LXII

Most clearly he taught how we ought to understand the mystery of the blood and body of Christ. For when he had said that our fathers ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink—although no one can doubt that the manna which they ate and the water which they drank were corporeal—he adds, concerning the mystery now enacted in the Church, defining in what respect the body is Christ’s:

> “For the body of God,” he says, “is a spiritual body.”

God, certainly, is Christ; and the body which he took from the Virgin Mary, which suffered, was buried, and rose again, was truly a real body—that is, one which remained visible and tangible. But the body called the mystery of God is not bodily, but spiritual; and if it is spiritual, it is no longer visible or tangible. Hence blessed Ambrose adds:

> “The body of Christ,” he says, “is the body of the divine Spirit.”

The divine Spirit, however, is nothing corporeal, nothing corruptible, nothing tangible.

But this body which is celebrated in the Church, according to its visible appearance, is both corruptible and tangible.

### LXIII

How, then, is it said to be the body of the divine Spirit? Certainly, inasmuch as it is spiritual—that is, inasmuch as it exists invisibly and intangibly, and therefore incorruptibly.

### LXIV

Hence, in what follows (ibid.):

> “Because Christ is Spirit, as we read: ‘The Spirit before our face is Christ the Lord.’”

> **[Note: [Col. 0153B]** He plainly shows in what respect the body of Christ is possessed, and so forth. Ratramnus explains by what reason and in what manner we possess the body of Christ as food and nourishment for our soul. Since it is certain that nourishment of this kind does not feed the soul as ordinary and customary nourishment feeds the body—namely, through the natural conversion of one substance into another—he teaches that the body of Christ remains in our souls insofar as it is extended to us in the Eucharist, endowed with the power of the Word. This power not only nourishes but also purifies and frees our soul from sins, according to the fact that the Spirit of Christ is in it, that is, the power of the divine Word. In all this, nothing appears to contradict the view that establishes the true presence, or what theologians call the reality, of the true body. In this conviction and persuasion, we do not hesitate to say that, by receiving the truly true flesh of Christ in a manner not subject to bodily senses, the nourishment of our soul is effected in no other way. For the power of the divine Word, united and hypostatically joined to the body, fosters in us the gift and grace of God and purges us from the crimes and contaminations we have committed.

> These are Ratramnus’s exact words at the end of section 65: “But to show what food or what drink he is speaking of, he added pointedly: ‘This food’ or ‘this drink.’ What food is this? Or what drink is this? Clearly, the body of Christ, the body of the divine Spirit; and, to make the point still clearer, Christ the Spirit, of whom he speaks: ‘The Spirit before our face is Christ the Lord.’ By all this it is plainly shown that nothing in this food, nothing in this drink, is to be apprehended bodily, but everything is to be considered spiritually.”

> Paschasius said almost the same thing in his letter to Frudgard; with Albertinus and almost all Protestants today agreeing, he expressly accepted the reality and transubstantiation as doctrines to be maintained without suspicion or doubt.]

He plainly shows in what respect the body of Christ is possessed—namely, according to the fact that the Spirit of Christ is in it, that is, the power of the divine Word, which not only feeds the soul but also purifies it.

### LXV

For this reason the author himself says immediately afterward (ibid.):

> “Finally, this food strengthens our heart, and this drink gladdens the heart of man, as the Prophet has recalled” (Ps. 103:15).

Does bodily food strengthen the human heart, and corporeal drink gladden the human heart? But to show what food or drink he is speaking of, he added pointedly: “this food,” or “this drink.”

> “What food is this? Or what drink is this? Clearly, the body of Christ, the body of the divine Spirit; and, to make the point still clearer, Christ the Spirit, of whom he speaks: ‘The Spirit before our face is Christ the Lord.’”

By all this it is plainly shown that nothing in this food, nothing in this drink, is to be apprehended bodily, but everything is to be considered spiritually.

### LXVI

For the soul—which here is signified by the human heart—is not nourished either by corporeal food or by corporeal drink, but is fed and invigorated by the word of God. The same teacher affirms this more clearly in Book V of *The Sacraments* (chapter 4):

> “This is not the bread,” he says, “which passes into the body, but that bread of eternal life which supplies the substance of our soul.”

### LXVII

That Saint Ambrose said this not about ordinary bread but about the bread of Christ’s body is made unmistakably clear by what follows in the reading. For he is speaking of the daily bread which believers ask to be given to them.

### LXVIII

For this reason he adds:

> “If it is daily bread, why do you take it after a year, as the Greeks in the East are accustomed to do? Receive, therefore, daily what benefits you daily; live in such a way that you may deserve to receive it daily.”

It is therefore clear what bread he is speaking of: the bread of Christ’s body, which sustains the substance of our soul not because it passes into the body, but because it is the bread of eternal life.

### LXIX

> **[Note: [Col. 0153D]** From the authority of this most learned man we are thoroughly instructed, and so forth. From these passages it may seem to some that Ratramnus did not hold the opinion of those who persuade themselves that the body of Christ born from the Virgin, nailed to the cross, dead, and buried is not the same as that which is received in the Eucharist, and that he therefore decisively ended here the second part of the proposed question, in a manner of writing and argument wholly opposed to the opinion of Paschasius and to the persuasion of the Catholic Church. The Church does not doubt that it belongs to the Christian faith that, in the sacred mystery of the Eucharist, under a veil, we receive the same body that was nailed to the cross, and that we drink the same blood poured out for all human beings.

> But Ratramnus intended nothing less than this by his words. Whether, therefore, in Ratramnus’s time as in ours, the name “body of Christ” was applied to consecrated bread—that is, to something subject to our eyes after consecration, white, round, extended by the hands of the sacred minister, as the author of the books attributed to Saint Ambrose says in *On the Sacraments* (Book IV, chapter 4): “This bread is bread before the words of the sacraments; when consecration has been added, from bread it becomes the flesh of Christ.” And below: “It was not the body of Christ before consecration; and after consecration I tell you that it is now the body of Christ.”

> Even if such roundness, whiteness, and extension are not properly the body of Christ, but rather a veil or curtain by which it is hidden and removed from the sight of our eyes and the apprehension of our senses, this does not mean that bread is properly his body and the cup his blood. Rather, they contain within themselves the mystery of his body and blood, as Facundus, bishop of Hermianum in Africa at the beginning of the sixth century, once said in Book IX of *In Defense of the Three Chapters*.

> By the same name of Christ’s body and blood, the true body and true blood of Jesus Christ were called, hidden beneath the appearances in a spiritual manner and not subject to the senses—not bodily or circumscribed, as the schools put it. Ratramnus calls this in the present treatise Christ’s proper body, the true flesh concealed and wrapped beneath this mystery.

> Behold, friendly reader, two bodies of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist worthy of consideration and reflection. One exists in name only, in the appearances alone and in the expressed images which remain from the substance of bread and wine after consecration; the other is true and proper, into which bread and wine are changed, which exists and remains there in a manner and mode not subject to bodily senses, beneath the veils and expressed images or appearances of bread and wine.

> This is the very body that was crucified, and this is the very blood poured out for us; nor will Ratramnus anywhere be found to have said anything contrary to this. I shall not hesitate to say that Ratramnus readily and abundantly agrees with this everywhere, especially in section 24, where he says:

> “The Apostle added in sequence: ‘They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ.’ He said this so that we might understand that in the desert Christ was present in the spiritual rock and offered the people a stream of his blood—the same Christ who afterward took a body from the Virgin and was hung upon the cross for the salvation of believers, and who in our age has been displayed and poured forth a stream of blood from it, by which we were not only redeemed but also given drink.”

> He does the same thing frequently in other passages, where he expressly acknowledges the change of bread into the true body of Jesus Christ and of wine into his own blood.

> As for the other thing called the body of Christ in name only, subject to the senses and friable in the Eucharist, it is not, in some respect, the same as what was nailed to the cross. Nevertheless, it is again useful to observe that this bread and this wine after consecration are only veils and curtains—whiteness, roundness, and extension—which strike the eyes. They are called by this name collectively only because, through a wondrous mode of operation, they are the spiritual and divine body of Jesus Christ: namely, insofar as they express and form in our memory the true flesh and proper blood of Jesus Christ. These possess within themselves the virtue and power of the Word for nourishing souls and cleansing those contaminated by the stain of sins, as we observed above, and for granting us grace while preserving innocence and the redemption of sins.

> Since these things are so, these appearances of bread and wine after consecration, insofar as they are veils of the true flesh and proper blood of Jesus Christ poured out for the salvation of the faithful, are a spiritual and figured body, expressed in an image of the death and passion of Jesus Christ. In this respect they truly differ from the true body of Jesus Christ, which they conceal and hide from our eyes.

> But all these things signify nothing other than what the scholastic or disputatious theologians have expressed since the time when Aristotelian and Peripatetic reasoning occupied the Christian schools. Namely, everything externally seen in the mystery of the Eucharist—whether called accidents or appearances—is not the true body of Jesus Christ born from the Virgin, nailed to the cross, dead, and buried, but is its veil, covering, curtain, appearance, memorial, expressed image—in a word, its name. For names are customarily imposed upon sacraments from the names of the things which they contain and shadow forth.

> Thus blessed Algerus, the theologian of Liège and adversary of Berengar, speaks in Book I of *The Sacraments*, chapter 17: “With regard to the visible sacrament, the appearances and likeness of those things are the names which formerly belonged to them—namely, of bread and wine, not of the body of Christ. But the body and blood of Christ are now called by designation, in that mode of speech by which the signifying thing is accustomed to be called by the name of the thing signified.”

> Ratramnus clearly indicates that he intended nothing else by these carefully formulated words, copied continuously from section 69:

> “For this bread and this drink do not exist as the body or blood of Christ according to what they appear to be, but according to the fact that spiritually they supply the substance of life. But that in which Christ suffered once did not present another appearance than that in which it existed; for this was what was truly seen, touched, crucified, and buried. Likewise, his blood flowing from his side did not externally appear as one thing while concealing another thing within; true blood therefore flowed from a true body. But now the blood of Christ which believers drink and the body which they eat are one thing in appearance and another in signification; one thing feeds the body with bodily food, and another fattens the minds with the substance of eternal life. This is insofar as they are a figure and veil of the true body of Christ, to which the divine Word has been joined by a wondrous hypostatic union and which, through its power, effects grace and the remission of sins in us.”]

By the authority of this most learned man we are thoroughly instructed that the body in which Christ suffered and the blood which, while he hung upon the cross, he poured from his side are separated by a great difference from this body which is celebrated daily by the faithful in the mystery of Christ’s passion, and from that blood which is taken into the mouths of the faithful, so that it may be a mystery of the blood by which the whole world was redeemed.

For this bread and this drink do not exist as the body or blood of Christ according to what they appear to be, but according to the fact that spiritually they supply the substance of life. But that body in which Christ suffered once did not present another appearance than that in which it existed; for this was what was truly seen, touched, crucified, and buried. Likewise, his blood flowing from his side did not externally appear as one thing while concealing another thing within; true blood therefore flowed from a true body. But now the blood of Christ which believers drink, and the body which they eat, are one thing in appearance and another in signification: one thing feeds the body with bodily food, and another fattens the minds with the substance of eternal life.

### LXX

Concerning this matter blessed Jerome writes in his commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians:

> **[Note: [Col. 0156D]** On the words, “In whom we have redemption through his blood.”]

> “The blood and flesh of Christ are understood in two ways: either as that spiritual and divine flesh and blood of which he himself says, ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink’ (John 6:56), or as the flesh which was crucified and the blood which was poured out by the soldier’s lance.”

### LXXI

This teacher made no small distinction between the body and blood of Christ. For while he says that the flesh or blood which is taken daily by the faithful is spiritual, the flesh which was crucified and the blood which was poured out by the soldier’s lance are not said to be spiritual or divine.

> **[Note: [Col. 0156D]** He plainly indicates, and so forth. From Saint Jerome we understand with complete clarity that there is as much distinction between this body and that body, and between this blood and that blood—that is, between the Eucharistic body and the body nailed to the cross—as there is between corporeal and spiritual things.

> Since the question discussed by Ratramnus at this point chiefly concerns whether what is presented to our eyes and perceived externally by the senses in the Eucharist is itself the body of Christ, and since he clearly establishes that there is some figure, especially because the external things of bread and wine are only veils and coverings concealing the body and blood poured out for the salvation of the human race, he proves here that these external symbols, lacking the qualities subject to human senses with which the body nailed to the cross was endowed, can be nothing other than a spiritual body—that is, a body existing in mystery, appearance, figure, and signification—and therefore differ from the true body as spiritual things differ from corporeal things.

> In the following section he offers an invincible proof of this distinction, openly demonstrating that, once this distinction between Christ’s Eucharistic body and the body nailed to the cross has been properly established, by the Eucharistic body he understands only that to which the name “body” has been applied because sacraments—or that external part subject to the senses—are accustomed to be called by the names of the things they contain.

> Ratramnus intends to prove throughout this treatise that what is perceived and seen by the senses in the Eucharist—white, round, and extended—is not in reality Christ’s body itself, but the covering and veil which conceals the true body and removes it from the eyes of mortal human beings.

> This is plainly contrary to the opinion of those against whom he was writing, who denied every kind or degree of figure in the Eucharist, defended that nothing at all was hidden or concealed in so great a mystery, and stubbornly maintained that everything subject to the senses and perceived by the eyes was itself truly the body of Christ. In the course of time, we observed that Abbaud and Walter, the great prior of Saint Victor in Paris, adopted this opinion.

> Ratramnus therefore speaks in precise terms in section 72:

> “For that flesh which was crucified was made from the flesh of the Virgin, joined together with bones and sinews, distinguished by the outlines of human limbs, and given life, with its own life and appropriate movements, by the spirit of a rational soul. But the spiritual flesh which spiritually feeds the believing people consists, according to the appearance which it displays externally, of grains of wheat fashioned by the hand of an artisan; it is joined together by no sinews or bones, distinguished by no variety of limbs, animated by no rational substance, and capable of exercising no proper movements. Whatever supplies the substance of life in it belongs to a special power, invisible efficacy, and divine virtue; and it exists as one thing according to what is seen externally and as something quite different according to what is believed in the mystery.

> “Moreover, the flesh of Christ which was crucified did not display externally anything other than what existed within, because it was the true flesh of a true human being—a truly real body existing in the appearance of a true body.”]

He plainly indicates that they differ from one another as much as corporeal and spiritual things, visible and invisible things, divine and human things differ; and that things which differ from one another are not the same.

The spiritual flesh which is taken into the mouths of the faithful and the spiritual blood which is offered daily to believers for drinking differ from the flesh which was crucified and from the blood which was poured out by the soldier’s lance, as the authority of this present writer testifies. They are therefore not the same.

### LXXII

For that flesh which was crucified was made from the flesh of the Virgin, joined together with bones and sinews, distinguished by the outlines of human limbs, and given life, with its own life and appropriate movements, by the spirit of a rational soul. But the spiritual flesh which spiritually feeds the believing people consists, according to the appearance which it bears externally, of grains of wheat fashioned by the hand of an artisan; it is joined together by no sinews or bones, distinguished by no variety of limbs, animated by no rational substance, and capable of exercising no proper movements.

Whatever supplies the substance of life in it belongs to a spiritual power, invisible efficacy, and divine virtue; and it exists as one thing according to what is seen externally and as something quite different according to what is believed in the mystery.

Moreover, the flesh of Christ which was crucified did not display externally anything other than what existed within, because it was the true flesh of a true human being—a truly real body existing in the appearance of a true body.

### LXXIII

It must also be considered that in that bread not only the body of Christ but also the believing people who believe in him are figured. Hence it is made from many grains of wheat, because the body of the believing people is increased by the many faithful through the word of Christ. (See sections 96 and 98.)

### LXXIV

For this reason, just as in the mystery that bread is received as the body of Christ, so also in the mystery the members of the people believing in Christ are signified. And just as that bread is called the body of believers not bodily but spiritually, so also the body of Christ must necessarily be understood not bodily but spiritually.

### LXXV

In the wine also, which is called the blood of Christ, water is commanded to be mixed, and neither is permitted to be offered without the other, because neither the people without Christ nor Christ without the people can exist—just as the head cannot exist without the body, nor the body without the head. Finally, in that sacrament the water bears the image of the people. (See section 81.)

Therefore, if that wine, sanctified through the ministry of the ministers, is converted bodily into the blood of Christ, the water also, which is likewise mixed with it, must necessarily be converted bodily into the blood of the believing people. For where there is one sanctification, there consequently follows one operation; and where there is a corresponding relation, there likewise follows a corresponding mystery.

But we see that, according to the body, nothing has been converted in the water; consequently, nothing bodily has been manifested in the wine either. Whatever is signified in the water concerning the body of the people is received spiritually; therefore whatever is indicated in the wine concerning the blood of Christ must necessarily be received spiritually.

### LXXVI

Again, things which differ from one another are not the same. The body of Christ which died and rose again, having been made immortal, now dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over it (Rom. 6:9); it is eternal and no longer subject to suffering. But that which is celebrated in the Church is temporal, not eternal; corruptible, not incorruptible; on the way, not in the homeland. They therefore differ from one another and consequently are not the same.

How, then, is it called the true body of Christ and the true blood?

### LXXVII

For if it is the body of Christ, and it is truly called this because it is the body of Christ, then in truth it is the body of Christ. And if it is in truth the body of Christ, then the body of Christ is incorruptible and impassible, and therefore eternal. This body of Christ, then, which is enacted in the Church, must be incorruptible and eternal.

But it cannot be denied that what is broken apart into pieces for consumption and ground by the teeth and transferred into the body is subject to corruption.

> **[Note: [Col. 0160D]** Saint Ignatius, *Letter to the Philadelphians*: **Εἰς ἄρτος τοῖς πᾶσιν ὁθρόφθη** [“One bread was broken for all”; the supplied Greek reading is uncertain].]

But one thing is what is performed externally, and another is what is believed through faith: that which belongs to the senses of the body is corruptible; but what faith believes is incorruptible.

> **[Note: [Col. 0160D]** What appears externally, therefore, is not the thing itself but the image of the thing; whereas what is received and understood by the mind is the truth of the thing. It is impossible to express more fittingly and accurately the faith of the Church, which teaches us that the veils and what is subject to the eyes in this mystery are not the body of Jesus Christ itself—the thing itself—which, concealed beneath veils and coverings, has joined to itself the power of the divine Word. Through that power it nourishes the soul and supplies it with the substance of eternal life, namely, grace and the remission of sins, as has often been said above. For all the testimonies of blessed Augustine set forth above tend toward this.]

What appears externally, therefore, is not the thing itself but the image of the thing; whereas what is perceived and understood by the mind is the truth of the thing.

### LXXVIII

Hence blessed Augustine, in his *Exposition of the Gospel of John* (tractate XXVI), speaking about the body and blood of Christ, says:

> “Moses also ate manna, Aaron also ate it, Phinehas also ate it, and many there ate who pleased God—and they died. Why? Because they understood the visible food spiritually; they hungered spiritually; they tasted spiritually, so that they might be spiritually satisfied. For we too today receive visible food; but the sacrament is one thing, and the power of the sacrament another.”

Again, later he says:

> “This is the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:59). “This bread was signified by the manna; this bread was signified by God’s altar. Those things were sacraments; they differ in their signs, but in the reality that is signified they are equal. Hear the Apostle: ‘I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink’” (1 Cor. 10:1–4). “Spiritual indeed, and the same; not bodily, however, for they had manna and we have something else, but spiritual—the same as ours.”

And he adds:

> “And all drank the same spiritual drink. Something different for them, something different for us, but in visible form; nevertheless, it signified the same thing by spiritual power. For how did they drink the same drink? ‘They drank,’ he says, ‘from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ.’ From the same source came the bread as the drink. Christ was the rock symbolically; the true Christ is in the Word and in the flesh.”

### LXXIX

Again:

> “This is the bread coming down from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he will not die.”

But this concerns the power of the sacrament, not the visible sacrament: the one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; the one who eats in the heart, not the one who presses it with his teeth.

### LXXX

Again, introducing the Savior’s words later on, he says:

> “Does this offend you, because I said, ‘I give you my flesh to eat and my blood to drink’? What, then, if you should see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?” (John 6:62–63).

What does this mean? From this point he resolves what had troubled them; from this point he opened up the matter at which they had taken offense. For they thought that he was going to distribute his body; but he said that he would ascend into heaven, certainly whole and entire: “When you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before.”

Surely then you will see that he does not distribute his body in the way you imagine; surely then you will understand that his grace is not consumed by bites. And he says:

> “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (ibid., 64).

### LXXXI

After inserting several intervening passages, he adds again:

> “But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ,” says the same Apostle, “does not belong to him” (Rom. 6:9). “It is the Spirit, therefore, who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:64).

What does “they are spirit and life” mean? They are to be understood spiritually. If you have understood spiritually, they are spirit and life. If you have understood carnally, they are still spirit and life—but they are not so for you.

### LXXXII

On the authority of this teacher, who is treating the Lord’s words concerning the sacrament of his body and blood, we are clearly taught that the Lord’s words are to be understood spiritually and not carnally, just as he himself says:

> “The words that I speak to you are spirit and life.”

These are plainly the words concerning the eating of his flesh and the drinking of his blood. For he was speaking of the very matter at which the disciples had taken offense. Therefore, so that they would not be offended, the divine Teacher draws them back from the flesh to the spirit, from bodily sight to invisible understanding.

### LXXXIII

[Note: “We see, therefore,” etc. That is, not in the carnal manner in which ordinary foods and drinks are consumed.]

We see, therefore, that this food of the Lord’s body and this drink of his blood exist as truly his body and truly his blood in a particular respect—namely, insofar as they are spirit and life.

### LXXXIV

Again, things that are the same are included under one definition. Concerning Christ’s true body it is said that he is true God and true man: God, begotten before the ages from God the Father; man, born at the end of the age from the Virgin Mary.

[Note: These things cannot be said of the body of Christ that is enacted in the Church through the mystery—that is, insofar as it is outwardly expressed and subjected to the senses. This is Ratramnus’s meaning, and he intends to prove nothing else, as is clear from the following words of this section: “It cannot be said, in a certain manner, that it is known to be Christ’s body; and this manner consists in figure and image, so that the reality itself may be perceived.”]

Yet when these things cannot be said of Christ’s body that is enacted in the Church through the mystery, it is nevertheless known, in a certain manner, to be Christ’s body; and this manner consists in figure and image, so that the reality itself may be perceived.

### LXXXV

In the prayers that are said after the mystery of Christ’s body and blood, to which the people respond “Amen,” the priest says:

> “Receiving the pledge of eternal life, we humbly implore that we may receive with manifest participation what we touch in the image of the sacrament.”

[Note: “Receiving the pledge of eternal life,” etc. A vernacular interpreter who wrote these words in French from the Latin rendered them badly in 1672: *Recevant le gage de la vie éternelle, nous te supplions de nous faire la grâce de participer rêeliement à ce que notre main reçoit sous l’image du sacrement*—“Receiving the pledge of eternal life, we beg you to grant us the grace to participate truly in what our hand receives under the image of the sacrament.”

The Latin reads: *Pignus aeternae vitae capientes, supplicamus ut ea gratia nos donari velis qua participemus REALITER ea quae recipit manus nostra sub imagine sacramenti*—“Receiving the pledge of eternal life, we beg you to grant us that grace by which we may participate REALITER [really] in what our hand receives under the image of the sacrament.”

For this reason, calling attention to the word so that it might be explained, he added an asterisk above it and wrote opposite it in the margin of the book this note: “that is, *realiter*.” I, however, maintain that this is a clear corruption of the text of the prayer as Ratramnus transmitted it.

First, because no reading preserved in ancient manuscripts can establish that the word *manifesta* was not adopted to signify a clear disclosure or open knowledge of any object.

Second, because this prayer was copied from the Sacramentary of Pope Gelasius, book II, at the post-communion for the feast of the octave of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. A few years ago Angelus Bernabo published it at Rome, in 1680, from the manuscript of the most illustrious Alexander Petavius, counselor of the august Senate of Paris and by then of the most serene Christina, queen of the Swedes. The manuscript had been written nine hundred years earlier, according to the judgment of the most learned John Morin, priest of the Oratory of Jesus, in his excerpts from an ancient Penitential, p. 52.

The same interpretation was adopted by the very learned Joseph Maria Thomasius of the Theatine order. The learned republic of letters owes him the greatest thanks for publishing the same manuscript. In book I, pp. 27 and 34, he teaches us that this prayer is addressed to God in order to obtain or acquire knowledge of the things hidden in the mystery of the Eucharist and believed by faith:

> “Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, to Christian peoples both to recognize what they profess and to love the heavenly gift that they frequent.”

The same meaning is readily understood from the preface of the Mass given in the same book, p. 91:

> “We humbly beseech you that we may be able to comprehend the manifest gifts of Jesus Christ our Lord, whose pledge we receive.”

Third, the use of this same prayer has been received in most churches for many centuries, with certain variant readings that do not impair the common faith of the churches. They confess that the word *manifesta* is to be understood as manifestation or disclosure, since *manifestata participatione*—“with manifested participation”—is read in place of *manifesta participatione*—“with manifest participation.”

This can readily be seen in the ancient Missals of the very ancient primatial and metropolitan church of Sens, which are used today with the greatest piety and devotion, without knowledge of novelties, in editions printed in 1485, 1509, 1529, 1542, 1556, and 1575.

The same is understood from two manuscript Missals that I believe were written between the twelfth century and the end of the thirteenth, since they mention the feast of Saint Thomas of Canterbury while omitting the celebration of—or perhaps preceding the institution of—the feast of Corpus Christi:

> “Receiving the pledge of eternal life, we humbly implore, O Lord, that, supported by apostolic patronage, we may receive, with manifested participation in the sacrament, what we have touched in image.”

(*Sacramentary of Gelasius*, at the post-communion for the octave of the apostles Peter and Paul, on the day before the Nones of July, book XI, p. 160, published at Rome in 1680 by the printer Angelus Bernabo. Ancient and modern Missals of Sens. The Ambrosian Missal has the same reading.)]

“Receiving the pledge of eternal life, we humbly implore that we may receive with manifest participation in the sacrament what we touch in image.”

### LXXXVI

For both a pledge and an image belong to another thing; that is, they look not toward themselves but toward something else. A pledge is given in place of the thing for which it is given; an image belongs to that whose likeness it displays. These things signify the reality to which they belong, but they do not manifestly display it.

[Note: Since this is so, it follows more clearly than daylight that the flesh and blood seen in the mystery are a pledge and image of a future reality, so that what is now set before our eyes through an expressed image may, once the screens and veils have been drawn aside, be openly and clearly disclosed to our senses.

Who could now find room for doubt that Ratramnus is thinking here of the outward part of the sacred mystery subjected to the senses? Certain theologians of his age considered this part to be the very appearance of Christ’s body and the manifestation of Jesus Christ’s body. On the contrary, as our Ratramnus says in section 9, it is the appearance of bread and the form of wine that previously existed.

In the following section he proves that this part subjected to the senses is called Christ’s body, its pledge and figure being a future manifestation of the aforementioned body of Christ with all its geometrical dimensions. Taking these into account, he establishes a complete distinction between the body celebrated by the Church and the body itself that we shall behold in heaven. “For this reason,” he says, “what the Church celebrates is both the body and blood of Christ, but as a pledge, as an image. The reality will appear when there is no longer a pledge or an image, but the reality of the thing itself” (section 87).

There can be no doubt that Ratramnus repeatedly and immediately understood from the word “reality” the body of Christ subjected to the senses and visible with geometrical dimensions and the other characteristics of a human body, with which Christ’s glorified body will be adorned in heaven after human beings have risen again.

That this was his own opinion is perfectly clear from section 87. There he explains the prayers of the Church in which we humbly ask God that, as a propitious deity, he may perfectly confer upon us what his sacraments contain:

> “Perfect in us, O Lord, we beseech you, what your sacraments contain, so that what we now enact in form we may receive in the reality of things.”

From these words of the prayer he understands that we possess the things themselves under an expressed image, though they are not absolutely disclosed to us as they truly exist in themselves. It is entirely true that we possess these realities under expressed images, and it is clear that what is lacking is only their complete disclosure.

The entire difference between Christ’s body in the mystery of the Eucharist and that same body in heaven, the body that was crucified, consists in this: one will be disclosed to us, while the other will remain concealed—thus, the difference lies in the manner of existence and not in nature or existence itself.

Indeed, it would have been better for him to say, instead of “what we now enact in form, may we receive in the reality of things,” “what we now truly do not have, may we at some time truly and actually perceive.”

It is therefore certain that Ratramnus held no other position than that of the true Catholic disciples who opposed Berengar—namely, Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury. In his *Dialogue against Berengar*, speaking of the mystery of Christ’s body, he says:

> “It may truly be said both that it is the very body taken from the Virgin and yet that it is not the very body: the same, insofar as essence, the property of true nature, and power are concerned; but not the same if you consider the appearance of bread and wine.”

The same view is held by Algerus in book I, chapter 17; by Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, in letter 11 to Finardus; and by Rupert, abbot of Tuy, in his *Letter to Cuno*. All of them embraced and defended the faith that we hold concerning the truly existing body of Christ in the Eucharist and the transformation of bread and wine into flesh and blood, that is, transubstantiation.]

Since this is so, it is evident that this body and blood are a pledge and image of a future reality, so that what is now shown by likeness will in the future be disclosed through manifestation. If they signify now but will disclose in the future, what is enacted now is one thing, and what will be manifested in the future is another.

### LXXXVII

For this reason, what the Church celebrates is both the body and blood of Christ, but as a pledge and as an image. The reality will be present when there is no longer a pledge or an image, but the reality of the thing itself appears.

### LXXXVIII

Again, elsewhere:

> “Perfect in us, O Lord, we beseech you, what your sacraments contain, so that what we now enact in form we may receive in the reality of things.”

[Note: Mass on the Saturday of the Ember Days, in the seventh month. *Book of the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory*, p. 135, edited by Hugh Menard.]

He says that these things are enacted in form, not in reality—that is, through likeness, not through the manifestation of the thing itself. Form and reality differ from one another. Therefore the body and blood enacted in the Church differ from that body and blood recognized as already glorified in Christ’s body. The former is a pledge and form; the latter is the reality itself. The former will be enacted until they reach the latter; when they have reached it, the former will be removed.

### LXXXIX

It is therefore evident that things are separated by a great difference, as great as that between the pledge and the thing for which the pledge is given,

[Note: And as great as that between form and reality. Apart from this passage, nothing else is needed to demonstrate to all people who have not exceeded the powers of their minds that, by “form,” Ratramnus in this treatise *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* understood nothing other than an expressed image or the outward part of the Eucharist; and by “reality,” he understood the natural mode of Jesus Christ’s body, subject to the senses, with its properties and geometrical dimensions.

For what doubt could arise upon hearing these words?

> “We see, therefore, that the mystery of Christ’s blood and body, which is now received by the faithful in the Church, and that which was born of the Virgin Mary, which suffered and was buried, are separated by a great difference” (section 89).

These words clearly confirm what we have already abundantly said. The conclusion that follows from them is that Christ’s body, which according to Ratramnus is only figure, veil, expressed image, pledge, and form, differs from the body of Christ born of the Virgin Mary, dead and buried. In that condition it possesses all its natural properties, subject to the senses and sight, as well as its dimensions.

By contrast, in the mystery it is received by the mouths of the faithful without those properties and dimensions, spiritually and through faith. By faith we believe that beneath these veils subjected to the senses the true body of Christ is received by us, hidden beneath them and concealed, and that united or joined to it is the power of the Word, which supplies our souls with the substance of eternal life, nourishes them, and cleanses and removes the stains of sins.

According to Ratramnus’s teaching, therefore—as we may perhaps already have noted at excessive length—two bodies of Christ must be distinguished in the Eucharist. One is present in figure, form, or image; the other is hidden beneath the veils and forms. Both are received by the mouths of the faithful spiritually, because through the power of faith the one is believed to be concealed beneath the other. Thus, whichever of the two you see, you always receive both, because faith believes that one is hidden within the other; and in receiving one, the power of the Holy Spirit attached to it communicates eternal life to our souls.

The first is called “mystery” and “sacrament,” and is the body of Christ by designation, as Algerus says in book I, chapter 17, distinct from Christ’s body born of the Virgin.

The second does not differ from him and is not other than he is. Rather, in reality it is the true body of Christ itself, but concealed, neither veiled nor breakable or torn into pieces by the teeth; in a word, it is in a condition lacking physical properties and geometrical dimensions, although it remains in its proper nature and substance, into which the bread and wine have been changed. This is what Ratramnus calls Christ’s own body.]

and as great as that between the image and the thing of which it is the image, and as great as that between form and reality.

We see, therefore, that Christ’s mystery of blood and body, which is now received by the faithful in the Church, is separated by a great difference from that which was born of the Virgin Mary, suffered, was buried, rose again, ascended into heaven, and sits at the Father’s right hand.

For this thing enacted here on the way is to be received spiritually, because faith believes what it does not see; it spiritually nourishes the soul, gladdens the heart, and gives eternal life and incorruption. It does not attend to what feeds the body, what is pressed by the tooth, or what is broken into pieces, but to what is received spiritually in faith.

But that body in which Christ suffered and rose again is his own body, taken from the body of the Virgin Mary, tangible and visible even after the resurrection, as he himself said to his disciples:

> “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

### XC

Let us also hear what blessed Fulgentius says in his little book *On the Faith* (chapter 19):

> “Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that the only-begotten God the Word, having become flesh, offered himself for us as a sacrifice and victim to God as a pleasing fragrance. To him, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, animals were sacrificed by patriarchs, prophets, and priests during the time of the Old Testament. And to him now, that is, in the time of the New Testament, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, with whom he has one divinity, the holy Catholic Church throughout the whole world does not cease to offer the sacrifice of bread and wine in faith and charity.

> “In those carnal victims there was a sign of Christ’s flesh, which he himself, without sin, was to offer for our sins, and of the blood that he was to pour out for the remission of our sins. In this sacrifice, however, there is thanksgiving and commemoration of the flesh of Christ, which he offered for us, and of the blood which he shed for us.

> “Concerning this, blessed Paul the Apostle says in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood’” (Acts 20:28).

> “In those sacrifices, therefore, what was to be given to us was signified figuratively; but in this sacrifice what has already been given to us is clearly shown.”

### XCI

When he says that in those sacrifices what was to be given to us was signified, but that in this sacrifice what has been given is commemorated, he plainly indicates that, just as those sacrifices had the figure of future things, so this sacrifice is a figure of past things.

[Note: Just as those sacrifices were figures of future realities, so this sacrifice is a figure of past realities. Since the Lord Christ instituted the sacrifice of the Eucharist in memory of his death and passion, the doctrine of the Catholic Church has always been that the mystery of the Eucharist is a figure of the sacrifice of the cross.

But Ratramnus does not say that it is merely a figure, as the Protestant heretics claim for themselves. He proves only that there is a figure in it—namely, in what appears outwardly. But he openly acknowledges that something else exists inwardly, to be understood by faith.

Section 92 says:

> “This is mystical: outwardly displaying one thing through figure, and inwardly representing another through the understanding of faith.”

And in section 49 he says:

> “They truly exist as the body and blood of Christ.”

Here, then, are two perfectly clear things in the Eucharist: one outward, namely, the figure; the other inward, which is the object of faith and truly is the body and blood of Jesus Christ.

But since the object of faith in the Eucharist is not simply present in figure, it must be acknowledged that the body of Christ which we believe to be in the mystery, and which is the object of faith, does not exist there merely and solely in figure. Our Ratramnus was therefore always entirely alien to the position of the Protestants.

Indeed, the participle *repraesentans*—“representing”—does not here mean what the verb *exhibere* means: to present and set before us, or effectively to make and render a thing present. For example, when Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the Second Philippic:

> “Indeed, I would gladly have offered my body, if liberty could be restored to the state through my death,”

he did not intend that his death would be a mere image or empty representation devoid of Roman liberty, but that liberty would be effectively and truly restored through his death and fall.

Nor can anyone deny that this is Ratramnus’s genuine meaning, since, in opposition and parallel to this participle *ostentans*—“displaying”—he uses *repraesentans*—“representing”—to express the character of a figure, which simply forms an image and does not actually render anything present effectively.]

Just as those sacrifices had the figure of future things, so this sacrifice is a figure of past things.

### XCII

By these statements he has made perfectly clear how great the difference is between the body in which Christ suffered and this body which exists for the commemoration of his passion or death. The former is proper and real, having in itself nothing mystical or figurative; the latter is mystical, displaying one thing outwardly through figure and representing another inwardly through the understanding of faith. (See section 91.)

### XCIII

Let us set forth one further testimony of Father Augustine, which both establishes the truth of our statements and sets a boundary to our discussion. In a sermon that he preached to the people concerning the sacrament of the altar, he begins as follows:

> “What you see on God’s altar you also saw last night; but what it was, what it signified, and how great a reality its sacrament contained, you have not yet heard. What you see, therefore, is bread and a cup, as your own eyes also tell you. But what your faith, which must be instructed, demands is this: the bread is Christ’s body, and the cup is Christ’s blood.

> “This has been stated briefly, in a way that perhaps suffices for faith; but faith desires instruction. For the prophet says: ‘Unless you believe, you will not understand’ (Isa. 7:9). You may therefore say to me: ‘You have commanded us to believe; explain it so that we may understand.’

> “A thought such as this may arise in someone’s mind: We know where our Lord Jesus Christ received his flesh—from the Virgin Mary, of course. He was nursed as an infant, nourished, and grew; he reached young manhood; he suffered persecution from the Jews; he was suspended on the wood; he was killed; he was taken down from the wood; he was buried; on the third day he rose again. On the day he willed, he ascended into heaven; he lifted his body there; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead; now he sits there at the right hand of the Father. How, then, is the bread his body? And how is the cup, or what the cup contains, his blood?

> “These things, brothers, are called sacraments for this reason: in them one thing is seen and another understood. What is seen has a bodily form; what is understood has a spiritual fruit.”

### XCIV

By saying this, the venerable authority instructs us what we ought to think both of the Lord’s own body, which was born of Mary, now sits at the Father’s right hand, and in which he will come to judge the living and the dead, and of that which is placed upon the altar and shared with the people.

The former is whole and undivided; it is divided by no cutting and covered by no figures. But this which is contained upon the Lord’s table is also a figure, because it is a sacrament; and what is seen outwardly has a bodily form that nourishes the body.

[Note: But what is understood inwardly has a spiritual fruit that gives life to the soul. The meaning is not that what is understood inwardly is a spiritual fruit, but that it has a spiritual fruit.

For Christ’s body, which is truly present beneath the veils subjected to the bodily senses—namely, beneath the forms of bread and wine—does not nourish the soul through the conversion of its substance in the way that ordinary foods nourish and sustain our bodies. Rather, it does so through the power of the divine Word, joined to it and multiplied by an infinite increase of graces; fostering innocence, it grants and produces the remission of sins.]

But what is understood inwardly has a spiritual fruit that gives life to the soul.

### XCV

And wishing to speak more openly and clearly about this mystical body, he says in what follows

[Col. 0168B] (ibid., at the end; the letter of Saint Fulgentius to the deacon Fernandus):

> “If you wish to understand the body of Christ, hear the Apostle saying: ‘You are the body of Christ and members of it’ (1 Cor. 12:27). Your mystery is placed upon the Lord’s table; you receive your mystery. To what you are, you respond, ‘Amen’; and by responding, you subscribe to it.

> “You hear, then, ‘The body of Christ,’ and you respond, ‘Amen.’ Be a member of Christ’s body, so that your Amen may be true. Why, then, in bread? Let us bring nothing of our own here; let us hear the Apostle himself speaking of this sacrament. He says: ‘Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body in Christ’ (1 Cor. 10:17),”

and so forth.

### XCVI

Saint Augustine sufficiently instructs us that, just as Christ’s body is signified in the bread placed upon the altar, so also the body of the receiving people is signified. Thus he clearly shows that Christ’s own body is that in which he was nursed, in which he suffered, in which he died, in which he was buried, in which he rose again, in which he ascended into heaven, in which he sits at the Father’s right hand, and in which he will come to judgment.

[Note: “But this which is placed upon the Lord’s table,” etc. He repeats the same point in section 98:

> “But in this which is enacted through the mystery, there is a figure not only of Christ’s own body but also of the people who believe in Christ.”

He does not say that in this body which is possessed through the mystery there is only a figure of Christ’s own body, as though it were no more than a solitary figure of the faithful people. Rather, he says that the figure of both Christ’s body and the faithful people is present. This is sufficient for Ratramnus to establish what he intends to prove: namely, that everything present in the mystery is not merely what is subjected to and appears before our eyes, but that, in addition, an imposed figure and expressed image are present.

Meanwhile, since he recognized that these modes of speaking and writing might seem to some people harsher and more difficult, and that placing the true body of Jesus Christ under such an interpretation would make it as alien to the Eucharist as the body of the people themselves, he explains his meaning in section 101 as follows:

> “And because we say these things, no one should suppose that in the mystery of the sacrament of the Lord’s body his body or blood is not received by the faithful.”

It should also be observed that he calls the body into which Christ changed the bread and wine at the institution of this sacrament his own body—the body that was to suffer—as is stated above in section 28:

> “Thus, shortly before he suffered, he was able to change the substance of bread and the created substance of wine into his own body, which was to suffer.”

No learned person can entertain the slightest doubt that Ratramnus was persuaded and believed that Jesus Christ’s own body—the body born of the Virgin and affixed to the cross—exists in the mystery of the Eucharist, although he maintained that whatever is subjected to our eyes in this sacrament and is called Christ’s body is its simple figure, expressed image, and representation—not in Cicero’s sense, as we observed above, but in the usage accepted by deteriorated Latin.

For that reason he says, in continuous discourse, that the name “body of Christ” was imposed upon the bread, and the name “blood” upon the liquid—or the wine mixed with water—in the chalice, and that they truly exist. Thus we understand that, in his view, Jesus Christ’s body did not subsist in the Eucharist merely through designation or naming, but truly and effectively—or, as others immediately said, really.

See section 99. Let us add also that this bread and cup, which is named and exists as Christ’s body and blood, are mentioned repeatedly in the preceding section 29. But according to the invisible substance—that is, through the power of the divine Word—they truly exist as Christ’s body and blood.

We frankly admit that the adverb *vere* there sounds in Latin like what the barbarous word *realiter* signifies. Nevertheless, the Protestants will say that the words *et existit*—“and exists”—do not occur in the manuscript codices on whose authority this treatise of Ratramnus was prepared for printing. But they cannot deny that they are found in the manuscript codex of the Abbey of Lobbes, as the very learned Father Mabillon had already observed in the preface to the second part of the *Acta Benedictinorum*, p. 64, §130, placed at the beginning.

The reading written in the Lobbes manuscript is wonderfully confirmed as admissible by the fact that the same Ratramnus used it in section 16. There, distinguishing the forms of bread and wine from the body and blood of Jesus Christ, which are hidden and concealed beneath the veils in a spiritual manner not subjected to the senses, he says, together with Paschasius in his letter to Frudgard:

> “Because beneath the covering of bodily bread and bodily wine there exists the spiritual body of Christ and the spiritual blood of Christ.”

Moreover, no room for doubt remains that the manuscript codex of the Abbey of Lobbes ought to be preferred to all the others, given its antiquity and elegance, as we noted in the preface.]

But this which is placed upon the Lord’s table contains the mystery of Christ’s body, just as it repeatedly contains the mystery of the body of the believing people, as the Apostle testifies:

> “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body in Christ.”

### XCVII

Let your wisdom, most illustrious prince, observe that, once the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures and the sayings of the holy Fathers have been set forth, it has been demonstrated with complete clarity that the bread which is called Christ’s body, and the cup which is called Christ’s blood, are a figure because they are a mystery; and that there is a considerable difference between the body that exists through the mystery and the body that suffered, was buried, and rose again.

For this latter is the Savior’s own body. In it there is no figure or signification, but the manifestation of the reality itself is recognized, and believers long to behold it. It is our head, and when it is seen our desire will be satisfied—he in whom the Father and the Son are one, not according to the body that the Savior possesses, but according to the fullness of divinity that dwells in the man Christ.

### XCVIII

But in that which is enacted through the mystery there is a figure not only of Christ’s own body but also of the people who believe in Christ (see section 116). For it bears the figure of both bodies: of Christ’s body, which suffered and rose again, and of the people reborn in Christ and given life from the dead.

### XCIX

Let us also add that this bread and cup (see section 96), which is named and exists as Christ’s body and blood, represents the memory of the Lord’s passion or death, just as he himself said in the Gospel:

> “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19).

Explaining this, the Apostle Paul says:

> “Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. 11:26).

### C

We are taught by the Savior and by Saint Paul the Apostle that this bread and this blood, which are placed upon the altar, are placed as a figure or memorial of the Lord’s death, so that what was done in the past may be recalled to present memory; and so that, having been made mindful of that passion, we may through it become sharers in the divine gift by which we have been freed from death.

We recognize that, when we have reached the vision of Christ, we shall have no need of such instruments to remind us what immense goodness endured for us. For when we contemplate him face to face, we shall not be moved by an external reminder involving temporal things, but through contemplation of the truth itself we shall see how we ought to give thanks to the author of our salvation.

### CI

And because we say these things, no one should suppose that, in the mystery of the sacrament, the Lord’s body or his blood is not received by the faithful (see section 96). Faith receives not what the eye sees but what it believes, because this is spiritual food and spiritual drink, nourishing the soul spiritually and granting the life of eternal satisfaction.

Thus the Savior himself speaks in commending this mystery:

> “It is the Spirit who gives life; for the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:64).

### CII

Desiring to obey the command of your greatness, I, a small man, have presumed to discuss matters of no small importance. I have not followed the presumption of my own judgment, but have looked to the authority of my predecessors.

If you approve these things as expressed in a Catholic manner, attribute the credit to the merits of your faith, which, laying aside the glory of royal magnificence, was not ashamed to seek an answer concerning the truth from one who is humble.

But if they have pleased you less, let that be attributed to my foolishness, which was not sufficiently capable of explaining what it desired.

# Dissertation on the Book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*
