By James Boileau, theologian of Paris. The book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* is asserted to be by Ratramnus and is defended against John Hardouin, priest of the Society of Jesus, as free from every suspicion and invention of novelty or Calvinist heresy.

When, in the year 1689, a theological writer of the Society of Jesus published at Paris, from the press of François Muguet, bookseller to the Most Christian King and the illustrious Archbishop of Paris, a letter of Saint John Chrysostom to the monk Caesarius, to which he added notes and a dissertation on the sacrament of the altar, he persuaded himself—whether by an opportunity given or seized, through a counsel unknown and inconceivable to me—that the priest Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, was not the genuine author of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, written eight hundred years earlier and addressed to the emperor Charlemagne or Charles the Bald. With all his strength he then undertook to prove that this book existed polluted by many lapses into heresy and stained, indeed profaned, by the reproach of errors.

When I, for my part, perceived that such a dissertation-writer had seen fit to attack and demolish the arguments by which I had freed Ratramnus’s persuasion or faith from every suspicion of heresy and had expunged all the reproaches directed against the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*—in the Latin-and-French edition produced through my own study and care at Paris, at the house of Jean Boudot under the Golden Sun in 1686, which I had adorned with an apologetic preface and enlarged with additions to the notes—I applied myself to writing this response. In it I undertook to establish two propositions that have always seemed to me not merely probable but absolutely certain: namely, that Ratramnus is the true and sincere author of this book, and that it cannot be defiled by any reproach of heresy or error.

Rise, therefore, learned reader, and, setting opinions aside—opinions that have for the most part already occupied the minds of theological writers, both learned and unlearned, concerning this matter—judge this case. I make this pledge: I shall never appeal from your judgment.

The best kind of evidence for attributing and adjudicating a book to its author is drawn from ancient manuscripts in which the author’s name is prefixed—manuscripts that are genuine, not fabricated, and not adulterated either above or below. Among the learned, titles or inscriptions of this kind appear to be the cardinal authorities and decisive instruments of the case and dispute; nor do rights supported by them perish through the passage of time.

There is, however, no room for doubt that such autograph codices were written and transcribed in Ratramnus’s own age and attributed to him, since they are found adorned with his name. From an eight-hundred-year-old copy belonging to the Abbey of Lobbes, whose use was granted me by the most learned Mabillon, an illustrious monk of the Order of Saint Benedict—distinguished by his sincerity and lofty humility in diplomatic scholarship and most skilled in distinguishing genuine from false manuscript codices—I published the text together with a French translation. Mabillon mentions another manuscript, seven hundred years old, belonging to the Abbey of Salem-Weiler, in his *German Journey*; Ratramnus’s name is likewise inscribed in it.

Moreover, unless such documents are proved to be forged, they cannot be disparaged or contradicted. Since, therefore, the dissertation-writer does not place the manuscript codices inscribed with Ratramnus’s name under suspicion of forgery, he must necessarily appear to have voluntarily surrendered the opportunity of contradicting or refuting them.

The most illustrious Peter de Marca, Archbishop of Paris, whose opinion the dissertation-writer, struck by its novelty, willingly adopted, had neither seen such manuscript codices nor understood that they still existed. In fact, he would not have persisted in the opinion that the treatise *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* had falsely been attributed to a man named Ratramnus, nor would he have vindicated it for John Scotus in his letter to Dom Lucas Dacherius, the most learned and illustrious monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the year of Our Lord 1659, if such codices had reached his ears. Of so great a man—so learned and of so good a reputation among scholars—this is a very credible supposition.

For my part, I reasonably believe that he returned to his former opinion, or rather to the defense of his former opinion, as can easily be understood from the treatise *On the Eucharist* published by his associate and kinsman, the Abbot Faget, and from the free confession made by the aforesaid prelate to Dom Lucas Dacherius before he addressed that celebrated letter to him, published in the second volume of the *Spicilegium*. The most learned Mabillon left no room for doubt concerning the sincerity of this most illustrious prelate in the preface to the second part of the fourth century of the *Benedictine Centuries*, p. 45, § 6. There, in words whose authority admits no exception, he explains the man’s mind from this confession:

> “Dacherius had asked what the most learned prelate thought about this book of Ratramnus. He replied that he thought well of it; but when asked to state his opinion, he went over to the other side.”

Furthermore, with what appearance of truth could John Scotus assume the person and mask of Ratramnus, a man perhaps still living and well known and familiar among scholars—one who could easily have denied the charge, checked the insolence, torn away the mask, and reproached him for falsehood? What protection could he secure for himself under a concealed name when the Emperor Charles the Bald was publicly inquiring into the learned men’s opinions concerning Christ’s body in the Eucharist? When Catholic men held differing opinions, with no one accused or accusing another of the crime of heresy, why was there any need to release into public circulation a pseudonymous, anonymous writing under a fabricated name?

These facts are clearer than midday from the second section of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, from which we understand that this entire controversy took place among faithful and Catholic men. Yet when, two hundred years after Ratramnus’s book had been published, the heresy of Berengarius arose—he having given his name to such a sect—its adherents brought out John Scotus’s book in support of their cause, but never said that the name Ratramnus or Bertramus, instead of John Scotus, had been attached to the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. Nor did the Catholic men who undertook to defend the Catholic faith against Berengarius object to any such alteration or inscription of the name.

Indeed, certain Catholic writers, out of humility, formerly sent their works into the public under concealed names. This happened with the author of the books *On the Imitation of Christ*, with the books *On the Sacraments* of Saint Ambrose, with the *Commonitorium* of Vincent of Lérins, and with many others. Such concealment of names gave rise to the inscription and substitution of false names, and from this arose innumerable entanglements among learned men and empty conjectures about many authors in the minds of people.

But scarcely had the art of printing been discovered when a practice was deliberately developed of attaching fabricated names in place of genuine ones; and learned cuckoos began laying their eggs in another bird’s nest. Before those times, pseudonymous writers were a difficult invention, with few exceptions, although anonymous writers were not lacking—namely, writers who concealed their own names and imposed a false and supposititious one on their works. Indeed, in the history of antiquity one scarcely finds anything besides the *Apology of Origen*, which, although inscribed with the name of the martyr Pamphilus, is believed by most to be by Eusebius of Caesarea.

Everyone agrees that the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was written at the command of the Emperor Charles the Bald, and that its author was a learned man in whom lofty humility contended with wisdom, whose opinion concerning this mystery the king had asked. Moreover, with attentive mind and will, he takes precautions lest he put forward anything of his own, but everywhere brings forth and breathes the judgments of the Fathers.

What, then, had he to fear, and what reason was there for attaching a fabricated name to a work filled with so many judgments of the Fathers? What advantage was there in concealing the identity of a man writing at the emperor’s prompting and command? None of this suits John Scotus. It would also be improbable and unbelievable that he had invented and appended the claim that he had been compelled to write the book by imperial command. No sane man’s sense of shame has ever been so completely lost that, while a king and emperor was still alive, he would dare publicly to pretend that he was writing on the supreme matter of religion at the command of a great prince, bringing himself into imminent danger and risking his life and reputation, or at least enduring the accusation of forgery—a charge that would pass beyond every limit of impudence.

It also seems the product of an imaginative brain to suppose that the name Bertramus was transformed into Ratramnus by copyists or scribes at the end of the ninth or beginning of the tenth century. At that time the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, whether heretical or Catholic, circulated in everyone’s hands. If it was Catholic, why would John Scotus need to release it under a concealed name? But if it was regarded as tainted with heresy, by what plausible reasoning could the name of an author distinguished by eminent service to the Catholic religion be inscribed on it—a man most illustrious for holiness and learning, namely Ratramnus, monk and priest of Corbie and, as Flodoard reports, Abbot of Orbais, through whose assistance the Gallican bishops had thought the Church of the West should be defended against the Greeks, and who had vigorously defended Saint Augustine’s doctrine of predestination at the command of Charles the Bald, King of France?

It is therefore necessary to admit that this fiction and imposition of Ratramnus’s name cannot be defended in the book *On the Blood of the Body of Christ* except by a reckless critic. From this it follows above all that Erigerus cannot be credited with having called Ratramnus the author of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* in the eleventh century because of this supposed transformation of the name Bertramus into Ratramnus. For no such statement ever appears among Erigerus’s genuine works, nor does it occur in any ecclesiastical writer of the eleventh century, when the disputes and controversies of Berengarius were contested and renewed; mention of this book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* is everywhere absent and buried in the deepest silence.

In fact, the anonymous writer published by Cellot, a theologian of the Society of Jesus, in an appendix to the *History of Gottschalk*, expressly lists Ratramnus among the opponents of Paschasius, Abbot of Corbie. But there is a great difference between this anonymous writer and Erigerus. On the contrary, Erigerus himself wrote against Paschasius, as we understand from the continuator of the Chronicle of the Abbey of Lobbes, who copied these words from the Chronicle of Sigebert, Abbot of Gembloux:

> “Erigerus also collected many writings of the Catholic Fathers concerning the Body and Blood of the Lord against Radbertus.”

These words may be seen in volume VI of Dacherianus’s *Spicilegium*, fol. 591.

Nor was Sigebert deceived by any transformation or mixture of the names Bertramus and Ratramnus, as the dissertation-writer claims. Sigebert, a writer of the twelfth century, attributed this book *On the Body and Blood of Christ* to its true and genuine author in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*—namely, explicitly to Ratramnus—which appears clearly to have been expressed on the authority of ancient manuscript codices.

Indeed, if some manuscript codices of Sigebert should be found in which the name Bertramus appears instead of Ratramnus, they are more recent and commercial productions. I do not think the dissertation-writer read this anywhere except in printed copies of Sigebert produced carelessly and without fidelity.

From these points it is easy to understand how weak the dissertation-writer’s criticism is when, on page 166, he imagines that Paschasius Radbertus, Abbot of Corbie, intended to signify the author of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* in these words from his letter to Frudgard:

> “Although some err through ignorance concerning this, no one yet openly contradicts that this is so, which the whole world believes and confesses.”

The dissertation-writer interprets these words as follows:

> “By these words, he doubtless indicates that a certain volume was known to him whose author would not dare to meet his opponents γυμνῇ κεφαλῇ—‘bareheaded,’ as they say—but would proceed masked. Paschasius wrote this letter around the year 860.”

But if Paschasius truly wrote this letter to Frudgard in the year 860, it is improbable that he was referring to Ratramnus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, since that book was evidently composed about fifteen years after this date, at the time when Charles the Bald attained the imperial authority of the West. This is clear from the title of the book’s preface, which reads:

> “To Charles the Great, Emperor.”

This title occurs in the ancient manuscript codices on whose authority the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was first printed in 1532.

For from all the chronicles we understand that Charles the Bald, the person designated by this title, did not attain the imperial authority before the year 875, when he was crowned by Pope John VIII after defeating by force of arms King Louis of Germany, called the German. Louis died at Frankfurt on 28 August of the following year, 876. It is also agreed by everyone that Charles the Bald reigned as emperor for only two years, dying on 6 October 877.

It is therefore abundantly clear how rashly the dissertation-writer was led into error when he maintains that Paschasius wrote the letter to Frudgard in the year 860. For by that time several more years had elapsed since Paschasius’s death than had elapsed before the event that must have occurred prior to the year 853—namely, the succession of Odo, Abbot of Corbie, who subscribed to the second Council of Soissons and had succeeded Paschasius.

The dissertation-writer may perhaps say that Paschasius resigned the administration of the Abbey of Corbie in the year 852 or 853 and had not yet died. But however the matter may stand, he will not prove that Paschasius lived beyond the year 859 or 860. It will therefore be even clearer that Ratramnus’s book could not have entered Paschasius’s mind in his letter to Frudgard, since it was composed only under the reign of Charles the Bald, to whom it was inscribed under the title “To Charles the Bald, Emperor”—that is, between the year 875, when Charles attained the imperial authority, and 877, when he was killed by poison administered to him by his physician Zedekiah.

From this it follows clearly how wrongly the dissertation-writer has persuaded himself that Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, mentioned this book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, which we vindicate for Ratramnus, in the year 859, in book I of his work *On Predestination*, chapter 21, p. 232. There he expressly says that it was not Ratramnus but John Scotus whom everyone openly and publicly regarded as the author of the propositions that Hincmar had undertaken to refute.

Moreover, the statements that Hincmar had transcribed in his book *On Predestination* against the faith of the Church from the teaching and book of John Scotus do not occur at all under the name of Ratramnus in the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. For where, in Ratramnus, are these statements—or their meaning—known?

1. That the Godhead is threefold.

2. That angels are corporeal by nature; that the human soul is not in the body.

3. That the sacraments of the altar are not the true body and blood of the Lord, but only a memorial of his true body and blood.

In fact, Ratramnus says in sections 99 and 100:

> “That this bread and cup, which is named and exists as the body and blood of Christ, represents the memorial of the Lord’s passion, just as he himself said in the Gospel: ‘Do this in remembrance of me.’”

This is wholly true and entirely consonant with the Catholic faith. Ratramnus does not say that it is not the true body; rather, he says that it is named and exists as the body and blood of Christ. Nor does he say that it is only a memorial, for the monstrous poison of heresy lies precisely in the word “only.”

Furthermore, lest Catholic men take offense at Ratramnus’s words, he immediately and prudently avoids every poison and evil of heresy, saying:

> “Nor, because we say these things, should it be supposed that in the mystery of the sacrament the body of the Lord or his blood is not received by the faithful, since faith receives not what the eye sees but what it believes.”

Indeed, if what the eye sees is not received in the Eucharist—or if it is not believed to be received—but what faith believes is received, then it is necessarily to be believed that the true body of Christ is received. For faith believes that the true body of Christ exists there: it is named as such and exists as such.

Moreover, Hincmar observes that the propositions he refutes were, in his own age, openly attributed, without anyone objecting, to John Scotus and Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes, but not at all to Ratramnus, whose virtue and faith, ignorant of sordid heresy, shine with unstained honors. Read Hincmar’s *On Predestination*, chapter 21, p. 350:

> “The authors of these propositions,” he says, “or rather those who contend with themselves, and in certain matters attack the truth, are said by many to be Prudentius the bishop and John Scotus.”

The dissertation-writer is no more justified by reason or right when, on page 167, he persuades himself that Adrevald, a monk of Fleury in the time of Charles the Bald, uncovered the face or removed the mask of the author of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* in a short work written for that purpose against the absurdities of John Scotus and reported in volume XII of Dacherianus’s *Spicilegium*.

Adrevald’s short work, written in the time of Charles the Bald, was composed either before he assumed the imperial authority or afterward. If before, Adrevald could not have removed the mask from a book that had not yet been completed. If afterward—that is, between the years 875 and 877—how could he have removed the mask? For, according to the dissertation-writer, no one at that time could have doubted that the author of the book was John Scotus; and Adrevald himself wrote not against the absurdities of Ratramnus or Bertramus, but expressly against those of John Scotus.

Furthermore, if Ratramnus had been the author of the absurdities that Adrevald refutes under the name of John Scotus, such absurdities ought to be found, either wholly or in part, in Ratramnus’s book. Yet they nowhere meet the eye of a careful reader. Adrevald therefore did not even have Ratramnus’s book—or the book we defend, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*—in mind.

The dissertation-writer says, however, that in the time of Berengarius the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was known under no other name than that of John Scotus. The solitary Sigebert, he adds, once again attributes it to Bertramus.

The answer is easy: Berengarius’s followers did not bring Ratramnus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* out in support of their error, but only John Scotus’s book, as being more favorable and useful to Berengarius’s errors.

Moreover, in the same continuous argument the dissertation-writer adds, in order to prove that the work attributed to John Scotus really belongs to Ratramnus and ought to be assigned to him, the letter of the monk Ascelinus to Berengarius, transcribed and published among Dom Lucas Dacherius’s notes to the *Life of Lanfranc*, Archbishop of Canterbury, p. 25. There he maintains that the following words designate the book of Ratramnus that we defend:

> “I take up John Scotus neither thoughtlessly, nor impiously, nor in a manner unworthy of my priesthood. I see him directing all his effort and entire intention solely toward persuading me of this: that what is consecrated on the altar is not truly Christ’s blood.”

But it is as unjust as it is disgraceful to attribute such an opinion to Ratramnus, especially since he never spoke in this way. Nothing seems farther from ordinary human understanding than to imagine and construct a man who does not believe that what is consecrated on the altar is truly the body and truly the blood of Christ, yet who persuades himself—and has no doubt—that through the mystery of the Eucharist bread and wine are changed into the substance of his body and blood and are to be received by the faithful.

What does the faith of the Church teach us? What do we believe and confess by that faith? Is it not that, through the mystery of the Eucharist, the bread and wine consecrated on the altar are truly changed into the substance of Christ’s body and blood and are received and taken by the faithful?

Our Ratramnus, or Bertramus, said precisely this with his mouth and wrote it with his hand in the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, section 30:

> “Then you will understand that my flesh is not to be eaten by believers as unbelievers imagine—that is, as he teaches above in the same section, not to be distributed and torn apart in pieces, fragment by fragment, but truly, through the mystery, bread and wine changed into the substance of my body and blood are to be received by the faithful.”

It is incredible, inconceivable, and wholly ἀδύνατον—“impossible”—unless every law of natural and rational equity is to be violated, that a man who does not believe that what is consecrated on the altar is truly the body or truly the blood of Christ should sincerely believe that, according to an invisible substance—that is, through the omnipotence of the Word—the body and blood of Christ truly exist on the altar. These propositions contradict one another so completely that they appear utterly incapable of existing together in an undisturbed mind.

Yet the final words explain Ratramnus’s mind completely, since they are transcribed from section 49 of the same book. Read:

> “From all that has been said thus far it has been shown that the body and blood of Christ, which are received by the mouths of the faithful in the Church, are figures according to their visible appearance. But according to their invisible substance—that is, through the power of the divine Word—they truly exist as the body and blood of Christ.”

He repeats the same point in section 99:

> “Let us add that this bread and cup, which is named and exists as the body and blood of Christ…”

But so that nothing may be lacking from our additional proofs, I gladly ask the dissertation-writer whether he can imagine a man who utterly rejects the faith of the Catholic Church—who persuades himself that what is consecrated on the altar is neither truly the body nor truly the blood of Christ—yet considers it impious not only to deny that the body and blood of Christ are present in the Eucharist, but even to think such a thing.

These propositions are no less contradictory and incompatible. Nevertheless, there is no room for doubt that Ratramnus expressly says in section 15:

> “They are compelled to deny that it is the body and blood of Christ, which it is impious not only to say but even to think.”

Since this is so, it is clearer than midday that the book of John Scotus mentioned by Ascelinus in his letter to Berengarius must in no way be attributed to Ratramnus, but must be restored to its author, John Scotus Erigena.

The dissertation-writer replies that what occurs in John Scotus’s book recurs word for word in Ratramnus’s book, section 88, as is easily understood from Ascelinus’s letter:

> “He endeavors to establish this—that it is neither truly the body nor the blood—on the basis of the little works of the holy Fathers that he expounds. It is enough here to note that prayer of Saint Gregory: ‘May your sacraments, O Lord, we beseech you, accomplish in us what they contain, so that what we now perform in outward appearance we may one day receive in the truth of the thing itself.’ In expounding this, the aforesaid John says among other things contrary to our faith: ‘These things are performed in appearance, not in reality.’ If I know your vigilance well, you do not fail to recognize that this is not a Catholic statement.”

The dissertation-writer could easily have omitted this fragile objection. This prayer from Saint Gregory’s Sacramentary is indeed read verbatim in Ratramnus, but he brought it forward in defense of the Catholic meaning and in a sense utterly alien to John Scotus’s opinion.

For John Scotus defended from these words—“what we now perform in outward appearance, we may one day receive in the truth of the thing itself”—the claim that Christ’s body exists only figuratively, and that its existence, reality, and substance are not at all found in the Eucharist. Ratramnus, however, derives from this prayer a meaning wholly different and opposed to that.

He believed that the body and blood truly exist in a figure—that is, beneath the veil and curtains of an invisible appearance—but not in a figure alone. By the words “we may receive in the truth of the thing itself,” he understood the manifestation and open disclosure of Christ’s body and blood, free and devoid of every figure.

For this reason he explains Saint Gregory’s prayer as follows:

> “He says that these things are performed in that appearance, not in reality—that is, through a likeness, not through the manifestation of the thing itself.”

If John Scotus had added the words “through a likeness, not through the manifestation of the thing itself,” Ascelinus would never have accused him of heresy. For the word *truth* suffers from a certain ambiguity, that is, equivocation, as we observed in the preface to this work of Ratramnus.

It signifies not only the existence of a thing that may remain beneath figures, veils, and coverings, but also a disclosure or manifestation incompatible with every figure, trope, veil, or covering. Therefore, in order to explain the sense that he had undertaken to defend from Saint Gregory’s prayer, Ratramnus adopted another prayer in section 75 from the Gelasian Missal, in which these words are read:

> “So that what we touch in the image, we may receive through the manifest participation of the sacrament.”

John Scotus did not produce this prayer, which was unsuitable and inconvenient to his position. Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury and a most vigorous defender of the Catholic faith against Berengarius, adopted the Catholic meaning that Ratramnus attached to the word *truth*, as we understand from his *Dialogue against Berengarius*, where we read:

> “The priest asks that the body of Christ, which is now performed under the appearance of bread and wine, may one day be received through manifest vision as it truly is; for in sacred writings ‘truth’ is found in the sense of manifestation.”

Who, then, would say that the words of John Scotus are found in Lanfranc’s book in precisely the same syllables?

The dissertation-writer presses his argument beyond what it can bear when he claims that Berengarius, in his letter to Lanfranc, says that John Scotus’s opinion was opposed to Paschasius and would be opposed to Saints Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine, or to anyone who wished to oppose John Scotus; and that Ratramnus’s work had no difference from John Scotus’s book, since Ratramnus cites the same Fathers—namely, Augustine, Jerome, and Ambrose.

He also adds that Erigena lists Ratramnus among Paschasius’s opponents. But what of it? Nothing prevents John Scotus’s opinion from being opposed to Paschasius while Ratramnus taught a position consistent with Paschasius. Indeed, it is highly probable that this is how the matter stands.

Furthermore, if Ratramnus’s citation of Augustine, Ambrose, and Jerome means that he does not differ from John Scotus, then Lanfranc will agree with Berengarius, Sanctesius with Calvin, and Perronius with Plessis-Mornay. Is it permissible to abuse reason and common sense so intemperately?

There might perhaps be some basis for such reasoning and conjecture if Ratramnus brought forward no Fathers other than Augustine, Jerome, and Ambrose. But he also expressly cites Saint Isidore of Seville in sections 40, 45, and 47; Saint Fulgentius in section 89; the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory in section 88; and the Gelasian Missal in section 85. Apart from the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory, none of these is mentioned by John Scotus.

Moreover, Erigerus did not say that Ratramnus was an opponent of Paschasius. This was said by Cellot’s anonymous writer, whom it is unjust to confuse with Erigerus. Even if, in some manuscript perhaps five hundred years old, the anonymous work bears Erigerus’s name, a better argument must be found before attributing to a wise man and deserving member of the Church so futile and empty a work.

Finally, on page 168 the dissertation-writer says that Berengarius, in his letter to Richard, reported in volume II of Dacherianus’s *Spicilegium*, says that John Scotus wrote at the prompting and request of Charles the Bald, under whose command many also believe Ratramnus wrote around the year 855—a year in which the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* reported that many things contrary to the Catholic faith occurred in Charles’s kingdom, without Charles himself being unaware of them.

There are several easy answers to this.

**I.** Since requests and commands differ greatly, the book of John Scotus must also differ greatly from that of Ratramnus, since John Scotus wrote at Charles’s prompting and request, whereas Ratramnus wrote by command. Ratramnus’s book begins with these words: “You have commanded, glorious prince.” From Berengarius’s letter we understand that John Scotus wrote at the prompting and request of the emperor.

Ratramnus, a humble monk hidden in the darkness of his cloister, obeys the emperor’s and king’s commands and comes forth into the light. John Scotus, exalted by a doctor’s pride, yields to the prince’s admonitions and entreaties.

**II.** The heresies that agitated the state in the year 855, which the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* mention, could not have arisen from Ratramnus’s book. Since that book was inscribed to Charles the Bald as emperor—“To Charles the Great, Emperor”—it could not have been completed and released into the light before the period between the years 875 and 877, when Charles the Bald’s imperial rule ended, since this title is copied from ancient manuscript codices as “To Charles the Bald, Emperor.”

Yet the dissertation-writer immediately says on the same page that the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was condemned at the Councils of Vercelli and Paris in the year 1050 and finally burned at the Roman Council under Nicholas II in 1059, with the name of John Scotus inscribed on it. He says that by that time the true author had been identified and recognized, and that for this reason only very few copies survived under the name of Ratramnus or Bertramus, since during the period of those councils the substituted name had been recognized as false. He adds that for this reason the book was not seen under the name of Ratramnus before the year 1526, until which time there had been a profound silence among everyone concerning it.

If matters are so, let the dissertation-writer tell us how it could have happened that so many councils and so many illustrious men—Lanfranc, Ascelinus, Durandus—were so completely lulled into silence that they passed over this ἐτερωνυμία, this “different naming,” without comment; that they did not reproach John Scotus for so outrageous a substitution of names; and that they did not vindicate the memory of Ratramnus, a learned and pious man who had deserved infinitely well of the Gallican Church, from the reproach and disgrace of such heresy.

For my part, I confess that I cannot understand how the dissertation-writer persuaded himself that, after copies of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* had been burned, it was not seen before the year 1525 under the name of Bertramus or Ratramnus. For Sigebert, in the twelfth century—namely, forty years after the Roman Council—lists the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* under the name of Ratramnus among Catholic and orthodox writings. Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, in the fifteenth century, does the same in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* and repeats Sigebert’s testimony.

Earlier, the Cellotian Anonymous—or, as the dissertation-writer thinks, Erigerus—identifies Ratramnus as the author of the same book. John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, does so as well, in the very year 1526. Nothing, therefore, is farther from the truth than the dissertation-writer’s assertion that until the year 1526 there had been a profound silence among everyone concerning this book under Ratramnus’s name.

Moreover, if anyone reads attentively John Scotus’s books *On Predestination* or *On the Division of Nature* (*Περὶ φύσεων μερισμοῦ*), he will notice such a great difference in style and will find so many Greek Fathers, mystics, and ascetics cited—of whom no trace or furrow can be discerned in Ratramnus’s books—that it seems both outrageous and superfluous to assign the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, circulated under Ratramnus’s name, to John Scotus Erigena.

Nevertheless, I cannot pass over one point which appears altogether decisive for this controversy. For it is established that John Scotus considered Christ’s body after the resurrection neither perceptible to the senses and tangible nor corporeal, as we understand from Book V of *The Division of Nature*, p. 293, no. 37:

> “Whoever examines more carefully the statements of Saint Ambrose and Gregory the Theologian will certainly find that they teach not a transformation of an earthly body into a heavenly body, but an altogether complete passage into spirit itself—not into that which is called ether, but into that which is called intellect.”

For Ambrose removes every composition, so that after the resurrection body, soul, and intellect are one and the same, one simple thing, not compounded from three; and what here appear to be three become there one intellect. Gregory likewise, and without hesitation, asserts a transformation at the time of the resurrection: of body into soul, of soul into intellect, and of intellect into God; and thus God will be all in all, just as air is changed into light.”

And in no. 38 of the same book:

> “If, then, Christ’s flesh has been transformed into the power of God and into the spirit of incorruption, plainly that flesh itself is power and incorruptible spirit. And if the power of God is spirit, it is everywhere—not only beyond places and times, but also beyond everything that exists. No one can doubt, therefore, that this very flesh, transformed into power and spirit, is contained in no place and changed in no time; but that, like the power and spirit of God—that is, the Word, which He had also received into unity with His substance—it universally surpasses all places and times and every limitation.”

Who, then, would attribute such opinions to the author of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*—an author who teaches things wholly contrary and diametrically opposed to them, and who, especially in no. 30, places these words in Christ’s mouth:

> “When, after the resurrection, you shall see me about to ascend into heaven, with the fullness of my entire body or blood.”

And in no. 99:

> “That body in which Christ suffered and rose again is truly his own body, taken from the body of the Virgin Mary, tangible and visible even after the resurrection, just as he himself says to his disciples: ‘Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have.’”

There is therefore no need to dwell on these matters any longer; rather, it is fitting to proceed lightly and calmly in defending and vindicating the credibility and orthodoxy (*ὀρθοδοξίαν*) of this book.

The dissertationist says, on p. 166 and p. 288, in the inner column of the new Amsterdam edition, no. 166:

> “I greatly wonder that, after this book, which is attributed to Ratramnus, has recently been marked with a censure by the Tridentine censors and the supreme pontiffs, some men have nevertheless been found in this age willing to undertake its defense.”

## RESPONSE

If the dissertationist finds it so astonishing that certain theologians have undertaken to defend Ratramnus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, even though it was censured and consigned to the Index of Prohibited Books by the examiners appointed by the Council of Trent and by the Roman pontiffs themselves, his astonishment will be increased by the ancient Latin Mass which Matthias Flacius Illyricus recently had printed at Strasbourg. Indeed, it first came to public light through the assistance of a heretical man, just as Ratramnus’s book did, and it was likewise entered by the examiners of the Council of Trent in the Index of Prohibited Books, as can easily be seen in the second appendix to the Index. Nevertheless, today that Mass of Illyricus is regarded as Catholic and orthodox by all learned ecclesiastical writers, while even the Protestants reject it as strongly contrary and opposed to their own doctrines.

Its credibility and orthodoxy (*ὀρθοδοξίαν*) were vindicated by the most eminent Cardinal Bona in *Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chapter 12; Bona also arranged for a new edition in the appendix to *On Liturgical Matters*. Father Pierre Cointius, priest of the Oratory of Jesus, likewise arranged a more corrected and carefully revised edition in the *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, just as we have faithfully and carefully reproduced a more corrected edition of Ratramnus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* from an ancient manuscript.

The same Latin Mass was censured by the Spanish inquisitors under Philip II, at the instigation of Ferdinand of Toledo, Duke of Alba—a man not merely ardently devoted to the Catholic religion but actually raging with that zeal. The Jesuit Famianus Strada says that he was cast from the mouths of war engines at Antwerp and cast back into the same war engines.

There is therefore nothing astonishing if the works of learned men, judged and condemned by judges of such tribunals, to whom no infallibility has been handed down from heaven, require assistance and defenders. Among the writings of the most illustrious and learned Claude d’Espence, doctor of theology at Paris, which would have been admitted among the purple-robed Fathers had wicked counsels not prevented it—as D. Jacques-Auguste de Thou and Espence himself testify—his commentaries on the Epistle to Titus and his treatise *On Continence* stand out above the rest. They are filled not only with the highest learning but also written in a spirit of counsel and courage against the abuses and vices by which nearly everyone in that age was disfigured. Yet the treatises of so great a man unfortunately figure in the Index of the examiners of the Council of Trent together with our Ratramnus and the Latin Mass of Illyricus, though they remain no less worthy of esteem among all learned men.

Nor can there be any doubt that our dissertationist himself would count Espence among Catholic doctors who are complete in every respect of doctrine and faith. I would gladly ask the dissertationist whether he thinks that the Articles of the Gallican Clergy concerning ecclesiastical authority, presented to the Most Christian King in 1682—which he certainly knows were condemned by Innocent XI—could be defended. Would he endure, whether fairly or unfairly, the censures issued by the Faculty of Paris against Vernantius or Amadeus Guymenius being condemned? Would a defender of such censures cause him astonishment? Yet everyone knows that these censures were not only placed in the Index of Prohibited Books but also forbidden and proscribed by Pope Alexander VII in an authentic bull issued at Rome against them, under penalty of automatic excommunication, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July in the year 1665, the eleventh year of Alexander VII’s pontificate.

No author’s books were more harassed by censure than those of Origen Adamantius. More than once, indeed many times, pontiffs and even general councils proscribed Origenist doctrines. Nevertheless, the Jesuit Peter Halloix of Liège, a man of no humble intellect, defended Origen in a large folio volume of the same thickness as the major books and pleaded his case before Pope Innocent X. Four celebrated Jesuits, distinguished for piety and learning, approved this defense of Origen and examined it in obedience to the command of R. P. Carafa, superior general of the entire Society, at the Roman College in 1646. Finally, this defense of Origen was published at Liège in 1648 with the permission of the visitor of the provinces of Flanders, England, and Gallo-Belgium.

Nevertheless, the defended Origen entered the path of the universal Inquisition at Rome and obtained a highly honored place in the Index of Prohibited Books—but a still more honorable place in the libraries of the Jesuits; for nowhere does he crawl along in the series of prohibited books.

Finally, the famous book of the Jesuit Luis de Molina, *On the Harmony of Grace and Free Will*, condemned by the University of Salamanca on 22 July 1595 and declared dangerous and erroneous by the bishops of Spain, is defended every day by several Jesuits and by more than a few theologians of no mean reputation. The same is true of Cardinal Bellarmine’s books *On the Roman Pontiff*, as reported by another Jesuit, Jacques Fuligati, in chapter 11 of his *Life of Robert Bellarmine*.

Since these things are so, there is no doubt that books marked with censure and judicial decisions remain subject to re-examination, or can be referred to a renewed judgment; and thus cases that have fallen into a state of decay may be restored to the course of judicial proceedings. This is of no concern to the Church or to religion: it has always been, and always will be, permissible to vindicate certain authors from the accusation of violated faith. Indeed, nothing prevents us from clearing the letters of Pope Honorius I from the insult of the Monothelite heresy.

By this right Facundus, bishop of Hermiane in Africa, vigorously and forcefully defended the Three Chapters in favor of Ibas of Edessa, Theodore of Mopsuestia, and Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus; by the same right we undertake to defend Ratramnus’s doctrine. Molina and Bellarmine, once thrust into the Index of Prohibited Books, easily obtained release from it. But if we confine our arguments to refuting the calumny by which Ratramnus’s reputation and name have been stained, arguments that are probable and strong enough to establish the truth, it is far more astonishing that Ratramnus found unjust judges than that he found favorable defenders.

## THE DISSERTATIONIST’S WORDS

“Indeed, it will soon be said that he had long ago been condemned by plenary synods and by the universal Church and committed to the flames, and that more recently, in the preceding age, he was detected openly teaching heresy by the most illustrious and learned bishops Sanctesius of Évreux and Perronius, cardinal and archbishop of Sens.”

## RESPONSE

We certainly do not deny that a book under the title *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was condemned at the Council of Vercelli under Leo IX and burned at Rome under Nicholas II in the year 1055. But we absolutely deny that Ratramnus or Paschasius was the author of this book, since it is known to everyone that the book which was burned bore the name of John Scotus without anyone objecting, and that it was circulated under that name by the followers of Berengar in support of their errors.

For the rest, Cardinal Perronius and Sanctesius yielded to the common opinion of the writers of their age. Allowing themselves to be overly influenced by the very empty arguments of Protestant men, they rashly and excessively persuaded themselves that this book was favorable to the errors of the Calvinists. Yet this does not prevent the book from rightly deserving defense and patronage, since the dissertationist himself undertakes to defend the letter of Saint Chrysostom to the monk Caesarius, which Cardinal Perronius considers a spurious work fabricated by Peter Martyr Vermigli, a Florentine heretic, in favor of Calvinism, just as Perronius himself and Sixtus of Siena had thought Ratramnus’s book was fabricated by Oecolampadius.

This can easily be seen in Perronius’s treatise *On the Eucharist*, pp. 381–383, and in the *Bibliotheca* of Sixtus of Siena. The dissertationist differs from Ratramnus’s defenders in one further respect, which should not be passed over in silence: he was the first person in the Christian world to defend the doctrine of this letter to the monk Caesarius, and he confers the right of authenticity upon a work regarded by all learned men as suspect of being spurious and illegitimate; he vindicates it for Saint Chrysostom, who wrote in Latin rather than Greek, and assigns it to him despite his not inconsiderable resistance.

By contrast, numerous ecclesiastical writers, illustrious by right of learning and piety, have upheld the orthodoxy (*ὀρθοδοξίαν*) of Ratramnus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, both before and after Cardinal Perronius. Among them were John Fisher, the most illustrious martyr of Christ; Sigebert, abbot of Gembloux, in the twelfth century; John Trithemius of Sponheim, in the fifteenth; the doctors of Louvain after the Council of Trent; Jacob Gretser; Antonio Possevino; Gilbert Mauguin; Godefridus Hermannus, a doctor and associate of the Sorbonne, under the name Jerome ab Angelo Forti; Jacobus Samboevius, royal professor of sacred theology at the Sorbonne; Dom Jean Mabillon, the most learned monk of Saint Benedict; and countless other Parisian theologians who, in their theses, furnished the innocence and integrity of Ratramnus with the strongest support both before and after the Latin-French edition with a preface and notes which we arranged in 1686.

Among these I shall not hesitate, in honor, to name the distinguished Pierre Berthe, associate of the Sorbonne, already the most skilled librarian of our Sorbonne and the highly esteemed rector of the University of Paris, in the thesis which our predecessors called the minor ordinary thesis, dedicated and inscribed to Louis the Great in the name of the University of Paris. It was presided over and signed, with the authority proper to the president and moderator of the disputation, by the most illustrious and reverend François de Harlay, archbishop of Paris, commendatory officer of the royal orders, provost of the Sorbonne, and director and superior of the royal college of Navarre, on 20 September 1685. In it these words are transcribed in column 6:

> “Therefore neither Anastasius Sinaita nor Damascene among the Greeks, nor Paschasius—or his verbal opponent, Ratramnus—in the work of his that survives, introduced anything new; rather, just as they vigorously defended the faith, so they preserved it wholly undefiled.”

What remains, then, except that I should set the dissertationist himself against himself and restrain or moderate his astonishment? For although he considers that Cardinal Perronius’s authority concerning Ratramnus’s book should be obeyed so readily, he vehemently resists and contradicts him concerning the heresy of the Stercoranists, and, setting aside Perronius’s reputation and eminence, he fully embraces our judgment concerning the fictitious nature of this heresy on p. 171 of his dissertation.

Everything we have said up to this point concerns, in general terms, Ratramnus’s person and the author of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. We must now examine the doctrine of this book and free it from every suspicion of heresy, and consequently vindicate it from every insult.

## I

The dissertationist says, p. 174 of the first edition, line 8:

> “Ratramnus indicates both in the preface and at the conclusion of his book that he is revealing not what the Church teaches, but what he privately thinks.”

## RESPONSE

On the contrary. When the emperor ordered him to write his opinion concerning the body and blood of the Lord in the Eucharist, he openly professed that he wished to take nothing from his own private resources, but always to cling to the footsteps of the holy Fathers and not depart from the furrows traced out by the ancients, or by his forebears. This is clear from the words recorded in no. 5, which require neither commentary nor expanded explanation:

> “I shall attempt to disclose what I think about this, relying not on my own ingenuity but following the footsteps of the Fathers.”

And at the conclusion, no. 102:

> “Desiring to obey the command of Your Greatness, I, a small man, have presumed to discuss matters of no small importance—not following the presumption of my own judgment, but looking to the authority of my forebears.”

## II

From the fact that Ratramnus admits in no. 30 that he has many opponents, the dissertationist argues that he disputed against the doctrine of the Church.

## RESPONSE

Let us grant that Ratramnus admits this. But the multitude of his opponents consisted of those who maintained that there was no figure, but that everything was openly manifested in the Eucharist. This opinion is altogether erroneous, opposed equally to Paschasius and Ratramnus, and contrary to all the ancient doctors of the Church.

This is abundantly clear from the words of no. 32:

> “Here now arises the question which very many put forward when they say that it occurs not in figure but in truth—that is, manifestly. Those who say this are demonstrably contradicting the writings of the holy Fathers.”

But what then? Does not Paschasius also admit that he has many opponents, just as Ratramnus does? We understand this from the following words of his letter to Frudgardus, p. 1625:

> “Nevertheless, I have stirred up many toward an understanding of this mystery.”

And at the beginning of the same letter, p. 1619:

> “For you ask about a matter concerning which many are in doubt.”

In the same letter Paschasius expressly agrees with Ratramnus, namely on p. 1620, letter E, where he appears to have copied Ratramnus’s text from this no. 32:

> “And therefore, if anyone says that this flesh and this blood are simply and literally what they are, without mystery and sacrament, and that they are not to be taken in part as a figure—as those carnal people then understand carnally—he destroys everything.”

It is therefore difficult to understand what advantage the dissertationist derives from no. 52 in attempting to prove that Ratramnus opposed the Catholic Church.

## III

For this reason the dissertationist continues in the same uninterrupted argument, p. 175:

> “First, then,” he says of Ratramnus, “in no. 8 he distinguishes figure from truth insofar as something other than what is said is understood in a figure. Thus Christ is not the vine, nor the apostles the branches, even though the sacred writings give them those names. And when Christ is said to have been born or to have suffered, he is understood to have truly suffered and truly been born. This, he says, is truth in a narrative—that is, the bare and open meaning of the words. Since he denies there and throughout the work, especially in no. 32, that what is on the altar is truly the body of Christ, and says that it exists only in the figure of a mystery, he denies that the words ‘body of Christ’ have their bare and open meaning; he denies that what is said should be understood as signifying anything other than the body which you see.”

## RESPONSE

Such a circuit of words is unnecessary, nor is it necessary to extract oil from flint in order to perceive what Ratramnus means by figure and truth. He makes his meaning perfectly clear in nos. 7 and 8:

> “Figure,” he says, “is a kind of shadowing forth, displaying something under certain coverings. For example, when we wish to speak of a word, we call it bread, just as in the Lord’s Prayer we ask for our daily bread. Truth, however” (no. 8), “is the manifest demonstration of a thing, covered by no images of darkness, but conveyed by pure and open—and, to speak more plainly, natural—significations, as when it is said that Christ was born of a Virgin, suffered, was crucified, died, and was buried.”

Consequently, when in no. 32 and elsewhere Ratramnus says that certain people persuade themselves that Christ’s body is in the Eucharist not in figure but in truth, he must be referring to people who believed that there was no shadowing, veil, or figure at all in the Eucharist, but that everything was manifest and clear.

The question Ratramnus was discussing was not whether Christ’s body truly or really—as theologians say—existed in the Eucharist, or whether it existed only figuratively. No one seemed to have any doubt about that doctrine. Rather, the question was whether it was presented and divided manifestly and clearly before the eyes, without a veil, trope, figure, or shadowing; or whether the true body, existing secretly and concealed beneath shadows or figures, came before the eyes.

We understand that Charles the Bald proposed precisely this question to Ratramnus for examination from no. 5:

> “Your Excellence asks whether the body and blood of Christ which is received by the mouths of the faithful in the Church occurs in mystery or in truth—that is, whether it contains something hidden which is disclosed only to the eyes of faith, while the bodily appearance which the external sight beholds is, without any covering of mystery, the same as what the sight of the mind beholds internally, so that everything being done shines forth in the light of manifestation.”

Thus, when Ratramnus repeatedly denies that Christ’s body is in the Eucharist “in truth,” he does not thereby deny the real presence. He denies only a visible presence that enters the human senses—one that is clear and manifest and wrapped in no coverings, cloths, veils, or figures.

In this he is not distant from the mind and opinion of Saint Paschasius. For, as Ratramnus says in no. 49:

> “According to the invisible substance—that is, according to the power of the divine Word—there truly exist the body and blood of Christ.”

In no. 77:

> “What appears externally, therefore, is not the thing itself but an image of the thing; but what is perceived and understood by the mind is the truth of the thing.”

In no. 15:

> “It is not lawful to deny that it is the body of Christ—not merely to say so, but even to think so.”

And in no. 30:

> “Then you will understand that my flesh is not to be eaten by believers as unbelievers suppose, but that, through the mystery, bread and wine have truly been changed into the substance of my body and blood and are to be received by believers.”

Paschasius likewise teaches that figure and truth remain in this sacrament, in almost the same words, in Book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 4, p. 1564:

> “Truth, therefore, is present when Christ’s body is made through the power of the Spirit in his Word from the substance of bread and wine; but figure is present when the priest, bearing externally something else, sacrifices daily on the altar, in remembrance of the sacred Passion, the Lamb who was sacrificed once. But if we examine the matter truthfully, it is rightly called both truth and figure: figure or character of the truth is what is perceived externally; truth is whatever is rightly understood or believed inwardly concerning this mystery.”

Paschasius and Ratramnus, therefore, did not hold different and conflicting opinions, nor did they fight against one another. Even if Paschasius believed that there was some figure in the Eucharist, he was nevertheless Catholic. That Ratramnus too was Catholic is beyond doubt. He never said that Christ’s body was present in the Eucharist only in figure, as the dissertationist falsely attributed to him on p. 175. The dissertationist himself invented the word “only”; nowhere does it occur in the furrows of Ratramnus’s entire learned work.

## IV

“Therefore,” says the dissertationist, “he denies that it can truly be said: ‘This which you see on the altar of God is truly the body of Christ which was born of the Virgin.’ He expressly denies this in nos. 50, 59, and 101.”

## RESPONSE

Even if there is one substance in the Eucharist—as Ratramnus says in no. 16—and even if there are not two existences of mutually different things, nevertheless Christ’s body itself cannot be said to be seen in the Eucharist or presented to the sense of the eyes. Paschasius and all Catholics acknowledge this.

Even if Ratramnus had roundly denied that Christ’s body is seen in the Eucharist, he would thereby have incurred no criticism. For what is seen in the Eucharist is visible; but Christ’s true body, which truly exists in the Eucharist beneath visible species, is not in itself presented to sight. Therefore what is seen in the Eucharist is not Christ’s body, since that which is visible and can enter the senses is not Christ’s body but the veil, shadow, covering, and figure which conceals and hides Christ’s body.

Everyone knows that Christ’s body in the sacrament surpasses the grasp of the senses and the eyes, because it is spiritual and wholly spiritual, as Paschasius says. Only dimension, whiteness, taste, and odor are perceived by the senses—unless one should approve the opinion of certain recent philosophers, which R. Father Magnan of the Order of Minims of Saint Francis of Paola has discussed at length.

[Note: Appendix to the *Sacred Philosophy*.]

Magnan believed that God, through the concurrence which he had supplied to the bread before consecration, continued afterward to exercise the same motion upon the eyes, or to produce the same impression, which the bread and wine had produced before consecration. Or unless one should approve the opinion of the distinguished D. Rohault, a Cartesian philosopher, in a book written in the vernacular, in which he teaches that, since Christ’s body occupies in its entirety the place formerly occupied by the body of the bread, and is bounded by the same surface—that is, terminated by the same *περιφέρεια*, or circumference—it must affect the eyes in exactly the same way as the bread affected them before consecration.

If the matter were so, without a doubt the whiteness and roundness which are seen would be Christ’s body itself, which would be seen and would enter the eyes. But, unless I am mistaken, the dissertationist does not find this opinion pleasing. Rather, he favors another scholastic subtlety: he persuades himself that, since what truly exists—or lies hidden and concealed—in the sacrament is Christ’s true body, or rather the very substance of Christ’s body, that which is seen is likewise Christ’s body itself.

But the answer is easy. The substance of Christ’s body truly exists in the Eucharist, but it does not therefore become subject to our eyes and senses, since in a wondrous manner, superior to the powers of nature, it remains hidden from them and cannot in any way be perceived by the senses.

It remains to inquire how Ratramnus expressly denied in nos. 50, 52, and 101 that the body which is on the altar is the very body that was born of the Virgin. I deny, and emphatically deny, that Ratramnus ever denied in these passages that the body hidden in the Eucharist is the body born of the Virgin, which suffered and was buried.

But it must be frankly acknowledged that, when considered under different aspects, he establishes a significant distinction between the same body as it is celebrated in the Church through the mystery and its proper body—that is, the body endowed with its bodily properties—which was born of the Virgin Mary, fastened to the cross, buried, afterward wondrously restored to life, and ascended into heaven.

This is not difficult to understand from no. 88, where he says:

> “Therefore, the body and blood which is enacted in the Church differs from that body and blood which is recognized in Christ’s glorified body; this body is a pledge and likeness, whereas that is the truth itself.”

In no. 89:

> “We therefore see that the mystery of Christ’s body and blood, which is now received by the faithful in the Church, is separated by a great difference from that body which was born of the Virgin Mary, which suffered, which was buried, which rose again, which ascended into heaven, and which sits at the right hand of the Father.”

In no. 97:

> “It has been demonstrated most clearly that the bread which is called Christ’s body and the cup which is called Christ’s blood are a figure because they are a mystery, and that there is no small difference between the body which exists through the mystery and the body which suffered, was buried, and rose again.”

These are the words which the dissertationist ought to have transcribed from Ratramnus’s writings with some show of reasoning. From them he could have proved, without violating the laws of dialectical reasoning, that Ratramnus did not believe that the body celebrated in the Church was the very body formed in the Virgin’s womb, fastened to the cross, buried, and afterward restored to life.

It is therefore useful to introduce this point into the dissertationist’s mind and submit to his understanding this distinction concerning the same body, while the Catholic faith concerning the presence of Christ’s true body and blood in the Eucharist remains untouched and unimpaired.

No one can doubt that Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury and the strongest opponent of Berengar—at whose urging Berengar recanted his errors and burned his books before Pope Nicholas II in the year 1059—was a true and outstanding defender of the Catholic faith, endowed with a faith placed beyond every suspicion. Yet he says the following in his *Dialogue against Berengar on the Eucharist*:

> “It can truly be said to be both the body taken from the Virgin and yet not that very body, insofar as essence, the property of true nature, and power are concerned—but not if you consider the appearance of bread and wine.”

If such words were found in Ratramnus, they would move the dissertationist to the breaking point. It is enough that Ratramnus introduced some distinction between one body and another. He never said that it was not the very body taken from Mary.

But Blessed Algerus, an excellent defender of the faith against Berengar, seems to speak still more appropriately in accordance with Ratramnus’s mind, Book I of *On the Eucharist*, chapter 17:

> “Christ’s blood and flesh,” he says, “are understood in two ways: either that spiritual and divine flesh of which he himself says, ‘My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink’; or that flesh which was crucified and that blood which was poured out by the soldier’s spear. It must be believed that this was not said with reference to a double substance, but with reference to the double form of the same substance, which is now understood under the human form of bread and wine.”

A little farther below in the same chapter:

> “The species and likeness of those things are the names which existed previously—namely, bread and wine—not the body of Christ. The body and blood of Christ are now called by appellation, in the manner of speech by which the thing signifying is accustomed to be called by the name of the thing signified.”

And in chapter 18:

> “It has already been said above concerning the sacrament of bread and wine that it signifies and is called, by appellation, the body of Christ.”

That the true invisible body of Christ after the resurrection is the sacrament of Christ’s visible body in his Passion is attested by Augustine in the *Book of Sentences of Prosper*:

> “His flesh is that which we receive in the sacrament, covered by the form of bread; and his blood is that which we drink under the species and taste of wine—flesh, namely, the sacrament of flesh, and blood, the sacrament of blood.”

It therefore by no means follows that Ratramnus did not believe that the body taken from the Virgin existed in the Eucharist, even though he established a distinction between the body taken from Mary and that same body as it is celebrated in the Church. For he expressly teaches that the substance of bread and wine has been changed into the body and blood of Christ; that it is wicked not only to deny but even to think that it is not Christ’s body; and, as we have shown above, he says that the body is named and exists.

The same teaching is found in Ivo of Chartres’s letter to Finardus and earlier in Rabanus Maurus’s letter to Heribald of Auxerre, which the most learned Baluzius published and which the reverend Father Christian Lupus of the Order of Saint Augustine, professor of sacred theology at the University of Louvain, vigorously defended against every suspicion either of heresy or of error in a dissertation devoted specifically to explaining certain testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning the heresy of Berengar. It is reproduced in volume V of his notes to the Councils, p. 317, printed at Brussels in the year of Christ 1672.

## V

The dissertationist says in no. 10:

> “It is clear that that bread and wine exist figuratively as Christ’s body and blood.”

## RESPONSE

Who doubts that, in some manner or mode of speaking and writing, bread and wine exist figuratively as Christ’s body and blood? Paschasius, Lanfranc, Guitmund, and all ancient and recent Catholic men freely acknowledge this, provided that Christ’s body is truly recognized as contained inwardly and beneath the species.

Ratramnus expressly teaches this in no. 9:

> “Externally, the form which had previously been bread is displayed; its color is shown and its taste is received. But inwardly something altogether different, far more precious and far more excellent, is intimated.”

And in no. 10:

> “The wine, too, which through priestly consecration becomes Christ’s blood, externally displays one sacrament on its surface, but contains another thing inwardly.”

## VI

The dissertationist says, p. 291 of the Amsterdam edition, line 18, in the outer column:

> “And in no. 19: ‘They are not the same as what is believed.’ This statement, if considered precisely and by itself, may have a probable meaning; nevertheless, if it is uttered with the intention of opposing this Catholic proposition—‘What is seen on the altar is Christ’s body’—it is a pestilential heresy.”

## RESPONSE

From where did the dissertationist learn, and from which words of Ratramnus did he understand, that Ratramnus wrote “They are not the same as what is seen and what is believed” with the intention of opposing this Catholic proposition—“What is seen on the altar is Christ’s body”? Ratramnus wants nothing other than this: Christ’s body, which truly lies hidden and exists beneath the species on the altar, does not enter the eyes, that is, is not subject to the sense of sight and is not visible.

Apart from certain recent philosophers, all theologians—and indeed all people who are neither mentally nor physically blind—frankly acknowledge this.

The matter can easily be settled by an example. Suppose, for instance, that instead of the words “They are not the same as what is seen and what is believed,” Ratramnus had said, “They are not the same as what is corrupted and what is believed”; or “They are not the same as what is sent away into the privy and what is believed”; or “They are not the same as what is broken and what is believed.” The dissertationist would certainly not dare object to these propositions, even though they might have a probable meaning if considered precisely and by themselves, on the ground that they were uttered with the intention of opposing these Catholic propositions:

> “What is broken on the altar is Christ’s body.”
>
> “What is sent away into the privy is Christ’s body.”
>
> “What is corrupted on the altar is Christ’s body.”

That would be a pestilential heresy, since Christ’s body cannot be corrupted, sent away into the privy, or broken.

But Ratramnus wants nothing other than this: Christ’s body, which is believed truly to exist in the Eucharist, is not seen, just as the species which are broken, corrupted, and sent away into the privy are not the very body of Christ, which is believed to lie hidden and exist beneath those species.

From this it is abundantly clear how unnecessary it is to distill one’s brain into so many clouds of subtleties and ambiguities in order to establish this Catholic proposition:

> “What is seen on the altar is Christ’s body.”

The proposition contrary to it would plainly be heretical, since the former proposition is understood to signify nothing other than:

> “What is broken on the altar is Christ’s body.”

In that proposition, the word “this” does not signify Christ’s proper and natural body lying hidden and enclosed beneath the species, but a body called by appellation, as Blessed Algerus puts it—a body in figure which conceals the proper and natural body itself, which has become invisible to our eyes, *ἄφαντον ἐγένετο*.

## VII

The dissertationist says, p. 291:

> “But—and this is the chief point—he teaches most openly in no. 15 that it is not something in truth, that it is the same as not being such according to its proper essence.”

## RESPONSE
Nothing is more alien to the truth than this interpretation by the disputant. For these words, “not to be something in truth,” by no means signify “not to be such according to its proper essence”; rather, they necessarily acknowledge that a change has taken place in the Eucharist—not in those things that are outwardly seen or visibly apparent, but in those that exist inwardly and do not enter the external senses. By this method Ratramnus demonstrates that some things are seen and others believed: some exist inwardly, while others are visibly apparent outwardly.

“Therefore,” says Ratramnus, “they will have to admit either that they have been changed in some respect other than with regard to the body, and consequently that this is not what is truly seen, [Col. 0188A] but something else, which they discern not to be according to its proper essence.”

From this we understand that Ratramnus did not reject transubstantiation. Indeed, he uses this very point to conclude that those who refused to acknowledge that a change had taken place on earth in the Eucharist—but certainly not in the things outwardly manifest—were forced into the untenable position of denying that Christ’s body exists in the sacrament, something that cannot be said or conceived without guilt.

“Or if,” he says, “they refuse to confess this, they are compelled to deny that the body is the blood of Christ—which it is impious not only to say but even to think.”

For my part, I readily confess that I have never understood anything more consonant with the Catholic faith than this: that one must acknowledge that a change has taken place in the sacrament of the Eucharist which does not in the least fall within the range of the human senses—or else deny that Christ’s body truly exists in this sacrament, which it is impious not only to say but even to think.

## VIII. (Same place.) Thus, in no. 18, he opposes the mystery to property—that is, to the proper essence of things. When, therefore, he denies that Christ’s body exists “in truth” on the Lord’s table, he denies that it exists in its proper essence.

### RESPONSE

He by no means opposes property to the mystery in that passage. On the contrary, he demonstrates and confirms that the two can be joined, using baptism as an example: in baptism, water remains in its natural property while inwardly concealing the power of sanctification and immortality. By this argument he proves that the Eucharistic species, while remaining in their natural property, conceal Christ’s holy and immortal body like coverings and curtains.

“Therefore,” says Ratramnus, “in property there is corruptible moisture, but in the mystery there is saving power.”

The disputant has drawn a superfluous conclusion from this passage. “When,” he says, “he denies that Christ’s body exists in truth on the Lord’s table, he denies that it exists in its proper essence.” For by “truth” he understands only the manifestation or external disclosure of a thing, which excludes every association with figure or shadow, and not the proper essence of things, which does not reject such association.

Since this is so, even if I granted it—which, however, I would be very far from conceding—namely, that Ratramnus denied Christ’s body to be in the Eucharist “in truth,” he would have denied nothing other than that this body is palpable or exists wholly without any figure or shadow. For it is inconceivable that he intended to say that the body does not exist when, in no. 96, he states expressly that “it is called and exists as Christ’s body.” He also acknowledges that an inward change takes place which the external senses do not perceive, and that Christ’s body cannot be denied to exist in the Eucharist without great sacrilege.

## IX. (Amsterdam edition, p. 291; first Paris edition, p. 175.) Every sensible person will understand that this one interpretation of the expression “IN TRUTH” pleased John Scotus—that is, Ratramnus—and indeed pleased all Catholics, if he remembers that Berengarius was condemned because he likewise asserted that everything took place “in figure” and “in the sacrament,” but nothing “IN TRUTH,” especially since John Scotus appears to have been Berengarius’s almost adopted and favored authority. In support of this, the disputant produced a fragment of Walter, prior of Saint Victor, included in volume III of Mabillon’s learned *Sacred Analects*, p. 450.

### RESPONSE

Berengarius was rightly and wisely condemned, since by the expression “IN TRUTH” he understood a thing in its proper nature or essence. Accordingly, he persuaded himself that everything in the sacrament took place in figure, and that nothing took place in the reality and essence of Christ’s body.

But it is absurd to introduce Berengarius as the interpreter of Ratramnus, who had died long before, two hundred years earlier. Ratramnus himself testifies and openly indicates that by this expression “IN TRUTH” he understands the external manifestation [Col. 0189A] or disclosure of a thing, free from and wholly opposed to all figures and shadows, as we established above from no. 5.

## X.

Next, Ratramnus says in no. 10 that the substance of wine is seen. So says the disputant on p. 176 of the first Paris edition of Claudius Muguet, published in 1699—that is, p. 291, no. 176, section 11, of the Amsterdam edition of 1709 by de Lorme—at a time when Catholics openly professed that the substance of bread was converted into the substance of Christ’s body, as did the previously cited Haymo of Halberstadt, p. 99. They also said that what we see on the altar is not the substance of bread but the very body born of the Virgin.

### RESPONSE

Ratramnus by no means says that the substance of wine is seen. If he said only this, he would seem to imply that after consecration the substance of wine would be changed. Rather, he says that nothing other than the substance of wine is seen on the surface:

“For what else is seen on the surface than the substance of wine?”

He observes and teaches that, through consecration, wine becomes the sacrament of Christ’s blood, showing one thing outwardly on the surface while containing another inwardly:

“That which through priestly consecration is made the sacrament of Christ’s blood shows one thing on the surface and contains another inwardly.”

And so that no one might suspect that he meant anything other than the substance of wine enclosed by this surface and external appearance, he says expressly in the preceding section that the form of the bread that had previously existed is seen—and therefore no longer exists; that its color is displayed and its taste perceived; but that inwardly something much more precious and excellent is contained, because it is divine. He does not say that it is merely the power of sanctification, but that it is the very body of the Lord Christ, which cannot be perceived by the eyes, taste, or any sense, but is seen and eaten by the eyes of the believer’s mind.

“Outwardly,” he says, “the bread is what it was before” (therefore after consecration it is no longer so); “its form is presented, [Col. 0189C] its color is displayed, its taste is received. But inwardly something altogether different, much more precious and much more excellent, is intimated, because it is heavenly, because it is divine: that is, Christ’s body, which is seen or eaten not by the senses of the flesh but by the contemplation of the faithful mind.”

These statements must also be joined to what he says in no. 30:

“But truly, through the mystery, bread and wine are converted into the substance of my body and blood, to be received by believers.”

I utterly do not know by what words or expressions the faith and conviction of the Church could be signified, unless they are understood most clearly from these statements.

As for the rest, Haymo of Halberstadt does not say, “What we see on the altar is the very body born of the Virgin,” but rather, “What we believe on the altar is the very body born of the Virgin.” For he knew that what we see is visible, whereas what is hidden in the Eucharist as Christ’s true body is invisible.

Thus Haymo says expressly in volume XII of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*:

“Therefore the invisible priest changes his visible creatures, by a hidden power, into the substance of his flesh. In this body and blood of Christ, for the sake of the communicants’ horror, the taste of bread and wine remains, and the form is changed into substance, nature into Christ’s body and blood. But one thing is reported by the sense of the flesh, another by the faith of the mind.”

Moreover, these statements do not differ from those made by Anastasius Sinaita in book XII of the *Anagogical Contemplations on the Hexaemeron*:

“Οὐ περὶ τῆς ὁρωμένος αὐτοῦ σαρκὸς καὶ αἱμάτος λέγει·”

“He is not speaking of his flesh and blood as they are visibly seen.”

And before him, Saint Dionysius, chapter III of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, p. 286, whom we cite in the preface:

“Ἀλλὰ, ὁ θειοτάτη καὶ ἱερὰ τελετὴ, τὰ περικειμένα σοι συμβολικῶς ἀμφιέσματα τῶν αἰνιγμάτων ἀποκαλυψαμένη τηλαυγῶς ἡμῖν ἀναδείχθητι, καὶ τὰς νοερὰς ἡμῶν ὅψεις ἡμῶν ἑνιαίου καὶ ἀπερικαλύπτου φωτὸς ἀποπλήρωσον.”

“But, O most divine and holy rite, reveal to us with radiant clarity the symbolic garments of riddles that surround you, once they have been unveiled, and fill our intellectual visions with a single and uncovered light.”

## XI. (p. 291, section III, under no. 176, Amsterdam edition, 1709.)
