To prove that no change of substance took place, Ratramnus, in no. 12, appeals to the judgment of the eyes and senses and says that “the appearance of the creature remained.” In no. 14 he says that the appearance and form have undergone no change in themselves—that is, their proper essence; or, if anyone prefers the expression, the external form, which that school regarded as inseparable from substance.

### RESPONSE

Would that the disputant had not cut anything from Ratramnus’s words! From no. 12 he would have understood most clearly that Ratramnus himself established the change of the substance of bread into the substance of Christ’s body. For he does not simply say that the appearance of the creature remained, but that outwardly the appearance of the creature that had previously existed was recognized as remaining.

According to truth—that is, according to external manifestation—the appearance of the creature that had previously existed is recognized as remaining. This is entirely true and thoroughly Catholic, since unquestionably the appearance of the bread and wine that existed before—and therefore no longer exists after consecration—remains.

Consequently, no change can be seen or recognized through the operation and ministry of the senses. Here also, this transition is not recognized. For, as he himself says in the same no. 12, in this sacrament, if it is considered only in the simplicity of truth—that is, in what appears outwardly and is perceived by the senses—and if nothing other than what is seen is believed, no change is recognized as having taken place.

He does not say, “It is proved” or “demonstrated that no change has taken place,” but “no change is recognized”—namely, it is not seen by the ministry of the senses and eyes. But if something other than what is perceived by the senses is believed, a change has taken place, as he says in no. 30:

“But truly, through the mystery, bread and wine are converted into the substance of my body and blood, to be received by believers.”

Moreover, the words from no. 14 cited by the disputant—“the appearance and form have undergone no change in themselves”—are truncated and distorted. For he makes it seem that Ratramnus means by “appearance” the matter and substantial form of bread and wine, which suffer no change. Yet if the words are presented in full and honestly, they convey the entirely opposite meaning: according to the appearance and form of the creature, or of visible things that lie within the senses, the bread and wine that previously existed have undergone no change in themselves. This is entirely true.

“For according to the appearance and form of the creature, both—that is, bread and wine—have undergone no change in themselves; and if they have suffered no change, they exist as nothing other than what they previously were.”

In the immediately following argument, he firmly proves that one must acknowledge that a change has truly taken place inwardly, although it is by no means seen outwardly or perceived by the senses:

“For bodily, nothing is discerned in them to have been changed” (no. 15).

And he rightly does not say that nothing has been changed, but that nothing is discerned by the senses to have been changed. Otherwise they would be compelled to deny that the body is Christ’s—something that it is impious not only to say but even to think.

“Or if they refuse to confess this, they are compelled to deny that the body and blood are Christ’s, which it is impious not only to say but even to think.”

The blessed Algerus, a thoroughly Catholic man and a most resolute opponent of Berengarius, said the same in his own time, as we understand from chapter 17 of book I, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*:

“The saints have noted this doubleness as belonging not to substance but to form, whenever they have said of Christ’s body ‘the same and not the same’: it is the same according to substance, but not the same according to form.”

And in chapter 18:

“Just as the imaginary immolation is figuratively called death, the crucifixion of Christ, and the form of bread and wine is figuratively called Christ’s body, so the sacrament of faith, namely baptism, is figuratively called faith. It must be noted that in one of these likenesses he called the heavenly bread, which is truly Christ’s flesh, Christ’s body not in a common but in its own, almost proper, manner, because he saw that body as not corporeal but spiritual and divine, uniquely above all others. In the other case, he called the sacrament of Christ’s body—that is, the form of bread—absolutely, in a certain sense, Christ’s body, because he observed that by a common figure the body of Christ is called what does not exist as such. But when he called the invisible body of Christ the sacrament of Christ’s visible body, this is to be understood intellectually through some outward action, and not sensibly.”

## XII.

Understand Ratramnus’s statement in no. 56 that what is seen exists as Christ’s body and blood, not in appearance but in power. This attacks the Catholic declaration that what is seen is Christ’s true body.

[Col. 0191B] ### RESPONSE

From this aphorism of Catholic men it must not be understood that the substance of Christ’s body is perceived by the senses. That is plainly false. Rather, the veils and shadows by which Christ’s true body is covered are seen and perceived by the eyes.

Thus the meaning of this maxim is:

“What is seen is Christ’s body”—that is, the substance which truly exists invisibly beneath these sensible coverings is itself Christ’s true body.

Therefore Ratramnus rightly says:

“Understand that what is seen is Christ’s body and blood, not in appearance but in power.”

For we truly believe that Christ’s body exists there; and when we believe it, it necessarily follows that we do not see it. If we saw it, we would say, “We see it,” and would not say, “We believe that it is Christ’s true body and blood.”

“You faithfully believe Christ’s body and blood; but you perceive that what you believe you do not yet see. For if you said, ‘I see,’ you would not say, ‘I believe that it is Christ’s body and blood.’”

From this power with which Christ is adorned in the mystery, he argues that this power must be venerated: by it Christ creates whatever he wills, and changes what has been created, in whatever manner and whenever he wills, into that which previously did not exist.

“Thus he says that the order of nature must not be considered here, but Christ’s power must be venerated: whatever he wills, in whatever manner he wills, into whatever he wills, he creates what did not exist and changes what was created into that which previously did not exist.”

## XIII.

“The Catholics,” says the disputant, p. 291, section 176, Amsterdam edition, but p. 176, section 4, Paris edition, “did not wish faith, which lies inwardly hidden in the mind, to perform anything in the mystery. What was seen on God’s altar they said was Christ’s body; the substance of the creatures remained unchanged, with the appearance preserved, according to the understanding of appearance that we explained in chapter 4; nor were they now symbols after consecration of what they had previously been. An inward change did indeed take place, but in the symbols before it took place in the minds of believers.”

In these statements the author presents Ratramnus as teaching five propositions exactly contrary to those five, namely, in no. 54:

“Let those who want to receive nothing here according to the inwardly hidden power, but wish to judge everything that appears visibly, say in what respect a change has taken place here. For according to the substance of the creatures, what they were before consecration, that they remain afterward. Bread and wine existed previously; they appear to remain in that same appearance even after consecration. Therefore what has been changed inwardly by the powerful operation of the Holy Spirit is what faith beholds, nourishes the soul, and supplies the substance of eternal life.”

[Col. 0191D] ### RESPONSE

It is impossible to derive from these words of Ratramnus the five propositions contrary to the five asserted by the disputant.

1. “The Catholics did not wish faith, which lies inwardly hidden in the mind, to perform anything in the mystery.”

“If only,” says Ratramnus, “faith, which lies inwardly hidden in the mind, were to perform something in the mystery!”

Here the disputant will construct the opposite of his fifth proposition, namely: “An inward change takes place, but not in the symbols before it takes place in the minds.” On the contrary, Ratramnus demonstrates throughout his work that this change is the object of faith, and therefore precedes it.

Indeed, he says in no. 11:

“But if, according to certain people, nothing is received figuratively, but everything is seen in truth, then faith performs nothing here.”

But this means nothing other than that faith has nothing to consider if nothing is hidden—if everything is manifested and uncovered outwardly and inwardly. In that case, I believe, one ought not to say “I believe,” but “I see,” as Ratramnus observes in no. 54:

“For if you saw it, you would say, ‘I see,’ and you would not say, ‘I believe that it is Christ’s body and blood.’”

What heresy is suggested by these words? What alien from the Catholic faith emerges here? What does it mean here to say that faith, which lies inwardly hidden, performs something in this mystery, unless “performing something in the mystery” means performing something with respect to the object of the mystery? For faith performs its work in contemplating this mystery: it believes and affirms that beneath the species of bread and wine the true body and blood of Christ are hidden and concealed through the marvelous conversion of the substance of bread and wine, as we have observed Ratramnus teaching from nos. 49 and 30.

“But according to the invisible substance—that is, by the power of the divine Word—Christ’s body and blood truly exist . . . . . . but truly, through the mystery, bread and wine are converted into the substance of the body and blood, to be received by the faithful.”

However the matter may stand, Ratramnus never said, “Faith, which lies inwardly hidden, performs something in this mystery.” He said only:

“Faith performs nothing here if, according to certain people, nothing here is received figuratively, but everything is seen in truth.”

This is entirely true and plainly Catholic, since in the Eucharist there are both figure and truth. It is equally false to say either that everything is figurative or that nothing is figurative.

[Col. 0192C] It remains to inquire what Ratramnus means by these words:

“For according to the substance of the creatures, what they were before consecration, that they remain afterward. Bread and wine existed previously, and they appear to remain in the same appearance even now after consecration.”

I maintain that by “the substance of the creatures” he by no means understands a self-subsisting entity, as the Peripatetics speak, but the external affections and qualities of substance which existed previously and now no longer do, although they nevertheless appear to survive and remain. This is what the words signify:

“Bread and wine existed previously, and they appear to remain in the same appearance even now.”

Indeed, the word *species* in Ratramnus does not signify the thing itself, but the thing’s covering, shadow, and likeness, as in Horace, book II, *Satire* 2:

“Appearance leads you on, I see.”

Apart from the examples by which I could prove that ancient ecclesiastical writers used “substance” to signify the affections of a thing and the qualities of things, rather than the things themselves—examples of which I provided in the preface to the Latin edition of Ratramnus that you have before you—there can be no doubt that Ratramnus intended by these words to signify such affections of the soul, not the soul itself:

“Therefore what has been changed inwardly by the powerful operation of the Holy Spirit, what faith beholds, nourishes the soul, and supplies the substance of eternal life.”

For the substance of eternal life is not the soul itself as a self-subsisting entity, but blessedness itself, or the complete and perfect possession, all at once, of unchangeable life.

## XIV.

In no. 4 he compares the Eucharist with baptism. In nos. 17, 18, and 19, p. 292 of the Amsterdam edition and p. 176 of the Paris edition of 1699, he says that in baptism there are two things: the element that outwardly washes, and the power of sanctification—or the faith of the one who is washed—which cleanses inwardly. Thus, in appearance or property, there is nothing but water; in the mystery, or in the understanding of the believer, there is healing power.

[Col. 0193A] ### RESPONSE

I frankly admit that Ratramnus compares the Eucharist with baptism. But by “the Eucharist” he understands not bread and wine alone, but the whole Eucharist in its entirety—namely, Christ’s true body and true blood beneath the species of bread and wine.

This must be Ratramnus’s meaning, since he acknowledges a true change of substances, does not assert two existences, and regards it as a great sacrilege to think that Christ’s body, which is named and exists there, is absent.

If, then, he compares the Eucharist understood in this sense with baptism, what false or harmful thing can be charged against him? For just as the power of sanctification is joined to the element of water in baptism, so much more does the power of immortality and sanctification accompany Christ’s true body, hidden beneath the species, and provide us with immortality and the substance of eternal life.

Yet unless we approach this mystery with faith and charity, Christ’s hidden flesh itself profits nothing:

“It is the spirit that gives life.”

In the same way, water is of no benefit if it lacks the power of sanctification—that is, unless the adult who has been initiated through holy baptism believes and persuades himself that eternal life can be obtained through this power of sanctification.

It is therefore not merely wonderful that Christ’s body exists in the Eucharist, but that it exists there for our sanctification. It remains equally in the mouths of the wicked and the good:

“But to the wicked it is nourishment of death, and toward the good nourishment of life—life to the good and death to the wicked.”

[Note: [Col. 0193] Prose for the Feast of the Blessed Sacrament, whose author is Saint Thomas.]

Moreover, this comparison is neither new nor unusual. It was used by the most resolute defenders of Christ’s presence and of transubstantiation, as we learn from Paschasius’s letter to Frudgardus, p. 1621, letter B, and from chapter 3 of the treatise *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, p. 1562.

The blessed Algerus made the same comparison in chapter 10 of book II and chapter 8 of book III. He considers that what appears to have a bodily form is understood to bear spiritual fruit, just as Ratramnus does in no. 19.

“For according to what is seen, the corruptible things themselves nourish the body; but according to what is believed, the immortal things themselves nourish souls destined to live forever.”

## XV. (Amsterdam edition, p. 292; Paris edition, p. 177, line 2.) Nos. 4 and 19.

“In baptism,” says Ratramnus, “whether of the old or the new covenant, there are two things: the water that is seen and the spiritual power that is believed inwardly. From both the mystery is made, when it is understood what the symbol signifies.”

Here he says not only that the Eucharist, like the water of the saving washing, becomes a mystical reality because, when the symbol is seen, the mind understands something other than what it sees, and from this understanding through faith the mystery is said to be and become what it is; he also reduces the sacraments of the New Law to the same meaning in which the sacraments of the ancient covenant exist.

He likewise compares the ancient sacrifices with the new sacrifice and confirms the point again in no. 91:

“Just as those things possessed the figure of future things, so this sacrifice too becomes a figure of past things.”

[Col. 0193D] ### RESPONSE

Ratramnus says nothing about the Eucharist in that no. 21, nor in what follows does he say that the mystery is said to be and become such through the understanding of faith. Rather, he observes that the mystery arising from Christ’s body and blood enveloped in the species of bread and wine, together with the accompanying power of sanctification, is to be received worthily for the benefit of the faithful and becomes the object of faith. This applies equally not only to the Eucharist but also to all the sacraments of the Old and New Law.

Nor is it peculiar to the Eucharist that the power of sanctification is added to bread and wine, as it is added to water in baptism. Rather, that power is added when it is joined to Christ’s true body, concealed and hidden beneath the species or figures.

There can be no doubt that this is Ratramnus’s meaning, since in the immediately following discussion, no. 24, he says that the blood drunk by the Jewish people in the desert was a figure of the blood taken from the Virgin’s womb and poured out on the wood of the cross—not merely so that we might be redeemed by it, but also so that we might drink it:

“So that we might understand,” he says, “that in the desert he stood in the spiritual rock and gave the people a stream of his blood, and that afterward, in our age, he displayed the body taken from the Virgin and suspended on the cross for the salvation of believers, and poured forth from it a stream of blood by which we might not only be redeemed but also given to drink.”

However the matter may stand, if the blood poured out by Christ for us from the wood of the cross so that we might be redeemed is the true blood of Christ taken from the Virgin Mother, then that blood poured out and given to us to drink must likewise be true and identical blood:

“By which we might not only be redeemed but also given to drink.”

It is easy, indeed, to confirm—and even demonstrate—the orthodoxy of Ratramnus in this passage. If we ask all the ministers of Calvinist superstition whether the blood poured out on the cross for our redemption was the true blood of Christ taken from the Virgin Mary, they will all undoubtedly answer that it was true and proper blood.

But if the same question is asked concerning the blood poured out by Christ so that we might drink it, they will answer that it is not the same blood, but merely represents the true blood in figure, or presents it in figure—a heretical interpretation.

If, however, we asked Ratramnus the same question, he would answer in the Catholic sense:

“Christ stood in the spiritual rock in the desert and gave the people a stream of his blood, and afterward displayed the body taken from the Virgin and suspended on the cross for the salvation of believers in our age, and poured from it a stream of blood by which we might not only be redeemed but also given to drink.”

Therefore, according to Ratramnus’s meaning, just as we are redeemed by the true blood of Christ taken from the body born of the Virgin, so we are given to drink by that very same true blood.

Ratramnus would further answer that we are redeemed and given to drink by the blood whose figure was present in the manna, the Red Sea, and the rock of the desert. Since this blood now lies hidden beneath the veils and figures—that is, the species—of wine and bread, and truly exists there, it becomes the object of our faith and spiritual understanding. Through the wondrous union of truth and figure, it also became a figure of the past manna, Red Sea, and rock of the desert, just as the manna, Red Sea, and rock of the desert possessed the figure of future things.

“Just as those things,” he says in no. 91, “possessed the figure of future things, so this sacrifice becomes a figure of past things.”

## XVI. (p. 292, no. 177.)

“Therefore,” says Ratramnus in no. 30, “do not suppose that my flesh or blood is to be eaten or drunk by you bodily, divided or to be divided into portions, since after the resurrection you will see me ascending into heaven with the fullness of an entire body and blood.”

Who among the Catholics ever dreamed that Christ’s flesh was to be cut into pieces? Certainly no one.

### RESPONSE

It is highly credible and very probable that Ratramnus’s opponents were Catholics. Since he calls them “the faithful” in no. 11, he abundantly indicates that they were free from every suspicion of heresy:

“For while certain of the faithful say that the body and blood of Christ, which is celebrated daily in the Church, are made with no figure and no revelation…”

Who could persuade himself that by “certain of the faithful” people tainted with heresy are meant?

Those opponents believed that Christ’s true body was truly seen or perceived in the Eucharist, in the condition and form in which it actually existed, enclosed by no figures or shadows of the mystery:

“which is made with no figure and no shadow.”

Such opponents, as far as they could, rejected and defended themselves against the foul consequence into which they were entangled and by which they were convicted of believing that Christ’s body was corrupted and, through the action of natural heat and spirit, agitated like food, dissolved after being moistened by the fluids in the chest and stomach of those who received it—even though they did not doubt that it was truly Christ’s body and blood.

Abbot Abbaudus, an author of uncertain date, adopted the same position concerning the breaking of Christ’s body. Walter, prior of Saint Victor in Paris, followed him. The learned Mabillon published their fragments in volume IV of the *Sacred Analects*, along with many Catholic writers before and after Berengarius’s time, or after his recantation, as Mabillon himself observes in his notes to Abbaudus’s treatise on the breaking of Christ’s body.

However the matter may stand, there was no sect of men who persuaded themselves that Christ’s flesh and God could ever be sent into a sewer. Christians had not forgotten what is related in Exodus, chapter 32, verse 20:

“When Moses seized the calf that the Israelites had made, he burned it and crushed it to dust, scattered it upon the water, and gave the Israelites drink from it.”

On this subject Peter of Rheims, an ancient writer called de Riga, composed the following not entirely contemptible verse in his *Aurora*. John Selden testifies that the work was held in the Cotton Library in his *Syrian Gods*, syntagma 2, on the golden calf; and I myself saw it in the library of the chapter of the metropolitan church of Rheims:

“He crushes it, mixes it with water, and gives the Hebrews the drink,

So that the foul god may pass out through foul places.”

## XVII. (Same place, p. 292.)

“But that old trickster,” says the disputant—who enjoys rubbing this salt into Ratramnus—“wanted it to be understood that Christ’s body is neither seen on the altar, nor eaten, nor broken; and that, once the body had been taken up into heaven, it no longer exists on earth.”

### RESPONSE

If Ratramnus had persuaded himself that Christ’s body did not remain on earth after the ascension into heaven, [Col. 0195C] he would never have said in no. 99:

“This bread and this cup, which are called and exist as Christ’s body.”

Nor would he have said in no. 24, concerning the blood poured out on the tree of the cross:

“By which we might not only be redeemed but also given to drink.”

Nor would he have warned his readers, lest they be deceived by a preconceived opinion concerning the very words he used. He would not have added what is found in no. 101:

“Nor, because we say these things, should it be thought that in the mystery of the sacrament the Lord’s body or his blood is not received by the faithful, since faith receives not what the eye sees but what it believes.”

Faith, however, believes that the true body is hidden in the Eucharist, not a body existing merely in figure; therefore it does not first perceive something false or figurative.

Nor would Ratramnus have said in no. 10:

“Wine also, which through priestly consecration is made the sacrament of Christ’s blood, shows one thing on the surface and contains another inwardly.”

For what does it contain inwardly besides wine, unless Christ’s blood is placed there in the wine’s stead?

Furthermore, what need would there have been for him to say in no. 30:

“But truly, through the mystery, bread and wine are converted into the substance of the body and blood, to be received by the faithful,”

if he had rejected the Catholic Church’s doctrine of transubstantiation?

Nor should there be quibbling over the expression “through the mystery,” which signifies nothing other than that Christ’s true body and blood remain hidden beneath the species of bread and wine. For Ratramnus means nothing else in that passage than what he had said in no. 28:

“Before he suffered, Christ could have converted the substance of bread and the creature of wine into his own body, which was to suffer, and into his blood, which was afterward to be poured out.”

## XVIII.

“Nowhere does it exist,” says the disputant, p. 177 of the Paris edition and p. 292 of the Amsterdam edition, “unless it is palpable.” He repeats this in no. 89 and consequently concludes in no. 17:

“Where the body is not seen by the eyes and is not manifest, there it is altogether absent.”

[Col. 0196A] ### RESPONSE

Nothing of this sort ever appears in Ratramnus, nor is it credible that a man who had not departed from his senses could be so utterly contradictory. Everywhere he says—or is understood to say—that Christ’s body, in which he suffered death, exists in the Eucharist, as we have already shown in several places. It would be superfluous to repeat them.

Nor does he conclude in nos. 89 and 97 that wherever Christ’s body is not seen by the eyes and is not manifest, it is altogether absent. He merely observes that there is a difference between the mystery of the body celebrated in the Church and Christ’s proper body in which he suffered and died. The difference consists in this: in the mystery the body is veiled beneath figures and is not palpable, whereas the body that suffered and was buried is manifest and palpable.

Meanwhile, he does not say that there are two existences of things. On the contrary, he expressly teaches:

“Not that there are two existences of things distinct from one another, namely, of body and spirit, but one and the same thing: according to one aspect, it consists as the species of bread and wine; according to another, it is the body and blood of Christ.”

(No. 16.)

## XIX. (Amsterdam edition, p. 292.)

Ratramnus interprets the Lord’s statement “It is the spirit that gives life,” in no. 31, as referring to the spiritual action of believers—that is, faith—which gives life and makes the mystery what it is. Without this faith and action, the mysteries nourish only the body, and are not even mysteries, but merely the substance of bread and wine.

### RESPONSE

Ratramnus truly maintains that those who receive the Eucharist must possess faith. Moreover, Paschasius and all Catholic men require this in accordance with Saint Paul:

“Let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood, not discerning the Lord’s body” (1 Corinthians 11:29).

Ratramnus means nothing else when, explaining these words in no. [Col. 0196C] 31, “The Spirit is the one who gives life,” he says:

> “Thus, in this mystery there is a spiritual operation of the body and blood which grants life; without its operation the mysteries are of no benefit.”

Indeed, these mysteries not only confer no benefit but also bring harm and death if received without faith and charity. For this is why theologians teach that the Eucharist is the sacrament of the living, not of the dead. Yet none of this signifies that spiritual activity alone gives life and effects the mystery. Ratramnus never spoke in that way in no. 31; rather, he taught the contrary in these words:

> “He says that the flesh profits nothing, in the manner in which unbelievers understood it; otherwise, it grants life, just as it is received by the faithful through the mystery. And why is this so? He himself makes it clear when he says: ‘The Spirit is the one who gives life.’ Thus, in this mystery of the body and blood there is a spiritual operation which grants life; without its operation those mysteries are of no benefit, since they can indeed nourish the body, but they cannot nourish the soul.” [Col. 0196D]

Who, on the basis of these words, could understand that it is only the faith of the recipient that effects the mystery, and fail to recognize the Christian and Catholic truth—namely, that the flesh and blood of Christ in the Eucharist grant life to the soul, that is, grace, to those who worthily receive this sacrament, to persons properly prepared, ready, and suitable, adorned with faith, charity, and the virtue of repentance?

## XX. The disputant says (p. 292 of the Amsterdam edition) that Ratramnus says the mystery is enacted spiritually because the spirit of faith effects it; faith nourishes, gladdens, and gives life inwardly, while what is external nourishes the flesh. For this, he says, is the pure and unadulterated doctrine of the Sacramentarians.

### RESPONSE

I should gladly ask the disputant by what reasoning he persuades himself that the mystery can be effected except spiritually. [Col. 0197A] As though this meant that the mysteries are effected by the operation of faith, and not by the power of the Holy Spirit, through which the mysteries become objects of our faith. In agreement with Ratramnus, Paschasius speaks in chapter 5 of his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*:

> “Christ, therefore, is the food of angels, and this sacrament is truly his flesh and blood, which man eats and drinks spiritually. Accordingly, by that through which the angels live, man also lives, because everything in what man receives is spiritual and divine.”

And at the end of the same chapter:

> “We too drink and eat spiritually the spiritual flesh of Christ, in which eternal life is believed to exist. Otherwise, to think according to the flesh is death; yet to receive the true flesh of Christ spiritually is eternal life.”

He observes in the immediately following discussion, chapter 6, that this spiritual flesh of Christ pertains to the good, and in no way to the wicked:

> “Behold,” he says, “all alike frequently receive the sacraments of the altar; yet one spiritually eats the flesh of Christ and drinks his blood, while another [Col. 0197B] does not, although he may appear to receive a morsel from the priest’s hand. And what does he receive, since there is one consecration, if he does not receive the body and blood? Truly, he receives it unworthily as one guilty, just as the Apostle Paul says: ‘He eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not having first examined himself and not discerning the Lord’s body’ (I Cor. 11:29). Behold what the sinner eats and what he drinks. Certainly not flesh and blood beneficially for himself, but judgment. And why? Because he does not examine himself and does not discern the Lord’s body. For the unbeliever thinks that an unworthy person can receive what is worthy and holy, attending to nothing except what he sees and understanding nothing except what is perceived.”

For the same purpose, Ratramnus quotes Saint Isidore of Seville:

> “This same doctor also says: ‘A sacrament is present in some celebration when the event has taken place in such a way that it is understood to signify something which must be received in holiness.’”

In this definition of a sacrament he agrees with Paschasius, chapter 3 of *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*:

> “A sacrament, therefore, is whatever is delivered to us in some divine celebration as a pledge of salvation, when a visible event inwardly effects something altogether different and invisible, which must be received in holiness.” [Col. 0197C]

Blessed Algerus, the most formidable opponent of Berengarius, follows the footsteps of Ratramnus and Paschasius in book II, chapter 1, of *On the Eucharist*:

> “In that sacrament Christ is present, because it is Christ’s body; therefore it is not bodily food but spiritual food. If, then, it is spiritual and not bodily, how can it be subject to bodily digestion?”

In the immediately following discussion of the same chapter he proves that the bodily fast is not broken by the Eucharist, which is spiritual nourishment:

> “But far be it from the hearts of the faithful to believe that the fast is broken on days of fasting, no matter at what hour Masses are celebrated; for since it is not bodily but spiritual food, bodily abstinence is not broken by spiritual food.”

There is therefore no room for doubt that the mystery is enacted spiritually. Ratramnus, however, intended something quite different from what the disputant puts into his mouth when he says that the spirit of faith effects it: “Faith nourishes, gladdens, and gives life inwardly, while what is present nourishes the flesh.” For faith is very far from doing everything inwardly; rather, it presupposes the mystery as the object of its persuasion. This is the solitary meaning of Ratramnus and of all Catholics.

## XXI. (p. 292, no. 178, in the margin.) The disputant says that Ratramnus most explicitly denies in no. 52 that what is received by the mouth at the altar can bestow eternity, for the life contained in the mystery comes from the invisible power of the Word, which produces faith in us; and that the efficacy and power of the Lord’s body reside in this faith.

### RESPONSE

It is plainly evident that these three statements do not occur in Ratramnus at no. 52.

1. In explaining Saint Ambrose’s words [Col. 0198A] about the bread of life that descended from heaven, he openly acknowledges that it is received by us at the altar. For he expressly speaks of the spiritual nourishment by which the faithful are fed in the Church, the food which the faithful receive in the Church, and he teaches that bread and wine not only can give us eternal life but actually do so. This living bread, which descended from heaven, supplies the substance of eternal life. He says that whatever in the Eucharist is subject to the senses or palpable can nourish only the body, and in no way the soul. This is so true that among all Catholics it is placed beyond every possibility of doubt. By this line of argument he proves that those are gravely mistaken who persuade themselves that there is no figure in the Eucharist, but that everything consists in an open and manifest presentation.

2. Ratramnus did not at all say that the life contained in the mystery comes from the invisible power of the Word, which produces faith. The disputant has forgotten that he reproached Ratramnus for saying that the mystery is enacted spiritually [Col. 0198B] because the spirit of faith effects it. Indeed, if Ratramnus said that faith effects the mystery, on what grounds can the disputant say that the life which is in the mystery produces or effects faith? Whichever direction the disputant takes, he will not easily escape this snare. For if Ratramnus’s meaning is that faith effects the mystery, he is wrongly reproached for saying that the mystery effects faith. In any event, Ratramnus was far removed from such subtleties, since he fully acknowledges that the Eucharistic mystery is effected by the power of God’s Spirit and is the credible object of our faith, that is, of the persuasion of Christians. Nothing wiser or more orthodox than this doctrine of Ratramnus can be put forward.

3. It necessarily follows from these points that Ratramnus did not teach that the efficacy and power of Christ’s body reside in this faith. On the contrary, he maintains that in this bread there is a life which does not strike the eyes but is recognized by faith alone; that this bread descended from heaven and exists; and that it was said that whoever eats of this bread will be immortal:

> “There is therefore in that bread a life which does not appear to bodily eyes but is seen by the gaze of faith. That living bread which descended from heaven also exists, and of it it is truly said: ‘Whoever eats this will not die forever’; and it is the body of Christ.” [Col. 0198C]

Who could persuade himself that these words mean that the efficacy and power of Christ’s body reside in this faith? For just as, when the eyes are said to see colors and light, it is not said that the efficacy of colors and light resides in sight, so to say that faith looks upon or believes in the body of Christ in the mystery—“it is seen by the gaze of faith”—is not to say that the efficacy and power of Christ’s body reside in this faith. But I fear that in this matter there may be an instance of *ὑπερ νικᾶν ἐπιφθώνον*—“to win too complete a victory is offensive” (Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, letter M, chapter 18, p. 633).

## XXII. The disputant says (p. 178 of the Paris edition, p. 292, no. 178, of the Amsterdam edition, and p. 178 of the first Paris edition) that when Ratramnus denies Christ to be present corporally at the altar and says that he must be understood spiritually, Ratramnus himself explains what notion and force he intends by both expressions in no. 76:

> “Just as in the mystery that bread is understood to be the body, so also in the mystery the members of the people who believe in Christ are signified; and just as that bread is said to be the body of believers not corporally but spiritually, so also the body of Christ must be understood not corporally but spiritually.” [Col. 0198D]

### RESPONSE

Since Ratramnus wrote with the purpose of proving that there is some figure in the Eucharist, he could not have produced a better line of argument than the one he derives from the body and blood of the faithful people, which are signified by the mingling of water with wine in the chalice. For just as, through the mingling of water, the people are figuratively united to Christ, and the blood of the people is figuratively signified, so through the species of bread and wine the body and blood of Christ are signified in figure. For insofar as these species are veils and curtains of Christ’s body, they are regarded as its figures and shadows, [Col. 0199A] by which the true body present deceives the eyes and senses of those who look upon it. Sight, touch, and taste are deceived in you, but by hearing alone you are securely led to believe.

Indeed, Algerus calls these species the body of Christ by designation, because they conceal and enclose Christ’s proper body. Once this has been established, I do not doubt that everyone will easily understand the comparison between the body of the people and the body of Christ in the Eucharist. Ratramnus means nothing other than that the body of Christ, by designation, is a figure of the body and blood of the people. But this does not prevent the true body from being believed to lie hidden beneath the species, even though the body and blood of the people are understood only figuratively. For Paschasius, the most invincible defender of the real presence and transubstantiation of Christ’s true body in the Church, makes the same comparison; and he says that the body of the people, like the body of Christ, is present figuratively in the Eucharist, although he had no doubt whatever that Christ’s body is truly hidden beneath the species in real presence. Thus he speaks [Col. 0199B] in chapter 11 of *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*:

> “And therefore it was rightly provided that water should flow together with the blood, so that in this mystery water might be mingled with the true blood, in order that we too might be in him and, through this sacrament of salvation, might mystically be offered as united with him in the divine sight. For if wine is offered without water, the blood of Christ begins to be without us; but if water alone is offered, the people already appear to be without Christ. When, however, both are mingled and joined together, then the mystery of the Church is rightly completed spiritually.”

And later in the same chapter:

> “Let the faithful therefore rejoice when they understand that through grace they have been joined to so great a unity with Christ and advanced to so great a fervor of charity. Thus, how fittingly our figure is admitted into this mystery through water, so that each person may understand that he has been received into that blood of Christ and transformed for the better. Hence, although wine and water are first mystically mingled, after consecration nothing but blood is drunk, because, having first been received into him through the water of baptism, we again drink him whom we daily drink while hungering and thirsting.”

And further below:

> “For this reason water is also not inappropriately consecrated for this same purpose—not that the water remains water, but that it is changed into blood, so that it may signify what faith receives.” [Col. 0199C]

From these words it is easy to understand how superfluous is the disputant’s conclusion drawn from Ratramnus’s words:

> “For this,” says the disputant, “is to say clearly and unambiguously that neither is the body present in the consecrated bread corporally, that is, according to its substance, but only spiritually, through the understanding of faith.”

For he could just as easily derive such a conclusion from Paschasius’s similar, if not identical, words. Why, then, should he derive it from Ratramnus, especially since Ratramnus did not lack the intellectual care necessary to prevent the fiction born in Calvin’s brain [Col. 0199D] from being attributed to him throughout the ages, as is evident in no. 101:

> “Nor, because we say these things, should it be thought that in the sacramental mystery the Lord’s body or his blood is not received by the faithful, since faith receives not what the eye sees, but what it believes.”

Nor did the disputant produce a more relevant passage from Ratramnus, taken from no. 75, in these words:

> “But we see that nothing has been changed in the water; consequently, nothing corporal has been manifested in the wine. Whatever is signified in the water from the body of the people is received spiritually; therefore whatever is signified in the wine from the blood of Christ must necessarily be received spiritually.”

For these words signify nothing other than that Christ’s blood is not perceived by the senses in the species of wine, and that such species are the body of Christ spiritually and by designation, just as in the mingling of water the blood of the people is not perceived, but the water is only by designation and spiritually the blood of the people. Nothing prevents the matter from being so even though Christ’s true body lies hidden in the Eucharist, while the body of the people is present only figuratively. Nor is it necessary for the comparison to hold in every respect in order to prove what Ratramnus chiefly intends: that there is some figure in the Eucharist, and that not everything is disclosed by open and manifest revelation. [Col. 0200A]

Up to this point, we seem to have explained sufficiently the things in Ratramnus’s book which the disputant accuses and vehemently attacks as abhorrent to the Catholic faith and chargeable with heresy. Let us now investigate what he denounces as more concealed and disguised, and pursue the case of the innocent and undefiled Ratramnus by what jurists call a restitutory action.

## XXIII. The disputant contends (p. 292, no., or section 179, no. 1, of the first Paris edition, p. 179) that Ratramnus—or the author of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*—so entangles the question that it can scarcely be discerned even by experts. For he says that in no. 5 one must inquire:

> “Whether the body and blood which are received in the Church by the mouths of the faithful are effected in mystery or in truth—that is, whether they contain something secret which is disclosed only to the eyes of faith; or whether the bodily exterior of the body is perceived by the outward sight without any veiling of the mystery, while the inward eye of the mind sees it inwardly, so that everything enacted shines in the light of manifestation; and whether it is the very body which was born of Mary, suffered, died, and was buried, and which, rising again and ascending to heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father.” [Col. 0200B]

### RESPONSE

It is difficult to understand what appears obscure or complicated in this formulation of the question. Since there can be no doubt that in Ratramnus’s time there were faithful people who persuaded themselves that everything in the Eucharistic mystery was open and manifest, and who believed that Christ’s body and blood were placed under no figure or shadow—as we see from no. 11 of the said book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*:

> “For when some of the faithful say that the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood celebrated in the Church is enacted under no figure and under no shadow, but through the bare manifestation of the truth itself, while others testify that these things are contained under the figure of a mystery, and that one thing appears to the bodily senses while another is seen by faith, a considerable difference between them is discerned.” [Col. 0200C]

Furthermore, Ratramnus cannot justly be accused of obscurity and entanglement in the question proposed. He was not the author of the question; it was the emperor Charles the Bald, at whose command Ratramnus undertook to investigate and discuss it, as we understand from the words in no. 5, which the disputant deliberately omitted. Ratramnus does not say:

> “It is asked whether the body and blood of Christ received in the Church by the mouths of the faithful are effected in mystery or in truth,”

and so forth. Rather, he says:

> “That the body and blood of Christ which are received in the Church by the mouths of the faithful are effected in mystery or in truth is what the excellence of Your Greatness [Col. 0200D] asks to be investigated.”

Let Ratramnus therefore not be accused of having proposed an entangled question. That insult must be directed back at the emperor himself.

By these words, “the excellence of Your Greatness asks,” he by no means understands the author of this question to mean by “the secret” something held inwardly in the mind of each believer; nor does he mean the veiling of the mystery, the symbol which each person, looking upon it, believes in his mind, together with the Word of God, concerning Christ’s body. Nor does he in any way intend to inquire whether it is merely a figure and sign which, joined to the faith of the observer, bears the name of mystery, and whether the bread is the body of Christ only through thought, or whether it is truly and in reality so that, even before the operation of faith and the mind, what is seen may truly be said to be the body born of the Virgin.

Ratramnus investigated and examined only whether this sacrament was entirely without any figure and empty of it. He proved that some figure exists in it, one capable of being associated and joined with the truth, in accordance with Paschasius; and he always regarded what is inward and secret in the Eucharist, deceiving the eyes of men, as an object and prospect of faith, not as something brought into existence by faith. It always seemed inconceivable to him that Christ’s body should be regarded as a fiction of reason. Rather, he did not doubt that it subsisted in itself as a real object around which reason, faith, and understanding operate.

Nor does Ratramnus anywhere teach that the mystery is made from two things: symbols as signs, and the faith of the believer, which completes the mystery by believing—the claim which the disputant falsely attributes to Ratramnus on p. 179 of the Paris edition and p. 292 of the Amsterdam edition, no. 179, while omitting the passage, because there is no passage from which he copied it. Nevertheless, Ratramnus continues in the immediately following discussion, section 11.

## XXIV. There is a similar abundance of deceit in what Ratramnus says in no. 9:

> “That in which nothing is hidden, nothing removed from bodily senses, and nothing covered by some veil cannot be called a mystery. But that bread which, through the ministry of the priest, is made the body of Christ displays externally one thing to human senses, and proclaims inwardly another thing to the minds of the faithful . . . . . because what is heavenly and divine—that is, the body of Christ—is shown, which is seen, received, or granted not by the senses of the flesh but by the contemplation of the faithful soul.” [Col. 0201A]

[Col. 0201B] The learned men were misled by the words “INWARDLY” and “OUTWARDLY.” For this man does not understand “inwardly,” which also occurs below in nos. 10 and 21 and elsewhere, as signifying something within the symbols themselves. Rather, he says that the mystery is effected in the minds of believers, and denies that it can be called a mystery unless, prompted by the symbols as by an admonition, the mind believes something other than what the eye sees. The mystery, he says, is made from both—the symbol and the faith of the believer.

### RESPONSE

It is not easy to detect deceit or cunning in these words of Ratramnus. Indeed, if he really explains clearly and openly in this passage, setting aside every ambiguity, what he understands by “inwardly” and “outwardly,” and honestly indicates what is within or outside the object of our faith’s mystery, while nowhere suggesting or insinuating that such a mystery is effected in the minds of believers, then it is highly probable that his words are entirely free of deceit and fraud.

[Col. 0201C] Moreover, from the words of no. 9 we can easily understand and grasp his meaning—words which the disputant was not afraid to omit, or rather to expunge:

> “OUTWARDLY, the form that the bread previously had is displayed, its color is shown, and its taste is perceived. But INWARDLY something altogether different, much more precious and much more excellent, is signified, because it is heavenly and divine—that is, the body of Christ is shown, which is not perceived by the senses of the flesh,” and so forth.

Who in his right mind could persuade himself or understand from such a discourse that faith effects Christ’s body, or that it exists in the Eucharist only through the power of the mind’s thought? What deceit or fraud is there in the construction and coherence of these words, and what could Ratramnus have meant except that sight, touch, and taste are deceived in this mystery, while it is securely believed by hearing alone?

If there is any craftiness, therefore, it belongs to the disputant, who slyly omitted these words; the force belongs to the lion—that is, to Ratramnus—who vigorously and clearly sets forth his mind concerning the Catholic faith. Truly, foxes are cautious, but those who catch foxes are more cautious.

## XXV. Ratramnus does not say, the disputant claims (p. 180 of the Paris edition and fol. 292, no., or section 180, of the Amsterdam edition), that the symbols are changed “INWARDLY.” Rather, “INWARDLY,” that is, in the innermost mind, the Lord’s body is intimated or signified by the symbols, where the faithful soul sees, receives, and grants what Ratramnus, as the disputant cunningly argues, denies can be said: that the sight looks upon Christ’s body and the mouth eats Christ.

### RESPONSE

Three things in these words are plainly and manifestly false.

1. It is false that Ratramnus does not say that the symbols are changed inwardly, since he expressly says in no. 9: “THE BREAD WHICH PREVIOUSLY HAD BEEN.” For if it truly was bread before, it is no longer so; consequently, a change has taken place inwardly, since no change appears outwardly. Moreover, does Ratramnus not say in no. 30:

> “Truly, through the mystery, bread and wine have been changed into the substance of Christ’s body and blood, to be received by believers”? [Col. 0202A]

2. Ratramnus does not at all say that Christ’s body is signified by the symbols to the innermost mind. For he expressly says that bread and wine, since they are now other than they previously were, have undergone a change; that this cannot be denied; and, in the immediately following discussion, he proves that the change has not taken place in what lies before our eyes or appears outwardly. Bread and wine must be something other than they appear through outward manifestation—or else, something which cannot be said or thought without sacrilege must be denied: namely, that, according to Ratramnus’s mind in no. 15, the body and blood of Christ exist in the Eucharist:

> “They will therefore necessarily admit that they have been changed in some respect other than with regard to the body, or that they are not what they truly appear to be, but are something else which, according to their proper essence, they are seen not to be; or, if they refuse to confess this, they are compelled to deny that it is the body and blood of Christ—something which is impious not only to say but even to think.” [Col. 0202B]

3. The disputant falsely attributes to Ratramnus the cunning denial that the sight looks upon Christ and the mouth eats Christ. Ratramnus prudently and simply denies that Christ’s sacred body, which is celebrated in the Church, is visible and palpable to the senses in such a way that it is cut into pieces, as food is, and crushed by the teeth. But, with Paschasius, he readily confesses that the substance of Christ’s body and blood, which does not strike the eyes, is truly hidden, visible only as enclosed and wrapped in the coverings of the species of bread and wine, and exists beyond the reach of the senses—invisible.

## XXVI. Yet the disputant says (p. 180 of the Paris edition and p. 293 of the Amsterdam edition) that Ratramnus is displeased with the very confession which Catholics freely make. He proves this by five propositions which, he maintains, Ratramnus deliberately contradicts and strongly rejects.

1. [Col. 0202C] Consecrated bread is truly the body of Christ who was born of the Virgin. According to the mind of the pseudo-Ratramnus, he says, no figure is acknowledged in the expression “body of Christ”; nothing there is received figuratively; everything is taken in truth; and, as he says in no. 14, it is freely confessed that the whole is seen “in the simplicity of truth,” with everything understood corporally.

2. Catholics freely asserted: “What we see is truly the body of Christ.”

3. Anathema to anyone who says that faith effects the mystery; for, according to the disputant, before faith, consecration through the mouth of the priest of God—God himself—effects the mystery in the symbols.

4. Nothing spiritual is enacted in that mystery; nothing hidden, nothing secret.

5. We do not receive what faith effects, but what has been effected by the Word of God and the mouth of the priest, which faith thinks and believes.

### RESPONSE

[Col. 0202D] The first proposition nowhere conflicts with Ratramnus, who confessed, with Paschasius and all Catholics, that figure and truth are found in the Eucharist. He truly denied that the body by designation—that is, the visible species of bread and wine—was born of the Virgin Mary. But he never doubted that the true body itself, hidden under designation, or concealed by the species and veils, was truly formed from the purest blood of Mary.

In the first part of his book he proved that Christ’s body is present in the Eucharist with some figure, under the veils and shadow of the species of bread and wine. In the second part he admits—or rather demonstrates—that these species, which must be called Christ’s body by designation and which are like the veil and canopy of the hidden true body, are not the body born of the Virgin Mary, dead, and buried. Rather, he shows that they differ from Christ’s true body. His opponents were necessarily driven to this conclusion because they defended the view that there is no figure and no veil in the Eucharist, but that the very body of Christ born of Mary is presented openly and manifestly.

Such are certain recent philosophers today, as were formerly Abbot Abbaudus, Walter, prior of Saint Victor of Paris, and many others, perhaps misled after Berengarius’s retraction by understanding the words of that retraction too literally. The second proposition also seems capable of being accommodated easily to Ratramnus’s mind, if by the words “What we see is truly the body of Christ” we understand that the substance hidden beneath the Eucharistic veils, or visible species—*ὁρωμέναις*, “visible”—is the true body of Christ. For this is the true position of Ratramnus, Paschasius, Lanfranc, and the Catholic Church.

But if we understand this hidden substance to be palpable and capable of being perceived by the senses, the proposition is contrary to Ratramnus and is the position of his opponents, which he repeatedly shattered and refuted with all his strength throughout the work we are defending. [Col. 0203A]

[Col. 0203B] Ratramnus does not refuse to subscribe to the anathema attached to the third proposition, since he regards Christ’s body present in the Eucharist as an object of faith, not as something effected by faith, as we observed above. He expressly admits in no. 11 that faith operates, but when he says that it therefore operates or effects Christ’s body, he means that faith gives assent to Christ’s presence. Just as an artisan does not effect the material but works upon the material by refining it, so faith does not effect the Trinity, the Incarnation, or the Eucharist; rather, it operates with regard to these mysteries by believing them, assenting to them, and bringing the understanding into captivity in obedience to faith—not by effecting them or forming them through the power of belief.

All the faithful utterly oppose the fourth proposition. Ratramnus rightly says that faith would effect nothing if nothing secret or hidden were found in this mystery. For nothing would remain to be believed if everything were made known through open and manifest revelation. Paschasius goes beyond Ratramnus with particular force when he says in his letter to Frudgardus: “Everything is spiritual.” But if by the words “spiritual,” “hidden,” and “secret” the disputant wishes to signify that the mystery depends on understanding and is regarded as effected through it, he could not be farther from Ratramnus’s meaning. We confidently assert that he will not be able to produce any passage from Ratramnus composed and explained in those terms. [Col. 0203C]

The fifth proposition explicitly explains Ratramnus’s mind. For what does it mean for something to be effected by the Word of God except through the power and force of the divine Word? Thus he says in no. 49:

> “The body and blood of Christ, which are received by the mouths of the faithful in the Church, are figures according to visible appearance. But according to invisible substance—that is, through the power of the divine Word—they truly exist as the body and blood of Christ.”

Can figure be recognized more clearly together with truth, or can the existence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist be demonstrated more powerfully through the force of the Word? Nevertheless, there is nothing to prevent us from reinforcing this passage with another. From no. 44:

> “We confess that whatever is received outwardly in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood is suited to the nourishment of the body; but the Word of God, who is the invisible bread invisibly existing in that sacrament, invisibly nourishes the minds of the faithful through participation in himself.” [Col. 0203D]

## XXVII. The disputant says (p. 180) that Ratramnus appears to deny only in no. 10 that, according to what is seen, the appearance of flesh is recognized in that bread. But who was ever so insane as to imagine or believe this?

### RESPONSE

Ratramnus knew that no human being could deny this without having departed from his senses. By this device, therefore, he proved that some figure must necessarily be acknowledged in the Eucharistic mystery. In no. 10:

> “Since no one can deny that these things are so, it is clear that that bread and wine exist figuratively as the body and blood of Christ.”

Nevertheless, who doubts that Ratramnus wrote against the supporters and defenders of such a position, as is evident from no. 5, quoted so often above? Who could think that most of the Catholic opponents of Berengarius were strangers to that opinion? Who could deny that Abbot Abbaudus or Walter, prior of Saint Victor of Paris, undertook to defend this opinion? Finally, who does not know that the more recent philosophers—and especially Father Magnan, a man never troubled by any mark of Catholic censure, a highly distinguished theological professor of the Order of Minims in the province of Toulouse—deliberately wrote an appendix to *Sacred Philosophy* against the Jesuit Théophile Raynaud, in order to prove that God, through his concurrence, when the substance of bread is lacking after consecration, causes the same impression to be made upon our eyes and senses as bread and wine made before consecration? And thus, that Christ’s very body is seen in the appearance of bread, without figure or shadow. [Col. 0204A]

## XXVIII. The disputant says on p. 293, no. 180, IV (p. 293 of the Amsterdam edition):

> “But Ratramnus was plainly infected with that heresy according to which, where the appearance of flesh is absent, flesh is absent—a question which Paschasius addressed in his letter to Frudgardus.”

### RESPONSE

How can a man infected with such a heresy—that is, believing that Christ’s flesh is absent wherever the appearance of flesh is absent—explain in express and unmistakable words what is inward and outward in the Eucharist, and teach that outwardly nothing is perceived by the senses except the species of bread and wine, while inwardly Christ’s very body and blood truly exist?

For who could fail to understand this from Ratramnus’s words in no. 10?

> “For what else is seen on the surface than the substance of wine? . . . But if you consider what is inward, it is no longer the liquid of wine, but the liquid of Christ’s blood.” [Col. 0204B]

For my part, I take from these words a firm argument for proving that Paschasius did not write against Ratramnus when he wrote against those who thought that no flesh could exist without the species and appearances of flesh.

## XXIX. “With precisely this understanding,” says the disputant (p. 181 of the Paris edition and p. 293 of the Amsterdam edition), “the pseudo-Ratramnus”—for so he chooses to deform the true author—says in no. 88:

> “These things are enacted in appearance, not in truth; that is, through likeness, not through the manifestation of the thing itself.” [Col. 0204C]

For he takes as certain and established what is utterly false: that Christ’s body cannot exist anywhere except in one of two ways—either through conspicuous manifestation or merely through likeness, that is, through figure. For when appearance is opposed to truth, mere likeness and mere figure are understood.

### RESPONSE
He does not say in that passage that these things are enacted “in appearance, not in truth,” that is, “through resemblance rather than through the manifestation of the thing itself.” Rather, he says that this meaning is expressed and signified by this prayer of the Church: “May your sacraments, O Lord, we beseech you, perfect in us what they contain, so that what we now enact under an appearance we may receive in the reality of the things”; and rightly so. For in this prayer “appearance” and “figure” are neither opposed nor contrary to the truth of Christ’s body in itself, that is, to the true substance of the body, but to its open manifestation and declaration, freed and released from every covering. Therefore, in explaining this word, Ratramnus prudently says “not in truth,” that is, “not through the manifestation of the thing itself.”

Nor does he in any way say, as though it were certain and established, that Christ’s body cannot exist except in one of two ways: either through conspicuous manifestation or merely through resemblance or figure. On the contrary, from this prayer of the Church he takes an argument to confirm that Christ’s body in the Eucharist is hidden beneath figures and shadows, namely, beneath the appearances of bread and wine. For in that petition we ask that Christ’s body, which is enacted under the appearance of bread and wine, may be seen by manifest vision, just as it truly is in heaven.

Blessed Algerus, that well-known opponent of Berengar, reported the same prayer in order to defend Ratramnus’s understanding and position, in Book I of *On the Eucharist*, chapter 5, around the middle of the Antwerp edition of 1536. “For the priest,” he says, “asks that Christ’s body, which is now enacted under the appearance of bread and wine, may at some time be received by manifest vision, just as it truly is.” Now who, unless he wished to make a laughingstock of blessed Algerus, would attribute to him such a doctrine as this: that it was certain that Christ’s body could exist anywhere only in one of two ways, either through conspicuous manifestation or merely through resemblance or figure?

### XXX. 

After the disputant, on page 181 of the Paris edition and page 293 of the Amsterdam edition, did not hesitate to maintain that Ratramnus taught the transformation of bread and wine in section 15, he strains beyond all bounds to prove that Ratramnus spoke fictitiously and deceptively, understanding by “body” in the Eucharist nothing other than something figurative and existing through mental apprehension. He cites words taken from section 16:

“But because they confess that it is the body and blood of God, this could not have happened except through a transformation for the better; and since this transformation did not take place bodily but spiritually, it is now necessary that it also be said to have taken place figuratively, since beneath the covering of bodily bread and bodily wine there exists the spiritual body of Christ and the spiritual blood.”

### RESPONSE

From this we understand that Ratramnus proved that the transformation took place figuratively, not bodily, or in a manner accommodated to the human senses. But who would therefore persuade himself that he believed Christ’s body to exist only figuratively? The reason for which he recognizes some figure in this mystery is decisive and accepted by all Catholic men:

“For plainly beneath the covering of bodily bread and bodily wine there exists the spiritual body of Christ and the spiritual blood.”

But these words do not mean that Christ’s body and blood exist in the sacrament merely as a solitary mental conception aroused by symbols. When Paschasius says in his letter to Frudgard that “the whole thing is spiritual,” the disputant would hear this as the speech of a deceitful and treacherous man. Blessed Algerus would be subjected to the same insult, since he says in Book I of *On the Eucharist*, chapter 5, in accordance with Ratramnus’s understanding:

“What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit. Therefore, since the bodily thing that is seen is one thing and the spiritual thing that is understood another, the sacrament is consequently one thing and the reality of the sacrament another.”

And in Book II, chapter 30:

“What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit.”

### XXXI. 

The disputant admits, on pages 181 and 182, section 6, of the Paris edition, and page 293, section 6—or section 6—of the Amsterdam edition, that Ratramnus used the word “conversion” in sections 24, 25, and 27. But, in order to convict him of concealment and fraud, he produces the comparison which Ratramnus made in those sections between the manna and the Eucharist. He claims that Ratramnus there places the conversion of the manna into Christ’s body on the same level as the customary conversion of bread and wine into flesh and blood. But since the opinion defending the presence of Christ’s body and blood in the manna is false, extraordinary, and abandoned by everyone, the disputant argues that Ratramnus’s opinion concerning the presence of Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist ought to meet the same fate.

### RESPONSE

Nothing is more common and familiar among the Fathers and teachers of the Church than this comparison between the manna and the Eucharist, whose resemblance is especially proper and fitting. Indeed, just as the manna was a figure representing the future Eucharist, so the Eucharist is also a figure presenting the manna of the past.

Nevertheless, it does not follow from this that the Fathers regarded the Eucharist as a mere figure, or that they did not regard or believe Christ’s body to be truly present in the sacrament. The disputant is a teacher in Israel, and he does not fail to know how easily I could demonstrate the faith of the Fathers if he pressed this comparison more eagerly against them and treated them, like Ratramnus or the author of *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, as his opponents. For since they taught the true presence of Christ’s body in the sacrament in countless passages, he would understand that this comparison could cause them no harm.

But I would gladly ask him why he violates this right in the case of Ratramnus and does not grant him the same standard of fairness, since Ratramnus did not cease to testify to his faith in this presence in several passages previously cited by us, and especially in section 24. There, after mentioning Christ, he says:

“He who later displayed the body taken from the Virgin and hung upon the cross for the salvation of believers in our own age, and poured it out through a stream of blood, by which we were not only redeemed but also given to drink.”

Thus it is beyond all suspicion and dispute that Ratramnus believed that human beings were equally redeemed and given to drink by the true blood poured out by Christ:

“By which we were not only redeemed but also given to drink.”

The disputant cunningly took care never to produce words of this kind, and always separated and omitted them from the writings containing them, as though they were a fable.

### XXXII. 

What of the fact that he himself expressly denies, in section 62:

“This manna which they ate,” says Ratramnus, “and the water which they drank—no one doubts that these were bodily.”

Here, just as in the case of the Eucharist, he maintains that what is eaten is bodily, and that this was also the case with the manna.

### RESPONSE

I now ask the disputant whether he imagines that anything is eaten bodily, gradually and perceptibly, through the bodily mouth in the reception of the sacrament, except that which is accommodated to and subject to the senses. Does he wish to persuade us that Christ’s true body is eaten in the manner of ordinary food, torn into pieces by the teeth and swallowed portion by portion?

No one can firmly hold or carefully defend this opinion. What, then, troubles him in these words of Ratramnus? Are not the sacramental appearances alone eaten bodily—or crushed by the teeth—and gradually and perceptibly lowered through the passage of the throat into the chest, just as the manna was? Or do Paschasius, Algerus, and all Christian and Catholic men in general explain another doctrine?

### XXXIII. 

“Therefore,” says the disputant, “in section 26, on page 293 of the Amsterdam edition, he teaches that in both symbols Christ is merely indicated, feeding the minds of believers; and, through his cunning as an old deceiver, he conceals—or rather precisely denies—that in one Christ is merely indicated, while in the other he is also contained. There is not even the slightest trace of this matter in the whole work. He also denies that Christ is received by the teeth of the wicked, since he feeds only the minds of the good.”

### RESPONSE

Ratramnus certainly does not teach in section 26 that Christ is merely indicated in both symbols. In fact, he says that Christ is indicated in both. But the words “merely” and “only” were invented in the disputant’s brain, occupied and overheated by preconceived opinions against Ratramnus; they occur nowhere in Ratramnus’s work. Had he used them, he would have contradicted himself.

For in section 9 he says:

“Outwardly, the form of the bread that existed before is displayed, its color is shown, and its taste is perceived; but inwardly something altogether different, far more precious and far more excellent, is intimated, because what is shown is heavenly, divine—that is, Christ’s body—which is seen, received, or eaten not by the senses of the flesh but by the contemplation of the faithful soul.”

And in section 10:

“The wine also, which through priestly consecration becomes Christ’s blood, displays one sacrament on its surface but contains another inwardly.”

Who would be so deranged as to imagine that Christ is denied in one of these words? He says in the same continuous work:

“But if you consider what is within, it is no longer the liquid of wine but the liquid of Christ’s blood that, when tasted, is perceived by the minds of believers.”

And in section 43:

“Therefore they are called the blood and body of Christ, because they are received not as what they appear outwardly to be, having been made by the operation of the divine Spirit; and because by invisible power they exist as something far different from what they visibly appear to be.”

What could be devised more consonant with the Catholic faith?

“Where,” says the disputant, “does even the slightest trace of this appear in the whole work?” By what right does he imagine that Ratramnus denies that Christ’s body is pressed by the teeth of the wicked, while feeding only the souls of the good? Does he mean that it feeds the souls of the good and the wicked equally, and thereby stain himself with the manifest disgrace of heresy? Does he not know that the Lord’s body, when discerned and received with holiness, is life for the good and death for the wicked, and that whoever receives it unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord?

What purpose would there be in exercising such preparation for receiving the Eucharist, and approaching God’s altar with such provision of grace and spiritual readiness, if it fed the souls of the good and the wicked equally? Or if it meant denying that Christ’s body is truly received by the wicked in respect of its substance, since it is said to be nourishment and life only for the good, but death and destruction for the wicked?

### XXXIV. 

Finally, in section 28, a similar dishonesty and cunning appears. He uses Catholic words so that he may also seem to breathe faith, while nevertheless, by adding the same comparison with the manna and the water, he overturns the genuine meaning of those words:

“Therefore, just as shortly before he suffered he was able to transform the substance of bread and the created substance of wine into his own body, which was about to suffer, and into his blood, which was afterward to be poured out, so also in the desert he prevailed to transform the manna and the water from the rock into his flesh and blood.”

Will Calvin not readily subscribe to this statement?

### RESPONSE

Since Ratramnus was not writing with the intention of proving the true presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist—a presence to which no one in that age was opposed—but only that some figure was to be found in it, which was denied by his opponents, who insisted that everything was externally clear in an elevated and open manifestation, without any figure or shadow, it is not surprising that Ratramnus, in proving a simply figurative conversion, drew an argument from the Eucharist’s true conversion and its one figurative conversion.

That is Ratramnus’s purpose and intention, and I strongly doubt that Calvin would have wished to endorse it. In any case, he reasons as follows: Since, without doubt, the Lord Christ was able to convert the substance of bread into his own body and the substance of wine into the blood that was soon to be poured out for the salvation of humankind, he was also able, through a figurative conversion, to transfer the manna in the desert into his own body and the water from the rock into his blood.

But who would suppose that Calvin would find this favorable? Moreover, although I do not hesitate to regard as false the opinion defending the true presence and existence of Christ’s body and blood in the manna and in the rock of the desert, it is nevertheless not so unbelievable or unimaginable that Ratramnus might have approved it. For John Duns Scotus, in Book IV, distinction 10, question 4, adds two corollaries that are no less related to such an opinion.

In the first, he maintains that before the incarnation of the divine Word the Eucharist could have existed in the same way as it does now, both with respect to the signification and with respect to the thing signified and contained.

In the second, he teaches that after the incarnation Christ’s body could cease to be present under its natural mode, while the Eucharist would nevertheless truly remain, both with respect to the truth of the sign and with respect to the truth of the thing signified and contained.

For existence under the natural mode is not of the essence of existence under the sacramental mode, nor is it its cause. Accordingly, the latter does not depend upon the former, because nothing depends upon something that is neither of its essence nor its cause.

Indeed, if such opinions of Scotus appear orthodox and tolerable within the Catholic Church, what strange or extraordinary thing will it seem that Ratramnus said in section 28, in these very words:

“Therefore, just as shortly before he suffered he was able to transform the substance of bread and the created substance of wine into his own body, which was about to suffer, and into his blood, which was afterward to be poured out, so also in the desert he prevailed to transform the manna and the water from the rock into his blood.”

For if, as the disputant Hardouin imagines, Calvin does not refuse to subscribe to Ratramnus’s opinion, by what right will he refuse to agree with the views of Scotus? And if in this matter he accepts the Scotist school’s defense of the truth, who will accuse Ratramnus of falsehood or deceit?

Indeed, who would not understand from these things—as I observed in the notes—that Ratramnus saw nothing false, impossible, or absurd in the mystery of transubstantiation, since he believed that the incarnation could have existed in the manna and water from the rock in the desert, just as Scotus believed the Eucharist could exist, both with respect to the signification and with respect to the thing signified and contained?

To some, it may seem superfluous to advance these arguments from the Scotist school against a minister of Calvinist superstition, since they customarily call the opinions of John Scotus and the subtleties of Scotus, together with Francis Rabelais, mere fantasies. But let the reader remember that I am writing against the Jesuit Hardouin, to whom the Scotist school has always seemed rational and theological, after whose model they have attempted almost from their beginnings to establish and raise up the Molinist school.

### XXXV.
