“But,” says the disputant, “in section 30,” on page 293 of the Paris edition and page 293 of the Amsterdam edition, section 7, “he truly says that through the mystery bread and wine are converted into the substance of the body and blood, to be received by believers.” What an ingenious heresy for deceiving mortal minds! Why, then, did he take such care not to say that the substance of Christ’s body is received by the mouth? Why did he write *sumenda*—‘to be received’—rather than *sumendam*, unless he understood that bread or wine had not been bodily changed?”

### RESPONSE

It is difficult to understand the ingenuity of a heresy designed to deceive human minds from these words:

“Truly, through the mystery, bread and wine are converted into the substance of the body and blood.”

If Ratramnus had said only that the conversion took place through the mystery, there might have been some room for suspicion. But if he further says that the conversion truly takes place through the mystery, what suspicion or entanglement can such a proposition involve?

For what does Catholic Church doctrine teach in the mystery of transubstantiation, except that through the mystery bread and wine are truly converted into the flesh and blood of Christ, not merely figuratively, as the patrons of Calvinist superstition stubbornly and obstinately defend?

Paschasius spoke in express accordance with Ratramnus’s meaning, and the disputant does not place Paschasius’s faith under suspicion, in his book *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, chapter 4:

“Thus, through him, the same body and blood of Christ are mystically consecrated from the substance of bread and wine.”

And in chapter 11:

“Who does not know that it is truly the Lord’s body and blood according to truth, although it is received in the sacrament through faith?”

Second, by what right does the disputant demand so vehemently the reason why Ratramnus took such care not to say that the substance of Christ’s body is received by the mouth? Does he not admit in section 5 that the entire question and discussion were instituted concerning this body, namely, the body of Christ which the faithful receive with their mouths?

Concerning this body, Charles the Bald asked Ratramnus for advice and judgment:

“Your Excellency asks whether the body and blood of Christ which are received in the Church by the mouths of the faithful occur in the mystery or in truth.”

What advantage could Ratramnus gain by cunningly and deceptively concealing a word that necessarily belonged to the exposition of the question proposed? Nor do I see what it matters whether Ratramnus said *sumenda* or *sumendam*, since they always amount to the same meaning. The manuscript codex of Lobbes has *sumenda*; other contemporary or nearly contemporary copies have *sumendam*. Let the disputant therefore explain to us what abundant fruits he derives from a brain dripping with such tangles and subtleties.

### XXXVI. 

In section 42 he falsely ascribes the same force to the word *transponendi* (“of transferring”):

“The bread that is offered,” he says, “is transferred into Christ’s body when it is sanctified. Likewise, when the wine has flowed from the vine, it nevertheless becomes Christ’s blood through the divine sanctification of the mystery—not visibly, but invisibly, through the operation of God’s Spirit, in the souls of the priest or of the people, in whom faith contemplates the mystery and, by contemplating it, brings it about.”

For he appears to deny that this occurs visibly alone. Such is the cunning of this dishonest man: he denies that something can be a body unless it is palpable and visible, as we previously heard from Paschasius; and consequently, where it is not such, he says that there is no body at all.

### RESPONSE

This is what the disputant must prove: that he has persuaded himself that this conversion takes place in the solitary mind of the believing person, and that it is not the object to which faith is applied but its effect. But this is altogether impossible (*ἀδύνατον*, adýnaton).

He could attribute the same deception to Paschasius, who says in chapter 3 of his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, page 1560:

“That which is a sensible thing is transferred intelligibly, by God’s power, through the Word of Christ, into his flesh and blood.”

“Transferred” and “transposed” are synonyms and mean precisely the same thing.

It is also pointless to say that Ratramnus deceitfully denies that this occurs in a manner accommodated to the senses, on the ground that he denies that anything can be a body unless it is palpable and visible. Paschasius said precisely the same thing in chapter 5 of his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*:

“Christ, therefore, is the food of angels, and this sacrament is TRULY HIS FLESH AND BLOOD, which a human being eats and drinks spiritually. Thus, from what gives life to the angels, the human being also lives, because everything in what the human being receives is spiritual and divine.”

And at the end of the same chapter:

“We too drink and eat spiritually the spiritual flesh of Christ, in which eternal life is believed to exist. Otherwise, to savor according to the flesh is death; yet to receive Christ’s true flesh spiritually is eternal life.”

### XXXVII. 

Again he continues in the same deception in section 42:

“Therefore,” he says, “they are called the blood and body of Christ because they are received not as what they appear outwardly to be, but as what they have become inwardly in the souls of believers, through the divine Spirit operating through faith. And because by invisible power they exist as something altogether different from what they visibly appear to be, plainly through the power of the Word, which creates and implants faith in our souls; and when that Word is believed, it has the power of Christ’s body and blood, so that it may feed the soul and give it life.”

### RESPONSE

Nothing is lacking from the interpretations and meanings which the disputant draws out of Ratramnus’s words except the force of a certain argument by which they could be defended and sustained. This would proceed easily and successfully if the words “in the souls of believers” and “through the spirit of faith,” which have been wrongly sewn onto Ratramnus’s text, were found in the autograph rather than in the disputant’s brain.

But since they were fabricated in the disputant’s workshop, he could equally well insert them, as a forger would, into Paschasius’s text and accuse him of Ratramnus’s heresy and sophistries. This is readily understood by the following words of Paschasius, in which the reader will find the additions, taken from chapter 4 of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*:

“But because it is not lawful for Christ to be devoured by teeth, he willed that in the souls of believers this bread and wine should truly be created as his flesh and blood through the consecration of the Holy Spirit of faith, in power.”

Could one egg be more like another?

### XXXVIII. 

Again, in section 42—page 294 of the Amsterdam edition, page 184 of the Paris edition—he says:

“What else are we thoroughly taught by this than that the body and blood of the Lord are called mysteries because they possess a secret and hidden disposition: that is, because they are one thing in what they indicate outwardly and another in what they invisibly effect?”

The disputant takes this from Ratramnus in order to attribute to him the opinion that he believes the mysteries are effected inwardly through faith acting invisibly in the mind of the believer.

### RESPONSE

This is what the disputant must prove, but he sweats in vain over such a small task. For what is gained by attributing to Ratramnus something that he cannot attribute to Paschasius, who reports the same thing in express words?

For Paschasius speaks thus in chapter 3 of his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*:

“But it is called a mystery because it has within itself a secret and hidden disposition. In the divine Scriptures, a sacrament exists wherever the Holy Spirit inwardly works something effectively by speaking through them. But instructed by the sacrament of the Scriptures, we are inwardly nourished by God, and, once nourished, we are instructed for Christ’s work and discipline.”

And at the end of this chapter:

“Therefore it is not surprising that the Holy Spirit, who created the human Christ in the Virgin’s womb without seed, also daily effects the substance of bread and wine as Christ’s flesh and blood by invisible power, through the sanctification of his sacrament, although it cannot be grasped outwardly either by sight or by the taste of flavor. But because they are spiritual, they are most fully received with the certainty of faith and understanding, just as the Truth foretold.””

If these words occurred in Ratramnus—“Christ’s body and blood are received because they are spiritual, through faith and understanding”—the disputant would spare him nothing, but would utterly destroy him.

### XXXIX. 

“Let us now,” says the disputant Hardouin in the same place—the first Paris edition, page 184, and the second Amsterdam edition, page 294, section 184, subdivision VIII—“go through the remaining frauds of this man,” in section 56:

“Now, since faith beholds the whole of whatever that whole may be, while the eyes of the flesh apprehend nothing, understand that Christ’s body and blood exist not in appearance but in power, which are believed [in the latest Amsterdam edition: ‘which are seen’]. Hence Ambrose said that here one must not consider the order of nature but venerate Christ’s power, which creates whatever it wills, however it wills, and into whatever it wills; which creates what did not exist and changes what was created into what it previously was not.”

But since transubstantiation could not be explained in more explicit words than these—not Ratramnus’s words, but those of Saint Ambrose from the book *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*—the disputant was pleased to heap upon them additions from this gloss, namely, “in the souls of believers,” in which the power of the divine Word creates faith in Christ’s body and blood through the powerful operation of the Holy Spirit, as he says in section 54. That is how he understands it.

He cannot stomach anyone’s saying that what we see on the altar is Christ’s true body. He says that it is a body not in appearance, or in propriety—that is, in its own essence—but in power. Paschasius rightly censures this word of his and of those like him in chapter 26 of his commentary on Saint Matthew:

“Therefore I marvel,” he says, “what has prevented certain people from saying that the truth of Christ’s flesh or blood is not in the reality but in the sacrament; that there is a certain power of the flesh and not flesh, a power of the blood and not blood; a figure and not truth, a shadow and not a body. This power belongs only to the sign, since the symbols represent the body and blood to the mind.”

### RESPONSE

The disputant draws horrifying conclusions from these passages. Indeed, there would be no room for doubt if the explanations that suitably and faithfully fit them were rigorously deduced according to right reason: Ratramnus—or the author of the book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, whose defense prompted us to write this treatise—would then certainly hold Calvinist heresy tightly.

For no heresy of this kind could be expressed or stated more precisely or elegantly than in these words:

“Understand that Christ’s body and blood, which are believed, exist not in appearance but in power.”

However the matter may stand, if “the body and blood which are believed in the Eucharist exist in power and not in appearance, with the word ‘appearance’ taken to mean essence and the propriety of nature,” then here we see pure and unalloyed Calvinist heresy.

But I do not know by what misfortune the disputant unhappily gouged out his own eyes—the eyes he applied to section 56—in which these words, “which are believed,” do not occur at all. On the contrary, the words are “which are seen,” and they signify a very different and Catholic meaning.

For what is seen in the Eucharist is whiteness, roundness, and extension—in short, visible objects readily accessible to human senses. These are not the appearances and manifestations of Christ’s body and blood, but of the bread and wine that existed before and that God changed into his body and blood, as Ratramnus says, citing Saint Ambrose’s book *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 9:

“He changes what was created into what previously did not exist.”

Yet I would not wish to accuse the disputant, otherwise a pious man and not of the lowest intelligence, of such a foul interpolation or corruption that he would consign the unfortunate Ratramnus among the fraudulent heretics. Especially since, in order to receive him favorably among those same heretics, Peter Allix, a minister of Calvinist superstition, did not resort to such crude methods or such gross ineptitude in our French temple at Charenton.

This is readily apparent from the Latin-French edition prepared under his direction at Rouen by Lucas in 1672, and from the English-Latin edition prepared by another man of a different confession at London in 1686. Although the ministers are stubborn and obstinate defenders of their superstitions, they did not dare to replace the word “which are seen” with “which are believed.”

How superfluous and disgraceful it is to deform Ratramnus’s text by such an interpolation is amply and repeatedly demonstrated by the doctrines scattered throughout this book, which are contrary to it:

“Therefore, the things that are seen and the things that are believed are not the same. According to what is seen, they feed the corruptible body—the things themselves being corruptible; but according to what is believed, they feed souls that will live forever—the things themselves being immortal.”

Let the disputant now apply his will and read Ratramnus, and with open eyes let him see that in section 56 the word is not “believed” but “seen.” Then let him keep before his eyes, in one continuous view, the most delightful spectacle of the defenses, interpretations, inferences, and glosses which he wrongly drew from this passage immediately collapsing and gaping open with cracks on every side.

Since this is so, the following can nowhere be true:

1. That the transformation which takes place in the Eucharist exists in the souls of believers, in which the power of the divine Word creates faith in Christ’s body and blood through the powerful operation of the Holy Spirit. Such a creation of faith has no trace whatsoever in Ratramnus’s work.

2. Ratramnus in that passage does not oppose the essence or natural propriety of Christ’s body to “power” by the words “not in appearance but in power.” He opposes only the outward appearance, which truly does not appear in the Eucharist or present itself to the eyes.

On the contrary, in agreement with Paschasius, he says in section 49:

“Christ’s body and blood, which are received by the mouths of the faithful in the Church, are figures according to visible appearance; but according to invisible substance—that is, through the power of the divine Word—they truly exist as Christ’s body and blood.”

What person in possession of a sound mind would place Ratramnus’s sincerity of faith under suspicion on the basis of these words? From them it is readily and plainly understood that by the word “appearance” he did not mean nature or propriety, but outward appearance and manifestation.

It is therefore pointless to imagine that Paschasius wrote against Ratramnus in his commentary on Saint Matthew, chapter 26, and that in section 56 Ratramnus understood “appearance” to mean something other than outward manifestation, when he says:

“Not flesh in appearance, but in the sacrament; and this, which now contains in the mystery a likeness of that flesh, is not flesh in appearance but in the sacrament.”

For in the immediately following speech he explains his meaning and abundantly testifies that by “appearance” he understood the outward disclosure of the bread and wine, beneath which—that is, in the sacrament—he teaches that Christ’s true body and blood exist:

“For in appearance it is bread; in the sacrament it is Christ’s true body, as he himself cries out: ‘This is my body.’”

With Ratramnus’s position standing thus, how wrongly the disputant exclaims that Ratramnus is “fighting with ghosts,” and says:

“Who said that Christ’s body is visible upon the altar? Was this dream to be refuted by the testimonies of the Fathers?”

A ready answer could be given: he himself went toward this position, since he repeats in countless passages that what is seen is Christ’s body. Does anything appear except what is visible? And can something be seen that cannot be seen?

But let us grant that the disputant’s reasoning recoils from this opinion, struck by the evidence of his own senses. There is no doubt that the opponents whom Ratramnus refutes persuaded themselves that no figure or shadow subsisted in the Eucharist, but that everything was manifest and open. They were followed by Abbot Abbo, Walter, the prior of Saint Victor of Paris, and, in our own age, more recent philosophers who, although they all professed the Catholic faith and religion, were somewhat alien to the positions of Aristotelian philosophy and had no conception of accidents inhering in no subject.

### XL. 

Why does he say in sections 5, 49, and 96, and elsewhere, that what has been placed upon the Lord’s table, what is celebrated and preserved on the altar, and what is received by the mouths of the faithful, is Christ’s true body only in mystery or figure?

### RESPONSE

Ratramnus never said in sections 5, 49, or 96, nor anywhere else, that the body of Jesus Christ received by the mouths of the faithful is Christ’s true body only in mystery or figure. This proposition, as the schools say, would involve a contradiction in terms. It is inconceivable that a true body could exist only in figure and mystery; for it would then be both a true body and not a true body.

### XLI. 

And indeed Erigerus, or the Cellotian Anonymous, says that there were only two parties; Paschasius likewise, and Ratramnus:

“Some,” he says, “say that what is taken from the altar is the same as that which was born from the Virgin; while others deny this and say that it is something else.”

### RESPONSE

From the words of the Cellotian Anonymous I claim the right to make everyone understand that the various and conflicting opinions of faithful people concerning the matter of the Eucharist are not to be regarded as parties—that is, as different sides opposed to the truth of the faith.

Ratramnus observes in section 11 that this entire controversy arose among the faithful. But whatever the case may be, since the Cellotian Anonymous is a writer of the lowest intelligence and no merit, and since the solitary testimony on which rests the conviction of those who imagine that Ratramnus and Paschasius fought against each other, this entire controversy can easily be resolved by a careful reading of the books of Ratramnus, Paschasius, and the Cellotian Anonymous. From these the reader will see that this Anonymous understood neither Ratramnus’s meaning nor Paschasius’s.

For since the Anonymous failed to notice that Ratramnus never denies that the body born from the Virgin Mary is present in the Eucharist, but only distinguishes it from the body celebrated in the Church—namely, from the body so called, beneath which the true body is concealed and lies hidden—and since Ratramnus denies only that this so-called body was born from Mary, the Anonymous persuaded himself that Paschasius, who asserts that the true body born from Mary is in the Eucharist, and Ratramnus, who denies that the so-called body was born from Mary, were opposed to one another.

In reality, once a distinction is made between the so-called body and the true body—that is, between the true body hidden beneath the shadow of the figurative body—they can easily be reconciled and brought into agreement.

The disputant says that Ratramnus, in order to placate the faithful, referred equally to the supporters of both opinions, whether those asserting that everything was open and manifest or those asserting that there was some figure in the sacrament of the body received by the mouths of the faithful in the Church. Nothing seems more alien to ordinary human judgment than this claim, since Ratramnus was bound to respond at the emperor’s command, and those whom he was to include among the heretics had to be counted as such, by the common judgment of all Catholics, if they truly denied the real and true presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist.

### XLII. 

First, he misuses the word “mystery” in an improper way. For in sections 73, 74, and 98 he teaches that consecrated bread is a mystery, both of the body in which Christ was born and of the body of the Church—something which we have shown by many proofs to be utterly contrary to the truth.

### RESPONSE
Neither in these passages nor elsewhere does Ratramnus teach that the consecrated bread is a mystery, but rather that it is a figure and veil which covers and conceals Christ’s body. Paschasius taught the same thing in countless places, especially in chapter 4 of his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. Halmo of Halberstadt, whom the disputant cites against this passage of Ratramnus, says nothing contrary or opposed to it; indeed, he is highly favorable to it in his treatise *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, published by the most learned monk Dom Luc d’Achery in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 28, where the following words may be read—words that wonderfully explain Ratramnus’s meaning:

> “In this body and blood of Christ, because of the horror felt by those who receive it, the taste and figure of bread and wine remain, while the nature of the substances has been wholly changed into the body and blood of Christ. But the sense of the flesh reports one thing, while the faith of the mind reports another: the sense of the flesh can report nothing other than what it feels, whereas the understanding and faith of the mind report and confess Christ’s true flesh and blood.”

### XLIII [Cols. 0213B–0214A]

Nor do the two ecclesiastical prayers which he cites in numbers 85 and 88 lend support to the error of the pseudo-Ratramnus.

### RESPONSE

We have already spoken of these prayers of the Church above, in the explanation of Ascelinus’s letter to Berengar. Ratramnus presented them for no other purpose than to refute the opinion of those who had persuaded themselves that everything in the Eucharist was open and exposed to the view of the senses and the eyes, with no shadows or figures concealing it. For in these prayers God was asked that we might receive, through the manifest—or manifested—participation in the sacrament, what we touch in the image; and that what we now bear under an outward appearance we might receive in the reality of the things themselves. That is, “by manifestation”: for, as we have shown above and in the preface, this word “manifestation” is expressed in Ratramnus’s style by the phrase “the reality.”

The blessed Algerus likewise used “the reality” to signify manifestation in book I, chapter 5, *On the Eucharist*:

> “Hence,” he says, “at the end of a certain Mass it is prayed and said:
>
> ‘May your sacraments, Lord, we ask, accomplish in us what they contain, so that what we now bear under an outward appearance we may receive in the reality of the things themselves.’
>
> The priest asks that Christ’s body, which is now borne under the appearance of bread and wine, may at some time be received in a manifest vision, just as it truly is. Concerning this vision we have been taught in the Gospel according to John: ‘Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.’ Concerning this same sacrament we read in the passion of the blessed Dionysius that, while he was celebrating the sacred mystery in prison, the Lord appeared to him and, giving him the holy sacrament, said: ‘Receive this, my dear one, which I shall soon complete for you together with my Father.’ It was as though he were saying: ‘What I give you I give as provision for the journey. I shall not change it into something else as a reward, but I shall complete that very same thing by manifesting myself,’ and so forth.”

I observed in the preface that these prayers were translated from the Greeks into Latin, as we understand from the words of Saint Dionysius which we cited earlier in our response to objection 10. Yet prayers of this kind, thus explained, cannot lend support to any error. Therefore, Ratramnus must be recognized as free and innocent of every charge of heresy.

Nevertheless, the disputant endeavors to prove that Ratramnus was profoundly mistaken by appealing to the authority of Saint Augustine, who, in *Tractate XXVII on John*, interprets “manifest participation” as extending to participation in the spirit. But what follows from that? It is certain that these prayers were composed long after Saint Augustine, during the pontificate of Gelasius or Saint Gregory the Great, since they are found in the sacramentaries of those men, but nowhere in Saint Augustine’s works. These arguments are so feeble that they require no answer.

The disputant’s interpretation of the other prayer is no more satisfactory:

> “May your sacraments, Lord, we ask, accomplish in us what they contain, so that what we now bear under an outward appearance we may receive in the reality of the things themselves.”

With a stubborn heart he insists that the meaning of this prayer does not differ from that of another prayer composed in Paschasius’s time:

> “Pour into us the spirit of your charity, so that those whom you have satisfied with the Paschal sacraments you may make united through your loving-kindness.”

He might just as easily prove that the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* has the same meaning as Psalm 109, *De profundis*.

### XLIV [Cols. 0214A–0215A]

Disputation, p. 295, Amsterdam edition, and p. 188, Paris edition. This perverse acceptance of the term “mystery” leads the pseudo-Ratramnus to maintain everywhere that Christ’s body which is on the altar is separated by a great interval from the body in which Christ was born—just as there must be a distinction between the sign of a thing and the thing signified.

### RESPONSE

Ratramnus does not give the word “mystery” either a vain or a perverse interpretation. He explains his meaning openly and clearly in number 9; to add anything to it or subtract anything from it would be dreadful and alarming:

> “If that mystery is not enacted under a figure, then it is not rightly called a mystery. For that cannot be called a mystery in which nothing is hidden, nothing is removed from bodily senses, and nothing is covered by some veil.”

Who would not recognize in these words the broadest traces of truth? Who could doubt that they apply to the Eucharist, in which faith and understanding have as their object Christ’s body and blood, hidden, while the senses perceive only the outward appearances of bread and wine remaining, as Ratramnus says in the same number 9?

For the rest, nothing contrary to the laws of right reason or of the Christian religion prevents us from recognizing a distinction between Christ’s veiled body and that same body when set forth and manifested; between the body located circumscriptively, as the philosophers say, and that same body existing spiritually and definitively. This distinction concerns not the substance of the body but its various modes of existence.

What prevents us from recognizing a great difference between our living bodies and those same bodies restored to life after the resurrection? Did not the apostles recognize the greatest difference between Christ’s glorious and radiant body on the day of the Transfiguration and that same body, torn and mutilated, on the day of his passion and death?

There is therefore no obstacle to admitting the greatest distinction and interval between Christ’s body, born of the Virgin, suffering and nailed to the cross, made a spectacle to the world and to human beings, and that same body veiled, hidden, and wrapped in figures and shadows in the Eucharist, imperceptible and inaccessible to all the senses.

The blessed Algerus, Berengar’s opponent, said that this body is “THE SAME AND NOT THE SAME”; Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, said the same.

Moreover, according to Algerus, we must not omit that Christ’s body existing in the sacrament of the Eucharist is of two kinds: one is the nominal body, consisting in the shadows and figures of the species of bread and wine; the other is the true and proper body assumed from the Virgin Mary, hidden and concealed beneath the nominal body, deceiving the eyes and senses of human beings.

Of these Ratramnus says:

> “Not that there are two existences of things.”

And this is entirely clear and true, since he himself teaches in number 30 that the substance of bread and wine has been changed into the body and blood of Christ, and says in number 28:

> “For we do not suppose that any of the faithful doubts that that bread was made Christ’s body, which, giving it to the disciples, he says: ‘This is my body, which is given for you’; nor that anyone doubts that the cup contains Christ’s blood, concerning which he says in the same place: ‘This is the cup,’ and so forth.”

The disputant may perhaps reply that all these things do not signify the body born of the Virgin Mary, dead, and buried. But it is not difficult to return this objection upon him, since Ratramnus himself says that the blood poured out for salvation was drunk by the faithful, by which we were not only redeemed but also given to drink, as we observed above from number 24.

### XLV [Cols. 0215A–0215D]

Page 295, Amsterdam edition, and page 198, Paris edition. But the pseudo-Ratramnus rightly distinguishes and separates the body which exists through the mystery—that is, the body which exists in the understanding of faith after the figure, symbol, or mystery has been pointed out—from the bodily and proper, or human, body of Christ. He falsely thinks that this is the divine, spiritual, and invisible body indicated by Jerome. Yet he impiously denies that the proper body has a place on the altar.

### RESPONSE

Ratramnus by no means imagined that Christ’s body exists in the Eucharist through the mind or through the operation of the understanding. Such a chimera, or entity of reason, never entered his mind. He therefore does not distinguish or separate the true and natural body from that phantasmal body; rather, he distinguishes it from the nominal body, which, as Algerus says, hides and covers the true and proper body.

Nor does Ratramnus in any way deny that Christ’s true and proper body exists in the Eucharist. Concerning this he says in number 49:

> “That body and blood of Christ which are received by the mouths of the faithful in the Church are figures according to visible appearance; but according to invisible substance—that is, through the power of the divine Word—they truly exist as Christ’s body and blood.”

But if they truly exist, they do not exist through the mind. To exist through the mind is to exist fictitiously and phantasmally:

> “A woman fair above ends in a fish.”

Moreover, Ratramnus does not impiously deny, as the disputant falsely attributes to him, that the proper body has a place on the altar. For he explicitly teaches in number 24:

> “He displayed in our times the body taken from the Virgin and hung upon the cross for the salvation of believers, and from it poured out a stream of blood, by which we were not only redeemed but also given to drink.”

Indeed, since we were redeemed not by fictitious or imaginary blood but by true blood, we are not given to drink fictitious or imaginary blood but true blood—namely, the same blood poured out for the redemption of the human race.

If by “proper body” one means a body with its own properties—weight, dimensions, affections, palpable and accessible to the senses—then such a body truly has no place on the altar. But if “proper” means true, spiritual, and beyond the grasp of the senses, then Ratramnus believed that the true body of Christ, born of the Virgin, is present in the Eucharist just as all the faithful believe that the bodies we now use will be restored, glorious, and spiritual after the resurrection.

### XLVI [Cols. 0215D–0216A]

Ratramnus errs, says the disputant, p. 187 of the Paris edition and p. 295 of the Amsterdam edition, in thinking that the sacrament is composed of complete symbols untouched by any change, while the thing of which they are sacraments is the very body in which Christ was born.

### RESPONSE

Ratramnus says that no external change is perceived in the Eucharistic species, or in the symbols of bread and wine—and rightly so. But he teaches with complete clarity that the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Jesus Christ, in numbers 15 and 30, where he says:

> “Bread and wine, changed into the substance of the body and blood, are to be received by believers.”

The Magdeburg Centuriators themselves acknowledged this.

As for his statement that “the thing of the sacrament is the very body in which Christ was born,” the blessed Algerus said the same in book IV, chapter 5, *On the Eucharist*:

> “The sacrifice is made up of two things: the sacrament and the thing of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body.”

And below:

> “The sacrament, therefore, is one thing, and the thing of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body, is another.”

Who, nevertheless, would say that Algerus was mistaken in this?

### XLVII [Cols. 0216A–0216B]

Amsterdam edition, p. 295; Paris edition, p. 189. Connected with this first error is another, namely, that he considers the whole mystery to be enacted by faith. As he said in the passage cited immediately above, the bread which is figuratively and mystically called Christ’s body is received by the mouths of the faithful in order that it may be a mystery—that is, so that faith may understand that this sign is Christ’s body.

### RESPONSE

Ratramnus never held that the whole mystery is enacted by faith, nor can such a perverse doctrine be understood from his books. According to Ratramnus, the mystery is the object of our faith, because inwardly it contains what surpasses the powers of the outward senses.

Nor did he ever say that the body is received figuratively in order that it may be a mystery. To prove this, the disputant can appeal to nothing except, and then only contemptuously, the very words excerpted from Ratramnus’s work.

### XLVIII [Cols. 0216B–0216C]

Amsterdam edition, p. 295; Paris edition, p. 189. In number 44 he says that the sacrament or mystery consists of two things: visible bread and the word of God. Christ’s body, which is intimated by that bread, is believed through the understanding; thus the mystery is enacted through understanding and faith.

### RESPONSE

To convict the disputant of falsehood, the words of number 44 must be transcribed, for they readily show the contrary:

> “We confess that whatever is received outwardly in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood is suited to the nourishment of the body; but the word of God, who is the invisible bread invisibly existing in that sacrament, invisibly nourishes the minds of the faithful by participating in himself and bringing them to life.”

Can anything else be understood from these words than that the Word of God, Christ the Lord, is the invisible bread received by the faithful in the sacrament of the Eucharist?

Paschasius stated this very clearly in chapter 8 of his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*:

> “O man, learn to taste something other than what is perceived by the mouth of flesh; learn to see something other than what is shown by these eyes of flesh. Learn that, as God is spirit, he is everywhere without being confined to a place; understand that these spiritual things, just as they are not local, are likewise not carnal, but are borne aloft before the sight of the divine majesty.”

And earlier, in chapter 5:

> “We too spiritually drink and eat the spiritual flesh of Christ, in which eternal life is believed to exist.”

And in chapter 6:

> “That sacrament of faith is rightly called the truth. It is therefore the truth when Christ’s body and blood are made from the substance of bread and wine through the power of the Spirit and his Word; but it is a figure when the priest, as though carrying out something outwardly different, sacrifices daily on the altar, in remembrance of the sacred passion, the Lamb who was offered once.”

You will find the same teaching at the beginning of Algerus’s book *On the Eucharist*.

### XLIX [Cols. 0216D–0217A]

Number 95: The sacrament contains something secret, and what appears visibly is one thing, while what must be received invisibly is another—that is, according to his mind, it is not in the consecrated bread that is seen, but in the spirit of believers, in the faith that lies hidden.

### RESPONSE

This conclusion—namely, “that the sacrament contains something secret, and that what appears visibly is one thing while what must be received invisibly is another”—is orthodox and catholic. Ratramnus took it from Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, book VI, chapter 19 of the *Etymologies*, where these words occur in continuous text:

> “A sacrament is present in some celebration when the thing enacted is such that it is understood to signify something which must be received in a holy manner.”

Paschasius gave the same definition of a sacrament at the beginning of chapter 3 of his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*:

> “A sacrament, therefore, is whatever is handed down to us in some divine celebration as a pledge of salvation, when a visible event produces something altogether different and invisible which must be received in a holy manner.”

He explains this definition according to the mind and intention of Ratramnus in the whole of chapter 3. There is no need to transcribe it here.

It is therefore just as vain and insulting to attribute to Ratramnus the belief that Christ’s body exists in the Eucharist solely through the operation of the understanding as it would be unnecessary and futile to attribute the same belief to Paschasius.

### L [Cols. 0217A–0217C]

Likewise, in number 49, says the disputant, p. 190 of the Paris edition and p. 295 of the Amsterdam edition:

> “The body and blood of Christ, which are so called and are figuratively, he says, and which are received by the mouths of the faithful, are figures according to visible appearance; but according to invisible substance—that is, through the power of the divine Word—they truly exist as Christ’s body and blood.”

For the pseudo-Ratramnus, the power of the invisible substance is the power of the divine Word in which the mind believes. Thus this wicked man—namely Ratramnus—by abusing catholic expressions such as “invisible substance” and others, which he miserably and violently distorts, deceived French translators, who rendered this passage as **par la puissance du Verbe divin**—“through the power of the divine Word”—whereas he said not “through the power” but “according to the power of the Word.”

### RESPONSE

Of all the French translators of this treatise of Ratramnus, I alone, as a catholic, translated the words *secundum potentiam Verbi*—“according to the power of the Word”—as **la puissance du Verbe**. Petrus Allix, minister of the Charenton temple of Calvinist superstition, translated it according to the disputant’s intention in the edition printed at Rouen in 1672. Earlier, in 1561, Augustine Marlorat had rendered it **selon la puissance**—“according to the power.”

But since a faithful translator ought to take greater care to render the meaning than the word literally, and since I did not undertake to produce a gloss or an interlinear version but an accurate and corrected translation, there can be no room for doubt that by the words *secundum potentiam* he understood “through the power.” He uses this very manner of speaking in number 443:

> “And because they exist in a wholly different manner through invisible power from the way they appear visibly…”

Thus he indicates what he wished to say in number 49:

> “Namely, that according to the invisible substance—that is, through the power of the divine Word—they truly exist as Christ’s body and blood.”

### LI [Col. 0217C]

Amsterdam edition, p. 296; Paris edition, p. 190. And through faith he changes the substance of the bread into the substance of the Lord’s body.

### RESPONSE

This is false and fictitious. Our Ratramnus never spoke in this way. We have demonstrated above, with the clarity of midday, that he always regarded Christ’s body and blood in the mystery of the Eucharist as the object, not the effect, of faith. Therefore, the presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist precedes the operation of faith—

### LII [Cols. 0217C–0218A]

The same Amsterdam page 296 and Paris page 190. In the same sense, in number 68 he says that the bread of Christ’s body embraces two things: that which passes into the body and that which is the bread of eternal life, namely, the Word of God; and when the mind believes in it, it is nourished and given to drink by Christ’s body.

### RESPONSE

Everyone knows that the nourishment of the soul takes place through communion in the body, not through the conversion of that body into the substance of the soul.

But it is false that Ratramnus understands Christ’s body to be nothing other than what enters the mouth in a sensible manner, is swallowed, and passes into the stomach, together with the Word of God in which one believes. On the contrary, in that same number 68 he observes that Saint Ambrose, whose words he cites, wishes to speak of the bread which is Christ’s body and supports the substance of our soul—not insofar as it enters the body, but insofar as it is the bread of eternal life:

> “Therefore it is evident,” he says, “which bread he is speaking of: namely, the bread of Christ’s body, which supports the substance of our soul not by what passes into the body, but by the fact that it is the bread of eternal life.”

This is thoroughly catholic and orthodox. It does not mean that Christ’s body is the Word of God, by believing in which the mind is nourished and given to drink. Nevertheless, it is necessary to believe the Word of God and love God with one’s whole heart and whole soul in order to receive Christ’s true body beneficially.

### LIII [Cols. 0218A–0218C]

Amsterdam edition, p. 296. In number 72 he says that Christ’s spiritual flesh is composed of two things: the outward appearance it bears and the spiritual power of the divine Word, an invisible efficacy and divine virtue of the Word of God in which one believes.

### RESPONSE

All this is fictitious. In that passage he is not considering the composition of Christ’s spiritual flesh. He merely explains the different and distinct modes in which Christ’s body is understood to exist—namely, in the womb of the blessed Virgin and on the cross. He then speaks of the nominal body of the Eucharist.

In the continuous text he shows that Christ’s spiritual flesh—that is, the glorious flesh assumed from the blessed Virgin, which supplies immortal life to the soul—is the effect of spiritual power, invisible efficacy, and the virtue of God, and that what is presented to and perceived by the senses is different from what is believed and understood by faith:

> “For whatever in it provides the substance of life is spiritual power, invisible efficacy, and divine virtue; and it exists in one way according to what is seen outwardly, and in a wholly different way according to what is believed in the mystery.”

Paschasius says the same thing, together with all the defenders of the catholic faith, in chapter 11 of *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*:

> “And it will enable the priest who attends to it to understand the whole sanctification of the mystical sacrifice and its efficacy: how a sensible thing is intelligibly and divinely transformed by the power of God through Christ’s Word and his flesh and blood.”

And in chapter 4:

> “But it appears to be a figure when it is broken; when, under a visible appearance, something other than what is perceived by the sight and taste of the flesh is understood; and when blood is mixed in the cup together with water. That sacrament of faith is rightly called the truth. It is therefore the truth when Christ’s body and blood are made from the substance of bread and wine through the power of the Spirit and his words.”

### LIV [Cols. 0218C–0218D]

Amsterdam edition, p. 296; Paris edition, p. 191. Ratramnus says in number 77:

> “It is the true body, he says, which the mind perceives by thinking. It exists in the understanding of faith, invisible indeed and spiritual, but perceived by the mind itself. Thus Christ’s body exists in the mystery, in the minds of believers through the Word of God; outside the mind, it does not exist on the altar.”

### RESPONSE

It is enough to transcribe the precise words from number 78, so that the reader may see how unnecessary it is to attribute such an opinion to Ratramnus, or the claim that Christ’s body is not outside the mind on the altar. He says:

> “One thing is what is enacted outwardly, another what is believed through faith. Is this not true, when outwardly only the appearances of bread and wine are seen, while inwardly Christ’s body is truly believed to exist? What pertains to the senses is corruptible; but what faith believes is incorruptible.”

Is there anything fictitious or false in these words, since the appearances are corrupted daily, while Christ’s body, which is the object of faith, suffers no corruption?

What appears outwardly is not the thing itself. Are the whiteness, roundness, and taste of bread, or the smell of wine, Christ’s body? Yet are they not truly the image, figure, veil, or covering of the thing, by which it deceives human eyes?

What is perceived by the mind, however, is the truth of the thing. Since the thing itself is Christ’s body, the truth of the thing is the truth of Christ’s body. And since it is truth, not a chimera or an entity of reason, does it exist merely through the mind’s thought and not as the mind’s true and substantial object?

### LV [Cols. 0218D–0219C]

Amsterdam edition, p. 296; Paris edition, p. 191. In numbers 89 and 94 Ratramnus says that the soul is spiritually nourished by faith, when attention is not given to what nourishes the body, what is pressed by the tooth, and what is broken into pieces, but to what is spiritually received in faith. You clearly imply that outside faith there is nothing except what nourishes the body and is pressed by the tooth. Nor, he says, can one affirm what the Church of God confesses with Paul and Augustine, indeed with Christ the Lord: “What you see is my body.”

### RESPONSE

We have already observed that the nourishment of the soul provided by Christ’s flesh and blood does not occur, like natural nourishment, through the conversion of his flesh into the substance of the soul, but through the infusion of the grace of faith, hope, and charity. Yet this does not prevent Christ’s body from being real, through whose mixture and reception our spiritual nourishment is provided by the spiritual power and virtue of God’s Spirit.

Since this is so, it is necessary to observe how profoundly the disputant was mistaken when he asserts that Ratramnus meant that, apart from faith, nothing is found in the Eucharist except what can contribute to bodily nourishment. Ratramnus does not say this; he says that what is received spiritually together with faith provides nourishment for the soul.

There is a very great difference between faith and what is perceived together with faith, just as there is between sight and the object of sight.

Paschasius agrees wonderfully with Ratramnus in establishing a distinction between those who approach the sacred communion of Christ’s body worthily and those who approach it unworthily:

> “Behold, how often all indiscriminately receive the sacraments of the altar. They certainly receive them, but one spiritually eats Christ’s flesh and drinks his blood, while another does not, although he appears to receive a morsel from the priest’s hand.”

As for the disputant’s statement that Ratramnus teaches in this passage that one cannot affirm what the Church of God confesses with Paul and Augustine, indeed with Christ the Lord—“This which is seen is my body”—although we have already explained this maxim in countless places, we can give no better answer than the following words of the blessed Algerus, book I, chapter 11, *On the Eucharist*:

> “Likewise Augustine to Irenaeus: ‘You are not going to eat this which you see; it is the same and yet not the same, the same invisibly and not the same visibly.’ Hence it is added: ‘If it is necessary that it be celebrated visibly, it is necessary that it be understood invisibly.’ Therefore, since the Lord’s spiritual body is not bodily food but spiritual food, it is necessary that it be understood invisibly.”

Thus speaks that most powerful defender of the catholic faith against Berengar, entirely appropriately for defending the mind and judgment of our Ratramnus. No catholic person could accuse him of error or heresy on account of saying that what is seen in the Eucharist is not Christ’s body itself, because it is neither visible nor palpable; rather, it is that very body which is truly hidden and concealed beneath visible species—the bread and wine that existed previously and have now been changed into the substance of Christ’s body and blood, to be received by the faithful.

### LVI [Cols. 0219D–0220A]

The same work. For this reason, in number 15 he denies that the body of the bread has been changed. Why? “For bodily,” he says, “nothing is perceived to have been changed in them.” Certainly—but it is nevertheless believed.

### RESPONSE

In number 15 he does not deny that the body of the bread has been changed. Rather, he proves this in the numbers that follow and says only that the external change is not perceived by human senses:

> “For bodily,” he says, “nothing is perceived to have been changed in them. They must therefore admit either that they have been changed in some respect other than bodily.”

And at the end of this number, after proving that some change must take place in the Eucharist, he says:

> “Or, if they wish to profess this, they are compelled to deny that it is the body and blood of Christ—which it is impious not only to say but even to think.”

What could support the doctrine of the catholic Church more forcefully than these words? I marvel that the disputant has never considered them with attentive mind.

### LVII [Cols. 0220A–0220C]

The same work. And in number 16 he says that the change is figurative and spiritual, as we have said, taking place through the understanding of faith.

### RESPONSE

This is false. Ratramnus never spoke in this way, nor did he say that this change occurs through the understanding of faith. On the contrary, he adds that this change must take place from bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood, as he says in number 30:

> “Bread and wine, changed into the substance of the body and blood through the virtue and power of the divine Word.”

In truth, he teaches that this change does not take place in a sensible and bodily manner but spiritually and in a way removed from the senses, as Paschasius, Algerus, Lanfranc, and all catholic writers have said.

Therefore Ratramnus speaks thus in number 16:

> “Beneath the covering of bodily bread and bodily wine there exists Christ’s spiritual body and spiritual blood.”

For although the body is real and subject to no mental conception, it is nevertheless spiritual and glorious, like our bodies when they rise again after the resurrection. They will indeed be the same bodies that are alive today on earth, although restored to life in heaven and glory, and differing from their mortal condition through the substance of immortality.

The words that Ratramnus immediately continues to speak confirm the sincerity of his faith so clearly that nothing can weaken them:

> “Not that there are two existences of mutually different things, namely, body and spirit, but one and the same thing: in one respect it consists as the species of bread and wine, but in another respect as Christ’s body and blood.”

Nothing more compatible with the catholic faith could be said. Nor can I understand why the disputant, provoked by these words, thinks that they signify that on the altar there is only the substance of bread, by the reminder of which the body of Christ that is believed nourishes and gives life to the minds of believers, and that, by what is conceived, it is called Christ’s spiritual body.

On the contrary, since he acknowledges the change of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood, and since he recognizes that the bodily and sensible species do not have an existence different from Christ’s spiritual or glorious body, it clearly follows that Ratramnus could not have meant:

> “That in this mystery there is only the substance of bread, by the reminder of which the body that is believed nourishes and gives life to the soul, and by what is conceived is called the spiritual body.”

### LVIII [Cols. 0220C–0220D]

Amsterdam edition, p. 276; Paris edition, p. 191. From this it necessarily follows that he freely and openly says in number 40 that the Lord’s body and the Lord’s blood are called symbols, because they take their designation from the true body and blood in which Christ was born, whose sacrament they are, and whose memory and faith they arouse.

### RESPONSE

The symbols are not called Christ’s body simply because they recall that body or arouse faith in it, but because sacraments and mysteries take their names from the things they contain.

For this reason the blessed Algerus calls the Eucharist the nominal body of Jesus Christ, because in it there are Christ’s figure and veil. These species and figures approach the likeness of Christ’s body and present its image, not because they recall it, but because they nourish the body—just as the Word of God, which is the living bread descended from heaven, nourishes and refreshes the souls of the faithful through participation in itself:

> “For just as the substance of this visible bread and wine outwardly nourishes and inebriates the human being, so the Word of God, which is the living bread, refreshes the minds of the faithful through participation in itself.”

### LIX [Cols. 0220D–0221C]

Amsterdam edition, p. 296; Paris edition, p. 192. Nor must it be overlooked that, with remarkable boldness, the pseudo-Ratramnus corrupted the testimonies of the Fathers which he abuses, especially those of Ambrose and Augustine. Concerning Ambrose, the most illustrious bishop Petrus de Marca had already warned that, in the testimony which the impostor cites in number 59, the following words had been removed:

> “This body which we make is from the Virgin.”

### RESPONSE

Ratramnus neither defiled nor corrupted Saint Ambrose when he cited this passage from book *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 9. Nor did the most illustrious and learned Petrus de Marca ever accuse him of this crime of corruption. This is readily understood from his letter to Dom Luc d’Achery, reported in volume V of the *Spicilegium*.

He merely observes that Ratramnus could well and wisely have cited these words of Saint Ambrose from the same chapter:

> “This body which we make is from the Virgin.”

They occur above in the same chapter, fifty lines earlier. Paschasius could have cited the same words, and yet he would not thereby be called a corrupter of Ambrose.

But if we act in good faith, can an ecclesiastical writer rightly be accused of alteration and corruption, and charged with being an expunger and impostor, because he omitted certain words separated from the cited passage by an interval of fifty lines? God forbid.

If I were to ask all the Fathers of literary scholarship what it means to corrupt an author’s text, they would unanimously answer that it means removing a word from the text and, by means of that removal, introducing a heretical meaning in place of a catholic one and attributing it to the author.

The reader will find abundant examples of this crime in the *Critical Colloquy on the Errors of Illustrious Men in Literary Matters*, included among the works of Marcellus of Ancyra.

Meanwhile, let him observe the disputant’s boldness on p. 184. Having taken these words of Ratramnus from number 56:

> “Understand that what is seen exists not in appearance but in reality as Christ’s body and blood,”

which convey a catholic and entirely orthodox meaning, the disputant removed the word *cernuntur*, “are seen,” and wrote *creduntur*, “are believed,” in Ratramnus’s text, so as to convict him of Calvinist heresy, as we have already observed in our response to objection 39. It would be tedious and superfluous to repeat that response here.

### LX [Col. 0221C]

Paris edition, p. 193; Amsterdam edition, p. 296. He is somewhat more careless in the words of Augustine. For when the holy Doctor said in the sermon to infants cited above, “You receive your mystery,” the pseudo-Ratramnus appears to have read, in number 95, “You receive the Lord’s mystery.” Thus all editions of his book have it, from the first, published in 1522, except the latest, published in 1686.

Nor did he interpolate this passage of Augustine in this way without a purpose. He did so in order immediately to conclude that the consecrated bread is as much a mystery by name as it is “our mystery”—that is, that it is merely as much a sign of the Lord’s body as it is merely a sign of the believing people.

### RESPONSE
It is easy to answer this. The edition of Ratramnus of 1686, in whose correction I took no small part, is to be preferred to the others, especially since it was accurately and faithfully reproduced from an eight-hundred-year-old manuscript of the Abbey of Lobbes. But if Ratramnus is to be sullied by the reproach of interpolation because of the words “you receive the Lord’s mystery” in place of “you receive your mystery,” then the same charge must be brought against the sermon of Saint Fulgentius found at the end of his letter to the deacon Ferrandus, where the reading is “you receive the Lord’s mystery.” This is readily established from the edition of Saint Fulgentius’s works produced at Lyons by the care and scholarship of Father Théophile Raynaud, a Jesuit neither unlearned nor lacking in ability.

However the matter may stand, if—apart from the authority of the antiquity of the Lobbes manuscript—there can be room for conjecture among learned men, I think “you receive your mystery” should rather be read than “you receive the Lord’s mystery,” since Ratramnus himself had said in the preceding line, “your mystery is placed upon the Lord’s table.” Accordingly, it seems more just and reasonable to judge Ratramnus’s faith from an ancient manuscript of eight hundred years than from more recent editions corrupted and interpolated by heretics, the first editors of this book. In any event, the dissertation writer’s conjecture is so deceptive that it is not difficult to see that he was carried away by excessive zeal against Ratramnus.

### LXI. (Page cited above)

Thus again, in no. 33, when the Augustine whom we cited said that “the mystery of the Passion” should be “pleasantly and profitably stored in the memory,” he himself, having removed and deleted the first two words, presented the reading “faithfully stored.” Although this interpolation might elsewhere appear slight in itself, it was nevertheless introduced by him with the purpose of concluding from it that the mysteries are performed by the faithful through their own faith, and not by God himself in the consecrated symbols.

### RESPONSE

It is the dissertation writer’s responsibility to prove that Ratramnus interpolated Augustine for that purpose. But such an interpolation is so slight and futile a fault that the Calvinists regarded it as nothing and did not think it could in any way serve their cause. For in the editions of Ratramnus whose preparation they undertook, they printed “pleasantly and profitably,” not “faithfully,” as is especially clear from the most recent edition, published in London in the very year 1681, from the edition of Monsieur Pierre Allix, minister of the Charenton temple, published in 1672, and from all the others published through the care and labor of Protestant scholars since 1532.

Moreover, if the dissertation writer wishes obstinately to maintain such a conjecture, however slight and futile it may be, I appeal to the common sense of learned men. Who could persuade himself that the flesh of Christ, fastened to the cross for the salvation of humanity, can be recalled to our memory “pleasantly and profitably”? If not “faithfully,” then how? If not “pleasantly and profitably,” what can the dissertation writer mean except, through some sort of idiosyncrasy, to draw water from a pumice stone?

[Col. 0223]

# FOUR BOOKS OF RATRAMNUS, MONK OF CORBIE, AGAINST THE OBJECTIONS OF THE GREEKS WHO DEFAME THE ROMAN CHURCH

*(In Acherius, volume I of the Spicilegium, p. 63.)*

## NOTICE

The following final words of the fourth book seem to persuade us that Ratramnus labored over these books at the urging or command of the bishops: “We have acted as best we could, answering those things that you sent to us in writing. If they have pleased you, we give thanks to God; but if they have displeased you, we await the judgment of your correction.”

For Nicholas I, supreme hierarch of the Church, had warned the bishops of Gaul by letter that they should answer the objections of the Greeks, adversaries of the Roman See, as Frodoard testifies in *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims*, book III, chapter 17:

“Pope Nicholas sent a letter to him [Hincmar] and to the other archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of Charles, making known that the aforementioned Greek emperors, as well as the Eastern bishops, were calumniating the holy Roman Church—indeed, every Church that uses the Latin language—because we fast on Saturdays; because we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; because we forbid priests to anoint the foreheads of the baptized with chrism; for the Greeks themselves say that we Latins make chrism from river water; because they reproach us Latins for not abstaining, as they do, from eating cheese and eggs for eight weeks; and because they also say that at Easter, following the custom of the Jews, we bless and offer a lamb upon the altar together with the Lord’s body; and because they are angry with us because our clerics shave their beards; and because they say that among us a deacon, without having received the office of the priesthood, is ordained a bishop,” and so forth.

Then he appends the words of Nicholas’s letter:

“When your charity, Hincmar, has read this letter, as soon as it has also been conveyed to the other archbishops who are established in the kingdom of our son, the glorious King Charles, you should strive with the utmost diligence to ensure that each of them, in his own diocese, together with his suffragans—wherever they may be situated, in whatever kingdom—properly discuss these matters, and that you do not neglect to urge them to report to us what they discover,” and so forth.

This was, in sum, the schism stirred up in the East by Photius, the false patriarch of Constantinople, and his associates, and fostered by the Greek emperors Michael and Basil.

Accordingly, our Ratramnus carefully, elegantly, and with complete learning carried out the task imposed upon him in four books. In the first three he is wholly occupied both with the sacred Scriptures and with the opinions of the Greeks and Latins, in order to repel the blasphemies of the innovators and establish the Catholic truth concerning the Holy Spirit. In the fourth book he deals most successfully with the differing observance of Lent and the differing use of foods; with the Latin fast on Saturday; with the beard and head-shaving of clerics and with celibacy; with the sacrament of Confirmation, which is to be conferred by the bishop alone; with the supreme right of the Roman pontiff over the patriarch of Constantinople and indeed over all the prelates of the Christian world; and with other rites of the Church.

Those who read through these four books will readily perceive how deeply versed Ratramnus was in the sacred Scriptures and in the writings of the ancient Fathers and councils. The narrow limits of a preface do not allow me to review the praises of so great a man in a more extended style; I have thought it sufficient to append here only a few testimonies from writers.

Before proceeding farther, however, it will not be out of place to warn the reader that Jacques Sirmond, worthy of immortal memory, while publishing certain minor works of Saint Fulgentius and, at the end, listing fragments of works that had until then remained hidden, attributed these very books of Ratramnus to Hincmar of Rheims in the final fragment, in the following manner: “From book III of Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, against the objections of the Greeks, to Odo of Beauvais.” He then appended the very words of Ratramnus: “Fulgentius, a bishop highly learned in literary studies,” and so forth, which you will see below in book III, chapter 5. Finally, he produced two previously unpublished passages of Fulgentius cited by Ratramnus in the places mentioned.

What persuaded Sirmond to father this offspring upon a stranger, I simply do not know, since otherwise he ought to have counted this by no means insignificant work among the other works of Hincmar which, over nearly forty-two years, he had sought out with the greatest zeal and diligence. Let us now bring forward the testimonies.

**Sigebert**, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 95:

“Bertramus, or Ratramnus, wrote a book on the Body and Blood of the Lord, and a book on Predestination to Charles.”

**John Trithemius**, abbot, *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, book II, chapter 48:

“Bertramnus, a monk devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly instructed in secular letters, wrote booklets worthy of considerable attention, in which he magnificently exercised his intellect. Among them I have found only one book on the Body and Blood of the Lord and one book on Predestination to Charles. He flourished in A.D. 870.”

**Claude d’Espence**, doctor of Paris, *On the Eucharist*, book IV, chapter 19, near the middle:

“And deservedly so, since that true Bertramus, so to speak, for seven hundred whole years was neither accused by anyone of heresy nor censured as having written badly, but was entered in the catalogue of ecclesiastical writers as a man distinguished no less in life than in doctrine, intellect, and eloquence.”

**Claude de Saintes**, bishop of Évreux, *On the Controversies of the Eucharist*, second repetition, chapter 14:

“Yet for seven hundred whole years no one censured that true Bertram as having written badly on the charge of heresy; rather, he is listed in the catalogue of ecclesiastical writers as a man distinguished and Catholic no less in life than in doctrine, intellect, and eloquence.”

**Aubertus Miraeus**, in his scholia on the aforementioned chapter of Sigebert:

“Bertramus wrote a book on the Body and Blood of the Lord, printed at Cologne in 1532, at Basel in the *Mycropresbyticon*, and elsewhere, but condemned by the Tridentine censors. Thus Molanus in the manuscript library. Heretics were the first to publish it in print, and they seem to have inserted into it whatever is read there that is obscure or apparently sounds wrong. Certainly, in very many passages it asserts the true presence of Christ and teaches transubstantiation, so that even the interpolator himself does not conceal this toward the end, saying that many things do not cohere and that earlier statements contradict what follows. Among others, Bartholomeus Petrus Lintrensis, doctor of theology, observed this.”

**Dionysius Petavius, S.J.**, *Theological Dogmas*, volume II, book VII, chapter 2, near the end, makes use of Ratramnus’s authority as that of a Catholic and distinguished writer while explaining the word *Filioque*, added to the Constantinopolitan Creed:

“Indeed Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, in book II, *For the Roman Church against the Greeks*, which he wrote around the year 868, in the time of Photius, dissolves, as though it had been brought by them, the charge of corruption of the Creed,” and so forth.

He adds:

“Ratramnus wrote, as has already been said, after receiving Nicholas’s encyclical, which he had sent in the year 867 to Hincmar and the other bishops established in the kingdom of Charles the Bald, in order to urge them to refute the calumnies directed against the Roman Church by the emperor Michael and Basil in a certain letter addressed to him.”

**John de Launoy**, doctor of Paris, in his dissertation *On the Ancient Choice of Foods*, and so forth, page 13:

“Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, answers the objection of the Greeks in this way, in the work which that highly learned man then composed against the Greeks by the authority of the bishops. From book IV of this work,” and so forth.

From there he excerpted a lengthy passage.

**Gilbert Mauguin**, counsellor to the king, in chapter 17 of his *Historical and Chronological Dissertation*, under the year 850:

“In this year also Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie and a soldier of no slight strength in the Church of Christ, obeying a royal command, composed two books on Predestination.”

He was the first to bring them to light.

**Jacques de Sainte-Beuve**, a Sorbonist associate and royal professor, while himself lecturing on the treatise on the Eucharist in the schools of the Sorbonne, vigorously defended Ratramnus in a work filled with much learning, and not ordinary learning. First, after Sigebert, Trithemius, Espence, and Saintes, he shows that Ratramnus held a place among ecclesiastical and orthodox writers; then he shows that he composed a Catholic work on the Body and Blood of the Lord. He relies not only on the testimonies of Sigebert and others, but is led especially by these arguments.

The first is that for seven hundred years Ratramnus was accused of heresy by no writer, much less condemned. The second is that you will find him praised nowhere either by Berengarius himself, the heresiarch, or by his disciples. To this is added the fact that Ratramnus’s book escaped the censure of the Council of Vercelli, at which the impious doctrine of Berengarius, together with the works of John Erigena, or Scotus, of the same sort, were struck by an eternal anathema.

Finally Sanbovæus adds:

“Even if that work on the Body and Blood of the Lord, which bears the name of Bertram, were his genuine offspring and entirely uncorrupted and uninterpolated, the heretics nevertheless try in vain to persuade us that our Ratramnus belonged to them or favored their heresy because of the blemishes contained in that work. For he lived continuously in the bosom of the Church and peacefully fell asleep in her communion.”

For Facundus says, book X, chapter 5:

“What is said must be judged not from the slight sound of the words but from the intention of the speaker. But when the speaker is already dead, his intention is judged more religiously from his communion.”

And indeed Ratramnus could be defended in a Catholic manner against the calumny of the heterodox, just as Athanasius once vindicated Dionysius of Alexandria:

“This is certainly a powerful argument,” he says in his letter on the opinion of Dionysius against the Arians, “that even in this matter they do not speak the truth, but oppress the man with calumnies: he was never convicted of impiety by the other bishops, nor did he withdraw from the Church by defending heresy, but fell asleep in it with piety; and his memory has continued to be celebrated with the Fathers and entered in the catalogue. If he had shared their opinion, or if he had not rendered an account of his writings, there is no doubt that he would have suffered the same things as they did.”

Finally, since the aforementioned work of Ratramnus so clearly and openly proves the real presence of Christ’s Body and Blood under the Eucharistic species, as well as transubstantiation, its more obscure and difficult passages can therefore be kindly elucidated in an orthodox sense, according to the rule of Facundus, book IX, chapter 5:

“Just as it belongs to heretics who slander to interpret badly, from doubtful and obscure matters, things that are certain and manifest, so it belongs to Catholic prudence and piety, from things indubitable and evident, to establish what is ambiguous and clarify what is hidden. But if some who are also orthodox should think that something else ought to be done, the prudent must not imitate them in this.”

This is what Acherius says. He also notes that he published these books from the Thuaneus manuscript. Baluzius later collated this manuscript in the Colbert Library, and he reported as the fruit of his diligence that in several places he discovered Acherius’s copyist to have indulged his own ingenuity too freely while transcribing Ratramnus’s work.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0225]

## CHAPTER ONE. Answer to the objections of the emperors Michael and Basil. The objections of the Greeks.

[Col. 0225D]

The objections by which Michael and Basil, the Greek emperors, attempt to defame the Roman Church are known to be either false, heretical, superstitious, or irreligious. They therefore ought rightly to be despised, unless one considers that they might inflict the scandal of injury upon the simple and less capable, in accordance with that saying of Solomon, uttered by the Holy Spirit: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself” (Prov. 26:5).

When they say that we make chrism from water and that on the holy day of Easter we place a lamb upon the altar, to be consecrated together with the Lord’s body, after the manner of the Jews, are they not plainly lying? And do they not fear the Psalmist’s words, spoken by the Holy Spirit: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5:7), or what the Holy Spirit elsewhere threatens: “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Prov. 19:5, 9)?

Again, when they try to blame not only the Roman Church but the entire Latin Church because we confess, in accordance with the Catholic faith, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, while they say only that he proceeds from the Father, are they not condemning themselves by the perversity of heresy, removing themselves from communion with the Church, and blaspheming against the Holy Spirit—a sin which the Savior declares in the Gospel to be unforgivable (Mark 3:29)?

Unless perhaps they can show that this was at some time denied by their forebears, who were Catholic men. For when they say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, they do not deny that he also proceeds from the Son. If they wish to follow their forebears, they will embrace the Catholic statement that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, just as their forebears embraced it; those men, instructed in the sacred writings, knew perfectly well that he belongs to both—that is, to the Father as well as to the Son. This will be demonstrated more clearly below.

## CHAPTER II. Again concerning the objections of the Greeks. — What duty belongs to emperors.

As for the charge they try to bring against us—that we fast on Saturday, or that we do not celebrate the Easter fast according to the same rule as they do—who does not see with what swelling arrogance and what stupidity they say such things, puffed up or blinded as they are?

They accuse those who fast, and then again reproach those who do not fast. Either fasting is good or it is bad. If it is good, why do they accuse it? If it is bad, why do they practice what they accuse? Perhaps the matter is not to be sanctioned on its own merits but judged according to the persons involved: the fast observed by a Latin is to be condemned, while that observed by a Greek is to be revered. So they judge, deceived either by pride or deprived of knowledge.

Who, moreover, could tolerate their eagerness to censure those pursuing continence, withdrawing from intercourse with women and striving after holiness of flesh and soul? Such qualities, which deserve to be exalted in all mortals with a proclamation of praise, deserve this especially in the ministers of the sacred altar, whose duty is always to attend upon holy things, continually to offer the service of obedience to the Divinity, and every day to appease the divine majesty with unceasing prayer on behalf of the peoples entrusted to them.

Because our priests, following the custom of their ancestors, do not fail to do this, they are defamed as condemning marriage. What are they attacking by this, except religion? What are they trying to destroy, except the sanctity without which no one can please God?

Who does not see how ridiculous it is to censure us for the shaving of the beard, or because our priests do not anoint the foreheads of those whom they baptize with chrism, but leave this privilege to bishops? Is any transgression of the divine commandments recognized in shaving or retaining the beard? Or, if the priests do not anoint with sacred unction the foreheads of those whom they baptize, does this mean that they do not complete the grace of baptism when they perform the threefold immersion through invocation of the Holy Trinity? These things are recognized as superstitious, not as belonging to any religious consideration.

What wonder if such calumnies proceed from men versed in the sacred law, supported by secular power and relying upon the arrogance of empire? It belonged to bishops, not emperors, to debate sacred doctrines and ecclesiastical ritual. Their ministry in the Church was entrusted to them for learning, not for teaching. For although they excel in imperial dignity, the public affairs of the world, not the episcopal ministry, have been entrusted to them.

Emperors ought to deal with the laws of the secular world; bishops, however, ought to debate divine doctrines. Let them strive to keep within their own limits and not seize the episcopal office, lest what happened to King Uzziah, when he presumed upon the priestly ministry, happen to them. He was struck with leprosy by divine judgment and is known to have been expelled not only from the temple but also from communion with the people (2 Chron. 26:17).

Why, then, do these recent and, so to speak, monstrous teachers attempt in their own time to bring into accusation what their predecessors—if indeed they are sons of the Church and followers of Catholic unity—have always considered worthy of reverence?

No new worship is now practiced in the Roman Church; no new religion, no new doctrine, no new institution. Whatever our ancestors held, taught, and left to their descendants as things to be preserved, we hold and preserve—adding nothing to it and taking nothing away. What they believed concerning the Holy Spirit, we believe. They received it from the apostles, and the apostles received it from Christ.
