The Church, both in the East and in the West, has always remained in the same faith. For the apostles knew the saying that there is “one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5). And although heresies frequently arose, breaking apart the nets of Christ like bad fish, Christ’s tunic nevertheless remained whole.

The institutions of our ancestors, established in their several places, just as they were not identical in all churches, nevertheless in no way divided the unity of faith; nor, because of changes in reciprocal custom, did they lose the communion of mutual fellowship. For it is one thing to distinguish people by dress and manner of life, and another to think alike concerning the unity of faith.

But more on these matters later. Let us now come to the proposed topics and discuss each of them as the grace of the Holy Spirit grants. We shall not follow the order of the questions proposed, for it has been arranged with little prudence and is recognized as having been organized through levity of mind rather than the gravity of prudence.

First, let us speak of what the Holy Spirit himself has granted concerning the Holy Spirit. This is both the first and the chief matter, and it belongs to the strengthening of the Catholic faith. We must show to the mind that we think and confess concerning him what our Fathers also thought and confessed; and that they thought and professed what the apostles thought and taught. But if anyone prefers to accuse the teaching of the apostles, he must necessarily reject the teaching of Christ and refute the oracles of the prophets.

## CHAPTER III. It is proved that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Greeks are likened to Arius. The Savior is the truth. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth, that is, of Christ. Charity is called the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0229A]

You object that we say the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, while you say that he proceeds from the Father alone. Let us consider the Gospel reading and derive the character of our answer from it. The Savior speaks in the sermon that, according to John, he delivered to his disciples on the night when he was to be betrayed. Among other things he said:

“When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26).

You read the words “who proceeds from the Father,” but you do not wish to hear the Son saying, “whom I shall send to you from the Father.” Say how he is sent by the Son. For you do not deny that the Son said this, if you read the Gospel, or if you believe the Gospel.

Either, then, acknowledge this sending as a procession, or else—you would be saying something impious—call it service [Note: Col. 0229D: “You will call it service” is the very correct reading; previously the text read “impium dicenti, obsequium” (“service to the impious speaker,” uncertain)]; and, God forbid, you will be with Arius, who in his perverse doctrine asserted that the Holy Spirit was lesser than the Son.

Far be it from you to support the party of Arius; far be it from you to affirm that the Holy Spirit is lesser than the Father and the Son. Therefore, when the Son says that he will send the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he plainly confesses that the Spirit proceeds from himself as well, since he confirms that he himself sends him.

Perhaps the question arises from the fact that the Savior did not simply say, “whom I shall send to you,” but added, “from the Father.” The Arians were the first to raise this objection, wishing to establish a gradation within the Divinity. But the truth of the Gospel displays the consubstantial unity of the entire Trinity.

The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father because he flows from the Father’s substance. The Son also sends the Spirit of truth from the Father, because the Holy Spirit was born from the Father in order that he might proceed from the Son; and just as the Son received his substance from the Father by being born, so likewise he received from the Father the power to send the Spirit of truth as proceeding from himself.

Otherwise, when he says, “who proceeds from the Father,” he does not deny that the Spirit proceeds from himself, since the sending of the Son is the procession of the Holy Spirit—not as though the Son, being greater, commands the Spirit as one who is lesser, but because the word “sending” shows that just as the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father, so also he proceeds from the Son.

Hence, in what follows:

“He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:14).

What will the Holy Spirit receive from the Son, since they are of one substance and one power? “He will receive from what is mine,” he said—that is, “he proceeds from me,” because just as the Father and the Son are of one substance, so the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, has received an existence consubstantial with them.

Nor should it trouble anyone that he said “he will receive,” using the future tense. This refers to what was to happen in the future, namely, that the Spirit would be sent to the disciples, not to the fact that he proceeds from the Father and the Son. For he proceeds timelessly from the Father, and he proceeds also from the Son, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three persons but have existed and continue to exist as one and the same substance.

It follows:

“Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:15).

If everything that the Father has belongs also to the Son, then just as the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father, so he is also the Spirit of the Son. Otherwise, if he belongs only to the Father and not also to the Son, then not everything that the Father has belongs to the Son. But the Son has everything that the Father has. Therefore, just as the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father, so he is also the Spirit of the Son.

Yet we must not suppose that this possession is a lowering through deposition or an addition of created status. Rather, it is made clear that just as the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, so he also proceeds from the Son.

A little earlier Christ said:

“When that Spirit of truth comes”;

and previously he had said:

“When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth.”

The Savior is the truth. He himself testifies to Philip:

“I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

If, therefore, the Savior is the truth, and the Savior is the Son of the Father, what else is meant by saying “the Spirit of truth” than “the Spirit of the Son”? Thus the Spirit of the Father is recognized as the one who proceeds from the Father, and at the same time the Spirit of the Son, whom the Savior confesses to be the Spirit of truth.

If you ask from whom the Spirit of truth comes, ask at the same time from whom the Spirit of the Father comes. By proceeding from the Father he is the Spirit of the Father; and, by proceeding at the same time from the Son, who is the truth, he is the Spirit of the Son.

These things are not said to indicate subjection but to signify one and the same substance. For just as the Father and the Son are of one and the same substance, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from both.

Do not suppose that the Holy Spirit has two fathers because he proceeds from the Father and proceeds from the Son. The Holy Spirit is not the Son, and whoever is not a son cannot have a father.

The Holy Spirit is also said to be charity. Hence blessed John says:

“God is charity” (1 John 4:16).

Commending this charity, he writes to the faithful:

“Let the anointing which you received from him remain in you, and you have no need for anyone to teach you; but as his anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2:27).

The Savior says something similar:

“When he comes, that Spirit of truth, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:16).

Whether, therefore, you say, “God is charity”; or, “As his anointing teaches you about everything”; or, “the Spirit of truth, who teaches all truth,” you signify the Holy Spirit.

He is the charity of the Father, by which he loved us; he is the charity of the Son, by which he redeemed us. But the charity is not thereby different because it is said to belong to the Father and to the Son. For by the charity with which the Father loves the Son, the Son loves the Father with that same charity.

The Holy Spirit is the charity of the Father; the Holy Spirit is also the charity of the Son. The charity of the Father proceeds from the Father in order to love the Son; the charity of the Son also proceeds from the Son in order to love the Father. Therefore the charity of both is one, because the Spirit of both is one, proceeding from both.

Christ cried out, saying:

“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37).

“Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

The evangelist adds:

“He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:39).

Following the evangelist’s teaching, we understand the rivers of living water as the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, by which the Savior teaches that those who believe in him are to be watered. From where, then, do the rivers flow, unless they flow from the faith of Christ? And from where does faith come, unless from Christ’s teaching?

Therefore, just as Christ’s teaching comes from Christ, and faith in that teaching comes from Christ, so the rivers of living water—that is, the Holy Spirit—proceed from Christ. For Christ is both perfect man and perfect God.

As perfect God, he grants and pours into those who believe in him the Holy Spirit who proceeds from him. His streams flood the hearts of believers with the fountains of eternal life.

He also says to the Samaritan woman:

“Whoever drinks from this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks from the water that I shall give him will never thirst. Rather, the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water leaping up into eternal life” (John 4:13).

What he had earlier called rivers of living water he now calls a fountain of water leaping up into eternal life. In both cases he wishes the Holy Spirit to be understood, whom he most clearly says is given by him when he says:

“The water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water.”

For what he gives, he gives from himself. He gives a fountain of water leaping up into eternal life—that is, he lavishly grants the Holy Spirit to those who believe in him. Thus he demonstrates that the Spirit proceeds from him, since he says that he himself gives him to believers.

After rising from the dead, when the disciples were sitting in a room, after greeting them with peace and entrusting them with the mission of peace, he “breathed upon them and said: Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22), and so forth.

What does this breathing signify, except the procession of the Holy Spirit? Not that the bodily breath taken from the air and emitted through the organ of the mouth by the service of the lungs was the substance of the Holy Spirit; rather, by this action he wished to teach us that the Holy Spirit proceeds from himself and that the substance of the Holy Spirit flows from the substance of the Son.

In the same way, wishing to show that the birth of the Son was propagated from his own substance, and thereby that the Son was consubstantial with him, the Father speaks to that Son in the Psalm:

“From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

This does not mean that God the Father had a womb from which he begot the Son before the ages; rather, it testifies that he begot the Son not from nothing, nor from the subsistence of some other thing, but from his own nature and substance.

Thus, too, when the Son breathed forth the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, he showed that the Spirit proceeded from his substance, whom he wished to give through that breathing.

Speaking to his disciples about the sacrament of his Body and Blood, he said:

“The words that I have spoken to you are Spirit and life” (John 6:64).

From where, then, do words proceed, unless from the innermost part of the mind? Therefore, the words that Christ speaks are Spirit and life, because the Spirit who proceeds from Christ’s heart is life.

This does not mean that there is a heart in the Divinity, namely, a bodily part of flesh; rather, by this term he wished to display the mystery of the inner substance, from which he says that the Spirit who is life proceeds.

Therefore the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son and is of one and the same substance with the Son.

## CHAPTER IV. Testimonies are brought forward from the Gospel and Paul’s Epistles.

In the Gospel of Luke we read:

“Christ went out in the power of the Spirit into Galilee” (Luke 4:14).

The Savior is said to be the power of the Father, and now the Spirit is called power. Is Christ one power and the Spirit another? Certainly not. Both are called power, so that the unity of their substance may be shown.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “in the power of the Spirit”? Did he wish to show that the power of the Holy Spirit was greater than the power of the Son? Not at all.

What, then, does “in the power of the Spirit” mean? He did not wish to show a power external to Christ, as though it had been granted from elsewhere, but his own power. Since it belongs to the Holy Spirit, it also belongs at the same time to the Son, because in one nature the essence is not different; and, while both remain together in one [the transmitted wording is syntactically uncertain], one proceeds from the other—namely, the Holy Spirit from the Son; while both are from the Father, the Son by being born and the Holy Spirit by proceeding.

This does not mean that he proceeds from the Father or the Son at alternate times, but that, without any intervening time, he proceeds simultaneously from the Father and the Son.

The blessed apostle Paul writes to the Galatians:

“Because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4:6).

He does not say, “God sent his Spirit.” If he had said this, he would not have entirely excluded the Son, since the Son is also God, just as the Father is God; and the two are not two gods but one God. For what person separates, substance joins.

But, wishing to remove every question, he specifically mentioned the person of the Son and said that God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts.

Is the Spirit of the Son other than the Spirit of the Father? If the Spirit is the same Spirit of both, then he certainly proceeds from both. For he is not called the Spirit of the Son as though he were lesser than the Son; whoever thinks or says this is not a Catholic.

Therefore there is no reason for him to be called the Spirit of the Son except that he proceeds from the Son, just as he is called the Spirit of the Father because he proceeds from the Father.

Writing to the Philippians, he says among other things: “For I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ” (Phil. I, 19). Jesus Christ is God and man. Was the Apostle speaking of the human spirit when he said this? For on the cross Jesus Christ surrendered his human spirit, as the Evangelist testifies, saying of him: “And bowing his head, he gave up the spirit” (John XIX, 30). And he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John X, 18).

But this Spirit of whom the Apostle now speaks (I Cor. XII, etc.), through whose provision he confidently hopes that he will in no way be put to shame concerning the ministry of Christ, is God. He is also called the Holy Spirit, to distinguish him from the Father and the Son. Concerning him the Apostle testifies that he distributes the divisions of graces, working all things as he wills. This, then, is the Spirit of Christ—not by servile subjection, but by divine procession, equal in nature, majesty, and dignity to the Father and the Son.

Saint Luke writes in the Acts of the Apostles: “When they had come to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts XVI, 7). Of which Spirit he is speaking, he explains above, saying: “And having passed through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia” (ibid., 6). The one whom he had previously called the Holy Spirit he later called the Spirit of Jesus, plainly indicating that the Spirit of Jesus is none other than the Holy Spirit. The reason he is called the Spirit of Jesus has often been stated: it is because he proceeds from Jesus—not according to that nature by which, in mercy, he became man, but according to that by which, born from the Father, he is equal to the Father.

He also says to Titus: “According to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior” [Col. 0233C] (Titus III, 5). How did he pour out the Holy Spirit through Jesus Christ? Was it as though the lesser were poured out through the greater? This is what the Arians wanted. But he says that the Father poured out the Holy Spirit through Jesus Christ in order to show that the outpouring of the Holy Spirit took place from Jesus Christ—not as though he received him from elsewhere, but as though he sent him from himself. For he did not mean to say that the Father poured out the Holy Spirit through Jesus Christ as water is poured through a pipe, so that the Son’s role in this outpouring consisted only in service or conveyance or passage. To think this is impious.

Rather, the Father poured out the Holy Spirit upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior because he proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father. By saying that he poured him out through the Son, he showed that the Spirit proceeds from the Son, yet he did not deny that he proceeds from the Father; for when he proceeds from the Son, he also proceeds from the Father.

Blessed Peter also testifies in the Acts of the Apostles concerning this outpouring of the Holy Spirit, speaking to the Jews about the Lord Jesus Christ: “Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out this whom you see and hear” (Acts II, 33). Concerning this, Luke testifies in the same Acts:

“When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together in the same place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven like that of a rushing mighty spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, and one rested upon each of them; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in various languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts II, 1–4).

And later:

“And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord, that I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons shall prophesy” (ibid., 17), and so forth. A little later:

“And indeed upon my male servants and my female servants in those days I will pour out from my Spirit, and they shall prophesy” (ibid., 18).

We have set all this down so that, through blessed Peter’s teaching, we might recognize that the Holy Spirit was poured out by Jesus upon the apostles and the other believers who had been gathered together on the day of Pentecost. Hence it is written: “This Jesus God raised up, of which we are all witnesses” (ibid., 32). Then he added: “Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God, he poured out this”—that is, the Holy Spirit—“namely Jesus, whom God raised up, whom you have seen and heard” (ibid., 33).

You saw him in the fiery tongues; you heard him in the variety of languages. For the Holy Spirit, in his proper nature, cannot be seen with bodily sight or heard with bodily hearing. Rather, he assumed an appearance—the form of fire under the image of tongues—in order that he might be seen, and he took possession of the disciples’ voices in order that he might be heard.

When he says that, having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, he poured out this Spirit, he commends not the grace of divinity but of humanity. For according to his divinity he did not receive a promise, since everything the Father has belongs to him—not by receiving it temporally, but by possessing it eternally.

## CHAPTER V. What the Outpouring of the Holy Spirit Is. The Holy Spirit Breathes.

[Col. 0234C]

Let us compare with these things the statement of Paul already cited, in which, speaking to Titus about the Holy Spirit, he said: “Whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior” (Titus III, 6). Paul testifies that the Father poured out the Holy Spirit through Jesus Christ our Savior. Peter, however, says that Jesus poured out this same Holy Spirit when he rose from the dead. By this we are taught that both the Father and Jesus Christ pour him out, so that we may learn that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, whom both pour out.

We must not imagine that this outpouring was spatial, as though, flowing from the Father, he passed spatially to Christ as if leaving the Father; or as though he could come to the Son by extending himself, so that one part of him touched the Son while another remained in the Father. Similarly, when he was poured out by the Son upon the disciples, we must not imagine that he left the Son and came to the disciples, or that, by some extension, he irradiated the disciples’ hearts by a proportionate part of himself while some part remained in Christ—as when one considers a ray of the sun, with one part illuminating its sphere and another touching the earth.

But such things belong to bodies. In the divinity of the Holy Trinity none of these things is found. Rather, without an interval of time or place, the Holy Spirit is poured out from the Father, and likewise from the Son. He is poured out [Col. 0235A] from the Father into the Son because the Father begot the Son; and he is poured out from the Son because the Son possesses everything that belongs to the Father.

The Holy Gospel also testifies that “the Spirit breathes where he wills” (John III, 8). What does “breathes” mean? Clearly, it means that whenever and wherever he wills, he pours himself out. Let us observe the one operation of the whole Trinity. The Father pours out; the Son pours out the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit, breathing where he wills, pours himself out.

How fittingly, then, does the Apostle say that the Holy Spirit was poured out through Jesus Christ, through whom God the Father made all things! And how appropriately does the Apostle Peter testify that the Son poured out the Holy Spirit, of whom the Gospel says that “whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John XVI, 15). The Father therefore pours out the Holy Spirit, and the Son also pours him out, since just as he is given by the Father, so he is given by the Son.

Let the emperors of the Greeks therefore not accuse the Latins because they confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father. Rather, let them learn the truth of the faith from Christ, and let them learn it from his apostles.

Again, in the Acts of the Apostles Peter says: “And we are witnesses of these words, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him” (Acts V, 32). Which God does he mean has given the Holy Spirit, except the one of whom he said above: “Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God, he poured out this whom you see and hear” (Acts II, 33), indicating that Jesus Christ is to be understood?

But how did God give the Holy Spirit to those who obey him? Was it as though he were lesser? Certainly not. For the Son says: “The Spirit breathes where he wills.” God therefore gives the Holy Spirit by infusing him into the hearts of those who obey, not so that he leaves the one in whom he remains through the unity of substance, but so that he illumines those whom he had not previously irradiated.

No one can give what he does not possess. Thus the Son testifies that he possesses the Holy Spirit, whom he gave to all who obey him. And just as he possesses him through unity of substance, not through the acquisition of possession, so, when he gives him, he does not bestow something belonging to another as a gift, but imparts what is his own as his proper gift. The Son could not do this in any other way if the Holy Spirit did not also proceed from him.

In what follows, blessed Peter teaches how Cornelius, a gentile, and the believers who were with him received the grace of baptism. After other matters he says:

“If, then, God gave them the same grace as he gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God?” (Acts XI, 17).

Here “God” may be understood as the Holy Spirit, who filled the hearts of the believers and gave them knowledge of languages, or certainly as the Father. Yet if we consider Peter’s earlier words concerning the sending of the Holy Spirit upon believers—namely, that the Son poured him out, as was stated above—then here too God must accordingly be understood as the Son, who gave Cornelius and his companions the same grace that he had previously given by pouring out the Holy Spirit upon the disciples in fiery tongues, while Peter was speaking.

It has plainly been shown that the outpouring, or giving, of the Holy Spirit belongs both to the Father and to the Son, because he proceeds from both. Here too, therefore, when he says that the same grace was recently given to believers as had previously been given to the apostles, he clearly signifies the Holy Spirit. The Son could give him because he proceeds from the Son; and he could not do this at all if he did not proceed from him.

## CHAPTER VI. Testimonies from the Scriptures.

Writing to the faithful at Rome, blessed Paul says: “But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his” (Rom. VIII, 9).

Consider whose person you wish to understand when he says: “If the Spirit of God dwells in you.” If you understand the person of the Father, he consequently testifies that this same Spirit is the Spirit of Christ. By this statement he plainly proves that the Spirit of the Father is the same as the Spirit of Christ; and, by not concealing that he is the Spirit of both, he confesses that he proceeds from both.

But if you wish to understand both expressions as referring to the person of Christ—which the order of the passage seems more readily to allow, since Christ is God—we are likewise taught that the Spirit of Christ is the Holy Spirit, and thereby instructed that he proceeds from Christ.

For the person of the Father is marked more clearly below, where he says: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you.” Yet the Son too may be understood here, since he himself, together with the Father, raised the man whom he had assumed, as he says in the Gospel.

But whether you prefer this interpretation or the other, we are plainly taught that the Spirit of the Son is the same as the Spirit of the Father. Hence what the holy Apostle says below—“For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God” (Rom. VIII, 14)—can without hesitation be understood of both, that is, either of the Father or of the Son. For he is the Spirit of both, proceeding from both, as has already been demonstrated in many passages.

And further: “For you have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (ibid., 15).

Writing to the Galatians, he says: “And because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. IV, 6).

Observe that he calls the Spirit of adoption as sons the same Spirit whom he confesses to be the Spirit of the Son. Thus the Apostle teaches us that the Spirit of the Father is the same Spirit whom he calls the Spirit of adoption, and that the Spirit of the Son is the same Spirit whom God sent into our hearts. In this one Spirit, shown to be the Spirit of both the Father and the Son, we cry, “Abba, Father.” We could never do this if the Holy Spirit did not proceed from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father.

In his Second Epistle he writes to the Corinthians: “You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all people; it is manifest that you are the letter of Christ, ministered by us and written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God” (II Cor. III, 2–3).

When he says that the Corinthians are Christ’s letter, written by the Spirit of the living God, he demonstrates the one operation of the Holy Spirit and Christ. But whom does he call the living God here? Clearly, Christ, whose letter he says the Corinthians are, thereby revealing that the Spirit who wrote the letter in the Corinthians’ hearts is the Spirit of Christ—not with bodily ink, but by his own illumination.

Since Christ and the Holy Spirit write the same letter, they are shown to be of one substance just as they are of one operation. What Christ writes, the Holy Spirit writes; and what the Holy Spirit writes, Christ writes—not by alternation of time, exchange of places, or variation of work. For just as they have the same will, so they have the same operation and the same power, because they are not of differing essence.

How the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of Christ has often been stated: not as though he were a part of Christ, a quality, or some subject belonging to him, but as proceeding from Christ.

Again, in the same Epistle to the Corinthians: “To this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart; but whenever anyone turns to God, the veil will be taken away” (II Cor. III, 15–16).

Whom he means by “God” he makes clear a little earlier, when he explains how this same veil is abolished in Christ. If, therefore, the veil of the old reading is abolished in Christ, it is clear that, when anyone turns to Christ, the veil will be removed.

Blessed John says the same in his Apocalypse: “And I wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book or to look at it. And one of the elders said to me: ‘Do not weep; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered so as to open the book and its seven seals’” (Rev. V, 4–5).

The opening of the book is the removal of the veil. Who is to accomplish this needs no explanation, since it is clear that the Lion of the tribe of Judah and the Root of David signify Christ, who is also said to open its seven seals.

By these seven seals the Holy Spirit is signified, on account of the sevenfold grace of his gifts. For he is the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety; he is also the Spirit of the fear of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah says (Isa. XI, 2).

The Root of David, that is, the Savior, opens the seven seals of this book because the spiritual mysteries contained in it are disclosed in Christ, when the veil that is shown to have been sealed in the book of the Old Testament is removed and revealed in Christ.

The Apostle continues: “Now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (II Cor. III, 17).

Whose Lord? Clearly, the one in whom the veil is removed—the veil that remains unrevealed when Moses is read in the reading of the Old Testament. The removal of the veil is the removal of slavery, which is contained in the letter of the law, so that the liberty administered through the Spirit of the Lord may come about. This occurs when one passes from the letter to spiritual understanding and from slavery to the flesh enters into the liberty of the Spirit.

We see in these words that the Spirit of the Lord is called the Spirit of Christ. Hence, in what follows, he says: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. III, 18).

Therefore, since the unveiling of the face takes place through Christ, and we are transformed from glory to glory by the Spirit of the Lord, the common operation of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit is shown. Thus, when he says “from the Spirit of the Lord,” he undoubtedly indicates the person of Christ. Although the Spirit is his Spirit, he nevertheless works together with the Savior in the revelation of the old reading.

By their working together, their fellowship of one substance is shown. By his being called the Spirit of the Lord, it is indicated that he proceeds from him. For the circumstances of the passage plainly show that “the Lord” here signifies the Savior.

## CHAPTER VII. Other Testimonies.

Blessed Peter the Apostle writes to believers in his First Epistle: “Concerning this salvation the prophets inquired and searched carefully, who prophesied of the grace destined for you, searching to discover what person or what time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating” (I Peter I, 10–11).

The chief of the apostles—to whom the Savior says, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18)—does not hesitate to say that the Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets is the Spirit of Christ. And yet I do not know by what worldly dignity certain people, puffed up with pride, presume to criticize what they learned from the apostles of Christ’s Church!

If, then, the Holy Spirit does not proceed from Christ, how is he called the Spirit of Christ? He proceeds from Christ, therefore, because he is said to belong to him not by subjection or by division into parts, but because he proceeds substantially from his substance.

Observe also that blessed John agrees with the same judgment and proclaims that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Christ. For he says in the Apocalypse: “And I saw in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes” (Rev. V, 6).

Explaining what he had said, he added: “These are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth” (ibid.).

I suppose no Catholic will deny that the slain Lamb must be understood as Christ. Of him John the Baptist says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I, 29). This Lamb of God was sacrificed for the sins of the world and rose for the justification of the world.

This Lamb is said to have seven eyes, by which, as John teaches, the seven spirits of God are signified—not because there are seven enumerated persons, since there is one Holy Spirit within the unity of the Holy Trinity, but they are called seven because of the sevenfold distribution of gifts. In substance he is one.

Therefore, when he says that the Lamb has seven eyes, it is clear that he confesses that Christ possesses the Holy Spirit—not as some bodily member or bodily part, but because the Spirit is substantially in him and also proceeds substantially from him.

We say that he is in him not as in a place or as in a subject. He is not contained by Christ as though he were less than Christ, as is ordinarily the case with things contained in places—for things that contain are greater than the things contained. We do not say that the Holy Spirit is in Christ in this way, since he is equal, not lesser.

Nor is he said to be in Christ as in a subject. He is not an accident that cannot exist without its subject. Rather, he is in Christ as one consubstantial with him, just as we see heat present in the brightness of fire: fire both shines and is hot; likewise, it both illuminates and kindles.

You also have this in the prophet Zechariah: “Behold, I am bringing my servant, the Orient; for behold, the stone that I have set before Jesus: upon the one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. III, 8). And below: “These seven are the eyes of the Lord, which range throughout the whole earth” (Zech. IV, 10).

This stone is the Savior, of whom the Psalmist says: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Ps. CXVII, 22). God the Father also calls him his servant, the Orient: servant because of the assumption of humanity; Orient because he is himself the sun of righteousness.

Upon this stone he says there are seven eyes of the Lord, ranging throughout the whole earth. In the eyes the Holy Spirit is to be understood. They are called seven for the reason stated above, since the Holy Spirit is one but the gifts of grace are many.

What does it mean that there are seven eyes upon the stone? Clearly, it means that the Holy Spirit remains in Christ. And just as the eyes are said to belong substantially to the one in whom they are, so you should understand that the Holy Spirit belongs to Christ.

The same prophet signified this under the image of a lampstand, saying: “I saw, and behold, a wholly golden lampstand, and its lamp upon its top, and its seven lamps upon it” (Zech. IV, 2).

Understand the golden lampstand as the incarnation of Christ: golden because it is without stain or any mixture of sin, wholly bright and wholly shining. The lamp upon its top is the divinity in the man. For the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (I Cor. XI, 3).

The seven lamps upon it—that is, upon the lampstand or upon its head—are the fullness of the Holy Spirit. He rests upon him according to the oracle of the prophet Isaiah:

“And the Spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI, 2).

If, then, the seven lamps of the Holy Spirit rest upon Christ, the Holy Spirit rests in him, being represented by the seven lamps. And since he rests in him by substantially indwelling him, he is the Spirit of the one in whom he substantially rests. Hence he is rightly called the Spirit of Christ.

It should also be noted that concerning this Spirit signified by the seven eyes it is added that they range throughout the whole earth.

[Col. 0240A]

And after the Apocalypse had said that the seven spirits of God are the seven eyes of the Lamb, it added: “Sent into all the earth” (Rev. V, 6). What Zechariah calls “ranging,” John in the Apocalypse calls “sent,” indicating the procession of the Holy Spirit by the term “sending.” Although he is substantially in Christ, he does not range or get sent unless he proceeds from Christ—not locally, but substantially.

For in order to exist, he receives being from both the Father and the Son, just as the Son essentially received being from the Father. But this does not work conversely, so that, because the Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Son and the Father, the Son would likewise be born equally from the Father and the Holy Spirit. His birth is from the Father alone; his procession is from both—that is, simultaneously from the Father and the Son.

The Apocalypse says that the seven spirits of God were sent into all the earth, and Zechariah that the seven eyes of the Lord range throughout the whole earth, on account of the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit, diffused through the apostles and the successors of the apostles among all nations. Through these gifts the faithful who believe in Christ are sanctified and receive cleansing from their sins.

John also signified that the Holy Spirit himself is the Spirit of Christ when he said that he saw, in the midst of the seven lampstands, “one like the Son of Man” (Rev. I, 13). After some intervening words he said: “And his eyes were like a flame of fire” (ibid., 14).

Who is this Son of Man? Clearly, the Lord Jesus Christ, who very often calls himself the Son of Man in the Gospel, as in the passage: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. XVI, 13). Ezekiel too frequently hears himself called “son of man” under his figure.

By saying that the eyes of this Son of Man shone like a flame of fire, he signifies the Holy Spirit. For the Spirit appeared over the apostles as fire sent from heaven. By calling them his eyes, he signified that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Christ.

There is no other reason why he is called the Spirit of Christ except that he proceeds from him and is substantially in him.

John also says, when speaking of the future glory of the saints, that neither the sun nor any heat would afflict them, and he adds: “For the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will shepherd them and lead them to the fountains of the waters of life” (Rev. VII, 16–17).

What are these fountains of the waters of life? They are the streams of the Holy Spirit, by which the faithful are both washed through cleansing and given life through irrigation. Concerning these streams the Savior says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 38), signifying the Holy Spirit whom believers were to receive. This was first fulfilled in the apostles on the fiftieth day after the resurrection.

The Lamb, therefore, will lead them to the fountains of the waters of life because he will intoxicate them with the streams of the Holy Spirit, so that they may never be able to lose the joys of eternal life.

Let us not suppose that these fountains of the waters of life exist outside Christ. For he himself said to Philip: “I am the life”; and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 6, 9). Thus whoever sees Christ also sees the Holy Spirit, who is in Christ. To lead believers to the fountains of the waters of life is to lead them to himself, so that those who believe in him and gaze upon him may continually be satisfied from the fountains of the Holy Spirit proceeding from him.

Again, in the Apocalypse John says: “And the angel took the censer and filled it with the fire of the altar and cast it into the earth; and there were thunderings and voices,” and so forth (Rev. VIII, 5).

This angel is Jesus Christ, who is called the Angel of the Great Counsel. The censer is his humanity. The altar, from whose fire the censer is filled, is the divinity of Christ. The fire from the altar is the Holy Spirit taken from Christ’s divinity. For both the altar and the censer are Christ.

He is the altar because upon him the holocausts and sacrifices of the saints are offered, and the earthly altar bears his image. The vows of the saints are not otherwise received unless they are placed upon Christ the altar.

The censer is so called because the prayers of the saints are received through him. Or certainly the censer is the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the Apostle testifies: “We do not know what we should pray for, but the Spirit himself pleads for us” (Rom. VIII, 26)—that is, he makes us plead “with inexpressible groanings” (Luke XII, 49).

The fire of the altar is the Holy Spirit, concerning whom the Savior says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, which I wish to burn.”

The angel therefore sent the censer, full of the fire of the altar, into the earth, because, having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, the Savior poured out the grace of the Holy Spirit upon believers.

Accordingly, it follows that there were thunderings, voices, flashes of lightning, and earthquakes, in accordance with what the Savior says in the Gospel:

“It is expedient for you that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment” (John XVI, 7).

What the Apocalypse says about the fire of the altar—that the angel sent it into the earth and there were thunderings—is what the Savior says: “I will send him to you; and when he comes, he will convict the world.”

The whole world has recognized what thunderings and voices of preaching resounded after the coming of the Holy Spirit, how greatly they shook the hearts of mortals with fear, what flashes of miracles shone forth, and what earthquakes arose to shake the hardness of mortals.

The fire of the altar, then, is called the Spirit of Christ, whom he himself promises to send to the apostles. The Apocalypse testifies that he sent him into the earth, plainly teaching that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son and that he was sent by him upon the apostles after his ascension. For how is he sent by the Son except by proceeding from him? And he proceeds from the one whose Spirit he is.

Again, in the same Apocalypse John says: “And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse; and the one sitting upon it was called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and fights. His eyes were like a flame of fire” (Rev. XIX, 21).

The white horse is the body of Christ, suffused with the brightness of holiness and having no stain. Its rider is the divinity of Christ, which governs and inhabits the man he assumed in such a way as to make one Son: from his divinity containing the substance of the Father, and from his humanity containing the substance of his mother.

His eyes are like a flame of fire because the divinity and fiery splendor of the Holy Spirit dwell in him. From his fullness light shines forth like the light of his eyes. Under this figure it signifies—or rather teaches with complete clarity—that the divinity of the Spirit proceeds from the divinity of the Son. And just as light is said to belong to the one whose eyes they are, so the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Christ, in whom he dwells and from whom he proceeds.

## CHAPTER VIII. Testimonies from the Gospel and the Councils.

We believe that it has been sufficiently demonstrated by the testimonies of the divine Scriptures that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Let us add two further testimonies from the Gospel, by which the hardness of those who contradict this may be crushed.

After the woman who suffered from an issue of blood had been healed, the Savior said: “Who touched me?” When everyone denied it, Peter and those who were with him said: “Master, the crowds press upon you and overwhelm you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” And Jesus said: “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke VIII, 45–46).

What is this power which the Savior says has gone out from him? Clearly, it is the grace of the Holy Spirit. For the Apostle says: “To one is given the grace of healings in the one Spirit, and to another the working of miracles” (I Cor. XII, 9).

What, then, does it mean for the Savior to say, “I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke VIII, 46), except: “I know that the Spirit proceeds from me, the one who bestows healings and works miracles”? He says that the Holy Spirit went out from him in the same way in which he elsewhere says of himself: “I came forth from the Father” (John XVI, 28). For the Son’s coming forth from the Father means his being born from the Father. Likewise, the Holy Spirit’s coming forth from the Son means his proceeding from him.

Again, in the same Gospel of blessed Luke you have: “And the whole crowd sought to touch him, because power went out from him and healed them all” (Luke VI, 19). The power going out from Christ heals all because the Holy Spirit proceeding from him grants the grace of healing to everyone.

Let the critics, the malicious, and the ignorant therefore cease reproaching the Church of Christ because it confesses that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. This is what the Gospels teach; this is what the apostles profess; this is not concealed by the prophets.

Let them first learn what the Church learned from Christ, and, having become disciples of the Truth, let them confess the Catholic faith, lest, deceived by arrogant presumption or ensnared by ignorance of error, they nourish a heresy long since lulled to sleep. For they are sliding into the madness of Arius, who, while derogating from the Son’s consubstantial equality with the Father, also taught that the Holy Spirit was lesser than the Son, attempting to assert both that the Son was not born from the substance of the Father and that the Holy Spirit was a creature.

Consider, illustrious emperors, where your profession leads when you say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father but not from the Son. You have never read this either in the divine Scriptures or in the ecclesiastical teachers.

The holy synod of Constantinople, refuting and condemning the madness of Arius, did indeed say that the Son is consubstantial with the Father and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father (Constantinople I, in the Creed). But did it deny that he proceeds from the Son? Or does it follow that, if he proceeds from the Father, he does not proceed from the Son?

Rather, if you wish to be sons of the Church and to follow the teaching of the Fathers, recognize that when the holy council gathered at Constantinople spoke of the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father, it did not deny that he also proceeds from the Son. Since the whole Trinity is consubstantial, and since the Son is born from the Father, and since the Holy Spirit is the love of both, no one can deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son without denying that the Son possesses the love with which he loves the Father.

Since this would be madness, it must be held and faithfully professed that the Father loves the Son, the Son loves the Father, and that the love with which the Father loves the Son proceeds from the Father; while the love with which the Son loves the Father likewise proceeds from the Son. This love is the Holy Spirit.

The Spirit therefore proceeds from the Father and from the Son. It is now time to confirm the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son by the testimonies of the holy Fathers, so that those who hold different opinions may be moved to reverence and corrected by salutary respect, lest through foolish obstinacy they slip into the pit of destruction.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0243]

## CHAPTER ONE. The Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son Is Proved from the Fathers.

[Col. 0243B]

We are discussing the question of the procession of the Holy Spirit, which the emperors of the Greeks deny to be from the Son. They say that he proceeds from the Father alone, and for this reason, refusing communion with the Roman Church, they did not receive the legates of the Apostolic See. They charge the Roman Church with guilt because the Latin Church says something different from them about the Holy Spirit, professing and believing that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, whereas they say that he proceeds from the Father alone.

First, we see laymen acting against all ecclesiastical regulations and imposing decrees upon the faithful. Although they are not permitted to establish any statute concerning ecclesiastical law without the counsel of the bishops, they themselves attempt to formulate laws concerning the faith. According to their decrees, some are admitted to communion while others are excluded.

If, indeed, they had decided that anything should be enacted concerning the content of their faith, they ought to have summoned a council of bishops, sought the decrees of the Fathers and the oracles of the holy Scriptures, and, after consulting the bishops, determined by common agreement what ought to be followed and what ought instead to be rejected. If they discovered that in certain Churches, or in some part of the world, practices were being held or professed which ought rightly and properly to have moved them—whether on grounds of faith or of custom—they should first have written to those communities, and the reason for the practice should have been investigated. Then, if the discipline of sound reasoning required it, a judgment should have been issued. And even this should have been done under their own governance and supervision, with the Churches established under their authority. Otherwise, what right did they have to judge, according to custom, peoples who did not belong to the care of their administration, or Churches that did not reside under their rule, or to investigate a matter of the faith’s doctrine—and, if those communities did not think or hold everything precisely as they did, to strike them with the sentence of excommunication? Did the Savior grant the Greek emperors the power to bind and loose? Did he say to them, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14)? Did he command them to teach all nations and baptize them in the name of the Father, [Col. 0244B] and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19)? But if you say that the Holy Spirit proceeds only from the Father, refusing to confess that he proceeds from the Son, although the entire Latin Church—or certainly the Catholic Church of the whole world—professes that he also proceeds from the Son, on what grounds do you prove that your opinion is preferable and fortified by the authority of truth? Or perhaps has the truth of the Gospel reached you alone and remained with you alone?

The apostle Paul says that he was called an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of Christ (Rom. 15:19), and that he had filled the whole region from Jerusalem to Illyricum with the Gospel of Christ. He also went to Rome and Spain, and traversed the entire Roman world, fully preaching Christ either through his bodily presence or through his writings. Does he say that he preached Christ only to the Greeks and disclosed the truth of the Gospel only to Greek emperors? Throughout the whole world the Gospel of Christ shines forth; the writings of the apostles are read; the oracles of the prophets are recited. By these the teachers of the Churches, just as they were instructed from the beginning through the apostles, learn daily what they ought to think and profess concerning the Holy Trinity; what they should teach the peoples entrusted to them; by what morals they should instruct them; by what manner of life they should shape them; and by what religious observance they should order them.

Neither do the sacred pages speak, nor do the institutions of the ancients commend, nor do the precepts of the apostles judge, that the Greeks should be the teachers of the whole Church of Christ, or that it should be shown or taught by them to their emperors what must be observed throughout the entire world of Christ’s Church, whether in outward practice, religious observance, or doctrine. If this is recognized as exceedingly foolish and excessively presumptuous, the Roman Church ought not to have been so lightly reproached for preserving the institutions of its own ancestors and not following the institutions of the Greeks in every respect. For whatever it holds or practices concerning the Holy Trinity or any religious observance has flowed from the fountain of Christ’s disciples. What it believes, teaches, and carries out is neither contrary nor inconsistent with the pages of the holy Scriptures. Therefore you attempt to reproach us [Col. 0245A] because we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, while you say that he proceeds from the Father.

## CHAPTER II. The opposing claims of the Greeks are refuted by the authority of councils.

First we ask you for the authority of the ancients—namely, of the Catholic bishops—by which you maintain the decree that you are trying so strenuously to defend. The Council of Nicaea, comprising three hundred and eighteen bishops and assembled against Arius under the first Emperor Constantine, after composing the Creed concerning the Son’s consubstantiality with the Father, says this when it reaches the Holy Spirit: “We believe also in the Holy Spirit,” determining nothing either greater or lesser concerning his substance or procession. Where, then, is the rule by which you think yourselves protected, or the Latins bound, so that you may say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, while the Romans may not say that he proceeds from the Son? If, by following the authority of the Council of Nicaea, you do not wish to add anything further, remove the words “proceeding from the Father,” because they are not contained in the Nicene Creed; and perhaps it would likewise be permissible to remove what the Romans added concerning his proceeding from the Son.

But if you reply that this was included in the Council of Constantinople, where one hundred and fifty bishops gathered, we answer that it was not permissible either to subtract from, add to, or alter anything in the Creed of the Council of Nicaea concerning the faith. If you say that nothing concerning the Son’s consubstantiality could lawfully have been added to what had been determined in that assembly, but that, because little had been said there about the Holy Spirit, additions were permitted on account of future heretical controversies and in accordance with the authority of the holy Scriptures, we reply that the Romans were likewise permitted to do this on account of future heretical controversies and in accordance with the authority of the divine Scriptures.

Nor can you prove that the authority of the city of Constantinople was greater than that of the city of Rome, which is the head of all the Churches of Christ; this is confirmed by the testimony both of your ancestors and of ours. Nor is the authority of one hundred and fifty bishops so great that it could prescribe to all the bishops of the entire world that what was permitted to them should not be permitted either to the Roman pontiff or to all the Churches of Christ.

They also added to the aforesaid Creed, saying that the Holy Spirit is to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, that he spoke through the holy prophets, and several other things. By adding these statements they did not prescribe them to the Churches of Christ, but gave an example: if anyone wished to add something concerning the Holy Spirit in accordance with the holy Scriptures—something that would overcome heretics and strengthen the faith of believers—this could be done.

But if you prefer to object that the statement that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father cannot be found written in the holy Gospels or in the other divine books, and therefore you refuse to accept what is not found written in the holy Scriptures, just as the Arians refused to accept that the Father and the Son are of one and the same substance because the sacred Scriptures did not contain that expression, tell us where you have read that the Council of Constantinople placed in its Creed the statement that the Holy Spirit is to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son and that he spoke through the holy prophets.

If you say that these things are not found in the holy Scriptures in bare words, but that the power of their meaning is contained there—so that, because the Holy Spirit is of one substance with the Father and the Son, of one power, and of undivided majesty, he is therefore to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son—then grant the same to the Latin Churches. Although the Gospels do not state in bare words [Col. 0246B] that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, they nevertheless demonstrate in many ways that he is the Son’s Spirit, just as he is the Father’s Spirit, and that he proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father. We believe that this has been sufficiently demonstrated in the preceding book.

Since these things stand thus, and since the Catholic faith, founded through the Savior and the apostles, has always held and has never ceased to preach that the Holy Spirit is of the same power and the same substance as the Father and the Son, and that he proceeds from both, what is this that you now attempt to reproach in the Catholic faith, and what are you trying to contrive against Catholic doctrines? Perhaps you are attempting to revive Arius or Macedonius and bring into the Church the ashes of their wicked doctrines, long since laid to rest.

Did your ancestors not know what the Roman Church taught concerning the Holy Spirit? Yet they never withdrew from communion with the Roman See, knowing that the truth of the Catholic faith consisted in what it held and preached, and that what rested upon the authority of the holy Scriptures was not legitimately open to reproach.

Until the time of Arius, no confusion disturbed believers concerning the consubstantiality of the Father and the Son, nor was the term *homoousion* (“of one substance”) preached. Nevertheless, the force of that word was present in the minds of believers, because they believed that the almighty Son was in no respect unlike the Father, recalling the Savior’s well-spoken saying: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9). Nor did they know Christ as anything other than the Creator of all things, since it is written through John that “all things were made through him” (John 1:3). Yet the Creed composed in the assembly of the apostles contained nothing beyond what we all know: that we ought to believe in God the Father almighty and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord. This faith was sufficient for the salvation of believers; throughout the whole world it was both approved and commended by the blood of many martyrs and the innumerable voices of confessors.

But when Arius, the opponent of truth, began to rage against Christ’s divinity and to hurl many blasphemies, the minds of the faithful were stirred to piety, and they brought forth the weapons of truth against the error of impiety. Together with its author, they struck down the impious doctrine that blasphemed the Son of God as a creature rather than one begotten from the Father, and that likewise declared the Holy Spirit lesser than the Son.

After him Macedonius arose. He agreed with the Catholics in his thinking about the Father and the Son, but did not acknowledge the person of the Holy Spirit. The Catholic bishops contended against him and proved that the Holy Spirit is one within the Holy Trinity, consubstantial with both the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father, and to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son.

Then, when the Arian madness sprouted again and sought to establish that it was not orthodox to say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father—because this appeared blasphemous, since it would make the Father the Father of two, namely, of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—the teachers of the Churches determined that this blasphemy also had to be driven away, and they added to the Creed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well. Otherwise, if he were said to proceed only from the Father, the Son might be thought to be the Holy Spirit, and he would not be called the Son’s Spirit; this would be impious and blasphemous and contrary to evangelical and apostolic teaching.

For if you wish to say that the word “proceed” sufficiently distinguishes the Holy Spirit, so that he will not be thought to be the Son, know that the same word is also proclaimed concerning the Son. For he himself says in the Gospel of John: “I proceeded from God and came” (John 8:42). If, therefore, the Son proceeds from God the Father, and the Holy Spirit also proceeds, what will silence the Arians, so that they may not blaspheme by making the Holy Spirit the Son of the Father?

## CHAPTER III. Testimonies from Athanasius and Gregory of Nazianzus.

Keeping this matter in view, the teachers both of the Latins and of the Greeks said that the Son alone is begotten from the Father, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. They understood this because they had been taught by the instruction of the divine Scriptures that the Spirit is the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son, and therefore proceeds from both.

Accordingly, blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, who endured much from the Arians for the steadfastness of the Catholic faith, was often driven into exile by their faction, and, while serving as deacon to his bishop, blessed Alexander, at the Council of Nicaea, fought alone against the madness of Arius. In the book on the faith that he composed and proposed for all Catholics to hold, he says among other things:

> “The Father is made by no one, created by no one, begotten by no one. The Son is from the Father alone—not made, not created, but begotten. The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son—not made, not created, not begotten, but proceeding.”

The Latin prelates, recognizing this truth of the faith, considering it a singular defense against the wicked Arian doctrine, and understanding it to have been derived from the holy Scriptures, added to the Creed of the faith the words concerning the Holy Spirit: “Who proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

From those times—namely, from the time of Constantine, under whom the council of three hundred and eighteen bishops was assembled at Nicaea—down to our own age, the Western Church has held this faith. Nor has the Catholic Church of the Greeks repudiated it, because it did not wish to become alien to the doctrine of truth, as their writings make clear. [Col. 0248A] Yet now you accuse this faith, moved, I know not by what frivolity or deceived by what error.

Tell us: do you profess that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Christ? If you deny it, the apostle Paul cries out against you, saying: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). Saint Luke also cries out, saying: “The Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16:7). Peter cries out as well: “Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God, he poured out this Spirit whom you see and hear” (Acts 2:33). The Savior himself cries out, speaking to his disciples: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you” (John 16:7). Likewise, after his resurrection he breathed upon the disciples and said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22).

All these passages profess that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Christ. Since you cannot deny this, necessity compels you, whether you wish it or not, not to deny that he proceeds from the Son. For your profession that he proceeds from the Father bears witness against you if you call him a creature with Arius or deny his existence with Macedonius. Since you say that he proceeds from the Father, how do you attempt to deny that he proceeds from the Son, when he is of the substance of both—the Father, namely, and the Son—and cannot be of the substance of both unless he proceeds from both?

Let us hear what Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, says in his sermon on the Holy Spirit, which he delivered before the people in the Church of Constantinople on the day of Pentecost:

> “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “was always, and is, and will be, having neither any beginning nor any end, but coeternal with the Father and the Son. For it is not fitting either that the Son should at some time have been absent from the Father, or that the Spirit should have been absent from the Son.”

By saying that the Holy Spirit is coeternal with the Father and the Son, he refutes the Arians, who taught that he was a creature. By saying that he always was, is, and will be, he refutes Macedonius, who denied that he exists. But by confessing that the Son was never at any time absent from the Father, nor the Spirit from the Son, he refutes you, who deny that he proceeds from the Son.

For if, according to your opinion, he had wished the Holy Spirit to proceed only from the Father, he ought to have said that neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit was ever absent from the Father. But since he says that the Son was never absent from the Father, nor the Spirit from the Son, he plainly teaches that the Son was born from the Father without any interval of time, and that the Spirit proceeded from the Son before all time. Yet he did not deny that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, a matter about which there was no controversy; rather, he said that the Spirit was never absent from the Son, which was the point at issue.

Later, speaking of the Spirit himself, he says:

> “He sanctifies and is not sanctified; he makes gods and is not himself made God; he is unchangeable, immutable, always present to himself, to the Father, and to the Son; invisible, beyond time, of his own power, all-powerful.”

When he says that the Spirit is always present to himself, to the Father, and to the Son, he does not demonstrate the attendance of a servant in obedience. Rather, he shows that he is unchangeable and immutable, existing in his own nature as he does in the substance of the Father and the Son. He is in his own nature because there is no alteration in him; he is immutable with respect to the Father and the Son because the Father and the Son are of the same nature as the Holy Spirit.

He is unchangeable and immutable with respect to the Father, who is the fountain and first origin of all things; and with respect to the Son, because he proceeds from him, is not unlike him, and is not of another substance than the Son. He is also said to be “of his own power, all-powerful,” because he subsists in his own person and does whatever he wills throughout every creature.

Further on Gregory says:

> “He is also life, giving life; light and illuminating; good and goodness; he is Lord of all, sending the apostles; inspiring wherever he wills; distributing gifts as he wills; the Spirit of truth, the Spirit of wisdom, through whom the Father is known and the Son is glorified.”

We pass over many things, gathering only those that bear upon the present question. The Spirit is said to be life; and the Son says of himself: “I am life” (John 14:6). The Spirit is said to give life; and the Son says of himself: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21). Therefore, if the Spirit is life, the Son is also life; and if the Spirit gives life, the Son also gives life. They are of one substance and one operation.

But the Son is life from the Father, while the Spirit is life from the Son. Likewise, the Son who gives life is from the Father, while the Spirit who gives life is from the Son.

The Spirit is also light and illuminating; and the Savior says of himself: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). The evangelist John says of the Son: “He enlightens every person coming into this world” (ibid. 1:9). Therefore, if both are light and both illuminate—the Son, namely, and the Holy Spirit—they are of one substance and one operation.

But for the Holy Spirit to be light, he receives from the Son who is light; and for him to illuminate, he receives from the Son who illuminates, as the Son himself testifies: “He will receive from what is mine” (John 16:14). He receives, not as though he previously lacked what he receives, but as proceeding.

Likewise, the Spirit is good; and the Son says of himself: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). No sound-minded person will deny that Christ is goodness as well. Yet good and good are not two good beings, but one good being; goodness and goodness are not two goodnesses, but one goodness, because there are not two gods but one God, and the Godhead does not know an increase through multiplication into number.

Therefore the good Spirit proceeds from the good Son; he is not born from him. The goodness of the Spirit comes from the goodness of the Son, not by being born but by proceeding. Otherwise, if the Spirit proceeds only from the Father and not from the Son, how are the things that belong to the Son also the things of the Spirit? Or how does the Spirit receive from the Son?

Now, when Saint Gregory says that the Holy Spirit is Lord of all, this pertains to the Spirit’s omnipotence, because he is Lord of all things created by the Father through the Son—not by receiving lordship in time, but by proceeding eternally from the Father and the Son.

The Holy Spirit is said to send the apostles; and the Savior speaks to those same apostles: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. 10:16). The one operation of both is shown, since the Son and the Holy Spirit cooperate with one another. Hence it is made clear that they are neither of different substances, nor of different wills, nor of different powers, since their operation in all things is the same. Nevertheless, the Son is referred to the Father, from whom he is born, and the Holy Spirit to the Son, from whom he proceeds.

Blessed Gregory continues concerning the Spirit:

> “Inspiring wherever he wills; distributing gifts as he wills.”

And concerning the Son:

> “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” (Eph. 4:8).

These words show the majesty of the Holy Spirit: that he is not subordinate, imperfect, or less powerful, but equal to the Father and the Son in nature, greatness, every power, and every virtue.

The fact that he distributes gifts in the same way as the Son—not different gifts, but the same ones; not at one time the Son and at another time the Holy Spirit; not to some people the Son and to others the Holy Spirit—clearly demonstrates the effect of one operation and the movement of one will. Since this is so, the Son cannot exist without the Holy Spirit, nor the Holy Spirit without the Son, because both are of one substance and because the Spirit proceeds from the Son.

Gregory also calls the Holy Spirit the Spirit of truth; and the Savior says of himself: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). Therefore, by saying that the Spirit is the Spirit of truth, he plainly teaches that the Spirit of Christ, who is the truth, is meant.

This blessed man further says that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of wisdom. The apostle Paul testifies that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24). Therefore, the Spirit of wisdom is the Spirit of Christ, who is the wisdom of God.

Thus he clearly shows that the Spirit is Christ’s Spirit by calling him the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of wisdom. How, then, is he Christ’s Spirit, since he is Lord of all—as the same blessed Gregory testifies? Clearly, because he proceeds from Christ. If you deny this, you will confess that he is subordinate, and consequently either a creature or lesser than the Son. Both alternatives are blasphemous and far removed from Catholic piety.

Let what the truth possesses therefore be said: the Spirit is Christ’s Spirit, namely, the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of wisdom, because he proceeds from Christ—that is, he proceeds from truth and proceeds from wisdom.

Gregory adds:

> “Through whom the Father is known, and the Son is glorified, and by whom alone he himself is known.”

The Son says to the Father: “Father, I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me” (John 17:6). If the Father is known through the Spirit, and the Son manifests the Father’s name to human beings, they are shown to have one operation.

Gregory also says that the Son is glorified by the Holy Spirit; and the Son says: “It is my Father who glorifies me” (John 8:54). He also says to the Father: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself” (John 17:5). If the Spirit glorifies the Son and the Father glorifies the Son, the Father and the Spirit perform one and the same work; and if they operate together, they are shown to have one will, one essence, and one power.

The passage continues: “And by whom alone he himself is known.” If the Holy Spirit is known only by the Father and the Son, then plainly he proceeds from both and is consubstantial with both.

Observe also what Gregory says: the Son is glorified by the Spirit, just as we read that the Son glorifies the Father. What does it mean for the Father to glorify the Son except to make manifest to human beings that he was begotten from the Father? Likewise, the Son is glorified by the Spirit when the Spirit shows that he proceeds from the Son.

In many ways, therefore, blessed Gregory proves that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son and is of one and the same substance with the Father and the Son. In conclusion he says:

> “What need is there,” he says, “of more words? Everything that the Father is, the Son is also, except that the Father is unbegotten. Everything that the Son is, the Holy Spirit is also, except that the Son is begotten.”

What does this distinction and sequence of order mean: that the Son is what the Father is, except that the Father is unbegotten, and that the Holy Spirit is what the Son is, except that the Son is begotten?

He could have said that everything the Father is belongs to the Son and the Holy Spirit, except that the Father is not born and does not proceed from another. But instead he says that the Son is everything the Father is, and that the Holy Spirit is not everything the Father is, but everything the Son is, except for the privilege of birth. By speaking thus, he clearly shows that the Father is from no one, that the Son alone is begotten from the Father, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son.

That the Spirit also proceeds from the Father he stated somewhat earlier, saying:

> “And to the first origin of all things, which is the Father, everything is referred, just as everything belonging to the Only-Begotten is referred to him, so also everything belonging to the Holy Spirit.”

By saying this he shows that everything belonging to the Son has a relation to the Father, and that everything belonging to the Holy Spirit is referred to the same Father as the first origin of all things. For although the Spirit proceeds from the Son, the Son received this from the Father: namely, that, as the Son was born from the Father, the Holy Spirit should proceed from him; so that everything belonging to the Son belongs to the Father, and everything belonging to the Holy Spirit also belongs to the Son. Consequently, all this belongs to the Father, from whom the Son—begotten rather than created, not diminished but equal in power, and of not another but one and the same nature—received that the Holy Spirit should proceed from him.

Likewise, later Gregory says:

> “For it was truly fitting that, when Jesus had come to us bodily, the Spirit should also appear to us bodily; and when Christ had ascended to him, he should descend to us. He came indeed as Lord in power, but he is sent as one who is not opposed to God.”

Here also this teacher shows one operation and the will of one concord between Jesus and the Holy Spirit. He says that it was fitting that, because Jesus had come to us bodily, the Holy Spirit should likewise appear to us bodily.

From this the likeness of their one will is shown: the Holy Spirit wished to manifest himself bodily to mortals because Jesus wished to display his coming bodily to mortals. Since the Spirit proceeds from Jesus, he has one will with him; he is not different from the Son in operation, from whom he is not separated in nature; and he is always joined to him in action, since through his coeternity he is never absent from him, but continually cooperates with the one from whom he proceeds.

When Gregory adds, “And when Christ had ascended to him, he should descend to us,” he does not wish to show the Son’s diminution, but the assumption of humanity. Through this assumption Jesus ascended not only to the Holy Spirit but also to himself, because the one who through his humanity was within all things was, through his divinity, above all things.

He continues:

> “He came indeed as Lord in power, but he is sent as one who is not opposed to God.”
