He says two things: that the Holy Spirit came and that he was sent. His coming belongs properly to his own power, and therefore Gregory said, “as Lord.” His being sent reveals another relation, and therefore he said, “as one who is not opposed to him by whom he is sent.”

Being sent does not signify subjection, but procession. He is sent by Christ, to whom Christ ascended, and he is sent as one who is not opposed to God—that is, to Christ, who is indeed God, whose will he always shares. He is sent by Christ because he proceeds from him.

Gregory adds:

> “Therefore, after Christ, so that one Paraclete—meaning advocate or comforter—might never be absent from us. He is called another Paraclete so that you may recognize equality of nature and power. For ‘another’ means ‘another I’; and ‘another I’ is not said of one who is of another kind, but of one who is of the same substance or nature.”

By calling Christ the Paraclete and the Holy Spirit likewise the Paraclete, and by saying that the Spirit comes when Christ departs so that the faithful may not be without a Paraclete—whether Christ or the Holy Spirit—Gregory plainly shows that they have one office, since they share one name. They succeed one another because they are shown to have one will and one operation; when Christ ascends, the Spirit descends, and the Spirit is plainly sent by Christ, whose place he represents.

This sending is procession, since it signifies neither diminution nor subjection. The Holy Spirit is called “another,” that is, “another I,” and by this the complete likeness between them is shown. For “another I” cannot be said of one who is of another kind, but of one who is of the same substance or nature. The Spirit is therefore shown to proceed from the one whose nature or substance he possesses. For the Spirit cannot be of the same nature or substance as the Son unless he proceeds from him.

Gregory also adds farther on:

> “God is therefore fire [Note: [Col. 0251D] ‘God is therefore fire.’ Here Ratramnus copies Gregory of Nazianzus in such a way that he attaches Gregory’s meaning rather than his words, as Acherius himself pointed out. Moreover, Gregory’s words are falsely interpreted. For when he wrote that God the Father is fire, and likewise that God the Son is fire, and then added that the Holy Spirit is also fire, without attributing the name ‘God’ to him, we know that this was done because, although all Catholics believed that the Holy Spirit was equal to the Father and the Son, many nevertheless refused to call him God in Gregory’s time because he is nowhere called God in Scripture. Since every prudent prelate understood that this was so erroneous that nevertheless no harm to the Christian faith could result from it, he refrained from calling the Holy Spirit God; and not Gregory alone but also Basil the Great, his close friend, provides an example of this indulgence.] and the Holy Spirit is fire.”

It is read concerning God that he is a consuming fire—not natural and bodily, but spiritual and invisible. God the Father is therefore fire, God the Son is fire, and God the Holy Spirit is fire. Yet God the Father is fire from no fire, because he derives his origin from no one; God the Son is fire from the fire that is the Father, because he was born from him; and the Holy Spirit is fire from the fire that is the Son, because he proceeds from the Son.

By saying, therefore, that God is fire and that the Holy Spirit is fire, Gregory shows the one substance of the whole Trinity. He joins the persons of the Father and the Son by speaking of them together under the name of God, saying, “God is fire”; then he mentions the Holy Spirit separately, saying, “And the Holy Spirit is fire.”

Why he placed the persons of the Father and the Son together under the common designation “God,” but preferred to distinguish the Holy Spirit separately, is obvious. By this distinction he wished to show that the Holy Spirit, who is fire, proceeds from the Father and the Son, who are fire.

When Saint Gregory had discussed such matters concerning the Holy Spirit in the Church of Constantinople and committed them to writing, proving that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son and proceeds from the Son, without either concealing or diminishing his procession from the Father, but equating his omnipotence and lordship in every respect with those of the Father and the Son, was he expelled from the Church? Was his sermon rejected? Was he refused communion either by the citizens or by the emperor?

Certainly this venerable teacher lived in the time of the Roman emperors Gratian and Theodosius the Great. From then until our own time more than five hundred years have passed, and the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son has never been denied. No controversy arose among Catholics concerning it until your own times. Rather, both the Eastern and Western Churches always maintained the same and identical profession of faith concerning the Holy Spirit.

You may determine what has now, after so many centuries, produced this proposal for controversy. No reason either of integrity or wisdom can justify your having arrived at this point, since by saying such things you oppose the Catholic faith, resist the truth, and run contrary to the sacred pages.

## CHAPTER IV. From Ambrose.

Ambrose, bishop of Milan, a man adorned with every splendor of virtue, who fought many battles against the Arians and suffered no small number of injuries from their persecutions, wrote eloquently against Arian perversity in his books on the Holy Spirit and strengthened his arguments with evangelical truth. He says (*On the Holy Spirit*, book I, chapter 3):

> “If you say ‘Christ,’ you have designated God the Father, from whom the Son was anointed, the Son himself, who was anointed, and the Spirit, who anointed. And if you say ‘Father,’ you have likewise indicated his Son and the Spirit of his mouth—provided that you also grasp this in your heart. And if you say ‘Spirit,’ you have indicated God the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Son, because the Spirit is also the Son’s Spirit.”

Blessed Ambrose teaches that, when one name is uttered—whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit—the whole Trinity is comprehended. He demonstrates such a great likeness of equality among the three that the three persons are contained under one name: not through a distinction of sound, but through the equality of their unity.

When he says that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, there is no controversy between us, for you admit this with us. But when he says that, if the Son is named, the Spirit is likewise named because he is the Son’s Spirit, here you separate yourselves from us. For those who shrink from professing that the Spirit proceeds from the Son likewise shrink from saying that he is the Son’s Spirit. If he does not proceed from the Son, he is not rightly called his Spirit. He is called the Father’s Spirit because he proceeds from the Father; and consequently, when the Son is named, the naming of the Holy Spirit is not understood along with him. He cannot be shown to be included under the Son’s name if he is not the Son’s Spirit; and he is not the Son’s if he does not proceed from him. But Saint Ambrose says that he is the Son’s Spirit. Therefore he proceeds from the Son.

In what follows he speaks in the same way: “Whoever will deny the Holy Spirit will also deny God the Father and the Son, since the Spirit of God is the Spirit of Christ; and no one will doubt that there is one Spirit.” He shows how great is the unity, how great the consubstantiality of the Spirit with the Father and the Son, when he says that whoever denies the Spirit likewise denies the Father and the Son, because there is one Spirit of both. From where, then, is he the Father’s? Because he proceeds from the Father. Hence likewise he is the Son’s, because he proceeds from the Son. For there are not two Spirits, but one; nor is one said to be the Father’s Spirit and another the Son’s, but one Spirit of both. Therefore he proceeds from both.

Later (chapter 10): “Therefore the Spirit is not sent, as it were, from a place, nor does he proceed, as it were, from a place, when he proceeds from the Son, just as the Son himself says: ‘I proceeded from the Father and came.’” He plainly testifies that the Spirit proceeds from the Son. But lest this procession be measured by bodily distances, the Son himself, excluding such an interpretation, says of the Father: “I proceeded and came” (John 8:42). The Son proceeds from the Father, not by spatial distance, but by the departure involved in birth; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son neither by spatial distance nor by the departure involved in birth, but by a procession of existence.

Speaking below of the Son’s procession from the Father, he begins as follows: “Nor, when he goes forth from the Father, does he depart from a place, and are they separated like body from body. Nor, when he is with the Father, is body enclosed in body, as it were. Likewise, when the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son, he is not separated from the Father, nor is he separated from the Son.”

This eminent teacher and most illustrious confessor of Christ, by saying that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and proceeds also from the Son, removed from the Arians against whom he was contending the opportunity for blasphemy, lest those who said that the Spirit was a creature and inferior not only to the Father but also to the Son should carry off the palm of victory. Rather, hearing that he proceeds from both, they would recognize him as consubstantial with the Father and the Son, and as equally worthy with them of adoration and glorification.

And later he testifies that the Son said: “Whoever loves me will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). “Thus, then, the Spirit comes in the same way as the Father comes, because where the Father is, there also is the Son; and where the Son is, there is also the Holy Spirit.”

What does he mean by saying that where the Father is, there also is the Son, except that the Son was born from the Father, from whom he is never separated? And what does “where the Son is, there is also the Holy Spirit” mean, except that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, from whom he is never separated? He thereby displays the ineffable consubstantiality of the whole Trinity, when he testifies that the Son is always in the Father and that the Holy Spirit is always in the Son, so that where the Father is, there is also the Son, and where the Son is, there is also the Holy Spirit—not divided by place, time, will, action, or essence.

Again, later (chapter 12): “Just as the Father handed over the Son, and the Son himself handed himself over, understand that the Holy Spirit handed him over. For it is written: ‘Then Jesus was led into the desert by the Spirit, to be tempted by the devil’ (Matthew 4). Therefore the loving Spirit also handed over the Son; for the love of the Father and the Son is one.”

By saying that the love of the Father and the Son is one, he testifies that the Spirit of both is one, for the Spirit is love. The Apostle says: “The fruit of the Spirit is love” (Galatians 5:22). Thus it is shown that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, whose love he is. For the Father’s love cannot exist unless it proceeds from the Father, since it receives its love from no other source; nor can it be the Son’s love unless it proceeds from the Son, just as the love by which he loves proceeds from him. And just as the love of the Father and the Son is one, so the Spirit of both is one, proceeding from both.

In the second book (chapter 12) he says: “The Holy Spirit received from the Son. He received through unity of substance, just as the Son received from the Father.”

By saying this, does he not most clearly teach that the Holy Spirit received from the Son? And what he received, he received by proceeding, just as the Son received from the Father by being born. Could the Holy Spirit have received from the Son something that he did not previously have, since he is of one substance with the Son and of one power, and since whatever the Son has, the Holy Spirit also has?

Saint Ambrose adds testimony from the Gospel: “He,” he says, “will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you. Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said: ‘He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you’” (John 16:14–15).

He continues: “What, then, is clearer than this unity? What the Father has belongs to the Son; what the Son has, the Spirit also received.”

These words of Saint Ambrose most plainly testify that the Holy Spirit proceeded substantially from the Son. For he says: “What the Father has belongs to the Son”—that is, since the Son was substantially born from the Father, what belongs to the Father belongs also to the Son. Likewise, since the Holy Spirit substantially proceeds from the Son, he received from the Son, so that whatever the Son has, the Spirit also has; that is, so that he may be of the same substance as the Son, just as the Son is of the same substance as the Father.

Again, in what follows: “What the Son speaks, the Father also speaks; and what the Father speaks, the Son also speaks. And concerning the Spirit the Son of God said: ‘For he will not speak from himself’—that is, not without my communion and the Father’s, for the Spirit is not divided or separated—‘but whatever he hears, he will speak’ (ibid., 13), hearing, namely, through unity of substance and particularity of knowledge.”

When this catholic teacher confesses that the Holy Spirit does not speak without the communion of the Father and the Son—that is, when the Spirit speaks, the Father speaks and the Son also speaks—he testifies that the Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son and of the same operation, neither divided nor separated. And what he adds, “Whatever he hears, he will speak,” implies the Spirit’s procession. For, since he is of the same substance, the Spirit does not hear the speech of the Father and the Son through intervening distances or through some openings.

And just as the Son says, “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15)—namely, by being born from the Father and remaining in the Father’s substance, not by perceiving the Father’s speech at some interval—so also the Spirit speaks what he hears, namely by proceeding from the Father and the Son, because, substantially remaining in both and proceeding from both, he hears what he speaks through unity of substance and particularity of knowledge.

And below: “The Son has everything that belongs to the Father; he says: ‘Everything that belongs to the Father is mine’ (John 16:15). And what he himself received through unity of nature, the Spirit received from him through the same unity, just as the Lord Jesus himself declares concerning his Spirit, saying: ‘Therefore I said: He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you’ (ibid., 14).”

By saying that the Son has everything that belongs to the Father, and again that everything he himself received from the Father the Spirit received from him through unity of nature—that is, from the Son—does he not plainly declare that, just as the Son was born from the Father, that is, from the Father’s substance, so also the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, that is, from the Son’s substance? And just as the Son, by being born, received everything that belongs to the Father, so also the Holy Spirit, by proceeding from the Son, received everything that belongs to the Son?

And below: “Therefore what the Spirit speaks belongs to the Son; what the Son gave belongs to the Father.”

Thus, if what the Spirit speaks belongs to the Son, this teacher plainly testifies that whatever the Spirit has, he received from the Son, because he proceeds from him. And if what the Son gave belongs to the Father, to whom did he give it? Clearly, to the Holy Spirit who proceeds from him. And if what he gave belongs to the Father, the Son received it from the Father by being born, so that the Holy Spirit might proceed from him.

He added: “Thus neither the Son nor the Spirit speaks from himself, because the Trinity speaks nothing outside itself.”

The whole Trinity consists in the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. The Son speaks nothing from himself because he is not from himself but from the Father. Likewise the Spirit speaks nothing from himself because he is not from himself but from the Son; the Father alone is from no one. Therefore, when the Son speaks, the whole Trinity speaks; when the Spirit speaks, the whole Trinity speaks; and when the Father speaks, the whole Trinity speaks, because the Trinity speaks nothing outside itself, since it is neither divided from nor separated from itself.

Again, in the same work, in the third book (chapter 1): “For according to divinity the Spirit is not above Christ but in Christ, because just as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, so the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ is in the Father and in the Son.”

By saying that according to divinity the Spirit is not above Christ but in Christ, blessed Ambrose distinguishes Christ’s humanity from his divinity. We read in the Gospel that the Holy Spirit came upon the Savior and remained upon him, and the Father says to John: “Upon whoever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him” (John 1:33). Thus, according to his humanity, the Spirit came upon Christ and remained upon him; but according to his divinity he remains in Christ, since he is equal to him and of the same substance with him, as is also written concerning the Father, that he remains in the Son and the Son in the Father.

When he added that the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ remains in the Father and in the Son, he testified that the Spirit of both is one, because he proceeds from both and remains in both through consubstantiality.

He added: “For he remains in God because he is from God, as it is written: ‘We did not receive the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God’” (1 Corinthians 2:12). “And he remains in Christ because he received from Christ and is in Christ.” For it is written again: “He will receive from what is mine” (John 16:14).

From where, then, is the Spirit from God? Clearly, because he proceeds from God. And from where did he receive from Christ? Certainly because he proceeds from Christ. And from where does he remain both in God and in Christ? Entirely because he is consubstantial with both.

In what follows (chapters 7 and 8), speaking of the Antichrist, he says: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the Spirit of his mouth” (2 Thessalonians 2:8). “Here there is not an acquired grace, but an undivided unity remains, because neither can Christ exist without the Spirit nor the Spirit without Christ; for the unity of the divine nature cannot be separated.”

Here too Saint Ambrose shows the distinction between Christ’s humanity and divinity—not that Christ is one thing as man and another as God, but that the one Christ is perfect God and perfect man. The man, however, became God by grace; God exists as God by nature.

Therefore, when he said, “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the Spirit of his mouth,” and added that this was not an acquired grace, he excluded the humanity, so that the Spirit of the mouth by which the Antichrist is to be killed might be understood as the Spirit of divinity, namely the Holy Spirit, who is one person in the Holy Trinity. Thus, when he says, “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the Spirit of his mouth,” understand the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of the Lord Jesus.

It must likewise be observed that, when the same Spirit is called the Spirit of the Lord’s mouth and is now called the Spirit of the mouth of the Lord Jesus, it is plainly shown that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the mouth of the Lord Jesus—not because he has a mouth according to his divinity, but because the Spirit proceeds from his substance, just as he is called the Spirit of the Lord’s mouth because he proceeds from the Father’s substance. Thus it is shown by the clearest assertion that the Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son, since he is called the Spirit of the mouth of both the Father and the Son.

Blessed Ambrose continues (chapter 8) that the unity both of Christ and of the Spirit remains undivided, because “neither can Christ exist without the Spirit nor the Spirit without Christ.” Christ cannot exist without the Spirit, as one consubstantial with him and proceeding from him; nor, again, can the Spirit exist without Christ, as one consubstantial with him and having received from him everything that Christ has.

He connects the reason why this is so, namely “because the unity of the divine nature cannot be separated.” By saying this, he acknowledges that Christ’s nature is the Spirit’s nature and that the Spirit’s nature is Christ’s nature, and that the bond of unity cannot in any way be separated, except that the Son is born while the Spirit proceeds. But these distinctions do not establish substance; they indicate relation.

He speaks below: “It has been read that the sword of the Word is the Spirit; likewise it has been read that the sword of the Holy Spirit is the Word of God” (Ephesians 6:17).

After inserting several matters by way of explanation, he concluded as follows: “Since, then, the sword of the Word is the Holy Spirit and the sword of the Holy Spirit is the Word, there is certainly a unity of power.”

But what is the sword of the Word except the Word itself? And what is the sword of the Spirit except the Spirit himself? From this it follows that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Word, whose sword he is, and that the Word belongs to the Holy Spirit, whose sword it is. For neither does the Word exist without the Holy Spirit, nor the Holy Spirit without the Word, because they have one operation and the same power.

Since this is so, their substances cannot be separated, nor can they be divided by will. Therefore, since the Son and the Holy Spirit exist as one substance and one will, one proceeds from the other—that is, the Spirit from the Son—because the Son, born from the Father, gave to the Spirit everything that he received from the Father by being born, not as to one inferior or foreign, but as to one proceeding from himself.

It must be observed, however, that when the Word is called the sword of the Holy Spirit and the Holy Spirit the sword of the Word, the persons are not joined together; rather, the joining of substance is shown, so that they are of one substance although they are not one person. One is from the other, namely the Spirit from the Son; but the Son is not from the Spirit, but from the Father.

In this way Saint Ambrose, thinking and arguing about the Holy Spirit, was not regarded as ungrateful or heretical by the Greek emperors—namely Gratian and Theodosius the Elder, under whose reign he flourished—but was honored by them with complete affection and always held in the highest reverence. His argument and his tireless labor on behalf of the Catholic faith defeated, conquered, and crushed the Arians who were attacking the Church.

Now look to which emperors you are striving either to defend the faith or to imitate in religion. Behold: by denying that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, you have raised your hands against the catholic bishops who crushed the Arians when they held wicked opinions concerning the Holy Spirit; and you overturn the piety of your ancestors, namely the Roman emperors, who always cherished this faith and, fighting on its behalf, loved it with great reverence.

## CHAPTER V. From Didymus

[Note: Didymus of Alexandria. Aeneas of Paris, Ratramnus’s contemporary, testifies that Jerome rendered this book of Didymus into Latin word for word, in the work that we append to Ratramnus. Anselm of Havelberg later wrote the same in *Dialogue*, book II, chapter 24.]

Didymus of Alexandria—blinded in his bodily eyes from childhood, but highly distinguished by spiritual vision—speaks as follows in the book that he wrote about the Holy Spirit:

“Therefore whoever shares in the Holy Spirit immediately shares also in the Father and the Son. And whoever has the love of the Father has received it as contributed by the Son through the Holy Spirit; and whoever is a participant in the grace of Jesus Christ has that same grace given by the Father through the Holy Spirit.”

From all this it is approved that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have the same operation.

Let us carefully reconsider what he says. He says, then: “Whoever shares in the Holy Spirit”—and one shares in the Spirit who becomes a participant in him—“immediately shares also in the Father and the Son.” For through participation in the Spirit he has become a participant both in the Father and in the Son.

From this it is shown that the Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, and so fully their companion that no one can possess the Spirit without likewise possessing the Father and the Son.

He adds: “And whoever has the love of the Father has received it as contributed by the Son through the Holy Spirit.”

Previously he showed only the consubstantiality of the Father and the Son; now he begins to teach the procession of the Spirit. He calls the Holy Spirit the love of the Father, as is confirmed by what follows, when he says that this love is contributed through the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit contributes nothing except his own proper gift when he contributes love. And it is written that love is God. Therefore, when the Spirit contributes love, he contributes himself, because he himself is love.

But this love is said to be the Father’s because the Spirit is the Father’s Spirit. And from where is he that Spirit? Because he proceeds from him. For he is not one of the spirits of creatures, so that he could be of a substance other than the Father’s. Therefore he is not said to belong to the Father as one created by him, but as one consubstantial with him and proceeding from him.

He says that the person who has the Father’s love has received it as contributed by the Son through the Holy Spirit. How, then, does the Son contribute the gift of the Holy Spirit? Clearly, as a co-worker with the Father and the Spirit. But how can he contribute one equal to himself, or the gift of another—that is, of the Holy Spirit? Certainly because the love that belongs to the Father and is contributed by the Son through the Holy Spirit also belongs to the Son, since whatever belongs to the Father belongs also to the Son.

But is the love that is the Holy Spirit the Son’s in such a way that it is a creature? Certainly not. Rather, it is contributed by the Son because it proceeds from him, and it belongs to the Son because it is consubstantial with him.

It is added: “And whoever is a participant in the grace of Jesus Christ.”

In this passage he calls the grace of Jesus Christ what above he called the Father’s love. What, then, is meant by his now calling it the grace of Jesus Christ, when it is established that it is the gift of the Holy Spirit? Without doubt he shows that it is contributed by Jesus Christ, whose grace it is. Thus, just as it is called the Father’s love because it proceeds from the Father, so the same love, which he calls the grace of Jesus Christ, is understood to proceed from Jesus Christ.

Whoever possesses this same grace of Christ, he says, has received it through the Holy Spirit, so that we may see the whole Trinity working together and hold that the Holy Spirit, who is the love of the Father and the Son, proceeds both from the Father and from the Son.

He continues: “From all these things it is approved that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have the same operation.”

Those who have the same operation also have one will; and those who have one will have one substance. Hence he adds: “Those who have one operation also have one substance, because things that are of the same substance, *ὁμούσια* [consubstantial], have the same operations; whereas things that are of another substance have discordant and different operations.”

He approves that the Holy Spirit is of one substance with the Father and the Son because he has the same operation as they do. But it was shown above that the Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Son because he proceeds from both the Father and the Son.

Later he says: “When he had said, at the time of answering”—namely, the Son had said that the disciples would be taught by the Spirit what they ought to answer—“he says in what follows: ‘For I will give you wisdom that they will not be able to resist or contradict’ (Luke 21:15). From this it is shown that the wisdom given to the disciples by the Son is the wisdom of the Holy Spirit, and that the teaching of the Holy Spirit is the teaching of the Lord.”

How, then, is the wisdom given by the Son the wisdom of the Holy Spirit? Only because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, whose wisdom is also the wisdom of the Holy Spirit. And how does he say that the teaching of the Holy Spirit is the teaching of the Lord? Clearly because everything that belongs to the Holy Spirit also belongs to the Lord Jesus Christ, since the Spirit proceeds from him.

Therefore he adds: “And that the Spirit shares with the Son one fellowship of nature and will.”

These words testify that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, since the Spirit has with the Son one fellowship both of nature and of will. Otherwise, if the Spirit did not proceed from him, he would not have the same will as the Son, for those who are separated in fellowship are also separated in will.

He also says: “And since it was shown above that the Spirit is by nature the companion of God the Only-Begotten and of God the Father, while the Son and the Father are one, according to the saying: ‘I and the Father are one,’ the Trinity has been shown to be undivided and inseparable according to nature.”

If the Spirit is by nature joined to God the Only-Begotten and to God the Father, he proceeds from God the Only-Begotten. But if he proceeds only from God the Father and does not proceed from God the Only-Begotten, then he is indeed joined to the Father by nature, but he is not joined to the Only-Begotten God. For he cannot be joined by nature to one from whom he does not proceed.

But this author testifies that the Spirit is by nature the companion of God the Only-Begotten. Therefore he acknowledges that the Spirit proceeds from God the Only-Begotten. And since he says that the Trinity is undivided and inseparable according to nature, he acknowledges that the Son is begotten from the Father, while the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

But if you teach that the Spirit proceeds only from the Father, then the Trinity is no longer undivided and inseparable, because the Spirit is divided from the Son, from whom he does not proceed, and separated from the Only-Begotten, whose Spirit he is not.

Far be such an impious opinion from catholic members. The Holy Trinity is undivided and inseparable according to nature, because the Father is from no one, the Son is begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

He also says: “In another Gospel it is likewise written: ‘For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you’ (Matthew 10:20). If, then, the Spirit of the Father speaks in the apostles, teaching them what they ought to answer, and what is taught by the Spirit is wisdom—which we cannot understand as belonging to anyone other than the Son—it plainly appears that the Spirit is of the same nature as the Son and as the Father, whose Spirit he is. Moreover, the Father and the Son are one.”

This author says that the wisdom by which the Spirit of the Father teaches the apostles is the Son. If the Son is wisdom, and the Holy Spirit speaks in the apostles the wisdom that is the Son, then he receives from the Son. How does he receive? Certainly by proceeding, not by participating in something he previously lacked. For the Spirit was never without wisdom; rather, he received from the Son that he should always be wise, proceeding from him, because he is of one nature with the Son and with the Father, whose Spirit he is.

He did not say this in such a way as to exclude the Spirit of the Son, whose wisdom he said the Spirit speaks. Rather, he said it because he had stated above: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father.” For he says later: “Moreover, the Father and the Son are one.” If the Father and the Son are one, the Spirit who belongs to the Father belongs also to the Son, and consequently proceeds from both.

Later in the same work (book II), after treating at some length the consubstantiality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he concluded:

“From these things it is gathered that, although the substance of the Trinity is undivided, the Father is nevertheless truly the Father of the Son, the Son truly the Son of the Father, and the Holy Spirit truly the Spirit of the Father and of God; and, moreover, the Spirit of wisdom and truth, that is, of the Son of God.”

If, then, the Father is the Father of the Son because he begot him, and the Son is the Son of the Father because he was begotten by him, and the Holy Spirit is truly the Spirit of the Father because he proceeds from him, then he is consequently also the Spirit of wisdom and truth—that is, of the Son of God—because he proceeds from the Son. He proceeds from truth, he proceeds from wisdom, he proceeds from God, that is, from the Son.

For this reason, after calling the Holy Spirit the Spirit of truth, he added, “and the Spirit of God,” intending the person of the Son to be understood. But lest hesitation confuse the reader, he said in what follows: “The Spirit of wisdom and truth, that is, of the Son of God.”

Later he says: “We have already frequently shown that the Spirit has the same operation as the Father and the Son, and that in the same operation there is one substance; and, conversely, that among those things that are *ὁμούσια* [consubstantial], the operation is likewise not different.”

The Spirit’s operation is the same as the operation of the Father and the Son because he is consubstantial with both, proceeding from both. For he cannot be joined to them in the same operation unless he proceeds from both. Substance is divided from those with whom it is not joined by procession; nor can the Spirit otherwise be substantially joined either to the Father or to the Son, because, in order to be of their substance, the Spirit received this by proceeding both from the Father and from the Son.

Again, below: “In what follows, concerning the Spirit of truth who is sent by the Father, the Savior says, although he is the Paraclete: ‘For he will not speak from himself’ (John 16:13); that is, without me and without my will and the Father’s, because he is inseparable from my will and the Father’s. For this very thing—that he subsists and speaks—is from the Father and from me. I speak the truth, that is, I inspire what he speaks, since he is the Spirit of truth.”

[Note: “Since he is the Spirit.” We have transferred the entire marginal matter into the text, for previously only this was read: “that he subsists and speaks, I, truth, speak, since,” which was plainly incomplete. Nevertheless, it is sufficiently clear from what follows that Ratramnus preferred the corrupt reading.]

This teacher plainly instructs us that the Holy Spirit is from the Son. For when he says, “He will not speak from himself,” he shows that the Spirit is not from himself. Explaining what he had said—“that is, without me and without my will and the Father’s”—he shows from whom the Spirit is, namely from the Father and the Son, without whom and without whose will he does not speak.

And when he says, “For this very thing—that he subsists and speaks—I, the truth, speak,” he shows that the Spirit’s subsistence is from the Son. If, when the Spirit speaks, truth—that is, the Son—speaks, he shows that what the Spirit speaks and what he is in his subsistence he received from the Son.

And repeating the same point as though more openly, he says: “That is, I inspire what he speaks.” How does he inspire? Clearly because the Spirit proceeds from him and is joined to him. “Since he is the Spirit of truth”—that is to say, the Spirit of the Son.

By all these statements it is demonstrated that he is the Spirit of the Son and that he is inspired by the Son—that is, that he proceeds from him. And because what the Spirit speaks and what the Spirit is in his subsistence he receives from the Son, he receives it not as one inferior but as one consubstantial with him and proceeding from him.

Again, below: “Therefore the Father’s speaking and the Son’s hearing—or, conversely, the Son’s speaking and the Father’s hearing—is an indication of the same nature in the Father and the Son and of their agreement. The Holy Spirit also, who is the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of wisdom, cannot, when the Son is speaking, hear what he does not know, since he himself is what is brought forth by the Son.”

By saying that the Son hears the Father speaking, he indicates the Son’s birth from the Father. Likewise, by saying that the Father hears the Son speaking, he intimates that the Father begot the Son. And because the Father and the Son are of one nature, they are also of the same agreement, so that the Father’s speaking to the Son, or the Son’s speaking to the Father, means their coming into one agreement of will and their not thinking anything different.

By confessing the Holy Spirit as the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of wisdom, he declares him to be the Spirit of the Son. He says that, when the Son speaks, the Spirit cannot hear what he does not know, because, since he is of the same substance as the Son and proceeds from the Son, what the Son speaks the Holy Spirit also speaks. For, according to the teacher now before us, this very thing that the Spirit is is the Son’s speech to the Spirit.

After saying that the Holy Spirit cannot, when the Son is speaking, hear what he does not know, he immediately adds: “Since he himself is what is brought forth by the Son.” That is, the Son’s bringing forth is the Spirit’s substance. For when he says, “since he himself is this,” the Spirit is understood; and “what is brought forth by the Son” means what the Son speaks.

If what the Son speaks is the Holy Spirit, as this teacher testifies, it cannot be denied that the Spirit proceeds from the Son. For the Son’s speech proceeds from the Son. Therefore, since the Spirit is the same as what is brought forth by the Son, the Spirit proceeds entirely from the Son.

He adds: “Finally, lest anyone separate him from the will and fellowship of the Father and the Son, it is written: ‘For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak’ (John 16:13). The Savior also says something similar concerning himself: ‘As I hear, I judge’ (John 5:30).”

The Father’s will is the Son’s will, and the fellowship of both is the Spirit of both, because love, which is the Spirit, joins the will of the Father and the Son. The Spirit’s will cannot be separated from the will of the Father and the Son; but just as he is the fellowship of both, so also he has the same will as both.

And just as the Son’s will is born from the Father, so the Spirit’s will proceeds from the Son. Hence he says concerning the Spirit: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak.” From whom will he hear? Clearly from the Son, from whom he proceeds.

For the Spirit’s hearing is his proceeding from the Son, just as the Son’s hearing is his being born from the Father. Hearing the Son is not one thing and being born another; both are the same. Likewise, hearing the Spirit is not one thing and proceeding another; both are one and the same.

And below: “For it is written: ‘Whatever he does’”—there is no doubt that the Father is meant—“these things the Son also does in the same way. If, then, while the Father and the Son are working, all things that are made subsist in the same and similar manner, not according to the order of a first and a second but according to the same time of working, and if the Son cannot do anything from himself because he cannot be separated from the Father, so also the Holy Spirit, in no way separated from the Son because of the fellowship of will and nature, is believed not to speak from himself, but speaks all things according to the word and truth of God.”

The Father and the Son perform the same works—not the Father at one time and the Son at another, but both together and at the same time. Nor can the Son work while separated, because he is not divided from the Father, having been born from the Father and being of the same substance as the Father.

So also the Holy Spirit does not speak from himself while separated from the Son, because, proceeding from the Son, he shares the Son’s nature and the same will as the Son. Nature joins them, and will does not distinguish those whom nature joins. Therefore he speaks all things according to the word and truth of God, because, proceeding from the Word and the Truth, he perceives what he is to speak.

For what proceeds is not one thing and the reception of speech another; rather, the reception of speech is the existence of procession, just as the procession of existence is the reception of speech.

And below: “How, then, above, when discussing incorporeal natures, we understood the matter, so now it must be recognized that the Holy Spirit receives from the Son that which belonged to His own nature; and this signifies not one who gives and another who receives, but one substance. For the Son also is said to receive from the Father the same thing, which is He Himself subsisting; indeed, the Son is nothing other than those things which are given to Him by the Father, nor is the substance of the Holy Spirit anything other than that which is given to Him by the Son.”

He confirms that the procession of the Spirit takes place from the Son, and says that the Holy Spirit receives from the Son that which belonged to His own nature—that is, that the nature of the Spirit is from the Son—and that for the Spirit to receive from the Son means nothing other than to proceed from the Son. Nor should “the one giving” and “the one receiving” be understood as though they were of different substances, but rather as the person of the Son giving existence to the Spirit, and the person of the Spirit receiving it, so that He proceeds from the Son.

He confirms his position from the fact that the Son is said to receive from the Father. For the Son is not one thing and that which He receives from the Father another; rather, the Son’s reception from the Father is His subsistence. He states this more clearly as he continues: “Indeed, the Son is nothing other than those things which are given to Him by the Father.” That is, it is not permissible to separate from the substance of the Son those things which are given by the Father to the Son; rather, what is given by the Father is the substance of the Son, since by being born He received all that belongs to the Father.

So also concerning the Holy Spirit he acknowledges that the substance of the Holy Spirit is nothing other than that which is given to Him by the Son. That is, the Holy Spirit is not one thing and that which is given to the Holy Spirit by the Son another; rather, the Son’s gift is the substance of the Holy Spirit. In this way he manifestly teaches that the Holy Spirit is from the Son—not as a part, but as the whole that the Son is—for whatever belongs to the Son also belongs to the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit receives from the Son, proceeding from Him [Col. 0264D] as one consubstantial with Him and possessing all that belongs to the Son.

Further on: “Finally, when he explained how He had said, ‘He will receive from what is mine,’ he immediately added: ‘All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you’ (John 16:13–14). He was speaking, in a certain manner, as follows: although the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father, and God gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him, nevertheless, because all that the Father has is mine, and this very Spirit of the Father is mine, He will receive from what is mine.”

In saying this he teaches that the Spirit proceeds from the Son just as He proceeds from the Father. For He is the Spirit of truth, that is, of Christ, who is truth; and because the Son possesses everything that belongs to the Father, this very Spirit of the Father bears witness that He is also the Son’s, and receives [Col. 0265A] from the Son. What does He receive? Entirely, subsistence, by proceeding from Him.

Further on: “The same Spirit, however, is the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ, bringing and joining to the Lord Jesus Christ the one who has possessed Him. Hence it is said below: ‘But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to Him’ (Romans 8:9).”

If the one who is the Spirit of God is also the Spirit of Christ, as this author acknowledges, there is no doubt that there are not two Spirits—one of the Father and another of the Son—but one and the same Spirit of both. And if the Spirit of Christ is the one who is the Spirit of God the Father, then just as He proceeds from the Father, so He proceeds from the Son. For He is called the Spirit of God the Father for no other reason than that He proceeds from God the Father; likewise, He is called the Spirit of Christ for no other reason than that He proceeds from Christ. He is not a creature, to be possessed as something inferior, but consubstantial.

Likewise, by adding that the one who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Christ, he acknowledges that the Spirit proceeds from Christ, whom he calls Christ’s Spirit; and that the one who does not have His Spirit cannot belong to Christ. For where the Spirit of Christ is not, Christ is not; for those who are joined in substance are not separated by indwelling. From this we learn that the fellowship which the Spirit has with Christ He also has with God the Father. For He cannot fail to have fellowship with those with whom He is consubstantial and from whom He exists.

Further on: “But also in the Epistle of Peter the Holy Spirit is proved to be the Spirit of Christ: ‘Searching and investigating,’ he says—that is, the prophets about whom he had spoken above—‘what time or what circumstances the Spirit of Christ who was in them was indicating, testifying to the sufferings in Christ and to the decrees that were to follow afterward.’”

And shortly afterward: “This same Holy Spirit is also called the Spirit of God, as in the passage: ‘No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God’ (1 Corinthians 2:11).”

Thus he acknowledges as the Spirit of Christ the one who is the Spirit of God, and consequently as proceeding from both; for there is no other reason why He should be called the Spirit of both. He is equal and consubstantial.

Again, below he says: “By saying, ‘But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to Him’ (Romans 8:9), and adding, ‘But if Christ is in you’ (ibid., 10), he most clearly demonstrated that the Holy Spirit is inseparable from Christ, because wherever the Spirit is, Christ is also [Col. 0265D]; and wherever the Spirit of Christ departs, Christ likewise departs.”

This fellowship of the Spirit and Christ which he teaches is not merely one of will, but also of substance; and it is not only one of substance, but also of procession. For things can be united by will while being separate in substance, as in Christ’s saying to the disciples: “Behold, I am with you all the days” (Matthew 28:20), or in what he said in the present passage: wherever the Spirit of Christ is, Christ is also.

Where Christ and the Spirit of Christ are, they are indeed together, but by will, not by substance. For God and man are not of one substance but of different substances. Again, things can be joined in substance and united at the same time by birth, as the Father and the Son are. The Son and the Spirit, however, are joined in substance, though not by birth but by procession.

Therefore, when he says, “Wherever the Spirit is, Christ is also,” and “Wherever the Spirit of Christ departs, Christ likewise departs,” he shows that this fellowship consists not only in will and substance, but also in procession: the Spirit is not merely consubstantial with Christ, but also exists from Him.

Later, taking up another testimony of the Apostle, he says: “You have not received a spirit of slavery in fear” (Romans 8:15); that is, you do not abstain from vices in the manner of slaves, through fear and terror of punishments, because you have received the Spirit of adoption, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is also called the Spirit of the Son and of Christ, and of truth and wisdom.

What does he imply by this? Truth and wisdom are Christ, as Scripture testifies and has often confirmed; and Christ is undoubtedly the Son of the Father. He affirms that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, from Christ, from truth, and from wisdom—not because these are different Spirits, for the things of which He is said to be the Spirit do not signify different substances.

Wisdom and truth, and Christ, proclaim the Son: Christ because of the man whom He assumed; truth because He Himself said, “I am the truth”; wisdom because Paul testifies concerning Him (1 Corinthians 1:30) that He was made Wisdom for us by God.

What do all these statements establish? Without doubt, that He proceeds from the Son, whose Spirit He is said to be. For He cannot be either a part of the Son or something subject to the Son. From where, then, is He the Son’s? By procession, or by consubstantiality. But consubstantiality shows equality, and equality is not subordinated but shared. From where, then, is He the Spirit of the Son? Without doubt, because He proceeds from the Son.

Let these brief excerpts from Didymus’s book suffice. While he held and wrote such views concerning the Holy Spirit at Alexandria, he was neither reproved by the Greeks or by the Greek emperors, nor suspended from communion. Those who were emperors at that time—who ruled not only at Constantinople but also at Rome—understood that this was catholic dogma, apostolic faith, the impiety of the heretics which it defeated, and the doctrine of truth which it affirmed.

But you, modern emperors, now establishing a new sect of error, consider whose faith you possess and whom you have had as teachers in Christ’s doctrine. For you are convicted of not being disciples of those who preceded you, who strengthened the catholic faith and always attacked the inventions of false doctrine.

## CHAPTER VI. From Paschasius

Let us join to these what the Roman Church believed concerning the Holy Spirit during the same period, so that we may prove that the sect he proclaims is not new, but was commended long ago by the Fathers, defended throughout the entire body of the Church, and attacked by those who held contrary opinions. Let it likewise be shown that he is now unjustly reproached as preaching a new dogma, when it has always been preached by our predecessors.

Paschasius, an ancient teacher and deacon of the Roman See, in the little book he wrote on the Holy Spirit, following the footsteps of Didymus of Alexandria, begins as follows (Book I, chapter 2):

“Do not investigate how God is, when it is manifest that He is God. Here reason lies hidden; truth does not lie hidden. Why do you ask how He is the companion and equal of the King, when it is established that He belongs both to the King’s honor and to His lineage? It is superfluous to investigate the name where there is no doubt concerning the majesty.”

In this, truly refuting you, he opposes the Arians, who denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit and refused to confess Him consubstantial with the Father and the Son, but called Him a creature subject to the Son as something lesser. He proclaims that the Spirit is true God and consubstantial with both the Father and the Son.

He also makes clear what he thinks concerning procession when he adds:

“Therefore, because the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, he says: ‘But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Him’ (Romans 8:9). And elsewhere: ‘He breathed on them and said: Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20:22).”

He testifies that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and strengthens his assertion from both the Apostle and the Gospel. He shows equally that the Spirit cannot otherwise be Christ’s unless He proceeds from Christ Himself. Nor does Christ give the Spirit by breathing Him forth for any other reason than that He sends Him from His own substance, since, when He is called the Spirit of Christ, He is shown to have a relation to Christ—not as a slave, for He is not a creature, but as receiving existence from Him by proceeding, not by being created or generated.

Likewise, when Christ sends Him by breathing Him forth, He does not send someone foreign, nor someone from any source other than His own nature. The Spirit’s procession from the Son cannot be denied, since the Son sends Him forth by breathing Him from the depths of His own divinity.

He continues, still speaking of the same Spirit:

“Do you ask whether He is begotten or unbegotten? The sacred Scriptures have sung nothing concerning this; it is impious to break into divine silences. What God did not deem necessary to indicate in His Scriptures, He did not wish you to ask or know through superfluous curiosity. He judged that this should reach your conscience: that which pertains to your salvation.”

Here he speaks against those who, disparaging the person of the Holy Spirit and the holy Trinity, did not accept that He was God, as though, if He were acknowledged as God, He would have to be confessed either unbegotten or begotten. If begotten, there would be said to be two sons, and the Savior could no longer be called the only-begotten; this would contradict the catholic faith, which confesses belief in God the almighty Father and in Jesus Christ, His only-begotten Son.

If He were confessed unbegotten, there would then be shown to be not one Father but two, which would likewise be utterly contrary to the catholic faith. For we believe in one God, the almighty Father.

To those devising such perverse arguments this catholic teacher responds with due piety and caution, saying that the Holy Spirit should be called neither begotten nor unbegotten, since the holy Scriptures do not speak in those terms; but that what they affirm should be professed: namely, that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son and proceeds from both.

Later he says (chapter 10):

“In the Acts of the Apostles, Peter, speaking about the Lord Jesus Christ, says: ‘Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, He poured out this whom you see and hear’ (Acts 2:33). In ‘the right hand’ the Son is designated; in ‘God,’ the Father; in the distinct property of His name, the Holy Spirit.”

By this testimony he proved that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, whom he said was poured out by Him. For Christ poured out only what He contained in Himself—not as though it were enclosed in a place, but as remaining substantially in Him. Nor did He pour Him out in such a way as to empty Himself, as a vessel becomes empty when what it contained is poured out. That belongs to bodily things; in divine matters it is not the same.

When either the Father or the Son pours out the Spirit, He does not empty Himself, but communicates the grace of His gift to whomever He wills without loss to Himself.

And below, offering the Apostle’s testimony, he says:

“But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to Him” (Romans 8:9).

When he says “the Spirit of God” and immediately adds “the Spirit of Christ,” observe that here he designates the person of Christ under the name of God. Or if here he signifies the Father, whose Spirit He is, under the title “God,” behold: through the unity of substance this Spirit is declared to be the Spirit of both the Father and the Son. He is rightly recognized as proceeding from both, and is clearly seen to have a distinct person within the bond of the Trinity. The one who does not have the Holy Spirit is shown not to have Christ either.

Thus the Holy Spirit is God; and when He is denied, Christ also is denied, who said: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). Whoever is empty of the Holy Spirit does not belong to Christ and has lost the way by which one reaches the Father.

By many arguments he shows that the Holy Spirit is both God and consubstantial with the Father and the Son, and that He proceeds from both; nor can He be separated from the bond of the Trinity, since He has the same nature as the Father and the Son. He repeatedly insists that no one can have Christ who does not have the Holy Spirit. Since the Holy Spirit is God, whoever denies the Spirit consequently denies Christ also. This would not happen if the Spirit did not remain in Christ and were not consubstantial with Him.

That the Spirit remains in Christ and is consubstantial with Christ demonstrates that He proceeds from Christ. For He cannot remain in and adhere consubstantially to the one from whom He does not proceed. Since Christ is the way to the Father, whoever does not have the Spirit cannot have Christ as the way. No one can have one without the other, since they are divided neither in substance nor in indwelling.

Therefore, whoever is empty of the Holy Spirit is also found to be empty of Christ, because whoever does not have the spring is not flooded by the spring’s irrigation. By all these arguments it is clearly shown that the Holy Spirit proceeds from Christ.

And below (chapter 11):

“Let the Holy Spirit therefore be thought of as in no way incomplete, since He is compared with fullness; for He who is given in the place of God, as a pledge, must not be believed to be anything other than God.”

Anyone who denies that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son regards Him as incomplete; and whoever does not attribute procession from the Son to Him denies that He is given as a pledge in the place of God. For God cannot be understood as full if the Son’s consubstantiality with Him is denied, nor can He represent God’s place if the Son is not consubstantial with Him.

But no catholic holds such a view. Rather, he confesses the Spirit to be fully God and consubstantial with the Father and the Son. He should know that the Son proceeds from the one from whom He also receives His substance; and whoever is joined in substance to the Father and the Son must necessarily proceed from both.

Again he adds, introducing a passage of the same Apostle to Titus:

“He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom He poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ” (Titus 3:5). “Behold, here too, under a manifest Trinity, the Father pours out the abundance of the Holy Spirit through the Son. And what must be observed above all is that he attributes to the Holy Spirit Himself the power of regeneration and renewal.”

The Father poured out the Holy Spirit abundantly upon us through Jesus Christ, to show that the Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from Jesus Christ. When He is poured out upon us, the Father pours out the Holy Spirit because He is sent by the Father; He pours Him out through Jesus Christ because the Son cooperates with the Father in pouring out the Spirit. For he does not say that the Father pours Him out through Jesus Christ as though Christ did not pour Him out. The Father and the Son are not separated in operation. Rather, the Father pours Him out through Jesus Christ because, when the Father pours Him out, Jesus Christ also pours Him out, since He is sent by both, because He proceeds from both the Father and the Son.

This author testifies that the power of the Holy Spirit is equal to that of the Father and the Son when he says that the power of regeneration and renewal is attributed to the Holy Spirit. He thus shows that the Spirit possesses the same power as the Father and the Son; and consequently He is affirmed to be consubstantial and to proceed from both.

Again, later (chapter 12), introducing the testimony of the Psalmist, who says:

“Where shall I go from your Spirit?” (Psalm 138:7)—that is, “Where shall I hide myself from His presence, when I have no doubt that He is present everywhere, both within and outside?”

And below:

“From this it is clearly understood what is said: ‘Nor is there anyone who can hide from His heat’ (Psalm 18:7). His ineffable greatness enters, fills, and transcends the depths of the underworld, the expanse of the waves, the breadth of the earth, and the heights of the heavens. He is said to be sent by the Father and the Son, to proceed from their substance, and to perform one work with them.”

By all these statements the majesty and procession of the Holy Spirit are shown. When he testifies that no place is removed from the presence of the Holy Spirit, he compares Him with the divinity of the Father and the Son, which penetrates and contains all things.

Then, adding that no one is untouched by the fire of His heat, he testifies to what is also said of the Son: “He enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). He shows that the Spirit possesses the same power as the Son, since the Son enlightens every person and no one is excluded from the Spirit’s heat.

When the Spirit is said to be sent by both the Father and the Son and to proceed from their substance, it is shown simultaneously both from whom the Spirit is and of what power He is. In every respect he shows Him to be God, equal to the Father and the Son in both power and substance, and to proceed from both.

And below, introducing the Son as speaking, he says:

“The Paraclete who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26). He did not say, “who was created by the Father,” but “who proceeds from the Father”—that is, from the fellowship of the Father’s power and from the property of His nature. The very expression shows that, when He is said to proceed from the Father, He does not have His beginning together with the Father.”

Do not suppose that he intended to deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son because he said that He proceeded from the Father. Above he said that the Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son, that He proceeds from their substance, and that He performs one work with them.

Now also, when he says that He proceeds from the fellowship of the Father’s power and from the property of His nature, this is because, just as the Father and the Son are not separated in power or nature, so they are not separated in the Spirit’s existence. Since He is the Spirit of both, He proceeds from both; and those whom nature and power make equal are not separated by procession.

[Col. 0270C] Further on he says:

“What, then, is the distinction between the Son, who is said to be born from God the Father, and the Holy Spirit, who is signified as proceeding? If you ask what difference there is between being born and proceeding, the distinction is clearly this: the one is born from one, while the other proceeds from both.”

By this he professes that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. He also gives the reason why He proceeds from the Son. For if we say that He proceeds from the Father alone, we do not escape danger to the faith. How can the Son be called the Father’s only Son, when it is also not denied that the Spirit is the Father’s? And how can it be established that the Spirit is not a Son, when He exists from the Father as though He were a Son?

Such blasphemy must be avoided—indeed, overthrown—lest the catholic faith be exposed to the missiles of its enemies. Let us therefore say what our ancestors said: the Son was born from the Father, alone from the alone, and therefore is only-begotten; but the Holy Spirit proceeds indeed from the Father, yet not alone from the alone, because He also proceeds from the Son. Otherwise, if we confess that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, we appear to proclaim two Sons.

Therefore this teacher, following the teaching of his own ancestors, transmitted to his descendants what he had received from those who preceded him. Although he proved that the Roman Church believed concerning the Holy Spirit as it believes today, he nowhere showed that, while remaining in this faith, it was ever separated from the Eastern Churches or that it ever held or taught anything different concerning the Holy Spirit.

But now it is astonishing to consider what the inventors of the new dogma are arguing. Why do they separate themselves from the communion which their ancestors always maintained? Why do they pass judgment before acquiring knowledge? Why do they accuse before they hear? This is not a judgment of equity but a prejudice of iniquity.

If they think it sufficient that they know with certainty that the Roman Church teaches that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and therefore refuse to inquire into what they plainly know is taught, let them know that they must judge their own ancestors along with the Romans. While they seek to deprive the Romans of their communion, let them likewise excommunicate themselves from the fellowship of their own ancestors. Let them not be shown to be in communion with any catholic Church, since by making themselves strangers to Roman communion they have alienated themselves from it.

Let them quickly consider what evil this action entails and not delay correcting their error, lest, if they refuse communion with the Romans, they fear that they will be excommunicated by the whole catholic Church.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0271]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the procession of the Holy Spirit—That the universal Church embraces the whole world

[Col. 0271B]

Scripture says: “Do not move the boundaries which your fathers established” (Proverbs 22:28). If the rulers of the Greeks had wished to observe this command, the Roman Church would not have suffered any reproach concerning the Holy Spirit, nor would they have attempted to devise anything new. Instead, they would have been content with the boundaries of the faith which the catholic Fathers established and which the sacred Scriptures, produced through the Holy Spirit, set in place.

But, afflicted by the disease of vainglory or weakened by the plague of envy, because they cannot be content with the boundaries of their ancestors, they seek their own glory and transgress the boundaries which their predecessors established.

While they seek to bury the glory of their ancestors [Col. 0271C], they fall into the pit which, according to the Psalmist’s words, they dug (Psalm 7:16). They ought not to have raised any question in our time concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit if they had either paid attention to the teachings of their ancestors or diligently undertaken to examine the sacred Scriptures.

For the catholic teachers clearly demonstrate what we ought to believe concerning the Holy Spirit. Through both their repeated disputations and their abundant writings, they not only understood the perverse inventions of the heretics concerning the supreme Trinity—including the procession of the Holy Spirit—but also attacked them with the most evident assertions. We have already presented no small portion of their authority above, and through them we believe it has been clearly shown what we ought to believe concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. Whoever attempts to contradict them, or rather refuses to accept them, is plainly shown to be a contradictor of the catholic faith and a blasphemer of the Holy Spirit.

We have learned from the mouth of Truth what punishment such a person deserves: He said that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matthew 12:32).

It was also appropriate to join to the preceding the writings of Father Augustine, that outstanding teacher and most accomplished of ecclesiastical masters. He maintained a continual struggle against the heretics; and not only did Arian impiety yield to his teaching and eloquence, but also the ferocity of the other heretics—namely, the Macedonians, Manichaeans, and Pelagians.

[Col. 0272B] Perhaps Greek arrogance will object that it refuses to accept the authority of the Latins. But what will it say about its own authorities whom we presented above? What will it say about the authors of the sacred Scriptures? Will they also refuse to accept them because they see them as severe enemies of their error and fierce attackers of their impiety?

It would be most foolish to say that they refuse to accept the authority of the Latins and, by refusing to agree with them, construct the novelty of a schism and make themselves strangers to the catholic Church. Far be it from them either to say or to think such things, or to wish to prefer their own opinion or custom to the universality of the whole Church.

For either to imagine or to decree such a thing is an evil of boasting, so wicked that it is intolerable and must be struck down by the general authority of the entire catholic Church. For when the Savior said to His Apostles, “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15), He did not commend the Greeks alone, but referred to the fullness of the whole world, to which He commanded the Gospel to be preached.

It is the height of arrogance to wish to claim as something special for oneself what is plainly bestowed generally upon all nations, peoples, and languages.

For the Holy Spirit, speaking through the prophet to Jerusalem, says: “From the East I will bring your offspring, and from the West I will gather you. I will say to the North, ‘Give’; and to the South, ‘Do not withhold’” (Isaiah 43:5). Are these words spoken only of the Greeks? Or is the people of Jerusalem to be prophesied as being gathered solely from Constantinople?

The universality of the nations spread throughout the whole world is announced, and from them the heavenly Jerusalem is thoroughly taught to be gathered. Let them not therefore attribute to themselves what has been bestowed upon all nations; let them not usurp, through the privilege of their special position, a gift which plainly belongs to universality.

Let them look upon the catholic Church of Christ, spread throughout the breadth of the whole world and extended from East to West, from North to South. Let them rejoice that Christ rules throughout the whole world, in fulfillment of David’s prophecy, in which he introduces the Father speaking to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8).

And another psalm speaks in the person of Christ: “And he shall rule,” it says, “from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the world” (Psalm 71:8). Nowhere does it mention either the Greeks or Constantinople. Yet it does not omit them altogether, since it includes them within universality. It removes the privilege of special status, so that they may not become inflated; it places them within the generality, so that they may be humbled.

Thus they may know that they are not the entire magnitude of the Church’s body but a portion of it, and may venerate the mother exalted with royal splendor from the rising to the setting of the sun. Let them rejoice that they are her sons, not boast that they are her fathers.

For the Savior says: “And do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matthew 23:9). The Savior, as He was about to ascend into heaven, also promised His disciples: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

We hear Christ’s promise as given to all believers, that is, to the universal Church, not specially to the Greeks or to the people of Constantinople.

Therefore, in whatever language and among whatever people Christ speaks, let the Greek emperors receive Him reverently, lest, if they despise Him, they be judged to despise the truth and thereby become deprived of salvation, because they have rejected Christ speaking the truth to them.

For when the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles in tongues of fire, He did not teach only the Greek language; rather, He bestowed knowledge of the languages of all nations, to show that the Church would speak in the languages of all peoples and that the distribution of the Holy Spirit would be divinely granted to every nation.

Let the glorious rulers therefore receive the Holy Spirit through the teachers of the Church, speaking from Himself in the Latin language, so that in humility they may learn from where they may advance and, by the swelling of pride, may not despise the light of truth and fall into the darkness of error.

## CHAPTER II. Heretics refuted by the authority of Augustine

Augustine, bishop of Hippo, an outstanding teacher and exceptional defender of the catholic faith, says the following concerning the Holy Spirit in his book of Questions, which he wrote to the presbyter Orosius (Question 2):

“Certain faith declares that the Holy Spirit is neither unbegotten nor begotten. For if we say that He is unbegotten, we will seem to affirm two fathers; but if we say that He is begotten, we will be accused of believing in two sons. What certain faith holds, however, is that He is neither unbegotten nor begotten, but proceeds from both—that is, from the Father and the Son.

“And to establish this by testimonies, hear our Lord Jesus Christ Himself teaching His disciples: ‘When the Paraclete has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, He will bear witness concerning me’ (John 15:26).

“And again, our Lord Jesus Christ Himself, after His resurrection, to show that the Holy Spirit proceeds from Him as from the Father, breathed upon the disciples and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20:22).

“Thus there is one Spirit of the Father and the Son, one Spirit of both. That He is the Father’s Spirit, our Lord and Savior Himself said to His disciples: ‘For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you’ (Matthew 10:20). And that He is also the Son’s Spirit, the Apostle Paul bears witness: ‘But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to Him’ (Romans 8:9).”

What do you, rulers of the Greeks, judge worthy of reproach here? He says that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. He proves this by the testimony of the Gospel. He says that the Spirit belongs to both the Father and the Son, and affirms this from both the Gospel and the Apostle.

If you do not wish to believe the Latins, believe the Gospel. If you do not wish to lend your ears to Augustine’s words, lend them to Christ and to the Apostle. But if you despise Christ and the Apostle, beware lest you yourselves be despised. For whoever does not follow the teaching of these men rejects from himself fellowship with the disciples of Christ; whoever rejects ecclesiastical teaching will not be a participant in the Church; and whoever does not embrace Christ’s teaching will not have a share with Christ.

Gregory, bishop of the Roman See, an apocrisarius during the reign of Tiberius Constantine—at that time a deacon, and afterward an eminent bishop—was greatly loved and familiar to the emperors Tiberius, Maurice, and Phocas. While he was living at Constantinople as deacon and legate of the Roman See, he defeated and refuted Eutyches, bishop of Constantinople, who was teaching an extremely perverse doctrine concerning the resurrection of the flesh, in the presence of the emperor, by the authority of the divine books and by the truth of the matter itself.

Concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit he speaks as follows in a homily delivered to the people during the octave of Easter (Homily 26 on the Gospel):

“For the Son Himself declares that He will send from the Father the Holy Spirit, who, although equal to the Father and the Son, was nevertheless not incarnate, saying: ‘When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father’ (John 15:26).”

If “being sent” were to be understood solely as incarnation, the Holy Spirit would certainly in no way be said to be sent, since He was not incarnate. Rather, His sending is His very procession, by which He proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Therefore, just as the Spirit is said to be sent because He proceeds, so the Son is also appropriately said to be sent because He is generated. If you attempt to disregard this bishop’s authority, consider to what height of arrogance you are raising your horn.

He was held in the greatest reverence by your predecessors for both holiness and wisdom. While he was a legate of the See and performing the office of deacon, he crushed the perverse doctrines of the bishop of your Constantinople with such authority that he not only defeated the man himself but so completely overthrew the strength of his doctrine that afterward it was unable even to recover its power to breathe.

But what he says concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit he confirms by the force of reason, saying that for the Paraclete to be sent by the Son is nothing other than for Him to proceed from the Son, just as, when the Son is said to be sent by the Father, His birth is indicated.

Augustine, bishop, says in his *Treatise on the Gospel according to John* (Treatise XCIX):

> “Here someone may perhaps ask whether the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son: for the Son is the Son of the Father alone, and the Father is the Father of the Son alone; but the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of one of them [Col. 0275A], but of both. You have him himself saying: ‘For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you’ (Matthew 10:20). You also have the Apostle: ‘God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts’ (Galatians 4:6). Are there therefore two spirits, one belonging to the Father and another to the Son? Far be it. For, when he was signifying the Church, he says: ‘We are one body,’ and immediately adds: ‘And one Spirit’ (Ephesians 4:4).”

And in what follows he adduces many further testimonies by which he establishes that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son—not one Spirit of the Father and another of the Son, but that whoever is the Spirit of the Son is also the Spirit of the Father. Whoever here attempts to contradict these evident testimonies will plainly be proved to contradict Holy Scripture.

And below:

> “If, therefore, the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son, why did the Son say, ‘He proceeds from the Father’ [Col. 0275B] (John 15:26)? Why do you think, unless because he customarily refers to him even what belongs to himself, from whom he himself is? Hence also that saying: ‘My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me’ (John 7:16).
