If, then, this teaching is understood to be his, although he said that it was not his but the Father’s, how much more must the Holy Spirit also be understood to proceed from him himself, when he says, ‘He proceeds from the Father,’ without saying, ‘He does not proceed from me.’”

The teacher Augustine, by the clearest reasoning, shows that the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son, and he confirms his opinion also by that Gospel testimony in which the Son says of the Spirit that he proceeds from the Father. For he says that the statement “He proceeds from the Father” must be understood in such a way that he is understood also to proceed from the Son. He did not wish to deny that the Spirit proceeds from himself [Col. 0275C]; rather, by naming the person of the Father, he likewise wished his own person to be understood—as also in the statement, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.” By saying this, he shows that the teaching is likewise his, but says that it belongs to the Father because, just as he is from the Father, so his teaching is said to belong to the Father; for whatever the Son possesses, he received by being born from the Father. Likewise, when he says that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, he does not deny that the Spirit proceeds from himself as well. He nevertheless shows from whom the Son has what enables the Spirit to proceed from him—namely, from the Father, from whom, having been begotten, he received that the Spirit should proceed from him.

Accordingly, Saint Augustine says:

> “But from whom does the Son have that he is God—for he is God from God? From him, certainly, he has that the Holy Spirit should also proceed from him. And therefore the Holy Spirit has from the Father himself that he should proceed also from the Son, just as he proceeds from the Father.” [Col. 0275D]

With altogether remarkable subtlety, the distinguished teacher indicates both the Son’s nativity and the Holy Spirit’s procession, saying that the Son received from the Father both that he should be God, as God from God, and that the Spirit should proceed from him. He likewise says that the Holy Spirit received from the same Father that he should proceed from the Son, just as he proceeds from the Father. In saying this, he confesses both the Son and the Holy Spirit to be from the Father, who is the source of divinity: the Son received generation and that the Holy Spirit should proceed from him; while the Holy Spirit received procession from both the Father and the Son, but not generation, which belongs solely to the Son from the Father alone.

Here he adds the question that commonly troubles some readers: whether the Holy Spirit is said to have been born. He therefore says:

> “Here, too, as far as such matters can be understood by persons such as we are, it is to some extent understood why the Holy Spirit is not said to have been born, but rather to proceed. For if he were also called a son, he would certainly be called the son of both, which is utterly absurd; for no one is the son of two except of a father and a mother. Far be it from us to suspect anything of this kind between God the Father and God the Son. Nor does a human son proceed simultaneously from his father [Col. 0276A] and his mother: when he proceeds into his mother from his father, he does not at that time proceed from his mother; and when he proceeds into this light from his mother, he does not then proceed from his father. But the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father into the Son and from the Son toward the sanctification of creation; rather, he proceeds simultaneously from both, although the Father has given this to the Son: that, just as he proceeds from the Father, so also he should proceed from the Son. For neither can we say that the Holy Spirit is not life, since the Father is life and the Son is life. Accordingly, just as the Father, having life in himself, gave the Son also to have life in himself, so he gave him that life should proceed from him, just as it proceeds from himself.”

With the truest reasoning he proves that the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son, and yet is not the Son of both [Col. 0276C], since he is the Spirit of both. A son belongs to two, mother and father; but spiritual procession knows nothing of such a thing. There is no distinction of sex here, because there is no carnal offspring fashioned from flesh and bones. Nor does this procession take place through intervals of time, so that at one time he proceeds from the Father and at another from the Son, but simultaneously from both.

Nor does it occur in the manner customary in carnal generation. There is no discharge here such as normally occurs of seed from a man into a woman, nor offspring such as proceeds from a mother into the generation of a son. In all these cases there is a movement of alteration; but such movement is far removed from spiritual procession.

[Note: [Col. 0275D] “From spiritual procession.” No person of sound judgment could deny that this is the correct reading. The former reading, “from special procession,” disrupted the entire sentence. If the reader wishes to know the origin of the error, we will not hesitate to inform him that it may have arisen because a copyist wrote “from spiritual procession.” [Col. 0276D]]

The Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son, without any movement, without any alteration, and without any discharge. This procession is effected by the power of will, not by any temporal change, extension, or generation as from a father or mother, but as one light proceeds from two subjects—not that the Father and the Son are subjects beneath the Spirit, but because the Father and the Son are two persons of one essence, from whom the third person, the person of the Holy Spirit, proceeds. He proceeds not as a quality of the two, but as the consubstantiality of both.

As blessed Augustine says: the Father is life, the Son is life, and the Holy Spirit is life. The Father is life, receiving life from no life; the Son is life, receiving life by taking life from the Father; the Holy Spirit is life, proceeding as life from the Father and the Son and receiving life. For the Trinity could not be a Trinity of perfect consubstantiality in divinity if the Holy Spirit were not what the Father and the Son are.

There is indeed no dispute at present that the Spirit proceeds from the Father. But that he proceeds from the Son is attested by the Son himself, who says: “He will take from what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16:14).

From this, heretics wished to construct ranks within the divinity, saying: “If the Son receives from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from the Son, then the Holy Spirit is lesser than the Son.” Blessed Augustine opposes this perverse proposition while treating the chapter cited above (*Treatise* C, near the end):

> “As for what he says, ‘He will take from what is mine and declare it to you,’ hear it with catholic ears and receive it with catholic minds. The Holy Spirit is not lesser than the Son for the reason some heretics have supposed—that the Son receives from the Father and the Holy Spirit from the Son, according to certain degrees of natures. Far be it from us to believe this, far be it from us to say this, far be it from Christian hearts to think this. Finally, he immediately resolves the question and explains why he said this: ‘All things that the Father has are mine; therefore I said that he will take from what is mine and declare it to you’ (John 16:15). What more do you want? Therefore the Holy Spirit receives from the Father what the Son receives: for in this Trinity the Son was born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. The Father alone is born from no one and proceeds from no one.” [Col. 0277A]

What he now says—that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father—is not contrary to what he said earlier, namely, that the same Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Rather, he removes the inferiority that heretics were chattering about and commends the equality that Catholics believe. For if the Holy Spirit were said to receive only from the Son and not also from the Father, the Arians would be given an opportunity to invent ranks within the divinity. But now, when he says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, there is no basis for their inventing inferiority, because the Holy Spirit also receives from the Father that he should proceed, just as the Son receives from the Father that he should be born. Since both receive from the Father—the Son, nativity, and the Holy Spirit, procession—there is no basis for one to be preferred to the other.

Nevertheless, this does not mean that we must deny that the Spirit also proceeds from the Son. For the Son says:

> “All things that the Father has are mine. Therefore I said that he will take from what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16:15).

The Father has that the Holy Spirit should proceed from him; consequently, the Son also has that the Spirit should proceed from him. Therefore the Holy Spirit proceeds from both.

## CHAPTER III. Further Testimonies from Augustine

In the first book of *On the Holy Trinity* (chapter 4), he says:

> “Although the Father begot the Son, and therefore the Son is not the one who is the Father; and although the Son was begotten by the Father, and therefore the Father is not the one who is the Son; the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Spirit of the Father and the Son, himself also coequal with the Father and the Son and belonging to the unity of the Trinity. Yet it was not the same Trinity that was born from the Virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, buried, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven, but only the Son.” [Col. 0278A]

He clearly indicates the distinctive properties of the individual persons in the Holy Trinity and shows that the Incarnation belongs to the Son alone. The Father is not the same as the Son, because he begot the Son; and the Son is not the same as the Father, but is only the Son who was begotten by the Father. The Holy Spirit likewise is neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Spirit of the Father and the Son. Since he is called the Spirit of both, it follows that he must be confessed to proceed from both. For just as he is said to belong to the Father because he proceeds from the Father, so he is also professed to belong to the Son because he proceeds from the Son. The reason for his belonging to both is therefore similar, and Augustine likewise confesses that he proceeds from both.

Although he is coequal with the Father and the Son and belongs to the unity of the Trinity, the Incarnation of the Son nevertheless belongs neither to the Father nor to the Holy Spirit. It belongs to the Father alone to have begotten the Son; to the Son, to have assumed complete humanity; and to the Holy Spirit, to have proceeded from the Father and the Son.

Again, in what follows (chapter 5):

> “It also causes us to ask how the Holy Spirit exists in the Trinity, whom neither the Father nor the Son nor both have begotten, although he is the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son.” [Col. 0278B]

By these words he removes generation from the Holy Spirit, who is said to have been begotten neither by the Father alone, nor by the Son alone, nor by both, although he is the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son. He clearly indicates that, although he is not the Son by being born, he is the Spirit of both by proceeding. For where nativity is excluded and he is said to belong to both, procession is undoubtedly signified—not from one alone, that is, either from the Father or from the Son, but from both, since he is proved to be the Spirit not of one alone but of both.

Again, below (chapter 12):

> “For we have already shown that in this Trinity, through many modes of divine speech, what belongs to all may also be said of individual persons, because of the inseparable operation of one and the same substance. Thus of the Holy Spirit he says: ‘When I go, I will send him to you’ (John 16:7). He did not say, ‘We will send him,’ but spoke as though only the Son would send him and not the Father. Yet elsewhere he says: ‘I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you; but the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will declare all things to you’ (John 14:25–26). Here again he speaks as though the Son would not send him, but only the Father.” [Col. 0278C]

It has frequently been stated that the sending of the Holy Spirit is his procession. Therefore, when the Son testifies that he will send the Spirit, he signifies the Spirit’s procession from the Son. Likewise, when he says that the Father will send the Holy Spirit in the Son’s name, he again signifies the Spirit’s procession from the Father. Since the Spirit is said to be sent by both, he is proved to proceed from both.

Augustine also gives a general rule concerning the Holy Trinity, saying that what belongs to all may be said of individual persons “because of the inseparable operation of one and the same substance.” [Col. 0279A] By this statement we are plainly taught that, when the Spirit is said to proceed from the Father, it must likewise be understood that he proceeds from the Son. Similarly, when he is said to be sent by the Son, it must at the same time be understood that he is sent by the Father, because the Father and the Son, just as they are of one and the same substance, are also of one and the same operation.

Therefore, whoever denies that the Spirit is sent by the Son while admitting that he is sent by the Father undoubtedly denies that the Son cooperates with the Father. In doing so, he says that the Father and the Son are no longer of one and the same operation and consequently denies that the Father and the Son are of one and the same substance.

The same applies to the Son’s testimony that the Spirit proceeds from the Father. Whoever prefers to deny that the Spirit also proceeds from the Son likewise denies that the Son is not of the same operation as the Father and consequently says that the Father and the Son are not of one but of different substances. Since we see that this proceeds from the source of Arian impiety, let us confess with Catholics that the whole Trinity cooperates with itself and that, concerning everything, what is said of one person is to be understood of each, because the whole Trinity is of one and the same substance and cannot be separated in operation. Therefore, when it is said that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, it must likewise be understood that he proceeds from the Son.

Again, in book 15 of *On the Holy Trinity* (chapter 6):

> “Christ is indeed called in the holy Scriptures the power of God and the wisdom of God. But how this is to be understood, so that the Son may not appear to make the Father wise, was discussed in the seventh book. The reasoning reached the point that the Son is wisdom from wisdom, just as light is from light and God from God. We could find no other explanation of the Holy Spirit than that he too is wisdom, and that all three together are one wisdom, just as they are one God and one essence. What are we taught by this except that the Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son, and that this Trinity is of one substance? [Col. 0279B]

> “He says that the Father is wisdom, the Son is wisdom, and the Holy Spirit also is wisdom. But the Father is wisdom from no wisdom. He did not receive from the Son that he should be wise, because, since he himself is the source and beginning of all things, he is wise from himself, not through participation in another. Just as God is light not from another but from himself—for he has nothing higher or prior to himself, since otherwise he would not be the beginning of all things—so God is neither imperfect nor in need of anything, but full, true, and perfect God. Therefore he is wise from himself.

> “But the Son is wisdom from the Father, because the Father begot what he is. The Spirit also is wisdom, but not wisdom from no wisdom, for the Father alone is from no one. From where, then, is the Spirit wisdom, unless from wisdom? The Father is wisdom, and the Son is wisdom; therefore the Spirit is wisdom from the Father and the Son, who are wisdom. The Father and the Son are not separated by diversity but joined by unity. Therefore both send the Spirit, wisdom proceeding from both.” [Col. 0279C]

Again, later (chapter 7):

> “Behold, then, those three things—memory, understanding, and love or will—in that supreme and immutable essence which is God. They are not the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but the Father alone. And because the Son too is begotten wisdom from wisdom, just as neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit understands for him, but he himself understands for himself, so neither does the Father remember for him nor the Holy Spirit love for him, but he himself remembers and loves for himself. For he himself is also his own memory, his own understanding, and his own love. But that he is so is from the Father, from whom he was born. [Col. 0280A]

> “The Holy Spirit also, because he is wisdom proceeding from wisdom, does not have the Father as his memory, the Son as his understanding, and himself as love. For he would not be wisdom if one remembered for him, another understood for him, and he alone loved for himself. Rather, he himself possesses these three, and possesses them in such a way that he himself is these three. Yet that he is so—whence is it for him, if not from the one from whom he proceeds?”

With exceedingly subtle and divine insight he indicates the distinctions of the persons of the Trinity. He says that the Father is wisdom, the Son is wisdom, and the Holy Spirit is also wisdom; but the Son is begotten, wisdom from the Father, who likewise is wisdom; and the Spirit proceeds and is also wisdom, but from the Father, who is wisdom, and from the Son, who likewise is wisdom. [Col. 0280B]

To make his meaning clearer, let us set forth the analogy given above. He establishes three things—namely, memory, understanding, and love—as an image of the Trinity placed in the inner person. He discusses these at length both in the fifteenth book and elsewhere in the same work, affirming that understanding and love are contained in memory, that understanding is born from memory, and that love proceeds from both memory and understanding; [Col. 0280C] and that these three exist together and are of one substance.

For we remember what we understand; and when we wish to contemplate our understanding, we cannot do so unless it proceeds from a certain hidden place of memory, as though it were generated. When we approve our understanding as having been brought forth from memory, a kind of love arises that embraces both understanding and memory. Understanding takes delight in what it approves, and memory takes delight in the understanding that it knows to have been born from it and that it loves. Thus love arises both from memory and from understanding.

For if there were no understanding, there could be no love of it; and if there were no memory, there would be no source from which understanding could arise. We understand nothing of which we have no memory. These three are nevertheless distinguished by the proper limits of their operations. Memory does not understand by itself but through understanding; nor does understanding remember itself by itself but through memory. Likewise, love does not love without memory or understanding. When understanding is removed, there is nothing for memory to retain; and when memory is removed, love remembers nothing. Therefore love would no longer exist, since there would be nothing to love or anything for it to remember and toward which it might extend itself. [Col. 0280D]

Thus these three both exist together, arise from one another, are distinguished by their own limits, and mutually need one another.

But the Holy Trinity is not understood in the same way, as this venerable teacher indicates. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the whole Trinity, as memory, understanding, and love are. The Father is like the source from which the Son is born, just as memory exists as a kind of principle from which understanding is formed. The Son, since he is wisdom, is born from the Father, as understanding is generated from memory. The Holy Spirit, also wisdom but nevertheless love, proceeds from the Son and from the Father, as love proceeds from understanding and memory. [Col. 0281A]

Yet although this is so, the distinction of the persons is not such that the Father is wise only through the Son, or that the Son loves only through the Holy Spirit, as we see in the human Trinity within: memory understands not by itself but through understanding; understanding remembers not by itself but through memory; understanding loves not by itself but through love; and love neither understands nor remembers by itself, but remembers through memory and understands through understanding. [Col. 0281B]

The Trinity that is the supreme and immutable essence, that is, God, is not memory, understanding, and love in such a way that these three are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the Father as memory, the Son as understanding, and the Holy Spirit as love. Rather, the Father alone is these three, and the Son likewise is these three, and the Holy Spirit likewise is these three.

The Father remembers, understands, and loves from himself. He did not receive understanding from the Son, for otherwise he would be said to be born from the Son, which is not catholic teaching. Nor did he receive love from the Holy Spirit, for he would then appear to proceed from him, which is perverse. Rather, he remembers, knows, and loves from himself. [Col. 0281C]

The Son too, since he is wisdom begotten from wisdom, does not have the Father remembering for him, but he himself remembers for himself; nor does the Father understand for him, but he himself understands for himself; nor does the Holy Spirit love for him, but he himself loves for himself. For he remembers, understands, and loves from himself.

The Holy Spirit also, who is wisdom proceeding from wisdom, does not have the Father as memory for him, the Son as understanding for him, and himself alone as love. Rather, he possesses all three together—memory, understanding, and love. He remembers by himself, understands by himself, and loves by himself. Yet that he is these three he has from the one from whom he proceeds, that is, from both the Father and the Son, for he proceeds from both. [Col. 0281D]

We see that by the most subtle and truthful reasoning it has been shown—so that no prudent person could contradict it—that the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son. Although he is the Spirit of both, he is nevertheless not the Son either of both or of one of them. For love, which we say is born from memory and understanding, is not thereby called the daughter either of both or of one of them.

Again, in what follows (chapter 17):

> “Now we must speak of the Holy Spirit, as far as God grants us the ability to see: according to the holy Scriptures, the Holy Spirit is neither the Spirit of the Father alone nor of the Son alone, but of both. Therefore he signifies the common Trinity by which the Father and the Son love one another.” [Col. 0282A]

The Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone or of the Son alone, but of both, because he proceeds from both. Thus he signifies the common Trinity by which the Father and the Son love one another, joining the two together as proceeding from both—not as a quality of both, but as the third person in the Trinity, consubstantial and coequal with them.

Again, later:

> “For the Father is God, and the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and all three together are one God. Yet it is not without reason that in this Trinity only the Son is called the Word of God, only the Holy Spirit the gift of God, and only God the Father is called the one from whom the Word was begotten and from whom the Holy Spirit principally proceeds. I added ‘principally’ because the Holy Spirit is also found to proceed from the Son. But the Father gave this also to the Son—not to one who already existed and did not yet possess it, but by begetting him he gave him whatever he gave to the Only-begotten Word. Thus he begot him in such a way that the common gift would also proceed from him, and the Holy Spirit would be the Spirit of both.” [Col. 0282B]

By this testimony also he proves that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Nevertheless, he assigns something proper, as it were, to each person of the Holy Trinity, since the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, while all three together are one God.

It is proper to the Word of God that only the Son be called the Word; it is proper to the gift of God that only the Holy Spirit be called the Gift; and the one from whom the Word was begotten and from whom the Spirit principally proceeds is called God the Father alone. These are the distinctive properties of the individual persons in the Holy Trinity.

He said that the Spirit proceeds principally from the Father because he is also found to proceed from the Son. The Father gave this to the Son not as to one who existed first and did not yet possess it, but he gave it by begetting him, since whatever the Son has he received from the Father by being begotten. The Father did not first beget him and afterward give him the ability for the Spirit to proceed from the Son; rather, by begetting him he conferred on him that the common gift should also proceed from him—that is, the Holy Spirit, whom Augustine calls the gift of both the Father and the Son, because he is the Spirit of both. [Col. 0282C]

Again, below (chapter 19):

> “If among the gifts of God nothing is greater than love, and no gift of God is greater than the Holy Spirit, what follows more appropriately than that he himself should be love, who is also called God from God? And if the love by which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father ineffably demonstrates the communion of both, what is more fitting than that he should properly be called love who is the Spirit common to both?” [Col. 0282D]

Above, he had called the Holy Spirit the gift of God and by this property had distinguished the person of the Holy Spirit from the person of the Father and the Son. Now he calls this gift of God love, which is the chief gift among the gifts of divinity, because, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 13:3), the other gifts are nothing without love.

He calls this love “God from God,” signifying the Holy Spirit proceeding from God. Since “God” is a common name of both the Father and the Son, and it is not immediately apparent from whom he says the Spirit proceeds, he explains this in what follows:

> “And if the love by which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father ineffably demonstrates the communion of both, what is more fitting than that he should properly be called love who is the Spirit common to both?” [Col. 0283A]

In saying this, he both calls the Holy Spirit love and confesses that he proceeds jointly from both, namely, from the Father and the Son. For he could not otherwise be common to both unless he proceeded jointly from both.

Again, later (chapter 23):

> “In that supreme Trinity, which surpasses all things incomparably, there is such inseparability that, although a trinity of human beings cannot be called one human being, in that Trinity both ‘one God’ is said and is the case. Nor is that Trinity in one God, but it is one God. Nor again is that Trinity like this image, which is a human being possessing those three things and is one person; rather, there are three persons: the Father of the Son, the Son of the Father, and the Spirit of the Father and the Son.” [Col. 0283B]

By saying that the Father is the Father of the Son alone, that the Son is the Son of the Father, and that the Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone or of the Son alone but of both, he clearly testifies that the Spirit proceeds from both. For the Father is the Father of the Son because he begot him, and the Son is the Son of the Father because he was begotten by him. Consequently, the Spirit is called the Spirit of the Father and the Son because he proceeds from both the Father and the Son.

In this Trinity he teaches such great inseparability that, although a trinity of human beings cannot be called one human being—for it consists of three human beings, just as a trinity of bodies consists of three bodies, and therefore a trinity cannot be called one human being, since a single, indivisible singularity belongs to one number—in that supreme Trinity the Trinity is both called God and is one God. [Col. 0283C]

Yet this does not mean that the Trinity is in one God in the sense that each individual person is himself the Trinity: neither the Father alone, nor the Son alone, nor the Holy Spirit alone is the Trinity. Rather, since the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, the Trinity is one God.

Nor is the situation in the supreme Trinity like that of the image of the Trinity, which possesses three things—memory, understanding, and love—and is therefore a Trinity in one person. It is not that one human being is a trinity, but that in one human being there are those three things. The supreme Trinity is instead three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; yet these three are one God, and therefore the Trinity is one God.

There is such fellowship among the three persons and such consubstantiality that the three are one and one God is predicated of the three. They are distinguished only by relation, but joined in substance. The Father is relative to the Son, and the Son is relative to the Father; the Holy Spirit, however, has the Father and the Son as the terms of his relation, from which it is proved that he proceeds from both. [Col. 0283D]

Again, below (chapter 26):

> “Furthermore, in that supreme Trinity, which is God, there are no intervals of time by which it could be shown, or at least inquired, whether the Son was first born from the Father and afterward the Holy Spirit proceeded from both, since Holy Scripture calls him the Spirit of both.”

He is the one of whom the Apostle says:

> “And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Galatians 4:6). [Col. 0284A]

He is also the one of whom the same Son says:

> “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

And by many other testimonies of the divine utterances it is proved that he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, who is properly called the Holy Spirit in the Trinity.

Of him the Son himself also says:

> “Whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15:26),

and elsewhere:

> “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26).

That he proceeds from both is taught in this way: the Son himself says:

> “He proceeds from the Father.”

And when he had risen from the dead and appeared to his disciples, he breathed upon them and said:

> “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22),

so that he might show that the Spirit also proceeds from himself. He is also the power that went out from him, as we read in the Gospel, “and healed them all” (Luke 6:19). [Col. 0284B]

What room for contradiction remains here? By the authority of the divine Scriptures it is shown that the Holy Spirit belongs both to the Father and to the Son and that he proceeds from both. If this is to be denied, let the Apostle be denied, and let it also be denied that the Son said these things.

We believe the Son when he says that the Spirit proceeds from the Father; let us also believe that he sent the Spirit from himself when he breathed upon the disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” Furthermore, the power that healed them all, going out from Jesus, testifies that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son.

It is therefore clearly shown that the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son. Yet an even clearer testimony to that procession from both is the statement that he is the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son: he is the Spirit of both. This is not because he was created by the Father through the Son, which is impious, but because he proceeds substantially from both.

Nor can any intervals of time be demonstrated as to when the Spirit proceeded either from the Father or from the Son, or whether, after the Son was begotten, the Holy Spirit proceeded from both. What precedes all time is contained by no measure of time. Therefore no order of procession is to be sought within time, since all time encompasses paternity. [Col. 0284C]

The Father was never without the Son; the Son was never without the Father; the Holy Spirit was never without the Father and the Son; and the Father and the Son were never without the Holy Spirit.

Again below: “Can we therefore ask whether the Holy Spirit had already proceeded from the Father when the Son was born, or had not yet proceeded, and whether, after he was born, he proceeded from both, where there are no temporal intervals? Just as we could ask where we find temporal intervals when the will first proceeds from the human mind, so that what is found may be called offspring, and, once it has been brought forth or generated, that will is brought to completion, coming to rest in this end: that what had been the desire of the seeker becomes the love of the one enjoying, which now proceeds from both—that is, from the generating mind and from the generated conception—as from parent and offspring? These things absolutely cannot be sought there where nothing begins in time so as to be completed in time. Therefore, whoever can understand the generation of the Son from the Father without time should also understand the procession of the Holy Spirit from both without time.”

Blessed Augustine testifies that the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son. But he raises the question mentioned above: whether the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Father before the Son’s birth, and, after the Son had been born, proceeded also from him. This question is prompted by the analogy in which the will is said to proceed from the human mind before the word is formed from the mind, so that a certain desire of the will arises in the search for what, once it has been found, is called, as it were, the mind’s offspring. Once this offspring has been generated, the will that first proceeded as a desire to seek is brought to completion. Yet this will was first born from the mind, before what was desired was sought and found; once it has been found, the will is completed and filled, being increased by the thing discovered. For one rejoices at having found what one sought. Thus the will, born from both—from the mind and from what has been found—proceeds from both: first from the mind and afterward from what has been found; from the former, namely, toward seeking, and from the latter, toward delight in what has been discovered.

Yet this is not a twofold will, as though one belonged earlier to the mind and the other later to what was found. It is one will of one thing—namely, of what has been found—having its beginning in the mind as a desire to seek, but its completion in the discovery of what it sought: what was first a certain desire to seek afterward becomes love for enjoying what has been found.

These things occur in created realities, which are contained within time. But in divinity, where no time exists, nothing of this kind can be found. For it is not said there that the Father existed earlier or that the Son was generated later; rather, the Father has always remained in the Son and the Son in the Father. Nor could the Holy Spirit, by proceeding, precede the Son’s birth, since where no time exists neither “before” nor “after” can be found. What has no beginning in time cannot be completed afterward in time. Therefore, whoever can conceive the Son’s generation from the Father without time should also conceive the Holy Spirit’s procession both from the Father and from the Son without time. Just as one must not ask when the Son was born from the Father, so one must in no way ask when the Holy Spirit proceeded from both, or whether he preceded the Son’s birth by proceeding from the Father. For where eternity is present, the order of time is absent. Nor is any law of divinity to be judged from the condition of human creatures, since created things, being made within time, observe time’s order; but the one who created time is governed by no law of time, for he precedes all things contained within time.

He adds something else by which he proves that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son without time, just as it is established that the Son was generated from the Father without time. He says:

“And whoever can understand what the Son said—‘As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son to have life in himself’ (John 5:26)—should understand that the Father did not grant life to the Son as though the Son already existed without life, but generated him without time in such a way that the life which the Father gave the Son by generating him is coeternal with the life of the Father who gave it. Let him understand that, just as the Father has life in himself so that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him, so he gave this to the Son, so that the same Holy Spirit proceeds from him also—and both without time. Thus the statement that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father is to be understood as meaning that he also proceeds from the Son, and that he is from the Father and the Son. For if everything the Son has he has from the Father, then certainly he has from the Father also that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him. But let no temporal intervals be imagined there—intervals involving ‘before’ and ‘after’—because there are absolutely none there.”

He testifies that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father. Yet what proceeds from the Son was given to the Son by the Father—not to one who existed previously, but by generating him. For whatever the Father gave the Son, he did not give as to one who was inferior or who already existed; he gave it by generating him.

He offers an analogy by which what he affirms may become clearer:

“Whoever can understand,” he says, “what the Son said—‘As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself’—should understand that the Father did not give life to the Son as though the Son already existed without life.”

The Son would exist without life if he had existed in some way before he lived, so that life was afterward bestowed upon him once he already existed. Thus Genesis speaks of the first Adam, saying: “Then God formed man from the dust of the ground” (Genesis 2:7). It subsequently adds: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life.” It first says that he was formed, and afterward that, once formed—that is, existing through the quality of his own formation—the breath of life was added to him.

But the Father did not give life to the Son in such a way that he first generated him and afterward gave life to one already generated. Rather, he gave life by generating him, because the Son is substantially life, and the Father gave him life by generating him. Man, in fact, first existed formed and afterward received life, because he received life by participation, not by birth. He was not substantially life, but lived through participation in life. The only-begotten Son of the Father, however, did not receive life by participation; rather, he was substantially generated from the Father as life. Life was not given to one who already existed as though he remained without life; rather, he was generated wholly equal and consubstantial with the life of the Father, who gave him life by generating him.

He continues:

“But he generated him without time, so that the life which the Father gave the Son by generating him is coeternal with the life of the Father who gave it.”

By saying this he shows that the Father is life and that the Son is life. Yet the Son received life from the Father so as to be life—not as one who first existed without life, but as one generated as life, coeternal and consubstantial with the life of the Father, who gave the Son life by generating him.

Whoever can understand how this is should also understand that, just as the Father has life in himself so that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him, so he gave this to the Son, so that the same Holy Spirit proceeds from him. For he wishes to establish that the Son received from the Father, by being generated, not only life, but also that the Holy Spirit should proceed from him—the same Spirit, not another, who proceeds from the Father.

And since no sane person can deny that the Son received life from the Father so as to be life, as the Father is life, one must consequently also admit that the Son received from the Father that the Holy Spirit should proceed from him. Both occur without time. For just as the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father without time, so he also proceeds from the Son without time, since this procession is not temporal but eternal. Just as the Son’s birth from the Father excludes all time, so the procession of the Holy Spirit from both excludes all time.

He adds:

“And thus the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father in such a way that it is understood that he also proceeds from the Son, being from the Father and the Son.”

He wants it understood that whenever the Holy Spirit is read or said to proceed from the Father, he is likewise signified as proceeding from the Son. Therefore, when the Father is mentioned, the Son is to be understood as well, since the Son has received from the Father that the Holy Spirit should proceed from him.

And because the reference is made to the Father as the source from whom the Son received that the Holy Spirit should proceed from him, whenever it is said that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, it must be understood equally that he proceeds from the Son. Hence he adds:

“For if everything the Son has he has from the Father, he certainly has from the Father also that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him.”

We know that the Son said that everything belonging to the Father also belongs to the Son. Yet since these things were given to him by the Father, they are rightly referred back to the one from whom they were given. Therefore, when it is said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, the statement refers back to the Father, from whom the Son received that the Spirit should proceed from him.

Thus, when the Son says in the Gospel, “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26), he wishes it understood that he also said that the Spirit proceeds from himself. But this is without any temporal sequence, since one must not inquire whether the Holy Spirit proceeded first and the Son was born afterward, or whether, once the Son had been born, the Holy Spirit afterward proceeded from both. One must not think in terms of “earlier” and “later,” since no time is to be posited here.

And later:

“How, then, could the Son not most absurdly be called the Son of both, since, just as generation without any beginning of time and without any change of nature gives the Son his essence, so procession from both gives the Holy Spirit his essence without any beginning of time and without any change of nature?”

He shows that the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son, but that one must not ask whether he proceeded first from the Father and afterward from the Son. Rather, one must understand that just as generation gives the Son substance without the intervention of time or any change, so procession gives the Holy Spirit substance apart from any temporal interval and apart from any change. One must not debate what came before or afterward, but understand the Son’s birth from the Father and the Holy Spirit’s procession from both.

He continues:

“For this reason, although we do not call the Holy Spirit generated, we nevertheless do not dare to call him ungenerated, lest, by this term, someone suspect either two Fathers in that Trinity or two who are not from another. For the Father alone is not from another, and therefore alone is called ‘ungenerated’—not indeed in Scripture, but in the custom of those who debate and express, as best they can, their thoughts about so great a matter. The Son, however, was born from the Father; and the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from the Father and, with the Father giving it without any temporal interval, proceeds jointly from both. The Son would be called the Son of the Father and the Son if, as is abhorrent to the understanding of all sound minds, both had generated him. Therefore he is not generated from both; rather, the Spirit of both proceeds from both.”

He continues to establish that the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son. In this statement he answers the argument of those who contradict him, saying that if the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, he must be the Son of both. First, however, he discusses the name by which the Holy Spirit should be called—generated or ungenerated—and denies that either term should be applied to him.

He gives this reason for his assertion: if the Spirit were called generated, he would be the Son of two, namely, the Father and the Son, which he says is abhorrent to Christian devotion. But neither may he be called ungenerated, since this belongs properly to the Father, who is from no other. He is the beginning of himself, existing from himself and having nothing preceding him; he is the beginning, fountain, and source of the universe.

Since the Holy Spirit cannot properly be called either generated or ungenerated, he is properly called “proceeding.” But he does not proceed from one alone as one alone: that is, he does not proceed from the Father alone so as to be called the Father’s Son, just as the Son is said to be born from the Father alone. Rather, he proceeds from both—that is, from the Father and from the Son—without time, and therefore eternally. Yet they are not said to have generated him, because he is neither the Son of the Father nor the Son of the Son; he proceeds from both. He is the Spirit of both.

Thus it is shown by evident reasoning that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. It is plainly taught that he does not proceed from the Father alone, lest he be called the Father’s Son; nor from the Son alone, lest the Son be blasphemously called the Father. Rather, the Holy Spirit is called both proceeding and proceeding from both.

## CHAPTER IV. From the same author.

Many are troubled by the question of what difference there is between generation and procession. Since this question appears insoluble in that incorporeal and invisible Trinity, it must be stated what the most distinguished author, Augustine, thought. He therefore adds the following, speaking in Book 15 of *The Trinity*, chapter 27:

“But because in that coeternal, coequal, incorporeal, ineffably immutable, and inseparable Trinity it is exceedingly difficult to distinguish generation from procession, let what we said on this matter in a certain sermon delivered to the ears of the Christian people, and what we wrote down after saying it, suffice for the time being for those who are unable to extend their understanding further.

“For among other things, when I had taught through the testimonies of the holy Scriptures that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, I said: If, then, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son, why did the Son say, ‘He proceeds from the Father’? Why do you think, unless it is because he is accustomed to refer to the Father even what belongs to him, since he himself is from the Father? Hence the saying: ‘My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me’ (John 7:16).

“If, therefore, the teaching is understood here to be his, although he said that it was not his but the Father’s, how much more should it be understood there that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from him, where he says, ‘He proceeds from the Father,’ rather than saying, ‘He does not proceed from me’?

“From whom does the Son have that he is God—for he is God from God? From him, certainly, he has that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from him. Accordingly, the Holy Spirit has from the Father that he proceeds also from the Son, just as he proceeds from the Father.

“Here, so far as such matters can be understood by people like us, it is also understood why the Holy Spirit is not said to have been born but rather to proceed. For if he too were called the Son, he would certainly be called the Son of both, which is exceedingly absurd. There is no son of two except of a father and a mother. But far be it from us to imagine anything of this kind between God the Father and God the Son. For even a human son does not proceed simultaneously from father and mother: when he proceeds from the father into the mother, he does not then proceed from the mother; and when he proceeds from the mother into this light, he does not then proceed from the father.

“The Holy Spirit, however, does not proceed from the Father into the Son and from the Son toward the sanctification of creation; rather, he proceeds simultaneously from both, although the Father gave the Son this: that, just as the Spirit proceeds from the Father, so he should proceed from the Son also.

“For we cannot say that the Holy Spirit is not life, since the Father is life and the Son is life. Accordingly, just as the Father, having life in himself, gave the Son to have life in himself, so he gave him that the Holy Spirit, life, should proceed from him just as he proceeds from the Father.”

[Note: “Life, the Holy Spirit.” These last two words are not found in Augustine; that they were added by Ratramnus is clear also from the fact that above, in chapter 2, where he cited the same passage of Augustine, only this was read: “that life proceeds from him,” and so forth.]

Blessed Augustine transferred these words from the sermon which he said he had delivered before the people into Book 15 of *On the Holy Trinity*. We have already presented above testimonies from that sermon and briefly stated what we thought about them; we do not now consider it necessary to repeat those remarks.

It need only be said that he identifies the difference between generation and procession as follows: generation belongs to the Son, since he is said to have been born from the Father; procession belongs to the Holy Spirit, who cannot be called generated. For if he were called born, he would be said to be the Son both of the Father and of the Son. Augustine says that this is utterly foolish and does not accord with divine generation. For when did anyone ever exist as a son born from both the Father and the Son?

Therefore, since these alternatives are entirely absurd, the Son should be called born from the Father, while the Holy Spirit should be called proceeding from both. Nor is this inappropriate. It has been said that the Father alone is from no one; from the Father come both the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Father is life, the Son also life, and the Holy Spirit likewise life. But the Father alone is life from no life; the Son is life from the Father alone, but generated; and the Holy Spirit is life not from the Father alone or from the Son alone, but from both.

Yet the Spirit does not proceed from the Father in such a way that he proceeds from him into the Son and then again from the Son toward the sanctification of creation. No temporal moments or order are to be imagined here. Rather, he proceeds simultaneously from both: when he proceeds from the Father, he proceeds from the Son; and when he proceeds from the Son, he proceeds from the Father, with no intervening time or order.

The difference, however, is that the Father received from no one that the Holy Spirit should proceed from him, whereas the Son received from the Father that the same Spirit should proceed from him.

Likewise, in the book of the disputation against the Five Heresies, bringing his discussion of the Holy Spirit to an end, he says:

“What else can I say, weary to the weary? Whoever separates the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in eternity, substance, or communion, and denies that he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, is full of an unclean spirit and empty of the Holy Spirit.”

Let the opponents of the truth hear these words, those who deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. By denying this, they deny that he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son. Let them fear that they are full of an unclean spirit and empty of the Holy Spirit, and that they cannot obtain pardon unless they renounce so great a blasphemy. If the malicious do not wish to hear this, let the friends of piety hear it and shudder at the blasphemy of impiety, so that they may be filled with the Holy Spirit.

Likewise, in the book *Against Maximinus the Arian* (Book III, chapter 5), he says:

“You say that you honor the Holy Spirit as teacher, guide, illuminator, and sanctifier; that you worship Christ as creator; and that you adore the Father with sincere devotion as author.

“If you call the Father ‘author’ because the Son is from him, while he himself is not from the Son, and because the Holy Spirit proceeds from him and from the Son in such a way that he himself gave this to the Son by generating him in such a way that the Holy Spirit should proceed also from him;

“if you call the Son ‘creator’ in such a way that you do not deny that the Father and the Holy Spirit are creators;

“and finally, if you call the Holy Spirit teacher, guide, illuminator, and sanctifier in such a way that you do not dare to take these works away either from the Father or from the Son—then these words of yours are also our words.”

These are the words of Saint Augustine against the Arians. Let the emperors and the Ariomaniacs see whose faith they wish to embrace. If they deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, they oppose the Catholic faith and become defenders of Arian doctrine. If they are Catholics and hate the falsehood of corrupt doctrine, they do not accuse the Latins, who confess, in accordance with the Catholic faith, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. To deny this is manifestly to agree with Arian perfidy.

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 14:

“You ask me”—addressing, clearly, Maximinus the Arian, to whom he was speaking—“if the Son is from the substance of the Father, and the Holy Spirit is from the substance of the Father, why is one the Son and the other not the Son? Here is my answer, whether you understand it or not: the Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is from the Father; but the one is generated, while the other proceeds. Therefore the one is the Son of the Father, from whom he was generated; the other, however, is the Spirit of both, because he proceeds from both.”

Maximinus the Arian, against whom blessed Augustine is arguing, denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. He said that the Spirit was inferior to the Son and not consubstantial with the Father, wishing to empty out what the Catholic faith maintains: that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son. Therefore he said: If the Holy Spirit were from the substance of the Father, just as the Son is from the substance of the Father, there would consequently already be two sons.

In reply, blessed Augustine says that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Father, because he is of the same substance as the Father. Yet he is not the Son, because he is not born but proceeds. The Son, who is born, is from the substance of the Father, and is therefore the Son because he is born. The Holy Spirit, however, although he is from the substance of the Father, is not the Son, because he is not generated. He proceeds from the substance of the Son, because he is the Spirit of both and consubstantial with both. Whoever denies this agrees with the Arians and contradicts the Catholic faith.

He continues:

“But for this reason, when the Son spoke of him, he said, ‘He proceeds from the Father’ (John 15:26): because the Father is the source of his procession, having generated such a Son and, by generating him, having given him that the Holy Spirit should proceed also from him. For if the Spirit did not proceed also from him, the Son would not say to the disciples, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20:22), and, giving him by breathing upon them, would not signify that the Spirit proceeds from himself also. By breathing, he openly showed what he was giving secretly by his inspiration.

“Therefore, if the Holy Spirit were born, he would certainly be born not only from the Father or only from the Son, but from both; and without doubt he would be called the Son of both. Since he is in no way the Son of both, he ought not to be born from both. He is therefore the Spirit of both, proceeding from both.”

He affirms that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son and that the Son wished to signify this when he spoke of the Spirit in the Gospel, saying, “He proceeds from the Father.” He did not say this in such a way as to deny that the Spirit proceeds from himself; rather, he referred the authority of the procession to the Father, who generated such a Son and, by generating him, granted him that the Holy Spirit should proceed not only from the Father but also from the Son.

He confirms this by another testimony. After his resurrection, the Savior appeared to the disciples and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit.” And so that he might give what he commanded them to receive not only through words but also through breathing, he says that he spoke to the disciples by breathing so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. By breathing upon them he gave the Spirit, openly signifying by his breathing that the Spirit proceeds from him, while secretly giving him by inspiration.

He likewise resolves the question raised by the Arians’ impiety: if the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, would he then be the Son of both? He says: “For if the Holy Spirit were born, he would be born not only from the Father or only from the Son, but from both,” because he proceeds from both. He proceeds, I say, but is not born. If he were born, he would certainly be born from both, because he proceeds from both, and he would without doubt be called the Son of both.

But the generation of the Spirit is excluded, since he is neither the Son of the Father nor the Son of both. Therefore he ought not to be born from both. Whoever has no birth rejects sonship, and whoever is not a son ought in no way to be born. He is the Spirit of both by proceeding from both.

Thus he overturns the Arian calumny, fashioned by the envy of falsehood and generated by the malignity of impiety. That calumny wished to assert that the Spirit is not from the substance of the Father, on the grounds that, if he were, he would be the Son. But this Catholic teacher demonstrates by Catholic reasoning that the Spirit is indeed from the substance of the Father and nevertheless is not the Son, because proceeding is not the same as being born.

He then adds:

“But who can explain the difference between being born and proceeding when speaking of that most excellent nature? Not everything that proceeds is born, although everything that is born proceeds, just as not everything that is two-footed is human, although everyone who is human is two-footed. This I know; but I do not know, cannot, and am not sufficient to distinguish between that generation and this procession.”

The outstanding teacher and most vigorous conqueror of heretics testifies that the Holy Spirit is not the Son: he is not born but proceeds, and he proceeds not only from the substance of the Father but also from that of the Son.

Since he is a sharer in the substance of both, being consubstantial, and is said to proceed from the Father, from whom the Son is also born, the question of what difference there is between birth and procession is not a minor one. Augustine confesses that, concerning that most excellent nature, it is possible not only for him but for no mortal to distinguish what the difference is between being born and proceeding. Nevertheless, it can be understood that not everything that proceeds is born, although everything that is born proceeds. For nothing can be born unless it proceeds from that from which it is born, as a son proceeds from a parent.

When a child proceeds from the hidden parts of the mother’s womb into the light, he is said to be born; but this is not said when he proceeds from the hidden parts of the father into the mother. We cannot deny procession, since the emission of seed into the mother’s womb takes place, from which the son afterward proceeds and is said to be born.

We do not say these things as though the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Father at one time and from the Son at another. Rather, we wish to show that not every procession is generation, whereas every generation is procession. This is like the statement that not everything two-footed is human, although everyone who is human is two-footed.

He gives this example to distinguish birth from procession. Yet he does not thereby signify precisely what being born or proceeding is, but rather offers an analogy such as the distinction between species and genus. “Two-footed” is the genus of the species “human,” and “human” is the species of the genus “two-footed.” If one considers the genus, both humans and birds are two-footed; if one considers the species, the human is two-footed.

For this reason he says, “Not everything two-footed is human,” because birds too are included under this general term. But when one says “human,” one includes every human being, though not everything two-footed; the term “two-footed” signifies more than “human.” Therefore this definition does not properly signify either human or two-footed. The same applies to procession and birth.

In procession, birth is shown, but not always. Thus it is said: “Honey proceeds from the mouth of the wise.” The Psalmist says of the sun: “And he himself, like a bridegroom proceeding from his chamber” (Psalm 18:6). The sun’s chamber signifies a certain secret place, removed from human sight, from which it proceeds each day to provide light to mortals.

Birth, however, always manifests procession, because it can never occur without procession. Whatever is born also proceeds. Therefore blessed Augustine does say what generation and procession are, but only in the manner of genus and species, not in the manner of what is proper. He says that he does not know these things and cannot distinguish them by their proper boundaries.

Why is this so? He adds the reason:

“Because both that and this are ineffable”—that is, the generation of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit.

Just as the prophet, speaking of the Son, says, “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8), so it is most truly said of the Holy Spirit: “Who shall declare his procession?”

By these words he shows that the Son’s birth, just like the Holy Spirit’s procession, cannot be declared because both are ineffable. Therefore one ought not to investigate what cannot be declared, since it cannot in any way be comprehended. It should be enough that holy Scripture testifies concerning these matters: that the Son was born from the Father, while the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father alone but also from the Son, as he indicates next:

“Let it therefore be enough for us that the Son is not from himself but from him from whom he was born; and that the Holy Spirit is not from himself but from him from whom he proceeds. And because he proceeds from both, as we have already shown, he is therefore called the Spirit of the Father, where it is written: ‘But if the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you.’ And he is called the Spirit of the Son, where it is written: ‘But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his’ (Romans 8:9).”

Here, arguing against Maximinus the Arian, Augustine shows that the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son. Those who persist in denying this confess themselves to be Ariomaniacs and do not acknowledge the Spirit as consubstantial with the Son. For if the Spirit does not proceed from the Son, he is not of the same substance as the Son. Consequently, such a person must either blasphemously call the Holy Spirit a creature or deny that the Son possesses everything that belongs to the Father.

He cannot deny that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son. For the Apostle says: “Because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4:6). If he is the Spirit of the Son, as the Apostle confesses, then either he will be subject—as the Arian wishes, since he numbers him among creatures—or he proceeds from the Son, as Catholics confess.

Let the Greek emperors choose, then, what they wish. They cannot deny that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son. Let them therefore explain how he is the Son’s Spirit if he does not proceed from him. For if they deny procession, they proclaim creation, which is clearly an impiety of the Arians, since the Spirit cannot be the Son’s Spirit unless he has either been created or proceeds from him.

Likewise, later in the same work, chapter 17:

“What does ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John 1:1) mean except that the Son was in the Father? And when the Jews asked the Son himself who he was, he replied: ‘The Beginning, who also speaks to you’ (John 8:25). The Father is beginning, not from a beginning; the Son is beginning from a beginning. Yet together they are not two beginnings but one beginning, just as the Father is God and the Son is God, while together they are not two gods but one God. Nor will I deny that the Holy Spirit proceeding from both is a beginning; but these three together, just as I say that they are one God, so I say that they are one beginning.”

He denies that the Holy Spirit is a creature, saying that he is a beginning, just as the Father is a beginning and the Son is a beginning. But the Father is a beginning from no beginning; the Son is a beginning, but from the Father as beginning; and the Holy Spirit is likewise a beginning, not from no beginning or from the Father alone as beginning, but from both—from the Father as beginning and from the Son. Yet there are not three beginnings but one beginning, just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three gods, although each individually is called God, but these three are one God.

Likewise, later, chapter 21:

“Light from light, the Son from the Father, and together both one light; just as God from God, and together both one God—and all this not without the Spirit of both.”

By saying this he testifies that the Spirit proceeds from both. For if the Spirit is the Father’s because he proceeds from the Father, then consequently he is also the Son’s because he proceeds from him. He is not called the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of the Son for different reasons, but for one and the same reason: namely, that he proceeds from both, just as he is the Spirit of both.

If you say that he is called the Spirit of the Father because he proceeds from the Father, what reason remains for calling him the Spirit of the Son except that he also proceeds from him?

These are the things blessed Augustine, arguing against Maximinus the Arian, thought, said, and wrote concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son. He condemned Arian perfidy and affirmed the piety of the Catholic faith. Whoever attempts to contradict him is found to be an enemy of the Catholic faith.

Here also, disputing in the dialogue against Pascentius the Arian (*The Debate of Pascentius with Augustine*, Letter 178, middle), he says:

“For if, in a believing human being, God himself in his entirety is believed to dwell, how can the Father not be believed to receive the whole Son into himself, or the Son the whole Father? Accordingly, he himself remains in the Father and the Father in him, and the Holy Spirit is to be believed not only to have proceeded from the Father and the Son, but always to proceed from them for carrying out the works of the Trinity.”

He says that the Holy Spirit is one co-worker from the holy Trinity, joined to the Father and the Son not only in substance but also in operation, as proceeding from both and working together with both. He could not do this if, by proceeding from both, he had not received and were not receiving his substance from both.

## CHAPTER V. From Gennadius and Fulgentius.

Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, a man learned through extensive reading of the ancients, speaks as follows in his book *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit:

[Note: Gennadius of Constantinople. Since those who published this book of Gennadius knew no writer of that name except the presbyter of Massilia, they attributed another man’s offspring to him. Ratramnus rebukes their ignorance in this passage. Gennadius succeeded Anatolius in 458, held office until 471, and was succeeded by Acacius. The Greek copy of his work has perished.]

“We believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God: the Father because he has a Son; the Son because he has a Father; the Holy Spirit because he is from the Father and the Son.

“The Father, therefore, is the beginning of divinity, the principal name, because just as he was never not God, so he was never not Father. From him the Son was born; from him the Holy Spirit is not born, because he is not the Son; nor is he ungenerated, because he is not the Father. Nor was the Holy Spirit made, because he is not from nothing, but proceeds as God from God the Father and God the Son.”

He states with sufficient clarity that the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, which means that he proceeds from the substance of the Father and the Son. For he could not otherwise be from both unless he proceeded substantially from both. Therefore he says in what follows that he proceeds as God from God the Father and God the Son. And although he calls him proceeding, he nevertheless denies that he should be called either born, because he is not the Son, or ungenerated, because he is not the Father.

Fulgentius, bishop, exceedingly learned in literary studies and distinguished for the holiness of his life, having also suffered much at the hands of the Arians for the Catholic faith, says the following in his book *Questions on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*:

> “Thus everything that belongs to the very nature is found to be common to the three Persons, while nevertheless something is found by which each Person is properly recognized—something that is neither separable nor capable of being common. For we say that what the Father has as his proper attribute is that he begot; we say that what the Son has as his proper attribute [Col. 0295C] is that he alone was born from the Father alone; and that what the Holy Spirit has as his proper attribute is that he proceeds from the Father and the Son. In these proper attributes, however, there is no separation of nature, but a certain personal recognition.”

Here this author states what the three Persons of the Holy Trinity have in common and what properly distinguishes each one. What is common to the three Persons is the consubstantiality of the one nature; what is proper to each is that the Father alone begot, the Son alone was born from the Father alone, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore, those who accept as the Father’s proper attribute that he is the begetter, and as the Son’s proper attribute that he is begotten, must also accept that the Holy Spirit’s proper attribute is that he proceeds from the Father and the Son. If they strive to deny this, let them say what is proper to him. For procession from the Father is also common to the Son, since everything that is born also proceeds. Therefore, according to the judgment of this teacher, what is proper to the Holy Spirit is that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, something that is seen to be common neither to the Father nor to the Son: for the Father is from no one, the Son from the Father alone, but the Holy Spirit from both.

Likewise, in what follows:

> “The divinity of the Son, therefore, could not have received the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit himself proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father, and is given by the Son just as he is given by the Father. Nor could that nature from which the Holy Spirit has his origin either await or receive a gift. That Spirit is wholly the Father’s and wholly the Son’s; [Col. 0296A] for naturally there is one Spirit of the Father and the Son. Accordingly, he proceeds wholly from the Father and the Son, and remains wholly in the Father and the Son; for he remains in such a way that he proceeds, and proceeds in such a way that he remains. Hence, by nature he possesses with the Father and the Son the fullness of unity and the unity of fullness, so that he is wholly possessed by the Father and wholly possessed by the Son. The divinity of the Son, therefore, did not receive the Holy Spirit, with which the Holy Spirit is of one nature and from which he has whatever he has—or rather, from which he is what he is—for what he has naturally, that he is.”

This passage concerns the fullness of Christ’s divinity and his humanity. He says that the humanity received the Holy Spirit, not indeed according to measure, since the fullness of divinity consists in it, as the Gospel testifies when it says of Christ: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I, 14). “Truth” refers to divinity, while “grace” refers to the gift. In order that the man born from the Virgin might be perfect God, just as he is perfect man, he received this not by merit but through the gift of divine grace. But divinity naturally possesses fullness and perfection: it lacks nothing, can receive no diminution, and can endure no increase.

According to this fullness of divinity, Christ the Son of God could not receive the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit himself proceeds from him just as he proceeds from the Father, and is likewise given by him just as he is given by the Father. Therefore the divinity of the Son, from which the Holy Spirit takes his origin, cannot receive the gift of the one who is the cause of his existence. For that Spirit is wholly the Father’s and wholly the Son’s; and although he is wholly of both—or wholly of either—this does not mean by any conversion that the Father and the Son are called the Holy Spirit, as though they received from him the cause of their being. Nor is the Son alone the Son of the Holy Spirit, as though he received existence from him, since naturally there is one Spirit of both the Father and the Son, receiving essence from them.

Accordingly, as blessed Fulgentius testifies, he proceeds wholly from the Father and wholly from the Son. No part of him proceeds from the Father and another part from the Son; nor does one part of him remain in the Father and another part in the Son. For he is indivisible and impartible, not composed of different things; and he remains in such a way that he proceeds, and proceeds in such a way that he remains. By nature he possesses with the Father [Col. 0296D] and the Son the fullness of unity and the unity of fullness; he is wholly possessed by the Father and wholly possessed by the Son.

The divinity of the Son, therefore, did not receive the Holy Spirit whom it previously lacked, since the Holy Spirit is of the same nature as the Son, being from him and receiving from him whatever he has—or rather, being what he is from him—for he is substantially from the divinity of the Son. By all these arguments it is plainly shown that the procession of the Holy Spirit is no less from the Son than from the Father. Whoever intends to deny this will likewise deny the subsistence of the Holy Spirit, since he cannot subsist unless he receives essence from the one from whom, by proceeding, he subsists.

Saint Fulgentius spoke in this way concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit while arguing against Arian perfidy. He most truthfully approves the statement that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both the Father and the Son, since he is the Spirit of both and receives essence from both. Whoever denies this is shown to be subject to Arian perfidy.

## CHAPTER VI. From Athanasius

But let us return to Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, whom at the beginning we placed first among the Catholic witnesses, so that the one who was the beginning may be the conclusion of the testimony concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son. In the second book *On the Proper Persons and the United Name of the Divinity, Against the Arians*, he says:

> “In this respect the Father is another in person, because he truly begot; and in this respect the Son is another from the Father in person, because he was truly begotten by him. But in this respect the principal Paraclete, the Spirit, is another in person from the Father and the Son, who was poured out upon the apostles at Pentecost, because he truly proceeds from the united divinity of the Father and the Son.”

Distinguishing here the proper attributes of the individual Persons and joining them through the unity of divinity, this author shows what is proper to each and what is common. He says that it is proper to the Father that he begot; in this the Son and the Holy Spirit have no share, for otherwise “Father” would not be his proper designation. The Son is distinguished from the Father in that the Son was begotten while the Father begot. Nor does the Holy Spirit have any share in the proper attribute of generation, since the Son is begotten whereas the Holy Spirit is proved not to be begotten.

The Holy Spirit, in turn, has this as his proper attribute: he neither begot nor was begotten, but proceeds from the united divinity of the Father and the Son. In this he shares with neither the Father nor the Son. For the Father is from no one, the Son from the Father alone, but the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. Whoever strives to deny this should show how the Person of the Holy Spirit is distinguished from the proper attributes of the Father and the Son.

Although these three Persons of the Holy Trinity are distinguished from one another by their proper attributes, they are joined by the unity of divinity, so that there is no difference among them in the common possession of divinity: there is propriety in the Persons, but undifferentiated unity in the divinity.

Likewise, in the seventh book:

> “Why does ‘He who sees me sees also my Father’ (John XIV, 9) indicate this, if there is not in them one invisible image of the nature of truth?” Why do you read that the truth of the Spirit is preserved in the bond of peace (Ephesians IV, 3), if you do not accept that he belongs to the very united divinity of the Father and the Son? Why do you read that the chosen vessel said, ‘We have all drunk one Spirit’ (I Corinthians XII, 18), if you distinguish him from the united and true nature of the Godhead?”

He testifies that the Son is of the same nature as the Father—a truth the Arians denied—since there is in the Father and the Son one invisible image of the nature of truth.
