He also testifies that the Holy Spirit is of the same substance as the Son, since he exists from the united divinity of the Father and the Son. By saying this, he plainly shows that the Spirit proceeds from both. For since the divinity of the Father and the Son is so united that it can admit no difference, the Spirit cannot proceed from the divinity of the Father without also proceeding from that of the Son. Nor can he proceed from the divinity of the Son without also proceeding from that of the Father. Otherwise the united divinity of the Father and the Son would no longer be undifferentiated: if the Spirit proceeded from the Father’s divinity but did not likewise proceed from the Son’s divinity, it would no longer be united. This is impious and Arian.

Therefore, according to the Catholic faith, let it be said—as blessed Athanasius confesses—that the Holy Spirit is from the united divinity of the Father and the Son. He also testifies that we have drunk one Spirit. By saying this, he approves that the Spirit of the Father is not one and the Spirit of the Son another, but that the one who is the Son’s is also the Father’s. He is from the united and true nature of the Godhead, that is, from the substance of the Father and the Son, which subsists in such unity that it is divided by no separation. Since the Holy Spirit is also one Spirit of that substance, it is clearly proved that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, with whom he is joined in the united nature of divinity.

Likewise, farther on:

> “[Note: [Col. 0297D] ‘Hypocrites,’ etc. These and the passages that follow do not occur in Athanasius’s books *On the Proper Persons*. Nevertheless, religious scruple forbids us to doubt that they were written by Athanasius. Since we know from other evidence that his books were badly handled by copyists, we readily believe that passages vainly sought in the places indicated by the ancients may be found concealed under other titles, if someone undertakes that labor.] Hypocrites, how do you accept the statement, ‘The same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills’ (I Corinthians XII, 11), if you separate him from the united operation of the Godhead? The united divinity belongs wholly to the Holy Trinity, in which the Person of the Holy Spirit likewise subsists, and without which there will be no Trinity.”

By saying that the Godhead is joined in a united operation, he testifies that the Father and the Son cooperate with the Holy Spirit; nature cannot separate those whom the same operation joins. Consequently, it is clear that the Spirit is from the united nature of the Father and the Son, with whom he is joined both in substance and in operation.

Likewise:

> “Hypocrites, how do you accept the statement, ‘The same Spirit, the same Lord, and the same God’ (ibid., 4, 6), if you do not receive him as the true God from the true nature, working wonders in all things?”

He calls the Spirit both Lord and God, and indeed the true God from the true nature. By saying “from the true nature,” he confesses that the Holy Spirit is not from himself but from the true nature of the Father and the Son. Just as the Father and the Son are not separated in the truth of their nature, so the Holy Spirit subsists from the true nature of both. For he cannot proceed from the nature of the Father unless he also proceeds from the nature of the Son, since the nature of the Father is the same as the nature of the Son.

When blessed Athanasius calls the Holy Spirit the true God from the true nature, without adding “of the Father” or “of the Son,” he clearly implies that the Holy Spirit is the true God from the true nature of both, working wonders in all things.

Likewise:

> “Hypocrites, through whom is the word of wisdom supplied, or the word of knowledge, or faith, or the grace of healing, or the working of miracles, or prophecy, or the distinguishing of spirits, except because he is from the united fullness?”

No believer doubts that all these things he lists are gifts of the Holy Spirit. By concluding that the Spirit can do these things because he is from the united fullness, he plainly confesses that he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

The united fullness is the divinity of the Father and the Son. Since the divinity of the Father is full, and the divinity of the Son is full—because each is perfect and cannot be increased—they are nevertheless so united that there are not two fullnesses but one fullness; just as there are not two divinities but one divinity, and this one divinity is spoken of and exists. From this united fullness of the Father and the Son the Holy Spirit proceeds, himself also subsisting as full God, since he cannot receive any increase in quantity.

For if, according to the new heresy, the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and not from the united fullness, then he does not proceed from the united fullness, since the Son’s participation is absent there, where the Father’s singularity is present. But this is false and full of heretical depravity. Therefore, according to the judgment of blessed Athanasius, let it be said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the united fullness, since he subsists as the true God from the true divinity both of the Father and of the Son.

Likewise, farther on:

> “Since he said, ‘By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their strength’ (Psalm XXXII, 6), understand that this substantive Word was born as the Father’s own Word from no one other than the Father; and he also called the Spirit of his mouth the Spirit who proceeded from that very united substance.”

The Arians denied that both the Son and the Holy Spirit were consubstantial with the Father. Therefore, throughout the present discussion, he strives to establish the consubstantial divinity of both the Son and the Holy Spirit with the Father. In the present passage, when he says that the heavens were established by the Word of the Lord, he signifies the divinity of the Son; and when he says that all their power was established by the Spirit of his mouth, he signifies the consubstantiality of the Holy Spirit. He adds that the Spirit proceeded from that very united substance, plainly indicating that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, whose substance is united.

He consequently says:

> “Thus we find him to be from no other nature than from that very one.”

The Holy Spirit is understood here. The Arians blasphemed by saying that the Holy Spirit was from a nature different from that of the Father, for they maintained that he was a creature. Blessed Athanasius refutes them, saying that he is not from a nature different from the Father’s and that he proceeded from the united substance of the Father and the Son. Thus he testifies that the substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is united; this is what the Greeks call *ousia* (οὐσία), “substance,” and that the operation of the same Trinity is united.

[Note: [Col. 0299D] “In the eighth book.” If you consult the published editions, you will find that this passage is not treated in the eighth book of the treatise *On the Proper Persons*, but in the tenth, *On the Unity of the Faith*. Should we therefore say that Athanasius’s passage was incorrectly cited by Ratramnus? By no means. For Aeneas, bishop of Paris, also appended the same passage, in the same words, from the eighth book *On the Unity of the Faith*, in chapter 15 of his book *Against the Greeks*, below. We therefore prefer to say that copyists later than Ratramnus and Aeneas reversed the order of Athanasius’s books; hence passages copied by the ancients from that great man are not always easily found.]

In the eighth book:

> “Just as two pieces of wood joined together and cast into a furnace produce from the two pieces an inseparable flame, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the power of the Son, possessing that very power of divinity.”

Let no one suppose that blessed Athanasius intended to say that God the Father and God the Son were like two pieces of wood placed beneath one flame belonging to the Holy Spirit. Rather, he drew an analogy from material things for something that is not material or divisible by place, and he did so only partially, not in every respect. For no creature can be found wholly similar to the Creator. We should therefore weigh the meaning more intelligently.

He says that because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, as one fire and an inseparable flame proceed from two pieces of wood, the Holy Spirit should not for that reason be regarded as divisible, or as two spirits—one belonging to the Father and another to the Son. Rather, he is one and the same Holy Spirit, possessing the one and the same power of divinity that the Father and the Son possess, from whom he proceeds. Nor should this appear impossible or incredible, since in material things something can be born from two sources that subsists as one and does not admit duality.

Likewise, in the same book:

> “The Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father; but the Holy Spirit is the divine bond and the unity of the Trinity.”

By saying this, he shows that the Holy Spirit is the love of the Father and the Son; for there is nothing else by which the unity of the Holy Trinity could be more powerfully or suitably perfected. Yet “love” must not here be understood as a quality rather than a substance, since the Holy Spirit is one Person of the Holy Trinity. He calls the Holy Spirit the bond, or the unity, of the Father and the Son because, proceeding from both, he joins both while himself remaining undivided, unseparated, and consubstantial, since he exists as one of the Holy Trinity.

Likewise, in the booklet *On the Faith* (Book II, *On the Unity of the Faith*, addressed to Theophilus), he says:

> “The true Father begot the true Son: God from God, light from light, life from life, perfect from perfect, wholly from whole, full from full; not created but begotten, not from nothing but from the Father, of one substance with the Father; and the Holy Spirit, true God, neither unbegotten nor begotten, not created nor made, but the Spirit of the Father and the Son, always in the Father and the Son.”

Here too he says that the Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, because the Son is begotten, as he said above, whereas the Father is unbegotten. Yet the Spirit is not for that reason created or made, since he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, always remaining in the Father and the Son. By saying that he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, yet not created or made, he shows that he proceeds from both, being consubstantial and coeternal with them, always in the Father and the Son. Thus the unity of the Holy Trinity exists inseparably, neither by place nor by time.

Likewise, in the tenth book, he gives the testimony of the Apostle:

> “For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ” (I Corinthians II, 16).

After presenting this, he adds:

> “The Apostle confessed the mind of Jesus Christ in his own substance to be the Holy Spirit.”

Blessed Athanasius calls Christ’s own substance his divinity, and he professes the Holy Spirit to be the mind of that substance. “Mind” here must not be understood according to the hearing or sight of the human body, but according to what we call the mind of the soul, meaning its understanding.

He calls the understanding of Jesus Christ the Holy Spirit—not because Christ does not understand by himself, so that his understanding would be the Holy Spirit, for he is the wisdom of the Father: “Reaching from end to end mightily and ordering all things sweetly” (Wisdom VIII, 1). Rather, he wants Christ’s mind to be understood as the Holy Spirit in order to instruct us that the Spirit is from Christ’s substance. Just as the mind of the soul cannot be separated from the soul and is born from no other source than the soul, so the Holy Spirit, when he is called by the Apostle the mind of Jesus Christ, is not separated from the substance of Christ’s divinity and proceeds from no other source than that substance. He is consubstantial with the Son, having his procession from the divine substance.

Later:

> “Hearing, therefore, the Savior say, ‘I am the life’ (John XIV, 6), and Paul write, ‘For the law of the Spirit of life’ (Romans VIII, 2), and again, ‘God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts’ (Galatians IV, 6); and seeing also the Only-Begotten breathe upon the faces of the apostles and say, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John XX, 22), we are taught that the breath of the Son, who remains in his own life and substance, is the Spirit. And let us not suppose that he was begotten or created by the Son.”

By all these statements we are instructed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son and remains in his own life and substance. Although he is breathed forth by the Son—which means that he proceeds from the Son—he is nevertheless neither created nor begotten by him. The Holy Spirit is neither the Son nor a creature.

These statements clearly teach that the Holy Spirit is of the same substance as the Son, since he proceeds from him. He is not one of the creatures but the sanctifier of creatures. Therefore, when he calls him, according to the Apostle, the Spirit of the Son, he does not want him understood as subordinate, since he is not created; rather, he wants him understood as proceeding, though not begotten, since he is not the Son. He nevertheless received his proper existence from the substance of the Son, since he is one Person of the Holy Trinity.

Likewise, in the book *Discussion Against Arius*:

> “The Holy Spirit is shown not to be alien from the substance of the Father and the Son, since he does and speaks those things that are common to the Father and the Son, not from himself as an alien and outsider, but as a companion of one and the same nature. For if he spoke of his own things, he would undoubtedly be regarded as alien not only from the Father but also as false and deceptive. For, as the Son says, ‘Everyone who speaks falsehood speaks from his own things’ (John VIII, 44). Therefore he speaks truth here because he does not speak from what is his own—that is, not from himself—but speaks the things of the Father and the Son that must be spoken: ‘He will receive from what is mine,’ says the Son, ‘and will announce it to you’ (John XVI, 14). And to show that receiving from him means also receiving from the Father, he says: ‘Therefore I said, He will receive from what is mine, because everything that the Father has is mine’ (ibid., 15). You see, therefore, that the Holy Spirit is not separated from the Father and the Son, since he speaks those things that are known to be proper to the Father and the Son.”

He shows more clearly than light itself that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and is consubstantial with both. He says that the Spirit is not alien from the substance of the Father and the Son because he is not from himself but from those from whom he proceeds. Since he is of the same nature and substance as the Father and the Son, he does not speak what is his own but what is common to the Father and the Son.

For he is not from himself, and therefore the things he speaks are evidently those of the ones from whom he received both his being and his action and speech. Just as he does not speak of his own things, but received from the Father what he speaks—“Everyone who speaks falsehood speaks from his own things” (John VIII, 44)—so blessed Athanasius says that the Holy Spirit speaks truth because he does not speak from what is his own. He is not from himself, but speaks what belongs to the Father and the Son. Since he is consubstantial with them, he received from them what he speaks—not by existing first and receiving afterward, but by receiving through proceeding.

He introduces the Son saying: “He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John XVI, 14). He explains why the Son said this when he adds: “To receive from the Son means also to have received from the Father, because the Father and the Son are not separated in substance and are likewise in no way divided in the procession of the Holy Spirit.”

Therefore he adds that the Son said:

> “For this reason I said, ‘He will receive from what is mine,’ because everything that the Father has is mine” (ibid., 15).

This shows that when the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, he also proceeds from the Son; and when he proceeds from the Son, he also proceeds from the Father. Thus, concluding at the end, he says that the Holy Spirit is not separated from the Father and the Son, with whom he is joined both in nature and in operation. He speaks and says those things that are known to be proper to the Father and the Son. Proceeding from both and receiving from both, he receives operation just as he receives essence, undivided from them in both will and power, since he exists as one of the one and same Holy Trinity.

In teaching these things concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, blessed Athanasius approves that the Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son. If the Greek emperors wish to contradict this, let them consider which authorities they follow in their confession of the Holy Trinity. For the whole Catholic Church of Christ embraces, venerates, and defends the authority of this most blessed and thoroughly Catholic man.

Let what we have said concerning the Holy Spirit suffice, following the authority of our predecessors and imitating the teaching of the holy Scriptures. We wish to affirm that he is God, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son, in every respect equal in power, equal in might, and of one and the same majesty.

This question was examined and settled through the disputations of the holy Fathers, who refuted the perfidy of the heretics who, holding an evil opinion of the Holy Spirit, denied that he was the true God. We have not therefore been under the necessity of arguing extensively about this, although we have said a good deal on the subject when the occasion arose.

More has been said concerning his procession, which is the subject on which the controversy arose. We believe that what has been said is sufficient for those who love piety, cherish the truth, and pursue the light of wisdom rather than the darkness of error. Concerning both groups the Holy Spirit speaks through Solomon:

> “Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you. Rebuke a wise man, and he will hasten to accept it” (Proverbs IX, 8).

And again:

> “Do not speak in the ears of fools, for they will not receive anything unless you say what is in their heart” (Proverbs XXIII, 9).

Therefore let the calumniators of the Holy Spirit beware lest, unwilling to receive the discipline of wisdom, they be compared with those who prefer to set their own folly before the rules of the holy Scriptures.

What shall we call these modern men—not disputants, since they neither refute nor establish anything by reason, but advocates of novelty? To whom shall we say that they are like? When they wish to deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, they offer no reasoning or authority by which to prove what they say. Their position therefore appears rather to be the swelling of levity than the gravity of prudence.

Indeed, they are so arrogant that whatever they assert seems to them to possess the authority of truth. They resemble blind men who, not seeing the light, swear that the sun is not present above the earth even while the day shines with clear brightness.

But let us say to them what the Savior says to the Jews:

> “Search the Scriptures, for it is they that bear witness about me” (John V, 39).

Let these men likewise search the volumes of the holy Scriptures. They are the Scriptures that bear witness to the Holy Spirit, showing that he proceeds from the Father and the Son. Let them examine the doctrines of the Catholic Fathers; they will find there grounds for correcting their error and laying aside the swelling of their folly by which they think that they should be believed rather than the truth, and that the authority of their predecessors should be subordinated to their madness.

Let them first learn what they desire to teach, lest, while they boast of their ignorance as the highest expertise, they become like the one of whom Solomon says that, after he was exalted on high, he appeared to be a fool.

But it is now time to pass to the remaining accusations that they put forward maliciously. In their eagerness to criticize the Latins, they clearly demonstrate how open they themselves are to criticism.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0303]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Various Customs of the Church; What All Must Hold Uniformly in the Church; Customs Are Sometimes Changed

[Col. 0303C]

The objections that follow, although they seem to contain little wisdom but no small amount of ignorance, could have been omitted if they did not appear capable of producing the scandal of error even among the less prudent. For although they are of such a kind as to seem to display the outward form of piety, they can deceive many who are incautious and unable to distinguish true religion from its imitation.

Since they contain nothing concerning the dogma of faith, in which the fullness of Christianity consists, but merely recount the custom of their own Church, there was nothing in them that our Church either needed to approve or to refute. For they do not contain what the Apostle says: “I appeal to you all to say the same thing, and let there be no divisions among you” (I Corinthians I, 10).

What it is about which the Apostle urges us to think alike and speak alike, so that no division may arise, he shows elsewhere when he says:

> “One Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in all of you” (Ephesians IV, 5–6).

Among these things there is no diversity among believers. We believe with the heart, so that we may be justified, and confess with the mouth, so that we may be saved: the confession of the Holy Trinity; the birth of our Savior Jesus Christ from the Virgin; his passion, death, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and sitting at the right hand of the Father; and his coming as judge of both the living and the dead. Likewise, all of us who are Christians hold and confess with equal confession one baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. In these matters the Apostle urges us to have the same mind and not to hold different opinions.

The customs of the Churches, however, are not all the same, nor can they be held uniformly by everyone. At the beginning of the nascent Church, the Acts of the Apostles testify that the believers who were in Jerusalem possessed nothing as their own. They sold the possessions they had, placed their proceeds at the apostles’ feet, and distributed them to each person according to his need; for everything was common among them (Acts IV, 34–35).

But the Gentiles who believed were not held to the same form of religious practice. For the same Acts of the Apostles record what they had received as commands through the apostles and what they were to observe in order to become participants in eternal salvation. These commands were that they should abstain from the worship of idols, from fornication, from blood, and from what had been strangled. They did not wish to impose anything more upon them, as the letter sent by the apostles to the believers of the uncircumcision makes clear. It said approximately this:

> “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and so forth.”

And in conclusion:

> “If you keep yourselves from these things, you will do well” (Acts XV, 28–29).

Who does not see that the religious customs were different: one group possessed nothing as its own but lived in common, while the other retained all its possessions and was subject to only a very few commands?

For it is one thing to attain the summit of perfection, as did those who sold all they possessed and distributed it to the poor, and, becoming poor themselves, followed Christ in poverty. It is another thing for those who, scarcely embracing a few commands, remained within the beginnings of religious life. Yet on this account they did not become strangers to those who held the highest things, while they themselves followed, so to speak, the least demanding commands. Although they differed in the quality of their observance, they were nevertheless joined in the unity of faith.

Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, writes in his *Ecclesiastical History* (Book II, chapter 16) about the believers who lived in Alexandria, saying that they were devoted to the fervor of religion and conducted themselves according to an exceptional philosophy of life. He says:

> “[Note: [Col. 0305D] ‘First of all.’ Here we have thought it necessary to warn that Ratramnus, following Eusebius’s account as though it were beyond doubt that the people whose customs Philo described were to be counted among Christians, accepted what Eusebius had copied from Philo. All who devote themselves to literary study know that this is certainly not so. Although men of great learning, both of the earlier age and of our own, subsequently agreed with Eusebius, I see not a few who still find nothing in those Therapeutae that indicates they were Christians rather than Jews; and one may reasonably say that the question is still pending.] First of all, they renounce all their possessions, those who have devoted themselves to this kind of philosophy, and give up the goods in which they had shared. Then, secondly, they cast far away all the cares of life, leave the city, and live in little gardens or on whatever small plots of land they can find, avoiding the company of those whose purpose is unlike their own and the companionship of a different way of life—for they know that such associations impede those who wish to walk the arduous path of virtue.”

And later:

> “In each place there is a consecrated house of prayer, which is called a *semnion*, or monastery. *Semnion* may mean a gathering-place of honorable people, in which those who withdraw celebrate the honorable and chaste mysteries of life. They bring in absolutely nothing connected with food or drink, nor anything required for the other needs of the human body, but only books of the Law, volumes of the prophets, hymns to God, and other things of the same kind. Trained in their disciplines and exercises, they grow through continuous study toward a perfect and blessed life.

> “From sunrise until evening, all their time is spent in exercises of study, by which they are instructed in divine philosophy through the sacred Scriptures. They lead the laws of the Fathers toward allegorical understanding, because they consider the things written in the literal text of the Law to be forms and images of some profound and divine mystery hidden within.”

And in what follows:

> “They place self-restraint in the soul as a kind of foundation, and only then proceed to build the remaining virtues upon it. None of them takes food or drink before sunset, associating the time of daylight with the studies of philosophy and the care of the body with the night. Some do not come to share food even after three days, being driven by the more voracious hunger of study. Indeed, those who are occupied with the education of wisdom and the deeper understanding of the sacred books, as though longing for abundant banquets, cannot be filled; and the more intensely they contemplate, the more they are inflamed, so that they do not indulge the body with food until the fourth or fifth day, but finally on the sixth day, when it is not so much desired as necessary.”

Writing this about the way of life of believers—not only those living in Alexandria, but those scattered throughout Egypt—he shows how far their manner of life differed from that of the other believers throughout the whole world. For they had been so inflamed by desire for their heavenly homeland that the words could rightly be said to them: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). Although they dwelt in the flesh, they lived, so to speak, an angelic life on earth.

For it is reported that they were instructed in this manner by the blessed evangelist Mark, whom the apostle Peter had sent from Rome to Alexandria to preach Christ’s Gospel to that region. But did they therefore deprive the other Churches of Christ throughout the world, which lived in a very different manner, of their communion, or did they eagerly desire to convert them to their own rites and customs? They knew that grace had been given not only to each person but also to each Church according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Yet, because they had established continence as something like a foundation to be consecrated first, they did not condemn marriage—unless perhaps one ought to suppose that bishops and presbyters married wives among them, when it is established that even their laypeople abstained from marriage.

Nor did they dine every Sabbath, since it is clear that they prolonged their fasts continuously until evening, and that many of them scarcely provided food for their bodies before the third or sixth day.

Let the wise men—or at least the leaders—of the Greeks therefore consider how justly they criticize Romans who fast on the Sabbath. Let them then criticize those who fast every day; let them also criticize those who continue fasting throughout the entire week. Since that is plainly foolish, I would at least have them recognize from this the error of their ignorance or fickleness and strive rather to become imitators of virtue than to disparage those who fast. For, as the Apostle says, “the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and piety” (Romans 14:17). And the Savior conquered the devil not by eating lunch, but by fasting (Matthew 4).

Nor should all the Churches of Christ wish to follow the custom of their own religious observance, since they see that in the times both of the apostles and of their disciples there were different forms of observance. Yet they were not different in faith, although they were diverse in practice.

## CHAPTER II

### Further concerning the different customs of the Church; the Lenten fast formerly celebrated in different ways; the use of various foods; different rites; and how many sects formerly existed among the Jews

The Apostle writes to the Thessalonians: “For you, brethren,” he says, “became imitators of the Churches of God that are in Judea in Christ Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 2:14). By saying this he shows that the Churches of believers from the Gentiles were not all of the same virtue, but possessed different ministries and therefore also different customs.

The blessed Jerome also testifies to this in the Prologue to his epistles of Paul, saying:

> “I do not arrange them in the order in which they were written, but according to a certain progression of degrees, so that the first place is occupied by the epistles sent to Churches in which there was less teaching or virtue of observance. The middle place is occupied by those sent to Churches that had already withdrawn from their beginnings, but had not yet attained the summit of perfection. The last place is occupied by those sent to Churches possessing the degree of perfection, which excelled both in knowledge and in virtue, so that they had many beneath them and none above them.”

For what is shown by these words except that Churches differed in knowledge and virtue, and that their religious customs consequently were not the same? Those who lived together at Jerusalem, sharing in the breaking of bread, persevering in prayer, and possessing nothing as their own, conducted themselves in one way; those who retained what they possessed and commended the Gospel of Christ by their life, conduct, and faith according to the grace divinely bestowed upon them conducted themselves in a very different way. Among these the Apostle greatly extols the Thessalonians, to whom it was granted to suffer from their fellow countrymen the same things that those who lived at Jerusalem suffered from the Jews.

Concerning the varied customs of the Churches, Socrates says the following in his *Ecclesiastical History* (Book V, chapter 21):

> “That Easter is celebrated according to a certain customary practice in the provinces, I judge from this: no religion appears to preserve the same solemnities. For although they have one faith, they nevertheless arrange many legitimate matters differently concerning Easter; therefore only a few things need to be said. Even in the fasts, you find that observance differs among them. The Romans fast continuously for six weeks before Easter, except on the Lord’s Day. The Illyrians and all Greece, and Alexandria also, fast for six weeks before Easter, and they call those fasts Lent. Others begin their fasts seven weeks before Easter.”

And shortly afterward:

> “They also do not practice the same abstinence from foods. Some abstain altogether from living creatures; others eat only fish among living creatures; some, together with fish, eat birds, saying that according to Moses these have their substance from the water; others are known to abstain also from vegetables and eggs. Some eat only dry bread; others do not even eat that; others fast until the ninth hour and then refresh themselves without distinction among foods. Countless customs are found among different peoples. And because no ancient reading is found on this subject, I think that the apostles left this to the judgment of each person, so that each might do what is good, not from fear or necessity.

> “There is also some diversity concerning the celebration of assemblies. For although throughout the Churches established across the whole world sacrifices are celebrated on the Sabbaths of each week, this is not done in Alexandria and Rome, according to an ancient tradition. The Egyptians near Alexandria and the inhabitants of the Thebaid do hold assemblies on the Sabbath, but they do not receive the sacraments in the customary manner. After they have feasted and filled themselves with every kind of food, they make an offering and receive communion toward evening.

> “Again, in Alexandria the Scriptures are read on the fourth and sixth days of the week, and the teachers interpret them; everything is done except the customary solemn prayer.”

Further below he says:

> “In that same Alexandria, readers and reciters of the psalms are appointed indiscriminately, whether they are catechumens or already Christians, although all Churches appear to have faithful people in these orders. I also learned of another custom in Thessaly. When a cleric had lawfully married a wife before entering the clergy, he was deposed if he had intercourse with her after entering the clergy, whereas in the East everyone abstains voluntarily, not under compulsion, even bishops. Many of them have had children from a lawful wife even during their episcopate.

> “I also learned that this is observed in Thessaly: they baptize only during the days of Easter, and consequently many die without baptism. In Syrian Antioch they have the altar not toward the east of the church, but rather toward the west. In Greece, Jerusalem, and Thessaly they have prayers at evening resembling those of the Novatians living in Constantinople. In Caesarea of Cappadocia and in Cyprus, on the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day, bishops and presbyters interpret the Scriptures toward evening with lamps. In Alexandria a presbyter does not deliver a sermon; this practice began when Arius disturbed the Church. At Rome they fast on every Sabbath. In Caesarea of Cappadocia those who sin after baptism are suspended from communion. The Novatians around Phrygia do not admit those who have married twice. In Constantinople they are neither openly admitted nor publicly excluded; in the western regions, however, they are openly admitted.”

It would take too long if we wished to collect everything that the Churches spread throughout the world are known to observe, or are found to have observed in ancient times, with manifold variety. But it is enough to have briefly gathered these examples from the history of a single writer—and he was a Greek—so that the Greek emperors may understand how unjustly and incompetently they reproach the Romans for not observing their customs in every respect.

Let them therefore compel the entire body of Christ’s Churches, spread throughout the world, to submit to the laws of their customs; then, if they can, let them judge the Romans concerning the variety of their religion, because they appear to differ from the custom of Constantinople. Or are they wiser than the apostles? Can they demonstrate from the reading of the ancients that their custom is preferable to the Roman one?

For their own historian testifies that the holy apostles left this to the judgment of each person, so that each might do what is good, not from fear or necessity, but rather according to the decision of his own will. Although all possess one faith, they arrange different matters both concerning the legitimate observances of Easter and concerning the practice of fasting, some celebrating more days of fasting and others fewer. Nor do they observe their fasts with uniformity or equality of foods or times; rather, each is content according to the custom of his province, the practice of his ancestors, or the strength of his body.

The Churches also do not all hold their assemblies—that is, gatherings of the people—at the same time or in the same manner. The Alexandrians and Romans celebrate them in one way; the Egyptians and Thebans in another. For neither Romans nor Alexandrians hold gatherings on the Sabbath, whereas the Churches of Christ throughout the East are known to do so. The Egyptians, or those living in the Thebaid, although they hold gatherings—that is, assemblies—on the Sabbath, do not receive the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood while fasting, but toward evening, after being filled with food, contrary to the custom of the whole world.

The Alexandrians also add to their custom the fourth and sixth days of the week, on which they hold gatherings, reading the sacred Scriptures and having teachers interpret them, but they do not perform the solemn rite of offering on those days. Yet on this account they are not excommunicated by the other eastern Churches, from which they appear to differ.

Thessaly likewise has a custom different from that of the other eastern Churches. For after receiving clerical status, no one there is permitted—as that historian testifies—to have relations even with the wife whom he had lawfully married before entering the clergy; if he does so, he is deprived of his ministry. Throughout the other Churches of the East, however, no one is bound by such a law. Rather, the matter is left to his own judgment and the discretion of his will, so that not only the remaining ecclesiastical ranks, but also presbyters and bishops, may retain, if they wish, their own wives whom they lawfully possessed before ordination. They may not, however, marry if they had no wife, nor take a second marriage after the death of the first.

Yet this diversity does not separate anyone from communion, since custom is what distinguishes them. The Church of Thessaly also differs from the others in the time of baptism, since it baptizes only at Easter, although the authority of the ancients has appointed two seasons for baptism, namely Easter and Pentecost.

What should I say of Syrian Antioch, whose custom is to have the altar not toward the east of the church, but rather toward the west? The same historian reports that the people of Constantinople do not hold the same view concerning the admission or rejection of those who have married twice, but are divided: some approving their admission, others dissenting and holding that the rejection should stand. The entire western Church openly admits them without opposition. Yet although they are divided from one another in custom, they are not separated in the unity of communion.

I ask what kind of wisdom or zeal for sacred religion this is: that the Greek emperors do not permit the Romans to uphold what the universal Church throughout the world accepts, and wish neither the Romans nor the westerners to differ from their custom, when the easterners themselves are divided by manifold variety. Is Constantinople itself content with the practice of only one custom?

It is little to have said that the customs of believers in Christ are diverse unless we also demonstrate that the religious observance of the Jews was not uniform. Although they rendered due worship to one God and were bound by the precepts of the Mosaic law, they did not conduct themselves uniformly with regard to their way of life and rules of behavior, as the historian Josephus records in these words (*Book XVIII, chapter 2, beginning*):

> “Among the Jews,” he says, “there were from the beginning three philosophical schools handed down by ancestral institutions: those of the Essenes, the Sadducees, and the third, whose adherents were called Pharisees.
>
> “The Pharisees lead a daily life that is modest and altogether austere, indulging neither in softness [Note: [Cols. 0309D, 0310D] “Neither in softness.” Cotelerius so emended it; see vol. I of *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, p. 762. Previously the reading was *multitudini* (‘the multitude’), ineptly.] nor in luxury, but following whatever they have discovered by rational judgment to be necessary. They do not in any way resist those set over them; they honor their elders with fitting respect, so that they never answer anything contrary. They believe that all things are governed by fate, but they do not remove human free will. They hold that God’s judgment will come, and that there each person will receive according to his own merits, both those who have lived virtuously and those who have been corrupted by wickedness.
>
> “They say that souls are immortal; and they also say that in hell appropriate dwellings are assigned to each according to the merit either of virtue or of wickedness, just as each person had directed his purpose while alive. Some souls, they say, are confined in eternal prisons, while others receive the ability to live again. For these reasons they are acceptable and credible to the people.
>
> “Whatever pertains to the worship of divinity, they proclaim that the celebration of prayers and the establishment of temples must be carried out according to their interpretations. Their reputation for zeal is so great that many cities and a very large multitude flock to them with great enthusiasm, persuaded by the opinion that they are better than the others.
>
> “The Sadducees, however, believe that souls are mortal and perish together with the bodies. They observe no practices other than the law, and they consider it glorious to contend and resist the teachers of their philosophy; but their doctrine and manner of discipline reach very few. Their leading men, however, are honored with dignities and distinctions.
>
> “The Essenes refer everything to God. They say that the soul is immortal, and they proclaim that justice is a precious thing for which one must fight even unto death. In the temple they prohibit votive offerings. They do not celebrate sacrifices or offerings with the people, because they think that they differ from them greatly and deservedly in purity and holiness. They separate themselves from the common assembly and offer sacrifices in secluded places; but in the cultivation of character and manner of life they are excellent, devoting themselves with complete diligence to cultivating the land.
>
> “They also possess a practice that is worthy and very remarkable, one not found among other peoples, whether Greeks or barbarians: all their possessions are held in common, and everything is owned jointly among them. No richer man enjoys anything more than the others, and nothing is withheld from the poor, as though no one possessed anything at all.
>
> “They number more than four thousand men. They do not marry wives, nor are they eager to possess slaves; they consider the one an opportunity for injustice and the other an opportunity for sedition. Thus they live apart among themselves, assisting one another and serving each other in turn. They appoint receivers of revenues and stewards, who administer everything produced by the land for necessary uses. They choose the best men as priests. Their food is simple, and their clothing is inexpensive and clean.”

This same Josephus further describes (*ibid.*, at the end) a fourth philosophical school that existed among the Jews, whose founder he says was Judas. We have omitted it either because of brevity or because, having arisen recently, it was regarded as inferior to the others.

We have set out these matters concerning the Jews in order to show that, with regard to the worship of divinity and observance of the Mosaic law, they had a similar practice and burned with equal zeal; but in their moral conduct and religious manner of life they maintained practices that differed greatly.

We do not approve their religion in our own times. Rather, we wish to show that although they were alike in the worship of one God and differed in the manner of their way of life, they did not therefore separate themselves from one another’s communion. Remaining in the fellowship of unity, they tolerated with the greatest patience the fact that the customs of everyone’s conduct were not identical, knowing that diversity in moral practice did not conflict with their faith, since they shared the same assent concerning God and observance of the commandments of the law.

And yet the Greek emperors take it grievously that the Romans do not live according to the same practice as they do, nor follow their custom—that is, the Greek custom—although such uniformity cannot be found either among the Churches of Christ or among the Jews, among whom, before the preaching of the Gospel, the distinguished form of the worship of divinity was observed.

From this it is proved that such criticism did not arise from zeal for piety, but from the malice of envy and the boastfulness of pride. We must now come to the individual matters they appear to have brought forward; while seeming to display either wisdom or religion, they reveal their own foolishness and irreligion.

## CHAPTER III

### The Greeks blame the Romans for fasting on the Sabbath; why the Romans fast; the purpose of observing the Sabbath fast; the Greek objection and the response

They blame the Romans and westerners for fasting on the Sabbath, since they themselves—or the easterners—eat lunch every Sabbath, apparently unaware that not all western Churches follow this custom, but only the Roman Church and certain other western Churches. The greater number of westerners do not fast on the Sabbath. Yet they do not therefore criticize the Romans who fast, nor are they themselves criticized by fasting Romans.

For they know the Apostle’s statement: “Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat; and let the one who eats not judge the one who does not eat” (Romans 14:3).

Nor are all eastern Churches found not to fast on the Sabbath. Alexandria, together with Rome, already agrees by ancient tradition concerning the Sabbath fast. For assemblies are not held in Alexandria on that day, just as they are not held at Rome. This shows that the Alexandrians do not eat lunch on the Sabbath, just as the Romans do not. On days of assembly it is customary both to celebrate and receive the sacraments and to break the fast.

Among the Thebans and Egyptians, however, it is customary to break the fast on the Sabbath but not to receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood until evening, after they have eaten their fill. Yet they are not on this account found to be criticized by the other Churches, although they find no Church whose custom in this matter they follow. Whether they are also criticized by these recent critics, we do not know.

We do know, however, that the Romans were instructed by the apostle Peter, according to the tradition of the ancients, to fast on the Sabbath. For it is written that the apostles Peter and Paul fasted on the Sabbath in order to fight against Simon Magus. For this reason the custom of fasting every Sabbath was established among the Romans.

Concerning this matter, as the historian Eusebius writes in the little book *The Life of Silvester, Roman Pontiff* (Book I, chapter 8), the Greeks assembled before the blessed Silvester and raised a dispute against the Romans concerning the Sabbath fast. He answered them as follows:

> “This ought to be sufficient for the authority of our position: we know that the earlier apostles observed it in this way. Nevertheless, since your charity demands a reason, it must be supplied. If every Lord’s Day is observed because of the Lord’s resurrection, it is just that every Sabbath should be taken up with the urgency of fasting because of his burial, so that, mourning with the apostles over the death of the Lord Jesus Christ, they may deserve to rejoice with them over his resurrection.”

But the Greeks said that there was only one Sabbath of burial, on which the fast ought to be observed once a year. To them Pope Silvester said:

> “If every Lord’s Day is believed to be adorned with the glory of the resurrection, every day that precedes it is subject to fasting because of the burial, so that the one who has wept over the death may rightly rejoice over the resurrection.”

[Note: [Col. 0311] “Is subject to fasting.” The word “fasting” was added from a manuscript in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in which this *Life of Saint Silvester* is found.]

I would call this weeping compassion, while preserving the truth that the Lord’s Passion is the fullness of our joy. When the Greeks had accepted the explanation, they fell silent.

We have set this out to show that it is not something new for the Romans to fast on the Sabbath, nor something insignificant, since it is confirmed by apostolic authority and strengthened by a sufficiently fitting reason. It is therefore astonishing what wisdom these recent wise men possess, that they do not accept what their own ancestors are proved to have accepted.

From the time when Peter, the chief of the apostles, and Paul taught at Rome and commended the truth of their teaching by the shedding of their own blood, it has been the custom of the Romans and certain westerners to fast every Sabbath. Yet the Churches throughout the East that are not bound by this custom have not therefore judged the Romans to be strangers to their communion, although they themselves have the custom of not fasting on every Sabbath, just as they do not fast on the Lord’s Day.

For this reason the teacher Augustine writes to the presbyter Casulanus (Letter 86, and Letter 118 to Januarius), who was asking about the same question, replying as follows:

> “The Sabbath follows, on which day Christ’s flesh rested in the tomb, just as God rested from all his works on that day at the beginning of the world. From this there arose in the Church this variety concerning eating: some, especially the peoples of the East, preferred to relax the fast in order to signify rest; others, like the Roman Church and certain Churches of the West, preferred to fast because of the humility of the Lord’s death.
>
> “On the one day when Easter is celebrated, however, all fast in order to renew the memory of the event, by which the disciples in human grief mourned the Lord’s death. Thus even those who dine on the other Sabbaths throughout the year observe the fast on that Sabbath with the greatest devotion. In this way they signify both the disciples’ mourning on the one anniversary day and the blessing of rest on the other Sabbaths.
>
> “For there are two things that cause us to hope for the blessedness of the righteous and the end of all misery: death and the resurrection of the dead. In death there is rest, concerning which the prophet says: ‘My people, enter into your chambers; hide yourselves for a little while, until the Lord’s anger has passed’ (Isaiah 26:20). In the resurrection there is perfect happiness in the whole human being, that is, in flesh and spirit.
>
> “For this reason it came about that both of these were thought to be signified not by the labor of fasting, but rather by the cheerfulness of refreshment, except on the one paschal Sabbath, on which, as we have said, the disciples’ grief was to be marked by a longer fast because of the memory of the event.
>
> “But since, as I have already mentioned, we do not find in the evangelical and apostolic writings—which properly concern the revelation of the New Testament—a clear command that fasts be observed on particular days, this matter too, like many others that would be difficult to enumerate, has found a place for variety in the garment of that daughter of the King, namely, the Church.
>
> “I will tell you what the venerable Ambrose, the bishop of Milan by whom I was baptized, answered me when I asked him about this. When my mother was with me in that same city, while we were still catechumens and paid little attention to such matters, she was concerned to know whether she should fast on the Sabbath according to the custom of our city, or dine according to the custom of the Church of Milan. To free her from this uncertainty, I asked the man of God the question mentioned above.
>
> “He replied: ‘What more can I teach you about this than what I myself do? When I am here, I do not fast on the Sabbath; when I am at Rome, I fast on the Sabbath. And wherever you come, follow the custom of that Church, if you do not wish either to suffer scandal or to cause it.’
>
> “I reported this answer to my mother, and it was sufficient for her; she did not doubt that it ought to be obeyed. We followed it as well. But since it happens, especially in Africa, that one Church, or the Churches of one region, may have some who dine on the Sabbath and others who fast, I think that the custom of those people ought to be followed whose congregation has been entrusted to their governance.”

This is what the blessed Augustine, the catholic teacher, thought and wrote concerning the Sabbath fast. He judged that no more serious dispute should arise from it, but that each Church’s custom concerning fasting or dining on the Sabbath should be followed.

For those who dine on the Sabbath also appear to have a pious reason for doing so: they signify that on that day God rested from all his works, or the rest of believers in which the saints will rest at the resurrection, receiving their bodies and enjoying eternal repose with the Lord.

Likewise, those who fast have a pious reason for following that practice: on that day the disciples were physically saddened because of Christ’s death, and some of the faithful fast on the Sabbath because they wish to imitate their sorrow.

Others do not fast, so that by dining they may demonstrate the joy of the Lord’s resurrection, the joy that the apostles experienced when they saw the Lord risen. For, in imitation of the disciples’ sorrow, all the Churches throughout the world fast once a year on the Sabbath preceding holy Easter, although on the other Sabbaths they may dine or not dine.

The Romans, however, chose to commemorate this by fasting every Sabbath, just as the memory of the Lord’s resurrection is celebrated by all the Churches on every Lord’s Day.

Since both those who fast and those who dine on the Sabbath have a pious reason for what they do, and since no precepts of the New Testament are found either commanding or forbidding it, there ought to be no serious disagreement about this in the Churches of Christ. Rather, each person should be left free to choose what he prefers, while following the authority of his ancestors and the custom of his own Church.

If the Greek emperors had considered this, they would have raised no dispute about it, but would have maintained what their own ancestors maintained. Should anyone rightly be judged because he appears to fast for the sake of piety?

There are also other days on which certain Churches have a weekly custom of fasting, such as the fourth and sixth days. A reason is given for this, as the blessed Augustine says: on the fourth day the leaders of the Jews assembled and took counsel to seize and kill Jesus by deceit. On the sixth day they crucified him.

He writes concerning these matters in this way (Letter 86):

> “Why does the Church fast especially on the fourth and sixth days? The following reason appears to be given. When the Gospel is considered, the Jews are found to have made their plan to kill the Lord on the fourth day of the week, which is commonly called the fourth feria.
>
> “After an intervening day, on the evening of which the Lord ate the Passover with his disciples—the end of the day that we call the fifth Sabbath—he was handed over during the night that already belonged to the sixth Sabbath, the day on which his Passion was made manifest. This was the first day of Unleavened Bread, beginning at evening.
>
> “But Matthew the evangelist says that the fifth Sabbath was the first day of Unleavened Bread, on the evening following which the Passover supper was to take place. At that supper unleavened bread began to be eaten together with the sacrificial lamb. From this it is gathered that it was the fourth day of the week when the Lord said: ‘You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified’ (Matthew 26:2 and following).
>
> “Accordingly, that day was assigned to fasting. For, as the evangelist continues and says: ‘Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the court of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas, and took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him.’
>
> “After an intervening day, concerning which the Gospel says: ‘On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples approached Jesus, saying, “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?”’ (ibid., 17), the Lord suffered on the sixth Sabbath, as no Christian doubts. Therefore that sixth day is rightly assigned to fasting as well.
>
> “For fasts signify humility; hence it is said: ‘I humbled my soul with fasting’ (Psalm 34:13).”

The blessed Augustine writes this to the presbyter Casulanus concerning the fast of the fourth and sixth days, explaining why it was instituted. Yet this fast, which is observed on the fourth or sixth day of the week, is not practiced by all Churches, whether eastern or western, but only by certain Churches that have chosen to observe it.

Those who fast on these days are not therefore criticized by those who dine, but each Church maintains the custom it received from its ancestors. It is therefore astonishing that the Greeks reproach the Romans concerning the Sabbath fast, when they do not reproach either the Alexandrians, who fast on the fourth and sixth days, or the other Christians throughout the East, although it is clear that the people of Constantinople are bound by no law or custom to fast on the fourth or sixth day of the week.

On the island of Britain people fast every sixth day, yet they are not excommunicated by those throughout the West who do not have the custom of fasting on that day.

The nation of the Scots, which inhabits the island of Ireland, has the custom in the monasteries of monks, canons, and any other religious communities of fasting at all times except on the Lord’s Day and feast days, and of allowing food to the body only at the ninth hour or in the evening: at the ninth hour during the summer, and in the evening during the winter.

Since no Church, whether eastern or western, is bound by this custom, those who fast in this way are nevertheless neither excommunicated nor criticized by those who do not fast in the same manner.

It has already been said above how great was the fervor of fasting among the believers in Alexandria when the Christian religion first began there. No one took food before sunset. Many ate on the fourth day, and some on the sixth, food that was not so much desirable to the body as necessary. Yet those who fasted in this manner, contrary to the custom of the other believers, were not excommunicated or criticized by those who did not retain this custom of fasting.

And yet the Romans are criticized for fasting on the Sabbath, whether because of the memory of the Lord’s burial, or because of the disciples’ sorrow over the Lord’s death, or because it is handed down that the chief apostles fasted on that day in order to fight against the deceit and trickery of Simon, and certainly against the devil and the madness of Nero.

Some also have the custom of observing the fifth day of the week by not fasting on it, just as they do not fast on the Lord’s Day.

Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, approves this in the book he composed concerning the deeds of Pope Silvester, saying:

> “And Pope Silvester said: We ought to celebrate the anniversary of the chalice as a solemn day in the same way as the Lord’s Day, on which the celebration of the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and divine blood took its beginning from the Lord himself.
>
> “On this day the holy chrism is prepared throughout the world. On this day penitents are assisted through pardon; those who are divided return to concord; the angry are reconciled; rulers grant pardon to criminals; masters forgive wicked slaves; judges spare robbers; prisons are opened throughout the world.
>
> “On this day those who had shut themselves away in tears because of the severity of their sins go forth to the joy of the feast—the very sins which they may perhaps have committed by laughing, becoming angry, or transgressing in some other way.
>
> “When the holy Silvester had said these and many similar things, all the opposition ceased. The Greeks, most Christian and learned men, are said to have opposed it, saying: ‘Truly the apostolic see learned this from Peter, and it cannot be refuted by any argument.’”

[Note: “The anniversary of the chalice.” In the San-Germain manuscript the wording is quite different: “Why is it thought that Thursday should be excluded from the festivals of Christians, when it is established that the Lord’s ascension was revealed to the apostles on that day? On this day also the sacrifice…”]

If the Romans are judged because they fast on the Sabbath, why are those who fast on the fifth day of the week not judged? Or why do the modern Greeks prefer to be wiser than their ancestors, so that they seek to criticize what those ancestors accepted and praised with worthy commendation?

They are not proved to be either more religious or more learned than their predecessors; let them beware lest they be judged more insolent. For why can what was observed peacefully for so many centuries now no longer be tolerated? Why is it instead heaped up into the scandal of discord by the manufacture of disputes?

Have they been so wrapped in the darkness of ignorance that they think the Churches of Christ will wish to change, because of the criticism of insolent men, what they preserved unshaken for many centuries?

Melchiades, the thirty-third apostolic bishop of the Roman See after the apostle Peter, decreed concerning Thursday that, under no circumstances, should any of the faithful fast on Sunday or Thursday, because the pagans celebrated those days as though with a sacred fast. And although the reason concerning Sunday’s meal seems the stronger—the reason observed by the whole Church, namely, that Christ rose from the dead on that day and that the rest of the age to come is signified by it—yet what the blessed Silvester, disputing with the Greeks, established concerning Thursday must not be despised either. For the Catholic Church ought rather to destroy the fasts of the pagans than imitate them, just as it rejects all their festivals, in which they are known to serve demons rather than the true God.

Thus it was fittingly determined that Christians should not fast on those days on which pagans are known to fast, lest superstition in demonic worship appear to stain the holy character of pious religion. Nevertheless, although Sunday is a general observance among all Christians, on which they do not fast, it is not customary for everyone to observe Thursday in the same way, since many fast on that day, especially during the Lenten fast before Easter. Yet no dispute therefore arises among the Churches of Christ, since each preserves the custom of fasting or dining that it received from its forebears. If the leaders of the Greeks would attend to this, they would not so lightly criticize Latins or Romans who fast on Saturday; rather, content with their own custom, they would marvel at the Queen standing beside Christ in a garment of gold, clothed all around in varied adornment, and would not try to subject her to fixed rules concerning something for which they possess no authority either from the New Testament or from the Old.

## CHAPTER IV

The Romans are reproved because they do not observe Lent according to the Greek custom. Why a forty-day fast is kept before Easter. The number of weeks is observed in various ways. Why some Westerners fast for thirty-six days. The number forty is explained.

[Col. 0317D]

Let us now turn to what they attempt to criticize concerning the Lenten fast before Easter. They say that we do not fast as they do, since according to their custom we do not abstain from meat for eight weeks before Easter, nor from cheese and eggs for seven weeks. In speaking thus, they act as though all the Eastern and Western Churches, except the Roman Church, preserved this custom of theirs. Yet there is great diversity both in the Eastern and in the Western Churches, as has already been shown above: some Churches fast for six weeks before Easter, apart from Sundays; others for six weeks; others begin their fast seven weeks before Easter. That is, some begin the Easter fast six weeks before Easter, some in the seventh week, and many in the eighth; others even add a ninth week.

Let these critics therefore see whom they have as companions or imitators. In the first place, they do not agree with the Romans, who fast continuously for six weeks before Easter, apart from Sundays; nor do they agree with those who begin the fast in the seventh week. For they say that during that week they abstain from eggs and cheese, but that they have not yet undertaken the complete observance of the fast, as do those who have devoted seven weeks to the Easter fast.

[Col. 0318B] They also say that for eight weeks before Easter they abstain from meat, practicing not the full but only half of their fast’s abstinence. In this they are far removed from those who begin the fast in the eighth week in such a way that they make no change in the variety of their abstinence. Nor do they appear to have any communion with those who anticipate the Easter season by fasting for nine weeks, since they acknowledge that during the ninth week they abstain neither from eggs, nor from cheese, nor from meat.

Since, then, they are found to differ in the observance of the Easter fast not only from Westerners but also from Easterners, let them say on what grounds they criticize the Romans, and why they do not fear being criticized by other Churches with which they themselves appear not to agree in the Easter fast. Or let them produce either Old or New Testament precepts, or some authority by which they may defend their own custom or rightly criticize the Roman custom.

Since they cannot do this, let the varied custom of the Churches concerning fasting at least teach them that this observance does not arise from any divine command by which those who fast are compelled by necessity. Rather, it remains a matter of each person’s purpose and free choice, so that, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, each may offer God what seems right and possible for him—not something imposed as necessary, but our voluntary good. Yet this does not mean that the matter rests solely on each individual’s private choice: each Church must preserve the authority and custom of its forebears, so that each person may guard what each Church received from its founders to be observed.

Unless, perhaps, the Greeks are to be considered superior on the ground that in the seventh week they eat neither eggs nor cheese—although they are far surpassed by those who eat nothing cooked throughout the whole of Lent, and still more by those who live on bread alone. They appear far inferior also to those who are nourished not even by this, but only by eating herbs. Nor can they in any way be compared with those who throughout the whole of Lent give food to their bodies scarcely once or twice a week.

Let them therefore cease exalting themselves above others, lest they fall; rather, let them humble themselves so that they may rise, and recognize that the harmony of peace and the unity of love are more important than the observance of fasts. [Col. 0319A] Let them also consider why this variety in fasting before Easter has arisen.

In the end, both evangelical and legal authority teach us that a forty-day fast ought to be celebrated. For we read in the Gospel that the Savior continued fasting for forty days and nights. In the Old Testament it is written that Moses completed this same number of days by fasting twice: once before he received the Decalogue of the Law, which the Lord granted him; and a second time after, provoked by the people’s transgression, he shattered the tablets at the foot of the mountain. For two reasons he again continued a fast of forty days and nights: first, so that he might render God’s anger against the transgressors propitiable; and second, so that he might once more be found worthy to receive the Law from the Lord.

Elijah too, fleeing Jezebel’s anger, fasted for forty days and nights as he traveled through the wilderness until he reached Mount Horeb, the mountain of God. From this arose the custom that took root in the Churches of continuing a fast for forty days.

Since, then, nearly all the Churches of Christ strive to celebrate this number by fasting, yet do not all agree on the number of weeks, this is caused by the varying succession of days. Among human beings, the number forty is acknowledged as the measure of the Easter fast, but not everyone fasts on all the days of each week. Some dine only on Sunday; others fast neither on Saturday nor on Sunday; some are found to break their fast on Thursday.

Because they do not fast on Sunday, while fasting on the other days of each week, they do not complete the number forty, since four days are lacking from the total. Therefore those who wish to complete forty days fast for seven weeks, not merely six, before Easter, although six weeks contain not only forty but forty-two days. When the six Sundays are subtracted from the forty-two days, thirty-six days remain on which the fast is celebrated; but in order to complete the number forty, they fast for four days in the seventh week. Thus in the seventh week they fast not six days but only four, which, added to the thirty-six days, complete the number forty.

[Col. 0319D] Those who fast neither on Saturday nor on Sunday, yet desire to complete forty days before Easter, must begin the fast in the eighth week. For they are shown to fast only five days in each week, and eight times five makes forty; thus the prescribed number forty is completed in eight weeks.

But those who add Thursday to the two days—Sunday and Saturday—on which they do not fast cannot fast for forty days before Easter unless they undertake a fast of nine weeks. For when three days are removed from each week—Sunday, Saturday, and Thursday—four days of fasting remain in each week. Nine times four makes thirty-six, not forty. Thus, although they do not complete forty days by fasting, they nevertheless say that they complete Lent.

For this reason the Greeks have nothing with which to reproach the Romans concerning the difference in the number of weeks. What the Greeks do in eight weeks, fasting no more than five days in each week, both the Roman Church and the Western Church are known to complete in six weeks, with four additional days in the seventh week. For if the Greeks fasted six days of the eight weeks, as the Romans, or nearly all Latins, do, they would fast not merely for Lent but far more than Lent: eight times six makes forty-eight days.

Let the Greeks therefore consider, if they fast for so many days before Easter, what authority they follow. For neither the Savior, nor Elijah, nor Moses observed this number by fasting. If they complete the total of their fast in forty days, so that they do not differ from the New and Old Testaments, they find nothing in the Westerners to criticize, since they fast for as many days before Easter as the Greeks themselves.

But if fasting is the practice of humility, according to what the Psalmist confesses: “And I humbled my soul with fasting” (Psalm 34:16), then both the Romans and the Westerners fast for more weeks than the people of Constantinople. For the Western Church does not solemnly celebrate during the nine weeks before Easter the customary hymns—namely, the Alleluia—or the festivals of the martyrs. [Col. 0320C] Rather, it abstains from every festive act of glorification that it is accustomed to practice throughout the year, so that it may rejoice more gloriously on the day of the Resurrection, having taken care to anticipate holy Easter by humbling itself for a longer period.

The Lord also commanded the children of Israel through Moses, after the making of the calf, to put off their adornment, so that the Lord might know what he would do with them—not because he was ignorant of the punishment with which the guilt of idolatry ought to be struck, but because, through the affliction of humility, the transgressing people might show how they acknowledged the guilt of their transgression and by what kind of satisfaction they wished to cleanse what they had done wrong.

What, then, are we to understand by the people’s adornment, which they are commanded to put off, except the splendor of joy in which they were accustomed to rejoice before they incurred the guilt of idolatry? Thus the Roman or Western Church puts off its adornment by humbling itself when it abandons the festive joy and the delight of hymns in which it was accustomed to exult throughout the year. Assuming the habit of humility, it lays aside the glory of exultation, so that, approaching the face of the Lord in the habit of humility, it may receive the Easter festivals with the joy of exultation.

The Greek emperors therefore have no grounds on which they can rightly condemn either the Romans or the Westerners because they do not fast for as many weeks before Easter as the Greeks do, since by the number of days they are made equal through fasting for forty days. Since fasting signifies humility, and humility is the laying aside of joy, the form of affliction, the habit of sorrow, and the removal of gladness, the Romans or Latins may rightly be said to fast more than the people of Constantinople, since they anticipate Easter by humbling themselves for nine weeks, although that is the principal consideration.

Therefore the critics of the Romans ought to criticize themselves—if indeed they wish to be subject to the laws of discipline—for the custom of fasting before holy Easter is not uniform among all Churches, nor are they compelled to these practices by any law of divine commands. Rather, each Church is permitted to follow the custom of its forebears. If they had known this, they would not appear so brazen in their criticism, especially of those whose practice is established by apostolic teaching and by the consideration of a sufficiently honorable reason.

[Col. 0321B] In fact, the Romans fast continuously for six weeks before Easter, apart from Sunday, on which they break the fast. Thus, if they are known to complete thirty-six fasting days—four fewer than forty—the reason why they do this is sufficiently pious and plainly evident to those who wish to consider it. The solar year consists of 365 days. If you take a tenth of these days, you have thirty-six days. We are commanded to offer the Lord the tithes of our labors. Therefore it is not without reason that we offer him also a tenth of our days: having lived for ourselves throughout the whole year, we live for the Lord by offering him a tenth of the year’s days, and we cleanse through serving the Lord during these days the sins that we committed while living for ourselves throughout the year.

[Col. 0321C] But because there are very few in the West who do not complete forty days of fasting before Easter, the reason must also be given why they are content with the number forty. Setting aside the evangelical or legal authority by which we are clearly taught to devote forty days to fasting, we may consider that there are ten commandments of the Law, which we are commanded to serve according to the institutions of the Old Testament, and four Gospels, by which we are led into newness of life. Four times ten completes forty; and every person who serves the Lord is understood to have reached the sum of perfection if he supplements the legal Decalogue with the perfection of the Gospel.

It is also established that the human being consists of four elements, just as the world does. And because we transgress the Decalogue of the Law in many ways, it is necessary that, by afflicting ourselves four times ten, we obtain forgiveness of our sins.

This, then, is the reason why the Romans or Latins have chosen to fast for forty days before Easter; it is shown to be both religious and mystical, as was demonstrated above. Therefore this criticism of the number of weeks of fasting before Easter is unjust and supported by no weight of reason. It should consequently be regarded as nothing—except that charity, which bears all things, compels us to answer such objections when they are found to have been made contrary to reason—so that, once they have learned the reason, they may not dare to criticize what they recognize to be observed with the authority of propriety and the dignity of religion, and may return peacefully to the harmony of unity, from which they had not feared to depart through foolish presumption.

## CHAPTER V

The matter of shaving the beard or head is discussed.

Let us now examine the fact that they do not hesitate to criticize the clergy for shaving the beard—not only among the Romans but among all the Western Churches of Christ. This practice is recognized as so trivial that it might rightly be judged to deserve no answer, lest those who choose to answer something without any basis be thought equal or even inferior in triviality to such men. For what does the shaving or preserving of the beard contribute—not only to the perfection of justice but even to its beginning?

Let those who criticize state, then, what command concerning this they find either in the New or in the Old Testament. And, to press the matter further, what can they indicate as having been determined concerning it in the writings of the apostles or in the decrees of ecclesiastical teachers? This matter, like many others, has been left to the custom of individual Churches, so that, out of regard for their forebears, they may either grow or shave the hair of the head or the beard.
