Some have the custom of shaving the beard or the head; others do not shave the beard but strip the head completely of hair; still others prefer to remove all the hair from the face, shave the crown of the head, and leave the portion of hair that lies between the shaved crown and the temples. Others, however, do not shave the beard, but shave the head in part and leave it partly shorn.

This clerical appearance is not uniform in all Churches but varies and differs according to the custom of their forebears. Nor has any dispute ever arisen on this matter between the Western or Eastern Churches. Each has retained what it received from its predecessors, or what the usage of its provinces approved.

The apostle Paul reproved the Corinthians because the men either grew their hair or covered their heads, while the women neither covered their heads nor grew their hair. The apostle rightly criticized this custom, because although it seemed plausible to the Corinthians, it nevertheless appeared contrary to nature. He clearly shows why he criticized it when he says: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (1 Corinthians 11:7).

He similarly explains why a woman ought either to grow her hair or cover her head, saying: “The woman ought to have authority over her head, because of the angels” (ibid., 10). Let the clergy therefore consider this—those who grow the beard but strip the head entirely of hair, and, being unable to endure the force of cold or heat, or rather wishing somehow to conceal such a disfigurement of their appearance, cover their heads with a garment [Note: [Col. 0321D] “They cover their heads with a garment.” Let those who discuss the clothing of monks consider this passage. [Col. 0322D] For when Ratramnus warns that the custom of those who shave their heads and cover them with a garment may in some way be criticized, and adds that he does not write this because he thinks that custom altogether deserving of condemnation, but to show the Greek leaders that among them there is something they could criticize more easily than what is practiced among the Latins, he sufficiently shows, in my judgment, that in these regions monks of his own age did not use the kind of garment that they now use.]—whether they are proved to act contrary to the apostolic command.

For they cannot deny that they act against Paul’s statement: “Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head” (ibid., 4).

We do not say this because we perhaps prefer to criticize such a custom. We know that this kind of appearance is also an indication of humility. Rather, we say it to warn the Greek emperors that they have nearby something they might criticize or correct, and that they should not lightly criticize those who are far away, the Romans or Latins. If these shave the beard, they nevertheless neither grow their hair nor cover their heads when prophesying or praying, even though they possess the authority of the holy Scriptures by which they can most effectively defend their custom.

In the Old Testament, the Nazirites had the custom, when they completed the period of their consecration, of shaving both head and beard and placing the hair in the fire of the sacrifice. By this they signified that they consecrated to the Lord not only their actions but also all their thoughts.

For this reason the divine word speaks to Ezekiel the prophet: “And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword, a razor for shaving the hair; take it and draw it over your head and your beard” (Ezekiel 5:1). He was a priest, not of a foreign stock, but born from priestly descent; therefore, according to the custom of the Nazirites, he is commanded to shave both head and beard.

In the Acts of the Apostles it is also written that Prisca and Aquila, Jews who believed in Christ, had their heads shaved at Cenchreae, for they had a vow, as Scripture subsequently indicates. At Jerusalem the elders also say to the apostle Paul: “We have four men who have a vow upon themselves. Take them and purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads, and everyone will know that the things they have heard about you are false, but that you yourself walk in observance of the Law” (Acts 21:23–24). Shortly afterward: “Then Paul took the men, and on the following day, having been purified with them, entered the temple, announcing the completion of the days of purification” (ibid., 26).

Following this custom, the clergy of the Romans, or of nearly all the Churches throughout the West, shave their beards and cut their hair, taking their form both from those who in the Old Testament were called Nazirites and from those who are read to have done such things in the New Testament.

Yet they do not strip their heads entirely of hair. Rather, by leaving part of it, they signify in this form both royal dignity and priestly distinction. For kings have the particular dignity of wearing crowns on their heads, while pontiffs wore tiaras on their crowns in the temple. A tiara bears the likeness of a hemisphere, whereas a crown, being circular in shape, is accustomed to encircle the head.

The blessed apostle Peter says to believers: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9). Wishing to signify this, the clergy of the Romans or Latins form on the crown of the head the likeness of a tiara through the shaving of the vertex, by which they indicate priestly dignity. The remaining hair, encircling the head but not touching the crown, represents the appearance of a crown, by which royal dignity is displayed. Thus royal priesthood is designated by both forms.

Christ is also expressed as king and priest, as the prophet testifies: “The Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king” (Isaiah 33:22). Again: “You will rule them with an iron rod” (Psalm 2:9). That he is a priest, the Father testifies to the Son, saying: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4).

Therefore, whether the clergy of the Latins wear this form on their heads in order to signify the priesthood and royal throne of Christ, or whether they signify by this appearance that the whole Christian nation excels in both royal and priestly dignity, this is what they represent.

By the exposure of the face, they show purity of heart, alluding to the apostolic statement: “But we, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18). The face of the head signifies the face of the heart. For just as the head is the citadel of the heart, so the mind—which in this passage is called the heart—is the summit of the soul. The face of the heart ought continually to be stripped of earthly thoughts, so that it may behold the glory of the Lord with a pure and sincere gaze and be transformed into it through the grace of contemplation.

The blessed apostle Peter also, as well as many others both among the apostles and among Christ’s disciples, is read to have shaved both beard and head. Indeed, even to this day the images that are fashioned by the art of painters in this form testify that Peter did this. Neither the Apostle nor the other disciples of Christ, who were not displeased to assume such an appearance, feared the criticism of the Greeks on that account.

Since no one before the Law or after the Gospel has hitherto raised this question, let the Greek emperors see why they attempt to criticize something that in no way deserves to be subject to the slander of criticism. If shaving the beard is a sin or any transgression of divine law, let them say why the prophet shaved his beard at the Lord’s command; why this custom existed among the Nazirites; and why, finally, the apostles did not recoil from it.

But let us set aside this objection, since we see that it rests neither on the strength of reason nor on any dignity of seriousness. If we did not think that it could mislead the less prudent, it would more rightly be judged that no answer or discussion should be made concerning it.

## CHAPTER VI

The celibacy of the clergy is defended against the Greeks. The celibacy of the clergy is asserted by ecclesiastical laws.

We must now consider their objection that the Romans condemn marriage, because they not only refuse to permit priests to take wives but completely forbid it. Although in their other objections they appear excessively superstitious, in this matter they seem either greatly astonishing or greatly pitiable.

They are astonishing if they are so far removed from the light of wisdom that they do not understand that in this action the Romans appear not merely free from blame but even worthy of praise. For the good of continence and the distinction of chastity are so manifestly excellent that they are admired even by pagans. Although this virtue is praiseworthy in every rank, it is especially so in priests and in the other ministers of the sacred altar. The other virtues make them distinguished, but the splendor of holiness and the outstanding dignity of chastity make them still more distinguished.

They are pitiable if, knowing these things, they nevertheless strive against their own conscience and do not hesitate to criticize what they know to be praiseworthy. They ought to fear what the Holy Spirit says through Isaiah: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isaiah 5:20).

How, then, do they decide that it follows that the Romans should be judged to condemn marriage if among them bishops or priests do not enter into marriage? If, on that account, they are to be regarded as condemners of marriage, then the fathers of both the Old and the New Testaments will be subject to the same judgment.

The prophet Elijah, at whose command heaven is opened and closed, and who is lifted to heaven by angelic ministry, did not take a wife. Jeremiah the prophet, sanctified in the womb, preferred the good of virginity and the purity of chastity to marriage. Daniel, called a man of desires, chose continence rather than conjugal union. Yet none of these condemned marriage, although they did not enter into its bonds.

The Savior chose to be born of a virgin; nevertheless, to approve holy marriage, he did not refuse to attend a wedding. John earned from Christ the privilege of love because he chose discipleship to Christ over marriage. The apostle Peter, before Christ raised him to the dignity of apostleship, did not reject marriage. But after he had been elevated to apostolic dignity and sent to preach the Gospel, although he did not reject his wife, he avoided conjugal relations. There is no doubt that the other apostles did the same. Yet no sound person will say that these men condemned marriage, although they embraced the holiness of continence.

Moreover, how can the Romans be accused of condemning the bonds of marriage, when marriages are celebrated among them and children are born from lawful marriage?

The blessed apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians: “I wish that all people were as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (1 Corinthians 7:7). What he meant when he said that he wished all people to be as he himself was, he explains slightly earlier, where he established instructions for married people concerning how they should serve one another, since neither man nor woman has authority over his or her own body, but preserves it according to the permission of the other. In conclusion he added: “I say this by way of concession, not by command” (ibid., 6). Immediately he added: “I wish that all people were as I myself am,” and the rest.

By this he plainly signifies that he was celibate and was not bound by the union of a wife. Elsewhere he writes: “Do we not have the right to take along a believing woman as a companion?” (1 Corinthians 9:5). He does not deny that Barnabas was his companion in this matter, saying: “Do Barnabas and I not have this right?” (ibid., 6).

Yet although the blessed Apostle makes this declaration concerning himself, he in no way condemns marriage. He both gave commands to married people and urged the incontinent to marry if they could not remain continent. The Savior and the blessed Paul so completely do not reject the bonds of marriage that they establish that a wife should not leave her husband, nor a husband his wife, except on account of fornication; and if they should separate, they are to remain unmarried.

Nevertheless, wishing to persuade them to continence, Paul writes to these same Corinthians: “This, then, I say, brothers: the time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep as though they did not weep; those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:29–31).

Earlier he had given the incontinent permission to marry, offering a remedy for salvation to the weak, saying: “For it is better to marry than to burn” (ibid., 9). Now he commands that the reins of lust be restrained even with one’s own wife. For what else does he mean by saying, “Those who have wives should be as though they had none,” except that the wantonness of desire should be restrained even from one’s own wives, and that one should serve the love of children more than the desire of the flesh?

For this reason he had said earlier: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (ibid., 1). But because this virtue is not present in everyone, he therefore says: “But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband” (ibid., 2). Wishing afterward to cut away what is here conceded to weakness, he says: “Those who have wives should be as though they had none.”

He warns that one should not always serve weakness, but should grow accustomed to the holiness of chastity, because the form of this world is passing away. The form of the world consisted in seeking carnal posterity, rejoicing in the generation of children, and exulting in a crowd of relatives. But because the world, placed at its end, awaits its conclusion, and, as the blessed John says, “It is the last hour” (1 John 2:18), one should seek not carnal offspring but rather spiritual succession: “So that those who live may no longer live for themselves but for Christ, who died and rose again for them” (1 Corinthians 5:15).

Therefore he says that those who weep should become as though they did not weep, so that through the hope of eternal joys they may be consoled for the ruin and tribulations of this world. Similarly, those who rejoice in temporal worldly advantages should become as though they did not rejoice, so that, despising the joys of temporal goods because of their fragility and changeability, they may rather rejoice and exult in eternal things, and thus be able to attain everlasting joys.

Likewise, those who buy should not desire to possess here, but should wish their possession to be in heaven, saying with the Psalmist: “What have I in heaven, and besides you what have I desired on earth?” (Psalm 73:25). Thus those who use this world should do so as though they did not use it, so that it may be for them something passed through, not something desired; a road, not a homeland; something viewed from the side, not something possessed out of a love of holding or enjoying it.

Therefore he subsequently says: “I wish you to be without anxiety. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided. The unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, so that they may be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (1 Corinthians 7:32–34).

Let the leaders of the Greeks, then, who seek to criticize the Romans concerning the continence of priests, consider in what condition they wish the ministers of the altar to be established: whether they want them to be without anxiety, as the Apostle wishes, or entangled in the anxieties of the world, which the Apostle does not desire.

If they are without wives, they are free from worldly anxiety and concern themselves with the things of the Lord, seeking at all times to please God and reflecting on the apostolic saying: “Whatever you do, do everything always in the name of the Lord” (Colossians 3:17).

But if they were to live with wives, they would necessarily become entangled in worldly anxieties and would seek to please their wives rather than God. Anyone of this kind is divided, because he stands between love of his wife and love of God, unable to say with the prophet: “The Lord is my portion; I have said that I will keep your law” (Psalm 119:57). Nor can he say with the blessed Jeremiah: “The Lord is my portion, says my soul; therefore I will wait for him” (Lamentations 3:24).

The Apostle says: “The unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Corinthians 7:34). Is it fitting, then, for the priests of the Lord and ministers of the altar to be inferior to unmarried women and virgins, so that while those women think about the things of the Lord and preserve holiness in both body and spirit, these men think about the things of the world and reject holiness of body and spirit?

For those who think about the things of the world, desiring to please their wives, are deprived of both kinds of holiness, since, as the Apostle says: “The married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (ibid.).

The Savior says that no one can serve two masters (Matthew 6:24). Therefore bishops or priests who think about fulfilling their obligation to their wives cannot at the same time think about fulfilling the obligation of service owed to the Lord.

And since clergy are called clergy because they are the Lord’s portion—for this is what the word itself is understood to mean—and their portion is none other than the Lord, priests who serve their wives and think about the things of the world reject the Lord’s portion, to which they ought to have adhered in a special way. The Lord is no longer their only possession, since by continually dwelling in the world through their thoughts they cannot adhere to the Lord.

For a mind that embraces the world in its thoughts and clings to the world cannot in any way embrace the Lord or cling to him.

For this reason, the Greek princes are to be wondered at for striving to condemn the Lord’s priests, who keep far away from the embrace of women so that they may not be detained by any necessity arising from the world, but, rejecting the world, may remain continually free to cling to Christ. How much, moreover, the marital bond impedes continual supplication of the Lord, blessed Paul indicates when he says immediately afterward: “Now I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but for what is honorable, and for what affords the opportunity to entreat the Lord without impediment” (1 Cor. 7:35). For by saying this plainly, he demonstrates that those who serve a wife have no opportunity to entreat the Lord continually, but only temporarily. Let these censors of marriage therefore consider what sort of priests they wish to have: whether those who preserve the purity of sanctity and, remaining holy, dwelling continually among holy things, despising the world and contemplating heavenly things, have the opportunity to entreat the Lord without impediment; or, certainly, those who are bound by marital ties, unable continually to dwell among holy things, to despise the world, or at all times to pray to the Lord for the people subject to them. Let them see how far their understanding is removed from the apostolic sense. Paul persuades to continence; they interpret the sanctity of priests—without which no one shall see God—as a condemnation of marriage, forgetting what the Apostle says: “I say this for your benefit,” he says, “persuading you to continence.” But, taking account of weakness, he immediately adds: “Not to cast a snare upon you.” For he shows what he desires, but recognizes that each person has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that. Again, exhorting them toward what is preferable, he adds: “But for what is honorable”—that is, inviting you to it. By saying this, he places honor—that is, continence—above marriage; not indeed so as to condemn marriage, but he clearly proclaims that marriage is good, while widowhood in continence is better; and above these stands virginal integrity.

[Col. 0328D] The Romans and Latins therefore are not to be blamed if they exclude bishops or priests from the marital bed, since the Apostle likewise cannot be considered worthy of blame when, persuading to chastity, he urges that the bond of marriage not be entered, so that the faithful may retain continual opportunity to pray to the Lord. Indeed, how can those who must at all times touch the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood serve marriage? For when David came to Abimelech the priest, he was not permitted to touch the sacred loaves until he had declared that he and his servants had been purified from contact with women for three days. And who does not know that the mystery of Christ’s body and blood is far more exalted than the loaves that were set out every Sabbath upon the table in the temple? If those who had not been sanctified from women were not permitted to touch them, how is it fitting for those who serve women and are enslaved to the marital bed to touch the sacred things of the Lord?

The Church of Thessalonica, carefully examining this mystery, therefore judged that clerics who had known wives lawfully married before their clerical ordination were to be deposed. Hence the Greek princes are to be wondered at for reproving the Romans for what they patiently permit among the Thessalonians. And if, in modern times, they have perhaps yielded to their own superstition, let them nevertheless be convinced and recognize that such was the custom of their ancestors.

But let us finally turn to the ecclesiastical decrees, so that we may learn what they preferred to decree on these matters. [Col. 0329B] At the Council of Nicaea, under the emperor Constantine, the first, this was decreed by three hundred and eighteen bishops (canon 3, from the version of Dionysius Exiguus):

> “The great synod has altogether forbidden that a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all belonging to the clergy may have a woman living with him in his house, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, aunt, or only such persons as escape suspicion.”

Let the emperors of Constantinople hear this and judge whether these ranks, concerning which this canon decrees, ought to enter into marriages when they are not permitted to cohabit with women except persons whom no suspicion can stain. For whoever takes a wife cannot avoid having other women besides his wife in the household, to supply the necessities of the wife and the care of the home. But when the cohabitation of all women is forbidden, except entirely those persons who are free from every suspicion, it is clear that conjugal intercourse is likewise forbidden, since it can in no way take place without the addition of other women.

At the Council of Neocaesarea it was decreed as follows (canon 1, from the same version):

> “If a presbyter takes a wife, he shall be deposed from his rank. But if he has committed fornication or adultery, he must be expelled altogether and reduced to penance.”

The Roman Church and all the Western churches have thus far striven to observe what these canons decree, knowing that all must observe what is plainly religious and worthy of those who worship God. Let the Greeks see whether they insist upon holding to what was established. If they do so, they reproach the Romans in vain, since they plainly recognize them as their equals in observing ecclesiastical councils. But if they freely violate this enactment, they are found guilty of violating ecclesiastical constitutions. Since this was established in the East, and is evidently observed by Easterners as a rule enacted for the discipline of the Church, it is surprising that they try to blame Westerners for what they do not hesitate to observe among Easterners. And if they are ignorant of ecclesiastical laws, who does not know that those are rightly to be despised whom not the gravity of wisdom but the frivolity of ignorance drives to speak?

[Col. 0330A] At the Council of Carthage (African Council, A.D. 424, canon 37):

> “Moreover, since in the case of certain clerics continence was being reported as lacking, even toward their own wives, it was resolved that bishops, presbyters, and deacons should, in accordance with the earlier decrees, abstain even from their wives. If they do not do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office.”

By this present canon, not only are the aforesaid ranks forbidden to take wives, but they are commanded to abstain from those wives whom they had before their ordination; and if they do not do so, they are ordered to be deposed. This decree agrees both with the Council of Nicaea and with that of Neocaesarea, for each commands presbyters to be separated from their wives. In this matter let the imperial critics consider how just it is to allow presbyters to take wives contrary to the decrees of their ancestors, when they are ordered to abstain from the wives whom they had married before ordination. If they prefer to observe these laws, let them recognize that they reproach the Romans unjustly. If they do not, let them reproach, together with the Romans, the provincial bishops of all Africa, and together with these also their own Easterners, who, observing the decrees of their ancestors, altogether decree that bishops, presbyters, and deacons live continently—unless they perhaps choose to be transgressors of their own decrees.

In the twenty-fourth chapter of the book of the Constitutions of the emperor Justinian it is decreed as follows:

> “He who becomes a bishop must have neither a wife, nor a concubine, nor children, whether legitimate or unrecognized by law. And if anyone acts contrary to these provisions, both the one who has been made bishop and the one who made him shall be expelled from the honor of the episcopate.”

[Note: [Col. 0329] This law is expressed in somewhat different words in *Novell. const. coll.* I, title 6, novella 6, chapter 1.]

Let the emperors of the Greeks now see, who slanderously condemn the Romans for condemning marriage because they do not permit bishops, presbyters, or deacons to take wives, where they wish to place their own laws—that is, those established by their ancestors. Behold, Justinian, emperor of the Romans, decreed by law that one who is to become a bishop must have neither a wife nor a concubine; yet you, on the contrary, establish that both bishops and presbyters should receive the rights of marriage. The laws established by your ancestors command that those who do this be deprived of the honor of their rank; yet you blame those who do not do it for condemning marriage and refuse to receive them into your communion. It is therefore evident that you oppose both ecclesiastical laws and your own enactments. Thus you are bound by the guilt of a double offense, as transgressors alike of divine and human law and of ecclesiastical constitution (Justinian, cited above, *Novella* 123, chapter 29):

> “But with regard to presbyters and deacons, and others enrolled in the clergy who do not have wives according to the divine regulations, we likewise forbid them to have a woman in their house, except a mother, daughter, sister, or other persons who avoid every ground of complaint. If anyone, contrary to this observance, keeps in his house a woman who may give rise to suspicion of disgraceful conduct, and, after hearing from his clerics that he ought not to live with such a woman, refuses to remove her from his house; or if, when an accuser comes forward, he is proved to have behaved dishonorably with such a woman, then the bishop shall remove him from the clergy according to the ecclesiastical canons, and he is to be handed over to the city curia of which he is a cleric.”

The preceding law had dealt specifically with the person of the bishop, although it likewise included the persons of presbyters and deacons. For what is not permitted to a bishop is consequently forbidden also to the ministers of the altar, who handle the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood. And if the earlier law did not there determine the matter of presbyters and deacons with complete clarity, the present enactment is recognized to remove every obscurity of doubt. It plainly forbids marriage not only to presbyters and deacons, but also to subdeacons and all others enrolled in the clergy, so that they are in no way permitted to have anyone living in their house except their mother and persons free from suspicion of disgraceful conduct. It decrees that transgressors, if convicted, are to be expelled from the clergy and commands that such persons be handed over to the city curia for offices involving the punishment of disgrace.

We do not believe that the churches of the Greeks hold opinions about the marriages of presbyters such as the princes of Constantinople are shown to hold. Let them therefore not presume to act against ecclesiastical enactments or attempt to criticize what the churches are known to have observed and guarded by perpetual right. If secular authorities, in their presumption, criticize such things as both ecclesiastical and human laws forbid and condemn, it is surprising that they do not perceive that their own sanction is condemned not only by the Western Church but also is not accepted by the Eastern Church—unless perhaps, exhausted by the cruelty of tyranny, some part of the East is going to accept it. But the Lord’s sentence ought to terrify them:

> “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea” (Matt. 18:6).

Yet firm stands the sentence of the Savior speaking to Peter:

> “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18).

Again, in the same book, at the end of the same chapter:

> “No bishop shall live with a woman at all; but if he is proved not to have observed this, he shall be removed from the honor of the episcopate, because he has shown himself unworthy of the priesthood.”

Let the glorious princes [Col. 0331D] of the Greeks say, therefore, relying on what audacity of presumption they do not fear to act against the constitutions of their ancestors, against the laws of the Church, and against the custom observed until now, while reproving Romans and Latins because they do not permit bishops, presbyters, levites, or subdeacons to take wives. For behold, they are convicted by imperial laws which, while enacting provisions for Romans and Latins, unquestionably condemn those who act against them. In the Old Testament, the Levites who served the tabernacle or temple, whether presbyters or otherwise, did not approach their wives, nor did they presume either to enter or to touch the holy things unless they had been sanctified. Yet you say that priests, whose office is to celebrate daily the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood and never to withdraw from sacred things, ought to take wives, and that there should be no distinction between laypeople and the ministers of the sacred altar. If you are asked where such an opinion originated, you can undoubtedly point to no authority other than ignorance and boastfulness, from which rashness is accustomed to arise.

## CHAPTER VII. The Greeks contend that the sacrament of confirmation can be conferred by presbyters. The author refutes them.—What distinguishes a priest from a bishop.

Let us now come to the objection that among the Romans presbyters do not anoint the foreheads of the baptized with chrism. This objection, like the others, has been advanced more through frivolity than reason, since they put it forward by following the custom of their own church, not any authority of divine law. Nevertheless, it is clear that this practice was adopted both among the Romans and among all Westerners from the Gospel and from the Acts of the Apostles.

For it is clear that the grace of the Holy Spirit is given by bishops through the anointing of the forehead with chrism, and evangelical authority testifies that this has been granted to no one except bishops. For when the risen Lord appeared to his disciples, he breathed upon them and said:

> “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:22–23).

Therefore, if the forgiveness of sins is imparted through the Holy Spirit, and this gift is known to have been specially bestowed upon the apostles, this grace is rightly reserved to bishops, who are known in the Church to have received the succession and ministry of the apostles. We also read that Moses, in Exodus, anointed Aaron and his sons for the priestly ministry with holy chrism. Thereafter, in the Old Testament, kings and priests were anointed with holy oil by high priests; these are known to have prefigured the true King and High Priest, our Lord Jesus Christ, concerning whom the Psalmist foretells:

> “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8).

It is clear, moreover, that the whole Church is the body of Christ—namely, of the King and Priest—and therefore we Christians as a whole are a priestly and royal race. For this reason we are anointed after the washing, so that we may be designated by the name of Christ; and this is done only by high priests, by whom kings and priests were anointed under the Law.

In the Acts of the Apostles you also find the following:

> “When the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had come, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. For he had not yet come upon any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit” (Acts 8:14ff.).

Observe that they had first been baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, which is “in the name of the Lord Jesus,” since the invocation of the whole Trinity is contained in the name of the Lord Jesus. Yet they had not thereafter received the Holy Spirit. But when the apostles laid their hands upon them, they received the Holy Spirit. This form is still observed in the Church: the faithful are indeed baptized by presbyters, but the grace of the Holy Spirit is imparted by bishops through the laying on of hands. This occurs when the bishops anoint the foreheads of the baptized with holy chrism.

Likewise, in the same Acts:

> “It happened that, while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples. He said to them: ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’ But they said to him: ‘We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.’ He said: ‘Into what, then, were you baptized?’ They said: ‘Into John’s baptism.’ Paul then said: ‘John baptized with a baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus.’ When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied” (Acts 19:1ff.).

Here too you see that Paul did not baptize them, but ordered them to be baptized. After they had been baptized, Paul laid his hands upon them, and only then did the Holy Spirit come upon them. We are therefore taught that the grace of baptism can be imparted through presbyters, but that the gift of the Holy Spirit, which is bestowed through the laying on of hands when the foreheads of the baptized are anointed with holy chrism, can be obtained only through bishops.

And indeed there is no small difference between priests and bishops. Priests, like the other ecclesiastical ranks, are consecrated through the ministry of bishops; but bishops are not blessed by priests. They themselves also sanctify the holy chrism and consecrate the oil, and every ecclesiastical rank is administered by their arrangement. Considering this, ecclesiastical men decreed that the foreheads of the baptized should be anointed with holy chrism not by presbyters but by bishops.

Thus it is read concerning Saint Sylvester in the *Acts of the Apostles* (*Liber Pontificalis* of Pope Damasus), where the following is written:

> “He established that chrism should be made by a bishop, and that it should be the privilege of bishops to seal the baptized with holy chrism, because of the accusation of heretics.”

Hence Pope Innocent likewise decrees in his *Decretals* as follows (letter 1, chapter 3):

> “It is manifest that the signing of infants may be performed by no one other than a bishop. For although presbyters are priests, they do not possess the summit of the episcopate.”

That it belongs to high priests alone either to sign the baptized or to impart the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, is demonstrated not only by ecclesiastical custom but also by that passage in the Acts of the Apostles which states that Peter and John were sent to impart the Holy Spirit to those who had already been baptized. For presbyters, whether outside the presence of a bishop or in his presence, may anoint the baptized with chrism when they baptize—but with chrism consecrated by a bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that same oil, since this belongs exclusively to bishops when they impart the Spirit, the Paraclete.

For this reason all Western bishops, following the institution of their ancestors, adopted the custom of not permitting presbyters to anoint the foreheads of the baptized with chrism, but reserving this privilege to themselves. They do not, however, make the chrism itself—as the Greeks falsely claim—from the baptismal font, but from balsam juice or olive oil. This is done not only by the Greeks but by all the churches of Christ.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Greek emperors tried to place the patriarch of Constantinople above the Roman pontiff. The Roman Church surpasses all others in dignity.

But they falsely accuse the Romans of this, as they do concerning the consecration of the lamb, and likewise when they object that levites are made bishops without first receiving the rank of presbyter. They do not consider that in these matters they undermine the authority of their own faith, since in them they lie so plainly, unafraid of what the Holy Spirit says:

> “The Lord abhors the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. 5:7).

And:

> “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (ibid.).

And Solomon says:

> “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Prov. 19:5).

But when they object that a levite is consecrated bishop, why do they not observe that the charge is directed against themselves, since they make bishops out of laymen who have suddenly been tonsured, contrary to ecclesiastical rules and imperial decrees? For the Apostle forbids a neophyte to become a bishop (1 Tim. 3:6). The emperor Justinian likewise decrees in his ecclesiastical constitutions (*Novella* 6, chapter 1, at the beginning):

> “It is not permitted to ascend immediately from the laity to the episcopate; nor is it sufficient merely to have held clerical rank at the same time. He who becomes a bishop must have neither a wife, nor a concubine, nor children, nor grandchildren, whether legitimate or unrecognized by law. If anyone acts contrary to these provisions, both the one who has been made bishop and the one who made him shall be expelled from the honor of the episcopate. Nor is it permitted to become a bishop by the giving of money. He who becomes a bishop must be either a monk or a cleric, and in such a way that he is shown to have been in the clerical state for not less than six months,” and so forth.

We see that not only ecclesiastical but also imperial constitutions are opposed to the immediate promotion of someone from the laity to the honor of the episcopate, since he ought first to be tested in the Church and instructed according to ecclesiastical enactments, so that, ascending by the royal road through succession of ranks, he may be found worthy to attain the summit of the highest dignity.

Yet the Greek emperors, transgressing both divine and human laws, suddenly make bishops for themselves out of laymen who have been tonsured, and raise to the summit of the highest dignity those who have not yet been worthy to receive the honor even of the lowest rank. While doing such things, they are not afraid to slander the Church of Christ, speaking falsehoods in place of truths and treating as nothing what the Savior says in the Gospel:

> “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea” (Matt. 18:6).

May the punishment of death therefore avenge this upon them, and may they be swallowed up by the waves of perdition—those whom charity has not made subject to holy fear.

[Col. 0335A] But from where has such innate presumption arisen, that they do not fear to assail the Roman Church with false accusations? Clearly, from this: that, ignorant of the measure of their own status, they strive to claim for themselves a primacy which neither Christ, nor the apostles, nor the teachers of the churches, nor any custom has granted them. They have instead become imitators of the one who said in his heart:

> “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven. I will set my throne upon the mount of assembly, on the far sides of the north. I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14).

For what else do these princes of the Greeks say in the pride of their hearts, when they usurp the primacy of the Church for themselves and claim for themselves the exalted status of the apostles—whom the prophet Isaiah calls flying clouds? They desire to establish the throne of their dignity above the stars of heaven, that is, to place themselves above the whole assembly of the saints, and to usurp the veneration due to patriarchs, so that, with every church subject to them, they may make themselves like Christ. Yet no authority of their ancestors grants this to them, ecclesiastical laws do not permit it, and human laws do not assign it to them. Their desire to claim all these things is especially demonstrated by their eagerness to place the patriarch of Constantinople before the Roman pontiff and their attempts to put Constantinople before Rome, as though it were within their jurisdiction to alter ecclesiastical laws and to arrange the summit of kingdoms.

They ought nevertheless to have remembered that Christ is the head of the whole Church, and that the Father said to him through the Prophet:

> “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8).

And that he is the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which will shatter and reduce to dust all the kingdoms of the world (Matt. 16:18).

And Christ himself said to Peter:

> “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

Paul likewise testifies:

> “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised also worked through me among the Gentiles” (Gal. 2:8).

That Christ placed these two men in primacy in the Church and sent them to Rome is shown both by ecclesiastical truth and by the authority of their own passion. For both princes were sent there where the primacy of the world stood out, so that, just as the city of Rome had subjected the whole world to itself through imperial power, so it might preside over the kingdoms of the whole world through the height of religion and the dignity of the apostleship.

And just as the Savior chose to make Jerusalem exalted through his birth, teaching, miracles, death, burial, and resurrection, so he also chose to make the city of Rome glorious through the blood, tombs, memory, and teaching of the chief apostles. For as Christ, the heavenly Jerusalem, seated at the right hand of the Father, is honored as King and Lord through the service of angels and all the saints, so Peter and Paul hold primacy over the pilgrim Jerusalem, with the churches of Christ throughout the breadth of the world subject to them.

[Col. 0336A] Antiquity itself confirms that this is so, and the monuments of literature bear witness to it. For Socrates, writing in his *Ecclesiastical History* about the Arians who had assembled a synod at Antioch in Syria for the subversion and destruction of the Council of Nicaea and the condemnation of Athanasius, after recalling the bishops by whose authority the synod had been assembled, added:

> “But Julius, bishop of great Rome, was not present, nor did he send anyone in his place, although ecclesiastical rule certainly commands that councils should not be held without the judgment of the Roman pontiff.”

[Note: [Col. 0335D] Socrates, book II, chapter 13, middle; but he expresses the sense in different words.]

Behold, this historian was a Greek, yet he does not say that Constantinople possessed such authority as Rome; rather, he testifies that no council can be held without either the assent or the command of the Roman pontiff.

At the Council of Sardica, the following was enacted in this manner (chapter 7, from the interpretation of Dionysius Exiguus):

> “It was resolved that if a bishop has been accused, and all the bishops of that region, having assembled, have judged him and deposed him from his rank; if the one who appears to have been deposed appeals and flees to the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church and wishes to be heard; if he thinks it just that the examination be renewed, let the Roman bishop graciously write to the bishops who are in the neighboring and nearby province, so that they may carefully investigate everything and determine all things according to the faith of truth. But if the one who asks that his case be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his entreaty to send presbyters from his side, it shall be in his power to decide what he wishes and judges appropriate. And if he decrees that those should be sent who will judge together with the bishops present, so that they may also possess the authority of the person by whom they were sent, it shall be in his discretion. But if he believes that the provincial bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, let him do what he judges by his most prudent counsel.”

This council, held by Eastern bishops in the province of Asia [Note: [Col. 0335D] “In the province of Asia.” Not at all, but in Illyricum: [Col. 0336D] Ratramnus confused Sardica, or Serdica, with Sardis.], thus decreed concerning the dignity of the Roman pontiff under the Roman emperor Constantine the Great, who built the city of Constantinople and wished it to be called New Rome. But is anything of this kind recorded as having been established by the bishops concerning the patriarch of Constantinople?

[Col. 0336D] We see that the authority of the Roman pontiff altogether surpasses that of all the churches of Christ, so that all bishops have him as their head, and whatever is arranged in ecclesiastical matters depends upon his judgment: according to his decision, an established matter either remains in force, an error is corrected, or whatever requires renewal is enacted.

This is also attested by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, who writes in his history concerning the life of Sylvester [the manuscript *Life* cited above]:

> “On the fourth day the emperor Constantine granted the privilege to the pontiff of the Roman Church that throughout the Roman world priests should regard him as their head, just as judges regard the king.”

This matter is confirmed by the acts of the councils. For every council known to have been held either in the East or in Africa always had either vicars of the Roman pontiff presiding, or received firmness for its decrees through letters issued by his authority. Thus the Council of Nicaea, venerated by all the churches of Christ, placed Victor and Vincent, presbyters of the city of Rome acting in the place of the Roman pontiff, first among the subscriptions of the bishops, immediately after Hosius, bishop of the city of Corduba in the province of Spain, who had been sent there by the Roman pontiff because the latter could not come, being hindered by old age.

So the remaining councils always placed the Roman pontiffs or their legates first, as vicars of the apostles. And indeed all the Eastern churches, together with the Western churches, have always venerated the bishop of the city of Rome as though he were the head of the bishops. They looked to his judgment, submitted to his decision whatever he decreed concerning doubtful matters, and obeyed his decree. Whatever councils were strengthened by his judgment remained ratified; whatever he condemned was regarded as nothing and could possess no authority.

Although the monuments of the ancient Fathers confirm that what we say is true, I wish nevertheless to demonstrate from the letters of one Roman pontiff what we have asserted. When Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, who had condemned Eutyches, the Constantinopolitan archimandrite, for holding an erroneous opinion concerning the Lord’s incarnation, had himself also been condemned by the synod assembled at Ephesus contrary to ecclesiastical rules, he appealed to Leo, the Roman pontiff, on this account. Leo wrote to the emperor Theodosius that the synod should be reconsidered and that what had been wrongly established should be annulled.

Since this could not be done under the emperor Theodosius, who was overtaken by death, it was carried out under the emperors Valentinian and Marcian, who succeeded Theodosius. Their letter, sent to Leo, the venerable bishop of the city of Rome, reads as follows (before the Council of Chalcedon, letter 33):

> “The victors Valentinian and Marcian, glorious triumphant emperors, always Augusti, to Leo, most reverend archbishop of the glorious city of Rome. By the providence of God and through the excellence of the most distinguished senate and of the entire army, we have come to this great imperial office. Therefore, on behalf of the revered and catholic religion and of the faith of Christians, by whose aid we trust that the strength of our power is governed, we believe that your Holiness, who possesses the primacy in the episcopate of the divine faith, should first be addressed by sacred letters. We invite and beseech you, for the stability and preservation of our empire, to entreat the eternal Divinity, so that we may have such a purpose and desire that, when every impious error has been removed through the celebration of a synod under your authority, the greatest peace may be established among all the bishops of the catholic faith.”

Likewise, in the second letter, after the salutation and introductory address, it is written as follows (ibid., letter 34):

> “It remains that, if it should please your Beatitude to come to these regions and celebrate a synod, your Holiness should graciously do so out of religious devotion. Your Holiness will satisfy our desires and determine what is beneficial for the sacred religion. But if it is burdensome for you to come to these regions, let your Holiness make this known to us in your own letter, so that your sacred letters may be sent throughout the whole East, and to Thrace itself and Illyricum, in order that all the most holy bishops may assemble at a certain fixed place and, according as your Holiness determines in accordance with the ecclesiastical rules, may declare by your arrangement what is beneficial to the religion of Christians and to the catholic faith.”

These letters of the Roman emperors do not show that the patriarch of Constantinople was regarded as superior to the Roman pontiff. Rather, they show that the Roman pontiff held primacy among the bishops, that a synod was to be assembled according to his judgment, and that the matters to be discussed were to be ordered according to his arrangement.

The letters of the emperor Valentinian to Theodosius, the August Father, also testify to the dignity and honor which the Roman pontiff ought to possess above all bishops. They are known to read as follows (ibid., epistle 25):

“To Theodosius, most glorious victor, most excellent triumphant emperor and father: Valentinian, glorious victor and triumphant, ever Augustus and son.

“When I had come to the city of Rome to appease the Divinity, on the following day I proceeded to the basilica of the apostle Peter. There, after the venerable night of the apostle’s day, I was asked by the Roman bishop and by others gathered with him from various provinces to write to Your Clemency concerning the faith, which, although it is the guardian of the souls of all the faithful, is said to have been disturbed. We ought to defend this faith, handed down to us by our ancestors, with every fitting devotion, and preserve in our own time the dignity of its proper veneration for the blessed apostle Peter, so that the most blessed bishop of the Roman city—upon whom antiquity conferred the primacy of the priesthood over all—may have the authority and power to judge concerning the faith and concerning priests, most sacred Lord Father and venerable Emperor. For this reason, according to the solemnity of the councils, the bishop of Constantinople also appealed to him by written petitions, because of the dispute that had arisen concerning the faith.”

Galla Placidia, mother of the Augustus, likewise sent a letter to her son the Augustus concerning the same matter and said, among other things (ibid., epistle 26, at the beginning):

“It is no small injury in view of what has taken place that the faith, which for so many ages was regularly preserved by our most sacred father Constantine—who was the first Christian to shine forth in imperial power—should recently have been disturbed at the will of one man, who is reported to have practiced hatred and contention rather than anything else in the synod of the city of Ephesus. By the presence and fear of soldiers he attacked Flavian, bishop of the city of Constantinople, because he had sent a written petition to the apostolic see through those who had been dispatched to the council by the most reverend bishop of Rome, who, according to the definitions of the Council of Nicaea, are accustomed to take part in such matters, most holy Lord Son, venerable Emperor.

“Therefore, resisting such great disturbances, let Your Clemency order that the immaculate truth of the Catholic faith be preserved and, according to the form and definition of the apostolic see—which we likewise venerate as pre-eminent—let him transmit Flavian, with his priestly status entirely unharmed, to the judgment of the council and of the apostolic see. There the first man who was deemed worthy to receive the heavenly keys established the primacy of the episcopate.

“It is therefore fitting that we preserve every reverence toward this greatest city, which is mistress of all. Take careful precautions lest what our generation guarded in ancient times appear to have been diminished under us, and lest schisms be generated among bishops and holy Churches through this present example.”

It is therefore evident from these letters that the Roman pontiff was never subject to the patriarch of Constantinople. Rather, whenever necessity demanded it, the latter sought the apostolic see and requested that his case receive its conclusion according to the Roman pontiff’s judgment. The Roman city is more honorable than all the cities of the Roman Empire, and the Roman pontiff holds the primacy of the priesthood over all bishops, since this city is mistress of all; and whoever presides as bishop over that city is, by the constitution of antiquity, regarded as the chief of all the Churches.

Relying, therefore, upon this authority, Leo, the venerable bishop of the Roman city, wrote to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople (epistle 46), explaining what form the council ought to follow in condemning Nestorius and Eutyches. He wrote:

“Although I hope that your Dilection is devoted to every work, nevertheless, so that your diligence may become more effective, it was necessary and advantageous to send my brothers Licentius the bishop and Basil the presbyter, as we promised. Let your Dilection be associated with them, so that in matters concerning the condition of the universal Church nothing may be handled either doubtfully or sluggishly. While you are seated there, having been entrusted with the execution of our disposition, everything may be conducted with moderation, so that neither the claims of benevolence nor those of justice may be neglected, but that divine judgment may be considered in all things without respect of persons.”

After some intervening material he adds:

“And because the evangelical and apostolic faith overthrows every error, casting Nestorius down on one side and striking down Eutyches and his associates on the other, remember that this rule must be observed: whoever in that synod—which neither can nor deserves to possess the name of a synod, and in which Dioscorus displayed his malevolence and Juvenal his zeal—offers satisfaction, let brotherly peace be granted to them: … in such a way that, by unequivocal professions, they condemn Eutyches with his doctrine and his associates by the consecration of an anathema.

“As for those who sinned more grievously in this affair and thereby claimed for themselves a higher place in that unhappy synod, so that they might burden the simplicity of humble brothers with the prejudices of arrogance: if they should perhaps repent and, abolishing the defense of their deed, turn toward condemnation of their own error, let their satisfaction be of such a kind that it does not appear worthy of rejection, but is reserved for the more mature counsels of the apostolic see. When everything has been examined and weighed, their own acknowledgments will determine what ought to be established concerning them. Nor, as we have already written to you, shall the name of any such person be recited at the altar in the Church over which the Lord wished you to preside, until the course of events shows what ought to be decided concerning them.”

A little later:

“Strive, therefore, dearest brother, to carry out faithfully and effectively with those brothers whom we have chosen as suitable agents what accords with the Church of God.”

These letters show that the Roman pontiff presides over the patriarch of Constantinople, to whom he entrusts the exercise of his authority at the council. He prescribes to him how each matter is to be carried out, indicates what is to be reserved for his own judgment, and defines what the pontiff himself must determine. Yet the patriarch is not permitted to possess the power of judging alone; rather, those who had been sent by the apostolic see are joined with him in deciding the affairs.

The same blessed bishop Leo also wrote to the holy synod established at Chalcedon (epistle 40), concerning the condemnation of the second synod of Ephesus, in which the venerable Flavian, patriarch of Constantinople, had been condemned not by justice but by violence. These are his words, preceded by a salutation:

“I had indeed wished, dearest brethren, out of the charity that unites our college, that all the priests of the Lord should persist in one devotion to the Catholic faith, and that no priest should be corrupted by favor or fear of secular powers or depart from the path of truth. But since many things often occur that can produce repentance, and since God’s mercy surpasses the faults of sinners—and therefore vengeance is suspended so that correction may have an opportunity—the deeply religious counsel of the most merciful prince must be embraced. He has preferred that Your Holy Fraternity assemble to destroy the snares of the devil and restore ecclesiastical peace, while the right and honor of the see of the most blessed apostle Peter are preserved. Indeed, he invited us by his letters to offer our judgment to the venerable synod. Neither the necessity of the time nor any established custom could permit this; nevertheless, let Your Fraternity judge me to preside over your synod through these brothers, the bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius and the presbyters Boniface and Basil, who have been sent by the apostolic see. And let my presence, which is not separated from you, be understood to be present now in my vicars, just as previously I was not absent from the preaching of the Catholic faith.”

After other material:

“Since we are not unaware that the condition of many Churches has been disturbed by wicked rivalries, and that very many brothers, because they did not accept heresy, were driven from their sees and deported into exile, while others were installed in the places of those who survived, let the remedy of justice first be applied to these wounds. Let no one be so deprived of what is his that another may use what belongs to someone else. If, as we desire, all abandon their error, no one’s honor ought indeed to perish; rather, for those who have labored on behalf of the faith, what belongs to them should be restored with every privilege.

“Let the statutes of the earlier synod of Ephesus, over which the bishop Cyril of holy memory then presided, remain specially in force against Nestorius, so that the impiety once condemned may not at last flatter itself in any respect—an impiety which Eutyches is struck down by a just execration. For the purity of the faith and doctrine that we preach in the same Spirit as our holy Fathers equally condemns and persecutes the depravity of Nestorius and of Eutyches, together with their authors.”

We clearly perceive that the pontiff of the Roman see is neither placed beneath nor ranked alongside the patriarch of Constantinople, but is set above him. For we see that the Council of Chalcedon was assembled with the Roman pontiff’s permission; that he preferred to preside over it through his legates; that in his own letters he also provided the form of what was to be decided concerning the second synod assembled at Ephesus; and that he prescribed what was to be done concerning those who, because of the truth of the faith, had been expelled from their own sees and deported into exile. He also prescribed what was to be done concerning those who, compelled by threats and terror, had pronounced and accepted judgment against the faith, if they preferred to return from their error and profess the truth of the faith. He established that the first synod of Ephesus, held under the blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, should in every respect be observed, condemning both Nestorius and Eutyches for their erroneous views concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Through all these things we are plainly instructed that the Roman pontiff was pre-eminent in honor not only over the bishop of Constantinople but over all the Eastern bishops, as one who ought to possess full concern for all bishops and upon whom in particular the vigilant care of all the Churches rests.

To make it still more evident how greatly the Roman bishop excels in honor all who are regarded as bishops throughout the East, I have decided to present an excerpt from the letter of the blessed Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, addressed to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica (epistle 84). After a salutation, he says:

“If you would truly perceive and justly weigh how many responsibilities have been entrusted to Your Fraternity by the authority of the most blessed apostle Peter, and what responsibilities have also been committed to you through our favor, we could greatly rejoice in your devotion to the care imposed upon you. For just as my predecessors entrusted their delegated authority to your predecessors, so I, following the example of those before me, have entrusted to your Dilection the exercise of my governance. Thus, by becoming an imitator of our gentleness, you might assist the care which, by divine institution, we principally owe to all the Churches, and might in some way extend the presence of our visitation to provinces far removed from us.

“You should readily recognize, through continuous and timely supervision, what matters you might settle through your own diligence and what you should reserve for our judgment. For although it was open to you to suspend greater affairs and the more difficult outcomes of cases while awaiting our decision, you had neither reason nor necessity to deviate into matters exceeding your measure. You have an abundance of the writings of our admonitions, by which we have frequently instructed you concerning moderation in all actions, so that through the exhortation of charity you might summon the Churches of Christ entrusted to you to the health of obedience.”

After complaining in similar terms about other matters, he adds again:

“And while they seek to dominate their subjects rather than to counsel them, honor pleases them, pride inflates them, and what was provided for concord tends toward harm. That we are compelled to speak in this way proceeds from no small grief of heart. I feel myself, in a certain sense, being drawn into blame when I learn that you have departed immoderately from the rules entrusted to you. If you were careless of your own reputation, you ought at least to have spared my good name, lest actions undertaken solely on your own judgment appear to have been undertaken by our decision.

“Let Your Fraternity reread our pages, and let it run through all the letters sent to your predecessors by the bishops of the apostolic see. You will find ordered by either me or my predecessors what we have learned was presumed by you. For our brother Atticus, metropolitan bishop of Old Epirus, came to us with the bishops of his province and complained in a tearful case, before your attending deacons, of the utterly unjust affliction he had endured. Since they offered no reply against his tearful complaints, they showed that the matters he brought before us were not without credibility. It was also being read in your letters, which those same deacons of yours brought to me, that brother Atticus had come to Thessalonica.”

And later:

“Thus the words of your letter gave testimony to the lamentations mentioned above, and by what was not concealed, what had been covered in silence was exposed: namely, that the prefecture of Illyricum had been approached and that the most exalted power among secular authorities had been incited against an innocent bishop. A terrible enforcement was sent, joining all the public offices to the execution of the command, so that a priest accused of no crime, or of a false one, might be dragged from the sacred entrances of the Church. No allowance was granted him either because of the burden of illness or because of the severity of winter; instead, he was forced to travel a rough road, full of dangers and blocked by impassable snows. The labor and danger were so great that some of those who accompanied the bishop are said to have collapsed.

“I am greatly astonished, dearest brother, and also deeply grieved, that you were able to become so savagely and vehemently enraged against a man concerning whom you had indicated nothing more than that, having been summoned, he delayed appearing and pleaded illness as his excuse—especially since, if he deserved such treatment, you ought to have awaited what I would write in response to your inquiries. But, as I see, you formed a good opinion of my character and most accurately anticipated what civil response I would make for the preservation of priestly concord; and therefore you hastened to carry out your impulses without delay, lest, after receiving letters disposing otherwise according to our moderation, you should no longer have permission to do what was done.

“Or had some crime of your brother become known to you, and was the metropolitan bishop burdened in your eyes with the weight of a new accusation? Yet you yourself confirm that this was foreign to him by bringing no charge against him. Even if he had committed something grave and intolerable, our judgment ought to have been awaited, so that you would decide nothing before learning what pleased us. For we entrusted our delegated authority to your Charity in such a way that you were called to share in the care, not to possess the fullness of power.

“Therefore, just as the things you have piously managed greatly rejoice us, so the things wrongly conducted distress us exceedingly. After the experience of so many cases, it is necessary to exercise more anxious supervision and more careful foresight, so that through the Spirit of charity and peace every occasion of scandal may be removed from the Churches of the Lord that we have entrusted to you. The height of your episcopate may indeed be pre-eminent in those provinces, but every excess of usurpation must be cut away.

“Therefore, according to the canons of the holy Fathers, established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces, whose care is entrusted to Your Fraternity by our delegation, retain inviolate the right of the dignity assigned to them from ancient times, so that they may depart from the prescribed rules neither through negligence nor through presumption.”

He then adds the other provisions that he established for the Thessalonian bishop to preserve in ecclesiastical affairs.

From these things we see that the bishop of Constantinople is in no way pre-eminent over the Churches of Christ except those of his own diocese. Rather, the care of this concern was entrusted from ancient times to the Roman pontiff, to whom all the Churches of Christ look, and whose office it is to dispose of individual ecclesiastical matters. Each province is to retain that form of ecclesiastical jurisdiction which the Roman pontiff has either established or granted. This is confirmed by the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, sent to all the Churches of Christ throughout both East and West; they are observed and revered by all the Churches as laws governing ecclesiastical affairs.

Who, then, would tolerate the patriarch of Constantinople being placed above all the Churches of Christ—a privilege conferred upon him neither by antiquity, nor by any decrees of the Fathers, nor by anything established as valid by ecclesiastical or human law? Unless perhaps the modern Greek emperors think that they may claim for themselves what the Roman emperors could not: that they may dispose at will of the Roman Church, which those emperors venerated as a mother, and alter the authority that both Christ and the whole Church, together with the principate of the entire world, conferred upon blessed Peter. For they see that the city of Rome, which holds the primacy of all the Churches, has been removed from their imperial rule, and that the whole of the West, Africa, and nearly the whole of the East have been taken from them, except for a very few provinces of Europe and Asia and the territories of a few islands.

What reverence the patriarch of Constantinople ought to receive—not on account of his own merit, but because it is called “the second Rome”—is testified by the pragmatic sanction of the emperor Justinian (Novella 131, chapter 2), which reads:

“Let the Roman pope sit first among all bishops and patriarchs, and after him the archbishop of the city of Constantinople.”

Here the patriarch of Constantinople is neither placed above nor ranked alongside the Roman pope, but is placed beneath him. It must also be considered that the honor of the see is granted to him, whereas the summit of authority is in no way conferred upon him.

Likewise, in the History of Socrates (book V, chapter 8), it is written:

“At that time they also established the rule”—namely, the bishops who appointed Nectarius at Constantinople to be bishop—“that the bishop of Constantinople should possess the privileges of honor after the Roman pontiff, because it is the new Rome.”

But here too no privileges of authority are granted to him; these are shown to remain with the Roman pontiff.

From where, then, do the Greek rulers derive the authority to place the bishop of Constantinople above all the Churches? Antiquity gives them no support; no decrees of synods support them; no imperial pragmatics support them. Even if some such documents could be produced, they could not possess the weight of authority without the assent of the Roman pontiff. By the grant of antiquity, such a right of authority remains with him that neither Constantinople nor any Eastern or Western city can obtain privileges of authority without his permission, except those privileges that have been either granted or confirmed by the Roman pontiff. To him belong the power and the care of all the Churches: to grant or arrange whatever, according to the ecclesiastical rules, has been approved as serving ecclesiastical welfare. This is confirmed by many records of Scripture sent by the Roman pontiff throughout all the Churches.

Thus Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, writing to Simplicius, bishop of the city of Rome (Simplicius, epistle 6), says:

“To the holy lord and father, the archbishop Simplicius: Acacius.

“Although, in accordance with the Apostle, you carry the care of all the Churches, you continually exhort us, even though we are watchful and anticipate matters of our own accord; yet you demonstrate that you are solicitous with divine zeal when you inquire more certainly into the condition of the Alexandrian Church, so that, in accordance with the paternal canons, you may undertake the labor and, as has always been approved, pour out your most pious sweat on its behalf,”

and so forth.

We learn that Acacius, the Constantinopolitan pontiff, testifies that the Roman pontiff, in accordance with the Apostle, bears concern for all the Churches, and that this responsibility has always been imposed upon him by antiquity. By saying this, Acacius in no way claims for himself the administration of all the Churches. He knows that this is far removed from his own office, and he does not presume to usurp what he knows himself to be far from possessing.

When Acacius was discovered to have acted against the ecclesiastical rules, doing what no just principle permitted him to do, Felix, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, wrote to him as follows (epistle 6):

“You are found guilty of many transgressions and have often been involved in contempt of the venerable Council of Nicaea. You have rashly claimed for yourself the rights of provinces belonging to others. You thought that heretics and perverters, those ordained by heretics, and those whom you yourself had condemned and had asked the apostolic see to condemn, ought not merely to be received into your communion; you even caused them to preside over other Churches, something that could not be done even in the case of Catholics, and you increased them with honors they did not deserve.”

After writing much concerning his transgressions, he concluded:

“Therefore, share your portion with those whom you willingly embrace, and recognize that, by the present sentence which we have sent to you through the defender of your Church, you have been separated from priestly honor, Catholic communion, and the number of the faithful. Your name and the office of priestly ministry have been taken from you; you have been condemned by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by the apostolic authority exercised through us, and you are no longer to be released from the bonds of anathema.”

Can anyone now be convinced that the Roman pontiff was subject to the patriarch of Constantinople, by whom he is sharply rebuked for his transgressions and condemned by a sentence of anathema? It would be an immense task to gather everything by which the Roman pontiff is shown to be pre-eminent over the Constantinopolitan pontiff. But what has been presented is sufficient: it clearly demonstrates that the patriarch of Constantinople must in no way be placed above all the Churches of Christ, but ought to be content with the measure of his own honor, lest, by acting against the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, he suffer the loss of his own honor.

We have acted as best we could in responding to what you sent us in writing. If it has pleased you, we give thanks to God; but if it has displeased you, we await the judgment of your correction.

(See the letter concerning the Cynocephali at the end of the volume.)

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 868. GOTTSCHALK OF ORBAIS, MONK.

[Col. 0345]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON GOTTSCHALK.

(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina medii et infimi aevi*.)

Among the poems of Walafrid Strabo there is a poem addressed to Gottschalk the monk, who is also called Fulgentius, in volume XV of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*, page 232.

This is that famous Gottschalk, a monk of the Benedictine order, of Orbais in the diocese of Soissons, who, because of the controversies he stirred up with excessive intensity concerning predestination, was condemned at the synod of Mainz in 848 and at the assembly of Quierzy in 849, and was confined in the monastery of Hautvillers. After more than twenty years of custody, he died around the year 870.

That Gottschalk was treated harshly by Hincmar of Reims, Rabanus Maurus, Amolo or Amalarius of Lyon, John Scotus, and his other adversaries is openly lamented by Florus in his work against John Scotus and by Remigius of Lyon in the book written in the name of the Church of Lyon concerning the three Letters, which appears in volume XV of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*, page 666 and following; also by Prudentius of Troyes, Ratramnus or Bertramnus of Corbie, and others.

[Note: See Bulaeus, *History of the University of Paris*, vol. I, p. 178 ff.; *Summary Notices of the Thomasius Library*, vol. I, p. 681 ff., 734 ff.]

James Ussher, in his *History of Gottschalk and the Predestinarian Controversy*, first published in Dublin in 1631 in quarto and reprinted at Hanover in 1662 in octavo, maintains that Gottschalk proceeded no farther than Augustine’s teaching. At the end of his work he published two Confessions of Gottschalk, one shorter and the other longer.

[Note: Ussher did not altogether persuade Vossius of this, although he had dedicated his book to him. See Vossius, epistle 156, thanking Ussher, and epistle 158, to William Laud, bishop of London; also Grotius, epistle 292; Vossius, *History of Pelagianism*, book VII, part IV, vol. VI of his Works, p. 812 ff. Yet Gilbert Manguin, in *Vindications of Predestination and Grace* and in his *Collection of Ninth-Century Writers on Predestination and Grace*, Paris, 1650, quarto, 2 vols., and Cardinal Noris likewise adopt Ussher’s view. Noris’s synopsis of the history of Gottschalk appeared in vol. IV of his Works, pp. 681, 720, Verona, 1732, folio.]
