In both, Gottschalk does not permit divine foreknowledge to be separated from the divine decree. In both, he repeatedly appeals to Augustine and Fulgentius of Ruspe and professes himself so firmly convinced of his position that on page 345 he declares that, if it could be done, he would choose a thousand times rather to die for the truth than once—to God forbid—to yield and succumb by giving way to anyone speaking otherwise.

[Note: It is suspected that Gottschalk acquired the surname *Fulgentius* from this Fulgentius, to whose books he appeals so strongly, although others say that he was so called because he seemed to shine above others in talent and learning. See Cave, *Historia litteraria S. E.*; Caspar Sagittarius, *Introduction to Ecclesiastical History*, vol. I, p. 970 ff.]

On page 353 he says that, taught by Truth itself and freely and sufficiently piously inspired, animated, armed, and at once mercifully and wonderfully aided, kept safe, strengthened, and supported by it, he faithfully believes in it, firmly holds it, and truthfully and patiently defends it; and that anyone whom he knows to teach contrary doctrine he flees as a plague and casts away as a heretic.

On page 354 he appeals to God himself in these words:

“And would that it might please you, almighty and most merciful Lord, that, just as I believe and hope in you, and since you have graciously granted me the ability—and have long ago deigned to grant it and daily deign also to will to grant it—before a multitude gathered from every side of peoples who fear you, in the presence also of the present ruler of this kingdom [Note: Charles the Bald, king of France], together with a venerable company of bishops and priests, monks and canons, I might be permitted, if they were unwilling to receive this truth of the Catholic faith concerning your predestination, to prove it openly, by your grace favoring me, through the test I shall describe.

“Let four barrels be placed one after another, each separately filled with boiling water, thick oil, and pitch, and finally let an immense fire be kindled. Then, having invoked your most glorious name to prove this faith of mine, indeed the Catholic faith, let me pass through each one in turn, until, with you going before me, accompanying me, following after me, extending your right hand, and mercifully leading me out, I might emerge unharmed. Thus at last, in your Catholic Church, the brightness of this faith might shine forth, falsehood disappear, faith be strengthened, and unbelief be avoided.”

[Note: Referring to this passage, John Scotus Erigena, in chapter 3 of *On Predestination*, page 123, says to Gottschalk: “Among those barrels, as I see, which you order to be prepared for you, you are already wrapped up and suffocating. For you deserved to burn in oil and pitch, since you were not afraid improperly to teach both the light of charity and the mystery of predestination.” Because of this unusual promise concerning the barrels, Gottschalk is sharply rebuked by Hincmar of Reims in his book *On the Non-Trinitarian Deity*, volume I, page 433.]

After Ussher, Gilbert Manguin presents both Confessions of Gottschalk in volume I, pages 7–25, of his *Vindications of Predestination and Grace in the Writers of the Ninth Century*.

In the same work, page 6 and part II, page 3 and following, are fragments from Gottschalk’s little book *On Predestination* and from the profession of faith submitted to Rabanus Maurus in the year 848, preserved by Hincmar of Reims, volume I of his works, pages 25, 26, 118, 149, 211, 224, and 226.

In volume II of the same Manguin, page 54, there are published verses—twenty-six leonine hexameters—from Gottschalk’s letter, written from Germany to Ratramnus, the monk of Corbie, which Sirmond had published in volume I of Hincmar’s works, page 555. He also produces other anacreontic verses from the preface to the same Ratramnus. Sirmond, in his note to the fifth book, letter 7, of Ennodius, writes: “Come, I ask you, proceed, Clio,” and so forth.

Labbe, on page 59 of his *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, had long ago led readers to hope that many more verses of Gottschalk would be brought to light by some learned man whose identity he did not know.

The same Hincmar presents several excerpts from Gottschalk’s *pitacium* addressed to a certain monk, pages 304–305, and from a letter to one of his associates, page 226.

A letter to Ratramnus appears in Ludovicus Cellotius’s *History of Gottschalk*, published at Paris in 1655 in folio, page 415.

The same Hincmar presents Gottschalk’s memorandum on the possibility of speaking of a “threefold Deity” in volume I, pages 415–418, and thereafter made it the subject of attack in his entire book *On the Non-Trinitarian Deity*.

Lupus of Ferrières responded to Gottschalk’s more subtle questions concerning the manner in which the blessed will see God in his thirtieth letter. Baluze also attributes to Lupus the book *On Three Questions*, although others preferred to attribute it to another Lupus and others to Amalarius.

Concerning Gottschalk’s case, besides Ussher, Cellotius, and the others whom I have cited, one may also consult Mabillon, the preface to volume III of the *Benedictine Annals*; Sirmond, in his *Predestinarian History*; Gilbert Manguin against Sirmond, in his *Historical and Chronological Synopsis of the Gottschalkian Controversy*; and his *Historical and Chronological Dissertation* in part I of volume II of the *Writers of the Ninth Century on Grace and Predestination*. Among our own authors one may also consult D. Paulus Roeberus, *Dissertation on the Errors of Gottschalk Condemned in the Ninth Century*, Wittenberg, 1646, quarto.

Excerpts from a manuscript history of the visions of Gottschalk of Neumünster in the year 1190 were published by the illustrious Leibniz in volume I of the *Brunswick Writers*, pages 870–875.

[Col. 0347]

CONFESSION OF GOTTSCHALK THE MONK AFTER THE CONDEMNATION OF HERESY.

(From Manguin, *Vindications of Predestination and Grace*, page 5, from a Corbie manuscript.)

[Col. 0347D] I believe and confess that almighty and immutable God foreknew and predestined the holy angels and elect human beings to eternal life freely given; and that he likewise predestined the devil himself, the head of all demons, together with all his apostates, and also with those reprobate human beings who are his members, because of their foreknown and certainly future evil merits, to deserved everlasting death by his most just judgment. For the Lord himself says in his Gospel: “The prince of this world has already been judged” (John 16:11). Blessed Augustine, explaining this to the people (Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate 95), openly stated: “That is, he has been irrevocably destined by the judgment of eternal fire.”

Likewise, concerning the reprobate, Truth itself says: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18), that is—as the aforesaid author explained (tractate 12)—“has already been condemned.” “The judgment,” he says, “has not yet appeared, but the judgment has already taken place.”

Again, explaining the words of John the Baptist, “No one has accepted his testimony” (John 3:32), he says (tractate 14): “No one: there is a certain people prepared for God’s wrath, to be condemned with the devil.”

Again, concerning the Jews: “These died in indignation and were predestined to everlasting death.”

Again (tractate 48): “Why did the Lord say to the Jews, ‘You do not believe because you are not of my sheep’ (John 10:26), unless he saw that they were predestined to everlasting destruction, not purchased for eternal life at the price of his blood?”

Again, explaining (the same passage) the Lord’s words, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them from my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them from my Father’s hand” (John 10:27–29), he said: “What can the wolf do? What can the thief and robber do? They do not destroy any except those predestined to destruction.”

Again, speaking of the two worlds (tractate 87): “The whole world is the Church, and the whole world hates the Church: therefore the world hates the world, the enemy hates the reconciled, the condemned the saved, the defiled the cleansed.”

Again (tractate 110): “There is a world of which the Apostle says, ‘so that we may not be condemned with this world’ (1 Cor. 11:32). For this world the Lord does not pray; for he is not ignorant of the end to which it has been predestined.”

Again (tractate 107): “Judas the betrayer of Christ is called the son of perdition, predestined to betrayal.”

Again, in the *Enchiridion* (chapter 100): “For the condemnation of those whom he justly predestined to punishment.”

Again, in the book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness* (chapter 13): “This good,” he says, “which is to be sought, there was no one to do; there was not even one—but among that class of human beings which was predestined to destruction. For upon these God’s foreknowledge looked and pronounced sentence.”

Again, in the books *On the City of God* (book 22, chapter 24): “What will he give to those whom he predestined to death?”

Blessed Pope Gregory likewise says (*Moralia*, book 34, chapter 2): “Leviathan with all his members has been assigned to everlasting torments.”

Saint Fulgentius, in the third book *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace* (book 3, chapter 5), likewise says: “God prepared punishments for sinners—namely, for those whom he justly predestined to undergo punishments.”

Blessed Fulgentius composed an entire book devoted solely to this question, namely *On the Predestination of the Reprobate to Destruction*, for his friend Monimus (book 1).

Hence Saint Isidore also says (*Sentences*, book 2, chapter 6): “There is a twofold predestination: either of the elect to rest, or of the reprobate to death.”

Thus, in every respect, together with these elect of God and Catholics, I believe and confess, insofar as I am divinely inspired, animated, armed, and assisted. Amen.

For a false witness is one who corrupts either the meaning or the surface wording of anyone’s statements.

[Col. 0349]

## THE MORE EXTENDED CONFESSION OF GOTTSCHALK

[Col. 0349C] Ruler, Lord God, my mercy, almighty King and incomparably compassionate, patient in your immeasurable kindness toward the human race, and wise with utterly unfathomable depth. All your elect always so greatly need you that they may continually be able to please you through you alone. They are like branches that need the vine in order to bear fruit, or the air and the eyes that need light so that the air may be luminous and the eyes may see. Otherwise the branches, without the vine, wither and consequently are thrown into the fire and burn; the air without light is dark; and the eyes remain open in vain.

Therefore I humbly invoke you, all-powerful, most merciful, and most glorious, triune and one Lord God: graciously consent to be my most loving helper and hearer, and graciously bestow upon me, who am most needy, through the unconquerable power of your freely given grace, that what I have long believed in my heart concerning your foreknowledge and predestination—as something proceeding from you, through you, and in you, thanks be to you—for righteousness, just as I have often confessed through your grace, I may likewise confess truthfully and simply with my mouth for salvation. May the unconquerable and eternally blessed truth at last be made manifest on my part to your elect, and may the defeated falsehood, as is fitting, now and henceforth be exposed and rightly accursed. Amen.

For I believe and confess that you foreknew before the ages everything that was to be, whether good or evil, but predestined only what was good. The good predestined by you are investigated by your faithful in two ways—or rather, it is evident that, through your revelation, they have been made known to them: namely, as benefits of grace and judgments of justice. For, as the Psalmist gives the most certain testimony, you, Lord, love both mercy and judgment (Ps. 33:5).

Therefore you predestined eternal life, freely given, for all your elect, and likewise predestined them to everlasting glory; for surely you would have predestined life for them in vain unless you had also predestined them to that life.

In the same way, you predestined for the devil and his angels, and likewise for all reprobate human beings, the everlasting punishment deserved by them, and similarly predestined them to that punishment. For you would plainly have predestined the punishment of perpetual death for them without cause unless you had also predestined them to it. They would not go there unless they had been destined for it, nor would they be destined for it unless they had been predestined.

For since you yourself have always existed before all the ages, and cannot now in any way be changeable even for a moment, and since throughout all the ages thereafter you will be proved to be immutable, no reprobate person would be destined there—God forbid—who had not been predestined.

Therefore, since you alone are the One who is, as you yourself testify (Exod. 3:4), and as David also says to you, “You are always the same” (Ps. 101:28), and as you say elsewhere, “You are the Lord, and you do not change” (Mal. 3:1); and since your outstanding preacher Paul likewise declares, “You alone possess immortality” (1 Tim. 6:16), that is, immutability; with you, as another apostle says, “there is no change or shadow caused by alteration” (Jas. 1:17)—it is entirely and plainly evident, and sufficiently clear to every sound-minded person, that you foreknew and predestined immediately, without any interval whatever, as one simultaneous and single act, before the ages, all and each of your works. For, according to what Isaiah said, “you have made the things that are to be” (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore, following David the prophet and most faithfully explaining him, your servant Augustine says: “God, according to that will of his which is eternal together with his foreknowledge, has certainly already made in heaven and on earth everything whatever that he willed—not only past or present things, but also things still future.”

Since, therefore, your will, Lord, is eternal together with your foreknowledge, as Augustine says here; and since, in relation to your omnipotence, concerning your works alone, to foreknow is the same as to will, as Orosius writes to that same Augustine; and since to have made your will is likewise to have made the thing willed, as Ambrose says—it is beyond doubt evident that whatever will appear outwardly as future in the work has already been made by you in predestination, according to what Pope Gregory dares to say, teaches, and writes.

Therefore, let no Catholic of yours presume that there was any interval, even for a moment, between the foreknowledge and predestination of your works, since he reads, hears, and believes that you made all the things you willed simultaneously. Especially since you did nothing whatever in actuality before you had incomparably foreknown the future and arranged it by predestining it in your eternal counsel.

But now it is time, Lord, to set forth the truthful testimonies of the divine books, by which it is taught without hesitation and declared without ambiguity that the reprobate have been predestined to the eternal fires of punishment.

First, I consider it right to present your unconquerable truth, Lord Jesus Christ, rightly so called. “Whoever does not believe,” you say, “has already been judged” (John 3:18), that is, as Augustine explained, “has already been condemned.” “For,” he says, “the judgment has not yet appeared, but the judgment has already taken place.”

Again: “The prince of this world,” you say, “has already been judged” (John 16:11), that is, as the same author explained, “has been irrevocably destined by the judgment of eternal fire.”

David also says: “Therefore the wicked shall not rise in the judgment” (Ps. 1:5). Augustine explains that they have already been destined for utterly certain punishments.

Again: “You have struck all those who oppose me without cause.” “This,” he says, “is rightly spoken in predestination concerning the devil and his angels.”

And lest anyone say that only the devil together with his angels has been destined for death—which is proved to be altogether absurd, namely, that the head should be separated from the body in predestination—David says again: “You have brought me down to the dust of death” (Ps. 21:15), that is, the wicked have been destined for death. No prudent person doubts that this is said of all human beings made from dust and likewise left to dust.

Solomon also says: “The Lord has made everything for himself, even the wicked for the day of evil” (Prov. 16:4).

The book of Ecclesiasticus likewise says: “Whoever turns from righteousness to sin, God has prepared him for the sword” (Ecclus. 26:27). This must plainly be understood as referring only to the people of the reprobate.

Hence Job also says: “Ask any of the travelers, and you will learn that they understand this same thing: the wicked is kept for the day of destruction and is led to the day of wrath” (Job 21:30). His commentator Gregory explains it thus: “Divine patience often tolerates for a long time those whom it has already condemned to punishments foreknown.”

When explaining the words, “He has counsel and strength” (Job 12:13), Gregory says among other things: “The hidden delay of judgment itself may also be signified by the word ‘counsel’: when he sometimes strikes sinners later—not because the guilt of the wicked is not seen, but so that the sentence of their condemnation, which is deferred in order that they may do penance, may be made to emerge, as it were, slowly and deliberately. Therefore what he sometimes judges outwardly by an open sentence was hidden before the ages in the counsel of almighty God.”

Again, explaining, “You have appointed his limits, which cannot be passed” (Job 14:5), he says: “Nothing comes upon human beings in this world without the hidden counsel of almighty God. For God, foreknowing all things that would follow, decreed before the ages how they would be arranged throughout the ages.”

Again, explaining the statement about the wicked, “They shall be like straw before the face of the wind, and like chaff which the whirlwind scatters” (Job 21:18), he says: “Before the eyes of almighty God the life of the wicked is chaff. Even if it appears green for a moment, it is nevertheless seen as already consumed by his judgment, because it has been assigned to eternal destruction.”

Concerning such people and their crimes you yourself, Lord, say through Moses: “Are not these things stored up with me and sealed in my treasuries? Vengeance is mine, and I will repay them in due time” (Deut. 32:34–35).

Again: “The day of their destruction is near, and the appointed times hasten” (ibid.).

Again: “I will raise my hand to heaven and say: I live forever. If I sharpen my sword like lightning, and my hand takes hold of judgment, I will repay vengeance upon my enemies and recompense those who hate me. I will intoxicate my arrows with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh from the blood of the slain and from the captivity of the enemies’ uncovered heads. Praise his people, nations, for he will avenge the blood of his servants and repay vengeance upon his enemies” (Deut. 32:40–43).

If anyone presumes to say that all these things, and innumerably many others scattered throughout the breadth of the canonical Scriptures, were indeed foreknown by you but in no way predetermined, make him, I ask, carefully consider how contrary he is to the truth and how he favors pernicious falsehood. For he subjects you so rashly to mutability that, as Saint Augustine says, “no mutable nature would reward anything unless you, Lord our God, remained immutable.” He would care little if the Church regarded—or rather believed and proclaimed—that you were mutable from eternity until the day of judgment—God forbid—and that on the day of judgment itself you were changed by doing what had not been predestined, namely, by sending the reprobate to punishments. Thus, thereafter, you would be proved to be eternally changed—that is, dead—God forbid; for, as the authority of Augustine, Gregory, and the other teachers testifies, how can one who is changed not die?

But far be it from us to suppose that you, Lord, who could not, cannot, and will not be changed in any way, might at some time—even for a moment—be mutable without beginning, up to the day of judgment, and then appear changed forever solely because of the condemnation of the reprobate and the punishment owed to them.

Indeed, Lord, it would truly have been better, consistently with your immutability, if none of the elect had been created—much less saved—while you were mutable, let alone changed. How much more must it be rejected as impossible that you should be changed because of the vessels of wrath and anger, upon whom your face is turned because of the evils they commit, “to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. 33:16)?

Concerning these people the faithful truthfully sing to you far and wide, day and night: “But you, O God, will lead them down into the pit of destruction” (Ps. 54:24).

The apostle Peter also says of them: “Their judgment from of old does not cease, and their destruction does not sleep” (2 Pet. 2:3).

And Paul says (Rom. 9:22): “Although God wished to show his wrath and make known his power, he endured with great patience vessels fitted or fashioned for destruction, according to Jerome; or prepared for destruction, according to Ambrose; or perfected unto perfection, according to Augustine”—that is, unquestionably, predestined, as Augustine himself is known to have explained it.

The same preacher also says: “They complete their sins continually; for the wrath of God has come upon them to the end” (1 Thess. 2:16).

Jude likewise says: “Certain people have slipped in, who were long ago written down for this judgment—ungodly men” (Jude 4). By asserting that they were written down not for this judgment but into this judgment—that is, into this condemnation—he wished them to be understood as not merely foreknown but also equally predestined.

For you, eternal God, had predestined them before any person born in time knew them to have been foreknown. Since you foreknew that they would persevere in damnable sins through their own misery, you, as the most just judge, predestined them to destruction, justly and deservedly enough. You not only predestined them, but, by predestining them, already destined them.

Hence David speaks as though of those already placed in hell by predestination, although they were still to be placed there at your command. For after he had said, “and afterward they will delight in their mouth,” he added: “Like sheep they have been placed in hell” (Ps. 48:14–15).

All this is most clearly in harmony with the apostle John, who says in the Apocalypse: “And the books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life; and the dead were judged from what was written in the books, according to their works” (Rev. 20:12).

Again: “And each was judged according to his works; and death and hell were thrown into the lake of fire”—by saying that death and hell were thrown into the lake of fire, he means the devil and his followers—“and whoever was not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire” (ibid., 13–15).

Again, a little earlier: “And the devil who deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur” (ibid., 9).

Again, a little later: “And he said to me, ‘Write, because these words are most trustworthy and true.’ And he said to me, ‘It is done’” (Rev. 21:5–6).

And lest anyone perhaps doubt this after hearing it from John, you yourself immediately follow, Lord Jesus Christ, and say: “I am the α and the ω, the beginning and the end. I will give the thirsty water from the fountain of life freely. Whoever conquers will possess these things, and I will be his God, and he will be my son. But for the fearful, unbelieving, accursed, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake burning with fire and sulfur, which is the second death” (ibid., 6–8).

Let unbelievers and liars therefore fear and beware, lest their portion be with the accomplices named above, if they have chosen to remain obstinate by resisting such evident truth.

Again: “Behold, I am coming soon, and my reward is with me, to repay each according to his works” (Rev. 22:12).

[Note: [Col. 0353D] Something is missing here.]

Unless this is in the predestination that you established by an immutable and irrevocable preordination.

You therefore continue and say: “I am the α and the ω, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have authority over the tree of life and may enter the city through the gates. Outside are dogs, sorcerers, the sexually immoral, murderers, those who serve idols, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood” (ibid., 13–15).

Let all liars in general hear this, but especially those who, in religious teaching, not only do not fear or feel shame but do not hesitate in the least to be deceitful. For nothing more serious than this kind of falsehood can ever be found—or rather, nothing is found so grave, although some regard it as light or even consider it pleasant. But let them hear what follows if they hold what came before in contempt.

“I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches” (Rev. 22:16). And a little later: “I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues written in this book. And if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his portion from the book of life, from the holy city, and from the things written in this book. He who testifies to these things says: ‘Yes, I am coming soon’” (ibid., 18–20).

Behold, Lord Jesus, in this holy book of yours I find that the devil and his angels, and also all reprobate human beings, have already been destined by you to be thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, as stated above.

I do not dare to deny you—that is, I do not dare to deny the truth—for I fear being denied by you, just as you yourself testify: “Whoever denies me before human beings, I will also deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:33).

Paul likewise says: “If we deny him, he also will deny us” (2 Tim. 2:12).

Therefore, as I said, I do not dare to deny you, because I fear being denied by you. But I do not presume to add or subtract anything, since I fear either that the plagues written in this very book may be added to me or that my portion may be taken away from the book of life.

Therefore, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I beseech you, Lord, insofar as I am able, that you graciously deign to support me as I need, and do not permit any of your elect—God forbid—to remain longer in doubt about this. Rather, do not delay in making the most health-giving truth known to them, since you see that it is wholly necessary for them.

For, according to the most truthful testimony of blessed Augustine, which he openly delivered to the people while clearly and faithfully explaining a difficult evangelical passage: “Those who build falsehood in human beings—what do they expel from them except the truth? They admit the devil and exclude Christ; they admit the adulterer and exclude the bridegroom—paranymphs, or rather procurers, of the serpent. For they speak in order that the serpent may possess and Christ may be excluded. When falsehood possesses, the serpent possesses; when truth possesses, Christ possesses. For he himself said, ‘I am the truth’ (John 14:6); but of the other it is said, ‘He did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him’ (John 8:44).”

Therefore, what that same blessed minister of yours, Augustine, truthfully endeavored to affirm—namely, that the reprobate are condemned by foreknowledge—while elsewhere he admits that they are condemned to death by predestination, is wholly true in both respects, because both are true here.

For, as the same author wisely and truthfully acknowledges, foreknowledge is sometimes used for predestination. Nor is this contrary—God forbid—but rather it appears to agree with the truth. Such is the statement of the Apostle: “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. 11:7), although elsewhere, joining the two together but distinguishing them from one another by a reasonable difference, he wonderfully defined the matter by saying: “By predestination God foreknew those things that he himself was going to do.” Hence it is said: “Making the things that are to be” (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint).

Again, connecting predestination more plainly and fully with foreknowledge, he says concerning the Trinity: “To arrange in his foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived or changed, the works that he himself is going to do—that, and nothing else, is to predestine.”

Again, more briefly but much more clearly expressing the same sense: after he had stated that the Apostle said, “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. 11:7), and had explained that in this passage he wished predestination to be signified by the term “foreknowledge,” he shortly afterward says: “To have predestined is to have foreknown what he himself was going to do.”

Therefore, as I have already said, both are true: namely, that the reprobate are condemned both by foreknowledge and by predestination; and it is entirely clear that they were justly predestined to destruction. The testimonies cited above prove this sufficiently and more than sufficiently. Catholics certainly do not doubt that these testimonies are unconquerable.

Even if the testimony for this matter had to be understood entirely through metalepsis—a figure by which what follows is understood through what precedes—it could and indeed ought to be understood in that way. Nevertheless, if they still desire to hear more about this, because they see the truth, which they love, being excessively attacked, I ask them to lend their ears to hearing and to devote themselves to defending the truth now and henceforth.

Let them hear, I say, Augustine still speaking wonderfully through the divine gift freely infused into him in abundant measure:

“This good, which is to seek God, there was no one to do; there was not even one—but among that class of human beings which was predestined to destruction.”

Again, speaking of the two cities: “One of them,” he says, “is predestined to reign eternally with the Lord; the other to undergo eternal punishment with the devil.”

Again: “If the Church were so certain about some people that it even knew who they were—people who, although they still live in this life, are nevertheless predestined to go into everlasting fire with the devil—she would not pray for them any more than she prays for the devil himself.”

Again: “What will he give to those whom he predestined to life, who gave these things even to those whom he predestined to death?”

Again, in the *Enchiridion*, which he wrote and published as an old man concerning faith, hope, and charity, with exceedingly subtle understanding, most practiced intellect, exceptionally pure expression, and brilliantly lucid style, wonderfully and uniquely favored by God:

“For the condemnation,” he says, “of those whom he justly predestined to punishment.”

The same work also says that the children of Gehenna were prepared not out of it but into it, just as the children of the kingdom are prepared into the kingdom.

What could be more evident? What could be more sufficient?

“As,” he says, “the children of the kingdom are prepared into the kingdom, so also the children of Gehenna are prepared into it.”

This is plainly nothing other than being predestined.

Indeed, if that great author had not recognized all these things, and many others besides, as utterly truthful and entirely consonant with the Catholic faith, he would in no way have left them uncorrected. Rather, when he carefully revised and reviewed his books, he would have tried to correct them. Nor would he have spoken about them so frequently to the people, fearlessly and undauntedly, freely, willingly, and openly, confidently and boldly, and joyfully, having put aside slavish fear and being suffused with luminous love for you, if he had known any danger to be involved.

I have already set out some of these passages above, and I have thought it appropriate to add a few here as well:

“There is a certain people prepared for the wrath of God, condemned with the devil.”

Again: “There is a certain people born for the wrath of God.”

Again: “Why did the Lord say to the Jews, ‘You do not believe because you are not of my sheep’ (John 10:26), unless he saw that they were predestined to everlasting destruction, not purchased for eternal life at the price of his blood?”

Again: “What can the wolf do? What can the thief and robber do? They do not destroy any except those predestined to destruction.”

Again: “These died in indignation and were predestined to everlasting death.”

Again: “The world,” he says, “hates the world, the enemy the reconciled, the condemned the saved, the defiled the cleansed.”

Again: “Judas the betrayer of Christ was called the son of perdition, predestined to condemnation.”

Again: “For this world he does not pray, since he is not ignorant of the end to which it has been predestined.”

Blessed Fulgentius likewise speaks in this way: “God also prepared punishments for sinners—namely, for those whom he justly predestined to undergo punishments.”

Here he plainly confesses both points: that punishments were predestined for the reprobate and that the reprobate themselves were in turn predestined to those punishments.

Hence he argued in a thoroughly Catholic and exceedingly comprehensive manner in seven books against the two books of Faustus, formerly a heretical monk of Lérins and afterward bishop of Riez. That same teacher wonderfully convicted him and crushed the devil’s inventions; together with fourteen other holy fellow bishops, he drove from the Church of Christ and eliminated the deadly poison of Antichrist.

He also wrote three other books *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, as well as that one book which he is known to have composed entirely on this single question for Monimus, who had consulted him about it.

The glorious Gregory also—some of whose statements I have already inserted above—spoke in this way among other things:

“The Lord saw the dark sacrifice when, entering the prison of hell, he struck the cruel spirits and, by dying, condemned the rulers of death.”

He says that this is spoken not of the future but already of the past for this reason: “Whatever was going to be future in action had already been accomplished in predestination.”

Again: “That Leviathan has been assigned to everlasting torments together with all his members.”

Again, he says that even the day of judgment itself has been predestined. Explaining the statement from the book of Job, “A lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich, prepared for the appointed time” (Job 12:5), he says: “The time of the despised lamp is the predestined day of the final judgment.”

Saint Isidore likewise says: “There is a twofold predestination: either of the elect to rest or of the reprobate to death.”

For he does not say, “There are two,” because there are not; rather, he says “twofold,” that is, divided into two, because you, Lord, spoke once: in one predestination, yet a twofold one, you freely justify and eternally save the elect, and also deservedly reject and justly condemn the reprobate.

“And,” as the aforementioned Gregory says, “looking upon some, you redeem them; abandoning others, you destroy them.”

This is what is meant by predestination being called twofold: it is divided between the elect and the reprobate, although it is one, even though it is twofold. It is like what blessed Augustine and the other Fathers frequently call charity or love twofold, although it is not two but one, even though it is also twofold because it is directed toward God and neighbor.

It is also like what Father Augustine says when he calls the work of God divided into two, wishing it to be understood as twofold, and when he likewise calls the world divided into four parts. Yet it is not four worlds but one. He also acknowledges that continence is divided into five parts, but does not teach that there are five continences; rather, there is one.

Hence Saint Gregory also calls the knowledge of the Jews twofold; nevertheless, although it is twofold, it is understood to be one.

This kind of expression is extremely common, including among authors of secular literature. Since it is entirely proper and truthful, it is not irrelevant to insert here some examples that may reinforce the defense of the opinion stated above. One of those authors called a tree twofold, intending not two trees but one; another called the quality of a name divided into two; another called the condition of all feet threefold; and the equally learned Priscian explained as “tripartite” what the other had called “threefold.”

Nor should it seem absurd to anyone who thinks piously that a twofold predestination is believed, recognized, and unequivocally said to exist in you, our Lord, who are naturally one but personally threefold.

Certainly, according to this twofold predestination of yours—as your Augustine faithfully believes and confidently asserts—you are good in the benefit bestowed upon some and just in the punishment of others. Moreover, as he consequently professes, you are good in all things, because it is good when what is owed is repaid; and you are just in all things, because it is just when what is owed is given without fraud against anyone.

All these things I both believe and confess here, thanks be to you, insofar as you have freely bestowed this upon me. And because I find these things spoken by you in your books—that is, in the books of your ministers, truthfully expounded through your grace—I do not dare, God forbid, to contradict such evident truth.

For I fear being denied by you, the Truth, just as you threatened, and I exceedingly fear that repeated statement of Paul: “If anyone announces to you something contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:8).

I owe you, Lord Jesus, such an enduring love of your unconquerable truth that, as Augustine, your faithful servant, truly declares, I must not—God forbid—be turned away from the truth either by the desire to please human beings or by consideration of avoiding any disadvantages.

As blessed Gregory also teaches, insofar as we can avoid giving offense to our neighbors without sin, we ought to do so; but if offense is taken at the truth, it is more useful to allow offense to arise than to abandon the truth.

Nor should the person of anyone be accepted against what must be received, when either Augustine or the Apostle, by announcing the truth, is struck with an anathema worthy of the Apostle’s own mouth.

For, as the aforementioned Gregory truthfully admits: “When the matter is conducted with faith preserved, it is a mark of virtue if whatever belongs to the earlier person is endured.”

Otherwise, if it were possible, I ought always, and would rather, fall a thousand times for the truth than once—God forbid—yield and succumb by submitting to anyone who speaks otherwise. I remember your statement: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I will also confess before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:32).

I also remember this: “Do not move the ancient boundaries which your fathers established” (Prov. 22:28).

As Gregory explains, heretics do this; they stand outside the bosom of the holy Church.

“They move the boundaries,” he says, “because by transgressing they pass beyond the constitutions of the Fathers. They also tear apart and feed the flocks, because they draw even the inexperienced to themselves by their perverse persuasions and nourish them with deadly gifts for slaughter.”

Blessed Job also rebukes them, saying: “Does God need your lie, so that you may speak deceitfully for him?” (Job 13:7).

God does not need falsehood, because the truth does not seek the support of falsehood’s assistance. But because heretics cannot defend from the truth what they perversely understand about God, they seek, as though to approve a ray of light, the shadows of falsehood.

They speak deceitfully for him when they deceive weak minds by foolish seduction, drawing them away from understanding him.

Again: “Will he be pleased with the one whom nothing can conceal? Or will he be deceived like a human being by your frauds?” (ibid., 9).

Heretics display frauds to God because they assert things that cannot possibly please the one on whose behalf they speak. While they seem to defend him, they offend him, falling into opposition to the one whom they appear, through their preaching, to serve.

Therefore it is said through the Psalmist: “That you may destroy the enemy and the defender” (Psalm 8:3). For every heretic is both an enemy and a defender of almighty God, because in attempting to defend him in one respect, he thereby opposes his truth. Since nothing can be hidden from God, he judges in them what they feel inwardly, not what they appear outwardly to profess. Since, then, God is not deceived like a human being by their deceptions, it is rightly added: “He himself will convict you, because in secret you show regard for his person. As soon as he stirs, he will trouble you, and his terror will fall upon you” (Job 13:10).

What he asserts about receiving the face of God in secret can be understood in two ways. There are some who perceive the truth in their hearts and yet speak outwardly what is false about God. So that they may not appear to be defeated, they recognize the truth inwardly and nevertheless attack it outwardly. Hence it is well said here: “He himself will convict you, because in secret you show regard for his person,” as though it were openly said: “The more you are reproved by him for falsehood, the more you see in yourselves what is true.”

What a heretic is, however—so that no one may be permitted to fabricate one thing in place of another—a certain Father, Cassiodorus, has defined most beautifully. He says: “A heretic is one who, driven either by ignorance or contempt of divine law, is found to be obstinately attached to some new error, or to be a follower of some sect; he prefers to oppose catholic truth rather than submit to it.”

I have thought this should be inserted here because I have discovered that many people are thereby both deceived and deceivers—those, namely, who wish, or, to put it more mildly, suppose that those are heretics who believe and confess as the truth—despite necessary opposition and contradiction, and with your help—this truth of the catholic faith concerning the predestination of the reprobate, and who, on the contrary, assert to be catholic those who are not afraid to whisper, indeed openly to preach, a falsehood hostile to so evident a truth. They make light of what blessed Basil says: those who are nourished by divine utterances neither corrupt the divine doctrines nor tolerate a single syllable of corruption; rather, if the occasion arises, they embrace every form of death for their sake. They also despise what Gregory Nazianzen says: “It is the mark of courage to persevere in the truth, even if someone is compelled to fight against things that are nothing.”

Falsehood and lying are indeed nothing; and hearts that are always truthful both avoid and dread them, as they ought, above all the bodily kinds of death. Especially in religious teaching they altogether avoid the precipice of deceitful speech.

This is, then—thanks be to you, Lord, nourishing Trinity—my inviolable faith and confession concerning your foreknowledge and predestination, which the Truth himself proclaimed, and which the disciples of that same Truth likewise proclaimed against false-speaking supporters, and—unless they are corrected—sons of falsehood and perdition, and against their pestilential poisons and heretical doctrines.

If, sprinkled with your grace, they carefully attend to, weigh, and ponder how, from the beginning of the angelic fall—as the apostle Peter says—you “did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them into the chains and prisons of hell and delivered them to the punishments of this air, reserving them for greater torments on the day of judgment” (2 Peter 2); and how you also destroyed the former world because of the wicked crimes of human beings; and how, moreover, you punished the unspeakable crimes and vices of the Sodomites, consumed and destroyed them by heavenly fire, and plunged them into everlasting punishments; and how you cast Pharaoh and his army into the sea and there utterly annihilated them, shaken out like straw—

if, I say, laying aside their hostility, they diligently examine these things and, with your help, wisely take them into consideration, they will very easily understand that you cast down those angels—who, as Jude, the brother of James, writes, “did not preserve their own principality, but abandoned their own dwelling,” and are “reserved under darkness in everlasting chains for the judgment of the great day” (Jude 6)—into this prison of the dark air, and reserved them for punishment throughout the ages, where they deservedly suffer even greater pains, as both of the aforesaid apostles testify, not without the everlasting counsel of your predestination.

They will also understand that you did not commit those things subsequently narrated concerning the reprobate without predestination—which God forbid. Otherwise you would be found to have been changeable before all ages and, at the beginning of the ages, according to their most deceptive doctrine, immediately changed—which cannot be the case even for a moment—although you alone are believed by all true catholics to be immutable and are known to be so, revealed by you more clearly than daylight.

Grant also, I beg you, Lord God, that they may consider again and again—not now as insolent, stubborn, obstinate, contentious, deceitful, and mendacious people, since such persons cannot be perceptive enough to behold the truth against which they struggle, however naturally clever they may wish to be—but rather, having become simple lovers of the truth, that with the whole spiritual vision of their minds they may consider the following:

If you, by your coeternal predestination, destined, and afterward and daily destine and will destine, the souls of the reprobate—from that first Cain down to the last person who will die before the day of judgment, souls drawn from their own bodies whenever they have died, are dying, or will die—to the torments deserved and entirely justly appointed for them; then you are not merely changeable before the ages, but also—which is altogether impossible—you have been changed repeatedly from the beginning of the death of those same reprobates, indeed from the beginning of the condemnation of the wicked angels. You have changed through innumerable alterations, and you are changed and will be changed through each day and night, and, once changed, you will undoubtedly remain so throughout the ages, solely because of the sons of Gehenna whom the enemies of the truth obstinately and deceitfully deny to have been predestined to everlasting punishment.

I beg you, Lord, make them attend to, weigh, and ponder these things as they ought, and at last see what they have hitherto pretended not to see: what and how great an evil they have long preached, continue to preach, and have asserted and continue to assert, openly and mendaciously, against you, our Lord God, who are always unchangeable—an evil destructive to themselves and to their associates alike.

And I beg you mercifully to recall them to the way of salvation, lest they persist in so deadly an error of heresy. Let them see, I say, what and how great an evil it is that, although all your elect have always done, do, and will do every good thing with counsel—insofar as they are aided by the gratuitous assistance of your goodness—they presume not only by lying but also by swearing falsely to affirm publicly that you, who are the author and fountain of all wisdom, indeed the triune, one, and eternal Wisdom, have wished, or been able, or even been obliged, to do anything without counsel—which God forbid.

I do not even speak of your having destined, from the beginning of the human race, the souls of the dying reprobate, or of your having destined those same souls at the end, together with their own bodies received on the day of judgment, with the devil and his angels, without the counsel of predestination.

When they have examined these matters keenly and understood them vividly, may they be salutarily confounded and put to shame, and so at last submit humbly to the truth and cease their opposition to me. But if, with brazen brow and without any sense of shame, they remain in falsehood rather than withdraw from so great an error as they ought, let them themselves see where, in their ruin, they may turn.

I beg you, Lord God, freely to guard your Church, lest they continue to pervert it by their falsehood and overturn it with the pestilence of their heresy and the rest of their depravity, even though they thereby sorrowfully overturn themselves and their own people with them.

But I, freely taught by the Truth itself—which the aforesaid teachers of your Church preached, and of which they were altogether its most faithful, devoted, and renowned ministers—here clearly set forth the catholic faith concerning your predestination. Freely and piously inspired, encouraged, armed, mercifully and wonderfully aided, protected, supported, trusting, and upheld by you, I believe it faithfully—thanks be to you—I hold it firmly, defend it truthfully and openly, and everyone whom I know to teach contrary doctrines I flee as a plague and reject as a heretic.

And—to express with the greatest sorrow what is consequently established concerning such people by the most blessed Augustine—I declare that anyone whom I hear obstinately resisting the unconquerable truth and whom I see teaching things contrary to it is a heretic and an enemy of the Christian faith, and for that reason must be anathematized by all catholics.

Moreover, if any of them, after reading and understanding these things once, refuses to yield, and, hardened like Pharaoh—in the manner of a heretic—scorns to submit to truth so manifest, I judge that his conflict should now be avoided, according to the counsel, or rather command, of the apostle Paul: “A person who is such, I see to be perverted and condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3:11).

Nevertheless, for the sake of the less knowledgeable, who have therefore been enticed by them and, unless corrected, are lost, I would wish—if it pleased you, Lord—that a public assembly be held, so that, with the truth openly established and falsehood utterly destroyed, we might together give thanks to you, who have deigned to grant us the long-desired outcome, indeed one more prosperous than we ask or understand.

For I suffer exceedingly great pain and endure the greatest sorrow day and night because, on account of the lowliness of my name, I see the truth regarded as lowly among human beings; and because those who ought to preserve sincere love toward you have not preserved it, since, merely so that they might appear to be my victors, they have loved and do love you not at all, or scarcely at all—you whom they did not shrink, and do not shrink, from denying because of me.

And would that it pleased you, almighty and most merciful Lord, that, just as I believe and hope in you—since you have freely given me the ability to do so, as you long ago deigned to give it and daily deign to give also the will—before an everywhere gathered multitude of chosen people who fear you, with the prince of this kingdom present, together with a venerable company of bishops, priests, monks, and canons, I might be granted, if they refused to receive this truth of the catholic faith concerning your predestination, to establish its truth before all who witnessed it by the test I am about to describe, with your grace favoring me.

Let four barrels be placed one after another and filled separately with boiling water, rich oil, and pitch, and let a very great fire be kindled in the last. Then, invoking your glorious name, may I be permitted, in order to prove this faith of mine—indeed, the catholic faith—to enter each one and pass through them one after another, until, with you going before, accompanying, following, extending your right hand, and mercifully bringing me out, I might emerge unharmed. Thus at last, in your Church, the clarity of this catholic faith might shine forth for the faithful, falsehood vanish, faith be strengthened, and unbelief be avoided.

May you deign, Lord, to inspire readers and hearers of this kind of work with such a desire that they earnestly implore you to bring this desire of my heart, as your Church requires, swiftly to completion. And if, with your support, I emerge unharmed from all of them, may they embrace the truth and curse falsehood.

But if I should tremble even to begin, or fear to complete, what I promise—in believing, confessing, hoping, and loving what comes from you, through you, and in you, secure only in you and certain only of your grace—then let them immediately cast me into the fire and permit me deservedly to perish there.

Nevertheless, I humbly beg you, Lord, in your sweetest name, that no catholic may rashly rebuke me in his heart—which God forbid—for daring to ask such things. As you yourself know best, I do not presume upon my own rashness to ask them; rather, I receive this daring from you through your goodness.

Indeed, whoever fears you truly and loves you sincerely, and deigns to read these things or hear them attentively, implores your gratuitous mercy with fraternal compassion and a doubled love, asking that you, who alone are a helper in times of need (Psalm 9:10), deign to help me earnestly in my tribulation as I believe and hope in your gratuitous mercy; that you enrich me with the means both to begin and to complete this work in perfect faith; that you strengthen me with solid hope; that you grant me the most sincere charity; and that you freely adorn me with the truest humility always before you.

Drive far from your orthodox Church the deadly falsehood of this doctrine, and grant that thereafter I may rejoice with your elect over the truth of the catholic faith revealed to your faithful. May our true and sincere joy, our highest and solid rejoicing, and our common glory in you alone henceforth be this: that, through your mercy, your people and nation have at last been freed from the grave treachery of the heretics.

For certainly none of your elect has ever been able, can, or will ever be able, to please you for anything of his own, even for a moment. Rather, all your own have hitherto pleased you, please you now, and will always please you through your gratuitous grace, because of what comes from you.

Thus, animated by this faith freely given, made firm also by hope, and likewise inflamed by charity, I humbly beseech you through yourself, O most good God, that, having granted me true humility, you may always cause me to rejoice in the solid joy of life.

Finally, to you and to your name is due glory throughout the ages: because of justice, since you deservedly humble, bend, and bow down the proud; and because of grace, since you freely exalt, raise up, and glorify the humble. Through both, I beseech you, almighty and merciful Trinity and Unity, to forgive completely and pardon all the debts of all your enemies—whoever they may be—whether through ignorance or knowingly they have harmed, indeed wished to harm, me because of hatred for your name; though without doubt they have harmed themselves more than me. Forgive them all their offenses and crimes together, and spare them entirely. Amen.

I give you thanks, O triune and one sovereign Lord God, however great those thanks may be, because you have deigned, and deign, freely to enlighten, inflame, and assist me so that the catholic faith concerning predestination may be believed and confessed—and, as I believe and hope, you will increasingly deign day and night henceforth to do so. Amen.

I beg, insofar as divine humility is granted to me, in the most immediate presence of the majesty of the triune Unity and the one Trinity, that whoever reads this not with black envy but rather with dove-like love may remember Gotteschalk the sinner before God and, with a fatherly or brotherly affection, simply implore his most kind mercy, asking that he deign freely in his goodness to grant me always and everywhere, before him, the excellence of true humility and the preeminence of sincere charity.

May he protect me continually in his tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues (Psalm 30:21)—that is, in the right faith of the catholic Church, from the calumnies of heretics—so that, for the name of the Lord our God and the love of truth, I may incomparably prefer to suffer all present adversities through their persecutions rather than deviate even for a moment—which God forbid—from love or confession of the truth, or from the catholic faith prescribed above, which has been declared both by the mouth of Truth himself and by the unconquerable authorities of his ministers.

For I owe my neighbor as much love as I owe myself; but I owe God love with my whole being, because whatever good we possess is either God himself or comes from him.

But you, whoever you may be, pious reader and learned interpreter, who wisely receive this faith and confession of mine, [Note: Col. 0363D: Something is missing here.] I earnestly ask you as a venerable father, or faithfully exhort you as a brother: if you wish to see the truth forever and to hasten to rejoice eternally in the truth itself with the holy angels, the chosen human beings, and the faithful witnesses of that same truth, dread above bodily death that most pernicious and destructive kind of lie which is committed detestably in religious teaching.

Thus, according to what was divinely spoken through blessed Augustine, let the most beautiful and modest charity poured into our hearts gratefully receive the kiss of doves, so that cautious humility may avoid, or solid truth blunt, the dog’s tooth.

By the kiss of the dove he evidently signifies the inspection of those who are upright and truthful in heart concerning themselves and their words. By the dog’s tooth he signifies the malicious and mocking criticism of the perverse and deceitful.

Therefore beseech and implore, I beg you, the Lord our God and his majesty, that against the barking of heretics we may have the truest, simplest, and most gracious love, and that, even to the end, we may blunt their teeth and their most biting falsehood by unconquerable—whether they wish it or not—and solid truth.

But if anyone becomes angry with me while I say these things, he will admit that they were said about himself—or another author asserts it.

Whoever, then, still damnably presumes such things and, fearing the truth and its judgment either not at all or only slightly, boldly denies—in opposition to it—that the reprobate have been predestined to everlasting punishment is someone who does not fear that the same truth will say to him on the last day, with everyone listening: “Behold, I now justly deny you, because you once unjustly denied me.”

Let such a person, I say, deny the truth if he wishes and dares—he who does not fear offending the truth, which he needs day and night together with us.

But we, hearing from that same truth, “The day of vengeance is in my heart” (Isaiah 63:4), and, “Behold, our God will bring vengeance and recompense” (Isaiah 35:4), should trample down this harmful falsehood and preach the truth, so that the same Truth—my God and God’s Son—may have mercy on us, both now and then, on the coming day of vengeance. For if we truly fear the fury of deceitful people [Note: Col. 0365A: Something is missing here.], provided only that we may be able to please him who governs and protects us and shields us forever against the rage of those who rage. Amen.

Lord God—blessed and unconquerable Trinity and Unity—pour out, I beg you, upon those who read these things the faith to believe, and grant to those who believe the power to confess. To those who believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation (Romans 10:10), grant the abundance of a rich reward and the blessedness of eternal light with you. Amen.

[Column 365]

# All the Surviving Fragments of the Booklet Delivered by Gotteschalk to Archbishop Rabanus of Mainz at the Assembly at Mainz, in the Year 848

(From Hincmar of Reims, in his work *On Predestination*.)

## Article I: On the Twofold Predestination

(Hincmar, *On Predestination*, chapter 5, p. 25.) Let us set forth what Gotteschalk, the standard-bearer, forerunner, and reviver of this perverse doctrine, writes concerning the first point at issue in the book of his contentious composition presented to Archbishop Rabanus, saying:

“At last,” he says, “I read your book, venerable bishop, in which I found it stated that the impious, or reprobate, have not been divinely predestined to condemnation.”

And a little later:

“He foreknew, I say, that they would have a most evil birth and a worse death; but he predestined them to endure everlasting torment and eternal destruction.”

And again, a little later:

“For truly, just as he predestined all the elect to life through the gratuitous gift of his grace alone—as the pages of the Old and New Testaments provide the clearest evidence to those who consider them carefully and soberly—so altogether he predestined every reprobate to the punishment of eternal death, through the most just judgment of his unchangeable justice.”

## Article II: On Free Will

(Hincmar, same work, chapter 21, p. 118.) Hence Gotteschalk, the modern Predestinarian, says in his booklet to Rabanus, Archbishop of Mainz, at the relevant passage:

“Concerning that free will which the Church of Christ ought to hold and believe, not only have the other catholic Fathers discussed it clearly—thanks be to God—but blessed Augustine is known to have inculcated it more fully and abundantly against the Pelagians and Coelestians in various little works, and especially in the *Hypomnesticon*.

“Therefore I would much rather rely incomparably upon the fruitful assertions of that same most catholic teacher than upon the erroneous opinions of Gennadius of Massilia, who in many passages presumed to resist both the catholic faith and the unconquerable authorities of the blessed Fathers, following the exceedingly pernicious doctrine of the unhappy Cassian.”

## Article III: On the Will of God

And Gotteschalk, the modern Predestinarian, says in his book to Rabanus, Archbishop of Mainz:

“All whom God wills to be saved are undoubtedly saved; nor can anyone be saved unless God wills him to be saved; nor is there anyone whom God wills to be saved who is not saved, because our God has done whatever he has willed.”

Gotteschalk, chief of the new Predestinarians, had written in the aforesaid booklet to Rabanus:

“‘All’ and ‘all’ must be understood to mean all who are saved. Concerning them the Apostle says, ‘who wills all human beings to be saved’; and also all who are not saved, whom God does not will to be saved.”

## Article IV: On the Death of Christ

Gotteschalk, standard-bearer of the new Predestinarians, says in his booklet to Rabanus, Archbishop of Mainz, at the relevant passage:

“Almighty God’s goodness wishes only those impious and sinful people for whom the Son of God came to redeem by the shedding of his own blood, predestined to life, irrevocably to be saved.”

And again:

“All those impious and sinful people for whom the same Son of God neither assumed a body, nor offered prayer, nor—I say—shed blood; for whom he was in no way crucified. Since he foreknew that they would be exceedingly wicked and most justly determined that they would be cast into eternal torments, he altogether does not wish them ever to be saved.”

Gotteschalk wrote in the same frequently mentioned booklet to Rabanus, Archbishop of Mainz:

“Therefore, what I most faithfully believe, I speak most confidently, and what I confess most certainly and fruitfully, I profess most truthfully: our almighty God, creator and maker of all creatures, has deigned to be the gratuitous restorer and renewer of all the elect alone; but he has eternally willed to be the Savior, Redeemer, and Crown-giver of none of the reprobate.”

Hence, in his written statement of faith addressed to the same Archbishop Rabanus, he says:

“I, Gotteschalk, believe and confess, profess and testify, from God the Father, through God the Son, in God the Holy Spirit, and I affirm and approve before God and his saints that there is a twofold predestination: of the elect to rest and of the reprobate to death.

“For just as the unchangeable God, before the foundation of the world, unchangeably predestined all his elect to eternal life through his gratuitous grace, so in every respect that same unchangeable God, through his just judgment, unchangeably predestined all the reprobate who will be condemned on the day of judgment, because of their evil merits, to a death deservedly everlasting.”

[Column 367]

# Letter of Gotteschalk to Ratramnus

(According to Cellot, *History of Gotteschalk*, p. 414.)

Come, I beg you; go forth, Clio,

with a faithful heart as you return.

Hasten, swift maiden;

turn back, wise offspring,

whose brother is Apollo.

Therefore, as though flying,

carry this rejoicing to my friend Ratramnus,

to the lord, father, and teacher,

in an unpolished metrical pen:

a poem which I gladly send back

to the celebrated and radiant man.

I love him very greatly,

with a pious and kindly heart,

since through him, though I am wicked,

good is given to me by God,

who will give to everyone who asks,

without whom, as is clear,

no pupil can accomplish anything.

Therefore, as though you had been requested,

go, and let no delay hold you back.

May you be held by him,

and behold the beautiful face of your companion.

For you come twice from him,

already beautiful from the teacher:

you remove gall, imprint honey,

and restore the pupil’s mouth [Note: Perhaps read: “your mouth”]

with a sweet feast and fragrant savor,

where you see him sitting,

teaching others well.

Let them ask powerful God

to grant these people pious rest.

I ask you: say perpetual greetings.

## 1

On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August,

the horses of the sun breathed forth their sweet fire among the clouds,

their heads and manes wet from the waves of Ocean,

as they hastened to turn the chariot toward its accustomed course;

when the bright stars had already yielded throughout the whole sky,

and pale Cynthia had likewise yielded to her brother Phoebus;

when he alone was already driving the four-horse chariot with swift reins,

and already pouring his lovely radiance upon the world divided into four quarters [Note: Divided into four parts: east, west, and so forth];

when he was already shining with new brightness and splendid brilliance,

and by his clear light was restoring to each thing its form;

when the whole earth rejoiced that the darkness had been driven far away,

and my mind, applauding me as though it anticipated good,

was exulting and triumphing more than usual,

and greater strength for rejoicing filled all my limbs;

then suddenly verses were given to me as a gratuitous gift,

brought by a companion from the High-throned King,

sweeter than honey and brighter than the sun’s light.

## 2

As my mind thirsted for them beneath the sign of Cancer,

as a reaper loves to be refreshed by the sweetness of a pure spring,

and the wasted man likewise wishes to be restored by bread because of hunger;

as the chilled man desires a fire, and the naked man clothing;

as the exile desires his fatherland, or the shipwrecked man the deepest land;

and as one buried in darkness longs for the gifts of nourishing light—

## 3

so now my needy state desired the excellent Muses

which your nobility, my friend, brought forth:

distinguished, beautiful, sweet, skillful, and graceful,

conspicuous in renown, and pure through a true pledge [Note: What is “a true pledge”? Or perhaps “pledges of truth”?];

strong in their figures and flashing with tropical charm;

you approve them through simplicity and adorn them with humble piety;

seasoned with salt and polished with the love of peace.

I believe that the Holy Spirit dictated them to you.

Indeed, beyond doubt, nothing is born from here, most humble man [the construction is uncertain];

for when I possess all good things, they are given to the one who receives them in poverty.

Therefore I ought to praise throughout the ages, with suppliant prayers,

this equal and equally pious Father,

the triune and one God,

through whom I have been joined to you as my protector,

without any merits of my own.

For he did this freely:

he wished to restore you through his blood poured out [Note: Therefore Ratramnus is exalted; for, in Gotteschalk’s view, he alone seems to have been redeemed by Christ’s blood],

enriched you with wisdom,

and also endowed you with the special honor

and the beauty of varied virtue through love.

He is worthy from this point onward of the favor of praise throughout the ages,

if he were to grant that this could be accomplished with equal and unending continuity.

Certainly he must always be loved in sincere affection

and everywhere reverently feared with chaste holiness,

since he continually asks that we be able to praise him with holy trembling.

If our hearts can offer him anything,

he has no need of us,

nor of any profit from us;

he does not need service, obedience, or hymnody.

For this reason alone he possesses the title “true Lord.”

And yet, you good teacher, let him be broadly both the author of these things

and of all other good things, whether ours or yours [Note: Read perhaps: “He is the author of these things and of all good things; or, you know, good teacher.”].

Therefore, if he grants it, I am certain that I should bless him with a humble mind,

because he has granted us such a pledge of love in you,

who are willing to preserve and compose poetic words:

words inspired by the Holy Spirit, not inflated by worthless noise,

which, with sweet-speaking expression and celebrated, radiant narration,

soothe the mind that lacks the rhythm of such music

and console it, sick with various languors.

You sing various poems for various evils.

Thus the most celebrated harpist of old strove

to calm a human heart by playing upon melodious strings—

the heart of a man who had already lost the honor of kingship,

whom a cruel dragon and wicked serpent tormented,

and deservedly so, because he had voluntarily abandoned the Lord,

lifted up by excessive pride and the cunning of savagery.

I would often call you like that Psalmist’s harpist,

my holy friend and noble poet,

for by your musical art you lighten the heavy heart of your pupil.

## 4

Would that the piety of my magnificent friend

had wished to sing in prose things so sweet, so beautiful,

so splendid, so pleasing, and so graceful,

so pious, so peaceful, and—what is more—so true to me!

Nevertheless, I obey this here, hoping to repay it elsewhere.

With God’s favor I shall write, although I shall not soon be able to do so, as I wish,

for many reasons. The first is that I wish your graciousness to know

that scarcely an hour remains

in which my rusticity can at least fashion three little letters,

because the Father’s command presses me to accomplish one thing,

then immediately another;

for this reason I cannot do this.

But I truthfully add that I am exceedingly afraid to answer you—

indeed, I hold this in my mind—

because I am sluggish in an unrefined heart,

full of ignorance and entangled in much error,

uncultivated in speech and also unversed in the old law,

although I have been occupied with it for only a short time.

For scarcely one year have I been subject to a teacher,

and thereafter I learned nothing;

uncertain amid doubtful byways,

leader of fools, precipitous and headlong in everything.

I had no guide, and therefore the light was not revealed to me,

enclosed by seven sins, except insofar as heavenly piety freely grants it.

To him be virtue, glory, and praise.

Rarely is this done through me;

through you I ask that it happen more frequently.

Therefore, since scarcely a tiny spark of knowledge can exist in me,

I greatly fear what I might mutter to a supreme friend,

sharp in understanding and exceedingly keen in speech.

For by practicing in this matter night and day,

you long ago rose to the very summit.

Considering, weighing, and pondering this,

I have resolved to set aside the knowledge that puffs up [Note: The Apostle speaks of knowledge, not virtue]

and gladly prefer what builds up,

and so far to remain silent,

until, with the Lord’s help, I can obtain something certain,

something that may delight the magnanimous ears of my companion [Note: “Magnanimous,” unless he intended to make an error in the case],

and move his heart,

lest squalor creep into his ears

and I offend again if I should pour forth something trivial.

To prevent this, my mind asks, however unwillingly,

and your piety humbly begs that you ask the same.

Finally, by the Lord’s gift, there are many teachers

located in this region, blessed with abundant talent;

many of them remain in the palace court.

To these and to others stationed throughout barbarian kingdoms,

I have eagerly stretched out my bowed-down writing in recent days,

earnestly asking that they deign to reply to me quickly,

since you know how greatly I am in need.

The opinion of blessed Augustine has been sent to them,

and I asked that it be clearly explained in accordance with its author.

Indeed, I strove to assign its proper meaning to three of them:

Matcaudus, Jonah, and Lupus, radiant in speech,

earnestly asking them to endeavor to report the truth.

A question has been proposed to all the others.

I have indeed set forth the objection, which is raised from both sides.

No one except one person has yet given me anything in reply.

He is cautious and clever at once, and moderate,

and has now weighed three answers of his little booklet [or: “letter”],

so that, without detriment to either side,

it agrees with neither side.

Therefore I have decided that both of these should be read to you,

while the others hasten to reply with discerning minds,

so that you may consider something concordant with your own judgment,

rather than with mine, dearest friend, if you see that anything is lacking.

Yet I continually ask this with a twofold prayer [Note: What does “with me two” mean? Perhaps “pray with me that the two together…”],

and remember to pray humbly with your whole heart

that an able speech may be granted to them,

and that, with the power of salt, they may become pious pledges of peace for us.

I rejoice in what has passed, venerable poet,

that although you are exalted, you shine with humble honor,

and although you ascend to heaven, you show that you creep upon the earth.

For this pleases the King, as you know, splendid man,

who for your sake deigned to become supremely humble in the depths,

even unto a kind of death that was worse than all others.

You do this, as it were, with your mouth; if you strive to accomplish it in your heart,

you will truly stand in the citadel of all virtues.

It is easy for a person to confess himself wretched with his voice—

perhaps as a pretender—

but to hold in his heart what is present there

belongs to the poor man who reigns in spirit upon high Olympus.

The former is very often done by the reprobate, who are to be lamented.

The latter is done by the elect,

chosen, certainly, from the foundation of the world—

not therefore because of merits,

but truly by the Father’s gift.

Blessed, brother, blessed, exalted teacher,

are those whom the Father chose in Christ according to his gracious will;

none of them perishes,

for the wave of the blood of the heavenly Lamb redeemed them

and gave them life.

Blessed will be the last of the lambs,

if neither lion nor predator,

wolf, dragon, thief, or devourer [Note: “Devourer” means the devil, as one who swallows human beings]

ever snatches any of them away by force or fraud.

Indeed, everything that the Father grants comes to him [Note: A few words seem to be missing.]

[lacuna]

## In the Year of the Lord 868. Lotharius

[Column 371]

# Three Letters of Lotharius

## First Letter: To Pope Nicholas

[Note: In Labbe, *Councils*, volume 8, p. 500.]

[The supplied source ends here.]

He complains that the pope believes his rivals far too readily. He indicates his grief at the excommunication of Theutgaud and Guntharius. Moreover, clearing himself of every charge, he declares himself ready to refute his adversaries’ accusations before the pope.

To the truly most blessed and most holy lord, supreme pontiff of the whole holy Church of God and universal pope, NICOLAS: Lotharius, by the preceding mercy of God king, sends peace and glory of the highest happiness and present prosperity.

After divine condescension, in its gratuitous mercy, entrusted us with the governance of the kingdom, following the custom of our predecessors, the most Christian kings, we have always and in every respect reverently loved the see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which ought rightly to be exalted, and we have been constantly prepared, insofar as it lies within us, to raise it up. Desiring always to draw salutary things from your governance as from that of the supreme spiritual Father, we recall that it was said to you by the voice of Truth: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21); and through the prophet: “I myself will feed my sheep, says the Lord God: I will seek what was lost, bring back what was cast away, bind up what was broken, and strengthen what was weak” (Ezekiel 34).

We greatly desire to present ourselves to you as soon as possible, so that you may fulfill with more certain experience what the same prophet adds shortly thereafter: “And I will judge them in judgment and justice” (ibid.). Indeed, our most serene and devoted affection of mind toward your pious fatherhood is grievously obscured by the fact that, believing too readily the false words of our rivals, you lend the ear of your most holy apostolate to our disparagement beyond what is necessary. Especially since our gentleness is entirely ready to resist every detractor by true and just reasoning.

Your legates, recently sent into these regions, could have informed you of this, had they wished: for, having given our accusers security, we granted them access to come, and we were ready to provide a reasonable satisfaction, as in your patience, to those sent from your side.
