We favored nothing belonging to our royal dignity, but, like one of the humblest persons, obeyed priestly admonitions.

Our rivals, understanding all this through sinister interpretation, burned with desire for the kingdom granted to us by divine condescension through hereditary right. They paid no attention to Scripture, which says: “The kingdom is the Lord’s, and he will give it to whomever he wishes” (Daniel 4); nor to the Apostle, who says: “There is no authority except from God” (Romans 13). Therefore, while we believe that his victorious right hand is fighting on our behalf—he who knows both the one who plunders and the one who is plundered—we pay little heed to their disguised hostilities. We ask only that the anchor of your pontificate, fixed upon the most solid foundation of holy Mother Church, may deign to grant us, who likewise petition, what is written by the finger of God in the commandments: “Judge your neighbor justly” (Leviticus 19).

Moreover, while we were staying in the furthest regions of our kingdom and keeping laborious watches against pagan attacks, we learned through reports brought by travelers that Theutgaud of Trier and Guntharius of Cologne had been excommunicated by your authority and canonically condemned by the testimony of your own mouth. We received this with profound sorrow and resolved to endure the news with patience and long-suffering, to retain hope of restoration, as has formerly been done in many cases, and, after all matters had been piously reconsidered and revisited, to await from your generosity an opportunity for reasonable mercy.

Meanwhile, we came to know that Guntharius did not hesitate to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass before he reached us, and presumed to prepare the episcopal chrism according to former custom and to administer the Paraclete Spirit [the Holy Spirit]. We bore this with great displeasure, and we abhor it in every way, as deadly poison, so that it might not be done. When he came to us, we refused to hear his Mass and judged that we ought not to communicate with him in any respect. In accordance with the voice of Truth, like an offending eye, we intend to remove this stain from ourselves until we can learn the definitive judgment of your most holy apostolate concerning him.

We also sent him a letter from your holiness addressed to the bishops of his diocese, so that, clearly learning the canonical and apostolic sanctions contained therein, he might see what he ought to do in the future.

For the rest, let your fatherhood know truthfully and sincerely that Theutgaud, a very simple and innocent man, humbly bearing your censure, presumed to have no dealings whatsoever with the sacred ministry. He preferred to suffer present dishonor in the eyes of men rather than, through disobedience, be separated from the members of him who is the head of the humble and says to his disciples: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11). He who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble will indeed be able, if Theutgaud is innocent, mercifully to look upon him from above.

In fact, we ordered our legates Theutgaud and Guntharius to say nothing of that kind during their embassy by which they might incur the mark of condemnation. Nor ought we or do we wish to pronounce any prejudgment concerning Ingeltrude, the wife of Boso. When we learned that she was bound by the bond of anathema, we commended her to Guntharius, because he was then in his own diocese, warning him to exercise his ministry concerning her; indeed, we judged that she should be expelled from all the regions of our kingdom. Later, when your legates sought her out and placed her in their midst, we do not know what conclusion they imposed upon her case.

The bishops of the diocese of Trier, the metropolitan see, and of Agrippina, Cologne, will be proved to be neither accomplices of the condemned nor supporters of vices, nor in any respect despisers of apostolic decrees or violators of canonical teachings, but worshipers of sound and catholic faith and of the true God.

Therefore, for God’s sake and for the sake of the holy and undivided Trinity, we humbly ask that you by no means readily admit the guilty to bring accusations against us. Nor, as the Apostle teaches, should you believe every spirit, but “test whether they are from God” (1 John 4). For we are ready, if reason should dictate it, personally to refute the false charges fabricated by the envy of our rivals.

May almighty God preserve the most holy summit of your episcopate, governed by the scales of equity, safe for a long time. Amen.

## LETTER II. TO THE SAME

[Note: In Baronius, under the year 867, from a Trier manuscript.]

To escape the excommunication threatened on account of his association with Waldrada, he announces his coming to Rome to Nicholas; and, in order to amuse him with good hope, he appoints bishops as an embassy to him, promising him assistance against the Saracens if necessary.

To the truly most holy and most blessed lord, supreme pontiff of the whole Church of God, acquired by the rose-colored blood of pious King Christ, and universal pope, NICOLAS: Lotharius, by the propitious mercy of God king and your most devoted son, sends everlasting glory with joy, prosperity, and happiness, and faithful service.

Christ, King of kings and prince of shepherds, who united priestly and royal dignity in himself in the ministry of our redemption, and who entrusted the care of his flock to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, instructed us by salutary decrees to love faithfully and venerate humbly the most sacred summit of your apostolate, exalted by God upon the foundation of the Church.

Hence the affection of our gentleness toward your eminence is inflamed by the fire of true charity and, for many days now, has not ceased desirously to invite us into your presence. For this reason we have sent these letters to your most eminent fatherhood, so that we may learn more quickly of your desirable health, which our body embraces as more precious than the radiance of every jewel and dearer than every treasure.

And because we confidently believe the same concerning your health, we have decided that it should be more suitably reported to you that, by the help of divine mercy, our gentleness is in excellent condition, and the whole body of our faithful, with Christ’s assistance, is making salutary progress in the necessary affairs of the state. Indeed, we humbly and faithfully await from the giver of every good a beneficial outcome of prosperity.

Know also that the kingdom entrusted to us by divine piety has thus far remained wholly secure from every pagan attack and the depredation of other enemies, while the right hand of almighty God fights for us, the merits of blessed Peter the apostle assist us, and your nourishing prayers lend their support.

Let your pious fatherhood know that at this time we have the most ardent desire, for the sake of prayer, to visit the thresholds of the apostles, to see your long-desired face, and sweetly to embrace your sacred footsteps. We have already twice and three times renewed the preparations for our journey after definite deliberation, and we desire to fulfill what remains our vow.

But if, God forbid, some change in dangerous times should thwart our vow, we shall arrange to send to your presence our most beloved uncle Gutfrid [Luitfridum], our faithful Waltarius, and also the venerable archbishop Theutgaud and our fellow bishop Atto [Hatto, perhaps of the Church of Verdun]. Through them your eminence will clearly learn how faithful we and our faithful are to you in every respect, and how faithfully we desire to obey your salutary counsels and spiritual admonitions.

Indeed, as a spiritual and devoted son ought to do toward a most reverent father and universal pope, we and the venerable bishops and our faithful, prostrate in heart, if not in body, before your sacred footsteps, humbly ask that, if any of our enemies should presume to report something sinister concerning us to your most holy ears in a lying declaration of falsehood, the apostolic authority should abhor it as serpentine poison.

Moreover, our bishops, proved to be disciples of truth, cannot be teachers of error; they will be shown to be true worshipers of the orthodox father’s catholic and apostolic faith.

Meanwhile, we have judged it appropriate to insert the following: if any pagan incursion should attempt to approach the borders of blessed Peter, divinely entrusted to you, or should perhaps presume to break into the territories of the most august emperor and our most beloved brother Ludovicus, as we have learned from a recent and unhappy report, we ask that this be communicated to us immediately and without any delay. For, setting aside every loss of temporal goods and disregarding the danger threatening the kingdom that is destined to perish, for the love and fear of God, for reverence toward the blessed apostles and all the saints, and likewise for your most holy fatherhood—which we have resolved to love and venerate above all mortals—we are ready to commit ourselves and our faithful to death and danger, knowing that it is written: “We ought not to fear death, which undoubtedly leads to life.”

Therefore, with every prayer of which we are capable, we implore the mercy of the Lord to present our gentleness at last, unharmed, to your most excellent holiness, so that, through more certain experience, your apostolate may purely learn whether the things spoken have proceeded from the fountain of truth.

May almighty God, mindful of us, deign for a long time to preserve and exalt, with prosperous success, the resplendent radiance of the summit of your most holy pontificate for the protection of the flock, most glorious and outstanding father.

## LETTER III. TO POPE ADRIAN II

[Note: In Baronius, in the same place.]

Having learned of Nicholas’s death, Lotharius writes this letter to his successor Adrian, asking to obtain from him what he could not obtain from Nicholas: permission to come to Rome.

To the most holy and most blessed HADRIAN, supreme pontiff and universal pope: Lotharius, by the preceding mercy of God king, sends peace and glory of eternal blessedness and present prosperity.

An unhappy report, hitherto remaining uncertain, has, so to speak, sharply pierced the ears of our serenity by announcing that the lord Nicholas, of blessed memory, universal pope, has departed from this valley of tears at Christ’s summons, to be crowned, as we believe, immeasurably among the saints.

Our gentle affection therefore, grieving greatly, is shaken by a double sorrow: first, because the holy and apostolic Church, mother of all the Churches of God, has been deprived of such a great father; and second, because in the heavenly Jerusalem a burning and shining lamp has been removed from the dark and evil bounds of our perilous times [Dei; perhaps *diei*, “day”]. Nor is it surprising that all Christian religion grieves over so great a pontiff and that every ecclesiastical order laments a pope so prudent and holy.

Indeed, we grieve especially because we entrusted the causes of our calumny—the insolent and fraudulent complaints of our rivals—to such a kind father, to be weighed and determined for a time and in part on the scales of equity and justice. But, as we sorrowfully repeat, the plots and feigned deceptions of our enemies prevailed more with his holiness than did our simple and pure defense.

For patiently and equably, beyond the endurance of all our predecessors, we humbly submitted our royal dignity and the authority divinely attributed to us to his reverence—or rather, to that of the prince of the apostles. We confidently obeyed his paternal admonitions beyond what could be believed, and, following the varied and manifold exhortations of his envoys for the love of God and the reverence of the saints, in some matters we departed from our royal position, in part contrary to what was proper.

Therefore, hoping and believing in every way, we placed the firm hope of our protection in the most holy pontiff. But we do not know through what suggestions—or perhaps excessive promises—it came about that an unexpected delay produced many hostilities, and for this reason our state suffered no small injury everywhere.

We, however, continually protesting in letters and words and repeating the same request through various embassies, humbly petitioned that we and our accusers might deserve a hearing before his pontifical court according to divine and human laws, presenting our presence as reason required. But after being rejected so many times, and finally compelled in many ways, we placed our judgment and refuge upon that rock of which the Psalmist, trusting, said: “The high mountains are for the deer; rock is the refuge of the hedgehog” (Psalm 103).

What especially clouded the sight of our mind was that we were driven away from the holy see itself, whose holy Mother Church our forebears and ancestors protected with pious and faithful patronage through divine assistance.

We rejoice beyond what can be expressed that the Bulgarians and other pagan peoples are invited to the thresholds of the holy apostles; indeed, that the holy Church, in accordance with the prophet’s prediction, enlarges the place of its tent, lengthens its cords, and stretches out the skins of its tabernacles (Isaiah 54). Yet we are greatly saddened that, though we so often hastened there with longing, we were unable to obtain an audience with your predecessor.

But setting these matters aside, let us return to the purpose of our mind and to the excellence of your apostolate, worthy of God; and, as is fitting, let us proclaim glory to God in the highest, who, mercifully regarding the flock acquired at the rose-colored price of his own blood, placed the radiance of your pontificate by his election in the seat of holy Mother Church, for the salvation of us and of the entire Christian people.

And since almighty God, prince of shepherds, has exalted the summit of your pontificate upon that holy see, we are ready, after the custom of our predecessors, to offer in every respect our salutary assistance for the defense, stability, and honor of your pontificate.

With the creator of all things as witness, no Catholic king and no Christian prince desires to be more devoted to your holiness or more eager for your welfare than our lowliness [alternative: greatness]. For if time should smile upon us, and, with divine mercy assisting, the scandals that have arisen enormously through the hostility and insinuation of our rivals, namely the members of Satan, should subside, we greatly desire your presence, to be encouraged by your conversations worthy of God and to receive your honey-sweet blessing.

Finally, we humbly ask your nourishing fatherhood not to decide in any way to prefer or place before our gentleness anyone similar to us in royal dignity and name. Nor should you permit letters of your blessedness intended for us to be sent through anyone except either our legate, or one whom you have sent from your holy side, or a messenger of our most august brother, the emperor Ludovicus. For, to speak truthfully, considerable hostility is known to have arisen in these regions through such an action, and, unless it is prudently anticipated in the future, it could generate some danger.

Meanwhile, we earnestly beseech you in every way to make our eminence certain through your letters of your desirable prosperity, and to deign to bestow upon us the gift of your dear sonship. Commend our serenity to the Lord through your nourishing prayers and render it acceptable and pardonable before him, so that, supported by the pious prayers of so great a father, we may be able, with Christ’s assistance, to govern the rule entrusted to us.

May almighty God deign to preserve your pontifical radiance, brilliant with splendor, and your angelic holiness safe for us for a long time. Amen.

# In the Year of the Lord 768: Guntharius, Bishop of Cologne

## Guntharius’s Diabolical Chapters against Pope Nicholas

[Note: Concerning these, see the *Annals of Hincmar of Reims*: “The emperor ordered Guntharius and Theutgaud, degraded as they had come with him, to return to Francia. Then Guntharius sent these diabolical and previously unheard-of chapters, with the following preface, to the bishops of Lotharius’s kingdom when he returned to Rome in the service of Ludovicus, through his brother Hilduinus, a cleric, together with his own men, sending them to the apostolic see and instructing him that, if the apostolicus [the pope] refused to receive them, he should throw them upon the body of blessed Peter.” But the apostolicus, having learned of them beforehand, refused to receive them. The aforesaid Hilduinus, armed and accompanied by Guntharius’s men, entered the church of the blessed apostle Peter without any reverence. As his brother Guntharius had ordered him, he wished to throw the diabolical writing upon the body of blessed Peter if the apostolicus refused to receive it. When the custodians prevented him, both he and his accomplices began to beat those same custodians with clubs, so violently that one of them was killed there. Then he threw the writing upon the body of blessed Peter, and, protecting himself and those who had come with him with drawn swords, left the church and returned to Guntharius after carrying out the mournful deed.]

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*.)

## Preface to the Bishops of Lotharius’s Kingdom

To our holy and venerable brothers and fellow bishops, Guntharius and Theotgaud send greetings in the Lord.

We humbly ask your most beloved fraternity, since we continually pray for you, earnestly to grant us the consolations of holy prayers, and not to be disturbed or terrified by what rumor perhaps reports about us and you in a sinister manner.

We trust in the most merciful goodness of our Lord that, with God’s assistance, the plots of our enemies will prevail neither against our king nor against us, and that our adversaries will not rejoice over us. For although the lord Nicholas, who is called pope and who counts himself an apostle among the apostles and makes himself emperor of the whole world, wished, at the instigation and desire of those with whom he is known to have conspired in favor, to condemn us, nevertheless, by Christ’s favor, he found us resisting his madness in every way, and whatever he did afterward caused him no small regret.

We have sent you the chapters written below, so that you may learn our complaint against the aforesaid pontiff.

After we had departed from Rome and gone some distance away, we were summoned back to Rome again. As we began to return there, we wrote you this little letter so that you would not be surprised that we are making a longer delay.

Visit and encourage our lord king frequently, both yourselves and through your envoys and letters. Reconcile to him as many friends and faithful supporters as you can. Above all, continually admonish and invite King Ludovicus, and carefully inquire with him into the common welfare, because in the peace of those kings will be our peace [alternative: in their kingdom will be our peace].

Be of even mind and tranquil heart, lord brothers, because, God willing, we hope to report such things to you that you will be able clearly to perceive the Spirit of the Lord teaching you what you ought to do and how you ought to do it.

Take every care only to urge the aforesaid king to remain unmoved amid the various insinuations until he himself learns the causes of the matters.

Moreover, most longed-for brothers, it is necessary and praiseworthy for us to preserve inviolate before God and men the faith we promised our king.

May almighty God preserve you in his holy service.

## The Chapters Begin

### Chapter 1

Hear, lord pope Nicholas. Our fathers and fellow bishops sent us to you, and we came of our own accord, namely to consult your teaching concerning those matters which, as it seemed to us, we jointly judged—after adding and approving what could be made known—while setting forth in writing the authorities and arguments we followed, so that, after examining everything, your wisdom might show us what it thought and what it wished.

And if your holiness should find something better, we humbly ask you to instruct and teach us in it, ready, together with our sound-minded brothers, to accept whatever you might indicate as more correct and plausible.

### Chapter 2

But after waiting three weeks for your answer, you expressed to us nothing certain and no teaching. You merely said one day in public that, according to the assertion of our little book, we appeared excusable and innocent.

### Chapter 3

Finally, when summoned, we were led into your presence, suspecting nothing hostile. There, after the doors had been bolted and a conspiracy had been formed in the manner of brigands, with a crowd gathered and mixed from clergy and laity, you attempted to crush us violently among so many people.

Without a synod or canonical examination, with no accuser, no witness, no strictness of debate deciding the matter, and no proof of authorities establishing our guilt; without a confession from our own mouths; in the absence of the other metropolitans and diocesan fellow bishops and brothers; entirely outside the consent of everyone; by your sole judgment and tyrannical fury, you wished to condemn us.

### Chapter 4

But we do not receive your accursed sentence, alien to paternal kindness and foreign to fraternal charity, pronounced against us unjustly and irrationally contrary to the canonical laws. Rather, together with the entire brotherhood, we despise and reject it as a curse pronounced in vain.

We likewise do not wish to receive you into our communion and fellowship, since you favor and associate with those who have been condemned and anathematized and who reject and despise sacred religion. We are content with the communion of the whole Church and the fraternal association that you, arrogantly exalting yourself above it, despise, and from which you separate yourself by making yourself unworthy through the swelling of your pride.

### Chapter 5

Therefore, through the rashness of your own frivolity, you inflicted upon yourself the plague of anathema by your own sentence, crying out: “Let him be anathema who does not observe the apostolic precepts.” Yet you are known to violate and to have violated them in many ways, emptying, insofar as lies within you, both the divine laws and the sacred canons, and refusing to follow the footsteps of your predecessors, the Roman pontiffs.

### Chapter 6

Now, therefore, we who have experienced your fraud and cunning do not act as though provoked by the insult inflicted upon us. Rather, we are inflamed with zeal against your iniquity, paying no attention to the person of our own lowliness, but keeping before our eyes the entire community of our order, against which you are attempting to use force.

### Chapter 7

We briefly repeat what the substance of our particular proposition was. Divine and canonical law proves most appropriately, and the venerable laws of the age also support it, that no one may give a freeborn virgin to any man as a concubine, especially if the girl has never wished to consent to an illicit union. And because she has been joined to her husband with the consent of her parents, in fidelity, affection [alternative: effect], and conjugal love, she must certainly be regarded as a wife, not a concubine.

## Guntharius’s Retraction Given to Adrian II

I, Guntharius, confess before God and his saints, before you, my lord Adrian, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and before the venerable bishops subject to you and the rest of the assembly, that I do not wholly reject the judgment of deposition canonically imposed upon me by the lord Nicholas, but humbly bear it.

Therefore I do not presume to touch the sacred ministry any further, unless you should wish to assist me through mercy. Nor do I wish ever to stir up any scandal or adversity against the holy Roman Church or its pontiff. Rather, I declare that I will present myself as devoted to that holy Mother Church and its prelate and remain obedient.

I, Guntharius, have subscribed this profession made by me with my own hand.

Given on the Kalends of July, in the second indiction, in the church of Saint Salvator, which is in the monastery of Saint Benedict at Cassino.

## Letter of Theotgaud, Guntharius, and Arduicus to Hincmar

(In Labbe, *Councils General*, volume VIII, column 762.)

To our desirable brother in Christ, Hincmar—[written] Igmar—Theotgaud, primate of Belgic Gaul; Guntharius, of Agrippina, Cologne; and Arduicus, bishop of the Church of Besançon, send greetings and peace.

We have reread, brother—and would that you were truly a brother, Igmar—the written accusation you made against Hilduinus, our beloved son and brother, whom we believe to be a suitable man, in which you assert that he is unworthy of the pastoral office and cry out that you know the reasons why he ought not to be elected and ordained.

Even if nothing else had restrained or moderated you from this wickedness, it ought to have been enough that he was your beloved lord and fosterer, had you wished to be mindful and not ungrateful of the fact that he bears both the relationship and the name of that man.

Now, since you wished to be an informer, do not omit what remains. You stripped yourself of judgment when you rashly presented with your own hand—something you cannot deny—the document of accusation, which, as we judge, was not fitting for your office and honor, to our prince Lotharius in the assembly of kings, and thereby rendered the aforesaid Hilduinus, and us likewise, suspect.

Therefore, since you have promised to prove the charges brought, it follows that you must carry out what you promised. Accordingly, we admonish you by canonical authority to pursue the execution of your accusation canonically.

But if you withdraw from the accusation and fail to provide proof, know that you will be subject to the canonical rules concerning accusers.

As for the calumnies that you attempted to cast into the shade by synodal decrees, they rebound upon you and upon your like-named nephew, who have been so advanced. Neither of you belonged to that church in which he is known to have been enthroned through ambition, favor, and power.

Since the synod requires this condition, you must be present at the synod that, with Christ’s grace, will be held on the Ides of March near the city of Metz. There the aforesaid brother will either be convicted by your proof or freed by his defense. There also we may answer you by giving reasons for all the matters that, in writing, you have mentioned and criticized concerning the Church of Cambrai.

We wish you prosperity in Christ.

## Their Letter to the Bishops Established in King Ludovicus’s Kingdom

To the venerable brothers in Christ, the archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of the distinguished king Ludovicus: Theotgaud, primate of Belgic Gaul; Guntharius, of Agrippina, Cologne; Arduicus, of Besançon; Rotlandus, of Arles; Tado, of Milan—archbishops of the Churches—and their fellow bishops send greetings and peace, and pray and wish for them.

We see and sigh daily that the Church of God is shaken and struck from without by various disturbances; but when we see it harassed and consumed inwardly by dissension among its members, we are overcome with profound horror and grief. For we cannot help grieving and mourning that we have learned that the holy priests of God—namely, Hincmar, an archbishop widely renowned for religion and wisdom, and Rothad, famous for a long and venerable life of holiness—have so fallen out with one another that the metropolitan did not hesitate to hurl a sentence of excommunication against that suffragan and, after depriving him of his office, consign him to custody.

But, surrounded at once by astonishment and bewilderment, we do not know which of the two we should deplore more: whether Rothad, for having so strayed from the truth that such penalties were deservedly inflicted upon him; or Hincmar, for having so overstepped the bounds of justice and dignity that, bound or overcome by some zeal of bitterness or ambition, he did not hesitate to inflict such treatment upon a holy and, as was believed, aged bishop. The former proclaims that he was unjustly condemned; among the other defenses of his cause, he persisted in an appeal to the Roman pontiff. The latter, however, among the other inventions of his attacks, declares that he rightly removed him from priestly office on account of his contempt and disobedience toward himself.

Since all this is entirely uncertain to us—for we have learned the case of neither party publicly—we dare neither readily believe rumors nor rashly judge the dissensions of absent men. Nevertheless, because many—indeed, almost all to whom this report has reached—have suffered scandal with us, we communicate this to your holiness with deep sorrow. We pray and implore your unanimity that, having observed the snares of the ancient enemy and considered the excesses of human frailty, you may examine and weigh more carefully how the discord of the aforesaid bishops began and grew; and that, coming together with us through the Lord’s help, we may diligently dispel the clouds of this uncertainty and arrive at the light of truth, with true light revealing it. Thus, if Rothad is proved to have been justly deposed, let him be silenced by the judgment of all; or, if he was unjustly condemned, let Hincmar rightly blush for it.

And may the scandal or murmuring that is battering so many in the holy Church over this controversy be destroyed and quieted by our vigilance, lest so great an offense disturb the Christian people any longer. This matter ought not, therefore, to be passed over on any pretext or deferred for any reason, since, as we believe we remember, the apostolic see once changed its own sentence for the better when it perceived that it had been misled concerning a certain man. Dioscorus also, because he had unjustly deposed the holy man Flavian of blessed memory, was condemned by the apostolic see and vanished, while the other bishops remained uncondemned—those who had consented to the deposition of the holy bishop not willingly, but as though under compulsion, because Dioscorus, a crafty and skillful contriver of arguments, had labored to deceive them in many ways.

Do not now delay while the danger grows and many insult and disparage the holy order, boasting that they confidently promise themselves they can harm us in every way while we bite and disagree with one another. We briefly append below the matters about which Rothad complains and which greatly move us.

Should a presbyter or deacon justly deposed by his own bishop be restored by a metropolitan or anyone else to his former rank without the consent of that bishop, when the Council of Antioch says the following about this (canon III): “If any presbyters or deacons excommunicated by their own bishop should dare …,” etc.? Likewise, in the same council (canon VI): “If anyone has been deprived of communion by his own bishop …,” etc.

Should a presbyter who has been accused and condemned be reconciled after four years, when the African Council says the following about this (canon XII): “If anyone has refused to clear his case within a year …,” etc.?

Should anyone retain a bishop’s ordained minister—how much less should he seize him or thrust him into prison—when the decretals establish the following on this matter: “No bishop shall presume to retain the parishioner of another …,” etc.? And somewhat later: “If any metropolitan bishop, except in what pertains solely to his own parish …,” etc.

Should a bishop invite in writing the ministers of another bishop, or solicit them in any way, or usurp the people of another’s authority for himself, when the African Council says the following about this (canon X): “No one ought to do an injury to his colleague …,” etc.? Many other provisions concerning these matters were also promulgated in that same council.

Should a bishop be heard by fewer than twelve men—how much more should he be condemned—when this is prohibited even more explicitly in the Council of Sardica?

Should a bishop who persists in an appeal to the Roman pontiff be condemned, or another bishop be substituted in his place, unless the appellant’s case has been determined in that pontiff’s judgment?

Can a judgment that is suspect and uncertain be renewed? Or may a suspect metropolitan summon neighboring provincial judges? Much is contained on these matters in synodal councils and in the decrees of the Roman pontiffs.

Should an innocent or unheard man be condemned?

Should someone be condemned because, detained by illness, he could not appear before the synod, with this being imputed to him not as impossibility but as contempt?

Should someone be condemned because he regards the metropolitan and the entire assembly as suspect, and, fearing or knowing that they have conspired against him, postpones entering the place of the synod, always appealing to the Roman pontiff?

Should the accuser be a witness or a judge? Or is it fitting for a bishop to carry out all these functions at once?

Therefore, priests of the Lord, fellow ministers of our God, who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, take care to search out and examine the pages of the divine authorities, and determine whether this is the wisdom from above which, according to the Apostle (James 3), is “first pure, then peaceable”—or, God forbid, whether it is that which he mentioned earlier, earthly, sensual, and demonic. Let the holy Church and fraternal charity, which seem to have been scandalized by the wickedness of others, return as quickly as possible to peace through your pious diligence and labor.

## In the Year of the Lord 868. Theudoinus, provost of Châlons.

## Notice from Fabricius

Theudoinus, provost of Châlons, wrote a letter in the year 868 to Almannus, a monk of Hautvillers near Rheims, asking him to compose the Life of Saint Memmius, the first bishop of Châlons. It was published by Mabillon, *Veterum Analectorum*, p. 423, from which we have taken it.

## Letter of Theudoinus to Almannus, Monk of Hautvillers

### On writing the Life of Saint Memmius, the first bishop of Châlons

To my most beloved brother Almannus, a monk by profession and, by the grace of God, a priest (*hiereo*).

To meditate on the law of the Lord day and night does not go unrewarded in the eyes of the divine majesty. Therefore I considered it worthwhile to admonish your charity. Since, from your earliest age, you were brought up in a religious place and devoted yourself especially to this purpose—that you should be lacking in no grammatical knowledge, and should also progress in this, so that you might in no way be ignorant of writing—leave the grove of Angitia and, with divine assistance, transfer your whole self into the vineyards of Engaddi.

You certainly know the vineyard of Sorek as well; you have also heard of the householder who went out early in the morning and, at the appointed successive hours, hired laborers for his vineyard. Indeed, my wishes in this matter are that, having been called with a calling according to God’s purpose, you should also labor according to the measure of your little spark in the Church of the Lord of hosts, without interruption, neither delaying nor burdening yourself with any postponement.

For death comes upon us with great speed, although we possess wisdom only very slowly [*f. tarda*, “slow”]. Therefore hasten, supported in every respect by the protection of truth, and fashion some little vessel in the house of the Lord [*elabora*, “work at it”]. For in it there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also wooden and earthen vessels: namely, in the holy Church, which, according to the prophet Hosea, was betrothed three times—first before the Law, in Abraham; second under the Law, through Moses; and third under grace, when the Lord himself came and assumed virgin flesh in the virginal womb, from which he proceeded “like a bridegroom from his chamber.”

You have also learned that the Lord determined to enter into a covenant with the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven, and the creeping things of the earth; and that the Lord also takes counsel for his vineyard through the shepherds of Tekoa. And, to make what we are saying clearer, know that it did not happen without the hidden providential disposition of God that, after the mausoleum had been removed and the mound of earth cleared away, we examined the tomb of blessed Memmius in a square, cemented grave containing his precious body. This was done at the command of King Charles in the year 868 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, which was the Wednesday before mid-Lent. His holy tomb was found not to adhere to the earth at any point; rather, by the power of almighty God, with whom the merits of so great a patron shine, it was hanging in the grave as though balanced in the air, four fingers above the ground.

At this miracle the hearts of mortals, struck with amazement, utter these words: “O how great a devotion to piety made him conform himself to heavenly life while he lived on earth, whose glory is now so great in heaven that the earth confesses itself unworthy to touch not only his body but even his tomb!”

We ask your devotion to renew the life of this most holy man, which through long age and negligence is almost worn away, as though on scraps of parchment. Come, then, and favor our request according to your strength, so that you may rejoice in heaven unto everlasting salvation because of so great an intercessor.

## Almannus’s Reply

To the venerable provost Theudoinus, Almannus, a sinner.

You command me, through the charity poured from heaven into the hearts of the elect by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, to undertake the renewal of the life of Saint Memmius, the first pontiff of Châlons, neglected through age and corrupted by ignorance, as though it had been dug out of the ashes; you command me to correct it through knowledge and strive to supply whatever appears to be lacking, driven by devotion to the truth.

But there are many grounds on which I can easily excuse myself from so great a task. First, because modern disputation is not suited to a man of such gravity and holiness. Second, because my conscience, itself a witness to my ignorance, relies on no testimony by which I may claim to be wise, since I am foolish; and therefore it is less fitting that I should presume to undertake a task beyond my strength. Third, and most important, the sorrowful remembrance of my sins, while it consigns me to bitterness alone in proportion to the debt of my offenses, strikes fear into me at the thought of setting down in writing the deeds of one whose apostolic preaching and most holy religion I have, alas, never shown myself to share or imitate.

I therefore confess that this work is owed to one worthy of the life, and to a wise man learned in charity—not to me, who am wholly foolish—lest that voice of righteous severity come upon me which says: “Why do you recount my justice and take my name upon your lips?” (Psalm 49).

But because, when you pray, charity commands, and when you exhort, Christ orders, I will not evade whatever small gift is ours, but will reveal what the Lord grants. For I know what is said: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80); and, “Work your land, and you will be satisfied with bread” (Proverbs 12:11).

Nor will I seek lofty language, since I have never attained it; rather, having before me material that is simple from antiquity, simple in words but shining more clearly than the sun in deeds, and surpassing by its own power and divine virtue the whole structure of the world, I will follow it as best I can. I shall seek assistance from your prayers, so that the spirit coming from the four winds may give life to my dead bones and deem me worthy to become such a man that he may not demand my debts down to the last farthing, but rather erase and forgive all my sins down to the last farthing.

In this may Saint Memmius be our pious intercessor. To him we endeavor to offer the service of our devotion, small indeed, but as much as the spark of our littleness and the material of truth, with divine assistance, have contributed to us. In this common little work, it will be yours to choose the judge whom we shall receive. For although testing is useful in all matters, as the Apostle says, “Test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21), it is especially necessary in matters that look toward the light of truth through the effectiveness of just examination. This alone is a major reason why we await the judgment of wisdom.

For in regulating this matter we pay little or no attention to the very safeguards of grammar, by which grammar itself judges that barbarism or solecism must be avoided, since truth is being sought, vanity must depart, and we desire to flee what is contrary while pressing forward, according to the strength of our mind, toward gravity [*read*: truth]. We do not say this in order to regard grammar as a fault, since it is itself the sole, or at least the greatest, virtue of knowledge; but because, for those devoting themselves to truth, other things become obscure, just as stars are obscured by the sun. Hence it is said: “I will not love darkness when I have seen the sun.”

Finally, how much shame I suffer in this matter I can scarcely, or not at all, express, fearing that I may become a laughingstock to the wise because I wished in this affair to consult readers. A refuge of modesty would remain, if it were possible for the writing in the work to survive without the name of its scribe. I leave this also to your judgment.

God is able to take away our reproach, and, as we truly trust in his mercy, he will do so, through the intercession of blessed Memmius, who looks upon us from heaven with kindly eyes: you exhorting through the devotion of your mind, and I writing according to the fidelity owed and the capacity of my heart.

I therefore desire that no small reward for this undertaking remain for you. Since I owe you everything, I could not refuse so arduous a task. I wish you every blessing and good health, even to the contemplation of heavenly glory.

## In the Year of the Lord 869. Paul Alvarus of Córdoba.

## Historical Notice

*(In Antonio, Old Spanish Library, vol. II, p. 475.)*

Alvarus of Córdoba was contemporary with all these men. Ambrosius Morales compiled everything that survives in memory concerning him in book XIV, chapter 3. We are not, however, satisfied with everything he reports as established about him.

Morales says that Alvarus was born at Córdoba of an illustrious family and therefore believes that Eulogius addressed him by the title “Serenity” and “Most Serene” [Note: Higuera uses the same argument in his notes to Luitprand, year 846]. But, if the author of a certain letter among Alvarus’s other letters to Eleazar—a Jew by religion, formerly an idolater—is not someone else—the letter begins, “Fabricated from falsehood …”—we must admit that the man who writes the following about himself to Eleazar is of Hebrew stock:

“Because our parents were formerly sprung from that very Israelite stock; but when he whom all nations desired came, we immediately recognized that he had already come.”

And more clearly and explicitly below:

“And we say these things so that your pride may be broken and the craftiness of your assertion blunted. Moreover, I have a freer and shorter—indeed, clearer—reply, since, descending from the stock of Israel, I claim as mine all the things you applaud yourself for having extracted. Understand prudently, gather wisely, and be a fair judge. Who is more worthy to be reckoned by the name of Israel: you, who after a long period of idolatry returned to the worship of the supreme God, or I, who am a Hebrew both by faith and by descent? But I am not called a Jew because a new name was imposed upon me, which the mouth of the Lord named. Surely my father is Abraham, because my ancestors descended from that very stock. For those who awaited the Messiah to come and received him when he came appear more truly to be Israel than those who awaited him and rejected him when he came, though they did not cease awaiting him.”

### 172

In some way he also seems to affirm that he is a Goth when replying to the same Eleazar in a letter that is mutilated at the end and begins, “The character of your exposition …,” namely, with these words:

“But so that you may recognize who I am and henceforth avoid me in silence, listen to Virgil” [Note: These verses are falsely attributed to Virgil]:

“The Getae despise death with a celebrated wound.”

And also this:

“Getes, he says, where does he proceed on horseback?”

Whence also the poet’s line is found:

“On this side may the Dacian press, on that side may the Getae confront him.”

“I am, I am the one whom Alexander declared must be avoided, whom Pyrrhus feared, whom Caesar dreaded. Jerome, who is ours, also says of us: ‘He has a horn on his forehead; flee far away.’”

Unless these words are referred to the writer’s lineage—as though, in playful fashion, he had boasted that Gothic ferocity was to be feared by an opponent who provoked it—I do not know what other suitable meaning they could have. As for what was earlier said about the salutation “Serenity” attributed to Alvarus, the style of that period was entirely different from ours: men who possessed no particular dignity of rank addressed one another with such titles as “Serenity,” “Excellence,” and “Sublimity.”

### 173

We have examples in these very letters of Alvarus and in letters addressed to him by others. One person’s heading reads: “To my most serene lord Romanus, most catholic of all,” whom the heading of the letter calls “the Roman physician.” To the same man he says: “Beginning with my earlier words, most serene lord, toward you …,” and somewhat farther below he calls this same man “most sublime.” Then: “My most sublime lord, my affection toward you …”

The address “Excellence” belonged to the same category. Speraindeus writes to Alvarus: “And I will return to what your excellence has set forth.”

It must nevertheless be observed that, whether because of Gothic origin or for some other reason, Alvarus seems to have been addressed by those who wrote to him with the surnames Flavius and Aurelius; yet in most letters he himself calls himself Alvarus Paulus by his proper name.

But whatever may be said about his Gothic or Hebrew ancestry, he speaks modestly of his studies in the *Luminosus Indiculus*, which is believed to have been written by him:

“Because I do not fail to recognize that my own study is not untrained in the discipline of the liberal arts, and I myself am not ignorant of my ignorance; and what I did not learn through human instruction, I was unable, being unlearned, to display to others.”

Although we may miss eloquence in a man immersed in the dense darkness of captivity, we admire his talent and learning. We know from other sources that under Speraindeus, together with the martyr Eulogius, he made considerable progress in a good disposition and in serious studies.

He is also said to have suffered misfortunes from adversaries. Concerning them he writes to Romanus the physician:

“I made all those who opposed me my closest friends; and, employing the skill of my mind through certain peaceful bonds, I embraced my opponents with the hand of affection, softening them by humility and soothing them by kindness.”

His friendship with Saint Eulogius the martyr was especially distinguished, as is clear from his writing of Eulogius’s Life and Martyrdom. At the beginning of that work he placed the following inscription, and made the condition of his lay status and attachment to the world known to everyone:

“I profess that I am recounting not things heard and uncertain, but things seen and tested by me—namely, concerning Eulogius. Since, by the cooperation of God’s grace, from the first flower of youth we were bound together by the sweetness of charity and the love of the Scriptures in one concordant bond, we bore the yoke of this life together in all questions, though not in equal rank, yet with equal affection. But he, adorned with the dignity of the priesthood and carried aloft on the wings of virtues, flew upward to greater heights; while I, smeared with the mud of luxury and pleasure, crawl along the ground and am dragged along to this day.”

That Alvarus was bound by marriage seems to be implied by John of Seville when writing to him:

“I presume to greet, through your mouth, all the beauty of your household. The lady Froisinda greets you,” and so forth.

It is pleasing to add here several passages from the beginning of the same Life of Eulogius concerning the common habits and pursuits of the two men under the direction of the abbot Speraindeus, since they concern their studies:

“We engaged,” he says, “to omit other matters that may be seen in the published works, in a delightful play with the Scriptures; and, not knowing how to guide an oar on the lake, we were thought to be exposed to the roar of the Euxine Sea. For our youthful disputes concerning doctrines by which we were divided—perhaps concerning the positions of philosophers—we conducted through letters against one another, not with hostility but with pleasure, and we soothed one another with praises in rhythmic verses.

“This exercise was sweeter to us than honey and more delightful than honeycombs. And, as we daily stretched ourselves forward to attempt many things inaccessible in the Scriptures, youthful and immature teachability drove us on, so that we composed volumes which later age, falling silent, decided should be destroyed lest they remain for posterity.”

A certain codex of the Church of Córdoba, apparently written seven hundred years ago, has happily preserved Alvarus’s works for us. Morales saw it and praises it in more than one place [Note: In the preface preceding book XI of the *History of Spain*, under the heading “The aids for what follows,” and in book XIV, chapter 3]. Thomas Tamayo also praises another codex belonging to the Church of Toledo [Note: In his notes to Luitprand, year 869, p. 209].

We possess a copy derived from that source of everything contained there, transcribed from another copy communicated to us from the extensive Roman library of Francisco Barberini, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. It is preserved there, having formerly been written out and presented to that great ornament of the purpled cardinals and most generous protector of learned men and learning, in Madrid, when he had come there as legate *a latere* of Urban VIII of holy memory, by Thomas Tamayo de Vargas himself, royal historiographer, together with other Spanish monuments of antiquity, from his own transcript.

We shall provide its description here, as it appeared from the copy belonging to the aforementioned Thomas Tamayo:

“Collected works of Aurelius Flavius Alvarus, illustrious patrician of Córdoba, friend and fellow student of Saint Eulogius, archbishop of Toledo and martyr—works long desired by many, never before published, faithfully transcribed for the first time from a very ancient codex of the Church of Córdoba written in Gothic letters, and willingly communicated from the library of Don Thomas Tamayo de Vargas, royal historiographer.”

The learned man had marked the body of Alvarus’s works, which he was preparing for publication, with this inscription. It contains the following.

### The *Luminosus Indiculus*

It begins: “In defense of your servants, Lord …,” etc.

It was written by the author in the year 854, as is clear from the following:

“For in this year of the Lord’s Incarnation, eight hundred and fifty-four, and in the era that is current, eight hundred and ninety-two, two hundred and forty Arab lunar years are reckoned, while the solar years are two hundred [lacuna] from which total sixteen solar years remain.”

There is no need to investigate this calculation more carefully, since we have the years of the Incarnation, the Spanish era, and the Arabs’—that is, the Hegira’s.

Morales once denied that this work was by Alvarus [Note: In his notes to the Life of Eulogius, at the end], chiefly because he found no mention of Eulogius in it, Alvarus’s closest friend—a subject that Alvarus could scarcely have omitted if he were treating the same matter. Nevertheless, he later abandoned this opinion when writing his *History* [Note: Book XIV, chapter 3] and, following his considered judgment, assigned this book to our Alvarus.

He was right to do so. The style itself, both in vocabulary and composition, is very similar to Alvarus’s other writings; the same events and the same period belong to Eulogius and Alvarus; and the mention in Eulogius’s Life that Alvarus wrote a work relating to the history of that persecution seems to establish that the author of the book was no one else.

For this reason, our sources frequently follow these positions [Note: Petrus Pontius in Morales’s notes to the Life of Eulogius, near the beginning; Ramirez to Luitprand, year 866, no. 309; Tamayo leans more strongly this way at year 869, p. 208], with the sole exception of Jerome Romanus de la Higuera, up to his own time. Yet the same inconsistency that appears in his other works is found here, especially in his assignment of the author of the *Indiculus*.

For if one consults Higuera’s work on Luitprand [Note: Year 866, no. 309], the author is Bonitus, bishop of Toledo; but if one consults his *Julian*, it is Wistremirus, who was likewise bishop of Toledo. The same Julian later presents this claim in his *Chronicle*, while in the prefatory letter to the *Chronicle* he takes the position of Bonitus.

Many people nevertheless admire this man, of whom one might aptly say with Ennius: “We go this way, we go that way; when we have arrived there, we wish to go elsewhere”; or with another Greek saying: “I say yes and no, and I do not know what to say.”

His authority, though utterly worthless, nevertheless kept Thomas Tamayo—whom such tricks were least worthy of deceiving—from settling the matter. At last, after every path had been tried, Tamayo turned to Alvarus. He was moved chiefly by the fact that the epithet “luminosus,” attached to the *Indiculus* as though it were its proper title, was characteristic of Alvarus’s own manner of expression in his other writings. He adduces several examples of this, from the Life of Eulogius and from a letter to Eulogius.

Beyond these, at the end of another letter to John of Seville, Alvarus writes:

“And may the revealed judgment of your mouth disclose all things to us luminously.”

Nor was the author of the *Indiculus* content merely to use this word in the title; he employs it frequently throughout. Eleazar, he says somewhere, “teaches luminously in the Second Book of Maccabees.” Elsewhere: “And blessed John teaches luminously in his First Epistle.”

Alvarus likewise uses the word *indiculus* in his letters: “And he sent us the friend’s desired little book.” Furthermore, he very often uses the word *invectio*, as though one were speaking of a discourse directed against someone; the author of the *Indiculus* uses it in the same way.

In the *Indiculus* one reads:

“To whom that invective of exaggeration among the Israelite people rightly applies.”

And shortly afterward:

“And although a carefully worked invective brings the whole matter out into the field in an extended work” [*read*: “in an extracted work”].

And again after a little:

“The seductive invective was not ashamed.”

Also:

“And against the foolish invective of criticism.”

Scarcely anyone other than the author of this *Indiculus* can be found to have spoken so frequently in this manner, as we read Alvarus doing in his letters.

In one of the letters he wrote to John:

“So that your entire invective may contend against these things.”

And in another to the same John, twice within a few words:

“For a reply is never brought to rest unless the invective is first refuted” [Note: In our manuscript it reads *converscatur*; I prefer the other reading].

And:

“Let there be a winding little chain, and a chain-like winding contention, which is neither eluded by invectives nor brought to an end by replies.”

In a letter to Romanus the physician:

“And I would blunt the invectives of my adversaries through an apologetic work.”

There are very many features in which the same author corresponds with himself in both works. Since these make it worthwhile to settle the matter beyond further doubt, it is useful to append them.

The *Indiculus* uses *sequipedes* in the nominative plural for those who follow at someone’s feet:

“And for the learned in doctrine, and the fellow-followers of Christ.”

And below:

“But we, evangelical servants, fellow-followers of Christ’s rustic disciples.”

Likewise, concerning the followers of Muhammad:

“Extending the sect of the most impure men, most impure fellow-followers,” etc.

Soon afterward, concerning the same people:

“Fellow-followers of their faith.”

A letter to an unnamed bishop uses the word in the same way:

“And therefore, my most sublime lord, vicar of the apostles, and fellow-follower of Christ, the creator of all things” [Note: In our codex it is *sequippede*], etc.

It is characteristic of the *Indiculus* to use *opus praecidere* for “to finish.” “Let us finish the little work at its proper end.” The letters use the same expression, especially the fourth letter to John of Seville, at the end of which he cuts off statements of this kind.

The author whom we believe to be the same frequently uses the adverb or preposition *tenus*. Concerning the blessed who enjoy the vision of God, the *Indiculus* says:

“Already rejoicing in eternal quiet and serving their king face to face.”

Likewise *coelo tenus*, meaning “up to heaven”:

“Thus today they abound in more perfect abundance, as they believe, and carry it up to heaven.”

Similarly *facietenus*, meaning “apparently”:

“They show the appearance of piety outwardly.”

And afterward:

“Pretending piety outwardly.”

Likewise in the Life of Eulogius, which certainly is by Alvarus:

“I crawl along the ground and am dragged along to this day.”

And in the second letter to John:

“He recounts it in words.”

And in the fourth to the same man:

“And by the name itself, what it is may be investigated more clearly outwardly,” that is, plainly.

And in the fifth to the same man:

“Let us extend it higher than the earth, up to heaven.”

And shortly afterward:

“Astrologers wished to fly on wings up to heaven,” that is, as far as heaven.

There are also very similar turns of phrase in the *Indiculus*, such as:

“Whenever an effort was available.”

And in the fourth letter to John:

“As much as it was possible for me,” meaning “as I was able.”

In both works we find deponent verbs such as *opinari*, *adversari*, and *praeconari* formed actively.

The *Indiculus* has:

“Perhaps someone may think that he ought to be avoided.”

And soon:

“They will have thought many things.”

The fourth letter has:

“To have thought so lightly.”

The author of the *Indiculus* says:

“As though they were proclaiming in a frenzy.”

And soon:

“They shout, repeat, and proclaim.”

Alvarus in the *Confession*:

“You detest sins.”

And below:

“He may strive to turn away.”

The *Indiculus*:

“They will return from his number.”

The second letter:

“God does not disdain man.”

The fourth letter:

“And they complain that they have not yet grasped it.”

And afterward:

“He did not arrange it according to the rules of Donatus.”

The *Indiculus* uses the Greek word *euphrasia*:

“With his own *euphrasia* (‘eloquence’) he fashioned a thousandfold sectarian rite.”

Just as Alvarus does at the beginning of the fourth letter to John of Seville—a passage corrupted in my copy, though not in the word *euphrasia*:

“Taking the *euphrasia* (‘eloquence’) of your *empeiria* (‘experience’).”

The author of the *Indiculus* uses the word *innumerositas*:

“He grants the license of innumerability,” referring to the license granted to Muslims to have several wives.

Alvarus uses it in the fifteenth letter to Eleazar:

“Through the innumerabilities of diversities they make use.”

In both works we believe *domui* should be retained as the genitive of *domus*. In the *Indiculus*:

“For it is shameful to set forth the madness of that household piece by piece.”

And in the second letter:

“The beauty of your household.”

To conclude, substantives of one gender joined with adjectives of another are read everywhere in both works, in the letters as well as in the *Indiculus*. From the *Indiculus* we have selected the following: *Imitare decuit factum probabilem* (“It was fitting to imitate a commendable deed”).

Likewise: *conjugium quem* (“the marriage whom”), etc.

From the fifth letter: *Ad illum flectere articulum congruit, quod mentem macerat* (“It is fitting to turn toward that point which torments the mind”), etc.

From the seventh: *Apostoli eum dictum* (“the Apostle, him said”).

From the ninth: *Abundantiorem pretium* (“a more abundant price”).

This grammar is Alvarus’s, and it is extremely difficult to find such a combination of features common to any other two authors. There is therefore no need to investigate further the author of the *Indiculus*.

Nor should we yield to the recent opinion of our friend Don Joseph Pellizerius. Merely because Alvarus begins a certain letter written to Eulogius with the words, “The luminous document of your work,” he suspects that Alvarus may have been referring to the work of Eulogius called the *Luminosus Indiculus*.

The eminent man, whom I have always treated with the greatest honor and shall continue to do so, is plainly mistaken. Alvarus is speaking, using his customary word *luminosus*, of the *Martyrial Document* dedicated to the virgin sisters Flora and Maria, a book that Eulogius had sent him with the immediately preceding letter for him to inspect.

Nor shall we easily find in Eulogius the kind of freedom of expression that appears in Alvarus. Nor is it weighty enough to compel us to insist that the author of the *Indiculus* could not have failed to mention Eulogius, such a man and one who had formerly undertaken the same work. The *Indiculus* could have been written by Alvarus before Eulogius completed his *Memorial* of the saints.

For it is established that the *Indiculus* was composed in 854, as was noted earlier, whereas the third book of the *Memorial* was written at least after 856. It is not impossible that Alvarus modestly suppressed his own *Indiculus* so that it might not come to Eulogius’s attention.

But concerning what we have heard about the Toledan bishops Bonitus and Wistremirus: Higuera himself—and, to use Alvarus’s word, his fellow-followers—was especially troubled by the idea that the author of so useful and learned a little work was someone other than a bishop of Toledo. Provided that they maintained this claim, they were equally willing to accept either Wistremirus or Bonitus.

Certainly the *Indiculus* has reached us mutilated. Not only is the end of the part we possess missing, but the entire other, or second, book is also wanting, as is clear from the following:

“And how universal this belief of ours is, the authority of our ancestors established in the second book of this work.”

And elsewhere:

“And in the second book let us gather the judgments of the teachers and confirm our laborious little tales by the dripping of truthful testimony.”

The subject of the work is a defense of those who in Córdoba offered themselves for martyrdom without having been sought out, on behalf of whom Eulogius also contended; and afterward an explanation of the prophecies concerning Muhammad and his abominable heresy.

The following appears next in the Córdoba codex.

### Alvarus’s Confession

It begins: “Exalted God, ineffable …,” etc. It bears the unmistakable signs of a most humble spirit, truly crushed by the hammer of repentance, modeled on that of Isidore.

### The Book of Letters

Of these:

#### I

It is addressed to John, or Flavius John, by Paul Alvarus. It begins:

“You know, most beloved, the source of sweetness.”

#### II

It is addressed to John, whom he here first calls “of Seville.”

The heading reads:

“To Aurelius Flavius John, Paul Alvarus.”

It begins:

“Thus far in the manner of friends …”

### III

This is John of Split’s, with the following heading: “To Aurelius Flavius Alvarus, an illustrious man: the petition of the least John.” You see how John and Alvarus call one another Aurelius and Flavius, presumably as a matter of honor, not because they were actually so named. It begins: “O great lord.”

### IV

“To the same John.” It is Alvarus’s, with the same names. Its opening has been corrupted by age. In my copy it reads, not far from the correct reading: “Taking the epitome of your imperial experience, or rather running through the epitome of your energy, the soul became joyful” (*Enclocae, emperiae vestrae sumentes euphrasia imo energiae percurrentes epitoma, jucunda facta est anima*). I would gladly read: “Taking the eloquence of your experience”—that is, “taking in hand the eloquence of your sweet-flowing expertise” (*Englocae empeiriae vestrae sumentes euphrasiam*).

In Greek, ἐγγλύσσω means “I sweeten” (*indulcoro*), “I bring sweetness” (*dulcedinem affero*), while ἐμπειρία means “experience,” “expertise,” or “prudence.” And perhaps beginning the letter with these three Greek words, when his eloquence was already weakening, was not inelegant. This letter, however, is longer than the others.

[Note: More simply, *enclocae* or *englocae* derives from the Greek and Latin ἐγλογὴ, *egloga*, that is, “a short work,” “a little book,” or “a letter.” For the Greeks pronounce the letter γ (*gamma*) similarly to the Hebrews’ *hain*, as though they placed the liquid Latin *g* before *n*, and from both formed something like the double letter *ng*. I observe Gallaecians pronouncing vernacular names ending in *-on* in this manner: *sermon*, *oracion*, *confession*, as though they were saying *sermong*, *oraciong*, *confessiong*. Nor is the transition from Greek Υ, or ὕψιλον, to the small Ο, or omicron, otherwise easy, so that *enclocae* or *englocae* might descend from ἐγγλύσσω.]

### V

“To the same,” similarly addressed. Its heading is: “After the discussion of our ignorance.”

### VI

This is John’s letter to Alvarus, with the following heading: “To the illustrious, exceptional, and exalted Alvarus, John, least of all and lowest in everything.”

### VII

Alvarus’s letter to the abbot Speraindeus, with this title: “To my most beloved lord and father in Christ, Speraindeus the abbot: Alvarus, his servant.” It begins as follows: “The all-knowing and omnipotent God,” etc. We have said in the Life of Eulogius who this abbot Speraindeus was, and how much both Alvarus and Eulogius, the martyr of Córdoba, advanced in their youth under that teacher.

### VIII

The mutilated reply of the abbot Speraindeus, with this address: “To my most illustrious and venerable lord, or rather to renowned Alvarus, to be embraced with every affection in the charity of Christ: Speraindeus.” The letter begins: “While from tribulations.” We have already spoken of it in the account of Speraindeus.

### IX

Alvarus’s letter to the physician Romanus, with this heading: “To my most serene lord Romanus, foremost among all Catholics: Alvarus.” It begins: “My ancestors.” In this letter there is mention of the Romans of Córdoba, of a certain prince, and also of Count Servandus.

### X

This has no title and seems to have been written to a bishop whom he calls “the vicar of the apostles” and “the follower of Christ, the maker of all things.”

[Note: This is not by Paul Alvarus, but by an uncertain bishop—perhaps Saul of Córdoba—and was addressed to another uncertain bishop. At its very beginning our words are read: “And therefore, my most exalted lord, vicar of the apostles and follower of Christ, the maker of all things,” etc. These words cast some suspicion as to whether it was written to the Roman pontiff. It is extant in Flórez, volume XI, beginning on page 156.]

### XI

Alvarus’s letter to Bishop Saul, with this heading: “To my most holy lord Saul, bishop (of Bishop Saul): the petition of Paul Alvarus.”

[Note: The repetition seems to concern the same matter.]

[Note: My manuscript does not correctly read *suggestio* but *suggressio*.]

After receiving absolution at the extreme danger of his life, Alvarus, now freed from illness—as was right—returned by this letter to Bishop Saul, to be absolved once more, according to canonical practice, from certain censures of which I know nothing.

### XII

Bishop Saul’s reply to Alvarus. It begins: “We had many [reasons].” He refuses to absolve Alvarus and sends him back to those from whom he had received penance during his illness.

He denies that this had been done properly while a bishop was present in the city and without that bishop’s permission. Moreover, he implies that Alvarus had adhered to the party of a certain pseudo-bishop.

### XIII

Alvarus’s letter addressed to Bishop Saul. It begins: “The letter written in your name.” He reproaches Saul for having denied him the ministry of absolution that he had requested, persuaded by the words of some insignificant man, a disturber of peace and sower of heresies. He also complains that Saul had failed in many matters to act as a minister of the true God.

### XIV

Alvarus’s letter addressed to the convert. Its heading is: “To Eleazar, beloved by me: Alvarus.” It begins: “First of all, my beloved.” Eleazar was a Gaul by nation, but a Hebrew in faith, having been a Christian; therefore Alvarus calls him a transgressor (an apostate). The whole letter concerns the promises and prophecies already fulfilled concerning the coming Messiah.

### XV

The convert’s reply addressed to Alvarus, with this salutation: “To Eleazar, beloved by me.” It begins: “You wrote to me.” Nevertheless, perhaps the religious scruple of someone close to superstition caused only a very small portion of this letter to survive, lest the writing of a Jew be read. In fact, the owner of the book crossed out the fourteen lines that followed on the page, cut out the entire following leaf, and finally deprived the page that continued the volume of the four additional lines that concluded the letter.

### XVI

Another letter of Alvarus addressed to Eleazar: “Alvarus to beloved Eleazar.” It begins: “Your reply.” In it he blunts Eleazar’s arguments on behalf of the errors of the Synagogue. It was written in the year 840.

### XVII

Two fragments of another letter, opposed to Alvarus by that same Eleazar. The owner of the book likewise sacrificed to oblivion as much of it as he could without damaging Alvarus’s other letters.

### XVIII

Another letter of Alvarus addressed to the convert. It begins: “A fabrication founded on falsehood.” Everything in it is most worthy of being read concerning Christian truth against Jewish unbelief.

### XIX

Another, very brief letter from the convert to Alvarus.

### XX

A reciprocal letter of Alvarus addressed to the convert.

Before these letters, our manuscript contains certain poems under the following inscription: “The poems begin.” There follows a philomelic poem in praise of the nightingale; a fragment of another poem; distichs about a rooster; “poems”—for they are always called *versi*, not *versus*—of praise or prayer; the “poems of Epimenides,” concerning his own illness; a personal metrical lament; poems in the library of Leovigild; a poem in praise of the cross; and heroic poems in praise of Blessed Jerome.

All these are found both in our copy and in the Cordoban manuscript. In addition, as we have already seen in the Life of Eulogius, Alvarus wrote:

The Life or Passion of the most blessed martyr Eulogius, priest and teacher, who suffered in the Spanish era 897, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 859, under King Muhammad, on the fifth day before the Ides of March. Morales published it from a manuscript of the church of Oviedo, distinguished by this title and serving, as it were, as a forerunner of Eulogius’s works; after him Schott published it in the fourth volume of *Hispania illustrata*, with Morales’s own notes.

In the same manuscript and editions this is followed by a hymn for the feast of Saint Eulogius:

> Now the fruitful  
> festivals return—

and likewise by his epitaph. All these works, except for this last Life of Eulogius, still lie hidden.

[Note: All these works are found in Flórez, volume XI, beginning on page 275—indeed, unless I am mistaken, increased by two poems: one mutilated at the beginning, which seems to concern a peacock proudly scorning the other birds, especially the nightingale, though defeated by its song; and another in which the colors of flowers are compared with the colors of little stones. In these poems Alvarus seems, as we indicated shortly before, to have attempted to imitate Isidore of Seville and Eugenius of Toledo, as is clear from their related headings and subject matter.

As for the epigram “In the Library of Leovigild,” which we mentioned shortly before, with the same opening—“Here are many sacred things,” etc.—I have read it in Isidore’s library. We now add the metrical lament, which resembles Isidore’s rhythmic *Lament of Repentance*: “Hear, Christ, the sorrowful weeping.” In the *Diary* concerning his own illness, he seems to have closely followed Eugenius of Toledo’s title, or complaint, of nearly the same subject, “Concerning His Own Illness.” Likewise, in the philomelic poem, the opening “Your voice, O nightingale,” etc., is read three times in both authors.]

Neither Don Laurentius Ramírez nor Don Thomas Tamayo, both exceptionally diligent scholars of our affairs, ever fulfilled their intention of preparing an edition. Perhaps, if leisure permits us to complete the notes, we shall do so. The following work is also attributed to our Alvarus:

The *Book of Sparks*, in a parchment manuscript of the library of the monastery of Saint Facundus—commonly called Sahagún—in Spain. There, after Saint Gregory’s exposition of Ezekiel, this book appears with the following inscription: “In the name of Christ, here begins the *Book of Sparks* of Alvarus of Córdoba, collected from the sayings of the holy Fathers.” It is said to have been written on the fifth day before the Kalends of October in the Spanish era 1213. Here the work of the copyist is praised, not the date of the author.

Morales, who was also the first to see this copy, mentions two other exemplars in an account of his still-unpublished journey, undertaken by royal command to visit the archives and *cemilia* of Galicia, Asturias, and Old Castile, and in his *History*.

[Note: Book XIV, chapter 3.]

He says that one exemplar, written in the Gothic script and extremely old, is preserved in the Cistercian monastery of La Espina, fifteen miles from the city of Valladolid; the other in the city of Mondoñedo. The work was published at Basel without the author’s name.

[Note: Two codices of Paul Alvarus’s *Book of Sparks* exist in the Royal Library of Madrid. One is Gothic and seems to have been written at the beginning of the eleventh century; the other is at least three centuries more recent. Flórez mentions both in volume XI, page 47, note 68, as well as other short works contained in the famous Cordoban manuscript repeatedly mentioned by our author, though he himself denies that Paul Alvarus wrote them.

Among these, Flórez, note 69, lists fourth: “The Book of Genealogies,” beginning: “There are two Adams: one is the first-fallen Adam, the other is the second Adam, Christ.” We included this, or something similar, among the works of Isidore of Seville when writing about him, without making any certain determination about its author.

In the Library of the King of France, part III, page 281, manuscript 2444, this treatise of Paul Alvarus’s *Book of Sparks* is noted as being attributed in other manuscripts to the Venerable Bede. In the Alnensis collection, class IV, division 6, page 245, Bousquier attributes it to John the Defender. In the Bodleian Library, class IV, manuscripts 1383 and 1393, it is attributed to Cassiodorus.

In the Escorial manuscript of Isidore’s *Etymologies*, apparently written in the eleventh century—digramma and shelfmark I, no. 14—at the place where the text of Isidore’s Book VII reads, “The sacred Scriptures testify that there are nine orders of angels,” there is in the margin an ancient note in the Gothic manner: “ALVARUS.”

I do not recall ever having read in any ancient teacher that there are nine orders of angels, except in Saint Gregory and in Lord Isidore; this may perhaps have come from our Alvarus. It should also be observed that Gregory is honored with the title “saint,” whereas Isidore is given the title “lord.”]

The year [is lost].

Other works have perished, namely the letters to Eulogius, or the scholarly disputations held with him. Yet, as we have already quoted from that author, the age, mute and intent on obliterating them so that they might not remain for posterity, decreed their destruction, along with the rhythmic poems.

He also planned to write deliberately against the Qur’an, as can be gathered from these words of the *Catalogue*: “All these matters we shall discuss more fully and with a more polished invective in another work, if God grants us life.” And later: “For I am ashamed to set out one by one the madness of his house”—[Note: Thus for *domus*, concerning the house mentioned above, evidently some idol]—“nor is it appropriate to attack briefly with a few darts some of the many things deserving ridicule, since the whole matter is held in our minds, to be made public one day to all the faithful.”

We have no certain information concerning Alvarus’s death.

[Note: The learned Flórez, volume XI, page 30, note 33, assigns Alvarus’s death to the year of Christ 861 or approximately that time.]

Nor should one give even the slightest weight to what the pseudo-Liutprand said [Note: Under the year 859.]: that the holy patrician Alvarus died at Córdoba on the fourth day of May, in the Spanish era 907, but in the year of Christ 869.

John Tamayo, believing him rashly, consequently introduced Alvarus as a saint into the Spanish Martyrology on that day. These are Toledan apotheoses; for the recently mentioned Liutprand [Note: Under the year 846, no. 290.] and his fellow secretary Julian [Note: In the *Chronicle*, no. 433.] call him, in round and emphatic language, a saint flourishing at Córdoba in the reputation of sanctity.

I can never sufficiently marvel at John Tamayo’s carelessness. In his eulogy he had said of Alvarus that he was, as some believe, the brother of Saint Eulogius; yet in his notes, or acts, he did not hesitate to confuse our Alvarus with Alvarus, the brother of Eulogius, who traveled in Germany together with their other brother Isidore. Eulogius speaks of them in his letter to Wiliesindus of Pamplona, as we stated in the Life of Eulogius.

He must indeed be blind who does not see Alvarus himself confessing that Eulogius was bound to him not by any bond of blood but by a single bond of friendship and mutual association. He says most clearly in the Life:
