> From the first flower of adolescence, bound together by the sweetness of charity and the love of the Scriptures in one harmonious bond of this life, we took up the yoke, etc.

And below, after saying that Eulogius had been accustomed to visit the house of the abbot Speraindeus:

> There, he says, I first deserved to see him; there I clung sweetly to his friendship; there I was bound to him by an indivisible bond of affection.

And what follows.

Do you suppose that actual brothers could by chance have first come to know one another in this way? Yet does not Alvarus himself mention Eulogius’s brothers’ journey?

> Nor was it enough for him, he says, to visit the monasteries of his homeland; rather, on account of his brothers, who at that time were exiles in the regions of France, he undertook an untrodden road.

We make these remarks not without indignation at Tamayo when, astonished, we notice that he placed this colophon at the end of Alvarus’s acts:

> You will note one thing: although Alvarus and Isidore are called the brothers of blessed Eulogius, they were brothers not by a bond of flesh but by a bond of companionship.

What a judgment from a man devoted to frivolities! Once he had truly been driven into the narrow predicament of making one and the same person out of two Alvaruses, perhaps seeing the testimony quoted above concerning the friendship—but certainly not the blood relationship—between our Paul Alvarus and Eulogius, he did not hesitate to disown the other Alvarus, the true brother of Eulogius, and exclude him from that kinship.

The following passages from Eulogius will establish, in accordance with the natural brotherhood of both Isidore and Alvarus with Eulogius, the vindication of their relationship. In his letter to Wiliesindus, where he describes their journey into the regions of Gaul clothed in a toga, he says:

> Thus, in my exile, I longed for nothing except the affectionate presence of my pilgrim brothers and my abandoned family.

Whose family? He shows below:

> Therefore, when affection for returning to my own fields, and for my devout mother Elisabeth, or my sisters Niola and Anullona, and my younger brother Joseph, urged me on, you compel me still to remain and do not allow me to depart in sorrow. But my heart, struck by both wounds, you could no longer heal, since both the exile of my brothers and the desolation of my household brought me daily lamentation.

Even if we grant that Eulogius could have called both men “brothers” because they were bound to him by charity—just as he is also found often to have called a father, mother, sisters, and other brothers by those names on that basis alone—this excuse does not apply to the other Alvarus, who, speaking of Eulogius in his Life, as we have already said, would foolishly have called Isidore and Alvarus Eulogius’s brothers unless they were actual brothers.

## Works of Alvarus of Córdoba

First published from the Gothic manuscript of the venerable Church of Córdoba, written eight hundred years ago.

*(In Flórez, Sacred Spain, volume XI.)*

## Here Begins the Confession of Alvarus

[Note: In this manuscript Alvarus’s name is written with *b*, not *v*.]

### 1

Exalted God, ineffable and invisible, from whom comes the good and through whom whatever shines with holiness is made; whom no one can worthily beseech, yet whom every speech dares to beseech, however unworthily; without whom nothing exists and apart from whom all impiety proceeds:

God, who are good without quality, great without quantity, present without location, diffused everywhere without the spreading of form;

God, who are not corporeal [Note: The manuscript reads *corporalem*, “corporeal.”] and yet are everywhere through your uncircumscribed substance;

who, seated above, govern, sustaining below, are present, surround outside, are beneath [Note: *Infra* frequently stands for *intra*, “within,” among ancient writers.] and penetrate all things;

God, who hate all evils and, by a hidden but certainly just plan, generally permit them;

God, who, just as you hate evil, which is nothing, so love the good, which is something;

who condemn not the nature of evil, which does not exist, but those who do evil;

God, who rule all things with compassion but never leave sin unpunished;

God, who strengthen some part of your work through eternity, without any preceding merit, while justly corrupting another part through mortality, without any sin having first appeared;

God, who did not wish that the creature whom you had willed to be first in dignity, strength, or beauty, once corrupted by its own fault and fallen to lower things, should remain what it had been created to be, justice requiring otherwise;

God, who, just as you created the human race when no goodness yet existed, so preferred us to other creatures through reason, without any preceding merit;

God, who justly destroy the mass devoted to perdition, while choosing the mass of the kingdom mercifully, solely through the goodness with which you overflow;

God, who restore part of Adam’s offspring solely through goodness, while justly condemning the part you allow to perish because of ancestral fault;

[Note: The manuscript reads *parentalem*, “ancestral,” rather than *parentale*.]

God, who gave the knowledge of faith to those whom you knew would believe before the foundation of the world;

God, who, although you have done many hidden things, nevertheless justly made all that has been made;

God, without whose will no word proceeds, and against whom the very word often presumes to act;

God, whom no one fails to know, yet whom no one fully knows as you are in yourself;

God, whose greatness is incomprehensible, whose glory is immeasurable, whose command is powerful, whose ordering is just, whose judgments are true, whose mercy is extended over your works;

God, whom no one reaches except one purified in heart; whom no one finds except one approved by works; to whom no one cleaves except one chaste in mind and body;

in whom there is no iniquity, in whom there is the highest [something is missing], in whom there is great mercy;

[Note: Something is missing.]

God, author of light, river of piety; you are sweet to one who believes in you with a steadfast heart;

[Note: The manuscript reads *dulce es te firmo corde credentis; caecorum oculus*: “You are sweet, [of] one believing in you with a steadfast heart; eye of the blind.”]

eye of the blind, mind of the weak, truest salvation of the sick, foot of the lame, tongue of the mute, strength of all ages.

You are the way of life. You are the life of salvation. You are the unconquerable right hand of all who ask you. You are the wealth of the poor. You are the consolation of the afflicted. You are the one who raises the humble. You are the destroyer of those who exalt themselves.

From you the righteous receive increase; through you the perfect are sanctified; by you the one who has been brought to completion in a good work is crowned.

You hate the wicked, condemn the unjust, cast down the proud, confound the arrogant; you grant forgiveness to the penitent and life to those dead through sin, nor do you deny your accustomed mercy to those who ask you.

You do not despise sinners, but condemn sins. You do not hate those who sin, but detest sins. You do not destroy the human being, but by attacking crimes you consume them. You do not eradicate the creature, but the fault. “For our iniquity commends your justice” (Romans 3:5). Our crimes affirm that you are just.

Our deeds, deserving of crimes, are evidence of your justice, because in the very respect in which you are just, you hate the unjust. In the respect in which you are holy, you punish sinners. In the respect in which you are true, you condemn liars. In the respect in which you are gentle, you detest the proud. In the respect in which you are merciful, you do not investigate everything so strictly.

[Note: Perhaps read *non totum*, “not everything.”]

From the beginning you nurture your creature with singular mercy, rule it with powerful strength, and order it by ineffable counsel and power.

God, who do not despise the prayers of the contrite, nor reject the cries of those who beseech you with a true heart;

who kindle cold minds with the fire of your love and often, by certain occasions unknown to us, form the beginning of a good work;

from whom virtue has its beginning, from whom its increase, and from whom and through whom its perfection is begun;

who give strength to the weary for action, grant those who act the resolve to complete, and instill in the sluggish the desire to begin;

who never desire the death of a sinner, but always truly call those who transgress to life.

### 2

Be present, be present, Father of the poor. Assist the weary, O Emmanuel. Help the contrite, Holy Spirit. Raise up the fallen, just Creator. Heal the sick, good Jesus. Visit the languishing, kindly Paraclete. Bestow strength, holy God. Grant power, O light of Nazareth. Make whole the one torn apart, O gift of the Father; and make me, whom the dominion of vices has possessed everywhere, your devoted servant, O God Trinity.

It is enough, Lord, that I have served the devil until now; that I willingly fulfilled the service of the enemy of the world; that I offered service to the enemy through the work of iniquity; that I obeyed the one lying in wait for me [Note: The manuscript reads *me*, “me,” rather than *mihi*, “for me.”]; that although I understood his hidden snares, I did not avoid them; that, ignorant of myself, I carried his weapons against myself and even made myself, as though by obligation, his bearer, because I never ceased to store in myself, as in a sheath, the weapons with which he completely shattered me.

[Note: Read “I served the devil.”]

But it is already a long time, Lord, since I preferred to reject his dominion from me. I was unable to do so, as my guilt deserved, because, as though by right of power, he claims as his subject the one whom he held captive by a terrible bond from the beginning of birth [Note: The manuscript reads *a nativitate*, “from birth.”].

And the one whom he claimed as his captive by his own right for so long, now that he breathes again, he keeps deeply entangled in his yoke; and the one whom he never detected resisting him, he now binds, groaning, with unbreakable chains.

Lord, kind and merciful God, look upon your works. With that force of compassion by which you receive the prodigal son, protect me also in my misery, because it is in no way right to leave the work of your hands under the dominion of the most wicked enemy:

that I, created by you, should be the devil’s servant;

that I, created by you, should be a pasture-ground for the robber [Note: That is, *pascui*, “of pasture.”];

that I, enriched with many good things by the best Lord and loving Father, should be handed over to a cruel, horrible Ethiopian.

[Note: The manuscript reads *eziopo* instead of *ethiopi*.]

Blinded by the devil, I chose this cruelty, this voraciousness, and this brutality for myself of my own will. I brought this terrible torture upon myself. I plunged the sword into my own throat. I handed myself over entirely to death, so that I might entrust your possession, owed to you alone, to the worst enemy; so that I might surrender to a horrible plague the field [Note: The manuscript reads *utrus*.] established under your dominion; and so that I might choose as lord the one whom I knew to be an enemy of my father.

For what we long ago read as having happened in the first-formed man [Note: The manuscript reads *proto plausto*.] has happened in me, Lord God. Just as he, created immortal by your gift, was plunged into death through his own fault by eating the forbidden tree, so I, already washed in the bath of living water, cleansed from my father’s offense through regeneration, or redeemed by your dew-flowing blood, have through disobedience to your commandments fallen into the ruin of death that must be mourned.

I cannot discover how I may escape from it, because by walking along forbidden paths I made you, the Lord God whom I ought to have entreated and whose commands I ought to have fulfilled, angry with me.

And so, feeling my prolonged captivity, I grieve, and I perceive no redeemer present to redeem me. My enemy rejoices when he sees that you are angry. He exults when he feels that I have been expelled by so great a Father. He triumphs when he recognizes me so utterly abandoned.

But you, God, who are exceedingly powerful and generous in mercy toward your works, who seek not the death of the sinner but his return to you after his fall (Ezekiel 33:11), who love compassion more than vengeance and display mercy, not judgment, toward sinners, be present to me, a miserable sinner, and rescue me as I seek you with a contrite heart.

Send me help from above, by which I may be able to reject the yoke of my enemies. Repel their customary dominion. Break apart the bonds of entanglement. Restore, Lord, the works of your making, and restore to me your likeness, which the enemy has invaded.

Do not despise me, my God, whom you wonderfully created and redeemed still more wonderfully, beyond all comparison. You made me so that I might look uprightly toward heaven, in which you had promised me an everlasting reward. But my iniquities have plunged me into the depth of hell, and there is no one to rescue me now that I have been plunged down [Note: The manuscript reads *diversum*, “divided” or “different.”].

Can this crafty and cunning enemy stand against you, the true Lord?

[Note: “Against,” that is, “contrary to” or “opposed to.”]

Far be it from that. Nor would he continue to exist unless he received from you the condition of continuing to exist. [Note: The word *quem* is superfluous, or something else is missing.] He who, created by you, was once in blessedness but did not wish to remain there because of the swelling of pride, is even now ruled by you, although he attempts to oppose you.

For whatever he thinks he exercises against us through his wicked will, he agrees with you even in this, serving you unwillingly and unknowingly. Your just power restrains his evil will. And what we, blinded by iniquity, consider unjust, we do not deny to have been justly permitted by a just Judge.

With you, everything has its proper order, and nothing enters the world disorderly. For it is equitable, Lord, that those who have willingly subjected themselves to the devil’s dominion [Note: The reading may be *diabolico*, “diabolical,” or *diaboli*, “of the devil.”] should remain subject to the choice they made of their own accord. Whoever among us has been plunged down is greatly mistaken if he thinks that he is to be released by you again, not willingly but against his will.

For the free will once given by you to human beings ought not to be annulled, so that the one who subjected himself to the servitude of his own will might be restored solely by your command.

In this also, Lord God, you know what concerns me.

[Note: One manuscript adds *dux*, “guide.” Something also seems to be missing afterward.]

Do not remain concealed from me in the pit of my danger. But because the enemy bound me willingly by various arts and at different moments of deception, while my mind did not resist him as it ought, but like an obedient servant gave its hands to bondage, therefore, most merciful God, assist me now in my misery as I repent and groan over my sins.

Now redeem me in particular from the terrible robber whom you have already redeemed generally at the price of your blood.

I shall speak, Lord—hear me. Grant me the power to speak, and deign yourself to accept what I say.

Do you, Creator, not know [Note: The manuscript reads *Nam quid*, “for what?”] the things that press upon me from every side? Do you not see beforehand what I desire to ask? Is anything hidden from you, or are not all things, even those obscure to us, placed in light before you?

Certainly you are the one who sees the hidden things of the heart, who knows what lies concealed by looking into it, who examines and punishes thoughts. For you created all things by saving counsel and, by knowing all things, have weighed them all.

But you await the sinner’s confession. You do not need a narrative, but seek the profession of the mouth. You accept not so much the humility of the tongue as that of the heart; and, since you are incomparably pure, you first taste true purity by sanctifying it from a pure heart.

Behold, Lord, I confess my sins with a pure heart, as you yourself most truly know, and with my whole mind I desire to draw myself away from their enticement.

[Note: The manuscript reads *toto mentis*, “with the whole of the mind,” rather than *tota mente*, “with my whole mind.”]

But bound by the treachery of my chains, I cannot fulfill what I promise. Consequently, I remain daily a transgressor of my vow. Instead of watering myself with tears and cleansing myself entirely through continual weeping, I become more soiled and pile up nothing but an increase of guilt.

Thus, whatever my mind rejoices to grasp even slightly through your gift [Note: The manuscript reads *domo*, “house,” rather than *dono*, “gift.”], it repeatedly laments that, through the enemy’s overthrow or the sluggishness of my heart, it has been deprived of it, and it does not perceive that the means of recovering it are present within me.

For the light of knowledge implanted in me by you naturally remains active, through which I am not unaware [Note: The manuscript reads *Qui*, “who.”] that what I do is wrong. This causes me severe grief even after the preparation of my desire.

But because, while committing things for which I ought to repent, I do not mourn what I have committed, I myself inflict immense harm upon myself. Therefore I do not count myself as seeing even those things that ought not to be despised but embraced in work and in mind, and the things in which I involve myself—not unwillingly, but willingly—I later detest greatly after the pleasure of the filth.

I am my own witness that, though unjust, I never put an end to my injustices. And I grieve all the more that I shall be punished without forgiveness [Note: The manuscript reads *veniam*, “forgiveness,” rather than *venia*, “without forgiveness.”] in the future because I plunge myself wholly into the abyss not unknowingly but knowingly.

What am I to do amid such great crimes? What medicine shall I apply to such a blow? What soothing remedy shall I use for this wound?

[Note: The manuscript reads *hujus se . . . adhibeant*; the passage is uncertain.]

I plainly do not know, because through transgression I fail to know the very thing I know. And this is most truly to know: to weep most bitterly. For to know what ought to be known and in no way fulfill it in practice is not to call it knowledge, but certainly the madness of great folly.

For I know, Lord God, that you are inclined toward mercy and do not desire the sinner’s punishment. I also know that you are supremely powerful in majesty, and that, just as you will, so you are able to act.

[Note: The manuscript reads *magestate*. Spaniards likewise say *magestad* in the vernacular.]

And from my knowledge that you prevail over all things, confidence of some kind arises in me, because you have always called the sinner back. But when I consider your justice and contemplate the examination of your judgment in my mind, I immediately melt away like wax.

Does your justice approve injustice? Does your truth crown liars? Does your holiness reward the wicked, so that I might believe that I, an unjust, impious, and lying man, would escape unpunished?

Far from it. Rather, without any doubt, I shall firmly believe that you hate or punish those like me with the utmost severity. Darkness does not share in the fellowship of light, nor does stench possess the sweetness of a good fragrance.

And if no one of evil mind dwells near you, and no one reaches you except one holy in heart and body, what shall I say about myself, a most foul goat, whom habitual iniquity, like a cruel and most savage mistress, draws almost violently toward the perpetration of crimes?

What can I say amid such misery and unhappiness, except that I should disclose everything to you alone, who know all things before they occur?

3. Be present, Lord, from the most exalted seat of your throne, [Col. 0403C] and free me from this savage dragon who holds me captive: for you alone have bound the strong one, and have powerfully shattered his vessels, and from the sides of the north have often made a holy city for yourself, O great King. Build, Lord, in my heart an urn shining with the brightness of life, and an ark in which you may deign to dwell forever; in which knowledge of your law may continually flourish, and in which the mind itself, by you who are the true way, may never proceed through steep places into byways.

Restore, Lord, the ruin of my body, renew the vigor of my mind, and let that heavenly antidote remove from my inward parts the countless pains that the tongue cannot recount. For if I wished, by enumerating them, to declare even briefly all the things into which I have fallen or in which I still lie—[Note: Manuscript, “in which” (in quo).] as you know—the end of my speech would never come. For I ought to have set out, one by one, my inexplicable vices, and for each offense to have specially entreated you, the Lord, and against those very illnesses to have implored your medicine, most loving Father.

But do you examine sufferings as a physician, or rather, as Creator, do you mercifully bestow remedies upon those who labor? For while we do not know the nature of our diseases, you alone cleanse us, who are the author of our members; and you who see the wounds of souls yourself prepare for them their particular soothing remedy. Pious and merciful God, patient, long-suffering, and exceedingly placable toward human wickedness, raise up him who has been consumed by beasts, and tend with the oil of mercy him who has been wounded by robbers. Build up what is half-ruined, and mend the garment eaten away by moths.

For if a fuller can restore filthy garments to their former beauty through water, how much more can you, good Craftsman beyond comparison, cleanse me if you will? For I know that you desire to save all [I Tim. 2:4]; but those who perish render themselves unworthy of this your most holy will. For according to our works, either we are devoured by the beast [Note: Manuscript, “we are stripped by the beast”: the letter *f* is used for *v*, as in *proflema* for *prolevamus*.] or we are thrust down into Gehenna.

[Col. 0404B] Behold, I have taken up the voice of that leper, because I feel myself bound to a worse plague than he was. For I say: “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean” [Matt. 8:2]. Speak the word, and I shall be healed of this deadly disease. But surely your hand has not been shortened, so that you cannot save, nor your ear become heavy, so that you cannot hear? Far from it. Rather, my iniquities have multiplied, and my sins have weighed me down exceedingly. Because of these things, my words, pressed down by their own weight, cannot travel straight to you. [Note: “Straight” is understood as “by the straight way”; unless one reads *recta* in a more classical sense. In Gothic manuscripts *a* and *u* are often found without any distinction.]

Speak now, Lord: “I will.” Say: “Take up your pallet and walk” [John 5:8]. Say to the wretched man: “Go, and do not sin any more” [John 8:11]. For the jaundiced skin recovered its former color [Note: Manuscript, “received its former color.”] when it heard your will; and the paralytic immediately walked on his feet when he recognized that the burden of his sins had been dismissed by you [Note: Manuscript, “dismissed to you”]; and the adulteress immediately escaped unharmed [ibid.] when she understood that both her past and her future sins had been forgiven her by you.

Is “do not sin any more” anything other than “you shall sin no further”? [Note: Manuscript, “Sin.”] And what else is “Take up your pallet and walk” than “Cast away your sin and henceforth walk in the footprints worn smooth by the feet of the saints”? For your saying, Lord Jesus, is your doing.

O happy would I be if you infused some one of these voices from yourself into my breast! [Note: Literally, “if some voice of these, infused, were to sound”; or, “if some voices of these, infused, were to sound.”] Then, joyful, then secure, then cleansed by the command of my Lord, I would believe myself to be your most faithful servant, because you would not have caused such things to sound to me unless you already foreknew me cleansed and obedient to you—or rather, unless you had prepared me to be led from darkness into the true light.

Let your mercy, Lord, be upon me, and direct your face in the illumination of my heart. Show me your face, and have mercy on me, who need mercy above all. Behold, Lord, not only in deed but also in thought I fall every hour; and from how many directions arrows strike me, I neither count nor weigh. [Note: The reading is uncertain: *consuanter*; the manuscript reading is discussed as *consuantur*, with *e* for *u*, as also below *videnter* for *videntur*. The meaning of *consuantur* or *consuanter* is better learned from the context than from our commentary.]

For I pass over counting those things that are accustomed to deliver the soul, weighed down by their gravity, to the unending fire of Gehenna [Note: Manuscript, *suete*, “are accustomed”]; but now I shall bring forward those that seem light to those who do not weigh them in an even balance. For if I lament only the commission of lesser offenses, their quantity will surpass the state of greater evils. Yet when, with the eyes of my mind and with you as witness, I turn back into myself, I find nothing there that is light, nothing that is not grave.

For what is heavier than lust? What more burdensome than fraud? What weighs more heavily than empty boasting [Note: Manuscript, “empty boastings”]? What is worse than murder? What evil is like false testimony? What is more unjust than the despoiling of the wretched? What is more criminal than the denial, for the detriment of others, of a matter known to be true? [Note: Manuscript, “more heavenly”; the contextual sense requires “more criminal.”]

And yet I have committed all these things, and others that, because speech fails, I have not been able to proclaim—as you know, who are the knower of consciences—partly in deed and partly in will; indeed, in action I, most unjust of men, have fulfilled everything that not even the devil ought to fulfill.

If it is lust, then, wretched that I am, I serve it even to this day through various kinds of enticement. If fraud, then, with conscience alone as witness, I serve it in mind as well as body until today. If bloodshed, then I stand as the actual murderer of my own soul, not merely in appearance. If false testimony, then, by repeatedly serving perjury, I have never imposed a limit upon my tongue to this hour. If swelling pride, I recognize no one as my equal in this corruption. If envy, at every moment I burn as though with fire, begrudging my brothers’ happiness. If injustice, like an unbridled horse I, wretched man, leap upon falsehood. If greed for possessions, then from my longing for them I see myself acquiring golden mountains even in dreams.

Finally, if I should conceive even some slight thought that is right, I immediately hand it over to be gnawed by the worm of empty glory; besides the other forms of the soul’s destruction conceived in the heart and not properly set out as they are. For even in the very history of your sacred reading, or in the divine sacraments of heaven that you grant us for salvation, who could count or draw out how many forms of deception and how many snares of destruction are opened to me without my knowing, or how many shapes of enticement arise on every side? [Note: Manuscript, *per dictionum*, for *perditionum*, “of destruction.”] Who could proclaim so many and such great pits? [Note: Manuscript, “so great”; the contextual reading is “so many and such great.”]

Because I do not doubt that these things are known to you [Note: Manuscript, perhaps *esse*, “to be,” for *ecre*.], I therefore cry out to you, most loving Father, simply for mercy concerning them all. For in slips of speech and in playful conversation, how often I fall, and how innumerably I defile myself, I cannot even perceive with my understanding, much less recount with my tongue. In walking itself and in the manner of my gait I often stumble. And if one sins while silent and not even thinking, what does one do while speaking or deliberating, except multiply the offense a hundredfold?

For when the very medicine with which you heal our wounds produces wounds in me rather than a soothing remedy, what else must my illness be called but mortal, when heavenly care does not benefit me but rather kills the one who suffers? For you, Lord God, brought down to earth for our benefit the Holy Scripture, full of medicines compounded from life-giving juices drawn from your most excellent glory.

But from the very source where I have seen others made wholly sound, I have wasted away in fearful sickness, wounded myself; and I have not proved the medicine powerless, but have lamented myself, the sick man, as incurable and not properly. For if I were to cover myself sufficiently with floods of tears [Note: The corrected reading may be *compluerem*, “were to drench myself”], I would cease seeking a soothing remedy elsewhere, nor would I seek in another place a remedy that I possess within myself.

But could Peter have wept unless you had looked upon him [Luke 22:61], Lord God? Look upon me, Lord, and see me clinging to thorns; and by looking upon me, break my bonds. Grant by your customary clemency what my tongue cannot reach, my God, cleansing me; for the things that you brought to us from heaven through the prophets in your Testaments know how to heal not by themselves but through you.

And unless you, most pious God, are present, and unless you have prepared those antidotes once brought forth by you, through that finger with which you healed the demoniacs, they do not impart the remedy of health. Just as they are known to be life-giving in your presence, so in your absence they are avoided as harmful; for without you nothing in the world is good, and nothing good is good of itself apart from you.

For you are good, O guardian of all, and all goodness received its beginning from you. But how can those wondrous heavenly sacraments be said to exist without you, when your majesty has been set forth in them—not as great as it is, but as much as mortals can hear? Hence it is necessary to believe, certainly, most truly, and fully, that you are present in those readings, and that through them you always heal not the unworthy but the worthy.

For the one who is not healed by those readings is the one who proceeds in the arrogance of pride, not obeying but examining them; who does not subject himself to your word but wishes to scrutinize it according to his own understanding; and while, puffed up, he wishes to exalt himself above you, deceived by himself he struggles against himself. Thus he is afflicted all the more by the disease through which he thinks he is examining the one who examines.

Truly wretched, and rightly to be called unhappy, are we who believe that the words of the Creator are our own and wish rationally to weigh them—as though anything else in the nature of things were reason than the command of you, the most just; or as though man could have obtained the very power of reasoning from anywhere but you, who gave it to him without any preceding merit of his own.

And if he truly possessed reason, rather than a rational part corrupted by his own fault [Note: Manuscript, “corrupted rational part”], he would never seek reason in matters set forth by his Creator, from whom he knows that reason itself was given to him. For truly our great folly directs its daring toward knowing what is forbidden [Note: Manuscript, *ausos*, “daring” in the plural]; and while it desires to know what may in no way be known, it offers itself as a plaything to its enemies. For by frivolously seeking what you did not grant it to know, it seeks to discover what it did not rationally receive from you in the beginning.

For if a human being carefully considered himself, and profitably balanced against himself the reason he seeks, then, since he does not know what is daily done beneath him or within him, he foolishly wishes to weigh the works of his Lord [Note: Manuscript, *liberare*, “to free,” for *librare*, “to weigh”], while he remains perpetually ignorant of himself.

And when we most wretched beings fulfill our desires through beasts and four-footed creatures, and by your gift command even birds and fish, and either capture or kill them, partly for food and partly for assistance [Note: Manuscript, *in adjumento*, “for assistance,” in both occurrences], without rendering an account to those whom we oppress as to why we do this, or why some and not others are killed, or why these and not those are spared from slaughter for assistance, we seek an account from you, wretched men, of your deeds—although we cannot learn through anyone but you what it means to understand rationally.

4. Did you receive anything from us as a reward, that you should create? Or did we give you the price of our labor, that you should redeem? Certainly, in our creation this human and utterly deceptive reasoning comes to an end, since vain presumption cannot explain how it sees itself to have been made. For if someone is ignorant of the reason for his own creation, how does he attempt to inquire into the reason for your other works?

Or let the inquiry of the vain reasoner set forth the quality of the body, or the harmonious structure of the members cohering with one another, or the place of habitation of the soul; and let him investigate its origin, if indeed he has enough wisdom to ask from where it exists. Then let him dare to scrutinize you, the highest Good, and to weigh your judgments [Note: Manuscript, “signs.”]

You know, Lord, why I have brought these things forth, and that I wished in this matter to destroy myself. I preferred to disclose—not as though you were unaware—the agitations of others no more than my own, known to you [Note: Manuscript, *estos*, for *aestus*, “agitations”]; but I have recounted them in obscurity as a penitent. For although your mercy makes it useful for me to know these things, nevertheless doubt again arises unexpectedly concerning matters properly set forth, and I perceive that I need the protection of your defense itself, which, by feeling it, I opposed to my errors.

Teach, therefore, Lord, the mind inwardly, and remove from it the heat of hesitation concerning those things you have taught. [Note: Manuscript, *estos*, “heat.”] Be the guide of the journey for your little servant, the royal way for the wandering fugitive, medicine for one wounded by various illnesses; for you are the light of all ages, the sweetness of the saints, the strength of the weak, the healing of lepers, the life of the dead, the fortitude of the righteous, the example of subjects, the way of believers, and the joy of angels.

Through you princes reign [Prov. 8:15]. To you angels minister. You the archangels proclaim. You the Virtues adore. The Cherubim and Seraphim with unceasing voice proclaim you, the Triune Lord, to the heavens and to human beings.

You are the rest of the patriarchs, the praise of the prophets, the exultation of the martyrs, the hymn of virgins, and the reward of confessors. You are truly the Sabbath [Note: Manuscript, *sabbatus*, “Sabbath”] of the elect, because the kingdom of heaven is yours and is in you.

Lord God, may it please you to snatch me from the condemnation of the most wicked enemy and restore me beneath the yoke of your most gentle power. And if my iniquity opposes me in this very matter, may your abundant mercy shatter that iniquity of mine.

For I know, Lord, I know that you are ready to have mercy on all, and that you are accustomed to grant the way of salvation even to those who do not deserve it. But my iniquities, like a heavy burden, have weighed heavily upon me [Ps. 37:5]. By their density [Note: Manuscript, “thickness”] they have set a cloud between you and themselves. Nor can prayer ascend to your throne when the weight of darkness presses it to remain clinging to the earth.

Send, Lord, the ladder of your mercy, and by its steps make me, crawling, ascend to you [Note: Manuscript, *grados*, for *gradus*, “steps”], though the weakness of my feet does not permit me to stand even upon the first step. And let him whose whole body is shaken by trembling, and who is not permitted by that foul trembling to remain steady in one place, be made firm by your power.

For you are the one, Lord, who gave us your cross as a ladder, which you commanded us both to lift upon our shoulders and to follow you with a pure mind. You are the ladder of believers, because for those who climb through you, you offer yourself as the reward.

By this ladder Judas descended, while Paul, called by you, climbed upward, leaning upon you. By it the Jews slipped down to the earth, while the nations were taken up to heaven. By it sinners, at your command, cleanse themselves and climb daily toward the heights, while those who presume upon their own righteousness fall headlong into the depths.

Make me, Lord, so that just as by faith I have been worthy to reach the steps of this ladder, so by my deeds I may be able continually and firmly to remain upon them. For you are the one who strengthens the wavering, who makes the weak firm, and who crowns the strong by establishing them.

Could Paul have seen you unless you had first called him? So Abraham also, certainly the father of the nations, did not go forth without your call; but just as he received from you the beginning of good work, so he offered the obedience of his will.

For it could not happen that the one whom the life of the dead was calling should be held by unrighteous death; nor could darkness retain in obscurity the one whom the light itself had illumined.

Call me, Lord, and say to me: “You follow me” [John 21:19]. And after you have called me, graciously deign to inspire my heart to obey your voice. Although your calling is nothing other than a true regard. I seek this calling; I desire this regard; I thirst exceedingly to hear such an effective voice.

But surely you have not called? Surely you have not invited us to your grace? Surely you have not sent us the voice of your calling every day? Indeed, every hour, every moment, you call and cry out. And not only through your prophets, but you yourself came in order to call us to you.

Therefore, every day through your Gospel you cry out to us, undeserving though we are: “Let the one who thirsts come and drink, and whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall not thirst again” [John 4:7]. And truly, Lord, whoever thirsts for you with a true heart receives from you a draught of life that does not die; nor does the mind that drinks the cup of your fountain ever know thirst.

But your water, Lord, just as it grants life to those who cease from sinning, so to those who still sin it supplies fire, not satisfaction. [Col. 0409A] [Fragment: *strat.*] And certainly whoever unworthily approaches this fountain does not refresh himself but burns himself.

Be present, Lord, to me who thirsts without knowing you. [Note: Manuscript, “to be thirsted for.”] Cleanse me, so that I may be able to drink you without unworthiness. Behold, my God, this fountain lies open to all who dwell in Jerusalem for the cleansing of sins and of the menstruating woman [Zech. 13:1].

But how do I receive drink in you, when I do not hasten toward it with the step of my soul? And since, with broken legs and clinging to a pallet, I cannot enter Jerusalem, how will I be able to cleanse myself by drinking from its saving fountain?

For if I were one of the inhabitants of the most holy city, I would believe that I was receiving the remedy of health, because salvation has occupied its gates and praise its walls [Isa. 60:18].

But you, my God, who healed by a word the paralytic who had no one to put him into the pool when it had been stirred [John 5], speak the word and deign to cleanse the wretched man from his wounds.

Was that pool healing without you? Or did it display the powers of healing apart from you? Far from it. For you are the salvation of the sick, and through you, wherever or through whomever it occurs, there is healing for the sick.

But to show the manifold greatness of your power, and to bestow healing upon those who labor according to their merits, and to show that you grant us your effective compassion through various occasions, you heal some through themselves as they walk toward life, while you cleanse others, negligent of their own salvation, through gratuitous mercy.

Thus you show us, most exalted God, that our presumption does not find salvation where it thinks it will obtain it, but that you, as a loving Father, graciously bestow salvation precisely where you minister it.

Bestow, Lord God, as God, immeasurable grace upon man, and multiply your overflowing mercy toward the wretched, as the all-powerful one. Irrigate, Lord, my barren earth, so that, watered by your rain, it may bear a fruitful tree. Sprinkle me, God of sweetness, with the dew of your sweetness, and rain upon my mind with the showers of your grace.

For I ask, most pious God, because you commanded me to ask; and this slender spark of your fear has been implanted in me by you. I beg you to increase it by enlarging it, and, once enlarged, to accept it within my inmost heart, as you know.

For behold, my iniquity has grown so dense [Note: Manuscript, “thick”] that it has closed off from me the very access to seeing you; and it is divided into so countless forms that from one mother, pride, many stronger daughters arise daily.

And since I can neither count nor weigh them, how will I be able to destroy them? Certainly every iniquity takes its beginning from pride, because every vice that is committed has its origin in contempt for your commandments. And therefore whatever is wrongly done by a human being who contradicts you is rightly attributed to pride.

For unless he attempted to be proud against you, the Almighty, he would never commit what is forbidden in deed or thought. And therefore the proud and arrogant person cannot find how to come to you, the humble one, because he knows that you do not approve the proud but detest them.

I desire, Lord, to cast away the pride that contradicts your commandments; but, bound by its constant presence and hindered by [Note: Manuscript, “this sluggishness.”] sloth, I am unable to fulfill in deeds what I eagerly desire.

But if I desired rightly and prayed to you with my whole heart to be my helper in this, would you not bestow help upon me, since you are often a helper even to those who do not pray? Surely you are the one who brought water from the rock in the desert for those who did not deserve it? Are you not the one who gave manna to a people who despised it?

Are you not the one who, to this day, makes your sun rise upon sinners and the wicked, and in the mercy with which you overflow pours your rains not only upon human beings but also upon beasts? Are you not that same God whose loving care burns for all? Do you not fill the storehouses of the impious? Do you not permit even slaves to rule as kings? Are you not the one who grants prosperity even to those who resist you?

Certainly you are the one who bestows many worldly goods upon those who deny you, who feeds and sustains even those who blaspheme you—not merely in deeds, as I do, but also with a viperous mouth.

For the one who does not fulfill your commands disparages you by deed, while the one who mocks and does not believe what he ought to believe attacks you with tongue and deed. Even what is blasphemous for those who confess it to recount, you see: the foulness of the Jews, whom you daily nurture not through vengeance but through immeasurable goodness.

Or must it perhaps be confessed that you are the creator of another world, not of this one, where you condemn the impious according to what they deserve by judging them, and crown the pious by glorifying them? Far from it. Rather, with a pure heart and open mouth it must be firmly confessed that you are the creator of both this glorious world and the other.

Here you show goodness toward creation; there you distinguish by judging in accordance with truth. Here your mercy sustains both the worthy and the unworthy; there your justice crowns the worthy and justly condemns the unworthy.

Here you often test the righteous through torments, whom there you crown by assigning them heavenly dwellings. Here you also often reward the saints, so that by showing them a taste of the good reward you may not break them through despair. And often, my God, you afflict the wicked even with these scourges; and through the sentence justly inflicted upon them, you frighten away others like them.

Here what is sown is reaped there. Nor is it right to believe that the light-filled world receives sinners, in which you deigned to dwell by sustaining it and which you have determined to be the place of the recompense of justice.

And if you perform daily in the undeserving all these things that I have set out, and other greater things that I have omitted, why do you not cleanse me, King of kings, small and counted as almost nothing?

Here I seek cleansing; here I ask mercy; here I implore forgiveness of sins, because I am convinced that in hell no confession is profitable.

But if perhaps you await me to stretch my smallness toward contemplating your greatness, I beg you to grant strength for stretching out [Note: Manuscript, *tentendi*, for *tendendi*, “for stretching”] and provide a foothold for extending myself farther forward—or rather, for raising my feet on high.

For although Zacchaeus was small in stature [Note: Manuscript, “Zaccheus”] and stretched himself out, he could not see you at all unless he climbed the height of the sycamore [Luke 19]. And truly, the one who holds to the height of your commandment sees you with his own eyes; the one pure in heart climbs into the tree of life.

But will he climb to the heights when iniquity goes before him to the depths? Far from it. Rather, through you, who are the true way, he is able to walk and through you to climb to eternal life, which you are; and you deign to direct his steps by making them firm. [Note: That is, “deign.”]

Direct my steps, Lord, and let your word be a lamp to my feet [Ps. 118:105], so that, illumined by your light and fortified by the protection of your right hand, I may be able to sing sweet hymns at the gates of the daughter of Zion. [Note: Manuscript, “daughter.”]

Lord my God, compassionate and merciful, look upon me with the regard of your loving-kindness, and with that gaze of your mercy by which you are accustomed to look upon sinners and call them back to yourself from their wandering path.

Have mercy, Lord, have mercy, and grant forgiveness to me who pray to you. Hear, Lord, hear, and forgive my iniquities yourself. Break, Lord, the bonds of my sins, so that I may sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise.

I ask, Lord, forgive me, and blot out my sin, known to you alone. Behold, Lord, I wished to wash myself in this river; but my filth remains exceedingly hardened by its oldness, and can scarcely be washed away by any river [Note: Manuscript, *nullus*, for *nullo*, “by any”] except perhaps by the dew of your grace.

Since you washed Naaman the leper in the waters of the Jordan [2 Kings 5]—[Note: Read *aquis*, “with waters,” instead of *augit*.] are you not able to wash me with your word alone? You are powerful, Lord, and your mercy is above all your works.

Say to me, Lord: “Lazarus, come forth” [John 9:43]. And immediately, although I lie bound, although I already stink as a four-day-old corpse, at your voice I shall receive both release and fragrance together with life.

Anoint the eyes of my heart, Lord, with that clay with which you anointed the bodily eyes of the blind [John 9:6], so that, just as he was worthy to receive bodily light, so I may be worthy mentally to enjoy your light. For truly, Lord, with saliva you illumine those whom you enlighten with your grace.

And if you see me unworthy of a mild medicine, and recognize that I must be cleansed by iron—or rather, by cautery—apply the medicine of cautery to your servant, in whom the enemy has driven a great wound; and in whatever way you yourself will, heal the one who suffers. Only do not cast away one who believes in you with a steadfast heart and cries to you, God, from his inmost heart in every deed.

Spare, God, spare, and in your goodness forgive my crimes. Pardon, most merciful God, and in your mercy wipe away my evils. I have sinned, Lord, I have sinned, and I myself acknowledge my iniquities [Ps. 50].

I ask, Lord, forgive me, and sprinkle my wounded inward parts with the hyssop of your word. Help, Lord, the lost, wandering fugitive, and protect him by your holy gift, so that through the thousandfold snares of our enemy and the manifold deceptions you may lead me to yourself, who are the true protection, without separating me from yourself; and strike down with unconquerable power the one whose deceptions you are able to overcome, since you can accomplish whatever you desire.

Take me, Lord, away from myself, and return me to yourself. Take away my evil, so that I may enjoy your good. Take me away from myself, place me beside you, and let any hand then fight against me [Job 17:3].

Take away what is mine, conceived through my fault and completed through my weakness. Take away what I possess from myself, and confer what I tearfully ask from you. Strip me of my own things, and let me be clothed in yours. Remove me entirely from myself, so that I may be restored entirely to you; so that, when my enemy sees what is yours clinging to me [Note: Perhaps read *haerere*, “to cling,” for *aere*], he may command his feet to flee rather than hasten to pursue me.

Behold, Lord, I have believed [Note: Perhaps *credidi*, “I have believed”], and you have given me the ability. Have I spoken a thousandth part of my evils, or explained more than a slender fragment of my crimes? For I have said not as much as I ought, but as much as you permitted me to say and commanded me to say.

Command, Lord, that what has been said be accepted, and grant your little servant whatever has been set forth through your gift. And just as you see me trembling from myself and recognize that I presume upon nothing except from you, so, merciful Creator, defend me wholly, because I have wholly committed myself to you.

For just as, created by you and by your gift receiving this vital breath, I exist wholly from you and wholly subsist, and, wholly redeemed through you, live in this mortal world, so may I, wholly possessed by you in the future and devoted to your dominion with everlasting and most sweet submission, be worthy, by your gift, to receive your gifts—those which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the heart of man [I Cor. 29:9] [Note: Manuscript, *quam*, for *quae*, “which”]—and to enjoy you as the true Sabbath in place of every gift.

By your favor, you who reign, Three and One, throughout ages of ages that shall never end. Finished.

[Col. 0411]

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF ALVARUS’S LETTERS. (C)

### I.

[Col. 0411D]

**Paulus Alvarus to Aurelius Flavius John.**

1. You know, my most beloved, that charity is the tinder of sweetness and that true affection is the bond of genuine friends. For that concord is rightly called true, and that affection rightly approved as gratuitous, which is joined not by the necessity of fleeting things but by the spontaneous goodness that binds together eternal rewards [Note: Manuscript, *que*, for *quae*, “which”]; which the nourishment of the Holy Scriptures unites [Note: Plural neuter words here frequently take singular verbs], and which the love of divine understanding binds inseparably.

This is true charity, which knows no downfall, which shines with radiant splendor only among the well-mannered, which does not know how to end with the world, and which even after the world’s destruction shines with greater light and indescribable brilliance.

Let us desire, most reverend one, to embrace with every effort of our endeavors the ineffable glory of this sweetness, scarcely conceived by mortals in its full magnitude, and, by increasing charity between us, to make it ours as far as we are able. For I believe, my most exalted friend, that the beginnings of our friendship did not take their origin from perishable things but began from eternal things [Note: Manuscript, *et* for *set*, or *sed*, “but”]. Hence it is fitting that the intention of our minds should strive toward the end at which this affection was first begun, so that, increasing still further, our devotion may be enriched by an everlasting gift.

Moreover, compelled by the sweetness of your charity and driven by the knowledge of your more illustrious mind, I searched through the volumes of great men for what I discussed with you in words; and whatever I was able to find concerning these matters I myself wrote down in readiness with my own hand.

It is yours, most illustrious one, either to enter with your feet into the opinion of my understanding or immediately to reject it as unworthy of such men. For if you do not see that what I have said ought to be followed, then without doubt you judge it worthy of rejection together with those whose path I have followed.

I ask you to allow me to err freely with such men, with such men, without whose work no truth has been established—unless perhaps your most subtle and keen examination should prove that they said these things in another manner. If I learn this, and clearly establish it through your writings [Note: Manuscript, *per scriptis vestris*, “through your written works”], I shall immediately and swiftly ask pardon. For I am more ready to learn the truth than to defend falsehood.

2. First, concerning what I said: that holy and apostolic men do not devote themselves to arrangements of words but rejoice in the truth of meanings, and that they proceed not by Donatus’s art but by the simplicity of Christ—let your patient kindness command us to hear what Blessed Jerome said about this, what he thought, and what he instilled into us in his own writing; and, if another view ought to be held, let it not weary you to explain it to us.

For in the book addressed to Algasia [Note: Read “Algasia.” The words that follow were written by Jerome in Letter 131 to Algasia, question 10, where he recalls the Apostle’s statement to the Colossians, chapter 2: “Let no one deceive you,” and immediately adds the words quoted here: “That which we have often said,” and so forth], in the Epistle to the Colossians, it is written:

> “For that which we have often said—‘And if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge’ [II Cor. 11:6]—we also approve as having been said by Paul not from humility but from the truth of his conscience. [Note: Manuscript, *adprofemus*; Jerome’s text reads *etiam nunc approbamus*, “we now also approve.”] For the tongue does not express profound and hidden meanings. And although he himself understands what he is saying, he cannot transfer it in pure speech into the ears of others.”

The same teacher says to the Galatians:

> “Those who think that Paul spoke according to humility, and did not truly say, ‘And if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge,’ should defend the sequence of this passage. He ought indeed, according to the order, to have said: ‘You who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourselves, lest you also be tempted’ [Gal. 6:1], and not introduce a singular subject after a plural number. Therefore, a Hebrew of Hebrews, and one who was most learned in his native language, was unable to express profound meanings in a foreign tongue; nor did he care greatly about words, since he had secured the meaning.”

[Col. 0414B] **3.** I have likewise briefly and repeatedly noted here what the teachers judge concerning the matter which I sharply refuted and about which I heard you speaking almost with an unbalanced mind. It is for you also to weigh this usefully and then freely present to the weak what you have weighed. [Note: Ms. reads *tritunare … tritunata*.]

Blessed Augustine says the following in his exposition of Psalm 37:

> “Lord, my God, do not depart from me. If he did not depart from the body, did he depart from the head? Whose voice, then, was it, if not that of the first man? For, showing through him that he truly bore flesh, he said: ‘God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ (Ps. 21). God did not abandon him. If he does not abandon you when you believe in him, would the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit abandon Christ? But he had transformed himself into the person of the former man. We know, as the Apostle says, that ‘our old man was crucified with him’ (Rom. 6). Yet we would not be rid of our oldness unless he crucified us in weakness. He came for this purpose: that we might be renewed in him; for by desiring him and [Note: Augustine’s text adds at the end of *super psal. XXXVII*: ‘imitating his passion’.] his passion we are renewed. Therefore it was the voice of weakness, it was our voice, by which it was said: ‘Why have you forsaken me?’ Hence it is said there: ‘the words of my offenses,’ as though he were saying [Note: We read there also: ‘as though he were saying: These words have been transformed in me from the person of the sinner: Do not depart from me.’]: ‘They have been transformed in me from the person of the sinner.’”

**4.** Likewise blessed Ambrose, disputing in the ninth book *Against Arius* concerning the Incarnation of the Lord:

> “[Note: In Ambrose, *De Incarnatione*, chapter 5; but there the text has *qui audit* (‘the one who hears’).] Let the one who hears the words ‘Why have you forsaken me?’ not be misled, but let him understand [Note: In the same place, *intelligat* (‘let him understand’).] that these things are said according to the flesh, which are far removed from the fullness of divinity. For the words ‘of my offenses’ are foreign to God [Note: The manuscript reads *ad verba*, perhaps indicating *per d Deum*, according to the customary notation of scribes.], because offenses are also foreign to the words. But [Col. 0414D] since I have taken upon myself the offenses of others [Note: Ms. reads *suscepit* (‘he took upon himself’); Ambrose’s text more suitably has *suscepi* (‘I took upon myself’).], I have also taken upon myself the words of the debts of others, so that I may say that I have been abandoned by God the Father, although I am always with God.”

Likewise he himself, in the seventh book *According to Luke*:

> “Therefore I shall not blush to confess what Christ did not blush to proclaim with a loud voice: the clear manifestation of the God who testifies to the separation of divinity and body. [Note: Ambrose, *In Lucam*, book 10, chapter 24, has the following elsewhere.] For you have this passage: ‘Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ (Mark 15). The man cried out, dying through the separation of divinity. For since divinity is free from death, death could not exist unless life departed, because life is divinity. This saying must be understood in this way—not because humanity was bearing the passion.”

**5.** Likewise, from the book of the Blessed One against Elipandus:

> “When he says: ‘He who sent me is with me, and he has not abandoned me,’ and elsewhere: ‘God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ it is one and the same person: in both natures he says ‘me’ and ‘me.’ When he says, ‘He has not abandoned me,’ it is divine; when he says, ‘You have abandoned me,’ it is human. Because God had taken up man, and that man was to die, while divinity, which was life, was an exile from death, therefore through the death of the cross he was to be abandoned until his resurrection. This does not mean that divinity abandoned its flesh, but that it was not to die together with its flesh. For he did not abandon his flesh by remaining with it in the tomb, just as he formed it by being conceived together with it in the Virgin’s womb. [Note: The word *non* is absent from the editions, but the omission is marked at the page margin in vol. 4, part 2, of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, col. 523, quarto edition, Paris 1624.] It therefore accords with our faith that the human Son says: ‘Why have you forsaken me?’ while God the Son, who is equal with the Father, says: ‘He who sent me is with me, and he has not abandoned me.’ And since there is one Son from both, care must be taken lest anyone say: ‘A man died, and God raised him.’ This is what those say who proclaim him adoptive according to the flesh and proper Son according to divinity.”

**6.** Likewise Saint Fulgentius, in his book addressed to Peter:

> “The same God-man, he says, came forth from his mother’s womb made man; the same God-man hung upon the cross; the same God-man lay in the tomb; and the same God-man rose from the underworld on the third day. Yet in the tomb the same God lay only according to the flesh, and into the underworld he descended only according to the soul [Note: Ms. reads *in inferno*; Fulgentius, *De fide ad Petrum*, chapter 2, has *in infernum* (‘into the underworld’).]. When that soul returned from the underworld to the flesh on the third day, the same God rose according to the flesh in which he had lain in the tomb. And on the fortieth day after the resurrection, the same God-man ascended into heaven, sat at the right hand of God, and from there will come at the end of the age to judge the living and the dead.”

[Col. 0415D] **7.** Likewise the aforementioned blessed Libanensis:

> “If you wish to examine this and presume to give an account of God and man, you will immediately be plunged into the snare of perdition. Therefore we must not say that one is God and another man [Note: The editions read *nos ergo* (‘therefore we’).]. We have and worship one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. We must not introduce a fourth person by naming one separately, but with that very flesh of his we must worship one Christ, the Son of God, God, according to the true confession of faith of the Council of Ephesus, which says [Note: Ms. reads *qui* (‘who’)]:
>
> ‘We take care not to say of Christ: “Because of the one who was assumed, I worship the one who assumed him,” or “Because of the invisible one, I worship the visible one.” It is also dreadful to say: “The one who was assumed is not named God together with the one who assumed him.” Whoever says this again divides the one Christ into two: placing the man separately on one side and God likewise separately on the other. For he plainly denies the unity according to which one is not co-worshiped with another or named together with another, but one Christ is understood: Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, to be venerated with one service together with his own flesh.’ [Note: From book 1 of the Blessed One’s work against Elipandus.]”

**8.** Likewise Saint Augustine:

> “The author and the work are the same. Since he made flesh in the Virgin’s womb, the author of the work is present. Since he himself deigned to be born in this flesh, the work of the author is present: he who, coming to his mother by a movement that is not local [Note: That is, ‘by a non-local movement,’ as the book of Augustine cited below says. From that text several readings have been corrected: *gignendus* (‘to be begotten’), *plenitudine* (‘in fullness’), *servata* (‘preserved’), *patienti, facienti* (‘while suffering, while acting’), where the manuscript has *gignendo*, *plenitudinem*, *servatam*, *patientis*, *facientis*.], filled his mother’s womb, to be begotten, by ineffable power, yet did not deprive the whole of the fullness of his substance. Thus, at one and the same time, he was wholly in the underworld and wholly in heaven: there suffering injury in the flesh, here not abandoning the glory of divinity. Finally, among those below was the resurrection of the dead, while above the heavens was the life of the living: truly dead, truly alive—in him mortality’s assumption received death, while divinity’s life, remaining intact, did not lose it. In him, while humility is ascribed to the one who suffers and power to the one who acts, the same Christ is taught to be weak when he suffers and omnipotent when he acts, at one and the same time, through one and the same work.” [Note: Augustine’s words are somewhat fuller in the latest Paris edition, appendix to volume 8, chapter 14 of *Against Felicianus the Arian*. From it, *servata, patienti, facienti* has been restored; the manuscript has *servatam, patientis, facientis*.]

He united both operations or wills, understandings and wisdoms, or the natures of divinity and humanity, without confusion and without separation, in the unity of his person, so that they cannot be divided from one another, as the admirable Cyril says. Therefore everywhere, with rapid and insistent speech, we proclaim the one Lord of the Holy Trinity, our Lord Jesus Christ, true God, believing him to be without confusion and undivided even after the Incarnation.

**9.** Likewise the aforementioned distinguished teacher Fulgentius:

> “Thus Christ joined and united both natures indissolubly in the unity of his person, so that in the one person of the only-begotten God neither divinity can be separated from its humanity nor humanity from its divinity. The union of the Word and flesh was made indissoluble when the Word became flesh [Note: Ms. reads *verbo* (‘to the word’ or ‘by the word’).], in whom the natural unity remained in such a way that the proper character of the natures could neither be divided nor confused.”

**10.** Likewise Saint Athanasius:

> “We confess that he himself is the Son of God and God according to the Spirit, and the son of man according to the flesh—not two natures, one to be worshiped and the other not to be worshiped, but one incarnate nature of the Word, to be worshiped with his own flesh in one act of veneration; nor two sons, one truly the Son of God and to be worshiped, the other from the Virgin Mary and not to be worshiped, but made a son of God by grace like the rest of human beings.”

**11.** Likewise from the Council of Ephesus:

> “If anyone dares to say that the man is *Theophoros*, that is, ‘God-bearing,’ and does not rather truly call him God as Son by nature, insofar as the Word became flesh and likewise shared flesh and blood as we do, let him be anathema.
>
> If anyone says that the Word of God the Father is God or Lord of Christ, and does not rather confess that the very same one is simultaneously God and man, because the Word became flesh according to the Scriptures, let him be anathema.
>
> If anyone says that Jesus, as a man, was joined to the operation of the Word of God, and attributes the glory of the Only-begotten as though to another existing apart from him, let him be anathema.
>
> If anyone does not confess that the Lord’s flesh is life-giving and proper to the very Word of God the Father, but says that it belongs to another joined to him by dignity or as though possessing a divine indwelling, and does not rather confess—as we have said—that it is life-giving because it has become proper to the Word, who is able to give life to all things, let him be anathema.”

[Col. 0417C] **12.** Likewise blessed Jerome:

> “How the one who is said to have been made according to the flesh from the seed of David is Jesus, the Son of God, ‘through the resurrection of the dead’ (Rom. 1), is not difficult to perceive for anyone who reads what is written: ‘It was fitting that he, through whom and in whom all things exist, while bringing many sons to glory, should make the author of their salvation perfect through suffering’ (Heb. 2). The end of Christ’s sufferings is the resurrection; and since, after the resurrection, he dies no more, death no longer has dominion over him (Rom. 6). Again it is said: ‘Although we knew Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer in that way’; therefore everything that is in Christ is now the Son of God.
>
> “But how these words are to be referred to him who was appointed Son of God in power constrains your understanding—unless it is because, through the indissoluble unity of the Word and flesh, everything belonging to the flesh is ascribed to the Word, while what belongs to the Word is proclaimed in the flesh. We often find Jesus, Christ, and Lord referred to both natures, as in the saying: ‘There is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist’ (1 Cor. 8). And again: ‘If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory’ (1 Cor. 2).”

**13.** Hence our present teacher Vincentius likewise says, imploring in these words:

> “May the very Word of the Father, through whom the Father founded the ages, who afterward was silent before the judge for our sake, and who is to be crowned with the lot of the saints for eternal reward, raise you up [Note: I would read: ‘may he raise you, who are to be crowned’; for he is speaking to a people, as the following context shows]. May that right hand which made heaven and earth, and which afterward, unjustly judged by Pilate, was bound in chains, command that at the time of judgment you be joined by its own embrace in the presence of the saints. May that face which, after midday, the cultivator of paradise could not bear to see and therefore fled, and which afterward was befouled by the spittle of unbelievers for the transgression of that man and his offspring, command that it show itself to you in the appearance of tranquility and peace when it comes in fire to judge the world.” [Note: Ms. reads *quem post meridiem colonis* (‘whom after midday to the guardians’).]

**14.** Behold, I have gradually written down what I have found discussed concerning both questions. I do not prejudge those who are better, but set forth what I have carefully sought. It is for you to sift all the opinions I have set down here, and thereafter to sift me thoroughly in that matter [Note: The word is uncertain in the manuscript], and not to regard me as presumptuous, but from this day forward to esteem me more as lovable and beloved. The end.

## II. ANOTHER LETTER ADDRESSED TO JOHN OF SPALATO

**Paul Alvarus to Aurelius Flavius John.**

**1.** Thus far I have written in the manner of friends and, as is customary with those who are dear, have sent the arrows of affection. But since I have not received a reply from your sweetness, I have now attempted to write harshly: perhaps threats will succeed in obtaining what love was unable to secure.

Tell me, O inhuman one among the men whom the fields have produced, why, although rooted in love through affection for the Scriptures, you do not hesitate, through a certain sluggishness, to tear it apart; and why you are not afraid to erase that letter which the blessed Apostle says is written in the hearts of Christians? Truly you bear a heart cut from flint, nourished on the milk of a he-goat or a tiger [Note: Ms. reads *ircanum tigrinumve* (‘of a he-goat or a tiger’)].

I shall no longer lash you with words, but with clubs; not with maxims polished by Donatus’s art, but with knotty tree trunks [Note: Ms. reads *nodociis*]. Thus, at least when wounded, you may come armed to meet us—you who prepare no joyful banquets for the one who desires you. And lest you despise the light course of my uprising, I shall now tear you apart entirely with the fiercest bite.

Why are you so swollen with authority of mind that you refuse to visit your brother through your writings? Why, with an arrogance detestable to God and the Church [Note: Ms. reads *exacranda*], do you despise the small words of your brother? Was Christ crucified for you alone? Does the world serve you alone in its ministry? Why do you disdain to be warmed by the brighter light of one who was redeemed with you at the same price?

The Father sent five books through Moses to the Jews [Note: That is, the Pentateuch], in which he narrates verbally the friendships binding him to their ancestors and instructs them by certain rules to preserve those friendships. Christ, as God, did not disdain to return Abgar’s correspondence as a man; and the Holy Spirit, sending through the apostles to all nations writings that instruct them in their affairs, does not reject human beings. Is there anyone so swollen with the corruption of pride that he cannot answer his fellow servant in words? If you have suffered offense in some matter, why have you not pursued even that matter in a letter?

Do you lack the charming eloquence of the rhetoricians, or the thorny intricacies of the dialecticians, which I know? Where is that liberal talent for letters, as though born with you? Have the precepts of the philosophers slipped from you, and has the discipline of so many arts that cultivated you escaped your mind, so that, even when angry, you cannot perhaps smooth the fury conceived within?

An enemy must be opposed either with hands or with feet. If you honor me as a friend, send golden apples [Note: Ms. reads *malas aureas* (‘golden apples’)]. If you regard me as an adversary, attack me with a drawn blade. For behold, with strong hand and all my strength I drive a staff into you. Either prepare a shield in your defense, or cast your body half-alive upon the ground. Thus I shall either hand you over, captured, to physicians for treatment, or return you, dead, to the earth for burial.

But if, wounded by such a blow, you still refuse to awaken, and continue to maintain Pythagorean silence, and refuse to withdraw from the purpose you have begun [Note: Ms. reads *accepto proposito* (‘the purpose accepted’)], then I shall call you an insensible piece of metal, since you neither feel the wounds inflicted [Note: *inflicta* would perhaps be the better reading] nor grow soft at the touch of handling.

**2.** Mountainous hollows return the voice sent into them along their winding sides, and the upright pinnacles of rocks; bronze ringing without understanding gives a sound wonderfully pleasing to the ears. Thus an axe striking trees gives the voice that nature gave it, and often a stone struck against stone sends forth a cry with fire.

Nothing created has existed that, according to the order assigned to it, does not praise God by its own activity. Chattering creatures produce sweet melodies in their throats. Four-footed animals, weak in their jaws and cries, break their speech with their mouths in distinct and varied utterance; and although they make it unintelligible to us, they perform for themselves the service customary to them.

The serpent has its own hiss, and the fish that creeps through the depths cuts the waters with a rasping sound. The murmur of the billowing sea rejoices through the pools, leaping and laughing; and nothing created in the world appears that does not, by its own motion, unfold the affection proper to the quality allotted to it.

You alone have been found rational and unfeeling throughout the whole world: you neither produce words in considered speech with rational beings, nor strike up a sound by bellowing with creatures without reason, nor are you softened by feeling with insensible things. Therefore, because until now you have not wished to nourish affection through writing, material has been given you for tearing it apart—if, in anger, you should prefer to thunder against us.

**3.** I wrote these things with a heart full of affection, and in them I have seemed to jest with you while trying to frighten you. Cast them far away and turn, I beg you, to our former affection—or return us an answer, even one of abuse. It will be a great consolation to me if a reply is returned even by an angry spirit.

I desire through you to greet the beauty of your household, and to have those books—or *glossomitae*, or *eprimerides* [Note: From the final words of the following letter one should read *glossemata* and *ephemerides*. By “those” understand a book or volume.]—sent to me. I await the greeting of our common father John at his home [Note: Ms. reads *commune domun* (‘common house’)], and kiss all our relations on my behalf [Note: Ms. reads *omnique cognationi nostrae* (‘to all our kin’)].

## III. THE LETTER OF JOHN OF SPALATO TO ALVARUS BEGINS

**To Aurelius Flavius Alvarus, illustrious man, the submission of the least John.**

**1.** O great lord, and wisest of many wise men, the reply is late, and the opportunity for answering has been granted me only tardily, because affliction has risen upon me as my sins have increased [Note: Ms. reads *que*].

Now, although worn down by a hundred griefs and a hundred cares, after a long succession of time, awakened, so to speak, from the heaviness of an unexpected sleep, I desire to discharge the duty of greeting and to offer the assent of heart and body in humility. I beseech the wisdom of your serene sweetness to command that the special friend whom you received and accepted entirely—not from banquets or temporal things—you continue to hold in your care to the end.

For I am tormented by deep pain—he knows it, who knows the secrets of my heart and knows all things before they happen—that after so long a period I do not even now deserve to see your joyful and delightful face, so that together with you I might weigh the secrets of my heart and, through your honey-sweet words, turn deeply hidden griefs into joy.

For, as Christ knows, seven weeks ago [Note: Ms. reads *ebdomade monomade*. D. Thomas Tamaio, p. 211 in Lu​​itprand, cites *hebdada monomade*. I think it should be read as I have restored it, namely, ‘seven units of weeks’; both the subject of the preceding letter and the reasons presented here sufficiently prove that the reply had long been delayed.] I had resolved to write back to your serenity, had I not been surrounded by a multitude of sin and polluted myself with sordid business. Nor could I find any other suitable bearer through whom I might immediately write to your glory.

**2.** Finally, when I, the least of men, wished to be carried in a small vessel and to touch the tranquil shore [Note: Perhaps *attingere*, ‘to reach’], and to gather little fish from the small pools of Latin [Note: *parvos* is perhaps preferable], you compel me, most exalted lord, to spread my sails upon the deep, abandoning the work in which I had been minimally occupied, so that, as you urge, I might make a reciprocal turn toward great matters [Note: That is, a reciprocal transformation], in which, while I remain a follower of your thought [Note: Ms. reads *sensum*, ‘sense’, and *pelagum*, ‘deep’], I am carried into so deep a sea that there is great fear of entering it, lest I be overwhelmed by the magnitude of the matters and the monstrous force of the waves.

Moreover, you do not consider that my spirit is too slight to fill your magnificent trumpet of speech. Yet this is not a matter of my own skill in composition, but, as you believe, perhaps a divine gift, since you demand these things.
