Therefore, first beseeching God, who teaches human beings knowledge and gives the Spirit the word of wisdom (Ps. 93), who enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1), we ask that he deign to make us worthy to write back what is worthy and to dispel what is doubtful.

**3.** First, concerning what you noted—that the most blessed and apostolic men did not devote themselves to elaborate arrangements of words or run by Donatus’s liberal art [Note: Ms. reads *partem liberalem Donati* (‘the liberal part of Donatus’), but the sense is ‘art’], but proceeded through the simplicity of Christ—we have observed what blessed Jerome thought about this.

For when the Apostle says, “Although unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (2 Cor. 11), he was not always unskilled. Indeed, when he wrote his first Epistle to the Corinthians, as the most blessed Jerome reports, he had made considerable progress, yet he speaks of himself as though still wavering when he says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found rejected” (1 Cor. 9).

But also, when writing to the Philippians, he shows that something of that perfection which he later attained was still lacking in him when he says that he is being conformed to Christ’s death, “if somehow I may attain to the resurrection from the dead” (Phil. 3). For he would not have said “if somehow” if the matter had already seemed certain to him.

He shows the same thing in what follows in that Epistle when he says: “Not that I have already obtained it or am already perfect; but I pursue it, so that I may take hold of that for which I have also been taken hold of by Christ. Brothers, I do not consider myself to have seized it yet” (ibid. 12–13).

But if some think that this was said out of humility, let them consider in what follows how greatly he speaks of his progress when he says: “But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (ibid. 13–14). And afterward he says: “Therefore, let all of us who are perfect think this way” (ibid. 15). In this he shows that perfection is twofold: one is the perfection that consists in the completion of virtues; the second is that by which someone makes such progress that he cannot fall. For is not proficiency also one of the virtues?

How, then, are words not to be pursued through liberal art, when blessed Jerome, writing to the great Orator, says:

> “For who does not know that certain things were taken from the books of the Gentiles in Moses and in the volumes of the prophets, and that Solomon both proposed certain matters to the philosophers of Tyre and answered some of them? Hence, at the beginning of Proverbs, he admonishes us to understand discourses of prudence, subtle turns of speech, parables [Col. 0422A] and obscure sayings, the utterances of the wise, and riddles—things that properly belong to dialecticians and philosophers.
>
> “The Apostle Paul also made use of a verse of the poet Epimenides. [Note: Epimenides, in his work *Oracles* (*χρησμῶν*). The verse taken from him by the Apostle is: ‘Cretans are always liars’ (Titus 1:12).] What wonder, then, if I too wish, for the beauty of expression and the elegance of its members, to make wisdom an Israelite woman from a slave and captive? The presbyter Juvencus, under Constantine, explained the history of the Lord and Savior in verse, nor did he fear to subject the power of the Gospel to the law of meter. [Note: The passage is mutilated and should be completed thus: ‘Nor did he fear to submit the majesty of the Gospel to the laws of meter.’ I say nothing of the others, dead or living, whose writings display both their powers and their intentions. Jerome, Epistle 84, to the great Orator of Rome.]”

**4.** Origen, that eminent teacher, argued as follows in his commentaries:

> “And if the prophecies of Balaam were inserted into the sacred books [Note: I restore the passage thus: ‘The prophecy of Balaam by Moses.’ From Origen, Homily 130 on Numbers], how much more did those who were then dwelling in Mesopotamia also possess this prophecy: that ‘a star would arise from Jacob’ (Num. 24:17), and that ‘a man would rise from Israel’?
>
> “The Magi had these writings among themselves. Therefore, when Jesus was born, they recognized the star and understood that the prophecy was being fulfilled—more than the people of Israel, who despised the words of the holy prophets. Thus, recognizing from what Balaam had left written that the time had arrived, they came; and when they had sought him, they worshiped him. To show that their faith was great, they honored the little child as a king.”

Blessed Augustine, when he treated three heresies with extraordinary skill [Note: In the treatise *Against Five Heresies*, chapter 2], says concerning Mercury:

> “Mercury, he says, is the son of the blessed God and of good will, whose name cannot be expressed by the human mouth.”

And again:

> “He exists. Who is he? The son of the ineffable one, the word of wisdom, Christ the Holy One [Note: The Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur reads: ‘Holy, holy, Christ without a voice.’]. Is this not: ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John 1)?”

Origen likewise, in his *NENTATEOFAS* [Note: These words occur in Origen, Homily 18 on Numbers. The barbarous expression perhaps designates homilies on the Pentateuch]:

> “Behold, I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the divine Spirit of wisdom, understanding, and skill, so that he may understand every work and be an architect for working silver, gold, and bronze, and stone for setting, and every work of craftsmanship; and in wood, to work according to every work for which I have appointed him. And Eliab, son of Ahisamach, from the tribe of Dan; and I have given understanding in the heart to every skillful person, so that they may make everything that I have commanded you (Exod. 34:2–6).
>
> “Consider, then, from all these things how craftsmanship comes from the Lord’s wisdom, whether in gold, silver, or any other material, and even the wisdom of weaving. And observe that it may rightly be said of all these things that their knowledge comes from the Most High.”

Concerning the three boys he likewise says:

> “Nebuchadnezzar placed these boys for three years in the art of grammar. The Lord gave them wisdom, understanding, and prudence in every grammatical art; and he gave Daniel understanding in every word, power, and dream. He was before the king in every word, wisdom, and discipline. In whatever matter the king questioned them, he found them ten times better than all the sophists and philosophers who were in his entire kingdom (Dan. 1).
>
> “These things are indeed found in the copies of the Septuagint [Note: The words are truncated and should be completed from Origen, Homily 22 on Numbers: ‘These things are found in the copies of the translators of the seventy; but in the Hebrew codices something else is found,’ and so forth]. But in the Hebrew codices I find something even stronger; although we do not use them, for the sake of recognition we shall also report what we read there:
>
> “‘God gave them,’ he says, ‘understanding and prudence in every grammatical wisdom; and Daniel understood every vision and dreams’ [Note: Ms. reads *danielo … somnis*].
>
> “And shortly afterward: ‘They stood in the presence of the king, and in every word of wisdom about which the king questioned them, he found them ten times superior to all the enchanters and magicians who were in his entire kingdom.’”

From all these things it may be understood how Balaam also said of himself: “Who knows the knowledge of the Most High?”—namely, so that it may be understood that the origin of all knowledge began from him.

**5.** The most holy Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius, when he treated in a distinctive manner the subject of the three leeches, argued as follows:

> “To know wisdom and discipline, to understand the words of prudence, to grasp subtle turns of speech, to understand true justice and love judgment, so that he may give craftiness to the innocent and sense and thought to the young. When these things have been heard, the wise man will become wiser; but who will understand parables and obscure speech, the sayings of the wise and their riddles? Yet who is so wise, and who so prudent, that he can clearly comprehend these things without the Spirit of God? These are the matters which we command you to investigate, comprehend, and know fully.”

Blessed Pope Gregory of the City, in the third book according to the literal sense concerning the Apostle Peter, where he rebukes Simon with the words “May your money be with you for destruction” (Acts 8:20), says that because he does not say “is” but “may it be,” he indicated that he spoke these words not in the indicative but in the optative mood.

Hence Elijah said to the two captains of fifty who came to him: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you” (2 Kings 1). Observe that he used this same art.

There were many testimonies that could be written concerning these matters, but lest this seem excessively tedious to the wise, let a few examples from many suffice for the learned. I shall also, at my own prompting, set down a few things as best I can.

The apostolic and most holy men did not always give milk as drink, nor did they frequently give solid food. They did not always offer simple things, nor did they long remain with lofty things, but they spoke as the Spirit granted utterance. Hence the Psalmist says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. 84:9).

Observe what Saint Gregory, Pope of the City, says:

> “For the Spirit comes upon all the faithful, but remains in the Mediator alone: it never abandoned his humanity, and it proceeded from his divinity. In him, therefore, he remains who alone and always has power over all things; for the faithful who receive him cannot always possess the gifts of signs whenever they wish.”

There is also what Paul wrote in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “In your seed, which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16). He did not write this according to liberal art, as you say, but, as I think, expressed it through allegory, because in the titles of Abraham’s Song it is thus noted:

> “The blessing with which God blessed Abraham in the promise of his seed, which is Christ, and in the calling of the nations.”

For there it is written: “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore” (Gen. 22:17). He spoke tropically and hyperbolically. For who does not see that the number of grains of sand is incomparably greater than the number of all human beings from Adam himself to the end of the age—much more, then, than the one seed of Abraham? This is certainly a trope, not a literal statement.

### 6

As for what you seemed eager to refute sharply, and almost unwilling to hear from one who was speaking without hostility—[Note: See above, Letter 1, no. 3.]—we read what the most blessed Augustine thought in his exposition of Psalm 37:

> Therefore it was the voice of weakness, it was our voice, because of which it was said: “Why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). [Note: The manuscript reads *quia*, “because.”]

What the most blessed Jerome wrote about this, and what he handed down for us to observe, he set forth to a certain person in these words, among others:

> “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation” (Romans 10:10). The Son of God is not the son of man: he is the Son of God, not the son of man. He is the Only-begotten of God; but whoever is the son of man is the First-born, and because of the one who assumed him he is also called First-born, since the Only-begotten is in him. Therefore the Apostle says of the First-born: “First-born among many brothers” (Romans 8:29), namely, among those who believed in him. He is not First-born by the nature of the Only-begotten, but because of his fellowship with the Only-begotten God he is the Only-begotten. The First-born, however, is First-born by nature, not because of fellowship, since no one from the dead rose to immortality except he himself first, and by his resurrection set an example for all who would follow. Therefore the Apostle says: “Who is the First-born from the dead” (Colossians 1:18). Again, to the Romans: “So that he himself might be First-born among many brothers.” And because the Only-begotten and the First-born are two natures, divine and human. For the difference between these natures is also shown in the wording of the Gospels.

Therefore it does not accord with our faith that Jesus Christ should lie, because he himself is the truth. Since this is so, he says of himself: “He who sent me is with me, and he has not abandoned me” (John 8:29); and elsewhere: “God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). Since God had assumed a human being, and through the death of the cross he was to be forsaken by God until the resurrection, it therefore accords with our faith that the human being should say to his God: “Why have you forsaken me?” But the Only-begotten God, who is inseparable from the Father, should say: “He who sent me is with me, and he has not abandoned me.”

Saint Augustine, against the Priscillianists:

> For in that assumption neither of them was converted or changed into the other; nor, indeed, was the Divinity changed into the creature, so that it would cease to be the creature. For if the substance of the human being had been converted into the Divinity, it would have increased the Divinity in some respect. But far be it from us to suppose that the ineffable fullness receives increase. Therefore both natures of the Son and one person remain.

The blessed Leo, bishop of the apostolic see, to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople:

> And just as the form of a servant did not take away the form of God, so the form of God did not diminish the form of a servant.

And shortly afterward:

> And just as the Word does not depart from equality with the Father’s glory, so the flesh does not abandon the nature of our race.

Likewise Jerome, in his Commentaries on the Gospels according to Matthew:

> “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Psalm 109:1). This was said not according to the fact that he was born from David—that is, from David—but according to the fact that he was eternally born from the Father, preceding him who was the father of his flesh. [Note: The words are corrupt. They should be emended as follows: “that is, from David, but according to …,” from Jerome, Book IV on Matthew, chapter 22, verse 44, where he says: “Therefore he is called David’s Lord, not according to the fact that he was born from him, but according to that which he was always born from the Father, preceding him who was the father of his flesh.”]

Likewise, from the holy Athanasius, bishop of the see of Alexandria and holy confessor, to Epictetus, bishop of the Corinthians:

> How, then, did those who are called Christians dare even to doubt, unless the Lord who proceeded from Mary is indeed, in substance and nature, the Son of God? But according to the flesh, he is from the seed of David and from the flesh of holy Mary.

Likewise, in the book of Saint Ambrose, confessor and bishop of the Church of Milan, which he sent to the emperor Gratian, in the second book, among other things:

> “From this comes what has been read: ‘The Lord of majesty was crucified’ (1 Corinthians 2:2), let us suppose; but because the same one is both God and human being:” God through his divinity, and, through the assumption of flesh, the human being Christ Jesus; therefore the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified.”

[Note: Here the material found in Ambrose, Book II, To Gratian, chapter 4, is lacking: “The Lord of majesty was crucified; let us not think that he was crucified as he existed in his majesty,” and so forth.]

And shortly afterward:

> “Let us preserve,” he says, “the distinction between Divinity and flesh. The Son of God speaks as one in both, because he exists in both natures. And although the same one speaks, he does not always speak in the same manner: recognize in him now the glory of God, now the sufferings of the human being. As God he speaks what is divine, because he is the Word; as human being he says what is human, because he was speaking in that substance.”

Likewise, from the same author’s book On the Incarnation of the Lord against the Apollinarians:

> “But while we refute these people, others emerge, who say that the Lord’s flesh and Divinity are of one nature. What sacrilege has hell vomited forth? The Arians are now more tolerable, since through these people the strength of their unbelief grows, so that they assert with greater insistence that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not of one substance. [Note: The manuscript reads *substantiam*; but Ambrose’s text, chapter 6 of *On the Incarnation*, has *substantiae*—‘of one substance.’] For these people have attempted to say that the Lord’s Divinity and flesh are of one substance.”

Again, below:

> “And these people frequently tell me that they hold to the teaching of the Council of Nicaea. But in that teaching our Fathers said that it was not the flesh but the Word of God who was of one substance with the Father: they confessed that the Word proceeded from the Father’s substance, but that the flesh was from the Virgin.”

### 7

Since you anticipated writing to us what is contained in the Council of Ephesus, where the following is noted at the relevant place:

> “If anyone confesses that the flesh of God is life-giving and proper to the very Word of God the Father, but as though belonging to another, joined to him in dignity, or as though possessing a divine indwelling, and not rather, as we have said, that it is life-giving, let him be anathema.”

For if you say that it is proper to God the Father—something which I scarcely believe the holy Fathers said—then you will appear to be following the Sabellian heresy, since you say that the flesh is proper to God the Father and, again, proper to the Word. This the holy Council of Ephesus certainly did not decree.

For, among other things, our Vincentius, you say, appealing to someone, speaks in this manner:

> “May that face which, after midday, the gardener of paradise endured carrying away in flight, and which afterward, on account of the transgression of him and his offspring, was sullied by the spittle of unbelievers, command that it display itself to you in the appearance of tranquility and peace when it comes in fire to judge the world.”

See that this does not appear contrary to what was proved above by the holy Fathers. If that face which the gardener of paradise fled from was a subjected creature, and a corporeal creature—but it was not born from the seed of David; rather, Divinity had not yet been embodied from David’s lineage, nor had it yet been born in time—what, then, should we think about what the Apostle says: that he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, and was predestined as the Son of God (Romans 1:3)?

For, as the distinguished Jerome says, one is predestined who does not yet exist. And what should we think about Jesus’ soul, of which he says: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matthew 26:38); and again: “I have power to lay down my soul” (John 10:18); and again: “My soul is troubled unto death” (John 12:27)—a soul which did not descend from the seed of David? Was that soul also already placed in that face at that time?

How, then, shall we say that he is true God and true human being, born from his mother in time but eternal from the Father? And: He put on flesh but did not remove his majesty; true flesh, taken from his mother’s womb alone, without sin.

### 8

As for the fact that you are seriously vexed with us, and that you ordered me to be punished not merely with fists and kicks but with rough beams because of the delay in my reply and in sending your book, I confess that I have made no slight error.

“Better are the wounds of a faithful friend than the kisses of an enemy who deceives” (Proverbs 27:6).

We read among the ancient philosophers that, when Antisthenes accepted no disciples and could not drive away the persistent Diogenes, he threatened him with a club unless he left. [Note: The manuscript reads *Antistitenes*.] Diogenes is said to have placed his head beneath it and said:

> “No staff is so hard that it can separate me from your service.”

And I shall say the same with him:

> “No speech can be so harsh that it can tear me away from your affection and your sweetness.”

### 9

I heard fully from the mouth of our common father about the departure of your three maidservants:

> “Do not grieve, as the others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:12).  
> “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord forever” (Job 1:21).  
> “We must come to Christ through many tribulations,” as the Lord says: “The world will rejoice, but you will grieve; yet your grief will be turned into joy” (John 16:20).

May we deserve, united with you, sooner to stand together in what is common to us [the text is corrupt or incomplete]. [Note: The editor proposes *sistere*, “to stand” or “to be established.”]

Through your mouth I presume to greet every ornament of your household. Lady Froisinda greets you with her children, healthy and unharmed, and rich in an abundance of wheat.

I have sent you that book of glosses and the ephemerides, continually returning thanks. May I deserve to receive your pleasant written reply.

The end.

## IV. Likewise, a Letter of Alvarus Addressed to John, the Same Person Mentioned Above

**Paulus Alvarus to Aurelius Flavius John.**

### 1

Taking up the eloquence (*euphrasia*) of your sweet-flowing expertise (*englocae empeiriae*) [Note: *Englocae empeiriae vestrae sumentes euphrasiam*: “taking up the eloquence of your sweet-flowing expertise.” In Greek, ἐγγλύσσω means “I sweeten, I bring sweetness”; ἐμπειρία means “expertise, practical knowledge, prudence.” See Nic. Ant., Book VI, no. 190.]—or rather, running through an epitome of its energy (*energia*)—my soul became joyful when it was permitted, even late, to learn of the beloved man’s welfare.

Since your extended eloquence seemed to practice rhetoric after the manner of orators, and since, against the great ignorance of our weakness, you employed the rivers of learned men [Note: Read *inscitiam magnis … fluminibus*, “ignorance with great … rivers.”], lest I serve hyperbatonic constructions [Note: *Hyperbaton* is a figure of speech, in Latin *transgressio*, “transposition”], and fail to express what I desire but instead obscure it, I shall briefly and concisely begin weaving the thread of my defense.

### 2

I pass over the praise of your more polished sweetness of speech, with which, while anointing my head, you strive to inflict a honeyed sword upon me. And lest I become burdensome to readers by saying too much, my speech shall weave, however sluggishly, only those points which show that the opinions of the learned, prudently arranged by you, agree with me, and do not show themselves to be opposed to me in the manner you desire.

First of all, beloved, take this answer from me, and remember that the opinions of the learned which I sent to you have been preserved by you in their entirety. Until now you have not shown them to have been stated in any other manner; rather, just as I learned them and sent them to you, most reverend, so far they have remained faithful to their own tenor.

I marvel at your excellent judgment [Note: The manuscript reads *vestro*, “your”; the context may require *vestram*, “your.”] and at the remarkable diligence that I know well in you: why did you not examine the testimonies themselves with more refined attention and prove them arranged in another manner through the energetic investigation of the skill of our elders? Unless perhaps you failed entirely to see that something else appeared to you to be understood there.

Since they remain undefiled and have never, through you, been bent toward another meaning, if you wish, now tear apart thousands upon thousands of testimonies [Note: The manuscript reads *miliorum*, an obvious corruption; *millium*, “thousands,” is intended.]—inflicting, as I believe, no harm on me by questioning them, since you have fought against me with no other weapons than those by which you yourself were assailed.

And while they testify on my behalf, and again, as you think, furnish support to you, I do not think that any prudent person will suppose them to be false in what they provide no support, and truthful in what favors you. Unless perhaps you are throwing their opinions into quarrel and maintaining that they have spoken contrary things against one another. If you think this, then you certainly dissent from our Catholic peace.

I wished to arrange these matters at the beginning as though they had perhaps already reproached me in battle.

### 3

But since it is clear that in many passages they have not been placed suitably, what harm does it do me if you draw up their entire battle line, while destroying someone else’s army, not mine? For from Saint Jerome I received certain passages, and from the same author likewise received these very things. [Note: The manuscript reads *migi … issa*, evidently corrupt.]

But did he teach things contrary to himself, or, as though he had forgotten himself, produce one thing here and another there? If he did so, your eloquence did not thunder against me, but his own words themselves rose up against him.

Listen, therefore, most prudent man and head of Roman dialectic: our predecessors did not employ this method [Note: The manuscript reads *hunc morem*, “this custom.”], nor did our elders wander through such contradictions. First they weakened the objections, and only then did they strive to strengthen the arguments of their own assertion. And if it had perhaps pleased them first to establish their own position, nevertheless afterward they destroyed the adversary’s counterarguments and in no way left them untouched.

### 4

But now let us return to the subject and examine all the opinions one by one.

You say:

> “For concerning what the Apostle says: ‘Even if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge’ (2 Corinthians 11:6), he was not always unskilled.”

Behold: if you say “not always,” you affirm that he was at least sometimes unskilled; yet you do not clearly explain whether in speech or in knowledge—unless someone who is skilled examines your whole statement and plainly recognizes that you said he was unskilled in knowledge.

But he immediately denies this about himself by saying:

> “Even if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge.”

Since he says that he was not unskilled in knowledge but in speech, who, possessed by such great dullness, would dare to assert the opposite—that he was unskilled not in speech but in knowledge?

### 5

You say:

> “Yet he was making great progress, and he speaks of himself as though somewhat wavering when he says: ‘I discipline my body and enslave it, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found rejected’” (1 Corinthians 9:27).

Indeed, we know that the most blessed Jerome said this, but we prove that it has nothing to do with the matter begun.

For when he says, “He was indeed making great progress,” he shows that he lacked nothing in perfection. And when he adds, “Yet he speaks as though wavering,” this is not about ignorance but about humility. For holy and perfect men, although they advance to the summit of virtue, always complain that they have not yet attained it. [Note: The manuscript has *conquerunt*, “they conquer”; the intended word is *conqueruntur*, “they complain.”]

Here, since he is placed in a struggle, he spoke as though doubting about himself. He set forth nothing here either about knowledge or about the discipline of words, but only arranged the contests of his works.

Therefore he added:

> “I discipline my body and enslave it, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become rejected.”

For he disciplines his body through those things by which, in another Epistle, he unravels the trophies of his triumphs: through dishonor and good repute, through glory and disgrace (2 Corinthians 6:8), and through all those things to which he was subjected—in fasts, vigils, dangers, losses, beatings, and countless other disciplines. [Note: The manuscript reads *per quem*, “through whom”; *per quae*, “through which,” is intended.]

### 6

What here corresponds to the matters that have been acted out between us, what agrees with you, or what appears there to oppose me, I plainly do not see, nor do I suppose that anyone else sees it.

You add in what follows, saying:

> “And when writing to the Philippians he shows that he still had something less than the perfection he afterward attained.”

Behold, here again you proclaim and affirm him imperfect, as though you were arguing with us about his perfection or imperfection. Unless perhaps you think that holy men possess no perfection apart from knowledge of grammar.

He says:

> “That I may be conformed to his death, if somehow I may attain the resurrection that is from the dead” (Philippians 3:10–11).

He would not say “if somehow” if the matter already appeared to him at that time to be certain.

I certainly do not understand why you included this, unless perhaps you wished to place a suspicion before your readers—something far removed from your mind, most reverend. For when you say, “If somehow I may attain the resurrection that is from the dead,” and add, “He would not say ‘if somehow’ if the matter had already seemed certain to him,” you show that the Apostle did not believe in the resurrection upon settled conviction, but tempered it with this language of doubt.

Yet that saying must be understood very differently by that teacher; we have not undertaken to debate it here. I shall say only this: you have labored over this empty matter and have introduced opinions incongruously into the argument.

Again you say:

> “But in what follows in the same Epistle he shows the same thing when he says: ‘Not that I have already obtained it or am already perfect; but I pursue it, to grasp that for which I have been grasped by Christ’” (Philippians 3:12).

I should like you to answer me here. Did he say that he was pursuing grammar? Or does he recognize that he was grasped by Christ in Donatus’ art, so that your diligence, while we are contending about grammar, may produce this statement for us—something which that great man professes as the summit of virtue?

He continues:

> “I myself, brothers, I myself do not yet consider that I have grasped it” (Philippians 3:13). [Note: Above and in the Apostle’s text we read *fratres*, “brothers,” not *rater*, “brother.”]

What, I ask? Grammar and the liberal art according to your Donatus? Are you not ashamed, beloved, to use testimonies so weak for your side and to adapt to our present assertion passages that suit an entirely different matter?

### 7

Your letter continues:

> “But if some think that this was said out of humility, let them see in what follows how much he recalls concerning his progress, when he says: ‘Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, according to my purpose I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus’” (Philippians 3:13–14).

I do not know against whom you are fighting here, or whom you hasten to slaughter with the golden rod of this sentence. [Note: *Ancila* means “a golden rod,” according to Papias in the glossary of Cange, edition of the Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur.] Was our dispute about perfection or imperfection, so that your entire attack should contend against these things? Unless perhaps you say that the things he sees behind him and has forgotten are grammar. [Note: The manuscript reads *tutius*, “more safely”; the context may require *totius*, “the whole.”]

You say:

> “Let all of us who are perfect think this way” (Philippians 3:15).

In this he shows that perfection is twofold: one kind consists in the completion of virtues, according to which he says that he too is perfect.

Behold the perfection concerning which he himself says:

> “Even if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge.”

For perfection in knowledge is mastery of the knowledge of virtues.

Name the other perfection—the one you mean. Is mastery not also among the virtues? But what mastery you wish to signify here I scarcely understand: whether of works or of words, I do not sufficiently discern.

If it is mastery of works, I do not refute it. If it is mastery of words, I reject and refuse it so completely that I establish its folly through divine speech.

For the Apostle says:

> “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19).

And again to the Corinthians:

> “God chose the foolish things of the world in order to confound the wise” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

Which wise people, certainly? Our most holy Fathers? Or rather grammarians, philosophers, and rhetoricians? You see that those whom you praise as worthy to be followed are shown to be confounded, while you raise them up with much praise.

And elsewhere the same Apostle says:

> “When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with excellence of speech, as a wise man proclaiming to you the testimony of Christ” (1 Corinthians 2:1).

For what is excellence of speech except the rules of Donatus through metaplasm and tropes?

You see that the Apostle does not shape his course according to those same things, but knows the Lord Jesus Christ through the simplicity of Christ. Therefore he added in what follows:

> “Not in learned words of human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things” (1 Corinthians 2:13).

Pay attention to what he says:

> “Not in learned words of human wisdom.”

What is this human wisdom, through whose most learned expressions the Apostle cannot proceed, unless it is this praiseworthy rule of yours, in which you think the sum of all perfection exists? [Note: The text’s *nisi in haec tua laudabili* is to be read *nisi haec tua laudabilis*.]

You see that the Apostle calls human wisdom what you inopportunely insist is divine. For, as the Apostle says, our faith is not in the wisdom of human beings but in the power of God.

> “We speak wisdom,” he says, “among the perfect; yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the rulers of this world, who are being destroyed. Rather, we speak God’s wisdom, hidden in a mystery, which none of the rulers of this world has known” (1 Corinthians 2:5–8). [Note: Read *in mysterio*, “in a mystery,” rather than *in ministerio*, “in ministry.”]

I ask you to answer me: what wisdom of this world, or of its rulers, are we to believe this is, from which Paul turns us away, while he is not ashamed to proclaim himself unknown to these disciplines?

For the Lord says through Isaiah:

> “You will not see an impudent people, a people of profound speech, whose language you cannot understand, in whom there is no wisdom” (Isaiah 33:19).

That is—and, as our Jerome says in this passage [*destina*, “a column or support,” is a corrupt or uncertain reading]—the philosophers and orators of the world, who applaud themselves in secular learning and eloquence, whose entire adornment lies in words.

[Note: The text here reads *destina*, “a column or support.” Saint Braulio likewise says in his *Eulogy of Saint Isidore* that God placed him, as it were, as a certain support for restoring the monuments of the ancients. See also the authority of Corippus, volume V, page 469.]

You see your Donatists portrayed here and proved foolish by God, who is true wisdom.

### 8

As for the fact that you produce Saint Jerome speaking to a great orator, you ought to consider the beginning of the letter and explain more clearly how this matter came about.

He says:

> “As for what you ask at the end of the letter—why in our little works we sometimes insert examples from secular literature and pollute the purity of the Church with the filth of the pagans—take this brief answer.”

Notice what he says: “Sometimes we insert examples.” By this he shows that it is not always or everywhere, but only when necessity compels it, and not without some danger.

Thus, in what follows, he reports concerning the most blessed Cyprian:

> “Cyprian, a man distinguished by eloquence and martyrdom, tells Firmianus—and is reproached for it—that, when writing against Demetrianus, he used testimonies of the prophets and apostles, which Demetrianus falsely called fabricated, rather than those of philosophers and poets, whose authority, as a pagan, he could not oppose.”

This is the statement of Jerome that you arranged for my assistance, though with hostile intent, where you say that the captive woman’s head, eyebrows, and all the hairs of her body must be shaved and cut off, and that afterward she should be embraced and brought forth into spiritual matters. [Note: The manuscript reads *tradendum*, “to be handed over”; *radendum*, “to be shaved,” is intended.]

It is enough for me that you call her a captive, and not a citizen, native, or colonist.

Nor, most reverend, was this said about leaves of words [Note: *Pro foliis*, “about leaves,” as the following phrase immediately says: “for the reading.”], but was spoken about the reading of pagan books. We must use these books not for the elegance of their words but for the fruits of their meanings or opinions. [Note: The proposed reading is *quibus uti non debemus*, “which we ought not to use.”] And whenever I find in them something fitting for the Christian faith, I claim it wholly for myself; having drawn the sword from Goliath, I cut off the head of that most impious man with his own weapon.

So also with what you excerpted from the books of blessed memory Augustine concerning Mercury as a vain idol, or with what you read with me from the prophecy of the Sibyls.

Thus the Apostle too, compelled by necessity, used many passages from those writers against those same people—not directing himself by their rule, but reducing them to his own standard. He made an Israelite woman out of the maidservant, as he himself declared, rather than instituting a captive slave as an Israelite from the womb.

But tell me, I beg you: do you hold the whole rule of this errant Donatus, or only half of it, shaved and full of spiritual hair, yet bristling with the stiff hairs of the head? And if you shave the head, eyebrows, and nails, explain what the head, eyebrows, nails, and the hairs themselves are thought to signify, which you read must be shaved before your aforementioned writing style. [Note: The manuscript has *praedixit legis stylum*, “he foretold the style of the law”; the wording is corrupt.]

If you sow or graft anything from this woman, you will no longer be a perfect grammarian. Listen to how the Apostle Paul shaves the hairs of this captive.

To the Athenians he says:

> “As I passed through and observed your objects of worship, I found also an altar on which was inscribed: ‘To an unknown god.’ Therefore, what you worship without knowing it, this I proclaim to you” (Acts 17:23).

The inscription on the altar, however, was not as Paul stated it—“To an unknown god”—but rather:

> “To the gods of Asia, Europe, and Africa; to unknown and foreign gods.” [Note: So Jerome says in his Commentary on the Epistle to Titus, chapter 1, verse 12.]

But because Paul did not need many unknown gods, but only one God, he used the singular expression, so that he might teach them about his God, whom the Athenians had marked beforehand in the title of the altar.

### 9

As Jerome says, Paul did this rarely, when the opportunity of the place rather than display demanded it.

You see that he did this rarely and not always, according to the opportunity of the place, not according to a rule that must always be followed. Take the statement as referring to the confirmation of his arguments through pagan books, not to Donatus’ art.

For your testimonies do not provide support for you but for me.

If you carefully examine all the Apostle’s Epistles, through conjunctions and propositions placed in unsuitable positions, you will immediately and clearly see that he was ignorant of this art of Donatus.

As for what you presented about Solomon, you did not prove him to have been a grammarian; rather, you asserted that he had taken certain things from books of rhetoricians or dialecticians.

For it says that he both proposed some things and answered others. Wherever it says “some things” and “certain things,” it is clear that, according to the opportunity of the place, he excerpted not everything but certain matters relevant to the subject, as he wished. [Note: The manuscript reads *excepta*, “excepted”; *excerpta*, “excerpted,” is intended.]

Nor should it be believed that a Hebrew man, supremely learned in the vernacular language [Note: The manuscript has *tavernaculo*; read *vernaculo*, “vernacular.”], followed the rules of a Latin man or proceeded through the rhetorical flourishes of Donatus [Note: “Through the ornament of resounding expressions”], abandoning the rivers of the most holy language—even the sacred language not yet at the cross of the Lord—to seek help from a foreign one.

Paul did not serve the laws or feet of pagan meters, as you say. Rather, he used a verse of Epimenides, composed by another but borrowed by him for his own necessary purpose.

These arguments are foolish and frivolous. Rather, show where the writings of the apostolic man himself have been adorned by this discipline of yours.

### 10

As for your assertion that Juvencus placed the Gospel under the law of meter, listen: he did this to the praise of Christ, so that whatever sordidness he felt to be present in it might be made beautiful and refined through the praise of God.

At that time, because anyone who devoted himself to verse did so especially for the beauty of eloquence and, under the pretext of verbal refinement, served pagan error, Christians were at risk when they read Virgil’s *Aeneid* and wept over Dido, dead and pursued to the end by the sword; or over the insult to her beauty; or over the honors of the abducted Ganymede; or over Minerva’s deceptive gift; or over the trickery of unjust Juno.

To prevent Christians from being defiled by these errors and impurities, it was planned that the miracles of Christ should be sung in meter. Thus, attracted by the sweetness of meter, they might cling not to falsehood but to truth, savoring a honeyed flavor, while rejecting the filthy and most foul stench of the pagans, in accordance with what Sedulius says prosaically in the preface to his *Paschal Work* to Chalcidius. Your own sagacity, if it prefers, will be able to find this.

As for your producing the ancient heretic Origen as a testimony, calling him a pre-eminent teacher, although you yourself know that he was condemned by the Fathers, know that I am not frightened by his statements—even if they stood against me with greater weight. For he is the one who said:

> “The term ‘magic art’ does not seem to me to be the name of anything that exists; but even if it does exist, it is not an evil work, nor something that can rightly be held in contempt.”

I think that you, most prudent man, do not approve these statements of his, nor, I do not doubt, do you fail to refute with the greatest force the other things he set down in the books of *Periarchon*.

Those Magi, however, were most certainly moved by Balaam’s prophecy. [Note: In accordance with what was noted above, read “the prophecy of Balaam.”] But that prophecy was inspired by God, not invented through Donatus’ art.

As for Bezalel [Note: The manuscript has *elehel*; read “Bezalel,” the son of Uri, son of Hur], who was filled with the divine Spirit (Exodus 31), I do not understand what you wish to establish. Did I say that wisdom had been given by God to no human being, or deny that all knowledge had been brought down from heaven by God to his creature, so that you might recount the deeds of this man and of Eliab, son of Ahisamach. [Note: The Vulgate has “Oholiab, son of Ahisamach.”]

Did I say that wisdom had been given by God to no human being, or deny that all knowledge had been brought down from heaven by God to his creature, so that you might recount the deeds of this man and of Eliab, son of Ahisamach?

On the contrary, I freely profess:

> “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

This too was a perfect gift, because it was consecrated for the honor of God’s sanctuary.

Can you establish Donatus’ art as a perfect gift? But, to agree with your opinion, let us suppose that it is a perfect gift and an excellent endowment. Did I say that it was entirely and in every respect to be rejected?

Are these not the words of my letter?

> “Holy and apostolic men do not serve the composition of words but rejoice in the truth of meanings; they do not proceed through Donatus’ liberal art but through the simplicity of Christ.”

If this displeases you, and you prefer to refute rather than follow it, state the contrary opinion [Note: The manuscript reads *formam*, “form”; the proposed reading is *forma*, “state.”] by saying that holy and apostolic men do not rejoice in the truth of meanings but serve the composition of words; that they do not proceed through the simplicity of Christ but through Donatus’ liberal art.

Then, plainly, I would not labor in my response for only one day, but for the whole span of my life. [Note: The manuscript reads *temporis*, “of time”; the context requires *tempus*, “span.”]

The human mind—which Plato locates in the brain, but which Christ shows to be in the heart—discovered all these things; it was not discovered on account of them. [Note: The manuscript reads *ab easdem*, “from the same things”; the intended reading is uncertain.]

Thus it is plainly evident that whoever carries understanding as his support [Note: The manuscript reads *colomen … colome*, corrupt forms; *columen*, “support,” is intended] will never seek assistance elsewhere from an art which he foresaw to be within himself and for himself.

Let the one who seeks Donatus’ help do so whose weakness impairs his step.

But as for us, whose understanding Christ—who is true wisdom—instructs, nourishes, and teaches, why should we wander through the shrines of the pagans, when it is clear that our vital faculties are filled from the fountains of every kind of learning?

Therefore, although holy and apostolic men may appear to speak through mastery of Donatus, they should not be believed to have been instructed by him, but by the one who bestowed even this modest ability upon that pagan.

For the apostles and prophets did not, as though engaged in a craft, serve human rules; rather, with sound understanding, they foresaw through divine instruments how things ought to be expressed.

### 11

As for your claim that the three young men taught grammar, I am astonished that you, a prudent man, should have formed so light an opinion as to assert that the Chaldean discipline was grammar, when grammar is said to be Greek, and its very name makes clear, at least on the surface, what it is. But since you have used Symmachus’s edition in place of the Hebrew, and seem, as though introducing what is unknown in place of something else, to have transformed the profane command of King Nebuchadnezzar into a doctrine for us—ordering us, who are free, to do what he did to captive boys—hear what our most holy Jerome thinks about this:

> “Observe,” he says, “that God gave the holy boys knowledge and secular literary learning in every book; for this Symmachus interpreted ‘the art of grammar,’ so that they might understand everything they read and, by the Spirit of God, judge the learning of the Chaldeans. And although the gentile king placed them in school for the sake of education, God gave them manifold wisdom for refuting the wise men of the Chaldeans. Notice that God gave them understanding and knowledge so that, by the knowledge of the Chaldeans, he might refute the Chaldeans themselves. It should also be noted that they were not taught by that discipline or by those same deceivers, but were enlightened tenfold by God, so that you may understand that they did not attain this through art, but were inspired by God’s gift for the purpose that was necessary. They learned,” as Jerome says, “not in order to follow, but in order to judge and refute.”

How could anyone, writing against mathematicians while ignorant of mathematics, not expose himself to ridicule, or dispute against philosophers while not knowing the doctrines of philosophers? [Note: [Col. 0434D–0435D] The passage is perhaps to be corrected thus: “How could anyone, writing against mathematicians while an unskilled mathematician, expose himself to ridicule, or, disputing against philosophers, fail to know the doctrines of philosophers? And we, etc.”] And we, Reverend Father, say that we pursue grammar in this way [Col. 0435A]: that we destroy and refute it. Whoever does not direct his steps by these means destroys the path he has cut.

Daniel is granted more, since the interpretations of visions are added to him, so that by this he might be adorned with the royal tiara and regarded as more exalted for the work required of him. For they are said to have been ten times superior to all the diviners and magicians. And surely I do not think you would fail to reject the idea that God’s boys served the arts of magicians. Yet he is said to have been ten times superior because what those men had learned through arts and wicked arguments, these men attained by God’s inspiration through contrary paths—that is, not by the same method by which the others had attained it. Thus divine wisdom might refute human knowledge and destroy what is thought to consist wholly in learning.

### 12

As for your proving that Saint Gregory knew the indicative and optative moods, know that he was by no means ignorant of these disciplines [Note: [Col. 0435D] The manuscript reads, “was by no means ignorant of these disciplines” with a different case construction.], but that he both knew this art most thoroughly and guarded against it most cautiously. For he himself is the one who, at the beginning of his discourse, says:

> “Far be it from me to compress the words of so great an oracle within the words of Donatus.”

Yet whenever the occasion required, he did not serve that rule, but rather refused to use the rule itself in his own case. I have professed this most firmly, and continue to profess it: he did not subject himself to that rule [Note: [Col. 0435D] F. reads, “that he himself did not subject himself to the same rule.”]. Nor did he care about correctness of expression, provided that he could preserve the meaning safely [Note: [Col. 0436D] F. reads, “so that he could preserve it.”].

### 13

At the end of your discussion you say: “Apostolic and holy men are not always simple in their expressions, nor always sophisticated.” I, on the contrary, answer you openly: Apostolic and holy men are both always simple in their expressions and always sophisticated.

They are always simple because they utter pure words, wholly unmixed with anything but the most sincere truth; they are always sophisticated because not a single iota was uttered by them without mystery. Their words are veiled and open, plain and lofty, small and great, mystical and concise. They shine, as the great Jerome says, on the surface, but in the marrow they are sweeter. Whoever wishes to reach the kernel breaks the nut.

Yet, according to the clear-sighted Gregory, Scripture is not so closed that it ought to be feared, nor so open that it becomes worthless. Hear, finally, what the most blessed Augustine thought about this:

> “I resolved to turn my mind toward the holy Scriptures and to see what they were like; and behold, I see a subject not discovered by the proud nor laid bare for children, but humble in its gait, lofty in its progress, and veiled in mysteries.”

But if they are not always simple and not always sophisticated, as you yourself seemed to affirm, it is clear that they did not run through Donatus’s rules, since in some passages they spoke simply. You see that your whole arena labours in my favour, and that your attack prepares the palm of victory for me. Here it appears that, moved by the divine Spirit, they adapted their steps to rules as the occasion of the passage permitted [Col. 0436A].

### 14

Nor is it right that one who proceeds regularly and by any art should at some point wander astray by departing from the formula he has established for himself. For you say:

> “They did not frequently give milk to drink, nor often solid food; they did not give simple things only occasionally, nor lofty things for long, but according as the Spirit supplied utterances.”

As I infer [Note: [Col. 0436D] The manuscript reads *coniceo hista*.], you are trying to derive all this from grammar. You want “lofty things” and “solid food” to signify Donatus’s art, while “milk” and “simple things” signify our ignorance. You do not notice the purpose for which you cut off these words when you say: “But according as the Spirit supplied utterances.”

My most Reverend Father, you must not understand these words as rhetorical displays, nor as the pomp of frothy and insane bladders [Note: [Col. 0436D] F. reads “the pomp of extravagant displays.”], but as referring to the difference of teachings by which he became all things to all, in order to save all (I Cor. 9:22). For, as the Most Chaste says, he gives the Corinthians milk rather than solid food (I Cor. 3:2), when he says that he was among them in weakness, fear, and much trembling.

### 15

As for the testimony of the Prophet that you use here—“I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. 84:9)—I plainly cannot keep from laughing. Did the Prophet, with reference to the grammar now under discussion, say, “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me”? Rather, it would be more fitting for him to say, “I will hear what the profane Donatus speaks within me”—unless perhaps you claim that Virgil, Homer, or the other poets spoke by the Holy Spirit, and maintain that idols were praised through divine inspiration; and thus [the remainder of the corrupt text is uncertain].

As for your assertion that Saint Gregory said, “The Spirit comes in all the faithful, but remains in the Mediator alone, who never abandoned his humanity,” and so forth: you repeat and insist upon the same things, and by repeating something once stated incongruously you press your argument. We are not disputing about the Spirit’s inspiration, so that you should fight against something we never remember having been alleged.

### 16

For what you say—that the apostle Paul brought forth “seeds” allegorically—is true, because everything he brought forth he brought forth allegorically, and by understanding all things mystically he taught them thoroughly. But is allegory introduced in such a way that something erroneous is uttered, and that it is compared not in Latin but, according to you, through faulty usage [Note: [Col. 0436D] *Citer* is an obsolete word, related to *citerior*. F. reads *vitiositer*, “faultily.”]?

Yet allegory, or at least mystical interpretation, was not arranged in this way by Donatus’s rule. Or perhaps allegory occurs only where there is error, while things are simple and bare where there is grammar? If I establish through Donatus’s art the force of an erroneous statement, and you immediately say that the very thing you call erroneous must be understood allegorically, I ask you to say repeatedly whether, without allegory, you prove his assertion to have been thoroughly correct everywhere.

### 17

But since you cannot deny that he spoke this without the aid of art, you wish to weaken it by means of some unknown device. For you assert:

> “This is the blessing with which God blessed Abraham in the promise of his seed, which is Christ, and in the calling of the nations. For it is written: ‘I will multiply your seed’ (Gen. 22:17), and so forth.”

You add: “He spoke tropically and hyperbolically.” For who does not see that the number of grains of sand is incomparably greater than the entire multitude of human beings from Adam to the end of the age—how much more than Abraham’s race alone?

While you devote yourself excessively to contradiction and wish to oppose everything that is said, you do not see, my dear one, that you are answering one thing in place of another. You do not affirm that the Apostle’s statement was arranged through Donatus’s art, but turn aside by some dizzying trick to the blessing of Abraham [Col. 0437B].

And although in this passage you have used the opinion of a teacher, it must not be reconsidered in the way you think, but otherwise. Hear, however, what your Isidore says, more truly and more appropriately than the version you set before us [Note: [Col. 0437D] F. reads “than the teacher whom you set before us.”]:

> “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven”—that is, the Christian people, whose father in faith you remain; thus I will make it shine with the light of the resurrection. Then he showed him the sand of the sea and said: “Thus I will multiply your seed” [Note: [Col. 0437D] In Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 12, the text is not exactly this, but rather: “Thus shall your seed be in multitude”; those words alone agree with what follows.]. That is, there will indeed be a numerous Jewish people, but it will remain barren and unfruitful like sand.

Thus “so shall your seed be” does not refer comparatively to the number of multiplication represented by the sand or the stars, but to the effects of their works. He did not say, “So shall your seed be in the number of the stars or the sand of the sea,” but marked the effects of those things that he showed him: “So shall your seed be.” In one respect it will shine with brilliance, and in another it will be utterly barren and unfruitful [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscript reads, “they will be entirely barren.”].

And although it is spoken tropically and hyperbolically, by an excessive trope [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscript reads, “by an excessive trope.”], nevertheless its mystical and allegorical meaning is readily disclosed to those who understand.

### 18

There were many things I could set out in confirmation of my statements, but I hesitated to burden my readers with weariness. It is enough that the most blessed Augustine, in the first book of his *Confessions*, so laments the expertise in this art that he had acquired that he mourns, not with dry eyes, the fact that nearly all those skilled in this art have fallen into the greatest error.

And the blessed Cassian, together with his distinguished companion Germanus, received such a remedy for those who wept over the guilt of this discipline from Abba Nesteros [Note: [Col. 0437D] The manuscript reads *A Nesterote*; he was called Abbot Nesteros.] in the Fourteenth Conference, in the following exchange [Col. 0437D]:

> “Concerning this very matter,” he says, “from which the greatest despair of purification arises for you, a sufficiently swift and effective remedy can emerge if you are willing to transfer to the reading and meditation of spiritual Scriptures the same diligence and persistence which you said you had devoted to secular studies. For it is necessary that your mind be occupied with those poems for as long as it takes to seek, with equal zeal and assiduity, other things within itself for remembrance, and in place of those unfruitful and earthly matters to bring forth spiritual and divine things. When it has conceived them deeply and profoundly and has been nourished by them, the earlier things may gradually be driven out or entirely abolished.” [Note: [Col. 0438D] The manuscript lacks *ad*, “to,” but it has been restored from Cassian, *Conference* XIV, chapter 13, as have the following words: “which he may seek within himself”; the manuscript has a different wording, but the text should be read as in Cassian.]

### 19

As to what you applaud yourself for having established, according to Jerome, concerning the great orator—and which you know has already been said in another way—look more carefully at what that same man says to Eustochium:

> “Do not wish,” he says, “to seem abandoned by the multitude, nor to play with lyric verse in festive meters [Note: [Col. 0438D] The manuscript reads several corrupt forms; Jerome’s text is as translated here.]. Do not pursue the delicate spittle of languid matrons, who now with clenched teeth, now with relaxed lips, regulate a lisping tongue with mutilated words [Note: [Col. 0438D] The manuscript preserves corrupt forms; Jerome’s text is as translated here.], considering everything rustic that comes forth; hence even the adultery of the tongue pleases them. For what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial (II Cor. 6:14–15)? What has Horace to do with the Psalter, Maro with the Gospels, Cicero with the Apostle? Is a brother not scandalized if he sees you reclining in an idol’s shrine? And although all things are clean to the clean (Tit. 1:15), and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, nevertheless we ought not to drink at the same time from the cup of Christ and the cup of demons (I Cor. 10:20, 30).” [Note: [Col. 0438D] The manuscript lacks *moderantur*, “regulate”; it is found in Jerome, Letter 22, well after the middle.]

After these words, so strong and powerful, he adds others still much stronger. He says that the revelation granted to him by the Lord was not delivered through false dreams but through real blows. In it, he asserts, he was led before the tribunal of the judge and severely beaten in the presence of angels and all the heavenly powers for his frequent reading of gentile books.

### 20

Let us look again at what the extraordinary Augustine thinks about this also. He says:

> “The person who teaches should not care how eloquently he teaches, but how clearly. Someone who diligently seeks such clarity will sometimes neither read more cultivated words nor care what sounds good, but rather what indicates well and makes clear what he intends to show.”

He also says:

> “Good teachers ought to be so concerned with teaching that, if a word cannot be Latin unless it is obscure or ambiguous, but is used by ordinary people in order to avoid ambiguity and obscurity, it should not be spoken as it is by the learned, but rather as it is customarily spoken by the unlearned.”

You see, excellent man, that teachers did not care about grammatical faults in words when their meaning and usefulness were secure. Is not this assertion of the most holy teacher like my own profession, against which you speak—that holy and apostolic men do not serve the arrangement of words, but rejoice in the truth of meanings, and proceed not through the liberal art of Donatus but through the simplicity of Christ?

His statement has the same force: “It should not be spoken as it is by the learned, but rather as it is by the unlearned,” so that the truth of the meaning may be revealed and the arrangement of words may not swell with pride.

### 21

But if you perhaps assert that the Psalms and the Book of Job exist among the Hebrews in metrical form, know that you have not brought against us an insoluble problem. For just as the Hebrew language was holy and renowned, consecrated by the Author of human beings himself at the beginning of the world, so the metrical form of that language is not the rule of a profane worshiper of idolatry [Note: [Col. 0439D] So also frequently in other authors, instead of *idololatriae*, “of idolatry.”], but either an invention of Moses, the author of letters, or something promulgated to later generations through God’s inspiration by some holy man [Note: [Col. 0439D] More appropriately, “of some holy human being.”] or prophet.

We are demonstrating [Note: [Col. 0439D] That is, “we are directing our argument toward.”] the art of this Donatus and destroying it with all our strength; we are not trying, by any impulse, to invalidate the character of the most holy language. For we hold this certain within ourselves: every language possesses a rule of its own correctness, through which it extends itself rationally and directly [Note: [Col. 0439D] Better, “directed,” or “in a straight manner.”] into the minds of learned men. But the utterance of divine inspiration [Note: [Col. 0439D] L. reads *eloquentia*, “eloquence.”] is so great that it does not, as though compelled, submit to alien forms of expression, but rests upon a certain authority in its own strength.

Now hear what the most holy Isidore says:

> “The sayings of the gentiles shine outwardly with the eloquence of words, but inwardly remain empty of the wisdom of virtue [Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscript has corrupt forms; Isidore’s text is as translated here.]. But sacred utterances appear outwardly unpolished in their words, while inwardly they shine with the wisdom of mysteries [Note: [Col. 0439D] Isidore has *eloquentia*, “eloquence,” here; Alvarus immediately resumes it in this form.].”

Pay attention to what he says: sacred writing is unpolished in eloquence, and is not adorned by you through Donatus [Note: [Col. 0439D] L. reads “through the art of Donatus.”]—or, as some writers of late Latin say, “cultivated” [Note: [Col. 0439D] *Cultare* is used for *colere*, “to cultivate,” also by other late Latin writers.].

He also says:

> “The holy Scriptures please the fastidious and talkative less because of their simple language; compared with gentile eloquence, they seem unworthy.”

Here too, I ask you to consider carefully how he calls the language of the holy Scriptures simple. He also says:

> “The embellishment of grammatical art should not be preferred to simpler writing.”

You see that here simplicity is preferred in words to Donatus’s art.

### 22

Listen to what Jerome says to Damasus:

> “The food of demons is the poetry of poets, secular wisdom, and the pomp of rhetorical words. All these things delight people by their sweetness; and while they seize the ears with verses flowing in sweet modulation [Note: [Col. 0439D] The manuscript reads “ears”; Jerome has “to the ears” in Letter 146.], they also penetrate the soul and bind the inner parts of the heart.”

As I think, secular learning has been proved to be the eloquence (*euphrasia*) of demons [Col. 0439D]. Listen also to what he says in what follows, continuing the matter already mentioned [Note: [Col. 0440D] See above, no. 1 of this letter]:

> “But when they have been read through with the greatest zeal and labor, they give their readers nothing except an empty sound and the clamor of words. No satiety of truth, no refreshment of justice is found there. Those devoted to them remain hungry for truth and in poverty of virtues.”

And do you say that holy and apostolic men were occupied with empty sound, hunger and emaciation of truth, and poverty of justice? After many manly statements [Note: [Col. 0440D] Read “that man,” namely Jerome, whose words follow, as do those above.] that cut down you and your assertions, he repeats the Apostle’s words:

> “For if someone who has knowledge sees one reclining in an idol’s shrine, will not his knowledge, since it is weak, be built up to eat? And will the weak person perish through your knowledge, brother, for whom Christ died?” (I Cor. 8:10) [Note: [Col. 0440D] *Replicat*, “he repeats,” should be read instead of *replicas*, “you repeat.” The passage is not found above in the letter of John of Seville, but in the cited letter of Jerome.]

Does he not seem to say in other words:

> “Do not read philosophers, orators, or poets; do not rest in reading them.”

If there is scandal in reading them, there is much more sacrilege in teaching them.

And later:

> “But now,” he says, “we see even priests of God, having abandoned the Gospels and the prophets, reciting comedies [Note: [Col. 0440D] Jerome has “reading,” not “reciting.”], singing the love-words of bucolic verses, holding Virgil, and willingly making into a crime for themselves what is a necessity in children” [Note: [Col. 0440D] L. reads “pleasure”; this is also Jerome’s text.].

You see that even in children this crime arises from necessity; yet you wish to place us, who have been freed by grace and have already reached mature age, under condemnation.

Again, admit into your arguments the teacher already mentioned, speaking to Algasia [Note: [Col. 0440D] L. reads “Algasia.” See Letter 1, no. 2.], when he wished to explain the Apostle’s statement, “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle,” all of which perish through use according to the precepts and doctrines of men, “which indeed have an appearance of wisdom” (Col. 2:21–23). He says:

> “In this passage the conjunction is superfluous, something we find the Apostles to have done in many places because of their lack of skill in grammatical art. For it does not follow [Note: [Col. 0440D] The manuscript reads “we follow.”], but rather another conjunction, or one of the conjunctions that normally corresponds to that preposition, wherever it is found” [Note: [Col. 0440D] Add “where it is indeed found,” from Jerome, Letter 151, to Algasia, question 10, near the end.].

Do you have any further means by which to stretch the sinews of your loquacity? Behold: in plain words and almost tangible facts, you subject the unlearned Apostle to your grammatical law. And certainly you cannot deny that he was wiser than the other apostles.

### 23

But if you do not accept the opinions of our teachers concerning the holy writers, yield to the very philosophers in whose disciplines you have been trained, with their emasculated [Note: [Col. 0440D] The text is corrupt; the precise force of *eviratis veribus verbis et clivosis* is uncertain.] and tortuous words.

For Porphyry, looking upon us in his books of insults against the Church, says:

> “They cling to the absurdities of the Jewish Scriptures, in which there is no complete or satisfactory explanation, and turn to certain incongruous and unsuitable narratives. These are not so much explanations of what is obscure as a means of winning praise and applause for those who discuss them. For they affirm that what Moses wrote in rustic and simple language was divinely sanctioned and covered with figures and riddles, and, puffed up in mind and swollen with pride, with the judgment of human reason disturbed within themselves, they consider them mysteries—things which the rustic writer is unable to explain.”

Behold the philosopher, noble among his own people and a distinguished extemporaneous declaimer, attacking Moses in his own terms as an unskilled and rustic writer unable to explain himself. If he had seen Moses’s statements proceeding by the art of grammar, or had judged them to be eloquently and skillfully unfolded through secular wisdom, he would not have thought him deserving of such a designation. But because, like a true gentile, he did not see outward ornament in his words, he could not search out their inward splendor.

Did he pass over the words of the holy Apostle, who says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. 4:7)?

### 24

I would need many days before I exhausted the opinions of teachers, if I wished to gather together all the opinions of learned men that strongly accord with our assertion. Since these are numerous, and since scarcely any of them can be fully explained by the wisest of men, I shall be content with the testimonies already set forth [Note: [Col. 0441D] F. reads “already,” rather than the transmitted form.] and arm myself again with the weapons of the fathers who are defending this cause [Note: [Col. 0441D] F. reads “defending,” rather than “departing.”] for the second objection.

You therefore try to undermine the opinions of the teachers that we have arranged in support of the union of the Son of God, drawing from those same writers their statements concerning the distinction of natures. Without hesitation, you point out statements that seem to contradict one another. You do not destroy the words of the blessed Augustine, but set against him the statements of Saint Jerome, throwing the opinions of both into conflict and showing them as though they had risen against one another and spoken against themselves.

But far be it from anyone with even a little understanding to believe this—much less you, a man so great and so distinguished by knowledge and liberal arts. For what we have said we have said in defense of the union of person; and we have rightly established that Christ is one in two natures.

What you maintain the blessed Jerome thought, you should understand him to have said concerning the properties of the natures, not concerning the union of person, since nowhere in any writing do you read of two distinct Christs. He says:

> “Therefore the Only-Begotten is not firstborn by nature, but because of the fellowship of the Only-Begotten God he is Only-Begotten.”

You see that he explained the property of the natures, not distinguished the unity of the person. For, according to divinity, he is God, and according to humanity, he is truly human.

Yet again I freely and firmly profess that in both natures there exists one Christ, and that there is one proper Son—not two, as the heretic Elipandus seems to have named him.

As for the statement that God had assumed a human being and that, through the death of the cross, this human being was to be abandoned by God until the resurrection, he does not say this because he affirms that the man was abandoned; that is far from our understanding. Rather, as the blessed Libanensis the presbyter said:

> “Not that the Divinity abandoned its flesh, but that it was not going to die together with its flesh; for it did not abandon its flesh by remaining with it in the tomb, just as it established it by being born together with it in the Virgin’s womb” [Note: [Col. 0441D] The manuscript reads “by being born”; not only in Libanensis but above, Letter 1, no. 5, we read “by being born together.”].

Thus it accords with our faith that the human Son should say, “Why have you abandoned me?” (Matt. 27:46), while the divine Son, who is equal to the Father, should say, “He who sent me is with me, and has not abandoned me” (John 8:29). And since there is one Son from both, care must be taken lest anyone say: “The human being died, and God raised him.” This is what those say who preach him as adoptive according to the flesh and proper according to divinity.

### 25

The statement of Saint Jerome that you, my dear one, have introduced must undoubtedly be understood in this way: humanity was abandoned by its own divinity, which is itself the third person in the Trinity. But because divinity could not die, humanity therefore bore the passion, as it were, naturally in itself alone.

I am nevertheless astonished that he dared to say here that he was abandoned by God, since in your letter, while you say something else, he never seems to have affirmed that he was abandoned. There our assertion is confirmed by the distinguished Gregory. For you say that he stated:

> “For the Spirit comes in all the faithful, but remains in the Mediator alone, who never abandoned his humanity.”

If it was not abandoned, then it was certainly not forsaken.

As for what you intend to establish from Saint Augustine against the Priscillianists—that divinity is not subject to change or transformation—you are indeed arguing truly, but against no one in particular. For we do not say that humanity was changed into divinity or divinity converted into flesh; nor do we attribute increase to that most simple nature; nor have we ever contested such blasphemies with anyone.

Rather, with truthful insistence we affirm that God became man, Christ the Redeemer of all, one and not two sons separated and distinguished from one another by a difference of persons, but one Son, proper through the union of person and not adoptive.

I have long and carefully examined the words of blessed Leo, the venerable statements of Saint Jerome, and the opinion of the distinguished Athanasius, and I have found them not opposed to one another but entirely harmonious. For I have recognized that they were arranged not with regard to the person of Christ, which is one, but with regard to the properties of the natures, which are two in him [Note: [Col. 0442D] The manuscript reads, “with regard to the properties of the natures.”].

You likewise bring forward blessed Ambrose making similar statements, and set him against the Apollinarians, as though I were saying that divinity and flesh are of one substance, while I openly distinguish two natures in him [Note: [Col. 0442D] Read “I distinguish two natures,” not “I do not distinguish.”]. You dissolve what no one objects to, and give no affirmative answer to the matters about which you complain [Col. 0443A].

### 26

As for your attempt to weaken the statements of the Council of Ephesus, I am astonished that you should even have wished to consider such a course, much more to discuss it at length in writing. For you say:

> “If you say that the flesh is proper to the Word of God the Father—which I scarcely believe the holy Fathers said—then you will seem to follow the Sabellian heresy [Note: [Col. 0443D] The manuscript’s copyist omitted the word “heresy.” It is found above, Letter 3, no. 7, and immediately below.], since you say that the flesh of the Word of God the Father is proper to him, and that it is the Word’s own, whereas the holy Synod of Ephesus certainly did not teach this.”

You surely recognize that I have not expressed my own opinion but that of the Council of Ephesus, as you yourself testify. How, then, did you dare to say, “which I scarcely believe the holy Fathers said”? Were those holy men not Fathers who presided in person at the Council of Ephesus?

You say, therefore: “You will seem to follow the Sabellian heresy.” Why do you attach this to me [Note: [Col. 0443D] The manuscript reads “to the title.”] and hasten to punish me for another person’s opinion? Did I say anything of my own? Their words sounded through my writing.

Say, then: “The most holy Fathers of the Council of Ephesus followed the Sabellian heresy when they said that the flesh is proper to the very Word of God the Father and that it is proper to the Word.” But listen, O Aristarchus of our age, with what intention they said this: it is proper not only to the Word of God the Father but also to the Father, because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us—not changed into flesh, or transformed as you say, but made one proper Son in the flesh.

The flesh is proper to the Father through the property of his Word. This does not mean—far be it from us—that flesh was taken from the divinity of the Father; rather, the flesh was assumed from Mary, ever Virgin; and the Word, together with his divinity, is the third person in the Trinity.

### 27

But if he is proper to the Father according to the Word and adoptive according to the flesh, then Elipandus, long ago dead, has risen again on your side.
