We do not preach Sabellianism; we believe in three persons. Nor do we assert Christ’s flesh to be adoptive, but truthfully preach one proper Son, not two. If you do not call him proper to the Father, you will consequently seem to affirm him adoptive with respect to the Father.

But hear how you slay yourself with your own sword. At the time when the plague of Elipandus was ravaging our province in its mad fury and was violently scattering deadly hearts with the cruel barbarian sword [Note: [Col. 0443D] Alternatively, “cruelly.” Bravo, *Catalogue of the Bishops of Córdoba*, p. 107.]—with its powerful blade [Note: [Col. 0444D] That is, *romphaea*, “sword.”]—your bishop Teudula, now summoned for judgment, after many varied and venerable statements concerning the property of Christ, concluded the summary of his entire argument with these words:

> “If anyone calls Christ’s flesh adoptive with respect to the Father, let him be anathema. Amen.”

### 28

Hear what Basiliscus says to Elipandus:

> “Someone adds,” he says, “‘God the Father did not beget flesh.’ I myself admit that he did not beget flesh, but he begot the Son whose flesh it is” [Note: [Col. 0444D] The manuscript reads “son.”]. “Nor does any human father beget a soul in a son, but he begets the flesh whose soul it is. There God the Father, being Spirit, begets Spirit, not flesh. Here a human father, being flesh, begets flesh, not spirit. There God the Father begets both nature and person; here the human father begets nature alone, not person.

“Before he assumed human nature, the subsisting divine person obtained an increase of dignity, so that he might be acknowledged as the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0444D] That is, “might be called.”]. Here, so that he might be acknowledged as a human son, he possessed much less, since he received from the father only the nature of flesh, without a person.

“Therefore, one must either divide every human son completely, or proclaim Christ as one from both. Every human being created in the image of God, through whom the image of God descends, is generated dissimilarly from both parents. First he is born from the father and remains unknown for a time. Then he is born from the mother and appears as a human being. The father alone generates nature without person; the mother generates both nature and person.

“Yet in one person she transmits both substances: by giving birth to one from her own entrails, she brought forth the other—not from her entrails—when she gave birth to the one who had been conceived. Hence, among those who beget, flesh alone is known to be born from flesh, while the soul is propagated from God.

“Therefore, if neither parent generated the soul in the Son from his own substance, he was adoptive with regard to the soul. Consequently, if anyone wishes to divide Christ, according to the distinction of natures, into a proper son and an adoptive son, let him divide every human son completely [Note: [Col. 0444D] Perhaps “every human son,” as written shortly above.]. But because the reasoning of truth resists this, let the proper Son be recognized as coming from both with respect to God the Father, from both and in both with respect to his parents, because in both cases only one Son is shown personally to be either the Son of God or the son of man.”

### 29

As for the statement of our Vincentius that you seek to weaken, you must consider the intention with which it was spoken. He did not produce it to affirm that Christ’s flesh was created before the ages, but to show that the person of the Word and the flesh is one.

For you say:

> “That face which the cultivator of paradise fled was a created being subject to God, but it was not born from David’s seed; rather, the divinity had not yet been embodied from David’s line, nor yet born in time.”

Behold, you plainly bring forward and confirm what you rejected shortly before, when you say: “But the divinity had not yet been embodied from David’s line.” What divinity was embodied from David’s line? If it was the Son’s, then it became proper to the Father.

You criticize Vincentius, who had an excellent understanding of the property of the Son’s person, and you do not notice that the Gospel confirms the same thing more clearly:

> “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

And also:

> “When you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before” (John 6:63).

Tell me: where was the Son of Man before he received flesh? If he was in heaven, why did he receive flesh when he already had flesh, since he says “Son of Man”? He says this both to show that through the union of person he existed from the beginning and to show that he had been named a human being.

For when he says “Son of Man,” he shows that he is the son of Mary. Cast those things which you object to Vincentius, that most learned man, upon the most holy Gospel, and consider again that Gospel’s statement:

> “Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56).

And recognize that Abraham saw a created being subject to God, not an incarnate form. Know that this is not spoken according to the nature of the flesh, but is established according to the unity of person [Col. 0445A].

For far be it from us to proclaim that the incarnate Son existed before the ages from any other source than Mary, ever-virgin. And again, far be it—and let it be far from our understanding—to give him, through the union of person, a beginning from Mary.

### 30.

I would like you to answer me here whether you present Christ, in both natures, as the true and one Son, God; or whether in one nature you present him as God, and in the other separately as a mere and pure man. Do you say that Christ’s flesh is the creator of all things according to the union of the person, or do you openly defend it as a creature? For if you maintain him to be merely a creature and do not assert him to be the Creator, you prove yourself a transgressor, bowing your neck to the creature while passing over the Creator. “For the gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish from under heaven.” And where will be that which we read: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, God blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. 9:5)? And that of blessed John: “We know that the Son of God has come, and for our sake has put on flesh, and has suffered, and has risen again: this is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). And Paul again: “Let it be known to you, brothers, that the Gospel which I preached is not according to man, nor did I receive it from man; nor did I learn it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1:11).

But if you believe him to be the Creator in every respect, you will prove him to have existed before Adam, whether you wish it or not; indeed, you will defend that he existed from the beginning without a beginning.

### 31.

You argue about Christ’s soul, and contend that it is not from the seed of David, as though we had said that it descended from David’s seed, or held a different view concerning the proper nature of his humanity. For we do not say that humanity—that is, body and soul—was embodied from the beginning, but that, through the indissoluble conjunction of the Word of God, it existed and acted as one in him from the very beginning.

How this happened, I do not know, because I cannot grasp it intellectually—[Note: The manuscript lacks *non* (“not”); from what follows, however, the negation appears necessary.]—in accordance with what blessed Augustine says:

> “Let faith believe this,” he says, “and let it not demand understanding, lest it either judge what has not been discovered to be incredible, or, once discovered, fail to believe it unique.”

In the same way Saint Jerome, eloquent in expression, says:

> “You wonder if I am ignorant of the mystery of the divinity [Note: *de* (“of”) appears redundant in the manuscript.], when I do not know myself. You ask me how divinity and incarnation are one, when I do not know how I live. To understand God is to believe him; to know God is to adore him. It is enough for me to know what I believe; I neither want nor desire anything more. If I should want to know more, I would begin to lose even what I believe.”

For earlier he had stated:

> “I do not understand one thing as seated and another as the footstool, but the whole in Christ is the throne. He asks and says, ‘Why?’ or ‘For what reason?’ I do not know how it is; nevertheless, I believe that it is.”

You ask: How shall we say that he is true God and true man? Hear how: according to the flesh, man; according to the Word, God [Note: The manuscript reads “God … flesh … one,” and so forth]. But flesh and Word are one Son, true and certain God. Born from a mother, as you say, in time, but eternal from the Father. Yet follow the whole concluding statement: “In two substances there is one person of the Godhead.”

That he was not abandoned by the divinity I have already established as clearly as I was able in the preceding letter, through the streams of the teachers; and I saw that reviewing the whole matter would be burdensome to readers, especially since you, my beloved, had neither weakened it nor rashly violated it in any part. I interwove the strong statements of Saint Fulgentius, blessed Jerome, illustrious Augustine, and others—statements that you neither wished, nor ought, perhaps nor were able, to undermine.

I have arranged these matters according to the measure of my abilities, not as much as I ought, or as much as the dignity of the subject demanded, but as much as I was able. Especially since, as you know me more fully, I am held back by dullness of speech and hindered by slowness of intellect. It is yours, most reverend sir, to approve what I have said and henceforth not to proceed into something that cannot be defended.

### 32.

Bring back to mind once more that saying of Junillus: distinction, union, alternation. Distinction is what speaks according to the natures, so as to show their properties without confusion. Union is what asserts the unity of the two natures in one person. Alternation is what assigns divine things to the human and human things to the divine—both in one Son—just as without confusion, so also without division.

Since you yourself know this, why do you seek to pass over this alternation in order to win your case? Understand the statements of our Vincentius according to this alternation, and plainly you will not say that he erred.

Therefore I ask, and ask again, that you remove such assertions of yours from your mind forever, and that you not discuss matters of such difficulty abruptly and lightly, lest—God forbid—you lose the name of Catholic and cause scandal to the weaker. For the audacity that devises these evil assertions is a mass of perfidy and impiety, already long ago cut out by the roots by illustrious teachers.

### 33.

The Nestorians, as our light Isidore says, were named after Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who asserted that blessed Mary was the mother not of God but of a man, so as to make one person of the flesh and another of the divinity. He did not believe in one Christ, the Word of God and flesh, but preached them separately and apart: one of God, the other of man.

Remember the eloquent statement of the distinguished Augustine’s response:

> “The very person whom the Father begot before the ages, the Virgin begot with flesh.”

And heed that saying of Saint John:

> “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, who was dead, and behold, I am alive for ever and ever. Amen” (Rev. 1:17).

And the prophet:

> “If a man affixes his God, because you have affixed me?” (Mal. 3:8).

Thus we also read that “the Lord of glory was crucified” (1 Cor. 2:8), although it is certain that, insofar as he is the Lord of glory, he suffered no loss through the cross.

### 34.

Review the decrees of the Council of Ephesus, and those of the distinguished Jerome, or Fulgentius, or others, especially the nearly contemporary blessed Libanensis, priest. You will plainly never venerate the one who was assumed on account of the one who assumed him, nor adore the visible on account of the invisible; rather, you will at once venerate the assumed and the one who assumed him, the invisible and the visible, as one—your Redeemer, and the Redeemer of all.

This is the faith of the Council of Ephesus; this is also our confession. For this, if the matter should require it, I will offer my neck to the sword.

I suggest only one thing, in a brotherly spirit, at the end of this letter: that what has been set out not be received harshly, since I descended into these words not with the intention of victory but with the intention of truth. It is yours to season my words, which may lack sufficient salt, and to grant pardon to my verbosity or ineptitude. For I have already confessed that I do not proceed by Donatus’s art, but rely upon the ignorance innate in me.

Nor is it right that, when I rise against someone’s rule, I should proceed by the rhetorical device of that very rule which I am destroying. Yet I wonder why, following Varro, you wanted to say *lac* (“milk”), when Caesar says: “No noun ends in two mute letters.” But this and other matters elsewhere.

### 35.

Now let us return to the subject, and judge that everything written was said out of love. I arranged everything not with hostile intent but with loving desire; in what you call cruel beams I soothed you, and, as I think, beneficially. For it was not useless: the severity—or rather the rusticity—of one who had long owed a response caused him, though silent and long devoted to silence, to burst forth into speech. He accomplished what flattering eloquence could not [Note: *blandiloquacida* means “flattering eloquence” (*blandiloquentia*).], and sent us the little message from a friend that we desired.

Do not assert that I am the philosopher Antisthenes and that you are Diogenes, since in everything you approve me as being not the disciple but the teacher: you do not offer your head to the one striking and submit it, but attack me with a very sharp and cruel blade.

This is indeed the Antisthenes who, after teaching rhetoric gloriously and hearing Socrates, is said to have said to his disciples: “Go away and seek a teacher; for I have already found one.” But what can be harsh, I ask, among those who love? What can be severe among friends, since not even death can tear apart those whom the indissoluble love of Christ has joined?

### 36.

We received your second letter sad and almost plunged down to the realm of the dead, and we recognized that, however little, we had possessed some consolation in the writings of a friend. We could reply to it with nothing but tears, since we have also read what the elders said: “Music in mourning is an untimely or inopportune narrative” (Sir. 22:6).

We answered only this, as if in battle array [Note: The manuscript reads *procincte*.]: If Christ’s flesh is therefore not proper to the Father because it was not assumed by the same Father, then neither is the Son wholly proper in divinity, because he is not one person with the Father, nor did he likewise put on human form [Note: The manuscript reads *induli*; the intended reading is evidently *induit*, “put on”].

But if you say that the Son is wholly proper to the Father, and do not declare him adoptive from the Father, then, whether you wish it or not, you will call the flesh proper to the Father, without which you cannot believe a third person in the Trinity. For that very person is perfect and complete God and man, the third person, and, as I believe, in no respect inferior to the Father and the Holy Spirit—unless perhaps you believe that only the Word is the proper Son, and say that the body assumed by him was laid aside again, like a garment, from the place from which it had been taken.

Or you assert that human nature is a fourth person and openly defend not a Trinity but a quaternity.

### 37.

As for your charge that the scribe made an error, I do not know why you wished to introduce this. For we set out the judgment of the Council of Ephesus intact; we neither augmented it by adding anything of our own nor diminished it by taking anything away.

If you find a syllable omitted or added in the very judgment of the Ephesian synod that you attack, you should know that this was caused by the scribe’s haste, not by the intention of the one dictating something foreign. For it is incongruous, and nearly characteristic of a foolish and deranged person, to use the testimonies of teachers in support of one’s own position and then pollute that judgment with one’s own material, sharpening more fiercely, through one’s own stupidity, the language of the response against oneself in debate.

Do not think us so foolish, most reverend sir, that you suppose we would diminish anything in another’s edition [Note: The manuscript reads *minuare*] or rashly and insolently appropriate the words of our elders otherwise than they were set down. This is the conduct of the profane and of a sacrilegious mind, not of a Catholic or even a minimally faithful person.

If you have found anything omitted or added in the decrees of the holy synod excerpted by us, attribute the fault to the external limb that served the work [Note: The manuscript reads: “from the excerpted decrees: attribute the fault of the limb serving externally”], not to the mind presiding within.

Farewell, my lord, and always pluck joyful grasses from the fruits of the Scriptures.

## V. ANOTHER LETTER ADDRESSED TO THE SAME JOHN

**Paulus Alvarus to Aurelius Flavius John**

### 1.

After the discussion of our ignorance concerning two questions—not sufficiently, as was fitting for so great a subject, but moderated in every direction, though not moderately, by the mediocrity of our intellect—I remained silent until now, and had decided to remain in the silence I had begun [Note: The manuscript reads *incepto*.], until I should either be beaten back or approved by a written response from your eloquence.

But because inward love—or, if it is more suitably called so, affection, which in the divine books is more appropriately called charity—boils up within, possessing the interior self, and in boiling over observes no measure, I therefore fail to preserve the proper order of letter-writing. In an unusual manner, and knowingly, I make myself entirely adorned with words, and approach as the first, middle, and last writer, verbose, so that I who impelled matters at the beginning and discussed what I had begun in the middle may bring them to a conclusion at the end.

I could easily believe this if I were disputing with an ignorant breast [Note: The manuscript reads “with an ignorant breast,” rather than “with an ignorant mind”]. But since it is clear that the stream of Latin eloquence—indeed, the force of a torrent—has rushed against the glassy element, how can the facility of closing be granted to me, when the abundance of the disputant’s fertility [Note: The manuscript reads *copia* (“abundance”).], the slowness of my own intellect, and the smallness of my entrusted talent all stand in my way? And although the will of God exists implanted in natural places [Note: The manuscript reads *exit at voluntas*; the text is corrupt], nevertheless the power of reinforcement is removed from one to whom weakness in every respect is imposed as an obstacle.

The beginning is weighed out according to our own will; the conclusion remains in the judgment of both. For a response is never quieted unless the attack has first been turned back [Note: Niccolò Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book 1, chapter 6, no. 181, reads “is engaged”; *converscatur* may mean “is exchanged” or “is turned about”].

And so a winding little chain is made, and a chain-like, winding contention, which is closed neither by attacks [Note: The same source reads “eluded,” but *cluditur* should be retained] nor ended by responses. This is often intensified among men of outstanding eloquence, frequently investigated, and repeatedly brought forward as a pretext.

It has the benefit of equal contest when this same rope is stretched between equals. But when a cord is drawn between unequals, the weak man is thrown down, the strong man is raised up, strength rejoices, and weakness groans.

There is also a third thing—not to be awaited [Note: The reading *expetendum*, “to be sought,” is also found], but to be detested: the quarrel of slander, which habitually arises among insolent and tumultuous gatherings. The person involved lacks the abundance of eloquence and yet holds fast, with ill-placed force, to the verbosity of abusive speech [Note: The manuscript reads *decacitatem*, apparently for *dicacitatem*, “biting wit”]. He does not know how to speak at all, yet, making an inconvenient din, never knows how to be silent: loudly shouting in verbosity and verbosely shouting.

A chattering jackdaw [Note: The manuscript reads *Gragule*] and, with the mouth and roar of beasts, enormously bellowing [lacuna] gaping open on every side [Note: The manuscript has the corrupt reading *ritu barrituque inormi, iatibus undique iulca* (“with manner and enormous roaring, gaping everywhere with jaws”).].

When such a quarrel has arisen among the most obstinate minds, the tongue’s rivalry turns into blows with a sling. A matter that, when settled by speech, gives pleasure, when ended by hands, staffs, and knotted rakes, causes sorrow by maiming the limbs.

### 2.

Among the wise and well-mannered, disputation possesses the sweetness of flavor; among fools and uncultivated people, it produces the bitterest and most acrid pain. Among the wise, the honey of wisdom is sweetly tasted; among the senseless, gall rolls about amid tumult.

What takes place among the wise is called discussion; what takes place among the senseless is more truly called tumult. The quarrel of the wise ends in affection; the love of the foolish ends in fat and sweet things [Note: Another reading is “in punches and kicks”].

The former advance toward better things through argument; the latter fall toward worse things through brawling. For the former, charity supplies eloquence; for the latter, strife brings a knotted cudgel. From the former peace and fragrance flow; from the latter hatred and stench exhale.

The memory of the wise benefits those who come after; the error of fools perishes with them. The wise man dies, and after death flourishes; the fool dies, and after death rots. The contention of the wise is a delight for those who follow; the division of fools is the horror of those who remain.

The quarrel of the prudent offers a honeycomb; the struggle of fools crushes lime. The one grows through knowledge at its sources [Note: It may be necessary, from the context, to read “fronts” rather than “sources”]; the other grows hot through slaps and punches.

Both have their own boundaries and different heats [Note: The manuscript reads *estos*]; according to their own quality, each produces offspring. Let us therefore generate, most reverend sir, mature sons, invigorated by truth, who may enrich their parents with unbroken rewards.

And with the Prophet let us say concerning our own work: “From fear of you we conceived, and we brought forth the hope of salvation.” Let us imitate the example of the wise in our conduct and emulate in everything the behavior of the truest philosophers—not allowing the rivalry of victory to accuse our understanding [Note: The manuscript reads *accusat*, “accuses,” rather than *accuset*, “may accuse”], but letting the zeal for improvement guide the conduct of our entire work.

Let there be pure concord and undivided chastity, and let the struggle of words immediately be counted as nothing. Believe me, brother—or rather, in age, Father—that what I poured out in affection, and everything that I completed in the course of the work, was done without any envy, God forbid, but in charity, which may eternally remain with us.

Therefore, recognize that whatever was harsh in the more severe eloquence was drawn forth by the necessity of defense, according to the custom of defense, and was not composed out of the zeal of contention [Note: The manuscript reads: “the harsh things were … elicited … completed”]. Love poured the ink into me [Note: The manuscript reads “poured in”], and the stylus of composition was not a feather or a reed, but affection.

Indeed, the letters were written not so much by hand as by the mind, and all were composed through charity. Yet the words, the delivery of the speech itself, and the meaning of the statements as a whole were nothing other than affection sprinkled with dew from the heart.

I ask that, even if they were ineptly arranged, my whole offense be left aside, so that your offenses may likewise not be sought [Note: “Offenses,” that is, “faults” or “crimes”]. For the rest, my beloved, there were many secret and mystical matters which I would have shared with your kindness, if the prosperity of this world smiled upon me, or if I sensed an end to the scourge.

### 3.

But because divine and just judgment does not gently wear away our evils on every side only to the extent that we deserve, we are not permitted even briefly to breathe amid those things that were for us matters of the soul’s advancement [Note: The manuscript reads “in that”]. We are unable to search out the secrets of wisdom and extend the wings of our discussion higher from earth all the way to heaven in the loftier questions.

Thus, leaving earthly things behind and despising the serpent’s food, dust, let us take the wings of that dove which has wings more clearly spread before the eyes, silvered, as it were (Ps. 67), and unfolded with the bright whiteness of purity and innocence for all who look upon them, almost inviting them to itself.

Yet it discloses a more hidden meaning in the pallor of gold, as though inwardly—not to everyone, but to those who look within. For this reason it also bears golden feathers on the back.

For what is the dove except the all-holy Spirit, in whose likeness it was seen to appear? And because Holy Scripture stands written by the Spirit of God, it therefore bears a silver exterior and golden interiors. Accordingly, I would say that its wings are everything it contains historically, everything it teaches morally, and everything it forms actively. Its back, however, is not improperly understood as everything mystical, everything spiritual, and everything raised up under the cloud of allegory [Note: Perhaps “veiled”].

Thus Holy Scripture consists of an outer body and spiritual power. Just as it appears outwardly, limb by limb, to less perceptive readers, so to the more prudent it shines through invisible spiritual power.

### 4.

> “It was rightly arranged,” says blessed Eucherius, worthy of being proclaimed with outstanding praise, “that the chastity of those expressions should be concealed from the indiscriminate eyes of all by its own kind of veil of modesty [Note: The manuscript reads *additu*; *abdito*, “hidden,” is required by Eucherius’s preface to the *Book of Spiritual Formulas*]. For divine providence wisely arranged that the writings should be covered in this way, overshadowed by heavenly mysteries, just as the divinity itself was concealed in its secret [Note: Eucherius has *operiebatur*, “was concealed”; the manuscript reads *operabatur*, “was working”].”

The worldly writings do not know the form of this silver-and-gold dove; philosophers are ignorant of it, and your grammarians have not been able to know it. Only our ordinary people, peasants, and those who bear calloused hands from their labor know it [Note: The manuscript reads *tante* for *tantum* (“only”).].

Thus our peasant, while grafting a fig tree, found what the sophists did not know:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1).

The learned Plato did not know this; the eloquent Cicero was ignorant of it; the fiery Demosthenes never fully investigated it. The twisted Aristotelian thickets do not contain it [Note: Another reading is *spineta*, “thickets,” rather than *pineta*, “pine groves”]; the winding subtleties of Chrysippus do not retain it.

It was not investigated through Donatus’s art and its rules, nor through the whole olive grove of grammatical discipline. The geometers, so called from the earth, pursued earthly and dusty matters. The verbose rhetoricians, superfluous, filled the air with empty wind. The dialecticians, constrained by rules and entangled everywhere in syllogisms, crafty and clever, were more truly deceivers of words than builders of things in their speech.

The arithmeticians tried to investigate the causes of numbers, but could not perceive their marrow—how much less express it [Note: The manuscript reads *dici*, “to be said,” rather than *dicere*, “to express”]. The musicians, vain blowers of wind, pursued breathy airs, and could never raise their wings to the truth of that musical art.

The astrologers, for their part, wished to fly with wings all the way to heaven. Yet they could not ascend there by the guidance of their temples; instead, they placed an earthly order in heaven rather than a heavenly one on earth.

For when they placed rams and bulls, scorpions and crabs, lions and bears, goats and fishes in the region of heaven, what else did they do but raise earthly things into the heavens? Not knowing the nature of heaven, they rashly attempted to discuss what they did not know and ventured toward famous undertakings; but they produced nothing worthy of such a subject, because they investigated the spirit through the human, rather than these things through the divine Spirit.

### 5.

If anyone says that the writings of these men were composed through spiritual power, he unquestionably asserts something contrary to our faith and is an enemy and defamer of divine Scripture. He thereby asserts that the tongue of Leviathan, already bound by Christ’s hook, and the tongue of the Egyptian sea, laid waste by the Redeemer’s coming, still possesses strength by whatever effort; and he claims that the divine Scriptures were composed in the same style as the empty and false doctrines of the philosophers.

And where will be that saying of our Psalmist:

> “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested in fire, proved on the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11)?

Concerning this the superior teacher, the distinguished Eucherius, also says:

> “Nor is it surprising that the divine speech, uttered by the mouths of the prophets and apostles, departed greatly from that customary manner of writing among human beings, possessing easy things on the surface but containing great things in its depths. For it was truly fitting that sacred sayings should be distinguished from other writings, both in merit and in appearance, lest the dignity of heavenly mysteries be indiscriminately and without distinction open to everyone, exposing what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine” [Note: The manuscript reads “from true writings”; Eucherius, in the passage cited above, has “from other writings.”]

And because secular knowledge does not prophesy even in riddles, the Psalmist says:

> “You broke open the springs and torrents; you dried up the rivers of Ethan” (Ps. 73).

The Lord broke open springs and torrents when he opened the streams of truth in the hearts of his apostles. Thirsting, we proceed toward their teaching, and soon carry back our little flasks full of truth [Note: Another reading is *lagunculas*, “small flasks,” the same as a little bottle; Spanish *jarro*]. But through the opening of these springs the rivers of Ethan have been dried up, because, when the truth of the teaching appeared through faith, it closed the mouths of the false knowledge of the gentiles.

### 6.

But in order to prove the venerable expressions of our Christianity and to establish the gentiles’ execrable doctrine as hateful to God and to human beings, we turn the hearts of many teachers into one [Note: The manuscript reads “we strive for one heart”]. We have read many little flowers of the teachers’ writings, collected until now and in our possession, especially concerning that second question in which our response to you was composed about Christ’s divinity and our humanity. These will eventually have to be sent by us, if the stream of your response should again come before us.

But reserving these and other matters for a suitable time, and observing a measure of moderation in everything [Note: The manuscript reads “among human beings”], it is fitting to turn to that point which torments the mind and burns the soul. I can neither think about it nor speak of it. For this reason, the beginning of this inquiry now stands interwoven with it.

### 7.

Therefore I ask, beg, and demand that you prepare your heart and your marvelous mind for me, entirely free from worldly cares, and that you keep watch more attentively over the matters I inquire into, so that they may be searched out and clarified. Perhaps, through fraternal consolation, what has until now remained buried in a certain concealment of its own may be opened to me.

Finally, I know that questions about the human soul have been debated by many; I have read them discussed among many people, but I have never found clear and more revealing indications from them. What I have discovered, and what I have learned was debated among illustrious men, I will narrate here—not by reproducing all their words, but by gradually abbreviating them. I will also investigate, however rustically, the matters and their character that repeatedly trouble me concerning the soul, so that you may teach my ignorance in whatever way you can [Note: “In whatever way,” that is, “by any means”], or instruct me more clearly with proofs.

Know that blessed Augustine wrote two little books on the soul’s immortality, overflowing with learning and abundantly filled with clearer indications. In them he demonstrated its immortality most truly and fully, with every argument of which he was capable. In the books that the same blessed teacher entitled *The City of God*, he also inserted many strong arguments concerning the conflict of soul and flesh, and established most certainly that the very conflict between flesh and spirit arose from the sin of transgression. But he did not touch at all upon the matter I desire to know.

Likewise, blessed Jerome composed a small book *On the Nature of the Soul*. He fought variously and very forcefully against those who assert that the soul arose through transmission, and who argue that, just as body is born from body, so soul is born from soul. He affirmed with many testimonies of Scripture that new souls are made daily for those being born, and finally said that he did not know its origin.

In the *Dogma of the Holy Fathers*, the same most holy man also said:

> “The soul is not the Spirit of God, but the breath produced by creation, brought forth not by generation.”

There too he said that new souls are always created for those being born. He affirmed that they were neither created once for all at the beginning, as Origen imagines, nor sown through intercourse, as certain presumptuous Latins contend.

The distinguished Augustine, in the work already mentioned, *The City of God*, likewise repeatedly and elegantly demonstrated that the breath of God is the soul, not from the substance of God. Claudianus, again, composed three books against certain short works of Cassianus, whose name was suppressed, concerning the soul’s invisibility or incorporeality. In them he dared to criticize blessed Hilary, who had sound understanding.

With a sufficiently subtle and almost incomprehensible argument, worked out through dialectical art and ingenuity, he attempted through geometric formulas, with many and nearly superfluous efforts, to demonstrate that the nature of the soul is incorporeal and invisible even to God. No Catholic will be able to praise him for having done this.

Likewise, the distinguished and most blessed teacher Jerome replied in the following manner to a certain Marcellinus from Africa, who had asked about the origin of the soul:

> “There are five opinions about the soul,” he says. “The first is that it fell from heaven, as the philosopher Pythagoras, all the Platonists, and Origen think. The second is that it is from the substance of God, as the Stoics, the Manichaeans, and the Spanish Priscillianist heresy suspect. The third is that souls were formerly created and kept in a treasury, as certain churchmen contend in their foolish persuasion. The fourth is that it is transmitted, so that, just as body is born from body, soul is born from soul, and stands in the same condition as irrational animals; this is what Tertullian, Apollinaris, and the greater part of the Westerners maintain. The fifth, which is our opinion and the truer one, is that souls are created daily by God and sent into the body, according to the Gospel: ‘My Father is working until now, and I am working’ (John 5).”

### 8.

Likewise, the most blessed Augustine set forth four opinions in his books *On Free Choice*, but he confirmed none of them; rather, he withheld his agreement from all and left which was the truer to God’s knowledge. He omitted the fifth, that of the Priscillianists, which he confessed at that time that he did not know, in the letter sent to the blessed Jerome through Orosius. This opinion, therefore—that new souls are said to be created daily by God in bodies—the same Saint Augustine says was held by the blessed Jerome; and against it, in the same letter sent through Orosius, he fought with great vigor. For he says:

“Tell me: if souls are made individually today for each person being born, where do they sin in infants, so that they require remission of sin in Christ’s sacrament, sinning in Adam, from whom the flesh of sin has been propagated? Or, if they do not sin, why are they bound by another’s sin through the justice of the Creator, when, being inserted into mortal members propagated from that source, condemnation overtakes them unless the Church comes to their aid—although it is not in their power that the grace of baptism can come to their assistance? By what justice, then, are so many thousands of souls condemned which depart from the bodies of infants who die without the remission of the Christian sacrament, if they are new creatures, with no preceding sin of their own, but have been attached individually to those individually being born by the will of the Creator, who created and gave them to animate them, although he certainly knew that each one would depart from the body without Christ’s baptism through no fault of its own?

“Since, therefore, we can neither say of God that he compels souls to become sinful or punishes the innocent, nor is it lawful for us to say that those who have departed from their bodies without Christ’s sacrament—even infants—are drawn anywhere except to condemnation, I beg you: how is this opinion to be defended, by which souls are believed not to be made from that one first man, but, just as that first soul was made one for one, so individual souls are made for individuals?”

*Note:* The manuscript reads *qualitate* (“by what quality”). Augustine, *Epistle* 166, chapter 4, reads *aequitate* (“by what justice”).

And later, at the relevant point, he says:

“But when the matter comes to the punishments of infants, believe me, I am beset by great perplexities and find absolutely no answer. I do not speak only of those punishments which that condemnation has after this life, to which they must necessarily be dragged if they have departed from the body without the sacrament of Christian grace, but also of those very sufferings which, while they are in this life, pass before our eyes and afflict us. If I wished to enumerate them, examples would run out before time did: they languish through illnesses, are tortured by pains, tormented by hunger and thirst, weakened in their limbs, deprived of their senses, and harassed by unclean spirits. It must surely be shown how they can justly suffer these things without any evil cause of their own.

“For it is not lawful to say either that these things occur while God is unaware of them, or that he is unable to resist those who cause them, or that he either does or permits them unjustly.”

*Note:* The manuscript reads *puniantur* (“are punished”).

And shortly afterward:

“God is good, God is just, God is almighty: it is altogether the mark of a madman to doubt this. Let a just cause, therefore, be given for the many evils that occur in infants.”

*Note:* The manuscript reads *quod defit* (“which is lacking”).

Likewise:

“What shall I say about the diversity—or rather, the absurdity—of intellectual capacities? It lies hidden in infants, but, arising from their very natural beginnings, appears in adults. Some of them are so slow and forgetful that they cannot even learn the first elements of letters. Others are so foolish that they scarcely differ from beasts; such people are commonly called *murriones*.”

*Note:* Augustine has *moriones* (“fools” or “simpletons”).

“Perhaps the answer is that bodies cause this”—[namely, bodies which are newly created for each person being born].

*Note:* The words enclosed in brackets are to be added to the commonly published text of Augustine, where they are missing.

“But according to the opinion which we wish to defend, did the soul choose its body and, in choosing it, make a mistake when it was sent into it?”

*Note:* In the printed Fathers’ edition of the Congregation of Saint Maur, volume II, column 590, we also read *cum falleretur* (“when it was being deceived”), without any recorded variant reading. But the text as found in Alvarus is to be preferred.

“Or, when it was compelled to enter a body by the necessity of birth, did it find no other body because swarms of souls had occupied the others beforehand, and, just as one chooses a place at some spectacle, did it occupy not the flesh it wished for but the flesh it was able to obtain? Can we or ought we to say or think such things? Teach us, then, what we ought to think and what we ought to say, so that the rationale of new souls made individually for individual bodies may become clear to us.”

And finally:

“The blessed Cyprian, not framing some new decree but preserving the Church’s most firm faith, said, in correcting those who thought that an infant ought not to be baptized before the eighth day after birth, that it was not the flesh but the soul that must not be lost; and together with his fellow bishops he judged that a newborn could properly be baptized at once.

“Let each person think whatever he wishes, provided that he does not think against the apostolic faith, which proclaims that, because of the sin of one, all are led into condemnation; from that condemnation no one is liberated except by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, in whom all are made alive who are made alive.

“Let no one think against the Church’s most firmly established custom. For if people hurried to baptism in order to baptize only the bodies of infants, the dead too would be brought forward.

“Since these things are so, the cause must be sought and given: why are souls condemned if infants die apart from Christ’s sacrament? For both Holy Scripture and the holy Church testify that, if they depart from the body in this way, they are condemned.

“Therefore, if this opinion concerning the creation of new souls does not oppose this most firmly established faith, let it not be yours.”

*Note:* The passage is mutilated. It may be completed from Augustine as follows: “If it does not oppose this most firmly established faith, let it be mine as well; if it opposes it, let it not be yours.”

By this he shows that this opinion belonged solely to Saint Jerome. For in his letter to Evodius concerning the Holy Trinity and the dove, the same Saint Augustine says:

*Note:* Augustine, *Epistle* 166, formerly 102, chapter 4.

“I also wrote to the holy presbyter Jerome, consulting him about the origin of the soul: how that opinion could be defended which he had written to Marcellinus of revered memory as his own—that individual new souls are made for those being born—without undermining the Church’s most firmly established faith, by which we unwaveringly believe that all die in Adam and, unless they are liberated by Christ’s grace—which also operates through his sacrament in infants—they are drawn into condemnation.”

### 9.

I have said this in order to establish that this Catholic opinion concerning the creation of the soul first arose from Saint Jerome—or, if one puts it more suitably, was first approved by him. For it is easy and readily available to know what your distinguished—indeed, our common—Isidore says in *The Differences* concerning the blessed Fulgentius of Ruspe. There he brought forward two opinions held by the same man, each opposing and destroying the other, and balanced them with equal eloquence, confirming neither of them with any force. There is no doubt that he did not dare to affirm either one.

Just as the blessed Augustine in his book *On Free Choice* believed that four opinions should be examined in such a way that, weighing them all in an equal balance, he inclined toward suspending judgment rather than confirming any of them, so Saint Fulgentius strengthened two opinions—namely, that souls are newly created, or that they are sown together with the body through transmission—in such a way that they repeatedly destroyed one another more than either built up or established any single position. From this it is plainly evident that nothing definitive concerning this matter had been worked out by earlier men.

Yet because the question of blessed Augustine argues with the utmost sharpness and adequacy against this Catholic opinion which is now ours, and because it has battered and overthrown it as far as it could, I beg you: if anywhere you have read the response of the most blessed Jerome to that question, do not disdain to share it with us; or if you have come across, in the work of any other teacher, an appropriate response to the discovery of so great a doctor, do not withhold it.

For it is not fitting that Orosius, vigilant in ingenuity—[the manuscript reads *in lenio*, “in gentleness”; read *in ingenio*, “in ingenuity”]—who had been sent by the distinguished Augustine to the great Jerome solely to learn about the origin of the soul, and who returned repeatedly while that most holy Jerome was still alive, would have come back immediately without any evident indication or palpable reasoning; especially since he knew from Augustine that Jerome’s opinion had been very fully and clearly demolished by him.

And he, who was accustomed freely to release the fountains of eloquence and let the waters of life flow in streams from his gushing veins—would he now have rejected them most emphatically and grieved that his channels were blocked as though by some rocky mountain, when both the subject matter demanded it and the case urgently called for a specific response? But either the negligence of posterity has destroyed it, or it has not yet reached our hands.

Therefore, if you have seen his response anywhere, make known what it is, and that will suffice for us.

### 10.

If it is otherwise, do not delay in explaining what I desire. For I ask—and inquire with sufficient persistence—which of the two persons is cleansed by baptism: the body, which the Apostle calls the outer person, or the inner person, who is called spirit or soul?

And if only the body, and not the soul, is baptized, let me recall what Augustine said above: “Why, then, are the dead not baptized?”

But if the soul is baptized, what is cleansed in one that was not propagated from the first man, but was newly created by God individually for each person?

This argument readily shows that only the body was propagated from original sin, arising through successive generations from Adam’s stock by a kind of transmitted fluid. Yet the soul, which is new and infused into the body without any fault of its own, why is it cleansed by baptismal water, when it was neither wounded at the beginning by the transgression of the commandment in the first parent’s eating of the forbidden tree, nor, upon entering the world in a body, enclosed within the corruption compacted through the process of generation?

For it is absurd, far removed from the line of truth, and wholly alien to reason either to wash what has not been entirely defiled or to cleanse an insensible member of anything. If only the body is cleansed—which possesses a fixed and immovable condition and, unless animated by a life-giving spirit, would necessarily be found more like insensible metal than suited to anything—then it must be admitted that the Lord Christ descended from heaven not to redeem souls, which have not been infected with Adam’s original sin, but only to redeem bodies that continued to arise through transmission from the one who sinned.

*Note:* The F manuscript reads *manarunt* (“flowed forth”), rather than *manerent* (“remained”).

Who, then, would be so foolish as even lightly to dare think this?

But if he is rather the redeemer of souls than of bodies, the reason for the creation of that very soul must be supplied.

*Note:* That is, “of the soul,” so that no ambiguity may arise; *in* has perhaps been suppressed. Alternatively, read *redemptio* (“redemption”) immediately, where *redemptionis* (“of redemption”) is written.

If it fell, it is raised up; if it was stained with filth, it is washed clean; if it was taken captive by the serpent, it is redeemed. But if it neither fell in its parent nor was stained with original filth nor deceived by the serpent in the first human beings, why, if it is not washed in water, is it plunged into flames? Is it condemned for another’s sin and, on account of the body that has continued to arise from those same parents, plunged into everlasting fire? Why is one held by another’s sin who is free from its own?

Therefore, if anywhere you have read this question set forth and unfolded in this way by me, I ask you not to delay in replying to me. May you always flourish in perpetual bloom.

Or let your clearer pen and truthful testimony show what must be held or believed concerning it, and how God’s justice is to be defended in the condemnation of innocent souls; and, with luminous clarity, let your serene judgment reveal everything to us, drawn from the light of your mouth.

Thus may you deserve here and in the future to be rewarded by the heavenly gifts, with the ethereal strength and unbroken happiness of the heavenly homeland. Amen. Finished.

## VI. THE LETTER OF JOHN OF SPALATO TO ALVARUS

### [Col. 0458A]

To the illustrious, distinguished, and exalted Alvarus, John, least of all and lowest in every respect.

### 1.

Since every day and at every moment we have approved your pursuit of wisdom and your ever-watchful concern for the usefulness of the Catholic faith, we have given thanks to God because your light has long cast its fragrance in hidden places, shines continually in public ones, and often radiates with the beam of its splendor throughout the ends of the world. At times it gathers like rain in discourse and in all divine matters: frequently you send forth words like a shower upon the grass, and, like drops upon the herbs, you pour in excellent teaching.

And because in all these things you are a bishop, may the Lord cause you to complete a long span of days in years and show upon you the face of his mercy, so that, rescued from gloomy darkness,

*Note:* The manuscript reads *caliginis* (“of darkness”).

you may soon deserve to climb upward among your companions in heavenly places. Amen.

### 2.

Finally, whatever your wisdom has elaborated concerning the connection of the five causes of souls, and whatever questions defending different positions from one another and differing in many respects we have been able to observe, we have examined; and we have understood whatever our elder thought about these matters.

Yet your prudence adds that, if anywhere we have read the response of the blessed Jerome to the distinguished Augustine, we should not delay in sending it to your sweetness. The Lord lives, and may your soul live, because I have read no response on this subject—except that I have read only the teaching of the blessed Ambrose against those who do not confess that the soul is God’s creation, or who say that it arose through transmission, or who assert that it is proclaimed to be a portion of God.

What the aforesaid distinguished teacher thought about this, what he maintained, and what he taught should be held, we have sent to you briefly and summarily, because we believe that for a wise person a little from the many sayings of the wise is sufficient.

### 3.

For at the beginning of his discourse he addressed the matter as follows:

“‘A spirit shall go forth from me,’ says the Lord, ‘and I create every breath.’ Is this not the God who calls his boy Jacob and his servant Israel, who formed him in the womb? Is this not the maker of souls, of whom it is said: ‘He who forms their hearts one by one’? (Psalm 33:15.) And the Apostle says: ‘He who set me apart from my mother’s womb’ (Galatians 1:15). He who has the power to set apart also has the power to form in the womb.

“You see, therefore, that God is both the one who forms in the womb and the shaper of souls, because the Lord himself speaks in this way: ‘My Father is working until now, and I am working’ (John 5:17).

“And Moses, the bearer of the law, says: ‘If a man strikes a woman with the heel and she casts out what has been formed, he shall pay all the woman’s belongings according to the will of her husband. But if she casts out what has already been formed, he shall give eye for eye, bruise for bruise, soul for soul’ (2 Maccabees 7:22). You see, therefore, that a soul receives form in the womb.”

*Note:* The F manuscript reads: “if she casts out what has been formed by the heel, or has not yet cast out what has been shaped.” The following clause is then: “But if she casts out what has already been formed.”

### 4.

For the mother of the seven sons also says: “Nor did I myself join together your limbs in the womb, but God did.” And again she herself says: “Nor did I give you soul, but God, who joined together the body, who lined and shaped every flesh, gave you soul” (2 Maccabees 7:22).

And Isaiah says:

“The Lord God, who established heaven and solidified the earth and the things in it, gives breath to the people who are upon it, and spirit to those who tread upon it” (Isaiah 42:5).

Job likewise:

“Whom did you wish to teach? Was it not him who made your breath?” (Job 26:4.)

*Note:* The manuscript reads *Jacob* for *Job*.

And Isaiah:

“Your Lord God, who formed you as his servant in the womb” (Isaiah 42:24).

And Ezra:

“You alone are God, and we are your one creation, the work of your hands, as you have spoken. You visit the body formed in the womb, supply its limbs, and preserve it through fire and water. Your creation suffers for nine months the forming of your creature, that which has been created in it, so that it may be preserved. And when it again gives back to the womb what has been created in it, you command that milk be supplied in the limbs—that is, in the breasts—the fruit of the breasts, and that what has been formed in the womb be nourished” (4 Ezra 8:7 and following).

### 5.

Let the most perverse assertion cease, unsupported by any authorities. Let Plato cease, who says that he is the fountain of souls. Let Hermogenes cease, who says that nothing will happen to a human being after death. Let Epicurus cease, who testifies to their mutual [unclear: the manuscript appears corrupt]. Let the most impious sect of the Sadducees cease, denying the resurrection.

Let Aristotle cease, and likewise Manes, who resembles them and says that the body is a phantom. Let Priscillian cease, who confesses that the human soul is not God’s creation but a portion of God.

Our assertion, therefore, is this: we speak it not from our own will, but as believers in the divine Scriptures. God is the shaper of the human body in women’s wombs; and he who formed the bodies must necessarily make the soul for the bodies shaped by him.

Bracharius the bishop, too, in his doctrinal statements, which he says must be acknowledged throughout his entire Church, laid down the following among other things:

“Human souls did not exist from the beginning among the other intellectual natures, nor were they created all at once, as Origen imagines; nor are they sown together with bodies through sexual intercourse, as the Luciferians, Cyril, and many presumptuous Latins affirm, as though the succession of nature required it.

“Rather, we say that only the body is generated through the union of marriage; that, by God’s judgment, it is coagulated, fixed, and formed in the womb; and that, once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused, so that a human being consisting of soul and body lives in the womb and emerges alive from the womb, complete in human substance.”

As for what the blessed Jerome and the distinguished Augustine established concerning the different opinions about the soul, and how they treated opposing positions against one another: the illustrious Jerome says that the fifth opinion is the truer, and our Bracharius also affirmed it. Augustine, however, sets aside the fifth opinion of Priscillian while likewise withdrawing his approval from the other four and leaving the matter solely to God’s knowledge. In my judgment, he alone perceived this matter beautifully and distinctly.

### 6.

For it seems by no means doubtful, as far as the smallness of my understanding reaches, that the body, an insensible piece of matter, is regenerated only together with its soul, since it was made from Adam into a living soul; afterward he appeared as a transgressor, and after the sin he begot Cain.

### 7.

The Apostle Paul says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death.” Indeed, from the one Adam sin began to reign in this world, and it reigned over those who followed the likeness of Adam’s transgression; and therefore judgment came from one offense to condemnation (Romans 5:12–16).

And again: “Through one new Adam grace began to reign, and through righteousness it reigned in all.”

But since the distinguished Jerome mentioned above, together with his associates, preaches that new souls are created and inserted individually into individual bodies, and since blessed Augustine raises a doubt about this, the question is hard and obscure, an intricate, difficult, arduous, and inextricable knot, soluble by God alone.

### 8.

We have sent you the annotation concerning the heretic Mammet, appended at the end of this letter. We have also sent you that part of the discourse which we found among our elders, more quickly than you requested.

*Note:* *Maturius*, as Cicero says, means “more quickly,” “sooner,” or “more speedily.” You see that it is an adverb, from the verb *maturat*, meaning “he hastens” or “he accelerates.” Hence the adverb of the comparative degree *maturius*, just as *insipientius* means “more foolishly,” *stultitius* “more stupidly,” and *aptius* “more suitably.” These adverbs did not arise independently but were derived from other parts of speech.

### 9. Annotation concerning Mammet, prince of the Arabs

Mammet the heretic arose—the seal of the Arabs’ false prophets and the forerunner of Antichrist—in the time of the emperor Heraclius, in his seventh year, while the era was running at 656. At this time Isidore of Seville flourished in our doctrine, and Sisebut held the summit of royal authority at Toledo.

This wicked prophet, they say, and his followers, shone with such miracles that, even in the heat of his lust, he took another man’s wife and joined her to himself in marriage; and, as we read of no prophet having done this, he presided over a camel whose understanding he possessed.

When death intervened, and he promised that he would rise again on the third day, he was found and devoured by dogs through the negligence of those guarding him. He held the principate for ten years; when these had been completed, he was buried in hell.

* Aera 717.

The Moors came into Spain in the time of King Roderic, in the ninety-first year of the Arabs, in the era 1113, in the year 468 of the Arabs.*

*Note:* The passages marked with asterisks were written not by the first hand but by a second, though still an ancient hand, with a certain empty interval between the paragraphs.

### 10.

If you cannot send the book of Lord Eulogius, then send us at least those syllables which are arranged in order—that is, the *a* followed by what follows it, and whether that vowel is lengthened or shortened; likewise *e* through *u*, and then *ba, be, bi, bo, bu*, and the remaining syllables through the end of this work.

If you cannot send the book, write these syllables to us and order that they be sent quickly. May Christ thus grant you comforts and frequently bestow good things upon you. Amen.

May your wisdom remain happy for a long time. Amen.

If he has lent you that book, make known to us the number of days after which I should have it returned. If you grant permission, we greet every beauty of your household. May I soon deserve to behold your cheerful face and rejoice together with you. Amen. Finished.

## VII. THE LETTER OF ALVARUS TO ABBOT SPERAINDEUS

### [Col. 0461B]

To the most beloved lord and Father in Christ, Sperandeus the abbot, Alvarus, his servant.

### 1.

The all-knowing and almighty God, foreseeing the times into which we have fallen and the powerful hunger for the word of God that we suffer, has sent you to us as a strong provision,

*Note:* The manuscript reads *valida . . . destina . . .* The word *destina* is discussed above, letter 4, number 7, at the end.

so that you might feed our hunger and restore our hearts with the dishes of nourishment.

But since I now know that you are devoted to tribulations or oppressed by bitterness, I ask you to take up the Apostle’s saying as an expression of consolation. For he says, concerning the dangers of tribulations that he endured: “In dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness, in dangers among false brothers” (2 Corinthians 11:26).

And afterward, in another place, he said: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance; endurance, testing; testing, hope; and hope does not disappoint us” (Romans 5:3).

Therefore, venerable Father and best of all priests, do not keep silent about what has been requested because of the dangers of tribulations, but grant what your servant seeks, because the hand is increased by giving and diminished by refusing.

Moses the lawgiver instructed me when his discourse thundered: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will announce it to you” (Deuteronomy 32:7). And because I remember you as a spiritual father, I therefore seek spiritual aid.

The reason is that the heresy which my negligence long ago brought to your attention is tearing apart the Church of God and, through the assertion of the Itehalian band, dragging a crowd after it to death. For, in the Apostle’s words, “the speech of heretics spreads like a cancer through the hearts of the humble” (2 Timothy 2:17), especially since “the poison of asps is under their lips” (Psalm 13:3).

For this reason we earnestly request your assistance and support, so that their murky and abominable heresy may perish through heavenly power and the radiant doctrine of Christ’s bride may shine forth through you. Their objections are those which I have already communicated to you.

### 2.

The chief point of those most wicked men, which must be cut away by the sickle of truth, is this: they do not believe in three in unity and one in Trinity. They reject the sayings of the prophets and repudiate the teaching of the doctors; they say that they accept the Gospel, yet they misunderstand what is written:

“I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17).

They assert that Christ, our God and Lord, was merely human, on account of what they read about him in the Gospel:

“But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, except the Father alone” (Matthew 24:36).

Nevertheless, with every effort I ask that you oppose these old-womanish questions of the pagans,

*Note:* Supply “oppose,” or something similar.

because they produce deadly consequences for those who hear them, especially those who are inexperienced and do not examine the texts of Holy Scripture.

May you adorn these two responses, as you are accustomed to do in other cases, more fully with the flowers of Scripture. And through the one statement of the advocate which we have brought before you, may you publish an appropriate response.

Thus may you receive from the Lord a radiant dwelling in the holy heavenly kingdoms. Amen.

## VIII. THE LETTER OF SPERANDEUS TO ALVARUS

To my most illustrious lord, venerable and renowned Alvarus, whom I embrace with every affection in Christ and in charity, Sperandeus.

### 1.

While I was exceedingly occupied by the strongest tribulations, and my mind—or spirit—was in turmoil, entangled in the darts of rivals and pierced by their arrows,

*Note:* The manuscript reads *inredditus, telisque confossos*.

I sat wounded by the injuries of weariness, and my spirit, surrounded by bitterness, tossed like a ship amid the gulfs of the sea. Suddenly your messenger came in to me and brought me the gift of a letter.

I read the written message quickly, and immediately recognized the words of your serenity. As soon as they shone brighter than light, they illuminated me, already almost dead, and at once that inner person was raised up.

I began, astonished, to consider who I was, or who he might be through whom I, such as I was, deserved to be raised up; and I wondered why he should inquire about such difficult questions from the sacred Scriptures, when nowadays not a few people prefer to linger not over this, but over vulgar expressions, paying no attention to the Lord’s saying:

“Every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36).

Or they wish to extend their tongue in criticizing their companions, not remembering the sacred Gospel:

“You see the speck in your brother’s eye, but you do not consider the beam in your own heart” (Matthew 7:3).

Some immediately believe the harmful things that enemies spread for their brother’s ruin and do not recall the Psalmist’s words:

“The words of the enemy are iniquity and deceit” (Psalm 35:4).

The hearers themselves then quickly circulate the inventions of their enemies and expose them to others while insulting their brother, casting behind them the words of the holy Apostle:

“He who speaks evil of his brother and judges his brother speaks evil of the law and judges the law” (James 4:11).

We must carefully withdraw ourselves from such falls, lest the Lord’s voice through the prophet Jeremiah clearly thunder against us:

“I attended and listened, says the Lord: no one speaks what is good; there is no one who repents of his sin” (Jeremiah 8:6).

Therefore, contemplating our offense at every moment and awaiting the end of our former life, we ought, with most holy compassion, to offer a tearful groan for our brother’s fall and fulfill and proclaim the Apostle’s words:

“Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29.)

We must not therefore readily believe when someone’s ears are struck by slanderous words, unless they have first been usefully examined and faithfully recognized. We have an example in the words spoken by the Lord:

“The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave. I will go down, therefore, and see whether they have completed in deed the cry that has come to me; whether it is so or not, that I may know” (Genesis 18:20).

Why does the almighty Lord, who knows everything, seem to doubt before an inquiry, unless he is also setting before us an example of carefulness, so that we do not presume to believe evil about a person before testing it?

And therefore he says:

“I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the cry that has come to me; whether it is so or not, that I may know.”

### 2.

But I shall omit all these things which I have spoken through contrition of heart and return to what your excellence requests.

For who would dare say anything about so ineffable a matter, when the blessed Jerome says:

“The mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation and the sacrament of his birth are indescribable. Therefore we do not attempt to make known how great the birth itself is, but only as much as we are able to express in speech.

“Indeed, however great the birth itself is, we can not only not explain it fully, but even the holy evangelists were unable to state it completely. And if the holy evangelists, who were certainly inspired by the Holy Spirit, were unable to speak of it fully, then, from what they recorded in the books of the Gospels in an incomplete manner, it is better to remain silent than to assert, and rightly to believe the things as they were spoken than, by scrutinizing the letters, to commit something to writing, according to the true sentence of the doctor which has been set forth:

“‘We believe the Father with his Offspring, and the kindly Spirit, in three persons; we believe the Godhead one. How the untouched birth proceeded from the Virgin, or how the one born wished to suffer—let no one treat of this, but only believe it.’

“Even if treating of this is forbidden, who would then dare to write anything about it with a pen or utter it with his tongue?”

### 3.

And because, against these points recorded in your letter, you seek testimonies from the books of the Gospels and the Apostles in order to scatter their schemes and strongly confirm what is doubtful, your kindness is nevertheless better able to do this, since no tribulation or worldly adversity has ever wearied it.

Therefore complete integrity remains in your understanding and judgment, since the harshness of this world has already crushed me in almost every way.

But because, as I believe, you are fully sufficient for this work, you seek nothing else from me except that you may be able to recognize the text of my belief. I shall humbly set forth what I believe and simply explain what I think concerning the questions you have asked.

Whatever our lord, your father, may there perceive to be contrary to the rule of truth, let the speed of the scribe immediately correct it and secretly instruct me again, as he once instructed others, for the sake of your honor. Let your prudent skill conceal the fact that I am ignorant and uninformed, so that no one outside may notice the error. For this has been sent to your highness to correct, remove, or add.

Behold: as your excellence commanded, I, your servant, have discharged the service as best I could.

But I shall introduce those objections which are marked in your letter under the name of the advocate; I shall produce, from your text, testimonies of the holy Scriptures; and, together with the sayings of the doctors,

*Note:* Read: “together with the sayings of the doctors, and so forth.”

I shall connect what I write in response. Finished.

## IX. THE LETTER OF ALVARUS TO THE PHYSICIAN ROMANUS

To my most serene lord, supreme among all Catholics, Romanus, Alvarus.

### 1.

Recalling the friendly sweetness of my predecessors toward you, most serene lord, and frequently proving the affection of your glory amid our compassionate wounds,

*Note:* Read: “in the compassion for our wounds.”

I have decided to send to your presence these connected lines of my ineptitude, arranged in an uncultivated style and composed in an unpolished text.

*Note:* That is, *contiguos*, “adjacent” or “connected.”

Through them I may renew our charity toward our misery and blunt the attacks of our adversaries through an apologetic work.

At the beginning of our rustic letter, I ask that you receive with a cheerful face and peaceful mind the petition of your servant or son, and weigh whatever he says on a reasonable balance.

May you not, according to the law of the gravity of your exalted ears, which are chiefly adorned with the strength of moderation, open their hollow to light or empty whispers gathered from elsewhere, lest—God forbid—it drink falsity to its own scandal and, receiving what has not been approved, dissolve a charity rooted in antiquity.

Although the advocate may argue the first part of his proposition with copious insistence and think that he has established it by sufficient proof of his own, nevertheless an argument that rises in isolation is always considered ineffective before honest judges if it is not restrained by the barrier of an opposing party on the other side.

The defense of the second part is awaited; freedom and permission are granted; and a perpetual judgment is issued only after the final matters have been thoroughly examined and understood.

Let this much suffice to have been said in the preface; for a wise person, to have begun is enough to have advanced toward explaining the whole.

2. And thereafter, my most exalted lord, recall my affection for you and for all your people from the very beginnings of my infancy; and, since you yourself know me well, believe me rather than those who, speaking against me, make adverse reports about me [Col. 0465A]. My pride and rapacity—or rather, my life of insolence—are, as I think, known to you more fully than to others. Whatever has been done from my earliest age up to the present, as I believe, has not been hidden from you but is known to you. And certainly it remains plain and known to many that I have been entangled in numerous snares and addicted to a thousand evils up to this point. Often, too, the adversity of the times turns even the most patient spirit away from gentleness toward something else. But, with the most present and most high Creator helping me, I made all those opposing me my closest friends; and, employing the skill of my mind through certain bonds of peace, I embraced my adversaries with the hand of affection, smoothing them with humility and soothing them with love.

Yet my wickedness, and the fault of the ignorance of my youth, justly keep raising their heel against me. [Col. 0465B] Hence everything that was begun otherwise rises up in opposition. For, with God as my witness—God whom I await as the examiner of my conscience, indeed of this letter as well—whatever Manichaeus Felix [Note: The manuscript reads “Maniceus felix.”], whatever the confessor [Note: On the word “confessor,” see below, Letter 13, no. 1.], and Julianus repeatedly and importunately assert to you and thrust against me through false accusations, happened not by the intention of my mind but by accidental circumstance. That same religious man knows this truthfully, yet, trampling upon his own conscience, he disregards what is known, while asserting and defending what is unknown.

3. And, setting aside for a little the method of narration, let me state what must be observed about how the matter was handled. Certainly, before the deterioration of my illness and before the remedy of penance that I received in my final necessity, I enriched that holy monastery and place with many gifts and many possessions [Col. 0465C]. What my father, of blessed memory, had never done before me, nor had anyone else of our family done, I alone fulfilled of my own accord. The accuser himself cannot deny this, and the whole neighborhood bears witness to it.

And now, when the law of penance bends the most wretched man down, and weakness has overtaken one who is already at the point of death, would I have closed the door of life against myself and rushed headlong into the cavern of the abyss? But I shall make clear, with God and the present accusers as witnesses, how the matter was handled and by what arrangement the transaction was carried out.

4. I wanted to redeem that entire place for myself, and, fleeing the disturbance caused by the Romans [Note: Florez, in his Prolegomena, discusses this word: Aldrete, in book I, chapter 6, understood the name “Romans” here to mean Spaniards descended from Romans, in contrast with those descended from Goths. But to the Moors both groups were the same, all equally subjugated; and thus Gómez Bravo proceeded better when he said that they were soldiers from France who were in the service of the king of Córdoba, and were called Romans because western France was called Roman on account of its language, in contrast with eastern or Teutonic France. See the authors cited in Du Cange’s Glossary, under “FRANCIA,” or Pagi on the year 888, no. 5.], I preferred to seek out the very prince whom you know. For the confessor had rightly said that those who possessed things bought from my father or from me wanted to sell them; and our plan, together with him, was to send the prince to them craftily and not in truth, and through him to gather our possessions for ourselves, reckoning that we were advancing his honor and the place, and that no one could resist him in bringing the matter to an end.

When, during those days of my illness on which he had come to visit me, I made this request of him and explained everything I desired, he promised to fulfill it and said that he would bring it to completion without difficulty. We therefore immediately, suspecting nothing of what later happened, made the sale to him and confirmed it through witnesses, so that by his entry we might deceive the others and through him attach the whole territory to ourselves.

But, hindered by his preoccupations and not sufficiently concerned about what had been arranged, he began to consign our affairs to forgetfulness and to postpone his care for things in which he had no possession and had given nothing. The robberies increased, as did the privileges of the Romans, who, crossing the boundaries of our lands, threatened to invade the entire place [Col. 0466B]. We, however, were now thought to possess nothing there, while the man who had made the purchase wanted to claim the invasions.

Placed in such a conflict, afflicted by remorse, we lamented in contrition and sorrow. After six months or more, the prince himself came to me and requested that he should truly buy what he had supposedly purchased. At first, with God as my witness, I refused, and I begged him repeatedly not to transfer my inheritance to others. But he opposed his benefaction to me, asserting that, if he had received it from me as a gift [Note: The manuscript reads “donitum.”], it would be nothing in return for the many things [Note: The manuscript reads “pro tanta,” “for so much.”] he had done for us.

But when I came to myself and considered the sale that I had already made to him, and weighed his power against my weakness, I immediately resolved to consent, because I could do nothing else. I nevertheless pointed out the church’s boundary, which I, not my father, had given; I fixed it in the purchase document, with those present subscribing; I commended the confessors themselves many times; and, as far as I could, I did not cease to make representations on behalf of that place.
