Yet, through my offense and by my very foul merit [Note: From the word *olim*, “formerly,” some have derived *olitum* or *olidm* as a term for “ancient.”], the matter was handled otherwise than I had thought. He gave as much as he wished, whenever he wished, and in whatever manner he wished.

5. What must now be done, most serene lord? We have neither the ability to resist, nor the means of restoring, nor the abundance required to redeem. With God as my witness, I groan, roar, and lament what has happened; but I cannot heal or repair what has taken place. At intervals I made representations to him, and I promised a price far greater than what he had given, indeed a more abundant price [Note: The manuscript reads “abundantiorem,” “more abundant.”]; but until now I have remained suspended.

We are blamed and accused by everyone [Col. 0466D], but we ourselves detest ourselves still more. And although, according to the venerable pronouncements of our teachers, in every matter it is not the execution of the deed but the will to perform it that must be considered; and one must not immediately ask what someone did, but with what intention he did it; and it is not the deed itself that is performed but the quality of the mind and the purpose of the doer that must be judged; nevertheless, however the matter may have been conducted, we impute it to our own merits. With trembling heart we declare, amid no ordinary lamentations [Note: That is, “with no ordinary griefs.”], that the Lord’s judgment pursues us daily; we despair of our exceedingly evil deeds [Note: *Opera*, “deeds,” is equivalent to *opus*, “deed.”], yet we trust in his accustomed mercy.

Your prudence has now been shown the whole manner in which the matter was handled. I have taken care to recount each detail to you because I heard many things attributed to you, apparently in praise of that confessor, which I could not believe, since I have often sensed your own disposition toward me.

6. At the end of the letter, prostrate at your feet, I entreat you: since poverty and weakness have made me absent from you [Col. 0467B], may your goodness always make me present in your heart. Examine malicious reports with that paternal discernment in which I know you to be strong; pass by the incantations of discord with deaf ears; and hold us commended to your very heart.

Whatever Felix, son of the judge Gratiosus, has inserted into the ears of Lord Servandus the count together with that confessor, your fatherhood, if you wish, will entirely erase. For in your time it was permitted us to explain the causes of others; how much more should we not resolve our own affair? Recall, I beg you, the bond of friendship with our ancestors, and embrace your son in your inmost heart.

I had wished to compose more, even if in plebeian speech, by arguing at length; but I did not wish to exceed the proper measure of a letter, and I feared joining foolish things to the wise. [Col. 0467C] But I ask that what I wrote more in haste than with deliberation, and painted more with grief than with polish, not be examined scholastically or according to the liberal art [Note: The manuscript reads “per liberali arte,” “by the liberal art.”], but be read again purely and simply, just as it was written.

7. May the flourishing happiness of your fatherhood, increased through the passage of years, remain vigorous and prosper. Amen.

X. LETTER OF THE BISHOP (AND, AS IT APPEARS, OF SAUL OF CÓRDOBA) TO ANOTHER BISHOP [Note: See the notice above.]

1. By what calamities and by what miseries, as justice has demanded, I have been crushed up to now, and by what sharp and unbearable pain I am assailed from different directions, I believe has been spread abroad to your blessedness by widespread report and confirmed by more truthful evidence of your presence, as though established through personal compassionate mercy.

And therefore, my most exalted lord, vicar of the apostles and follower of Christ, the maker of all things, extend to me the fraternal aid of your support with a correspondingly more abundant outpouring of tears, insofar as you see me oppressed above all others by the weight of offenses and by the enormity of scourges. May divine compassion—which, offended by my countless crimes, has until now inflicted wounds in the most just moderation of punishments—moved by your worthy prayers, now wipe away with its accustomed clemency the faults that we have quickly accumulated [Col. 0468A].

For the constant prayer of a righteous person can obtain what the wickedness of a sinner cannot deserve. It is your task, my lord, to extend your hand to a suffering brother and to lavish the help of consolation upon one wounded by the weakness of illnesses, so that you may both grant us the remedy owed to us and bring to its glorious completion the office assigned to you for the whole Church [Note: *Ravo*, p. 149, reads “indictum,” “assigned.”]. Amen.

2. Furthermore, my lord, I do not think the calamity of our province is hidden from your prudence. Wounded by a manifold plague and a great ulcer—or rather, brought even to the end of life—it has until now been savagely torn by a ferocious tooth, with bestial jaws and the wild barbarity of a beast.

But because, through the regard of the Most High and Most Present Creator, it has now begun somehow to breathe again after dreadful and palpable darkness, and has been able somehow to look upon the light—not by human ingenuity but by divine command—it has come about that the admirable right hand which knows how to humble the lofty and raise the fallen higher has removed, through delayed mercy, the plague that extended anger had brought upon it.

Desiring to pursue with fuller praise the grace of his benevolent and praiseworthy administration in these works, and wishing by effective effort to match it in every direction insofar as ability has been entrusted to us; granting concord to unanimity and striving utterly to uproot the mass of discord from its roots; having at once obtained the opportunity to present our presence personally to our brothers and fellow priests, whether sons; and carrying out what is true, partly with the severity of judgment and partly with the gentleness of a sentence that was growing more lenient—they fortified themselves with such abundant proofs of testimony and established themselves with so many judgments of the Fathers, which had acted with compassion toward the common people, [Col. 0468C] that it is almost impossible for one who claims to bind everything by judgment and by the example of the Fathers to oppose them in anything [Note: *Obviare*, “to oppose,” that is, “to contradict,” just as *obvius* means “contrary.”].

I confess, most holy lord, that I was astonished at the writings which they produced through the industry of such men [Note: The manuscript reads “ostipui.”]; and, after a truer and better-attested investigation had confirmed the opinion I had previously sought in another direction, I changed it toward the better course in the universal assembly. I did this lest, God forbid, driven by obstinacy of mind, I should nourish the fuel of discord, and, cutting off a member from the head, should attempt by an unjust judgment—contrary to the understanding of the Fathers—to cast away those whom conscience had shown to be free and innocence to be exempt from guilt.

Thus the whole Church might be stained by an unwarranted decree of cruelty—or rather by the arrogance of ignorance—something far from the practice of the shepherds of God; and, agreeing with heretics in contemptuous contention [Note: *Contentia* is equivalent to *contentio*, “contention.”], and pleasing insignificant, inexperienced, and ignorant little men, it might retain the name of universality—that is, “Catholic”—in a part and not in the whole, as it ought to do [Note: F. reads “retinerem,” “I should retain,” instead of “retinere,” “to retain.”].

For, according to the most truthful canonical decrees, tested by all ages [Note: F. reads “universis,” “by all,” instead of “universalis,” “universal.”], that the sin of the people should pass unpunished [Note: The text is defective: something such as “we ought” or “we are commanded” is missing; the author immediately continues, “If it is commanded to pass unpunished …”], as the venerable Pope Innocent sanctioned in his most approved decrees when writing to Bishop Rubius [Note: “Rufus” should be read. That decree is found in title 6 of Letter 22 of Innocent to the bishops of Macedonia, the first of whom is there named Rufus.] [Col. 0469A]. But if a sin proven by the deed or by suitable witnesses is commanded to pass unpunished for the preservation of charity, how much more is that not brought under the heading of guilt which, after investigation of the truth and knowledge of the witnesses—not through rashness or the impulse of usurpation, but solely from fear and under the pressure of the savagery of the most terrible time—was moderated, not without consideration, but with exceptional discernment and honorable dispensation?

How much has been dispensed in due season by the most blessed authorities of our faith, namely the apostles, according to the law of moderation and the good of discernment, and how much they did, is related with the clearest light and evident brilliance in their deeds. The letters of the most holy Jerome, an admirable man worthy to be praised throughout all ages, also testify to it. And, setting aside for a little the testimonies and the authority of the Fathers, matters which must be considered according to pastoral governance and anticipated with paternal diligence should be examined with more attentive and polished care.

Certainly, in the judgment of this agreement, bishops are not regarded as inferior to those of our order; and not only bishops but also some metropolitans are produced as clear proofs, partly by episcopal decree in letters and partly by their present participation in communion [Note: Perhaps “*communione*,” “in communion,” is intended.]. It is attributed to insolence or frivolity to raise the heel of pride against the metropolitans’ primacy, which has been established within the bounds of equity, when there is continually held throughout the world that unalterable judgment which commands that the privileges of metropolitans be examined not by neighboring bishops but by the Apostolic See [Col. 0469C].

3. Is it not, according to the venerable eloquence of Blessed Julian, metropolitan bishop of Toledo, considered the mark of an insane and foolish head to raise its feet where the reasoning of the head has not given permission?

But there are some who, cold in the fervor of the Lord, swollen with the boastfulness of vain glory, naked of knowledge, and rigid with pride, sow the contagion of dissensions and quarrels. Against the commandments of charity and unanimity, and under the veneration of God’s mystery and the invocation by which it is consecrated, they attempt through certain trivial opinions to defame the sacraments, saying that they are holy only when they have been touched beforehand by the hands of holy men. They do this against the judgment of Blessed Augustine, which he brought forward in his exposition of the tenth Psalm against the false-speaking vanity of people of this kind.

“For,” he says, “they do not trust in the Lord who say that the holy sacraments are holy only if they are administered by holy men.” But the admirable teacher Isidore [Note: Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 19.] also cuts down and eradicates their utterly empty and detestable presumption by these truthful teachings:

“Sacraments,” he says, “are so called from secret or sacred powers. They are therefore performed fruitfully within the Church because the Holy Spirit, remaining in it, secretly brings about the same effect of the sacraments. Hence, whether they are administered within the Church of God by good or by wicked ministers, nevertheless, because the Holy Spirit gives them life mystically—the Spirit who once appeared to visible eyes in apostolic times—the gifts are neither increased by the merits of good ministers nor diminished by those of wicked ones, because neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God, who gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:7). Hence in Greek it is called *mystērion*, ‘mystery,’ because it possesses a secret and hidden arrangement” [Note: The manuscript reads “habeant,” “they possess.”] [Col. 0470A].

The venerable Pope Anastasius also sets this forth, in a sufficiently splendid authority, with the same meaning, because it was inspired by the same Spirit, and in carefully composed speech, in his letter to the Emperor Anastasius concerning those who communicated with Acacius, a heretical and condemned man. For in the seventh chapter of that same letter he says:

“For, according to the custom of the Catholic Church, let your most sacred and serene heart acknowledge that none of those whom Acacius baptized, or whom he ordained as priests or Levites according to the canons, is touched by any share of harm on account of Acacius, so that the sacraments perhaps seem less valid because they were unlawfully handed on. Indeed, baptism, whether administered outside the Church or by an adulterer or by a thief, reaches the recipient as an unimpaired gift. For that voice which sounded through the dove excludes every stain of human pollution, by which it is declared and said: ‘This is he who baptizes in the Spirit and in fire’ (John 1:33) [Note: Thus the letter of Anastasius; the manuscript reads “quia,” “because.”].

“For if the rays of this visible sun, when they pass through the most foul places [Col. 0470C], are not stained by any pollution from contact [Note: The manuscript reads “quacumque,” “through whatever places.”], much more is the power of him who makes this visible sun not constrained by any unworthiness of the minister [Note: The manuscript reads “mysterii indignitate conficitur,” “is impaired by the unworthiness of the mystery.”].

“And even Judas, although he was sacrilegious and a thief, whatever he did among the apostles by virtue of the office entrusted to him, received no diminution in the benefits given through an unworthy man. The Lord made this clear in the most explicit words: ‘The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Therefore do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do; for they speak, and do not act’ (Matthew 23:3).

“Whatever, therefore, any minister in the Church appears to perform in his office for the benefit of the Lord [Note: The letter of Anastasius reads: “for the benefit of men.”], all of this is contained in the effect of the divinity, which fulfills it [Note: The manuscript reads “implenda divinitatis affectum,” “the affection of the divinity to be fulfilled.”]. Paul, through whom Christ speaks, affirms this: ‘I planted, Apollo watered, but the Lord gave the growth.’ Therefore neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God, who gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:7).

“Now the Lord does not ask who or what kind of person preaches, so that he confirms that even the envious preached Christ well. By this evil the devil himself was deceived [Note: The letter reads “dejectus,” “cast down,” rather than “deceptus,” “deceived.”], and he does not cease to preach it [Note: The letter reads “praedicare,” “to preach,” rather than “praecipitare,” “to cast down.”].

“And again, in the eighth chapter:

“Therefore this man, whose name we must refrain from mentioning, harmed only himself by administering good things wickedly. For the inviolate sacrament that was given through him obtained for others the perfection of its power.

“But if the suspicion of some extends so far that, after the judgment issued by Pope Felix, they imagine that Acacius subsequently acted ineffectively in the sacraments he usurped, and consequently fear that the mysteries they received in consecrations or in baptism were invalid, lest the divine gifts appear to be void, let them remember that in this matter also the superior principle prevails in the same way. For he performed this act not without usurping the name of the priesthood. Since the mysteries retained their power, the guilty person did not harm others in this respect either.

“For what was said in the Davidic trumpet [Note: The manuscript reads “davit.”] belonged to him: ‘Yet God will crush the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins’ (Psalm 67:22). For pride always brings ruin upon itself, not upon others, as the entire authority of the heavenly Scriptures testifies. As it is also said through the Spirit in the Prophet: ‘He who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house’ (Psalm 100:7).

“Therefore, although the condemned man claimed for himself the name of priest, the swelling of pride was inflicted upon his own head; for it was not the people, who thirsted for his gift in the mysteries, who were excluded, but only that soul which had sinned and was properly subject to the just judgment of its own guilt [Note: The letter reads “judicio propriae culpae erat,” “was subject to the judgment of its own guilt.”]. The abundant teaching of the Scriptures everywhere testifies to this.

“Therefore, setting aside all human efforts [Note: The edition reads “hominum,” “of men,” for the manuscript’s “omnium,” “of all.”] and schemes in the present frailty of our circumstances, according to our prayers and with imperial authority, offer to our God one Catholic and Apostolic Church [Note: The letter reads “offerre Domino nostro unam,” “to offer one to our Lord.”], because this alone is the Church in which those established not only on earth but also in heaven may triumph without end [Note: The manuscript reads “in qua,” “in which,” rather than “in quo,” “in which.”].”

And because canonical instruction again proclaims through the mouth of the most blessed Pope Celestine, in repeated and celebrated words, to the bishops established throughout Apulia, that the people must be taught, not followed; and that, if they do not know what is permitted and what is not permitted, they must be admonished, not given agreement.

4. We judged it right to provide for necessity and to approve ecclesiastical dispensations foreseen for the time—not through presumption [Note: The manuscript reads “presumptionis,” “of presumption.”], but through necessity—formed by apostolic, indeed canonical, instruction and by the truest constitutions. Otherwise, by unjustly pursuing what is just, contrary to the sanction of Moses the lawgiver [Col. 0471D], we might be branded with the disgrace of excessive justice and intemperance, contrary to Solomon’s command.

At this point we must recall the judgment which the most illustrious Pope Innocent delivered to Rufus and Eusebius and the other bishops concerning the restoration of Photinus. His venerable words must be repeated here. After many matters had been splendidly treated, he concluded as follows:

“For I willingly admit that you are anxious for salvation [Note: Add *audio*, “I hear,” from Letter 22 of Innocent to the bishops of Macedonia, at the end.], but I do not willingly admit it against the head, even if it must be done.”

It is as though he were saying: “I command you, therefore, to act with prudent diligence for the advantage and peace of the Churches; but I judge that you must in no way rise up against the head, or against him who rightly holds primacy among you, even if he has committed things deserving of reproach.”

But if the oversight of bishops is bound by such a bridle of sanction, by what bit is it right to close the mouths of common people who, presuming to undertake what is unlawful and not owed to them, arrogate to themselves judgment concerning the offenses of priests?

Nor am I unaware that those general judgments are usually brought forward which, circulating in a free and tranquil time, are thought to concern the general arrogance of those who do not consult their country but assert scandals and controversies. Those judgments truly apply to people whose necks are swollen with the tumor of pride, who devote themselves to license, who insolently defend anyone who is most arrogant, or who, sitting on one side, attempt with rash audacity to abandon the assembly of the whole; to those who protect a curse through the obstinacy of unbelief and bring aid to any impious person.

But these men were overcome by the impious man with hated cruelty and harshness, crushed by prison restraints [Note: *Claustra* was then in use in the feminine gender.] and the burden of excessive censure. With conscience as their witness, they have always pursued the accursed with curses; not out of love or through the effort of a most stubborn will, but crushed solely by necessity and royal command, they have attempted, with discernment and at the daily risk of their own lives, to dispense certain matters for the time being.

Why they should be pursued by an unconsidered mind, or punished by another’s sentence of death [Note: Perhaps “a deserved sentence.”] [Col. 0472C], I do not see at all [Note: “*Animus ordine*.” Perhaps this means “outside order” or “without order.”]. Human consciences and weaknesses must be examined, and the lives of subjects must be shaped from our own.

If we are willing to weigh with useful and devout compassion how much each of us who is a bishop has usurped over the flocks entrusted to him for the sake of the time, for pressing necessity, or through fear of those in power, then at once those who appear to be most merciful toward our own people will be proved more severe in attacking the offenses of subjects, if we choose to examine their faults differently from our own. For by the judgment with which we judge, we shall be judged.

And therefore, according to the judgment of Blessed Julian, that outstanding teacher, it is no less a matter of prudence to provide for an impending necessity than to apply the rudder of complete discernment. It is therefore more praiseworthy to choose certain suitable measures out of necessity than to formulate choices among matters that are available. And it is much greater to supply what is lacking with an adequate substitute than to postpone judgment over the arrangement of an abundant resource.

For there is salvation, and complete fullness of salvation, if useful counsel is extended where complete fullness is perceived, because without breaking the general form of a command, a specific judgment is introduced, and provision is made for an outcome that generality does not provide [Col. 0473A]. We do not therefore overturn the primitive arrangements, but order present circumstances more prudently, since the former prevails by universal decree and the latter by a special judgment.

5. In saying these things, we are not repeating what is unknown to you, but bringing back to mind what you know and ought to remember. Thus, if from this day and time forward any of our priests should be brought by any worldly necessity into your presence, let him not be regarded as accursed—far be that from us—or as an exile from your fellowship. Let him be received as your own, embraced as a son, and admitted as suitable to every service of the altar. He will gladly receive consecrated offerings from you and will also administer, even personally, the mysteries that have been prepared.

This is especially so since our fraternity judges the flock entrusted to it, by the firmest decree confirmed by the subscription of our hands, to be perpetually preserved safe and free from the slander of all whisperers, with that strength of stability by which it is found to have been confirmed in the past and present by the sanctions of the metropolitans.

We wish to fortify ourselves with your reciprocal letters and to be strengthened by fraternal aid in matters of peace and charity. But if anyone from our congregation, through depravity of heart, envy of mind, or the arrogance of seeking advancement, attempts to bring any frivolous charges to our ears [Note: Read “to your ears.”], despite your distinguished knowledge of the divine books, then, with that natural ability in which I know you to be strong, hasten to denounce the madness of those who speak evil. They despise the fellowship of unanimity and attempt, by abrupt and crooked paths, to direct their step upward into the heights, where they will fall in a precipitous descent [Col. 0473C].

Farewell.

XI. HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF ALVARUS ADDRESSED TO BISHOP SAUL.

A petition of Paul Alvarus to my most holy lord Saul, bishop.

1. There were many things that ought to have been written to your holiness, if the storm of the world and the calamity of our time had not hindered the service of speech. But since the bitterness of our straits and the enormity of our scourges have closed the fountain of eloquence and driven away the material for speaking under their weight, I therefore briefly, with God as the witness of all consciences, offer the service of greeting to your fatherhood with a loving heart and pure mind, and set forth my own misery [Col. 0473D] and petition.

I think it was not unknown to you that this year brought danger and the deterioration of my illness, so that, when I was approaching the boundary of death, I sought the remedy of penance and, after no small despair, found healing salvation. For the Lord, who kills and makes alive, leads down to the gates of the underworld and brings back (1 Samuel 2:6), after much punishment of judgment and a deserved correction by the scourge, recalled from the door of danger, through wondrous clemency, praiseworthy compassion, and singular power, the man whom his crimes had justly been leading to Tartarus. Blessed be his name forever [Col. 0474A], whose just judgments shine, girded with justice and compassion.

2. I have briefly noted for your fatherhood what was done. Now I humbly wish again to implore what must be done. Certainly, from the time of my illness until today, I have remained excluded from the saving remedy. Although I could have enjoyed reconciliation from elsewhere, if I had wished, nevertheless, desiring to fulfill what has been consecrated by the authority of the Fathers, I wished to seek your permission and resolved to return to communion by the command of your fatherhood.

For this reason I did not seek it elsewhere, because, with the Lord Jesus, God and our Lord, as my witness, I feared his judgment. Therefore I ask that a letter from your fatherhood be sent, through whichever of your priests you consider earlier, better, and more suitable, and that it impose upon them my reconciliation in whatever manner you wish [Col. 0474B].

I am ready to obey in everything and to give myself wholly to your salutary commands. Only do not deprive me of the remedy of communion, because I am plainly afflicted by immense weariness while I grieve that I am excluded from the wedding-feast of the Lamb. Whatever rule of fasting, almsgiving, or temperance in good works you impose upon me, I wish to fulfill, and in nothing to depart from the rules of truth or of possibility.

For our mind is ready to fulfill everything commanded and, insofar as ability permits, to restrain with the reins of temperance the mind that has hitherto wandered along crooked paths, keeping it from all unlawful commands and from everything prohibited by paternal ordinance.

3. Therefore I beg and entreat with tearful prayers that your fatherhood promptly command any one of your priests to absolve me [Col. 0474C]. But if something else must be done for us, let him again promptly write this to his humble servant, because our weakness is prepared to obey you in all things and does not desire, through proud insolence, to cross the boundaries of the Fathers.

Nevertheless, I shall await your written reply this week. If I do not deserve to receive it, I intend to implore reconciliation itself from your brothers and bishops, because I cannot remain deprived for so long of the body and blood of my God.

I have made this known to you because I desire to see your prompt response, and, bound by uncertainty, I hesitate to keep this feast among the others. May I soon deserve happily to enjoy your joyful countenance amid gladness and delight.

The end.

XII. THE REPLY OF BISHOP SAUL ADDRESSED TO ALVARUS.

[Col. 0474D]

1. There were many things that it was necessary for us to write before your eyes, but, hindered by my offense, I am daily occupied with lamentation, so that neither can my tongue recount what our mind suffers, nor can written characters express what is owed. Scripture says: “The dwelling-place of the senses, while thinking on many things, has failed” (Wisdom 9).

But since, in the letter of your affection which I received, your pen there set forth, as I think, your condition more fully—perhaps anxiously [Note: Read “*anxiat*,” “may distress,” instead of “*auxiat*,” “may increase”]—and I learned that you were laid low by excessive bodily weakness, so that you say you have no means of coming to see us, but wished that a written instruction be sent by me to one of the priests of Córdoba, through which, once you had been instructed, he might restore you, released, to the body of Christ; you say that there were some who had been compelled unwillingly to give an account.

Source preparation: Supplied local source; translated as part of this section.

2. What are we to say about these matters, when today we are bearing the time of silence? For we prejudice no one, condemn no one, neither justify what we do not know nor punish what we are ignorant of. But you, who know their minds and weigh their intentions, since access to see us is denied you, receive absolution from those from whom you also received penance. For if their laying-on of hands was then worthy, their absolution, once received, will now likewise doubtless be valid. As we have informed you, it is not for me to judge such matters unless, with God inspiring it, their legitimate council and our case have been fully debated (Col. 0475B).

But, so that I might first make this known to your sweetness, I inform you that this matter is forbidden to all the clergy while the bishop is present. The rule then says that this is permitted to the person to whom it has been entrusted when either the length of the journey or bodily weakness has prevented the bishop from being able to do it. But now what can you bring forward against this, when you have me present? Why, refusing my presence, do you ask for letters, and seek through written words what you can hear from my living voice?

Yet plainly I do not know whom you call “salted,” and mark as almost Migentian Donatists and Luciferians. For this reason I am surprised that you, a prudent and industrious man, condemn those who have thus far preserved conciliar censure, and who are said not to perish by the example of the multitude, but to retain unshaken in mind what the authority of the Fathers sanctioned, until the judgment of very many bishops either confirms the decree or moderates the decision adopted. Therefore, as we have said, they ought not to be regarded by us as rebels against the Church, since they appear to obey ecclesiastical laws.

Earlier, indeed, I wrote to you most affectionately but only partially, because I did not recognize the characters of your letter. But now, since we have found your own writing and recognized your hand, I have written to you in friendly affection for the remedy of your soul, earnestly wishing that you seek what is holy and avoid the company of the wicked. For it is said: “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Ecclus. 13:1). What absolution for receiving the sacraments can be available to you (manuscript: “could be”) if tomorrow you are seen in any way to be attached to a pseudo-bishop?

This is the Lord’s judgment, not ours: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot harm the soul” (Matt. 10:28). Solomon says something similar: “Whoever fears human beings will quickly fall; but whoever hopes in the Lord will be strengthened” (Prov. 29:25), and so forth—things that are not hidden from your prudence.

I ask that you first always discuss these and similar matters with yourself, and then admit the sacrament of reconciliation. But if you prefer something else, do what seems good to you, or what your prudence, when it teaches you, perceives. With these matters dismissed, I have said as much as I could; from many things I have learned, I have sent only a little to your charity. The saints of God remember you; so do I, in everything. We greet with a holy kiss all whom the enclosures of your house retain. May I deserve to see you in joy. Amen.

[Col. 0475D] That is, “I have made it known.”

[Col. 0475D] Concerning the errors of the Migentians, see *Hispania Sacra*, vol. V, p. 540 onward. See also vol. X, chap. 8, no. 10.

[Col. 0475D] Perhaps “by the decree.”

[Col. 0475D] *Cortis* here has the same meaning as “house.” See Ambrose de Morales, *On the Works of Saint Eulogius*, book II, chap. 8; and the Glossary of Du Cange, Maurist edition. *Claustra* is singular and feminine, as above in letter 10, no. 4.

## XIII. Likewise, Alvarus’s Letter Addressed to Bishop Saulus

1. We received a letter sent to us in your name, and recognized that its wording was not yours but that of that little man whom we have often proved to be an expeller from his homeland and a sower of many heresies. While we write purely and simply in our own hand, seeking remedies for our soul, you, by contrast, bite us maliciously and deceitfully—not from your own mind, but from a stomach wounded by many potions. You offer us not cups of life but poisons, and cast your son far away from your charity.

2. And not merely one person, but the entire flock, you judge to be diseased by I know not what counsel; you tear it apart not with medicinal remedies but with rasping teeth, and destroy your own members with your own hands. O, how many weapons ought to have been hurled against the destruction of that wicked man, if he had fought face-to-face, like a vigorous man, in battle, and had not secretly, like a tortoise and after the manner of women, sharpened his sword in the shadows! Condemned by his own judgment, he is properly neither a confessor nor a priest. His dress makes him a confessor, while his tongue proves him a mocker; his warp-threads and sheep’s wool present him as religious, while the length of his beard declares him a layman; the pretense of his conduct displays him as holy, while his rivalry in slander shows him to be arrogant.

What wonder if he slanders the priests of our time, when he attempts to overthrow teachers? If he strives to condemn clerics, when he does not hesitate to mutilate the struggles of the martyrs? Father, how many testimonies ought to have been brought forward for the destruction of that not most wise but most foolish little man, and how many arguments against his disorderly letter, if reverence for your honor did not restrain us!

[Col. 0476D] The antithesis between “mocker” and “confessor” suggests that *confessor* here means a singer, that is, someone belonging to the lower clerical order appointed to sing divine praises. Since “to confess” frequently means “to sing God’s praises” in Sacred Scripture, singers were called “confessors.” Thus the First Council of Toledo, canon 9, says: “Let no professed woman or widow, in the absence of a bishop or priest, perform antiphons in her house with a confessor or with her servant.” See Du Cange’s Glossary.

3. For the end destroys the beginning, and, without considering how he began, he wrote contrary things at the conclusion. The foolish editor, seeking holiness and wisdom, did not avoid foolish speech; and while accusing the condemned, as he strives to release one who is bound, he himself did not discover the person whom he would release by his attack.

I, my lord, having called upon the testimony of the divine majesty, set forth the misery of my danger and asked for a remedy. You, however, did not answer purely from yourself, but looked for some sophist to answer me as though I were an enemy—or rather, not a sophist but a solicitor—and you stir us, though we are at rest and grieve for your blessedness, toward the goad.

We have taken note, moreover, of Solomon’s sayings, and have learned from you that they were long ago scattered. Contrary to the institutions of the Fathers and the decrees of those who came before, we have seen you repeatedly associate with a certain anathematized man before our episcopal dignity, and we have proved that, after your elevation, you communicated with priests who communicated with him, without any fear of terror or occasion of dread, solely by the will of your mind and the affection of your love.

Surely you remember when you supplied him with a chasuble for the offering of Mass as clothing, and how much I suggested to you in those very days, moved by my love for you. You certainly do not fail to know how many were, by your command, irrationally released without a council from the anathema imposed by the Fathers. Recall, I beg you, the not-unblemished beginnings of your consecration, bordering almost upon the error of simony. For the beginnings of your canonical initiation could have been defended by anyone who made the claim, if four hundred solidi had not openly been paid to eunuchs or others—but not secretly: they were distributed by Arabic documents from the Church’s treasury, which is unlawful for debtors—and collected from that ministry from which it is not lawful to distribute anything even to faithful laymen, since the little possessions of the Church are divided among priests alone.

How many priests, I ask, were ordained without testimony? How many consecrated without the consent of the clergy or the sons of the Church? How many churches were divided by a doubled priesthood—that is, by two pastors—against the institution of the Fathers? How many were appointed by you to different ranks throughout all the basilicas, contrary to the canons? Look into these matters yourself, I beg you.

[Col. 0477D] Manuscript reading: *invectionem suam*. Bravo suggests *insectionem*.

[Col. 0477D] Manuscript: *a vos*.

[Col. 0477D] Possibly “Honorius?” At “only among priests,” the printed text has *super solos sacerdotes* (accusative after *super*), while the manuscript reads *super solis sacerdotibus* (ablative/dative: “upon/among priests alone”).

4. But you cast all these things behind your back and keep your eyes open only against the priests of our time. Nor do you do this at any other time, except when our suggestion obtains it from you. For you saw the honorable abbot Athanagild face-to-face and wished to say this to him in person; you ordered Eulogius to offer sacrifice at the first onset of the persecution; and now you fight against yourselves only because of our intervention.

O fortunate—indeed, very fortunate—will be the man whom the council you await shall find! Would that serenity might now return and the storm depart! I think that the tongues of many would fall silent, and that those mouths would impose a bridle upon themselves—those which, unable to speak, have hitherto hissed through caves.

For when you say, “Whoever fears human beings will quickly fall, but whoever hopes in the Lord will be strengthened” (Prov. 29:25), or that evangelical saying, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot harm the soul” (Matt. 10:28), you speak truly and religiously. But I wonder why one who teaches such courage hides himself, and, separated from his own people through fear of human beings, wanders about in various places.

As for what you ironically ordered at the beginning—that I be released by those who bound me—adding, “If their laying-on of hands was then worthy, their absolution will now also doubtless be valid”: that little scholar could never perceive what he said against himself in this passage alone, and, avoiding the saltiness of Sardis, does not know how he has fallen into brine.

If he said this sincerely and not ironically, why did he finally forbid us the company of the wicked and affirm that those who touch pitch are defiled? But if, as the text of the letter shows, he introduced this at the beginning in mockery and attempted by it to taunt us, let the sinewy man listen, that he may applaud himself as an advocate, and the woodland man, not a courtly dictator:

“What, then, does your pastor himself seek to release here and now, when transgressors, having no authority to bind, never bound him at all? How, then, can one who was not bound be released? For if you take away from them the power to bind, cease seeking to release one who was not bound.”

Let this also be said in answer to him: “As for the rest, we have the Lord of all as judge of our conscience, who can heal the weak without reproach. For although the Levite and the priest left the man wounded by robbers, that merciful Samaritan carried the half-dead man to the inn, poured oil upon his wounds, and paid the innkeeper.”

Nevertheless, my lord, I will seek no further judgment flowing from another’s mouth, because we are thoroughly weary of serving the judgments of others, and not your own pure judgments.

## XIV. Alvarus’s Letter Begins, Addressed to the Transgressor

[Col. 0478D] He mocks Eleazar, a Gaul by nationality and a Hebrew by faith, though a Christian.

### Alvarus to Eleazar, My Beloved

1. First, my beloved, I discharge the duties of salvation lovingly and sweetly, and, if it suits the rite and practice of your sect, I repeatedly offer you salutary obligations in fellowship. For the rest, I ask that the offering of our affection not become burdensome to you, since I desire to win you for the Lord.

2. But if you love as I love, strive repeatedly to win me by your zeal; for “whoever converts a sinner wins his soul and covers a multitude of his own sins.” David likewise pays what are almost vows in return for a great gift: “I will teach transgressors your ways, and the ungodly will be converted to you” (Ps. 50:15).

Therefore, favor my efforts: examine attentively the text of this little page, and look carefully not at the words but at the meaning. For we do not desire to scatter torches of ornamented phrases, but to bring forth for you the words of the simple and pure. Our assertion is not colored with a twofold cloak, nor does the speech of this discourse smell of Attic salt, but it proceeds in plebeian—or, so to speak, common—language.

Here Thucydides or Sallust does not arrange the path of knowledge, but Jacob and David lead their little ones to the sheepfolds. Here Cyrus does not lead an army by fighting, but Moses, with hands raised, turns aside the phalanxes of the Amalekites by prayer. Nor do we sing Memnonian hymns, or fashion verses in the song of the Aeneids; I do not lead forth the milky river of Libya, nor chant the war-song of the Iliads.

For the viperous tongue of Demosthenes is far from me, of whom Aeschines (the note corrects the printed *Oscines*) is reported to have said: “What if you had heard the beast itself uttering words with its own mouth?” My letter does not seek the favor of pagans, nor does it derive its coloring from the Athenian; rather, it is fragrant with the flavors of the prophets and bears on its surface the dishes of the patriarchs.

Indeed, if the birth of Christ were said to be destined at any definite point in the reckoning of years, the dispute between Christians and Jews would immediately have ended. For, once the years from the beginning of the world had been calculated, his coming into the world would be known without any impediment, so that neither the faithful would endure delays in asserting it nor the unbeliever find opportunities for rejecting it.

And because, as some think, Scripture left his coming uncertain, touching it almost as something untouched rather than predicting it, the opinion of all therefore deceives itself. This does not mean that everyone’s faith is enveloped in blind darkness, but rather that faith which is held more by opinion than by truth. I have discussed these matters according to the questions of those who are contentious.

For the rest, according to the knowledge of my littleness, I judge that Christ’s coming can plainly be learned from the legal sayings, if the prophecies of the seer are carefully investigated—prophecies that are brighter than light and life-giving. For although the years are not found fixed from the beginning of the world, they are nevertheless found most clearly numbered from the prophetic period onward.

I believe that divine judgment, foreseeing human madness and acumen, which differs in its reckoning of ages, preferred to insert the number from the time when it foresaw the sinew of contention to have been cut away. For you know the disagreement between the Hebrews and the Septuagint interpreters in calculating the total from the first man to the time of the Flood—so great that, according to the Hebrew truth, six hundred and fifty-six years are found from Adam to the Flood, while from the Flood to Abraham two hundred and ninety-two years are found.

3. According to the Septuagint interpretation, however, two thousand two hundred and forty-two years are counted from Adam to the Flood. From the Flood to Abraham, one thousand seventy-two years are calculated.

The divine Spirit, inserted into the hearts of the prophets, foresaw these disagreements long beforehand. He did not wish to assign the total from the time of Christ’s birth, since from that point he also protected the assertions of those who extend frivolous inventions. For although he did not express the number by naming it, he never left untouched the time in which Christ was destined to be born.

So that you may not think that I am recounting this in bare words, I shall now take care to bring forward living proofs. But before our argument is legally established, I ask you willingly to attend to what I say. Do not sharpen your understanding with the desire to win a contest; rather, with the intention of making progress, polish your judgment—both mine and yours—knowing that faith does not rest upon reasoning but upon truth and simplicity of heart.

Whoever is pure in mind sees the Lord. Therefore, if what I have brought forward is accepted, what I have suggested is welcome. But if what I have written is burdensome, I have not concealed my goodwill toward you. You likewise ought to show the same toward me, and, when you see someone whom you think to be in error, strive with all your strength and persist so that he may not perish.

[Col. 0480D] At “strive” the main text reads *cona*; the manuscript reads *conare*, likewise “strive/endeavor.”

Nor ought I to burden your mind, already occupied with many testimonies, knowing that a person for whom small things are not sufficient will find even a thousand insufficient. A wise man does not consider how many people are speaking, but knows usefully who those speakers are. Hence the prophet declared blessed the one who utters words into the ear of a listener, because hearing is said to deceive when the sluggish sense has not kept watch.

I could extract abundant testimonies concerning your rejection and the election of the nations, if I did not remember that this had already been done by highly learned men, your predecessors. Therefore, leaving aside what they—men distinguished in eloquence and holiness—wrote long ago in a more polished or eloquent style, as I said, I shall bring out brief testimonies that are not weak but strong, and by questioning you shall inquire what you think about them: whether you can teach me that I have been ignorant of what I firmly hold, or teach yourself that you do not know what I know without dishonesty.

4. Moses, the editor of the Pentateuch, the lawgiving author of Scripture and announcer of the world’s origin, when he introduced Jacob consulting his sons and, in place of a testament, declared by blessing what they should possess by hereditary right after their father’s death, spoke as follows:

“Jacob called his sons and said to them: ‘Gather together, so that I may announce to you what will happen to you in the last days’” (Gen. 49:1).

And, so that they might know what those last days were, he explained more openly in the blessings of Judah:

“The ruler shall not fail from Judah,” he said, “nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (ibid., 10).

Pay attention, my most beloved, open your understanding, and show me throughout the whole world even one leader from the tribe of Judah. I do not wish to thrust upon you the childish songs of frivolous people or their fictitious doctrines—those stories with which they habitually weave long tales on account of a single word.

And because they cannot find a king in the regions of human beings that are clearly known, I do not know why they seek a ruler beyond the sea. Even if that were true, he would less readily have been from the tribe of Judah, since the tribe of Judah was not led away by Sennacherib or by Artaxerxes, who was also called Ochus, but was dispersed throughout the lands by Vespasian and Titus.

For just as the prophet proclaims with a clear trumpet that no temple, no altar, and no ruler remained for you:

“The children of Israel shall sit for many days,” he says, “without king, without prince, without sacrifice, without altar, without priests, without manifestations” (Hos. 3:4).

Do you understand that these are the days which the prophet Hosea foretold? Or perhaps the blind opposition of the Jews says that they are still awaiting worse days.

Here we must review the kings—not from the time of Judah, those who are known and who proceed in a straight line through David and Solomon down to Zedekiah, but from the time of Daniel and after the Babylonian captivity had been released, when they proceed through rulers.

Therefore, as I said, I shall enumerate your kings from the time of Daniel and briefly indicate when they came to an end. If that people had anyone afterward, under whom it existed as a ruler, please state his name.

5. The first to rule after the prophecy of Daniel, once the people had returned from Babylon, were Jesus son of Josedec and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel. After them, Joachin son of Jesus succeeded to the high priesthood. Eliuth succeeded him; Joiada succeeded him; then John; afterward Jadus. After him, Onias; then the high priest Eleazar ruled. Another Onias succeeded him. Then Judas, succeeded by his brother Jonathan. After him came Simon, the brother of both. Then John, after whom came Aristobulus. Alexander succeeded him; he was both king and high priest.

After him, his wife Alexandra ruled the people with her sons Hyrcanus and Aristobulus. At that time Herod, son of Antipater, after killing Hyrcanus, received the kingdom of the Jews by decree of the senate.

Your charity does not fail to know that our Christ was born in his time. If you attempt to await another, show us rulers from the tribe of Judah in your nation even to this day. Then you will establish that you are awaiting redemption, when you have supplied the lack of the tribe of Judah with rulers.

But if you can find no king who has provided leadership by his voice up to the present, examine the prophecy of Daniel more attentively, and then you will more truly prove that the confusion already owed to the Jews has arrived, beginning at the place where the angel speaks to Daniel, saying:

“Daniel, now I have come forth to teach you and to make you understand” (Dan. 9:22).

From the beginning of your prayers the word went forth, until it concluded with this statement:

“After sixty-two weeks Christ will be killed, and the people, together with the coming leader, will destroy the city and the sanctuary; its end will be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed.”

You see that after Christ’s death divine Scripture promised devastation to all the Jews. And if you still await Christ—that is, the Messiah—you must surely fear an even greater desolation, because from his coming until the end of the world he announces to you not redemption, as you vainly suppose was promised, but devastation, as the angel said to Daniel.

And where then will the daughter of Zion be left, since she exists nowhere? Where is the sanctuary that the people destroyed together with the coming leader, who has been reduced to ashes? Let the Jews restore the state in which Christ will find it. Let them build the temple where the angel of the covenant may suddenly come.

Behold, your sacrifice too has ceased, so that your sins may be blotted out without any aid, since you no longer burn the offerings that you used to burn. The Law commands that, in captivity, it is not permitted to prepare royal anointing oil. From where, then, will your messiah be anointed, so that he may truly be believed, according to Daniel, to be the Anointed One?

6. But now we must come to the reckoning of years; and it must be calculated not according to our custom but by legal testimony, since the Lord says to Moses:

“You shall count seven weeks of years for yourself” (Lev. 23:15),

that is, seven times seven, which amount to forty-nine years. Therefore seventy weeks produce four hundred and ninety years. For seventy times seven is four hundred and ninety.

Accordingly, run briefly through Greek, Latin, and barbarian histories from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, to Christ the ruler, and you will find that the full number of the weeks was completed according to the Jewish reckoning of lunar months, by which they assign twenty-nine days to each month.

For from the twentieth year of the aforesaid Artaxerxes to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, four hundred and seventy-five years are found; these make four hundred and ninety Hebrew years, because the Greeks and Jews make intercalations of three months every eight years.

Therefore, as I said, the reckoning must begin from the twentieth year of this Artaxerxes, because in that year the word went forth that Jerusalem should be rebuilt, when Nehemiah the cupbearer made his request, as the angel said to Daniel.

But if you wish to calculate again from the first year of Darius, who was also called Melas, the successor of Cyrus, in whose reign the vision was revealed to Daniel, you will find Christ’s birth to have occurred in the sixty-second week.

7. If, after Christ’s birth, you prefer to calculate the remainder of the number of weeks, you will find it completed in the first year of Vespasian, when your captivity occurred.

I could have shown these things one by one by the names of the kings and the years of each ruler, just as I could have proved the legal successions through the books of the prophets. But although they may be proved by a truthful and manly assertion, they nevertheless require a faithful listener. Therefore I will not laboriously construct a lengthy tale about the periods of numbers or emperors; it is enough to have touched briefly upon what our elders thought about these matters, and to ask you, in a brotherly manner, what the leaders of the Synagogue have discussed concerning them. Thus I may learn what is true, and you may take pleasure in rejecting what is false.

Above all, I ask that you explain to me without the bitterness of gall what benefit there is in knowing these things. Do not refuse, in a more eloquent style and according to your judgment, to explain fully both the blessing that I brought forward from Jacob concerning Judah, and also what was declared by Daniel and the prophets. Explain it either according to what you think or according to what is set forth by the teachers of the Jews, and write the whole matter to me with friendly zeal.

For although the sayings of the prophets contain many splendid testimonies favorable both to us and to you, nevertheless, when all have been usefully sifted, they do not seem to me—or to us or to you—to break mouths against a rock or crush mouths with a hook. These alone are presented with such force that, once their interpretation has been received, none of us can even murmur.

But if you foresee that this interpretation must be rejected and not followed, draw out what ought rather to be held, asserted in a more enduring and stronger argument. Do not construct your rejection of this interpretation with bare words alone. After you have proved soundly that it is false, produce another interpretation that does not allow those who follow it to go astray, so that you may conquer your opponent and teach your friend as a disciple.

I wish you always good health, most reverend and beloved one—my brother by nature, though not by faith. Finished.

## XV. The Transgressor’s Reply Addressed to Alvarus

### Eleazar to Alvarus, My Beloved

You wrote to me, good man, about how I and the leaders of my Synagogue understand the words: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs,” and what follows. This is as clear as daylight to us. If you were present now, I would ask you what sort of scepter the children of Israel had, or which leader they had, during those seventy years when they were in cap[lacuna] Nebuchadnezzar, and as yours …

*(Fourteen lines on this page have been so completely erased that not a single word can be read. The owner of the manuscript cut out the following leaf so that the transgressor’s ravings would not be read.)*

## XVI. Likewise, Alvarus’s Letter Addressed to Eleazar

### Alvarus to Eleazar, My Beloved

1. I have read the letter of your response, most reverend brother, and I have recognized that the attack brought against me was arranged in reverse order. For my objections have in no way been weakened, nor was an answer offered to each of the objections. Instead, the style merely drove souls headlong into blasphemy, and the writer of the Synagogue composed mocking little works. As lovers of Christ, we shall cast against him not missiles of ornamented words, but shall openly and purely investigate the rule of truth.

Yet I am surprised that you, a prudent man and, as your style proves, thoroughly trained in the liberal arts, should have thought so superficially—at least in divine matters—as to try to equate the seventy-year captivity with the lifetime of one king alone, after so many and such long periods have already passed.

Leaders and royal scepters from the tribe of Judah never ceased, because Jeconiah, who was led away to Babylon, had a son, Shealtiel, from whom Zerubbabel was born. To him the word is directed through the hand of Haggai:

“The word of the Lord came through the hand of Haggai, in the second year of Darius, to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, ruler of Judah, and to Jesus son of Josedec, the high priest” (Hag. 1).

You see that rulers from the tribe of Judah never ceased. Even while in captivity, that tribe never lost its precedence.

As for your new argument—that the Hebrew does not have it this way, but signifies something altogether different in other words—I am amazed at the speed of your learning in the Hebrew language. After eight hundred and forty years, you attempt to console the folly of the Jews, although this interpretation had never before entered their minds.

They were accustomed to seek a king beyond the sea, not to overturn the words of the prophecy by another interpretation. For if this is so in Hebrew—*Sabet* and *Amhokek*, which sound in Latin as “tribe” and “teacher”—why has it not been brought against us throughout all these years, when they admitted that they had a king or ruler across the sea, and had a freer and easier assertion available to them: that this was not found at all in Hebrew? Unless perhaps you, a Gaul, have understood in their writings what the leaders of the Synagogue had hitherto ignored, and a Latin has found in Hebrew writings what a Hebrew did not know.

Truly, the assertion of this frivolous investigation must be blunted by the reckoning of faith. For both our teachers and your elders used to tell us nothing other than that you sought a king for yourselves from transmarine regions. Examine the interpretation of this remarkable teacher, our Jerome, and, if you wish, prove it from other passages of Scripture.

2. But before I begin comparing the editions of the individual interpreters, is it fair, good man, for you to tear apart with dog-like bites not only one who is absent but also one who is enjoying eternal rest? Did Moses the lawgiver teach you to bring before judges, against an absent man, testimony not proved by your own eyes, and to say that one whom you know to have left his parents’ estates and abundant wealth was driven by love of money? Do you also assail with malicious accusations a man whose conscience is chaste—a man who, for devotion to virginity, rejected fasting, austerity, and the pleasures of worldly wealth? For one who abandoned his own possessions—how could he have sought another’s out of love of money?

But you, my brother, how do you dare accuse another in the very matter which you proclaim to everyone to have abounded in you within our doctrine, boasting that, through intercourse with various women, you enjoyed embraces sweet to you in our temple?

That abyss of knowledge and unfathomable ocean, Jerome, if he were alive today, certainly would not let you breathe. He would strip bare the thorns with which you are covered and, like a victor—as he was accustomed to triumph over everyone—would either bring you into his own ranks or throw you half-alive into the remotest lands. And when you boasted of the doctrines of philosophers or Jews, he would cast you down so completely that, with his accustomed firmness, he would sing those words to you:

“Have you any further place to stretch the sinews of your loquacity?”

[Col. 0484D] Corrected to *Sabet et Amhokek*. The printed form is *Seber et Amohkec*.

[Col. 0478D] At “almost vows,” the manuscript reads *nota* (“note”); [Col. 0479D], at “arrange the path of knowledge,” it reads *scientiam*; at “does not seek the favor of pagans,” it reads *non ad ethnicorum* (“not [for] the favor of pagans”); at “legal sayings,” this means *in dictis legalibus* (“in the legal pronouncements”); and at “calculating,” perhaps *in calculorum* (“in the calculations”). [Col. 0480D], at “strive,” the main text reads *cona* and the manuscript *conare* (“strive/endeavor”); at “small things are not sufficient,” the manuscript reads *sufficit parva* (“small things suffice”); and at “utters,” it reads *proferit* rather than *profert*. [Col. 0481D], the manuscript omits “many days”; [Col. 0482D], perhaps read *ad tempus* (“at the time”), and the manuscript reads *si* for “just as”; at “from Jacob concerning Judah,” it reads *quam a Jacob jube*; [Col. 0483D], perhaps read “what I have declared from the prophets,” and, at “go astray,” perhaps *errare* (“err”).

### 3

We must now come to the editions of the Seventy Interpreters and add a few brief chapters by way of example. For in Zechariah (chapter 11) the Septuagint rendered the passage as follows:

“If it is good in your sight, give me my wages, or refuse. And they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: ‘Put them into the furnace, and see whether it has been proved, as I have been proved by them.’ And I took the thirty pieces of silver and put them into the house of the Lord, into the furnace.”

Our luminary Jerome translated it thus:

“If it is good in your eyes, bring me my wages; and if not, refrain. And they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: ‘Cast it to the statuary, the handsome price at which I was valued by them.’ And I took the thirty pieces of silver and cast them into the house of the Lord, to the statuary.”

[Col. 0485B] [Note: Manuscript reading: “cast it to the statuary, of whose price that.”]

Although the sense is the same, the wording is reversed and almost entirely different.

Likewise, in Isaiah:

“Behold, the virgin shall receive in the womb and shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isa. 7).

In place of this Jerome has:

“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and she shall call his name Emmanuel.”

For “you shall call” is one thing, and “she shall call” another. Decide for yourself who translated better, although the other Interpreters rendered it “young woman” or “young girl.” But you will find the Hebrew word *almah*—“virgin”—used of Rebekah while she was still a virgin, and of Mary, the sister of Aaron, before she was joined to a man. It signifies one who is hidden and carefully guarded.

Therefore, in the title of the psalm where *alma, noth* is written, the Septuagint said: “For the hidden things.” Likewise, in the Book of Job, where it says, “and it is hidden from the eyes of every living thing” (Job 28:21), the Hebrew has *almah*, differently formed because of the inflection of the verb. And in the Books of Kings it is written in the person of Elisha speaking to Gehazi: “And the Lord hid it from me” (4 Kings 4:27)—something similar, although it is inflected in the masculine gender.

If, then, you are willing to regard Rebekah and Mary as virgins, for whom you never read the word “old woman,” what impudence is it to deny to this one virgin what you concede to the others, whether you wish to or not? Show me anywhere that *almah* means a young woman and not a virgin, or anywhere that a married woman is called by this word, and I shall admit that I am ignorant or defeated.

The Punic language also, which derives from the sources of the Hebrews, properly calls a virgin *almah*. But whoever wishes to know the variations among the translators, or desires to disparage the inventions of the Jews, should read Jerome’s *Hebrew Questions* or his other works.

And plainly, as he himself declared, “despise the burps” [Note: Read: “burps,” for *ructus*.] and nausea of the Jews, and pass over their shouting with deaf ears. For this Jerome of ours, truly worthy not only of the world but also of heaven, whom you irrationally detest—why, I do not know—why do you gnaw him with your ravenous tooth, when you do not yet know his edition?

Recognize that this edition which you strive to prove false belongs to the Septuagint Interpreters, not to Jerome. He himself also criticized it in many of his works and proved, not without evident reason, what they had added and what they had omitted. Because of the variations among these editions, he learned the Hebrew language and soon gave the churches his own truthful edition in the Latin tongue.

You see that, while you wish to prove Jerome deceitful, you display your own ignorance. Moreover, you attempt to condemn your own Jews as wiser than the Septuagint and the others. If, as you say, he expressed everything in the Psalms word for word, why would one who was faithful in a small matter prove unfaithful in a great one? Unless it is because the edition of the Psalms is Jerome’s: consider from that edition how differently he rendered it from the Septuagint, so that by this you may recognize the faithfulness of the great teacher Jerome and the zeal and labor with which he strove to hand on the precise meaning of the Law to the churches of Christ.

### 4

But your people have distorted this testimony with as perverse a mind as they rejected from the canon the Book of the Wisdom of Solomon, which foresaw the testimony concerning Christ’s crucifixion. For after Christ’s death, where it reads:

“The ungodly said among themselves: ‘Let us oppress the righteous, because he is useless to us and opposed to our works. He professes to possess knowledge of God and calls himself a son of God’” (Wis. 2:12–13);

and below:

“For if he is truly God’s son, he will receive him and deliver him from the hand of his enemies” (ibid., 18);

and thereafter:

“Let us condemn him to a most shameful death, so that we may know his reverence and test his patience” (ibid., 19–20),

they cut it away from the prophetic books, lest our people at the sacred assembly reproach them for so evident a sacrilege, and they permanently forbade their own people to read it.

For those who did not hesitate to separate an entire prophetic book from the prophetic writings and to deny that it had been produced by that same Solomon were even more ready to publish passages of words differently from the way they had been arranged. Therefore your fabricated stories must by no means be heeded; only this should be held true: what the prudent Jerome, interpreter of our language, gave to everyone. [Note: Perhaps read *vero*, “true.”]

No one is unaware that the Hebrew books were falsified after Christ’s coming, so that they might remove the clearer testimonies concerning Christ, by which they knew they would be convicted. [Note: Manuscript reading: “by which they used to know that they would be convicted.”]

For it is established, and clearer than daylight, that those who insulted the author of the Law did not fear to corrupt the Law itself—the only means by which they could be refuted.

Run through all the curses of the Law which you know to have been pronounced against human beings, beasts, serpents, and lifeless metals. You will see that nowhere is anyone called “cursed by God” except in that passage where you wished to understand the words, as though to disgrace Christ:

“Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Deut. 21:23).

Here the leaders of the synagogue added “by God” from their own source, so that by this they might deny that he was God.

If the eyes of faith are open to you, examine the whole history of the Old Testament. You will never see “cursed by God” written there, and from this you will be able to learn the genuine faithlessness of that people and their incurable rage against their own life.

You too can mock us because you know that we are ignorant of the Hebrew language, exploiting the variations of Hebrew manuscripts wherever you foresee that you have been defeated. By this argument you are able to defend yourself in all the Scriptures, thinking that you can clear yourself by words when facts press you hard.

### 5

Come now, let us approach the second chapter and approve your response, seasoned with very little salt. For you say that the seventy weeks are confused among the Latins, as though I had declared that they should be calculated according to the reckoning of the Latins—or as though you, a Hebrew, could be overcome by a calculation derived from the Latins. [Note: Read “a Hebrew” (*Hebraeus*).]

Legally I established the number of one week as seven years; I did not, as you did, scatter an uncertain interpretation in different directions, so that, having no sure footing on which to plant your step, you limp with both feet.

You count seventy days, or seventy weeks, or seventy moons, or seventy years according to—I do not know whose own interpretation—and, proceeding everywhere under suspicion through the numerical diversity of your alternatives, I ask you to tell me: whose interpretation do you wish to follow?

Jerome’s? I am astonished that you impose my interpretation upon me and wished to teach a Latin from the diversity of Latins. You seem to me to have assumed the role of a teacher rather than of an advocate.

But I complain again: why, in the above-mentioned cases of days, weeks, moons, and years, did you prefix to each one the phrase “according to his explanation,” when it is certain that you have never read the explanations he gave, and especially that he did not apply this particular expression, “seventy times seven,” to them? Unless, perhaps, after rejecting the others, you have learned that these are the two interpretations of the Hebrews.

Nevertheless, since you fortify your final position with prophetic testimony, there is no doubt that you wish to prove that one alone. [Note: The manuscript reads *aut*, “or.”] For you say:

“The days, when multiplied, make one thousand three hundred and thirty.”

The same number is found at the end of Daniel, for he says:

“Blessed is the one who waits and reaches one thousand three hundred and thirty-five days” (Dan. 12:12).

And because you saw that the five days—which you take as years—went beyond the number, you immediately added, as though it were a clever point of your own:

“For during these five years the Lord will separate those who remain from all the nations upon the earth for the service of Israel.”

By your slippery wording you darkened the reader’s mind, so that he could not know at all what sort of years you meant by the five, or at what time they should most truly be calculated.

### 6

Coming to the matter in brief, I grant that there are indeed one thousand three hundred and thirty-five years. Therefore, from the second year of Darius, who was also called Melas, in which the vision was revealed to Daniel, until Vespasian, who completed the captivity of the Jews, four hundred and ninety years are counted.

If you add to these the eight hundred and forty years of the Lord’s incarnation, the total will be one thousand three hundred and thirty years. If from this sum you subtract forty, because the war of Vespasian occurred in the fortieth year after the Lord’s passion, one thousand two hundred and ninety years remain. [Note: Manuscript reading: “one thousand two hundred years remain.”]

Subtract thirty-three years, the age of the Lord, from these, and there will be one thousand two hundred and fifty-seven years from Daniel’s time to the 878th era, which is now in progress, in the 840th year of the Lord’s incarnation and the 1040th year of the world.

### 7

But if you wish to calculate from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes—the year in which the word went forth that Zerubbabel’s temple should be rebuilt—you will find four hundred and ninety years up to Christ’s birth. If you add the years of the Lord’s incarnation to these, there will be one thousand three hundred and thirty years, and the five years which you oppose to us for the service of the nations will still remain.

You yourself shatter this frivolous interpretation of yours when you say:

“For you are, my brother, imbued with such great stupidity and such foolishness of spirit that you wish to know what Daniel did not know, when the angel said to him: ‘Go, Daniel, because the words are closed and sealed until the appointed time’” (Dan. 12:4).

Truly this is a strong argument, one that would press me with both horns, if the author’s subsequent wording did not break its force when you add: [Note: Read *premeret*, “would press,” for *promerent*.]

“Therefore you open up a field of response for me and allow me to suffer no narrowness, when you say: ‘Count from the first day on which Nebuchadnezzar placed swine’s flesh in the temple until one thousand two hundred and ninety years have been completed; then that book will be opened and its seals will become known.’”

If the prophet spoke of words closed and sealed because of the marvel of the entire vision, who opened this number of years for you, so that you know what Daniel could not know? He spoke of days, whereas you interpret them as years. And I do not know by what such an authority you read part of the sealed book, if the whole book is under the seal.

Therefore these one thousand two hundred and ninety days too are included in the same number. Why do you say that part is sealed and part open? You are permitted to interpret the appointed number of the sealing not as days but as years; am I not permitted to prove that, according to the preceding statement, they are not years but days?

You claim greater things for yourself when you interpret days as years, clearing the clouds and making the sky bright; you grant me no lesser privilege, so that I may expound the words of the prophecy plainly, without hesitation, in terms of days.

If the words are sealed, how did you calculate above, after one thousand three hundred and thirty years, five years for the servitude of the nations? Who gave you this authority, to impose five years of service upon all the nations? Why do you try to explain what Daniel did not explain? Why do you hurry to handle what he left untouched?

But you say:

“We, however, are today in the 1363rd year.”

By this you hasten to show that only twenty-seven years remain until your Messiah is released from fiery or iron chains. [Col. 0489A] All effort would be futile here if life remained for both of us: for, counting twenty-seven years from the era now called the 878th, the advent of your Zabulus would be recognized in the coming 905th era.

Nevertheless, let us both bind ourselves by a decree of such a definition that, if life accompanies us and we both reach that span of years, the one whose charge proves false may transfer his step into the faith of his opponent.

### 8

But if your redemption has not occurred at that very time, I fear that perhaps you will turn the number of one week into the course of seventy years and say that 3,900 years must run until the advent of that most wicked enemy.

[Col. 0489B]

### 9

Observe with what words Daniel sealed the book:

“Many shall be chosen, made white, and tested as though by fire; and all the ungodly shall act ungodly. But the learned shall understand” (Dan. 12:10).

You see that from among the many, a few will be chosen and made white; and again, not all but many will be tested. The ungodly will not understand, because they denied God; but the learned will understand. For he did not forbid knowledge of the book to those whom he foresaw would be learned in faith.

You applaud yourself again, because, if you had the opportunity, you would teach me and my own Egesippus himself to have erred greatly. [Note: Read “Egesippus,” of whom mention is made immediately below.]

And what you cannot demonstrate, you threaten almost in passing, so that the reader may think that you spare me, when by lying you spared not even your own soul, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11)—your own much more than another’s.

This is a rhetorical device: when someone cannot prepare answers, he pretends voluntarily to omit what, as though he were powerful, he could have proved, in order to show everyone that he lacks not diligence but only the desire to do so. Thus, while he promises golden mountains, he produces not even a bronze coin.

You have been imbued with such disciplines, and therefore you boast that you can do what, with your conscience as witness, you are entirely unable to perform.

### 10

Know that I quoted nothing to you from the words of Egesippus, but from those of your own teacher Josephus. From the Babylonian captivity until Herod, a foreign descendant, he handed down in his books all your rulers and kings, who were both kings and priests, usurping the priesthood after seizing the kingdom. From this it cannot be doubted that they endured a deadly fall.

Do not oppose me by saying:

“An outsider who approaches shall die, unless he is from the tribe of Aaron” (Num. 1:51).

But recall the obstinacy of the Jewish people and their recklessly bold strength, and then you will know who could usurp greater things.

For I established that Alexander was a leader from the tribe of Judah, and that he usurped the priesthood for himself. If you wish, say that he was not a king either; but you will not be able to do so, because a witness from your own household rises up against you: Josephus, who also confirms in his own words that his brother Aristobulus did such things.

For he says:

“Aristobulus, older in age among the brothers and more headstrong in mind, converted the primacy of the priesthood into royal power for himself and arrogantly usurped the diadem.”
