Let us see who this Josephus was, or from what tribe of the Jews he arose. For he says:

“Josephus, son of Matthias, and priest of Jerusalem, who himself first fought against the Romans in the war and afterwards, compelled by necessity, took part in the battles.”

And elsewhere:

“Indeed, I am not Aaron, but nevertheless I am not degenerate from him.” [Note: Read “degenerate,” for *deneger*.]

But let us produce from the fifth book of his *History* what testimony he offered concerning his own people.

After he had been captured by Vespasian and condemned to death because he had been leader of the Jewish faction and had exhausted the Romans through many wars, he finally prophesied to Vespasian concerning Nero’s death and Vespasian’s rule. Immediately he received not only the favor of release but also a position of no small friendship with him.

Nevertheless, he was ordered to address in his ancestral language the Jews whose leader was John the Sicarius, the parricide. Josephus spoke to him as follows:

“It is no wonder, John, if you persist until the destruction of your country, since the divine protections have already abandoned it. But I wonder whether you do not believe that it will perish, when you have read the prophetic books in which they announced to us the destruction of our country and its restored heights, which were again to be destroyed by the Roman army.

“For what else does Daniel proclaim? He was not prophesying what had already happened, but the future. [Note: Perhaps read *pro futuro*, “for the future.”] What is the abomination of desolation that is to be when the Romans come, if not this very thing that threatens? [Note: The manuscript reads *venientis*, “of the coming one.”]”

You see that at that very time your Josephus believed that the seventy weeks had been fulfilled.

And shortly afterward he added this as well:

“Nor am I free from this danger. I know too that, together with your people, my most holy mother, my noble wife, my not ignoble lineage, and my once illustrious household are in danger. Perhaps you think that I urge this on account of my family. Kill them, and take my blood as payment as well. I willingly pay this price for your salvation, if after me you are able to become wise.”

You understand, my brother, that you can never become wise according to the words of your own teacher. Truly you trust in the winds [Note: Manuscript reading: “in things stretched out,” or possibly “in intentions”] and place your confidence in nothing.

For you said that he was born and anointed on the very day on which Jerusalem was destroyed. It is enough that his birth pronounced your destruction and perpetual ruin.

### 11

You see, my brother, that you are better off than your Messiah. You are free; he is bound. You are young; he is already old. And perhaps that is why he grows old, unless you say that he does not experience the increase of age, thereby asserting that he is an insensible metal.

For the title reads: “Do not falsify the metals.” Would that you were not reluctant to write to me who bound him, who guards him while bound, in what latrine he lies infected, in what portion of the earth he is submerged in a sewer teeming with worms.

Call to him in a louder voice, because perhaps your Messiah is cleansing his bowels, relaxing his bladder by an outpouring of urine, silently exhaling the stench of excrement from his anus, or at least digesting by the bloating of his belly something tasteless [Note: Perhaps “insipid”?], and for that reason he does not hear your sighs, prolonged for so long.

Are you not ashamed to pursue so ridiculous a madness? [Note: The manuscript reads *putet* for *pudet*.] Truly, my brother, you follow the winds and feed upon air. Holding the sinews of mist, you place your trust in the smoke of houses; you even await release from one who has not been released. [Note: Manuscript reading: “from one who is not released, await it.”]

At the end you write:

“Go, and hold on to your Jesus, both here and forever.”

Receive this brief answer: Amen; and again, amen; and a third time, amen; amen in heaven, amen on earth. And let not only the angels but also the whole people say:

“Let it be, let it be” (Ps. 105:48).

Thus, just as I willingly embrace him while he breathes through faith, may I be held by him, so that I may not be led away from him by the faith or the deceptive work of anyone’s invention.

And so may Jesus rightfully claim my mind for himself forever, so that no obscene impulse may thereafter awaken in my thoughts. May he so preside over my mind through faith that he governs my body in its actions; and, freeing me by the gift of his right hand from evil hearing, may he make me share in joy.

He himself, whom I worship as the one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the Trinity, to whom be glory forever and ever.

## XVII

Here traces of red letters appear, apparently the title of another letter, namely that of the transgressor. The lower part of the leaf, in which it began, was therefore cut away. But on the reverse page the following text is present:

### 1

Israel, as it is written in the Book of Deuteronomy:

“Place these words of mine in your hearts and in your souls,” and so forth (Deut. 11:18).

And elsewhere in the same book:

“Moses commanded us the Law, the inheritance of the multitude of Jacob” (Deut. 33:4).

And again in the same book:

“Beware lest you forget the words which your eyes have seen, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life” (Deut. 4:9). [Note: In the Vulgate we read *excidant*, “fall away.” In Alvarus below, *excedant* appears for *excidant*.]

Listen, detractor, to what is written: “All the days of your life.” Pay close attention and beware lest, while seeing, you fail to see, and while hearing, you fail to understand.

See, then, how I confirmed my law with the truest . . . .

[From this point the sheet is missing; we stated below that it had been cut off. The three following leaves were also cut away. On the fourth succeeding leaf, where Alvarus’s eighteenth letter begins, the transgressor’s letter ends as follows:]

### 2

“Deserted places filled with flocks of people, and they shall know that I am the Lord” (Ezek. 36:38).

And shortly afterward:

“Son of man, all these bones are the whole house of Israel. They say: ‘Our bones are dried up, our hope has perished, and we have been cut off.’ Therefore prophesy and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: ‘Behold, I will take the children of Israel from among the nations to which they have gone, and I will gather them from every side and bring them to their own land. I will make them one nation in the land, upon the mountains of Israel, and one king shall rule over them all.

“‘They shall no longer be two nations, nor shall they be divided any further into two kingdoms. They shall no longer defile themselves with their idols, their abominations, or any of their transgressions. I will save them from all their dwelling places in which they sinned, and I will cleanse them. They shall be my people, and I shall be their God.

“‘My servant David shall be over them, and there shall be one shepherd for all of them. They shall walk in my judgments, keep my commandments, and do them. They shall dwell upon the land that I gave to my servant Jacob, in which your fathers dwelt. They and their children and their children’s children shall dwell upon it forever. And my servant David shall be their prince forever,’” and so forth (Ezek. 37:11–24).

See now that you can find no occasion for saying that all these things will not take place upon the earth. The end.

## XVIII. ALVARUS’S LETTER ADDRESSED TO THE TRANSGRESSOR

### 1

We have seen your letter, blackened with lies, foul with insults, and stained with filth. We examined it for a short while and immediately recognized how crooked it was. It was not laziness that delayed my reply; rather, circumstances brought matters to this conclusion, since, having been driven into [an uncertain or corrupt phrase] [Note: Corrupt words], I was not held in my proper place.

For that reason we prefixed this apologetic preface, so that you might not complain that I replied too late.

At the very outset we were astonished at your Jewish manner of lying and shuddered at the habitual faithlessness of your trustworthiness, when you say:

“A certain note of ours came into our hands, and it was full of blasphemies against the true and living God.”

It is clear that you are deceitful when you try to attribute to me things which, with your conscience as witness, you never appear to have read in my letters.

But since, as you say, you did not wish to answer me unless the command of your instructors and teachers compelled you, I beg you, laying aside your rancor for a little while and driving away the error of obstinate faithlessness, to attend to what I say.

Since, according to the prophet’s testimony, all have been struck with blindness, with what presumption do you claim to have teachers whom you know to be blind by the prophetic judgment? And the prophetic word resounds this openly to everyone, so that it even investigates the time of blindness with no small diligence, saying:

“How long, O Lord?” (Isa. 6:11).

The divine response immediately declared perpetual blindness by its oracle. But that is another matter.

Nevertheless, I shall follow the traces of your letter and bring out the error by the lines along which it entered, omitting the wounds of the most foolish insults that you produced from your shameless, serpent-bearing wisdom. I shall mention only briefly those things which will both restrain your tongue with a bridle and lead it, by the bit of justice, into the track of the right path.

### 2

For you say that, on the contrary, you have abandoned a faith that is rejected, cast off, false-speaking, accursed, dreadful, despised, abominable, and worthless, and have taken up a glorious and true one.

I am astonished at the hardness of your brow, that, while the world protests, you uttered such unspeakable things as Virgil says:

“Neither easy to behold, nor gracious in speech to anyone.” [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.621.]

You ought to consider the force of the words that you have crudely uttered and understand that you yourself are divided in two ways.

For a thing is called “faith” because it has been established. Hence people who are firm in truth are called *fideles*, “faithful.” [Note: Read *fideles* for the printed *fides*.] If it is faith, it is not rejected, nor is it any of the other disgraceful things that you attached to it with your shameful mouth. But if you attach such great and such serious reproaches to it, I ask you to remove the name “faith.”

For when you call it rejected, you unknowingly destroy yourself with your own mouth. That is called “rejected” which was previously chosen and afterward rejected for some reason. To confirm this by legal instruments, hear what follows:

“Call them rejected silver, because the Lord has cast them away” (Jer. 6:30).

You perceive that the passage has spoken against you and that your own sword has been turned back against you. “Cast off” means the same as “rejected,” because what is cast away is found to have belonged to someone before its rejection. This applies to you, not to the nations, and to your law, not to ours.

For who, O most foolish of men, babbling against himself with such mad speech, has killed himself in a peaceful mind?

Although you have uttered many foul things in the manner of the insolent rather than the eloquent, and have not, as your people boast, displayed the refinements of Chrysippus through the thickets of syllogisms and solecisms, you should at least not have called it despised, nor called it worthless, when you foresaw it as royal and thunderous with your eyes.

You ought to blush at forcing upon us things which you cannot fail to know abound in you yourself. For today it is not the faith, which once existed in a small measure of holiness, that is trampled down, but the monstrosities of your transgression; every false fabrication is crushed beneath the foot.

And do you dare to call worthless what you see flourishing in glory, swelling with honor, and shining far and wide?

Indeed, your people are now so despised that they are proclaimed throughout all kingdoms like the cloth of a menstruating woman, so that it is considered a great insult to say that someone is a Jew.

As for your boast that the Law was written by the finger of God, add, if you wish, many miracles as well—miracles which divine power performed not for you but for your fathers. All these were the mighty works of almighty God, not the mad insolence of your people.

The Law is specifically said to have been written on stone tablets because it was to be given to your exceedingly hard hearts. And, so that this may be certain and clear to you, its entire text is declared to be the writing of God’s finger, by which the power of the Holy Spirit is indicated in the most explicit terminology.

For he is not composed of bodily members, so that his finger could be called bodily; rather, whatever is marked by the finger has been written by the Spirit of God.

If you wish to understand the Law carnally, you ascribe not only limbs to God but also establish him as like yourself. And while you refuse to call Christ God, you will prove every human being altogether equal to God.

For thus he says:

“Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:29).

The one who says this is certainly God, who exercises the authority to create. Now answer me: to whom does he say “Let us make,” and whose power to create does he seek as assistance?

If he means the angels, then the angels are like him and likewise creators of human beings; and while you proclaim the worship of one true God, you fall into the servitude of many gods.

### 3

You see that, if the Law is observed carnally, it has been destroyed. I could demonstrate, in the manner of the Manichaeans, the whole history of the Law attacking itself; but observe that you introduce not only several gods, but also assert that your creator is like the other creatures.

If you ask me how I understand this, you will not grasp the judgment of my mind, because “wisdom does not enter a malicious soul” (Wis. 1:4).

But since you labor in vain to confirm the Law, and hasten to fetter me with deaf ears and an untamed heart, do not applaud yourself with lips spread wide over testimonies, knowing that I do not deny the command of the Law but venerate it through divine understanding.

Am I like you, so that I would make things brighter than daylight uncertain by proclaiming them? Far be it from me that, worshiping the truth, I should speak falsehood.

For I believe that the Law was given not only to you but to all the nations, and that it was inserted into the tablets of the Decalogue.

Look upon the first tablets, broken because of your fault, and understand that they signified your false insanities. You were initially chosen, but because of your fault you were cast away.

Observe, I beg you, the second tablets covered with veils, so that your hearts, covered with a useless veil, might not be illumined by the ineffable light from above. Therefore Moses is also reported to have veiled his face, because he signifies your understanding, blind to this day.

You continue this Jewish practice to the present day when you cover the *Eptaticum* with a silken veil and read the legislator’s words to everyone while they remain covered. [Note: *Eptaticum*, that is, the *Heptateuch*, or seven first books of the Old Testament: namely, Moses’ Pentateuch, the books of Joshua, and Judges.]

The testimonies themselves, which oppose one another, were specifically arranged for this purpose:

“Beware lest you forget the words which your eyes have seen, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life” (Deut. 4:9).

Pay attention, enemy of the Most High God, and carefully consider the force of the words: [Note: The manuscript reads *Averte inimici*.]

“Do not forget the words which your eyes have seen.”

Certainly words are heard rather than seen. Words belong to the ears, not to the eyes. But if you know how these things are said, explain them; and if you do not know, I warn you: beware of what you do not know.

Instead, assume the role of a disciple: ask, seek, knock. Although I am not unaware that you have plundered the volumes of teachers, from whose flowing stream you appear today to shine.

As for your seeming to admonish me to hear this “all the days of my life,” and, like a little scholar, openly to warn me with my eyes to beware of blindness, I regard in an instant the madness of your impudence—the insolence that does not allow you to think rightly and that, with your conscience trampled down, forces upon me the things which are present in you and in your people.

In this too you appeared to me to be a declaimer. But hear what our eloquent discourse produces, and blush at your blindness through at least one example.

For the great wonders of God, which stand written in the Law, never fall from our heart—not even those terrible events by which unheard-of power struck Egypt. [Note: The manuscript reads *qua* for *quibus*, “by which.”] We also read there of your acts of defiance, and every day we lament and grieve over you.

But you not only have now forgotten those things; even then you treated them as nothing and despised them. For those footprints that had trodden the dry sea with a dry foot soon danced before the calf, clapping their hands. [Note: Manuscript reading: “the sea trod,” “danced.”]

And, imitating in theatrical fashion the movement of their bodies [Note: Read *flexus*, “movements,” for *fluxus*.], they sang—not with a truly exalted voice, but with one sunk low:

“These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. III, 24).

And the prophetic word rightly says:

“Let them not depart from your heart all the days of your life.”

It said this not to signify a perpetual practice of the deed, but only to indicate the duty of remembrance. For who, O madman, would not recall these things daily in his heart, as the prophet says, and even read them publicly aloud on appointed feast-days—things which stand known to your condemnation? [Note: The manuscript reads *cognita*, “known,” for *cognitum*.]

### 4

As for your boast that you have confirmed your law with truthful testimonies: who has even denied to you that it is God’s, so that you explain away what no one alleged? For we say that you have taken up a rejected law—not because it was rejected at that time, but because, when the light had already arrived, the shadow came to an end. For your entire law—or rather, mine even more than yours—announces Christ, whose coming all Jews do not deny. You certainly know that all the ancestors of old awaited the Messiah and that his presence was desired daily by the fathers. The books of the prophets openly proclaim this, and all the blind men and leaders of the blind cannot deny it.

For you once confessed it, and cannot deny it: compelled by the commands of your teachers, not with the intention of faith but through the envy of unbelief, you hissed forth your dog-like eloquence with a viper’s mouth. And therefore, since your words flow from another’s stomach and you bear the name not of teacher but of disciple, you ought willingly to inquire of the leaders of the Synagogue:

“Whether this Christ of ours, whom you appeared to disparage with your most filthy mouth—when the light arose in the world—any one at all among them recognized as the Messiah.”

And certainly you will not be able to deny that many Jews believed in him, so that he arranged their sacred banquets in gatherings of thousands of people. For not merely many, but nearly all the Jews believed in him. While awaiting the Messiah, some recognized him as the way of those who were wandering; to others, however, he became a stone of stumbling.

And therefore we do not say that we are Gentiles, but Israel, because our parents of old arose from that very Israelite stock. But when the one desired by all the nations came, we immediately recognized that he had come—the one whose coming we had previously read as prophesied over many ages:

> “The multitude of the sea has been turned toward us, and the diversity of the nations has returned to us” (Isaiah 60).

The Lord has arisen over us, and his honor has been seen in us. “And the nations shall walk in our light, and illustrious kings in the splendor of our countenance,” because “the Lord has made his salvation known; before the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness” (Psalm 97)—which is Christ.

For what David sang long beforehand has been fulfilled:

> “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight” (Psalm 21:28).

We are Israel, who once awaited the Messiah together with you. But when the fullness of the nations came, the multitudes of peoples increased. The utterances of the prophets were fulfilled, because the glory of the Lord has filled the whole earth.

Whoever from among the nations believed in our Jesus immediately passed into the number of Israel. And, to establish what I say in clearer language, look upon yourself, poor little man, and see how you have passed into the ranks of the Jews—so that you are no longer counted among the nations, but applaud yourself as arising from Israelite stock, because you have adhered to their madness.

[Note: Col. 0496D, manuscript L reads: “you adhered” (*haesisti*).]

Whatever the prophecies of the prophets once sang and, as though by a pledge, promised was spoken to us believers, not to those who denied. Therefore do not exalt yourself with puffed cheeks and an inflated throat over the promises of the lofty throne, when you know that all these things are mine, not yours.

### 5

As for your statement that all people before God are like a drop from a bucket (Isaiah 40:15), and as though they did not exist, and are reckoned as nothing: I am astonished that you, a prudent man, have thought so pointlessly. Surely you know that before God no one is anything—or do you not know what he himself reported concerning Moses? For he says:

> “I am who I am”; and you shall say to the children of Israel, “He who is has sent me” (Exodus 3:14).

You understand, surely, where this narrative is going. For it is not an outstanding and singular praise if you grant that anyone besides God exists.

And rightly the prophet added not merely “the nations,” but “all” (Isaiah 40:17), because he included the Israelite nation among the number. He said “all”; he excluded none. But if all nations are before him as though they did not exist, and as nothing, and are reckoned as vanity—and Israel is among all the nations—then Israel too is as though it did not exist and is reckoned as nothing and vanity.

[Note: Col. 0496D, manuscript reading: “into this” (*in hanc*).]

We say this so that your pride may be broken and the cunning of your assertion blunted. Otherwise, I have a freer, shorter—indeed clearer—reply: since I descend from Israelite stock, I boast that all the things you applaud yourself as having selected belong to me.

Understand prudently, reason wisely, and be a fair judge. Who is more worthy to be counted by the name of Israel: you, who, as you say, have returned from idolatry to the worship of the highest God and are a Jew not by nation but by faith; or I, who am a Hebrew both by faith and by nation?

[Note: Col. 0496D; Nicetas Antonius, I. VI, no. 171, reads: “by race” (*genere*).]

But I am not called a Jew, because a new name has been imposed on me, the name which the mouth of the Lord called me (Isaiah 62:2). Surely my father is Abraham, because my ancestors descended from that very stock. For those who awaited the coming Messiah and received him when he came appear to be Israel more than those who awaited him, rejected him when he came, and nevertheless did not cease hoping for him—you have awaited him even to this day, although it is certain that you have already rejected him.

The Gentiles who daily return to the faith of Israel are grafted into the people of God, just as you appeared to have clung to the error of the Jews.

And if you complain that we do not observe the ceremonies of the law, hear Isaiah sounding the trumpet to all:

> “Do not remember the former things, and do not consider the ancient things. Behold, I am making new things” (Isaiah 43:18–19).

So that he might leave you no opportunity for quibbling, he used the future tense, not the past. And to indicate that this was given not only to the Gentiles but also to the Jews—which is what we are—the following is added:

> “And now they shall arise; surely you shall know them” (ibid.).

He confirms deliberately that the Jews—the people that we are—would know them.

And to show more openly the salvation of the nations, he added:

> “I will place in the desert a way that had not been subdued by cultivation under the Lord’s plow”—that is, Christ, who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (Isaiah 14:6)—“and rivers in the trackless place.”

[Note: Col. 0497D, manuscript reads *domatum*, “of a tamed thing”; the received text has *domata*, “subdued.”]

Truly he placed rivers in the trackless place when he made the nations, who were ignorant of the way of the law, come to know themselves. And when the fleece, which had previously been full of dew while the world lay dry, had been dried, the moisture of truth filled the ends of the whole world, while dryness clung to the fleece alone.

[Note: Col. 0497D, manuscript reads “which” (*qui*) for “which had” (*quod*).]

> “The beast of the field shall glorify me, the dragons and the ostriches” (Isaiah 43:20).

[Note: Col. 0497D, manuscript reads *instructiones* in place of *struthiones*, “ostriches.”]

All these things apply allegorically to the nations, which had been consecrated to the idolatry of beasts through various errors.

[Note: Col. 0497D, manuscript reads *congruit, qui*, “fits, which,” for *congruunt, quae*, “apply, which.”]

He repeats the calling of the nations in order to show it more firmly:

> “For I have given waters in the desert, rivers in the trackless place.”

And so that he might not exclude Israel—but rather show that the nations had already become his people—he says:

> “My people, my chosen” (ibid.).

You see that the waters of the Gospel and the rivers of the apostles have been given to us for drinking—that is, to the Jews who, while awaiting Christ, received him when he came—or to all who, repenting even to this day from the snares of the devil, insert themselves into the members of the Church.

Concerning this people it is added:

> “I established this people for myself; it shall declare my praise” (ibid. 21).  
> [Col. 0498D, manuscript M reads: “I declared” (*narravi*) rather than “it shall declare” (*narrabit*).]

The remaining things that follow promise us many matters, some already accomplished and others still future.

### 6

As for your claim that I am going into darkness, and your attempt to prove this by Isaiah’s testimony:

> “For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gloom the peoples” (Isaiah 60:2),

I am astonished that you, a clever man, have thought so carelessly as to count me among the peoples while removing yourself from the people.

For I have already confessed above that the Lord has arisen over us and that the nations walk in our light.

### 7

And so that you may know that neither you nor your followers will ever be joined to the people of God, but will always remain scattered and never return to the way of peace, hear Isaiah proclaiming, in the person of Christ, words fitting the human nature:

> “And now the Lord says, forming me from the womb as a servant for himself, to bring Jacob back to him; and Israel shall not be gathered” (Isaiah 49:5).

Pay attention to what the divine word says: “forming me from the womb as a servant for himself.” That is, I am his servant from the time when I am cast forth from the womb, so that the hearer may not be scandalized when he hears the Lord called a servant. For just as he is God from the Father, so he is a servant from his mother: one Lord, Jesus Christ, in both natures.

But we have not undertaken to discuss these matters here. Let us hear what this servant of the Lord—who is himself Lord—says:

> “The Lord created me from the womb as a servant for himself, to bring Jacob back to him.”

And immediately he pronounced a deliberative sentence, saying:

> “And Israel shall not be gathered.”

He openly and absolutely declared that Israel would not be gathered.

Do you perceive, I ask, how with such small words I have melted your icy coals, and with a very little finger scattered so many of your phalanxes?

[Col. 0498B] **8.** Yet in the meantime you raise your broken neck and perhaps object that this is not found in the Hebrew. But observe that the Hebrew word **LO** is not written with *lamed* and *waw*. If it were, it would signify what Aquila rendered: “he shall be gathered to him” or “to that one.” But it is written with *lamed* and *aleph*, which does not properly produce that meaning.

[Manuscript E reads “EO.” It should be written **LO**, with *L*, not *E*, for the author himself says that *lamed* is the first letter of the word.]

Since, therefore, Jacob was not brought back to the Lord and Israel was not gathered, Christ speaks:

> “Though you did not believe, I have been glorified in the eyes of the Lord; for the whole world has believed in me, and my God has become my strength” (Isaiah 49:5).

He says “my God” according to the human being. For just as, against you, I must establish by the sentences of Scripture that he is God, so against anyone who denies that he is human it is fitting for me to take up the battle of Scripture and produce all those examples of his humanity by which I may confirm that he is truly human. For if I deny one of these, I shall not be a Christian.

But let us return to the order of the passage and examine still another prophetic sentence:

> “And my God has become my strength,”

the one who consoled me in my sorrow over the rejection of my people, just as it is also read in the Pentateuch:

> “It repents me that I made man upon the earth.”

And, touched by inward grief of heart, he says:

> “I will wipe out the man whom I made from the face of the earth” (Genesis 6:6).

But if you raise the heel of contradiction, explain how you understand what you read in the prophet Ezekiel spoken in the person of God:

> “And in all these things you were grieving me.”

It follows:

> “It is a small thing for you to be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob that fell through their own fault and to restore the dregs—or the remnants—of Israel” (Isaiah 49:6).

The Hebrew word here sounds like **nesure**, “remnants.” For them I gave you as a light to all the nations (ibid.), so that you might illuminate the whole world and bring my salvation—through which all may believe and be saved—to the ends of the earth.

And what follows:

> “It is a great thing for you to be called my child,”

refers to the human being and to the child, who in comparison with God is small.

Those testimonies which you set down through empty labor in order to establish unity we have read attentively and found to be congruent with us, not opposed to us. For we do not worship three gods, but assert and venerate one in the Trinity.

We can establish this for you with suitable witnesses and the thunderous utterances of the prophets:

> “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,”

says the divine Scripture (Genesis 1:26). And so that this voice might be understood as directed not to angels but to the Son, it immediately added:

> “And God made man; according to the image of God he made him.”

Hear, faithless man and enemy of holy faith: God making man according to the image of God. Recognize the mystery of the Trinity at the beginning of your own creation.

> “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 2:6).

So also Isaiah, foremost among the prophets, repeating “Holy” three times (Isaiah 6:3), demonstrates the Trinity; but by saying “the Lord God,” and not “the Lords God,” he declares the unity.

### 9

But what need have I to linger long over so obvious a matter, which ought to fill not the memorial of one volume but those of many volumes?

Let me state briefly this much: if you should wish to examine the history of the entire law with the utmost keenness, you will either believe in a threefold God or lead many and more people into the error of idolatry. For when you read in the sacred writings, “Let us make,” and “Let us go down,” and “Who will go for us?” and many other such expressions; when you find in Zechariah that God was sent by God; and when you observe a plurality of gods in many passages—

[Note: “The Trinity in God.”]

—we leave these matters for you to investigate, so that you may hear and be silent, understand and then speak.

We have come to your epilogues—that is, to your curses—where you call me wretched. Forgetting the old proverb, while saying one thing you destroy your strongest argument:

> “Liars ought to remember.”

Earlier, in order to establish me not as a son but as a nation, you set down Isaiah’s testimony:

> “All nations are like drops from a bucket, and as though they did not exist.”

But now, forgetting your own purpose, you undermine yourself by saying:

> “You have abandoned the God who begot you” (Deuteronomy 32:18).

For if he begot me, he is my father, and you are not his only son.

Moreover, by subtly calling Israel “firstborn,” he declares that he has others after the firstborn. For “firstborn” is not said unless he has brothers, of whom this one is the first; and rightly he is called “firstborn,” not “only-begotten.”

But if, as you say, I abandoned him, it is clear that I knew him beforehand. This applies to Israel, not to the nations, because the nations did not abandon one already known; they received one not yet known.

Either you will establish that I am a Jew and the Son of God, so that you may confirm that I abandoned the one who begot me, or you will establish that I am a nation and will grieve that you have set down all these things in vain.

But while you wear yourself out rolling entirely amid attacks and insults, you do not correct your own nonsense. You see yourself bound by the lanterns of your own words, not by the little bundles of spiderwebs but by something rightly fastened with the strongest and most solid bonds.

And you have turned, you say, to a mortal man. For you repeat the same things, and it is not enough once to have demonstrated the stupidity of your sluggishness.

You say:

> “You have turned to a mortal man.”

Therefore you yourself testify to me that I worshiped the living God: I received the long-awaited Messiah as the eternal shepherd. For when you say “you have turned,” you show that I was not a nation but a people, who for a long time awaited with you the Messiah, the Redeemer of all.

### 10

You see that you labor in vain, since you see nothing, and grope while attacking your own statements.

Do not now oppose to me promises and counter-promises, or call the nations hateful and rejected before God, because you confirm that I am not a nation but a Jew.

But the thing you belch forth from the sewer of your belly, sprinkling filthy gall upon the Redeemer as you cast it at him, displays the treasure of your heart,

[Note: Col. 0499D, a variant reads *spurca*, “filthy things.”] because “the evil man brings forth what is evil from his evil treasure” (Matthew 12:35), and “every bad tree produces bad fruit” (Matthew 7:17).

For, according to Isaiah:

> “The foolish man speaks foolish things, and his heart understands vanity, so that he may complete iniquities and speak falsehood against the Lord” (Isaiah 32:6).

Let the one who can commit filthy deeds speak filth, in accordance with Jerome’s statement. For:

> “In the mouth of the fool is the rod of pride.”

Therefore the Psalmist says of you and those like you:

> “They have set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue has traversed the earth” (Psalm 73:9).

And elsewhere he says of them:

> “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue” (Psalm 12:4).

And another says in reply:

> “A fool does not receive words of wisdom unless you say what turns over in his heart” (Proverbs 18:2).

And the one quoted above says:

> “Why do you boast in wickedness, O Judah, you who are powerful in iniquity all day long?” (Psalm 52:3).

And the whole continuation of the psalm, up to the words:

> “And he prevailed in his vanity.”

This is your perversion and your harsh contention, which is expiated neither by sacrifice nor by offering.

Of this the prophet says:

> “The sin of Judah is written with an iron pen, engraved with a diamond point” (Jeremiah 17:1).

Thus, by both iron and unyielding diamond, he signified its permanence.

### 11

But because, being polluted, you have spoken many polluted things, and I cannot pass over the insult against the highest God with a deaf ear, hear what truth—not pride—says.

Hear, enemy of the Most High God; hear, profaner of divine law; hear, violator of the sacred sanctuary; hear, thief of the Lord’s vessels.

[Note: Col. 0499D, manuscript: “laws . . . sanctuary” (*jura . . . sacrarium*).]

For who has ever drunk so deeply from the vine of Sodom and tasted the wine of envy, of dragons and asps, that you—who dared to raise yourself in pride against the Most High—should prepare an accusation against the Son of God together with the devil?

Who has ever been struck with such blindness as to say that purity is conquered by pollution?

[Note: Col. 0500D, manuscript reads *vinceri*, “to be conquered.”]

Look, wretched man: the rays of Phoebus penetrate a sewer, yet they neither lack their own light nor take on the sewer’s uncleanness.

[Note: Col. 0500D, manuscript reads “their own light” (*lumen proprium*).] Rather, the sewer is dried up, while the sun’s lights always remain bright.

And if the eye of heaven, the servant above the stars of the Thunderer—the sun—does these things, how much more does the one who created the sun?

Do you distrust the power of God, whose wondrous works you see every day?

You say to me: How did flesh beget flesh and not become violated? I answer you: How did Aaron’s staff produce nuts without being planted? How did the sun, abandoning its natural movement, prolong the day by shining farther? How did the wave of the sea, forgetting the flowing of its nature, stand like a firm wall, with its margins raised and its currents solidified with icy rigidity? How did the she-ass, a beast of burden, properly produce human speech? By what means did the sun turn backward fifteen degrees on the horologe?

[Note: That is, “clock.”]

When you recognize that all these things were accomplished not rationally but by power, willingly or unwillingly you will bind your tongue in silence.

[Note: Col. 0501D, manuscript reads “us” (*nobis*) for “unwillingly” (*nolis*).]

And while with your poisonous mouth you utter many poisonous things—while you assert that you kissed the genitals with your own lips through the virgin’s barriers and the polluted passage, what shameful things you have brought forth with your shameless and brazen brow, when you declared the receptacles and inner folds of your mother’s womb accursed—

hear, criminal, filled with every curse and abomination, unclean and dreadful spirit: you dared horribly to blaspheme the living God, and attempted to fabricate inventions through empty novelties of speech.

[Note: Col. 0501D, manuscript M reads *est*, “is,” for both instances of *es*, “you are/have.”]

And first of all, trembling in my whole body, I condemn my ill-fated eyes with curses and outcries, because they perceived such things by reading.

[Note: Col. 0501D, the text reads *funes*, “ropes”; F reads *funestos*, “ill-fated.”]

For if Isaiah testified that he had polluted lips (Isaiah 6:5), because he dwelt in the midst of a people possessing polluted lips, what should be said of me? I stand polluted not only because my deserts demand it, but also because of your nonsense and fabricated frivolous tales, which I have heard with my eyes and ears.

Woe, woe, woe to you, wretched and unhappy man, who impiously dare to examine one whom you are unable rightly to entreat.

But tell me: who fashions the bodies and grants the living spirit to adulterers, to those who gaze like maddened horses upon the wives of their neighbors, and to those born from that very incest? Is it not God?

If God does this, then he not only puts the hands of his creative work into filth, but also—far be it from us—becomes a collaborator in evil, since he grants animal breath to those born from such contamination.

[Note: Col. 0502D: something is missing.]

Our prudent and great Jerome explained this under such an image that he compared seed taken from the fruit and placed in furrows. He says:

> “Should the earth therefore not bear fruit from such sowing because the sower cast it with an unclean hand?”

[Note: Col. 0502D, manuscript reads *quia asatorea*; the text has *quia sator ea*, “because the sower [cast] it.”]

But we have not undertaken to discuss these matters here.

### 12

Do you not know, wicked man, that God stands in every place, whether clean or horrible?

[Note: Col. 0502D, F reads *assistit*, “is present,” for *astitit*, “stood present.”]

It is not the uncleanness of the place that overflows upon the Lord, but the Lord’s purity that overflows upon the place.

Or do you not know that nothing is unclean to God, who can make clean from what is unclean? Do you not consider that God penetrates even the infernal place, more horrible than every place smelling of foulness?

Either you will affirm that God the Creator fashioned our body, or you will defend the existence of another creator besides God.

For David dares to say:

> “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Psalm 119:73).

And elsewhere he says:

> “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother brought me forth in sins” (Psalm 51:7).

You see that the Lord’s hands made those very genitals which you call hateful; you behold the receptacles of the womb fashioned by the hands of the lofty throne.

Hear also another passage:

> “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26).

And you call the image of God polluted?

You recognize that man was formed according to the image of God, line by line, distinguished through his members; yet you call the nature reproachable whose divine form you see?

Nor can you say that the soul was formed according to the image of God. For “man” is said from *humus*, that is, earth, from which our body was formed—not from the soul, whose origin no created being knows.

And therefore the virgin’s virgin barriers were touched by his own lips not disgracefully, as you assert, but gloriously, as we truthfully say: he not only touched the likeness of God but received it in his own limbs.

And he deigned to be born in time in that form in which it is known that, before time, he had been shown to all—not specifically but in the ordinary manner. For the one who at the beginning chose man, more beautiful than all the beasts, made him according to his image only after deliberation.

I have said all these things, without prejudice to the other sense in which Christians are accustomed to treat them, in order to overthrow Jewish errors, not to construct a doctrine for Christians.

As for the insult which, with swollen mouth, puffed up like a bladder and inspired by a diabolical spirit, you have repeatedly directed against God, although it contains many indecent matters unworthy of a response, it signifies nothing greater than the cross, or death, or descent into the underworld.

We not only do not deny these things; we also proclaim them as monuments of glory, raising them like victorious and triumphal weapons with one of the friends of the Bridegroom.

[Note: Col. 0502D, the corrupt reading is emended to *adorearum tropaea*: “trophies of glory,” that is, monuments of glory.] We have said, and shall say:

> “Far be it from us to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14).

All the things you have said, and much greater things, the prophet Isaiah set forth concerning you and those like you, prophesying that you would say all these things—from the place where he says:

> “Behold, my servant shall understand” (Isaiah 52:13),

to the point where he concludes:

> “And he himself bore the sins of many and prayed for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12).

### 13

You add another extremely serious argument, saying:

> “Cursed is the one who trusts in man” (Jeremiah 17:5),

as though I believe him to be man because he is man, and do not rather worship him because he is God.

You would rightly say this if you had often heard me believe him to be a mere man and not God. But since, in your excess, and through love of contradiction, you do not know how to restrain your evil-speaking tongue from insults, you kill yourself with your own sword.

Tell me, I ask you—if you are ever able to answer: Do you believe that this Messiah whom you await is a man, or do you believe that he is God?

If he is a man, then you are all accursed, because you trust that flesh is your arm. If he is God, then he is not David, nor his son, nor bound by fetters, because God is free and is no one’s servant.

Are you not ashamed, most wretched of mortals, to pursue such ridiculous fictions, awaiting as your refuge a monstrous portent whom you hear to have been bound with bonds and fettered with iron chains?

And therefore you are accursed in the house and accursed in the field, while the Psalmist likewise resounds:

> “Let sinners vanish from the earth, and the wicked, so that they may no longer exist” (Psalm 104:35).

### 14

The remaining things you set down I judge unworthy of a response, because you chose to set against me things which your sluggishness has never heard me deny.

As for your statement:

> “He has not dealt thus with every nation” (Psalm 147:20),

I have already established that I myself am the nation to which he did so much.

Nor is it necessary for me to pursue at greater length what I briefly proposed above. Repeated things generate weariness, and things said many times obscure understanding.

But, scattering the smoke of your blindness and the darkness of your houses with which you wish to obstruct our light, you say that in the palace of the king of the Franks you saw fourteen men differing among themselves in dress.

As though we did not know, you seem to flaunt your learning. What harm does it do me that you saw what you report to me—something which, even if you had not seen it, you could have claimed to have seen?

Do I not know the errors of novelties and the depravity of the seventy-two heresies? Indeed, I learned even their various rites by reading, although I never had you as my informant.

But why do you continue by enumerating the names of the pagan gods, none of whom at this time wages war?

You say:

> “Do you make greater houses for your Jesus than they made for their gods, when one of them laments the ruin of his shrine in this way?”

> Alas for me! Now I see the long-established fame  
> Of the temple’s noble sanctuary destined to fall  
> In sudden ruins.

To this we add:

> You babble something rancid from a stammering nose,  
> And trip your words upon your tender palate.

[Note: In Persius: “He liquefies and trips the words upon his tender palate,” *Satire* 1.35.]

Tell me, wretched—but not deserving of pity—what advantage has this invective of narration brought you? Do you wish me to answer you in your own language and say:

> “Can you raise for your god greater houses than the gods of men are able to build for their gods?”

If you wish, I shall add something else from Jeremiah’s alphabetic lament, comparing this pagan’s fall with the idols he mourns.

This is not our fault but yours, since you compelled us and brought forth words full of insults.

### 15

As for your daring to call Christ worse, you are the murderer of your own soul. Neglecting the truth, you wish to clear yourself by words, although facts press upon you, when you say:

> “They did not have the law, nor will God require anything of them that he never commanded.”

By this argument of yours, therefore, the nations too are free from the punishment of the raging Gehenna, because he commanded them nothing concerning the riches of his laws. Israel alone will endure the enormity of punishments, because to Israel alone the utterances of the prophets were entrusted.

[Note: Col. 0503D, manuscript reads “was entrusted” (*est*) for “were entrusted” (*sunt*).]

And while the whole world has departed in freedom, Israel alone will mourn—the people in whom his great and wondrous name was established (Psalm 76:2).

You see that while you favor the idols—Jupiter, Mercury, and Juno—you burn yourself; and while you strive to kill Christ, you choose Barabbas, the servant of your ancient father’s enemy.

You say:

> “He was a Jew, and fulfilled circumcision,”

[Note: Col. 0503D: “Who” (*qui*), or perhaps “and you say” (*dicisque*).]

along with the other things by which you close off your own path of return, while slandering the works done by Beelzebub and never fearing to blaspheme the Holy Spirit.

But I shall tell you why you considered him worse than all these: because you knew him as one who loved the chaste and virgins.

I would ask you why he was circumcised, if I did not know that you understood it. For what need is there to brandish weapons in a vain labor and to instruct one who knows that he is lost?

I grieve over you, my fellow servant, and, as God knows, I sympathize with you from a truthful heart, since after so many and such great things you have attempted to toss about empty trifles.

### 16

As for your setting out the sentences of the prophets in cola and commas—

[Note: That is, what I punctuate in our fashion with a *y* and *coma*, namely, a comma with a point.]

—know that I have examined them carefully and that everything in them agrees with me. For many things there are already narrated as accomplished; others are woven as future for me, who am Israel.

Some are brought forward for your conversion at the end, at the preaching of Elijah, when one hundred and forty-four thousand shall have returned to the faith of the true God, Christ, and shall follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Revelation 14).

For the non-lying God will present everything he promised in its proper times, to us, not to you—though to you also, when you have been converted to the shepherd and guardian of your souls (1 Peter 2:25).

But I ask you to present truth to me in a brotherly manner, not falsehood. For you say:

> “These sentences compelled me to Judaize.”

And why does your tongue disagree with your heart? Why does your mouth not agree with your mind? Why do your lips roll forth one thing and your heart another?

You surely know who compels you to Judaize: the one who drove Adam from paradise; who made Solomon, *Idida*—the beloved of the Lord—go astray; who took Samson’s eyes; who shook Elijah repeatedly with fear.

[Note: Col. 0504D: *Idida* is a Hebrew word meaning “beloved,” as the Complutensian Biblical Vocabulary indicates. Hence perhaps *Idithum* in the line recorded in Du Cange’s glossary of medieval Latin: “and the psalms of the prophets, and the little books of Idith,” where “the little books of Idith” appears to mean books of Solomon—as though one said “of the beloved.” Alvarus here calls Solomon *Idida* of the Lord; in Poem VIII, v. 35, he further states: “Idida, who now signifies Christ himself, Solomon.”]

[Note: Col. 0504D, L reads *pereumque*, “repeatedly,” from 3 Kings XIV.4.]

Do you wish to know who is the author of so great an evil? A woman, the moth of soul and body.

And since you began badly, why do you complete it by an even worse deed? Why, pursuing sexual pleasures, have you become the servant of Venus?

If lust delights you and virginity and flourishing chastity horrify you, seek not Jews but “Mammetians”—

[Note: That is, those whom we commonly call Muslims.]

—where you may shine according to the world, take not one wife but several, and, like an unbridled horse driven everywhere by desire for women, rush in different directions; where, in the manner of a brothel, you may be satisfied with lust and stained by the filth of badly disciplined greed, and fattened through the incestuous path of concubines.

Why do you destroy both this world and that one? Or at least make this one profitable, if you are destroying the heavenly one.

I ought to have written much against your madness; but, with God as my witness, I descended reluctantly even to these small matters. Not, as you say, by the command of my teachers, but from weariness at hearing you: for the more I perceive you through reading with my ears, the more deeply I grieve that I am sinning.

17. But as for the many things which you set forth at the end of your letter, where you say that David will reign forever, I scarcely deem them worthy of a reply, because I proclaim the spiritual meaning of the whole Law. But let us see what the prophet says about your conversion: “They shall no longer defile themselves with their idols and with their abominations” (Ezek. 37:23). It is therefore evident that you now worship idols, from whose uncleanness you will be washed. [Note: F. reads “a quorum” (“from whom”).] And you bring forward as suitable witnesses for Christ men whom you know the prophetic word has called idolaters? At least blush at this, unhappy man.

The rest that follows applies to that part which was washed through the waters of baptism, which pure water has continued to wash to this day [Note: The manuscript has the singular, “applies.”]; not to that part which, as though claiming the mire as its own, wallows in filth and mud.

David, however, signifies Christ allegorically as a shepherd, whose kingdom will have no end. He also killed the giant and the lion—that is, the devil—and was strong-handed or desirable. But if, in their foolish contention, they say that this applies to David, let them prove where they read that David is greater than all. Or how can they grant him authority over Moses, whom everyone presents as greater than all in Israel? Or how is this David proclaimed a shepherd, when elsewhere he is said to be a son, where it is written: “And when you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up from your loins” (2 Sam. 7:12)? Certainly Solomon did not arise from him only after his death, but was chosen for the kingdom even before his death.

You perceive that the prophetic utterance is enigmatic and does not agree with your interpretation. For if he is from David’s loins, it is clear that he is not David, but that another who will already arise from ash and decayed embers will come into existence. But if you assert that he has already been born, tell me where you have read this; and just as you show David as his father, so you must declare his mother as well. If he has no mother, he will not be David’s son, because he is not a son whose maternal office is absent and whom the womb’s embrace does not carry. Either he is David, and he is not dead; or, if he is dead, he is not bound; or, if he is bound, he is not David.

If he is David’s son, it is necessary to inquire when David begot him. For if he existed before David died, he is not the Messiah whose birth was foretold after David’s death. But if he was born after David’s death, it must be asked where, when, from whom, and in what manner he was born. It is certain that a dead man cannot have a son. If he did have one, the conclusion follows: either David was not dead—which would mean that his son is not the Messiah, whose birth is proclaimed after David’s death—or he was dead and had no son; or he was not dead and had another son, for he does not have the Messiah. From all this it is concluded that the Messiah is not his son.

You see that, according to your own historical account, your position has collapsed. But if you insist that he is David’s son because you expect him to arise from David’s lineage, why may I not also call Christ the son of David, since he sprang from David’s origin? For when they insist that his kingdom is everlasting, they are proclaiming Christ’s power throughout the whole earth. If this David of theirs reigned forever, he would never see paradise, because he always reigned not in heavenly things but in earthly ones.

You see that you pursue earthly, perishing, passing things, all of which tend moment by moment toward their end, rather than heavenly things possessing enduring strength; you pursue fragile, transient, and limited things. Take care lest you become food for the serpent, lest you be dust cast away from the face of the earth, since you seek an earthly rather than a heavenly kingdom.

As for the bones which Ezekiel calls the house of Israel and whose resurrection he proclaims at the end of time, although I recall that some of them have already been raised in the Lord’s resurrection, nevertheless they say that they will again be raised at the end of all things. I do not mean that I shall bring them once more into the promised land, but into the land of the saints, the land of the living, of which the Prophet sighingly said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13). Indeed, he was already living in the land of the living when he sighed for another land of the living.

For all the saints are said here to be pilgrims and strangers—not because, possessing the heavenly region as their homeland, they have descended to earthly lands, but because, for a long time, they have lived as pilgrims in this valley of tears, separated from the Father of all and the heavenly Creator—not in body, but in spirit, and not by the spirit’s nature, but by desire and the affection of love.

18. But let us see whether your promise can stand according to the literal sense. “I will make them,” he says—that is, the Jews—“into one nation” (Ezek. 37:21). Were they divided among the nations? And how does he say elsewhere: “He shall not be reckoned among the nations” (Num. 23:9)? If at the end they will still be gathered into one nation, how have they been divided among many?

It follows: “And one king shall be king over them all, and there shall no longer be two nations” (Ezek. 37:22–23). Therefore Israel alone will exist, and it will have no one over whom to rule. Either all the Jews to whom these promises were made will then exist, and no unbeliever from the nations will remain, or certainly this statement will not stand. [Note: The manuscript reads “was not firm.”] It follows: “They shall no longer be divided into two kingdoms,” that is, into Israel and Judah, “nor shall they defile themselves any longer with their idols” (ibid., 22–23).

You see that you have clung to the worship of idols, from which you will be cleansed at the end of all things. Observe what he says: “with their idols”—not with the idols of the nations, but with their own. I could dry up the streams of your opinions in a single moment by the sun of the Church, but I shall be content and reply only to your assertions.

If you provoke me further to anger, you will depart covered with spittle like phlegm. For we have given you a taste of our manner, so that through these small matters you may fear those that are great, since these small matters have already crushed you so thoroughly.

Could I not have brought forward the whole history of Daniel, the root of our faith and a mighty shield, where not only the Holy of Holies is killed, but also the periods of years are numbered by fixed weeks, and the desolation is said by the prophetic mouth to persist until the consummation and the end? Here I could have unfolded the passage concerning the issuing of the word, for the rebuilding of Jerusalem until Christ the ruler (Dan. 9:22), set out the years of the reigning emperors until Christ’s coming, and shown that what you foolishly suppose still remains to be fulfilled has already been fulfilled.

I would also have affirmed that the removal of the royal authority, which Jacob foretold by sacred prophecies, occurred in the time of Herod, who was of foreign rather than Jewish descent. I would establish this not by my own words, but by the testimony of your own teacher from long ago—not only Josephus, but also Philo.

But because you contend not from a desire for instruction but rise up from envy in order to destroy, I have therefore found it necessary not to disclose all my mysteries to you, but only to dismantle whatever your naked speech has produced. I opposed your assertions, for I did not attempt to establish myself as though I were uncertain; I have always known myself to be firm. And therefore your own speech answered you, and your own tongue was turned back upon you.

Accordingly, if anything harsher flowed forth, it was the fault of the sick man, not of the physician. Hence my style advanced more mordantly in places where it pressed down sacrilegious opposition with a pious answer. But from now on answer us those things which you know to be pleasing to God. For you know that our dispute will be examined in the presence of the angels, or of all the heavenly powers, so that not even a single iota will pass without the disposition of mind with which it was written being known, and each matter will receive its due recompense, whether rewards or blows.

19. It pleases me, finally, to answer you in either case. If you desire peace, lay down your weapons; but if torments delight you, prepare your missiles. However much you wish, rise against the shield; whirl whatever storms you prefer. The spear is strong and, in disputes, is recognized as a knotted texture, and it fights [Note: The reading is uncertain: perhaps *textum* (“texture”) or *textus*; compare Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.626, “and the indescribable texture of the shield.”], with a sharp point, wounding the enemy and not merely injuring him but cutting him to pieces.

Of such things Virgil says:

[Col. 0507D] “Accustomed, in the Aetnian [reading uncertain] manner, to hurl little chains…”

We have thought it appropriate to note here the small prophetic sayings, in order to demonstrate the state of our faith and yours.

The Lord says through the prophet Malachi (Mal. 1:10–11): “I have no will in you, says the Lord, and I will not accept an offering from your hand.” Why? “Because from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great.” Among whom? It follows: “Among the nations.”

And why is an offering not accepted from your hand? Why do you ask me? Consider what follows: “Because in every place an offering is sacrificed and presented to my name, not polluted but clean.” This belongs properly to Christians. And so that this utterance might not be disregarded, he repeats it again, as though with glory: “For my name is great,” not among peoples, but “among the nations.”

Likewise Isaiah [Note: The manuscript reads “Jeremiah.”] says: “The house of Judah has acted treacherously against me.” He made the treachery more explicit: “They denied me and said: ‘It is not he’” (Jer. 5:12). Who is “he”? “This one who has come is not the Messiah; we await another.” You see how openly the prophet depicted your madness.

The same prophet also says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will make with the house of Judah”—that is, with the two houses—“a new covenant” (Jer. 31:31). [Note: The Vulgate reads, “with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah a new covenant.” Our text too reads “Israel” (besides “Judah”), though it immediately applies this to two houses.] How could it be new unless an old covenant preceded it? And therefore it is a new covenant, so that it might abolish the old; and so that you may know that this covenant was established not as Law but as Gospel, not only for the nations but also for the Jews, who are we, listen:

“Not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers, when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt”—that is, the covenant of the Law.

You see that the Law has been abolished and made, as it were, rejected. And rightly did the prophet foretell that this would happen after that time, because he foresaw that the testament of the Gospel would be given not in his own day but in the days to come.

Hear Ezekiel again: “I gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments by which they should not live” (Ezek. 20:20).

Isaiah, moreover, dares to say: “Hear, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the Law of your God, people of Gomorrah. Of what use to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?” says the Lord. “I am full. He did not desire the burnt offerings of rams, nor the fat of fattened animals, nor the blood of calves, goats, and lambs” (Isa. 1:10–11). Thus he showed that all your sacrifices, in which you trust as your remedies, have been rejected.

Hence he continues: “Who asked these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts? Do not continue to offer sacrifice in vain” (ibid., 12–13). Look more carefully at the words “continue” and “in vain.” “Do not continue to offer”—that is, ever again—“a sacrifice in vain”—that is, without cause, without benefit.

But if you wish to offer in vain, as he said, learn what follows: “Incense is an abomination to me. The new moon—not mine, but yours—and the Sabbaths, likewise yours, and the festivals, similarly yours, I will not endure.” Why? “Because your assemblies are wicked. Your new moons and festivals, which are not mine, my soul has hated; they have become burdensome to me; I am weary of enduring them. And when you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply your prayer, I will not hear” (ibid., 13–15).

You see that his ears are closed to your prayers—and yet you await redemption? Why are they closed? “Because your hands are full of blood” (ibid.). With what blood? With that by which you yourselves condemned yourselves: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25).

The same prophet also says: “They shall be ashamed of the idols to which they sacrificed, and you shall blush over the gardens which you chose, when you are like an oak whose leaves are falling, and like a garden without water. And your strength shall be like tow, and your work like a spark; both shall burn, and there will be no one to extinguish them” (Isa. 1:29–31).

Observe, drunkard with the wine of God’s fury, that your works become a flame which offers you destruction, not atonement. Consider carefully: you will be consumed more by your own works than you will gain any benefit of assistance from them.

20. And when the prophet—or rather, God through the prophet—says, “There will be no one to extinguish it,” who, I ask, is so senseless as to think that what the Lord presents as burning and unextinguished will be extinguished? For he did not say, “There is no one who extinguishes it,” but “There will be no one.” He used the future tense, not the present, to establish that you would be consumed by everlasting fire.

Likewise Jeremiah, after saying, “The house of Judah has acted treacherously against me; they denied me and said: ‘It is not he, nor will evil come upon us; we shall not see sword and famine’” (Jer. 5:11–12), added: “These things will therefore happen to them. Thus says the Lord of hosts: Because you have spoken this word, behold, I make my words in your mouth fire, and this people wood, and it shall consume them” (ibid., 13–14).

You see, fool, that the words of the Lord are not a support for your salvation but the completion of a devouring flame. [Note: The manuscript has the singular, “is.”]

But observe the following carefully, impious man, and grieve at being pierced on every side. For after many things which bravely cut you down, he added this as well: “The bellows have failed; the lead has been consumed in the fire; the refiner has refined in vain, for their wickedness has not been consumed. Call them rejected silver, because the Lord has cast them away” (Jer. 6:29–30).

Do you understand, wretched man, that this affliction and captivity are less than your iniquity? Behold, the prophet says that you have been cast into the fire in vain, because by this he did not see your wickedness being purged.

And again, after many things which freely punish you and your people, the divine word also added this: “Therefore do not pray for this people, nor take up praise and prayer on their behalf, nor oppose me, because I will not hear you” (Jer. 11:14).

21. How, then, do you expect liberation, ignorant man, when you read these things? Why do you remain like a hard stone, never becoming soft? You see that the omnipotent God, whose saying is doing, is immediately present in your devastation; and yet you claim to expect redemption, although you know that the prophet was forbidden to pray.

Behold, he forbade the prophets to raise prayer on your behalf; he forbade the clouds to sprinkle upon you the rain of grace. From where, then, do you vainly promise yourselves that salvation will come, when so many examples lead to death?

He added also: “And if you pray, I will not hear you.” He who foretold that the prayers of the prophets for your restoration would be futile—will he regard your prayers, those of transgressors, as something great? [Note: “Yours,” that is, prayers.]

And the Lord said to me: “Do not pray for this people for good, because when they fast, I will not hear their voices; and if they offer burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not accept them. With sword, famine, and pestilence I will consume them” (Jer. 14:11).

You see that the Lord forbade his prophets to raise prayer on your behalf. You perceive that your prayers and burnt offerings are rejected. You hear that the Israelite people have been consumed by sword, pestilence, and famine—and with what face do you expect restoration after consummation? For what has been consumed is never restored.

Perhaps you complain: Why are you being so utterly consumed? Listen not to me but to the prophet himself: “If you say in your heart, ‘Why have these things happened to me?’ it is because of the multitude of your iniquity that your shameful parts have been revealed and your feet have been defiled” (Jer. 13:22).

And to affirm your perpetual and innate madness, he next expressed it allegorically: “If the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard his spots, you too will be able to do good when you have learned to do evil” (Jer. 13:23). [Note: Add “or the leopard his spots,” as it is read in the prophet; the following context also shows this.]

Therefore, if you can at some time show an Ethiopian becoming white, or a leopard no longer variegated in color, then you too will be able to obtain the good of redemption that you expect. Since you know this is impossible, it is fitting that you now admit, though unwillingly, that you have perished forever.

It follows: “And I will scatter them like straw carried away by the wind in the desert” (ibid., 24). When God scatters you, who is this person who will gather you together by collecting you?

He added: “This is your lot and the measure of your portion, says the Lord” (ibid., 25). You hear of your lot and the measure of your portion: dispersion. Why are you not ashamed to seek the gathering that belongs to another’s lot?

The same prophet also said elsewhere: “If Moses and Samuel were to stand before me, my soul would not be toward this people” (Jer. 15:1). After forbidding Jeremiah to pray for you, lest he alone be made to appear rejected in his intercession, he immediately joined companions to him, through whose remembrance he demonstrates your ruin, declares it perpetual, and proves the insoluble guilt of your crime.

The divine word cries out and says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, the house of Israel has become dross to me. All these are bronze, tin, lead, and iron in the midst of the furnace; they have become the dross of silver. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have all become dross, behold, I will gather you in the midst of Jerusalem, in a gathering of silver, iron, tin, and lead, in the midst of the furnace; and I will kindle it with fire to melt it. Thus I will gather you in my fury and in my wrath, and I will rest, and I will melt you” (Ezek. 22:18–20).

You see that God says that your smelting will be his rest. And he added: “And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have poured out my indignation upon you” (ibid., 22).

22. And to show more clearly that no benefit would come to you from this testing, he added shortly afterward (Ezek. 24:9–14):

“Woe to the city of blood, for which I myself make a great fire. Heap up the wood; kindle it without fire; the flesh shall be consumed, and the whole mixture shall be boiled, and its bones shall decay. Place it empty upon the coals, so that it may grow hot and its bronze may melt, and its uncleanness may be melted within it, and its rust may be consumed.”

Immediately the divine word answered itself: “It has been exhausted by much labor; yet its excessive rust has not gone out of it, nor has your accursed uncleanness gone out through the fire. Because I wished to cleanse you, and you were not cleansed; nor shall you be cleansed until I cause my indignation to rest upon you.”

And so that he might leave you no avenue for drawing breath, he said: “I, the Lord, have spoken. I will come and act; I will not pass over it, nor spare, nor be appeased. According to your ways and according to your inventions I will judge you, says the Lord God.”

God says, “I will not be appeased, nor will I spare”—and you consider him a liar?

The divine word goes on still further, declaring your insensibility: “The ox knows his owner, and the ass his master’s manger; Israel has not known me. My people does not understand” (Isa. 1:3).

You see that your oxen and asses have been placed before you.

Hear Jeremiah again: “The kite in the sky knows its appointed time; the turtledove, swallow, and stork have observed the time of their coming; but my people has not known the judgment of the Lord. How can we say, ‘We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us’? Truly, the lying stylus of the scribes has worked falsehood” (Jer. 8:7–8).

23. You perceive, rival, that even birds have been placed before you in understanding and knowledge; and yet you produce teachers for me from among those whose lying stylus you find everywhere when you read? You know also through Isaiah that they are blind and do not see.

But I think that the very blindness foretold there covers the light of your eyes with darkness; and therefore the blind mind does not lament that blindness is present within it.

For after the Lord of hosts—whom the Seraphim never cease to praise with triple sanctification—commanded the prophet’s lips to be cleansed with a coal held by tongs, he spoke to the prophet in this manner (Isa. 6:8–10):

“Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?”

The prophet, already cleansed from the pollution of those dwelling among them, answered: “Here am I; send me.”

Immediately the Triune Lord said to him: “Go and say to this people: ‘Hear with hearing, and do not understand; see the vision, and do not know.’ Make the heart of this people blind, and make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest they perhaps see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them.”

O how openly this passage demonstrates the holy and ineffable Trinity, if the foretold blindness did not obstruct the senses by failing to present itself voluntarily to them.

Do you understand, fuel of madness, that the omnipotent Lord of hosts hates your conversion as a kind of crime, and does not offer you opportunities for conversion but removes them? See what he says: “Lest they perhaps see with their eyes.”

And when God has no desire at all for your conversion, who is so foolish as to proclaim that you will one day be converted?

You could have observed this vision of Isaiah, recognized it in your heart, and believed in the Trinity repeated in triple sanctification, if the divine word had not said: “Make the heart of this people blind, and harden its heart.” And to designate that the blindness would be perpetual, the prophet asked: “How long, Lord?” And he said: “Until the cities are desolate without inhabitant, and the houses without human beings, and the land is left desolate” (ibid., 11).

You see that your blindness was foretold to last until the end of the world.

And through Jeremiah he says: “Behold, I will give this people over to ruin, and fathers and sons shall fall among them together, neighbor and kinsman alike, and they shall perish” (Jer. 6:21). And: “I will feed them wormwood, and give them water of gall to drink; and I will scatter them among nations which neither they nor their fathers knew; and I will send the sword after them until they are consumed” (Jer. 9:15–16).

You hear of consummation, and yet you expect redemption? You see that the virgin daughter of Zion has fallen and will not rise again. Why? Because there is no one to raise her. The one who was accustomed to lift them up has flown away from them.

He added: “And if they say to you, ‘Where shall we go forth?’ you shall say to them: ‘Those destined for death, to death; those destined for famine, to famine; those destined for captivity, to captivity.’ And I will visit upon them four kinds of punishment, says the Lord: the sword for slaughter, dogs for tearing apart, birds of the sky for scattering, and beasts of the earth for devouring” (Jer. 15:2–3).

All these things have been fulfilled among you from the time of Vespasian and Titus down to the present through various kinds of torments and captivities. Add this captivity to the others, if you can, and you will see by how many years this terrible devastation surpasses them.

24. Therefore I beg you not to be reluctant to write back to me concerning what manifest guilt has been committed—a guilt not expiated even by so long a passage of time. For all your captivities, dispersions, and servitudes under various kingdoms are known and require no witness beneath the sun. Indeed, even before they occurred, they were fixed by divine speech in predetermined times, so that no servitude existed beyond what the divine word had announced for its servants.

This captivity alone is imposed without an end, and it is unknown by how many years or in what times it will be relieved. The recognized guilt of others had an end to their scourging. This alone, as you say—not specifically but generally—extends in its entirety through the ages.

If you show me a predetermined time, I shall admit that I have been defeated. I wish to have peace with you through Christ, if you desire it. If you are considering the matter otherwise, you are a madman and a trifler, closing the end with a most evil boundary and, despite such great and terrible things, remaining hard and unsoftened.

May God open the eyes of your heart—he who reigns forever throughout infinite ages. Amen.

XIX. ALSO, THE LETTER OF THE TRANSGRESSOR ADDRESSED TO ALVARO

For the sake of eternal reward I have devoted myself diligently to standing in the Law of the Lord. Therefore I considered it superstitious to answer the barking of all rabid dogs.
