Yet if I had perceived in you some fuel in which the little spark of faith might be kindled, perhaps I would have written something back to you, so that you might recognize clearly that you, who are a compiler, and those from whose books you have drawn these things, are in error.

For this deceitful little letter of yours we may say what Virgil says [Note: *Bucolics*, Eclogue 8, verse 108]:

[Col. 0513A] “Do we believe it? Or do lovers themselves invent dreams for themselves?”

And elsewhere [Note: Eclogue 3, verse 90]:

“Whoever does not hate Bavius, let him love your songs, Maevius;

and let him also yoke foxes and milk he-goats.”

May God almighty, creator of heaven and earth, the merciful and glorious God whom you reviled, be your avenger and vindicator because of what you said against him . . . [lacuna].

XX. ALSO, ALVARO’S REPLY ADDRESSED TO THE TRANSGRESSOR

What your pen’s argument elicited, my watchful eye read ahead of it, and it wisely admired you for avoiding danger. But because you play with prudent rhetorical skill, and, through a Pisonian fault, do not know how to be silent while you speak, and because, as the stories tell, you hold the wolf by the ears and can neither hold him nor let him go, the poet aptly sings to you:

[Col. 0514A] “Attempt what you can, lest, pressed down by the weight of the work,

the labor overwhelm you and you abandon what you have attempted in vain.”

But so that you may know who I am and avoid me still further by keeping silent, hear Virgil [Note: These verses are falsely attributed to Virgil]:

“The Getae despise death with a celebrated wound.”

And also this:

“Getae,” he says, “where does he proceed on horseback?”

Hence this too is found among the poet’s words:

“On this side let the Dacian press, on that side let the Getae advance.”

I am he, I am he whom Alexander declared must be avoided, whom Pyrrhus greatly feared, whom Caesar shuddered at. Our own Jerome also says of us: “He has a horn on his forehead; flee far away.”

Therefore do not call us rabid dogs, but recognize yourself as a yelping fox. Nor should you call me a compiler of the ancients, since that requires great strength.

[Col. 0513]

THE LUMINOUS LITTLE INDEX [Note: See the *Notice* above, col. 387.]

[Col. 0513B] In defense of your servants, Lord, I do not trust in the frail judgment of a human being, nor rely upon a subtle refuge of my own; neither am I lifted up by the unjust swelling of pride nor inflated by the zeal of envy. Rather, trusting in the aid of your free mercy and relying upon your most merciful and unconquerable arm, I, wretched man, ascribe to you—my God in the beginning and Jesus Christ, Lord of all things—all the good that I know.

At the beginning I invoke you; throughout the whole text I implore you; to the end of the book I entreat you, bending the knee of my heart. I firmly believe that you are the light of all ages, without end; from you I know that the fountain of all virtues flows forth; in you I know that an ineffable sweetness is securely hidden for the saints. You are the way without error for believers, the life without death for the living, and the rest without end for those who enjoy you.

I invoke you, inexpressible light, fountain of true knowledge and of the teaching of saving life, so that, when your light comes upon me, you may brighten the darkness of my heart, and may abundantly satisfy and fruitfully enrich the soil of my breast, which is rough with the weeds of filth, by the stream of your Law, the fourfold-flowing river of paradise.

Thus may the true rising sun illumine our dark inward parts, and the river that makes the city of God glad irrigate the thorn-covered soil of my heart, so that the tongue of me, a wretched dog, which desires to please you through these things, may not contract the fault of loquacity while attacking errors, but, with your inspiration, may utter only those things which, in the age to come, may run through all the ages’ volumes for the benefit of souls, the advancement of readers, and the eradication of every insolence before the sight of the glory of your wondrous throne.

May this very small offering of your servant be accepted, Lord God, before the mercy of your majesty, and may the votive offering of this earthen vessel not be rejected. And although it may be stained by any human filth [Note: Read *inficietur*, “be stained,” for *infinietur*.], may it be cleansed by that gracious and blessed regard of yours, though I do not attend to it intently.

Be, Lord, a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths, and teach me your judgments (Ps. 118:103, 12); defend your understanding with my mouth. You, Lord, cause your words to sound through my mouth. Feed your dog, barking for you against the rabid wolf, with crumbs from your table.

For I did not rise up for these things trusting in myself, but in you, who make the tongues of infants eloquent and loosen the reins of speech for those made mute by you. In my devotion I have offered these two mites, not as one who knows, but as one in need (Luke 12:2).

For what is a human being, Lord, deprived of your help, except a source of danger to himself, while he lies plunged in the fall—or rather, in the depths—of error?

And therefore, most merciful maker, most loving craftsman, most compassionate judge, bring to completion what you have inspired; fulfill what you have commanded; accomplish what you have granted me to consecrate; and, concerning the one whom you have made worthy of this talent, arrange that through it he may incur not the boldness of presumption but obtain a fruit of humility most acceptable to you, in accordance with that immeasurable goodness with which you overflow.

For you have given me, pious creator, strength to understand; you have implanted faith in my inward parts; and from my mother’s womb you have preserved me not as a pagan but as a believer—not because any merit preceded, nor because any righteousness followed, nor because any work deserved it. For what did not yet exist could not have earned merit, nor could what was formless have been retained by right.

Even what my sordid action and my lot—which is nothing—denied me, your abundant kindness granted. But lest, because of what you have granted me, most excellent Lord, I should be accused as reckless, exposed as wicked, or condemned as a usurper, I therefore sigh trembling, pale, fearful, and groaning.

May I not daily walk through crooked paths and precipices, through empty and perishing things, through swollen and foolish things, through shameful and exalted things, through frivolous and inflated things, by serving sinister works; nor, even when speaking of things I consider acceptable to you, contract likewise a blemish of iniquity. May I not, from the very place where I ought in some measure to have lightened the burdens of my wickedness, heap up crimes a hundredfold—something which, under your ordering, is far from me.

Be present, Lord, be present to your most wretched and needy servant, and direct him, filled with the zeal of your faith. Cut away, Lord, the foreskin of my tongue, fashioned from worldly filth, and cleanse the secret fire of my mind with that fire by which you know how to melt the hearts of the saints and by which, above all, the affections of the martyrs are believed to be kindled.

Thus, with your inspiration, may I introduce into this work only those things sufficient for it, so that on that day of your fearful examination and just judgment they may not form a heap of sins erected against me, but may crush and overthrow the thousand ranks of offenses opposed to me by their own advance.

Go before me, unconquerable Lord Christ, and be a guide to your servant, already redeemed by the grace of your holy Gospel, as you went before the Israelite people through the desert in a pillar of cloud and light (Exod. 13:21–22). Under your leadership, may the ranks of the Amalekites [Note: Read “the ranks of the Amalekites.”] be destroyed; and may your cross, placed upon our shoulder, destroy all the dark horrors with its light, overwhelm the faithful with a single stroke of battle like a flashing star, and crush or drown the impious with that power by which you crush the demons.

Through you, Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit are one God and reign through the never-ending ages of ages. Amen. The end.

This book is therefore called the *Luminous Little Index*, because it teaches by illuminating the things that must be followed, and by clear indications reveals the enemy of the Church, whom all Christianity ought to avoid. The end.

[Col. 0515C] **1.** It has been enjoined upon the minds of the most skilled Catholics of the Church, from the very beginning of the faith, to rise up with special vigor against the enemies of the Lord and, with a two-edged sword, to cut down with the evangelical sickle all errors springing up in opposition—so that, with the axe laid at the root of the fruitless trees (Matt. 3:10), and with the hatchet balanced by a strong arm, the tall branches barren of stature, green with leaves but not with fruit, may be cut down with fitting legal severity and the evangelical double-edged blade, and appointed to be burned in eternal fire and everlasting conflagration.

Although, being among their number, [Note: Perhaps *olidi gestu*, “of foul bearing”? *Ollitus* is said to mean “foul” in the Glossary published by the Congregation of St. Maur.] frail in action and brutish in instinct, striving to prove ourselves in the age to come, and desiring to bark like dogs for the Lord, moved by zeal for God and love of religion, we discharge the service of this ministry of ours [Col. 0515D] and offer to our Creator what he has granted in us from his own generosity. In this we presume nothing from ourselves, and we acknowledge that by his gratuitous kindness we possess whatever strength he has established in us, though we are unworthy.

We do not rise up against the common fellowship of the faith through the jealousy of conquering them [Note: That is, “not against those who share faith with us.”]; rather, brandishing the horns of the Chaldeans, we trample them down with the truthful threshing of earthly things [Note: The manuscript reads *veracia*, “truthful.”]. We place this as a preface and set it before the opening of our disputation, lest the malicious chatter of slanderers and the customary insolence of brothers accustomed to disparaging others should proclaim that we have waged wars against the Church [Col. 0516A], by which they might suppose that, in disgracing us, they have confirmed their own laborious nonsense.

Far be it from us that the Catholic and universal Church should fight against her own members. Far be it again that sons should take up arms against their mother. The Church does not reject martyrs, but receives them; she does not defame them, but praises them; she does not disparage them, but exalts them. And we, following the mind of that venerable mother herself and praising the glory of the beauty of our Redeemer’s bride, venerate and honor those whom we rejoice to have laid down their lives for Christ and for the truth; nor do we mutilate the deed of a single work by the variation of times. And the authority of our elders has confirmed how universal this belief of ours is in the second book of this work. [Note: Perhaps “the greater authority of the elders.”]

**2.** But since there are some who are unworthy of special fervor, [Col. 0516B] cold in their love of the faith, terrified by earthly fear and the blow of the sword, who, not with compressed voice but with hoarse throat, loose lips, and twisted tongue, detract from or sneer at the martyrdom accomplished in our time with an inadequate denial, and who do not refuse, insofar as it lies within them, to hand the palm of victory to the devil, let them not accept this while remaining true to their own senses.

Our favor, most reverend brethren, even if—God forbid—it errs, agrees with truth and with Christ. But truth supplies the knife of vengeance to the demon, the minister of those who assert something else. And I wonder by what kind of reasoning truth can be named truth where error is ascribed to those who have fallen for Christ and for the truth.

At the beginning of the work we must therefore undertake, not arrogantly but steadfastly, as with brothers, to join battle and discuss whatever accords between the two sides [Note: Perhaps *discutere*, “to discuss.”]. Let the weak and infirm flee; let the strong and those girded with honorable courage contend. Certainly Christ did not command them to suppress the truth, but to offer their backs to their persecutors because of the sowing of the Gospel: “They shall flee from one city to another” (Matt. 10:23)—preaching what is true and honorable, not—God forbid—concealing what is holy and modest.

These are the foremost fugitives, worthy to be proclaimed with no ordinary praise throughout all ages. Although they may appear fearful and fleeing, nevertheless, wandering throughout the whole world and darting about like flashes of lightning, they sing the mercies of the Lord in synagogues and assemblies of peoples; with eloquent and distinguished speech they proclaim what they know will benefit holy hearers. They are driven out so that they may be silent about the mighty works of the Lord; yet they embrace exile so that they may more freely proclaim to diverse nations, and not merely to one people, what they are forbidden to say.

And lest what we say appear to be entirely our own, let us state what that holy man and abyss of knowledge, Jerome, thought about this matter with us. He says:

> “This must be referred to that time when the apostles were sent out for preaching, to whom it was specifically said: ‘Do not go into the roads of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans’ (Matt. 10:5)—that is, they should not fear persecution and yet should withdraw from it. We see that believers did this at the beginning, when, after persecution arose in Jerusalem, they were scattered throughout all Judea, so that the occasion of tribulation might become the sowing of the Gospel. Observe and consider carefully in your hearts that they were commanded to withdraw for no other reason than that the occasion of their departure might become the seedbed of the kingdom in every city.

> “For the true Teacher could have said, if he had followed your understanding, chilled by divine frost: ‘Suppress the truth; conceal justice; and when your fear has shaken your mind, retain what is true only in your heart, so that you may live secure, terrified by no one.’ [Note: *Tulta* means “removed.”] For when preaching was removed, all persecution ceased. Once persecution is removed, there will be no flight. Thus everyone remains safe who does not contradict the Gentiles, who does not attack error, who does not expose fraud, who does not oppose sinners, who does not break the bonds of heretics. Blessed Gregory explains this clearly in the twenty-first book of the *Moralia*:

> “‘Often we are left in peace and unchallenged [Note: Gregory has *inconcussi*, “unshaken,” in place of *indiscussi*, “unchallenged.”] if we do not take care to oppose the wicked for the sake of justice; but if the soul has already burned with desire for eternal life, if it already beholds the true light within, if it has kindled in itself the flame of holy fervor, then, insofar as the place permits and the cause demands, we ought to expose ourselves in defense of justice and oppose the wicked when they break out into injustice, even when they do not seek us out. For when they strike the justice that we love [Note: *quam*, “which,” is absent from the manuscript but occurs in Gregory at the cited place.] in others, they nevertheless pierce us by their blow, even if they appear to be honored.’ [Note: Gregory has *venerari*, “to be venerated,” here.] Since, therefore, the holy man opposes the wicked and evildoers even when he is not sought out, it is rightly said of the horse of God [Note: The manuscript reads *de eo quod*, “concerning that which.”]: ‘He advances into the encounter armed’ (Job 39:21).”

**3.** The apostles and apostolic men, all teachers and preachers, were commanded to attack the errors of Jews, Gentiles, and every heresy in speech, with true reasoning and strong, demonstrative argument. [Note: Perhaps *probabili*, meaning “probable” or “approved”; in the Glossary of Du Cange it signifies what is correct and approved, something resting on true proof.]

The strongest athletes contended unto death. They continually endured persecution for the sake of the justice they openly defended, and they were crowned and adorned. Is it not obvious, and clear to all who see the light, that persecution did not arise first from the Gentiles, but that preaching first arose among our own people?

Read the struggles of the holy martyrs in their various passions: the armies of the Lord fighting, cutting down the Lord’s enemies with the sword of the word. You will clearly see that many rushed forward of their own accord, without waiting for the orders of persecutors or for the snares of informers who sought to ensnare them in their frenzy. Instead, following the Lord’s example, they voluntarily offered their own welcome offerings and brought themselves as a pure sacrifice upon the altar consecrated by the blood of Christ, the eternal God. And—what you are accustomed to criticize even more—they wearied governors and rulers with many insults.

Those were especially the ones who stood first in the contest, fortified by the goodness of confidence; whose hearts possessed unrestrained courage, and whom no fearful fantasy had invaded; whom spiritual fervor, burning with zeal for the Lord [Note: The manuscript reads *extant*, perhaps for *aestuans*, “burning.”], and the love of Christ, moving freely in every direction, held more firmly and drenched manfully, compelling them outwardly to bring forth the flame hidden within, as a holocaust. Although savage persecution attacked most of them, nevertheless—and this you cannot deny—you read that innumerable people contended voluntarily. In this they fulfilled to the highest degree what is said: “I will sacrifice to you willingly, O Lord” (Ps. 53:8).

You say: “It is not a time of persecution.” Rather, I say more: “It is not the time of the apostles,” because apostolic vigor has diminished, though it ought always, in the shepherds of Christ, to kindle spiritual flames against adversaries through steadfastness and zeal for justice until the end of the age, and, having kindled the fuel of illumination, to brighten the darkness of the world with the flashing star of the eastern sky.

I fear that those who see the persecution of Antichrist established for the final times and yet remain silent will take offense at an answer based not on rashness, as they think, but on truth, as Catholics judge it. Whoever today denies that persecution exists in these regions either carries the yoke of servitude in the deepest sleep of negligence [Note: Read *somno*, “sleep,” for *summo*, “highest”], or, puffed up with the Gentiles in the pride of his foot, tramples upon Christ’s subject recruits.

Are we not bound to the yoke of servitude, weighed down by an unbearable tax, stripped of our possessions, crushed beneath bundles of insults, and made a proverb and a song—made a spectacle to all the Gentiles? [Note: Read *theatrum*, “spectacle,” as in the Apostle, 1 Cor. 4:9: “We have been made a spectacle.”] They say that this is not a time of persecution; I reply in opposition that we have encountered deadly times. They assert that these men proceeded without hostile provocation; I shall establish, by their own testimony, that they were oppressed by Gentile zeal.

Let us first look upon the priest Perfectus, slain by Gentile zeal, adorned with steadfastness in the faith, crowned with martyrial glory, and truly numbered among the elect. Let us sincerely set forth how he came to his death.

As he was going elsewhere and attending to other secular matters, thinking nothing about what had happened, he was provoked by the assertions of idolaters. From them, cautiously and circumspectly, as they suppose—but, as I see it, fearfully—he was asked to give his faith. He prayed that he not be hindered by his own answers, saying:

> “I had many arguments by which I could utterly shatter your nonsense or destroy your old women’s tales, if I did not fear rushing headlong into the judgments of your vengeance, which run this way and that with an avenging sword.”  
> [Note: The manuscript reads uncertainly: “from which … to fear … avenging … I have run.”]

When they had given him their word and, after imposing an oath, urged him to explain what he thought, he accepted the confidence to speak, taking their lies as though they were a true oath. After many and varied struggles of debate, he reproached, as far as he could in speech, their prophet’s wanton [Note: The manuscript reads *voluntuosam*.] licentiousness and the passive debauchery of his procuring [Note: Morales, in his scholia on book II of the works of St. Eulogius, chapter 1, omitted *passivam*, as he also omitted *factionis* shortly below; the author repeats *passivam libidinem* (“passive lust”) in section 28, at the end.], and demonstrated it with an eloquent argument.

After some verbal contest concerning the mockery of his fornication, or the collusive plot of the adultery of married women, they gnashed their teeth, raged with doglike jaws, hissed with viperous mouths, and roared with the fierceness of lions. Yet, because of the oath they had recently given, they allowed him to depart unharmed. [Note: Morales substitutes “permitted” for “allowed.”]

But after some time had passed, while they always retained the poison of pain in sinful hearts, and, as though time had rendered it obsolete, regarded their former deceitful pact with him as annulled, they surrounded and seized him by trickery. They maliciously brought him before a judge, eagerly pressing a falsehood [Note: The manuscript reads *iniantem*.], claiming that he had impiously destroyed their religious rite; and they confirmed, by the testimony of a contemptible little man, that he had cursed their prophet.

Terrified by this unexpected turn of events and perplexed by this unheard-of deception, ignorant of the fraudulent plans that their treacherous plotting had devised against him, he denied with a sufficiently weak defense that he had said any such thing. But when he had been thrown into prison and turned his attention inward, he began, with bold purpose and manly engagement, to break their entire law. He not only said what he had said the day before, as their ignorant faction alleged against him, but also advanced other, more important matters, looking forward more to the glory of death than to destruction.

Then, on that very dreadful day of his, when they were accustomed to enjoy carnal feasts and to provide abundant food for belly and lust, they led him out and killed him with the avenging sword. As though they had gained victory over their enemies, they went to the assembly for prayer, believing that they had rendered service to God; carried away and drenched in the blood of an innocent man, they proceeded, as was their custom, to complete their rite.

**4.** Now be just judges and pronounce not a favorable, windy, and shifting sentence, but a true judgment of reason, bound by the chains of justice. From whom, I ask, do you now see that persecution has arisen?

Is it not evident that they themselves are the instigators of evil, the advocates of errors, and the inflictors of suffering? They did not fear, because of the zeal of their faith, boldly to shatter, insolently to mutilate, and, in Gentile fashion, skillfully to destroy [Note: Perhaps “destroy” should be read] the pact first offered to an innocent man, a pact prepared by the fraud of poison, preceded by fury, inflamed by anger, and filled with iniquity.

Behold the boldness—or rather, the steadfastness—which you drag into condemnation and bring forward as a crime. This priest did not possess it. Timidly he went to war; through the zeal of the devil he came to his death. He received his passion not from worshipers of God, but from disciples of Antichrist. Is it hidden, concealed, or covered over that persecution arose, was discovered, begun, defended, and completed by them?

**5.** Let us proceed to explain once more the second case. After the turning of a year, or somewhat more, that eye of Gentile envy did not rest. As was their custom, they tried to mock the most Christian of men and insult all of us who worship Christ. They attempted to harass this John—whom they had held for a long time in the confinement of prison [Note: *Claustra* is feminine, singular, in writers of Late Latin]—while he was increasing the wares of trade at market. Burned by envy on account of the trade, they heaped many reproaches upon him [Note: Perhaps *ingessere*, “heaped upon.”], saying:

> “You make light of our prophet and are always using his name in mockery. By oaths of our religion, as it seems to you, you repeatedly affirm to ignorant ears, falsely and without knowing it, that you are a Christian.” [Note: Morales, in his edition of St. Eulogius, reads *te ignorantium*, “to the ears of the ignorant.”]

When he, confidently and suspecting no deceit against himself, wished to show that he was free from the charges they brought against him, bursting fury and headlong anger repeated, pressed, and continually reiterated the things they had often said, and threatened him.

Then, unable to endure this cloud of such generations, and girded with a sufficiently witty urbanity, he answered them with elegant and exalted thought:

> “Cursed by God be anyone who wishes to name your prophet.”

Immediately there arose a great outcry. A packed crowd of the lost, a hated gathering of iniquity, like bees gathered into one mound of treachery, sprinkled with the mixture of a single mass of wickedness [Note: Morales reads *conspiratione*, “conspiracy”; *conspersione* or *consparsione* should nevertheless be retained. The ancients used *consparsum* for “sprinkling.” See the Glossary of Du Cange], dragged him, half alive, before the judge. Producing witnesses of little authority, arising from that same mass of faithless men, they brought stronger and greater accusations against him by their own testimony.

He denied all of it and openly exposed their jealous envy against him. But the unjust judge beat him with four hundred blows of the whip and had him led through all the churches of the saints, while a herald proclaimed:

> “Such things must be suffered by anyone who disparages the prophet of God.”

Then he handed him over to prison under strict guard, threatening to inflict still greater torments upon him.

**6.** Is there still anyone possessed by the cloud of error, sprinkled with the dregs of iniquity, who denies that this is a time of persecution? What greater persecution could there be, or what harsher downfall could be expected, when what is rationally believed in the heart cannot be spoken publicly with the mouth?

Behold, the public law is in force, and legal commands [Note: *Legalis jussa* is feminine singular, like *claustra*. One might read *legalis jussio*, “legal command,” unless the verb is also taken to continue, as Morales does] run throughout their entire kingdom, so that whoever blasphemes is scourged and whoever strikes is killed.

Behold also how, daily, in the hours of day and night, from their towers and mist-covered mountains [Note: *Caligosus* means the same as *caliginosus*, “misty” or “dark,” according to Du Cange], they curse the Lord, while with a voice of testimony they exalt, together with the Lord, an immodest, perjured, rabid, and wicked prophet. [Note: Perhaps read *eum*, “him,” for *una cum*, “together with.”]

Alas, and woe to this age of ours, poor in the wisdom of Christ and full of zeal for the devil! In it no one is found who, according to the command of the thundering heavenly Lord, raises the banner of the faith of the cross over the mountains of Babylon and the dark towers of pride, offering the evening sacrifice to God.

We not only receive poisons with joyful mind, tranquil acceptance, and composed regard; we drink their potions and taste beforehand their death-bearing shoots. But what is more destructive, we oppose those who resist them and who, like Elijah, are zealous with zeal for God; with deaf ears we form friendships with the enemies of the Most High God, and, to please them, disparage our own faith.

Certainly, in our view it is more acceptable to contend like Elijah with the sword than, like our heroes, to oppose them with the tongue. Every day, crushed beneath reproaches and a thousand bundles of insults, we say that we do not suffer persecution. [Note: These words and others would better be closed with a question mark. Since the manuscript never marks this, and since they may be understood as spoken from the mind of the adversaries, we have not altered them.]

To say nothing of other matters: when they see the bodies of the dead being carried by priests, according to ecclesiastical custom, to be given to the earth, do they not say in open voices and with the foulest faces [Note: Morales reads *gemitibus*, “with groans,” in his edition of St. Eulogius. The manuscript has *genis*, “faces,” which we do not reject. Below, in sections 20 and 24, the author repeats “with impure faces”]: “God, do not have mercy on them”? Do they not attack the priests of the Lord with stones, mark the Lord’s people with disgraceful words, and cover Christ’s worshipers with the filth of their dung, scattering them with unspeakable stench and snarling while threatening worse things?

And again, a third time, innumerable woe to us, who endure this mockery and derision of theirs and doubt whether this is the time of the persecution of Antichrist.

Likewise, when they encounter priests of God traveling along the road, do they not roll stones and the driest potsherds [Note: Morales reads: “Whenever they meet anyone on the road, they pile stones before them and place the driest potsherds ahead,” adding words of his own. The reading “the driest potsherds,” which is better than the manuscript’s form, is restored here] before their footsteps, disparage them with an insulting and infamous name, and sneer at them with a vulgar proverb and indecent song? Do they not stain the sign of faith with a disgraceful epithet? [Note: Morales wrongly printed *detruncant* (“cut down”) for *decolorant* (“stain” or “disfigure”).]

But when they hear the signal of the basilica—that is, the sound of ringing bronze struck at all the canonical hours to gather the church’s assembly—they hunger for derision and contempt. They shake their heads, repeat and redouble their unspeakable words, and attack and mock every sex, every age, and the entire flock of Christ the Lord, not with a single uniform sneer but with a thousand infamies of insult.

**7.** Are these not the men who curse Jerusalem and destroy and burn the walls of holy faith, concerning whom it is said:

> “Cursed are all who despise you, and all who blaspheme you. Cursed are all who hate you, and all who speak a harsh word against you. Cursed are all who cast you down, and all who destroy your walls, and all who overthrow your towers, and all who burn your dwellings.”

[Note: These are the curses that the Church regularly and openly poured out upon those who hated her, as the author immediately recalls.]

Although they fulfill all these things, as we have said, through contempt, derision, or hatred, they also perpetrate them bodily every day against the dwellings of the Lord and the buildings of the sanctuary, while the churches of God are destroyed and temples established upon ancient foundations are leveled to the ground.

Is there still anyone who will not declare those worthy of a curse whom, together with the teaching Church, he has so long sung as accursed? The Church proclaims this curse every year over those who hate her—not secretly, but openly and resplendently—and with a lofty voice and gentle sweetness sufficiently exalts the mouths of her faithless enemies.

For the angel of the Lord commanded the inhabitants of that land to be cursed because they did not come to the aid of the strong men of the Lord. And we declare that those who trample upon the strong men of the Lord and mock the sacred things of God and the truly Holy of holies are not worthy to be assailed by curses, but that this should be considered indiscriminate or unjust.

**8.** The prophetic—indeed, divine—sentence thunders:

> “Curse Meroz, says the angel of the Lord; curse its inhabitants, because they did not come to the aid of its strongest men. Bless Jabel, the wife of Barcennae [Note: The Vulgate has “Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite”], who gave milk to one asking for water and offered butter in the prince’s bowl. She put her left hand to the peg and her right hand to the smith’s hammer, and struck Sisara, seeking a place on his head for the wound, piercing his temple powerfully.” (Judg. 5:23 ff.) [Note: Read *tempus*, “temple,” that is, the part of the head which in Spanish we call *la sien*.]

And, as I think, it is a greater deed to pierce a temple with a hilt than to wound the enemies of the Lord with truthful words. It is also a greater reward to fight spiritual battles [Note: The manuscript reads *pugna spiritalia*.] for the truly Holy of holies, as I have already said, and for the state of eternal life that will exist without end, than to contend with nails and hammers for the typological and carnal Jerusalem or for an earthly kingdom that will eventually be cut off within a brief span.

But at that time the prophetic spirit blessed her, and today the whole chorus of the Church proclaims her in the same way that the holy universal congregation then praised her.

Certainly, whoever affirms that the enemies of the Church are accursed when they curse her, recoiling from the truth, detests sacred religion. It remains for him, after defaming those of the present, to attack the celebrated contest of the saints of former times.

Let him curse Jahel, whom prophetic inspiration blessed in the assembly of the peoples. Let him curse Judith, who, according to the sense of those who mock, deceitfully killed the army [Note: Perhaps “the king.”]. Let him also curse the countless other fathers who, fighting unto death through zeal for the Lord, cut down the enemies of God not only with words but with swords.

And if they do not accept that battle must be undertaken for the faith from true and vigorous men of severity, let them at least learn from women to raise a manly trophy of victory over their enemies. [Note: The manuscript reads *ad ore harum*, “at the mouth of these women.”] Let the stronger sex be ashamed to be surpassed by the female sex.

Finally, something that will appear sacrilegious to everyone: if so great an adversary curses the holy Church, which curses those who curse her every day, then certainly the one who curses the Church is a defamer of the Church’s members—indeed, he is a profane slanderer of that very Church, which is reckoned no less in the martyrs themselves than in others.

Did not our teacher, Paul, the master of Christ’s churches, the apostle of the Gentiles, the chosen vessel of Christ, marking this angel with his finger, curse him in the prophetic spirit, saying:

> “If anyone proclaims to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed. Amen. Even if an angel from heaven should proclaim to you a different gospel, let him be accursed. Amen.” (Gal. 1:8)

Behold that accursed angel is revealed: he who attempts, by another authority, to destroy Paul’s instructions by another way—unless, perhaps, you say either that the good angel was cursed by so great an apostle, or that, with insolent chatter, you proclaim before the world that this most impure man, who offered himself to dwell with the most impure angel [Note: The manuscript reads *in purissimo*, “in the most pure”; the sense requires “with the most impure”], preached the very thing Paul preached.

And it is true that, from the time of that supreme teacher just mentioned, no one else under the name of an angel dared to bring forward a deviation from his preaching and something opposed to the evangelical sect, except this man who, under the name of Gabriel, falsely claimed to have brought another law from God to humanity.

Although many founders of heresies had been deceived by the invasion of angels of darkness, none of them presumed to usurp a testament in the place of God. But if an angel from heaven who brings forward deviations from our faith is anathematized by the Apostle’s mouth, what should be thought appropriate for that most wicked vessel [Note: That is, Muhammad], if its inhabitant is condemned by so bitter a wound of cursing?

But these and other matters. [Note: The manuscript reads *Elias*, “Elijah”; read *Haec et alias*, “these and other matters.”] [Note: The manuscript reads *Elias*, “Elijah”; read *Haec et alias*, “these matters and others.” The phrase is familiar to Alvarus.]

**9.** Let us now turn back to the section of our narrative concerning the lukewarmness of our people, and set forth in brief words the condition of our entire tepidity, in order to establish the just divine judgment.

Are not our own people, who serve their commands through the office of the palace, publicly entangled in their errors? For when they do not pray openly before the Gentiles, they do not fortify their foreheads with the sign of the cross while yawning [Note: Here is evidence of how ancient was the custom of signing oneself during the act of yawning. Today, however, we fortify the mouth, not the forehead, with the sign]; they do not openly proclaim Christ God before them, but utter him in evasive speech, professing the Word of God and the Spirit as they assert them, while keeping their confessions in their hearts, as though they were aware that God sees everything.

What do all these things show, except that they possess the mottled variety of the leopard while being zealous for God, since they defend Christianity not wholly but only halfway? Yet we defend all these things as good and proclaim them not damnable but excellent.

We do not curse or detest Christians who fight against the companions of their faith for the king’s favor, for saleable gifts, and in defense of the Gentiles; rather, we strike with anathema and defame religious men who contend for the true God. And we do all this under the pressure of fear of an earthly king, whom we confidently believe and hold to be destined for a swift end; while we cast behind us and trample underfoot the fear of the eternal King, to whom we truly believe and hold that we shall soon be led. And those who contradict their errors we judge to be heretics and ignorant.

Our weapons fight against us, and our iniquity descends upon our own head (Ps. 7:17). Excellent preachers, admirable chosen shepherds of flocks, good and “nonnus” [Note: *Nonnus* is a term by which elders are addressed as a sign of reverence. See the Glossary of Du Cange. It is also a word in the Tagalog language of the Philippine Islands with the same sense. The author repeats it below in section 34, “the nonn of Hilary.”], is this how Christ taught us? Is this how all the apostles and teachers taught us? Is this how all those taught who, laying down their lives for the truth, labored through diverse contests?

**10.** I ask: whence has this new clemency arisen in the churches, which has vomited forth these infernal doctrines? Or, if you think this statement rash, tell us which pious Apostle commanded these things.

If error must not be openly attacked, why did the Lord Jesus Christ descend? Why, when no one questioned him or asked about his conversion, did he voluntarily bring light to the blind? Why prophets? Why apostles sent out? Why teachers? Why shepherds appointed beforehand? Was it not so that ignorance might be subdued and every perfidy receive punishment?

How will what the Lord foretold come to pass, if no preaching thunders among the Gentiles: “When this Gospel has been preached in the whole creation, then the end will come” (Matt. 26:13)?

Attend to and examine the words of so great a craftsman: “When this Gospel has been preached in the whole creation.” Preaching is certainly introduced among the ignorant and unbelieving; it is not repeatedly imposed upon those who already know, honor, and worship the things that must be believed. For among the faithful, the communication or teaching of what is known is called a contribution or instruction. Preaching, however, if I am not mistaken, is properly called that which, as though in the course of a work, as all the apostles did, is thrust upon people opportunely and inopportunely, even at the risk of one’s life; and which is sought out frequently, even when danger may arise, so that unbelievers may receive the light of faith.

He did not say openly that every creature would receive the preaching of the Gospel, but that the preaching of the Church would shine clearly throughout the whole world. Through this ministry, a due reward is brought to preachers, and a most just, eternal, and unending punishment to those who despise it.

Nor is the preaching of the faith to be confined only to those apostolic times. Rather, until every nation and tongue believes the Gospel of Christ, the preaching of the Church must be sown throughout every age.

I think that until now no preacher has existed among this Ishmaelite people through whom they might be held accountable as debtors to the faith. These men [Note: Read *sed nos*, “but we,” that is, the Christians who disapproved of the martyrdom occurring at that time. “These” are those who voluntarily offered themselves to the judges at Córdoba, concerning whom and on whose behalf this apologetic speech of the author was written] fulfilled among them, so to speak, the role of the apostles and the preaching of the Gospel, and made them debtors to the faith. But we, covered by the thick cloud of ignorance, do not see the mystery of the eternal Gospel running its course. And when they proclaim justice to a people for whom no one’s preaching has hitherto opened a way [Note: That is, among the Saracen people], we cry out that it is the madness of folly, not the fulfillment of the foreknown design of the evangelists.

For the more they glory in being philosophers above all other peoples, the more deservedly they are despised by the humble, by those who know nothing except Christ—and him crucified. Against them, appropriately and in the customary manner, Truth itself sends unlearned disciples, uncultivated in worldly learning, so that rustics and those who appear contemptible to the world may attack philosophers adorned with royal insignia in words, trample them beneath their feet, and regard all the swelling of their power as nothing beneath the heel of faith.

This is what the distinguished teacher Arnobius explained in the eighteenth psalm. He says:

> “There is no one who can hide from his heat. No nation, he says, will exist in the world to which the heat of Christian faith does not reach—the faith in which the law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls, inviting them from error to the straight path and from falsehood to truth, where there are joys that gladden hearts.”

Truly, this Ishmaelite people is ignorant of the heat of Christian faith and until now did not know the ministers of the Lord, sprinkled with consuming fire.

We have become, O companions in our faith—if indeed you deign to be such—mute dogs, unable to bark. [Note: The manuscript reads *impetum*, “attack”; the context requires *impetus*, “the attack” or “the force.”] Against us is directed the statement of the most holy Jerome, lover of the heavenly library, in which he explains the prophetic word:

> “All the watchmen are blind; they are all mute dogs, unable to bark.” (Isa. 56:10) [Note: The manuscript reads *nullut*, perhaps *illud*, “that.”]

We are mute when it comes to speaking against adversaries, yet rabid dogs against our own people. But let us rather follow the ways of God. The wolves, however, because they rage around the sheepfolds, have raised against us the voice of rebuke. In an unheard-of and hated fashion, wolves and dogs have returned to peace.

### 11

Let us examine this pride, which our humble men praise as something to be maintained in the causes of God, by reference to the histories of our ancestors, and let us establish how true their claims are. Is not Elijah regarded by all as a great prophet? And indeed he is the one who, out of zeal for God, did not fear to gird himself not only with words but also with a sword, and to cut down more than four hundred worshipers of Baal who were prophesying (3 Kings 18). He also consumed two captains of fifty with fire, while he spared the third—not because of any softness of mind, but because the man humbly entreated him—and left him unharmed (4 Kings 1). By the merit of this action he provoked the merciful Lord to vengeance, consuming the wicked with fire before the day of judgment.

Is he not also the one who, out of zeal for God and for the neglected faith, shut up heaven, restrained the clouds, and afflicted the land of idolatry with an irremediable scarcity of bread, withholding the rains for three years and six months and suspending the most merciful God from his customary compassion by prayer? He showed mercy to no one, but persevered in harshness, and was rigidly cruel according to the demands of the case, sparing not even an old woman’s age (3 Kings 17). And what could have been a stronger sign of cruelty and irreligiousness than for so great and distinguished a prophet not to hesitate to cut down, according to your view with excessive severity and zeal against the judgment of God, the innocent childhood of infants because of their parents’ faithlessness, contrary to the divine sentence that commands that a child’s soul not be punished for its father’s wickedness (Deut. 24:16)?

Moses, the lawgiver of God and, for forty days, a pupil in the school of the Most High, employed zeal for God not only against the Egyptian (Exod. 2:12), but also acted with rash yet most holy and generous courage against the tablets written by God’s finger, which he did not hesitate to break; and for this he earned not God’s anger but his favor (Exod. 32:16). Perhaps the gentlest of men was imbued with this severity during the forty days he remained with the Lord. For immediately afterward he descended to the transgressing people, broke the tablets of God, as I have said, and, coming to the people, said:

> “Let each man place a sword around his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate through the middle of the camp, and let each man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.”

And on that day about twenty thousand men fell (Exod. 32:27).

Moreover, when he saw Dathan and Abiram, who had risen up improperly against him, swallowed by the earth, he was not moved by his customary compassion, with which he had often entreated the Lord on behalf of the transgressing people; rather, he was stirred to action (Num. 16). But because he was looking toward the future purification of many, he endured the death of a few with equanimity.

Examples of these cruel acts abound. The divine pages, written by these cruel authors, while instilling gentleness in us, urge us to persecute the enemies of God with perfect hatred, and loudly proclaim, both in words and deeds, that this cruelty—which you consider acceptable—is preferable to sacrifice. Hence Samuel, cruel—or rather, a faithful servant of the Creator—cuts down the exceedingly fat king whom your pious king Saul spares (1 Kings 15:33). But God, approving the cruel man and rejecting the mild one, rejected the pious Saul and chose the fierce Samuel.

For Samuel knew what came of approving undisciplined softness, and knew that Eli the master had been expelled and that the people of the Lord had reduced the ark of the law to the power of foreigners. David also says:

> “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and do I not waste away over your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me” (Ps. 138:21–22).

Is the zeal of Phinehas unknown, or his intercession that mitigated the Lord’s anger (Num. 27), so that the divine Spirit says of him through the prophetic voice:

> “Phinehas stood up, and made intercession, and the plague ceased” (Ps. 105:30).

And certainly that intercession, celebrated beforehand in the Psalmist’s words, was a sentence of the merciless sword against those who despised God. Let our “merciful” men see that this cruelty became intercession, and let them cease to put forward piety and humility in matters consecrated by divine speech—piety for which they read that Saul was rejected from the kingdom and Eli removed from the priesthood and from life (1 Kings 3–4).

Let them recall the severity of Peter and Paul against the magicians Simon and Elymas, and against Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5, 8, 13). And let those who are proud, arrogant, haughty, and unbending in their insults against their own people, but appear humble, gentle, simple, and quiet against the enemies of God, learn both from Christ, the God of all things, and from all the prophets, apostles, and Fathers: in the face of insults directed against themselves they must be humble and abject; but in avenging contempt for the divine majesty they must be strong and rigid. They should employ not the inappropriate piety of these men, but this holy cruelty.

“For cruelty is not piety on behalf of God,” as blessed Jerome says. I shall establish this in the second book with clearer indications and more evident proofs from the testimonies of the teachers. But let us now return to the matter at hand.

### 12

It has been clearly set out from where the persecution arose; therefore let us hasten to our voluntary martyrs. Isaac, a religious man, was moved by zeal for God, not by human instigation. He walked a path unfamiliar in our times but long since obliterated, and, unable to endure with equanimity the ancient smoke of persecution, he approached the judge. What he, when harassed by a dreadful scourge, denied—what the weak accuser claimed amid the blows that he had not said—the strong athlete and soldier in the warfare confirmed by a fuller prosecution, undertook in a greater battle, and began with a free mind; he carried it through, completed it, and fulfilled it. [Morales reads: “he began it, and completed it by an honorable death.”]

Thus he showed to all that he had been moved by zeal for the faith, not overtaken by fear of necessity, so that the Church militant might openly and plainly bring its battles into the field with steadfast confidence, and firmly establish what they had been striving to support by certain indications. [The same source adds: “also.”] The Lord thereby brought the victory of his athletes before the world, proclaimed the steadfastness of his soldiers to the inexperienced world, [Manuscript: “to the rude world”; Morales: “to the rude age,”] and showed that in the last times he would also have victors who would wage the Lord’s battles with the same impulse with which the men of old had undertaken them. [The same source adds: “would fight the battles they had first undertaken.”]

What do you consider blameworthy in this? Behold, we have proved that the persecution arose from the pagans. Behold, we have also established that our own men rose up out of zeal for God, not for men. What do you consider blameworthy in this? I ask you not to delay in declaring it.

They saw the battle of combat. Clad in the breastplate of faith, they undertook a most splendid war; with rapid course and tireless step, after they had seen one man killed and another wounded [namely, Saint Perfectus killed and John scourged], they ran to the field of combat to win the palm of glory.

### 13

They were vigorous men and warriors, desiring the contest of spiritual warfare, where the action proved to be such as the opportunity had been expected to provide. They could not restrain their course, because they sought to fulfill the command of their eternal Lord.

Why do you oppose the weakness of the feeble, and, lest the weak be frightened, break the strong? If you are weak, feeble, empty, timid, and puffed up, be quiet, and do not fight against those who are contending with their fellow citizens. Sit still, await the outcome, and learn to bridle your tongue by keeping silent. But if you are capable, strong, bold, steadfast, and suited for God’s war against his enemies, hurl your darts as a vigorous man, not as a coward against your own people.

Why do you not perceive the marvelous and fiery resolve, the confidence in the astonishing resurrection, the steadfastness of glorious hope, and the zeal for the glory of faith and Catholic religion? Why do you, by your persecution, shatter the purpose set before them, the sacred order, the prolonged ordering of confession, the soul’s long inward battle, and the banner raised against the devil and the ranks of the Amalekites?

Why do you impose the stain of falsehood upon Catholics, upon the sons of the holy Church, upon those instructed in pious doctrine, upon the followers of Christ, upon those excluded from worldly affairs, and upon those who cling to God alone? Why do you not fear opposing those who choose the good portion like Mary, and consenting, as far as lies within you, to the sentence of vengeance pronounced faithlessly against the saints by Christ’s rivals?

They killed with swords those whom they judged hostile to their faith; you kill with sentences those whom you know to agree with your faith. They attempted to remove them from worldly life; you strive to separate them from eternal life. But far be it from us that those who lost their lives for life should be separated from life.

Far be it, and far removed from our thoughts, that worshipers of truth and confessors of Christ for so long should, with the devil mocking them, bring their course to an end in the lie. Let this be said by the faction of ignorance, and by the hardened multitude rendered insensible by Christ’s hidden and just judgment. Let whoever, in the end, insolently casts himself before the devil while seeking the highest rank of the most Christian order explain to us, if he can, what he thinks about the other orders.

But our simplicity, poor in guile, and the Church’s pure and chaste sincerity that is with us, celebrate the order of confession as directed by the divine Spirit, and maintain that those who announce the truth to kings have been enlightened by Christ’s happy refreshment.

### 14

But you object: “Because of them, the basilicas of God remain deprived of priests, and while persecution rages, the continual sacrifice has been forbidden.”

To this a truthful confession responds: “Our sins—our sins—have done this: sins which dared to rise up against the martyrs of God, or rather against the Lord himself.”

Let your fraternal assembly [that is, your gathering] recall what a great and terrible storm of madness, stirred up against God, seized weapons in rebellion [possibly: “rebellion”]; and then let it impose this stain upon the holy martyrs, if it can. Did not those themselves who seemed to be pillars, who were thought to be the rocks of the Church, who were believed to be chosen—without anyone compelling them and without anyone provoking them—approach the judge [manuscript: “heard”], and, in the presence of Cynics, or rather Epicureans, defame the martyrs of God?

Did not the shepherds of Christ, the teachers of the Church, bishops, abbots, priests, nobles, and magnates publicly proclaim them to be heretics? And did they not, in a public declaration, without examination and without inquiry, utter of their own free will and by the unforced judgment of their minds things that ought not to have been said even under sentence of death?

With conscience trampled and faith despised, all served falsehood—alas, what grief! They affirmed that those whom they knew to have been born in the Catholic faith and nourished at the breasts of Mother Church had been fed by adulterous intercourse and the food of adulterers.

### 15

Is there anyone who can still complain worthily about the scourge, when he sees plainly the cause of the scourge itself? Is it not obvious that all these men professed falsehood and, according to the saying of Truth, which indicates the danger of this final time, “the elect were scandalized” (Matt. 24:24)?

They were elect because they were overseers of God’s flock and adorned with sacred orders; but they were scandalized because, fearing to testify publicly to the truth, which is Christ, they tried to strengthen falsehood.

“You will destroy those who speak falsehood,” says Scripture (Ps. 5:7). And: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11)—its own soul all the more than another’s. For just as Christ the Lord is the Truth, so the devil Antichrist is falsehood.

“Rejecting the truth,” as the Apostle says (Rom. 1:25), they will receive falsehood—that is, the final enemy himself, condemned at the last judgment, the instrument of the devil and the most fitting title of every falsehood. Nothing opposes truth except falsehood. Nor is there any doubt that whoever speaks falsehood immediately departs from God, who is truth.

We do not fall into falsehood only in trivial and moderate matters [that is, mediocre matters], but also in the highest matters consecrated by the principal name. When, under the pressure of persecution, we were especially constrained in the very truth of the faith, we infected ourselves with much bitterness of gall, and clothed the worshipers of Christ in the scandal of heresy, whenever that stinking skin arose among us.

What was done publicly outside, before the authorities who savagely ravaged us, may perhaps appear unpunished somewhere. But what defense can be offered concerning those whom we ecclesiastically prohibited, and from whom we extorted an oath that they should never rise to the palm of martyrdom? We forbade them to refute the errors of the pagans, and wickedly forced them by oath not to attack the Gospel and the cross with curses, threatening unheard-of punishments and promising monstrous mutilations of their limbs—various scourges horrible to speak of or hear.

And woe to us! We used the Gospel against the Gospel. For whoever forbids cursing necessarily commands blessing.

Let us consider here, if it seems just to you, our public falsehoods and their truthful confessions. They said what the whole Church proclaims; we said what all Christianity condemns. They cursed the false prophet; we disparaged the worshipers of Christ. They were persecutors of pagans; we were persecutors of Christians. They were bold and upright against the devil; we were proud against the Lord. They grew proud against an earthly king; we against the immortal and eternal King. They confessed with their mouths what they held in their hearts; we confessed one thing in our hearts and another with our mouths. They were, as I have said, truthful confessors and witnesses; we—woe to me!—were deceitful fabricators.

To the carnal and less knowledgeable, the scandal arising at the time of martyrdom is announced by blessed Isidore, our light, in his book On the Nature of Things, with clear eloquence and an apt image concerning a certain star, Orion. “The Orions,” he says, “signify the martyrs. For just as these stars arise in heaven in winter, so martyrs arise in the Church during persecution. When the Orions appear, the sea and the land are disturbed; but when martyrs arise, the hearts of earthly people and of the faithful are tossed by the storm.”

### 16

But perhaps someone maintains that simulation in such matters is a worthy form of administration, and frivolously attempts to affirm this by the authority of the apostles or of the law. Let them briefly run through those very administrative examples, and they will clearly find that no one regularly employed an expedient falsehood in matters of principal importance. They did not use it to endanger the soul, but where they knew that it would most beneficially bring forth the salvation of many and the proper ordering of their own future.

The simulation of the king of Israel [namely, Jehu] makes this clear. He professed that he wished to worship the idol so that he might easily overthrow the priests hiding in various places, saying:

> “Gather all the priests of Baal for me. If Ahab served Baalim a little, I shall serve him greatly” (4 Kings 10:18).

Likewise David, seeing that bodily death, not death of the soul, threatened him, feigned madness (1 Kings 21:13), and avoided the deadly danger into which he had fallen—not a danger to his faith, but to his bodily person.

In this way Paul and the other senior apostles are to be understood as having feigned the observance of the ceremonies of the law (Acts 21), so that through this accommodation provision might be made for the salvation of the Gentiles. They treated their private loss as insignificant in comparison with the whole world, for which a remedy was thereby impending. They were not bent toward worshiping idols, but turned to the ceremonies of the living God, although by that time those ceremonies had already been abolished.

### 17

These authorities are to be invoked at another time, not, as we have said, to be used in the principal worship of the holy faith, but subsequently to be approved in matters concerning bodily and human welfare, without harm to the faith.

That falsehood and simulation must be entirely avoided in divine matters is taught with luminous clarity by the sacred authority Eleazar in the Second Book of Maccabees. When his friends advised him to eat privately other meats instead of sacrificial meats, or pork, and to pretend that he was eating the forbidden foods that the impious king insistently urged him to consume—so that he might escape death and not transgress the decree of the law—he rejected the deceitful pretense. He chose instead to endure a public triumph, thereby offering to future ages an exemplary lesson of his virtue.

> “It is not worthy of our age,” he said, “to pretend, lest many young men, thinking that Eleazar at ninety years of age had passed over to the life of foreigners, should themselves, because of my simulation, be deceived for the sake of this brief and corruptible life, and I should thereby bring stain and execration upon my old age. For even if at the present time I escape the punishments of men, I shall not escape the hand of the Almighty, whether alive or dead. Therefore, by departing from life bravely, I shall appear worthy of my old age, and leave to the young a strong example if, with a ready and courageous spirit, I undergo an honorable death for the sake of the most weighty and holy laws” (2 Macc. 6:24–28).

He could have pretended without illicit transgression, and the lawful things could have been done without pretense; yet he refused. Desiring to meet a precious death for the Lord and for his lawful commandments, he said at the hour of his departure:

> “Lord, who possess holy knowledge, you clearly know that, although I could be freed from death, I endure harsh bodily pains; but inwardly, for fear of you, I willingly suffer these things” (ibid., 30).

We ought to imitate this commendable deed and contend, as that venerable old man did, not for pork but for the truth, which is God, even to the shedding of blood. [The note corrects the printed wording to “for pork,” and further explains that “meats” is required by the context.]

This is enough here concerning their feigned testimony of faith.

### 18

Now I turn back to what I had begun, and shall again endeavor to prove that the scourge was brought upon us through our own fault. These evils, brothers—our evils—were produced by our laziness, our impurity, our fickleness, and the obscenity of our morals, while we feared where there was no fear and treated matters lightly. Because the everlasting punishment was delayed, we followed dreadful death and an unpleasant hell.

Therefore the Lord, who loves justice and whose face decrees equity (Ps. 10), handed us over to be gnawed by the beast. For he raised up against us, as though it were his own particular curse, the one who crushed every rank of Christianity and the entire state of the Church; and he justly, rightly, and deservedly leveled us with the ground.

While our frivolity did not fear lightly cursing the saints of God, and our rashness, from an elevated position, attempted to defend the curse—or rather, to praise it daily in public speech in the Church—then immediately, as though brought up from hell, the very one whom we had almost praised while defending him with laudatory speech was, by the just judgment of God, set over us in a position of authority. We lamented him, not as gentle but as cruel and dreadful, sharpening the blade against our necks, which we have endured until now.

“Our iniquity has descended upon our own head” (Ps. 7), and “the wickedness of our heel has surrounded us” (Ps. 48). Nor should we complain about the uprising of certain Christians—or rather, publicans—who themselves rose up against the worshipers of our faith, and, insofar as we could, disgraced the saints of God by abusive words.

Although this publican persecutor of the Church, with God’s permission, rose up like a rabid dog against his own faith [something is missing; perhaps: “against his own faith”], and offered the pagans a sword with which to slaughter the people of the Lord, nevertheless, just as we must confess that this came upon the faithful justly and deservedly because of their transgression, so conversely we must confess that he clung to the members of the devil [manuscript: “limbs”] and sprang forward at the Lord’s prompting and the goad of sin, for the testing of the Church and the winnowing of the chaff.

Although his uprising is still displayed, as we have said, by permission of the Almighty, nevertheless, after the judgment of winnowing or testing has been completed, he will be punished by a more severe—indeed, a true—judgment, so that the Church of Christ may shine in the furnace of testing and its enemies may be darkened by a worthy sentence.

For what do the hardships of the air mean, what the harshness of the sky, what the vastness of the rains, what the famine of the peoples, unless they proclaim the Lord’s anger and threaten and announce that vengeance is already impending? The temples of Christ have been desolated of sacrifice, the holy places uprooted by the pagans, and those same places of God destroyed publicly; they will be avenged through the hardships of the seasons, the distributions of peoples, and the incursions of battles. [Bravo reads: “will be avenged,” rather than “is avenged.”]

For this entire plague benefits the faithful for reward and increases the punishment of the faithless. We are cleansed through the pressures of this age, provided that, repenting, we resolve to heal the faults we have contracted. Otherwise, if we persist in our former error with obstinate minds and untamable hearts, and trample crooked paths underfoot, we must beware lest we provoke the sentence of the most merciful Father to avenge greater matters, and incur not redemption but a temporal sword—or rather, everlasting death.

### 19

Yet I am astonished to find certain very small men—perhaps not men at all, but truly little homunculi, to be described with diminution—who defame the bishop as accursed, detest the martyrdom that he endured with equanimity, and revere the death-dealing sentences of the bishops rushing against the bishop, sentences full of curses and detestation. [Bravo reads “read sentences” rather than “death-dealing sentences.”]

With the same force of mind they oppose the decree of the bishops concerning the faith, which they regard as lightly filled with sacrilege and blasphemies against the little soldiers of Christ. They attend to human curses against the bishop and venerate human laws with the utmost care, but disregard divine ordinances, and condemn those who praise Christ’s martyrs. [Bravo omitted “praising”; the sense, however, is that those whom the author attacks condemn others who praised the martyrs.]

They do not see, with open eyes and unveiled light, that they have been justly handed over to the curse, since, by refusing blessing, they have despised the friends of Christ. Why they reject Bishop Biothenatus I do not know, while they maintain that the witnesses of Christ and ministers of truth are subject to real condemnation [manuscript: “true”] and to a fitting judgment.

Let us therefore open the eyes of our hearts and see that the Lord’s just judgment has raged against us. Let us cease insulting the martyrs, lest the vengeance of the eternal King lead us, uncorrected, into Tartarus. Let us take care that no boastful speech proceed from our mouth, and let us avoid setting our mouth against heaven (Ps. 72), knowing that mercy and anger quickly draw near from him, and fearing lest his fury suddenly come and destroy us.

Let the saying of Jeremiah not apply to us:

> “I have killed and destroyed my people, and they have not returned from their ways” (Jer. 15:7).

And again:

> “With great labor it was exhausted, yet its excessive rust did not come out of it, nor was your abominable impurity removed by fire; because I wished to cleanse you, but you were not cleansed from your filth” (Ezek. 24:12).

Considering these and similar things, weighing the deeds of many saints, and exalting the victories of the faithful, let us glorify the Lord and fasten a knot upon our crimes. Let us not attack with ravenous teeth those who, forgetful of us, already rejoice in eternal tranquility and serve their King face to face with the bites of beasts.

### 20

But if we do not proclaim the Lord’s faith as we ought, let us at least proclaim it secretly and offer the right hand of assistance. Let us ask the most merciful Lord, Jesus Christ, who customarily comes to the aid of sinners, to forgive both what has happened in the past and what has so often been attempted now, and to hold the invincible hearts of the weak by his power, lest reckless action, rushing forward in its customary way, fall again.

We have said these things to our own people not maliciously but peacefully. Against our opponents, however, we have spoken firmly, boldly, and in a Catholic manner, as has been enjoined upon the sons of the Church. In unpolished speech we have arranged briefly, as our effort permitted, what appeared to us to be necessary.

Although an uncomposed style weakens the reader’s understanding, the devotion of the one who is engaged in the struggle will nevertheless not be judged uncultivated, if the work is weighed according to the Christian spirit in which it was begun. For I am not held in such dense stupidity that, forgetting myself, I should think that through these things by which I fear displeasing vigorous men I have gained the glory of praise.

I know that my own study has not been cultivated in the discipline of the liberal arts; I myself am not unaware of my ignorance, and what I did not learn through human instruction I could not, as an ignorant man, display to others. Certainly the rusticity that clings to me as a native trait of my uncultivated tongue ought to have imposed silence upon me. Perhaps someone very wisely judges that I should have avoided intruding upon men most skilled and resplendent in eloquence.

But I, considering not how elegantly but how truthfully I should write, treated lightly the praise of all philosophers. My unlearned tongue did not prevent my lips from defending justice, because the foreskin of the mouth is not counted against one whose heart has been commanded to be circumcised.

For a deceitful and flattering attack has its foreskin, as do uncontrolled and exaggerated foolish anger that oversteps its limits, or a quarrel [possibly: “contention”] woven together with laughter. But even carefully composed and elaborated eloquence concerning perishable and fleeting matters, and speeches about worldly things opposed to the faith, are polluted, uncircumcised, and stained with the filth of uncleanness.

Rusticity, however, when fruitful, and ignorance when exalting sacred mysteries, though not elegant, does not swell with the mud of unbelief or with the roughness and chasms of filth. Rather, it shines distinctly of itself through humility and the beauty of truth.

Therefore, if I have perhaps discussed anything opposed to Catholic doctrine negligently [manuscript: “if I have been negligent in doctrine”], not by intention but under the pressure of blindness of mind, I ask my readers to wash it away with tears, wipe it away with prayers, and cleanse it with supplications. But I ask them to leave the faults of my speech entirely untouched.

For that Judge to whom I have offered this intention of devotion discerns not the leaves of words but the root of the heart; nor does he look for the dazzling treatment of prose, but for the end of the work.

Let philosophers pursue their belching questions. Let the Donatists, impure in their cheeks, belch forth with the barking of dogs and the grunting of pigs, their throats scraped raw and their teeth grinding, while grammarians, foaming with saliva, spew forth their utterances.

But let us, evangelical servants, disciples of Christ, followers of rustic people, to whom full things are entrusted, to whom strong things are commanded, and not empty, light, and inflated things, but marrow-filled whole burnt offerings, pursue what is solid and clear through the vitality of our judgments—not, God forbid, empty things swollen with deadly disease and smoky with human praise in every direction. Such things torment the mind of the author and of those who discuss them more than, by opening up the text for reading, they enlighten minds polluted by the dregs of a winding course. [“Conturnus” is sometimes used by Du Cange for a bend, deviation, or circuit. If “they torment and enlighten” is read, the following should likewise be corrected.]

Such writing proceeds everywhere without the bridle of reason, with loosened reins leaping beyond the limits of its boundaries rather than fulfilling them. With one blow of stubbornness it overthrows the editor and the attentive reader alike, since it takes its beginning from empty glory and pours itself out nowhere except into the breasts of those who praise it.

Let this suffice to have been said against the Donatists.

[Editorial apparatus: §11, after “left him unharmed”: the editor would read *non molledine mentis, sed humilitate se deprecantum, inlaesum dimisit*: “he spared him unharmed, not through softness of mind but because of those humbly entreating him.” §11, “written by these cruel authors”: manuscript, *ab hos auctores crudeles*, “by these cruel authors.” §11, “reduced the ark”: perhaps read *arcam … redactam*, “the ark … reduced.” §11, “intercession that mitigated”: read *mitigantem*, “mitigating.”

§12, “a path … obliterated”: manuscript, *antiquitus*, “formerly.” “Unable to endure”: manuscript, *non sufficerens*, an uncertain corrupt reading. “What he … denied”: Morales, in the Life of St Eulogius, fol. 55b; another manuscript reads *ille* (“he”); see above, no. 3, where the author says of St Perfectus, whom he appears to indicate here, “that he had said this absolutely not,” etc. “He began … fulfilled it”: Morales reads, *inchoavit, ingenua morte peregit*, “he began it and completed it by a noble death.” “Might openly … establish”: Morales adds *etiam*, “also.” “To the inexperienced world”: manuscript, *rude mundo*, “to the rude world”; Morales, *rudi saeculo*, “to the rude age.” “In the last times”: Morales again adds *etiam*, “also.” “The men of old had undertaken them”: Morales reads, *primi intentaverant praeliarentur*, “might fight the battles which the first had undertaken.” “One killed and another wounded”: namely St Perfectus, slain, and John, scourged.

§13, “suited for God’s war”: read *aptus*, “fit,” rather than *abjectus*. “Do you not perceive”: manuscript, *avertis*, for *advertis*, as elsewhere more than once *averte* occurs for *adverte*. “The purpose set before them”: preferably *propositum*, “purpose,” for *praepositum*. “Those who choose”: manuscript, *elegentibus*.

§14, “fraternal assembly”: that is, *collectio*, “gathering.” “Seized weapons in rebellion”: perhaps read *rebellio*, “rebellion.” “Approach the judge”: manuscript, *audierunt*, “heard.”

§15, “plainly”: manuscript, *prespicuum est quos*, a corrupt reading. “Which indicates”: manuscript, *designantem*. “Moderate matters”: that is, *mediocribus*, “middling matters.” “Most fitting title”: manuscript, *abtissimum titulum*. “Worshipers”: read *cultoribus*, “the worshipers.”

§16, “administration”: perhaps read *dispensatorie*, “by way of accommodation,” since accommodative reasons are immediately mentioned. “King of Israel”: namely Jehu.

§17, “Public triumph”: perhaps *praeparatum*, “prepared,” rather than *propalatum*. “For his lawful commandments”: read *licitis … legitimis*, “lawful … lawful.” “Harsh bodily pains”: manuscript, *dolos*, “deceptions,” an evidently corrupt reading. “Not for pork”: read *pro suillis carnibus*, “for pork flesh,” as the immediate context says, rather than *pro suillas*.

§18, “Against his own faith”: a word is missing; perhaps read *contra fidem suam*, “against his faith.” “Members of the devil”: manuscript, *membribus*, “limbs.” “They will be avenged”: Bravo, p. 134, reads *vindicatur*, “is avenged.”

§19, “Death-dealing sentences”: Bravo, p. 130, reads *lectas*, “chosen/read,” rather than *letas*. “While praising”: Bravo, p. 131, omitted *conlaudantes*; the sense is that those attacked by the author condemn others who praised the martyrs. On Biothenatus, see vol. X, treatise XXXIII, ch. 8, no. 8. “Real condemnation”: manuscript, *vero*, “true.” “Eyes of our hearts”: manuscript, *oculis*.

§20, “In a Catholic manner”: manuscript, *catholica*. “Perhaps someone”: manuscript, *aliquid*, “something.” “A quarrel”: perhaps *rixa, contentio*, “quarrel, contention.” “Anything opposed to Catholic doctrine”: manuscript, *dogmate neglegentur*, “they are neglected in doctrine.” “A winding course”: *conturnus* is sometimes used by Du Cange for a bend, deviation, or circuit. If *macerant* and *inlustrant* (“they torment” and “they enlighten”) are read, the following words must also be corrected.]

### 21

Now we must return to those matters which, after the withdrawal of our defense, may place the crown of perfection upon this very small work and may easily restrain or overwhelm the precursor of Antichrist, who must be supported in this slight little treatise only by a whole burden of testimonies [Note: He seems by these words to suggest a desire to shed light upon the matter by means of the testimonies.].

Let us take our beginning from Daniel and establish, from what the blessed Jerome has set forth concerning Antichrist, those things that agree with and approach this most impious man. Then let us examine what blessed Job says about Behemoth [Col. 0535B] or Leviathan, and similarly show this man what has been assigned to him, in agreement with the exposition of Saint Gregory [Note: F. *expositiones*, “expositions.”].
