In the third place, approaching the Apocalypse and discussing certain figures in a similar manner, let us leave all the material for discussion to the teachers and more distinguished writers who will follow. After gathering flowers [Note: *Deflorare*, “to gather flowers.”] from the oracles of certain prophets and saints, let us cut short this little work at its proper conclusion; and in a second book let us collect the opinions of the teachers and strengthen our laborious little tales by the starry radiance of truthful authorities [Note: F. *favillas*, “sparks,” so that what follows—“we strengthen by the starry radiance of the truthful”—has the same sense as: “by the firm and shining light of the teachers, we illuminate the truth of our assertion.”].

For if some have established Domitian and Nero as Antichrist because of the enormity of their crimes, and have said that Antiochus prefigured him, or if the most approved teachers have constructed the other plagues that rose up against the Church as precursors of that wicked beast, what have we improperly said after them today, we who seek to place a blemish upon the works of others?

Behold, as I first examine Daniel’s prophecy, I shall serve it with brief conclusions that possess their proper sequence. I shall not explain everything specifically, but only certain parts, and in doing so I shall not depart from the rules of the Fathers.

For he says concerning the eleventh horn of the beast:

> “The fourth beast which you saw shall be the fourth kingdom, which shall be greater than all the kingdoms” (Daniel 7:23).

There is no doubt that this signifies the Roman Empire, repeatedly raised up and extended more widely than the other kingdoms. Moreover, the ten horns of that kingdom are ten kings:

> “And another shall rise after them, and he shall be more powerful than the former; and he shall humble three kings, and he shall speak words against the Most High, and he shall wear down the saints of the Most High. He shall think that he can change times and laws, and they shall be delivered into his hand for a time, times, and half a time” (ibid., 24–25).

Porphyry placed all these matters historically and literally in Antiochus. Our writers, however, placed them typologically in Antiochus, and more truly and properly in Antichrist. Nevertheless, we say that some part of this applies to the precursor of that condemned man of our own time [Note: That is, Muhammad, the precursor of Antichrist.].

For, rising in the eleventh number—which is always inauspicious in the sacred Scriptures—he subdued three kingdoms, when he occupied the provinces of the Greeks and Franks, which flourished under the name of the Romans, and trampled the necks of the Western Goths beneath his victorious foot. Or this may be understood as applying when he attempted to destroy the decad—that is, universal religion and the number which is often inserted to signify the whole—and tried to rebel against the faith of the Trinity, fortified by hope, faith, and charity.

Fabricating insolent words against the exalted God, weighing out grand things, and weaving together those smoky claims that are truly precursors of Antichrist and sufficiently hostile to our humble religion, he thought that he could envelop the law of the Lord, radiant like the sun with miracles, in a cloudy darkness. As though by command of the Most High Lord, and with ridiculous audacity, he composed for his supporters light and laughable stories; with a false pen, an impure brow, and theatrical approval, he invented fabulous lies, girded by no strength of manliness or reason. He wore down the saints of God and trampled with a clownish foot upon part of the stars of heaven—that is, upon the sons of the Church. This is proved more by the evidence of our eyes than by the eloquence of our exposition.

Now the “time, times, and half a time” must be assigned specifically to the head of Antichrist, and it must be asked why the divine speech did not plainly say “three and a half years,” but used that obscure expression, by which the divine utterance customarily gives birth to differing meanings in the hearts of teachers. A year has four seasons, and the word “time” itself can signify a year; moreover, a short or long period of hours, days, months, and years is designated by the name “times.” The Hebrews understand one “time” as seventy years, according to the words:

> “The days of our years are seventy years” (Psalm 89:10);

or according to the number of years during which they were subjected to the yoke of servitude under Nebuchadnezzar.

And, led by this [lacuna] manner of interpretation, the Hebrews [lacuna] in this passage assign “time, times, and half a time” to the Ishmaelites as two hundred and forty-five years, after which they confidently expect, in a sufficiently audacious statement, that their kingdom will come to an end.

Indeed, in this year of the Lord’s Incarnation—854—and in the current era, the 892nd, two hundred and forty lunar Arab years are reckoned, but two hundred and twenty-nine solar years. From this total, sixteen solar years remain [Col. 0536D].

### 22

We, however, leave these matters to God’s knowledge alone, and to those who, touched by the divine Spirit, can ascend the cloud with Moses and, when God opens them, behold the hidden things of God with unveiled face.

Yet one must look carefully and foresee the matter with the diligence of legal exposition, lest an insane mind rashly attempt to explain this enveloping obscurity, and lest detestable madness presume to revise the manifold meaning that has been designated by the audacious and insolent.

For at the end of the book he says:

> “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be manifold” (Daniel 12:4).

By a prophetic spirit he announces the diversity of interpreters, and prefigures commentaries not of the foolish but of the wise. Knowledge will indeed be manifold, when many, not wandering into error but examining the matter, offer many opinions, and the causes of different times are revealed in a single utterance.

Therefore, I think that by the elevated meaning of figures and by the manifold introduction of problems, one and the same matter is very often repeated many times: in three or four places, under another figure of manifestation, far removed from the first, the very thing that was initially figured is again represented. This, I think, ought to be understood in all the works of prophecy: that under varied forms of repetition the causes of the whole age are marked out in a single prophetic book.

If this opinion is weighed with a worthy and friendly mind, it will not be rejected through the envy of the present generation, but will be confirmed by the events of evident causes. Strengthened by this manner of understanding, we can proceed without error, so that we may say not only that the prophets announced by the divine Spirit what took place in their own time, but also that they most clearly foretold what was to be accomplished in all the ages, so that the divine speech might explain the causes of the entire age in one continuous discourse.

Behold, in Habakkuk the speech is directed against Nebuchadnezzar, and everything nearby and agreeing with it is immediately opened to those who see clearly [Note: F. “everything … is clearly opened.”]. Nor will one stray from the path of truth if the prophecy directed against the Chaldeans is likewise expounded as applying to them. This is more fitting to the wisdom of God and to the catholic doctrine which we serve than to say that the history of this madman or of other kingdoms was not prophetically foreseen [Col. 0537C].

Indeed, as it seems to me, what is said specifically in the head of the aforementioned matters serves, for those who perceive sharply, as an enigmatic reference in the member—or, to speak more clearly, in his throat—and the catholic faith does not recoil from this sense of interpretation.

For what the prophetic Spirit says at the end of the book concerning that head of the proud, when clearly examined and sifted by subtle investigation, is declared to have been directed against this host of the most wicked spirit [Note: The manuscript reads *disseritur*, “it is discussed.”]:

> “He shall be lifted up and magnified against every god” (Daniel 11:36),

that is, against the gods of the nations, whom, as though by religion, but while magnifying himself over them, he crushed beneath the foot of contempt. “And against the God of gods he shall speak magnificent things” (ibid.).

He will speak against the Lord of lords, the God of heaven and earth, the eternal Creator, and against that law which, at the prompting of demons, he composed with poison in the Creator’s name; and, by a subsequent false deception, he wove a third false testament.

> “He shall not regard the God of his fathers” (ibid., 37),

that is, the idols of the Ishmaelites which they worshiped up to his own time.

> “And he shall be in the desire of women” (ibid.).

Who would not see that this impure man is specifically indicated by this sentence? Although this is read ambiguously in the Hebrew, namely whether he has or does not have desire for women, Aquila says:

> “And concerning the God of his fathers he shall not understand; and concerning the desire of women, and concerning every god, he shall not understand.”

By these words, as I said, he is understood both to have a desire for women and not to have one. I think that the statement was placed ambiguously for this reason: so that it might disclose both meanings in one sense to those who understand.

That is, in the former beast it affirms the desire for women, and in the latter it declares that it is absent; thus “to have” and “not to have” can be understood in one continuous sense. Nor is it permissible to assign discordant actions to one person. Rather, as I said, the speech indicates one thing in a single textual sequence without leaving the other aside: the prophetic speech strikes the former, while the divine Spirit does not leave the last untouched [Col. 0538B].

### 23

It is fitting—and, as I think, most fully appropriate—that the errors of these peoples, worthy of ridicule, be recounted here, and that their foulnesses, which the whole Church must regard as execrable, be exposed.

For they report, and babble as though with a distinguished exclamation among their untimely teachings, that this lover of women among them, occupied with womanizing, possessed a power of sexual pleasure surpassing that of other men. They say that his god granted him, as a gift, a more abundant desire for Venus than to all others [Note: Understand “pleasure.”], that he possessed a more copious emission from the most filthy act than the rest, and that he discharged it from others with greater ease. They also assert that the gods above bestowed upon him a flow and vigor—or rather an abundance—for the exercise of feminine lust equal to that of forty men.

Such filthy and swollen abundance of his stinking loins did not come, as the most wicked robber imagined, from God, the parent of all things, but from mockery-making Venus, the wife of Vulcan—that is, the wife of fire—who was also called Aphrodite because of her foaming fluid. To her the sexual act is assigned, which that impudent man called *alkaufeit*.

A truly splendid praise, and a very elegant gift for the carnal. To him aptly applies that denunciation against this generation among the Israelite people, which flows from the prophetic mouth concerning the Egyptians’ excess:

> “They raged over intercourse with those whose flesh is like the flesh of donkeys, and whose emission is like the emission of horses” (Ezekiel 23:20) [Note: The Vulgate reads: “of those whose flesh …”].

Or this:

> “They became mad for women; each one neighed after his neighbor’s wife” (Jeremiah 5:8).

This most impure prophet is said to have done these things and is praised for having proclaimed them, when, seduced and enticed by his own pleasure, he took the wife of his neighbor, who agreed with his faith; indeed, he falsely claimed that she had been joined to him through a revelation of Gabriel [Note: F. “by God.”].

By enlarging upon the sect of this most impure man, his most impure followers [Note: L. *amplectentes* or *ampliantes*, “embracing” or “enlarging upon.”] have all become pimps and adulterers. On account of marital rights, they tear apart a marriage which, with greater disgrace, they join again by committing adultery [Note: The manuscript reads *quem*, “whom.”]. By multiplying concubines and living as trigamists or quadrigamists, they are womanizers—or rather, they are all neighing stallions or braying asses [Note: Above in the text of Jeremiah they are called lovers of women and “emissaries”; here *amissarii*, that is, *admissarii*, “stallions.” This usage is especially acceptable to Latin speakers.].

For they are ashamed of nothing: they have withdrawn every restraint, make use of the natural law by claiming that women are permitted to them, and seek out new paths of lust; alas for me, they practice these things amid applause.

The blush of our cheeks does not permit us to hurl a rhetorical speech against the enemy, especially since modesty commands silence. Although a carefully composed denunciation might bring the whole matter out into the open and arrange what should be attacked with the weapons of combatants, the indecent action—and the parts of the subject, which are unworthy of the work—rather desires to be lightly touched by a subtle indication than for shameful things to be stripped naked before modest readers by the shameless exposure of the word, with uncovered speech and an immodest tongue. Otherwise we would lose in our speech the modesty which they lacked in their conduct.

### 24

No one was ever so ruined by lust, or so befouled by the filth of the mire, as this pimp polluted with foulness.

As we have said, he also enjoyed the wives of other men as a procurer, concealing the filthiness of his uncleanness under an angelic command. He promised those who believed him that prostitutes would be permitted to them and that, without any satisfying intercourse ever reaching an end, they would perpetually enjoy it in the paradise of their god as a reward. Thus the final heat, kindled by the impulse of a single hour, would not end after its customary duration, but would be prolonged through the pleasure of seventy men, the pleasure itself flowing forth in the special manner of asses.

Whoever that long-sleeping inhabitant of paradise may be, he is said to possess an enlarged emission and an extended desire for fatness; and, throughout every act of intercourse, virginity, lost through so prolonged a crime and pierced by so unyielding a rod, would be restored to those enjoying it in the same way. The growing severing of that torn membrane and the thin, rubbed-together covering of the lappet would not terrify them through the pain of the act, but would sweeten both parties with the sweetness of pleasure. By this means it would suggest to their minds a more eager desire to possess, and would not bring their most ardent appetite to an end through renewal, but would extend it.

And there are still other, greater things concerning both sexes and both natures which that seductive denunciation was not ashamed to fabricate with impure cheeks for the lost people, in the person of the Almighty Lord. All these matters we shall discuss more fully and with a more polished denunciation in another work, if God grants us life [Note: See the *Notice*, above, col. 587.].

### 25

It follows:

> “He shall care for none of the gods, because he shall rise up against all” (Daniel 11:37).

Clearly, because he despised the religion of the Gentiles, the Jews, and even the Christians, and rose up against everything.

> “But he shall honor the god Maozim in his place” (ibid., 38).

*Maozim* is said to mean “great” and “greater,” or “strong” and “strongest.” If someone says that it signifies not “greater” but “strongest,” we answer him that this religion pretends to honor the strongest—that is, God—in his place. But it does this in order to fortify Maozim “with the foreign god whom he has known” (ibid., 39) [Note: At this point the manuscript has been marked: “with the foreign god”—he means the demon.].

Theodotion explains this more clearly:

> “And he shall do this,” he says, “to fortify the strongholds with a foreign god; and with those whom he has acknowledged, that is, his own, he shall multiply honor, and he shall make him rule over many, and he shall divide the land for nothing. Therefore he pretends to worship the strongest God, so that he may introduce the foreign god to his own people, and by a perverse account of God may multiply his honor among the nations and increase his dominion.”

This is what they daily proclaim in their smoky towers with an enormous and monstrous bellowing, in the manner of wild beasts, with parted lips and open throats, crying out like those afflicted with the cardiac disease [Note: That is, those who suffer from heart disease.]. In their shouting, like madmen heralding a proclamation, they say:

> “That he may fortify Maozim with the foreign god whom he has known.”

That is, that he may fortify Maozim, whom they call *Cobar*, meaning “greater,” with the foreign god—that is, with the demon who appeared to him under the persona of Gabriel—under one name of veneration. By this means he hides his error in the hearts of believers, exalting by the name of the greater God the rite of his shouting, and infecting the souls of the noble with a superstitious effort and a wicked spirit.

But lest I seem to speak of these matters enigmatically rather than literally [Note: The manuscript reads *dici*, “to be said.”], and lest I be judged to have produced them as inventions of human ingenuity rather than as matters unfolded by the divine Spirit, clearer proofs must be introduced.

Behold, those devoted to the same rite still call the days on which they consecrate their madness in the house of the idol by the same name. Because of the difference of the Arabic language, which differs slightly from Hebrew in many names [Col. 0540C], they themselves call them *Almozem fairs* [Note: F. *ipsae feriae*, “the fairs themselves.”]. At the very time when, in ancient days, that people or nation gathered from all regions to the idol just mentioned, the same lost crowd now assembles annually. They perpetually serve the very demon whom they think has been uprooted from that place by the magnitude of their faith [Note: The manuscript reads *ipsoque daemone*, “and by the demon himself.”].

They still inhabit Maozim in his place, as the prophet reported by the divine Spirit, since they continue to call those days by the customary name, and the month which they call *almo arram* [Note: The carelessness of the copyist is apparent here: living among Arabs, he wrote the name of that month so awkwardly.]—just as worshipers of idolatry once exalted it, so these people today carry it up to heaven with greater abundance and perfection, as they suppose.

I am ashamed to set out separately the madness of that house. Nor does it suit me briefly to assail with darts some of the many things deserving ridicule, since the whole matter is held in our mind to be made public for the faithful at some time [Note: The manuscript reads *Putet … domui*, apparently “he thinks … concerning the house.”].

And:

> “His glory shall be multiplied, and he shall give them power over many, and he shall divide the land for nothing” (Daniel 11:39).

For he divided land, rather than heaven, among them, and gave glory for nothing when he established the law of which they had been ignorant up to that time. The Hebrews, however, assert that the text says not “for nothing” but “for a price,” that they sell the land. Theodotion explains it more clearly:

> “And he shall do this,” he says, “to fortify the strongholds with the foreign god; and when he has advanced with them, that is, with his own people, he shall multiply honor, and he shall make him rule over many, and he shall divide the land for nothing. Therefore he pretends to worship the strongest God, so that he may introduce the foreign god to his own people, and by a perverse account of God may multiply his honor among the nations and increase his dominion” [Note: See the same words noted above.].

By this, the activity of this people or kingdom is evidently and specifically disclosed. For they sell even the places established for commerce, where markets are customarily held—places without roofs, open to the sun and sky [Note: The manuscript reads *potentia*, “power,” instead of *patentia*, “open”]. Thus no bold presumptuous person dares, unless the price has been paid [Note: The manuscript reads *pretioso luto*, “with costly mud.” I understand it to have the same sense as the statement. From the glosses of Isidore. Here it seems to signify permission.], to undertake by any means the permission to trade which ordinary necessity demands.

All these things were established by the eleventh horn, “speaking great things” (Daniel 7:8). It arose from a small tribe and, growing not by power but by deceit and by something resembling zeal for the law, increased in greater strength and gradually invaded the kingdom. In certain places it subdued the Roman forces—that is, the garrisons of the emperor Heraclius.

Therefore, this entire prophecy applies to him in part, in which the beast is said to emerge from a small people. Hence the horns of the beast are said to have contained something like human eyes. For what is signified by the eyes, by which vision is directed, except that law which, at the prompting of demons and by the hidden judgment of God, he delivered to the lost?

> “The commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm 19:8).

But because they were revealed not in the number ten but in the eleventh, and were marked not as eyes but as something like eyes, it follows that it must not properly be called a law, but must be regarded as something usurped that resembles a law. Consequently, it must truthfully be proved hostile to the divine testaments.

This is that speech speaking great things against God; this is that strength raised up against the Most High; this is that presumption against the stars of heaven, part of which has been trampled beneath the foot of victory.

I pass over many things, because I am in great haste.

### 26

Let us come to blessed Job, and quickly explain the power of Behemoth from his most holy words (Job 40:10 and following). He said that it would rise like evening over the sons of the earth, and, with all its smoky light preceding the darkness of night and wrapping the hearts of all in gloom [Note: The manuscript reads “with darkness preceding … enveloping.”], he revealed through his open mouth what the divine Spirit showed him concerning the age to come [Col. 0541D].

At the beginning of these words the name itself must be considered with sufficient care, and the stupidity of its works must be explained from the term. It is called an animal, for *Behemoth* means “animal” when translated from Hebrew into Latin. It is plainly beyond doubt that his stupidity is proclaimed by this name.

For he was unlettered [Note: F. *inlitteris*, that is, “unlettered”; below, in section 28, he is said to have arisen “without letters.”], and can neither read nor write. In eating he also chooses hay, not wheat: proclaiming everything empty and possessing nothing of the solidity of religion, but clothed only in madness and the error of faithlessness.

Yet the hay which he will eat can also be understood as empty men, devoid of the law, whom he deceived [Note: F. *qua* or *quos*, “which” or “whom.”]. For all the nations were infected with the filth of paganism and the evil of idolatry; finding them empty, he devoured them and bound them to himself with an everlasting bond.

He possesses strength in his loins and power in his navel, as the exposition of the preceding text has shown more clearly than the sun. In both sexes these regions are especially held by luxury and headlong lust. Extending their seedbed with unrestricted and wandering freedom, he thought that he could enlarge his power through propagation, and by numerous branches of offspring he succeeded in possessing the age.

He tightened his tail like a cedar when, foreseeing the future, he strengthened his followers in the severity of his law and in diabolical rules. We have experienced this tail, for we are established in the final age and endure the more terrible persecution of that beast.

For he is that one:

> “A king shameless in lusts and adulteries, in countenance, and understanding the devices of wicked propositions” (Daniel 8:23).

### 27

He has the sinews of his testicles tangled, flowing with lusts and full of generation—or else he has preachers who, in their assertion of acuity against the humanity of God and of our Lord, are strong.

> “His bones are like tubes of bronze.”

All his strong men render the plausible sound of the Arabic tongue insensible. Indeed, as blessed Gregory says:

> “Like metal, they possess an insensible sound of speaking well, but they do not possess the sense of speaking well.”

His cartilage is like a plate of iron. Cartilage has the appearance of bone, but does not retain the firmness of the joints. In the same way, the ministers of this most wicked leader display to the lost, on the surface, the appearance of piety, but lack the fruit of that most chaste piety. They imitate not the strength of saints but that of hypocrites; they emulate not the virtue of the sincere and humble but that of the crafty. They are pretenders and schemers, who continually provoke the Lord’s anger.

After exposing their deceptions, he strikes the inspirer of the word with a sword:

> “He is,” he says, “the beginning of the ways of God.”

As though he were saying: The most wicked man is capable of such great and multiplied greatness because his inspirer, the devil, was created as the first substance in the nature of things.

But the most wise Creator, who made him first among all creatures, justly bent his sword in certain respects, since he did not permit him to rage against the elect as far as his evil will urged him.

> “To him the mountains bring forth herbs.”

The proud of the age and the most savage tyrants offer him their most wicked pleasures [Note: The manuscript reads *voluntates*, “wills.”]. Certainly the demons, who in Scripture are called dark mountains, as well as the rulers of the earth and the philosophers, offer him the food of falsehood: refined and cultivated deceits of various teachings.

> “All the beasts of the field will play there.”

These may be understood as the demons in the heart of the most impious man, or as the innovations of many heresies in his law. From these sects he draws in poison with his open mouth, and, infecting himself through his work, he fashioned his own *euphrasia* according to a thousandfold rite of sects [Note: L. *operose*, “laboriously.”]. He composed it from the teachings of heretics, philosophers, and Jews, clothing it in the color of faith among different peoples and offering to all the frivolous an enchanted covering [Note: F. *fascinatum*, “bewitched.”].

He sleeps under the shadow of darkness and death, or of gloom and error, and is not illumined even by a slender ray of light from Christ, who is believed to be the true and eternal sun. He sleeps in the secret place of the reed and in moist places, where there is grassy vegetation (?) [Note: Perhaps *gramminea*, “grassy.”], where there is flowing moisture and hateful mockeries, where unrestrained barbarism, execrable fury, tangled lust, propagation, and provocation to marriage exist, and where the dissolution and enervation of souls flow. There they gather who outwardly appear polished but inwardly are empty of marrow.

> “The shadows protect his shadow.”

All the wicked certainly defend his lie by their own lie and by their personal service. Just as truth exists in the body, so falsehood exists in the shadow of the body. For all the wicked, as I have said, filled with the dregs of savagery, protect his lie with their own lie. Where he perhaps stumbled through an inattentive or feeble step and did not take care to defend himself after being defeated by the truth, these eminent men, flourishing in worldly wisdom and powerful in the cunning of their arguments, defend him with ingenious skill, learned falsehood, and carefully chosen opinions; they arrange the matter proudly and color the obvious lie of his work with the disguised falsehood of their words [Note: The manuscript has *sapientiae*, “of wisdom”; *eruditate*, “with learning”; and *ornare*, “to adorn.” L. *patens*, “open.”].

The shadows may also be understood as other demons who pretend to protect this inhabitant of a most wicked body by their own service. For they report that he restored peace among the most wicked spirits who were at variance with one another, brought many demons under his faith, and handed down his law to them for them to remember and observe.

Hence, even in that horrifying law, speech of preaching is frequently introduced from the person of God, addressed either to demons or to men, and they are repeatedly urged to believe him.

> “The willows of the torrent will surround him”—

that is, fruitless beings who grow green through the flow of lusts. The seed of this tree, when taken as food, makes people sterile.

Such are the ministers of the enemy of the Church: dry through the sterility of faith and utterly killing the seed of teaching. In contrast, all the children of the Church who ascend from the bath produce twin offspring, and there is no barrenness among them.

> “He will swallow up the river and will not marvel.”

That is, he will devour at the root the multitude of the nations without knowledge of the law, and he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth. He thinks that by the venomous deceit of the serpent he can also consume those whom the wave of sacred baptism has washed and whom the royal mark—the sign of the cross—has consecrated to Christ our God and King.

28. Now what follows pertains more to the inhabitant prepared as a vessel of perpetual disgrace than to that “man slain by life” [Biothenatus], who, seeing the bait but not the hook, fixed his bite and was pierced through—since, sensing the Devil’s intrusion, he lightly believed him to be an angel of light, and was taken without knowing that he had been taken: “And he will pierce his nostrils with stakes.” Through the nostrils odor is drawn in, and things placed outside are immediately identified by smell.

But our Master and Lord pierces his nostrils with stakes even to this day, whenever through the prudence of the saints he weakens all the stratagems of their cunning. Now the divine discourse turns by apostrophe to another designation [that is, an apostrophe], and under a more explicit name reveals his arts and counsels. “Can you,” it says, “draw out Leviathan with a hook?” Leviathan is said to mean “their addition”: whose addition, that is, except that of proud men, who always desire to seem greater than they are? This most aptly suits him who, by his own rashness, devised something beyond what had been uttered from the mouth of God, as though introducing other, novel things. He is rightly designated by the name of serpent, because, proceeding in the manner of a serpent, he filled the whole world by crawling through it. He was truly caught by the hook of divinity when, desiring the body, he was pierced by the sharp point of the word.

He holds the ring placed in his nostrils, because, although he cunningly strikes at strong things, he nevertheless moves beneath the ring of the Creator. He neither tests as much as he desires, nor desires as much as he tests. His jaw is also said to have been pierced because, although he often attacks those whom his greedy mind assails, a more powerful ordering releases them. Once seized, he could not have escaped if the dragon’s jaw had not possessed a hole.

He multiplies prayers to God, while his members, each moment, intercede with the Lord on his behalf. Those prayers are to be understood as the laws that he wove with fabulous mockery [F: “with ritual”]. And he speaks smooth things, which through their mouths resound daily with much eloquent splendor and in words approaching compassion, while they constantly say: “Lord, spare that prophet.” They do not use the customary form of speech by which it is usual to speak on behalf of others, but speak tropically, in language adapted to many other matters: “May God sing over him,” they say, “and save him” [The same reading is found in Saint Eulogius, Book II, chapter 1].

And just as we, for every gesture and every utterance, taught by evangelical authority amid pressing storms, continually say, “Christ, save us,” so they, at every moment, incessantly repeat the aforesaid word. They do this familiarly, in a voice worthy of proclamation, crying it out, repeating it, and proclaiming it in houses and towers. He who overflows in many things and has transgressed is commended by many whom he himself has destroyed and by frequent prayer. Yet he cannot be cleansed by the prayers of transgressors, because, in the delusion of their error, he blinded those who prayed on his behalf so that they would not be heard.

All the doctrine contrived by his deceit consists nevertheless of smooth words: words that remain compacted with the seductive sweetness of the lips, promising things that perish and are fleeting [F: “promising perishable things”]. Or those smooth words are what he fabulously invented, dreaming in that horrible law with studied argument. And just as the law of God thunders authoritatively over angels and human beings, so, in opposition, these doctrines of the Devil offer a word of faith to demons and ruined men, repeatedly and constantly saying: “O multitude of demons, and of all …,” which is said in Arabic: *Lemahascar algen*.

And rightly the author of it has been made a plaything [Read: *inlusus est*, “has been mocked”; for Job’s text says: “Will you play with him as with a bird?”], as though a bird. For, desiring the bait and led on by appetite [L: “by the throat”], he did not foresee the snare of the trap. He is rightly called a bird because he is the king of this air, in which birds fly and the princes of darkness exercise power.

Because he arose as a brute and without letters, he was called *Behemoth*, that is, “animal.” Because he appeared deceitful, crafty, and cunning, he was named a serpent or dragon. He is also called a bird because he proceeded proudly, arrogantly, and restlessly, and armed himself with no bridle of self-restraint.

“His friends will cut him to pieces”—namely, the Lord’s friends, those who expose his deceits to the whole world and maintain by public profession that he has attacked the Church as her enemy. He is cut to pieces as often as he is marked with an anathema.

“Merchants will divide him”—holy men who, dividing the dragon’s members from its treacherous head, join them to themselves. “And you will fill the nets with his skin, or the fishpond with his head.” By the skin he indicates outward things; by the head, greater and more splendid things. Keeping the order, he asserts that he will first fill the nets, or the fishpond of fish—that is, his Church and the desires of the faithful—with his skin, and afterward with his head, because he first chose what was weak in order later to confound the strong. Within the Church of the faithful he first gathers, as though the Devil’s skin, the extreme and lowest members, and afterward subjects to himself through his head the wise who oppose him (1 Cor. 1:27).

“And the Lord will lay his hand upon him,” because he restrains him by powerful might and does not permit him to rage beyond what is expedient.

The Church is told: “Remember war; do not add further speech beyond what has been set down and solemnly received.” Recall to mind his inward battles against you, and do not accuse the Lord concerning the outward power that you see raised up so greatly. Or certainly remember that he is set against you for this contest of battle so that the one who has fought lawfully may be crowned.

If, however, he patiently endures the assaults of temptations and presumes nothing from himself above what he sees raised upon the lofty summit of the authority of the Lord’s law [Ms.: “my law”], and does not incur an addition upon pride [Ms.: “lest he incur an addition”], then the body of this Leviathan may rightly be represented. For he will be frustrated in his hope of escaping the hand of the Creator, and the dark angel will imagine that he is not held by eternal punishment. Or he will be frustrated in that hope by which he believes that, in the world to come, he may scatter passive lust through various paramours in abundant licentiousness.

29. In the sight of all—of the elect and the reprobate, or of those whom he deceived—he will be hurled into the pool of burning fire.

“I will not raise him up as a cruel being” (Job 41:1 ff.), since through him I rather inflict both the reward owed to the just and the punishment corresponding to the merits of the unjust. For who will be able to resist my face, from whom this sacred ordering and this just arrangement proceed in the world? Certainly no one, O merciful and patient Lord, over the wickedness of human beings.

“And who has given to me beforehand, that I should repay him?” Again we say to you in all truth, most just Creator and most loving God: no one. For every creature has received from you the strength by which it subsists. If, then, miserable beings cannot resist the Almighty, and, as creatures destined to perish, cannot retain an eternal creditor on the basis of our own work, let us not attempt to scrutinize the rationale of his works, which we see to be just in the punishment of sinners and gratuitous in the gift bestowed upon the just.

But lest despair pierce the souls of those listening, the divine judgment immediately proclaimed the sentence already imposed upon him, saying: “I will not spare him with powerful words, composed for entreaty.” As I have already said, the composition of words and the prayers of all his members, daily fashioned for him with elegant eloquence and graceful speech, we read even now in their books and often admire. Yet he is not spared by things so great and such as these, because the prayer of a transgressor becomes sin; and by continual bending and repeated pressing of the head, they most frequently press themselves to the ground in a display of ostentation, acquiring not a remedy but eternal punishment.

From this it is made clearly understood that every prayer or work not founded upon faith in Christ will be found empty and harmful at the time of judgment. For without Christ every virtue is a vice, as he says: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). And again: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Whoever does not possess the light, the truth, the life, and the way, walking in darkness, holding fast to falsehood, and wandering along byways, incurs eternal death.

“Who will uncover the face of his garment?” That is: who will strip away his wickedness, which outwardly pretends to piety? “And who will enter into the midst of his mouth?” Who will penetrate the cunning of the wicked law? Who will sift, by the sharpest examination, the error folded up within it and the arrangement of letters that he wove into certain fabulous passages of his law?

“Who will open his gates,” which he closed and shut up with poison? The understood answer is: no one but I, who openly manifest to all my elect and to the little flock—indeed, to those who are little in wickedness—the deceitful wisdom of his teachers, his subtle fraud, and the hidden delusion compounded by the Devil and poisoned by him.

“By the circuit of his teeth fear is proclaimed.” The terror of his power is declared by evident signs: with the severe vengeance of the law it rises to fortify his falsehood and the word of his most deceitful mouth.

“His body is cast shields.” Cast shields resist the blows of weapons but remain fragile when they fall. So too are the preachers of the most savage beast, obstinate in mind: hard toward those preaching the truth, and, through the conduct of their works, wretched [F: “miserable”] and transitory. They contradict the Church, puffed up by the wind of pride, and by the fall of the flesh destroy themselves by their own will.

“Compacted with scales pressing upon one another.” The dragon’s body is compacted with scales so that it may not be exposed to the darts of preachers. He opposes the Church with scales, so that the arrow of truth cannot pierce him. Yet he presses upon himself, not upon others, while he thinks that he is covered and protected by shields [Ms.: *clippeus*].

“One is joined to another, and not even a passage for breath proceeds through them.” The breath of life, plainly. For they are hardened and obstinately joined to evil, imparting to no one the fragrance of a good odor [In the vernacular, with the *c* suppressed, we Spaniards pronounce *olfactum* as *olfato*].

“One will cling to another, and, holding fast to one another, they will not be separated.” For they are joined by a strong connection and a tenacious bond of iniquity; united in mind and equal in vice, they are glued together [F: “equal, fastened together by greater vice”].

“His sneezing is the splendor of fire.” What is signified by sneezing [Since *sternutatio* occurs so shortly beforehand, one cannot help being astonished at the copyist’s yawning] except the swelling of the body and the shaking of the head? And what is signified by the shaking of the head and the swelling of the breast except pride, fury, anger, and firmness of mind?

That force of fury is called splendor because, as though through vengeance inflicted by the law, insane rage rages against the worshipers of Christ, pretending to possess the splendor of the law, although it retains not a torch of light but the blackest flame of burning. Yet, as I have said, it puts on the color of truth and pretends, in the eyes of those who look on, to defend justice. In reality it is the dark fire of Gehenna, because it does not illuminate the creature but burns it.

“His eyes are like the eyelids of dawn” [Ms.: *palfebrae*]. Through the eyes we draw in light. And what are the eyes of Behemoth except either his commandments, through which he deceitfully pretends to pour in light, or the wise through whom his extended cunning ranges?

They promise to drive away darkness and to announce the light of truth with shining signs, asserting that the faith of Christ is darkness and indicating themselves to believers as the true morning by certain deceptive signs.

They may also be understood to be called “like the eyelids of dawn” because he made a pretense of imitating the former, ancient law, as though through certain decrees of signs or severities of commandments, endeavoring to imitate it in some small matters [Here, when dealing with the past, he wrote *conabit* with *b*; he frequently marks future times with *v*].

“But from his mouth lamps proceed,” not luminous with the radiance of faith, but darkened before observers by the smoke of blackness. For it follows: “Like torches of fire kindled.” When a torch is kindled, it carries a dark fire, and, like a mass of clouds pouring forth and stretching through empty space, sends it toward heaven. So too his law is kindled by the fire of vengeance—not the Lord’s—but through the cunning of pretense it carries, in place of splendor, the darkness of error.

30. “From his nostrils smoke proceeds.” Through the nostrils odor is drawn in. And what is indicated through the nostrils except those who give off his odor—that is, the wise and distinguished, who do not smell of nectar, amber, and incense, but emit the stench of corpses, while continually fumigating themselves [L: *suffientibus*, from *suffio*, “I fumigate”; in Spanish, *sahumar*].

And rightly he is designated by the name of smoke, so that the substance of hypocrisy may be stripped bare by a more fitting term.

“His breath makes burning coals glow.” Breath is indeed the passage of life, and the life of human beings is the law of God, which corrects human conduct and, directing the condition of human salvation toward the desired peace, orders it rightly. But this lawgiving sanction makes burning coals glow because it fills its own worshipers with carnal desire and fleeting love, and by continual ambition teaches them, through certain examples and rules, to burn.

Their breath may also be understood as the burning sword that he threatens as it flashes, which he, as the true Antichrist proceeding along the path opposite to the Redeemer, most cruelly unleashed by universal persecution throughout the whole world, as we have said, after the Lord had ordered it in peace and patience.

The passage itself explains this more clearly, saying: “And flame proceeds from his mouth,” which, seeking to burn the worshipers of Christ and the servants of the Almighty Lord, makes their hearts burn with carnal lust and with the mingling of many impurities.

“In his place strength will dwell”: royal power and vigor, and a principal decree extending widely, strong through imperial authority [Ms.: “the principal decree … strong”].

“But want will precede his face.” Want either of the ability to promise anything, or certainly want of true doctrine, which has been diminished and broken since the day of the beast’s emergence; or else the signs of virtues and miracles [Ms.: *signia*], which shine moderately and not with the abundant flowering in which they shone at the beginning.

“The members of his flesh cling to one another.” The divine discourse frequently repeats the same point. And just as it designated the strong among them by the name of those who cling together through the mouth, so it distinguished the soft and weak by the members of the flesh. Thus it showed the entire mass of the lost united in the mire of iniquity here, and taught that in the future it would in no way be divided from punishment.

Everywhere they remain clinging to one another and not separated, because in this world they are joined by perverse will, and in the future condemnation they will not be divided from one another by the most just equity of the just Judge.

“He sends lightning bolts against him, and they do not travel elsewhere.” When the divine threats seize him and his members, they will not pass over to punish others, because they will abundantly possess what may burn them.

“His heart will be hardened like stone,” because none—or certainly very few—will return from his members to the faith of truth.

“And it will be squeezed like a smith’s anvil.” Bound by cords of sins, they will be hardened like a smith’s anvils. A smith’s anvil is bound so that it may be struck by repeated blows. These too are bound by obstinate faithlessness, in accordance with their preceding merits [Ms.: *precidentia*], so that by continual blows they may be hammered in the regions below.

“When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, will be cleansed.” The preachers of the Church sent by Christ, who at the end are cleansed from lighter sins by the sight of his terror.

“When the sword seizes him, neither spear nor breastplate will be able to stand.” He is seized by the sword because he will not master his anger. Neither spear nor breastplate will stand against him, because he cruelly killed those preaching the truth to him and relentlessly condemned those who endured.

Or spear and breastplate will not stand against him in the time of war, when fear terrifies even bishops distinguished by the office of preaching, and the strong members of the holy Church, shaken, consent.

What follows explains this more clearly: “He will regard iron as the strength of the Church, and bronze, the perpetual [Ms.: *jungis*] instruments ringing through the songs of the world [L: *cardina*], as straw and rotten wood,” while he crushes the strong and mocks the great whom he has deceived.

“The archer will not drive him away”—that is, the ecclesiastical preacher. This corresponds most conspicuously to our own time and, against the foolish attack of criticism, grants victory in glory to the Catholics.

“The stones of the sling have become straw to him”: stones, namely, of the sanctuary, which strike hearts in the manner of stones; or certainly stones by which the house of the Lord—that is, that heavenly Jerusalem—is beautifully built and adorned with everlasting fortification. Yet they are regarded as straw, because either through the sword they will be dissolved into nothing, or, through the traps of the snare [L: “through the casting of the snare”], those consenting to error will be reduced to the softness of hay.

But what wonder if he casts down stones, when he despises the hammer striking him? He will regard the hammer as straw and, having assumed humanity, its striker, the Lord Jesus Christ, master of all things. Is it not a hammer for him to regard the King of all ages as equal or similar to the first-formed human being?

31. “He will mock the flashing spear”—the threat of this holy law, which continually resounds to him of destruction—while he mocks the arrows of God, that is, the preachers, and despises their words, which foretell destruction for them, as the ravings of madmen.

“He spreads gold beneath himself as though it were mud,” either despising spiritual understanding as mud, or trampling the Christian people beneath the foot of victory, or profaning the holy things of God and persistently disparaging and trampling upon God’s law in mockery.

“He makes the deep sea boil like a pot” [In Job: “he will make it boil”], either while he provokes the world to wars, or while he sets the hearts of worldly people ablaze with desire, lust, or legal impulse and, as he has shown, with zeal for God.

“He makes it boil like ointments when they bubble up,” so that he may boast of twisting all these wicked deeds into zeal for righteousness and faith against his opponents and adversaries, fulfilling that Gospel saying: “Everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2).

We see this fulfilled in our own time, when we roll before the Lord the blood of the faithful as though it had been poured out in defense of the law, and behold with our own eyes the bodies of martyrs burned by the pagans. And what must be mourned with more abundant weeping: we have seen many fathers, while anathematizing such things, endure them.

“After him the path will shine.” This requires no evident exposition, and it is so open and clear that, since the matter itself shines forth, it needs no teacher. For after the shameful departure of that wicked one, the path shines with such great teachings and provisions that, unless the most merciful Judge governed the hearts of the citizens above through heavenly inspiration, all hearts would be deceived by that worldly splendor.

Nor is a lengthy exposition needed for a matter that stands clearer than light [Here perhaps the period should be closed and a new one begun, with the note of interrogation brought to an end], which has discoursed on cleanliness and on the superfluous and elaborate washing of the bath through the cleansing of all prayers, and on the most subtle discipline of many arts, which has been imposed only upon bodily limbs. With what eloquence could an orator disentangle this?

For their entire shining path shines most especially in those things that supply the flesh with nourishment for luxury and material for sin—not in those that restrain the soul from the stain of deception and from the flow of transgression by the correction of conduct.

“He will regard the abyss as though it were growing old.” Although blessed Gregory, in his customary radiant manner, discusses this against the Origenists, nevertheless, since the manifold meaning of Catholic doctrine does not conflict with it [that is, “does not oppose it”], and since Sacred Scripture often designates many things by one expression or figure, let us continue the order of our exposition.

In many passages of Scripture the abyss is understood as the law of God. Here he regarded the abyss as growing old, when, in derogation of the Gospel, he arranged for it a different and contrary testament, as though it were new.

“There is no power upon earth that can be compared with him”: such was his power that he raged through pretense of the law and oppressed through terror of authority. No one like him is found upon earth, because his inspirer was not one of those born from the earth but one of the apostate angels; and the wisdom that had fallen with him from heaven he twisted into the opposite by turning it toward cunning.

He was made such that he feared no one except God, who had filled him with such excellence and beauty. But, not content with the honor by which he had been placed above all creatures, always desiring to possess an addition [Ms.: *honorem*], he neither revered his Maker with the reverence due to fear nor, satisfied with the blessedness by which he excelled the others, kept his proper order. From there, falling to the depths, he plunged even beneath the creatures who fear God.

“He sees every lofty thing.” He does not desire to be within all things, but, swelling above all things, desires to be exalted by a power higher than all others, puffed up by the wind of vainglory.

But this clause may also appropriately be treated as referring to his member. For everything considered more precious among worldly things is subjected to their power and offered to them.

“He is king over all the sons of pride.” In its customary manner, Sacred Scripture frequently repeats and reinforces what it has once said; it was not enough to designate his pride and the swelling of his exalted mind once for weak minds. Nor does it simply call him proud, but confirms that he exercises leadership over all the proud.

For this author of wickedness ruled all heretics and all the unjust inventors of various errors [Ms.: “all … heretics … unjust”]. He who openly revealed himself through this mouth secretly hissed out great things through the former inventions of heretics [Ms.: *sivilavit*]. In those he lay hidden secretly under a disguise; in this one he stripped bare all his wars openly. Through their tongues he maliciously expounded the holy law; through this one’s instrument he composed new laws.

But he will be more aptly confirmed as king over all the sons of pride if all who are contained under his rule are examined clearly. For they are swollen with pride, exalted by the swelling of their hearts, fluid in the pleasure of carnal works, excessive in eating, rapacious and greedy in acquiring possessions and seizing the poor, grasping without piety, lying without shame, deceitful without discernment, brazen without mental modesty, cruel without mercy, aggressors without justice, without honor and without truth, ignorant of the affection of kindness [Ms.: *benignitatem*].

They are ignorant of the embrace of piety; affected, adorned, cunning, and crafty; or else stained not moderately but principally by the filth of every impiety. They mock humility as madness, reject chastity as filth, disparage virginity or regard it as the dirt of roughness [L: “virginity or the filth of scabies”], and trample the virtues of the mind beneath bodily vice, revealing their own customs by their bearing and dress.

32. These matters, which I have briefly touched upon from the book of blessed Job, I have treated while conscious of the weakness of my powers [*Imbecillatus*, a word to be added to the glossary of Late Latin: it means the same as *imbecillitas*, “weakness”]. I followed the commentaries of blessed Gregory. What he, eloquent in abundance and abundantly inventive, distributed among the members of the dragon, both generally and specifically, by means of certain figures, I have found occasion to explain continuously with reference to this beast arisen in our own times, relying upon that authority by which I know not to depart in any respect from the rules of interpreters [Ms.: *conticue*].

For I did not use rash originality or invent new meanings for matters, but followed my elders and served those meanings in which I have been instructed. Without disagreeing either with their sense or with the prefiguration of events, I have transferred the whole image of the Antichrist to this one.

For what else is Antichrist said to be except the adversary of Christ? And what is this man except Christ’s adversary, who has fought against Christ’s most holy teachings with arms outstretched? Let us examine at this point, if it is useful, part of his contrived scheme.

33. He rejects the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, giving it over to the pleasures of festivals, while he devoted the sixth day, the day of the Lord’s Passion, to mourning or fasting, to the belly and to lust.

Christ taught peace and patience; he sharpened and honed war and the sword against the necks of the innocent, so as to establish that the following had been said of him or of his followers: “Scatter the nations that desire wars” (Ps. 67:31). For they desire wars to such an extent that they wage them among all nations as though by God’s command.

Christ made the people devoted to him radiant through the gift of virginity and the good of chastity; he, as I have said, dirtied the minds and bodies of those who obeyed him with the richest delights, thick sensual indulgence, and incestuous intercourse.

Christ taught marriage; this one, divorce. Christ taught frugality and fasting; he, banquets and the enticements of feasts. Extending luxury and broadening pleasures, he restrained indecent behavior by no bridle of law.

Christ, in all the laws of continence and within the bounds of moderation, restrained natural impulse, without which human nature is scarcely found; this one, with reins broken, granted license to those lusting everywhere for countless sexual unions.

Christ orders that during the time of fasting one abstain from one’s own lawful marriage; he, especially on those days, consecrates Venus as a reward for his worshipers, together with lavish vows and offerings.

Christ promised his servants an angelic and spiritual state; he brings upon his ruined followers a bodily—or rather, equine—overflow.

Moreover, all heresies up to the present and all former errors, from the time of the birth of our Lord and God’s Son, the Redeemer, flowed forth from Judea and the Church—that is, from those whom the pure truth held under the dominion of the law.

No one else brought throughout the whole world a kingdom opposed to Christ’s renowned rule except this most wicked dreamer of empty vanities, this deceitful Antichrist, who extended himself evilly through the entire circuit of the world by a cunning and wicked intrusion.

And therefore, because he raised himself against Christ, the teacher of humility, and against Christ’s gentle and gracious commandments used defiance, the lash, and the sword, he was rightly called Antichrist. He was found to be the most open defamer and the most subtle overthrower of the Christian religion.

The Lord Christ had those who, before his bodily birth, would signify and confirm his coming through certain figures, by gesture and dress. He too has forerunners of his wickedness, who present him in full through the deceit of an upright manner of life [F: “through the deceit of evasion”].

If my readers wish to criticize this, let them first run through the books of the learned, let them grow further through the reflection afforded by reading, and let them not sneer at what has been plainly set forth.

34. What appears openly, I think, is expounded more readily than what is obscured by certain veils of problems. We follow more closely the history of present evils than the future of things expected, while we lament what was once announced under the laws of prophecy and which we now endure beneath the yoke of servitude that oppresses us [F: “deplore”; above, no. 21, we read *difflorata oracula*, “prophecies laid waste,” but that meaning now seems inappropriate].

And I think that through Antiochus, Nero, and the others whom the blessed teachers repeatedly mention, they established forerunners of the Antichrist. They would call this man the Antichrist’s instrument if they were to come down into our own times.

For our admirable teacher Jerome, although he disagrees with Porphyry concerning Antiochus and contradicts other very learned men concerning Domitian [Read *Domitium* for *Domitianum*, as above, no. 21], nevertheless did not deny that they presented, in part, a figure of the Antichrist. Rather, by a plausible refutation he disproved, as far as he could, that they were Antichrists in the strict sense, and confirmed that Antiochus himself prefigured the Antichrist in part, saying:

“Therefore, just as the Savior has Solomon as a type of himself, so he must be believed to have had other holy men as his types; and what preceded in part in him must be fulfilled in the Antichrist.”

The same admirable teacher says in Book Four of his work *According to Matthew* [that is, “in the section according to Matthew”], concerning all heretics:

“I consider all the founders of heresies to be Antichrists, and under the name of Christ to teach things that are contrary to Christ. Nor is it surprising if we see some being led astray by them, since the Lord said: ‘And they will lead many astray’ (Matt. 24:5)” [Jerome, *Commentary on Matthew*, Book IV, chapter 24: “if they lead some astray”].

Blessed John also says this most luminously in his Epistle: “You have heard that the Antichrist is coming; but now there are many Antichrists” (1 John 2:18).

There were also other works that could provide learned support for our assertion [F: “the support of learned men”], but since the matter shines more brightly through its own light, I avoided needless delay.

But lest it be said that we rely only upon our teacher Jerome and are not considered to be supported by the testimony of another, let us once more bring forward the eminent confessor Hilary and confirm ourselves by the testimony of two men who profess the truth.

### 35. That There Are Several Antichrists

“We have learned,” he says, “that there are several Antichrists, as the apostle John also proclaims. For whoever denies Christ as he was proclaimed by the apostles is an Antichrist. The proper meaning of the name ‘Antichrist’ is to be opposed to Christ.”

In passing, we point out to the prudent reader that, among the matters set forth by many learned doctors concerning the Antichrist—namely, that when he comes he will strive to restore the Mosaic law, instituting circumcision in order to injure the firmness of faith—this man appears in part to have renewed the knife of circumcision, plausibly sharpening it, and forbidding or restraining the adherents of his impious sect from pork-meat.  
[Col. 0553D] The manuscript reads *a carnes suillas*, “from pork-meats,” instead of *a carne suilla*.

As for what we promised to explain from the Apocalypse, in a manner suitable to this very modest work: although, as I have often said, the Antichrist displays all these things in himself in their present reality, nevertheless, if we treat these matters under the guidance of the Spirit, as ecclesiastical custom very commonly maintains, we shall demonstrate most clearly that they have already been fulfilled in part in the enemy mentioned above; and on this account we do not fear any malicious talker.

For none of us in the present age is found under their rule who is exempt from the mark of the most savage beast when he buys or sells.  
[Col. 0553D] The reference is to the Apocalypse, where it says: “so that no one may be able to buy or sell except the one who has the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of its name” (chapter 13). Hence, where the manuscript reads *inmunem omine*, it may perhaps be corrected to *immunis nomine*.

Everyone most frequently provides him a receptacle on his forehead, in his chief activity, or on his hand—that is, by eagerly yet sluggishly giving himself up to works.  
[Col. 0554D] The manuscript reads *in principale operis . . . in opera*.

We possess its mark when we pursue their neglected customs—the pestilential sects of the gentiles—in preference to the fathers’ most approved customs; and we bear its name upon our foreheads when, having erased the banner of the cross, we use the sign of that wicked one.

For when, in order to avoid the disgrace of those who reproach us, we practise circumcision, while despising the circumcision of the heart, which was principally commanded, and even inflicting no slight pain upon the body, what else do we do than carry his mark in our mind and upon our bodily member?  
[Col. 0554D] Thus the manuscript has *non medio* for *non modico*, “not a little.”

And when we delight in their poems and in their many tales, and serve them, or even comply with the most wicked among them for the sake of some reward, and thereby pass our life in the world or fatten our bodies, gathering greater riches through unlawful service and accursed ministry, and laying up for ourselves, our sons, and our grandsons, for long periods, the splendour, perfumes, and abundance of garments or other riches, while marking beforehand upon them, with our own hands, the name of the wicked beast with the honour and invocation customarily offered to it in their place—do we not openly carry the name of the beast in our right hand through these passions?
[Col. 0554D] The manuscript reads *solitum*, agreeing with “customary,” rather than the printed *solito*.

Likewise, when, for the sake of worldly honours, we accuse our brothers before impious kings, with guilt, and offer the sword of revelation to the enemies of the Most High for the slaughter of the Lord’s flock, and purchase with money their leadership and service for carrying out that very crime, what else do we do than conduct transactions with the name of the beast and the mark of the most cruel wild creature, sinning by exposing the Lord’s sheep, through the evil of our commerce, to wolves’ teeth?  
[Col. 0554D] The manuscript reads *crudelissime ferre*, apparently for *crudelissimae ferae*.

Likewise, when we investigate their sacraments and learn the sects of philosophers—or rather, of *philocompori*—not in order to refute their errors, but for elegance of wit and brilliant eloquence, gathering these things while neglecting the holy readings, what else do we do than place the number of his name in our chamber as though idols?  
[Col. 0554D] That is, not lovers of knowledge—which is what *philosophus* signifies—but lovers of boasting. From the Greek *φιλόκομπος*, “a lover of boasting.”  
[Col. 0555B] “The number of his name,” that is, six hundred and sixty-six (Apoc. XIII, 18).

Who, I ask, is found today among our faithful laypeople so diligent that, when he comes upon the Holy Scriptures, he looks at volumes written in Latin by any of the doctors?  
[Col. 0555B] Aldrete, *On the Origins of the Castilian Language*, book I, chapter 22: *inveniatur*, “is found.”  
[Col. 0555B] The same author: *recipiat*, “receives.”

Who is held by love of the Gospel, who by love of the prophets, who by love of the apostles? Are not all the Christian youths—handsome in appearance, eloquent in speech, distinguished in dress and bearing, renowned for pagan learning, exalted in Arabic eloquence—handling the volumes of the Chaldeans with the greatest eagerness, reading them most intently, discussing them most ardently, and gathering them with immense zeal, praising and disseminating them with broad and tightly controlled speech, while remaining ignorant of the beauty of the Church and despising, as utterly worthless, the streams of the Church flowing from paradise?  
[Col. 0555B] Aldrete reads *homines*, “men,” for *omnes*, “all,” and *lingua*, “tongue,” for *linguae*, “of speech.”  
[Col. 0555B] The manuscript has *gentilici eruditioni*, “to pagan learning.”  
[Col. 0556B] Aldrete reads *eructant*, “belch forth,” instead of *tractant*, “handle.”

Alas, what grief! Christians do not know their own language, and Latins do not pay attention to their proper language, so that throughout the whole fellowship of Christ scarcely one person is found among a thousand who can reasonably address a letter of greeting to a brother.  
[Col. 0556B] Aldrete reads *ex omni*, “from the whole,” for *omni*, “throughout the whole.”  
[Col. 0556B] The same author: *legem*, “law,” instead of *linguam*, “language.”  
[Col. 0556A] The same author: “And you may find.”

Yet an innumerable, manifold crowd is found that explains the ornate displays of Chaldean words with practiced eloquence.  
[Col. 0556B] Aldrete reads *Et reperias*, “and you may find,” for *Et reperitur*, “and there is found.”  
[Col. 0556B] The manuscript reads *multiplices turbas*, “manifold crowds.”

Thus, with a more learned metrical art, they adorn their final clauses by compressing a single letter, in poems taken from those peoples and made more elevated by beauty; and according to the requirements of that language—which closes every vowel sound in its commas and cola—many letters of the entire alphabet are rhythmically, or rather, as is proper to them, metrically, varied through different words and bound together by one ending or by a similar cadence.

Many other things existed that could provide firmness for this exposition of ours, indeed that could bring plainly into the light the matter we are explaining.  
[Col. 0556B] Up to this point the Cordoban manuscript continues. The second book promised by him (nos. 1, 11, and 21) is missing.

[Col. 0555]

## Poems Begin

[Col. 0555D] The manuscript consistently reads *versi*, “verses.”

### I. The Nightingale’s Song

[Col. 0555C]

Your voice, Philomela, surpasses songs of metre,  
and in wondrous measures overtops the mighty winds.

Your voice, Philomela, sweetly proceeds above the organs,  
for your great songs resound sweetly and brilliantly—[lacuna].

Your voice, Philomela, so surpasses the Muses in your throat  
that it conquers the hissing of zithers—[lacuna].  
[Col. 0555D] Morales: “it conquers the cicadas.”  
[Col. 0555D] The manuscript has *sivila*, apparently for *sibila*, “hisses.”

And thus, with the thumb directing the sweet lyres’ strings,  
you soothe and cherish the hearts of men—[lacuna].  
[Col. 0555D] Morales reads *ducunt*, “they lead,” for *ductus*, “directed” or “led.”  
[Col. 0555D] The following verses are absent from Morales. Above, on page 32, he remarks: “This first page, besides being torn and mutilated, had been so thoroughly destroyed by age that scarcely a few letters could be recognized. Those that were recognized were deciphered through the diligent investigation of Don Francisco Delgado.”

Let every other [voice] yield to you; let the chattering voice also yield:  
in my judgment, let all your song shine.

Certainly no bird now equals you in song—[lacuna]  
nor brings forth [anything] with a human voice—[lacuna].

Say—[lacuna]—gently—[lacuna].

[Col. 0555D] And—[lacuna]—pour forth melodies often from your accustomed throat.

Carry sweet sounds upon a joyful breast—[lacuna],  
and sweetly—[lacuna]—resound in song.

Glory—[lacuna]—to Christ throughout the ages,  
who has given us—[lacuna]—so great a gift.

### Another Philomelaic Song by the Same Author

[Col. 0556C]

Speak, speak—[lacuna]—sing for me with your throat—[lacuna].  
[Col. 0555D] “A good part of the lower section of the leaf,” says Morales, “was missing, where the beginning of this epigram was located. On the reverse leaf the following appeared: ‘Your songs joyfully…’—But most recently portions of the two preceding verses could be read:

“—[lacuna]—you, ceasing from singing,

“—[lacuna]—the days, leaving only the darkness of night.

“Your songs joyfully…””

Pleat your joyful songs with a rough whisper,  
and, I beg you, arouse your metrical praises for yourself.  
[Col. 0556D] Morales: *tui*, “of you,” instead of *tibi*, “for you.”

Behold, poetic responses run forth to your songs,  
and strive to surpass one another with varied step.  
[Col. 0556D] The manuscript has *te*, “you,” instead of *se*, “itself.”

Shake out your winged songs; raise them high with your voice:  
I do not wish you to be afraid; I do not wish you to be silent.

[Col. 0556D] Morales reads *exalta*, “raise”; the manuscript has the corrupt form *extulta*.

Let every kind yield; let the chattering voice yield; let it yield,  
and, in my judgment, let every breeze yield to you.  
[Col. 0556D] Morales and the manuscript read *cedat omne*, “let every thing yield.”

With feathered clamour, surpassing the deeds of those before,  
may you likewise surpass our new works.  
[Col. 0556D] Morales: *fata*, “fates,” instead of *facta*, “deeds.”

Great glory to our God, who reigns in an eternal seat,  
reigning forever, fostering us piously and justly.

### Distichs on the Cock

[Col. 0556D] The manuscript has *distica*, “distichs.”

The cock, shaking himself upon his wings, echoes with his voice,  
curling his throat and sounding beautifully with sweet sound.  
[Col. 0556D] Both Morales and the manuscript have *dulci sono*, “with sweet sound.”

[Col. 0557A] He repeats his lofty cries during the night,  
and, before the light, sings many songs.

He proclaims praises to the Lord through the hours of the day;  
often, crowing again, he awakens the sluggish.

### III. Other Verses

The part of the leaf that we said had been torn away had carried off the first eight verses. This was the beginning of the following leaf. —Morales.

[Col. 0557D]

And thus the peacock, quavering with varied voice, cries out,  
gleaming with tawny feathers and the purple *sicli* [the final word is corrupt].  
[Col. 0557D] Morales: *fores*; the manuscript: *pavus*, “peacock.”

He flourishes in beautiful form, lovely in appearance,  
and applauds the songs, painted with a jewelled star.

When he vibrates his smooth feathers and wonderfully unfolds his wings,  
and when his spread tail shines like the sun,  
the dense shields (*peltes*, a corrupt spelling of *peltae*) gleam with crescent-shaped brilliance.

[Col. 0557B]

When the beautiful and tranquil creature turns upon the earth,  
or raises his curled feathers, unfolding his wheels in order,  
a thousand lights shine serenely here and there,

while, resounding in melodious harmony, he looks down upon the *plume* birds [printed form corrupt]  
and repeatedly renews his songs.

Therefore you, swans, and peacocks splendid in beauty,  
lead the song with my sweet Philomela,  
and with metrical feet disdain the monsters of rhythm,

[Col. 0557D] Morales reads *mea cum*, “with my”; the manuscript has *meatim*, a corrupt or otherwise unclear form.

which—a sluggish, wandering flow—sound rancidly [the syntax is corrupt],  
and fashion songs with wandering lowing so as to make the Church’s song ugly,  
the Church which always shines brightly among the peoples.  
[Col. 0557D] Morales reads *Quae segnis errans fluxus … sanans*; the manuscript has the corrupt *harrans floxas* (perhaps *flexus*, “a bending/turn”) and *sannas* (perhaps *sonans*, “sounding”).  
[Col. 0557D] The manuscript has *plebisque semper fulgide claret*; Morales has the reading in the text. His transcript ends there, merely skimming the titles of the following verses.

### IV. Verses of Praise, or Prayer

O good Creator, good through piety, beautiful in splendour,  
strong King of the ages, bright and serene,

eternal power reigning with great authority,  
you shine forth radiantly throughout the whole world,

you extend over the sea, the lands, the heavens, and Tartarus,  
and, strong in power, you mark out and close the abysses.

Whatever you regard trembles; whatever you govern with piety  
you regulate, restraining the raging storms by your power.

You—[lacuna]—Lord of heaven, whose kingdom is power,  
and with a peaceful countenance you calm the storms;

you dissolve the Tartarean lands’ darkness with light,  
you beautifully loosen the tongues of infants,

and justly rule and adorn every kingdom.

You, most holy ruler, cleanse our sins,  
and in your mercy now make these voices worthy to be returned to you.

### V. Another Set of Verses

[Col. 0557D]

Here, the lilies of heaven shine with the light of whiteness;  
here, the golden roses imitate the flowering purple of earth;

and the violets glitter equally in place of the stars,  
while, united in varied colour, they breathe fragrance together.

Whitish lilies retain their color like a pearl in shells;  
and, like gypsum embracing the neck of a girl,

milky [necks], while *pingunt bilbant* [two corrupt or conflicting verb forms] the gleaming *selenci*.  
[Col. 0558D] The text has *conchis*, “shells”; the manuscript reads *conclis*. The printed *selenci* is corrected to *elenchi*, “pearls.”

The fiery carbuncle burns with wondrous flames,  
and a little stone, powerful in the color of heaven, is *acquescens* [corrupt; perhaps “resting” or “shining”].

Thus, precious in strength, it stands there, growing green among the others,  
which make the beautiful *celidrum* rise high about the neck.  
[Col. 0558D] The editor proposes *chelydrum*, a woman’s ornament, for the printed *celidrum*.

And the beautiful rose *flabescit* [corrupt; perhaps *flavescit*, “grows golden”] like topaz,  
while the rounded (*theretes*, for *teretes*) violets flash with gold in curling forms.

Necks gemmed with stones, like flowers of the field,  
shine brightly; the gems, bought at proud expense,  
remain exceedingly precious—prosperous in such a gift [the construction is uncertain].

Yet they possess like grace with flashing beauty.  
Mingled together, they flower, breathe fragrance, grow white, and redden.  
“A four-sided world with a thousandfold summit adorns” (*Quadratum apice mundum millene venustat*): the subject and syntax of this corrupt closing line are uncertain.

### VI. The Ephemerides of His Own Illness Begin

[Col. 0558D] The manuscript has *incipit versi Epimenides*, “the verses of Epimenides begin.”

#### Preface of the Prayer

[Col. 0558B]

You, Christ the Lord of all things, whom the tongue celebrates,  
whom the world fears, whom kingdoms proclaim brightly,

whom heaven, earth, the seas, and Tartarus serve;  
whom the sun, moon, and day obey, and all the abysses;

whom the blessed angelic host, through its power,  
serves with praises in shining beauty;

whom every power and every harmony praise,  
and the stars, and whatever is held within the convex centre;

whom light, air, day, heat, and fire resound,  
whom rivers, snow, ice, wind, and water echo—

the worthy prayer venerates you, Lord of all kinds of things.

In mercy, loosen for the wretched man his metrical songs,  
so that he may be able to sing praises in beautiful verse,  
and cover these bitter disasters of his in verse.

Though he deservedly suffers these disasters, subject to death and the tomb,  
you, God, in mercy call him back to the threshold of life.  
[Col. 0558C] The source has the irregular sequence *Quas … patiens subjectum morte sepulcri*; its masculine *subjectum* concerns the suffering speaker, while *quas* refers back to his disasters.

Now grant your servant abundant tears for lamentation in song,  
and, Christ, dissolve our darkness.
