Form the hearts of your servants with radiant, vigorous light,  
so that he may worthily return a beautiful hymn-bearing song,

by which, holy and peaceful, you may wipe away the sins  
we have dragged along while wandering astray and travelling on no straight path.

Thus I, repeating the paths of the first evils,  
am now bound by a just chain beneath the disaster of the guilty.

But to the wretched man whom guilt strips of pardon,  
may your grace, Christ, grant a crown;

whom the rope of guilt, stretched from our fathers,  
has bound, and who does not spring free even through weeping.

### VII. Another Personal Metrical Lament

[Col. 0558D]

Alvarus, O reader, composes this over a long span of time,  
and, with his resonant tongue, rises again with you after his deeds (*post facta*; the reading may be corrupt),

released into the air or certainly sunk into dust;  
turned into ashes, yet behold, he echoes metrically.

You, reader, reading again, now return the rewards of the voice,  
and, pouring tears before the Lord, answer these things in song.

[Col. 0559A]

All-powerful Father of all things, to whom glory will yield,  
whom the heavens praise and all the abysses serve,

whom the sun, moon, day, earth, and Tartarus serve—  
[Col. 0559D] The manuscript has *serbent*, perhaps the same as the Spanish *sirven*, Latin *serviunt*, “serve”—

whom the sweet birds praise when they pipe their songs,  
whom the murmur echoes as it swells along the watery shore,

whom the roaring deep storm of the sea celebrates,  
whom the wheel of all things proclaims in its meaning—

govern Alvarus in your customary and constant mercy.

May grace raise him up, whom harmful folly bends down.  
Thus, after death, may a truly serene prayer,  
worthy of the great, crown him with the lot of the saints.

Behold, I am he—I confess it—who once perhaps flourished,  
leading a living life and breathing forth from the body;

but the ashes withdrew swiftly into ashes,  
yielding as food to worms or being scattered by the wind,

[Col. 0559B]

returning to nothing, yet able one day to return,  
to be reshaped from nothing by the power of God.

I ask you now, recall yourself as bound by this fragile fate,  
and, when the soul has fled, as a sharer in our pains,

at some time enjoy these shadows of places in your heart.  
For I was what you, flourishing today, now shine as in your face,

boldly trusting in fragile, youthful bearing,  
thundering with raised neck and proud voice,

usurping what was forbidden, living with great guilt—  
yet, through God’s mercy, never drawn along the wrong paths.

I did not withdraw in faith or in mind  
from the holy standard of faith.

By the merit of that faith I believe that I may perhaps be blessed,  
if through your mercy I deserve to be helped with tears,

for what I am, you will be after the dark funeral of death.

Therefore, come: break your delays and rest in our end.

### VIII. Verses in the Library of Leovigild, by the Same Alvarus

[Col. 0559C]

Here are many sacred things, truly renowned in doctrine,  
which shine throughout the world’s hinges by God’s power.

Here new things and old alike are beautifully adorned:  
the golden sayings of God the Most High, the wisdom of the Father,

which the whole world celebrates with its four-sided summit.

The beginning of the book of Genesis unfolds the origins  
of the world, which surely reveals the natures of things.

Exodus leads the people from Egypt by the arm.

The third, Leviticus, adorns the distinguished head-coverings.  
[Col. 0559D] It seems to denote Aaron’s garments: *camilla* is a covering for the head, as Theodulf attests in book VI, poem 18, *On the Garments of Bishops*: “The flowing *camilla* covers the head; a black will covers the mind.”

The fourth is Numbers, powerful in the name of numbers;  
the Fifth repeats the law, setting its precepts in conclusion.  
[Col. 0559D] That is, “the Fifth,” the book of Deuteronomy.

The hero Navegius, Jesus in figurative name,  
[Col. 0559D] He is called Jesus Nave in Ecclesiasticus 46, as Moses’ successor.  
[Col. 0560D] Perhaps *figurato*, “in a figurative name.”

is followed by the book of Judges, revealing its deeds.

Ruth also; Samuel and *Malacim* follow,  
unfolding the deeds in four books in their proper order.  
[Col. 0560D] “Samuel” denotes the first and second books. The books which we call the Third and Fourth Books of Kings are called the first and second *Melachim* by the Hebrews. The printed poem has *Malacim*.

To these is joined the lofty prophetic utterance of the seers.

Isaiah, the first, cries out again; his companion, the second,  
Jeremiah, rises tearfully, a pious prophet;

and Ezekiel, covered at the head or shut off at the end,

then Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, shipwrecked Jonah,  
Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah;

then Haggai sounds out, and Zechariah resounds,  
while Malachi completes the end in the final word.

Isaiah, first of the prophets, exceedingly lofty,  
resounds more abundantly, brilliant with the mysteries of Christ.

This other one, Jeremiah, laments the holy matter  
with tears and such zeal of faith, portraying another thing in verse.

Ezekiel, shut in by a cloud or withdrawn in meaning,  
reveals not openly small matters of his own, but great things.

Then Daniel proclaims the stone that crushes kingdoms,  
and unfolds the coming of Christ in numbers and years.

I have kept silent about the words of the others, but in honour of meaning  
Job also shines here through his work, and his life flashes forth.

[Col. 0560B]

And sweet David makes sweet things metrical, sweetly.

Solomon himself is Idida [Jedidiah], who signifies Christ.  
[Col. 0560D] The manuscript has *quem*, “whom.” On Idida, see Letter XVIII, no. 16.

His three books shine wondrously and mystically,  
so that logically, physically, or ethically they reveal causes.  
[Col. 0560D] The printed form is *fistice*; the variant is *physice*, “physically,” as in *logice*, “logically,” and *ethice*, “ethically.”

Daniel then comes in proper order along the following path,  
followed by the words of the two books of Days—  
[Col. 0560D] That is, the two books of Chronicles—  
and then Esdras, beautifully restoring the law.

After him comes beautiful Esther; then Wisdom flourishes;  
Ecclesiasticus celebrates praises and the fathers.

After these Tobias shines, and Judith follows,  
and then the armed deeds of the two Maccabees.

These are the ancient sacred books, now the mystical gifts  
of God kept hidden for the ancient people beneath a sign,

which the servants of the Most High Lord, who rejoice in the name of Christ,  
hold unlocked through the great light.

[Col. 0560C]

Now I strive to unfold in verse the holy things of the saints,  
which Matthew, Mark, Luke, and the fourth, John,  
bring forth from the four-sided stream born of paradise.

[Col. 0560D] The manuscript reads *paradisi geno*, “born of paradise,” for *paradisigeno*.

They proclaim Christ and God to the fourfold world  
under the figures of a man, a lion, a calf, and an eagle.

Matthew shines with the face and appearance of a man;  
Mark gives forth a roar with the mouth of a lion;

Luke bellows like a bull with a great murmur,  
and swift John, like an eagle, climbs above the heavens.

For Christ is a beautiful man, born from the Virgin;  
he is a calf, having suffered as the Father’s consecrated victim;

he is a lion when, strong, he breaks kingdoms and powerful kings;  
he is an eagle, climbing heaven and the throne of the Thunderer.

After these, twice seven books of Paul shine forth,  
and seven catholic books follow them in number.

[Col. 0560D]

Here James sounds out gracefully, and Peter has two [epistles];  
John has three lofty books; then comes the page of Jude,

and here also the apostolic Acts, with their handsome texts;  
the flowering Revelation of John, small but densely figured, fittingly completes [the collection].

It sings the Alpha at the beginning and marks the supreme ω (Omega),

[Col. 0561A]

which it calls in Greek the Lord, King, and God.

Alpha and ω (Omega) clearly and serenely explain  
the one living God and man throughout the ages of ages.

These are the sacred things and gifts of God, flowering eternally,  
always shining like the lights of heaven.

These beautiful gems glow more brightly than the sun,  
and, while shining with light, renew minds or conquer darkness.

They hold the keys of the centre and reveal rewards;  
they refresh those born of paradise in the flower-bearing meadow.

Here, mystically, whatever lies hidden beneath the letter shines;  
simple history adorns those whom ethical teaching forms.

Here he drinks sweet drink who receives what is pleasant;  
here food satisfies hearts and refreshes them with nourishment.

These are the clear things of God, which certainly overcome  
the darkness of the world with flashing rays and make it serene.

[Col. 0561B]

The precious law shines, snowy with wondrous brightness,  
more luminous than the sun glowing with the purple of the sky.

All things together, whatever is fashioned by worldly art,  
these surpass deservedly, as they come from heaven’s summit;

through God’s piety they enlighten those whom darkness makes obscure.

This text is powerful through a single thousandfold path;  
with plain words it explains and reveals great things.

Thus it runs peacefully like water, so that it may portray deep things;  
thus it resounds deeply but briefly, so that it may revisit small things.

The wise seek obscure matters a hundredfold in meaning;  
the simple embrace what is open and conceal it in the mind.

This powerful teaching flashes with *ceneri* splendor [the printed form is corrupt].  
[Col. 0561D] The editor proposes *celeri*, “swift,” for *ceneri*.

Swelling, that thing yields to it which swells with a twisted ornament [the syntax is uncertain].  
He who, with zeal for faith, reads again the bright things of heaven—chaste, just, and pious—thrives with a thousandfold gift.

[Col. 0561C]

But whoever, rough and blind, unravels these things in his mind  
is darkened a thousandfold by a gloomy and distorted understanding.

The law of faith proceeds faithfully and is always faithful,  
but the perverse rebel in heart travels perversely.  
[Col. 0561D] Variant: *vitat*, “avoids,” instead of *viat*, “travels.”

As a pearl shines, grows white, and gleams in *conclis* [a corrupt form, perhaps “shells”],  
so God Christ is powerful, concealed beneath the letter.

He himself is the hyacinth, present to us and *aquescens* [corrupt; perhaps “shimmering with water”],  
cleansing what is obscene and renewing the redeemed in whiteness.

Here the fiery Lord burns, shining like a carbuncle,  
while he purifies disgrace with flames and flashes with light.  
[Col. 0561D] The manuscript reads *canbunculus* for *carbunculus*, “carbuncle.”  
[Col. 0561D] The manuscript has *humine*, apparently for *lumine*, “with light.”

And flourishing with eternal greenness like a true emerald,  
he is adorned throughout the ages by the twelvefold order of stones,

and by four times six elders, who venerate him,  
the Lord, the Lamb, and God, bending their knees.  
[Col. 0561D] The manuscript has *Populi te*; the reading is uncertain.

[Col. 0561D]

This eternal law endures while the ages return,  
sounding vigorously and enclosed by no limit,

while the sun brightens heaven and earth with its light,  
while Cynthia accompanies the nights and puts darkness to flight,

while the star-bearing centre flashes with varied stars,  
while the wind forms clouds and the water resounds,

while the great gate of heaven resounds with mighty force,  
while lightning flashes, hurled by a strong arm,

[Col. 0562A]

while the earth grows green and the woods blossom in darkness,  
while thickets hold wild beasts reclining in their lairs,

while the stag leaps lightly with his leap or his antlers,  
and the grim boar fights with his tooth, thrice fattened,

while the fish, creeping through the fluid, traverses the rivers,  
while birds extend themselves on wings through the empty air,

and pipe sweet songs through their throats with their beaks.  
[Col. 0561D] The manuscript has *rustro*, apparently for *rostro*, “beaks.”  
[Col. 0562D] The manuscript has *cantos*, apparently for *cantus*, “songs.”

While human beings live in the world and fall away through death,  
while the shadow follows the body—formed, perhaps, by lights—

while angels sound in heaven and the strength of peoples,  
through God’s eternal mercy, composes what is everlasting,

the law of Christ lives forever, blessed above the heavens.

This alone does not grow old with the world,  
while it lives, resounding among the saints in heaven after the end.

When the bodily mass, dissolved into decay, will fall—[lacuna],

[Col. 0562B]

for the spirit, carried above the heavens, lives by right.  
[Col. 0562D] The manuscript has *revectus*, “carried back.”

The words of the living revive through the life-giving breath,  
and after the world’s extinction rise again above the stars.

Thus whatever belongs to God never rots in the end,  
but, sent into the lands, always grows green through power.

Now it remains to see at whose command these things were written,  
or through whose work they were collected.

The strength of Leovigild gathered these things together in one work,  
placing seventy-two books beneath a sheath.  
[Col. 0562D] Perhaps *vagina*, “sheath.”

He shines with Getic light, or with abundance of speech;  
his offspring or language shines through the ages.  
[Col. 0562D] Variant: *gemina*, “double,” instead of *germina*, “offspring.”

After the sacred faith of the Lord has rightly been praised,  
it is fitting that this trumpet of ours sound for all:

Alvarus resounds these things metrically through long ages,  
and, turned from ash into ash, his tongue still sounds.

[Col. 0562C]

You who read, reader, at whatever time,  
recall that you will become our companion through death.

Break the delays of life, I beg you, and, shut within the tomb,  
tell beneath the shadows how great a salvation awaits us.

So that you may report the news of the world through dark dwelling places:  
who rejoices and groans well, badly, or moderately;

what the world now reshapes by savage, deceptive art (*sceva falens*; both forms are corrupt or uncertain);  
what error awaits the living, and how great a rebellious struggle

rises up in vain, rejecting these truths;

what hollow honour now destroys royal hearts;  
what pleasures are fluid, liquid, and fleeting,

which, while grasped by the fingers, flee like water.

Pour forth *pronsas* tears, reader [the adjective is corrupt],  
so that, before Christ the judge, you may be free from your own sins.  
[Col. 0562D] The editor proposes *pro nostros*, “for our [sins],” which may instead connect the tears with “our sins”; the supplied text does not permit a certain reconstruction.

[Col. 0562D]

And may you be able to climb to the lofty tribunal of the centre.

May that God grant it, who is powerful in the triune name,  
and grant us Christians rest throughout the ages. Amen.

### IX. Another Set of Verses in Praise of the Cross

From heaven, O Lord, flash forth with glorious power;  
the cross shines as a sign, happily gleaming above the heavens.

[Col. 0563A]

This strong palm establishes Christ’s trophies in the believing heart,  
by Christ’s power, with heaven as witness.

Let the treacherous sect of pagan errors yield;  
behold, the vault of the world shines with the sign of Christ.

No human hand painted this upon the heavenly hinge,  
but the heavenly hand of him who rules the world by his power.

For the moon’s golden form, most beautiful on its day,  
illumined by the cross, prevails with that full light

by which the Hebrew people customarily conduct the Passover [the syntax of *deducere pascha* is uncertain].

Look, wretched nation, upon the sign shining for the redeemed,  
and upon Cynthia on the fourteenth day, the *farsum* thus filled with Christ’s light,  
by which she displays the sign that flashes upon the forehead,  
always resplendent in beautiful splendor for the world.  
[Col. 0563D] The editor proposes *fassum* for *phasen*, “Passover,” behind the corrupt *farsum*.

Now recall, I beg you, the Lord “to have remained while it thundered” (*mansisse tonante*; the phrase is corrupt),  
who on the fourteenth willed to be suspended upon the wood of salvation

[Col. 0563B]

beneath this sign which the stars of heaven send.  
On that very day the moon’s image withdrew from heaven,

radiating beautifully—“by which the treacherous people, rejoicing …” [the sentence breaks off in the supplied text].

Therefore this beautiful form condemns the poisonous ones.

Look, I beg you, whoever you are, wretched in your evil mind,  
and again raise your eyes to the stars of heaven.  
[Col. 0563D] The manuscript has *ac*, “and,” instead of *ad*, “to.”

See why the arms shine with sidereal light:  
because this fourfold sign cleanses the whole world,

all that heaven and earth hold, created beneath the law.

All things are cleansed by the sign of the Cross; believe, wicked one.

Unhappy error, what mocking grimaces are you now fashioning?  
[Col. 0563D] That is, “mockery.”

If you can, cleverly disclose your murmurs to us.

Why does the moon now display a sign contrary to you?  
[Col. 0563D] Variant: *figurat*, “figures,” for *vigurat*, “displays.”

Why does the despised image shine again in heaven?  
Why does the golden palm of our forehead, victorious, shine thus?

[Col. 0563C]

The Cross, opposed to you, claims the vault of heaven.

This crown of our faith shines with light,  
which the servants of Christ always triumphantly bear from heaven.

But that which you persecute with weapons could [appear] in heaven;  
impious and cruel one, believe with your eyes—or from the heavenly body [the construction is uncertain].

Behold, our God Christ blossoms from the heavens;  
behold, the sign of the venerable cross above the heavens,

shining among the stars, now condemns the profane world.

Let the treacherous crowd, darkened by grief, depart;  
let the ranks of Christ rejoice in flowering beauty;

let the synagogue now withdraw in its own dark colour,  
and let the Church rejoice in its shining golden colour,

the Church whom Christ always joins to himself in beautiful love.

### X. Heroic Verses in Praise of Blessed Jerome

[Col. 0563D]

Jerome shines, resounding with lofty virtue,  
and, renowned in books, flourishes throughout the world’s hinges.

This man portrayed the Lord’s flower-bearing things as “born of paradise” (*paradisigena*),  
so that they might flash with celebrated radiance throughout the whole world.  
[Col. 0563D] The manuscript reads *paradisii gene*, “offspring of paradise,” for *paradisigena*.

Here he bound or adorned the sacred songs of the Lord who holds all things by his power  
with the sweet, heavenly poetry of the law [the force of *praestrinxit* is uncertain].

[Col. 0564A]

Here he poured new and old honey from his heart—[lacuna]  
—[lacuna]—do not doubt—[lacuna].

He wrote the sacred things that shine with double light, mystically,  
composed with great and pleasant power.

[Col. 0563D] The manuscript reads singular *resplendit*, “shines,” for plural *resplendent*, “shine.”

He displayed the golden sayings of God, the centre and ruler of all,  
showing what the tongue could achieve through so great a gift.

[Col. 0563D] The manuscript reads *Hos tendit*, “he extends these,” for *Ostendit*, “he displayed.”

While he shone with mighty pen in diverse brilliance,  
he poured forth Attic and Hebrew words in radiant origin,

and rendered in Latin whatever exists in Hebrew;  
moreover, he unlocked the Greek sources in due order.

The streams flow eloquently along the banks.

For this reason the servants of Christ always resound  
with the teacher, ever venerable, beneath the threshold of the Lord:

the splendor of the Church, the lamp of holy teaching,  
a heavenly cultivator of the richly fat olive tree,

driving away the heresies that, under the vast name of pestilence,  
devour the servants of Christ while barking beneath the tooth.

Here the sweet prophet shines in a varied path,  
and cuts off with his sickle the bristling, leafy branches.

the reddening dawn signifies excellent rains;  
here he is a glassy stream, peaceful and beautiful in radiance;

a rapid torrent to those whom error entangles.

Whatever has not been sprinkled with Jerome’s savour  
remains unapproved, totters, and withers limply.

The oracles not reheated in the fire of the holy flame-bearer hang limp:  
he shines with the light of faith, brighter and powerful in all things,  
whereby the grace of his tongue is *ortatur potuis*, flowering with a thousandfold doctrine [the two printed words are corrupt].  
[Col. 0564D] The manuscript has singular *rutilat*, “he shines,” where the syntax might suggest plural *rutilant*. The editor proposes *ornatur, potius*, “is adorned, rather,” for *ortatur potuis*.

[Col. 0564C]

While the sun and moon make the darkness serene beneath the sky,  
while the stars run in red brilliance to illuminate hidden places,

while they turn over an unseen dream or certainly reveal it,  
and in varied courses repeatedly attempt to balance the towers,

while the wind heaps up clouds and heat scorches,  
while hoary winter grows green upon the cold grass,

while fire flashes and fluid water runs back,  
while the sea’s wave resounds and swelling foam melts,

while wild beasts occupy the thickets and fish the waters,  
while the swift stag leaps with his branching body,

while the grim boar resists with crescent-shaped tusk,  
while birds pipe trembling voices from their throats,

while human beings perish in the world or certainly are born again,  
while the shadow follows the body—formed, perhaps, by lights—  
[Col. 0564D] The manuscript has *quem limina*; perhaps *lumina*, “lights.”

[Col. 0564D]

the servants of faith will always bless him beneath the heavens,  
whose tongue now shines through the ages,

while the Church retains the new and old things formed by his own mouth,  
singing without end through the days.

Therefore, great teacher, I beg you, from your heavenly seat,  
may your worthy prayer grant me a place of rest after life.

“Your lamp, O Lord, shone”—  
[Col. 0564D] These words no longer seem to concern Jerome, but an apostate angel, under another implied title, as the final verses especially show.  
—[lacuna]—

—[lacuna]—distinguished, and marked everywhere by light.

[Col. 0565A]

O finest work of the Lord, his glory and image,  
full of the delights of paradise and serene light,

shining with immense splendour, perfect in beauty,  
in form you surpassed the heavenly beings; you were above the stars.

[Col. 0566A]

While all marvelled at your splendour and beauty,  
you, the first image, fell, falling to the depths.

You cast yourself down because you lifted yourself above the stars.  
The grace of your splendour was the innermost cause of your pain.

[Col. 0565]

# Appendix to the Works of Alvarus of Córdoba

## Short Works of Leovigild and Cyprian, Priests of Córdoba

[Col. 0565]

### Leovigild’s Book on the Dress of Clerics

[Col. 0565B]

To the excellent and life-giving clerics who serve Christ the Lord under the protection of the blessed bishop and martyr Cyprian: your Leuvegild, everywhere your attendant.

When your serenity encountered folly in certain clerics, and saw the oppression of Christ’s worshippers by the Ishmaelites throughout all Hesperia, there was lacking the zeal by which they might have discerned the authority of clerical dress. Some of the ancient Fathers thought that this dress was intended only for the arrangement of their bodies [Note: *Antiquos* (“ancient”)]; and also, mystically, to disclose to our eyes each of its forms as an example for the faithful. Since your clemency was pleased to see the savage cruelty of the pagans prevailing over the Church of God in our regions—and lest, by arguing with us, our simplicity should in some measure be more clearly wounded on account of the dress of this order—you appointed me to set out and commit to writing the meanings of clerical dress, and to recite, before what I remember concerning these offices should slip more fully from our minds, whatever I recall from the admonitions of the Fathers about them, so that whoever among us, hindered by bodily weakness, cannot direct his steps to the teachers who remain, or whom an investigation, a tax, or the levy which we are compelled to pay every lunar month for Christ’s name has detained, may at least read it at night among his ecclesiastical duties, if he considers it necessary [Col. 0566B]. Thus, perhaps, through ignorance of the mystery of his dress, no one may put on the appearance of the impious and imitate the practices of unbelievers, in whom there is no wisdom.

O how devout was your excellence, if only, when such matters were commanded, suitable speech were present! Who would dare to proclaim the mystery of the priests’ dress without hesitation, or to disclose the mystical meaning of its explanation without fear? It would have been better for me to hear this work cautiously from you than to speak about it incautiously before men. And unless I certainly remembered my Lord’s truthful admonitions: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11); and: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20), I certainly would not have applied my knee to such matters [Note: “To such matters.”]. But since, through your intercession, I had put my trust in divine assistance, I leapt—not boldly, but obediently—into matters unlawful for me [Note: “Unlawful,” that is, beyond my strength], proclaiming with an inflated articulation and saying with the intention of my mind: “Make me understand the way of your justifications, O Lord” (Psalm 118:27). For whatever my rusticity has diminished from what was asked, may your most beloved holiness not turn back from fashioning it, by showing compassion toward one whom not laziness prevented from fulfilling the desired task, but whose mind was held fast by sluggishness in the face of sin.

[Col. 0567]

## The Epigrams of the Lord Cyprian, Archpriest of the See of Córdoba, Published at the Request of Adulfus [Note: Manuscript: *editi* (“published,” masculine plural).]

### I

[Col. 0567A]

This work shines forth through the illustrious count Adulfus,  
who, at his own expense, renewed the book-chest;  
in it are found the new books and the ancient books  
of the true Testament, preparing nourishment  
for one who longs to advance toward heaven and endure,  
and loudly proclaiming: whoever has been fed by this food  
does not burden his entrails,  
nor stuff his belly, but frequently nourishes the spirit.

From here a spring of Paradise rises in clear streams;  
here a sweet draught flows forth into the chamber of the heart;  
here it sends abundant waters along the roads of the world.  
Outside, it smiles with the bright metal of silver,  
and within it is renowned through the gift of spiritual grace.

The aforementioned Count Adulfus offered it to God  
as a memorial beside the blessed martyr Acisclus;  
he himself lies buried in the consecrated church where Córdoba stands.  
May the little servant, the patron’s now fortunate witness and fosterling [Note: *Faustus* (“fortunate”)],  
obtain that the great martyr deign to bestow so slight a gift,  
so that Christ, through his merits, may cleanse his sins  
and, once his soul has left its bodily prison,  
may gather it among the citizens of heaven in a blessed seat.

While you, reader, have gained these offered goods,  
I ask you, Adulfus, to incline yourself to God on my behalf.  
Now accept for safekeeping, child Fredenandus Kare,  
the book-chest which your own Adulfus himself adorned and completed,  
so that, when reading, you may reread it and preserve it with a pure heart.  
If you yourself willingly consent to his instructions,  
you will be able to ascend safely to the court of heaven.

### II. The Same Author’s [Epigram], at the Request of His Own Zoylus, for the Library [Note: By this word understand the place in which the books of the Old and New Testaments were kept—that is, the Bible], which he had written for Saturninus the archdeacon

I strive, grateful Zoylus, to pay you the vows of praise  
to Christ the Redeemer, the Creator, and my Lord,  
by whose help I have completed so great a labor.

When you have reached the end of this book-chest by reading,  
I earnestly ask you, attentive reader, to pray to God for me;  
thus may you safely enjoy Christ after this age has passed.

### III [Note: The title is absent from the manuscript]

[Col. 0567C]

Wipe away your grief, mourner; you see the green things brought forth,  
and the winged creatures chirp, their voices sounding in varied melody.  
And may the liquor of unmixed wine flow in the mouth of the intoxicated.

### IV. By the Same Cyprian as Above

[Col. 0568A]

The fan shines in the hand of the blessed count,  
inscribed in golden letters, as befits him—  
the count Guifredus, so named from the sacred font.

Count, gladly hand it over to your glorious wife,  
so that, with the breeze summoned by the fan, it may drive away the heat;  
in the same way may it disperse the heat weighing upon  
Guisinda, as she is called, and joined to your side.

### V. Another by the Same Author on the Fan

Adorn the right hand of the illustrious Guisindis, O fan;  
provide, though they are artificial, breezes to temper the heat,  
refreshing her limbs, relaxed in the summer season,  
and, spread out, fulfilling your service in every respect [Note: Manuscript: *imper* (“command”), rather than *imple* (“fulfill”).].

### VI. Epitaph Which He Composed in Heroic Meter for the Tomb of Lord Samson

[Col. 0568B]

Who, or how great, was the renowned abbot Samson,  
whose sacred limbs remain in this tomb in the church,  
while Hesperia, nourished by his utterance, resounds?

Bend God by your prayers, reader—now, I beseech you, bend  
heaven, so that he may ascend there with his sins cleansed.  
He departed, renowned and full of days,  
on the twenty-first day of the month of Sextilis.

On the twenty-first day of the month of Sextilis, under the sun.

Year 928 of the era.

### VII. Another Epitaph Composed by the Same Author

Here lies noble Hermildis, placed in this tomb,  
who, serving Christ and scorning the pomp of the world,  
ascended here, exulting and rejoicing, into the hall of the heroes.

### VIII. Epitaph over the Tomb of Saint John the Confessor

[Col. 0568C]

For love of Christ John endured prisons and grim iron chains; having completed his course,  
he rests in this hall.

## In the Year of Our Lord 870. Bernard, a Frankish Monk

[Col. 0569]

## Bernard’s Itinerary

Composed concerning the holy places in the year 870.

(Printed by Mabillon, *Acta sanctorum ordinis S. Benedicti*, vol. IV, from a manuscript in the library of Saint Remigius at Rheims.)

### 1

In the name of the Lord, for the purpose of visiting the places of the saints [supplied], I joined myself to two brothers in the devotion of charity. One was from the monastery of blessed Innocent of Benevento, the other was a Spaniard; France, however, is the place of my birth. Accordingly, when we reached the City, we obtained an audience with the lord pope Nicholas, together with his blessing and his assistance in carrying out the permission we desired.

### 2

From there we proceeded to Mount Gargano, where there is a church of Saint Michael beneath a single rock, above which stand oak trees bearing acorns; it is said that the saint himself dedicated it. Its entrance is on the north, and it can accommodate fifty people. Within, toward the east, it has an image of the angel; toward the south there is an altar, upon which the sacrifice is offered, and besides this no other offering is placed there. Before the altar hangs a certain vessel into which gifts are put. There are also other altars beside it. The abbot of this place was called Benignatus, and he presided over many brothers.

### 3

Leaving Mount Gargano, we traveled one hundred and fifty miles to the city of Bari, belonging to the Saracens, which formerly lay under the rule of the Beneventans. The city, situated above the sea, is fortified on the south by two very broad walls; on the north it projects toward and is exposed to the sea. There we approached the city’s ruler, named Suldanus, and obtained from him, with two letters, everything required for the voyage. The text of the letters explained to the rulers of Alexandria and Babylon the appearance of our faces and the purpose of our journey [Col. 0569C]. These rulers are under the authority of Amarmominus, who rules all the Saracens and lives in Baghdad and Axiam, which lie beyond Jerusalem.

### 4

Leaving Bari, we traveled southward for ninety miles to the harbor of the city of Taranto. There we found six ships containing nine thousand Christian captives from Benevento. Of the two ships that first departed for Africa, three thousand captives were aboard; the other two, leaving first, likewise carried three thousand to Tripoli.

### 5

Finally, boarding the remaining two ships, which also contained the number of captives mentioned above, we were carried to the harbor of Alexandria, sailing for thirty days. When we wished to go ashore, we were prevented by the captain of the sailors, who was in charge of more than sixty men. In order that permission might be given us to disembark, we gave him six gold pieces.

### 6

From there we proceeded to the ruler of Alexandria, to whom we showed the letter Suldanus had given us. It did us no good, although he said that he was familiar with all Suldanus’s letters. Under pressure from him, each of us paid thirteen denarii for himself, and he wrote letters for us to the ruler of Babylon.

Moreover, the custom of those people is that whatever can be weighed is accepted only by weight. Hence it happened that six solidi and six denarii among us amount among them to three solidi and three denarii.

Alexandria lies beside the sea. Saint Mark preached the Gospel there and exercised pontifical office. Outside its eastern gate is the monastery of that saint, in which monks live beside the church where he first rested. Later, Venetians came by ship, secretly took his body from its guardian, and carried it away to their island. Outside the western gate is the monastery called of the Forty Saints, where monks likewise live. To the north is the city’s harbor; to the south is the entrance of the Geon, or Nile, which waters Egypt and runs through the middle of the city, entering the sea at the aforementioned harbor.

### 7

Entering this river, we sailed southward for six days and came to the city of Babylon, where Pharaoh the king reigned, under whom Joseph built the sixteen granaries that still remain. When we disembarked at Babylon, the city’s guards led us to its ruler, a Saracen called Adelhacham. He questioned us about the whole business of our journey and about the letters we possessed for the rulers. For this reason we showed him the letter from the ruler of Alexandria, but it did us no good. Instead, we were sent by him to prison, until, after six days, when a council had been held with God’s help, each of us paid thirteen denarii for himself, as above.

He also wrote letters for us. Whoever saw them, in whatever city or place, thereafter dared demand nothing from us. For he was second in authority to the aforementioned Amarmominus.

After we entered the cities named below, we were not permitted to leave until we received a document or the impression of a seal, which we obtained for one or two denarii.

The patriarch lord Michael is in this city. By God’s grace he governs the whole of Egypt, arranging the order of all the bishops, monks, and Christians. These Christians have the following law among the pagans: each year, according to the means of his person, each must pay tribute to the aforementioned ruler, so that he may live safely and freely. This tribute is three, two, or one gold piece; from a poorer person he exacts thirteen denarii. If someone is unable to pay these thirteen denarii, whether he is a resident or a Christian stranger, he is sent to prison until he is either freed by God’s mercy through his angel or redeemed by other good Christians.

### 8

By way of the river Geon [manuscript: “Through the river”], we reached the city of Sitimulh. From Sitimulh we proceeded to Mohalla; from Mohalla we crossed over to Damietta, which has, on the northern sea, the city of Tanis. There are many Christians there, who are either religious persons or especially fervent in hospitality.

This city has no land except where the churches stand and where the field of Tanis is shown. In that field lie, in the likeness of three walls, the bodies of those who were destroyed in the time of Moses.

### 9

In the city of Faramea there is a church in honor of Saint Mary, at the place to which Joseph fled with the child and his mother when warned by the angel. That city has a multitude of camels, which resident owners lease to travelers for a price, so that they may carry their loads through the desert, whose journey takes six days.

The entrance to this desert begins at the city mentioned above. It is rightly called a desert, since it produces neither grass nor the fruit of any seed, except palm trees; it lies barren like Campania in the season of snow. Halfway along the route it has two hostels, one called Albara and the other Albacara, where Christians and pagans conduct the sorts of business necessary for travelers [Col. 0571D]. In their surroundings the earth produces nothing beyond what has been mentioned.

At Albacara the land becomes fertile, continuing to the city of Gaza, which was Samson’s city and was then the richest of all in every kind of possession [manuscript: *tumis*].

### 10

Then they came to Alarixa; from Alarixa to Ramla, near which is the monastery of blessed George the martyr, where he himself rests. From Ramla they went to the fortress of Emmaus; from Emmaus to the holy city of Jerusalem.

There is a hospice there in which all who visit that place out of devotion are received, provided they speak the Roman language. Beside it is a church in honor of Saint Mary, possessing a most distinguished library, established through the zeal of the aforementioned emperor [Note: That is, Charlemagne], together with twelve dwellings, fields, vineyards, and a garden in the Valley of Jehoshaphat.

Before the hospice is a marketplace, for which each person conducting business there pays two gold pieces annually to the one who maintains it.

Within this city, apart from the other churches, four prominent churches are joined to one another by shared walls. One is toward the east; it contains Mount Calvary and the place where the Lord’s cross was found, and is called Constantine’s basilica. Another is toward the south. The third is toward the west; at its center is the Lord’s tomb. It has nine columns around it, between which stand walls made of the finest stones. Of these nine columns, four stand before the face of the monument; together with their walls they enclose the stone placed before the tomb, which the angel rolled away and upon which he sat after the Lord’s resurrection.

It is unnecessary to write more about this tomb, since Bede is said to give sufficient information in his *History of the English*, which we too can report. This, however, must be said: on Holy Saturday, which is the vigil of Easter, the office begins in the church in the morning. When the office has been completed, *Kyrie eleison* is sung until, when the angel comes, a light is kindled in the lamps hanging above the aforementioned tomb. From this light the patriarch gives to the bishops and the rest of the people, so that each may illuminate his own place.

This patriarch was called Theodosius [supplied “was called”]. Because of his devotional merit, Christians brought him from his monastery, which lies fifteen miles from Jerusalem, and established him there as patriarch over all the Christians who are in the Promised Land.

Between the four churches mentioned above is a roofless Paradise—commonly called *le parvis*—whose walls shine with gold. Its pavement is laid with the most precious stone. At its center is the meeting-point of four chains, which come from the four churches mentioned above; in this center, it is said, is the middle of the world.

### 11

There is also, in the city itself, another church to the south on Mount Zion, called Saint Simeon’s. There the Lord washed his disciples’ feet, and the Lord’s crown of thorns hangs in it. In this church Saint Mary is said to have died.

Near it, toward the east, is a church in honor of Saint Stephen, at the place where he is said to have been stoned. Directly eastward is a church in honor of blessed Peter, at the place where he denied the Lord. To the north is Solomon’s Temple, containing a Saracen synagogue. To the south are iron gates through which the angel of the Lord led Peter out of prison; afterward they were not opened.

### 12

From Jerusalem it is one mile to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. It contains the village of Gethsemane and the place of Saint Mary’s birth, where there is a very large church in her honor. In the same village is a round church of Saint Mary, where her tomb is located. It has no roof above it and does not admit rain [Col. 0573A].

At that place there is also a church where the Lord was betrayed. It has four round tables belonging to his Supper. In the Valley of Jehoshaphat there is likewise a church in honor of Saint Leo, where the Lord is said to be coming for judgment.

### 13

From there they came to the Mount of Olives, on whose slope the place where the Lord prayed to the Father is shown. On the side of that mountain the place is shown where the Pharisees brought to the Lord the woman caught in adultery. There is a church in honor of Saint John, in which is preserved writing on a marble stone that the Lord wrote on the ground.

### 14

At the summit of the frequently mentioned mountain, one mile from the Valley of Jehoshaphat, is the place of the Lord’s ascension to the Father. There is a round church without a roof. In its center—that is, at the place of the Lord’s ascension—there is an altar open to the sky, on which the solemn Masses are celebrated.

### 15

From there they went to Bethany, which lies to the south, one mile from the Mount of Olives, on the descent of that mountain. There is a monastery whose church displays Lazarus’s tomb. Beside it, to the north, is a pool in which Lazarus himself, after being raised, washed at the Lord’s command. He is said afterward to have been bishop at Ephesus for forty years.

On the descent from the Mount of Olives toward the west, a marble is shown from which the Lord descended upon the foal of a donkey. Between these places, in the Valley of Jehoshaphat to the south, is the pool of Siloam.

### 16

From there they crossed into Bethlehem, where the Lord was born, six miles away. They were shown the field in which Habakkuk was working when the angel of the Lord commanded him to carry a meal to Daniel in Babylon, which lies to the south. Nebuchadnezzar reigned there; now serpents and beasts inhabit it.

Bethlehem has a very large church in honor of Saint Mary. In its center is a written inscription beneath a single stone. Its entrance is to the south and its exit to the east; the Lord’s manger is shown to the west of the inscription. The place where the Lord cried as an infant is to the east. There is an altar there on which Masses are celebrated.

Beside this church, to the south, is the church of the blessed martyrs, the Innocents. One mile from Bethlehem is the monastery of the holy shepherds, to whom the angel of the Lord appeared at the Lord’s birth.

Finally, thirty miles east of Jerusalem is the Jordan, over which stands the monastery of Saint John the Baptist. Many monasteries are situated in these places as well.

One mile west of the city of Jerusalem is the church of Saint Mamilla, in which many bodies of martyrs are buried. They were killed by the Saracens and carefully buried there by her.

### 17

From Jerusalem they entered the sea and came to the Golden Mount, where there is a crypt containing seven altars. A great forest also stands above it. Because of the darkness, no one can enter the crypt unless lamps have been lit. Lord Valentinus was abbot there.

### 18

From the Golden Mount they reached Rome. Within that city, on the eastern side, in the place called the Lateran, is a well-built church in honor of Saint John the Baptist, where the proper seat of the apostles is [read: “the apostolic seat”].

On the western side is the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, where he himself rests. No church throughout the whole earth is comparable to it in size; it also contains various ornaments. In that city innumerable bodies of saints likewise rest.

From there they came to Saint Michael at the Two Tombs. This place lies on a mountain that extends two leagues into the sea. At the summit of this mountain is a church in honor of Saint Michael. Around the mountain the sea rises twice every day, namely in the morning and evening, and people cannot approach the mountain until the sea has withdrawn.

On the feast of Saint Michael, however, the sea does not join together as it rises around the mountain; instead it stands like walls on the right and left. On that solemn day all who come to pray may approach the mountain at every hour, which they cannot do on other days.

## In the Year of Our Lord 870. Wandalbert, Monk of Prüm

[Col. 0573]

## Historical Notice on Wandalbert

(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*.)

[Col. 0573D]

Wandalbert, deacon and monk of the monastery of Prüm, lived around the year 850. He wrote a *Martyrology* in verse, which was formerly attributed to Bede. Philip Labbe promised a new edition in *Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum*, p. 64; Lucas Dacherius published the complete work in *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 39. In vol. V, p. 305, of the old edition, at the end of p. 62, there is added a poem on the Creation of the World, which was missing from the earlier edition of the *Spicilegium*. See also Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 316; Bulaeus, *History of the University of Paris*, vol. I, p. 447; Bollandus in the general preface to the *Acta Sanctorum*, before vol. I of January, p. 51; Baronius, *On Martyrologies*, ch. 9; and Sollerius, preface to Usuard’s *Martyrology*, ch. 1, article 3.

He composed the Life and Miracles of Saint Goar the priest at the command of Marcwardus, his abbot, around the year 939; it was published by Surius on 6 July and by Mabillon in the second Benedictine century, p. 281. Joan Pinius published only the miracles, omitting the Life, in the *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. II of July, p. 337. See Oudinus, vol. II, p. 149, and *History of Literature of France*, vol. V, p. 377.

It would be regrettable to pass over the fact that the *Martyrology of Wandalbert* published by Dacherius is interpolated—if anything ever was. It is read more completely and purely in the manuscript codex of the Library of the Canons of Saint Martin of Lucca. I consider it useful to give here one example, among many, of this interpolation, taken from the month of January. The Dacherius codex reads:

> Then on the day before the Nones, the feast of Augentus returns.

The cathedral codex reads:

> Then on the day before the Nones, the feast of Aggeus returns.

Wandalbert certainly wrote this, since the name of a certain martyr Aggeus occurs on this very day in the ancient Hieronymian martyrologies. Thus, after removing this lesser-known martyr, the interpolator substituted another, perhaps more celebrated, Augentus or Augendus—unless you would rather suppose that this fault belongs not to an interpolator but to an ignorant copyist.

As I recall these matters, the thought occurs to me whether I would be doing something worthwhile if I undertook a new edition of this *Martyrology*. I shall do so at the appropriate time, when a new edition of the *Martyrology* printed by my countryman Florentinus, fully revised by me and illuminated with new additions, has been brought to light.

## The Martyrology of Wandalbert, Monk of Prüm

(Printed by Acherius in vol. II of the *Spicilegium*.)

[Col. 0575]

## Notice

[Col. 0575B]

The most learned Bigotius copied the *Martyrology of Wandalbert* in his own hand when he visited the Netherlands, from a manuscript belonging to Isaac Vossius, a man of singular courtesy and distinguished by refined learning and knowledge of many things.

The Basle editors falsely attributed Wandalbert’s *Martyrology* to Venerable Bede, adding it to his *Ephemerides* in 1563. Later Molanus inserted it, distributed by days, into Usuard’s *Martyrology*, printed at Cologne in 1568, after removing several verses. Now it is brought to light restored to its complete form, its proper author, and its original purity, together with prefaces composed in both prose and verse, and with the materials that follow the *Martyrology*. Vossius himself copied these and sent them to the aforementioned Bigotius when I was bringing volume V of the *Spicilegium* to completion.

Of Wandalbert, Sigebert says briefly in chapter 128 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Wandalbert wrote a *Martyrology* in metrical style.” Trithemius, however, says more in chapter 36 of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*:

> Wandalbert, deacon and monk of the monastery of Prüm in the diocese of Trier, a German by birth, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and highly skilled in secular letters, an eminent rhetorician and poet, distinguished and polished in speech, and so forth. He also wrote metrically one book of the *Martyrology of the whole year*, as well as several other works that have not come to my notice. He flourished under the emperor Lothair, in the year of the Lord 854.

Miraeus repeats the words of Trithemius in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 316, under the year 840.

In his *Commendation to Caesar*, where Wandalbert praises Lothair, he rather clearly indicates the year in which he composed the *Martyrology*, especially in these verses:

> Five periods of five years  
> have passed around the world  
> since, renowned in name  
> and in arms,  
> you have held  
> the imperial rights.

Either Wandalbert counts the beginning of Lothair’s reign from the time when Louis the Pious wished his son crowned emperor in the year 817, or from the time when Lothair was inaugurated at Rome by Pope Paschal in the year 823. If from the earlier date, add five periods of five years, or twenty-five years, and you arrive at the year 842 of salvation; if from the later date, at 848.

He testifies in the Conclusion that he completed his *Martyrology* when he was in the thirty-fifth year of his life:

> Behold, through three decades  
> I have led my wretched life;  
> and, in addition, the fifth year  
> of life’s course comes and moves onward.

Molanus, in his preface to Usuard’s *Martyrology*, chapter 5, openly admits that Wandalbert borrowed his *Martyrology* from Bede’s *Ephemerides*. He then adds:

> In a catalogue of various libraries, written before the year 80 or thereabouts and kept at Louvain, I searched for manuscript copies of Wandalbert, but only one was listed, in the library of the Regular Canons of Louvain at Saint Martin’s Valley; yet it is not there now, however that may have happened. Therefore, candid reader, kindly make allowances for the fact that Wandalbert is being published without sufficient correction.

Finally, Florus, whom Wandalbert greatly praises in his preface, is not the martyrologist mentioned by Usuard, Ado, and others, but one younger than Wandalbert—namely, that vigorous defender, under Charles the Bald, of the Church of Lyons, of grace in Christ, and of free will. See Miraeus above, under Sigebert’s chapter 92.

Thus far we have copied Acherius, who, as usual, discusses Wandalbert’s *Martyrology* learnedly. We shall now mention the matters of which it is necessary to inform the reader.

First, we have appended the poem on the *Hexaemeron*, which Wandalbert himself says he added to his *Martyrology*. Since it was absent from the Bigotius codex used by Acherius, that diligent scholar later obtained another codex, from which the Reverend Father Edmundus Martene copied it and most courteously communicated it to us.

[Col. 0576D]

This was not the only benefit of the Bigotius codex; indeed, it was perhaps the least. With its help we corrected nearly infinite passages and restored not a few missing verses, just as from the very ancient royal codex with which Stephen Baluzius compared the earlier edition in the year 1676, as he himself notes.

Among these verses Baluzius found many names of saints copied by I know not whose hand. We judged that they ought to be published, since this diligence of ours could be useful for other purposes as well as for understanding Wandalbert and, sometimes, correcting him.

Among those names of saints, the copyist wished especially to note Saint Martial and Saint Leonard. He wrote the latter’s name in large letters and added to the former the title “most blessed.” From this I infer that the codex was brought to Rome from the province of Limoges.

## Author’s Preface

[Col. 0577A]

### Wandalbert Sends Greetings to Lord Otricus

An ancient and very old precept instructs us to strive to obey our elders, to accommodate our equals, and to advise our juniors. Since I cannot advise you [Note: The final little word, *tibi* (“you”), is added from the Bigotius codex. From the same codex comes *non valeo* (“I am unable”), where the earlier reading was *non video* (“I do not see”).], dearest, as a junior—something I judge sacrilegious even to contemplate—for I perceive that in you yourself, as befits a truly wise man, there is every counsel of assistance and the full abundance of prudence; nor can I accommodate you as an equal, because of the slowness of my sense and intellect; it is therefore clear that, as an elder, I desire with all my strength and every capacity to obey and serve you.

This is especially so because I understand that, after I began not so much to be exiled from my homeland and domestic affairs as to live far from them, I have been supported by your aid, advice, foresight, and generosity through your unceasing and indefatigable zeal and benevolence. Nor do I offend lightly if, when I cannot accommodate you, I refuse to obey according to the poverty of my intellect.

Accordingly, what you unexpectedly and insistently requested of me, with unavoidable and constant authority—that I should arrange in verse, for the whole span of the year, the festivals of the saints occurring on each day and the solemn celebrations of Christian vows from every place—I have done as I was able, relying not so much on artistic practice and skill [Col. 0577C] as on your devotion and, as I trust, on the undeserved favor of the saints who assisted me in completing it.

In this work, because the most certain enumeration of the solemn days was not easily or lightly established, owing to the variety of books, I made particular use of the help and assistance of the holy and famous man Florus, subdeacon of the Church of Lyons. Just as in our time he is distinguished by singular zeal and perseverance in knowledge of divine Scripture, so he is recognized as possessing no small abundance and variety of authoritative books [Note: “Abundance and variety.” We preferred this reading to the earlier edition’s “abundance and truth.” Not far below, the Bigotius codex adds *et addita post* (“and added afterward”); the printed editions incorrectly read *et edita post* (“and published afterward”). Immediately afterward we altered the construction in those words somewhat on our own authority: previously it read *distinctione ... usus Gallicos* (“by a division ... Gallic usages”); we now read *distinctionem ... usus Gallici* (“a division ... according to the arrangement of Gallic usage”).].

Taking old and corrected codices from him, I published in verse a martyrological book extending from the Kalends of January to the end of the year, with the festivals occurring on each individual day. As I judged appropriate, I prefixed an Invocation to God, an Address to all who might happen to be readers, a commendation to you, the encourager of the work, and an address to the most gracious Caesar Lothair, together with a description of the subject or proposition in a different meter.

After publishing the *Martyrology*, I added a Conclusion and a hymn to all the saints. To this work I also appended a clear and brief division of the individual months according to Gallic usage, as well as the ordinary measurement of the hours of daylight in our regions. I thought that neither of these differed at all from the preceding work.

Finally, at the end of the whole work, I added a short poem on the Creation of the World arranged according to the six days [Note: “On the Creation of the World.” This poem, which was missing from the earlier edition, was communicated by the Reverend Father Edmundus Martene; we shall publish it in its proper place], and appended an explanation of the mystical meaning understood in the human being, so that the explanation, repeated from the beginning of the world’s creation, might commend what I had described concerning the course of the whole year.

This work, since it consists of verses composed in various metres, I considered it necessary briefly to explain the kinds of metre themselves, so that I might make clear to all who will deign to read it not only the work itself but also the metres by which it has been arranged. Thus the Invocation, which I placed at the beginning of the whole little work because every form of knowledge, proceeding from God, ought rightly to be requested from him—for although others may wish the Proposition to be first in a poetic work—runs in choriambic, tetrameter, acatalectic Asclepiadics. The Asclepiad is named either after Aesculapius, who in Greek is called Asclepius, the discoverer of medicine, whose praises were frequently composed in this kind of metre, or after a poet of the same name. For metres are often named after their inventors, sometimes after those who frequently use them, and occasionally after those whose memories they celebrate. An acatalectic verse is one from which no syllable is lacking for its full measure, but which is concluded at the proper numerical ending. A tetrameter poem, moreover, is one that proceeds on four feet; this is understood in choriambic, dactylic, and anapaestic metres, in which we count dimeter, trimeter, tetrameter, pentameter, and hexameter by single feet. In iambic and trochaic metres, however, since they are shorter, we count the aforesaid numbers by double feet. Choriambic is so called from the choriambic foot, in which it properly proceeds. It consists of a spondee in the first foot, a choriambus in the second and third, and a pyrrhichius in the fourth. Since the choriambus has long syllables first and last and two short syllables in the middle, which together complete six morae, if we join the spondee to the pyrrhichius, we produce the same number of syllables and the same number of morae; and therefore this metre proceeds not so much through the pyrrhichius and spondee as properly through the choriambus. The Invocation, therefore, composed in this metre, consists of forty-four verses, which, joining together in groups of four, produce eleven longer verses.

The Address, which admonishes and invites those who will read, proceeds in dactylic tetrameter catalectic, named from its more frequent foot, from the number of its four feet, and from the one syllable lacking for the completion of its metrical number. For it consists of a spondee, a dactyl, a catalectic foot, then a dactyl and a spondee. Since this metre properly consists of dactyls, if the catalectic foot is added to the spondee, there will be, in terms of syllables, three dactyls and one spondee, and it will seem that only one syllable is lacking from the full number of dactylic syllables. In terms of morae, however, the dactyl, which consists of one long and two short syllables, is equal and equivalent to the spondee, which has two long syllables. Thus the Address, proceeding in the aforesaid feet, contains sixty-eight little verses, which, joined together in groups of four like the preceding ones, produce seventeen longer verses.

The Commendation, moreover, consists of Phaleucian pentameter hendecasyllables. It is called hendecasyllabic in Greek from the number eleven, Phaleucian from its inventor or frequent user, and pentameter from its number of feet. It proceeds with a spondee in the first foot, a dactyl in the second, and trochees in the third, fourth, and fifth; although the final syllable is accepted indifferently in all metres, and a trochee frequently passes into a spondee, a spondee into a trochee, an iambus into a pyrrhichius, and a pyrrhichius into an iambus through their final syllables. The first part of the Commendation, therefore, composed in this metre, is filled out by thirty-six verses, which are likewise known, through their grouping by fours, to complete nine longer verses. The latter part of the Commendation, addressed to the Caesar, consists of dactylic dimeter acatalectics, proceeding only through dactyls and spondees and requiring no syllable for completion. This part contains forty-two little verses, which, joined together six at a time, form seven verses through the larger conjunction.

The remaining work, up to the completed Martyrology, proceeds in heroic verse, which is so called from its frequent use in celebrating the deeds of brave men, and consists of six metrical feet. In this metre, apart from the last position, which admits only a spondee or trochee, and the penultimate position, which is filled only by a dactyl, the other positions freely admit either a dactyl or a spondee. From the beginning of the Proposition up to the completed Martyrology, this work contains nine hundred and forty heroic verses.

Next follows the Conclusion, belonging to the completion of the Martyrology, woven from mixed choriambic metres—that is, glyconics, Asclepiadics, and Alcaics. These metres are named after their authors or frequent users, Glycon, Asclepius, and Alcaeus. The glyconic proceeds through a spondee, a choriambus, and a pyrrhichius; the Asclepiad through a spondee, two choriambi, and a pyrrhichius; and the Alcaic through a spondee, three choriambi, and a pyrrhichius. The same Conclusion, containing twenty-four little verses through the aforesaid combination of metres, produces eight longer verses by joining them three at a time. This is followed by a hymn to all the saints, which consists of dactylic Sapphic pentameter. It is named after the woman called Sappho, who discovered this kind of metre; it proceeds through five feet—namely, a trochee, a spondee, a dactyl, and two trochees. After every three verses a heroic comma is added, consisting of a dactyl and a spondee. Thus three equal verses and a heroic member are produced in a different arrangement; this combination in the hymn mentioned above produces eight longer verses and twenty-four shorter ones, while also adding eight commas. These, as I said above, belong to the conclusion and completion of the preceding Martyrology.

Then follows a description of the twelve months, which displays the etymologies of their names, the names of the signs and stars, and the numbers and uses of time within the signs. Attached to this description is a measurement of the hours throughout all the months. The work is completed in four hundred and fifty heroic verses.

At the end of the whole little book there remains a brief and clear description of the creation of the world, with an addition concerning the mystical meaning to be understood in humanity from the creation of things. This description consists of Pherecratian metre, named after Pherecrates, its inventor or frequent user, and woven from a spondee, a dactyl, and a spondee, although, according to the nature of the final syllable, the last spondee frequently changes into a trochee. In this description, by joining three verses into one, two hundred and eighty-five shorter verses and ninety-eight longer verses are produced. Thus throughout this whole work there are, in verses of different metres and various measures, from the Invocation to God up to the account of the creation of the world, one thousand nine hundred and nineteen verses. I have brought these matters together in this way so that nothing here may remain unknown or doubtful to you, dearest friend, to whom the task of the entire little work, such as it is, will be assigned. Farewell.

[Col. 0579]

## TEXT OF THE FOLLOWING METRICAL WORK

## INVOCATION

[Note: Choriambic metre, tetrameter, Asclepiadic.]

[Note: “Making all things on high.” The Bigot manuscript has *celsi cuncte parens* (“parent of all things on high”); I do not hesitate to think that *celsi sancte parens* (“holy parent on high”) ought to be read. In verse 7, *lotaque sanguine* is the excellent reading of the Bigot manuscript; the reading of the earlier edition, *totaque sanguine*, is extremely poor.]

Making all things on high, creator of heaven,  
Beginning of the universe, giver of light,  
And nourisher, unfailing source of goodness:  
Hear what I, your little servant, ask and implore,  
You, head and glory of the radiant people,  
Which follows the Lamb, gleaming and clothed in white garments,  
And, washed in blood, is pleasing, purchased and given from all nations.  
The harmonious Church worships him on earth and proclaims him to all,  
Accumulating the best joys in its prayers,  
And soon joins its songs to the festive company of singers.  
Now, through the annual courses  
By which the days may stand out and return,  
I shall briefly set forth in trusted song,  
Gathering together the ranks and battles of the brave,  
For whose merits, Christ God,  
Grant me here pardon for all my sins.  
Bring aid to your servant, and let the hand sent down from above  
Now call back the blind man from the darkness;  
For, Ruler, nothing resists your power,  
No force is hard for your command.  
You can conquer with mighty weapons,  
Lest the deceitful wickedness of the Devil prevail,  
And so at last, through every crime,  
Every evil and every disgrace,  
It may wretchedly make its way to the lowest Tartarus;  
And let it delight me to live according to your laws.

[Note: “Nothing remains of hope.” Thus the Bigot manuscript correctly reads *spei nil superest*; the earlier edition has corruptly *spei vis sup.* Above, *regem praesidiis*; perhaps *regens* should be read, but even so the sense is not sufficiently clear.]

Happy is the everlasting life that abides among the inhabitants of heaven,  
Among whom the phrase *regem praesidiis* is unclear,  
When you, the highest good, abide with the godly,  
Whom love, thirsting for you, continually fills.

[Note: Dactylic metre, tetrameter catalectic.]

Nothing remains of hope for my forgiveness,  
Nor any better support of life, unless  
You raise me up, pressed down, sick and anxious,  
As I fall, succumbing to the depths of death.

Now, this offering of a very small work,  
Among the number of the saints, I offer to you,  
Ruler, and I ask that what I bring forth in your name  
May be pleasing, though in a barren song.  
Here let my humble mind sound a hymn to you,  
And let a devoted man sing of you in melody,  
To whom the shining host proclaims throughout the ages  
One glory with the Father.

## ADDRESS

[Note: “Whom he gathered into one.” In the printed editions, *in unum* (“into one [masculine]”) is incorrect; in the Bigot manuscript, *in unam* (“into one [feminine]”) is correct.]

You who desire to behold Christ and resolve  
To fix your mind in the high heaven,  
Seeing the sure signs of blessed hope,  
Follow here the deeds of great fathers.

They, often accustomed to behold God,  
Outstanding in wealth and strong in body,  
Supported by the offspring of a worthy line,  
Illumine the ages with holy merits.

They, freely abandoning their riches  
And despising all possessions in the green season of life,  
Beholding the realms above,  
Displayed hidden things to their own people through signs.

They, filled with life-giving speech  
And moved by heavenly visions and admonitions,  
Taught by their voices and various portents  
The Lord who was to come.

When he became man and came to save  
The lost world, he sent them,  
Instructed by word and hand, among every people,  
So that they might properly accomplish the salvation of the world.

True love of the King lifted them to the stars,  
Distinguished by the mark of martyrdom,  
Renowned by the flower of pious blood;  
Their triumphs now shine throughout the earth.

High learning and the glory of great merit  
Also adorn them: those who instructed the Church  
By word, by prayer,  
By signs, and by books.

They possess a particular splendour and honour,  
They who, strengthened by Christ’s snowy covering,  
With steadfast mind overcame the menacing and at once enticing love of the flesh.

They also possess everlasting fame,  
They who utterly trampled the experienced fire of the vigorous body by a celibate life  
And girded their loins with God’s covering.

Nor is the height of honour small for those women  
Who, preserving their marriage chambers,  
Properly adorned the shared bed with piety  
And freely dedicated their children to God.

Their fame through the ages surpasses the gaze of humankind: those who,  
Despising all the world, cultivated the desert,  
Are worthy to receive heavenly bread.

And their name shines, those whom sacred law  
Drew together into one mind,  
Who, bound by God’s law,  
Submitted necks and hands to the admonitions of the fathers.

Their piety shines no less with lofty merit—  
Those who gave their possessions to Christ  
And now, with distinguished courage, retain  
Everlasting treasures and the kingdoms of heaven.

Thus Christ calls us by many guiding standards;  
Thus the lights of the fathers shine  
Before the eyes of their lesser descendants.  
So numerous is the cause of blessed merit.

Nor shall it wrongly shame us to wish to follow them?  
The law and word of the gracious Father  
Will enable us to know what he wills, what he forbids, and what he commands;  
True faith, which purifies each person, will teach  
What the end will be, what rest of the blessed follows from this,  
And what return there may be.

[Note: “What return there may be.” This must certainly be read in this way; for the earlier edition’s *quive recursus* cannot be understood.]

Now this little book will recount the battles of the godly  
Through the course of the year,  
Showing them in a small body.  
If you, excellent reader, are willing to desire it,  
Make yourself willing to know it with a kindly mind.  
For no devout mind is guilty here  
Of anything that it has freely dedicated to Christ.

## COMMENDATION

[Note: Phaleucian metre, pentameter, hendecasyllabic.]

[Note: “Accept what is true.” We preferred this to the reading *vera summe* (“take the truth supremely”). Immediately afterward we wrote *hunc referans* from the Bigot manuscript, where the text had *hunc refonans*. Not far away, the same manuscript’s reading *de jusso inspicies* seemed more suitable than the earlier edition’s *de justo inspicies*.]

Accept this true book, consecrated in faith,  
Opening and reading it with a sincere mind.  
You, dear friend, command it to be written  
By your pious request and urging.

In this book you will see, briefly arranged for you,  
A work of knowledge, as you repeat and willingly undertake  
The task you have requested;  
At last you will look upon the labour that was commanded.

Once holy Jerome abandoned  
The quiet condition and manner of life  
And undertook, in Roman eloquence,  
To establish the books of the Old and New Law.

Augustine, your name, Father,  
Is borne throughout the world by the fame  
Of an everlasting age; you teach the Church of Christ  
And destroy and put to flight the whole crowd of errors.

Thus, martyr Cyprian, by doctrine  
And by pious blood, you proclaim Christ.  
Hilary shines with blessed mouth;  
Ambrose endures in his writings, and great Gregory  
Is powerful and shines by the praise of his words.  
Juvencus flies onward; Arator clings to him  
In joined passages; and Prudentius lives,  
Singing of God.

Thus honour recalls many whose fame  
Remains in their own writings and books,  
Which the world gladly reads and frequents,  
Although it sees that they have departed from here through death.

We possess only a small capacity for speaking  
And an inadequate talent for writing.  
The poverty of our speech denies us  
The place and rank of earlier poets.

Yet here we undertake to bring forth  
A new and pious song for God;  
And to you, friend, who ask it with a pious mind,  
We beg: favour our labour.

## TO THE CAESAR

And you, Caesar,  
Be present with favour,  
You who govern  
The sceptres of your fathers  
With piety  
And with benevolent law.

For God, ruler  
Of the world,  
Commanded you  
To bend the ancestral reins  
And the sceptres  
Of your father’s empire.

He himself once removed you  
From dangers prepared for you  
And often brought you back  
From the bloody slaughter  
Of raging men.

Golden Rome,  
Crowning you  
With a lofty name,  
Confirmed you  
As Caesar, soon  
To be king of the world.

Under your leadership  
Italy first  
Rose to prominence; afterward  
France next rose to prominence;  
The world adores you  
As you rule the sceptres.

Five periods have passed  
Throughout the world  
Since, illustrious in name  
And in arms,  
You have maintained  
The Caesarian laws.

May Christ govern you,  
Who behold long years;  
May everyone venerate you,  
And may the purple  
Both honour and tremble  
At you as king.

## PROPOSITION

I, who have often captured empty airs in song,  
Foolishly seeking the vain rumours of the crowd,  
Will at last undertake to seek true praise in song  
And to secure everlasting favour for myself,  
Briefly marking deeds, men, and days worthy to be seen,  
As they revolve in fixed return throughout the world,

[Note: “Revolving in fixed return.” The Bigot manuscript has *anni reditu* (“in the year’s return”). I read the following verse as it stands, in the order in which I believe each sun surveys the solemn observances.]

Writing in order which observances each one should survey?

Here and there the names of saints will exceed  
The limits of the song, but the constraint of naming them  
Must not be mutilated; through piety I shall earn  
The pardon of the good.

## ACCOUNT OF THE TIMES, MONTHS, DAYS, AND HOURS

Nature distinguished the world for suffering mortals  
Through various courses of things, under God’s governance,  
Constantly alternating night and day,  
Summer and winter, autumn and the warmth of spring,  
And the year divided at once into twelve months.

First, each period of the hours grows  
By its own appointed points; then twice twelve hours of time  
Complete the day with light and darkness from the beginning,  
When the shadows were dark.

Now the days and nights proceed in equal measure;  
Now, as the day hastens, night is stretched out  
On dark wings. At night, when it is short,  
The swift light again, on its tawny chariot,  
Carries the solar sphere to the highest axes.

[Note: “Now, as the day hastens.” We corrected this verse, formerly read as *nunc celebrante die f. vox tend. al.*, with the help of the Bigot manuscript, in which we also found *furvis*, where the printed edition had *furnis*.]

Hence a complete week embraces seven suns.  
Four weeks are said to roll around the ordinary month;  
But the months whose days the earlier authorities established  
Proceed in a different order and number.

June, April, September, and then November  
Consist of twice two weeks and two days.

The month of January, August, and December,  
March, October, May, and July, increased,  
Shine with four weeks and three days.

February alone, which Numa established as a month,  
Extends for only twice ten and eight days.

The four seasons that vary the solar year  
Are spring, summer, autumn, and winter:  
Flower, fruit, and honour play among the months,  
Moving in order through groups of three.

Nature gave these laws when the almighty Creator  
First formed the world and joined together  
The seeds of the earth in wondrous ways.

The learned fathers of old also observed these things  
And handed them down to their descendants,  
As the revolving year grew—  
Fifty-two weeks alike,  
And three hundred and sixty days each.

From this they established the Nones, Ides, and Kalends,  
So that the month, distinguished in varied order,  
Might properly lighten and soothe human labours,  
When festive leisure received the weary peoples  
And the people brought solemn gifts to the altars.

This the written account of the ancient law,  
Given through Moses, taught the people of Egypt  
Redeemed from death: it established Sabbaths,  
New moons, and the holy Passover,  
And appointed days of fasting to be observed  
At fixed times throughout the year,  
By an immutable law for ever,  
The people marked with the lamb’s symbolic blood.

He fed them with the lamb, unleavened bread,  
And wild lettuce.

All these feasts, which signified our salvation,  
Taught us that, redeemed through Christ’s death,  
We consecrate all our days to God under religion’s guidance.

Come, then, let us proclaim in song  
What solemn feasts the Kalends contain;  
What martyrs make the days illustrious throughout the world;  
Whom the holy praise and life of confessors crown;  
And what days and vows belong to virginal marriage chambers.  
Christ, fill the mind with piety.

[Col. 0585]

# HERE BEGINS THE MARTYROLOGY OF WANDALBERT

## JANUARY

### Day 1

Now let us sing what festivals January,  
Called by the name of Janus, brings,  
And whence its sacred name comes.

What the ancient fathers worshipped, and what the Law  
Established as a shadow of the future:  
Behold, the flesh of Christ, born of the holy Virgin,  
Circumcised, consecrates the Kalends of January.

And holy Basil shines with the honour of his merits.  
Euphrosyna likewise shines, and blessed Almachius.

### Day 2

Macarius dedicates the fourth day before the Nones,  
A holy inhabitant of the desert who preserved  
And taught the way of life there.

### Day 3

The third day before the Nones celebrates Genevieve.

### Day 4

Then, on the day before the Nones, the feast of Augentius returns.

### Day 5

Hence the holy confessor Simeon possesses the Nones;  
Pope Telesphorus likewise shines on that very day.

### Day 6

The holy Theophany is celebrated on the eighth day before the Ides.

### Day 7

The seventh day celebrates Christ returned from Egypt;  
The people of Antioch also commemorate their Lucian.

### Day 8

On the sixth day after the Ides, vows are offered to Eugenius.

### Day 9

On the fifth day, to Vitalis, Fortunatus, and Revocatus.

### Day 10

On the fourth day, Melchiades and Paul the hermit,  
Raised up through a blessed end, rejoice in the heavenly citadel.

### Day 11

Salvius consecrates the third Ides at Carthage.

### Day 12

The people of Italy commemorate their Cyriacus
