[Note: [Col. 0620D] “By divine gift.” We have followed the reading of the Royal manuscript; the earlier edition had “by divine will.”]

Then too the mother Felicitas, with her seven children,  
shines with a blessed triumph surpassing all.

Here too the contemptor of the world, Trudo, adorns his own people.

[Note: [Col. 0620D] “Here too his own.” This verse is absent both from the Royal and from the Bigot manuscript.]

## Day 24

Chrysogonus consecrates the eighth day by merits and death.

At Blavia, of Saint Romanus.

## Day 25

Bishop and martyr Peter beautifies the seventh day,  
under whose leadership the people of Alexandria, supported,  
scorn the crooked and blind paths of error.

## Day 26

On the sixth day the pope Linus is consecrated by rosy blood,  
and likewise Siricius and Cassianus.

## Day 27

Agricola and Vitalis honor the fifth day through martyrdom.

Of Severus and Beatus, bishops.

## Day 28

Silas, your companion, Paul, increases and adorns the fourth day.

Of Theophinus and Julius.

## Day 29

On the third day, Saturninus, we dedicate it to you, and to Maurus.

Likewise of Saturninus, Sisinnius, Chrysanthus, and Daria.

## Day 30

On the preceding day Andrew the apostle excels,  
shining throughout the world with broad rays and titles of virtue;  
by word and signs he subdued the unyielding Achaeans.

These vows of the peoples close November, the month of winter.

## DECEMBER

Let us call the final month of the year  
and report the festivals it celebrates in brief days.

## Day 1

Bishop Eligius marks December’s beginning for you,  
Noyon, in the first light, with fitting honor.

## Day 2

On the fourth day before the Nones, Verus and Securus shine through blood.

In Mauretania, of Saturninus, Fortunatus, and Maximus.

## Day 3

On the third day Africa makes offering to Cassianus the martyr.

In Africa, the feast of Saints John, Stephen, and Victor.

## Day 4

Then, on the preceding day, Heraclius excels together with Victorius.

In the metropolitan city of Laodicea, of Felix and Metrobius, and the translation of Saint Benedict the abbot.

## Day 5

Dalmatius the martyr and Crispina hold the Nones.

In Africa, the feast of Saints Candor, Privatus, Fulgentius, and Saint Amantius.

## Day 6

Bishop Nicholas adorns the eighth Ides.

In Africa, the feast of Saints Fortunatus, Hermogenes, and Rogatus.

## Day 7

Polycarpus holds the seventh day together with Theodore.

At Rome, the feast of Saint Eutychianus, bishop. And the octave of Saint Andrew the apostle.

## Day 8

Eutychianus, pope, you shine on the sixth day through blessed blood.

Zeno also holds this day with the honor of a joined martyrdom.

Of Eusebius, bishop; Uranius, bishop; and Successus, bishop.

## Day 9

On the fifth day we celebrate Sebastian, translated from the City,  
for whom the Gallic countryside rejoices in its own patron;  
a great temple and altar rise for him,  
whose heights shine and equal ancient splendor.

The virgin Leucadia also consecrates this day to herself through her merits.

In Alexandria, the feast of Donatus and Valentina.

## Day 10

On the fourth day we venerate Eulalia with holy love,  
whose blood and bones Spain at Mérida preserves.

And the feast of Saint Damasus, pope.

## Day 11

On the third day the solemnities of Damasus, the Roman pope, occur,  
and Victoricus and Fuscianus likewise possess  
the brightness of the festival and the vow;  
the fields of Amiens now grow green with their blood.

[Note: [Col. 0621D] “The Romans of Damasus.” Thus in the two Royal manuscripts and in Bigot; the earlier edition had “Rome offers sacrifice to Damasus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0621D] “Fuscianus.” In the Royal manuscript, *Faustianus*.]

At Rome, the feast of Saints Capitulinus and Praetextatus. In Spain, of Saint Euricus.

## Day 12

Hermogenes and Donatus shine twice on the tenth day,  
then on the preceding day, the two holy men joined by blood.

In the Spanish city of Mérida, the feast of Saint Hermogenes.

## Day 13

On the Ides Syracuse dedicated itself to you, Lucia,  
who endured the tyrant for Christ’s name;  
the Holy Spirit made you immovable before wicked men.

Judochus too is honored, an admirable priest,  
before whom the storms of the ocean often yield.

## Day 14

On the ninth day before the Kalends of January,  
the day customarily called the tenth, Bishop Nicasius increases its honor.

And Bishop Spiridion is celebrated on the same day.

At Lyon in Gaul, of Saint Viator, bishop.

## Day 15

Maximinus holds the eighteenth day,  
for whom the fertile fields of Orléans offer Bacchus.

## Day 16

On the seventeenth day the three boys are remembered,  
who despised the impious commands of the Assyrian tyrant,  
whom not even the crackling flame of the raging furnace  
could frighten from their faithful and steadfast spirit.

At the city of Orléans, of Saint Maximus, bishop.

## Day 17

Holy Ignatius triumphs on the sixteenth day,  
pastor of the city of Antioch and martyr,  
whose teeth of wild beasts made him living bread.

Rufus and Zosimus follow, having shed their blood for Christ.

And of Saint Valentinus.

## Day 18

On the fifteenth day, at last, the day blooms through the blood of Moysetes.

From here Capricorn carries Phoebus beneath a double constellation.

In Africa, the feast of Saints Victor, Honoratus, and Vincentius.

[Note: [Col. 0621D–0622D] “At last, the fifteenth day.” Since in the Royal manuscript the place of *demum*, which is entirely superfluous here, is occupied by *decimo*, I think the verse could be corrected as follows: “The fifth with the tenth,” or “with the tenth.” We have added the following verse from the Royal and Bigot manuscripts.]

## Day 19

On the fourteenth day Zosimus and Darius crown the calendar.

[Note: [Col. 0622D] “Durius also.” In the Royal manuscript, “Clarius also.”]

In the city of Nicaea in Bithynia, of Zosimus and Paul.

## Day 20

On the thirteenth day you shine, Bishop Zepherinus.

The feast of Saint Thecla.

## Day 21

The twelfth day celebrates the honor of Thomas translated;  
through him India, stirred by dreadful signs,  
deserved to know the golden glory of God the builder.

([Note: [Col. 0622D] At the solstice Phoebus here begins to return along the lofty axes, turning from here for the first time toward the cold Bear.])

## Day 22

Rome celebrates the eleventh day with the thirtieth martyr.

In Antioch, the feast of Saint Basil.

## Day 23

On the tenth day Victoria shines, the virgin of Christ.

At Rome, the feast of Saints Urban, Cornelius, and Victor.

## Day 24

On the ninth day, gathering gifts for the coming light,  
we prepare lamps, watchful altars, and temples.

On this day too forty virgins shine in heaven,  
who dedicated their lives to God by vow and virtue.

## Day 25

On the eighth day the Creator deigned to assume the form of a servant  
and came to call back wandering humanity;  
through a virgin birth he clothed himself in mortal limbs.

At that time we also remember Eugenia and Anastasia.

In Bethlehem, the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Accompanying Christ with a like mind and faith,

## Day 26

On the seventh day Stephen, the Levite and first martyr,  
excels—the blessed man who followed the newborn and suffering King,  
pursuing the Lord through a life of struggle and death.

## Day 27

The beloved of the Lord and observer of the divine Word,  
who deserved to drink from Christ’s breast  
the everlasting spring of Christ,  
consecrates and purifies the sixth day, John.

[Note: [Col. 0622D] “Divine.” In both manuscripts, “heavenly.”]

In Ephesus, the assumption of Saint John the evangelist.

## Day 28

We venerate on the fifth day the infants  
whom Herod’s cruel desire and thirst for kingship snatched from their mothers’ breasts,  
while he sought to destroy the Christ who had been born.

## Day 29

The prophet, pious king, and origin of the divine line,  
David marks the fourth day by speech and faith.

And the city of Arles, rejoicing in Trophimus as its shepherd, shines.

In Africa, the feast of Saints Saturninus, Honoratus, and Felix.

## Day 30

Mansuetus and Florentius adorn the third day together.

[Note: [Col. 0623D] “Adorn.” Both manuscripts have *aurant*.]

And the feast of Serenus.

## Day 31

On the preceding day Sylvester, pope, throughout the city of Rome  
subdues rejoicing peoples to himself with friendly prayers.

He was the first of the bishops to deserve to see peaceful times  
and to cleanse the rulers of the world in the laver.

At the same time, virgin Columba, accompanying Christ  
with blood poured out, receives the everlasting palm through courage.

Together with Potentianus, Sabinianus appears on the same festival,  
equal in altar and triumph;  
they were the first to teach the city of Sens its patrons.

These festivals at last close December, the final month.

## CONCLUSION

[Note: Choriambic meter; glyconic, asclepiad, and alcaic forms.]

Now, Christ, God, by your gift  
I have briefly written these songs,  
which steadfast faith sought with watchful devotion.

In them, arranged together, shine  
the hosts of the heavenly homeland and its warfare,  
which radiate in the highest heaven of perpetual light.

For these I, unworthy, ask you  
to grant pardon for my sins;  
for I am heavily oppressed by fear of everlasting punishment.

Behold, for three decades  
I have lived in misery; and now a fifth  
of the world’s course is present and passes through its paths.

Now, remembering no good  
that I have done, nor anything pious,  
I am greatly shaken; dreadful anxieties spur  
the innermost places of my mind.

Raise me up, now fallen, Father,  
and at last strip me of my past filth;  
my conscience is squalid, and my mind trembles  
with excessive anguish.

Here I have sung of the struggles of the saints  
and set before my eyes the glorious standards of the martyrs,  
the signs of those who triumph.

Their blood glorifies you, Father;  
their pious death continually speaks of you.  
For they live through your protection  
and forever in your light.

[Note: [Col. 0624D] Dactylic, Sapphic, and pentameter meters.]

## HYMN TO ALL THE SAINTS

Christ, whom the choir of heaven  
sings as it makes melody, praises, thirsts for, and desires,  
we ask you, looking favorably upon us,  
to behold the harmonious praises of your servants.

The heavenly choirs celebrate you as King,  
and the companies of the righteous resound your praise;  
the lofty palace of heaven, which retains them,  
shines and cherishes them.

The venerable blessed company  
of the patriarchs, continually praising you together,  
always receives, thirsting for life,  
the gifts of everlasting life.

The spirits of the speaking prophets  
resound you; the ministers sent throughout the world  
also proclaim you, servants of the Word,  
with voice and hand.

The blood of the martyrs, triumphing together  
with the voice of the priests, thunders;  
chaste virgins and widows join  
melodious drums and sistrums.

Every order, shining at the summit  
of the heavenly axis, points out and teaches  
the Lord, you;  
we sing you, his servants, with faithful devotion of heart.

Freely, we ask you: release our guilt.  
Breathe upon your servants,  
and by your gracious gift complete  
the pure and devout praise of our minds.

Let an exultant voice return everlasting  
glory to you, Father and Son,  
and to the Spirit, with whom, graciously equal  
in the kingdom, you live forever.

## HERE BEGINS THE ACCOUNT OF THE NAMES OF THE TWELVE MONTHS, THEIR SIGNS, AND THE QUALITIES OF THE AIR

We shall briefly set forth in order, reader,  
what is the origin of the system of the names of the months,  
which roll the great year twice through six constellations;  
what signs likewise illuminate the twelve Kalends;  
what the division of the months, joined to the earth, brings forth;  
what uses their cultivation generates,  
and what forms of possession it shapes.

## JANUARY

The month which Julius decreed should be preserved as the first of the year  
is called by the name of the king Janus,  
who ruled the race of Saturn in Latium  
and enlarged the city of Laurentum with scepters, people, and laws.

The constellations of Capricorn preside over it  
with a twofold monster,  
twice twelve stars shining together in one sign.

Then is the time to scour the snowy fields for hares  
and to capture, by varied arts, the variegated birds  
that fly across the fields, hills, and surrounding rivers.

While the capus and hawk are pleasing,  
and, freed from cares, one is at leisure to indulge in pleasure  
through the winter and at home  
to bring forth various occupations for the coming spring.

For then it is not useful to chase fleeing stags and does,  
nor to pierce the shoulders of foaming boars  
with a broad blade: the north wind restrains them,  
and leanness grips and wastes the limbs of the beasts.

Nor is it easy to entrust seeds to cultivated fields;  
frost burns everything, and dreadful ice stiffens the plains.

Then it is useful to fell oaks in the woods and cleave timber;  
then to prepare axes for houses and ships.

## FEBRUARY

[Col. 0625C] The year whose number the ruling Pompilius increased,  
under whom the city in the toga was customarily purified by dread rites—  
we retain the name derived from infernal Februus.

Aquarius marks this month with twice six stars;  
yet when it is seen pouring down showers from the southern sky,  
this watery sign shines with thirty lights.

This month holds the boundary between winter and spring:  
now it stiffens with cold, now it softens with kindly spring.  
Then is the time to break open the earth with drawn ploughs  
and to entrust seed to the favorable furrows.  
Then we sow foreign barley throughout the fields;  
after the bird, preeminent for its name of filial devotion, turns white,  
it is customary to tend the vines and prune them,  
so that, once the shoots have been cut back, they may put forth new buds.

The willows begin to grow gray with pale-green knots;  
[Col. 0626A] then, for the first time, the hazels leaf out for future nuts.

Then it is pleasant to drive the does found with dogs and spears,  
and to pierce the bodies of boars with stout iron,  
and, after the manner of hunters, to search out shapeless bears beneath their dens:  
then also to construct fish-weirs with embankments in the deep, fish-filled river.

[Note: [Col. 0625D] “After the manner of hunters.” We have printed this as the sense required; in the earlier edition it read *venatum* (“for hunting”).]

## MARCH

March, to which Romulus assigned the beginning of the year,  
bears its name from Mars, the lord of wars—  
him whom Quirinus, with his brother Remus, believed to be  
the founder of his race. The constellation of the Fishes,  
sparkling with thirty-six lights, presides over it.

[Note: [Col. 0625D] “Thirty-six.” Earlier it read *semisque* (“and a half”). Below, from the Bigot manuscript, we printed *diffundier* (“to be spread”), where the text had *diffundis* (“you spread”). [Col. 0626D] The latter was corrupt.]

Pleasant beginnings of spring cherish this month,  
which calms both sea and land with a lovely appearance.  
We see the great swells of Ocean first rising here,  
and the waters of the sea spread out beneath painted ships;  
we see new fish ascend the rivers.  
Then the chattering swallow shrills as it flies through the clear air,  
and we see the cranes settle again in the fields,  
while the hateful flock of geese departs.

Then is the time first to enclose gardens with fences as they are renewed,  
and to prepare them with foul manure and rakes,  
and to entrust different seeds to their proper furrows.

Then pleasure commands the searching out of does, roe-deer, and hares;  
then seats must be prepared for the bees in their spring station,  
when the desire for offspring and honey, acting as a spur,  
already invites them to leave their opened hives.

It is customary then to carry sterile root-stock from the first sites  
of trees and to set it down in unfamiliar pits.  
[Col. 0626C] Plants also, taken from a fruitful tree,  
receive the bark born from the shoot of another tree;  
opened by iron right up to the inner wood,  
it holds it in its bosom. From this graft the joyful fruits arise.

[Note: [Col. 0626D] “Manure and rakes.” Thus the Bigot manuscript. Printed editions had *rostris* (“beaks”); from the same manuscript we have written *plantas quin etiam* (“plants also”), where the edition had *plantis* (“to plants”), and so forth.]

## APRIL

The month which our predecessors called sacred and proper to Venus—  
because of the pleasure that invigorates and delights all things—  
we call April, a name derived from the Greek;  
or rather because it opens the lands, closed by winter’s cold,  
to various offspring and compels them to flourish through its fostering care,  
it is called by a name distinguished in the Roman language.

Aries, the first of the constellations shining along its oblique course,  
sparkles above it with thirty lights.  
For this month Phoebus first adorns its bright hair and delightful temples  
with flowers and green foliage.

For then all buds burst forth into their offspring;  
in this month the fields, woods, and fresh meadows  
turn green with grass, foliage, grain, and various shrubs,  
and send all the flocks from their stalls to pasture.

Then the nightingale, tireless, practices its songs,  
and the articulate swallow hangs its nest beneath the roofs.  
Then starlings, blackbirds, thrushes, and the birds accustomed to the woods  
fill the air with their many-voiced song.  
Then the turtle-dove with its groaning, and the hoarse wood-pigeons,  
delight the weary with rustic devotion and labor.  
The pleasure of hunting is the same in this month as in March.

Meanwhile farmers apply themselves to the task,  
and hasten to protect the future crops with cut fences or ditches;  
[Col. 0627B] they hurry either to water the meadows with diverted streams,  
or add stakes and forked supports to the vines,  
binding them with strips of bark so that they may easily withstand the blowing winds  
and support the hanging clusters,  
lest the vineyards lying beautifully spread out be disfigured,  
or alter and ruin their vigorous flavor by unworthy means.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] “To protect with ditches.” In the Bigot manuscript, *calatis*, incorrectly. Few are unaware that *caratum* is used in medieval Latin for a rampart or ditch. We immediately printed *prata* (“meadows”), where *grata* (“pleasing”) was read, without sense; shortly afterward, *vineta jacentia* (“vineyards lying spread out”), where the text had *vincta jacentia* (“bound lying”). The Bigot manuscript supports these readings.]

## MAY

May, named after Maia, the mother of Mercury,  
whom the falsely deceived age of our predecessors worshipped;  
or called from the name of the ancestors, the fathers—  
that more distinguished part of the people in the city of the toga—  
bears this name. For it the Bull, shining with fifteen stars,  
presents golden-haired Phoebus in his summer radiance;  
and the Maiads gild the forehead of the Bull,  
whose bent knee climbs toward heaven, with seven lights.

Here, as spring closes, the summer cycles begin.  
Displaying the earth’s new crops to suffering mortals,  
May is the first to mix its cups in baskets  
and to gather strawberries, exceedingly sweet, from modest herbs.

Then the seeds already growing green rise into ears,  
and the milk-white grains cover the bearded fields.  
Now it is useful to soften harsh wine with herbs  
and to avoid the poisons of stepmothers in the cups—  
poisons which the fields produce as remedies of various kinds.  
Indeed, when the air changes and snakes bring sickness,  
it is then easy to drive it away with medicinal care.

In this month too farmers turn over with yoked young oxen  
the backs of the fields where autumn crops are properly sown.  
This is also the month in which those who love and practice animal husbandry  
send a chosen male to the fertile flock,  
to produce a race that will serve its masters.

This month also, according to ancient practice,  
trains the recruit selected for the camp and the battle line;  
at the same time it teaches him to press the arms of the proud enemy  
with squadrons and legion,  
or to fit out a fleet for favorable winds.

Then the young swarm, released from the saffron-colored combs by the heat,  
plays beneath the open air; leaving the hives,  
the wandering colonies seek unfamiliar homes.  
[Col. 0628A] Often they even provoke battle with wings and stings,  
and rush with courageous breast toward beautiful death.

## JUNE

Julius made June the sixth month of the year after January;  
we retain the name said to derive from Juno.  
Or the younger people, traditionally ranked after the fathers,  
gave this month its name in due order.

The Twins mark it out, equal in radiance to Phoebus;  
the zodiac gilds them with fifteen stars.  
At the solstice it surpasses the other months  
and reaches the highest circles of heaven through its long days.

The scorching summer warms the crops in this month  
and first makes the fields appear to undulate like a river,  
filled with stalks. It also revisits the gardens with its care,  
and then it is useful to transplant vegetable plants,  
while they can grow tenderly into rich fruit.

Soon it is time to gather violets, then roses and lilies,  
and to combine hyacinth flowers in baskets.  
From this comes the custom of preparing sweet dinners with lettuce  
and lightening strong flavors with fragrant herbs.  
Garlic and onions are then especially pleasing for their juices;  
mint too is agreeable, and savory is healthful,  
while the sap has not yet thickened into vigorous herbs.

Then, for the fasting, it is pleasant to seek a spring of sweet water  
and avoid the heat by drinking from it.  
It is also the season to pluck cherries from the trees.  
Waxen plums follow the purple cherries;  
then gentle apples are added to the first pears,  
after the meadows have been deprived of their green by cutting,  
and the farmers, with the hay stored away, disregard the cold.

From this point the acorn-bearing tree clothes itself with blossom throughout the woods,  
and the vines nearby swell together with their blossoms.

## JULY

The fifth month, whose origin Mars marks for itself in the year,  
Quirinus ordered to be called Quintilis;  
now July, the seventh month after January, occupies the middle of the year,  
and is named in distinction after the great Caesar.

Under the solstitial, blazing Cancer,  
whose stars shine with fourteen lights,  
the golden light of the sun joins this month  
at equal intervals, sent down through the axis from the center.

In this month the fruitful crops begin to grow yellow  
at the tops of their stalks and to announce the hope of a ripe harvest.  
Barley sown beneath the first frosts of autumn does so.  
Since Phoebus also warms the fields with just fires,  
favorable breezes offer the wheat harvest.

Here too the capable hand seeks the crop of flax.  
For whatever was sown in the month of Mars,  
July returns ripe, bearing full pods;  
and what was entrusted to the sparse furrows in the month of Venus  
will itself give the month of August to the scorched field.

[Note: [Col. 0628D] “Throughout the month.” Thus the Bigot manuscript. Earlier it read *per mensis* (“throughout the months”); in the same verse we have added *quae* (“which”).]

[Col. 0629A] In this month too it is proper to adorn tables with pears  
and to pluck peaches of exceedingly sweet taste,  
the small ones that first ripen in the summer heat;  
it is certain that the rest yield to autumn.

Then there is leisure to pour offerings of spelt first soaked  
over the altars and to ask for the year’s joyful fruits,  
when their seasons do not yet pour forth a full harvest of crops  
and the appearance of a clear sky must be entreated.

The pleasure of hunting in this month is greater:  
to drive out the fat deer that have been found,  
and then to search the deep woods with dogs—  
the bodies now for the first time avoiding the long leanness  
which Venus and barren winters produced through scanty feeding.  
After the vineyards, with new blossom, produce certain clusters,  
this is the greater delight that accompanies the month.

## AUGUST

The sixth month, which Romulus, its author, decreed should be called Sextilis,  
Julius Caesar afterward judged to be the eighth month of the year.  
Rome, changing its name to August, named it illustrious after the prince Octavian.

Here it revolves through an equal span with May,  
guiding and diminishing the sun that had previously rolled  
its flaming lamp along a sloping course.  
The signs of Leo shine with eighteen lights,  
which pour out the last warmths of summer  
and compel golden Ceres to tighten her ripe ears,  
when every farmer girds himself for the harvest  
and all the fields produce crops for their sweating cultivators.

Although at times the golden sky may produce immense fires  
in this month, and heaven may tremble with mighty rumbling,  
while the poured-out rainstorms convulse the air,  
the joyful seasons join summer to autumn.  
Therefore the harvest must be tended by men with the greatest and swiftest labor,  
and the whole youth must be employed in the grain,  
lest a sudden shower overtake the ripened crops  
and the earth mock the unwary labor.

Nor is it only care for cutting the spelt  
that then drives the farmer’s zeal: all the fields alike demand attention,  
those cultivated earlier with various seed  
and afterward yielding different harvests at different times.

Here the field bears flax; there, rich legume;  
oats invite the sickle here, barley calls it there.  
Nor is the slender yield of vetch or tiny lentils despised;  
each is gathered into its own heaps.

Throughout this month too it is permitted to pluck ripe fruits from the branches  
and add them to the meals already served.  
We desire to mix pleasing flavors with sweet fig,  
plums, pears, and several kinds of nuts;  
to take from the vine modest clusters destined for the altars;  
to ask for fertile Bacchus, the source of autumn;  
to taste honeyed wormwood with the meal;  
and to add pure liquids to the sweet honeycombs.

[Note: [Col. 0629D] “And pears we desire.” The reading was *volemis*; I would prefer *voluptas* (“pleasure”). Below, from the Bigot manuscript, we wrote *sumere* (“to take”), where the edition had *tumere* (“to swell”), and, by conjecture, *mellita* (“honeyed”), where we had found *mel ita* (“honey thus”).]

## SEPTEMBER

Now we count September as the ninth month in order:  
the seventh from Mars, as Quirinus, the first, established it;  
it retained the ancient number from its old name  
and now also marks the autumn rains with the season.

Virgo, sparkling with eighteen stars,  
presents the lights of Phoebus, already bending downward.

In this month the farmer completes whatever labor  
August may have left behind, and fills the barns with the enclosed crops.  
This too is the time to set guards in the vineyards,  
who can keep wandering thieves away as they approach  
and catch crafty foxes with snares and knots.

Then, with a sling and its terrible crack,  
to frighten the birds—the varied plague threatening the carefully guarded grapes—  
while the exceedingly sweet clusters give off fragrance on the high hill;  
while the vintager, gathering, plucks the ripe grapes,  
until the vintage sweats with foaming must  
and pours forth full Bacchus under the press’s twisting force.

Although the vineyard, often warmed by rain-bearing heat,  
seeks the harvesting sickle beneath the light of the equinox,  
and the vintager, having cast aside his shoe, bares his legs  
to crush the piled grapes underfoot.

Here too it is customary to gather apples  
to be preserved beneath the cold of winter  
and to arrange them in sunny rooms.  
Here also it is useful to entrust spelt to its furrows  
and to commit future crops to rich fields.

Here deer seeking Venus in their fattened heat  
are pierced with arrows through groves and dense woods,  
when a favorable breeze known to dogs has descended:  
an eager pleasure in hunting taught the Franks this.

When Libra now governs the month as it declines,  
night and day are joined in equal measure.  
From this point dreadful night surpasses day  
in the length of its courses, joined in equal return  
beneath the equal springtime sun,  
until light again begins to hold greater stretches than darkness  
and presses down the fleeing shadow.

[Note: [Col. 0629D] “The carefully guarded grapes.” We preferred this to the former reading, *sollicitet, quarum* (“may trouble, whose”); yet we do not assert that Wandalbert wrote what we have conjectured.]

## OCTOBER

[Col. 0630D] The orbit of the year now turns October, the tenth month,  
which the ancient sphere established to be called the eighth.  
It too is known to retain its old name from its number  
and likewise to mark the frequent rains.

When Libra has made equal hours in the sky,  
Phoebus rolls the damp month along a shorter path;  
Scorpio, drawing back its four arms,  
extends them toward the burning one with flames,  
and leaves Erigone nearby.

The vintage, humbly, with full lips,  
and the tender vine that adorns every field,  
now fill this month. Throughout the vineyards,  
workers hired from every direction boil with activity.

Some cut the tender fruits from the branch with iron;  
others rejoice to carry the gathered clusters on their shoulders;  
others convey the vine’s gifts farther away on wagons;  
others strain with strong arms to twist the press  
and stretch the beams with sweet must.

Some also restore old vats everywhere,  
or supply new ones from solid oak,  
so that the watchful cellars may hold all the wine of the year.

The same love fires them all, and the same concern runs through everyone;  
even night can scarcely restore rest to the weary,  
and one common labor exercises them all: the labor of possession.

Then too the gathered must is cooked over a slow fire,  
which boils it with gentle heat and pours out foam  
from the swelling bronze vessel.  
Thus the clear wines preserve their exceedingly sweet flavor  
and, at last, provide an easy remedy for the fasting.

Then too it is useful to mix mustard, ground beneath the revolving millstone,  
with the first liquid of the grapes,  
so that afterward it may relieve the pleasing flavors of meals.

In this month too it is time to bring pigs into the light,  
so that they may break the winter acorn when it is ripe.

## NOVEMBER

[Col. 0631C] November now revolves as the eleventh month in the great sphere,  
which our ancestors of old called the ninth in the year,  
retaining its first name from its number and from the rain.

For it Scorpio shines with nineteen stars,  
but now four flames fill Libra—  
the Claws, which an age skilled in astronomy discovered;  
Scorpio now burns with only fifteen fires.

In this month autumn begins to withdraw before harsh winter,  
and the cold is forged from icy winds.  
But under an uncertain sky the earth assumes a changing form:  
now loosened into rains when the west wind blows,  
now hardened into a rigid shape when the north wind rages.

Therefore, when an opportunity is granted beneath favorable skies,  
it is useful to work the earth,  
to entrust seed to fields that have been ploughed,  
which may remain after autumn has passed;  
and to accustom herds of pigs to the fruitful woods,  
while the oak, shaken by the wind, grants its rich fall  
and the forests are strewn with scattered acorns.

Then too the greatest care is given to seeking the hard boar in the woods  
and drawing it from the dark grove with dogs,  
while hunters harden its strong shoulders with repeated blows  
and rub its ribs with ancient wood to make them firm.  
Nor do they fear the broad iron hunting-spears.

For what remains, festive care loosens cares  
and calls one to rest with sweet delights,  
after the harsh gusts of wind restrain rural labor.  
Then there are sweet games, then fire is most welcome,  
and it is delightful to invite sleep with new wine.

## DECEMBER

The final line now governs the twelfth month,  
which new Rome, under Quirinus as its author,  
wrote down as the tenth; it bears the same name  
to designate both the number and the rain,  
and now too December is called from the month of Mars.

The bow-bearing Archer carries Phoebus along narrow courses,  
shining with thirteen fires together.  
In this month the sun, sent down toward the southern axis of heaven  
and traversing our globe along a narrow path,  
turns its lofty lights back toward the north.

In this month too, when the winter cold burns the earth,  
the longest night, pleading for the gifts of a modest light,  
comforts farmers who have finally forgotten their labor,  
and gentle sleep bathes their limbs, now forgetful of their labor and ungrateful to themselves.

Nor is the rain-bearing month without its own gifts,  
nor does the season compel all labor to cease beneath the cold sky  
and the earth covered in a snowy appearance.  
Then too, when the field is wet with rain and wind,  
the fallen clod must be cut by the ploughshare.  
The farmer wishes then to sow barley  
or cultivate joyful legume  
and may scatter foul manure throughout the fields.

[Col. 0632C] But when the earth stiffens in dull torpor,  
there are still many tasks to hasten at home and beneath the roofs themselves,  
which may soon alleviate the cold of freezing winter.

From here it is possible to catch various sea-birds in nets,  
or to deceive them across the fields with fire and noise,  
or, as experience has discovered, to set spring-snares.  
It is also permitted to place wicker baskets in fish-filled rivers  
and to fix dense bundles along the banks,  
where the streams calm their swift course into the ford,  
so that the nets may easily capture prey carried by the current.

In this month it is customary to slaughter pigs,  
already dripping with acorn fat  
and displaying their full nourishment in their distended bellies,  
and to hang them in the warm smoke,  
after their backs have first been sprinkled with moist salt.

[Col. 0632D] The twelve months renew these practices in their revolution.

The Gallic countryside also retains this custom and way of life,  
which I, reader, have briefly marked out and arranged in verse—  
I, Wandalbertus, compelled by the urging of a friend—  
at the time when the sweet shores of the Rhine were nurturing me,  
where the great walls of ancient Agrippina stand.

[Col. 0631]

## THE HOROLOGIUM THROUGH THE TWELVE MONTHS’ POINTS

[Col. 0631D] The months whose seasons the sun joins in its course—  
now, reader, listen: I shall teach them briefly in verse.

[Col. 0632D] January, Janus, is the gateway of the year, and December its end.

The sun’s orbit turns these months equally by points:  
[Col. 0633A] the same orbit that turns February governs November;  
March is joined to October by the same interval;  
September meets April in the sphere;  
May looks toward August from the very center;  
the rising orbit of June draws Quintilis after it.

Observe, reader, which hours are joined to one another at the beginning,  
and remember to observe them equally in all the months.

In every month the first hour is joined to the eleventh.  
From there the second, in its course, joins the tenth by shadows;  
then the third embraces the ninth at these same points;  
the fourth, preceding it, is likewise joined to the eighth;  
the seventh follows the fifth in due numerical order.  
The sixth alone retains only its own measurements.

Joining these hours together in all the months, reader,  
observe by what interval the shadows exceed or fall short.

But first retain this knowledge: different parts of the globe  
also form different limits.  
Those scorched beneath the south by the nearby sun,  
because they shine with more light, can produce the smallest shadows;  
those that lie cold beneath the northern axis  
are more oppressed by the longer night and the dark shadows.

Those who stand midway between either axis  
also regulate light and shadows between the two.

Therefore, reader, if the following page moves you as you read it,  
you will test it in the region which, beginning at the Danube,  
turns toward the first risings of the West,  
and which, by the city of Lyons and the distinct streams of the Rhône,  
faces the Britons enclosed by the circuit of Ocean.

This measurement of the hours will also properly warn you  
not to wish to set down the movement of the shadows on the first Kalends  
and carry it through to the end of the month.  
For the boundary of the shadows that existed on the preceding day  
cannot pass beneath the night into various returns;  
but from the middle of the month to the middle  
we are taught, by true calculation, that the shadows  
increase or diminish gradually, as the rising of the signs revolves  
from midpoint to midpoint.

Now we shall set out in order the limits of the hours,  
which the shadow of the human body displays to those ignorant of it.

## JANUARY AND DECEMBER

[Col. 0633D]

The line that is first for January and likewise for December  
extends its shadow thirty-two feet;  
then, after eleven feet of shadow have been cut away,  
the following shadow appears extended only twenty-one feet.

The third line, with two feet cut away,  
[Col. 0634A] fixes ten feet and nine in the shadows at once.

Again, as the sun rises and the Twins are driven away,  
the fourth measure retains seven feet and ten.

As the shadow flees here too, with two feet cut away,  
its fifth line extends fifteen feet.

Then, with the sun governing the center,  
two feet are shortened; the sixth retains thirteen feet.

You will preserve this method of cutting away everywhere for the task.

## FEBRUARY AND NOVEMBER

The nature that governs February and joins it to November  
gathers the highest shadows at thirty feet;  
then the following ones stand at nineteen feet.

The third line stretches to seventeen feet.  
The fourth shadow likewise gathers fifteen feet;  
from there the fifth extends thirteen feet,  
[Col. 0634B] and the sixth soon restrains the rising wheel at eleven.

## MARCH AND OCTOBER

March, which equals October in its courses,  
sets the first line at eight feet and twice ten;  
the second completes and establishes seventeen;  
the third is held at fifteen as Phoebus rises;  
the fourth, recognized as exceeding ten feet, flees by three;  
then the fifth, extending eleven feet, withdraws;  
the sixth afterward spreads its lights over nine feet.

## APRIL AND SEPTEMBER

The orbit that joins September to flowering April  
teaches the first shadow at twice ten and six feet;  
it fixes the second at less than fifteen feet;  
the third also restrains its course at thirteen;  
[Col. 0634C] the fourth, increasing by eleven feet, then withdraws;  
the fifth closes the open course at nine feet;  
the sixth arranges its movements at seven.

## MAY AND AUGUST

The line that first joins August and May  
moves through the shadow at twenty-four feet;  
then the second rises to thirteen feet;  
the third concludes its bright course at eleven;  
the fourth, warmed by the sky, opens at nine feet;  
the fifth, completed beneath its own shadows, holds seven;  
and the sixth then ceases at five feet in the burning sphere.

## JUNE AND JULY

June, which equals Quintilis in its hours,  
[Col. 0634D] opens the first at twenty-two feet;  
the second is then displayed moving at eleven;  
the third soon completes nine feet, compressed;  
the fourth extends seven in the summer heat;  
the fifth line then climbs by five feet;  
from there, burning at the center, the sixth retains three.

[Col. 0635]

## ON THE CREATION OF THE WORLD IN THE ORDER OF THE SIX DAYS

## ON THE ONE AND TRIUNE GOD

[Col. 0635A]

Simple, pure, and one,  
the eternal Father  
and fountain of highest goodness,  
existing without end  
and without a beginning in time,  
God formed the universe.  
By the Word creating all things,  
the structure of creation stands,  
which the axis turns as it revolves.

Equal to the Father and the Begotten,  
the Spirit fills the world,  
illuminating all things.  
One and triune power  
governs everything  
by a distinct, comprehensive command.

[Col. 0635B]

### On the First Day

Here the first beginning arises:  
free from the bond of flesh,  
it possesses heaven’s court,  
and, beholding the King,  
it keeps the truly blessed law  
and its service.

This light, illuminated for us  
by the true light from an everlasting source,  
shines forth.  
That portion which freely abandoned it,  
while blindly exalting itself,  
now shudders in night and shadows.

But God the Ruler distinguishes the two  
and separates their origins according to their worth.  
To blind mortals this adds  
the poison of contempt, madness, and wickedness;  
but the other gradually pours out  
love of blessed life and kindly virtue.

Soon God created the lofty heaven  
and the earth, sunk under its weight  
and without form,  
which through the vast emptiness  
would initially have lacked  
the gift of light, covered as it was by waters.

[Col. 0635D] With these were combined  
the seeds of pure fire  
and the dry moisture of air.

[Col. 0636A] Certainly, when these were joined together,  
bodies move without sensation,  
set in motion by no breathing agent.

### On the Second Day

Next the part of heaven nearest to earth  
was created, often subject to dark vapors.  
For the upper waters, covering the earth,  
came rushing down in united mass.

Between them the Creator established  
a cloudy and cloud-bearing sphere.  
This power of the fluid, surging element  
moderates the fires of heaven.

### On the Third Day

At last, in this sequence,  
the Sower of the beautiful world  
uncovered the fields from the waters  
and spread the masses of water  
into great channels.

Soon springs, rivers, streams,  
ponds, and great waters  
flowed separately within their banks.

Suddenly the naked earth, rejoicing,  
clothed itself in the beautiful form  
of verdant foliage.  
Every tree’s seed,  
the productive offspring of grass,  
created these things at the urging of the Word.

### On the Fourth Day

So that all these things might not lack  
the honor and breathing warmth of light,  
the Creator of the sun fashioned fire,  
the lamp of the moon,  
and the brightness of the stars.

Some stars were ordered to remain fixed  
beneath the broad spheres;  
others were ordered to move.  
They were to preside over years and days,  
signs and portents,  
and over the seasons.

All the stars receive their light  
from the one Phoebus.  
[Col. 0637A] The dreadful night gives way.

The moon too, through a different course,  
wandering uncertainly in a changing orbit,  
now grows and shines, filled with the sun’s light;  
now, covered, withdraws.

### On the Fifth Day

After the law and structure of things  
had been illuminated in harmony  
by the full constellation,  
the Creator commands the origin  
of living nature and of things that breathe.

Suddenly from the waters there emerged  
a wondrous mass of innumerable species.  
Then all that fills the seas by swimming,  
and all that climbs the air on wings,  
appeared in different kinds  
and in bodies of great form.

Huge sea-creatures arose;  
then great and small fish,  
surpassing the waters by their leaps  
and their scales.  
Soon the closed-shell multitude also arose,  
and the immense power  
of the fertile sea.

Then painted birds,  
from the woods, the countryside, or the waters,  
flowed forth from their accustomed element.

### On the Sixth Day

Now the winged multitude gathered  
here and there, soothing the air  
with resonant applause;  
the rivers flowed with fish,  
and the Creator had adorned the elements,  
joined together in their natures.

A portion of the earth remained,  
which was commanded to produce  
living forms.  
The Creator ordered it also  
to undertake the task of producing  
a living and breathing species.

[Col. 0637D] Then different bodies arose  
throughout the earth,  
suddenly drawn from the mud.

Then came every form belonging to beasts of burden,  
every animal that distinguishes  
and diversifies the livestock of the field.

Whatever is wild,  
shaking its limbs with animal movement,  
runs forth, stirred by command.  
Every beast as well, fierce and untamed,  
came forth as a host  
with ravenous roaring.

All the figures that delight  
to proceed in a herd,  
and those that prefer to walk alone,  
then came into being.

## On the Creation of Humanity

Now the structure of the first world  
was pleasingly complete.  
Then the Sower of the universe said:  
“Now there is need of a work;  
now at last let us make one  
who can surpass all created things  
and whom the heavenly image may commend.”

Soon that Maker joined the clay  
and God shaped a stable fortress.  
Then, breathing into the completed work,  
he gave it life:  
a mind destined to remain eternal.

Indeed, this portion is of heaven  
and of the divine likeness;  
from it the lofty head shines.

No local movement constrains its power  
or its limbs, though they often slow it down.  
After the form, the Ruler makes the distinction  
so that there may be a man  
and so that woman may not be absent.

Sleep sent into the limbs  
immediately drenches them;  
from the bone taken from him  
the woman is formed.

[Col. 0638C] Nature varying,  
the supreme Creator commands humanity  
to rule over all things  
that move, fly, or now crawl,  
created in the waters, air, and earth.

Then he commands simple and innocent food  
to be prepared—food that the tree  
would provide from its branches.

For the Creator, provident long beforehand,  
had filled the broad paradise,  
rich in foliage, with abundant fruit,  
and with a river from an everlasting spring,  
so that eternal law might already hold  
the blessed future inhabitant and cultivator  
in this dwelling.

After the world had been completed  
through the six successive days,  
the excellent Author of nature,  
having seen that all things pleased him  
in their proper origin,  
rested on the seventh day.

## The Mystical Meaning of the World’s Creation as It Must Be Understood in Humanity

Seeing now how greatly  
so great a Creator loves you,  
know yourself by looking upon yourself.

All these things arose  
at the command of the One who willed them,  
through whom the order of things proceeds.

The supreme, wise, eternal Creator  
fashioned you from clay  
and, giving life to your formed limbs,  
raised you up so that your mind  
might behold all the structure of heaven.

For your sake the whole world was created.  
The whole world teaches you,  
and you too are called “world”  
by an ancient name—  
the one to whom this structure yields.

That everlasting light,  
brought forth at the first command,  
shows you as a child of light.  
For the Creator placed within you  
the light of the mind,  
the part that might make you blessed.

Therefore whatever portion of the senses  
wanders through the depths  
clings to blind shadows.  
The superior part must lift up  
the lower part and raise  
what lies inert.

The sphere of heaven, fixed through the waters,  
appears to teach this,  
as does the water, scattered abroad.

The earth too, which suddenly appeared  
fertile and brought forth offspring  
for the fields lying inert, teaches this.  
For this is the highest life,  
our virtue and our beauty:  
that which raises sluggish limbs,  
knows how to kindle torpid hearts,  
and to which the vicious part yields.

When you meditate on producing  
great or small virtues through action,  
the fruit-bearing herb or tree,  
bringing forth produce from mingled seed,  
flourishes in cultivated beauty.

Then the light of the sun  
begins to shine upon you from heaven,  
and a nourishing splendor arises.  
Then the mind, illumined, will see  
what is worthy of heaven’s favor  
to bring forth through action;  
then it will distinguish deeds  
to be adapted to light or shadows;  
then it will restrain shameful things,  
which, once inflamed, send out  
the hidden senses of the heart  
from beneath their covering into the air.

[Note: [Col. 0639C] Something is missing here.]

These rise to the heights of righteousness  
through the summit of the mind.  
With secret flight, revolving through cares  
and sustained by urgent labor,  
they pursue the welfare of the world.

Moreover, the very mass of the earthly body,  
heavy and sinking under its weight,  
either produces pure and innocent deeds  
together with the mind,  
worthy of the gift of life,  
or, by producing impure, foul, and bloody deeds,  
defiles the lofty honor.

Then at last that man will flourish  
with the true light of the mind,  
the man endowed with heavenly understanding,  
who governs all movements  
and, suppressing obscene acts,  
brings forth chaste deeds.

The flower and everlasting fruit  
of the eternal paradise,  
and the fountain of life,  
will sustain him.

## LIFE OF SAINT GOAR, BY WANDALBERT

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, vol. II, from Surius, according to the augmented and corrected manuscript of Saint-Remi at Rheims.)*

### In the Name of Christ

The prologue of Wandalbert, deacon, on the life, deeds, and miracles of the blessed Goar, addressed to the illustrious man Marcuvardus, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, begins successfully.

[Col. 0639D] **1.** We have learned from Holy Scripture, which admonishes us, and from the angel who gave this very instruction to the holy Tobias, that the miracles of divine works must always be received by the human race with complete faith and recounted with devoted glorification.

Yet many of the things which the power of Christ either accomplishes by itself or performs through holy men set before the world as examples are sometimes less known and celebrated in our own time. This happens either because, intent upon transitory affairs, we observe such matters only slightly and superficially, or because even those things that move us to admiration by their greatness we fail to transmit in writing to the age that will follow us—not so much through ignorance of the events as through laziness of spirit.

In this respect our fault is far greater than that of our ancestors, both because it is more evident and because it is less excusable. For in Gaul the study of letters lay dormant for many years, and few are readily found who, throughout the periods that have passed, exercised themselves in the liberal arts. Until, through the generosity of rulers and the diligence of the best men, the study of the disciplines advanced so far in our own age that we must now rightly incur the reproach of guilt if we allow the deeds of holy men—so far as they have been able to come to our knowledge—to perish from the knowledge of posterity.

Nor should we listen to those who assign so much to the age of the past that, with settled prejudice, they deny that anything worthy of writing can now be done. Divine Providence has always ordered the circumstances appropriate to the human race according to measure and reason in each period of the world, so that it is neither fitting for us to long for the happiness of ancient men, nor credible that they would have condemned the condition of our times had they been able to foresee it as it now exists.

For even now there are many in the Church illustrious for the virtue of their lives, and in the consecrated houses of the Churches astonishing miracles frequently occur to reveal the merits of the saints. Yet few, or almost no one, marvels at them, because their very frequency has made them cheap in the hardened hearts of men.

2. Since, therefore, holy and most beloved Father Marchuard, you compel me to lay my hand to a new work, so that I may more carefully expound the Acts of Goar, the holy confessor of Christ, which until now have survived in a very poor style and language offensive to many who heard them, adding anew miracles faithfully reported as having been performed by many at his shrine, I briefly satisfy those whom these writings of mine may perhaps move. I do not presume to claim the authority to correct a work to which the efforts of our predecessors have given precedence; nor do I arrogantly apply literary labor to composing a new account. Rather, I simply fulfill the obligation of obedience which I stated at the beginning: to consider that, according to Scripture, it is glorious to recount the works of God and to commit the deeds of the saints to writing for the benefit of those who will live after us (Prov. XXV, 2).

Indeed, in undertaking this work I am moved both by my great confidence in the merits of the holy man and by your command, to which I owe whatever I am able to do, and I do not consider that I need greatly esteem the rumors or prejudices of anyone, since, if the undertaking succeeds, I shall have among the well-disposed an unqualified testimony to its truth and fidelity.

**The Prologue ends in the name of Christ.**

# HERE BEGINS THE LITTLE BOOK ON THE LIFE AND DEEDS OF SAINT GOAR, WHOSE FEAST IS CELEBRATED ON THE DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF JULY

## [Column 0641]

### Goar’s homeland, parents, and virtues

3. Goar, then, was a native of the province of Aquitaine, which constitutes almost a third of all Gaul. He was illustrious by ancestry, with George as his father and Valeria as his mother. He lived in the days of Childebert, king of the Franks, who was descended from the line of the famous King Louis. Bishop Remigius of Reims was the first to convert Louis, together with his army, to the Christian faith by his preaching. Goar lived on into the time of King Sigibert, who made the city of Mediomatricum the seat of his kingdom.

Throughout his life Goar was upright and noble, distinguished in conduct, most dignified in appearance and pleasing in his bearing; humble in mind, chaste in body, sound in faith, and conspicuous in good works. From the beginning of his life he devoted himself to the religious and pious practices of an excellent way of life, and within a short time he rose to such a height of holiness that he became both a performer of wondrous deeds and a knower of heavenly mysteries.

As his love and longing for his heavenly homeland increased daily, and the fruit of his good works continually overflowed, his life began to serve as an example of salvation to others also. Many, admonished not only by his preaching but by his example as well, were turned from wickedness to a better life and more upright conduct; and those who had formerly served the devil began afterward to serve as soldiers of Christ.

### He becomes a priest, withdraws to Germany, and establishes a church

4. Since a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, the fame and life of the holy man advanced so far that, having received the rank of priesthood and the honor of the presbyterate, he became a steward of Christ’s mysteries and a dispenser of the divine word among the people.

**[Note: [Column 0641D] It is clear from the earlier Life that Goar was a presbyter; but whether he was ordained before his withdrawal to Germany we learn only from Wandalbert. In the very ancient Corbie Martyrology and in certain [Column 0642D] calendars, Saint Goar is called a bishop. He was indeed admitted to the honor of bishop, but was not promoted to it.]**

Then, as his mind grew toward a greater desire for heavenly goods, and, despising all visible things, he devoted himself wholly to the pursuit of invisible realities, he abandoned his homeland and parents and departed as a pilgrim from the world and a citizen of the heavenly homeland, traveling to the farthest borders of Gaul.

He came to the province adjoining the banks of the Rhine, now called Tricoria, which belongs to the diocese of Trier, within the boundaries of Wasaliacum. There he chose to serve God freely. In a certain place beside a stream now called the Wocara, with the permission and consent of the bishop then presiding over the city and people of Trier, a man named Felix [alternative reading: Felicius], he built a church with all the strength at his disposal and placed in it many relics of the saints—namely, relics of the holy Mother of God, of Blessed John the Baptist, and of other saints whom I have not thought it necessary to enumerate.

**[Note: [Column 0643D] Ober-Wesel; Surius is incorrect, reading “Vesalienses.”]**

### He excels in hospitality

5. In this place, then, he served God for many years, devoting himself day and night to vigils, prayers, and fasts, practicing patience and especially hospitality. He exercised this virtue at all times according to his strength, so that, although he excelled in every virtue of the soul, he was thought to possess hospitality as his particular and distinguishing virtue.

### He brings pagans to the faith

6. Meanwhile he began to proclaim the word of salvation among the pagans throughout the surrounding region, people devoted to the worship of images and deceived by the empty superstition of idols. Like a good evangelist who had abandoned everything for Christ, he became a teacher leading many to knowledge of eternal life.

Thus it happened that many neighboring pagans who had persisted in error until that time, admonished by his word and challenged by his example, rejected their error and turned to Christ, the way of life. And so that his preaching might not lack the authority of signs as well, and so that unbelieving minds—which reason could not move—might be led to faith by miracles, he began, through the power of Christ’s name, to perform from time to time acts of healing for the sick and for those afflicted by weakness of their limbs.

Even today we see that his merits grant these benefits in many ways to those who ask: at his shrine the blind receive sight, the lame the power to walk, the possessed soundness of mind, and those oppressed by other illnesses recover their health. Thus we see fulfilled in the holy man the Psalmist’s words: “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored; their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 17).

### His perseverance in prayer and his charity toward the poor

7. It was his established custom every day to celebrate the solemnity of Mass and offer the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood for the welfare of the Church, and to complete the entire Psalter in fervent prayer.

**[Note: [Column 0643D] This is not stated in the earlier Life, which says only that he celebrated Mass every day.]**

Afterward, he would receive at a meal the travelers and poor, from whom he was scarcely ever separated, according to the duty of charity. He commended them to God in prayer and refreshed them also with bodily nourishment, so that a traveler who happened to arrive might receive from him, together with the word of salvation and the help of intercession, food for the body as well.

He did these things mindful of the apostolic saying, “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX), and desiring to receive Christ in the poor and travelers, so that he might deserve to hear from him: “What you have done for one of the least of mine, you have done for me” (Matt. XXV).

### He provokes the devil’s envy

8. But because the ancient enemy, always envious of the progress of the elect, strives in many ways to obstruct their efforts, and because “all who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution,” the devil was deeply distressed that these works of charity and preaching were being performed by the holy man. He began to direct against him, now secretly and now openly, the deceits of temptation, and to labor by various means to turn him from his purpose.

Yet Goar endured all these things with equanimity, for he knew that “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” Therefore he could be restrained neither from preaching, so that he might always labor to win souls for God, nor from works of charity, which he knew to be especially pleasing to God. Thus, every day many people gathered around him, either fleeing from pagan emptiness to the sincerity of faith or desiring, by his example, to devote themselves voluntarily to Christ’s service.

### He suffers the harassment of his rivals

9. Just as it is characteristic of good people to rejoice in the deeds of others when they see them worthy of praise, and to use those deeds for their own improvement, so the minds of the wicked always attempt to obscure the upright works of the elect and to attack with malicious speech and intent what they neither wish nor are able to imitate.

It therefore happened that, at a certain time, two retainers of the bishop who then presided over the Church of Trier, a man named Rusticus, came to Blessed Goar under a false appearance of piety. One was called Albuinus and the other Adalwinus [another reading: Almannus]. They said that they had come to seek what was needed for the lamps of the Church of Saint Peter in the city just mentioned.

While they were seeking—or rather pretending to seek—the fuel for bodily light, they were unable to conceal the darkness of malice by which they had been blinded.

### He is accused before the bishop

10. For when they saw what the servant of Christ was doing—namely, that he immediately preached the word of God to those who came to him, that every day from the rising of the light he offered Christ the praises of the psalmody, and that afterward he celebrated Mass and dined with the travelers and poor who came to him—he certainly did these things from zeal for charity and the tireless practice of benevolence, not through any fault of intemperance.

**[Note: [Column 0643D] From this it may be inferred that the expressions “the course of the psalmody,” which the anonymous author of another Life of the same Goar uses here, had by Wandalbert’s time almost fallen out of use, although they occasionally occur in certain authors later than Wandalbert. Ekkehard the Younger, in chapter 3 of *On the Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, reports the following concerning Ratpert, who lived toward the end of the ninth century: “He generally neglected the courses and Masses, saying, ‘We have heard good Masses when we teach them to be celebrated.’” And Hariulf, an eleventh-century writer, says in *Chronicle of Centula*, book IV, chapter 35, concerning Abbot Gervin when he was near death: “The spiritual courses were recited continually in his presence.” It should be observed that the earlier authors who used this expression down to the time of Charlemagne commonly used *cursus* without an addition; later authors, however, used *cursus psalmodiae*, “course of the psalmody,” or *cursus spirituales*, “spiritual courses,” or something similar.]**

Since the life of good men is burdensome to the wicked, they thought they had found an opportunity by which they could accuse the servant of God and in some measure disgrace his life. Returning to their patron, they began to report one falsehood after another, saying that they had seen in Goar things that could greatly serve to condemn and destroy others; that Goar was more a glutton and wine-drinker than a priest of God, as the unwary might suppose; that he ate and drank in the morning and could not observe the customary and proper time and measure for eating; that he preached in order to conceal moral vices under the cover of words; and that he did many other things which, unless restrained by episcopal authority, would bring upon the bishop himself a stain of disgrace and reproach, as though he allowed such conduct by a foreigner and madman in his own diocese.

Goar, they said, ought to be brought before the public judgments of the Church and compelled to give an account of his actions, lest the permitted insolence grow among others and, the more people were allowed to act in this way, the more the authority of the episcopate be weakened.

This is what they said. But while they were constructing a calumny against the servant of Christ, by divine judgment they made the holy man’s life more renowned than that of other people, and made known how damnable they themselves were.

### He is summoned to the bishop’s judgment

11. When the bishop of Trier heard these things from his own men concerning the man of God—for sometimes the minds of prelates, especially worldly ones, are occupied with diverse matters, and the more they are divided among many concerns, the less capable they become of attending to each individual matter, so that they cannot easily discern why or for what reason people are speaking—the bishop, moved by their words, ordered them to return quickly to Blessed Goar and commanded them to bring him to his presence without delay, since he intended to hold an inquiry into his conduct.

They promptly returned to the holy man as they had been ordered. Wishing by a cunning pretense to conceal their deceit and accusation, although none of this was hidden from him, they greeted him in the name of their bishop and requested and commanded him to come to the bishop without delay.

When the holy man heard this, he, in his simple goodwill toward everyone, was filled with great joy and gave thanks to God. He rejoiced that he had been found worthy to receive a visit from his bishop and an invitation to hasten to him, saying: “May the Lord grant it—may he grant that I can go, for obedience must be offered without delay.”

Although he could have suspected the bishop’s command and could hardly have been unaware of why he was being summoned, he nevertheless considered the Lord’s authority addressed to the apostles: “Whoever rejects you rejects me, and whoever listens to you listens to me” (Luke X). He also considered the apostle Peter’s words: “Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake” (I Peter II).

### He lodges the bishop’s messengers overnight

12. Since, however, the day was drawing to a close and he could not immediately set out, he kept his escorts that night. Following the humanity he habitually showed toward everyone, he prepared a supper according to his means and refreshed them after the labor of their journey, while he himself, as was his custom, spent the night in hymns and praises of God.

At first light, as he did every day, he began to offer God the appointed prayers of the psalmody. Only after completing them did he begin and finish the solemnity of Mass. Then he ordered his disciple to prepare as best he could a meal for himself and the escorts.

“Son,” he said, “prepare a feast for us from our provisions, so that our bishop’s envoys may dine with us. Perhaps God will add some poor person who can receive food and drink together with us in Christ’s charity.”

When those men of malicious minds, already corrupted inwardly, heard this order, they could no longer conceal the poison of their malice. Showing what they had in mind, and as though they were rightly reproving someone who lived perversely, they said:

“Neither are you acting properly, since you disregard the lawful and canonical time for eating; nor do we agree with you in this matter, so as to endure the mature hours of the day before taking food. As though the kingdom of God were food and drink, rather than justice, peace, and charity! As though delay in eating were more important than moderation and temperance! Or as though the holy man were doing this for the sake of his belly and not out of benevolence—he who had ordered food to be prepared precisely so that those whom he thought wished to depart early might be refreshed in the morning for the labor of the journey, and so that he would not allow his guests to leave fasting, in whom, even though unworthy, he rejoiced to have received Christ.”

When he saw that they were obstinately and immoderately resisting him, the holy man, always calm in spirit, said: “It is an evil house in which the Lord is not feared. But if you truly feared God, you would certainly not refuse charity.”

While he was saying this, his servant came and announced that a traveler was standing at the door. When he heard this, he rejoiced. After receiving the traveler into the house, he said: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity!”

Then the table was set, and he himself ate together with the traveler.

### Blessed Goar supplies provisions for his rivals

13. When the escorts saw this, they hurried with great eagerness and activity to saddle their horses, saying that they had now certainly found a cause by which they could accuse Goar and charge him before the one who had sent them with an evident crime.

Nevertheless, they asked him to give them some food and drink, which they could consume on the road, for the labor and needs of the journey. He, always full of charity and ready to do good even to the ungrateful, received their request gladly and ordered that what they had asked for be placed in vessels for them.

Having summoned the servant who always accompanied him on his journeys, he set out with him toward the city of Trier.

### They are tortured by hunger and thirst through divine action

14. It was now midday, and the sun had climbed to the higher axis of its course as they traveled, when suddenly divine vengeance arrived to avenge his servant. Those who shortly before had rejected the supply of food and drink offered to them out of charity began to suffer severe hunger and thirst, and also became afflicted with such exhaustion as they had never before experienced.

Meanwhile the holy man meditated on divine praise and the Psalms, fulfilling the apostle’s command: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things” (I Thess. V).

When they had completed six miles of the road and had come to a place called Paul’s Field, Albuinus said to his companion Adalwinus: “I am afflicted by great hunger and thirst.”

Adalwinus replied: “But unless I drink more quickly, I shall die on the spot.”

They therefore stopped at a certain stream which they knew descended nearby, intending to drink from it and eat along its banks. But when they reached it, they found absolutely no water. For the stream had dried up, by the Creator’s command, for those in whom the force of malice had burned.

They then put their hands into their bags to take the food which they remembered having received from the holy man; but the bags too were found empty. And rightly so: those who were empty of charity, which is the fullness of all good things, found empty the vessels in which they had received food from a man full of charity.

### Saint Goar feeds them miraculously

15. Distressed by these events, though they still did not fully recognize their fault, and wondering what was happening around them, they continued their journey on horseback. Their exhaustion increased to such a degree that Albuinus fell from his horse as though lifeless. Adalwinus went to the man of God and begged him with earnest prayers to have mercy on himself and his companion.

Then Goar, who had read, “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Rom. XII), and who had heeded the Lord’s command, “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (I John III), answered the one who was entreating him:

“Son, you ought to remember that God is love, and that whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him. Therefore, when you saw me offering you food out of love for Christ and partaking of it myself, you ought not to have rejected the duty of charity. But now God is working this for your correction, so that, corrected by his warning, you may learn to embrace charity, which is the bond of perfection.”

As he was saying this, he saw at a distance three hinds of enormous size, as though prefiguring through their number the mystery of the Trinity. Immediately invoking the power of the Trinity, he ordered the hinds to stand still for as long as he wished.

They promptly obeyed, yielding even with brute understanding to the divine name, and silently accusing the hardness and disobedience of human beings. Goar took a small vessel, approached the hinds, and milked their udders. Then, permitting them to depart, he rubbed the milk he had drawn over the limbs of the men who were lying as if dead. Immediately he restored them to their former strength and health.

He then ordered them to return to the stream, draw water, take the food from their bags, and revive their fasting bodies. Thus it happened that those who earlier, because of their offense against the holy man, had found empty vessels and a dry stream, later, after obtaining his pardon, found sufficient water in the stream and the food they had placed in their vessels.

### He proves that prelates must be obeyed

16. While they were eating and marveling and being astonished at what they had seen happen to them, Blessed Goar began to inquire what reason the bishop might have had for summoning him, saying that he found it strange what business the bishop wished to have with him.

“For we must,” he said, “show obedience to prelates. Nor is it without reason that divine power has deigned today to reveal its purpose to us through wild animals: it has done so to show how he cares for his servants and does not abandon those who hope in him, because the Lord is powerful enough to prepare a table in the wilderness. How manifold are your works, O Lord!”

Overcome by fear and dread, they could answer nothing. They thought they would suddenly perish, since they had witnessed such an efficacy of power in the servant of Christ, whom they had dared in some measure to distress.

Afterward they continued their journey and reached Trier late in the day. When they arrived, the holy man, as was his constant custom, entered the church in order to commend himself and his cause to the Lord.

### The bishop drags him into a calumny

17. Those who had brought him came as quickly as possible to the bishop and reported in order everything that had happened on the journey and everything they had seen in the man of God.

The bishop ought to have been moved to admiration of the divine works and to praise God in his saint. Instead, inflamed with fury, he began to say to those standing around him that what Goar had done had been accomplished not by divine assistance but by magical art and sorcery. There could be no sign of true virtue in a man who was subject to flesh and belly, who ate and drank in the morning, and who could not tolerate fasting and abstinence, whereas the ancient saints and righteous men had pleased God through fasting, abstinence, and almsgiving.

These things were asserted as though anyone had ever become holy through abstinence alone, rather than through charity and sincere love of God.

### He hangs his cloak upon a ray of sunlight

18. While these things were taking place at the bishop’s residence in the presence of the church clergy, the venerable priest entered the house where the bishop was seated with his rustic attendants. He began to consider where either the disciple who had accompanied him might stay or where he himself could hang his hooded cloak.

Suddenly he saw in the corner of the house what appeared to be a wooden bar fixed to the wall. A ray of sunlight was entering through a small window. Approaching it—for, as stated, he thought it was a bar—he hung his cloak upon it and ordered his disciple to stand nearby.

There is no reason to wonder that a ray of sunlight offered the hardness of wood in the service of the holy man, since creation is subject, by the Creator’s will, to one who devoutly serves the Creator.

### He repels the charge of magic

19. When the bishop saw this, he began to ask what Goar intended by hanging his garment upon a ray of sunlight. It was not, he said, a divine miracle for a weak human being to presume such a thing; rather, Goar was doing this through boastfulness and the tricks of magical art, not through the merit of virtue.

He should therefore come closer and give an account of his actions. The bishop found it astonishing that a man in whom there was no excellence of holiness should milk wild animals and use a ray of sunlight in place of wood.

When these questions were put to the holy man, and calumnies were being constructed against the simple and pure conscience of the man of God, the holy man, conscious of his innocence, replied simply that he had never learned any evil arts:

“God, the just, strong, and long-suffering judge, the searcher of hearts and examiner of secrets, knows that I have neither ever known nor now know anything at all of magical art, nor do I wish in any matter to give consent to the opposing party.

“As for the wild animals, I milked them not by any incantations—of which I know absolutely nothing—but I fulfilled what divine mercy granted and ordained for the salvation of those who accompanied me. Nor do I know that I hung my garment upon a ray of sunlight, as it is said, but upon an oak staff.

“As for the claim that I eat and drink in the morning, let the one who examines and judges all things see whether I have ever acted from the fault of gluttony or from the duty of charity.”

### The custom of Trier regarding exposed infants

20. While he was saying this, a certain boy from the church clergy named Leobgisus arrived carrying in his arms a little infant. The child was thought to have completed only three nights since the hour of his birth, and his parents were unknown.

At that time it was the custom at Trier that, whenever a woman happened to give birth to an infant whose parents she did not want known, or whom she was entirely unable to raise because of poverty, she would expose the newborn in a certain marble basin established for this purpose. That basin now belongs to the water conduit at the monastery of Prüm, through the gift of the renowned King Pippin, and provides the brothers with water in front of the refectory.

Thus, when an exposed infant was found, there would be someone who, moved by compassion, might take it in and raise it. Whenever this occurred, the guardians or church matricularii took the child and asked among the people whether anyone might be willing to receive and raise it and afterward keep it as his own. When someone offered himself for this purpose, the exposed infant was brought before the bishop, and by the bishop’s privilege the authority to raise and keep the child was confirmed to the person who had received it from the matricularii.

### The infant’s speech defends Goar’s innocence

21. This is what happened at that time. The clerk mentioned above found the infant in the basin and brought him into the presence of the bishop and the church.

When the bishop saw him, he turned to his attendants and said: “Now we shall easily be able to prove whether Goar’s works are from God or from the adversary. Let him now reveal to us who the parents of this child who has been brought in are. If he relies upon divine power, let him cause an infant of three days to speak, contrary to the course of nature, and to disclose the names of his parents.”

The man of God was placed under this condition. The bishop ordered him to produce this miraculous work in order to demonstrate the innocence of his actions and the holiness of his simple mind. He ought, the bishop said, to do something of this kind so that the minds of those who hesitated to hear and imitate him might be strengthened.
