If he were unwilling or entirely unable to do so, then neither his former actions nor the innocence and purity he claimed for himself would be believed; everything he had done up to that point would immediately be attributed entirely to sorcery. Consequently, capital punishment would also be inflicted upon him as a magician and sorcerer.

Then the most blessed man began to grieve and suffer greatly because such things were being demanded of him by his own bishop. In attempting them there seemed to be some presumption; in refusing them, an extremely difficult necessity. His own conscience and the testimony of heavenly judgment had always been sufficient for him. Such things ought not to be commanded of him; miracles belonged not to him, who knew himself to be a sinner in all things, but to the saints.

Nevertheless, since he could not resist the bishop’s commands, and since he might also fear that the weak consciences of those accustomed to listen to him would be deceived in their judgment of him, he turned to prayer, stretched out his hands supplicatingly to God, and said:

“Christ, who emptied yourself for the redemption of humankind and deigned to take the form of a servant, show mercy to me, your client, unworthy though I am, and reveal the power of your strength in this necessity, so that this bishop and his people who are present may know that I love you, adore you, and desire to serve you sincerely, Creator and Redeemer of all.”

After saying this, he approached the man carrying the infant and asked how many nights the child had completed since birth. When the man said that the infant had already completed three nights from his birth, the man of God continued:

“Holy Trinity, I invoke you, and I adjure you, infant, in the name of the Trinity, to identify your parents clearly and by name.”

Then the infant, extending his hand toward the bishop, replied in perfectly clear speech: “This Rusticus the bishop is my father, and my mother is called Flavia.”

Thus, by the most just judgment of God, while that same bishop was devising calumnies against the servant of the Lord and attempting to obscure with a malicious fraud the works he ought to have admired, it became manifest to all what his deeds were and what kind of man he was in secret who publicly judged others.

### He exhorts the bishop to penance and promises to do penance for him for seven years

22. When the bishop saw that he had been exposed and that what he had believed could be concealed had been revealed to everyone, he fell in confusion at the feet of the blessed man. He said that he now undoubtedly recognized Goar as holy and pleasing to God, since by Goar’s virtue—or rather by divine vengeance on his behalf—the crime which he had thought no one knew or would ever know except himself, the woman with whom he had illicitly joined, and their little child had been disclosed by an innocent infant who had not yet learned to speak.

The holy man, reflecting upon what had occurred, stood stunned and speechless, drawing the deepest sighs from his heart. Turning toward the bishop, he began to lament that the bishop had been exposed through him. It would have been better, he said, for the confession to have been spontaneous and secret. Before being publicly exposed, the bishop ought to have cleansed the guilt of his conscience by voluntary correction and fitting satisfaction, since the sentence is true and immutable: “Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, and nothing hidden that will not be known” (Matt. X).

Therefore Goar advised him, yielding to salutary counsel, to accept for his guilt a harsh and lengthy penance according to the judgment of priests—one that would not consist merely in words but would proceed from the secret of his mind, and by genuine tears, sighs, and contrition of spirit would satisfy God, who desires the life of all.

Let him labor earnestly to bring sorrow and shame upon the devil, to whom he had brought profit and joy through so great a crime, by performing penance in a manner worthy of his actions. No one, and least of all the bishop himself, should despair of pardon, since the Lord himself cries out through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live; and on whatever day the sinner turns back, I shall forget all his iniquities” (Ezek. XVIII). And in the Gospel he says through himself: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke V).

Since heavenly mercy is ready to forgive, people ought to be most eager to repent. As for himself, he was so disposed toward the bishop that, according to his modest strength, he wished to undertake and complete seven years of penance for the bishop’s sin, and he desired to entreat God for him with continual prayers and lamentations. He did not doubt, however, that many good and better men would come who would mourn the bishop’s fall and strive to lift him up by their prayers, according to the apostle James’s words: “Pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James V).

With these and similar words he exhorted the bishop to penance and satisfaction. Compassionating his fall out of the charity with which he burned toward everyone, he asked the Lord to forgive him, mindful of the apostolic sentence: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death” (ibid.).

### He answers Sigibert modestly about himself and the bishop’s crime

23. After these events had taken place, news of them reached King Sigibert with the greatest speed. He immediately sent his envoys to Blessed Goar and had him summoned before him.

As soon as he learned that Goar had been brought into his presence, he questioned him about the matters whose report had reached him: the bishop’s envoys, the wild animals he had milked, the bishop himself, and the infant who had spoken before the proper time of life.

Goar answered nothing at all, lest he appear to boast publicly about himself. The king, moved by the obedience which the man of God owed to kings, princes, and priests, ordered him to disclose in sequence the matters about which he was being questioned.

At last, compelled by necessity, Goar asked the king what he wished to hear from him. When the king replied that he was asking about the envoys, the wild animals, and the bishop, the holy man requested that the king himself state how he had heard that the events had occurred.

When the king had done this and had explained in order how the truth of the events had reached him, Blessed Goar added:

“I must not neglect obedience. Nevertheless, you will hear nothing else from me except what you yourself have said; for [the Latin is incomplete or corrupt here: *aliis me factum*], as it has been related there.”

### [Column 0652A] He refuses the episcopate

24. Then the king, filled with admiration, began to recount publicly before everyone what he himself had learned about the holy man’s deeds.

As he continued, everyone acclaimed that Goar was worthy to become bishop of Trier once Rusticus had been expelled; that this had not occurred without divine ordinance; and that the man who could adorn the dignity of pastoral office in every respect through signs, virtues, and the merits of his life ought to preside over the Church.

The king too, with a joyful and eager spirit, desired to fulfill the acclamations of those present. Therefore, with the support of the priests and leading men of the palace who were present, he ordered Goar to accept the episcopate of the Church just mentioned.

But Goar did not seek his own interests, only those of others. He knew how to keep the saying of the wise man: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III), and the Lord’s command: “When you have done everything, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have done what we ought to have done’” (Luke XVII).

He therefore grieved and was distressed and took the king’s command hard. He said that it would be better for him to die than to seize the episcopal seat. The king ought to consider in a priest the divine knowledge expressed in the words: “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master” (Matt. X); and, “If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household?” (ibid.).

The bishop ought not to be denied a place for repentance. The king of all in heaven is the one who judges each person; just as the king himself wished his sins to be forgiven by God, so he ought to permit Rusticus diligently to seek forgiveness for his actions. A priest should not be so easily removed from office, since all mortals are fragile and, through the weakness of the flesh, inclined to sin.

### He asks for a delay when the king presses him
25. To these things that had been seen the king replied; yet the conclusion of his speech was that he would not refuse the bishop penance, nor wished to disobey the counsels of the man through whom such miracles had been performed; nevertheless, he could not oppose the judgment of the priests and the decision of the people, and therefore would have to promote him to the episcopate, as they requested. Then the most holy man, seeing that the king was obstinately opposing him, humbly and with tears begged him to allow him to go to his own cell, so that he might confer with the king more freely for a while and then be able to give him whatever answer seemed appropriate. The king immediately granted this permission, but ordered him to return to him at the city of Mediomatricum, now called Metz, after twenty days. Goar withdrew to his cell, meanwhile undoubtedly intending to undertake something by which he might evade the king’s proposal.

When he reached his cell, he prostrated himself in prayer and began earnestly and with groaning to beseech the Lord graciously to deliver him from so great a burden of pastoral care. It would be enough for him to serve God privately and in seclusion all the days of his life; he could not bear the burden that the king wished to impose. While he persisted in these prayers and afflicted himself, by God’s will he was seized by a severe fever, began to fall ill, and was worn down by a prolonged bodily illness. What more need be said? Matters turned out in such a way, and reached such an outcome, that the king, who had expected to see him after the passage of twenty days, did not see him even within the space of seven years. Thus divine Providence dealt with its servant: it enabled him to evade the king’s insistence that he be promoted to the episcopate, while also enabling him, although placed in sickness, to fulfill what he had promised the bishop—namely, to offer supplication on his behalf for seven years.

For throughout his whole life, and especially during those seven years, he devoted himself to prayer, praying, as the Apostle commands, for all human beings, for kings, and for all who were in positions of authority, that they might lead a quiet and tranquil life in complete piety and chastity (1 Tim. 2). When those same seven years had elapsed, he poured forth tears without ceasing and prayed constantly to the Lord, remembering his saying: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. 125); and knowing that the end of his life was not far distant, he desired “to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 2).

**He cannot visit Sigibert because of his illness**

26. When the period of seven years had therefore passed, King Sigibert remembered how pleasing the holy Goar had been both to himself and to the people and nobles of the palace. Immediately he sent envoys to him and asked that he come to him. But the man filled with the Spirit of God, knowing that the dissolution of his body was approaching, replied to the envoys in a prophetic voice:

“Tell your lord, my little sons, that in this present life he will not see my face, unless perhaps he himself wishes to come to our cell, since I am held by a very serious illness and cannot go anywhere; although these scourges of divine mercy are far lighter than my merits deserve.”

When the envoys had delivered this reply to the king, he began sadly to say that he was not worthy to have such a teacher, nor was the people worthy to possess so great a bishop. Nevertheless, he sent others and earnestly asked them to persuade the holy man to come as far as his presence, exhausted though he was, and not to refuse the prince who desired him so greatly.

When they arrived, they found the servant of Christ suffering from a much more powerful fever and a more prolonged illness, yet constantly persisting in the praises of God. [Col. 0653D] After they had been admitted into his presence, the most holy man said to them:

“Do not, my little sons, weary either yourselves or your king any further, for I am certain, and so trust through heavenly mercy, that I shall not leave this place again, nor undertake any other journey except to my own burial.”

Thus he remained steadfast in his resolve, fixed in the praises of God and in prayer.

**He asks the king for the place and ministers of his burial**

27. Then the envoys who had come to him asked what he wished them to obtain from the king on his behalf. [Col. 0654A] He replied:

“This alone is my request: that, if it pleases him, he may acquire for himself in the heavenly kingdom an increase of merit and a cause of eternal recompense from this place; and when my final day and appointed end in this life have come, let him, by his authority and command, cause the priests Agrippinus and Eusebius to come to me, so that they may commit my little body to burial.”

After receiving this answer, those who had been sent returned to the king, reporting in order the priest’s words and requests. When the king learned of them, he was deeply moved and groaned, and his countenance changed, because he saw that he was soon going to lose so great a man. Immediately summoning the priests named above, he ordered them, in accordance with the holy man’s wish, to set out for his cell, instructing them to fulfill with every diligence [Col. 0654B] and zeal whatever he commanded.

**He dies and is buried**

28. Thus, after the seven years mentioned above, the most blessed man—full of days, rich in good works, and perfected in deeds of righteousness—spent three years and three months in illness and in the praises of God. With the priests mentioned above and several other good and honorable men present, he died in his cell, where he had lived for many years in the service of God, on the day before the Nones of July, leaving behind in his bodily death the world whose pleasures and desires he had long ago abandoned for love of his heavenly homeland. He reached Christ the King, whom he had unceasingly desired, and the blessedness of heavenly life, to be there forever the possessor of eternal goods. While he had been able, he had refused to possess here the goods that are considered [Col. 0654C] those of the present age, and he was destined to have with Christ an eternal house not made with hands in the heavens, though during his life he had often made his poor earthly house a lodging for Christ in the persons of his members.

[Note: [Col. 0653D] According to the intent of the original author, the three years during which Saint Goar was afflicted with illness are to be counted among those seven years [Col. 0654D].]

Agrippinus and Eusebius, together with the other priests and noble men who were present, tended his now lifeless body with the greatest honor and reverence and committed it to burial in that same place and in the church that he himself had built.

**The author’s testimony and conclusion**

29. These are the things concerning the Life of the holy man Goar that I have undertaken to commit to writing, having received them from old and very ancient copies. Following with complete fidelity the truth in their narration of his deeds, I have endeavored, at your wish, most illustrious man and venerable father, to correct only the simplicity of expression, which might have offended educated readers to no small degree. I desire that both I myself and all who will read these things may always be aided by the intercession and merits of so great a man before the divine mercy, so that although, through the weakness of human flesh and the condition of mortal life, we daily do many things contrary to the divine laws, yet through the intervention of him who, as long as he lived, served the law of Christ with integrity, we may deserve both to be lifted from the burden of our sins and to receive help in living well. This is granted by the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

**The booklet on the Life and Deeds of the holy and most blessed confessor GOAR, published by WANDALBERT the deacon, ends successfully.**

[Col. 0655]

**HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOKLET, on the miracles that took place at the memorial of Saint Goar from the time his church began to be built, successfully.**

**The author’s prologue. The authority of this writing**

[Col. 0655A]

1. Having now brought to an end what I have found committed, however imperfectly, to writing by our predecessors concerning the Life and Deeds of Blessed Goar, and what I have attempted to correct as best I could at your urging, father whom I must embrace in all things, I see that I must undertake a new work. As I promised in the preface to the previous booklet, I ought to set down in writing for the memory of posterity what I have learned from the faithful concerning the miracles divinely performed at the most sacred memorial of the confessor mentioned above.

For I see that these events are so remarkable that I would judge it a serious fault if what has hitherto remained wholly unknown to all but the very few who witnessed them or heard of them from those who did witness them were not made known to the rest—unless the scarcity of writers and that custom which has crept in through the laziness and torpor of some offered an excuse: the custom by which we have grown negligent in contemplating the works of God and accustomed to regard lightly and undervalue the benefits granted to our own times. [Note: This is plainly a Ciceronian sentence, otherwise deserving the schoolmaster’s rod.]

In describing these matters, I shall follow with complete confidence the testimony of those who reported them to me, and shall include only what they affirm either that they themselves saw as eyewitnesses or that they received from those who had seen it. Yet these events too are so numerous and so great that, if I wished to commit them all to writing, I should plainly exceed the limits of a proper volume. From this we can easily estimate how great must have been the things that, through the merits and power of that man, could have taken place over the long periods of time preceding us, when such a quantity of events is known to have occurred and to have been reported to our knowledge within approximately the past seventy-seven years.

For it is not credible that the merits of the holy man first began to shine forth in the display of miracles in our own days, and that in earlier times he did not likewise bestow upon believers and the devout the benefits now granted through him, even though there may have been no one to commit those events to writing for posterity. I also wish all into whose hands this account may come to know that, in affirming these things, I have not placed my confidence in just anyone, but in men worthy of belief, whose truthful reports you yourself, venerable father, have been able to judge—especially Herirad, a monk and priest of your congregation, and Theodrad, a cleric of Saint Goar’s cell. Both were already advanced in age and had lived around that very place from childhood.

## I. ON THE TRANSLATION OF THE BODY OF SAINT GOAR

[Col. 0655D] **The cell of Saint Goar is granted by Pippin to Asuerus, abbot of Prüm. The church is restored not without a miracle.**

2. But to come to the narrative: many years after Saint Goar had died, when clerics who were to perform the divine offices were already maintained there at the expense of the church, and the daily gathering of the people was steadily increasing, the cell of Saint Goar was entrusted by the religious Frankish prince Pippin, father of the emperor Charles of august memory, to the venerable Asuerus, who at that time was first in charge of the monastery of Prüm—which you now govern as its third abbot after him, excellent father—so that through his efforts the place might be improved and the clerics who lived there might be instructed in religious observance and learning.

Desiring to cultivate and ennoble the charge he had undertaken with every effort, he began to build a basilica over the body of the holy man, one large enough to receive the people and sufficiently splendid to correspond to the merits of the blessed confessor. Previously there had been two churches there, not far apart from one another. The smaller of these was believed to contain the venerable body in the bosom of the earth, but the precise place of the grave was unknown to everyone. Leaving that church intact, and laying foundations all around it, the abbot named above constructed the church that remains to this day; the earlier church was not demolished until the whole present building had been completed.

At that time, those who knew the matter well testify that something remarkable occurred: until the basilica had been built, no rainwater at all, however abundant the rainfall, fell upon the whole area of the site. Whenever rain occurred, it fell around the surrounding space as far as the middle of the Rhine and the summit of the mountain, while the intervening area remained completely untouched. Thus, by a divine miracle, it was made plain how pleasing that work of construction was to heavenly regard, since the rains were prevented from hindering its progress in any way.

3. **The church is dedicated.** When the basilica had been completed and the time arrived for it to be consecrated to the divine name, the most excellent prince Charles sent Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, a man commendable in conduct and life and descended from the English people; Basinus, bishop of Nemeti, the city now called Speyer; and Mehingodus, bishop of the city situated beyond the Rhine and called in the barbarian language Wirziburc [Würzburg]. All had been ordained by the bishop and martyr Blessed Boniface. They were to consecrate the church and transfer the body of the most blessed man to the place where it now lies.

[Col. 0656D] **The relics of Saint Goar are sought through a three-day fast and prayer. Once found, they heal a cleric whose hand was disabled.**

4. They had arrived at the place, and, after the building had been consecrated, preparations were being made for the translation of the body. Abbot Asuerus was present [Col. 0657A] with several monks, and an immense crowd had gathered from every direction. The bishops decided first to seek the Lord’s will through a three-day fast and then to proceed to raise the bodily relics.

When everyone had devoutly completed this fast, Archbishop Lullus ordered his men to dig in the old building, so that the venerable relics might suddenly be raised and carried away. But when the entire ground had been excavated and examined, and no sign at all of the treasure they sought had been found, the troubled bishop asked the abbot whether there were any clerics serving God at the place. When the abbot replied that there were only six, the bishop summoned them and urged them to implore divine mercy for the discovery of their patron’s body. He instructed the others who were present to withdraw for a while to their lodging, and he himself departed with the abbot and his fellow bishops to take a meal.

The clerics who remained then earnestly begged Christ to enable them to discover where the venerable relics lay hidden. Among them was a certain cleric named Madalbertus, disabled in his right hand and in his walking. Taking up a mattock, he said simply:

“Now, if God wills, it will be clear where my lord lies.”

He immediately went beyond the area of the old building and, striking the earth with the mattock not far from its eastern wall, lifted a brick moved by the blow. When it had been lifted and a small opening exposed, he applied his disabled hand, grasped and drew out a silk cloth with which the sarcophagus containing the body was covered beneath an enclosure built of brick; and immediately his previously disabled hand was restored to health.

The sarcophagus was therefore quickly uncovered, and the bishops and people were summoned by the disturbance caused by this new sign. While everyone present gave praise and thanks to God, the body of the holy man was found inside the sarcophagus, in a small leaden coffin. It was immediately lifted, placed in a bier, and carried from that place to the oratory of Blessed Mary, which had stood nearby from ancient times. Shortly afterward, in full view of the people, it was to be brought back to the place prepared for it in the new building.

5. **The relics, initially immovable, are carried into the new church.** The bishops then decided that, since the narrowness of the site prevented the whole crowd from gathering in one place—for the Rhine surrounds it on one side and a very high mountain on the other—the people should be spread out lengthwise [Col. 0657D] around the foot of the mountain. Thus the venerable relics, carried somewhat farther because of the crowd and its desire, would be brought back into the new church along the upper road that runs around the foot of the mountain.

When the bishops wished to lift the bier after this plan had been announced, it became so heavy that it could not be moved at all. While everyone remained suspended in uncertainty and hesitated for a very long time, the archbishop, as later became clear, inspired by God, addressed the people. He said that Blessed Goar, throughout his life, had despised the empty glory of the world, human applause, and popular favor as fragile and fleeting things, out of love for eternal goods; and that even after his death he continued to despise these same things. His body ought therefore to be lifted simply [Col. 0658A] and with humble devotion and carried from the original church to the new building across the intervening space; it should not be led farther around, as they had planned, for the sake of popular favor.

The bishop had scarcely finished speaking when the bier immediately began to move and was lifted with such ease as though it had never carried any weight. The venerable relics were carried by the bishops and the abbot into the new building and buried with the greatest honor and reverence in the place where they are now venerated. Finally, the pallium that, as we mentioned above, had been found over the sarcophagus still remains incorrupt above the church’s altar. Thus, through the passage of a long age, that garment remains intact, just as his merits before God endure forever without failing.

When the basilica had been completed in all its work and the memorial of the holy man had been adorned as was fitting, miracles and divine benefits began to accumulate there in succession. Of these I shall now attempt, if I can, to touch upon some, recalling them in their proper order and according to the abbot under whom each occurred.

## II. MIRACLES PERFORMED DURING THE TIME OF ABBOT ASUERUS

**Concerning the wine that increased in the cask**

6. During the time of Asuerus, who was the first to preside over the monastery of Prüm, it happened—as often occurs because of the barrenness of the soil—that a smaller quantity of wine was produced in the regions of Gaul. The time of the new vintage was already approaching, and only a single cask of wine remained for the clerics living in the cell of the holy man.

When it began to be used, and every day cups were served from it both to those same clerics and to the guests whose frequent presence there was always considerable, nine or eight days passed. Although scarcely half or a third of the cask was thought to contain wine, it was suddenly found to have increased all the way to the top, so that the floor beneath was also wet with the wine as it overflowed. And rightly so: because the blessed man had practiced hospitality properly and sincerely throughout his life, it came about that neither those serving there nor the guests who arrived lacked wine to be provided for them.

**Concerning the wine that remained when the cask’s opening was left uncovered**

7. I shall add a similar miracle. At a certain time, when the cellarer of the place, named Horduinus, had drawn wine from a cask as night’s rest was already approaching, it happened that, distracted by something else, he closed the cask’s opening insecurely and went away. When he returned to the same cask the following day, he found the opening indeed open, with a spider’s web drawn across it; yet the wine had remained in the cask in such a way that not even the sign of a single drop having fallen from it could be found on the floor.

**Concerning the lame servant of a certain Wido, who was healed**

8. At about the same time, a lame servant belonging to a certain nobleman named Wido came to the place and was healed through the merits of the holy man. With his master’s permission, he devoted himself to the service of the church, and not long afterward became a priest; he was still alive when this was written.

**Concerning a certain Frecholfus who was mentally deranged**

9. Under the same Asuerus, a certain man named Frecholfus, the chief official of the royal estate called Wasalia, situated not far away, was mentally deranged. When his people brought him to the venerable memorial, he recovered his mental health.

**Concerning Waltarius, a noble man possessed by a demon**

10. A certain Waltarius, a man noble according to worldly status and still living to this day, suffered an extremely severe affliction and was undoubtedly driven by a demonic spirit. Sewn into leather, he was carried to the venerable tomb. After lying there for some time, he stretched out his hands and, in a loud declaration, subjected himself and all that belonged to him to Saint Goar. He also gave an excellent vineyard, which remains to this day in the possession of the same cell. Immediately he was freed from the madness that he had suffered for so long.

Although he now lives in his own freedom and is sometimes, as many accuse him, inflamed by the heat of avarice and seizes what belongs to others, he nevertheless openly declares that he is the servant of Saint Goar and that he was healed by him.

**Concerning Reginarius, the uncle of the same Waltarius, punished for his pride**

11. The uncle of the same Waltarius, named Reginarius, although a nobleman, was in character and conduct subject to cruelty and avarice. He despised the holy place and cursed all people of the Roman nation and language with such a kind of hereditary hatred that he would not even look calmly upon any of them; and whenever he happened to seize someone from that same people, he sometimes treated him cruelly.

With the same foolish hatred and barbarous spirit he detested the venerable Asuerus and several of his monks. By chance, while the abbot himself was staying in the cell, Reginarius was compelled by the necessities of travel to pass through the place. When he had already approached the church, he asked the servant accompanying him to lead him, if possible, along a route by which he might avoid seeing the basilica of Goar and the presence of Roman people—namely, Abbot Asuerus and his companions. Such innate stupidity, born of barbarous savagery, had seized his mind that he could not willingly look even in passing upon people of Roman language or nation, including good and noble men.

The servant promised that he could fulfill the request. After they had traveled some distance and reached the very site of the monastery and basilica, the servant warned his master that, if he wished to avoid seeing those whom he loathed, he should cover his head with his cloak for a very short time. When he had immediately done as instructed and had proceeded beyond the area of the place, the servant said:

“Now take care not to look back, for otherwise you will see those whom you asked to avoid if possible.”

The servant had scarcely finished speaking when, almost at that very moment, the aforesaid Reginarius was seized by a discharge of the bowels, and not long afterward, after only a few days, he ended his life. Thus he who, with a most foolish—indeed, most proud—mind, had dreaded the sight of the venerable place and of good men was deprived, by God’s just judgment, both of the light commonly granted to mortals and of life itself.

[Note: That is, Gallic; for we have observed more than once that the Gauls were called Romans in antiquity. And the town of Luxembourg, whose neighbors are the Trevirans, peoples of Belgic Gaul, is called Augusta of the Romans by Ptolemy.]

**Concerning the fish divinely provided on the feast of Saint Goar**

12. One year, when Abbot Asuerus had come from the monastery of Prüm for the feast of Saint Goar, accompanied by several monks, it happened that, because the Rhine had overflowed, there were no fish available to be served to the abbot and the brothers.

When the solemn feast day itself had dawned, and a few of the brothers were sitting in front of the church in the morning, a monk named Ansegilus, a man of good conduct, was sitting there with them and jokingly said:

“O blessed Goar, see how good you are at repaying service! We serve you and labor in vigils and psalmody for the sake of your feast; today you do not provide us with even a single little fish by which we may refresh ourselves.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when, shortly afterward, two sizeable fish were found in wicker fishing baskets made from willow branches. The baskets had recently been hung by a fisherman from a tree near the bank [Note: That is, in a place close to the riverbank; Odo, abbot of Glanfeuil, used the word in a letter prefixed to the Life of Saint Maurus the abbot, and Wandalbertus again uses it in chapters 11 and 28.] and had remained in the water when the river later rose. The fish, which we commonly call “selures,” were brought into the presence of the brothers at the very place where they were sitting.

The abbot, however, did not eat this fish because of his illness. Then the monk who had spoken earlier said:

“Now you have done well for us, providing fish for our refreshment, blessed Goar; but you must not neglect your old abbot, for he will not be able to use this fish.”

The monk had said this, and a short time had passed, when a baker was transporting flour by boat from a mill. A fish that we call a pike leapt into the boat, where the baker caught it and brought it out before the assembled monks—for they had not yet risen from the place.

“Now,” said the monk, “you have fulfilled the gift completely, blessed Goar, since you have provided suitable food both for us and for your old man.”

What a remarkable thing: the words of one who was joking rather than asking were heard so readily! Yet this is not unlike the merits of the blessed confessor, since while living in the flesh he had given his possessions to those in need for Christ’s sake and had always gladly offered hospitality and refreshment; therefore after his death he was rightly able to procure such things for those who served him.

How highly the virtue of hospitality, which the blessed man cultivated with singular devotion while he lived, is esteemed in the divine judgments, and how much reverence must always be shown to the place where his blessed limbs rest, is demonstrated by the things that, through divine favor, happen either to those who visit him frequently or, by divine judgment, to those who neglect him and pass by with some form of indifference. The examples that follow will show this even more clearly.

[Col. 0661A] **Concerning Count Heriwinus, warned by a divine scourge**

13. A certain count named Heriwinus, while passing through the place, turned aside there. Although his people urged him to pray, he postponed doing so because he was in a hurry on his journey. After proceeding a short distance, he fell from his horse and was crushed by a very serious fall. His attendants carried him back to the church in their arms; after lying there for a short time, he received the benefit of healing at the venerable memorial.

**Concerning Abbess Eufimia, corrected in the same way**

14. In the same way, a noble abbess from the city of the Mediomatrici, Eufimia, arrived there while traveling. She did not dismount to pray, as everyone was accustomed to do. Shortly afterward she fell from her horse and broke her leg. Against her will she was carried to the church, where she had refused to go voluntarily, and through the merit of the blessed man she recovered the health that she had lost through her own fault.

**Concerning Emperor Charles, who was endangered because of his neglect**

15. The power of his merits was no less evident in punishing and warning kings as well. For Charles, the emperor Augustus of most excellent memory, was once sailing from his palace, which he himself had built near the banks of the Rhine and which is called Ingilinheim, intending to descend to the fortress situated above the confluence of the Moselle and Rhine and to spend the night there. His sons Charles and Pippin followed him, each in a separate boat.

When the emperor reached the monastery of the holy confessor by boat, Abbot Asuerus came to meet him and asked him to visit Blessed Goar and, as the customary expression has it, take refreshment in his cell. The emperor refused to appear, and, turning back, signaled with his hand to his son of the same name that he should leave the boat and go to the church to pray, while he himself continued along his planned route.

When the son of Augustus had gone ashore, his other son Pippin, who was coming behind his brother in another boat, thought that the boat he saw drawn up at the shore belonged to his father. He too went ashore and, without knowing it, joined his brother in the church. Since there had previously been serious quarrels and hostilities between them, through the inspiration of heavenly mercy and the assistance of the most holy confessor’s merit they came together in fraternal concord and a bond of friendship.

After taking food and drink, they proceeded cheerfully and joyfully to the place mentioned above, which they had begun to approach with their father, and arrived there with all their men safe. But the emperor, who had remained alone in the boat with his attendants after his sons had gone ashore, wished to make for the same place. Suddenly a very dense cloud arose, followed by extremely dark fog, and he became so lost on the river that neither he nor any of his companions, nor even the boat’s helmsman, could in any way know or see where they should go or where they should steer the boat.

They were wearied on the open water for the remainder of the day. Only after the emperor began to acknowledge his fault and pray to Blessed Goar did they reach the mainland, by then late in the day and as night was coming on. Yet they came ashore three miles, or a little more, from the place where they had intended to disembark, and there the emperor was forced to spend that night without an adequate supply of necessities.

When day came, he publicly declared that it was owing to his sin and desert that he had been endangered on the river and had been kept so far from the convenience of the journey and the arrangements of the royal lodging. These things had not happened to him without cause: Blessed Goar had exacted the punishment he deserved for his contempt, and he had undergone the penalties he merited. He vowed and firmly promised that never again, however great the haste of his journey, would he avoid the place of the holy man if he came near it, since he had learned through such trouble that Goar could exact whatever vengeance he wished from those who thought the saint could be neglected.

In fulfillment of these vows he sent to the cell twenty pounds of silver and two silk pallia, and thereafter throughout his life never neglected for any reason what he had vowed. Finally, the man who was then the royal boat’s helmsman is still alive and gives indisputable testimony to what happened.

Nor is it without reason that the devotion and faith of kings are subject to him who, for Christ’s sake, despised not merely the great and desirable honors of the world but all worldly honors and fleeting dignities altogether. Although he could have become a bishop, he refused and chose instead to remain in a humble condition rather than be weighed down by the burdens of office. Yet among Christian rulers this attitude toward the servants of God is as spontaneous as it is devout, since they know that they will be all the more pleasing to God when, though they could be exalted for a time by the swelling of royal majesty, they choose inwardly to submit themselves to Christ’s servants.

**Concerning Queen Fastrada, healed there**

16. When Fastrada, the wife of the same prince, was tormented by an extremely severe toothache and came to the place to pray for relief from her pain, she was immediately freed from the affliction as soon as she had humbly prayed. On this account the emperor gave the estate called Nasonia, which remains to this day under the legal ownership of the place.

**Concerning the man who was endangered while walking on the ice and was saved**

17. At about the same time, it happened that the water of the Rhine froze because of excessive cold, so that it could bear the passage of all kinds of animals and vehicles. There was a tenant of the royal estate that we mentioned above, called Wasalia, whose vineyard adjoined the vineyards of Blessed Goar not far from the monastery. As sometimes happens, he used this opportunity from time to time to steal portions of those vineyards and add them, through human deceit, to his own.

One day, while walking across the ice of the river and having nearly reached its middle, he suddenly saw the ice break apart across the broad expanse of the river. As he lay upon the broken ice, he began to be carried downstream, trembling and anxious. It was a matter of the greatest danger and extreme desperation: a man was being carried on a very thin fragment of ice along a swift and extremely wide river, and there was absolutely no human means by which help could reach him.

He had no remaining hope or plan for escape and therefore began to implore only divine mercy, to call upon the merits of Blessed Goar for his deliverance, and to cry out loudly for pardon and help. Finally, when he had completely despaired of safety, he removed a sleeve from his arm and threw it down. Looking toward the basilica, he transferred his vineyard to the ownership of the holy man.

Immediately, by divine power, the ice carried the man to the bank like a little boat and set him safely on the mainland. Soon afterward he transferred the vineyard mentioned above to the church, under whose ownership it remains to this day. Thus the merit of the blessed confessor chastised the man for his fault as was fitting and miraculously rescued him from his distress.

**Concerning a certain Isanhardus, administrator of a royal estate, who was beaten and healed**

18. Isanhardus, royal fiscal administrator, was acting unjustly in many ways against the household of Blessed Goar. He was visited by the saint in a dream and, after being sternly rebuked, was beaten severely, so that on the following day he could not walk. He was taken by boat to the church, where he lay for some time and earned complete healing except for an affliction of the genitals; this remaining illness is certainly understood to have been left to him for his salvation.

These things, among others that I have suppressed for the sake of brevity, occurred through divine power at the place and through the merit of the blessed confessor during the time of Abbot Asuerus. In the days of Tancrad, who, after Asuerus was happily taken from this life, succeeded him in the governance of the monastery of Prüm and likewise of the cell of Saint Goar, the events that, by the gift of heavenly mercy, I wish to relate below took place. For the most part, those who gave me knowledge of these matters saw them with their own eyes.

## III. MIRACLES PERFORMED DURING THE TIME OF ABBOT TANCRAD

[Col. 0663C]

**Concerning the excessive overflowing of a stream and the miraculous preservation of a little tower**
19. Once, as a result of an abundance of rain, the stream which we said in the preceding little book was called Woccar, suddenly swelled so greatly that, rising into a vast mass, it tore away everything in its path, not without danger and considerable damage. For when it first began to overflow, its course was blocked by some obstacle—though it is uncertain what—and as waters descended from the hollows of the mountains, it grew to such an extent that at last, breaking through its barriers and rushing onward, it hurled even large and very solid houses, torn from their foundations, into the Rhine by the force of its current.

At that time something worthy of wonder occurred. In one of the houses that were torn away stood a little tower from which bells were hung [Col. 0663D]. It remains to this day set above the roof of the church. Although it was constructed much more weakly than the house itself on which it had been erected, and although, when the waters came upon it, it was exposed to nearly the full force of the current, it nevertheless remained completely unharmed. What was even more miraculous was that the house in which it stood, torn away with its walls intact and firmly joined together, could not drag the tower with it; and no one afterward was able to discover or determine through what opening or separation the water had passed around it. Finally, after that procession of waters had gone by, two small flasks containing oil were found at the bottom of the tower. To this day it is unknown which person had placed them there or from where they had been supplied.

### A woman of Scottish nationality healed there

20. A certain woman of the Scottish people, named Brigida, who was weak in her gait, was left there ill by her parents and fellow citizens as they were returning from the city. After she had spent some time there, on the day of the annual solemnity, in the presence of a multitude of the people, she was healed and stood upright.

### A certain Hadebald’s maidservant healed twice

21. Likewise, a maidservant of a certain well-known man named Hadebald, who was both blind and mute, was healed in the presence of the people at the venerable memorial. But when these things had become known, her master, who had sent the sick woman there, recalled her—now restored to health—to his service, and immediately her former infirmity returned. Thus, compelled by the evident miracle, her master had her freed and made her return to the place. Not long afterward, the health that had previously been granted to her, but had been hindered by the man’s presumption, was restored to the maidservant once her master had been corrected; she spent the rest of her life in that same place. Finally, her sister still lives there and stands as a most certain witness to what happened.

### Another blind woman

22. At the same time, another blind woman received her sight in the presence of Abbot Tancradus and afterward lived there for many years.

### The little son of a maidservant, blind and mute

23. Again, at a certain time, in the presence of the same abbot and the people, one of the monastery’s maidservants carried to the church her little son, who had remained blind and mute from birth [Col. 0664C]. As soon as the boy entered, he immediately began speaking with his mother and pointing out the paintings of the basilica to her with his finger. His mother was astonished, but because of the suddenness of the unexpected miracle, she did not dare publicly confess what she had seen.

As soon as she returned home with the child, however, his former infirmity immediately came back, so that it might become clear that his mother ought not to have suppressed in silence what had been granted to her by divine favor. Therefore, when she considered the matter and understood her fault, she quickly took her son back to the church and disclosed the whole event to the abbot and the people as it had happened. The favor that his mother’s timidity had hindered for a time was not delayed long; as soon as she had finished her account, the boy immediately recovered his health.

### A lame woman from the city of Mainz

24. From the city of Mainz, a lame woman came to the feast of Blessed Goar and was brought before Abbot Tancradus. While the clergy were completing the vigils with the evening psalmody, she was healed.

### Potters punished for contempt, and a child delivered

25. Let me now recall an event by which it may also be made clear how those who presumed in some measure to despise the merit and reverence due to the blessed man were either corrected or punished. At a certain time, some potters were carrying pots by boat on the Rhine to sell them. A faithful woman with her little son happened to be traveling upstream with them.

When they had reached the monastery, the woman asked her companions either to go with her to pray in the church, or, if they did not wish to do so, to bring the boat to shore, put her ashore, and wait for a little while at a designated place until she could return from prayer. She therefore went alone to pray, leaving her very young son in the boat with her companions.

They moved the boat to a place farther upstream and waited for her for some time; but, unable to tolerate her delay, they took the boat away and continued their intended journey. Divine retribution immediately followed, making it clear that they ought neither to neglect the opportunity for prayer because she had gone away, nor especially to despise the brief period of waiting for her.

For when they were driving the boat upstream and had come opposite the place where, because of the chasm formed by rocks hidden beneath the water and the violent collision of the waves, travelers often suffer grave dangers—a place in the river about one hundred paces, or somewhat more, from the church of Blessed Goar—the boat was seized and submerged, and they perished [Col. 0665B].

The devout woman’s prayer, however, could not have been fruitless. Although the water drowned her companions, it could not cause her son to perish; by divine power and through the protection of the saint’s merit, he was saved. When she returned from prayer and saw the pots being carried along on the water, she understood what had happened: her companions and the boat had perished. Anxious about her son, whom she supposed to have been lost with them, she cast her eyes about in every direction amid the greatest weeping. Suddenly she saw the little boy, lifted upon the crest of the waves, drawing near to the riverbank.

The clarity of the miracle was so great that, when the mother received the child, she found that he had reached the shore while only the middle of his little body projected above the water—a feat that not even any man, at any time, by swimming skill and bodily strength, could have accomplished.

### A child carried safely across the Rhine on a horse

26. In a different circumstance, a similar miracle occurred at about the same time, which I have added after the preceding account because of the resemblance of what happened. The mother of a child nearly five years old was going upstream by boat along the riverbanks with the man who had lifted the child from the sacred font. Both the mother and the godfather had arranged for the horse, with the boy mounted on it—for the child himself had asked this of his mother and godfather—to walk alongside them on the bank.

Then, free because he had no rider, the horse passed beyond the travelers and voluntarily entered the river with the child; no one could call it back. Everyone feared for the child’s safety, seeing him carried into a very swift, deep, and broad river on a horse that he could not restrain, and they earnestly sought the help of Goar. The horse, having swum across the river with the child unharmed, came out on the farther bank.

This event certainly occurred by a great miracle: the riderless horse crossed such a river, especially at a place made difficult and dangerous by rocks; and the child, who did not know how to sit on a horse even on dry land, escaped without any danger.

### A certain Willigelmus handed over to a demon and afterward delivered

27. But to continue my account: a certain Willigelmus, who still survives today, had withdrawn from the right and possession of the church of Saint Goar a vineyard given to him by his mother. He was handed over to a savage demon. Finally, tormented by it, he returned the vineyard and immediately deserved to be cured, so that by this example the others might be warned that possessions assigned by the vows of parents to the right of the church ought not to be withdrawn by their heir-sons.

### A certain priest named Wolvo

28. A certain Wolvo, who from infancy had been brought up there by his mother, later became a priest. He fraudulently leased for his own use the tithes that had long belonged by right to the church of Blessed Goar from the monastery’s fields [Col. 0666B]. Not long afterward he was made blind and mute and was brought by his people to the basilica of the most holy man. There he surrendered his patrimonial property together with the restored tithes, and, having appeased the one whom he had offended, he obtained his health.

### A merchant named Badoart who died because he had beaten a servant

29. A certain merchant named Badoart was going upstream on the Rhine by boat. One of his servants, who had happened to offend him and feared punishment, leapt from the boat and hurried to the church. The merchant followed the fugitive and began dragging him away from the church. A monk named Heriradus, who happened to be present there, forbade him to do this, invoking the name of Goar, while at the same time pleading and threatening him. I learned these details from Heriradus himself, who related the event.

But the merchant, inflamed with fury, disregarded the monk, who both pleaded and threatened him, and, to increase his contempt, struck down the servant whom he had dragged from the altar before the church doors. Not much time passed before he recognized whose judgment he had disregarded and whom he had despised. Handed over to an unclean spirit, he soon ended his life, wrung from him amid excessive torments.

### A certain Humfridus’s servant miraculously released from his bonds

30. Likewise, a servant of a certain cleric named Humfridus, having been bound by the arms behind his back and dragged away because of a fault committed against his master, dreaded inwardly the punishments that he knew were to be inflicted upon him. Since he could not otherwise escape his master’s presence, he looked toward the church and silently inclined himself toward it in prayer.

A deed worthy of wonder! Immediately the bonds with which he had been tied and led were loosened and broken more quickly than words can say. Freed from his bonds, the servant rushed into the church and, without being reclaimed by his master, escaped both the offense and the punishment. So powerful before almighty God was the silent supplication poured out to the holy man, and Christ did not allow him to remain bound who in necessity and in spirit had fled for refuge to the aid of the holy altar. Thus it was also made clear how greatly the saint’s intercession prevailed for loosening the bonds of souls, since the invocation of his name had dissolved the fetters of the body with such ease.

### Abbot Maximinus endangered because of his indifference, but saved

31. At a certain time, while Abbot Tancradus was staying at the cell, Maximinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gereon [Note: [Col. 0667D] The monastery of Saint Gereon, enclosed within the walls of Cologne, has long since been converted into a collegiate church. For this church, see Aegidius Gelenius, book III of *De Colonia Syntagma*, section 2.], which is situated near the city of Agrippina, now called Cologne, was traveling downstream from the vintage in the territory of the Vangiones [Worms], with a boat loaded with wine and carrying not a few companions.

When he had already drawn near to the monastery of Saint Goar, his companions urged him to bring the boat to land and go up to Saint Goar to pray. He replied that they were imposing upon him an unnecessary delay in this matter and that another time would offer a more suitable opportunity for prayer. Thus, after dissuading his companions, he continued on his intended journey. But divine retribution did not permit him to pass without punishment.

For as the boat was being propelled into sight of the cell, it suddenly sank through most of its length; the vessels it carried slipped into the water, and it struck fear into everyone because of the immediate loss and danger. All began to cry out and beseech help amid tears. The abbot confessed his fault and implored the merit of Goar.

Abbot Tancradus, observing the event from higher ground and considering the danger in which they all found themselves, immediately sent his men and ordered assistance to be brought to those in distress. Boats were at once sent down, and aid was supplied by whatever means were possible. Thus, through the abbot’s help and the exertions of many, but above all through the aid of Blessed Goar, the boat was recovered, its vessels and goods were retrieved, and the abbot reached the shore unharmed.

After leaving the boat, he hastened to pray, affirming that he would henceforth always be convinced that no one should ever pass easily by a place distinguished by the merits of so great a man without offering the service of supplication [Note: [Col. 0667D] “This custom,” says Gelenius, cited shortly above, “continues to the present day. For they consider it impious to pass by that place unless, after placing a bond around their neck, they have given themselves over to Saint Goar. The Innovators also do this, as does the common people, among whom the rationale of this religious practice is unknown.”].

### A certain Frisian similarly endangered nearby

32. In an almost similar event, when a merchant from the Frisian people was guiding a boat near the farther bank and did not intend to draw near the shore on which the monastery is situated, the boat reached those rocks of which we spoke above. Suddenly seized and dragged into a whirlpool by the violence of the waves, it threw everyone into immediate danger.

But when the boat’s master, repeatedly invoking the name and merit of Goar, sought help, the boat was immediately brought safely into port. As soon as he reached the mainland, he went to pray and, as a gift for his deliverance, presented a silk garment to the venerable memorial [Col. 0667D]. The garment was afterward brought to the monastery of Prüm by the cleric Theodradus, who related this event to me.

### A merchant’s servant miraculously rescued from the danger of the water

33. I shall now relate an event not wholly unlike those preceding, but one that contains something even more miraculous and has almost as many utterly trustworthy witnesses as there could have been inhabitants of the place itself at the time when it occurred [Col. 0668A].

A merchant from the Frisian people mentioned above was guiding a boat on the Rhine. Since he was traveling upstream, as is customary, he had arranged for his men to pull the boat along the bank by a rope. When he had already reached the vicinity of the cell, his men and others standing at the river’s edge urged him to leave the boat and go to pray. He replied that he had no opportunity then for such a thing: delay would obstruct the course he had begun, and he could not reach a suitable place for rest except by continuing his voyage.

Thus, with his mind made up, he guided the boat and sat in it at the rudder with one of his servants, while the others pulled the boat along the bank. Among them was one who, going ahead of all the rest, held the end of the rope, which was wrapped around his back and stomach.

They had reached that terrifying rapidity of the river of which we spoke above [Col. 0668B] when suddenly the waves, with tremendous force, seized the boat and dragged it far from the shore, no effort by the helmsman being able to resist them. When the boat was carried away, those who had been pulling it along the banks could no longer hold the rope and, overcome, let it go. But the man who had gone ahead of them all, unable to free himself from the rope quickly enough, was dragged into the whirlpool after the boat. The master of the boat, sitting at the stern and struggling, could not notice this.

The others, having escaped from the rope, cried out all the more loudly, asking that divine help and the merits of Blessed Goar come to the aid of the boat and their companion who was being dragged beneath the water. The force of the water and the chasm of the waves were so great that the boat could not be brought back into its course until, carried a very long distance away, it was taken to the farther bank amid the great fear and horror of many.

When the merchant reached land, he ordered a servant to gather up the rope that had remained attached to the boat and been dragged through the water. When the rope had been collected, the servant was found entangled at its far end just as he had been caught in it. He was examined and tested with the greatest care in various ways, but nothing other than death could be detected. Finally, a great quantity of straw was applied and a fire was lit all around him, yet he could feel no warmth at all and could give no sign of life.

What more is there to say? He was carried back to the nearer bank, and his master and companions concerned themselves only with his burial. The keeper of the church was asked to provide a place for burying the dead man. Once this had been granted, while they opened the grave, the body—believed truly to be lifeless—was placed for a time in the keeper’s dwelling.

Then, after not a long interval, it began to grow warm again [Col. 0668D], gradually opened its mouth, and drew breath. Thereafter, raising his whole body, he expelled a little blood from his mouth and immediately rose unharmed. After prayer had been offered and thanks returned by everyone, he hurried to go with his companions and guide the boat as before.

When the merchant saw this, he rejoiced greatly that he had been corrected and punished for his fault, paid a pound of silver to the sacred altar, and, then continuing the journey he had begun, departed with all his men safe.

Let others judge what they think about such a matter [Col. 0669A]. I would say with complete confidence that the merits of the blessed man are brighter after his death in proportion as, while he lived, he more earnestly avoided human praise and boasting. In displaying such signs and miracles, he should not seem inferior to any of the saints—except only the apostles and the most renowned martyrs of the Church. For in loving God and neighbor he could scarcely be judged inferior to any of them; and although in life he did not shine through many miracles known to human beings, he proved most illustrious through that charity which is superior to all miracles. Therefore, after his death, he shines each day in the faith of the living through so many and such great acts of power.

### A light kindled divinely in the church lamps

34. Moreover, the monk Heriradus—who, as has often been said, proved to be for me the most certain and truthful narrator of these miracles—asserts that twice, without anyone kindling an external fire, the lamp hanging before the venerable memorial shone with a light poured into it by divine power. Those who were present affirm that this also happened in the year immediately preceding and in the present year in which we have written these things. This, however, will be discussed in its proper place.

35. Thus far I have described those events reported among others to have occurred while Abbot Tancradus was still alive. Now, with Christ as my helper, I shall proceed to the time of the most illustrious Father Marcuvardus, who commissioned this very work, preserving the order I have proposed.

## IV. MIRACLES PERFORMED DURING THE TIME OF ABBOT MARCUVARDUS

### The Emperor Louis relieved there of pain in his feet

36. To begin these events with a somewhat clearer opening, setting aside their exact chronological order for a little: Louis, an emperor of outstanding piety, singular clemency, and greater devotion to the Christian religion than all other emperors—who, by the providence of heavenly mercy, still holds supreme power—was suffering from extremely severe pain in his feet, the illness by which that man, although not continuously, was nevertheless frequently afflicted.

As he traveled downstream by boat from his palace, which, as we said above, was situated on the bank of the Rhine and called Ingelheim, he went ashore to pray to Saint Goar. He could scarcely set his feet upon the ground because of the excessive pain and relied more upon those supporting him than upon his own steps.

When he reached the church, he humbly and devoutly prostrated himself before the venerable memorial [Col. 0669D] and prayed for a long time lying on the ground. When he had risen, he turned to the abbot and to the distinguished man Gerungus, formerly an official of the palace and now a monk, and said: “Thanks be to God! Now I feel that relief has been granted to me through the merits of Saint Goar, and I am no longer suffering from the pain with which I came here.”

Thus he returned from the memorial joyful and lively and spent the entire day in that condition. I learned these things from the abbot himself, who was present and related them, although I too was not far away: on the previous day I had seen the emperor suffering most severely in the palace from the pain mentioned above.

### A Scottish woman healed there of lameness

37. To place here an event that occurred somewhat earlier than this one: citizens returning from the city left there a sick woman of Scottish nationality who was weak in her gait. After she had spent six months in the place, on the day of the annual solemnity celebrated on the day before the Nones of July, she recovered the use of her feet during the evening psalmody.

### A demon-possessed child cured at Saint Goar’s memorial after his father’s promise of a bee swarm

38. In the preceding year, after the events I related concerning the emperor, it happened that one of the country people brought to the church, with weeping and supplication, his little son, filled with a demon. When he had laid the child before the memorial amid lamentation, in the presence of many, he said: “Saint Goar, now return my son to me, and heal him by driving out the demon who torments him. As a gift, I shall immediately bring you one *apis*”—for country people customarily call a swarm of bees an *apis* [Col. 0670B].

The simple petition of this countryman was not in vain. The father immediately carried the child home, completely healed, joyful and glad. Finally, he offered the swarm of bees, as he had promised, and it remains today in the gardens of the church. I learned these things both from the frequently mentioned Theodradus and from Ekkibaldus, the provost of that place, a man truly learned and truthful.

### A light kindled twice by divine power in a lamp

39. To add what I touched upon briefly above: last year, on the most holy day of Easter, when the provost Ekkibaldus wished to celebrate Mass at the very rising of the light, and likewise this same year in which we have written these things, when he was celebrating Mass during Lent, the church lacked a light. The keeper had taken down the lamp and found it without a flame and was hurrying to bring it away. Suddenly, while many people watched, a light spontaneously appeared and shone in the lamp. Several faithful men who were present testify that this happened repeatedly.

### A lame and deaf infant and a blind girl healed there

40. To conclude this present account of recently occurring miracles: at about the time when I began writing these things, before the little book had been published, a great multitude of people from every direction—as is customary—came together for the annual solemnity of the blessed man’s deposition. A woman known in the neighboring area arrived with her nearly seven-year-old son, who had remained from birth lame, mute, and deaf, bringing new grief and pain each day to his unfortunate mother [Col. 0670D].

With devout faith, the mother placed him before the venerable tomb during the nocturnal vigils. Near the end of the morning psalms, while the church’s clergy were singing the Gospel canticle, the little boy suddenly rose with a slow effort. Standing on feet that until that moment he had never set upon the ground, he called out repeatedly for his mother.

Weeping for joy, the mother immediately ran to him and received back her son, whom she had brought burdened with so many afflictions, now walking, speaking, and hearing. Nor was it difficult for Christ, through the merit of his confessor, at one and the same time to give the boy the ability to speak and to give him the knowledge that older people had never acquired through hearing. For Christ himself is the wisdom of God, who opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent.

Then the minds of all who were present were filled with astonishment at so great a miracle. The entire church cried out the praises of Christ, and the wondrous healing of one little child kindled the hearts of many toward faith.

41. On that same day, while the people watched the solemn celebration of the Mass and the priest was performing the divine mysteries, the same girl—nearly the same age as the child mentioned above—who had long been blind and had then been faithfully brought by her parents, recovered the light she had lost.

Thus, through a double miracle on a single day, the merit of the holy man shone openly before everyone, and the faith of those present recognized that Christ’s clemency, everywhere present, does not fail those who invoke him.

42. [Note: [Col. 0671D] This entire section is lacking in Surius; we have drawn it from the same Remigius. Cf. no. 36. [Col. 0672D]] I have arranged these few accounts of the miracles deservedly manifested and performed through Blessed Goar in brief and plain language, as far as I could, bringing the narrative down to the year 839 of the Lord’s Incarnation. As I noted at the beginning of this little book, I committed to writing only those things that I learned from the reports of faithful men, and that I found to be known not only to those who reported them but to nearly all who frequently visited the place.

Although I have not written down everything related by those whose testimony I considered especially worthy of belief—for otherwise I would either have exceeded the limits of the work undertaken or have been more lengthy and tedious for my readers than was proper—I have not by this work deprived others of the opportunity to write about these matters. Rather, those who wish may explain more worthily, according to their ability, even the things that I have set forth here, however inadequately; and they may describe events that perhaps occur in similar miracles, taking the example from you, most revered Father Marcuvardus, and from me.

For if divine works are most worthily set before us for glorification, then, as the benefit of divine power does not cease, the intention to write about it must not cease either. As long as there are people able to complete the task, matters worthy of wonder should be entrusted to writing. For this reason I have also chosen to append blank parchment leaves to this little book, so that, once the present work has been published, some prudent person may conveniently insert into it in future times whatever he judges ought to be added.

## V. COMMEMORATION: HOW AND BY WHOM THE CELL OF SAINT GOAR WAS JOINED TO THE MONASTERY OF PRÜM; BEGINNING HAPPILY

43. Having now completed what I undertook to write concerning the miracles of the holy man, it seems necessary to show briefly—after the publication of the two little books, as though in an additional section—how and for what reason the cell of Blessed Goar was joined to the monastery of Prüm, so that it too might at all times remain under the rule and authority of whichever abbot, by God’s appointment, presided over that monastery.

### The beginnings of the monastery of Prüm

44. King Pippin of the Franks, father of the most famous emperor Charles, a man of outstanding memory, after— as is known to almost everyone—being moved by love of Christ and at the request of his wife, Bertrada of holy memory, built the monastery mentioned above [Col. 0672A], installed in it monks who would serve God under the regular order, and appointed the venerable man Asuerus to its administration.

He presided over that place most successfully for forty-five years. Because he greatly honored him for the merit of his life, the king granted him authority of this kind: whenever he was traveling and came to a royal estate, he could freely take whatever necessities of the journey were required.

When, therefore, he was traveling from the monastery into the territory of the Vangiones [Worms], and turned aside on the way to Saint Goar, where a certain man named Erpingus was then in charge under the title of rector, he was unable to obtain any provision of the necessities he required. Shortly afterward he reported the matter to the prince as it had happened, saying that it was most deplorable that every form of hospitality should be denied in a place where that same virtue had once flourished in an exceptional manner under the blessed man.

The king promised that this would be corrected when a suitable opportunity arose. Not long afterward, while he was staying in the palace called Attigny [Attigny in Champagne on the Aisne], Abbot Asuerus came there for the general assembly of the people. The prince summoned him and reminded him of what he had said concerning the cell of the blessed man. He entrusted its administration to him, urging him to arrange it properly and to make it adequately hospitable, since he had not found it so.

### The dispute over the cell of Saint Goar settled by Charlemagne

45. This was the first union of the aforesaid cell with the monastery of Prüm, made by order and will of King Pippin. At that time the cell was not made subject to the monastery and its monks, but was legally entrusted as a benefice to the abbot alone for administration.

After Pippin’s death, when Charles the Great was reigning, a dispute arose over the same cell between Weomadus, then bishop of Trier, and Abbot Asuerus. The bishop asserted that it belonged by right to his Church; the abbot, on the contrary, maintained that it was a hereditary possession belonging to the king by royal law, and that the Church could claim nothing in it, since it had been entrusted to him by King Pippin and had passed by right of succession into the dominion of the illustrious Charles.

As they continued their long and intense dispute, and the matter was repeatedly brought into controversy, the king sent from his court, once, twice, and a third time, men of the greatest trustworthiness and truthfulness to investigate the case carefully and bring the litigation to a proper conclusion. When they examined the matter, they found nothing other than what the abbot had asserted: that possession of the aforesaid place belonged to royal rather than ecclesiastical right [Sup. rather than].

46. Since this did not satisfy the bishop, the most renowned prince undertook to examine the matter himself. He held a general assembly in Saxony beside the spring called Lippia [Sur. Lupia], in the presence of nearly all the leading men of the kingdom and of distinguished men of both orders [Col. 0673A]. By the judgment of all who were present, an oath was imposed upon the monastery’s advocate, then named Rabertus. He later confirmed, together with twelve others, that the aforesaid possession belonged not to the Church of Trier but solely to royal dominion.

The matter having thus been settled, and the bishop at last acquiescing, the famous king, with the consent of his people, handed over the cell of the holy man to the monastery of Prüm. He issued a privilege recording this transfer, in which he confirmed and testified that, for the love of Christ and as alms for his parents, namely King Pippin and Queen Bertrada, he subjected that cell to the aforesaid monastery under this condition: from that time onward, the rulers of that monastery were to hold it and freely use its resources for the necessities of themselves and of the brothers serving God, and without anyone’s opposition were to do and arrange from it whatever served the common good.

They were to enjoy not only the resources that the cell possessed at that time [Col. 0674A], but also those that it might acquire in future successions, under the strongest legal right.

47. Anyone who wishes may learn how these things were done and established by rereading the same privilege, which remains intact even today in the archives of that monastery. It will be enough for us to have recalled the matter briefly, lest we should rightly be accused of having completely silenced something useful to know and of having failed in our duty concerning Blessed Goar in this respect.

48. Finally, while we were writing these things, Tancradus had succeeded Asuerus, and Marcuvardus had in turn succeeded Tancradus, both in the administration of the monastery of Prüm and in the possession of the cell of Saint Goar.

49. Concerning Abbot Asuerus and the cell of the holy man, that the events we first related happened in this way, one of the elders, a man not unworthy of belief, declared that he had heard it from the same abbot.

[Col. 0673]

## APPENDIX. HISTORY OF THE TRANSLATION OF THE RELICS OF THE HOLY MARTYRS CHRYSANTUS AND DARIA FROM THE CITY OF ROME TO GAUL

(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, volume IV, p. 611.)

### Chapter I

[Col. 0673C]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 844, while Lothair Augustus, son of the most serene Emperor Louis, was reigning, Marcward, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, intending to go to Rome, obtained permission from the aforesaid ruler, together with letters to Gregory, pontiff of the Apostolic See. In these letters, by royal authority, it was required that the body of some distinguished martyr of more renowned reputation should be given to him—one whose passion and veneration no believer could doubt.

Having already set out on his journey, he learned that the aforementioned pope Gregory had died and that another, named Sergius, had been appointed in his place. After sending a report to the emperor and immediately receiving instructions for the newly created bishop, he at last entered Rome after covering the long distances of the journey. Finally received with honor by the apostolic pope, he handed him the royal letters.
