The pope, favorably assenting in every respect to the imperial commands and Marcward’s requests, promised that he would do everything he had proposed.

After this, he sent him, through Bishop Marinus, [Col. 0673D] a book containing the passions of the saints, and ordered him to commit to writing the passion of Saint Chrysantus and Saint Daria, promising that he would give him their bodies. Accordingly, when the appointed day arrived, Marcward proceeded to the Lateran church. When, as ordered, he had entered before the Roman pontiff, the bodies having been placed in a small chest upon the altar, with ranks of clergy standing on either side and singing, the pope handed him, with the utmost veneration and honor, the bodies of the aforesaid martyrs. Invoking the name of the Lord, he instructed Marcward to attend carefully to their veneration, so that each might escape offending Almighty God: the pope himself, if he failed to give what he had promised, and Marcward, if he failed to provide the veneration due to what had been given.

He also handed him the relics of forty-six holy martyrs and ordered that they be buried in the tomb of the aforementioned saints. Having received the bodies with the utmost veneration, Marcward hastened his departure, allowing no delay. Thus, with everyone safe and sound, on the fiftieth day after they had set out from the City, they arrived at the monastery’s possession, namely, at the cell of Saint Goar [Note: [Col. 0673D] Concerning the cell of Saint Goar and its donation by King Pippin to Asuerus of Prüm, see Wandalbert’s book on the miracles of Saint Goar, chapter 5, above.]. After remaining there for two days, he made arrangements with the brothers and sent the bodies, together with them, on ahead to the monastery of Prüm. When the brothers there learned of their arrival, they hastened out in sacred vestments to meet them with candles and crosses, in the greatest rejoicing.

[Col. 0674D] I shall recount, after completing the account of their translation, the miracles that God revealed during this stage of the journey in order to display the merits of his saints. Thus, having received the relics of the saints with immense devotion and joy, while all sang whatever was appropriate to the occasion, they carried them into the monastery of Prüm on the fourth day before the Nones of July [4 July]. They lay there in the bier in which they had been carried, to the right of the altar, until the eleventh day before the Kalends of November [22 October], namely, until part of the old church had been leveled and extended into a larger space, so that a tomb worthy of them could be constructed.

When this period had been completed, on the aforementioned day the bodies of the saints were transferred and, by Bishop Theganbert [Note: [Col. 0675D] This is Thegan, or Tegan, chorepiscopus of Trier, who wrote a history of the deeds of Louis Augustus and was praised in verse by Walahfrid Strabo, who seems to mention him in another poem addressed to Altger, a monk of Ellwangen.], on the eighth day before the Kalends of November [25 October], that is, on the day of their passion, they were buried with the greatest honor and amid universal rejoicing in the place where they are now venerated—namely, on the possession of Saint Savior, in the cell called the New Monastery. There Christ now hears those who pray through their intercessions, to the praise of his name, as is demonstrated by the miracles set out below.

But before the miracles performed after their burial are presented, it seems appropriate first to fulfill, at the beginning, what we promised somewhat earlier.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0675B] Accordingly, when they had departed from Italy and were directing their steps toward the basilica of blessed Goar, a certain woman, well known to her fellow citizens, was suffering from an excruciating pain in her kidneys. Having heard of the saints’ arrival, she asked to be brought out to meet them. Supported on both sides by two men, she had scarcely reached the place when, as soon as she touched the bier on which the sacred limbs were being carried, all the pain was driven away. Before everyone’s eyes she ran with free and unhindered steps ahead of the bier.

This was the first power of the saints to become manifest to us, although, while we were still in Italy, we had learned from the report of a faithful man that, in a similar manner, through their prayers, a certain crippled woman had been made upright.

## CHAPTER III

There was a certain woman, not of low status, the wife of a man named Waningus. Her feet and legs had swollen so greatly that she was almost confined to bed. Having heard the saints’ reputation, she was brought out to meet them on horseback, with the assistance of attendants. As soon as she had barely touched the bier, she became so completely well [Col. 0675C] that throughout the whole mountain—whose steepness and height are extreme in those regions—she was one of those carrying the bier.

On the following day, while the solemn celebration of the Masses was taking place, the servant girl of the aforesaid woman became so crippled during the celebration of the Mass that, although she had come on foot, she had to be carried away in another person’s arms. We do not know what the cause was. It was thought, however, that she had refused service to the saints, wishing her mistress to delegate that task to them.

Finally, after she had remained for three days in the same church where she had become crippled, and prayers had been offered for her, she was restored to health through the prayers of the saints. Likewise, when she was returning home, she became crippled again, but through the power of the holy martyrs she recovered her former health.

## CHAPTER IV

Likewise, a certain woman was held so tightly by weakness of her limbs that she had to be transported in a vehicle. She asked to be brought out to meet the saints. Through their prayers she rose so completely healed that, strengthened by her own steps, [Col. 0675D] she walked.

## CHAPTER V

When we were now deciding to carry the bodies of the saints to the place where they are presently adored, an innumerable crowd came out to clear the roads along which the martyrs’ relics were to be carried. As a certain tree was being cut down, it fell upon a man who had failed to take precautions. When he was thought to be dead, the tree was removed, and—so we believe, through the prayers of the saints—he was found so unharmed that it was as though he had suffered no injury at all.

## CHAPTER VI

After the blessed martyrs had been buried, a certain man [Col. 0676A] came there whose ears were afflicted by the swelling of perpetual deafness. While he devoutly awaited the saints’ aid there, through their most holy merits he deserved to recover the hearing that had long been denied him.

## CHAPTER VII

Likewise, a certain man had a disabled arm, so that it hung down, withered, from the shoulder; he was also condemned to deafness. When he approached the saints’ tomb with faith, his arm recovered its former function, and his obstructed ears regained their hearing.

## CHAPTER VIII

There was another man whose hand and arm were so weak that, always hanging down, they were useless for every bodily function. When he came to the martyrs’ memorial, as was proper, with a small bundle of flax tied to his withered hand, and placed it upon the altar, he was immediately released from his rigidity and recovered his former strength.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0676B]

A certain woman, wishing to assist God and the holy martyrs serving there with bodily provisions, was hurrying to the place, bringing with her a wagon loaded with bread and drink and other necessities. But when she was already close by, the wagon went ahead. When she saw that the tomb did not shine with gold or silver—as foolish and irreligious minds commonly expect—she despised and mocked the place. Then, quickly turning back to meet her people, she ordered them to return by the way they had come, saying that no holiness was contained there.

Then, through the punishment of the saints [al.: through a penalty inflicted by the saints], the wagon was shattered, its drink was spilled, and everything placed upon it was so scattered that it was rendered useless for any purpose. Finally, on the third day, she was punished with the penalty of death for her contempt.

## CHAPTER X

Likewise, another woman was afflicted over her entire body by a severe itch, so much so that it was thought to be leprosy; she was also confined to bed by a long illness and could not be cured by any medical skill. When she heard from her neighbors that a wax candle was being made in honor of the martyrs, she was moved by faith. Having purchased a piece of wax, she had it mixed into that candle.

When the candle had been carried to the martyrs’ tomb and was lit with fire, the sick woman, although far away, immediately felt its power in a marvelous manner. Rising from her bed, she recovered her body’s former health.

## CHAPTER XI

Likewise, another woman had her fingers closed together and rigid. Divinely warned to hasten to the martyrs’ memorial, she was led by faith and returned from the place so completely healed that it was as though she had never suffered any injury.

## CHAPTER XII

A certain nobleman, moved by love for the saints, wished to visit the place. He urged his wife to go with him, but she, on the contrary, rejected the proposal and said that she would rather attend to her own work, since what popular report had spread was not true. He completed the intention he had begun, whereas she remained in her unbelief. As she hurried toward the appointed place, she was thrown from her horse and broke her arm, which has remained in that condition to this day and cannot be cured by any medicine.

## CHAPTER XIII

A certain little boy had been so lame from his mother’s womb that birth itself denied him the ability to walk. When he was carried on his mother’s shoulders in faith to the saints’ tomb, he was so healed through the most holy merits of the martyrs that he who had come carried on another’s steps followed his mother on his own feet as they returned.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0677A]

Likewise, a certain woman had a hand and arm so crooked and weak that she could not bring anything to her mouth with it. After lying prostrate for a long time before the martyrs’ tomb, she was restored to her former health through their prayers on the day before Palm Sunday.

## CHAPTER XV

When the season returned in which the bodies of the most blessed martyrs had been carried to the place where they are now adored, and the day of the annual celebration was approaching, a certain woman arrived from the village of Tulpiacum [perhaps Tulpiacum], from the benefice of Odricus. amid the crowd of people who were then almost innumerably flocking there.

She had with her her only daughter, already five years old, named Ermenrada, whose eyes were covered by the darkness of blindness. Driven by grief, she devoutly brought the girl with her to be enlightened through the merits of the saints. When she asked the custodians that the girl be placed somewhere in the church to await the saints’ aid, she was permitted to lay her down in a corner of the crypt, where the saints are worshiped at their feet.

After she had been laid there all day and all night, as though rigid and motionless, while the morning office was being celebrated and the following night was beginning, divine power suddenly came through the prayers of the saints. Having received again the strength of sight that, as everyone knew, had been denied her for three years, she began to see clearly.

When this miracle spread through everyone’s mouths and they cried out praises to the Lord and his holy martyrs, the Lord also wished to double the spiritual joy of the faithful people through a twofold miracle and to show how great the saints’ merits were in his sight.

## CHAPTER XVI

For a certain woman named Bertrada, from the household of blessed Maximinus, from a village called Ocgisesheim, was afflicted by such extreme weakness that, with her sinews dried up, she had become crippled and weak in all her limbs. Hearing of the saints’ power, she came to this same celebration in hope of being healed.

As she devoutly implored the martyrs’ aid, she obtained health through their intercession. Thus, while the celebration of the Mass was being performed, the saints’ power came to her. She who had arrived crippled and weak, supported by the assistance of others, returned home strengthened by her own steps.

## CHAPTER XVII

There was also in a village called Sinciacum a certain woman named Gaminildis, from the household of Saint Peter, whose face was so deformed that it inspired no little horror in those who looked at her. For with her mouth twisted nearly to her ear and her eyes looking crosswise, she had become a kind of monster.

She begged her mistress, named Heritrudis, who was hurrying to the saints’ church, to carry with her a candle that she, as a poor woman, had made to the measure of her own head, so that through the saints’ intercession the mercy of Almighty God might come to the aid of her deformity.

Her mistress agreed to the servant’s request and carried with her what had been asked for. When she reached the sacred place, she lit the candle according to custom during the sacred vigils. Immediately divine power, looking upon the pitiable woman from afar, removed all deformity from her face. For when her mistress returned, she found her so completely healed and free of every deformity that not even a mark of her former affliction remained on her face. This miracle also occurred on the day of the saints’ birth [feast day].

## CHAPTER XVIII

There was another man named Freosbaldus, from Bonn, who had accumulated considerable wealth among his people—for he devoted himself to conducting business—but was oppressed by such severe weakness of his limbs that he was thought to be nothing other than paralytic. Bereft of the healthy use of his entire body, he used the steps of attendants rather than his own. [Col. 0678A]

Having heard of the saints’ power, which they conferred through their prayers upon the infirm, he asked to be carried to their memorial, so that they might grant him, as they had granted others, the aid of health.

Accordingly, he was carried there in a vehicle, since, as I have said, he could not come in any other way. When, however, after fulfilling his vows, he did not feel the requested strength returning to him, he had himself carried back to the place from which he had come, without abandoning hope in the saints’ power, intending to return again at a suitable time.

But the holy martyrs, not forgetting the faith of the man who was departing, wished to show that they could aid people through their prayers not only when present but also when absent. They therefore deigned to be present to him with their customary power. While the attendants were traveling with him, the sick man felt the saints’ power gradually coming to him through their merits.

When he reached home and was lifted down from the bier, he began to walk with his steps and all his limbs so firmly strengthened that he who had previously lain useless, wasted away by a long illness, was restored through the martyrs’ aid to usefulness in every respect.

Thus, praising and blessing God, [Col. 0678B] he received from him, through his saints, the health divinely granted to him, and to this day he enjoys the power he obtained.

## CHAPTER XIX

There was likewise a man from the household of Saint Peter, named Daguinus, in a village called Albiniacum. In the same year in which the sacred bodies were buried, his legs became so contracted that he could not walk at all. Remaining lame for the entire year, he crawled on his knees and hands.

He was carried by wagon to the holy place and, crawling, dragged himself through the church for three days, often sitting in the crypt near the saints’ memorial. On the fourth night, after the night offices had been rung, he was present as usual. When they were finished, the custodian ordered him to leave the church for a time. Obeying his command, he dragged himself into the vestibule of the church.

But, prevented by the excessive wind from sitting there, he went into another portico that led through the church to the hospice of the poor, and threw himself down at the entrance of the church. [Col. 0678C] After he had lain there for some time, he saw—as he himself related—two exceedingly handsome boys dressed in white emerge through the same doorway and proceed toward the guesthouse. After remaining there briefly, they returned through the same portico. As they entered the church, one of them touched his shoulder and said to him: “Rise, for you have been healed, and go to your lodging.”

He immediately awoke healthy, gave praise and thanks to God, who had healed him through his saints, so that he who had come in a vehicle proceeded to his own home on his own feet.

## CHAPTER XX

There was a certain little boy from the household of blessed Peter, namely, of the New Monastery, named Berefridus. His eyes were so filled with the darkness of blindness that, with light entirely denied him, he was led and guided by another.

When the day of the Lord’s Nativity arrived, his father—who, like his son, was called Berefridus—decided that the boy should be brought to the memorial of the illustrious saints. When the time arrived at which the nocturnal vigils were celebrated according to custom, he was laid in the crypt at the martyrs’ feet, there to await, through the saints’ prayers, the power of the Lord Savior.

When the vigils had been completed, the boy was carried back to the hospice of the poor, intending to return to the tomb in good hope when morning came. But the mercy of the Lord Redeemer, through the aid of the holy martyrs, unexpectedly came to him in the place of rest.

For when day had dawned and he rose from his bed, he began to see everything so clearly that, walking without stumbling before everyone’s eyes, he hurried to the basilica of the saints, giving thanks to him who rose on that day in the darkness for the upright in heart, and who, through the merits of those same saints, had enabled him to recover the sight of his eyes.

## CHAPTER XXI

Not far from the possession of the aforementioned monastery there is a village that antiquity chose to call Taberna. In it there was a certain man named Alvodus. Paralysis had so completely taken possession of his whole body [Col. 0679A] that, with nearly all his limbs dissolved in weakness, he could scarcely endure another person’s touch.

Accordingly, like that paralytic in the Gospel, he was carried by the hands of attendants to the saints’ memorial. In a short time divine mercy, through the martyrs’ aid, restored him so completely that, with his limbs made firm, he was carried home rejoicing and blessing God—he who had come on the feet of others.

## CHAPTER XXII

Another man from the same village, named Hibaldus, had been condemned to deprivation of the common light. When he heard that, through the martyrs’ power, his fellow villager had recovered the former strength of his paralyzed limbs, he was strengthened by hope and asked his brother to take him there.

His brother, moved both by his sibling’s blindness and by his confidence in the saints’ merits, began to travel with him toward the place. As an indication of the salvation that was to come, he who was being carried by another’s service began to move with remarkable agility.

When they were not far from the place, so that the ridge of the church could be seen, the brother slowed his following steps slightly and said: “Brother, if the power of sight were assisting you, surely you could see the roof and walls of the saints’ church.”

The blind man, silently imploring divine aid for himself through the martyrs’ prayers, began, in a marvelous manner, to see a little as the darkness was driven away. He marked the places in his mind, pointing them out with his finger.

When he reached the saints’ tomb, within a few days he recovered his former health so completely that he regained not only the full integrity of his sight but also the size of his eyes. These had become so small through the long blindness of the darkness that scarcely any pupil could be seen in them.

## CHAPTER XXIII

I shall add another miracle not greatly different from this one. A certain woman, likewise blind continuously, was tormented by the anguish of extreme despair. As she approached the place, she offered God and the holy martyrs a rope that she had made. If that rope were not suitable, she asked the custodian to give her its form, so that, on returning home, she could prepare an appropriate one.

Meanwhile, while the custodian delayed in tying it, she ordered the man guiding her steps to take her to the place where the signal-ropes were hanging, for she wished to weave her own rope for the same purpose.

And so it happened. As she felt the thickness of the rope with her hand, God’s magnificent power shone forth around the unfortunate woman, and with marvelous speed the blindness that obstructed her eyes departed, so that in the same instant she grasped the rope and recovered the clarity of light.

Rejoicing and exulting, she returned to the martyrs’ memorial and, as was fitting, offered them praises of thanksgiving, because divine mercy had deigned, through their intervention, to look upon her.

## CHAPTER XXIV

At the time when the relics of the saints were deposited in the place so often mentioned, there were in a village called Crupta two people joined by the bond of the flesh: one was named Wilhelmus and the other Engilsuindis. From the time of their union until then, they had always lived strengthened by good health.

At that time, however, something different occurred, and both were wearied by illness. For from the kidneys downward the severity of the disease consumed their entire lower bodies so completely that, unless they were carried by the hands of attendants, they could not move from the spot even under pressing necessity.

When frequent reports of the saints’ power and miracles spread everywhere and also filled the inhabitants of the aforesaid village, all of them, stirred by this report and having made an agreement, prepared to go together to the place to pray.

The two people already named, learning of the religious intention of their neighbors, desired to go in spirit, although they were unable to do so bodily. Taking wax and making candles, they arranged for their relatives and kinsmen to send them to the blessed martyrs’ memorial, so that, through the saints’ intervention, the mercy of the Redeemer might deign to assist their weakness.

While they were making these preparations, divine mercy shone wonderfully around them. Before they had even moved from the place, God’s power came to them more quickly than words can tell, so that at the same moment they rose completely healthy and set out on the journey with the others. They who had been going to seek health for others with their mouths themselves, through the glorious merits of the saints’ intercession, were enabled to carry out their vows in person.

## CHAPTER XXV

A certain woman from the region of the Ardennes, named Immina, from a village called Binuzfelt, had long been deaf and mute and was also weak in her hands. She came to the holy place to pray, accompanied by her neighbors and with the permission of her mistress, named Teotburga. After remaining there for an entire day, as soon as she began to return she first recovered the use of one hand, together with the faculties of speech and hearing. Then she obtained the use of the other hand as well as health of her entire body, so completely that even to this day her neighbors and relatives testify that she had never been healthy for a long period in the past as she was then.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Likewise, another woman who had seen the preceding woman in the illness described above, and who had accompanied her to the holy place and witnessed her healing, was named Grimilt. When her husband told her of the former woman’s recovery—a recovery she had seen with her own eyes—she asked to be permitted to come again to pray, but she did not obtain permission at that time.

At the very hour, as was later discovered, when the Mass of the Lord’s Day began to be celebrated in the monastery of the blessed martyrs, which Grimilt had vowed to attend, she was struck by weakness of the hands and heaviness of her entire body, so that, unable to walk, she had to be carried again to the monastery on a cart.

When she arrived and prayed for some time at the martyrs’ memorial, one of her hands was first released in the church. Then, while she was eating, the use of her other hand and the health of her entire body were restored. Thus she who had previously been the narrator of another woman’s healing afterward became both the possessor and the witness of her own.

## CHAPTER XXVII

It is the custom of the place that, on the day of the Easter solemnity, the clerics, [Note: [Col. 0679D] Two things should be noted here. First, as has often already been observed, the monks are here called “clerics.” Second, even at that time it was customary among monks, on solemn days, to wear not only white garments, as is done among us, but also other ornaments.] when celebrating the evening office, should be dressed in sacred vestments, as they are during the celebration of Mass.

It happened, therefore, that the custodian, dressed according to custom with the others, went out from the church to light the lamps. But as he proceeded carelessly, while he was standing beneath the lamps, the oil of a lamp fell and stained, not without disfigurement, part of the cloth with which he happened to be dressed.

The terrified custodian immediately withdrew to the sacristy, took off the garment, and, not without suitable faith, placed it there, saying: “Holy Daria, if you are able, restore this through your prayers.”

On the following day the custodian came to send the garment he had deposited to skilled women who could repair such a defect. But when he examined it carefully, he could not find on it even a slight stain that could have brought dishonor or loss.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

There is a village not far from the monastery’s possession called Wisa. Its inhabitants had all agreed to hurry together to the place. So that they would not seem to come empty-handed, they had, after making a collection, filled a vessel called a *cupa* with beer, intending also to fulfill their vows to God and the holy martyrs by offering a gift.

When they were already preparing to set out, they decided, after taking counsel, to test the quality of the drink before beginning their journey. They made a small opening, but not even a drop could be poured through it. Thinking that this had been done sluggishly by the servant, they chose another man to take his place, so that, after boring through the bottom of the *cupa*, he might draw out the drink.

When others succeeded one another and all their labor was completely frustrated, they came to their senses and realized that the drink had been prepared on that night which is called the Lord’s Day.

Recognizing their guilt and repenting of their sacrilege, they vowed to God and the blessed martyrs that they would never again attempt such a thing on that night, and that they would distribute the drink itself to the needy and the poor. As soon as the vow had been made, the drink began to flow out most abundantly through all the openings.

After distributing it to the needy in fulfillment of their vow and preparing another supply, they came, as they had planned, to the saints’ memorial. There they confessed the guilt of their offense and, having fulfilled their vows, returned home.

# A.D. 770. AENEAS, BISHOP OF PARIS

[Col. 0681]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(From Gallia Christiana.)*

[Col. 0681A] After Erchanrad’s death, the clergy of Paris and the unanimous community of the monasteries elected Aeneas, who had been proposed by King Charles. He was an outstanding herald of the divine word and a distinguished professor in the palace schools under Charles the Bald; at that time he was notary of the sacred palace, or, which is the same thing, chancellor.

Under this title he subscribed the charters granted by Charles for the monastery of Fosses on the seventh day before the Ides of October, in the eighth indiction and the sixth year of Charles’s reign, as well as the acts of the councils of Quierzy in 849 and Soissons in 853, although he was not yet a bishop.

They informed Wenilo, metropolitan of Sens, and the other bishops of the province of the election that had thus been completed, in a letter preserved among the letters of Lupus of Ferrières (letter 98). At the same time, they earnestly begged them, by responding as quickly as possible to their wishes, to set the lamp swiftly upon the lampstand.

The bishops responded to the wishes of the Parisian clergy, adorned the elected man with lavish praise, and unanimously subscribed to his ordination. For this purpose Archbishop Wenilo summoned the bishops of the province (letter 99 among the letters of the same Lupus).

But Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, unable to be present because of the known illnesses by which he was afflicted, sent a presbyter to act in his place and give his assent to the ordination, provided that Aeneas subscribed to four articles in which he believed the pure teaching of Saint Augustine to be contained. See Prudentius’s tractatoria letter among his works (*Patrologia*, vol. CXVIII).

The ancient documents do not tell us whether Aeneas subscribed, nor in exactly what year he was elected and ordained bishop. It is well established, however, that he took part in the synod held at Quierzy in November 858, in whose letter to Louis, king of Germany, the Fathers call him “the honorable bishop.”

Always devoted to King Charles, he not only publicly rebuked Louis for violating the treaty and trampling upon fraternal friendship, but also, at the council held at Saponaria in 859, did not fear to pass judgment on the metropolitan bishop of his own province, who had favored Louis’s invasion.

He attended the council held at Tusiacum in October 860 (*Councils*, Hardouin, vol. V, col. 490). Behold, now for the third time, in January 861, the Danes invaded Paris, gave it over to fire, and burned the church of Saint Germanus; they devastated everything around as far as the fortress of Melun.

In the same year, on the day before the Ides of July, in the twenty-second year of his reign, Charles the Bald subjected to the authority of Aeneas and his successors the great bridge that he had recently built over the territory of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, together with the road leading to the bridge (*History of the Church of Paris*, vol. I, p. 460).

At the council of Pîtres in 862, Aeneas subscribed the privilege that the bishops confirmed for the monastery of Saint-Denis, previously granted by Landeric, and another privilege for the church of Saint Martin of Tours (ibid., p. 431).

He attended the council of Soissons in the same year. There, in place of Rothadus, bishop of Soissons, another was substituted, and another privilege was granted to the monks of Saint-Denis at the request of Abbot Louis. Ormundus the deacon subscribed it on behalf of Aeneas, and Aeneas himself subscribed afterward (ibid., pp. 433–434).

When the body of Saint Germanus, after the Normans had been driven from the kingdom, was carried back to the city of Paris from the village of Novigentum in 863, Aeneas went out to meet it with the canons (ibid., p. 469).

He also attended another council of Soissons on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September [17 August] 866 and subscribed the synodal letter of the prelates to Pope Nicholas on the eighth day before the Kalends of September [25 August], as well as another of their letters to the supreme pontiff concerning the Breton bishops, dated the eighth day before the Ides of December [6 December] of the same year.

He subscribed the privilege granted to the monastery of Arras at the council of Vermer in that same year. In 867, when Aeneas petitioned him, King Charles returned to that city a certain island on its eastern side, adjoining it and nearer to the church of Blessed Mary, which had formerly been subject to a count. [Col. 0682B] The writ was issued on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April], in the twenty-seventh year of the king’s reign.

He attended the synod of Troyes on the eighth day before the Kalends of November [25 October] and subscribed the synodal letter to Pope Nicholas concerning the second expulsion of Ebo and the ordination of Hincmar.

About this time, delegated by the province of Sens and at the command and request of Pope Nicholas I, he refuted, in a learned and scholarly work, the slanders and insults of Photius against the Latin Church. The work was published in volume VII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 1.

In 868, King Charles returned to Aeneas the village of Nantriacum, situated in the region of Poitiers beside the river Clain. The diploma was issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April [18 March], in the twenty-eighth year of the king’s reign (ibid., p. 462).

In the same year, by order of the king, Aeneas went to the monastery of Fosses to receive the body of Saint Maurus. The king wished it to be brought from the estate of Count Audo, beside the Saône, to which the monks had transported it out of fear of the Danes, and returned to Fosses [Col. 0682C] (*Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, part II, p. 168).

On 7 April he carried the bier on his shoulders, solemnly brought it into the church of Blessed Peter, and placed it upon the altar of the Holy Apostles. For this reason, he granted one prebend in the Parisian church to the monastery of Fosses and established an annual procession (*Chartularium*, XIV, col. 13).

As usual, Launoius attempted wrongly to diminish the credibility of this donation, but Gerard du Bois will show better how futile the arguments he offers are (*History of the Church of Paris*, vol. I, p. 449).

Aeneas was present in 869 at the synod at Vermer, [Col. 0683A] where the case of Hincmar of Laon was first heard, and he subscribed the privileges of the monasteries of Carrofensis and Saint Vaast.

In the same year a synod was held at Pîtres. There, responding to the wishes of the metropolitan Egilo, Aeneas ratified the royal privilege that Egilo had obtained for the monastery of Saint Peter the Living, in which he had chosen his burial place.

In 870 Aeneas attended the council at Attigny, where the case of Hincmar of Laon was again heard, as is clear from chapter 33 of the synod of Douzy.

The old necrology of the monastery of Saint Germanus records the death of Aeneas of Paris on the sixth day before the Kalends of January [27 December]. Since Aeneas therefore attended the council of Attigny in 870, while his successor Ingelwinus attended that of Douzy in 871, it follows that Aeneas died on the sixth day before the Kalends of January in that same year.

In volume VIII of the councils of Labbe, appendix, p. [Col. 0684A] 1898, there are two letters, one from Hincmar to Aeneas and one from Aeneas to Hincmar. In the first, Hincmar asks Aeneas to allow a certain young man named Berno, entrusted to him by the abbot of Saint-Denis and already made an acolyte by Aeneas, to remain in his church for canonical instruction and be regularly ordained. Aeneas replied, but only the beginning of his response survives.

In another letter, Lupus of Ferrières, letter 119, commends to Aeneas the son of his niece, asking him to grant the young man a military benefice.

Although the arguments presented above sufficiently demonstrate Aeneas’s distinction in piety and faith alike, certain people nevertheless dared to undermine his memory. Gerard du Bois refutes them (ibid., p. 458).

[Col. 0683]

# AENEAS OF PARIS, BOOK AGAINST THE GREEKS

*(In Acherius, volume I of the* Spicilegium*.)*

## ACHERIUS’S NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING WORK

[Col. 0683B] This book of Aeneas, bishop of Paris, was recovered from the Thuanean library approximately twelve years ago. In it Aeneas adduces many testimonies both of Greek and of Latin Fathers.

Because of the ancient form of their interpretation, I have left the Greek testimonies intact. But the Latin testimonies, since they were both more extensive and more frequent, I have often abridged so as not to weary the reader, preserving nevertheless their initial and final words and referring the reader to the published works of the Fathers cited.

I compared both kinds of testimony partly with the printed books of the authors and partly with manuscripts, recording variant readings and noting several passages that do not appear in the editions.

During the reign of the emperor Charles the Bald, Aeneas lived, distinguished among the bishops of Gaul for piety and learning. Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, praises him highly in Letter 98, written in the name of the Parisian clergy to Wenilo, archbishop of Sens:

> “Aeneas, whose praises we have set forth above, we all unanimously choose; we desire to have Aeneas as our father, Aeneas as our bishop. For although our most excellent king possesses such great prudence and integrity that his judgment alone concerning the man in question could suffice, nevertheless, not ignorant of the human condition and concerned for the future, we ourselves first examined at length the purpose and conduct of the courtiers; and, among serious and worthy persons fervent in holiness, all of us who were able to know him have, as is now evident, without error numbered this man—whom we desire to have as our bishop.”

And in the reply of Wenilo, metropolitan, and the fellow bishops of the province of Sens, to the clergy of Paris, in Lupus’s Letter 99:

> “Who has lightly touched the palace without becoming acquainted with Aeneas’s labor and witnessing his fervor in divine matters? Therefore, with God’s favor, we gladly accept the election made in his case, and unanimously decree that he is to be promoted to the dignity of bishop, since he will benefit His people. Let him therefore be your shepherd, one who has been well pleasing to God by his merits; and, following his truthful teaching and imitating his holy works, hasten happily to the pastures of the heavenly kingdom.”

The bishops who were present at the synod of Quierzy likewise call Bishop Aeneas “honorable” in their letter to King Louis the German.

You will find one letter of Aeneas and a fragment of another in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 670.

Many writers have mentioned the schism of the Greeks, against whom Aeneas wrote this book: earlier writers such as Pope Nicholas I, in his letter to the bishops of Gaul; Ratramnus of Corbie, who composed four books against the objections of the Greeks; Frodoard, in Book I, chapter 17, of his *Ecclesiastical History of Rheims*; and more recent writers such as Baronius in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, and others. In our preliminary notice to Ratramnus, we too did not think it necessary to repeat here much of what must be said about it.

[Col. 0684C] Moreover, reader, observe that I was not wrong to attribute to Isidore of Seville the book *On the Order of Created Things*, which we publish in this *Spicilegium* and which Aeneas cites in chapter 94, even though none of those whom I have so far read remembers this work. I was guided only by the title of the manuscript: Aeneas, however, is an ancient and weighty authority, whose testimony I think should be accepted.

This is what Acherius wrote. His copyist, however, misled him in quite a few places. For when Baluzius, a man of distinction, later consulted the very manuscript that Acherius had used, he discovered, astonishingly often, that the reading embedded in the text was false and had been fabricated by the copyist. We have corrected the text with as much care as we could. Although we wished to provide examples of this care at the beginning of the work, it subsequently seemed less necessary to record each instance.

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

[Col. 0685]

[Col. 0685A] Aeneas, bishop of the city of Paris, over which Saint Dionysius first presided—consecrated archbishop of the Athenians by the apostle Paul, but appointed apostle of all Gaul by Saint Clement—sends peace and glory to the worshipers of the Catholic faith.

We read in the Book of Judges (chapter III) that divine foreknowledge permitted remnants of the Canaanites to remain in the renowned land promised to the seed of Abraham in reward for his immense faith, so that Israel might be tested by them and, perhaps, might not grow idle and ignorant of warfare. Its effective valor, with God leading the way, had previously won for itself by arms an outstanding kingdom, worthy of proclamation throughout all ages.

By this balance of equity, the Lord of heavenly, earthly, and infernal things wished to test with a victor’s laurel the holy Church—without spot or wrinkle, solemnly betrothed to Himself by royal right through the ring of His Passion—when she was assailed by the assertions of heretical depravity: as though standing in battle array and drawing her hands together for war, delighting in the embrace of her Bridegroom because of her repeated victories over her adversaries, she might exult greatly in the triumph that had been accomplished.

[Note: [Col. 0685D] “After the triumph had been accomplished.” This is how it is read in the manuscript, and I do not sufficiently know why Acherius wrote “with the triumph being open.”]

Rising to the wars of God through continual struggle, adorned with the knowledge of resistance and endowed with beauty, she might learn to repel powerfully those who attacked her with poisoned weapons, crying aloud to Him who crushed the helmeted head of the water-snake and acting confidently:

> “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me. Take up arms and shield, and rise to my assistance” (Psalm XXXIV, 1).

Thus, when enemies repeatedly defeated dare shamefully and disgracefully to renew their struggles, they are ground down even more miserably by the mouths of the great because of their sluggishness and worse reputation. They strive to raise themselves to loftier heights by means of cunning plots, but, as though weakened in strength and turning their backs, they fall disgracefully.

Thus, indeed, the poisonous destruction of perverse doctrine, wickedly sprouting from the Church’s beginning until the present, does not cease to creep forward: it seeks to seize the unwary, corrupt the peaceful through its teaching, attack secretly like a robber those who live well, and cunningly transform truth into falsehood.

But the holy Church, now almost wearied by old age, raises hands of intercession to the Lord with Moses, on behalf of her people, so that they may conquer. And Aaron and Hur fittingly support her weary hands—that is, the succession of the New and Old Testaments. The testimony of holy defenses quickly presents itself openly, lest those whom she has nourished catholicly and raised to the summit of perfection should yield to the arrows of their attackers. Rather, resisting manfully with the shield of truth, they should joyfully proclaim to the Lord of hosts and King of glory:

> “Let us sing to the Lord, for He has been gloriously magnified: horse and rider He has cast into the sea” (Exodus XV, 1).

Thus, in the time of the glorious and orthodox emperor Louis, Greece—which insists on being called the mother of words, the begetter of philosophers, and the patroness of all the liberal arts—attempted to consult the Roman Church, indeed the entire people who use the Latin language, about these superfluous superstitions. It is astonishing that she should occupy herself with such worthless questions, debated through a long age and clearly and fully elucidated, while she boasts that she is the source of all learning and eloquence, as though she were demanding the entire sea of dialectical subtlety and thought herself able to distinguish truth from falsehood reliably.

Therefore, as the Apostle, caught up to the third heaven, thunders: “If Jews seek signs and Greeks seek wisdom” (I Cor. III, 22), why does the sagacity of those who drink from the pure fountain cling to this? Why does dullness of understanding, by asking contemptible questions while attempting to grasp sublime things, shamefully darken those whom—so they falsely suppose—the summit of great intellect embraces and nurtures, flashing like lightning in the lap of its vastness?

Indeed, when the peoples of the East, as though seated especially beneath the Lord’s footstool, appear to dispute with Westerners concerning the articles of faith, it is as if the most beautiful sun, placed in the East at morning, were turning the rays of its light toward the West into darkness at evening.

Yet the climates of heaven do not make the dispositions of mortals worse, nor should the heavenly regions be blamed for the madness of various sects, since East and West alike contain both the just and the reprobate. Rather, humanity, created good at the beginning and powerfully established in free will, deserved to be moved from the right to the left by neglecting the Creator and obeying the deceiver. From then onward, the world began to yearn for a deviating path through its many byways.

Nor is it so surprising that such great errors should arise from Asia or from the borders of Europe, where Constantinople, the metropolis of Greece, is situated. For if the decrees of the holy canons are reviewed and the sequence of ecclesiastical histories examined, the offspring of vipers will be found to have arisen more from the regions of that kingdom than from those living under Roman rule—that is, very many inventors of perverse doctrines. To mention a few among many: Arius, Eunomius, Photinus, Marcion, Cerinthus, Manichaeus, Hebion, Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, and the other plagues of spreading heresy, who never rested from continually tearing apart and attacking Catholic minds.

Eutychius also, bishop of Constantinople, erred so greatly concerning the Resurrection that he asserted that our body, in the glory of that resurrection, would be intangible, subtler than winds and air.

[Note: [Col. 0685D] “Our body in it.” The reading of the manuscript is excellent and faithful: Acherius has “our body” in several places, incorrectly and against the Thuanean manuscript.]

But we, on the contrary, say and confirm with holy faith that, in the glory of that resurrection, our body will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but tangible through the truth of its nature.

For blessed Pope Gregory, who had once been stationed in that same city of Constantinople, held a celebrated dispute about this matter with the aforementioned Eutychius in the presence of the emperor Tiberius Constantine, as he himself more fully recalls in the fourteenth book of his *Moralia on Job*. Eutychius was so nobly defeated by him that he held the skin of his hand and said: “I confess that we shall all rise in this flesh”—something he had previously been accustomed to deny entirely.

It is lamentable to say that the same see, which attempts to raise its head toward the heights, once had as its rulers heretics who defiled the teaching of the bishops of the true faith. The *Tripartite History* records them, and the diligence of the holy Fathers condemns them in the canons.

But in the Roman See, under God’s governance, no such disgrace has ever occurred: no arch-heretic has ever presided over the see that the chief of the apostles illuminated by his presence and consecrated by the shedding of his blood, and to which the Son of God entrusted His sheep to govern with special care. Nor is this surprising, since it had been said to him:

> “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XVI, 18–19).

Therefore, could He who gave him the kingdom by His own authority fail to strengthen his faith? When He calls him “rock,” He indicated the Church’s foundation.

Liberius, however, the thirty-seventh pope after blessed Peter, although he did not deviate from the path of faith, was frightened by exile and the threats of the Arian ruler and did not resist the perfidious Arians manfully with the courage he ought to have shown.

To those who appear to deviate from the citadel of all Christianity and invent new questions, Paul rightly thunders in his Letter to the Galatians, whose origin is propagated from Greece:

> “I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from Him who called you in the grace of Christ Jesus to another gospel—which is not another gospel—except that there are some who trouble you and wish to overturn the gospel of Christ” (Galatians I, 6).

With equally great authority he repeats:

> “But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians I, 6).

And he added immediately:

> “As we said before, and now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed.”

It is therefore rightly that such words are brought apostolically against those who stray from the way of truth, by the ruler of the holy Church. They are also deservedly reproved with this rod of correction:

> “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you, that you should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed and crucified?”

At last, throughout all ages, an enormous offense is generated when those whose teaching ought to adorn the Church, make her flourish with the splendor of religion, and increase her salvation, strive to humble her through the zeal of wickedness. They attempt to inflict stains upon the one from whom every blemish ought to be far removed, so that she may no longer be free from defilement.

But because the holy Apostle says, “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (Psalm XXXIV, 1), the mockeries of deceit that the enemy of holy souls has attempted to bring against her must be repelled by the shield of her Redeemer. The more sacred and powerful divinity of visible and invisible things will not permit itself to be conquered by a creature that was created angelic but, through the swelling of pride, became more wicked of its own accord, without another compelling it, and fell into the abyss of everlasting damnation, desiring nothing except the destruction of the blessed.

For, with the Maker of all things granting it, wickedness will not conquer wisdom. Rather, the one who has always armed His own with spiritual teachings from the beginning will appear victorious in His own people:

> “All who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (II Timothy III, 12).

Thus it is now recognized that an age full of miseries is already present—an age which is perceived to embrace that span of time about which the Apostle foretold with lamentation:

> “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, itching in their ears; and they will indeed turn away their hearing from the truth, but will turn to fables” (II Timothy IV, 3).

Behold, we see these predictions spreading openly. Therefore, while the trumpet of war is sounding, weapons must be fitted to the limbs of the soldiers, lest the treacherous enemy forestall them through trained cunning.

Although the army of the Lord is shaken amid such storms of controversy, it is utterly unworthy that minds ennobled by courage should be twisted from the state of uprightness by heretical depravity. The more fiercely the devil approaches with cunning and savage craft, the more cautiously and readily must the foresight of the strong be fortified.

The Apostle, warning his disciple Timothy lest he be hindered by the snares of the wicked, gently exhorts him:

> “Avoid profane and empty babbling, for they will advance greatly toward ungodliness; and their speech spreads like cancer” (II Timothy II, 17).

He says likewise to Titus:

> “Avoid foolish questions, genealogies, contentions, and disputes about the law, for they are useless and empty” (Titus III, 10).

And, to make him more watchful and better instructed by holy sharpness, he adds:

> “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (ibid., 11).

Therefore, let us believe with holy Elisha that there are more with us than with them: namely, the most discerning Fathers of both Testaments, the most eager and unconquerable warriors for the defense of the true faith. With the most courageous Joshua, they strive to entreat God that the sun may stand still—that is, that the time of holy struggle may shine longer—until the true Israel avenges itself upon its enemies.

[Note: [Col. 0687D] “Of holy struggle.” Here too Baluzius removed the corrupt reading “of holy conduct” after examining, with more accurate eyes than Acherius, the very manuscript by whose aid the earlier edition had been prepared.]

“For God has not called us to uncleanness, but to sanctification” (II Thessalonians IV, 17), says the Apostle, after we have been renewed in the grace of Christ through the water of baptism and the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, we must not yield to our adversaries, but resist manfully, lest we be captured by the allurements of him who, through pride, fell from the heights to the depths and now strives with iniquitous efforts to tear apart the Church, which is the daughter of peace, through corrupt teaching and expose her to the bites of error.

To prevent these and similar things, Paul admonishes Timothy, who burns with love for the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit:

> “Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they generate quarrels” (II Timothy II, 22).

All believers in Christ must generally beware of these things, especially those who are to govern souls and be a mirror of good works and a model of holy virtues.

Hence those who live well must lament: from the very quarters where the honor of joy ought to shine in the holy Church, immense losses through scandal have arisen over the course of many centuries.

If iron is sharpened by iron, it would be fitting for the Greek language not to depart from the truth in which the Latin language holds the rule of the Catholic faith indissolubly.

These, then, are the superfluous questions directed more toward secular than spiritual matters. They do not seem to proceed from the experience of great intellect, but to arise from the reprehensible judgments of outward perception.

That sea, as it is vaunted, of distinguished eloquence brings these matters before Roman ears: Why do we profess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and not from the Father alone? Again, why do we fast on Saturdays? And why do we exclude marriage from the office of priests?

They also ask why Latin priests are forbidden to anoint the foreheads of the baptized with chrism, since the place for signing on the forehead properly belongs to bishops, and that on the crown of the head to priests.

Likewise, they inquire why, according to our custom, we do not abstain from eating meat for eight weeks before Easter, and from cheese and eggs for seven weeks.

They further object to why clerics shave their beards, and why deacons who have not yet received the office of the priesthood are ordained bishops, as is sometimes the Roman custom.

[Note: [Col. 0689C] “Are ordained bishops.” This is not a bad reading; but since the manuscript reads *in epm*, I do not know whether *in episcopatum*—“into the episcopate”—might be more correct. Here the reader should note that Aeneas refutes the same objections of the Greeks that we have seen Ratramnus refute with the greatest force above.]

They also complain about the transfer of the primacy of the Roman See, which they say was made to Constantinople, and therefore call it, together with its patriarch, the head of dignity.

To complete the heap and dullness of foolish absurdities, they prattle and inquire why we prepare our chrism—or rather, God’s chrism—from river water, and why at Easter we place a lamb together with the body and blood of Christ upon the altar and offer it in the manner of the Jews, although no one, not even any fool, has ever believed these things.

These two matters in particular seem so utterly unworthy that, in the judgment of the faithful, they should be completely excluded from hearing.

Greek cunning spreads these ravings throughout the Roman empire with haughty pretension. Standing against the Lord’s battle-lines and pouring forth from crafty deceit, it strives to provoke the peaceful.

But opposed to the leaders of those who undertake unjust things stand the armies of the heavenly powers. Indeed, the illustrious defense of the Fathers, the harmony of the canons, and the authority and victory of the most excellent bishops—proclaimed magnificently throughout the bounds of the Christian name and touching heaven by word and teaching—display from afar the shield of holy resistance.

In this brave encounter, raw recruits will not carry the standards, nor will exhausted old veterans raise their weary arms. Rather, a chosen youth, that is, those employing the most perfect understanding in the faith of Christ, will advance to glorious wars, bearing bodies and minds armed on every side with the weapons of sacred doctrines, and, with the Lord’s favor, will emerge victorious.

When the triumphal contest has been completed and the breath of the Holy Spirit supplies refreshment to the weary as though to exhausted limbs, the most glorious soldiers, having obtained their desire and rejoicing exceedingly because of the struggle, will raise their radiant faces toward heaven and acclaim praises to their King of kings and Lord:

> “The Lord is strong and powerful, the Lord powerful in battle” (Psalm XXIII, 8).

And:

> “The Lord of hosts is Himself the King of glory” (ibid., 10).

Then the Father of the entire Church—that is, the most blessed pontiff of the apostolic See—will rejoice and, raising his head on high with the apostle Paul, solemnly sound forth these words to God his protector:

> “But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the nations might hear; and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion. The Lord delivered me from every evil work and will save me for His heavenly kingdom. To Him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (II Timothy IV, 17).

## THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0689]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0689D]

Saint Athanasius, bishop of the Alexandrian See, highly experienced in the Greek language—the see over which the blessed evangelist Mark presided, and which, according to the decrees of the canons, is second after the first, the Roman See—says in his book *On the Unity of the Holy and Undivided Trinity* that the Son and the Holy Spirit are in the Father, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Father, without in any way excluding the name of the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0689] “In the book *On*.” In the published editions, the title of this book, which is *On the Unity of God*, is *On the Arian and Catholic Faith*.]

> “Christ the Son must therefore be served, because He is both perfect God and the true Son. Whoever faithfully serves the Son serves the Father and the Holy Spirit who is in Him. Whoever worships the Father worships in Him the Son and the Holy Spirit, because the Son and the Holy Spirit who proceeds from God are in the Father, as the Lord Himself says: ‘I am in the Father and the Father is in me’ (John XIV, 10).
>
> “Concerning the Spirit He likewise says: ‘The Paraclete Spirit who proceeds from my Father’ (John XV, 26).
>
> “When someone worships the Son, he worships in Him the Father and the Holy Spirit, because the Father is in Him. He says: ‘Whoever sees me sees my Father also’ (John X, 9); and again: ‘The Father, remaining in me, Himself does the works’ (ibid.).
>
> “Concerning the Holy Spirit He says: ‘He,’ He says, ‘has glorified me, because He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you’ (John XVI, 14); and: ‘Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said to you that He will receive from what is mine’ (ibid., 15).
>
> “The Spirit of the Father is therefore the Spirit of the Son, as the Apostle says: ‘Because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts’ (Galatians IV, 6); and again: ‘If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Him’ (Romans VIII, 9); and again: ‘For I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the assistance of the Spirit of Jesus Christ’ (Philippians I, 19).
>
> “In the Gospel the Lord Himself also says: ‘The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name’ (John XIV, 26).
>
> “And in the Acts of the Apostles we read: ‘As they passed through Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word. When they had come to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them’ (Acts XVI).
>
> “Therefore, by the clearest testimonies it is proved that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete Spirit, the Spirit who proceeds from the Father, is the Spirit of the Son, the Spirit of Christ, the Spirit of Jesus.”

## CHAPTER II

Saint Athanasius likewise says in his book [Note: [Col. 0691D] “On the Unity of the Trinity.” In Greek, *On the Unity of God*.] *On the Unity of the Trinity* that the Holy Spirit is the one God united in the Father and the Son:

> “Do you not know that the Father is one God, the Son is one God, and the Spirit is one God? Is there not one God, since the name is one in the nature of the οὐσία—that is, the substance? So also there is one Spirit, because His divinity is one.
>
> “For if, through the individual names of the persons, you have designated the one name ‘Spirit’ three times, ought one therefore to say that there are three Spirits? Certainly not. If this could be said, then it would likewise be necessary to introduce into the confession that three gods should be named in the plural, so that the nature of divinity would no longer be united in these persons, but each would exist in its own or different nature. May this never be.
>
> “Meanwhile, I repeat the same point and compare it with your words, and I report to you the meaning of my understanding: the Father is one God, the only-begotten Son is God, and the Holy Spirit, united in the Father and the Son, is God.”

[Note: [Col. 0691D] “United in these persons.” Acherius notes that elsewhere he found *in his one*—“one in these”—which he prefers. Below I reveal to you the understanding of my text.]

## CHAPTER III

The same author, in the same book, says that the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but, existing from the united nature, proceeds from God the Father and receives from the Son of God:

> “The blessed evangelist John says in his Epistle: ‘There are three who testify in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, and in Christ Jesus they are one’ (I John V).
>
> “Yet they are not one, because there is not one person in them. For when he said “one” of the two, what else is understood than that God the Father is called the selfsame Lord in the nature of divinity, and is likewise the selfsame Spirit; and that the Son is God, and likewise is Lord in divinity, and likewise is Spirit?
>
> [Note: [Col. 0691D] “And likewise is the Spirit.” Acherius notes that he found this reading elsewhere. In the text it read *sit in deitate*—“be in divinity”—which was not altogether bad, but it is sufficiently clear that the final two words are superfluous.]
>
> “The Paraclete Spirit also is God, and likewise is Lord in the nature of divinity; the Spirit is likewise the same. You see that in divinity and in the substance of fullness they are one in every respect, while in the persons there are three.
>
> “For what else is understood by their being three than that the one true Father, or the only one who begot, is not the same as the only-begotten who is from Him? And that the one Son, who did not beget but, as He Himself is, was begotten by the Father, is not the Father? And that this Holy Spirit is another, who is neither Father nor Son, who neither begot nor was begotten?
>
> “One person is He who begot, another person is the only-begotten who is from Him, and another person, as I have said, according to divine Scripture, is neither Father nor Son: this is the Holy Spirit. But He is plainly from the united nature; therefore His divinity is united.

[Note: [Col. 0691D] “The united name of divinity.” Acherius reports that elsewhere, instead of these words, he found “the common name belongs to Him.” Below, the words enclosed in brackets [Col. 0692D] have been added from an old published version. Shortly afterward, where the text read *in deitate divinitatis*—“in the divinity of divinity”—we have removed the final word, following the authority of the same old published version. It should also be noted that Acherius printed *divinitas*—“divinity”—in almost every place where we print *deitas*—“godhead.” He did this against his own manuscript and also against the authority of the ancients, who preferred the word *deitas*, as we learn from Anselm of Havelberg, *Dialogue*, Book II, chapter 17: “of the whole divinity, or, if it may better be said, godhead,” and so forth.]

> “The united name of divinity is one, just as, in the brightness of the Gospel Scripture, the Son testifies concerning the Paraclete Spirit, saying: ‘He proceeds from the Father’ (John XV, 26); and He continues: ‘He will receive from what is mine’ (John XVI, 14).
>
> “Therefore, wherever the persons are being considered, they are distinguished by their proper names. But wherever the divinity is being considered, the united name is indicated [in these]. Since we are speaking of the names of the persons in the plural, it is shown that in united divinity they are one, while in the names of the persons they are three.”

## CHAPTER IV

The same author, in the second book, concerning the proper persons and the united name of divinity, says that the Holy Spirit, just as He is sent by the Father, is likewise sent by the Son:

> “If the Son came in the name of the Father, is He Himself the Father who says, ‘I came in the name of my Father’ (John V), since the Father is God in whose name the Son plainly came?
>
> “Accordingly, in the united nature of divinity, one name is established, just as the Father Himself testified to the lawgiver Moses, saying: ‘Pay attention to Him, and do not be disobedient, for my name is in Him’ (Exodus XXIII, 19).
>
> “The patriarch David likewise says: ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord’ (Psalm CXVII).
>
> “And if the Paraclete Spirit came in the name of the Son, as He Himself says, ‘Whom the Father will send in my name,’ was He therefore called the Son Himself, although without doubt the name ‘Son’ is God in the one united nature of divinity? In this name, then, the Paraclete plainly came.
>
> “Therefore, according to each person, the united name has been declared to you in accordance with the substance of the nature of the Trinity.
>
> “The holy Isaiah, approving this, said: ‘The Spirit descended from God and led them out; thus You led out Your people to make for Yourself a name of glory’ (Isaiah LXIII).
>
> “The same prophet also indicates this: ‘They provoked the Holy Spirit, and He was turned against them as an enemy; the Lord Himself fought against them and remembered the days of old, He who led the shepherd of the sheep out of the land.’ And he added: ‘Where is He who placed His Spirit among them?’
>
> “You see, therefore, that this Lord, the Holy Spirit, is the glory of the Father and the Son according to the united name of the nature of divinity. He led the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt, as the Prophet says: ‘Thus You led out Your people to make for Yourself a name of glory,’ and He was turned against the sons of Israel as an enemy (Exodus XIII).”

## CHAPTER V

The same author, in the same book, says that the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father together with the Son:

> “But if the Paraclete Spirit had come only in His own name—that is, in the name called ‘Paraclete Spirit’—and not in the united substance of the Father and the Son, which is called God, then His own name would already appear to belong to Him according to His person, and not according to the united nature of divinity in both. Thus each person would display only individual names, while the united name of divinity would not be indicated.
>
> “But in this united name of the divinity of the Father came the true Son, in whom God is spoken of, in whom the name of glory is with the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0693] “In whom is charity.” Elsewhere the reading is “in whom He is the same in nature as the Father.”]

> “The Paraclete Spirit also came in the name of this nature, because in this most holy Trinity this name exists substantially, or in unity, just as I said above when the Father indicated concerning His Son: ‘My name is in Him’ (Exodus XXIII, 19).
>
> “The Son confirms these words: ‘I came in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me. When another comes in his own name, you will receive him’ (John XIV, 26).
>
> “And concerning the Holy Spirit He repeats the same thing: ‘Whom my Father will send in my name.’
>
> “Then hear Him exhorting the disciples concerning His own name: ‘Whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give you’ (Mark XI).
>
> “The Apostle Paul likewise bears witness to the same thing: ‘But you have been washed, but you have been sanctified, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God’ (I Corinthians VI).
>
> “Hear Isaiah declaring the united name of the glory of the Holy Spirit: ‘The Spirit descended from God and led them out; thus You led out Your people to make for Yourself a name of glory.’
>
> “Learn now that the name is united in the nature of the divine Trinity.”

## CHAPTER VI

The same author, in the same book, proclaims that the Paraclete Spirit is sent by the Father together with the Son:

> “In this matter the Father is indeed one person, who truly begot; and in this matter the Son is another person, who was truly begotten by the Father. But in this matter the principal Paraclete Spirit is another person, from the Father and the Son, who was poured out upon the apostles at Pentecost.
>
> “Therefore remember that these things are stated separately, so that the individual names might be distinct in the persons. You see that one differs from another, or one person from another, only in person and not in the fullness of the divinity of the οὐσία—that is, the substance—just as the Lord Himself says: ‘Another is He who bears witness concerning me, the Father who sent me’ (John V).
>
> “In another place the same Lord indicates the person of the Holy Spirit: ‘I will ask my Father, and He will send you another Paraclete’ (ibid., 14).
>
> “Know that one differs from another, or the one from the other, only in person, and not in the united fullness of the divinity of the οὐσία.”

## CHAPTER VII

The same author, in the same book, speaks as follows concerning the common sending of the Holy Spirit by the Father and the Son:

> “Therefore, if the Son came in the name of the Father, and the Paraclete Spirit came in the name of the Son, as the Son testifies concerning Him: ‘Whom the Father will send in my name’ (John XIV, 26), does it not seem to you that a twofold meaning is also contained here: namely, that there is distinction only in the name of the persons, while in divinity there is no distinction?”

## CHAPTER VIII
The same author, in this present book, says that the Holy Spirit is sent by God the Father and likewise by the Son of God, and that there is one power in them:

> “For concerning the person of the Holy Spirit the Son bears witness, saying: ‘Whom the Father will send in my name’ (ibid.). You see that the Son came in this name, which is also shown to exist unitedly in the Father’s divinity. And it is indicated that the Holy Spirit came in this name; while the apostles were sent to baptize all nations in the united or common name of the Godhead, which belongs to the invisible nature of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0694D] as it is written: ‘Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of your redemption’ (Gal. IV, 30). Or this: ‘And we were all given to drink of one Spirit’ (I Cor. XII, 13). Or receive the name of unity as it operates in baptism, when he says: ‘And you shall be to me as sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty’ (II Cor. VI, 18). Or accept this: ‘They were born of God’ (John I, 13). And also: ‘Let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ’ (Acts II, 38). And elsewhere: ‘But you were washed, but you were sanctified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God’ (I Cor. VI, 11).

> “John also bears witness that he was born of God: ‘He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name. They were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God’ (John I, 11). Learn, therefore, that this united name is everlasting in the Godhead of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, just as there is also one baptism of faith, which grants eternal life to believers. For just as there is one reality in the nature of the Trinity, so there is also one gift of divinity through baptism. The Apostle says: ‘One faith, one baptism.’ Therefore, because the name of the Father is in the divine nature, this same name is also the name of the Son in the nature of the Godhead; and likewise this name belongs to the Holy Spirit in the substance of glory.”

## Chapter IX

The same author, in the same book, showing the unity of nature between the one who sends and the Son who is sent, says:

> “O writing wholly unheard-of and utterly investigated! Therefore, with the Holy Spirit himself suggesting it, I give my answer concerning him. We must now offer one authoritative example relevant to many things. Remember that the power of nature is one in the sender and the one sent, since the one who has now been sent is found to have formerly sent the sender himself. Finally, through the holy Isaiah, hear the Son of the Lord God bearing witness: ‘Draw near to me and hear these things. From the beginning I have not spoken in secret. When they came to be, I was there; and now the Lord has sent me and his Spirit’ (Isa. XLVIII).

> “Learn at last that the nature of the divinity of the sender and the one sent is one, since the one who in the Gospel testified that he would send the Spirit the Paraclete nevertheless himself confessed, through the renowned prophet Isaiah, that he had previously been sent by him: the one who is sent by the sender is never divided from the sender, because their nature is undivided. Persons are shown to exist between the sender and the one sent, while there is no division in the Godhead, because this united fullness is present everywhere and fills all things within and without, from the summit of the heavens to the depth of the underworld.”

## Chapter X

The same author himself, in the book that he wrote against the objections of a certain Potentinus Urbicus, proceeds as follows:

> **[Note: “In the book which …” The title of this book, which is the fourth *On the Unity of God*, is given in the printed editions as *On the Individual Names*.]**
>
> “The Son,” he says, “cries out to the Father: ‘Father, glorify your name.’ And a voice came from heaven: ‘I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again’ (Luke VII). For elsewhere he himself repeats: ‘I came forth from the Father and came’ (John XVII). Certainly, if the Father and the Son were one person, he ought to have stated it in this way: ‘I came forth from myself and came into this world,’ whereas plainly one is the person who came forth and another is the one from whom he came forth.

> “But to this he added, concerning the person of the Holy Spirit: ‘When that Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father, he will bear witness to me’ (John XVI). Thus, is not the one who sends another, and likewise another in person he from whom he proceeds, and another he himself who comes? Indeed, if there were one person, from whom would he be sent, or from whom would he proceed?

> “The Apostle confirms these things in his greeting to the Corinthians, saying: ‘The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God—that is, of the Father—and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all’ (II Cor. XIII, 13). Did he not plainly distinguish, through the individual names, just as stated above, that individual persons are present?

> “Finally, accept these words of the Son himself: ‘Another is he who bears witness to me, the Father who sent me’ (John V, 32). When below he says of himself ‘another,’ you see that the Father is another person in relation to the Son, but is not another in divinity. And concerning the Holy Spirit he says: ‘I will ask my Father, and he will send you another Paraclete’ (John XIV, 16). Consider that the Spirit the Paraclete is another person, yet is not another in divinity. Therefore one differs from another only in person, and not in the divinity, the *ousia* [οὐσία].

> “Thus the Father is one person, who begot; the Son is another, who was begotten by him; and the Paraclete Spirit is another, who is from the united nature. But you say to me, heretic: How does the Spirit subsist from a united nature? Behold, the Son bore witness concerning him: ‘He proceeds from the Father’; and he continued: ‘And he will take from what is mine.’ The Father confirmed this testimony, saying: ‘The Spirit proceeds from me.’”

## Chapter XI

The same author, in Book V, *On the United and Everlasting Substance of the Trinity*, concerning the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son:

> “The Father’s eternity is his Son, because he was ineffably born from him before every beginning. And the Son’s eternity is his Father, because he himself begot him incomparably before all ages of ages. Thus the eternity of the Paraclete Spirit is his united divinity with the Father and the Son, which was not made, as the Son testified concerning him: ‘He proceeds from the Father, and he will take from what is mine.’ The Father also confirms these words through the prophet, saying: ‘The Spirit proceeds from me.’ And elsewhere: ‘I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh’ (Joel II, 28). Scripture testifies that this was fulfilled at Pentecost upon the apostles.

> “For just as the Father reveals his Son by his divinity, since he is true God, so the Holy Spirit reveals the Father and the Son in his united eternal nature, since he is true God. This united omnipotent eternity is the Trinity, to whose divinity no new dignity has been added.”

## Chapter XII

[Col. 0696D]

The same author, in the same book, concerning the Holy Spirit: that he subsists in the Father and the Son:
