> “The divine substance,” he says, “is neither extended nor stretched out in anything, nor cut into parts; nor is it comparable to the derivation of anything, because there is plainly no fluid in this nature, nor is it a kind of outflow, since it suffers neither loss nor increase. This is especially so because the fullness of the undivided substance of the Trinity is ineffable, as God the Son of God himself indicates: ‘I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.’ The Holy Spirit also subsists in the Father and the Son and in himself, as John the Evangelist testifies so explicitly in his Epistle: ‘And the three are one.’”

## Chapter XIII

The same author, in Book VI, *On the Blessedness of Faith*, concerning the fact that the Holy Spirit subsists unanimously in the power of the foreknowledge of the Father and the Son:

> “Although the united name of the Godhead has been spoken in many ways through the individual persons, what you have attributed to the Father you must confess to exist unitedly in the Son as well: God from God, light from light, whole from whole, and whole in whole, perfect from perfect, fullness from fullness, complete from complete, everlasting from everlasting, wisdom from wisdom, power from power, one from one, and one in one, true from true, Son from Father, born not made, of one substance with the Father.

> “And also the Holy Spirit, who subsists from the one Trinity: true God, true light, wholly perfect, wholly full, complete, everlasting; with the wisdom, power, and foreknowledge of the Father and the Son subsisting in him.”

## Chapter XIV

The same author, in Book VII, *On the Profession of the Catholic Rule*, recalls the Holy Spirit in this way, giving an example from the Psalmist:

> “‘By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power’ (Ps. XXXII, 6). Certainly he declared the Word to be the Son; he indicated that the Lord was his Father; and he demonstrated that the Spirit of his mouth was the principal Spirit. You see how briefly he distinguished, through each designation, that the persons are present: the Word, the Lord, and the Spirit; and he showed that their operation is one.

> “For if ambiguity still holds you in some respect, I repeat the same point. When he says, ‘By the word of the Lord,’ do not understand merely a word without substance, such as an echo commonly resounds from the mountains if someone emits his voice more powerfully—a sound heard only in the imagination of the one who hears the reverberation, but producing nothing. Rather, the divine Scriptures everywhere testify concerning this Word of our Lord and Father, who is our salvation, that the Son of God is God with substance, through whom all things were made.

> “Therefore, because he said, ‘By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power,’ recognize that this substantial Word was born properly from the Father and from no other source. And by ‘the Spirit of his mouth’ he meant the Spirit who proceeded from that same united substance, as we find authoritatively established—not from another nature, but from that very one. Accordingly, the substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is united; the Greeks call this *ousia* [οὐσία]. And the operation of this same Trinity in creation is united.”

## Chapter XV

The same author, in Book VIII, *On the Unity of Faith*, concerning the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son like one flame, concludes excellently in a few words:

> **[Note: “In Book VIII.” Not at all, but in Book X—unless perhaps Aeneas intended to cite the eighth book, *On the Individual Persons and the United Name of the Divinity*. It is certain from Ratramnus, Book III, chapter 6, that these passages were read in that book in Aeneas’s time, although they are no longer found there.]**
>
> “Just as two pieces of wood joined together and placed in a furnace produce from the two pieces of wood one inseparable flame, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from the power of the Father and the Son, possessing that same power of divinity. As the most blessed Paul said: ‘The mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus’ (I Tim. II, 5)—not ‘God as mediator of God.’ For there is one, even unto the Trinity.”

## Chapter XVI

The same author, in Book VIII, *On the Trinity and the Holy Spirit*, says:

> **[Note: “Book VIII, *On the Trinity*.” From this passage, just as from the preceding one, we learn how recklessly the titles of Athanasius’s works were shifted here and there by copyists. For this chapter and the following two are found in Book XI, *On the Unity of the Faith of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*. See Ratramnus’s *Book against the Greeks*, Book III.]**
>
> “The Lord significantly called the Holy Spirit ‘another Paraclete,’ because he himself is the Paraclete, as John says in his Epistle: ‘I have written these things to you so that you may not sin. But if we sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, and he himself is the expiation for our sins.’ Thus we are taught the equality of the Spirit with the Son.”

## Chapter XVII

The same author, in the same book, concerning the fact that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Lord Jesus, says:

> “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wishes. In the Epistle to the Romans he says: ‘If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you’ (Rom. VIII, 11).”

## Chapter XVIII

The same author, in the same book, concerning the fact that the Holy Spirit is the inspiration of the Father and the Son, and moreover that the Son is the fountain of the Holy Spirit; consequently, that the Spirit proceeds also from the Son:

> “The wisdom of Solomon expounds this in the Proverbs as follows: ‘The lamp of the Lord is the breath of human beings, searching all the inner parts of the belly’ (Prov. XX, 27). It is evident that the Spirit searches all things, as Paul writes. And God breathed the Holy Spirit into Adam’s face when Adam was formed at the beginning, as Moses says: ‘And God breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul’ (Gen. II, 7).

> “Nor is that which was breathed by the Lord a soul, according to the Jewish fabulists; otherwise, how could God condemn to eternal fire that which was breathed by him? Rather, it is the life-giving Spirit, concerning whom Paul also says: ‘The Spirit, however, gives life’ (John VI, 24); and: ‘God breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul.’

> “Therefore the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of life, and some who were living died when they fell away from him, as Paul writes: ‘She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives’ (I Tim. V, 6). Otherwise, how is Solomon to be understood when he says: ‘The lamp of the Lord is the breath of human beings, searching the inner parts of the belly’? If you say that the souls of human beings are the light of God, unless you believe that the Holy Spirit is the light of God, then Moses’s statement is meaningless: ‘God breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life.’ And the Son of God says: ‘I am life.’

> “Solomon’s wisdom also introduces the Savior saying: ‘Behold, I will declare to you the proclamation of my inspiration’ (Prov. I, 23). For thus he says in the Proverbs: ‘Wisdom will be proclaimed at the exit; in the streets she will speak boldly; at the gates she will stand before the powerful; and upon the walls of the city she will speak confidently. As long as the wise possess justice, they will not be ashamed; but the foolish, since they are desirous of insult and have become impious, hated understanding and became subject to rebukes. Behold, I will declare to you the proclamation of my inspiration; I will teach you my speech’ (Prov. I, 23).

> “And Isaiah, proclaiming the promise of the Holy Spirit, says: ‘Thus says the Lord, who made heaven and fixed it, who made the earth firm and the things in it, who gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who tread upon it’ (Isa. XLII, 5, according to the Septuagint). Tell me, what is the people that received breath? Do you say that here too breath is the soul, and will you claim that a people was established upon the earth without a soul? But it is not so. The prophet was proclaiming the coming forth of the Holy Spirit when he said these things.

> “Finally, Luke wrote of the fulfillment of this proclamation upon the believers who existed at that time: ‘When the day of Pentecost had been fulfilled, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty rushing Spirit, filling the whole house where they were sitting; and divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, and one rested upon each of them. And they began to speak in various tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance’ (Acts II, 1).

> “In a similar way, that great man Job, speaking against his friends when they had been deprived of the Holy Spirit and said nothing true, nor thought that they were speaking before God, said: ‘Do you not speak before God?’ And again: ‘To whom have you announced words? And whose breath is it that proceeds from you?’ (Job XXVI, 4). One of them, speaking grandly, said: ‘The Spirit is he who pleads for mortals; but the breath of the Almighty is what teaches me’ (Job VIII, 27). The Almighty is the Son of God, concerning whom Zechariah says: ‘Therefore thus says the Lord Almighty: After the glory he sent me against the nations’ (Zech. II, 8).

> “Thus, when Solomon says, ‘The lamp of the Lord is the breath of human beings’ (Prov. XX, 27), and when we have been instructed by Moses that ‘the Lord breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life, and he became a living soul’ (Gen. II, 7), and when we hear the Savior saying, ‘I am life’ (John XI, 25), and Paul writing, ‘For the law of the Spirit of life’ (Rom. VIII, 2), and again, ‘God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts’ (Gal. IV, 6), and when we also see the Only-Begotten breathing upon the faces of the apostles and saying, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John XX, 22), we are taught that the Son’s breath, remaining in his own life and substance, is the Spirit.

> “Let us not suppose that he was begotten or created by the Son, lest we believe that the Son, who was begotten, is the Spirit, or that the Lord is the Word of the Son. The Word of God, begotten by God and remaining in his own life and substance, is the Son of God, since the Son is life. The Spirit is not begotten by him, because he is not his Word. To call the Spirit created—far be it!

> “Nevertheless, we have learned from the holy Scriptures that he is the breath of the Son of God; and, hearing the Son of God, we call the Son the fountain of the Spirit: ‘For this people has committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water’ (Jer. II, 13).

> “The living water is the Holy Spirit, as John taught when the Savior said to the Samaritan woman: ‘If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, “Give me a drink,” you would surely have asked him, and he would have given you living water’ (John IV, 10); and again: ‘Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst’ (ibid. 13). And in the middle of the temple he cries out: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly’ (John VII, 37). And he interpreted it thus: ‘He said this concerning the Holy Spirit, whom those who were to believe in him were to receive’ (John XXXIX).

> “Isaiah likewise says that the Lord declared: ‘For I will give water to those who have walked in thirst through a dry land; and I will place my Spirit upon your offspring, and my blessings upon your children, and they shall spring up like grass in water and like a willow beside streams of water’ (Isa. XLIV, 3–4, according to the Septuagint). Therefore, from the holy Scriptures, which plainly declare that the living water is the Holy Spirit, we know this.

> “The Lord said that he is the fountain of the Spirit, in these words: ‘They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water’ (Jer. II, 13), just as David sings in Psalm XXXV, saying to the Lord: ‘For with you is the fountain of life’ (v. 10). Therefore, show another fountain of life besides the Lord, which is with him. For he did not say, ‘You are the fountain of life,’ but, ‘With you is the fountain of life.’ It is with God, and the Son is the fountain that exists as the source of the Spirit. Concerning this Paul writes to the Romans: ‘But the Spirit is life because of righteousness’ (Rom. VIII, 10), and thus he calls him not alien but proper to the Father.

> “For when he had confessed, ‘With you is the fountain of life,’ he added: ‘In your light we shall see light’ (Ps. XXXV), that is, ‘In your Son we shall see the Spirit.’

> “The Spirit is also shown to be called by the name of God’s power, and to be power and wisdom. For we heard the Savior saying in the Gospel to his disciples that he would send the Holy Spirit: ‘Behold, I will send the promise of my Father upon you. But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high’ (Luke XXIV, 49). In the Acts of the Apostles the same Lord says: ‘But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you’ (Acts I, 8). We find that this too was fulfilled when the day of Pentecost was completed.

> “Therefore, either confess that the Spirit is the power of God, or, like Sabellius, since he is the power of God, proclaim that the Paraclete is the very same person as the Son. And hearing Paul say, ‘The Spirit is life because of righteousness,’ we are again instructed that the Son is the fountain of the Spirit.

> “Hear Jeremiah crying out against the Jews: ‘For they have forsaken me, the fountain of life, God.’ Elsewhere, knowing that the Spirit is the Spirit of wisdom, hear Isaiah say: ‘And the Spirit of God will rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding’ (Isa. XI, 2).”

## Chapter XIX

The same author, in *The Catholic Faith*, concerning the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son:

> “The Father was made by no one, nor created, nor begotten. The Son is from the Father alone, not made, not created, but begotten. The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, not made, not created, nor begotten, but proceeding. Therefore there is one Father, not three Fathers; one Son, not three Sons; one Holy Spirit, not three Holy Spirits.

> “And in this Trinity there is nothing earlier or later, nothing greater or less, but all three persons are coeternal and coequal with one another. Thus, in every respect, as has already been stated, both the Trinity in unity and the unity in Trinity must be venerated. Therefore, whoever wishes to be saved must think this way concerning the Trinity.”

## Chapter XX

Ambrose, bishop of Milan, in the first book that he wrote to the emperor Gratian (*On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 10, beginning), treats the fact that when the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son he does not pass from place to place:

> “For if the Spirit proceeds from a place and passes to a place, etc., up to these words: ‘And you revealed them to infants,’ which bring the chapter to an end.”

## Chapter XXI

The same author, in his second book, concerning the fact that just as the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father, so he is sent by the Son, and the Son himself is sent by the Spirit:

> “Consider that our Lord Jesus Christ spoke through Isaiah, saying that he had been sent by the Holy Spirit. Is the Son therefore inferior to the Spirit because he was sent by the Spirit? You have it written that the Son says that he was sent by the Father and his Spirit: ‘I am the first, I am forever, and my hand founded the earth; my right hand established heaven.’ And below: ‘I spoke, I called, I brought him, and made his way prosperous. Draw near to me and hear these things. From the beginning I have not spoken in secret. When they came to be, I was there; and now the Lord has sent me and his Spirit’ (Isa. XLVIII, 13, 15–16).

> “Certainly the one who made heaven and earth himself says that he was sent by the Lord and his Spirit. You see, therefore, that the simplicity of the expression does not imply any injury in the sending. The one sent by the Father is himself the one sent by the Spirit.

> “And so that you may recognize that there is no difference of majesty, the Son also sends the Spirit, as he himself said: ‘When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father’ (John XV, 26). Above he likewise stated that the same Paraclete would be sent by the Father, saying: ‘But that Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, whom the Father will send in my name’ (John XIV, 26). Observe the unity: the one whom God the Father sends, the Son also sends; and the one whom the Father sends, the Spirit also sends.”

## Chapter XXII

The same author, in Book III, chapters 1 and 2, concerning the fact that the Holy Spirit was sent by the Father and the Son, where “sending” is understood as “proceeding”:

> “The Father also sent the Spirit, and the Son; the Father sent him, because it is written: ‘But that Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, whom the Father will send in my name,’ etc., up to these words: ‘The Spirit has been called the finger of God.’”

## Chapter XXIII

The same author, in the same book, chapters 20 and 21, concerning the fact that the river proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb is the Holy Spirit, where his procession from the Father and the Son is understood:

> “The Spirit therefore has what Christ has. He therefore has what God has, because everything that the Father has, the Son also has. For this reason he said: ‘All things that the Father has are mine’ (John XVI, 15).

> “Nor is it an insignificant matter that we read of a river going out from the throne of God. For the Evangelist John says: ‘And he showed me a river of living water, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb. In the middle of its street, and on either side, was the tree of life, producing fruit, yielding its twelve [fruits] each month, and the leaves of the tree for the healing of all the nations’ (Rev. XXII, 1).

> “This is plainly the river proceeding from the throne of God, that is, the Holy Spirit, which the one who believes in Christ drinks, as he himself says: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.’ He said this concerning the Spirit (John VII, 38–39). Therefore the Spirit is the river.”

## Chapter XXIV

Cyril, concerning the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, says in his letter to Nestorius:

> “When he says concerning the Spirit, ‘He will glorify me’ (John XVI, 14), those who understand this most correctly confess one Christ and Son, not as though he needed another’s glory, but that he received glory from the Holy Spirit; for his Spirit is neither better nor higher than he is. Rather, because, in performing wonderful works as a demonstration of his divinity, he used the Spirit’s own power, he is said to be glorified by him—just as someone might assert concerning human beings that one person’s power or discipline glorifies another.

> “Although the Spirit exists in his own substance and the property of his person is understood according to the fact that he is Spirit and not Son, nevertheless he is not alien to the Son. For he is called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is truth; therefore he proceeds from the Son in the same way as from God the Father.

> “Finally, this same Spirit, performing glorious miracles through the hands of the holy apostles, glorified God Jesus Christ after he ascended into heaven. For Christ was believed to be God by nature, accomplishing mighty works through his Spirit. Therefore he said: ‘He will take from what is mine and will announce it to you.’ But the same Spirit is not said to be wise or powerful by participation in another, because he is perfect in every respect and wholly needs no good.

> “The same Spirit of the Son is believed to be the power and wisdom of the Father; and therefore he is proved to be both substance and power and wisdom.”

## Chapter XXV

The same author, in the *Dialogue with Theodoret* contained in the *Tripartite History*, by Cyril the bishop, proceeds concerning the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and is not alien to the Son:

> “We remember Christ openly saying concerning the Holy Spirit: ‘He will glorify me.’ We know that the operation of the Holy Spirit overthrows the most wicked and unclean powers. But we do not say that he uses the Spirit’s power as each of the saints does, as though it were alien to him. For he was and is his Spirit, just as he is also the Father’s.

> “The most sacred Paul explains this sufficiently well when he writes: ‘Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his’ (Rom. VIII, 8–9).

> “The Holy Spirit proceeds from God and the Father, according to the Savior’s word, but he is not alien to the Son. For he has everything together with the Father, and the Son himself taught this when he said concerning the Holy Spirit: ‘Everything that the Father has is mine. Therefore I said to you: He will take from what is mine and will announce it to you’ (John XVI, 15).

> “Thus the Holy Spirit did glorify Jesus while he performed things beyond expectation; nevertheless, as his Spirit, he was not an alien power, nor superior to him insofar as he is understood to be God.”

## Chapter XXVI

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, concerning the mission of the Holy Spirit by the Son, in the book that he wrote to Germania, Gaul, Belgica, Lugdunensis, Novempopulana, Toulouse, and Britain, says:

> “We also believe in the Holy Spirit, that is, the Paraclete, whom, after promising him to his apostles, he sent after his return to the heavens to teach them and to bring all things to their remembrance. Through him the souls of those who sincerely believe in him are sanctified.”

## Chapter XXVII

The same author, in the same book:

> “If anyone, while calling the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, says that he is the unbegotten God, let him be anathema.
>
> **[Note: “An addition now.” Whatever is enclosed in parentheses in this chapter was absent from the older editions of Saint Hilary. The present addition concerning the Paraclete makes the proclamation that he is the unbegotten God liable to anathema. For it is most impious to call him the unbegotten God who was sent by the Son for our consolation.]**
>
> “If anyone, as the Lord taught us, does not say that the Paraclete is another than the Son—for he said: ‘The Father will send you another Paraclete, whom I will ask’ (John XIV, 16)—let him be anathema.
>
> **[Note: We remember that the Paraclete was sent by the Son, and the faith itself set this forth at the beginning. But because the Son often said, on account of the power of their undifferentiated nature, that his works were the Father’s works, saying, ‘I do the works of my Father,’ so also, although he frequently promised to send the Paraclete, he sometimes said that he would be sent by the Father, since he habitually referred everything he did piously to the Father. From this heretics frequently seize an opportunity to say that the Paraclete is the Son himself, although, in asking that another Paraclete be sent by the Father, he indicates a distinction between the one sent and the one who asks.]**
>
> “If anyone says that the Holy Spirit is the Father of the Father or of the Son, let him be anathema.
>
> **[Note: The foolishness of heretical madness compelled these statements to be included in Scripture—not an actual question. For the name of the Holy Spirit has its own signification, and the Holy Spirit the Paraclete has both the function and the order of his own substance. And since the Father and the Son are everywhere proclaimed immutable, how could the Holy Spirit be asserted to be a part of either the Father or the Son? But because, among the other kinds of madness, even this is commonly put forward by the impious, it had to be rejected by the saints.]**
>
> “If anyone says that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three gods, let him be anathema.”

## Chapter XXVIII

Saint Hilary, concerning the fact that it is one and the same thing for the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and to receive from the Son, or to be sent by the Son, reports in Book VIII *On the Holy Trinity*:

> “When that Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father, he will bear witness to me” (John XV, 26). “The Advocate will come, and the Son will send him from the Father, and he is the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father,” etc., up to the words: “the Son confesses that it is to be given by him.”

## Chapter XXIX

Jerome, in Didymus’s Book II, which he translated from Greek into Latin, teaches that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and is sent by the Son—not according to the ministry of angels, prophets, and apostles, but as it is fitting for the Spirit of God to be sent by the Wisdom of God—and thereby confesses that he proceeds from the Son just as from the Father:

> “Since the Holy Spirit, just as the Father and the Son, is taught to dwell in the mind and in the inner person, it is not merely foolish but impious to call him a creature. Disciplines—for I mean virtues and arts—and their opposites, disturbances, ignorance, and passions can dwell in souls, not as substances but as accidents. But it is impossible for a created nature to dwell in the mind.

> “If this is true, and the Holy Spirit, subsisting without any ambiguity, is the inhabitant of the soul and of the heart, no one can doubt that he must be believed to be uncreated together with the Father and the Son. From all that the preceding discussion has explained, the Holy Spirit has been shown to be incorruptible and everlasting according to the nature of the Father and the Son; he has removed every ambiguity and suspicion concerning himself, so that he may not be judged to be one of the created substances who is the Spirit of God. The Savior’s words in the Gospel declare that he proceeds from the Father: ‘When the Comforter comes,’ he says, ‘whom I will send to you, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness to me’ (John XV, 26).

> “He calls the Holy Spirit the coming Comforter, giving him his name from his operation, because he not only comforts those whom he finds worthy of himself, but also makes them strangers to every sadness and disturbance. Indeed, he gives them a certain incredible joy and gladness, so much so that someone, giving thanks to God for being considered worthy of such a guest, can say: ‘You have given gladness in my heart’ (Ps. IV, 7). Everlasting joy dwells in the hearts of those whose inhabitant is the Holy Spirit.

> “This Spirit the Comforter is sent by the Son—not according to the ministry of angels, prophets, and apostles, but as it is fitting for the Spirit of God to be sent by Wisdom and Truth, possessing an undivided substance with the Father and the Son.”

## Chapter XXX

The same author, in the same book, shortly afterward:

> “Although the Savior frequently says that he came forth from God, nevertheless, assuming from the name a property and, so to speak, a familiarity for himself from the Father, about which we have often discussed, he says,” etc., “up to the words ‘according to the truth of the operation.’”

## Chapter XXXI

The same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

> “Therefore, since the Holy Spirit is also sent by the Father in the name of the Son, possessing the Son’s property,” etc., “up to the words ‘the knowledge of divine things.’”

## Chapter XXXII

The same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

> “Finally, explaining how he had said, ‘He will take from what is mine,’ he immediately added: ‘Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said, “He will take from what is mine and will announce it to you,”’ etc., “up to the words ‘the Father also has these same things.’”

## Chapter XXXIII

The same author, in the same work:

> “‘But you,’ he says—plainly meaning Christ’s disciples—‘who have received the wisdom of the Spirit, and life and peace, are not in the flesh,’ that is, in the works of the flesh, ‘for you do not commit its works, since you have the Spirit of God in you. The same Spirit is both the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ, bringing and joining to the Lord Jesus Christ the one who possesses it,’ etc., “up to the words ‘the substance of the Trinity is demonstrated.’”

## Chapter XXXIV
Also the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

> “Since, therefore, Holy Scripture says nothing more about the Trinity than that God is the Father of the Savior, and that the Son was begotten from the Father—and since we must understand what has been written, and once it has been shown that the Holy Spirit is uncreated, consequently understand that he whose substance is not created is rightly joined to the Father and the Son.” [Col. 0706A]

## CHAPTER XXXV

Saint Augustine, in a homily on John:

> [Note: [Col. 0705D] ‘Here someone.’ Acherius remarks that he sought this homily in vain; but Theodulf also reported what Aeneas excerpted from it [Col. 0706D] in his book on the Holy Spirit.]

> “Here someone may perhaps ask whether the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son. For the Son is the Son of the Father alone, and the Father is the Father of the Son alone; but the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of one of them, but of both. You have the Lord himself saying: ‘For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you’ (Matthew 10:20). You also have the Apostle: ‘God sent,’ he says, ‘the Spirit of his Son into our hearts’ (Galatians 4:6). Are there then two spirits, one belonging to the Father and another to the Son? By no means. For when he signified the Church, he said ‘one body,’ and immediately added, ‘and one Spirit’ (Ephesians 4:4). And see how there he completes the Trinity: ‘As you were called,’ he says, ‘in one hope of your calling. One Lord.’ Here he clearly wished Christ to be understood. It remains for him also to name the Father. He therefore continues: ‘One faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all’ (ibid.).

> “Since, therefore, just as there is one Father and one Lord—that is, the Son—so also there is one Spirit, he is certainly the Spirit of both, since Christ Jesus himself says: ‘The Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.’ And the Apostle says: ‘God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts.’ In another place you have the same Apostle saying: ‘But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you’ (Romans 8:11). Here he clearly wished the Spirit of the Father to be understood; yet elsewhere he says of him: ‘But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him’ (ibid., 9). There are also many other testimonies by which it is clearly shown that the Spirit who is called the Holy Spirit in the Trinity belongs both to the Father and to the Son.

> “Nor do I think that he is called ‘Spirit’ in a special sense for any other reason than this: even if we are questioned about each of them individually, we can call both the Father and the Son ‘Spirit,’ since God is Spirit—that is, God is not a body but Spirit. Therefore, since they are each commonly called Spirit, it was fitting that the one who belongs not to one of them but in whom the common possession of both is manifest should be called Spirit in a special sense.

> “Why, then, should we not believe that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son, since he is himself the Spirit of the Son? For if he did not proceed from him, the Son would not, after his resurrection, have breathed upon his disciples when he appeared to them, saying: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20:22). For what else did that breathing signify except that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him also?

> “The same point is also indicated by what he said concerning the woman who suffered from a flow of blood: ‘Someone touched me; for I perceived power go out from me’ (Luke 8:46). That the Holy Spirit is also called ‘power’ is clear from the passage where the angel replied to Mary, who said, ‘How will this happen, since I do not know a man?’: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you’ (Luke 1:34). And the Lord himself, promising him to the disciples, said: ‘But you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high’ (Luke 24:49). And again: ‘You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses’ (Acts 1:6).”

## CHAPTER XXXVI

The same Saint Augustine, in Book XIII of *The City of God* (chapter 24): That the Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Only-Begotten, and is one Spirit belonging to both. Since this is so, there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both.

> “Accordingly, in what the Lord did when he breathed upon them, saying, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit,’ he clearly wished it to be understood that the Holy Spirit is not only the Spirit of the Father but also the Spirit of the Only-Begotten himself. For he is the very same Spirit of the Father and of the Son; and with him the Father and the Son constitute the Trinity—not a creature, but the Creator. For that bodily breath proceeding from the mouth of flesh was not the substance and nature of the Holy Spirit, but rather a sign by which we might understand, as I have said, that the Holy Spirit is common to the Father and the Son, since he is not separately the Spirit of each but one Spirit belonging to both.” [Col. 0707B]

## CHAPTER XXXVII

The same author, in Book I of *On the Trinity, Which Is God*: That the Holy Spirit belongs to both the Father and the Son, and is coequal, consubstantial, and coeternal with the Father and the Son, teaches as follows:

> “All the Catholic interpreters of the divine books, both old and new, whom I have been able to read and who wrote about the Trinity, which is God, intended to teach in accordance with the Scriptures that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, by an inseparable equality of one substance, signify the divine unity. Therefore there are not three gods but one God, although the Father begot the Son, and therefore the Son is not the Father; the Son was begotten by the Father, and therefore the Father is not the Son; and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but solely the Spirit of the Father and the Son. Yet he is also coequal with the Father and the Son and belongs to the unity of the Trinity.” [Col. 0707C]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

The same author, in the same book: That the Holy Spirit belongs inseparably to the Father and the Son; and since this is so, it is an act of great folly not to confess that he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

> “Finally, because of this very inseparability, sometimes the Father alone is sufficiently named, or the Son alone, as the one who will fill us with joy by his presence. Yet the Spirit of both is not thereby separated—that is, the Spirit of the Father and the Son—the Spirit who is properly called the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive (John 14:17).

> “For this is our complete joy, beyond which there is none greater: to enjoy God the Trinity, in whose image we were made. For this reason Scripture sometimes speaks of the Holy Spirit as though he alone were sufficient for our blessedness. And he is sufficient alone because he cannot be separated from the Father and the Son; just as the Father alone is sufficient because he cannot be separated from the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the Son is therefore sufficient alone because he cannot be separated from the Father and the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 0707D–0708A]

## CHAPTER XXXIX

The same author, in Book III of *On the Trinity*: That the Holy Spirit was sent by the Father and the Son.

> “When we had reached the point at which we wished to show that the Son is not therefore less than the Father because the Father sent him and the Son was sent, nor is the Holy Spirit therefore less than both because the Gospel says that he was sent both by the one and by the other, we undertook to investigate this question. The Son was sent to the place where he already was, because he came into this world and was in this world; and the Holy Spirit likewise was sent to the place where he already was, because ‘the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world,’ and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice (Wisdom 1:7).” [Col. 0708A–B]

## CHAPTER XL

The same author, in Book IV of the same work (chapter 20), clearly teaches that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son just as from the Father.

> “When the Father is known by someone in time, he is not said to have been sent. For he does not have one from whom he exists or from whom he proceeds. Wisdom says: ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High’ (Ecclesiasticus 24:5). And concerning the Holy Spirit we say: ‘He proceeds from the Father.’ The Father, however, proceeds from no one, etc., up to: ‘He works all things in all.’” [Col. 0708C]

## CHAPTER XLI

The same author, in Book VI of *On the Trinity*: That the Holy Spirit is the sweetness of the Son and the Father; hence whoever denies that he proceeds from both must consequently deny that sweetness proceeds from the Father and the Son.

> “That love, delight, happiness, or blessedness—if it can be adequately expressed in any human language—is called by him ‘use,’ and in the Trinity it is the Holy Spirit, not begotten but the sweetness of the begetter and the begotten, suffusing all creatures, according to their capacity, with the generosity and abundance of the Unbegotten, so that they may keep their proper order and rest in their proper places. All these things, therefore, which have been made by divine art, display within themselves a certain unity, as well as form and order. For whatever of these things exists is also one thing.” [Col. 0708C]

## CHAPTER XLII

The same author, in Book XV of *On the Holy Trinity* (chapter 17): That the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

> “I do not know why the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit should not each be called Wisdom, just as they are each called God, and why all three together should not be called not three wisdoms but one Wisdom, etc., up to: ‘This distinction of the Trinity.’” [Col. 0708D]

## CHAPTER XLIII

The same author, in the same book (chapter 26):

> “Moreover, in that supreme Trinity, which is God, there are no intervals of time by which it could be shown, or at least investigated, whether the Son was first born from the Father and afterward the Holy Spirit proceeded from both, etc., up to: ‘Because of the love of God.’”

## CHAPTER XLIV

[Col. 0709A]

The same author, in the same book (in the same passage and chapter 27):

> “Can we therefore ask whether the Holy Spirit had already proceeded from the Father when the Son was born, or had not yet proceeded, and whether, once the Son had been born, he proceeded from both—where there are no times, etc., up to: ‘May that which is held by faith be seen by the mind.’”

## CHAPTER XLV

Saint Augustine, on the point that the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son, says in the book he wrote against five heresies—that is, the Pagans, Jews, Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians:

> “We have spoken about the Father and the Son as we were able and as much as we were able, if indeed we were able to speak worthily of anything. We have kept silent about the Holy Spirit, but we have not passed him over. For whatever we have said about the Father and the Son, we have said about the Holy Spirit. He is in them and with them one true God, not a lesser or third God.

> “What more can I say, weary as I am, to those who are weary? Whoever separates the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in eternity, substance, or communion, and denies that he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, is full of an unclean spirit and empty of the Holy Spirit. For this reason it is said, ‘God is love’ (1 John 4:8): because he does not divide unity into parts but ineffably binds the Trinity together. For the Trinity itself is one God, a tower of strength against the enemy, who guards those who believe in him forever and ever. Amen.” [Col. 0709B]

## CHAPTER XLVI

Augustine likewise, in the disputation he held against Pascentius, an Arian count, in the presence of Laurence, the judge chosen by both parties (Letter 178, in the middle):

> “See what ‘consubstantial’ means, a term unjustly reproached. For it is not merely a word; the reality itself is present in the word. Nor is it merely speech sounding in the ears: one substance of God is to be believed in our minds.

> “If the whole God is believed to dwell in human beings who believe in him, how should the Father not be believed to receive the whole Son into himself, or the Son the Father? Thus the Son himself remains in the Father, and the Father in him; and the Holy Spirit must be believed not only to have proceeded from the Father or the Son, but always to proceed entirely for the accomplishment of the works of the Trinity.” [Col. 0709C]

## CHAPTER XLVII

Saint Augustine, on the point that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, says in Book II—rather, Book III, chapter 17—of the work he wrote against Maximinus the heretic:

> “You seem to yourself to be saying something important when you say: ‘The Son was in the beginning before anything existed, but the Father was before the beginning.’ Where did you read this, so as to believe it? From where did you presume to say it, when there is neither authority nor reason for it? For what does ‘before the beginning’ mean, since whatever existed before something else would itself be the beginning?

> “If, therefore, the Father is before the beginning, he is before himself, because he himself is also the beginning. But what does ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John 1:1) mean except that the Son was in the Father? And when the Jews asked the Son himself who he was, he replied: ‘The Beginning, who also speaks to you’ (John 8:24).

> “The Father, therefore, is beginning not from a beginning; the Son is beginning from a beginning. Yet both together are not two beginnings but one beginning. Just as the Father is God and the Son is God, while both together are not two gods but one God, so I will not deny that the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, is the beginning. These three together, just as they are one God, are likewise one beginning.” [Col. 0709D–0710A]

## CHAPTER XLVIII

The same author, in the same book:

> “You ask me: If the Son is from the substance of the Father, and the Holy Spirit is also from the substance of the Father, why is one the Son and the other not the Son? I answer, whether you understand or do not understand: the Son is from the Father, the Holy Spirit is from the Father, etc., up to: ‘But he is from the one from whom he proceeds.’” [Col. 0710B]

## CHAPTER XLIX

Saint Augustine:

> [Note: [Col. 0709D] In the book *On the Incarnation*. We know of no treatise by Augustine currently entitled *On the Incarnation*; for it is sufficiently established that the books *On the Incarnation* published among the works of Saint Augustine belong to another author. Since this chapter is not found in them, no one should doubt that it is a fragment of some lost work. [Col. 0710D]]

In his book *On the Incarnation of the Lord*:

> “The Holy Spirit likewise is neither unbegotten nor begotten, but proceeds from the Father and the Son, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son; he himself is consubstantial and coeternal with both. The Holy Spirit whom he gave by breathing upon them was not different from the one whom he sent after his ascension. For there is one Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit, the same God who works all things in all. Thus the Trinity is believed to be perfect because of the distinctness of the persons, and one God because of the inseparable Trinity.” [Col. 0710C]

## CHAPTER L

Saint Augustine:

> [Note: [Col. 0710D] In the book *On the Exposition*. Everyone now knows that the author of this exposition was not Augustine but Fulgentius; it was published among his works in 1684, p. 502.]

In the book *Exposition of the Faith to Peter*:

> “Therefore, just as the Son is neither later than nor less than the Father, so the Holy Spirit is neither later than nor less than the Son, etc., up to: ‘The Greeks call it οὐσίαν [ousia, substance].’” [Col. 0710D]

## CHAPTER LI

The same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

> “In that holy Trinity, therefore—a point that we repeat so that it may be impressed more firmly upon your heart—there is one Father, who alone essentially begot from himself one Son; and there is one Son, who alone was essentially born from one Father; and there is one Holy Spirit, who alone essentially proceeds from the Father and the Son.

> “One person could not do all this—that is, beget himself, be born from himself, and proceed from himself. Since, therefore, begetting is one thing, being born another, and proceeding is something different from either begetting or being born, it is clear that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.” [Col. 0710D]

## CHAPTER LII

[Col. 0711A]

The same author, in the same work (chapter 2):

> “For in that Trinity it would not be proper to the Father alone that he himself was not born but begot one Son; nor would it be proper to the Son alone that he himself did not beget but was born from the substance of the Father; nor would it be proper to the Holy Spirit that he was neither born nor begotten, but alone proceeds from the Father and the Son in unchangeable eternity.”

## CHAPTER LIII

The same author, in that work shortly afterward (chapter 11):

> “You should be completely certain, and in no way doubt, that the same Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeds from the Father and the Son, etc., up to: ‘Because he proceeds from his mouth.’” [Col. 0711A]

## CHAPTER LIV

[Col. 0711B]

Pope Hormisdas of the Roman Church, on the point that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, says in the letter he sent to the emperor Justin against the blasphemies of Nestorius and Eutyches (Letter 76):

> “Let us adore the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the undivided Trinity distinctly, the incomprehensible and ineffable substance of the Trinity. Although reason admits the number of the persons, unity nevertheless does not admit the separation of the essence [Note: [Col. 0711D] We have preferred *the separation of the essence* on the basis of the printed editions, rather than the earlier reading, *the separation of substance*.]

> “Let us nevertheless preserve what is proper to each divine person, so that neither the singularity of the divinity may be denied to the persons, nor what is proper to the names be transferred to the essence.

> “Great, holy, and incomprehensible is the mystery of the Trinity: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, the undivided Trinity. Yet it is known that it is proper to the Father to beget the Son; proper to the Son of God to be born from the Father as the Father’s equal; and proper to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son within one substance of deity.” [Col. 0711C]

## CHAPTER LV

Leo, pope of the Roman Church, on the point that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, says in the letter he sent to Turibius, bishop of Astorga (Letter 93, chapter 1):

> “In the first chapter, therefore, it is shown how impiously they think about the divine Trinity who assert that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same person, as though the same one were now called Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit; as though the one who begot, the one who was begotten, and the one who proceeds from both were not distinct, and as though the singular unity were to be understood in three names but not in three persons. They took this form of blasphemy from the opinion of Sabellius.” [Col. 0711D]

## CHAPTER LVI

Gregory, pope of the Roman Church, says in Homily 26, on the point that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son:

> “Accordingly it is said: ‘As the Father sent me, so I send you’ (John 20:21)—that is, I love you with the same love with which the Father loves me, when I send you amid the scandals of persecutors, with which love the Father caused me to come to endure sufferings.

> “Yet being sent may also be understood according to the nature of the divinity. For the Son is said to be sent by the Father precisely in that he is begotten by the Father. For the same Son also declares that he sends the Holy Spirit, who, although he is equal to the Father and the Son, was not incarnate: ‘When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father’ (John 15:26), etc., up to: ‘Should lead to the love of the Lord.’” [Col. 0711D–0712A]

## CHAPTER LVII

The same author, in Book II of the *Moralia* (chapter 27):

> “If the Spirit of prophecy were always present with the prophets, the prophet Nathan would never have granted King David’s request concerning the construction of the temple, only to deny it shortly afterward. Hence it is rightly written in the Gospel: ‘Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes’ (John 1:33).

> “For the Spirit comes upon all the faithful, but he remains uniquely in the one Mediator, because he never abandoned his humanity, from whose divinity he proceeds. He remains in the one who alone can do all things and can do them always.” [Col. 0712A–B]

## CHAPTER LVIII

The same author, in the same book shortly afterward (chapter 28):

> “In these gifts, therefore, without which one cannot attain life, the Holy Spirit always remains either in his preachers or in all the elect, etc., up to: ‘He remains for all things.’” [Col. 0712B]

## CHAPTER LIX

[Col. 0712C]

The same author, in Book V (chapter 26): That the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and receives from what belongs to the Son, whereby he is understood also to proceed from the Son.

> “‘And I heard a voice like a gentle breeze’ (Job 4:16). For what is signified by ‘the voice of a gentle breeze’ except knowledge of the Holy Spirit? Proceeding from the Father and receiving from what belongs to the Son, he is gently infused into the weakness of our knowledge, etc., up to: ‘By illuminating, he disturbs.’”

## CHAPTER LX

Fulgentius:

> [Note: [Col. 0711D] Fulgentius. Nothing survives from these books of Fulgentius except these fragments, which Theodulf also copied in his book on the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0712D]]

On the point that the Father alone begot the Son, the Son alone was begotten by the Father, and the Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son, he says in Book III, which he wrote against Fabianus:

> “For we truthfully confess that the Father alone begot, and the Son alone was born from the Father; we also truthfully say that the Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son.” [Col. 0712D]

## CHAPTER LXI

The same author, in Book V against the same Fabianus:

> “Behold, insofar as I have been able, though briefly, I have given the account by which we call the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit one God, and in the image of God I have shown a certain indication of divine knowledge.

> “In that image, memory, understanding, and will do not have separate and proper persons. For this image is not born but made; not begotten but created. The purpose is that, just as in this one image there is found a certain distinction of names, so in that one divinity the distinction of persons may be recognized; and that natural unity may show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, while the distinctness of the persons may demonstrate that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

> “The Father is another, not insofar as he is God but insofar as he is Father; the Son is another, not insofar as he is God but insofar as he is Son; and the Holy Spirit is another, not insofar as he is God but insofar as he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son. The Father is another because he begot; the Son is another because he was born from the Father; and the Spirit is another because he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

> “Yet the Father is not another God, the Son another God, and the Holy Spirit another God; rather, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. Unity does not confuse the Trinity, nor does the Trinity separate unity, because what is distinguished in the distinctness of the persons is shown to be one by the natural communion of the one essence.” [Col. 0712D–0713B]

## CHAPTER LXII

The same author, in Book VII of the same work:

> “‘For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you’ (John 16:13). First, he shows that the things of the Holy Spirit are none other than the things of the Son. Then, to show that everything belonging to the Father belongs to him, he adds: ‘Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you.’

> “Let us first attend to what he says: ‘He will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak.’ Who could comprehend what the speech or hearing of that simple nature is, where hearing is nothing other than being? The Holy Spirit therefore hears whatever the Father and the Son say, and likewise does these same things.

> “For in that nature where there is supreme and true simplicity, the Son sees in it what the Father does, and the Holy Spirit hears in it what the Son says with the Father, because by the communion of the natural essence the Son was born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

> “Thus, for the Holy Spirit, hearing means proceeding from the nature of the Father and the Son; and speaking means communicating ineffably to our hearts through grace.” [Col. 0713B–D]

## CHAPTER LXIII

The same author, in the same book:

> “‘No one will snatch them from my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father. I and the Father are one’ (John 10:28).

> “This, then, is the voice that his sheep hear: namely, in the fact that no one snatches them from the hand of the Son or from the hand of the Father, they understand that the Son and the Father have one power; and when they hear from him that he and the Father are one, they recognize the true unity of natural essence in the Father and the Son.

> “This is the voice of the Son; this is the speech of the Holy Spirit, because the Son was born from the nature of the Father, and from that source the Holy Spirit proceeds. The Holy Spirit also hears this from the Father and the Son, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son in the equality of their common divinity.

> “The Holy Spirit therefore does not speak from himself, because he is not from himself; rather, he possesses natural speech from the Father and the Son, and, proceeding naturally from them, possesses the truth of his origin. To this belongs what he says: ‘He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you. Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine.’

> “How well the very truth preserved the truth of his teaching! If he had not said this, he might have seemed to show that the Spirit belonged only to him. But by saying, ‘Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine,’ he showed that the Holy Spirit is one Spirit belonging both to the Father and to himself.

> “He also expresses this understanding when he says: ‘But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything that I have said to you.’ The Father sends him, but sends him in the name of the Son; the Spirit sent by the Father teaches, but the Son speaks.

> “This is also demonstrated in the passage where the Lord says: ‘But when the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.’ Behold, the Paraclete whom the Father sends in the name of the Son is the very one whom the Son sends from the Father; and he sends the Spirit of truth from the Father.

> “The Son therefore sends him from the Father because he himself is the truth; the Father sends him in the name of the Son because he is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son. The Son sends him from the Father because he proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father. This same Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of truth.

> “He therefore received from the Son, and everything that the Father has belongs to the Son, which the Holy Spirit received, because he proceeds not from the Father alone nor from the Son alone, but from both together.

> “Yet this term ‘procession’ is never found to have been granted to any creature in relation to the Father, so that this particular procession may be shown to belong solely to the natural essence. For we read that the Son was begotten from the Father; and although, when he is called ‘Only-Begotten,’ natural generation alone is indicated, nevertheless, because of the grace of adoption, God the Father also voluntarily begot us through the word of truth.

> “The Only-Begotten, therefore, is the one and only Son born from the essence of the Father. Yet we too are called sons of God by adoption and are said to be born from God, as the blessed Evangelist says: ‘But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of man, but from God’ (John 1:12).

> “Although the divine utterances show that we are children of God, begotten from God and born from God, no one can demonstrate that the term ‘proceeding from God’ has been granted to any creature. Why is this, except because natural birth could show the Only-Begotten Son to be true God, and demonstrate without doubt that he is not adopted or of another nature but consubstantial with the Father?

> “No creature is therefore said to proceed from God, so that he who proceeds from the Father and the Son may be believed to be God in the same way as the Father and the Son. This procession from the Father and the Son belongs solely to the Holy Spirit, whose nature is shared with the Father and the Son.

> “For he proceeds from the Father and the Son, but does not depart from them; nor is he in any respect lesser or subordinate, who proceeds inseparably and wholly as one from the immense Father and the immense Son. Thus what he wondrously accomplishes cannot be commanded to him.” [Col. 0713D–0715A]

## CHAPTER LXIV

The same author, in Book VIII of the same work:

> “The Son, therefore, was sent by the Father, not the Father by the Son, because the Son was born from the Father, not the Father from the Son. Likewise, the Holy Spirit is read to have been sent by the Father and the Son because he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

> “But since ‘mission’ is not used in only one way in the Holy Scriptures, in the mystery of the Incarnation the Son was sent not only by the Father but also by the Holy Spirit, because Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and human beings, was formed through the operation of the whole Trinity.

> “In another way the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son, because he naturally proceeds from the Father and the Son. For the Son and the Holy Spirit are sent by the Father when the effect of spiritual grace is bestowed by the Trinity itself, the one God.” [Col. 0715A–B]

## CHAPTER LXV

The same author, in Book IX of the same work:

> “We therefore confess God the Father to be the origin not of the whole Trinity but of the Son and the Holy Spirit; from him the Only-Begotten Son has the origin of eternal birth, and the Holy Spirit the origin of eternal procession.

> “Natural unity, however, signifies that the Son, the Creator, came forth by natural birth from the Father, the Creator, and that the Holy Spirit, the Creator, proceeds from the Father and the Son.” [Col. 0715B–C]

## CHAPTER LXVI

The same author, in Book X of the same work:

> “Having completed our confession of the true divinity and true humanity of the only Son of God, we confess that we believe in the Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father and the Son, naturally remaining in the Father and the Son, and naturally possessing from the Father and the Son the truth of one divinity.” [Col. 0715C]

## CHAPTER LXVII

[Col. 0715D]

The same author, to show that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son, testifies in the second book he wrote to King Thrasamund that the same Holy Spirit was sent by both the Father and the Son, and that the Son was sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit (*Book II to Monimus*, chapter 6):

> “Now we must also revisit the question of the mission of the Holy Spirit, etc., up to: ‘To any local coming.’”

## CHAPTER LXVIII

Isidore, bishop of Seville, says among other things in Book II of *The Offices* (chapter 23):

> “This, after the Apostolic Creed, is the most certain faith handed down by our teachers: that we confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be of one essence, and of the same power and eternity, one invisible God, while preserving the distinctness proper to each person. Thus the Trinity must neither be divided substantially nor confused altogether personally.

> “We also confess the Father to be unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten but proceeding from the Father and the Son; the Son proceeding from the Father by being born, while the Holy Spirit, by proceeding, is not born.” [Col. 0715D–0716A]

## CHAPTER LXIX

Isidore, in Book VII of the *Etymologies* (chapter 3), on the point that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, says:

> “The Holy Spirit is proclaimed to be God because he proceeds from the Father and the Son, etc., up to: ‘He does not belong to him.’” [Col. 0716A]

## CHAPTER LXX

[Col. 0716B]

The same author, in the same work shortly afterward (chapter 4):

> “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are therefore Trinity and unity. They are the same one and the same three: one in nature, three in persons. One because of the communion of majesty, three because of the distinctness of the persons.

> “For the Father is one person, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; yet they are different persons, not different things, because each is equally simple, equally an unchangeable good, and coeternal.

> “The Father alone is not from another; therefore he alone is called unbegotten. The Son alone was born from the Father; therefore he alone is called begotten. The Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son; therefore he alone is now called the Spirit of both.”

## CHAPTER LXXI

[Col. 0716C]

The same author, in the Book of *Differences* (Book II, chapter 3):

> “The persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinguished as follows: the Father was neither made nor born; the Son was born, not made; and the Holy Spirit was neither born nor made but proceeds from the Father, etc., to the end of the chapter.”

## CHAPTER LXXII

The same author, in the Book of *Sentences* (Book I, chapter 17):

> “The Holy Spirit is Creator, just as the Father and the Word are, as the prophet testifies: ‘The Spirit of the Lord made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life’ (Job 33:4).

> “The Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son; and this is why the Father and the Son are one: because the Father has nothing that the Son does not have. For one consubstantial reality belonging to two could not proceed from them and exist in them simultaneously unless those from whom it proceeds were one.” [Col. 0716C–D]

## CHAPTER LXXIII

Prosper, in the book *On the Contemplative Life*—or Julianus Pomerius, Book I, chapters 18 and 19—teaches that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as follows:

> “Since, according to the Apostle, we must not only present a model to the faithful but must also instruct those same faithful who have been entrusted to us by God for their formation, we must explain how the Father alone is called unbegotten; how the Son alone is called begotten; and how the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, can be called neither unbegotten nor begotten.

> “We must explain how these three are one, and how this one is not divided but distinguished into three, etc., up to: ‘May he act well.’” [Col. 0716D–0717A]

## CHAPTER LXXIV
Vigilius, African bishop [or: Vigilius, or Virgil, bishop of Trent, book I], demonstrates in the following words that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, in the books he wrote at Constantinople in defense of Pope Leo’s Tome against the Eutychians:

“Likewise they raise some question for us concerning the Trinity, alleging that, since there are certain properties belonging to the Father alone, which do not pertain either to the Son or to the Holy Spirit; and certain properties belonging to the Son alone, which do not pertain either to the Father or to the Holy Spirit; and also certain properties of the Holy Spirit, which are shown not to pertain either to the Father or to the Son, Catholics are accused of believing in three gods separated from one another. But, lest you perhaps be disturbed by an unexpected question, consider each aspect of the assumed humanity’s dispensation: it pertains neither to the Father nor to the Spirit, but to the Son alone. For it is properly the Son, not the Father, who was born of the Virgin. Again, the voice heard over him, ‘This is my beloved Son,’ pertains neither to the Son nor to the Holy Spirit, but to the Father alone. Likewise, the appearance of the dove that appeared in the Jordan, and the distribution divided into tongues of fire, are shown properly to pertain to the person of the Holy Spirit. But, lest you still doubt these properties, hear more plainly. It is the Father’s property to have begotten, and the Son’s property to have been born; but it is the Holy Spirit’s property to proceed from the Father and the Son. What is specially proper to each person is in no way transferred to another person. If, then, these three persons, each possessing their own properties by which they are distinguished more clearly, not separated, are one God, how is the Son not one Christ while the property of both natures remains intact?”

### CHAPTER LXXV

Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, teaches in these words, in a letter sent to the Armenians against the heretics, that the Holy Spirit proceeds inseparably from the essence of the Godhead:

“Let us therefore flee the counsels of deception—I mean the destructive and God-opposing streams of the heretics—the madness of Arius, who divides the inseparable Trinity according to substances; the audacity of Eunomius, who confines the incomprehensible nature within the limits of human knowledge; and the frenzy of Manichaeus and Macedonius, who separate the Holy Spirit from the essence of the Godhead, as though he proceeded separately.”

### CHAPTER LXXVI

Agnellus teaches in a letter to Menius that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son:

“Therefore the Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Nor does God, as some say, have two sons, Christ and the Holy Spirit; rather, he has an invisible Son, just as he himself is invisible. In order that he might be visible, the Son assumed the body of our weakness—not so that he would cease to be invisible, but so that, in Christ himself, he might remain invisible to unbelievers. For when he says, ‘Blessed are the eyes that now see what you see’ (Luke 10:23), then all the Jews and those who crucified him would have been blessed—for of them he says through David, ‘They themselves looked upon and saw me’ (Psalm 21:18). You see, therefore, that the invisible Father remains invisible and is perceived by a pure and believing mind. Thus the Father is invisible, the Son is invisible, and the Holy Spirit is invisible.

“And to bring you back to this point, from which it comes about that we teach this concerning a frail human being: these three things are invisible, undivided, gathered together into one, and overflowing with effective power: namely, the voice that generates the word; the power proceeding together with the voice from the word, which causes one man to become consul and another to be slaughtered. Tell me, Arius: are these three one, or are they not? If they are not one, then divide the voice from the word, and the power from the voice and the word. But if, in a frail human being, these three—the voice, the word, and the power—are so truly one that they are indeed three persons but one power of subsistence, then, as we have said, if such power exists in the most fragile human being, how much more does it exist in the omnipotence of God, so that the Father is the almighty begetter of the Son, and the power proceeding from the Father and the Son is the Holy Spirit.”

### CHAPTER LXXVII

Cassiodorus says in his exposition of Psalm 50 that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son:

“‘Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with your principal Spirit’ (Psalm 50:14). We should not think it accidental that the holy man, radiant with the illumination of his heart, named the Spirit a third time, unless it was because, devoted to the undivided Trinity, he asked forgiveness to be granted him by it. For, with respect to the essence of divinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are rightly called one God; but, in the distinction of persons, it is proper to the Father that he naturally begot the Son without beginning, before the ages; it is proper to the Son that he was naturally begotten by the Father; and it is proper to the Holy Spirit that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, because, through their ineffable love and cooperation, their consubstantial eternity and power accomplishes everything it wills in heaven and on earth,” etc., up to the point where he briefly discussed eternity.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII

Likewise, in his exposition of Psalm 61:

“‘For from him is my salvation,’ that is, the only-begotten Son, who rightly becomes salvation for believers. When it says, ‘from him,’ the Son is signified. For these are the distinctive properties possessed by the one God, the holy Trinity: the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son,” etc., up to the point where he demonstrated it with wondrous truth.

### CHAPTER LXXIX

Alcuin, in book I of *On the Faith of the Holy Trinity* (chapter 6), teaches that the Holy Spirit is the common Spirit of the Father and the Son:

“Therefore this gift of God, namely the Holy Spirit, who proceeds equally from the Father and the Son, is an ineffable communion of the Father and the Son. And perhaps he is called by this name because the same designation can apply to the Father and the Son. For he is properly called what they are called in common: the Father is rightly called Spirit, and the Son Spirit; the Father is holy, and the Son is holy. Therefore, so that the communion of both persons might properly be signified by names joined together which separately apply to each person, he is called the Holy Spirit, who is the third person in the Holy Trinity—equal in all things to the Father and the Son, coeternal and consubstantial.

“And this Trinity is one God, alone good, great, eternal, and almighty. Unity, divinity, greatness, goodness, omnipotence, and whatever is substantially predicated of himself belong to him alone. This is not to be understood or said in the same way of relative terms; for one cannot say ‘the Father is Father to himself,’ or ‘the Son is Son to himself,’ or ‘the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit to himself.’ These relative terms must without doubt be referred to another person.”

### CHAPTER LXXX

Likewise, in the same work (chapter 12):

“The Holy Spirit has this property: that he proceeds equally from the Father and the Son,” etc., up to the discussion of omnipotence and eternity.

### CHAPTER LXXXI

Likewise, in the same work (chapter 15):

“The Holy Spirit is nowhere called either unbegotten or begotten,” etc., up to the words “the Holy Spirit may proceed.”

### CHAPTER LXXXII

Likewise, in book II (chapter 9):

“These three are eternally three. That which is unbegotten is the Father alone, who derives his being from no one except himself. That which is begotten is the Son, whose being comes from the Father. That which is neither unbegotten nor begotten is the Holy Spirit, whose being is to proceed from the Father and the Son. And these three are the true, consubstantial, coeternal Trinity.”

### CHAPTER LXXXIII

Likewise, in book II (chapter 11):

“In Christ, according to the truth of the Catholic faith, we confess both divinity and a rational soul and flesh together in the unity of one person. Yet the divinity could not receive the Spirit, because, according to his divinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God. Therefore the divinity of the Son could not receive the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit himself proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father, and is given by the Son just as he is given by the Father.”

### CHAPTER LXXXIV

Likewise, in book II (chapter 19), on the unity of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son:

“The Holy Spirit, like the Father and the Son, is wholly and perfectly God; indeed, he is one God with the Father and the Son and one substance, as we stated above,” etc., up to the words “he breathes where he wills.”

### CHAPTER LXXXV

Likewise, in book II (chapter 20):

“The Holy Spirit exists in the same unity of substance and equality with the Father and the Son,” etc., up to the end of the chapter.

### CHAPTER LXXXVI

Likewise, in the same work (chapter 21), on why the same Holy Spirit was given twice by Christ God:

“Without doubt the Holy Spirit was given twice so that the two commandments of love might be commended,” etc., up to the end of the chapter.

### CHAPTER LXXXVII

Likewise, in book III, on how the mission of the Holy Spirit is to be understood:

“For just as the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father, so also he is sent by the Son,” etc., up to the end of the chapter.

### CHAPTER LXXXVIII

Likewise, in Alcuin’s *Faith*:

“We believe in the Holy Trinity, that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: one almighty God, of one substance, one essence, and one power; the Creator of all creatures. From whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things. The Father is from himself, not from another; the Son is begotten from the Father, true God from true God, true light from true light—not, however, two lights, but one light; and the Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and the Son, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son.”

### CHAPTER LXXXIX

Likewise, Alcuin, in his *Proposed Questions on the Holy Trinity* (answer to question 2):

“It is proper to the Father that he alone is Father, and that he is from no other except himself. It is proper to the Son that he is begotten from the Father, the only one begotten from the only one, coeternal and consubstantial. It is proper to the Holy Spirit that he is neither unbegotten, but proceeds equally from the Father and the Son.”

### CHAPTER XC

Prudentius, in his book *Against the Marcionites*, in heroic meter, in the peroration of the *Hamartigenia*:

“O almighty God, giver of the soul, O Christ God,

From whose mouth one God, the Spirit, came forth.”

### CHAPTER XCI

Likewise, in the same author’s book of Hymns, in iambic meter, in the hymn before sleep:

“O power, one light, of this Trinity,

Everlasting God from God,

God sent from both.”

### CHAPTER XCII

Likewise, in the same author’s book of Hymns, in choriambic meter, called Asclepiadic meter, in the hymn for the lighting of the Paschal candle:

“Good leader, author of the radiant light,

Who divide the times in their appointed turns,

When the sun has sunk and dreadful chaos presses in,

Restore the light to your faithful, O Christ.

Through Christ your begotten Son, highest Father,

In whom invisible glory stands before you,

Who is our Lord, your only Son,

Breathes forth the Paraclete from the Father’s heart.

Through him your splendor, honor, praise, wisdom,

Majesty, goodness, and piety,

Continue your reign under the threefold name,

Weaving age upon age forever.”

### CHAPTER XCIII

Likewise, in the Catholic Creed, which the universal Church of Gaul sings on Sunday at Mass, these words are sung among others:

“And I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, who together with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified, who spoke through the prophets.”

### CHAPTER XCIV

Likewise, Isidore says the following among other things in the Catholic Faith (*On the Order of Creatures*, chapter 1):

“One almighty God, the holy Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The almighty Father therefore derives his origin from no one, and he himself is the origin of the divinity; from him the almighty Son God was begotten without time. He was not created, for he is God. Apart from the fact that he is Son, everything in the divinity is common to him with the Father—in eternity, will, power, and wisdom. Likewise, apart from the fact that he is Father, everything is common to the Father with the Son.

“The Holy Spirit is almighty God. He is not begotten, because he is not the Son; nor is he created, because he is not a creature. Rather, he proceeds from the Father and the Son. Apart from the fact that he is the Holy Spirit, everything is common to him with the Father and the Son. For the person who is the Father is not here the Son or the Holy Spirit; nor is the person who is the Son here the Father or the Holy Spirit; nor is the person who is the Holy Spirit here the Father or the Son. But in essence, what the Father is, the Son and the Holy Spirit are also: one thing. What the Son is, the Father and the Holy Spirit are also. What the Holy Spirit is, the Father and the Son are also. Yet there is not a threefold number of gods in that Trinity. For, while the distinction of persons remains intact, everything belonging to the divinity is common.”

### CHAPTER XCV

Testimonies of the holy Fathers against those who, with profane intent, strive to attack the purity of Christ’s ministers—a purity which the beautiful virgin and true mother, the Church, without spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, has always chosen to preserve unstained in her service.
