Paul, the voice of thunder, speaks thus about purity when he permitted marriage to ordinary believers:

“Let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. This,” he says, “I say by way of concession, not by command. I wish that all people were as I myself am, but each has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that. But I say to the unmarried and widows: it is good for them if they remain as I do” (1 Corinthians 7:2, 6).

And shortly afterward, in the same First Letter to the Corinthians:

“I give advice as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful. Therefore I think this is good because of the present necessity, namely, that it is good for a person to be as he is” (ibid., 25).

The implied meaning is: to remain continent as I do.

And again shortly afterward:

“I want you to be without anxiety. The unmarried man is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please God. But the married man is concerned with how he may please his wife.”

But if he urges this chastity upon laypeople, he desires it to be present much more in the ministers of the Church.

Likewise, the Apostle says to the Galatians:

“Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. These are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law” (Galatians 5:16).

And again:

“The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, gentleness, continence, chastity; against such things there is no law” (ibid., 22).

And again:

“If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit” (ibid., verse 25).

When he had said concerning Christ, the great high priest, in the Letter to the Hebrews:

“Such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens” (Hebrews 7:26),

he set this purity of chastity before all priests and ministers of the Church for their observance. And if such things are praised among secular people, they appear all the more honorable among ecclesiastical persons.

Likewise, Paul says to the Colossians:

“Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire” (Colossians 3:5).

He also adds:

“Because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. In these things you too once walked, when you lived in them. But now you too must put away all these things: anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and shameful speech from your mouth.”

To increase these exhortations, the Son of God concludes and commands:

“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35).

And Paul says:

“It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Corinthians 7:1), as though danger were immediately present at the touch itself. If carnal people must refrain from touch and beware of it, spiritual people must abstain even more urgently and permanently from illicit embraces.

Likewise, Paul says:

“Fornication and every impurity or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or coarse joking, which are improper, but rather thanksgiving. For know this with understanding: no fornicator, impure person, or greedy person—which is idolatry—has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” (Ephesians 5:3).

And shortly afterward:

“For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light. For the fruit of light consists in every goodness, righteousness, and truth” (ibid., 8).

By these and very many other authorities, purity of mind and body is exalted even to the heavens.

### CHAPTER XCVI

At the Council of Nicaea, concerning women brought into the household of clergy (canon 3, from the first edition):

“The great synod absolutely forbade a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all who belongs to the clergy to have a woman brought into his household, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, aunt, or one of those persons who escape suspicion.”

The blessed Ambrose greatly extols this Council of Nicaea in his book *On the Trinity* (at the end of the preface to book I of *On the Faith to Gratian*) in these words:

“Of the councils, I shall especially follow this: that the three hundred and eighteen priests, chosen as though for Abraham’s judgment, victorious through the harmony of their faith, raised up a trophy throughout the whole world over the defeated impious, so that this seems divine to me: that in the councils we possess an oracle in the same number in which history gives us an example of piety.”

### CHAPTER XCVII

In the decretals of Pope Siricius, concerning incontinent clergy, chapter 7 (letter 1, chapter 7):

“Let us now come to the most sacred orders of the clergy, which, as your charity has informed us, we have found trampled upon and confused throughout your provinces, to the injury of venerable religion, so that we must say in the words of Jeremiah: ‘Who will give water to my head, or a fountain of tears to my eyes? And I will weep for this people day and night’ (Jeremiah 9). If the blessed prophet says that tears are not sufficient for him to mourn the sins of the people, how deeply can we be struck with grief when we are compelled to lament the crimes of those who belong to our own body? Upon them, according to the blessed Paul, daily urgency and concern for all the Churches continually press. ‘Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?’ (2 Corinthians 11).

“For we have learned that very many priests and Levites of Christ, even after long periods of consecrated service, have begotten offspring both from their own marriages and from shameful intercourse, and defend their crime by this argument: that in the Old Testament priests and ministers are said to have been granted the ability to beget children,” etc., up to the words “they have found the remedy.”

### CHAPTER XCVIII

In the same decretals, *On the Conversion of Clerics*, chapter 9:

“Whoever therefore devotes himself to the service of the Church ought, from infancy and before the years of puberty, to be baptized and associated with the ministry of the readers. If, upon reaching adolescence and up to his thirtieth year, he has lived commendably, he must remain content with one wife only—the woman whom he received as a virgin through the common blessing of a priest—and must be an acolyte and subdeacon. After this, if he first proves himself worthy, with continence leading the way, he may advance to the rank of deacon. If he serves commendably there for more than five years, he will suitably attain the presbyterate. Thereafter, after ten years, he may attain the episcopal chair, provided that during these periods the integrity of his life and faith has been approved.”

### CHAPTER XCIX

Likewise, in the same decretals, *Which Women May Live with Clergy*, chapter 12:

“We do not permit any other women to be in the houses of clergy except those whom the Council of Nicaea permitted to live with them solely because of the necessities of relationship.”

### CHAPTER C

Pope Innocent, in the decretals, *On the Incontinence of Priests or Levites*, chapter 21, to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse (letter 3, chapter 1):

“You have asked what should be observed concerning those who, placed in the ministry of the diaconate or in the office of the presbyterate, are shown by the children they have begotten to be or to have been incontinent. Concerning them there is both the discipline of the divine laws and the clear admonitions of Siricius, bishop of blessed memory, namely, that those placed in such offices who are incontinent should be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor and should not be admitted to a ministry which ought to be fulfilled by continence alone,” etc., up to the words “are thought to be seeking pleasure.”

### CHAPTER CI

Likewise, Pope Innocent, *That Those Who Have Begotten Children in the Presbyterate Must Be Removed from Office*, chapter 23 (letter 5, at the beginning):

“He is moved by zeal for faith and discipline and does not permit the Church to be polluted by unworthy presbyters whom he asserts to have begotten children while in the presbyterate. I would explain that this is not permitted if I did not know that your prudence possesses knowledge of the whole law. Therefore, dearest brothers, after examining the contents of the attached petition, order those who are said to have committed such acts to be brought forward publicly; and, after the charges brought against the presbyters themselves have been investigated, if they can be convicted, let them be removed from the priestly office. For those who are not holy cannot undertake holy things, and they become strangers to the ministry which they have polluted by unlawful conduct. We are astonished that their bishops conceal these matters, so that they may be judged either to connive at what is unlawful or not to know it.”

### CHAPTER CII

When Pope Saint Siricius was seated in council in the Church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and was setting out ecclesiastical laws for the brothers and fellow bishops throughout Africa, he introduced the following among other matters concerning chastity (letter 4, no. 9):

“Moreover, because it is worthy, chaste, and honorable, we urge that priests and Levites not have intercourse with their wives, since ministers are occupied with the daily necessities of their ministry. For Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: ‘Abstain so that you may have leisure for prayer’ (1 Corinthians 7). If abstinence is commanded to laypeople so that their prayers may be heard, how much more must a priest at every moment be ready, secure in the purity of cleanliness, lest he be required either to offer sacrifice or to baptize. If he has been polluted by carnal desire, what will he do? How will he excuse himself? With what shame, with what state of mind, will he presume to act? With what conscience, by what merit, does he believe that he will be heard here, when it has been said: ‘All things are clean to the clean, but to the polluted and unbelieving nothing is clean’ (Titus 1)?

“Therefore I urge, I admonish, I beg: let this reproach be removed, which even the pagans can rightly bring as an accusation. Perhaps this is believed because it is written: ‘The husband of one wife’ (1 Timothy 3). He did not mean one who remains in the desire to beget children, but one prepared for future continence. For he did not exclude those who were chaste when he said: ‘I wish all people to be as I am’ (1 Corinthians 7). And he declares it more openly when he says: ‘Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit’ (Romans 8).

“Therefore, brothers, if all these things are observed by everyone with complete vigilance, ambition will cease, disagreement will subside, heresies and schisms will not arise, and the devil will find no opportunity to rage. Unity will remain, iniquity will be overcome and trampled down; love will blaze with spiritual fervor, and the peace proclaimed by the lips will agree with the will—the peace, that is, of our God and Savior, which he commanded to be preserved near the time of his Passion and rightly left to us as an inheritance, saying: ‘My peace I give you; my peace I leave you’ (John 14). And in accordance with the Apostle’s command: ‘Let us remain of one mind, thinking the same thing in Christ; let us claim nothing for ourselves through rivalry or empty glory, and let us please not human beings but our God and Savior’ (Philippians 2).

“If we faithfully wish to obey all these commands, the Lord will guard our bodies and our souls on the day when he will repay each person according to his works. But if anyone, puffed up in the mind of his flesh, wishes to depart from this canonical rule, let him know that he will both be excluded from our communion and suffer the punishments of Gehenna. Moreover, mercy must be exercised with judgment. For a hand must be extended to such as are falling, in such a way that it does not drag one who is running into ruin.

“Given at Rome in a council of eighty bishops, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, after the consulship of Arcadius Augustus and Bauto, most illustrious consuls.”

### CHAPTER CIII

In the decretals of Pope Leo, *That Carnal Marriage Is to Be Denied to Subdeacons*, chapter 34 (letter 84, chapter 4):

“For while those outside the clerical order are free to devote themselves to the partnership of marriage and the begetting of children, nevertheless, in order to display the purity of perfect continence, carnal marriage is not granted to subdeacons. Thus those who have wives may be as though they did not have them (1 Corinthians 7:29), and those who do not have wives may remain single. If this ought to be observed in this order, which is fourth from the highest, how much more must it be observed in the first, second, and third orders, lest anyone be considered fit for Levitical honor, priestly honor, or episcopal excellence who is shown not yet to have restrained himself from the pleasure of a wife.”

### CHAPTER CIV

Pope Leo, sending a letter to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, and answering his questions, says among other things, chapter 3 (letter 92, inquiry 3):

“Concerning those who minister at the altar and have wives: is it lawful for them to have intercourse with them? The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and presbyters. When they were laymen or readers, they were permitted both to marry and to beget children; but when they reached the aforementioned ranks, what had been lawful for them began to be unlawful. Therefore, so that a carnal marriage may become a spiritual one, they ought not to dismiss their wives, but to have them as though they did not have them, so that the love of marriage may remain intact while the activity of marriage ceases.”

### CHAPTER CV

Likewise, Pope Leo, in his letter sent to the bishops of Mauritania, says among other things (in the edition, letter 87 to the African bishops through Mauritania, etc., chapter 1):

“The order of the entire household will totter if what is required in the body is not found in the head,” etc., up to the point where he says “they proved to be pure silver.”

### CHAPTER CVI

In the canons of the holy apostles, chapter 7 (canon 7; elsewhere 6; it differs from the edition):

“That priests and ministers of the altar abstain from secular concerns. A bishop, presbyter, or deacon must by no means undertake secular concerns; otherwise, let him be deposed.”

### CHAPTER CVII

Likewise, in the same collection, *That Ministers of the Altar Must Communicate after the Oblation Has Been Celebrated*, chapter 9 (canon 9, from the version of Dionysius Exiguus):

“If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all from the priestly order, after making the oblation, does not communicate, let him either state his reason, so that, if it is reasonable, he may obtain pardon; or, if he does not state it, let him be deprived of communion as one who has given the people cause for offense by creating suspicion that he who offered the sacrifice did not offer it correctly.”

### CHAPTER CVIII

Likewise, in the same collection, *Which Clerics May Be Joined to Wives*, chapter 27 (canon 18, from the same version):

“Concerning those who are unmarried and have been advanced into the clergy, we command that, if they wish, they may take wives, but only if they are readers or singers.”

### CHAPTER CIX

At the Council of Carthage, chapter 16 (Third Council of Carthage, chapter 17, from the first edition):

“That no unrelated women should live with any clergy at all, but only mothers, grandmothers, maternal aunts, paternal aunts, sisters, and the daughters of brothers or sisters, and any women from the household who, because of domestic necessity, were already living with them before they were ordained; or daughters-in-law, if their sons took wives after their parents had been ordained; or women whom it became necessary to bring in from elsewhere for servants who had none in the household whom they could marry.”

### CHAPTER CX

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 24 (ibid., chapter 25):

“That clerics or continent men must not visit widows or virgins except on the order or with the permission of bishops or presbyters; and they must not do so alone, but with clerics or with those whom the bishop or presbyter has ordered to accompany them. Nor may bishops or presbyters themselves visit such women alone, but only where clerics are present or where there are some reputable Christians.”

### CHAPTER CXI

In the canon of the Council of Ancyra, chapter 10 (canon 10; this version differs from three editions):

“When deacons are ordained, if at the ordination itself they have declared, saying that they wish to have wives and are unable to remain continent, then, if afterward they marry, they are to remain in the clergy only and are to be removed from the ministry. But those who kept silent and accepted the laying on of hands, professing continence, and afterward married, must cease from the ministry and from the clergy, receiving only lay communion.”

### CHAPTER CXII

At the Council of Laodicea, *Concerning Men Who Bathe with Women*, chapter 30 (chapter 30, from the translation of Dionysius Exiguus):

“That those devoted to sacred offices—whether clerics, continent men, or any Christian layperson—ought not to bathe together with women, because among the pagans this is the first reproach.”

### CHAPTER CXIII

In the same council, *That Clerics May Not Attend Amusement Spectacles*, chapter 54:

“Ministers of the altar or any clerics at all ought not to attend spectacles displayed either at weddings or at banquets; rather, before the theatrical performers enter, they ought to rise and leave the banquet.”

### CHAPTER CXIV

At the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 1 (chapter 1, from the translation of Gerard Mercator):

“A presbyter who has married a wife must be deposed from his order. If he has committed fornication or adultery, he must be expelled from the Church and, reduced to the status of a layman, must perform penance.”

### CHAPTER CXV

Likewise, Pope Innocent to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, chapter 10 (letter 2, chapter 9):

“Moreover, what is worthy, chaste, and honorable the Church must observe in every way: that priests and Levites not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with the daily necessities of the ministry. For it is written: ‘Be holy, because I too am holy, says the Lord your God’ (Leviticus 11:44 and 20). In former times the priests did not leave the temple of God during the year of their service, as we read concerning Zechariah, nor did they touch their own house at all,” etc., up to the end of the chapter.

### CHAPTER CXVI

Likewise, to the same man, chapter 12 (chapter 10, at the end):

“This rule is observed among clerics, especially since the ancient rule states that anyone who, after being corrected and baptized, wished to become a cleric had to promise that he would never marry a wife.”

### CHAPTER CXVII

At the Council of Laodicea, *That Those Who Are Ministers of the Altar Must Not Enter Taverns*, chapter 22 (chapter 24, from the translation of Mercator):

“Since those serving the altar—from presbyters down to deacons, and thereafter persons of the ecclesiastical order down to ministers, readers, singers, exorcists, and doorkeepers who have adopted a life of continence—ought not to enter taverns.”

### CHAPTER CXVIII

At the Council of Carthage, *On Continence*, chapter 3 (Second Council of Carthage, chapter 2):

“Bishop Aurelius said: When the previous council was considering the regulation of continence and chastity, it seemed fitting that these three ranks, which are joined by a certain written bond of chastity through consecration—namely, bishops, presbyters, and deacons—should, as is becoming for holy bishops and priests of God, as well as for Levites and those who serve the divine sacraments, be continent in all things, so that they may simply obtain from God what they ask. Let us also preserve what the apostles taught and antiquity itself has observed.”

### CHAPTER CXIX

Likewise, in the same council, *On the Abstinence of Various Orders from Their Wives*, chapter 4 (chapter 14, from another edition):

“Faustinus, bishop of the Church of Potentia in the province of Picenum, legate of the Roman Church, said: It is pleasing that bishops, presbyters, and deacons, or those who handle the sacraments, as guardians of chastity, abstain from their wives. All the bishops said: It is pleasing that chastity be preserved in all things and by all who serve the altar.”

### CHAPTER CXX

At the African Council, *That Clerics Must Abstain from Their Wives*, chapter 37 (chapter 7, and Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 3):

“Moreover, when the incontinence of certain clerics, even toward their own wives, was reported, it was decided that bishops, presbyters, and deacons should, in accordance with the earlier statutes, also abstain from their wives. If they do not do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office. Other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this, but the matter is to be observed according to the custom of each Church.”

### CHAPTER CXXI

In the synod presided over at Rome by the blessed Pope Sylvester with two hundred and eighty-four bishops, where Bishop Victorinus, Callistus, and the deacon Hippolytus were condemned, with bishops, presbyters, and Greek clerics present, the following is read among other things (Second Council, 19; it differs from the edition):

“No presbyter may take a wife from the day of receiving the honor of the presbyterate. If anyone, neglecting this, acts otherwise, we declare that he is to be deprived of his honor for twelve years. If anyone acts against this written decree, in its present and public form, he will be condemned forever.”

### CHAPTER CXXII

Ambrose says the following, among other things, in his Letter to Titus (on chapter 2):

“Younger men likewise,” etc., up to the words “he proves by deeds.”

### CHAPTER CXXIII
Also in the Epistle to Timothy:

“[He must be] the husband of one wife” (1 Tim. 3). Although having a second wife is not forbidden as a matter of number, nevertheless, for someone to be worthy of the episcopate, he ought even to renounce what is lawful because of the eminence of that order, since the one who desires that office must be better than the others: sober, chaste, hospitable, teachable, not addicted to wine, not violent but moderate; not quarrelsome, not harsh, managing his household well and having children subject to him with all charity (ibid.). He says that a man who observes these good qualities that he enumerates ought to be made a bishop. For these are the marks of episcopal dignity. But if someone, pursuing what is better, has dedicated both body and soul to God and therefore does not bind himself in marriage, he will become all the more worthy; for this reason he placed the lesser condition first, so that no one might doubt the superior one.”

## CHAPTER CXXIV

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“Likewise, deacons must be chaste, not double-tongued, not devoted to much wine, not occupied with shameful profits, holding the mystery of the faith with a pure conscience. Let these also first be tested, and then let them serve without blame. He who prescribes that deacons be chosen with such care—men who are plainly ministers of the priests—what sort of men does he wish bishops to be, except, as he himself says, irreproachable? They must not be engaged in public, shameful, or sordid business. For he knows that people engage in trade in order to receive profits, and that a person professes nothing other than what he practices. He calls these profits shameful when one pursues gain under the guise of a pious profession. For a person is found shameful when he displays himself as pure.

“Nevertheless, after the bishop he places the ordination of the diaconate. Why? Unless because the bishop and the presbyter have one ordination, since both are priests; but the bishop is first, so that every bishop is a presbyter, though not every presbyter is a bishop. For the bishop is the one who is first among the presbyters. Finally, he indicates that Timothy was ordained a presbyter; but because he had no one before him, he was a bishop. Hence he also shows how a bishop is to be ordained; for it was neither right nor permitted that an inferior should ordain a superior. No one gives what he has not received.”

## CHAPTER CXXV

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“Let deacons be husbands of one wife, etc., up to ‘they are stewards of God.’”

## CHAPTER CXXVI

Again, Ambrose, in the first book *On the Duties of Ministers* (this chapter does not occur in Book I of St. Ambrose’s *On Duties*):

“There is no need for younger men to visit the homes of widows and virgins except for the purpose of visitation; and even then, they should do so with older men—that is, either with the bishop or, if the matter is more serious, with presbyters. Why should we give secular people an opportunity for slander? Why should those visits also be granted such authority through their frequency? What if one of those women should perhaps fall? Why should we incur the odium of another’s fall? How many even strong men have been deceived by enticement? How many have not given opportunity for error, yet have given opportunity for suspicion?

“Why do you not devote the times when you are free from the church to reading? Why do you not revisit Christ, address Christ, listen to Christ? We address him when we pray; we listen to him when we read the divine oracles. What have we to do with other people’s houses? There is one house that contains everyone; let those who seek us come to us instead. What have we to do with stories? We have received a ministry to be offered to Christ’s altars, not service to human beings. We ought to be humble, gentle, meek, serious, and patient. Let either our silent expression or our speech announce that we maintain restraint in all things.”

## CHAPTER CXXVII

Again, the same author, in the same book (ch. 50, at the beginning):

“But what should I say about chastity, when even one marriage, and not a repeated union, is permitted, etc., up to the words ‘which belongs to self-control.’”

## CHAPTER CXXVIII

Jerome, in his Epistle to Titus (on chapter 1), says the following among other things concerning chastity:

“But he must also have a good testimony from those who are outside, so that he may not fall into reproach and the snare of the devil” (1 Tim. 3). As for what he says, “the husband of one wife” (ibid.), we must understand it in this way: we should not think that every monogamist is better than a man who has married twice, but that the person should be able to exhort his subjects to monogamy and continence who offers his own example in teaching, etc., up to ‘indulge the necessity of the flesh.’”

## CHAPTER CXXIX

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“Let the bishop also be chaste, whom the Greeks call σώφρονα (*sōphrona*), meaning ‘self-controlled’; but the Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, translated it as ‘prudent’ instead of ‘chaste.’ If laymen are commanded to abstain from intercourse with their wives for the sake of prayer, what should be thought of the bishop, who prays daily for his own sins and those of the people? etc., up to ‘let them be a rule of truth.’”

## CHAPTER CXXX

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward (on chapter 2):

“‘Showing yourself,’ he says, ‘as a model of good works.’ It is of no benefit for someone to be practiced in speaking and to have worn out his tongue in discourse, unless he teaches more by example than by word. Finally, if someone is impure, however eloquent he may be, when he urges his hearers to chastity, his speech is weak and he has no authority to exhort. Conversely, however rustic and slow of speech he may be, if he is chaste, he can by his example compel people to imitate his life, etc., up to ‘in incorruption and chastity.’”

## CHAPTER CXXXI

Jerome, in his *Apology to Pammachius*, discusses chastity among other matters as follows (Epistle 50, before the middle, vol. II, p. 133):

“At the end, we concluded our discussion by this comparison between marriage and virginity: Where there is something good and something better, the reward of the good and of the better is not one and the same; and where the reward is not one, the gifts are certainly different. Thus the difference between marriage and virginity is as great as that between not sinning and doing good—or, to put it more mildly, as great as that between the good and the better, etc., up to ‘each person can bear it.’”

## CHAPTER CXXXII

Again, Jerome, in the same *Apology*, shortly afterward:

“There is no doubt that the priests descended from Aaron, Eleazar, and Phinehas, who themselves had wives, would rightly be brought forward against us if we were arguing, in the error of the Encratites, that marriages ought to be rejected, etc., up to ‘I would place him in the third rank.’”

## CHAPTER CXXXIII

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“But now, since I have been more an interpreter of the Apostle than of a doctrine, and have performed the office of a commentator, whatever seems harsh should be attributed more and more to the one whom I have explained than to us who have explained him, etc., up to ‘rather than the obscure diligence of others.’”

## CHAPTER CXXXIV

Concerning virgins, married women, widows, monogamists, digamists, trigamists, and so forth, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“Married men are indignant against me because I said: ‘I ask you, what sort of good is that which forbids one to pray and does not permit one to receive Christ’s body? When I fulfill a husband’s duty, I do not fulfill the duty of one who practices continence,’ etc., up to ‘I changed neither the meaning nor the words.’”

## CHAPTER CXXXV

Again, the same author, at the end of his *Apology*:

“Therefore, in this final statement, I declare that I have neither condemned marriage nor do I condemn it; I have answered my adversary, and I have not feared the ambushes of my own people. But I exalt virginity to heaven, not because I possess it, but because I admire all the more what I do not possess. It is an open and modest confession to praise in others what one lacks oneself, etc., up to the end of the *Apology*.”

## CHAPTER CXXXVI

Again, Jerome, in Book I *Against Jovinian*, says among other things:

“Do you wish to know what the Apostle means? Join to it what follows: ‘But I wish all people to be as I myself am’ (1 Cor. 7:7). Blessed is the person who has been like Paul; happy is the one who hears the Apostle commanding, not excusing. ‘This,’ he says, ‘I wish; this I desire: that you be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ’ (1 Cor. 4:16). He was a virgin born of a virgin, incorrupt from one who was incorrupt; but because we are human beings and cannot imitate the Savior’s birth, let us at least imitate his manner of life, etc., up to ‘but I desire the good simply for its own sake.’”

## CHAPTER CXXXVII

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“What great happiness it is not to be the servant of a wife but of Christ; not to serve the flesh but the spirit. ‘For whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit’ (1 Cor. 6:17). And lest someone perhaps think that, in what he had said above—‘Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned; but even if you can become free, make use of it’ (1 Cor. 7:21)—he had mocked continence and handed us over to servitude to spouses, he adds a sentence that cuts off every quibble: ‘You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings’ (ibid., 23), etc., up to ‘the necessity that presses upon us.’”

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“For this reason Christ loves virgins more, because they freely offer what was not commanded them; and it is a greater grace to offer what one does not owe than to repay what is demanded. The Apostles, considering the burden of a wife, say: ‘If such is the situation of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry’ (Matt. 19:10). Approving their judgment, the Lord says: ‘You rightly perceive that it is not expedient for a man who is advancing toward the kingdom of heaven to take a wife; but the matter is difficult, and not everyone grasps this saying, but only those to whom it has been given’ (ibid., 11).”

## CHAPTER CXXXIX

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“At the same time we must examine the statement: ‘Those who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. 19:12). If eunuchs receive the reward of the kingdom of heaven, then those who have not made themselves eunuchs cannot receive the place of eunuchs. ‘Let the one who can grasp it grasp it’ (ibid.). It is a matter of great faith and great virtue to be God’s purest temple, to offer oneself wholly as a holocaust to the Lord, and, according to the same Apostle, to be holy in both body and spirit, etc., up to ‘free and finally released.’”

## CHAPTER CXL

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“I come now to husbands. ‘The time is short’ (1 Cor. 7:29); the Lord is near. Even if we lived nine hundred years, like the people of ancient times, nevertheless the time should be considered short if it would eventually have an end and cease to exist. But now, since the tribulation of marriage is short-lived no less than its joy, why do we take wives whom we are soon compelled to lose?” etc., up to “divided among the portions of anxieties and miseries.”

## CHAPTER CXLI

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“The first Adam was monogamous; the second unmarried: let those who approve digamy exhibit a third Adam who was a digamist, and let them follow him. But suppose that Paul permitted second marriages. By the same law he permits a third and a fourth, and as many as there are deaths of husbands. The Apostle is compelled to want many things that he does not want, etc., up to ‘according to the image of his Creator.’”

## CHAPTER CXLII

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“For a servant of a wife cannot serve in the Lord’s military service, etc., up to ‘he led them into the promised land.’”

## CHAPTER CXLIII

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“But now it is time for us to raise the standard of Jesus’ chastity, etc., up to ‘covered by the Savior’s help.’”

## CHAPTER CXLIV

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“And when the book that is called by Jesus’ name has been completed as far as his burial, he is again described in the Book of Judges as though alive and rising again, etc., up to ‘he begins to be crowned after death.’”

## CHAPTER CXLV

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“Do we not have the right to eat and drink, or to lead about believing women as sisters? Since eating and drinking, and the provision of expenses, are mentioned first, and then women are introduced as sisters, it is clear that wives are not meant, but those women who, as we have said, provided from their own resources, etc., up to ‘Scripture signifies nothing of the kind.’”

## CHAPTER CXLVI

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“We can say of Peter that he had a mother-in-law at the time when he believed, and that by then he no longer had a wife, etc., up to ‘the Virgin Mother is entrusted to the virgin disciple.’”

## CHAPTER CXLVII

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“As a worm in wood, so a wicked wife destroys her husband (Prov. 25). But if you maintain that this was said about bad married couples, I will answer you briefly. What necessity presses upon me to risk uncertainty about whether the woman I marry will prove bad or good? etc., up to ‘from his own dwelling, that is, from the Church.’”

## CHAPTER CXLVIII

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“Either allow priests to perform the duties of marriage, so that virgins and married men are the same; or, if priests are not permitted to touch wives, they are holy in this respect, because they imitate virginal chastity. This too must be added: if a layman or any other believer cannot pray unless he is free from marital duties, then the priest, who must always offer sacrifices for the people, must always pray. If he must always pray, then he must always abstain from marriage. For under the old law, those who offered victims for the people were not only absent from their houses, but were purified for a time by being separated from their wives, and they did not drink wine or strong drink, which customarily arouse lust.”

## CHAPTER CXLIX

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“Therefore the bishop must be irreproachable (1 Tim. 3), so that he is enslaved to no vice. ‘The husband of one wife’: one who has had one wife, not one who currently has one. ‘Sober,’ or, as it is better expressed in Greek, ‘watchful,’ that is, νηφάλιον (*nēphalion*); ‘chaste,’ for this is what σώφρονα (*sōphrona*) signifies; adorned both with chastity and with good character; hospitable, so that he may imitate Abraham and receive Christ with strangers—or rather, in strangers, etc., up to ‘not the one who is nobler, but the one who is stronger.’”

## CHAPTER CL

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, so that we may live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die, etc.,” up to “let us serve in the Gospel of the new Adam.”

## CHAPTER CLI

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“I think that the one who has a wife, as long as he returns to the same marital relation, so that Satan may not tempt him, sows in the flesh and not in the spirit, etc., up to ‘let us be joined to these and follow these.’”

## CHAPTER CLII

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“Let us pass to James, who was called the brother of the Lord, a man of such holiness, such righteousness, and perpetual virginity that Josephus, the Jewish historian, also reports that Jerusalem was overthrown because of his death, etc., up to ‘had dedicated himself as a virgin.’”

## CHAPTER CLIII

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3). And everyone who has this hope purifies himself, just as he is pure, etc., up to the words ‘to be defiled in comparison with this.’”

## CHAPTER CLIV

Again, the same author, in the same work, shortly afterward:

“It would be endless to expound from the Gospel the mystery of the five foolish and five wise virgins. For now I say only this: just as virginity alone does not save without the other works, so all works without virginity, purity, continence, and chastity are imperfect, etc., up to ‘we have offered examples from the divine books.’”

## CHAPTER CLV

Again, Jerome, in Book II *Against Jovinian*, says:

“Chaeremon the Stoic, a most eloquent man, relates concerning the life of the ancient Egyptian priests that, setting aside all the business and cares of the world, they were always in the temple and contemplated the natures, causes, and movements of the stars. They never associated with women; they never saw relatives or kinsmen, not even children. From the time when they began to devote themselves to divine worship, they always abstained from meat and wine, because of the weakness of their senses and the dizziness of the head that they suffered from eating little, and especially because of the impulses of lust that arise from these foods and this drink. They rarely ate bread, lest they burden the stomach, etc., up to ‘he published a work of his own.’”

## CHAPTER CLVI

Again, the same author, in the same work:

“We have spoken of married women, widows, and virgins; we have preferred virginity and widowhood to marriage, etc., up to ‘let the fear of the ruin of those who stand be present.’”

## CHAPTER CLVII

Origen, in Book III on Leviticus (or Homily 3 on chapter 3), says among other things:

“‘Any person who touches anything unclean, or the carcass of unclean animals, and is unaware of it, is defiled; or if he touches any human uncleanness, any uncleanness by which he is defiled’ (Lev. 5:2), etc. These observances are, among the Jews, sufficiently improper and useless. For why should the person who touches, for example, a dead animal or the body of a deceased human being be considered unclean? What if it were the body of a prophet? What if it were the body of a patriarch, or even of Abraham himself? What if he touched the bones of Samuel—would he be unclean? What if he touched the bones of Elisha, which raise the dead—would the one who touched them be unclean, and would the bones of the prophet make unclean even the one whom they raise from the dead? (2 Kings 13.) See how incongruous the Jewish understanding is.

“But let us first examine what it means to touch and what sort of touch makes one unclean. The Apostle says: ‘It is good for a man not to touch a woman’ (1 Cor. 7). This touch is unclean; for this is what the Lord said in the Gospel: ‘Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart’ (Matt. 7). The vice of desire has touched his heart, and his soul has become unclean. Therefore, if someone touches anything in this way—that is, either through desire for a woman, through greed for money, or through any other sinful desire—he has touched something unclean and has been defiled.

“You must therefore, if you have touched anything of this kind, know how to offer sacrifice according to what we recalled above, so that you may be made clean. Do you wish me to show you what sort of soul has touched something unclean and become unclean, and then touched something clean and become clean again? It is the soul of the woman who suffered from an issue of blood and spent all her resources on physicians without being able to benefit at all; through the uncleanness of sin she had been brought into this condition. She had touched sin, and for that reason had received the scourge of the flesh. But after she touched Jesus’ fringe, full of faith, the flow of her blood stopped, and she suddenly became clean—she who had previously lived unclean for so long.

“And just as, when she had touched the Lord and Savior, he said: ‘Who touched me? For I perceived power going out from me’ (Matt. 9), we understand without doubt that this was the power that healed the woman and made her clean; so we must understand that if someone touches sin, a certain evil power comes out of the sin itself, making the person who touched it unclean. This is truly what it means to touch something unclean. The same reasoning must also be applied to the carcass of a human being or to the carcass of a clean or unclean animal.”

## CHAPTER CLVIII

Again, the same author, in Book V on Leviticus (Homily 5):

“It follows that, according to the image of the one who gave the priesthood of the Church, the ministers and priests of the Church must also take upon themselves the sins of the people; and, imitating their teacher, they must grant the people remission of sins. The priests of the Church must therefore be so perfect and so trained in priestly duties that, in the holy place, in the courts of the tabernacle of testimony, they may consume the sins of the people without themselves sinning.

“But what does it mean to eat sin in a holy place? There was a holy place to which Moses came, according to what was said to him: ‘For the place on which you stand is holy ground’ (Exod. 3). Likewise, in the Church of God the holy place is perfect faith, love from a pure heart, and a good conscience. Whoever stands in these within the Church should recognize that he is standing in a holy place. For the holy place is not to be sought on the earth, concerning which God once pronounced the sentence: ‘Cursed is the earth in your works’ (Gen. 3). Whole faith and holy conduct are therefore the holy place. In this place, then, the priest of the Church should consume the sins of the people, slaughtering the victim of God’s word and offering the sacrifices of sound teaching, so that he may cleanse the consciences of his hearers from sins.”

## CHAPTER CLIX

Again, the same author, in the same book:

“Let the priests of the Lord who preside over the churches learn that they are given a portion with those whose offenses they have made propitious [to God]. But what does it mean to reconcile an offense? If you take a sinner and, by admonishing, exhorting, teaching, and instructing him, bring him to repentance; if you correct him from error, amend him from vices, and make him such that God becomes favorable to him after his conversion, you are said to have made propitiation for his offense.

“If, therefore, you are such a priest, and such are your teaching and your speech, a portion is given to you of those whom you have corrected, so that their merit may be your reward and their salvation your glory. Or does not the Apostle also show this when he says: ‘The one who builds upon it will receive a reward’ (1 Cor. 3:14)? Let the priests of the Lord therefore understand where their portion has been assigned, and let them devote themselves to this and attend to it. Let them not entangle themselves in empty and superfluous activities, but know that they will have a portion with God in nothing else except what they offer for sins—that is, in turning sinners back from the way of sin.

“It should also be noted that what is offered as a holocaust is internal; what is external is not offered to the Lord. The skin is not offered to the Lord, nor does it become part of the burnt offerings.”

## CHAPTER CLX

Again, the same author, in Book VI on Leviticus (Homily 6):

“For when a priest is ordained, the presence of the people is required, so that everyone may know and be certain who is more eminent among the whole people, who is more learned, who is holier, and who excels in every virtue. That person is chosen for the priesthood, with the people standing by, so that afterward no reconsideration may arise for anyone and no scruple may remain. This is also what the Apostle commands in the ordination of a priest when he says: ‘He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside’ (1 Tim. 3).

“Yet I see something more in what he says: Moses summoned the entire assembly, and I think that summoning the assembly means gathering all the virtues of the soul into one place and assembling the virtues together. Thus, when discussion is held about priestly mysteries, all the virtues of the soul may be vigilant and attentive, so that nothing of wisdom, nothing of knowledge, and nothing of diligence may be lacking in them; rather, let the whole multitude of the senses be present, and let the entire assembly of holy thoughts be present, so that within the sanctuary of his heart he may perceive what the high priest is, what the anointing is, and what his garments signify.”

## CHAPTER CLXI

Again, the same author, in the same book:

“The eighth kind is called the *campestre*, or, as we read elsewhere, the linen drawers, about which he was silent here among the other garments. What, then, shall we say? Shall we attribute forgetfulness to the words of the Holy Spirit, so that, when he has explained all the other matters a second time, only the one kind mentioned above escaped him? I do not dare to think this about sacred words. But let us see whether perhaps, because above we said that this kind of garment appears to signify chastity, by which the thighs seem to be covered or the loins and flanks bound, he may perhaps not be saying that these parts were always bound in those who were priests at that time.

“For at times permission is granted concerning the continuation of a lineage and the succession of offspring; but I would not introduce such an interpretation among the priests of the Church. For I see the sacramental meaning running in another direction. Priests and teachers in the Church can also beget children, as did the one who said: ‘My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you’ (Gal. 4:19). And again elsewhere he says: ‘Even if you have countless tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel’ (1 Cor. 4:15).

“These teachers of the Church therefore sometimes use bound drawers in begetting such offspring, and abstain from begetting when they find hearers in whom they know they can bear no fruit. Finally, it is also reported in the Acts of the Apostles concerning certain people: ‘We were not able,’ he says, ‘to speak the word of God in Asia’ (Acts 16). This means that they had put on the drawers and restrained themselves from begetting children, because their hearers were such that the seed would perish and no succession could result.

“Thus, when the priests of the Church see ears that are incapable of receiving, or when they recognize hearers who are pretenders and hypocrites, let them put on the *campestre* and use the drawers, so that the seed of the word of God may not perish; for the Lord also commands and says the same: ‘Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet and then turn and tear you apart’ (Matt. 7:6).”

## CHAPTER CLXII

Isidore, bishop of the Church of Seville, says in Book II of *The Offices* (ch. 5):

“That those who are chosen for the order of the episcopate should be of one virginal marriage was commanded also in the Old Law, and the Apostle writes more fully, saying: ‘The husband of one wife.’ For the Church seeks a priest either ordained from monogamy or made holy through virginity. A digamist is excluded from exercising the priesthood.

“As for the fact that a bishop is ordained not by one but by all the bishops of the province, this is understood to have been established on account of heresies, so that no tyrannical authority might contrive anything against the faith of the one Church. Therefore he is appointed by all who are assembled, with no fewer than three present, while the others give their consent through written testimony.

“When he is consecrated, a staff is given to him, so that by its indication he may rule or correct the people subject to him, or bear the infirmities of the weak. A ring is also given as a sign of pontifical honor, or as a seal of secret matters.”

## CHAPTER CLXIII

Again, the same author, in the same book:

“For the one who presides over peoples in educating and forming them toward virtue must be holy in all things and must be considered blameworthy in nothing, etc., up to ‘with secret distribution.’”

## CHAPTER CLXIV

Again, the same author, in the same book (ch. 17):

“Let virgins therefore proceed along the path of sublimity; let them follow Christ with the foot of humility, perseveringly holding what they ardently vowed, so that, having made their profession and preserved this integrity, they may also be suited to the other virtues, without which virginity undoubtedly remains idle and empty, etc., up to ‘they were able to conquer the flesh.’”

## CHAPTER CLXV

Again, the same author, in the same book:

“Before the coming of Christ, marriage pleased God; after his coming, virginity [pleased him], etc., up to ‘heaven may be filled.’”

## CHAPTER CLXVI

In the *Life of Blessed Basil, Archbishop of Caesarea*, which was faithfully translated from Greek into Latin, word for word, by a certain Greek named Euphemius, the following is read among other things (it exists in Surius, who altered the style):

“Accordingly, the assembled groups of bishops, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, elected Basil to the episcopal see; and, having been consecrated, he governed the Church by God’s providence.

“After some time he asked God to grant him the grace and understanding to offer to him, in his own words, the bloodless sacrifice, and for the coming of the Holy Spirit to descend upon him. After six days, when he had entered a state of ecstasy, and on the seventh day the coming of the Holy Spirit had taken hold of him, he began to minister to God every day.

“After some time, through faith and prayer, he began to write with his own hand the mysteries of the ministry. Then, in a single night, the Lord came to him in a vision with the Apostles; he placed the bread upon the holy altar and awakened Basil, saying to him: ‘According to your request, let your mouth be filled with praise, so that you may offer the bloodless sacrifice in your own words.’

“Unable to endure the vision with his eyes, he rose trembling and, approaching the holy altar, began to speak while writing on a sheet of paper as follows: ‘Let my mouth be filled with praise, so that it may sing a hymn to your glory, Lord God, who created us and brought us into this life,’ and the remaining prayers of the holy ministry.

“When the prayers had ended, he lifted up the bread, praying continuously and saying: ‘Look down, Lord Jesus Christ our God, from your holy dwelling, and come to sanctify us—you who sit above with the Father and are invisibly present here with us. Deign, by your powerful hand, to deliver to us, and through us to all the people, the holy things to the holy.’

“The people replied: ‘One is holy, one is Lord Jesus Christ, with the Holy Spirit, in the glory of God the Father. Amen.’

“And dividing the bread into three parts, he consumed one with great fear; he reserved another to be buried with him; and placing the third in a golden dove, he hung it above the altar.”

## CHAPTER CLXVII

A little farther on it is written:

“When the holy Basil elevated the holy sacrament, the sign that ordinarily occurred did not take place—namely, the movement of the dove, which hung above the altar with the Lord’s sacrament and was accustomed to move three times whenever the holy sacrifice was elevated. As he wondered what this might mean, he saw a deacon fanning the air and signaling to a woman bent down below. He removed the deacon from the altar and ordered him to be kept inside the church. Then, seeing the coming of the Holy Spirit, he urged all the people to remain there in prayer for seven days.”

## CHAPTER CLXVIII

**For increasing the splendor of complete chastity.** Blessed John the Evangelist concludes and develops the subject in this way, saying: [lacuna].

[Note: “For increasing.” This is the title of chapter 168, which was absent from the printed editions and has been restored from the table of contents. I do not know which passage of John Aeneas cited. From the same place we restored the title of chapter 169.]

## CHAPTER CLXIX

**Concerning those who dissolve the ecclesiastical fasts without necessity.** The following is written in the Council of Gangra: [lacuna].

## CHAPTER CLXX

Concerning the matter in which the Roman Church is criticized by the Greeks for fasting on Saturdays, Pope Innocent rationally defends it in the *Decretals*, chapter 4, saying as follows (Epistle 1, to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio):

“That one ought to fast on Saturday is demonstrated by the clearest reasoning. For if we celebrate the Lord’s Day because of the venerable resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ—not only at Easter but also by observing an image of that day in each cycle of the weeks—and if we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s passion, we must not pass over Saturday, which appears to lie between the sorrow and joy of that time.

“For it is certainly established that the Apostles were in mourning during those two days and hid themselves because of fear of the Jews. There is no doubt that they fasted during those two days to such an extent that the tradition of the Church holds that the sacraments are not celebrated at all during them. This practice must certainly be maintained in each week because the commemoration of that day must always be celebrated.

“If they think that one should fast only once, on a single Saturday, then surely the Lord’s Day and Friday should also be celebrated only once, at Easter. But if the image of the Lord’s Day and of Friday is to be renewed each week, it is foolish to observe the custom of the two-day period while omitting Saturday, since it has the same reason: Friday, on which the Lord suffered and also descended to the underworld, so that, rising on the third day, he might restore joy after the preceding two days of sorrow.

“We therefore do not deny that one must fast on Friday, but we say that this must also be done on Saturday, because both days brought sorrow to the Apostles and to those who followed Christ. On the Lord’s Day they rejoiced, and they wished not only that day itself to be most festive, but also that it should be observed throughout all the weeks.”

## CHAPTER CLXXI

In response to Lucinus, who had inquired about this matter, Jerome writes the following among other things in his reply (Epistle 28):

“Concerning Saturday, about which you ask whether one ought to fast, and concerning whether the Eucharist should be received daily—practices that the Roman Church and the churches of Spain are forbidden to observe—Hippolytus, a most eloquent man, did indeed write, and various authors have published brief treatments in different works. But I think I should briefly admonish you of this: ecclesiastical traditions, especially those that do not harm the faith, should be observed as they have been handed down by our predecessors; the custom of one group should not overturn that of another through an opposite practice.

“And would that we could fast at all times! We read that in the Acts of the Apostles the Apostle Paul and the believers with him did so on the days of Pentecost and on the Lord’s Day; yet they should not be accused of the Manichaean heresy, since carnal food ought not to have been preferred to spiritual food.

“We should also receive the Eucharist always, without condemnation from ourselves or a stabbing conscience, and hear the Psalmist say: ‘Taste and see that the Lord is sweet’ (Ps. 33:9). And with him sing: ‘My heart has poured forth a good word’ (Ps. 44:2).

“I do not say this because I think that one ought to fast on feast days or abolish the uninterrupted festivity of the fifty days; but let each province abound in its own judgment, and let it regard the precepts of its predecessors as apostolic laws.”

## CHAPTER CLXXII
Item Isidore, bishop of Seville, in the first book of the *Offices* (chapters 42 and 43), discussing among other matters the fasts of different days and seasons, writes as follows: [Col. 0740D]

“Besides these appointed seasons of fasting, some fast every Friday because of the Lord’s Passion. Likewise, Saturday is regarded by many as consecrated to fasting because Christ lay in the tomb on that day—namely, so that the Jews may not be granted cause for rejoicing over what Christ abolished by dying,” and so forth to the end of chapter 43.

## CHAPTER CLXXIII

At the Council of Laodicea, chapter 1 (chapter 50 according to the translation of Dionysius Exiguus): that the fast should not be broken on Thursday of Holy Week.

“It is not proper to break the fast on the Thursday of the final week of Lent and pass through the whole of Lent without due reverence; rather, it is fitting to honor the whole of Lent with strict fasting.” [Col. 0741A]

If, then, as this council judges, the fast ought not to be broken on Maundy Thursday, it is much more improper to do so on Thursday and Saturday during the remaining weeks of Lent.

## CHAPTER CLXXIV

The question is also raised why we do not abstain from eating meat for eight weeks before Easter, and from cheese and eggs for seven. The brief answer is that through the Lenten fast we imitate the Lord more perfectly: as the Son of God himself, we fast continuously for those same days, neither dividing nor interrupting the period of abstinence and fasting, as it is written in the Gospel: “And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry” (Matt. 4:2).

The evangelist did not say that he broke the fast every Thursday and Saturday of each week while abstaining on the other days, as the Greeks are said to do; rather, he fasted through those forty days completely and consecutively, and only then became hungry.

It should also be said that whether one fasts for eight weeks, breaking the fast on each Thursday, Saturday, and Sunday, or abstains continuously for six weeks except on Sunday, in either period thirty-six days of abstinence are found. Hence those act more reasonably who, imitating the Lord, practice the Lenten fast continuously than those who appear to carry it out with intervals between certain days. [Col. 0741B]

For blessed Pope Gregory, when calculating the Lenten period, begins counting it from the beginning of the six weeks, saying these words (*Homily 16 on the Gospels*):

“From the present day, then, until the joys of the Easter solemnity, there are six weeks: their days amount to forty-two. When six Sundays are subtracted from abstinence, no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence. Since the year consists of 365 days, while we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, we offer God as it were the tenth of our year, so that we who have lived for ourselves through the year we have received may mortify ourselves for our Creator in abstinence, as his tithe.”

## CHAPTER CLXXV

### On the varied practice of abstinence in different regions

[Col. 0741D]

As to the further question why we do not abstain from eating cheese and eggs for seven weeks before Easter, but only for six, the brief answer is that such an exacting requirement has no authority in the Holy Scriptures. For different practices of abstinence are observed in different regions.

Egypt and all Palestine fast for nine weeks before Easter. Moreover, part of Italy, which willingly embraces this practice, abstains three days each week throughout Lent from foods cooked by fire; using only various fruits of trees and kinds of herbs, with which Italy abounds abundantly, it fulfills the vow of abstinence through this food. [Col. 0742A]

Where such diversity and abundance of fruits are lacking, food cooked by fire is by no means forbidden.

Germany likewise does not generally abstain throughout Lent from milk, butter, cheese, and eggs, except where individual voluntary devotion leads someone to do so.

Finally, some have judged it reasonable to break the abstinence on Maundy Thursday and Good Friday, days which, because of the apostles’ grief, represent sorrow, and have foolishly and improperly indulged in eggs, cheese, milk, and butter.

Accordingly, until the glory of the Lord’s Resurrection solemnly draws near on Saturday evening, which dawns on the first day of the week; until the children of light are reborn through the water of baptism; until “Glory to God in the highest” and “Alleluia” proclaim the glorious victory of Christ’s Resurrection; and until the mystical candle shines spiritually with holy light, Mother Church considers it unworthy to use such foods, for she received the discipline of her teaching from the first Shepherd.

Since the order of abstinence during Lent is confused in these and other ways throughout many regions of the world, the Roman See has rightly and wisely chosen to continue and extend the fast before Easter to a total of forty days.

When thirty-six days have been counted as days of abstinence, and four more are added that begin at the start of the fast, we are admirably joined together and united without any reproach to the fast of our Savior, of which the evangelist says: “And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry” (Matt. 4:2).

## CHAPTER CLXXVI

[Col. 0742C]

Saint Faustinus, bishop, in a homiletic discourse on the Sunday before Lent, according to the custom of that period, explains the fast in various ways as follows:

“I believe that you are troubled, dearest brothers, wondering why we have been passing through Lent since the previous Sunday, and, although today is its beginning, why we began celebrating its feast a week earlier.

“This premature observance cannot be criticized. It is an indication of devotion to fulfill the law before one knows the law’s statutes, and to obey the commands before the commands of obedience compel one. The former is an act of love; the latter, of fear. The latter is demanded imperatively; the former is offered religiously. In the one case a gift is presented; in the other, a debt is paid.

“Therefore, when we fasted more, we offered God a religious gift. A hastened celebration cannot be criticized, for in matters of joy vows always precede the solemnity, and devotion, in desiring future gladness, anticipates it.

“Thus this was done not only without reproach but also cautiously. In uncertain matters one should always add something extra for safety, because what is extra can be cut back, whereas what is lacking cannot be prolonged.

“This is what happened in the present observance: lest, because we fasted more on account of Lent, we should diminish Lent, it remains complete for us. If we had fasted fewer days than the number required, we could not have restored them to the full number.

“But perhaps this is the reason why the fast we have undertaken does not benefit us as part of Lent. It will certainly benefit us, because even if it does not benefit us as part of Lent, it benefits us for salvation; if it does not benefit us in number, it benefits us in merit. For whom has prayer, reading, or fasting never been beneficial? For whom have chastity, sobriety, and gentleness not been beneficial?

“I consider those more deserving of reproach who, although prepared to fast, neglected to do so after hearing that the date of the solemnity was uncertain. They clearly demonstrated that they did not wish to live religiously but were compelled to do so. I suppose they feared that, if the fast of five days were prolonged, their flesh and body would fail them and, thin and weak, they would be unable to endure the abstinence of Lent.

“Let those who are refreshed and strong, as well as those who are thin and pale, hear that today is Lent. Let the former hear it, I say, so that they may begin to fast; let the latter hear it so that they may not cease abstaining. Let all hasten together to enter Christ’s ark—indeed, let them hasten all the more, because they began abstaining later—so that they may enter more disciplined and purer. For the Lord’s ark can sustain the fasting in times of danger; it does not know how to sustain the drunkard.” [Col. 0743B]

## CHAPTER CLXXVII

Likewise Augustine, in a homily on Lent, says among other things (*Sermon 69 on Time*):

“Holy, therefore, and saving is the course of Lent, by which the sinner is led to mercy through repentance and the righteous to rest. During these days divinity shows greater mercy than usual, sin implores pardon, and righteousness wins favor.

“For everything is open: the heavens to forgiveness, the sinner to confession, and the tongue to petition. The number forty, I say, is saving and mystical. For when human iniquity first possessed the face of the world, God, over the course of that many days, overwhelmed the entire earth with a flood by pouring down rains from heaven.

“You see, therefore, that even then the mystery was arranged in symbolic form. For just as it rained for forty days to cleanse the world, so now for forty days mercy is shown to purify humanity.” [Col. 0743C]

## CHAPTER CLXXVIII

### Why presbyters are forbidden to anoint the foreheads of the baptized with chrism

Pope Innocent says in the *Decretals*, chapter 3 (letter 1, chapter 3):

“As for marking infants, it is clear that this may be done by no one other than a bishop. For although presbyters are the second-ranking priests, they do not possess the fullness of the episcopate. That this belongs exclusively to bishops—that they should either mark the baptized or confer the Spirit, the Paraclete—is demonstrated not only by ecclesiastical custom but also by that passage in the Acts of the Apostles which states that Peter and John were sent to confer the Holy Spirit on those who had already been baptized.

“When presbyters baptize, whether without a bishop or in the presence of a bishop, they may anoint the baptized with chrism, but only with chrism consecrated by a bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that same oil, for this belongs exclusively to bishops when they confer the Spirit, the Paraclete. I cannot state the actual words, lest I seem more to disclose them than to answer the consultation.” [Col. 0744A]

## CHAPTER CLXXIX

It is also read in the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* that Pope Sylvester established that a neophyte should be anointed by a presbyter—namely, on the brain or crown of the head. For it is written there as follows, in the *Book of the Pontiffs*, falsely attributed to Pope Damasus:

“He established that the presbyter should anoint the baptized person with chrism after he had been lifted from the water, because of the danger posed by the passage of death.”

It is clear at what time Sylvester governed the Church of the Roman See: namely, when the Council of Nicaea was celebrated under the devout Emperor Constantine.

From this, as may be inferred, the holy Fathers established that neophytes should be anointed by presbyters with chrism consecrated by a bishop. [Col. 0744B] If this had already been done before, it seems superfluous to say that Saint Sylvester established it, since it was already being practiced by Catholics.

From this decree anyone may infer that in the earlier period the pontiff was awaited for the anointing with chrism, so that every anointing with chrism might be completed by the bishop’s hands.

Up to that time not everyone was baptized generally, especially since emperors and their rulers remained bound to paganism. It was therefore easy for a bishop to meet the neophytes, or for them to come to the bishop, because Christianity was still confined to a small number and practiced secretly.

## CHAPTER CLXXX

Pope Gelasius, in the *Ecclesiastical Institutes*, says that presbyters must observe the proper limits of their office and neither make chrism nor perform the episcopal signing, chapter 6 (letter 9):

“We also forbid presbyters to exceed the limits of their office and audaciously assume for themselves what belongs to the episcopal dignity, seizing for themselves the authority either to prepare chrism or to perform the episcopal signing.” [Col. 0744C]

## CHAPTER CLXXXI

Likewise, in the same chapter:

“Let him have no doubt that, if he should on his own initiative undertake anything specifically belonging to the episcopal ministry, he will immediately be deprived of the dignity of the presbyterate and of sacred communion.”

## CHAPTER CLXXXII

### On the objection that clerics shave their beards

[Col. 0744D]

Jerome explains this in the first part of his commentary on Ezekiel (book 2, chapter 5, beginning):

“And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword, like a barber’s razor—or one that shaves hair—and draw it over your head and your beard. Then take a pair of scales for weighing and divide them. Burn one third in the midst of the city, when the days of the confinement are completed; cut another third with the sword around it; and scatter the remaining third to the wind, and I will unsheathe the sword after them. Then take a small number from them and bind them in the hem of your cloak. Again take some of them and throw them into the midst of the fire, and burn them in the fire. From it a fire will go out over the whole house of Israel” (Ezek. 5:1ff.).

For the three portions of the hair and bodily hair—one of which is burned in the midst of the city, another cut down with the sword around it, and the third scattered to be carried here and there by the wind; from this third a small amount is taken and bound in the hem of the cloak, and again a little of that third part is cast into the fire, from which a flame proceeds over the whole house of Israel—the Seventy translated four portions.

After saying, “You shall burn a fourth part in the midst of the city, and strike a fourth part with the sword in its midst, and scatter a fourth part to the wind,” because another fourth part remained for them, they added on their own: “And you shall take a fourth part and burn it in the midst of the city,” as though this were not the same as the first and as though he had said one thing about the first and another about the added portion.

Finally, in what follows, the Lord himself explains through the prophet the riddle of the hair divided into three parts, saying: “A third part of you shall die by plague, and be consumed by famine in your midst”—identifying famine and pestilence with the fire. “And a third part of you shall fall by the sword around you,” describing slaughter and wars outside. “And I will scatter a third part of you to every wind,” showing that these are those who are to be led into captivity.

After them, he says that he will unsheathe or pour out his sword, so that captivity will not be the final evil. He will take some of the scattered and captive people and bind at the hem of his cloak those who are to return from captivity to Jerusalem; from these as well he will take some portion and consume it with fire and flame. This signifies the Macedonians, under whom the inhabitants of Judea, and especially Jerusalem, suffered harshly. [Col. 0745C]

When he says “from it”—that is, from the people—or, according to the Seventy, “from her,” with Jerusalem understood, “fire will go out over the whole house of Israel,” he recounts in the history of the Maccabees that a certain portion of the Jews surrendered themselves to Antiochus Epiphanes and stirred him up to persecute the people, along with many other events recorded in that same history and in the writings of Josephus—especially the conflict between Hyrcanus and Alexander, through whose circumstances Gnaeus Pompey captured Jerusalem and subjected it to Roman rule.

Afterward, under Titus and Vespasian, the city was captured and the temple overthrown. Then, fifty years later, under Aelius Hadrian, the city was burned and destroyed to its foundations, so that it even lost its former name.

Just as the hair on the head and beard is a sign of beauty and masculinity, and when it is shaved an ugly nakedness appears—and just as the outermost, so to speak dead, part of the entire body is found in the hair—so Jerusalem and its people, dead and separated from the living body of God, are handed over to famine and pestilence, slaughter and the sword, captivity and dispersion.

From that dispersion, under the figure of the hair, a portion is bound at the hem of the cloak, so that a small amount may again be delivered to the fire, from which an immeasurable flame, devastating almost everything, proceeds over the whole house of Israel.” [Col. 0745D]

## CHAPTER CLXXXIII

Pope Gregory, in the first book of the *Morals on Blessed Job* (chapter 19), says among other things:

“Jeremiah indicates that eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria, with their beards shaved, their garments torn, and themselves covered with filth; they had gifts and incense in their hands to offer in the house of the Lord. Ishmael, son of Nethaniah, went out from Mizpah to meet them, walking along and weeping. When he encountered them, he said to them: ‘Come to Gedaliah, son of Ahikam.’ When they came into the middle of the city, he killed them” (Jer. 41:6).

Those shave their beards who remove confidence in their own strength. They tear their garments who do not spare themselves in the rending of their outward adornment. They come to offer incense and gifts in the house of the Lord who promise to present themselves in God’s sacrifice through prayer accompanied by works.

Yet if they do not carefully watch themselves on this path of holy devotion, Ishmael, son of Nethaniah, comes out to meet them. For every malignant spirit, begotten in the error of pride after the example of its predecessor, Satan, sets himself before them as a snare of deception.” [Col. 0746B]

## CHAPTER CLXXXIV

Likewise, in the second book of the *Morals* (chapters 10 and 11):

“Then Jacob arose and tore his garments; and, falling to the ground with his head shaven, he worshiped. It was the custom of the ancients that anyone who preserved the appearance of his body by cultivating his hair should cut it off in a time of affliction,” and so forth up to “not to have had those whom we have lost.”

## CHAPTER CLXXXV

[Col. 0746C]

Isidore, bishop of Seville, says in the second book of the *Offices* (chapter 4, beginning):

“The practice of ecclesiastical tonsure arose, unless I am mistaken, from the Nazirite practice. After first preserving their hair, the Nazirites, when their great period of abstinence had been completed and their devotion fulfilled, shaved their heads and were commanded to place their hair in the fire of the sacrifice, so that they might consecrate the perfection of their devotion to the Lord.

“Accordingly, the apostles introduced the practice after their example, so that those who are devoted to the Lord and consecrated to divine worship, like Nazirites—that is, holy men of God—might be renewed by cutting their hair.

“This is also commanded to the prophet Ezekiel, when the Lord says: ‘You, son of man, take a sharp sword and draw it over your head and your beard’ (Ezek. 5:1). This was evidently because he too belonged to the priestly order and served God in the ministry of sanctification. [Col. 0746D]

“We also read in the Acts of the Apostles that those Nazirites, Priscilla and Aquila, were the first to do this; likewise the apostle Paul and certain disciples of Christ, who proved worthy of imitation in this form of worship.

“In clerics, tonsure is a certain sign represented on the body but enacted in the soul: namely, so that by this sign vices may be cut away in religious life, and we may strip ourselves of the sins of our flesh as of hair. Thus renewed in our understanding, we may shine with fresh locks, ‘putting off,’ as the Apostle says, ‘the old man with his deeds, and putting on the new, which is renewed in the knowledge of God’ (Eph. 4; Col. 3).

“This renewal ought to take place in the mind but be displayed on the head, where the mind itself is understood to dwell. [Col. 0747A]

“As for the fact that, after the upper part of the head has been shaved, a circular crown is left below, I believe that this signifies the priesthood and kingship of the Church. Among the ancients, a tiara was placed on the heads of priests. Made of fine linen, it was round, like half a sphere; this is signified in the shaved part of the head. The crown is the breadth of a golden circle that encircles the heads of kings.

“Thus both signs are expressed on the heads of clerics, so that what was written through the teaching of the apostle Peter may also be fulfilled by a certain likeness in the body: ‘You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood’ (1 Pet. 2).
