“It is asked why, as among the ancient Nazirites, the hair is not first allowed to grow and only afterward cut. Those who inquire into this should observe the difference between that prophetic veil and this revelation of the Gospel, of which the Apostle says: ‘When you turn to Christ, the veil will be taken away’ (1 Cor. 3:5).

“What the veil placed between Moses’ face and the sight of the people of Israel signified, the hair of holy men also signified in those times. For the Apostle too says that hair is given as a veil.

“Therefore, the heads of those consecrated to the Lord ought no longer to be veiled with hair, but merely revealed, because what was hidden in the mystery of prophecy has now been disclosed in the Gospel.” [Col. 0747B]

## CHAPTER CLXXXVI

### Why Latins do not grow their hair in the Greek manner, so that they may be distinguished from women by their hair

[Col. 0747C]

“Since the Greeks therefore reproach the Latins and Romans for shaving their beards—who certainly do this for cleanliness, which ecclesiastical ministry more expressly advances and requires—and since different nations observe their own customs in bodily appearance and clothing without guilt, provided only that these customs do not conflict with the Catholic faith, the Latins appropriately return the question by asking why the Greek laity, contrary to the prohibition of the thundering Paul, grow their hair like women.

“He threatens the Corinthians with apostolic authority in these words: ‘Does not nature itself teach you that if a man grows his hair, it is a disgrace to him, but if a woman grows her hair, it is her glory, because her hair has been given to her as a veil?’ (1 Cor. 11:14).

“Since the Latins consider it unworthy to grow their hair, so as not to conform to feminine adornment, it must be asked what the Greeks consider more holy, since they wear their hair as a covering, as though sharing one head with women.

“Corinth is in Achaea, which is one of the Greek cities situated in Asia. The Apostle did not wish its men to grow their hair—not just any apostle, but the one who was appointed not by men or through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead (Gal. 1:1).

“A certain man distinguished for holiness and eloquence as an orator said: If some holiness is implied in bodily beards, perhaps it could find a place among the larger goats.

“If, therefore, the wisdom of the Achaeans disregards the Apostle in growing their hair, the cleanliness of the ministers of Christ should certainly not on that account be judged inferior because they shave their beards. By cutting away what is forbidden, that cleanliness ought to shine more excellently in good works and be entirely free from the impurities of both mind and body.” [Col. 0748A]

## CHAPTER CLXXXVII

That the pontiff of the Roman See is regarded as first of all was clearly taught by blessed Pope Sylvester in the Preface to the Council of Nicaea, where the following is read:

“To the most blessed Sylvester, bishop in the city of Rome and head of the apostolic see: Constantine Augustus and Licinius; Paulinus and Julianus, most illustrious men, being consuls. In the 1034th year from Alexander, in the month of June, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, because of the heresies that had arisen, the Catholic faith was set forth at Nicaea in Bithynia. The holy and most reverent Roman Church embraces and venerates this faith, for 318 Fathers, through Victor and Vincentius, most devout presbyters of the Roman See, brought it forth under divine inspiration to destroy the poisons of Arius.

“Some rules were also appended, and the aforementioned Church, accepting them, confirmed them.

“All Catholics should know that the holy Roman Church was not placed first by any synodal decrees (from the decree of Pope Gelasius at the Roman Council, in the year 494), but obtained its primacy through the Gospel voice of our Lord and Savior, when he said to the blessed apostle Peter: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matt. 16:18ff.).

“The fellowship of the most blessed apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, was also added in that same city of Rome. He was crowned in glorious death, struggling under the emperor Nero with Peter on one and the same day and at one and the same time. Together they consecrated the holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord and placed it before all other cities throughout the world by their presence and venerable triumph.

“Although the prayer of all the saints is continually offered to God for everyone, the most blessed apostle Paul nevertheless promises the Romans in his own handwriting, saying: ‘For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I always remember you in my prayers’ (Rom. 1:9).

“The first see, therefore, by heavenly favor is that of the Roman Church, which the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul dedicated by their martyrdom.

“The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist, because he was sent by Peter to Egypt, where he first preached the word of truth and received a glorious martyrdom; the venerable Abilius succeeded him.

“The third see is honorably held at Antioch, likewise in the name of the blessed apostle Peter, because he lived there before coming to Rome, established Ignatius as bishop there, and there the first name of the new people, Christians, arose.

“The bishop of Jerusalem is also regarded as honorable by all because of the reverence due to so great a place, especially because there the first blessed James, called the Just and also named, according to the flesh, the Lord’s brother, was ordained bishop by the apostles Peter, James, and John.

“Thus, according to the definition of the ancient Fathers, Jerusalem is by no means called the first see, lest unbelievers or simpletons should suppose that the seat of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is in heaven, is on earth. His seat is heaven, while the earth is the footstool of his feet, because he is the one through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made; for from him, through him, and in him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever.

“At Ephesus, the most blessed apostle and evangelist John lived for a long time after the resurrection and ascension into heaven of our Lord Jesus Christ. There, by divine inspiration, he also composed the Gospel called according to John, and there he came to rest. For this reason, the bishop of Ephesus, in memory of so great an apostle and evangelist, holds a more honorable see than the other metropolitan bishops at synods.” [Col. 0749B]

## CHAPTER CLXXXVIII

Likewise, blessed Sylvester, at the end of the address he delivered in the synod held at Trajan’s on the third day before the Kalends of June, established ranks within the synod (*Canons of Sylvester*, chapter 20):

“No one shall judge the first see when it desires justice to be tempered; neither Augustus, nor the whole clergy, nor kings, nor the people shall judge it as a judge.”

## CHAPTER CLXXXIX

[Col. 0749C]

In the *Canons of the Apostles*, on the primacy of bishops, chapter 35 (canon 35, according to the translation of Dionysius Exiguus):

“The bishops of each nation should know who among them is regarded as first, whom they should consider as a head, and should undertake nothing beyond his knowledge except those matters that each one is responsible for in his own parish and in the villages belonging to it.

“Nor should he do anything without the knowledge of all. In this way there will be unanimity, and God will be glorified through Christ in the Holy Spirit.”

## CHAPTER CXC

At the Council of Nicaea, on the privileges belonging to certain cities, chapter 6 (canon 6 according to the first edition):

“Let the ancient custom be maintained throughout Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria has authority over all these regions, since a similar custom also exists for the bishop of the city of Rome.

“Likewise, in Antioch and the other provinces, let the privileges belonging to their Churches be preserved.”

## CHAPTER CXCI

Likewise, at the same council, chapter 7, on the bishop of Aelia—that is, Jerusalem:

“Since custom and ancient tradition have prevailed that the bishop of Aelia should be honored, let him have the precedence appropriate to that honor, while the dignity proper to the metropolitan see remains intact.”

## CHAPTER CXCII

At the Council of Constantinople, chapter 11 (canon 2; this version differs from the edition): on the order of the individual dioceses and on the privileges owed to the Egyptians, Antiochenes, and Constantinopolitans: [Col. 0750A]

“Those bishops who preside over dioceses must not at all enter churches outside the boundaries assigned to them, nor throw them into confusion through such presumption. Rather, in accordance with the canons, the bishop of Alexandria is to govern only what belongs to Egypt.

“The bishops of the East are to govern only the East, while the privileges granted to the Church of Antioch by the canons of Nicaea are preserved.

“The bishops of the Asian diocese are likewise to administer only what belongs to the Asian diocese; the bishops of Pontus only what belongs to Pontus; and those of Thrace are to govern what belongs to Thrace.

“Bishops who have not been summoned are not to go beyond their own diocese for the purpose of ordinations or other ecclesiastical administrations. Once the rule concerning these jurisdictions has been preserved, it is clear that matters belonging to each province are to be administered by the synod of that province itself, as the Council of Nicaea is known to have decreed.

“As for the Churches of God established among barbarian peoples, they should be governed according to the custom observed by the Fathers.

“Nevertheless, the bishop of Constantinople shall have the primacy of honor after the bishop of Rome, because that city is the younger Rome.” [Col. 0750B]

## CHAPTER CXCIII

At the Council of Sardica, chapter 3 (canon 3, according to the translation of Dionysius Exiguus):

“If a condemned man appeals to the Roman pontiff—as Ignatius, bishop of Constantinople, recently did, having been unjustly deposed, as is said—the decision of the pontiff himself is to be observed.

“Bishop Hosius said: It must also necessarily be added that bishops must not pass from their own province into another province in which they are not bishops, unless perhaps they have been invited by their brothers, so that they may not appear to close the door of charity.

“If in any province a bishop has a dispute with another bishop, neither of the two shall summon bishops from another province to act as judges.

“If a bishop has been judged in some matter and thinks that he has a good case, so that the council’s judgment may be renewed, then, if it pleases you, let us honor the memory of the holy apostle Peter by having a letter written by those bishops who remain in their own province to Julius, the Roman bishop. If he judges that the case should be reheard, let it be reheard, and let him appoint judges. [Col. 0750D]

“But if he determines that the case is such that the proceedings already completed should not be reopened, his decision shall be confirmed. If this pleases everyone, let it be established.”

The synod replied: “It pleases us.”

## CHAPTER CXCIV

Likewise, at the same council, chapter 4 (ibid., canon 4): that no one should usurp the see of an accused bishop, as Photios recently usurped the see of Ignatius, being a neophyte and an invader of the see of Constantinople:

“Bishop Gaudentius said: If it pleases you, something should be added to this judgment, which you have pronounced with complete holiness: when a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of bishops living in neighboring places and has requested that his case be heard in the city of Rome, no other bishop is to be ordained to his chair after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.” [Col. 0751A]

## CHAPTER CXCV

Likewise, blessed Pope Sylvester, in his address at the Council of Nicaea, established ranks within the assembly of the synod (*Canons of Sylvester*, chapter 3):

“That a presbyter may bring no accusation against a bishop, nor a deacon against a presbyter, nor a subdeacon against a deacon, nor an acolyte against a subdeacon, nor an exorcist against an acolyte, nor a lector against an exorcist, nor a doorkeeper against a lector.

“And a bishop, a prelate, shall not be condemned except on the testimony of seventy-two witnesses; nor shall the supreme prelate be judged by anyone, because it is written: ‘The disciple is not above his teacher.’

“A presbyter, however, shall not be condemned except on the testimony of forty-four witnesses.

“A cardinal deacon appointed in the city of Rome shall not be condemned except on the testimony of thirty-six witnesses.

“A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, or lector shall not be condemned except, as it is written, on the testimony of seven witnesses—those who have children and wives and who altogether preach Christ.

“Thus mystical truth is established.” [Col. 0751B]

[Col. 0751C] Pope Saint Gelasius condemned Acacius, bishop of the see of Constantinople, by apostolic authority, on account especially of his extreme presumption: he had excluded John, an otherwise ordinary man but nevertheless a Catholic, ordained by Catholics, from the city of Alexandria, which is regarded as the second see after Rome; and he had received Peter, already exposed and condemned as a heretic, without consulting the apostolic see. Moreover, after a synod had been held, he had boldly undertaken to depose Kalendion, bishop of the see of Antioch, contrary to reason, and had again admitted the heretic Peter, whom he himself had formerly condemned, without the knowledge of the apostolic see, with the heretical emperor Basiliscus consenting to this criminal presumption.

For this presumptuous exercise of power, Pope Gelasius addressed an admirable letter to the emperor Anastasius, so that unlawfully usurped power [Col. 0751D] might be restrained and the singular privilege of the holy Roman Church, together with its entire primacy, might be preserved unimpaired (To the Emperor Anastasius, Letter 8, beginning). This letter begins as follows: “Your Piety’s servants, my sons, the Master Faustus and Irenaeus, together with their companions, having returned to the City in the course of a public embassy, said that they had sought your Clemency: why I had not sent you written greetings, and so forth, to the end.”

Likewise Gelasius provided excellently composed explanations (Letter 13 of the same author, to the bishops of Dardania) that Acacius had rightly been condemned by the apostolic see. These explanations have the following opening: “We were greatly surprised that your affection, as though wishing to learn something new and apparently difficult, and something as yet unheard of, and so forth, to the end.”

[Col. 0752A] Again, Pope Gelasius gave an account of the same matter to the bishops of the East and sharply reproached them for not having resisted such presumptions. The beginning of this explanation is as follows (Letter 15 of the same author; this letter is not found among the editions): “What, then, are these wise men, with minds skilled in probing the inner matters of the whole religion, who are established in the regions of the East, etc., to the end of the discourse.”

Therefore, anyone who rereads all these things in order will be able to understand clearly and fully how greatly the apostolic see surpasses all the Churches throughout the world in dignity, and how eminent it is in power.

## CHAPTER 196

[Col. 0752B] Likewise, the *Commonitorium* of Saint Gelasius, sent to Constantinople through the Master Faustus, who was carrying out the office of ambassador (Letter 4), which begins as follows: “I too understood in my mind that the Greeks would remain in their obstinacy, lest what had already been foreknown should appear unexpected to anyone,” etc., to the end.

## CHAPTER 197

In this *Commonitorium*, among other things, he says:

“But if they say: ‘The emperor did this,’ by which canons, by which rules was this very act commanded? Why did Acacius consent to so wicked a deed, when divine authority says: ‘Not only those who do wicked things are guilty, but also those who consent to the doers of them’? (Rom. I.) By which canons, by which rules was Kalendion excluded, or [Col. 0752C] the Catholic priests of the foremost cities? By what tradition of our ancestors do they summon the apostolic see to judgment? Were the bishops of the second and third sees, and the other priests fully conscious of their duty, to be driven out, while the man who had proved himself an enemy of religion was not to be driven out?

“Let them see, then, whether they possess other canons by which to carry out their absurdities. As for those canons which are called sacred, ecclesiastical, and legitimate, they not only cannot summon the apostolic see to judgment; but should the bishop of the city of Constantinople—which certainly received no standing among the sees according to the canons—have been removed when he fell into communion with the treacherous? Or were those who are said to have lied to a human emperor, and those alleged to have injured the emperor, to be driven out, while Acacius, offending against God, who is the supreme and true Emperor, and seeking to mix the sincere communion of the divine sacrament with the treacherous, ought not to have been excluded according to the synod by which this treachery was condemned?

“But whether they wish it or not, the ancient canonical enactments are confirmed by his own judgment. Yet religious and perfect men, in accordance with the canons, are plainly attempting to wrest from the apostolic see the power granted to it, and are striving to usurp it for themselves contrary to the canons.”

## CHAPTER 198

Likewise, in his letter to the emperor Anastasius (Letter 8), among other things he says:

“Moreover, the authority of the apostolic see—that it has been placed before the universal Church throughout all Christian ages—is established both by the succession of the canons of the Fathers and by manifold tradition,” etc., up to “you think it makes a difference.”

## CHAPTER 199

Likewise, in the explanations he supplied, among other things he says (Letter 13, to the Dardanians):

“We certainly do not keep silent about what the entire Church throughout the world knows: that the see of blessed Peter the Apostle has the right to release a pontiff bound by the judgments of anyone whatsoever, since it is permitted to judge concerning the whole Church, while no one is permitted to judge its judgment. Indeed, if the canons should wish appeals to be made to it from any part of the world, no one is permitted to appeal from it.

“Therefore it is sufficiently clear that Acacius had no authority, as a pontiff, to release a sentence of the apostolic see without any knowledge of that see. By what synod, then, did he presume to do what even so he had no right to accomplish without the apostolic see? Whose bishop is he? Of what metropolitan city is he the bishop? Is he not the bishop of the parish of the Church of Heraclea? If it was certainly permitted to him, without a synod and without seeking any consultation from it, to overturn the sentence of the apostolic see, was it truly not permitted to the first see, carrying out the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon as was proper, to remove such a transgressor by its own authority?

“Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see frequently, as has been said, according to the custom of our ancestors, possessed the right, even without any preceding synod, to release those whom an unjust synod had condemned, and had the power to condemn those whom it was proper to condemn even when no synod existed.

“Thus the Eastern synod condemned Athanasius of holy memory; nevertheless, the apostolic see, having received him and not consenting to the condemnation of the Greeks, absolved him. Likewise, a synod of Catholic bishops had certainly condemned John of Constantinople, of holy memory; in the same way, the apostolic see alone, because it did not consent, absolved him. Similarly, it absolved the holy Flavian, condemned by an assembly of Greek bishops, because the apostolic see alone did not consent; and by its own authority it condemned Dioscorus, the bishop of the second see, who had been received there, and, by refusing consent to the impious synod, alone removed him; and it alone decreed that the Council of Chalcedon should be held.

“In that council, just as it alone had the right to absolve those whom synodal decrees had struck down, so it is also known to have condemned, without a synod, many metropolitans in this same matter. If anyone censures these actions of the apostolic see, whether performed according to a synod or otherwise, apart from the fact that he is refuted by the ancient proof of events, he will meanwhile admit all the more that Acacius was not permitted to do so.”

## CHAPTER 200

Likewise, the same Gelasius, shortly afterward in the same writings:

“We laughed at the fact that they wish a prerogative to be assigned to Acacius because he was bishop of a royal city. Was there not for many years an emperor at Milan, at Ravenna, at Sirmium, and at Trier? Did the priests of these cities ever, beyond the measure anciently assigned to them, usurp anything for their own dignities?”

## CHAPTER 201

Likewise, the same author shortly afterward:

“If the matter concerns the dignity of cities, the dignity of the priests of the second and third sees is greater than that of the city which is not only scarcely counted among the sees, but is not even reckoned among metropolitan rights. For when you say that it is a royal city, one power belongs to secular kingship and another to the distribution of ecclesiastical dignities.

“For just as a small city does not diminish the prerogative of the present kingdom, so imperial presence does not alter the measure of religious administration. Let that city be illustrious through the power of the present empire; religion under the same authority then remains firm, free, and advanced if, rather, in the presence of that power it retains its proper measure without any disturbance.”

## CHAPTER 202

Likewise, the same author at the end of his explanations:

“Just as the public transgression of all those who had fallen into the same act of treachery was made known through one writer of theirs, so, when the transgression was punished in the one man who had written on behalf of all, or who by writing had disclosed the wishes of all, all were punished.

“We judge that these matters are sufficient, and more than sufficient, for the instruction of your affection, although, if the Lord grants the opportunity, we shall endeavor to explain the same things at greater length [Note: [Col. 0753D] You will find this at the end of the letter.]; so that every one of the faithful may know that the apostolic see, God forbid, judged nothing rashly [Note: [Col. 0753D] In the printed edition you will see this joined with the words ‘all were punished’ above.].

“Nevertheless, although this sentence directed against Acacius is shown to have been drawn up only in the name of an apostolic bishop—whose legitimate authority it certainly was—especially since it seemed that it ought to be sent secretly, and a salutary arrangement obstructed by guards stationed everywhere [Note: [Col. 0753D] ‘With guards stationed everywhere.’ Thus it appears in the published letters of Gelasius, and correctly; in the codex of Aeneas, ‘the guard of the present one,’ incorrectly.], so that it could not achieve the necessary effect amid whatever difficulties might arise; nevertheless, since the orthodox had everywhere been cast down and only the heretics and their associates remained in the East, and Catholic bishops either no longer existed at all or enjoyed no freedom, an assembly of many Catholic priests in Italy reasonably recognized that the sentence against Acacius had been issued.

“That assembly of bishops did not meet against Chalcedon, nor as a new synod against the earlier and first one; rather, according to the tenor of the ancient decree, it became a participant in the execution of the apostolic judgment. Thus it is sufficiently evident that the Catholic Church and the apostolic see, since this could no longer be done elsewhere, omitted nothing whatsoever that could be undertaken, wherever it could and with whomever it could, for the sake of fraternal concern for undefiled faith and sincere communion.”

## CHAPTER 203

[Col. 0755A] Likewise, in the letter of Pope Leo to the emperor Augustus Marcian (Letter 6 in Part III of the Council of Chalcedon), which was sent through Bishop Lycinius and the deacon Basil, concerning the ambition of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, among other things we read:

“Knowing that your glorious Clemency is devoted to ecclesiastical harmony and gives the most religious assent to those things that accord with peaceful unity, I beg and earnestly beseech you to withdraw from every assent of your Piety the wicked attempts opposed to Christian unity and peace, and salutarily restrain the harmful ambition of my brother Anatolius, if he persists in it; lest, desiring things hostile to your glory and to your times, he wish to be greater than his predecessors.

“Let him be free to shine with whatever virtues he can, virtues of which he will not otherwise be a participant unless he wishes to be adorned more by charity than swollen by ambition. He ought never to have received within the secret recesses of his heart the conception of this wicked desire.”

## CHAPTER 204

Likewise, Pope Leo in the same letter:

“Do what belongs both to Christian uprightness and to royal authority, so that the aforesaid bishop may obey the Fathers and consult the peace, and may not think himself permitted to do what he presumed to do without any precedent against the Church of Antioch and contrary to the decrees of the canons: to ordain bishops. Out of love for restoring the faith and zeal for peace, we have not ceased to revoke this.

“Let him therefore refrain from injuring ecclesiastical rules and avoid unlawful excesses, lest, while he attempts things hostile to peace, he cut himself off from the universal Church. I would rather love him acting irreproachably than see him persist in this presumption, which could separate him from everyone.”

## CHAPTER 205

Likewise, Pope Leo writes to Anatolius the bishop, among other things, in another letter (Letter 5):

“After those blameless beginnings of your ordination, after the consecration of the bishop of Antioch which you claimed for yourself contrary to canonical rule, I grieve that your affection has advanced to this point, that you should attempt to violate the most sacred constitutions of the Nicene canons, as though this time had conveniently presented itself to you in which the see of Alexandria had lost the privilege of second rank and the Church of Antioch had lost the prerogative of third dignity, so that, with these places subjected to your jurisdiction, all metropolitan bishops might be deprived of their proper honor.

“You are carried forward by such unheard-of and never-before-attempted excesses that you drag into an occasion for ambition the holy synod assembled by the zeal of a most Christian ruler solely to extinguish heresy and confirm the Catholic faith, and compel it to grant you its connivance—as though what the multitude wished unlawfully could not be rejected, and as though the condition established by the holy Spirit through the Nicene canons could in any respect be dissolved by anyone.

“And let no synodal councils flatter themselves on account of the increase of their assembly; nor let any number of priests, however much greater, dare either to compare itself with or to prefer itself to those three hundred and eighteen bishops. The Council of Nicaea was consecrated with so great a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are celebrated by fewer or by more, whatever differs from the constitution of those Fathers is wholly empty of authority.

“These things, therefore, are exceedingly wicked and exceedingly perverse, since they are found to be contrary to the most sacred canons.”

## CHAPTER 206

Likewise, Pope Leo in the same letter shortly afterward:

“For I confess that I am bound by affection for the universal brotherhood, so that I should assent to no one at all in matters that he has set against himself,” etc., up to “you will deprive yourself of the peace of the universal Church.”

## CHAPTER 207

[Col. 0755] Shortly before the end of Act 5, in the Creed of the one hundred and fifty bishops, etc., in the middle. It differs greatly from the printed edition.

Likewise, in the Council of Chalcedon, the authority of the first see is recalled as follows:

“Therefore, making the testimony of the divine Scriptures more plainly manifest against those who attacked the mystery of the substance, asserting that a man had been created without divinity, shamelessly and crudely, from the venerable Virgin Mary—contrary to the letters of the venerable Cyril, formerly bishop of the Church of Alexandria, and to the fitting writings of the whole East against Nestorius’s madness, in which those desiring it seek a manifest expression of the sure and saving Creed—and setting forth the letter of Archbishop Leo of the first see, which seemed to have been sent and addressed to the venerable Flavian of holy memory in order to check Eutyches’s malignity: although it was seen to agree with us in Saint Peter’s confession and to be one and the same page, it was fitting clearly to instruct believers in the integrity of the faith against the audacity of detractors.”

## CHAPTER 208

Pope Leo writes in the letter which he sent to the holy synod at Chalcedon, among other things (in the Council of Chalcedon, Part III, or Letter 16):

“Dearest brothers, I also admonish your holiness concerning the observance of the statutes of the holy Fathers, which are fixed by the inviolable decrees of the Council of Nicaea, so that the rights of the Churches may remain as they were ordained by those three hundred and eighteen Fathers inspired by God. Let no wicked ambition covet anything alien, nor let anyone seek his own increase through the diminution of another.

“For however much the arrogance of vanity may equip itself with emerging flatteries and may think its desires strengthened by the name of councils, whatever differs from the canons of the aforesaid Fathers will be weak and invalid.”

## CHAPTER 209

[Col. 0757A]

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse (Book VII, Letter 64):

“A certain man from Sicily came and told me that some friends of his, whether Greeks or Latins I do not know, were murmuring, as though out of zeal for the holy Roman Church, about my practices, saying: ‘How does he propose to suppress the Church of Constantinople, when in every respect we follow its customs?’

“When I asked him, ‘Which customs do we follow?’ he replied: ‘Because you have made the Alleluia be said at Mass outside the season of Pentecost; because you have decreed that subdeacons proceed stripped of their outer garments; because you have decreed that *Kyrie eleison*—‘Lord, have mercy’—be said; because you have decreed that the Lord’s Prayer be said immediately after the Canon.’

“I answered him: ‘In none of these matters have we followed another Church. For the practice of saying the Alleluia here is traditionally said to have been brought from the Church of Jerusalem through the tradition of Saint Jerome, in the time of Pope Damasus of blessed memory. Therefore, in this matter we have rather removed the custom that had been introduced here by the Greeks.

“As for having subdeacons proceed stripped of their outer garments, this was an ancient custom of the Church. But what pleased one of our pontiffs—I do not know which one—led him to order them to proceed clothed. Did your Church, then, receive this tradition from the Greeks? From where, therefore, does it now have the practice that subdeacons proceed in tunics, unless it received this from its mother, the Roman Church?

“As for the *Kyrie eleison*, we do not say it as it is said by the Greeks. Among the Greeks everyone says it together; among us it is said by the clergy and answered by the people, and *Christe eleison*—‘Christ, have mercy’—is also said the same number of times, whereas among the Greeks it is not said at all.

“In the daily Masses we omit the other things that are customarily said; we say only *Kyrie eleison* and *Christe eleison*, so that we may remain somewhat longer in these words of supplication.

“We say the Lord’s Prayer immediately after the prayer because it was the custom of the apostles that they consecrated the sacrificial offering through that prayer alone. It seemed very inappropriate to me that we should say over the offering a prayer composed by a scholar, while we should not say over the body and blood of our Redeemer the very tradition which our Redeemer composed.

“Among the Greeks, moreover, the Lord’s Prayer is said by the entire people; among us, it is said by the priest alone. In what respect, then, have we followed the customs of the Greeks, when we have either restored our own ancient customs or established new and useful ones, in which we are nevertheless not shown to imitate others?

“Therefore, when the opportunity arises for your affection to go to the city of Catana or to the Church of Syracuse, let it teach, through conversation, those whom it believes or understands might have murmured about this matter; and, as though on another occasion, let it not cease instructing them.

“As for what they say about the Church of Constantinople, who could doubt that it is subject to the apostolic see? Both the most devout lord emperor and our brother, the bishop of that same city, constantly profess this.

“Nevertheless, if either that Church or another possesses anything good, I am ready to imitate it in goodness, both I and my inferiors, whom I restrain from unlawful practices. For he is foolish who considers himself first in such a way that he refuses to learn the good things he sees.”

“On the privilege of the primacy of the apostolic see, a few matters have been collected from many and diverse authorities of the canons and of the Roman pontiffs. In these, all the councils of the holy Fathers appear to agree unanimously and are recognized not to have erred in any respect.

“After the emperor Constantine, holding the monarchy of the secular world, received the sign of Christianity through the divinely inspired mercy of God, and for the love of God and in honor of the prince of the apostles voluntarily abandoned the throne of the city of Rome, saying that it was not fitting for two emperors to administer a common empire together in one city, since one was the ruler of the earth and the other the prince of the Church, he eventually, as is clear to all readers, went to Byzantium. There he built Constantinople after his own name and made it the royal see.

“On his departure, he subjected the Roman domain to the apostolic see, and subjected to it also the greater part of various provinces. Finally, after transferring authority and solemnly entrusting the royal power to the Roman pontiff, he withdrew and left to God and holy Peter the honor of a kingdom to be enlarged in the future for the acquisition of the heavenly empire.

“Thus he ordered a singular privilege and wondrous testament, then made known throughout the whole world, to be written for the apostolic see. He permanently assigned to it various estates of kingdoms, adding countless gifts in sacred laws of diverse orders and rites and in the adornments of ecclesiastical vestments; and he increased it most nobly and splendidly.

“Among these provisions he particularly wished this to be included: that the Roman pope should perpetually retain, as though by royal right, the summit of all primacy over the whole Church and its pontiffs.

“These and many other matters, too numerous to count, are read in that same privilege. The archives of the Churches established in Gaul possess complete copies of it.

“Since these things are so, it is exceedingly astonishing why the bishops of Constantinople have dared from the beginning to usurp what was not theirs, especially since in none of the councils is that city counted among the principal sees, except in the case of Constantinople, for which the royal favor of that same city always smiled.

“Although the reasoning of all justice resisted it, the consent of kings, secretly signaling its support for this foolish presumption, supplied strength to the attempt, since the empire had established its capital there.

“Many of the Constantinopolitans, desiring this eminence, which belongs by right to apostolic dignity, have been defeated so often with disgrace and dishonor whenever, inflated by the swelling of arrogance, they have attempted to pursue it.

“For the letter of blessed Pope Gregory to John, bishop of Constantinople, is recalled (Book IV, Letter 38), written against the ambition that was sufficiently ridiculous: John had caused himself to be called and recorded as universal pope in a synod over which he himself presided. Anyone who reads it there will be able to see more clearly with what severity apostolic authority condemned him, proving him insolent to such a degree that it unhappily compared him with the apostate angel.

“By pride stretching out his sides, that angel burst forth with this foul breath: ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne; I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the North; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High’ (Isa. XIV, 6).

“His arrogance is also woven throughout the whole letter with the greatest propriety, and Gregory promises that, unless John turned back from unlawful things, he would subject him to condemnation. Accordingly, he also sent a letter to the empress Constantina, so that neither she nor the emperor would ever give assent in such matters, lest perhaps one of the faithless should attempt in any way to violate the privileges of blessed Peter (Book IV, Letter 34; and to the emperor Maurice, Letter 32, in the same place).

“If the complete texts of these letters are read, those who study them carefully will be able to teach this sufficiently and abundantly. Indeed, in the records of the Roman pontiffs this same presumption is found to have been restrained repeatedly and most strictly.

“Therefore, concerning the claim that Ignatius, bishop of the see of Constantinople, was recently unjustly condemned when he canonically appealed to the apostolic see according to the statutes of the Fathers, and that Photius, a novice, was placed in his position contrary to ecclesiastical rule—so that he should not be called a bishop but rather an invader, immediately released from marriage and tonsured—anyone who is not ignorant of synodal definitions can plainly recognize how far this departs from reason.

“Because of a similar invasion, the Roman Church once suffered the ruin of a miserable loss, as happened in the time of Pope Vigilius, who most shamefully seized by force the see of Pope Silverius of venerable memory while he was still alive and had been carried away into exile.

“It also happened under Pope Stephen, the ninety-sixth after Saint Peter, when a certain duke named Toto suddenly had his brother Constantine tonsured; on the following day the same man was consecrated deacon contrary to the statutes of the canons; and on the next Sunday he was improperly acclaimed pontiff, although he ought rather to have been judged an invader of the apostolic see. He stained the Roman Church with the disasters of discord and bloody murders.

“Because of the abyss of such great ambition, he eventually reached the point where he was most shamefully thrown out of the see he had seized; shut up in prison, he was finally deprived of the light of his eyes by the sons of wickedness.

“When the Greek nation learns these things—or, if it did not know them before, is now able to learn them—it will be all the more astonishing why it placed a novice, immediately released from marital union, in the see of the falsely condemned Ignatius without any interval or period of examination.

“Hardly torn from a woman’s embrace and not yet perfectly cleansed from bodily pollution, he was raised up and honored as pontiff of complete purity.

“Shaken a hundredfold by these and other storms of tempests, the holy Church shudders at such unspeakable crimes, not only those completed in deed but also those conceived in the intention of carrying them out.

“Let this brief treatment of the privilege of the apostolic primacy suffice.”

## CHAPTER 210

Concerning the question why at Rome a deacon is often suddenly consecrated bishop by a kind of leap, without receiving the presbyteral blessing, it should be said in a spirit of simplicity that a rational response supported by such assertions is lacking, since truthful speech modestly refuses to utter what it does not know, especially when the tongue is stretched out in public discourse and cannot at all be supported by the aid of the holy Scriptures.

Nevertheless, with downcast countenance, one must modestly yield to the judgment of understanding, since perhaps those who approve this kind of ordination wish this to be understood: that whoever receives episcopal blessing is adorned with the honor of the other blessings as well; or because, in the consecration of the body and blood of Christ, the office of bishop and presbyter is mystically united.

“For just as different dignities are assigned to an earthly king—for emperors created from among consuls formerly did not, on account of the royal relationship, omit or change the name of consul and patrician—so it may be believed that in the exaltation of the greater pontiff there is also the honor of the lesser priest.

“Perhaps those who ordain a bishop from among the deacons, omitting the presbyteral blessing, seem partly to entrust themselves to the assertion of Blessed Jerome in his letter commenting on Titus. He affirms that the office of presbyter participates in some respect in the episcopal ministry.

“But lest we perhaps arouse some slight agitation among our greater lords, let us omit our own judgment in the importance of this matter and faithfully set down the words of Saint Jerome himself, without any words of ours intermingled” (Saint Jerome, Book I on the Letter to Titus, chapter 1, 5).

They are as follows in the aforesaid letter, where he elegantly explains this opinion:

“And appoint presbyters in each city, as I also appointed you. Let bishops who possess the authority to appoint presbyters throughout the individual cities hear under what law of ecclesiastical constitution the order is to be maintained. Let them not think that these are the words of the Apostle, but of Christ, who says to the disciples: ‘Whoever despises you despises me. And whoever despises me despises him who sent me. Likewise, whoever hears you hears me. And whoever hears me hears him who sent me’ (Luke X).

“From this it is evident that those who, disregarding the law of the Apostle, wish to confer an ecclesiastical rank on someone not on merit but by favor act against Christ, who through his apostle subsequently explained what sort of person is to be appointed presbyter in the Church.

“Moses, the friend of God, to whom God spoke face to face, could certainly have made his own sons successors to the leadership and left his proper dignity to his descendants. But Jesus, a stranger from another tribe, is chosen, so that we might know that leadership over peoples is not to be granted to bloodline but to life.

“Yet now we see very many people turn honor into a benefice, so that they do not seek those who can benefit the Church most and raise up its pillars, but those whom they themselves love, or whose services have won their favor, or for whom some person of influence has asked; and, to say nothing worse, those who obtained clerical office through gifts.

“Let us carefully attend to the words of the Apostle, who says: ‘Appoint presbyters in each city, as I also appointed you’ (Titus I, 5). Explaining afterward what sort of presbyter ought to be ordained, he says: ‘If anyone is without blame, the husband of one wife,’ and so forth. Later he adds: ‘For a bishop must be without blame, as God’s steward’ (ibid., 6).

“Therefore, presbyter and bishop are the same. Before rival factions arose in religion through the instigation of the devil, and people began saying, ‘I am of Paul, I of Apollo, and I of Cephas’ (I Cor. XII), the Churches were governed by the common counsel of presbyters.

“But after each person began to consider those whom he had baptized to be his own and not Christ’s, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be chosen and placed over the others, so that the entire care of the Church might belong to him and the seeds of schisms might be removed.

“Does anyone think that the statement that bishop and presbyter are one and the same, and that one is a name of age while the other is a name of office, is not a statement of the Scriptures but of us? Let him reread the words of the Apostle to the Philippians: ‘Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons: grace to you and peace,’ and so forth (Phil. I, 1).

“Philippi is one city of Macedonia, and certainly there could not have been several persons called bishops in one city. But because at that time they called the same persons bishops whom they called presbyters, he spoke indifferently of bishops as presbyters.

“Perhaps this still seems ambiguous to someone unless it is confirmed by another testimony. It is written in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XX, 17) that when the Apostle Paul had come to Miletus, he sent to Ephesus and summoned the presbyters of that same Church. Among other things he afterward said to them: ‘Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to shepherd the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood’ (ibid., 28).

“Here too observe more carefully how, after summoning the presbyters of one city, Ephesus, he afterward called those same men bishops.

“If anyone wishes to accept the letter written under Paul’s name to the Hebrews, there too the care of the Church is equally divided among several persons. For he writes to the people: ‘Obey your leaders and be subject to them; for they keep watch over your souls as those who must give an account, so that they may do this without sighing, since that would be unprofitable for you’ (Hebr. XIII, 17).

“And Peter, who received his name from the firmness of faith, speaks in his letter, saying: ‘Therefore I exhort the presbyters among you, as a fellow presbyter and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and as one who shares in the glory that is to be revealed in the future: shepherd the flock of the Lord that is among you, not under compulsion but willingly’ (I Peter V, 1).

“These things have been set forth to show that among the ancients the same persons were presbyters as were bishops; but gradually, so that the plantings of dissension might be uprooted, all care was transferred to one.

“Therefore, just as presbyters know that by the custom of the Church they are subject to the one placed over them, so bishops should know that they are greater than presbyters more by custom than by the truth of the Lord’s arrangement, and that they ought to govern the Church together, imitating Moses, who, although he alone had the power to preside over the people of Israel, chose seventy with whom he might judge the people.

“Let us therefore see what sort of presbyter or bishop ought to be ordained: ‘If anyone is without blame, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of dissipation or disobedience. For a bishop must be without blame, as God’s steward,’ and so forth (Titus I, 6).”

[Col. 0762C] But if the chance of controversy should make these things displeasing to anyone, let the haughtiness of pride not be imputed to Christ’s own servants, since no more evident rational answer could be found to the proposition stated above—one that would, indeed, be superior in the authority of its teacher.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 771. HERARD, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS

[Col. 0761]

HISTORICAL NOTICE FROM *GALLIA CHRISTIANA*
[Col. 0761D] Herardus is designated archbishop in the year 855, as is asserted in the brief summary of the chapters which he ordered to be observed at the synod by all the priests and clerics of his parish. He is mentioned in the chronicles of Vendôme and Maillezais, the latter assigning his ordination to the year 858. He was appointed a judge by the council at Saponaria in the petition of King Charles against Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, in 859; he addressed a warning to him and is recorded as a subscriber at Tusey in 862 and at the Third Council of Soissons in 866. At that council, in the synodal letter of the bishops to Nicholas, the supreme pontiff, the incursions of the Bretons are mentioned:

“We know, indeed, that the excellence of your blessedness is not unaware that the diocese of Tours, torn away and completely severed from its metropolitan see for a long time by the harshness of the Bretons, has been so treated that—as the same Herardus, metropolitan of Tours, and Actardus, bishop of Nantes, have repeatedly reported to us after careful investigation, and likewise in clear and extensive writing and speech at the aforesaid Council of Soissons—it is now nearly twenty years, or only a little less, since, having resumed their tyrannical violence, they neither celebrate provincial councils with the metropolitan of Tours nor show him any regard in the consecrations of bishops, nor in any way submit themselves to that see.”

He took part in the Council of Troyes in 867 and in the assembly of the bishops of the province of Reims under the metropolitan Hincmar, concerning the examination of Vuilibert, a native of the region of Tours, who was to be ordained bishop of Châlons. Pope Nicholas’s letter to him is addressed on this matter; see also chapter 10, Question 1, *Notum sit*. Hincmar’s letter is found in Flodoard, book III, chapter 20, and in Lupus of Ferrières, letter 118. He is also named in the charters of foundation of the abbey of Saint-Sauveur at Villalupe. He confirmed the donation made in 862 by the most pious King Charles to the brothers of the church of Saint Martin of Tours, of the estate of Lirado, to which they could flee for refuge if pagan incursions overwhelmed their community, as recorded in the archive of Saint Martin.

Meanwhile, when Nomenoius, duke of the Bretons, who had increased the four bishoprics of Brittany to seven by establishing three new ones to the prejudice of the archbishop of Tours, ordered that the see should be at Dol, and when the bishops of Armorica had withdrawn themselves from the jurisdiction of their metropolitan of Tours, the Franks and the bishops resisted—especially Nicholas. Writing to King Solomon around 866, in letter 56, Nicholas observes that no memory existed up to that time of the Bretons having had any metropolitan see in their own region. The schism, however, was settled under the pontificate of Innocent III, as Sirmond observes in his notes on the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*.

[Col. 0763]

# Chapters of Herardus, Archbishop of Tours

Collected from the capitularies of the Frankish kings.

(From Baluzius, *Capitularia*, vol. I, p. 1283.)

Chapters excerpted from the body of the holy canons, extremely necessary, collected by Herardus, archbishop of the holy see of Tours by divine command, to be memorized and observed at his holy synod by all the priests and clerics of his entire parish and by all who desire them.

[Col. 0763B] In the name of God alone. I, Herardus, unworthy bishop of the people of Tours, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 858, in the third year of our ordination, in the sixth indiction, seeing that the Church entrusted to me was afflicted by various and countless calamities, shaken by disasters, and—what we have discovered to be more grievous in word and deed—perishing through diverse snares laid for souls and through daily errors, partly because of negligence, sluggishness, or indolence, and partly because of the carelessness [reading: “of those preceding”] and cowardice of the priests in authority, have, as we believe, by the prompting of heavenly mercy, collected a very few but exceedingly necessary chapters of sacred admonitions. At the general synod of the priests of the whole parish entrusted to us, assembled in the city of our see on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, we had them publicly recited; and, so that they might reach the knowledge and understanding of all those present, we caused them to be read and reviewed before everyone. And since the sacred authority of the canons permits no priest to be ignorant of the canons, lest we should thereafter find anyone among those entrusted to us ignorant of the canons of this order, we have jointly decreed and imposed that each person should henceforth possess these brief and concise chapters, excerpted through the diligence of our labor.

[Note: See, among the works of Charlemagne, in volume 97 of the *Patrologia*, the collection of capitularies by the deacon Benedict, from which these passages have been taken in various places. — Editor.]

**I.** (Capitularies, book VII, chapter 264.) At a synod, let the general matters that concern the order of the whole Church first be settled; afterward let particular matters be examined.

**II.** (I, 15, 75, 139; V, 153; VI, 189, 205, 318; VII, 276.) Concerning Sunday: it is to be celebrated from evening to evening; and servile work, shameful speech, buying and selling, hearings of lawsuits, and public assemblies are to be prohibited, except for ecclesiastical matters.

**III.** (I, 16, 21, 62; V, 69; VI, 66, 215; Additions II, 21. See Regino, book II, chapter 364.) Concerning unknown names of angels and of other saints: they are not to be recited. Concerning sorcerers, enchanters, diviners, fortune-tellers, interpreters of dreams, weather-magicians, and written charms against cold, as well as women who practice magic and those who invent various portents: they are to be prohibited and punished with public penance.

**IV.** (I, 2, 82, 136; V, 40; VI, 217.) Let clerics proceed to ordination gradually at the appointed times, not confusedly; and let their faith and life, their freedom, and their ages be investigated.

[Col. 0764C] **V.** (I, 5; III, 90; V, 38; VI, 378; VII, 53.) All usury is to be prohibited for the faithful, clergy and laity alike. Let measures and weights be just and equal.

**VI.** (I, 22.) Let neither clerics nor monks enter secular business.

**VII.** (I, 28, 38; V, 70.) If clerics or monks have business disputes among themselves, let them settle them before the bishop, not before secular authorities. Otherwise, let them be excommunicated.

**VIII.** (VII, 210.) Let no layman, without the bishop’s permission, compel any cleric to go to a public court. Whoever does so is to be expelled from the fellowship of the Church until he corrects his behavior.

**IX.** (I, 32, 76; V, 72, 316 and following.) Let the priests preach the faith to all the faithful: the Incarnation, the Passion, the Resurrection and Ascension, the giving of the Holy Spirit, and the forgiveness of sins, which takes place in that same Spirit and in the water of baptism within the embrace of holy mother Church. Let vices, especially criminal ones, be forbidden, and let virtues be taught.

**X.** (I, 47; V, 151; VI, 106.) Concerning the fasts of the Four Times and other fasts established for various needs: they are not to be relaxed except for those who are certainly ill.

**XI.** (I, 48; V, 82; VII, 49, 113.) Those who sin irrationally, or with their relatives, are to be judged more severely, so that such vices may be cut off.

**XII.** (I, 61; III, 10; V, 196; VII, 101.) Perjury, sacrilege, and drunkenness are to be prohibited. Let witnesses swear while fasting, and first be warned about perjury. Let no one under fourteen years of age be accepted as a witness. [Col. 0765B] Those who have once committed perjury are not to be accepted as witnesses thereafter.

**XIII.** (I, 65.) Honor and assistance are to be shown to parents.

**XIV.** (I, 111; V, 165, 304; VI, 106, 409; VII, 132, 377, 435.) All incestuous unions are to be judged by priests according to the measure of the fault, without exception of persons. Public crimes are to be brought to the bishop’s notice at the appropriate time; especially on the great day of the Lord’s Supper, when the accused is to be reconciled or further suspended, the matter being brought before the bishop by his own priest or by that priest’s delegate—by the priest who has full knowledge of the case—lest the soul of a brother perish without reconciliation, through the negligence or idleness of the priest.

[Col. 0765C] **XV.** (I, 67; VI, 377.) All idle talk and every disturbance are to be avoided in church. Let no one leave before Mass is completed, and let him listen attentively to the word of God.

**XVI.** (V, 161, 170, 260; VI, 165, 290; I, 66; V, 86; VI, 173, 205, 376.) Let everyone know the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed by heart. Let the *Gloria Patri* (“Glory to the Father”), the *Sanctus* (“Holy”), the *Credulitas* (“Belief”), and the *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) be sung reverently by all. Let the psalms likewise be sung distinctly by the clerics. Let priests not begin the secret prayers before the *Sanctus* has ended, but sing the *Sanctus* with the people.

**XVII.** (I, 68.) Let priests maintain schools as far as they can and possess corrected books.

**XVIII.** (I, 70; V, 182; VI, 106; Additions III, 78, 98.) Above all, let them love hospitality; and let them care for widows, pilgrims, orphans, and the sick.

**XIX.** (VII, 376.) Let them detest the company of women and their access to them and service for them. Otherwise, let them be deposed from their order as despisers of the canons. For those whom they determine must be served with necessities, let them provide houses far away, where assistance is supplied not by the priests themselves but through ministers.

**XX.** (I, 88; V, 216; VII, 261.) Ecclesiastical vessels and vestments are not to be given as pledges without the bishop’s permission, nor are those given in this way to be accepted.

**XXI.** (I, 34; V, 73; VI, 106.) Those who are ill are to be reconciled without delay; while still alive, they are to receive the viaticum, and they are not to be deprived of the blessing of consecrated oil.

**XXII.** (VII, 394; III, 55; V, 104, 145.) Every year two priests from each ministry are to come for the chrism, so that, if one falls ill, the other may suffice. Let them likewise perform the sacred offices of that day. Let chrism be given to no one for overturning judgments, and let them keep it under seal.

**XXIII.** (I, 96; V, 222; Additions II, 13; III, 85.) No woman is to be veiled without the bishop’s permission. She is not to be veiled before the age of thirty, and this is to be done with the advice of her parents and neighbors.

**XXIV.** (I, 17; VII, 190, 262, 376; Additions II, 18.) Women and laymen are not to approach the altars, nor are they to touch the sacramental objects and the holy breads, except those which they themselves offer.

**XXV.** (I, 136; V, 40; VI, 217, 233.) No one is to be excommunicated lightly or indiscriminately. No one is to compel another to drink or to become drunk.

**XXVI.** (I, 151; V, 53.) No one is to compel a penitent to eat or drink, unless redemption has been permitted; even then, the redemption is first to be given on his behalf in his presence.

**XXVII.** (II, 46; V, 96.) Fathers and godfathers are to instruct and nourish their sons and godchildren: the former because they are fathers, the latter because they are sureties.

**XXVIII.** (Same, 159; Additions II, 9.) A priest is not to sing Mass alone, for he cannot say, “The Lord be with you,” “Lift up your hearts,” and the rest.

**XXIX.** (I, 147; V, 49.) No priest is to receive or presume to solicit another priest’s parishioner for Mass without his priest’s permission, unless the person is traveling or has a lawsuit there.

**XXX.** (VII, 16.) Let everyone remain content within his own boundaries and seek nothing from another’s.

**XXXI.** (V, 172; VI, 181, 183, 188.) No one is to accept a fee for baptism. Baptisms are to take place at the appointed times of Easter and Pentecost, and in villages, except in cases of illness.

**XXXII.** (II, 36, 47; V, 97.) Churches established from ancient times are not to be deprived of tithes or of any possession, unless the greatest necessity demands it.

**XXXIII.** (I, 145; V, 47, 267; VII, 260, 391, 424.) Churches or altars of doubtful status, and likewise infants, are to be consecrated and baptized; for what is not established to have been done does not appear to have been repeated for any reason.

**XXXIV.** (VI, 208; VII, 396; Additions II, 12.) In houses not consecrated by the bishop, no one is to celebrate Mass for any reason. Likewise, no one is to sing Mass using unauthorized vessels or vestments.

**XXXV.** (I, 143; V, 45, 154, 173, 194, 374 and following; VI, 407.) Let tithes be given faithfully by the people, dispensed canonically by the priests, and let the priests render an annual account of their administration to the bishop or his ministers, lest they become subject to the losses caused by fraud or—God forbid—become destroyers of the poor by withholding what is useful.

**XXXVI.** (Same, 209.) Let no marriage be contracted in the fifth or sixth generation, and let descent be observed up to the seventh generation.

**XXXVII.** (V, 180; Additions II, 17.) A woman may not in any way cast off a veil once received, whether voluntarily or under compulsion, even if she changes her clothing in her own house.

**XXXVIII.** (V, 167.) No one is to lift a son or daughter from the baptismal font, nor marry the woman whose son he has held at the font. If such persons are found, they are to be separated.

**XXXIX.** (V, 315, 322; VI, 99, 402; VII, 331; Additions IV, 8.) Let the people be taught to do nothing gravely or lightly against bishops, nor to slander them, but to obey them humbly and reverently in all things; and to understand that an injury done to them is referred to God, whose supreme legation they exercise. No one is to presume to curse or slander kings or princes, for whom we are commanded to pray and to whom, for God’s sake, we are commanded to be subject.

**XL.** (I, 85; V, 214; VII, 292, 468; Additions IV, 56.) An entire manse is to be given to each church without rent or temporal service. All endowments of churches belong to the rights of the bishop.

**XLI.** (IV, 17; V, 106, 233.) Whoever takes a widow, whether unwilling or willing, within thirty days of her widowhood is not to approach her thereafter and is to suffer the penalties of adultery.

**XLII.** (II, 39; V, 274.) The incestuous and those who do not pay tithes are not to be constrained by swords or oaths, but are to be corrected ecclesiastically.

**XLIII.** (Same, 325.) Priests are not to run about through markets, go indiscriminately from house to house, or take part in feasts and drunkenness, lest they incur a reputation for bad conduct.

**XLIV.** (I, 150; V, 327.) Let them leave to their own churches the goods they acquired while in sacred orders; but let them distribute inherited property according to their own free choice.

**XLV.** (Same, 372.) Let priests carry blessed water around the churches with their people, and let them not neglect the scrutinies at the appointed places and times.

**XLVI.** (Same, 382; Additions III, 72.) Concerning the construction of churches: let no one lay a foundation until the bishop has come and set up a cross in the middle; then, after receiving the endowment, let him grant permission to build.

**XLVII.** (I, 131; V, 266; Additions III, 83.) Let neither bishop nor priest, nor any cleric of a lower order, pass by ambition from an ignoble place to a noble one.

**XLVIII.** (VI, 200; VII, 245.) If a priest or deacon abandons his church, let him be deposed, unless this occurs at the request of the people, with the bishop’s permission, and for a greater advantage.

**XLIX.** (VI, 73, 75; Additions II, 10.) A priest is to have no more than one church, just as a man has one wife.

**L.** (VI, 61.) If priests or deacons go forth to war with weapons, let them be deposed in such a way that they do not even retain lay communion.

**LI.** (Additions IV, 54.) If anyone has been excommunicated by a synod or by his own bishop and performs anything of the sacred ministry, let him find no hope of restoration whatsoever.

**LII.** (VI, 77.) Whoever wishes to receive consecrated water on Holy Saturday or Pentecost is to take it before the chrism is poured in. For the mixing of chrism pertains to regeneration.

**LIII.** (II, 40; VI, 170, 191; VII, 472.) Let the people be taught to offer oblations to God and to receive communion every third or fourth Sunday, abstaining from sexual excess, from their own wives, and from other illicit acts—unless perhaps they are involved in criminal offenses.

**LIV.** (VI, 169, 171.) Let the bells be rung at the canonical hours. No one is to put himself ahead of another through ambition; all are to recognize the time of their ordination.

[Col. 0768B] **LV.** (Same, 175, 193.) No one is to receive anyone from the sacred font unless he knows the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed according to his own language and understanding. Let all understand the covenant they have made with God.

**LVI.** (Same, 178.) Let priests always possess chrism, oil, and the Eucharist, so that they may be found ready.

**LVII.** (Same, 29, 195.) Let all firstfruits of crops be brought to the church for the sake of blessing.

**LVIII.** (Same, 197 and following.) Let funerals be conducted with hidden mourning and groaning of the heart. Those who do not know the psalms are to sing “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*) there; and for thirty days let friends and relatives act on their behalf.

**LIX.** (Same, 206.) By order of the bishop, let priests reconcile penitents concerning hidden matters; and, as stated above, let them absolve and give communion to the sick.

**LX.** (Same, 207.) After childbirth, a woman may enter the church as soon as she wishes, unless she is an adulteress, and give thanks to God.

**LXI.** (I, 158; II, 35; VI, 189.) Concerning the festivals of the year on which there is to be a holiday: the Nativity of the Lord; Saint Stephen; Saint John; the Holy Innocents; the Lord’s Octave; Epiphany; the Purification of Saint Mary; the Assumption; the Ascension of the Lord; Pentecost; the Mass of Saint John the Baptist; the apostles Peter and Paul; Saint Michael; All Saints; Saint Martin; Saint Andrew; and those whose bodies and due veneration are observed in particular places.

**LXII.** (Same, 187, 330; Additions II, 23.) On feast-days and fast-days, married couples are to abstain from one another because a wife is not granted for the sake of lust but for children. All illicit acts are to be prohibited, and they are to abstain even from what is permitted.

**LXIII.** (VI, 103, 112, 394, 404, 407.) Let privileges granted to churches remain undiminished; whoever violates them is to suffer the penalties of sacrilege.

**LXIV.** (V, 403; VI, 393; VII, 199.) No authority is to be granted to laymen, however religious, to administer the affairs of the church, since this pertains to their condemnation.

**LXV.** (VI, 404, 405, 407; Additions IV, 57.) Everything offered to God is considered consecrated: vineyards, lands, forests, utensils, vestments, livestock, and other possessions. Whatever belongs to the Church is undoubtedly Christ’s, since he is her bridegroom.

**LXVI.** (VI, 421.) Spiritual union with a godmother (*commater*) is especially sinful; therefore the parties are to be separated and condemned to death or exile.

**LXVII.** (Same, 230, 240, 432; Additions II, 23.) Husbands ought to love their wives and, as they would a weaker vessel, provide them with protection and everything necessary.

**LXVIII.** (V, 23, 59; VII, 4, 78, 155, 163, 275.) Let the whole order of clerics remain subject to its bishop and come to his judgments, presuming nothing without him. Whoever acts otherwise is to be degraded.

**LXIX.** (V, 25, 26, 62; VII, 10, 474.) No one is to associate with the excommunicated or join himself to those who disturb churches.

**LXX.** (VI, 364; VII, 85, 100.) A criminal is not to have the right to accuse; whoever does not establish one crime is not to be admitted to another accusation.

**LXXI.** (VI, 381; VII, 116; Additions IV, 3.) No one is to bring an accusation before his own affairs have been restored.

**LXXII.** (V, 147; VII, 166.) No one is to accept a church without the grant and consent of his own bishop.

**LXXIII.** (V, 2; VII, 130, 231.) During Lent, priests are to come to the city or to appointed places for the sake of learning.

**LXXIV.** (VII, 106, 433; VII, 132, 336; Additions II, 23.) Let priests show complete concern and care for the incestuous, the sick, penitents, and the dead, and let them altogether prohibit concubines.

**LXXV.** (Same, 6; Gratian, *De consecratione*, distinction 50, canon 6, “That the fasting.”) Let those who come for confirmation be fasting and of mature age. They are first to be urged to make confession, so that they may receive the gift of the Holy Spirit in purity.

**LXXVI.** (VII, 129, 130, 147, 148, 465.) Let bishops visit the parishes every year, and let priests render to them an account of their entire ministry and of everything entrusted to them.

**LXXVII.** (*Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, title VII, chapter 72.) Concerning the sale of graves and those who demand gifts for burials: let them be severely punished and constrained.

**LXXVIII.** (VII, 225; Additions IV, 71.) Let no priest presume publicly to pour out a blessing over the people.

[Col. 0769D] **LXXIX.** (VII, 248.) Whoever has possessed a church by the right of thirty years is not thereafter to have it taken away from him.

**LXXX.** (Same, 253.) The accuser is to suffer the same penalty if unable to convict as the accused if he is defeated.

**LXXXI.** (Same, 261.) Those who invade, devastate, or plunder church property are to be excommunicated if, after being warned by the bishop, they do not correct themselves.

**LXXXII.** (VI, 371; VII, 279.) Let laymen not stand within the chancel rails, and let the offering be received from the people outside the enclosure.

**LXXXIII.** (Same, 280.) Those who do not fast from Easter Saturday until the beginning of the night are to be excommunicated and excluded from Easter communion.

**LXXXIV.** (Same, 357; Additions IV, 14.) In every capital or status case, proceedings are to be conducted by the person himself, not through an advocate.

**LXXXV.** (VII, 378.) Let priests guard themselves from all vices and provide those subject to them with guidance toward heavenly life.

**LXXXVI.** Let priests have respectable houses and clean clothing.

**LXXXVII.** (V, 138; VII, 379.) Let them assign penances according to rule, maintain equity in judging, and demand no gifts in connection with it.

**LXXXVIII.** (Same, 382.) A woman who smothers her son while asleep is to do penance for six years. If her husband was in the house, he is to do penance for four years. If he was in the same bed, likewise two years on bread and water, and the remaining time at the priest’s discretion, according to the person’s condition and the penitent’s tears.

**LXXXIX.** (Same, 463.) Let the bridegroom and bride be blessed by the priest with prayers and offerings; let them be betrothed and endowed according to law; let them be guarded by wedding attendants (*paranymphs*); and let the marriage be publicly and solemnly celebrated. Let them abstain for two or three days, and let them be taught to preserve chastity between themselves and to have intercourse at the appointed times, so that they may produce children—not illegitimate but hereditary—for God and the world.

**XC.** (I, 6; VI, 120.) Concerning those who sing Mass and do not receive communion: how can they say, “The sacraments which we have received,” and so forth?

[Col. 0770C] **XCI.** (I, 13, 127.) Let councils be held twice a year, and let no one remain at any one of them for more than fifteen days.

**XCII.** (VII, 40, 122.) Concerning prohibitions: whoever scorns observing canonical prohibitions is to be subject to the peril of his rank. Likewise, if any priest or cleric acts against the prohibitions of the canons, he is to be removed from his office.

**XCIII.** Concerning the anniversary of Easter, let it be commemorated.

**XCIV.** (VI, 74.) Concerning the Roman Litany on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, let it be commemorated.

**XCV.** (V, 150; Additions III, 122.) Let the days of Rogations be celebrated reverently and diligently, without shameful jokes or words. No one is to presume on those days to hold lunches, feasts, or various drinking parties in different places.

**XCVI.** (Council of Aachen II, title II, chapter 9.) Concerning the readings for the vigils of Easter and Pentecost.

**XCVII.** (II, 35.) Concerning the eight days of Easter, how they are to be observed as holidays, and concerning Pentecost.

**XCVIII.** (VII, 42.) Concerning the delays in the stages of those advanced to sacred orders. Whoever desires to devote himself to divine service is to remain for five years either among the lectors or among the exorcists. Thereafter he is to serve for four years as acolyte or subdeacon; then, if worthy, he may advance to the blessing of the diaconate. In that order he must remain for five years if he has conducted himself blamelessly; afterward, once tested, he is to become a priest.

**XCIX.** (V, 37; VII, 43.) Concerning confession of crimes. It is clear that the person confesses the crime who does not use the means of clearing himself in the judgment granted and delegated to him. For it makes no difference whether, in the present inquiry, everything said against him is proven: his very absence stands as a confession.

**C.** (VII, 62.) A penitent ought not to engage in profit-making trade. Let an unjust demand of the people be deprived of effect.

**CI.** (Same, 107.) No one is to accept or hear slanderous or suspicious accusers.

**CII.** (Same, 307.) Accusers and accusations which the laws of the world do not admit are likewise excluded by the decrees of the canons.

**CIII.** (VI, 359, 362; VII, 112.) Those whose faith, life, and freedom are unknown cannot accuse priests; nor can persons of low standing, except in their own cases.

[Col. 0771B] **CIV.** (*Capitularies*, VII, 436; Additions IV, 27.) If a cleric is accused in a criminal or lesser case, or summoned into danger of capital punishment, the person who could be accused is not immediately considered guilty, nor do we subject innocence to condemnation. Whoever brings the charge is to come to the episcopal judgment, state the name of the accused, and take up the bond of written accusation. Let him first understand the assessment of rank by comparison, and know that he has no permission to lie about the matter. Let the equivalence of punishment exact a like penalty from calumniators.

**CV.** (I, 9; V, 323, 371; VI, 194, 369; VII, 225, 260, 423, 424.) Let priests recognize their proper limits: they are not to desire what belongs to another, remove altars, or do other prohibited things. Let churches be adorned with lights and other ornaments. Let priests celebrate Mass wearing sandals.

[Col. 0771C] **CVI.** (V, 396; VI, 206, 313, 381; VII, 379, 436; VI, 402; VII, 331.) Priests are not to presume to judge matters unknown to them before they have truthfully heard everything that occurred. They are not to injure or slander anyone, condemn anyone before a just judgment, or judge by their own will. Let them first establish the facts and then judge; for it is not the one accused but the one convicted who is guilty. Let them not permit anyone to be injured or slandered without cause, following the example of Miriam, who slandered Moses on account of the Ethiopian woman and was punished with the uncleanness of leprosy. David, although he knew that Saul had been rejected and condemned by God, feared to lay his hand upon the Lord’s anointed. Likewise, let us withdraw the hand of reproach from all the faithful.

**CVII.** (VII, 63, 452.) Just as priests are holier by their order, so let them be more reverent in speech, conduct, and action, since the loftiness of rank makes the accumulation of sin more serious.

**CVIII.** (Additions III, 41; IV, 90, 152.) Let priests and clerics not permit shameful jokes to be made in their presence. Let them have the poor and needy at table with them, and let a reading be given to them.

**CIX.** (V, 156; Additions III, 32.) Secular lawsuits are not at all to be conducted in churches, in their houses, or in their courtyards.

**CX.** (VII, 395.) Those who abduct, steal, or seduce women are not to have them as wives, even if the women and their parents agree.

**CXI.** (VII, 382, 406.) No layman is to have more than two wives. Anything beyond this pertains to adultery. The same applies to a woman.

**CXII.** Christian weddings are not to include dancing, and weddings are not to take place from Quinquagesima until the octave of Easter.

**CXIII.** (VII, 217, 398; Additions III, 17.) If clerics carry weapons in any rebellion, after deposition they are to be confined in prison under severe penance. Otherwise, if they have used weapons, military cloaks, or swords, they are to be deposed.

**CXIV.** (VI, 196; VII, 205.) When the people come to the churches on solemn days, let them either sing “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*) together or say the prayer individually. Let them stand silently in the church and pray for themselves and for all God’s people, always lifting their hearts toward heaven. Let them be urged to bring lights, incense, small loaves, and the firstfruits of their crops, as it is written: “Honor the Lord from your substance” (Prov. 3:9). On those same holy days, let them not perform shameful or lustful songs, dances, or demonic games in the streets or houses. Instead, let them meet some wise and good person and attend to good readings concerning the salvation of the soul. When returning from church, let them likewise sing, and let their pastors go out or return to the fields, so that true Christianity may be recognized in them.

**CXV.** (Same, 347.)
