Let all the faithful be instructed concerning charity and hospitality, so that they may know that true charity is to love God more than oneself, one’s neighbor as oneself, and to wish to do nothing to another that one does not wish done to oneself. Whoever thinks charity consists in food and drink, or in giving and receiving things, is in error, as the Apostle says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace” (Rom. 14:17). Yet if these things themselves are done with charitable zeal, they are good and are to be counted among the virtues. Otherwise, they are acts of the world.

**CXVI.** (VII, 407.) Concerning prayers, almsgiving, and the celebration of Masses to be performed for the faithful departed: the impious are to be deprived of these, since neither their alms are to be accepted by priests or other faithful people, nor is burial among the faithful to be granted to them.

[Col. 0772D] **CXVII.** (Same, 346.) Scripture cannot prevail against the decrees of the canons or the enactments of the pontiffs.

**CXVIII.** (VI, 342; VII, 71, 247.) Lawsuits and contentions, quarrels and disputes, as well as discord and hatred, are to be prohibited, and peace and harmony are to be preached.

**CXIX.** (III, 31; V, 183; VII, 163, 291, 450.) No one is to dare reopen settled crimes.

**CXX.** (VII, 242, 243.) Penitents are to abstain from banquets, adornments, and white clothing. Those who are at odds are to be expelled from the church until they return to peace.

**CXXI.** (I, 7; V, 25, 6; VII, 10, 295, 474.) Concerning those whom a priest has excommunicated: no other priest is to receive them.

[Col. 0773A] **CXXII.** (I, 62; VI, 374; Additions III, 94.) Christians are to guard themselves against idle speech and oaths.

**CXXIII.** (VI, 303; VII, 149, 457; Additions IV, 60.) Whoever acts against canonical statutes is to be deprived of communion if a layman, and of honor if a cleric.

**CXXIV.** (Additions III, 21.) Let the faithful abstain from intercourse with pregnant wives and during menstruation.

**CXXV.** (I, 68; Additions I, 5; VI, 259.) Let priests learn the computation.

**CXXVI.** (VII, 203, 237.) Proud clerics and laymen are to be excommunicated. Patience and humility, chastity and humanity are to be preached by all.

**CXXVII.** (Additions IV, 55.) If any powerful person strips or oppresses anyone, he is to be recalled from this conduct through the preaching of priests.

[Col. 0773B] **CXXVIII.** (I, 24; V, 28; VII, 13.) Let each person remain in the place in which he has been appointed and not move to another.

**CXXIX.** (V, 55; Additions III, 30.) Concerning accused persons who flee to churches or their courtyards: they are not to be dragged away from there.

**CXXX.** (I, 100; V, 226; VI, 133; VII, 179; Additions IV, 188.) No one is to contract a secret marriage or marry a consecrated virgin or widow.

**CXXXI.** (VII, 237, 311.) Clerics who are late for the office are either to be flogged or excommunicated.

**CXXXII.** (VI, 192; Additions IV, 155.) No priest is to receive tithes amid lawsuits and quarrels, but through preaching and admonition.

**CXXXIII.** (V, 60; VII, 34, 460.) Those summoned to a synod are to arrive without fail; otherwise, they are to be condemned.

[Col. 0774A] **CXXXIV.** (Additions IV, 81.) For those who inflict death upon themselves through any negligence, or who are punished for their crimes, no offering is to be made, nor are they to be carried to burial with psalms.

**CXXXV.** (I, 157; V, 276; Additions IV, 100, 166.) Those who remove tithes from the church to which they belong and give them to another because of gifts or some other occasion are to be expelled from the fellowship of the church until they restore them.

**CXXXVI.** (V, 112.) A layman ought not publicly to recite a reading or “Praise the Lord” (*Alleluia*) in church, but only psalms and responsories.

**CXXXVII.** (VII, 383.) Let everyone devoutly come to the bishop’s preaching and confirmation, faithfully serve him, and obey him.

**CXXXVIII.** (Same, 271.) Those who use violence against churches or presume to insult clerics are to be anathematized.

**CXXXIX.** Whoever attempts to defend or excuse another in his guilt is to be excommunicated.

**CXL.** Let no priest be ignorant of what has been established at the synod; rather, once all matters are known, let them obey eagerly.

We have established that these chapters, collected by us for the sake of brevity, as stated above, are to be possessed by all our priests, since we know that, when properly retained and understood by them and by the sheep subject to them, they will be beneficial in every way.

[Col. 0773]

# Warning of Herardus, Archbishop of Tours, to Wenilo, Archbishop of Sens

(From Labbe, *Councils*, vol. VIII, p. 694.)

[Col. 0773C] To the venerable Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, Herardus, by the grace of divine mercy, although unworthy, bishop of the metropolitan see of Tours: greeting in the Lord and perpetual peace.

Your Belovedness’s sagacity should know for certain that we ourselves, by common decree, undertook the embassy of the entire synod that had assembled in the vicinity of Toul, to your fatherhood. We also received from that same synod letters to be delivered to you, according to ecclesiastical custom, in connection with the synodical summons.

Know thereafter that our insignificance has been weighed down by a serious affliction. And since it is now clear that, because of our present incapacity, we cannot fulfill the synod’s instructions as we would wish, we have, in fraternal fashion, sent word to and likewise requested our brother and fellow priest Robert, bishop of Le Mans, who is attached to our see by the honor of his office, to go to you in our place on the embassy entrusted to us [Col. 0773D]. He will endeavor to carry out before you, fearlessly and in accordance with the resourcefulness divinely granted to him [Col. 0774C], everything reverently enjoined upon us by the holy synod.

I also obtained this from the aforementioned synod: that if, as is the condition of human frailty, I were detained by any illness—as indeed happened—I might send him to you in my place, after he had received from that synod the authority and command of all. We therefore ask—and, as a dearest father and most familiar brother, presume to admonish you—that, after carefully and cautiously considering everything conveyed to you, you not refuse to take counsel for yourselves. With sound and wise judgment, see to it that you do not expose yourselves, and our entire order, to the reproach of childishness.

And if, in the matters brought against you, anything is judged reprehensible, or perhaps condemnable, with conscience as witness, strive in every way to forestall it and, at the proper time, wipe it away. Since every rank of the pontifical order [Col. 0774D], and the entire synod mentioned above, is scandalized, sympathizes, grieves, and groans because of the calumny of this kind imposed upon you, we exhort you—and faithfully urge you—whom we have discovered to be the cause of this injury, and who, according to the Apostle, ought to have a good reputation even among those outside [Col. 0775A], not to regard it as burdensome to satisfy, for the time being, either one bishop on behalf of all or several on behalf of everyone, by your sacred letters.

At the same time, we earnestly entreat you—and pray in sincere charity, sharing your distress—to strive to secure the royal favor, acceptable to you, as is expedient for you and for your entire flock, by giving satisfaction and humbly obtaining the gracious goodwill of that prince [Col. 0776A]. We ask with all our wishes that your fatherhood may prosper, and we pray that you receive our petition effectively. We admonish you, in our humble request, most blessed father, to endeavor to bring our unanimity, because of this matter of yours, to some measure—or rather to complete—joy.

[Col. 0775]

## HERARD, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS: ANNOUNCEMENT

*(Made by order of the king, Charles the Bald, and of the synod, the Third of Soissons.)*

[Note: [Col. 0775D] Herard’s announcement. The first part of this address concerns the case of Wulfad and his associates, for whose sake the synod had been assembled; the latter part concerns the coronation of Queen Ermentrude, which took place at the same synod. J. Sirmond.]

Why it should not seem strange that a case already settled should again be reopened in this synod, and why the king should now, only so late, request that his wife, the queen, be blessed by the bishops.

[Col. 0775B] Sacred authority and the watchtower of the ministry, from which we ought to announce your salvation to you, brothers, remind us that we must always be ready to give an answer to anyone who asks us for an account of the hope and faith that are in us (I Peter III). We must make known to those entrusted to our ministry—whether they ask simply or otherwise, or do not ask—what intention and faith govern the things we do, and with what hope we believe that the things we perform with right intention will be rewarded to us by God. Thus neither the simple will take offense at our actions through evil suspicion, nor the impure, finding an opportunity to disparage us, will commit wrongdoing.

For this is the duty of watchmen, by whose name we bishops are called by the Lord—not on account of merit, but by grace: that, seeing the dangers that threaten, we announce them to those whose salvation we have undertaken to protect [Col. 0775C].

Therefore, brothers, we have thought it good to satisfy the thoughts of some and the words of others—those who perhaps think and say that, although some of us, together with certain of our predecessors, held a synod in this same place several years ago, and then settled the same case, we have now changed what we settled, as though it had not been properly settled, even though it had also been concluded by the Apostolic See. For that reason, they may think our judgment contemptible, as though we changed our judgments in response to the fickleness of human favor—or, to put it more plainly, sold them.

It is not so, brothers. For in the episcopal ministry there is not “Yes” and “No,” but always “Yes”; that is, there is stability in it. This sacred ministry is rooted in Christ, who never changes his counsel but often changes his judgment, both through himself and through his faithful servants, among whom his clemency has numbered us. To them he promised in truthful speech: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them”; and, “If two of you agree on earth about any matter, it shall be done for them” (Matthew XVIII).

And because God often changes his judgment, we have considered it necessary to set forth, from many testimonies, one statement that all of us should embrace. The Lord says: “If I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ and that wicked man turns from his evil way and does judgment and righteousness, he shall live by living and shall not die; all his iniquities that he committed shall be forgotten before me” (Ezekiel XVIII).

After the severity of the Law that he gave through the angels by the hand of Moses, he also gave the grace of the Gospel through the apostles and their successors to be preached to all. For, as Saint Leo, the great adornment of the Apostolic See, says (Letter to Rusticus of Narbonne):

> “Just as there are certain things that cannot be changed for any reason, so there are many things that ought to be moderated either in consideration of the ages or because of the needs of circumstances; yet in such a way that what is found to be necessary to follow is neither contrary to the evangelical commandments nor opposed to the decrees of the saints” [Col. 0776C].

We have followed this principle in the present case, just as we find it in the sacred authorities. We sing in the psalm: “Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have kissed” (Psalm LXXXIV). And mercy always exalts itself above judgment, as the Apostle says: “I will show you a still more excellent way” (I Corinthians XII)—that is, charity, which desires to show mercy to all and wishes to benefit everyone in common.

The things pronounced by episcopal judgment for the correction of men and the exercise of due severity are indeed perfect. But more excellent are the measures by which, through the kindness of love, we provide for the salvation of our subjects and for the common usefulness and welfare of the churches [Col. 0776D].

Therefore, while the earlier statutes remain—those established according to authority through the severity of justice—it is lawful for us, by those same superior authorities that extend mercy, to alter harsher judgments by means of correction carried out through the more excellent way, namely charity [Col. 0777A]. And just as we consulted the Apostolic See concerning the earlier statutes, so we await from that same mother of all the churches a response concerning this decision of ours. If it agrees and consents to what, under its earlier admonition—which brought us together here—we have mercifully determined through indulgence, then let us favor the welfare of the churches.

For the rest, brothers, we wish you to know that our lord and senior, the glorious King Charles, asks the devotion of our humility that, by the authority of the ministry conferred upon us by God, just as he himself was anointed and consecrated king by episcopal authority through sacred anointing and blessing—as we read in Scripture that the Lord commanded kings to be anointed and consecrated for royal power—we should likewise bless his wife, our lady, in the name of queen, just as we know that this was previously done by the Apostolic See and by our predecessors for other women.

And so that you may not wonder why he makes this request, we hasten to give your fraternity an account. It is because, as many know, almighty God by his grace wondrously gathered this kingdom into the hands of his ancestors. Those predecessors governed it nobly, and their descendants have ruled it through successive generations down to the present time.

God has given sons to this present lord of ours, as you know. In the nobility of these sons, his faithful subjects have rejoiced, placing the greatest hope for the holy Church and for the kingdom that God entrusted to him to govern. Of them he offered some to God, so that he might offer to God an offering from the fruit of his womb; others God, by his grace, while they were still of immature age, snatched from this world, lest, as it is written, wickedness should change their hearts (Wisdom IV); while others, as you know, he permitted by his judgment to suffer such a trial as his faithful subjects are known to lament [Col. 0777C].

For this reason he asks that episcopal blessing come upon his wife, so that the Lord may deign to grant him from her such offspring as will provide the holy Church with consolation, the kingdom with necessary defense, his faithful subjects with the aid they desire, this Christian people with practical tranquility, and law and justice—with those whom he still has—with the Lord’s assent and cooperation.

We have authority for this in the holy Scriptures. Just as the Lord said to Abraham, “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Genesis XXII), and gave him Isaac, when he was already a hundred years old, from a wife of ninety; so he also caused Isaac to take a barren wife, in order that in this too, as in many things, he might display the generosity of his mercy. Scripture therefore says that Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren, and she conceived (Genesis XXIII).

Nor should you wonder why he did not do this earlier. For, as sacred Scripture says, at the beginning of the union of male and female the Lord said to Eve: “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis III). And when Abraham and Sarah were already mature in character for legitimate union and advanced in age, and, as Saint Peter says, “Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord” (I Peter III), the Lord said to Abraham something that we do not previously read him to have said either to Abraham himself or to any other man: “Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice” (Genesis XXI).

For Abraham was already rightly called an elder, and Sarah’s womanly faculties—that is, all wantonness—had failed. Then they received from the Lord the blessing of blessed offspring, in whom all nations are blessed. Amen.

Supported, therefore, by these authorities, we who have been appointed ministers of God for distributing his gifts must not, as Leo says, be difficult or neglect the petitions of the devout—especially when we see that those petitions have been conceived through God’s inspiration and are confirmed by evident judgments.

For God’s manifold mercy has decreed to assist human salvation in such a way that salvation itself should be obtained especially through the supplications of priests. In this work, as we read in the sacred writings, the Savior himself intervenes, and he is never absent from the tasks that he has entrusted to his ministers, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days” (Matthew XXVIII).

And if, through our service, we accomplish anything in good order and with a grateful disposition, let us not doubt, as Leo says, that it has been given to us through the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, brothers, since this is so, and since our ministry for you and your joined devotion toward us may become one supplication before the Lord, let your common prayer also accompany our common vow. For we read that priests were appointed to pray first for their own sins and then for those of the people, and that “prayer was made without ceasing to God for” (Acts XII)—that is, for the entire choir of bishops.

As we pray for our common need, indeed for the need and salvation of the whole Church and people, may your common prayer pursue our common request before him who makes people of one mind dwell in a house, and who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## In the Year of Our Lord 771. Iso, Monk of Saint Gall

[Col. 0779]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(In Fabricius, Bibliotheca of Medieval and Late Latin.)*

[Col. 0779A] Iso, master, monk of Saint Gall, and a most renowned teacher, died in the year 871, on the day before the Ides of May, according to Hermann the Lame in his Chronicle and Hepidanus in his Annals, in Goldast’s first volume of *Rerum Alemannicarum*. In that volume the monk Radbertus is also encountered. In his book *On the Origin and Fortunes of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, much is written in praise of Iso on page 12, and especially on pages 22 and following and on page 77, where his disciples are praised: Marcellus, Notker the Stammerer, Notker the master of theoretical art, Ratbertus, Tutilo, Hartmannus, and others.

Two books by the same Iso, *On the Miracles of Saint Othmar, Abbot of Saint Gall*, are extant in the same first volume of *Rerum Alemannicarum*, pages 180–189, and in Mabillon, *The Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Third Century, part II, page 162.

A centuria of charter formulae, from the time of Abbot Grimald and therefore before the year 872, not 913 as Goldast states on page 5, is found in the same Goldast, volume II of *Alemannica*, pages 28, 30, 33, 36, 48, and 54 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0779A] It would be superfluous to reprint Iso’s glosses on Prudentius after our highly learned edition of Prudentius’s poems, prepared according to Arevalus. In those scholia the reader would find nothing other than what is more fully supplied in Arevalus’s commentaries. Besides, what use would glosses be without the text being commented upon? Editor.]

John Weitzius published at the end of his Prudentius, from two manuscripts belonging to Charles Widmann and Jacob Bongarsius, the *Glossary on the Poet Prudentius*, pages 771–904, Hanover, 1613, in octavo.

No one has yet brought to light the Latin lexicon collected from all the ancient glossaries under the name of Salomon, bishop, which Goldast, page 144, attests is preserved in the monastery of Saint Gall and in the cathedral library at Constance.

He is also said to have composed certain poems, themselves not yet publicly seen.

[Col. 0779]

# TWO BOOKS OF ISO ON THE MIRACLES OF SAINT OTHMAR

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, volume III.)*

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

[Col. 0779B] Thus far the virtues and miracles divinely revealed on account of the holiness of the blessed Othmar, abbot, have been written down by Walafrid, a learned and wise abbot, who was considered distinguished among our people above others in knowledge of letters. He gave credence to the reports—or also the writings—of the elders living in the monastery of Saint Gall, whose accounts were exceedingly full of truth, and composed his work in a sufficiently lucid style and with truthful assertion.

But because we brothers, serving Christ in the same monastery, learned that many notable miracles had been divinely manifested around the body of that same man after the account of these virtues had been written, we have taken care to commit some of them to memory by the service of the pen, for the praise and glory of almighty God [Col. 0780B]. Thus all who possess sound understanding may clearly gather from this how worthily he is honored by men on earth who is daily glorified in heaven by such manifest testimony of signs.

We have not, however, been led by affection for him to record anything doubtful or liable to falsehood; we have resolved to put into writing only what is clearer than daylight in its occurrence and is known to have been truthfully confirmed by the reports of many.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0781]

## CHAPTER ONE. By what miracles the holiness of Blessed Othmar shone forth in the basilica of Saint Peter

[Col. 0781A] While the little body of the blessed man rested for many years, removed from the approach of the crowd, in the oratory of the prince of the apostles, clear indications of his holiness frequently appeared around his tomb through the manifestation of numerous signs.

For many brothers of our congregation, who were accustomed to rise before the vigils of the nocturnal celebration, affirmed that, when they entered that same oratory for the sake of prayer, they frequently found burning candles and glass lamps kindled there of their own accord.

There was also heard there a most sweet harmony of angels leading choirs among themselves. Their presence was accompanied by such a great brightness of light that the windows of the church itself shone with an extraordinary illumination, and the places nearby were flooded by the immense radiance.

A very sweet fragrance is also often reported to have been spread there. It was unfamiliar to the noses of those who smelled it, yet was regarded as highly fragrant by its own pleasantness.

All these things plainly show how great was this man’s merit before God: beside whose tomb the immense greatness of the light that shone forth spontaneously from candles and lamps was accompanied by the sweetness of angelic music, and an unfamiliar fragrance was perceived by mortal smell.

## CHAPTER TWO. How Bishop Salomon, touching upon his sanctity in a synod, instituted a three-day fast

[Col. 0781C] With such signs of miracles, therefore, God’s man Othmar, honorably buried behind the altar of Saint Peter, rested in peace for thirty-four years and one hundred and ninety-four days.

[Note: [Col. 0781D] Namely, from the translation made in the year 830 to the basilica of Saint Peter, above, chapter 16; for what is reported here took place in the year 864, as Hepidanus, Hermann, and others testify.]

But when almighty God wished to place upon a lampstand, for the example and illumination of the faithful, the lamp kindled by works of light and long kept hidden through human negligence, and to administer the grace of its light to all who remained in the house of God through the splendor of his holiness, the community of brothers serving Christ devotedly under the rule in the monastery of Saint Gall began to hold continual discussions about the excellence of his merits.

In these discussions the brothers encouraged one another, and, as we believe, by divine prompting, all together began to desire that the little body of the holy man be brought again to the church of Saint Gall, which, with God’s help, now shone forth, suitably adorned.

But since considerations of justice dictated that they should not presume to do this solely on their own decision, they entrusted to the venerable bishop Salomon for reading a little book of his life, which the diligence of our predecessors had once composed with numerous testimonies recorded in it and which had come down to us. They also disclosed to him the desire of their will, with which the entire congregation of that place was fervently animated, and declared themselves ready in every respect to obey his judgments and counsels.

[Note: [Col. 0781D] Concerning the dedication of the new basilica of Saint Gall, which took place before the year 860, see Notker in the Martyrology, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, and Ratbertus, chapter 6, from whom Hepidanus differs somewhat regarding the year.]

The benevolent pontiff, having examined the examples of his life, rendered manifold thanks to the author of every good thing, because he had revealed his warrior, fighting bravely for zeal for justice, through such clear manifestations of miracles [Col. 0782B].

Having also removed every doubt concerning his holiness—although he himself was certain of it—he nevertheless wished to define nothing rashly and nothing disorderly on his own authority. Rather, following his customary prudent practice, he solemnly announced an annual synod concerning ecclesiastical doctrines and ordered priests, deacons, and clerics of various orders to assemble at the town of Constance.

When they had gathered together, the venerable pontiff rose in their midst. After silence had been made, he recounted before all, as circumstances permitted, the account of the holy man’s life, which had already somewhat charmed many of those residing there with its sweet reputation.

When a great multitude of clergy had acclaimed the praises of God’s man, the bishop first admonished the abbot of the monastery of Reichenau—who at that time had also come there with certain brothers very dear to us—and then all the clergy of that council, to abstain through a three-day fast and pray together to the source of every good, so that by the gift of his mercy he might deign to accomplish the disposition of his will in these matters.

When he had spoken, the synod praised the bishop’s judgment and loudly declared that it would gladly act accordingly.

## CHAPTER THREE. How the same bishop lifted the holy body from the tomb and found the offerings there unharmed

Having therefore taken the synod’s decision and completed the three-day fast, the venerable prelate arrived at the same monastery with his companions and approached our elder Grimald, rector of that monastery and archchaplain of King Louis, to discuss the matter [Col. 0782D].

[Note: [Col. 0782D] Grimald, a secular abbot, presided for thirty-one years from the year 841. Under him the monk Harmotus held the office of provost and later became his successor. See Ratbertus, chapters 8 and following.]

After the duties of friendly greeting, as they frequently recalled among themselves in conversation the strictness of his life and the miracles repeatedly displayed as evidence of his holiness, they ordered the monks of the same monastery to assemble. Sitting among them, they unanimously decided, with equal resolve and common counsel, that the holy body should be removed from the tomb where it had hitherto lain and placed in the church of Saint Gall.

The venerable abbot Grimald, perceiving that the minds of certain people had been disturbed by fear and apprehension, became more confident than the others. By consoling the minds of the weak he strengthened them, and, with fatherly affection, instructed the hearts of those who trembled. He asserted that it proceeded from the disposition of the divine will that so many desired to remove the little body of the holy man from that same tomb [Col. 0783B].

When the distinguished prelate saw the abbot conducting himself in these matters with such confidence, he took with him Harmotus [also Harmodus], the dean, together with the other brothers.

[Note: [Col. 0783D] He later succeeded Abbot Grimoald in the year 872. He is praised by the monk Ratbertus in the book *On the Fortunes of the Same Monastery*, chapters 9 and 10; later he became an enclosed monk, according to the Anonymous of Saint Gall in book II of *The Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 15.]

Approaching the tomb, he ordered the stone placed above it to be removed and the sarcophagus itself, in which the treasure of the precious body lay, to be opened.

When this had been done, he gazed upon the limbs full of holiness and urged the monks to sing the litany and persist in devout prayers. Then, humbly kissing the venerable relics of the holy Father, he lifted them from the tomb with every mark of reverence and placed them in a litter that had shortly before been constructed to receive them.

Under the man’s head and around his breast, the same bishop found certain small rounds of bread, commonly called offerings [Col. 0783C] [Note: [Col. 0783D] Concerning offerings, or oblations, which they call hosts, see the discussion in the Preface to the first volume of this century.], so unharmed and untouched by any corruption that, although they had not lost their color or appearance in any part at all, they appeared to the eyes of those looking at them to have been made within the space of that very week.

By what order or at what time they had come to that place is unknown to us, but we know that it is manifest to God. We all know this with certainty, however: for thirty-five years no mortal had opened his tomb before the present bishop, relying upon the authority of his ministry, enjoined the brothers of the congregation to do so.

The same bishop nevertheless reverently took them up, placed them beside the sacred body, and honorably entrusted the body, carefully wrapped, to the litter mentioned above.

## CHAPTER FOUR. The translation of Blessed Othmar and the celebration appointed for his feast

[Col. 0783D] After this, when an interval of about one hour had passed, the devout prelate, at the urging of Abbot Grimald, ordered the holy man to be transferred from the same oratory with the honor due to him [Col. 0784A].

Then the entire congregation of monks, immediately clothed in white garments and bursting forth in sweet harmony into the praises of God, joyfully accompanied the body of the blessed man. Thus, escorted with great honor through the crowds of the numerous multitude whom love for his translation had drawn together, it entered the church of Saint Gall and was placed beside its altar, on the right-hand side.

The bishop noticed that the crowds, who had come there from various regions, wished to hear something about his holiness. But because he himself could not speak to them, being hindered by hoarseness of the throat brought on by the sudden onset of cold, he ordered an archpriest to climb the ambo [Col. 0784B] and deliver a sermon to the people in his place.

[Note: [Col. 0784D] Balbus, in the *Catholicon*: “Ambo,” a pulpit where there are steps on both sides; the same word is incorrectly written “Amo, Amonis.” More correctly, it comes from Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀμβαίνειν, “to ascend.” The *Tripartite History*, book X, chapter 4: “sitting upon the ambo, where he was accustomed previously to deliver his sermon,” etc.]

The arrangement was that the priest himself, standing in a somewhat higher place, would say only what the bishop, stationed nearby, indicated that he should say.

After some examples and virtues from his life had therefore been briefly recited before the people, the solemnities of the Mass were celebrated, and the people returned to their homes with joy. The bishop, however, remained that night in the monastery.

When morning came, he gathered the brothers together and, among other instructions of sacred discipline, being certain of the merits of the holy man, confidently ordered them that, when the day of his deposition came around, they should honorably celebrate the vigils and solemnities of the Mass, and that both they and the entire household established within the monastery should keep that day as a festival in honor of Blessed Othmar, with the joy of spiritual gladness.

When all this had been completed as we have related, the kind prelate, fortified by the prayers and blessing of the brothers, happily left the monastery [Col. 0784C].

## CHAPTER FIVE. A summary of the periods in which the events mentioned took place

If anyone wishes, in pious inquiry, to learn during what period or under which royal rulers these events occurred, he will easily be able to find what he seeks in the sequence of our account.

We have written down the dates of the periods here for this reason: so that they may preserve the faith of readers and, through their notation, display greater force in written form for posterity.

Therefore, in the early years of Charles, the father of Carloman and Pippin, blessed Othmar was brought by Waltramnus, a noble and powerful man, into the presence of that same Charles. From him Othmar received the administration of the cell of Saint Gall, and over many years nobly increased and expanded its possessions in various ways.

After Charles died, not many years later his son Carloman, moved—as is believed—by divine love, abandoned the pleasures of worldly pomp, handed the reins of the kingdom over to his brother Pippin, and, after first building a monastery at Rome on Mount Soracte beside the church of Saint Sylvester, submitted his neck freely to the institutions of the regular life. Then, withdrawing into the province of Samnium out of love for a more secluded life, he spent the remainder of his life in religious conduct in the monastery of Saint Benedict, situated in the fortress of Cassino.

[Note: [Col. 0785D] Except for the final period of his life, which he completed at Vienne in Gaul. See his *Eulogy* under the year 755.]

Pippin, the father of the emperor Charles, after King Childeric had been deposed and tonsured by the authority of Stephen, the Roman pontiff [Col. 0785B], was made king from prefect of the palace and began to rule the Franks alone in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 754, in the seventh indiction.

[Note: [Col. 0785D] The deposition of Childeric and the inauguration of Pippin by Boniface, following the decision of Zachary, the Roman pontiff, had taken place two years before he was anointed by Pope Stephen together with his two sons, Charles and Carloman.]

After these events, the aforementioned Waltramnus, to whose possession the cell of Saint Gall seemed to belong by almost hereditary right, learned that Pippin had been placed upon the throne of the kingdom with the consent of the Franks. He again took God’s man Othmar, as the earlier book of his life teaches (chapter 1), brought him to the palace, and requested that the king entrust the title of that place to Othmar.

When this had been done, the holy man, having received many gifts of royal generosity for the administration of that place, returned to the monastery rejoicing and exulting [Col. 0785B].

In the seventh year of Pippin’s reign, unjustly oppressed by the power of Warinus and Ruadhardus, full of days and also full of the merits of holiness, he was delivered from the anguish of this life and brought, for his good works, to the joys of eternal blessedness.

Ten years later, he was transferred by his monks to the monastery and honorably placed between the altar of Saint John the Baptist and the wall of the church, on the right side of the altar [Col. 0785C]. Then, after no fewer than sixty years had intervened, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, on the holy day of Good Friday at Easter, he was brought to the oratory of Saint Peter.

After this, in the thirty-fifth year, namely in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 864, in the thirteenth indiction, under the most pious King Louis, Grimald, the king’s archchaplain and abbot of that monastery, together with Salomon, bishop of the Church of Constance, carried out the translation described above on Wednesday, the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

And, as we have been able to investigate with diligent care, from the seventh year of Pippin, when the holy man departed from the tribulations of this world, until the translation, one hundred and four years are reckoned.

[Note: [Col. 0786D] Rather, almost one hundred and five years: for it is established that Othmar died in the year 759, counting from the seventh year of Pippin, whose reign Iso incorrectly places as beginning in the year 764.]

## CHAPTER SIX. An unfamiliar fragrance spread around his body

[Col. 0785D] Having described the periods in which the events mentioned above took place, let us now turn to the miracles that, after the translation we have related, we learned were manifested around the relics of Saint Othmar by the power of almighty God.

When the venerable relics of the holy Father had been carried to the basilica of Saint Gall in the manner described above, that very night, while the bishop was still within the monastery, a great sweetness of fragrance was discovered to have spread throughout the basilica of Saint Gall, especially near the body of Blessed Othmar, where it overflowed as though floating about in the form of a cloud [Col. 0786A].

Although the fragrance lasted there continuously for three days and nights, it could not be perceived by everyone. Certain brothers of our congregation, however, who appeared to be more religious, tasted its sweetness and, on the authority of their religious character, commended the truth of the matter to the others.

Although the odor itself was unfamiliar and previously unexperienced, it could nevertheless, as they asserted, partly imitate the sweetness of balsam.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. A glass lamp kindled there before him by heavenly power

[Col. 0786B] On the following Saturday, that is, the fourth day after the translation of the blessed man, the holy body was meanwhile placed behind the altar of Saint John the Baptist, until a new basilica could be built for its dwelling and dedicated in his honor.

That same Sunday night, when the custodian of the church rose to anticipate the vigils of the nocturnal celebration, he entered the basilica as usual and found all its lights completely extinguished.

A certain priest of our congregation, secretly following in his footsteps, left the enclosure of the basilica and prostrated himself there to pray before the sacred body. Rising from prayer, he saw a glass lamp burning there of its own accord.

When he saw this, he applied himself still more attentively to prayer. After leaving the oratory, he decided not to report the management of that light so quickly to anyone [Col. 0786C].

None of the church custodians extinguished the same lamp, because each thought that another had lit it. It shone more brightly than the others and, throughout the whole Sunday, was continually filled with a greater abundance of light, almost at each successive hour.

The priest to whom that heavenly administration of light was first revealed, fearing that the miracle of so great a sign might be suppressed by silence, reported it to the other brothers after the evening assembly had ended.

Then many of our brothers, desiring to see the light itself, approached more closely. Just as it had appeared to them, they discovered that the fire itself, which had continued burning as though from midnight onward, had consumed absolutely nothing of the oil.

Then, when the lamp itself began to burn as though more intensely, and the oil was gradually diminishing, the same light, always growing greater in itself and flooding the entire basilica of Saint Gall throughout the following night with the immensity of its radiance, prolonged its burning almost until the eighth hour of the day, into Monday.

Then the custodian of the church, seeing that it had diminished somewhat, carelessly loosened the rope from which the lamp hung after the Mass had ended and lowered it; thus the light itself went out.

Then, in a marvelous manner, beneath the lead to which the papyrus wick [Col. 0787A]

[Note: [Col. 0787D] Thus the ancients called the wick customarily used in a glass lamp. Paulinus, in *Natale* 3:

> “Bright altars are crowned with dense lamps,”]

Lumina are burned with fragrant papyrus wicks. And Gregory the Great, in Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 5: “He filled all the lamps of the church with water and, as usual, placed papyrus in the middle.” Aldhelm speaks more clearly in his prose work *On Virginity*, where he discusses Saint Narcissus the bishop, in these words: “Then the man devoted to God, exorcising the clear waters of the springs and making them fruitful through the abundance of sacred blessing [Col. 0788D], caused them to grow thick in a wondrous display of power—so much so that the liquid poured into the lamp-funnels was swiftly changed into the consistency of oil, and the papyrus placed at the center, like tinder soaked in fat or tallow, shone more brightly than usual.” Finally, Gregory, bishop of Tours, in Book III of *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 50, “found two candles made of wax and papyrus.”] … was placed upon it; you could see that its fire had consumed from the oil an amount equal to one finger’s measure, yet had caused no loss or injury whatever to the lead placed above it. Here I cannot easily determine what is astonishing—or rather, what ought especially to be admired: that the light itself shone forth of its own accord; or that, burning for so long, it diminished nothing of the liquid oil; or even that the fire itself, by the power of its heat, did not melt the softness of the lead placed above it.

## CHAPTER VIII. On another lamp that shone forth of its own accord on the eve of his feast

After this manifestation of the miracle, when the feast of his deposition was approaching, we diligently celebrated the vigils of the evening solemnity. When these had been duly completed, one of the church’s attendants extinguished the crown that had been lit before the holy body for the joy of his feast. When he wished to relight the lamp hanging in the middle of that crown, he suddenly saw that it had been illuminated of its own accord. Many—not only members of our household, but also students and guests who had come to the monastery at that time—testified that they had seen this. The heavenly origin of this light’s kindling also appeared from the fact that, although no mortal replenished it, it nevertheless did not lose the grace of the light it had received before the middle of the following night, but continued to burn moderately.

## CHAPTER IX. The labor of workmen frustrated on his solemnity

[Col. 0787C]

The devout congregation of the brothers, obeying the bishop’s commands, was properly performing the solemnities of the nocturnal office while persevering in the praises of God. They had also decreed that all who were within the monastery should keep the day itself as a holiday in honor of Saint Othmar. Yet, at the cellarer’s direction, three woodworkers—men who seemed superior to the others even in mastery of this craft—went to work in the storeroom constructed above the monastery. There they began to join together a certain barrel that had fallen apart through age and neglect.

When they had gathered the boards together and had joined its bottom only with considerable difficulty, they began to raise the carefully fitted boards around it. Yet, although they labored for almost the entire day, they could not secure them by any ingenuity whatsoever. In a wondrous fashion, the boards always sprang back from their proper position and seemed to reject every joining effected by the craftsman’s hand.

[Col. 0787D] Then the workmen themselves, as the day was already declining, saw that their labor was accomplishing nothing and recognized that they had acted wrongly. Returning to the monastery after vespers, they prostrated themselves in the church and begged that their folly not be held against them, asking pardon.

## CHAPTER X. How one afflicted by an aversion to bread was overcome by a desire for it

A young man born in the district called Elisazia [Note: [Col. 0788D] Goldast calls it *Elisaza*, that is, Alsace, the district or region on this side of the Rhine, near the Vosges.] claimed that from the beginning of his birth—or, to speak more cautiously, from as far back as he could remember—he had never eaten bread. Coming to the monastery, he remained there for nearly half a year without eating bread or ever tasting anything made from it. If, unknowingly, he swallowed even a little bread in food or drink, he immediately vomited up what he had taken, mixed with blood [Col. 0788B].

On the eighth day after the feast of Blessed Othmar, he entered the basilica of Saint Gall. As he went around the altars in prayer and reached Saint Othmar, he earnestly begged to be helped through the saint’s intercession. At first he was shaken in the chest by an excess of cold; then his head was surrounded by a heaviness and extreme stupor like that of a drunken man. When he reached the steps adjoining the sacred body, by which one enters the crypt, he began to be tormented by so great a desire for bread that, returning immediately from the crypt, he asked a certain priest who lived in the monastery to give him bread.

The priest, knowing for certain that the man had never before eaten bread, entered the small basilica dedicated in honor of the holy Mother of God and blessed some bread. [Col. 0788C] He then offered the man a small fragment, as though it were to be eaten as a blessing. When the man swallowed it while standing beside the altar, it immediately leapt from his mouth, bloodied, and fell onto the pavement beyond the basilica door.

The priest, astonished, asked what he was attempting and why he wished to eat bread that had until then been denied him. When he first learned that the man had been overcome by this desire beside the body of Blessed Othmar, he quickly handed him bread and said: “Go to the place where you first began to desire bread, for perhaps God will deign to grant you the help of his mercy there.”

The poor man obeyed his command and returned to the church. Before he arrived there, he consumed by eating the bread he had received from the priest. [Col. 0788D] When he entered the church, the miracle having quickly become known, many of our people gave him bread, and he sat before the holy man’s body and ate quite eagerly. He has remained with us up to the present and now eats bread without aversion, in the customary human manner; and he proclaims aloud that this miracle was performed in him by divine mercy.

## CHAPTER XI. A certain man restored to health

A poor man born in the province of Gaul carried his left knee, together with his foot, contracted from birth, with the foot flaccid, twisted toward the left, and raised from the ground. Rather than serving as a support, it was a burden that he carried. Supported by two crutches beneath his armpits, he used to go around the houses of the faithful seeking alms.

That same year, after the solemnities of the Lord’s Nativity had ended, while he was staying in the district called Linzgowe, he claimed that a venerable man, dressed in a priestly stole and distinguished by the dignity of his appearance, had stood before him in a dream and addressed him in these words [Col. 0789B]:

“If you were to visit my dwelling, poor man, I would give you a staff. Supported by it, you would be better able to walk along the difficult paths.”

He replied: “Lord, I do not know your dwelling, and I have no idea in what region I should seek it.”

The other said: “Cross to the far side of this pond and diligently search for it in those places. Know for certain that, if you reach it, you will rejoice at receiving the staff. And so that you may find it more easily, know that I am still staying in another man’s house and do not yet have a dwelling of my own.”

Moved by this vision, the poor man crossed the pond and one evening arrived at the house of a certain priest. That same night he again saw the man of the aforesaid appearance standing before him [Col. 0789C] and asking why he had delayed so long in coming. When the crippled man replied that, because he did not know the place and because of the difficulties caused by his disability, he had previously been unable to come, the other threatened to cut off his foot unless he went quickly to the same place.

Prepared to obey commands of this kind, the poor man, when daylight had been restored to mortals, hastened to the monastery, with the priest directing him along the way. There, on that very night—which was still regarded as the Lord’s Day—he devoutly kept vigil through the celebrations.

When morning came, after the Gospel had been read at the public Mass [Note: We call this Mass “conventual” or “solemn,” which the ancients called “public,” in the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Bercharius*, no. 19, of the second century; “private” was sometimes called “minor,” in the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Columbanus*, chapter 7.], he reached the steps that, as we have mentioned, adjoined the sacred body. The joints of his sinews and veins were broken, the skin having been ruptured and blood immediately following [Col. 0789D]; his limbs, which had long been contracted, were suddenly straightened by the effect of divine action.

Unable to endure the tension and breaking, the sick man collapsed on the steps and, making a dreadful uproar with his cries, terrified everyone standing in the church. Many of them ran together, immediately lifted him up, and, having recognized the miracle, offered due thanks to almighty God. The poor man himself was carried out of the church, gradually recovered his strength, and after a few days left the monastery in good health.

## CHAPTER XII. A mute man granted the faculty of speech

[Col. 0790A]

Three weeks after this miracle of healing, a certain mute man, born and raised in the neighboring territory, whom many of our people knew to have been deprived of the faculty of speech from earliest childhood, likewise came to the monastery on a Sunday. He approached the body of Saint Othmar and, as an act of pious devotion, placed a small ball of linen upon his coffin.

After this, by a sudden impulse, he was thrown face down upon the ground in a state of mental ecstasy. The restraints of his tongue were loosened, and he poured a quantity of blood from his mouth. Taking it in his own hands so that it would not fall onto the pavement of the basilica, he immediately cast it outside the church.

Overcome by immense fear and terror, and telling no one what had happened to him, he departed from the monastery with all haste. Reaching his home quickly, he addressed his acquaintances there with joy, having been granted the power of speech. When they heard him speaking and answering their questions, they were greatly amazed and quickly spread the miracle by reporting it to the others.

Then you could see many inhabitants of that place, men and women, gathering together, astonished that speech had been granted to the mute man. With him placed in their midst, you could see him recounting how it had happened to him and where and when his tongue had been loosed. The following day a certain cleric from the same place took him and brought him back to the monastery, and reported to us in due order the truth of this event.

## CHAPTER XIII. A man contracted in all his limbs from birth is restored through the merits of the saint

[Col. 0790C]

That same year a certain citizen of Orléans brought to Rome, out of pious devotion, a small boy whose joints were almost entirely contracted and knotted together. He placed him in a small cart, sometimes pulling it, sometimes pushing it before him, and sometimes carrying him on his own shoulders.

After spending a few days there, he returned from Rome and—as we learned from his own mouth—was warned at night in a vision to seek Alamannia and visit the monastery of Saint Gall. Wishing to comply with this vision, he crossed the Alpine passes with very considerable effort and, one day as evening was already approaching, entered the long-desired monastery in exhaustion.

The shoulders bore witness to how many hardships and difficulties he had endured on the journey: we found them so badly chafed by the poles of the same cart that many of our people could see hardened calluses on them.

At his first entrance into the basilica, therefore, he reached the body of Blessed Othmar. As the restraints of his joints stretched, the boy fell from the cart and rolled onto the pavement. Filling the church roof with dreadful cries, he made known by an unusual tumult of shouting that he was being pressed by immense pain.

[Col. 0791A] At that time our elder Grimald was staying in the monastery. As he stood within the cloister before the doors of the basilica, he heard this kind of uproar. Taking with him Bishop Solomon and the abbot of the monastery of Reichenau, who had come together there that very day, he entered the church and asked the cause of so dreadful and unusual a cry.

What more need be said? The abbots and the bishop drew nearer and saw the boy rolling back and forth on the pavement with mournful howling. They perceived him tearing and almost ripping his own flesh with his fingernails, driven by the pain.

[Col. 0792A] After a long period of such torment, his left hand, which had been contracted into a fist, was extended; his bent neck was raised; his left knee, together with his foot turned backward toward the shin, was loosened; and the sole of his right foot, which had been pressed against his buttocks, sprang forth when the knee broke, with an outpouring of blood. In the presence of the bishop, who was singing the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, God”), it was restored to proper form.

As time passed, the boy himself began to walk. Now using his newly acquired steps in the monastery, he remains a reliable witness to this miracle.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0791]

## PREFACE. On the miracles displayed in his basilica after the second translation of Saint Othmar

[Col. 0791B]

The miracles of our holy Father have thus far been set forth by us in a humble form of words. Although we do not doubt that they suffice for benevolent readers to make known the praises of his holiness, nevertheless, since mention was made somewhat earlier of the basilica to be built in his honor, we wish briefly to hand down to our successors—lest they perish through forgetfulness—how, after its construction had been completed, the holy man was translated into it, and by what manifestations of miracles divine mercy later revealed his holiness there.

We do not seek, through pompous composition, the empty glory of praise. Rather, we wish by the simplicity of our statements to show the truth of events to those who seek it. For it is not our glory, but his, that we ought chiefly to pursue: he who first grants his chosen ones the will to do good, then enables them to begin, afterward supplies the strength to complete their work, and finally rewards them with a worthy recompense, deigning openly to display their holiness through their virtues and signs.

Therefore, in every respect, we desire to praise him as the source of all goodness and the giver of every good thing in the miracles of our blessed father, saying with David: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Psalm 113).

## CHAPTER ONE. On the consecration of the church itself, and how, during the translation, a mute man was granted the gift of speech

[Col. 0791D]

After the translation mentioned above, when nearly three years had passed and the basilica of Blessed Othmar had been suitably completed through the devoted efforts of those building it, our elder Grimald, archchaplain of King Louis, asked the aforesaid bishop of Constance to come to the monastery to perform the solemnities of its consecration.

When the people living nearby [Col. 0792B] learned this through widespread report—namely, that the holy man was to be carried from the basilica of Saint Gall to his own oratory—they began to come to the monastery in crowds, wishing to take part in his sacred obsequies.

The bishop arrived on the appointed day and solemnly dedicated the church under the saint’s name. He then undertook the sacred body’s members, setting aside certain portions to be given afterward as relics. Wrapping the rest honorably in his own hands, he placed them in a new sarcophagus.

He also marveled that the offerings which, as we related in the preceding narrative, had been found in his tomb had remained until then incorrupt and entirely unharmed. He placed some of them, wrapped, upon the sacred body, while he deposited others in a reliquary and ordered them preserved for future times [Col. 0792C] as testimony to the saint’s holiness.

After this, when all of us had solemnly prepared ourselves in sacred vestments, the bishop himself, having offered an elevated prayer, instructed the priests standing by to lift the man of God to be carried outside. Without delay, the holy man was carried from the church with crosses, candles, and censers. At that same hour a certain mute man, as we believe through his merits, was granted the faculty of speech.

Because this man was of humble status and had previously been unknown to us, we initially pretended not to believe the miracle that he reported as having been performed in him. But when he claimed to be from the district called Arigewe [Note: Goldast calls it *Aragoewe*. This corresponds to what Hepidannus says in Book II, chapter 9, of the *Life of Saint Wiborada*: in the district called *Erigowe*, which the river Aar flows past on one side and the Rhine on the other. Hence Ekkehard calls it the district of the Aar, commonly l’Aar, which the Latins now call the Arola.], we later learned through inquiries made by our people of his parents and others who knew him well that this was true.

Then all of us, singing praises and melodies [Col. 0792D], accompanied by a large multitude of people, we followed the body of our beloved Father with due veneration. In a meadow situated toward the east, we halted briefly, prostrated ourselves face down in worship, then rose and began, one by one, to approach his holy remains and devoutly kiss the coverings laid over them.

After this, we proceeded with the greatest reverence to the monastery and, introducing his holy relics into his basilica, returned due thanks with praise to God, who had deigned [Col. 0793A] to grant us such great joy. We cannot at all describe how many tears of those rejoicing and how many sobs of those exulting arose there; indeed, interrupted by repeated sobs, we could not utter the praises of God themselves without tears.

Above all, our venerable father Grimald, moved by the joy of those rejoicing, could not restrain his tears. He gave thanks to God that in his own time, and in a place entrusted to his care, he had been deemed worthy to see such honor and such benefits of almighty God.

To add to this joy, the abbot of the monastery of Reichenau arrived at that same hour with some brothers from his community. Brothers sent by their abbot from the monastery called Kempten also rejoiced that they had taken part in such obsequies and such joys.

Meanwhile the bishop [Col. 0793B] placed the sacred remains of the devout father in a stone chest and set it beneath the altar. [Note: [Col. 0793D] Observe the custom of placing the relics of saints beneath the altar. Read the Preface to the second century.] After the celebration of the Mass had been solemnly completed, he blessed the people and dismissed them.

These things took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 867, under the most pious King Louis, while the princes mentioned above were diligently exercising pastoral responsibility in the governance of the churches of God: on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, a Wednesday, in the first indiction. [Note: That is, the first indiction beginning on 24 September; this explains how the thirteenth indiction above in Book I, chapter 5, is to be understood.]

On the following day, so that the honor of the blessed man might be further extended, the bishop first took for himself some of his relics which, as we stated, he had previously set aside for this purpose. He then entrusted some portions of them, according to his judgment, to the abbot of Reichenau, to the brothers from Kempten, and to the other religious and venerable men [Col. 0793C]. In our presence he carefully admonished them all to treat them in every respect honorably and worthily.

When this had been done, he consecrated the church of the blessed archangel Michael. After confirming many with sacred chrism, he took leave of the brothers and departed from the monastery joyfully with his companions.

On the following day, we escorted the abbot of Reichenau and the brothers from Kempten outside the monastery with praises and songs. [Note: [Col. 0793D] In ancient times pious men were received and escorted in this way with sacred songs, especially bishops. When Athanasius of Alexandria approached the monastery of Tabennesi, Pachomius came out to meet him with his monks and welcomed him with psalms and hymns. It was also customary for monks to receive abbots returning from a distant or lengthy journey with solemn procession. In the ancient *Acts of the Monastery of Corbie*: “When the abbot has gone to Rome or to other lands and has remained away for a year, upon his return he is received in procession, everyone being entirely dressed in cloaks.” Udalricus gives a similar account in Book II, chapter 3, of the *Customs of Cluny*, from which the monks of Corbie borrowed their practices.] After exchanging words of fraternal affection and giving the kiss of peace, we allowed them to return joyfully to their own homes.

## CHAPTER II. That many miracles occur in numerous places around his relics

[Col. 0793D]

Having finished the account of how the blessed man was translated to his basilica, and lest a speech prolonged at length should perhaps trouble the bored reader and bring a wrinkle to his brow, we have decided to append briefly and succinctly at the end of this work some of the indications of his holiness which we saw later manifested there through the radiance of his merits.

[Col. 0794A] We are not inserting in this little work everything that we ourselves saw happen or learned from others to have been truthfully accomplished. Rather, we wish to gather together a few examples from the many, especially those witnessed by us.

For we do not believe that all these things can easily be recounted, particularly since in very many places—not only those belonging to us but also those belonging to others, which were enriched by his sacred relics—so many signs of miracles have shone forth daily that neither eloquence of speech nor the strenuous labor of the pen can express or encompass them without difficulty.

Therefore, setting these matters aside for the present, we shall turn to writing only those things which we know to have occurred in every respect among us and which we trust will suffice, among those free from envy, as testimony to his holiness.

## CHAPTER III. A wounded and swollen foot obtained healing at his tomb

[Col. 0794B]

A certain head of a household, very well known among us to many people, had a servant who, while doing some work, accidentally injured his foot. The foot immediately became swollen and was so weakened by the contraction of the veins that he was entirely deprived of the ability to walk.

For nearly a full year, he supported a step which the infirmity of his foot denied him by placing a kind of support beneath his knee and artificially assisting his movement. When he came to seek the intercession of Blessed Othmar, he prayed prostrate before his altar. At once his foot was released, he abandoned the support, and he departed healed.

## CHAPTER IV. A suspended leg is extended

Not long afterward another man carried a foot and lower leg raised high above the ground and contracted backward, not as an aid for traveling but rather as a burden by its heaviness. One day he came to the monastery supported by staffs. Entering Blessed Othmar’s oratory, he prayed while standing before the altar. Then the foot and lower leg were released and extended; making a crackling sound like that of a broken piece of wood, they were restored to proper form.

Without delay, restored to its place, the limb carried the man who had previously carried it, and repaid with a welcome recompense the one who had borne it.

## CHAPTER V. The celebrated miracle of a nun who received sight

[Col. 0794D]

Within that same year, a certain nun from the town called Basula [alternative reading: Basilea, Basel], who four years earlier had been deprived of sight in both eyes, reached the monastery under the guidance of her sister. She remained there for nearly three weeks, still enveloped in the darkness of blindness.

When the annual feast approached in which the Catholic Church throughout the world rejoices at the coming of the Holy Spirit, on the Saturday preceding it—which was also drawing near—many people came to the monastery as usual for the sake of prayer. At about the fourth hour of the day, the nun herself, among the others who had come, prostrated herself before the tomb of the blessed man to pray. There, after praying for a while, she received back the light she had lost, and, when many people gathered together, the evident reality of this miracle became the cause of very great joy.

[Col. 0795]

## In the year of the Lord 872. Grimald, abbot of Saint Gall

[Col. 0795]

# BOOK OF SACRAMENTARIES EXCERPTED FROM THE WORKS OF THE HOLY FATHERS

(According to Jacques de Pamel, *Liturgicon Ecclesiae Latinae*, volume II.)

## PAMEL’S NOTICE

[Col. 0795B]

The *Micrologus*, *On Divine Observances*, chapter 60, mentions this book together with the preceding one [Note: Understand the Gregorian Sacramentary, which Pamel places before Grimald’s book and which is reprinted in our edition of the works of Saint Gregory the Great, volume IV. Editor of the *Patrologia*.] in these words:

“Nevertheless, that same Albinus produced a work in the holy Church that should not be despised. For he is said to have collected the Gregorian prayers in the books of the Sacramentaries, adding a few others, which he indicated should be marked with an obelus. Then he collected other prayers or prefaces which, although not Gregorian, were nevertheless suitable for ecclesiastical celebration, as the preface testifies—a preface that he placed in the middle of the same book, after the Gregorian prayers.”

Thus far the *Micrologus*. Although he attributes the work to Alcuin—for that same Alcuin was surnamed Albinus Flaccus—we have preferred to follow the authority of the most ancient manuscript codices. There may indeed be an error in the *Micrologus*, made by scribes who were unfamiliar with the name Grimald.

Whether it is attributed to this man or to the other, Amalarius certainly seems to allude to it in Book I, chapters 22 and 24:

“On his behalf,” he says, “the priest prays in the Sacramentary: ‘That, reborn as a new creature from the immaculate womb of the Lord’s font, a heavenly offspring may emerge.’”

[Col. 0795C] For it is not in the earlier book but in this one that the consecration of the Paschal candle is contained, whose words he explains at greater length in both chapters.

Some people wrongly attribute its original institution to Pope Zosimus, although long before that Prudentius had celebrated it in Spain in the hymn that we still use, and Saint Ambrose at Milan had likewise used a special blessing of the candle.

[Col. 0796B] Thus Amalarus correctly says about this matter in Book I, chapter 18:

“While the Romans were doing this, we too were commanded by Pope Zosimus to bless the candle.”

That is as if he said: “It was already customary at Rome, but Pope Zosimus decreed that it should also be performed in all the other churches.”

Although these remarks were made incidentally (παρεργῶς, “by the way”), they nevertheless confirm what Grimald writes in the aforesaid preface: that the materials he arranged in this work are almost more ancient than the Gregorian ones.

“But since,” he says, “there are also certain other things which the holy Church necessarily uses, and which that same Father, seeing that they had already been published by others, omitted, we therefore thought it worthwhile to pluck them like spring flowers blooming in the meadows and gather them together. After correcting and emending them and marking them with their respective chapters, we have placed them separately within the body of this book, so that the reader’s diligence might find in this work everything that we have judged necessary for our times.”

It is certain, moreover, that this book contains several prayers for Sundays after Epiphany, Easter, and Pentecost borrowed from Saint Ambrose.

[Col. 0796C] Elsewhere, too, Amalarius alludes to chapter 102 of this book:

“We have it written,” he says, “in a certain Sacramentary that offices for the dead should be performed around the third, seventh, and thirtieth days.”

He then explains these words beautifully and at length and confirms them by the authority of the Scriptures.

# GRIMALD’S PREFACE

[Col. 0797]

[Col. 0797A] Up to this point, the preceding little book of the Sacramentaries is known to have been edited by Blessed Pope Gregory, except for those passages which the reader’s diligence will find slaughtered in the same book by strokes placed before them, concerning the Nativity or Assumption of Blessed Mary, and especially concerning Lent.

For, as we have learned from the report of certain people, the apostolic lord entirely abstains from station services on those days because, wearied by observing stations on the other weekdays, he rests on those days. His purpose is that, being free from the tumult of the crowds, he may distribute alms to the poor and arrange external affairs more freely.

As for the Mass bearing the title “On the Nativity of that same blessed Gregory,” which has likewise been slaughtered by strokes placed before it, there is no doubt that it was inserted into his work by his successors out of affection, or rather out of veneration for him.

The aforesaid little book of the Sacramentaries, although many people possessed it in a corrupted form because of the errors of scribes and did not have it as it had been edited by its author, we nevertheless undertook, as far as our ability allowed, to correct it with a craftsman’s pen for the benefit of many.

When a prudent reader has carefully read it, he will immediately confirm that we speak the truth—unless it is again corrupted through the fault of scribes.

But since there are also certain other things that the holy Church necessarily uses, which that same Father omitted because he saw that they had already been published by others, we therefore thought it worthwhile to pluck them like spring flowers blooming in the meadows and gather them together. After correcting and emending them and marking them with their respective chapters, we have placed them separately within the body of this book, so that the reader’s diligence might find in this work everything that we have judged necessary for our times, although we had also found many more items inserted in other books of Sacramentaries.

For the sake of distinction, we placed this little preface in the middle, so that it might be both the conclusion of one book and the beginning of another. In this way, with the books arranged in proper form on either side, everyone may know which materials were published by Blessed Gregory and which by other Fathers.

Since we judged that it was neither right nor possible to exclude those seeking such great and varied holy institutions, we wished at least to satisfy the worthy desires of all of them through the evident abundance of this work.

If anyone is pleased to accept what we have gathered with the utmost care and devoted affection, without arrogant vanity, we ask that he not be ungrateful toward our labor, but rather give thanks with us to the giver of all good things.

If, however, he judges these things superfluous or unnecessary for himself, let him use only the little work of the aforesaid Father, which he cannot reject without danger to himself; and let him allow those who seek these additional materials and wish to use them with pious devotion to make use of them.

We have not gathered these things, therefore, for the ungrateful and the fastidious, but rather for the studious and devout. In them, anyone whose mind is properly disposed can find what will enable him to offer his fitting vows and the worship of God worthily and acceptably to the Lord.

Let the reader’s discernment know that we have inserted nothing else into this work except what was written out with great care by the most approved and learned men.

From many sources, therefore, we gathered many things, so that we might provide for the benefit of many.

As for the prefaces that we have placed at the end of this book, we ask that those who like them receive them with charity and sing them. But from those who understand them and nevertheless do not enjoy them, as well as from those who want them but do not understand them, we ask that they neither adopt nor sing them.

We also add blessings to be spoken by the bishop over the people, as well as material not found in Blessed Gregory’s aforesaid book concerning the establishment of the lower orders in the Church.

We therefore beseech all of you who take up this book to read or transcribe it to pour out prayers to the Lord for me, who have labored to collect and correct these materials for the benefit of many.

We also ask that you transcribe it so carefully that its text may delight the ears of the learned and prevent the simpler from going astray.

For, as Blessed Jerome says, it will be of no benefit to have corrected a book unless the correction is preserved through the diligence of scribes.

## I. Blessing of the Candle

[Note: [Col. 0799D] It is read that Pope Zosimus instituted the consecration of the Paschal candle. This must either be referred to the fact that he was the first at Rome to imitate the custom of Saint Ambrose, or certainly to the fact that, since the Ambrosian usage had previously been in force, he himself wrote down this form of consecration. For it is established that it had already been observed in the Milanese Church by Saint Ambrose, and that it was also attested in Spain at that period by Prudentius, who composed a hymn concerning it.]

**BLESSING OF THE CANDLE.**

Let the angelic host of heaven now rejoice; let the divine mysteries rejoice; and, for the victory of so great a King, let the saving trumpet resound. Let the earth, irradiated by such great splendors and illumined by the brilliance of the eternal King, rejoice and know that it has lost the darkness of the whole night. Let Mother Church also rejoice, adorned with the radiance of so great a light, and let this hall resound with the great voices of the peoples.

Therefore, dearest brothers, while you stand here before the wondrous brightness of this holy light, I ask you: invoke with me the mercy of almighty God, so that he who has deigned to enroll me, not by my merits, among the number of the Levites may, by pouring in the grace of his light, enable me to complete the praise of this candle [alternatively: “command me to complete the praise”].

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns as God with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit.

For ever and ever.  
R. Amen.

[Col. 0801B]

The Lord be with you.  
R. And with your spirit.

Lift up your hearts.  
R. We have them with the Lord.

Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.  
R. It is right and just.

D. For it is right and just to proclaim, with the whole affection of heart and mind and with the ministry of our voice, the invisible God, the almighty Father, and his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, [and also the Holy Spirit]. He paid to the eternal Father the debt of Adam for us, and wiped away, with compassionate blood, the bond of the ancient offense.

For these are the Paschal feasts, in which that true Lamb is slain and the doorposts are consecrated with his blood. This is the night in which you caused our fathers, the children of Israel, after they had been led out of the land of [Col. 0801C] Egypt, to cross the Red Sea on dry ground. Therefore this is the night that cleansed the darkness of sins through the illumination of the pillar. This is the night that today, throughout the whole world, restores to grace and joins to holiness those who believe in Christ, separating them from the vices of the age and the darkness of sins. This is the night in which, after the bonds of death had been destroyed, Christ rose victorious from the underworld.

For it would have profited us nothing to be born unless it had profited us to be redeemed. O wondrous condescension of your compassion toward us! O ineffable love of charity! In order to redeem a servant, you handed over your Son. O blessed night, which alone was worthy to know the time and hour in which Christ rose from the underworld! This is the night of which it is written: “And the night shall shine like the day,” and, “The night is my illumination in my delights.”

Therefore the sanctification of this night drives away crimes, washes away sins, restores innocence to the fallen, and joy to the sorrowful. It drives away hatred, prepares concord, and bends rulers. Therefore, in the grace of this night, receive, holy Father, the evening sacrifice of this incense, which the holy Church, through the hands of her ministers, solemnly renders to you in this offering of the candle, from the works of bees.

But now we know the proclamation of this pillar, which the shining fire kindled in honor of God. Although divided into parts, it suffers no loss from the light shared among them. It is fed by liquefying [Col. 0802A] wax, which the mother bee brought forth as the substance of this precious lamp.

O truly blessed night, which stripped the Egyptians and enriched the Hebrews! Night in which earthly things are joined to heavenly, and human things to divine. We beseech you, Lord, that this candle, consecrated in honor of your name, may persevere without failing in order to destroy the darkness of this night, and, accepted [alternatively: kindled] as a sweet offering, may be mingled with the lights above. May the morning Lucifer find its flames—that Lucifer, I say, who knows no setting; he who, having returned from the underworld, shone serenely upon the human race.

Therefore we beseech you, Lord, to preserve in the peace granted by the times, amid these Paschal joys, us your servants, all the clergy, and your most devoted people, together with our pope N. and our most glorious king N., and also our bishop N.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns as God with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit.
