## For the Sick

Eternal God, who therefore chastise your servants bodily so that they may advance in mind, and patiently show what the splendid salvation of your loving-kindness is, while you grant that even illness itself may work medicine for us: we therefore earnestly beseech your clemency to deign to grant your servant N. health of mind and body and continual growth in prosperity. Through Christ.

## For the Deceased

[Col. 0923C]

Eternal God, through Christ our Lord, through whom is the salvation of the world, through whom is the life of all, through whom is the resurrection, etc., as in Amb[rose].

### Within the Canon

Therefore, this offering, Lord, which we offer to you for the soul of your servant N., whose day of deposition we celebrate—the day on which, after the body had been laid down, he returned to you, the Creator, the soul which you had given—we ask that you graciously regard it. For him we ask your divine mercy, that, released from the bonds of death, he may deserve passage into life. Through Christ.

## For a Deceased Abbot

Eternal God, although the condition of death imposed upon the human race [Col. 0923D] grieves our hearts, nevertheless, by the gift of your mercy, we are raised up by hope of future immortality; and, mindful of eternal salvation, we do not fear to endure the loss of this light. For, by the benefit of your grace, life is not taken away from the faithful but changed, and souls freed from the prison of the body shrink from mortal things while they attain immortal ones. Therefore we ask that your servant N., established in the dwellings of the blessed, may rejoice that he has escaped bodily constraints and await the day of judgment with confidence and the hope of glorification. Through Christ.

### Within the Canon

Therefore, this offering, Lord, which we bring to you for the deposition of your servant and priest N., [Col. 0924A] we ask that you graciously regard; for him we pour forth humble prayers to your majesty, that you may cause him to be counted among the number of priests who have pleased you.

## At the Passing of a Bishop

Eternal God, we earnestly beseech your devoted mercy to command that the soul of your servant and bishop N. joyfully stand among the number of your chosen pontiffs, so that he who here served your altar humbly on their behalf may there deserve to share with them in your glorious praise. Through Christ.

### Within the Canon

Therefore, this offering which we offer to you in commemoration of the deposition of the soul of your servant and bishop N., we ask, Lord, that you graciously accept; and him whom, while he was established in the body, you willed to preside over the apostolic [Col. 0924B] see, place among the number of your chosen ones.

## At the Passing of a Monk

Eternal God, who through Christ your only-begotten Son, our Lord, have granted us the hope of blessed resurrection: grant, we ask, that the soul of your servant N., for whom we offer this sacrifice of our redemption to your majesty, may, cleansed from every stain of sin, by your mercy deserve to reach, with your servants, the rest of blessed resurrection. Through the same one.

### Within the Canon

Therefore, this offering which we offer to you for the soul of your servant N., a monk whom you freed from bodily corruption, we ask, Lord, that you graciously [Col. 0924C] accept; and whatever fault he contracted through the intrusion of human condition, wipe away, so that, purified by your remedies, he may reach everlasting joy.

## For Several Deceased Persons

Eternal God, who through Christ your only-begotten Son, our Lord, have given us the hope of blessed resurrection: grant, we ask, that the souls for whom we offer this sacrifice of our redemption to your majesty may, by your mercy, deserve to reach the rest of blessed resurrection with your saints. Through Christ.

### Within the Canon

Therefore, Lord, graciously regard this offering which we humbly present to your mercy for the souls of all the faithful [Col. 0924D] departed, so that, released from all sins through these holy mysteries, they may be made participants in eternal blessedness.

## For Several Persons

Eternal God, through Christ our Lord, who offered himself to be sacrificed for us, by whose death eternal life has been given to us, who is the hope of the souls of the holy faithful and the same rewarder of good merits as he is ruler: therefore, we ask that the souls of your male and female servants and of all the faithful departed may deserve to be rewarded with eternal glory when that same Lord Jesus Christ comes in his glory with his angels. Through him.

[Col. 0925A]

### Within the Canon

(A.) Therefore, this offering which we humbly [Col. 0926A] sacrifice to you for the commemoration of the souls sleeping in peace, we ask, Lord, that you graciously accept and, by your mercy, grant that this expression of devotion may benefit us and obtain everlasting blessedness for them.

[Col. 0925]

# Letter of Grimald and Tatto to Reginbert, Master of the Monastery School of Saint Gall

(Apud Baluz., *Capitularia*, vol. II, col. 1382.)

[Col. 0925B]

To the most excellent and ineffably beloved Reginbert, our teacher: Grimald and Tatto, disciples of your foremost students, send greetings of everlasting happiness.

The memory of your love, diligently clinging to our minds, does not permit us to be forgetful of your requests or of our promises. Would that we had been able to fulfill your pious wish as successfully as willingly! Behold, we have sent you the Rule of blessed Benedict, that outstanding teacher, which your benevolent spirit had always desired with the greatest longing. It is lacking neither in meanings and syllables nor even in letters arranged, if we are not mistaken, by the aforesaid Father. It has been transcribed from that exemplar which itself was copied from the codex that the blessed Father, with his holy hands, took care to write for the salvation of many [Col. 0926B] souls. Therefore, those words which the aforesaid Father, according to the method—as some assert—did not insert into the text of this Rule, we collected from other Rules corrected by modern masters and took care to insert in the margin of the page opposite the relevant passage, with two dots. Other words dictated by Benedict which are not at all found in the newer copies we marked with an obelus and two dots. We did this because we wanted you to possess both versions: the one according to the tradition of the pious Father and the modern one. Choose for yourselves whichever pleases your desirous mind. Farewell in the Lord.

Hail, flower of the young, beautiful in graceful form,

while retaining the desired path and a wholesome life.

Behold, your humble servants send you gifts,

which your spirit long desired to possess.

May the almighty Father, who contains the whole world,

guide you and preserve you everywhere, always in good health.

## In the Year of the Lord 872. Milo, Monk of Saint-Amand

[Col. 0925]

# Historical Notice

(Apud Fabricium, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*.)

[Col. 0925C]

Milo, monk of Saint-Amand, or Amandopolitanus, situated on the river Elnon in Belgium, in the diocese of Tournai, of the Benedictine order, distinguished for his knowledge of letters, flourished around the year 840 and thereafter until 871, when he died.

While still young he wrote, in four books of hexameter verse, a Life of Saint Amand, bishop of Tongeren, who died in A.D. 684, based on the Life composed in prose by Baudemundus, for Haiminus, a monk of Saint-Vaast. Henschenius published it in the *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. I of February, pp. 873–888, with notes; and Mabillon published it in the second volume of the *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, p. 719 and following. It begins with the prefatory elegy:

[Col. 0926C]

“The venerable feasts of our Patron were drawing near.” Book I:

“Almighty ruler, creator of human beings and of all things.”

He wrote a sermon on the translation of the body of Saint Amand and on the establishment and dedication of his church in the *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. I of February, pp. 889–891, and another on the elevation of Saint Amand’s body, pp. 891–893; it is also found in the works of Philip of Haveng, Paris and Douai, 1621, folio.

He wrote a sermon on Saint Principius, brother of blessed Remigius of Rheims, bishop of Soissons, who died in the year 506, published by Surius on 27 September [Note: [Col. 0925C] The sermon, or rather encomium, referred to here is read under the name of Sidonius Apollinaris among his letters [Col. 0926C]. See *Patrologia*, vol. LVIII, col. 612, editor’s note.].

[Col. 0927A]

Two books on the praise of chastity and sobriety, preserved in manuscript in the Cambridge library and incomplete at the beginning in the Leiden library. Sigebertus mentions them, chapter 105. They begin: “To the glorious king Charles [the Bald], Milo, suppliant.”

“To ancient princes the Muses of poets were pleasing.”

Magnus Crusius published the prologue in his *Epistola Dissertatio*, p. 42 and following.

*The Contest of Spring and Winter.* It begins:

“All suddenly they meet, all from the lofty mountains.” Oudinus published it in vol. II, pp. 326–328.

A double hexameter poem on the Holy Cross, ingeniously composed in the form of a sphere, preserved in manuscript at Elnon for Saint Amand, according to Miraeus, in Sigebertus, chapter 105.

[Col. 0927B]

*Poems on the Praise of Frugality*, which Hucbaldus, his kinsman and pupil, presented to the same King Charles the Bald after Milo’s death, in verses published by Edmund Martene [Col. 0928A] in vol. I of the *Anecdota*, p. 46:

Your poet Milo, who was also our teacher,

whose talent this work displays so well,

once described in verse the Life of Amand,

the eminent bishop, and presented it to you.

While he desired this little book, too, written in your honor,

to celebrate his vow,

he died, paying the debt owed by human life, etc.

Valesius mentions a book *On the Art of Meter* in Andreas’s *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 676.

Letters to various people: Trithemius, chapter 283, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and *On Illustrious Benedictines*, II, 50.

Milo’s epitaph is in the *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. III of June, 16 June, p. 16. I suspect that Hucbaldus composed it for him:

The poet and sage Milo lies enclosed beneath this marble,

sweet-speaking in verse, who published the book *On Sobriety*,

and beautifully depicted holy Amand,

adorning him with flowers and beautifying him in meter and prose,

[Col. 0928B]

the palm, head [Note: [Col. 0928B] Valesius Andreas and Oudinus read *capit* (“head”).] and crown of so great a pontiff.

[Col. 0927]

# The Metrical Life of Saint Amand, by Milo

(From the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, February, vol. IV.)

[Note: [Col. 0927D] Thus our manuscript reads. It begins: “The Letter of Milo the Levite,” etc.; but the Amandine manuscript reads: “The Letter of Milo the Philosopher to the venerable Father Haiminus,” etc.]

## Milo’s Letter to Haiminus

[Note: [Col. 0928D] We discussed Haiminus, priest and monk of Saint-Vaast, in the Life of Saint Vaast.]

[Col. 0927C]

To the most reverend Father Haiminus, Milo, the most devoted of sons, sends imperishable joy of eternal happiness.

Once I enjoyed the most gracious conversation of your gentleness, namely at the time when, received by you, I, though unworthy, deserved to rejoice in your address and to be cherished by its honeyed sweetness. I now return thanks. For such was the kindness of your excellence toward my smallness that thereafter the fire of love for you, once kindled in my heart, did not cease to burn. And not without reason: for, eructating deeds of heart and body full of the honey of the most sincere affection—deeds that had the inner chambers of your breast as their dwelling—you easily secured that your beloved memory should never slip from my inmost fibers by any course of time, but should be preserved, renewed forever, and endure with unfading bloom.

Therefore, trusting in such praiseworthy fatherhood, like a son I placed in your hands the foolish little songs of my inexperience—namely, the preliminary exercise (*praeexercitatem*, sic) of my tiny talent in the Life of the most blessed Amand—humbly begging that, if you should find in them anything less consonant with the Catholic faith or unsuitable to metrical usage, you mercifully bring it back to the standard of a firm rule in the manner of a father, and do not abandon me to my error. I call upon you and beseech you by the blood of Christ, which was poured out for the salvation of the Christian people.

But if, with the mercy of the heavenly majesty [Col. 0928C] going before, the equal portions of my poetic text should prevail, then, together with me, render due praises of thanksgiving with joyful exultation to the giver of this gift, namely the Holy Spirit, by whose gift I was able somehow to piece together so great a work.

It is necessary, however, to pardon my rusticity, because, as someone says, rusticity was created by the Most High. And although I could have used more difficult circumlocutions of words in certain places, I was forbidden to do so, since I also believed that this work would be more pleasing if it were open to the hearing of all the brothers. May your excellence therefore favor not my faults but my labors, so that you may receive in heaven what mortal eye has not seen. We wish you eternal health for the advancement of all the faithful.

## Haiminus’s Reply to the Same

[Col. 0928D]

Haiminus, the least servant of Christ, sends greetings to his Milo.

I read with eager mind the poem which you, dearest brother, offered me; but since it is not enough to have read it once, I was glad to continue examining it. Thus, beginning again from the start, not without critical judgment, I reconsidered what I had previously touched only superficially; reading and repeating the whole work anew, I applied all the powers of my attention to it.

At first, I confess, I thought that I had set my foot upon level ground. But when I discovered that my littleness would not merely be watered by a cup from the spring but would be overwhelmed by the waves of eloquence, I thereafter showed the brothers [Col. 0929A] who are with me, not without caution, how one ought to navigate the whole river.

And because I encountered in it neither a rock that obstructed the faith nor anything contrary to metrical usage, I urge our brothers who do not shrink from such studies willingly to accept this gift. I also entreat them to prefer being summoned to similar study rather than being consumed by the torches of envy.

For we know that citizens always envy their fellow citizens, and, according to the Savior’s saying, no prophet—or, as you are accustomed to say, no poet—is accepted in his own country (Luke II, 34). But because envy kills the little one, the person who envies is known to be lesser than the one who is envied.

Wonderful! I marvel that he has been able to prepare a splendid banquet for the rich, whom I thought scarcely capable of offering even a taste to the poor. I attribute this entirely to the merits of the most beloved Amand, [Col. 0929B] whose praises I do not cease to celebrate and whose Christ I do not cease to praise.

The eloquence is therefore sweet, and the poem is delightfully seasoned with wit; the discourse flows with a gentle movement and plain speech. What more is there to say? Let my companions speak and judge as they wish; but I reveal the secret of my heart: my dear one, you have sufficiently and abundantly illuminated the praises of so great a Father in your poem.

Nevertheless, I beg you, do not desist from what you have begun; do not succumb to laziness or inert leisure; do not neglect the grace that attends you. While you have the opportunity, always exercise yourself in good studies; and do not deny to others what you received freely. Do not wish to possess the common good by yourself. This is the only wealth that knows how to increase by expenditure; this alone grows when scattered and yields profit when distributed. It is also the wealth [Col. 0929C] that condemns its hoarder to punishments and adorns its good steward with the glory of an eternal reward.

Be strengthened by new virtue; farewell, excellent Milo, poet; say: “God, have mercy on your Haiminus.”

[Note: [Col. 0929C] The following stood before it: “In the name of the Lord begins the Life of Saint Amand, confessor of Christ, transferred from prose into heroic meter in metrical style, consisting of four books, published by Milo, monk of that same monastery.”]

# Prologue to the Following Work

The venerable feasts of our Patron were drawing near,

and the celebrated day for earthborn people was approaching.

[Note: [Col. 0930C] Behold the adornment customarily used for the celebration of saints’ feasts for more than eight hundred years.]

The holy company of the flock, watchful with care,

adorned the lofty chambers of the gleaming temple.

They placed shining tunics and ornaments upon the altars,

woven with purple thread.

As usual, the pavements were decently prepared

with varied rows mixed with marble.

[Col. 0930A]

One group fitted fragrant lights into wax

and the sweet-voiced choir composed songs.

Another, hanging vessels from olive-bearing wreaths,

poured forth radiant light from heart and hand.

Then, anxious lest I should appear empty-handed amid such great crowds,

this work seized me,

so that I might sing in sweet-sounding meter

the fitting praises and flourishing deeds of the noble bishop.

Love of the faith persuaded me to compose in verse

the sweet glory and pious work of the bishop’s life.

Compelled by the advice of certain brothers,

I undertook an immense burden with slender strength.

Ah, the ancient poets were not ashamed to relate

those in whom there was vain, fleeting, and trivial learning—

those whose desire to deceive beguiled the whole age,

and whose entire life was devoted to crimes—

[Col. 0930B]

to bear themselves in a distinguished poetic cothurnus of words

and seek a name for praise through wrongdoing.

While they wandered through errors by various winding paths,

they accomplished nothing else but the work of death.

Deceived by it and laid in tombs in hell,

they pay for such deeds with continual tears.

My tongue will be mute and languish against my dry palate:

I who condemn falsehood—can I remain silent about the truth?

For a sure hope urges me, in view of the gift,

to celebrate Christ’s triumphs by a better path,

so that the highest praise may be given to God,

due veneration to the Holy One,

and an example may likewise be offered to Christ-loving peoples.

May my reward also grow with accumulated interest,

and may the prayer of this Just One transfer me to the stars.

[Col. 0930C]

Yet this work has not previously been attempted in this form,

and I try, through love, to speak of what I have not learned.

Therefore, trusting in God’s goodness and the gift of the holy

Spirit, I begin this journey, ignorant though I am.

Whoever there may be who prefers to gnaw at our poem

is gnawed by the fierce worm of righteous envy;

but whoever desires to rejoice together in so just a labor,

born of God the Father, is a lover of the Father.

Therefore it is pleasing first to run through the Gospel text

and its seven sacred seals.

Then I shall be better able to hasten through the deeds of the Saint,

if pious members possess such a beginning.

[Note: [Col. 0930D] We assign these headings to the margin and distinguish them according to our custom; it is enough to indicate them here.]

# Book One

[Col. 0929]

## Chapters of Book I Prefixed by the Author

1. The human birth of Christ is explained, and how all the elements recognized that he would be Lord of all.

2. The election of the apostles, Christ’s passion and resurrection, his ascension into heaven, and the sending of the Holy Spirit are briefly indicated.

3. The places in which the apostles preached the Gospel.

4. After the successors of the apostles have been mentioned, blessed Amand is introduced.

5. The editor of the work, confessing his ignorance, asks for the grace of the Holy Spirit.

6. The homeland and parents of the blessed man are described.

7. Where the Saint, leaving his relatives, went to Ogygia.

8. Where he drove away a powerful serpent by prayer and the standard of the cross.

9. The reply to his father.

10. How, while praying at the tomb of Saint Martin, he shaved his head.

11. [Col. 0931] How he went to Bourges, and concerning his abstinence and manner of life.

12. Where he set out for Rome in the ardor of faith.

13. Where he was driven from the church by its guardian.

14. When Peter appeared, he was admonished to return to Gaul.

15. The Saint’s return is related, and the little book is brought to an end with a prayer.

# Chapter One

## Poetic Introduction, from Christ and the Apostles to Saint Amand. His Origin

[Col. 0931A]

### 1

Almighty ruler, Creator of human beings and of all things,

taking pity on the world as it perished in the darkness of error,

he entered the chamber of a virgin and prepared an untouched

dwelling for himself—whose closed door, Ezekiel marks by name,

no created being enters [Note: [Col. 0931D] Ezekiel XLIV, 2],

except the one for whom closed habitations lie open: Christ.

And, so that you may marvel still more at what is wonderful to say,

the heavenly door passed through a closed gate.

From this Mary, becoming the mother of her own parent,

washed away the ancient virgin Eve’s sin

and brought forth for the world, without seed,

the true fruit.

[Col. 0931B]

Therefore, when the Redeemer came forth in conspicuous honor

and shone upon the world more brilliantly than Phoebus himself,

the shepherds of the flocks, the first to hear,

pressed by fear, heard conspicuous citizens

singing a heavenly song with ears raised toward the stars:

that the Author and Restorer of all things had come to earth,

and that at his birth heavenly glory would be in the kingdom

and holy peace on earth for the willing human being.

The stars of heaven judged that their own Creator was present,

and sent a shining star to his cradle.

The sea recognized him as its Lord,

for it offered itself to be trodden beneath his feet.

The kindly sun too grieved when it saw the Lord

fixed upon the wood—the servant weeping,

clothed in a dark garment.

The earth recognized him when it was shaken by horrible trembling

[Col. 0931C]

and the holy tombs were duly broken open.

Hell too trembled in fear when it saw its barriers torn away,

its gates drawn together by conspicuous light.

### 2

But because the earthborn still did not believe

that he was King above all things,

thinking, alas, that abominable images were gods,

he could no longer allow these things to continue

or behold the harms wrought by the ancient ruin.

He chose certain men whom grace alone blessed,

through whom he would save the nations beneath the fourfold hinge of the world;

to them he showed great miracles,

giving life to the dead and giving sight to the blind.

And since the Redeemer had come from his seat above

to save the whole world by his own blood,

he was mocked, beaten, condemned, stripped,

the most just Judge under an unjust judgment,

the herald of justice,

crucified at the end and then buried.

From there he raised abundant spoils

to the upper air.

Then, piercing heaven, he sent back to his disciples

the gifts he had promised them;

the Holy Spirit came to them in the form of fire,

granting the gift of tongues,

so that they might proclaim to the world the great things they had seen.

### 3

These men too, completing his commands through wakeful labor,

[Col. 0932A]

went to the regions of the earth assigned to them.

Shining with conspicuous light like lamps,

the foremost exalted leaders, Peter and Paul,

hasten to the lofty walls of Romulus’s city,

and wash the Romans more effectively than the waters of the Tiber.

There they establish the first foundation of honor.

From there Andrew, hastening with manly strength, seeks Achaea

and manfully fulfills the significance of his own name.

From there the two Jameses adorn Judaea

with their twin laws.

They teach the old things to resound in a similar manner among the new.

From there Asia approaches, converted by John’s exhortations;

thirsting for a paradisiacal river, he gives it drink.

Philip shone in Scythia with lamp-like speech,

and there he fulfilled what his own name signifies.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Milo understands Φίλιππος, “Philip,” as signifying one who loves horses and is warlike and noble.]

Matthew washes the Ethiopians,

scorched by torrid heat,

as the distinguished Gihon [Note: Gihon, the second among the four rivers of Paradise, Genesis II, 13, flows around the whole land of Ethiopia.] washes the land of Ethiopia in its sacred stream,

and makes those washed shine white as snow.

[Col. 0932B]

Bartholomew dispelled the darkness of the Indians

and made them flash with the splendid light of his brilliance.

Thomas, solicitous for the Parthians, examines with his fingers, in a manner akin to the blessed, and recounts the wounds that he saw on the Lord’s living body after death.

Simon, accompanied by his kinsman Jude,

subdued Persia, which had been warlike,

with the sword of the word.

Mark also fills the land of Egypt,

better than the overflowing Nile,

with the rich fruit of the Gospel,

bearing holy seeds.

Luke, with heavenly speech,

cleanses the peoples with life-giving baptism.

[Col. 0932C]

Their duly sent teachers followed these men,

scattered throughout the world,

and spread the words of salvation.

Their acts, recorded in prose,

remain even now and will remain for all ages;

moreover, the deeds of some of them are sung in poetry

and are bound in brief verses, never to be abridged.

### 4

Among their number the Confessor Amand shone forth,
To whose deeds we now apply a new hand and pen, and with tightly constrained effort touch upon things of immense greatness, God inspiring us; for a great share of praise belongs to repeating with one’s pen his manifold labors.

And whether one writes his lineage and homeland, or his mighty deeds, all of which he accomplished to the praise of the Lord by whose power he performed them—for whatever a servant’s pen [reading uncertain] does in praise of the good, it refers to the Lord. By his gift, those who rightly bring forth the saint’s just and laudable deeds do so with mind, hand, and tongue: by meditation, action, and speech,

[Col. 0932D] without whom man is dust, and with whom nothing more precious exists.

### 5.

For however great was he whose deeds are being described; whatever his virtue in this world, whatever his piety and devotion—no one could express it with a hundred tongues, even if a thousand-throated tongue roared like thunder:

Still less shall I be able to recount these things in my slender speech, since I am unskilled and have scarcely now learned the beginnings of letters,

[Col. 0933A] dry and lacking both learning and the stream of eloquence. What shall I do? Shall I speak or remain silent about the holy deeds of my Patron?

Since I cannot forge these things into a worthy poem, that hope comforts me and confidence strengthens me: the saint himself may grant me the power of speech, he who was able to give speech to the mute through his holy prayers, when steadfast hope asked it of him. In whose beautiful hands the royal infant [Note: Saint Sigebert, as stated above and under 1 February.] learned speech, although he never answered through the use of his body; and when he had learned to utter a few Latin words, he nevertheless brought forth from the speech of the Hebrew tongue the sweet word “Amen,” fulfilling the holy prayers of the sinful man.

Therefore, so that I may properly record the praises and deeds of the great bishop, I humbly beg the aid of the divine Spirit, who contains and completes all things,

[Col. 0933B] filling the stars, the heavens, and the sea and lands, by whom all things are governed; with whom the tongue has power, and without whom eloquence is mute.

If what I recount is yours, God, I now beg you, as I pray: grant to me, who am without eloquence, the gift of an honorable tongue.

### 6.

But first love desires to celebrate the lineage sprung from a radiant height and swiftly to record the blessed

[Note: Another manuscript: “to touch.”]

and to recount its ancestry from the beginning, so that the page, preserving the firmly planted root of this exceptional tree, may finally raise its lofty offspring of branches and its high crown toward the stars.

There is a region called Aquitania by the ancient inhabitants, a land mighty in war, rich in crops, and populous. Yet it is more distinguished and far more fertile for this reason: that from its revered origin it produced such fruit.

This land sent you Amandus, whom Gaul rightly honors. His father was noble, who was rightly called Serenus, since he deserved to beget one serene.

His excellent mother was called Amantia. I marvel, foolishly astonished, at what has been accomplished by divine favor: that father, mother, and son correspond in names worthy of the gifts they bear.

For since Serenus rejoiced and his mother Amantia flourished, it is no wonder that they rightly begot such a boy, who in his name, Amandus, would be remembered for holy love.

O fortunate region, which deserved to see, bear, and nurture such a man! If you had retained him, such storms would not now be shaking you on every side.

Therefore, father Serenus, hail, having such a pledge; illustrious mother, hail, who flower through a noble offspring.

## CHAPTER II. The monastic life of Saint Amandus on the island of Ogia. The serpent driven away. His father’s promises rejected.

[Col. 0933D]

### 7.

Although still a child, perhaps refusing to take lesser beginnings from the cradle, he gave a sign that he wished to follow nothing imperfect. As he grew in age, blessed Amandus raised his step to the highest citadel of righteousness.

Burning with an excessive love of Christ, he left his homeland, like venerable Abraham,

[Col. 0934A] and, leaving his relatives, sought a foreign land.

There is a place in the Ocean, equally distant, as is reported, forty miles from the great shore. There the island of Ogia offers a harbor to those who arrive. When a lamb came there, white with shining wool, it was kindly welcomed by a snow-white flock rejoicing with it; and within a short time he shone forth with the highest merits.

Because he took care to learn the sacred Scriptures—for this is labor at first, but afterward has precious rewards, to be filled with the manifold fruit of virtues, which feed souls burdened with mortal flesh, sanctify, heal, save, give life, and adorn them—the protection of Christ did not fail his holy desire. Rather, it raised Amandus, who sought, thirsted for, and loved such things, to the highest summit of honor.

### 8.

From this point I shall relate the greater miracles of his works: what battles the devoted lover of the Lord first undertook, and how many triumphs he won after overcoming the enemy of body and mind.

By chance a certain day arrived on which the business of the monastery mentioned above had to be conducted. The excellent brothers, wishing to occupy the boy, assigned him tasks, which he immediately and diligently carried out, ready to serve all things and swiftly obedient in every service.

But while the saint was perhaps exploring places less familiar to him, he encountered a huge serpent of dreadful body—fierce, scaly, hideous, vast, and savage. When the boy saw it, and at once trembled with horror, he was terrified, amazed, and anxiously stood there,

[Col. 0934C] stunned and trembling, uncertain where to turn his steps [Note: “Angit” is used neutrally for “is distressed” or “is troubled.”].

But as soon as the heavenly grace of the Lord shone upon him, he fell facedown and pressed his body to the earth, prostrate in supplication but lifted in mind toward the stars.

Then he firmly opposed the serpent with the banner in which the fullness of our salvation consists, and commanded it to return to its familiar hiding place.

The deadly serpent, driven back by the power of the sign, fled and returned, slipping back into its known cave. It never again appeared to any human being, and the place mentioned above was delivered from so great an enemy.

It is said that the Marsi are accustomed to trouble serpents by making for themselves a small rampart of earth, which a large troop of harmful creatures cannot cross.

[Note: It was formerly believed that the Marsi, an Italian people—said to be descended from the son of Circe—had a natural power against serpents. Pliny, Book VII, chapter 2. Milo seems here to use the term for enchanters.]

But by a far better and much more excellent way, this holy man, prostrate upon the mound of earth, drove back the serpent’s fiery-opened jaws with divine speech,

[Col. 0934D] through the standards of the cross that he traced in the fields with his fingers. This was his first deed; having properly recorded it, we leave it for another page to recount in the future.

Therefore, Pastor Amandus, we pray you with humble devotion: drive away the ancient serpent, who, without caring to tear our bodies, desires even more fiercely to pour bitter poisons through his wounding tooth into our souls—he who vomits flames and breathes fire.

[Col. 0935A] The serpent who sent his own savage pupil to you, holy Father—a serpent sending a serpent, though the latter became more savage by sowing savagery, and was his servant—to the city of Centumcellae. When I reach that place, with Christ as my guide, I shall properly set it down in its order.

Now I proceed along the journey I have begun and leave the serpent behind. Grow, boy, in new virtue; thus you shall go to the stars.

### 9.

While blessed Amandus was still growing in the flower of youthful age, intent upon the honorable pursuits of virtue, he was young in body but old and gray in conduct.

His father approached him with many words: he pleaded, admonished, exhorted, coaxed, asked, and prayed that, leaving the sacred halls of the monastery, he should turn back and attend to worldly affairs.

What labor is found there, and what things are without repose? Fraud, rage, envy, violence, anxiety, and turmoil plunge human minds into various misfortunes.

The saint rejected his father’s words as though they were poisonous arrows, relying upon the shield of faith that he set against them.

But when his anxious father saw his words scattered to no purpose, he sought to overcome the man with threats of this kind:

“If he does not renounce the work he has begun and abandon his religious habit,”

[Col. 0935B] and quickly turn himself to worldly affairs, “I shall make him, in all those things that by paternal custom ought to be provided for him, an heir of nothing.”

But the holy boy, scorning these blows of words and full of the teaching of the divine Spirit, said:

“Remember, dear father, that nothing is so truly mine as to serve the supreme God as long as I live. When he becomes my portion, I shall deserve to be part of him.

“The sacred voice of the Gospel book [Note: Matthew 19:27–28.] recalls that God promised such things to Peter, who sought them:

“‘You who, having rejected everything and followed my commands, have scorned all the heights of perishable honors—when God, at the end of the world, has sat upon his heavenly tribunal, and swift fire has overturned the whole world, burning the lands, the sea, and the heavens, then he will make you twelve sit upon thrones and judge the world with righteous judgment.

“‘For everyone who, won over by my love, places the world or the beloved names of parents after me will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.’

“Therefore, father Serenus, I do not listen with deaf ears to what the sacred page of the excellent book records. The Psalter also briefly cites these words for you, where it sings: ‘The Lord alone is my portion’ [Note: Numbers 18:20].

“The law inscribed upon tablets hewn from the rock commands the Levites not to take a portion among their brothers [Note: Psalm 118:57].

“Therefore, father, I care for and seek nothing of my own. I reject earthly things, gleaming and shining metal. Let the earthborn possess the lands held by the earth.

“What have I to do with the world, father, since I am dead to it?

“Blessed Mary enclosed the veiled God, clothed in flesh, in a cradle beneath the covering of a poor cloth. And must a garment for me be woven with shining metal?

“Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have shelter;

[Col. 0936A] but our Lord, who created the entire world, has no small roof under which to rest his limbs. Must I have a great house painted in many colors?

“For a good soldier is not one who abandons beneath an airy roof the King whom he is bound by right to worship, and himself, as a fugitive, seeks the shady heights of a roof.

“He cannot be preferred to ten cities; and the palm that has no palm for a handle must be denied.

“My King is Christ, and his kingdom is Olympus. But I, Amandus, am a soldier who can never be conquered, if I preserve my military service. I embrace him and rightly follow him, after whose name I am called.

“Do not begrudge me such great honors, father, I beg you. Christ is my love, my clothing, my possession, my food,

[Col. 0936B] my house, my homeland, my place, my substance, and my gold.

“While I live, he is life to me, and to me who die he is gain. Without him I desire nothing; with him I shall possess every good.”

Blessed Amandus spoke these words to his astonished father, gathering flowers from the stock of Scripture as a bee does.

For the sake of brevity I pass over very much and hasten in swift speech to what remains.

## CHAPTER III. Saint Amandus’s clerical life. His anchoritic life. His first journey to Rome.

### 10.

From this point, as the desire with which he had begun increased, Saint Amandus went to Tours and sought the sacred tomb of Martin. Prostrate upon the holy ground, he wept with heartfelt emotion, beat his noble breast with blows, and drew long sighs.

[Col. 0936C] Praying, he poured these words from the depths of his heart:

“O holy Martin, whom the heavenly kingdoms hold, I beg you to obtain from him whose servant you are, to whose service you are continually joined and cling, that I may not return to my native land and my abandoned acquaintances, and that he may direct my steps along a saving path, so that as a pilgrim and exile I may complete the course I have begun, until at last I am released from the prison of the flesh.”

Clinging to the tomb of the sacred body, the saint uttered these many complaints in varied speech, shedding tears from his eyes and words from his mouth.

Then, there in that place, he cut off the hair of his head with iron and changed his clothing, receiving the dignity of the clergy.

And just as a soldier in the court of an earthly king, receiving his belt, is accustomed to bear the burden of service beneath an iron garment, so this warrior, ready to endure whatever evil might attack him in the world,

[Col. 0936D] took up the victorious weapons of the Cross as a blessed standard-bearer. Strong against the enemies of body and mind alike, he rightly brought back manifold triumphs from every side.

And just as a prudent bee, intent upon rich flowers, seeks the violet that rises close to the earth, yet offers an excellent color for dyeing and makes kings purple and terrible to peoples,

[Col. 0937A] so he kept a humble mind, which is close to the earth, yet when preserved offers angelic beauty. It accompanies the excellent heavenly assembly, and, adorning the inner chambers of his beautiful heart, he moved from lilies to roses, returning through each camp by turns.

Whatever he saw flourishing in the conspicuous flower of virtue, he drew into his own thirsty conduct.

### 11.

As he pursued his journey along a fortunate path, he came to the walls of the city of Bourges. There Saint Austrigisilus flourished in conspicuous episcopal office, sanctifying its people—a magnificent bishop, distinguished by honorable deeds. Associated with his service in the church was Sulpitius, then archdeacon, who afterward became an illustrious bishop through his merits and rank.

[Note: This is explained more fully in his Life, 17 January, chapter 5.]

He knew how to calm raging fires with his fingers

[Col. 0937B] and restrain enormous flames with the sign of the cross.

They both kindly received Saint Amandus, honoring him with devout affection. They graciously built a cell for him in the city wall, in which the man of God, enclosed for the love of perpetual life and striving toward lofty things, lived clothed in sackcloth and sprinkled with a heap of ashes.

What ruins could the city then fear, since you were supported by such strong pillars? What weapons of combatants could you fear, since you shone forth defended by such patrons?

You know what the others accomplished, for this warrior stood firmly in your citadel for fifteen years; his steadfastness strengthened your walls.

But although you shine, trusting in conspicuous teachers,

[Col. 0937C] you do not surpass us. Here shines the beautiful Amandus, whiter than Phoebus and more radiant than all gold. Enclosed within you, he expelled wine from his mouth; he was satisfied neither with sleep nor with any nourishment of life.

He took barley as his sparse food, and afterward, thirsty, drank small cups of thin water. He steadfastly lived a heavenly life on earth; and while tormenting his body, he fed his soul with the honorable dishes of virtue, following Christ’s commands.

For Christ he endured manifold labors by land and sea—anxious, afflicted, despised, needy, and breathless—humbly rendering praises to Christ. Therefore he now enjoys everlasting light.

He often hungered; now he is fed with the bread of heaven.

[Col. 0937D] He was often thirsty; now he drinks from the heavenly spring.

Once naked, he is now clothed in the fleece of the Lamb.

Once poor, he is now rich through the gift of the kingdom.

We pray with body and heart that he may remember us.

### 12.

Since holy love always knows how to grow and to heap up sheaves through its labor, the man of God always burned with great love, strong in the power of his mind though wearied in body.

He hastened toward the walls of lofty Rome, where Peter and Paul possess lofty tombs, beautiful in earth and heaven and shining throughout the world like the Church’s radiant leaders;

[Col. 0938A] their tongues have power to open and close heaven.

Therefore, beginning the journey with a certain servant as his companion, traversing squalid and remote places, he reached Rome, inflamed with wondrous love.

Consider now what companions he sought to have: Peter, to whom the key of the starry gate was entrusted, and Paul, the outstanding teacher of the world throughout the ages.

O, if only the fires of his love could be described, or writing knew how to express the sighs of his heart!

I would attempt to say how greatly he loved them, upon whose sacred doorposts he pressed his kisses.

What do you think he would have done if he had seen them in the flesh?

Meanwhile, every day he ran through the various churches, joining many companions to himself in honor. But he entered the church of Peter the Prince breathlessly,

[Col. 0938B] when the sun was dipping its light-bearing robes into the sea.

### 13.

Having passed over these events, let us sing of what follows: the first part of the book is now hastening toward its end.

While fervent in faith he went around the sacred churches, he entered Peter’s most beautiful basilica, bowing low.

The flame-haired sun was already preparing to swim into the great Ocean, and Hesperus was shining in its ruddy rising.

Meanwhile, the care of the temple guardians drove out the assembled crowd and closed the open doors.

The holy man remained for a little while in the church, wishing to spend the entire night in prayer. But while the temple guardian was inspecting the sacred altars, he found the blessed man keeping vigil in psalms and prayers.

Moved by anger, he violently attacked the gentle man, beating him madly, though he bore everything patiently,

[Col. 0938C] and expelled him, sending him outside through the open doors.

Yet the man’s swelling anger could not disturb one filled with sweetness, because he willingly endured all these things.

### 14.

Meanwhile, while the blessed man sat before the temple doors, his mind in ecstasy and penetrating the heavenly throne, Peter the Apostle, gatekeeper of the heavenly hall, soon appeared to him in lively dress, with a gentle face and pleasant speech.

He comforted him with soothing words and exhorted his friend with words of affection to retrace the journey by which he had come, returning from there, and to sow among the peoples of Gaul the seeds of eternal life with divine words; to cultivate and water them; and to wash the converted in the stream of holy baptism.

Thus, approaching the Lord as a fruitful laborer with the reward of so great a task and carrying sheaves of the harvest,

[Col. 0938D] he would receive more abundantly the rewards of the heavenly kingdom.

### 15.

At last, having received the Apostle’s message, the saint left distinguished Rome, lofty in its exalted dignity, and went to the Gauls as a healing remedy.

What hope, I ask, enabled one man confidently to approach peoples shut off by distant boundaries, so savage—to penetrate the fierce Vacceans, Gauls, and Slavs?

What this one laborer accomplished in so great a harvest is evident. For, coming amid many trials of labor, he endured evil and uprooted everything impious.

Thus he fashioned the peoples for evangelical practices,

[Col. 0939A] and, bearing holy words, carried profits back to heaven. There he enjoys eternal gifts for his merits throughout the ages.

Although, in singing of his deeds, I shall complete a foolish poem in foolish speech, I wished to finish this little book about what he did while still young, though not in youthful fashion.

I deserved, as a young man, to praise a young man, if I were free from the burden of immense guilt. Yet I trust that I can be lifted from it by the Lord through this bishop’s prayers and blessed merits, for he benefited not only himself but the whole world.

I earnestly beg, ask, pray, and repeatedly entreat with ceaseless vows that Christ almighty, Redeemer and Author of humankind, may have mercy on his least pupil and, by forgiveness, break the bonds of my guilt.

[Col. 0940A] I ask this before the golden thread of my own life runs out, and before the silver cord, fleeing away, breaks the vessel of the flesh and spills all its contents.

I fear justice; I hasten to merciful kindness. I beg that he be gracious to me and prove himself most just toward the just.

Therefore, may those who are good possess the deserved palm as their reward.

But for myself, it is enough to have passed through the flames of Gehenna and to have earned pardon for a great crime.

Spreading black seeds across white fields, weary beneath a heavy burden at the completion of the day, I now cease to sow, and here I bring my work to rest. 

[Note: The following was added: “Book II ends here; it contains 450 verses,” followed by the following chapter headings of Book II.]

## BOOK TWO

### Contents of Book II

1. The author, setting aside his own abilities, says that for the common benefit he has divided his books into parts; rejecting the poets’ dirges, he humbly asks the Holy Spirit to grant entrance and progress to his little book.  
2. When the holy bishop is ordained.  
3. The editor of this work addresses Gaul.  
4. Concerning purchased boys and their instruction.  
5. The author addresses the saint with praise in the verses of this meter.  
6. The saint saved a boy from the devil at Centumcellae.  
7. After rebuking the enemy, the author of this work returns to the narration of the saint’s deeds.  
8. Concerning the storm that arose at sea while the saint was sailing.  
9. The Apostle Peter speaks to him in the ship and calms the troubled sea.  
10. The saint proceeds to the district of Gandavum.  
11. After the prince of error has been overcome by him, the people believe.  
12. Due mention is made, with deserved praise, of blessed Bavo, his disciple.  
13. The writer of this book exhorts the people of that region and also commends himself.

## CHAPTER ONE. The episcopal office conferred upon Saint Amandus. Captives redeemed and instructed by him.

[Col. 0939B]

### 1.

Since my powers are slight, reader, as I sing the renowned deeds of pious Amandus, looking equally to the shared labor of writer and reader, I wished to divide these same deeds properly into four small books, so that you might gain relief from the arrangement and lighten the labor by dividing the burden.

For a prudent reader, if you wish, you will be able to recognize that the language does not proceed according to grammatical law, but that rustic poems are woven from foolish words.

I do not send this work to the teachers of the world for recitation—those whose speech flows like the torrent of a deep whirlpool, who, belching forth Maronian grandeur,

[Col. 0939C] produce the harmony of a swan’s voice from their throats, and who, while matching their poem to the sweet Muses, display something vain and suited to no useful gain.

I do not send my verses to such men for recitation, but to monks, upon whose lips rests the saving treasure of psalm, hymn, and song, which they sing through the churches, bellowing like thunder with their mouths in praise of Christ.

Peter the fisherman, fishing for peoples, is preferred to all poets: filled with the Holy Spirit, he turned countless crowds with a single utterance. By this he taught that the kingdom is not obtained by speech, but is raised firm by the power of the Lord.

Go, go, my poem. You, gracious Spirit, come; enter fully into the inner chambers of my heart,

[Col. 0940B] so that I may be able to write, in worthy narration, the deeds of the man that must be spread throughout the whole world.

### 2.

Meanwhile, as the holy man returned from the city of Rome, he went under heavenly direction toward the peoples of Gaul.

And just as a shining lamp hidden beneath a basket offers no benefit to human eyes, but, placed upon a stand, drives away darkness with the light of its radiance and displays its gifts to those entering the house,

so Amandus, shining with the light of Christ, so illuminated all the ministers in that church that he might remove many people from foul darkness.

Compelled by the commands of the prince and overcome by the admonitions of the bishops, he was made a bishop; what he had long possessed through his merits, he then received in due order.

He did not take possession of a fixed episcopal see. Rather, like Paul, who approached the eastern peoples,

[Col. 0940C] he was sent to the western regions and entered them, spreading among the scattered peoples the holy words of salvation.

### 3.

Gaul, rejoice gladly: this distinguished Apostle has been given to you.

When the Lord sent the lights of teachers into the world, shining like stars, he then, by a gracious lot, preserved our Amandus for you.

Through him, irradiated with the holy light of virtues, you have become splendid among the inhabitants enclosed beneath the four regions of the earth.

Through him, believing forever in the high-throned King, you will always be a holy, beautiful, and noble kingdom.

When he, the conspicuous Judge of the world, comes, he will lead you, gathered from every side like a shepherd leading his flocks, to the throne of Christ. As you come there, the great princes of the Lord will bring their gifts, with so great a Patron going before them.

[Col. 0941A] Amandus will hear the voice of the supreme Shepherd:

“Good servant, rejoice in eternal triumphs. You who were once faithful to me in a little, I shall set you over much; enter fully into our joys.”

Then the King will say such things to you, his dear people:

“Blessed flock, come; now receive the kingdom prepared for you, sought through sacred merits from the foundation of the world.”

Then, Gaul, you will receive such gifts from your King if you now imitate the magnificent deeds of Amandus.

He taught whatever he completed by his own conduct. Constantly preserving holy love, and with the goodness by which he was filled making his face serene, he displayed by his expression what the treasury of his heart contained.

Sober in mind, he shone forth chaste in heart, and kindly offered generous gifts to the poor.

[Col. 0941B] Here and there, adapting himself to all, he was rich among the wealthy and associated with the poor among the needy.

Vigilant and wakeful, devoted to prayer at every moment, he was sparing in speech and gentle in spirit.

### 4.

When this saint properly loosened the chains of human beings, if he happened to see some boys held captive, or if he could see them transported across the sea and offered for sale, he immediately, eager to pay the price, redeemed them for a substantial sum, breaking the harsh chains of the bound through compassion.

Nor did he lack diligence or abandon the labor he had begun. Those whose bodies he released from bonds he also freed from the inner darkness of their hearts by shedding light upon them all, and he drove away every impurity through holy baptism.

Pouring the sacred liquid into shining vessels, he inserted sweet honey into dew-bearing baskets,

[Col. 0941C] sprinkling the newly born with the fountain of instruction.

The saint left them among friendly churches, though permission for their freedom was granted according to a salutary custom.

From these men, many held distinguished episcopal sees; we have heard of men beautiful in holy conduct and speech, and that gracious abbots were multiplied.

Such gifts the saint scattered throughout the whole world.

### 5.

O memorable Father, I do not know with what praise I should now celebrate you, marveling at the marks of such great deeds.

You distribute the price, release captives from their chains, and by this art make money ascend to heaven. You place both the price and those bought with the price above the stars.

You empty your purse while filling heaven with your gift; and since you had been a merchant, it was fitting that you should be such a one.

[Col. 0941D] For if religious men send you gifts, you do not prepare larger chests for storing money.

Nor is it enough for you, holy Father, to serve the heavenly duties alone, to gather peoples called from every side, and to renew them in the sacred and living fountain.

Beautiful France no longer fills your love, and the hunt over the narrow bounds of the earth has become too confined for you.

[Col. 0942A] You also gather those brought across the sea and carried over vast waters. Your eagerness for the price does not delay, nor is any seller too dear for you, celebrated Father.

The seller takes a drachma stamped with the king’s name; you return a drachma stamped with the name of Christ.

The seller carries away his profits for earthly things; you preserve your profits for heavenly things.

He loses his money or hides it in locked chests; you fashion your money into an excellent crown by preserving it for Christ the King, and place it upon his lofty head.

You turn cruel wolves into gentle lambs and command them to stand in the sacred folds as singers [Note: That is, singers. Ausonius uses the term in *Professors of Bordeaux*, poem 16, addressed to Nepotianus:

“You would not leave the storyteller, Ulysses,

who left the singing maidens,” that is, the singing Sirens.

Likewise Sidonius, Book IX, Letter 15: “to sound with melodic strokes.” Prudentius, *Hymn 9 of the Cathemerinon*:

“Give the boy the plectrum,

that I may sing among the faithful

a sweet and melodious song,

the glorious deeds of Christ.”].

You make fierce robbers, whose former life had been devoted to plunder, into gentle doves without gall, so that they may spend what they had devoured from others.

## CHAPTER II. Saint Amandus’s second journey to Rome. A boy rescued from drowning. The storm calmed.

[Note: The Roman journey itself is not explained, but the miraculous events that occurred on the return journey are.]

[Col. 0942B]

### 6.

Nor do I pass you by, city, but visit you in my poem—you who are called by the name Centumcellae; you who are accustomed often to relieve the dangers of the sea, restore sailors, and raise up weary limbs.

Nor did you escape the notice of the saint when, departing from Rome for the second time, he set out from there by ship and reached you, destined to undergo his customary struggles.

There, as was his custom, he prayed alone amid the darkness of the shadowy night. Surely now you recognize that, after the example of Jesus, he bore a labor like his.

[Col. 0942C] A night full of terror came, darker than the earth’s darkness, desiring to blacken with harmful smoke the lamp shining by the Lord’s radiance.

Although the customary savage enemy always rebels and the wicked one desires to extinguish the righteous rays, even then he did not dare to touch the excellent Amandus.

Perhaps he remembered that once he had sent a serpent against the boy and had seen it quickly turn back, trembling on winged feet, when the saint traced with two fingers the sign of the cross, penetrating all walls.

Therefore the reckless enemy seized one of the servants and dragged him toward the sea. Why? To drown him.

And just as a savage wolf drags a woolly sheep torn from the snowy flock with dark jaws, intent on devouring it, so this robber, burning with desire for prey, carried the boy cruelly toward the dangers of death.

The boy repeatedly uttered these words:

“Christ, help me; Christ, help me.”

Then the insolent one said, “What Christ?” The youth, overcome, dared not answer a word. But the warrior Amandus,

[Col. 0943A] not allowing the beast to devour his disciple in his presence or drown him beneath the black waves of the sea, took up his weapons, seized his quiver, and shot a saving arrow at the boy—yet one wounding Satan in his pride—overcoming the victor by the force of a blow from the word:

“Boy whom you are dragging,” said Amandus, “tell the enemy: ‘Christ crucified is the Son of the living God.’”

The enemy heard the sound and, trembling with supreme horror, was terrified. He did not dare remain in that place, but fled and vanished, wandering into the empty air.

The prey remained unharmed, once the enemy had been driven far away.

Thus the distinguished warrior, the saint, triumphs in the world.

### 7.

Idle, accursed, fierce, cruel, unjust enemy—whose name, rebelling with its customary savagery, you now despise—he once took from you, savage tyrant, the dominion over the world which you held by deceit.

There is no place for you in heaven, and earth is denied to you. Tartarus alone lies open to you; its thresholds, once open to you as you entered, now remain closed when you wish to leave.

There you burn in the endless heat of a flame-vomiting furnace, bound in harsh chains amid pitch-black horror. Woe, woe! Groaning and weeping, you shall cry out.

And if, as a cunning deceiver, you now deceive some and join them to the beast to be burned in the fires of the cauldron, know that as your gains grow, so your punishments grow in equal measure—more harmful to you, thrice-accursed devourer.

That place is worthy of you; these are fitting rewards.

Those who bravely oppose you prepare these kingdoms for themselves.

And although anyone who desires to climb to heaven must be bound to wage continual wars against you,

[Col. 0943C] nevertheless, so that you would not depart from this poem without being praised, I have produced for you, in fitting fashion, songs black as coal.

And deservedly so, since you remain a coal burned throughout the ages.

Flee, seeking the kingdoms prepared from the foundation of the world.

Thus far, Father, we have heaped upon our common enemy insults, slaps, laughter, anger, curses, and mockery,

and spittle; we have not offered verses.

Now we all ask that, as once you were the protector of the boy, so you may always be the saving salvation of your servants everywhere.

Our Shepherd, be present: this is your most devoted flock.

Protect us, care for us, guard us, love us, and save us from the wolf’s tooth, from the jaws of the ancient serpent.

And since, relying upon the Lord’s power, he could not conquer, frighten, overthrow, possess, or devour you,

[Col. 0943D] rescue, Shepherd, the sheep whom you reverently feed in the fold from the snares of him who circles these enclosures.

Do not, through us, once become conquered by him who was conquered by you, if the enemy devours us, though we are powerless.

### 8.

Once, while cutting through the middle of the sea in a ship, blessed Father, you went on your way, teaching the sailors divine words and sowing holy seeds throughout the wave-tossed sea. Nor were you idle in your work.

You believed that the example of your Teacher was to be imitated: once he sat in a boat and taught the crowds.

While you were intent upon such deeds, as the events themselves relate,

[Col. 0944A] an enormous fish appeared to the sailors’ eyes and poured abundant joy into their astonished minds. They cast their nets and caught a watery haul.

What fish, gracious Father, would not serve your purposes?

Perhaps the whole joyful company would have hastened forward to offer its service, if it had thought this fitting; that fish would have been fortunate.

The sailor rejoices at the broad-spotted catch; he is voracious, since prey has been found for him, and the fish rejoices because it has come into your food.

The oars rejoice; the net brings forth joys. Everyone is cheerful, because no one lacked a share.

But the envious enemy, unwilling to let those holy joys remain with the men, attacked the sea with his trident and stirred it from the depths.

An unexpected storm rushed upon them, and a great tumult arose. The waves surged up, the keel was shaken;

[Col. 0944B] the sailor flew upward, borne by the wave to the stars, and then plunged toward the depths, cutting through the thirsty sands.

Joy changed into sorrow. Their companions scattered everything in grief, casting out the ship’s equipment, while the bodies struggled at least to withdraw from death.

But this gift was preserved for the saint as a reward, so that his virtue and merit might shine forth greatly.

Although all were shaken by violent movements, and the master of the ship [Note: The *proreta* is in charge of the forward part of the ship.] could not provide assistance to his damaged boat, they did not entirely lose all counsel.

Instead, with one accord they quickly approached Saint Amandus and begged him to bring them aid.

Accustomed to encourage the frightened with sweet speech, he comforted the sailors, promising that the merciful Lord would be tested and that the danger would be driven away in peace.

At last, exhausted, they lay down in helpless sleep.

The righteous man himself also sat in the stern and rested.

### 9.

Yet, lest, overwhelmed beneath the immense waves of the sea, he should perhaps remain hidden, lesser in merits though dear to the stars,

the illustrious Peter, key-bearer of the heavenly hall, soon appeared. He would not allow the waves to carry them without him.

Greeting the man reclining in the stern with a brotherly voice, he came to him, and, made more secure amid so great a danger, he began in this way, cast into a similar shipwreck:

“Brother Amandus, beloved of your King throughout the ages, do not fear, for it is shameful for you to have feared through fear.

“For although the swollen waves are raised to the heavens,

[Col. 0944D] they will not engulf you. Believe me: neither you nor your sailor, who is now sailing upon this sea, will perish.

“The right hand which once kept me from being drowned in the waves, …”

He rescued you then and now saves you from this peril.

Soon the wind too departs, every storm is driven away;

the sea is quickly calmed, peace having been sent across the waters,

and then joyful things return when the dark night withdraws.

The unharmed sailors swiftly pressed their wet feet onto the sands. Singing the sea-song,

with their voices they applaud God, and the servants magnify in praises the gracious One

at whose command the storms yielded, the deep stood still, and the wave was quiet. [Col. 0945A] But if the wave of the blue deep terrified them,

it did not swallow any of them in its greedy throat.

## CHAPTER III. The People of Ghent Converted to the Faith by Saint Amandus. His Disciple Bavo, Celebrated for Holiness.

### 10

As the Saint went onward with saving steps,

he scattered the word among the peoples and taught holy things,

disclosing to the nations the rewards of the eternal kingdom,

what gifts are prepared in heaven for the companies of Christians,

and what punishments are reserved in the caverns for the wicked.

Thus he went eagerly throughout every region,

diligent to bring a harvest of souls to Olympus;

he considered these his own groves, and took care to lead them with him.

[Col. 0945B] Therefore, while the Blessed One eagerly travelled through these fields,

he heard that the district of Gandavum, which the river Scheldt flows past,

was held fast by the enemy in the bonds

of sin and weighed down by an excessive burden of wrongdoing;

nor did those blinded by ancient darkness acknowledge

the true light that shone upon the whole world.

They worshipped idols, fit for the flames of hearths, made from the strength of the forests,

and images adorned by craftsmen’s hands,

with suppliant vows under the name of divine honor.

Alas, it is shameful to worship gods whom fire can turn, once burned,

into embers and thoroughly consumed ashes;

and reverently to bend proud necks to the stiff branches of a tree,

submitting them to the malignant enemy.

For no one had ploughed this land of faith with a plough;

no one had cast into it the seeds of the divine word.

[Col. 0945C] For the fierce region and unfruitful land drove away all bishops,

and no one dared approach

the forest-dwelling boars, those savage bands in their ferocity.

But this difficult labor had been reserved for our Amandus.

Seeking, therefore, a way by which he might remove so many peoples

from the enemy’s snares, and how he might shake the prey

from the savage tyrant and carry off the spoil,

he sought Aycharius, who governed the flock of Noyon,

so that he might go bowed into the court of the king—

for at that time Dagobert was directing with powerful reins

the prosperous kingdom of the Franks—

and by his command might bring back instructions for himself:

that anyone among them who wished not to wash himself

in the sacred font should be compelled to cleanse himself there.

With God granting it, Amandus soon obtained what he desired.

[Col. 0945D] He hastened to Gandavum, trusting in heavenly power.

### 11

With what kind of writing could I show the labors

which he endured there, while bringing the Word to cruel crowds,

being repeatedly plunged into the waters of rivers?

Yet he could never be compelled to abandon what he had begun,

nor could the raging people drive him away;

he did not care about wounds, nor refuse to endure blows,

until, when the darkness had been driven away by heavenly light,

he washed the people, transformed, in the life-giving font.

[Col. 0946A] For when the Saint, exultant, boldly took up his weapons,

he sought the savage enemy and mighty tyrant

in the fortress already mentioned, where he then held the citadel;

he who, once driven from all the territories of Gaul

by the various commanders of Jesus and by many trophies,

had come there, enclosed on every side by walls and rivers.

Yet he was not wholly deprived of his customary craft.

For, having gathered countless companies here and there,

and himself accompanied by four times two leaders,

he brought his arms outside, displaying his left hand

wet with blood. Fierce, he sounded the savage trumpets

with all his strength and entered the battle—conquered yet to be conquered—

ready for every evil. The enemy, savage in close combat,

came out to meet him in open warfare;

then, like a snake confused by various tricks and a thousand colors,

[Col. 0946B] trembling, exhausted, overcome, and panting,

he opposed him with poisons turned back and hidden behind him,

waging his wars by ambushes, so that perhaps, secretly creeping up,

he might prepare a joyful attack through unseen darts.

What more can I say? When the wars had everywhere been withdrawn,

and so many enemies had been subdued under Christ’s direction,

the victorious Amandus departed, leading a noble captive column,

and, with Satan’s tyranny destroyed, washed the people

in an eternal baptism, better than the Scheldt,

[Col. 0945D] augmented by the Legia, flowing into it from the left side.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] In the margin Milo wrote: “Perhaps creeping up.”]

[Note: [Col. 0945D] “Legia” was added in the margin for explanation: Legia, or Lisa, is a river that flows past Kortrijk and joins the Scheldt at Ghent.]

And lest the enemy rise again, revived,

and, like the three-mouthed Cerberus, burning with the desire to devour,

raise his deadly head against the Christians,

he clothed them in the breastplate of faith, helmeted them with hope,

imbued, equipped, strengthened, and consolidated them;

[Col. 0946C] he established the city and raised substantial towers,

foreseeing what was to come, and set up sacred standards in the midst.

He did not prepare a dragon breathing fire from its open jaws,

but impressed on their foreheads, with his fingers, the sign of the cross;

and instead of the sound of a trumpet, an abundance of standards was made,

where Christ the King possesses servants and holy faithful people.

### 12

Afterward he entrusted this camp also to his friend,

hastening to go as a warrior to other regions,

where a strong leader might not be lacking for the peoples there.

Blessed Bavo of God, this page marks you:

once recruited by the Lord’s commander Amandus,

you despised the world and trampled transient time beneath your feet;

taking up the weapons of the cross, you hastened on foot to battle,

and carried away much spoil from the savage enemy.

Among that spoil was the prey which he joyfully seized and desired,

if it had been possible, to shut up in the fiery caverns

of his own kingdom:

you, blessed one, shedding holy tears, pious vows, and prayers,

roaring in battle and fighting for blessed things,

saved them and gave your gifts to the supreme King.

You recognize what I am saying, since your deeds are sung:

namely, that when that enemy, brandishing a missile,

threw it from a wagon and struck down

[Note: [Col. 0946D] This is Artimus, raised through Saint Bavo’s prayers; he is discussed in the *Life* on 1 October.]

one of the servants, and made him prey for savage dogs,

he nevertheless spent his efforts in vain.

[Col. 0947A] For afterward, along the returning road, by praying,

you brought the herdsman back from the darkness of death into the light.

Having used many other holy arts as well,

through this one thing he learned that you could never be overcome.

O how magnificent a teacher Amandus, holy one, was for you,

and with what signs your instructor, that Amandus of yours, shone!

What things made you such a minister?

For in your deeds we behold the gracious Teacher,

excellent, beautiful, admirable, and worthy of glory.

It is sweet for me to run through the text of your life;

but the melody of what remains to be completed draws my step back,

lest these verses be poured out for you without return.

Repay the favor, and guide me, I beg, by your prayers;

obtain pardon for my offenses by having pity on me,

and, joined to your King, remain well through the ages.

### 13

And you, fortunate place, region brighter than gold,

illumined by the holy light of the just, hail;

and you, an excellent people, gathered through much labor

by two fathers, it is right that you should follow with love

those whom the Almighty, in his goodness, assigned to you as beloved patrons

and gave you as such merciful friends.

And although our Amandus, departing from here in body,

has left you, he governs everywhere by his merits, if you believe.

While he also protects us by holy prayers and merits,

remembering you, he opens for you the gates of Olympus.

Sing hymns with sweet sounds to such shepherds;

do not let your sheepfold appear ungrateful to the other flocks.

Mixing songs with written pages, as the Muse runs on,

I shall sing again with you, offering signs of my love

and reminders of my devotion, which remains without end,

toward those whom the feather of virtue has raised,

renowned, to the starry kingdom.

They have shown you, as you hasten there,

that the gates of life can mercifully stand open.

But I, bristling with sins like a goat rough with bristles,

stripped of covering and naked of a bright fleece,

am dragged, pitiable, toward the cruel courts of wretched death.

Stretch out your hands, I beg, and lift me from the devouring throat;

for, once seized, I cannot return by my own strength.

Although this creature has a mouth wide open,

perhaps I can pass through it

[Col. 0948B] if, by your aid and prayers, I am brought back.

This too, I ask, must be done in Christ’s name.

When your wise industry, joined to the heavenly seats,

has come into being, I beg that I, trembling,

may at last be sought out and enclosed by the key of blessed Peter.

When life, salvation, and the everlasting palm of glory

shall happily be yours through every age,

then, I pray, let there be at least indulgence for me, wretched as I am,

through Christ the Lord, who reigns through all ages.

[Note: [Col. 0947B] Added: “Book II ends; it contains 418 verses,” and the headings of Book III followed.]

# BOOK III

[Col. 0947]

## Contents of Book III

1. The poet rejoices that he has reached the midpoint of his poem; showing that he is writing a difficult work, he both urges his reader in speech and teaches by example to meditate on Christ’s life-giving commandments. — 2. Concerning a dead man raised. — 3. That he wished to conceal that deed. — 4. Concerning shrines destroyed and peoples converted and baptized. — 5. That he went to the Slavs for the sake of preaching. — 6. A speech of praise addressed to him. — 7. How he was rejected after rebuking the king. — 8. He forgave the same ruler’s crime when the ruler sought pardon. — 9. That the same king, wishing to entrust his son to the Saint, was unable to obtain his request. — 10. The same king’s little son speaks while being catechized by the Saint. — 11. The same event celebrated in praise. — 12. Where the Saint undertook the Church of Traiectum to govern. — 13. That, rejected by it, he went to the island of Calolo. — 14. A speech addressed to the Saint’s despisers.

## CHAPTER I. A Dead Man Raised by Saint Amandus

### 1

With God’s help, as I swiftly describe in verse

the holy life of the excellent bishop Amandus,

which rightly ought to have been recorded in long periods,

if only abundant or great eloquence were granted to me,

I now hasten onward by a shorter road,

placing two feet alternately

and counting three pairs as I run along the shortcuts.

Thus the journey has been measured out; the remaining praises,

for which rhetorical speech is insufficient and eloquence grows faint,

I, rash judge of these matters, attempt to compose

in brief little verses, though no account could complete them.

If the world, flowing with words, were to join in this undertaking,

[Col. 0947D] and all poets were to gather beneath one roof,

arguing, composing melodies, and philosophizing,

I confess that not all would be able to set forth in verse

the praises of his virtues as they deserve.

And even if they could somehow report his outward deeds,

I confess that with no modulation of voice

would they be able to express according to his merits

the rewards he received in heaven.

He flies higher than a chattering tongue can follow.

Look: poets sing fabrications in lyrical speech.

Why do you reread them, loving reader,

when they bring no profit of salvation to souls—

the labor of the mouth, the feeding of wind?

What can warlike ranks provide for you?

With what garment will torn Discord clothe you?

Why should you grieve over those companies cut down in slaughter?

Let the dead sing of dead things; you who live, compose what gives life.

Behold, better deeds are told in my song:

it does not recount swords, weapons, or Camilla’s quiver,

but remembers death conquered beneath Christ and his bishop,

[Col. 0948D] and what gifts the flesh honorably gave to its friend.

I shall recount, foolishly awed by fear of so great a deed,

how once Amandus, beloved of the Lord,

still remaining under the law of death and weighed down by flesh,

bore the rights of death,

[Col. 0949A] and also snatched a man from the closed prison of Avernus

and restored him to life in the customary manner.

### 2

There was once a city, as its remaining traces still show,

Tournai, now laid low by ruin upon ruin,

[Note: [Col. 0949D] This event seems to have occurred during the earlier wars among the Franks themselves. Yet later, too, they report that the monastery of Saint Bavo in the town of Ghent was burned by the Normans in the year 850, according to the *Deeds of the Normans before Rollo*; and the *Annals of Bertin* report that part of their territory—the Menapians, whose capital was Tournai, the Tarvisii, that is, the Tervani, and other coastal peoples—was plundered in that same year, 850. But Milo did not touch upon these matters, unless perhaps he revised and enlarged his poem after the death of Haiminus, to whom he dedicated it.]

completely, and lamenting the fall of its proud towers.

Yet it is still crowded with people, since it abounds in water and commerce;

and it rests on twin columns, no longer destined to fall.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] In the Amandine manuscript the margin contained: “The column itself has fallen from it now, alas!”]

For, with a beautiful church rising in the middle of the citadel,

it possesses an episcopal throne; and not far away

[Note: [Col. 0950D] Molanus writes under 14 December, concerning Nicasius: “A certain bishop of Noyon obtained some relics of this martyr and brought them to his own city. They are reported to have been made illustrious by clear miracles both at Noyon and at the fortress of Tournai, where they are said still to be preserved. We shall discuss them on that day.”]

the bishop of Reims, Nicasius, a precious martyr, rests in an urn—

happy was he, for life gave him a crown

and a shining palm in exchange for the blood he poured out.

[Col. 0949B] What then? Surrounded by a great number of Frankish soldiers at the fortress,

the stern Count Dotto, sent from the royal court,

had arrived, and the court was filled with complaining crowds.

Look: a thief was being dragged along, surrounded by a great throng,

bound with many knots for a great crime.

Everyone shouted; the whole people standing nearby

proclaimed in song that he was guilty;

none of them admitted that he deserved pardon.

Into the midst of these crowds Saint Amandus thrust himself:

he wept, groaned, implored, grieved, lamented, entreated, and prayed
