that they should pity and spare this wretched man,

so that the Almighty Christ might show mercy to him.

But the Saint did not obtain what he asked for with tears.

For Count Dotto was swollen with pride,

more cruel than any beast,

and ordered that the thief, fastened to a stake,

pay the punishment he deserved for his crime.

[Col. 0949C] Meanwhile he was led away and hanged;

then, overcome by savage death,

[Note: [Col. 0950D] Another manuscript has approximately the same reading.]

he sent his soul into the gloomy shades.

What are you doing, holy Father, worthy to be remembered throughout the world?

[Note: [Col. 0950D] Elno manuscript: “Then.”]

You cling prostrate at the feet like a little lamb

of the savage wolf—flee, lest he devour you yourself.

Rise up to the Lord; for what you ask, he himself will graciously grant,

and will mercifully bestow lasting honor.

Thus Dotto returned home with the people accompanying him.

The Saint, panting, hastened swiftly to the man,

and when compassion saw the wretched dead man,

strengthening his spirit with the breath of life,

he quickly carried the deposited body to the familiar church,

where he had been accustomed to knock at the heavenly gate.

Here he lies prostrate on the fields, there nearer to the stars,

and pours forth both prayers and rivers of tears.

[Col. 0949D] Although these, near at hand, stiffen the boundaries of the earth,

they fly higher as they climb toward the lofty tribunal,

carried beyond the heavens while the angelic choir applauds.

[Col. 0950A] These words are proved by deeds; fulfillment confirms the utterance.

For the Saint devoted himself to prayer, prostrate on the ground,

and the blessed prayer did not reach its end

until both, rising together at different but corresponding hours,

stood side by side—wonderful to see—

the dead man from death, and the Saint from the dust of the earth.

### 3

O how visibly the Lord loved his disciple,

to whom he granted so many signs of his love.

Finally, as the present writing reveals to us,

he prevailed, through holy prayers and blessed merits,

to restore to the dead man the life

that had been torn away by such a great crime;

and he obtained, through Christ’s mercifulness, saving pardon

for the soul that was already slipping into Tartarus.

[Note: [Col. 0950D] This does not mean that a sentence of condemnation, once issued, is revoked; rather, in similar cases the judgment had not been absolute.]

Let highest praise be given to God, who, adding gifts to the faithful,

so that souls may be able to leave the prison of Avernus,

burst open Tartarus and tore away every obstacle.

[Col. 0950B] Meanwhile, after the dew had been shaken from her damp hair,

Aurora, preceding the Sun that would soon follow her light,

had revealed herself to the inhabitants of earth in her rising.

But the power that filled the limbs of the revived body

had added returning strength through solid vigor.

Therefore the victor, joyful and the restorer of life,

the confessor of the Lord distinguished by honorable signs,

asked for water.

They hurried, thinking that the man’s limbs ought to be buried,

since he was asking for water as if for the customary washing.

They entered and found him unharmed—wonderful to tell—

and, with the order reversed, saw him sitting reverently.

The greatness of the event reveals what astonishment there must have been.

For the thief, restored to life, tells again of his life and pardon,

[Note: [Col. 0950D] That is, he rejoices that he has been heard by God, not that he rejoiced because of the honor bestowed upon him by the brothers.]

and the Saint rejoices at the honor granted to him.

[Col. 0950C] Then Amandus solemnly adjured the brothers and the people

in Christ’s name not to make the deed known among the peoples,

until the appointed time of life had been completed.

While his holy hand touched each wound,

blessed medicine restored swift health;

no furrow remained wherever the honorable finger passed.

Tell us, learned speakers; eloquent men, bring forth what is worthy.

What kind of physician is this?

When he touches, no scar appears on the wounds,

all of them being closed everywhere.

Where does this salvation travel? From what ointment does its power flow?

Be silent, talkative tongue; this is the work of the Almighty,

through whom whoever serves him is able to accomplish such things.

## CHAPTER II. The Faith Spread by Saint Amandus. The Slavs Added. The Penalty of Exile Inflicted.

[Col. 0950D]

### 4

Therefore, when flying Fame spread the memorable sign,

a great crowd of people suddenly gathered around him;

[Col. 0951A] just as you marvel to see bees swarm through meadows and gardens

toward purple flowers, and gather with their bites

what they will carry on their curved feet to their dear hives.

You would see these peoples likewise pressing around Amandus,

a conspicuous flower, green in winter and summer,

so that they might carry away the sacred baptism,

and bring back the food of virtues like sweet honey—

the food by which the Lord of the world is nourished with an exceedingly sweet draught.

Afterward the profane shrines were stripped of their empty honor,

and those whose labor had caused them to grow fell.

When the shrines had collapsed, the holy man restored temples,

establishing basilicas and monastic cloisters;

with faithful sharpness he crushed perfidy before the faith.

O how great a grace was granted to the just man,

who earned multiple fruit from a single seed!

[Col. 0951B] The inhabitant, reborn in the life-giving font, is consecrated,

and the splendid walls of the lofty Church rise.

Fortunate is that death in which a great plague dies;

yet far more fortunate is the salvation

by which, when one rises, many rise again in their hearts.

This, unless I am mistaken, is the transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High.

Love for the Saint grows, and praise of Christ is celebrated.

While he preaches the word of the One whose help he possesses to everyone

among the people, a fruitful harvest rises from the soil

and returns a hundredfold crop on the grass of virtues.

### 5

You should not lament, land of Sclavinia,

that no man passed through you who had been purified by the apostolic axe

or cultivated by the furrows of faith and by any plough.

For just as money silently increases for a miser,

and increase generates the fulfillment of his greatest hunger,

[Col. 0951C] so here—if it is permitted to compare benevolent things with foolish ones—

he prepared to increase the profits of good virtues

wherever they had grown, accumulating them,

and becoming still more eager to possess them.

When a renowned harvest began happily to rise here and there

in many regions, with the seed of the word scattered,

he learned that the Slavs were bound by the enemy’s error.

Confident that he could earn martyrdom for Christ,

the Saint crossed the icy Ister,

[Note: [Col. 0951D] That is, the Danube. The Slavs were discussed above.]

and began to cut open the clods of the hard earth.

From there he scattered the seed of the Gospel everywhere,

casting it through places, houses, fields, and crossroads.

He poured water from heavenly springs over the dry fields,

supplied it, sent it in, enclosed, drenched, and surrounded them.

Nothing remained undone that he considered worthy of doing.

Yet when he saw that the harvest did not answer his hopes

with a full crop,

[Col. 0951D] and, grieving that his labor was fruitless,

saw the conspicuous iron of the plough spring back from the stones,

and, looking through the emptiness, sought a harvest among thorns,

unable to grasp even the pious palm of martyrdom,

he returned again with Christ accompanying him,

a shepherd and a lamb, himself the leader of his own sheep,

lest he regret having poured out such great labors in vain

and having hastened over so long a road,

[Col. 0952A] without being able to gather even a small amount of fruit.

He gathered a few grains and placed them in the heavenly granaries.

### 6

You too, holy Sower, while we accompany you as you go

and follow your happy course in song,

we pass through an unknown road, travelling in speech,

where none sent by Jesus from that thousandfold host

shot the life-giving arrow with the bending bow.

Neither Peter nor Paul, nor the former sower of the word,

who was mistakenly called because of his customary work,

nor anyone else, however confident in powerful weapons,

hurled the distinguished sharpness of a spear at him.

But this contest was reserved for you, Amandus:

you could not subject stiff-necked peoples to the yoke of the King,

and love held these things; an honorable will led you.

[Col. 0952B] So that, drenched in a stream of blood for the Lord,

you might return defeated in death, but victorious in love.

What kind of steadfastness, perhaps, covered your breast?

What kind of courage, retaining unconquered strength,

made your feet advance into an unknown region?

From that region wounds came to the Franks in exchange for gifts;

the king, protected by a powerful defense of arms,

gave his back and fled, with a fierce Frank accompanying him.

You, without a companion, rushed through the borderlands

and the narrow passes.

[Note: [Col. 0951D] *Marka*, a Germanic word, signifies the boundary of a province. It is frequently found in the *Annals of Fulda* in the period of Milo’s writings, namely under the years 788, 827, 861, and others. The term was extended to signify an entire territory or province; hence the several *Markae*, or *Marcae*, in Germany and Italy, and the border officials called *Markisi* and *Marchiones*.]

[Note: [Col. 0952D] *Clusae* are narrow passages of entry, which open and close a region. In Einhard’s *Annals*, under the year 817: “King Bernard of Italy fortified with garrisons all the entrances, that is, the *clusae*, by which Italy is entered.”]

But pardon me, I beg, because I, your humble servant,

dare as a suppliant to bring my plaintive speech before you.

Accept the votive prayers of your devoted servant,

since we now enter the palace court.

Look upon me, holy one, I beg, as I now go on my way.

Guide our pen, so that it may not utter empty things;

lest, while we wish properly to narrate your triumphs,

the royal rod find some offense in our little place.

Here let the brotherly company gather with prayers for the singer.

### 7

Dagobert was king and held the laws of the Franks;

but he oppressed the peoples with a proud and harsh rule.

He surpassed in the height of power all those

who before him had held the scepter over that people.

He was harsh toward rulers, a pupil subject to vices,

shamefully stained everywhere by obscene luxury,

and carried in his bones the fire infused by Venus.

Yet lest the thorn’s prick rise in this harvest

and disfigure the work begun,

our bishop’s steadfastness could not tolerate

these and similar behaviors; moved, he brought forth a plaintive speech.

[Col. 0952D] Nor did he fear the sharp edge of the hostile sword,

for he had learned to trust in victory through many wars;

nor did he fear the savage fury of an earthly king,

whom he sought to strike with these words:

namely, that if he cared to reach the threshold of the eternal kingdom,

he should make the conduct of his life better,

removing sin, lest perhaps, rejected,

he suffer the torments of his crimes in infernal chaos.

And because the words of the just are goads to the wicked,

as soon as the king, raging, heard the words with ears pricked up,

wishing to believe that he was permitted to do whatever pleased him,

he gravely rejected the Teacher who admonished him rightly,

mocking him, and deprived his kingdom of such a guest.

The man who had been rejected departed, carrying the Lord also to the Gentiles.

## CHAPTER III. Saint Amandus’s Return from Exile. The Baptism of Saint Sigebert

### 8

And although the Prince scattered royal seed at the crossroads,

no ear of offspring arose for him;

unless drops should come from the clouds onto the dry field.

When at last he was able to recognize this,

he humbly sought help from the heavenly seats, praying

that a child might be born to him to rule after his scepters.

[Col. 0953B] With God granting it, he obtained what his devoted mind had asked.

When a joyful messenger reported to the royal halls

that a boy had come forth from his mother’s womb into the light,

he worshipped the Author of the child with praises and vows.

Yet uncertainty continued to burn his joyful mind:

who should raise the little boy from the holy font?

When the King’s captive memory returned to itself,

he ordered swift ministers to hurry through the kingdom

and commanded that the Saint be brought with the honor he deserved.

At last he was found and instructed to go to the palace.

He presented himself before the eyes of the aforesaid king.

As soon as the king saw that the man was present,

he immediately descended from his lofty throne,

and, lowering his shining head, still crowned with a diadem,

to the ground where the foot of the pious peacemaker happened to stand,

he bent his rigid neck to the holy feet.

[Col. 0953C] Then the purple garment prostrated itself upon the dusty ashes,

and he who issued laws to various ranks

asked that holy indulgence forgive his crime.

But the man was gentle, for whom it was sweet to forgive offenses,

free from bitterness and always burning with calm sweetness.

He quickly raised the king, who was prostrate on the ground in the dust,

and promptly released him from the sins he had committed.

### 9

Then the Prince addressed the Saint with these words:

“Holy Father, Teacher, I repent of having rejected your speech.

It displeases me that an injury was done at my command.

But now, I beg, let those merciful entrails relent.

By God’s gift I have one son, though I do not deserve him.

I ask that your holy blessing consecrate him;

deign to renew him in Christ’s life-giving font,

and, as Teacher, instruct him in divine law.

And you, Father, deserve to be called the boy’s second father,

as you bring forth offspring from the glorious twin font.”

But the holy man, after these words had been poured forth with supreme effort,

opposed the request, recalling that he had been ordered

to scatter the seeds of the word and consecrate peoples

in the river of baptism,

and that he had been sent not for one alone but for many.

He went out, and the king’s request remained unfulfilled.

Since he was unable to win the favor of the man whom he had despised,

he believed that the Saint could be moved by the guardians of his own side.

He sent friends of familiar affection,

so that you might think them one soul beneath two breasts:

the illustrious Dado, accompanied by the kind Eligius,

whom the Prince’s court then held in lay dress.

But later, after they had cast transient time beneath their feet,

as pillars they built two enduring churches.

The former was installed first; under his episcopate

lofty Rouen flourished in blessed titles.

His equal was Eligius, chosen by divine favor.

As Noyon shone as a city while its bishop lived,

so it shines at his tomb, enriched by many virtues.

Faithful faith preserved, happy concord, hail;

holy bishops, radiant in the light of merits.

My speech about you would not be so slight

if I did not know that you had nourished conspicuous poets,

who can chirp for you in triple measure with the Camena.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] *Pipare* is used especially of the sound made by hens.]

And sing noble poetry on golden reeds.

Yet we ask you, reveal our labors,

and let the little drop of my tongue resume its course.

### 10

Therefore the messengers pour forth prayers from devoted hearts,

that he wash the Prince’s offspring in the consecrated stream,

and educate him through books darkened with ink.

If he should perhaps not reject these prayers of the Prince,

their union might grant much to this friendship:

it would allow profit to be sought among the wandering people,

and the divine word to be scattered among many nations.

At last, overcome by the speech of his beloved friends,

he agrees.

He enters unwillingly the lofty palace of the king,

who at that time was residing in the villa of Clypiacum.

[Note: [Col. 0953D] Rather, at Orléans, as stated above and in the *Life of Saint Sigebert*.]

The child is brought to him, carried in the arms of others—

he for whom the sun had already shone forty times.

[Col. 0954C] When the gracious Bishop took him in his sacred hands,

and an excellent prayer had been poured forth in the customary manner,

the infant was enrolled among the catechumens,

and no one gave an answer at the conclusion of the prayer.

There was no confused sound of words striking against the palate;

rather, with open lips and a clear voice, crying out,

he quickly uttered in the hearing of the astonished people:

“Amen.”

Then, renewed in the stream of saving baptism,

he carried back from the life-giving waters the name Sigebert,

and afterward subdued the Austrasian hosts by his rule.

### 11

Here, reader, join me in recounting the praises,

if the spring of your speech flows abundantly,

and your tongue’s rain compares itself with a shower.

Who taught the child? What understanding, I ask, prompted him

to utter unknown *fritillos*—rattlings—in a Hebrew sound?

[Note: [Col. 0954D] *Fritillus* is a gaming board. Here Milo seems to take the word for a sound.]

[Col. 0954D] who instructed him to cry out in this voice,

when childish age still held him in its wailing?

Tell me, I beg: what school gave him utterances

he did not know? Under what teachable master did he flourish?

No whip ever tormented his tender limbs,

nor did slender fingers ever hold a little rattle;

and already he surpasses grandiloquent sophists in understanding.

He speaks in foreign voices and rejects Latin ones.

He teaches by nature. What inspiration pours these things forth?

With this new wine, O Judaea, accustomed to wander astray,

those who learned all languages in a brief time were inflamed.

Here, etymology, your order is confounded:

while the infant speaks, that name is taken from him.

Do not doubt that he rebuked Balaam’s foolish she-ass;

come here—this deed must be celebrated with everlasting praise.

## CHAPTER IV. Saint Amandus’s Bishopric of Traiectum

### 12

When these matters had thus run their course,

an angel sent from above carried away, as he died,

the bishop whose seat was at Traiectum,

beyond the stars of the lofty heaven,

so that he might receive the rewards of his merits in their proper order.

When the king learned this,

[Note: [Col. 0955D] King Sigebert, Dagobert having died several years earlier, as shown above.]

he summoned the holy Amandus,

bringing with him a very great company of bishops,

and joined them to the solemn honors of so great a bishop.

[Col. 0955B] Meanwhile the holy man was led and dragged in sacred procession

into the lofty citadel and placed in the aforementioned see.

He resisted and loudly declared himself unworthy of such an act.

But when, in his customary manner, he travelled through towns,

fields, cottages, villages, and fortresses,

surveying them in beautiful light,

those who ought first to have recognized the sad wickedness

and shown the people the word of the Lord to be followed—

the ministers properly placed in authority over the steps of the Church—

rejected, spurned, scorned, and despised him.

They set aside and drove away the worthy patron through insults,

from whom they had gained no profit for themselves,

but suffered the greatest losses.

For the dust shaken from righteous feet

will accuse them when that time comes

when the righteous will receive rewards

and the wicked punishments.

### 13

The island called Calolo gleams beside the holy Scheldt,

[Note: [Col. 0955D] We approved this reading above, where the Caloani were discussed, § 4.]

[Col. 0955C] beside the Scheldt, which with curved winding turns

offers a retreat, a river most pleasing to sailors.

When the Saint departed from those shores, driven away by their words,

he found it and, believing that it would suffice for him

at so sad a time, to restore the purity of his mind,

he remained there in seclusion for a while

and devoted himself to relieving his many labors.

Yet while he enjoyed this pious activity granted from heaven,

and desired with constant prayers to climb toward heaven,

like a white dove resting on twin wings,

just retribution did not delay to strike those rejecters,

the savage ones, according to their merits,

repaying them suitably because they had preferred

to drive away rather than honor the man.

They were oppressed by punishments of many kinds,

so that they might learn how beloved by Christ

was the one they had despised and driven away.

[Col. 0955D] For a blow descending from heaven and resounding through the earth

crushes and bends the rebels with stiff necks,

and overturns their houses.

The sound and great weight of their fall testify

that their ways have collapsed.

The field, deprived of its crop and stripped of its ear,

returns to them the sharpness of the deserved thorn

along with thistles.

Such exchanges are reported by the earth,

[Col. 0956A] which lacks so great a cultivator,

and whose inhabitant does not feed upon it,

because he has ceased to receive food from his mother’s breast.

### 14

You too, people—if you wish briefly to touch upon ancient things—

feel these wounds brought forth from ancient disasters.

Massive calamities do not spare strong walls;

they are thrown down upon the ground like dust before the wind,

and the houses collapse when no guard supports them.

Nor is it surprising that the structure should fall

if the lofty towers are utterly torn away,

when Amandus leaves it—

the stable defense of our Church,

the lofty column,

the enduring protection against destructive roars.

When he is offended, death comes to you;

salvation came to us while Servatius was alive,

[Note: [Col. 0955D] Saint Servatius is commemorated on 13 May. He died when the devastation of Belgium by other barbarians was imminent; the Poet alludes to this here.]

and afterward, so that he might not receive the sorrowful funeral

or mournful grief of heart

[Col. 0956B] at seeing your final ashes,

he passed to the Lord, leaving you bereft in death.

Afterward, pitying you, he sent Amandus to you,

like a sun gleaming with the radiance of his works.

But you, bleary-eyed, turn your eyes away from him,

and return to the dense darkness of night’s horror.

You hold mud in your hands while wiping your eyes,

and attribute to the light what you see less clearly because of it,

if you have been abandoned by your prayers in a blind prison.

Yet unless you return here and lovingly seek the light

which, by driving him away from yourselves, you mercifully gave to us,

we return no insults or quarrels to you here;

rather, we rejoice exultantly at his return.

Now, now, therefore, let your songs wipe away your guilt;

remember to call back, with worthy praises, the one who was driven out.

[Col. 0956C] Let your offense now repent; these are remedies.

And if, as I believe, the wounds have appeased your guilt,

and the holy man’s goodness has forgiven your enormous crime,

join your own song to my rhythms,

for these are not merely poems.

You can sing; you are skilled at applauding in verse.

You know how to touch the strings with the lyric plectrum,

and, powerful, to resound in a hundred meters with the Muses.

Like nets with threads, you weave books with words.

But from my mouth there runs scarcely a faint whisper,

although the gracious Muse is fitted to your little books.

Lest I fail to praise God, when I am an obvious debtor,

I ask that our little book be enclosed in God’s honor.

[Note: [Col. 0956D] The Elno manuscript reads *labellis* (“with little lips”).]

Praise, distinction, dominion, blessing, glory, victory,

majesty, honor, veneration, grace, and virtue;

May there be to the Father and the Son, together with the life-giving Spirit,

[Col. 0956D] now and forever, while the future ages endure:

To Him who glorified the holy Amandus for his merits,

Bright companion, confine the reed of care within the cloisters.

For the thirsty man has drunk his fill; take away the dew.

And lest the mournful breath be broken any longer,

Fix your step here; while I stretch out my fingers, you will rest a little.

[Note: [Col. 0956D] Added: “The third book ends here; it contains 436 verses,” and these chapters of Book IV were joined to it.]

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0957]

## Chapters of Book IV

1. The poet, about to write by what end the Saint sought the stars, trembles greatly; joining his little books to the four books of the Gospels, he moves toward the conclusion of the holy Amandus and of his own work both in prayer and in verse. — 2. How the Saint, preaching the word of God to the Basques, was rejected, and concerning a mimic seized by a demon. — 3. Concerning a blind man illuminated by water in which the man of God had washed his hands. — 4. Concerning his return to Gaul and the monastery he built. — 5. How, because he had obtained the town of Nantes from the king, Mummulus laid an ambush for him. — 6. How the man of God escaped death when the executioners were miraculously blinded. — 7. A conversion of praise through the Saint’s power. — 8. Concerning a blind woman who was illuminated. — 9. The same event is repeated allegorically. — 10. Concerning a monk released from paralysis for his disobedience and healed by the Saint’s word. — 11. Concerning his death and burial. — 12. Praise of the place and concerning the elevation of his body. — 13. Prayer of the author of this work. — 14. The final conclusion is completed with a prayer.

## CHAPTER ONE. The Basques instructed by Saint Amandus. A blind man illuminated.

[Col. 0957A]

### 1

Thus far I have dealt with the Saint’s eminent deeds,

And, though with a limping foot, I have been able to run through those of the bishop.

But now a matter far too fearful must be handled; it allows me

To fly beyond all strength, seeking what lies above the stars,

So that I may follow in speech where no pedestrian may go.

For my first little books hasten under this condition:

That the labor and merit of the holy Amandus may be known.

This is now the fourth, which must be forged in my hands,

To which I have properly appended the four Gospels.

Matthew, first, endowed with his gift, poured forth

God born in the flesh, who sucked at the Virgin’s breasts.

[Col. 0957B] Here too, as he enters the innermost chambers of our mind,

I wrote of the man born who touched his mother’s breasts,

Perfect, pure, just, worthy, and immaculate.

Then Marcus, exalted by the proclamation of his command,

Said that the voice of a lion crying through deserted fields

Resounded—the lion who slept in death with open eyes.

Following him, as far as I was able, I declared in verse

That the fourfold holy word had been scattered throughout the world.

Then Luke, rising, whose name signifies what he represents,

Introduced the laws of the ancient priesthood in his words

[Note: [Col. 0957C] The Codex of Elnon has *effert*.]

By which Christ, like a calf, was slaughtered upon the altar.

After reading him, I showed that he had ascended the pontifical seat—

The man who had been a living victim.

And because the grace of the sacred Spirit was poured out upon John,

He flies, borne on eagle’s wings, above the heavens,

[Col. 0957C] He sings of the Beginning, the Word before all ages.

It is likewise necessary for me now to hasten forward:

For I must recall the journey by which the holy Amandus

Went to the Lord, to receive honors he had earned,

And visited the rest prepared for him upon the heavenly summit—

To which no wing of good deeds lifts me.

Desire burns my spirit, but ability holds it back.

My tongue longs to run, but, ignorant of speech, it hisses.

Yet if that little whistle echoes in the ear of my heart,

And fills the mind with the fluid in which I dip my pen,

Which makes a she-ass form human speech

And confounds an unlearned man with plaintive rhythm,

I shall note in compressed verse the deeds that remain.

### 2

[Col. 0958A]

Come now, my Muse—cow roaming broadly, trusting in the reins and wielding weapons in your arms—

And mark it for the people in an ordinary voice:

If you remove and alter the letters, it is said to be Wasconia.

That race, sufficiently fierce, pressing on with varied attacks,

Returning hostile weapons with blows and repeated strikes,

Had been an enemy at the farthest borders of the Franks.

But then it was subdued and made peaceful by wounding arms,

And at last, guided by wholesome counsel, its reins were brought under control;

It does not tear with its bite but draws them toward kisses of peace.

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Peter de Maria discusses Wasconia, subject in the age of Milo to the kings of Aquitaine, near the end of Book I and the beginning of the following book of his *History of Béarn*.]

At that time this people, which had remained fiercely rebellious against the Gauls, was likewise rebellious against Christ, who had subdued the rest of the world.

For it lay stripped of the beauty of religion,

[Col. 0958B] In the darkness of night, lit by no lamp,

And, practicing a dreadful crime to which every harmful thing yields,

By which the remnants of plagues usually grow,

It turned worship suitable for Christ toward mute images

And believed that idols possessed the divine power.

When Bishop Amandus discovered these mad acts of error,

Inflamed against those whom he had made worthy of the name of brothers,

He swiftly approached their warlike lands,

So that he might wage Christ’s battles

And, an unconquered soldier, impress the standards of his King

Upon those fields.

Even if he could not rightly defeat their countless hordes,

Or might gain a glorious death through wounds,

While he drove life-giving spears into them,

Striking many level with the ground

And steadfastly overthrowing the false religion of the gods,

An idle, easy, slippery, and arrogant man,

Ugly and impure, muttering scurrilous insults,

Whom the common people rightly called by the nickname “mimic,”

Unhappy, opposed him with foolish, drunken laughter.

But soon the wretch was seized by a terrible demon, filled

With the same thing with which he had earlier been filled,

When he mocked the fosterer of life.

With his own hands, in unsound madness,

He tore, ripped, broke apart, scattered, and burned his limbs.

Before he crossed the open gulfs of Hell,

He gave clear indication under whose leadership he was departing.

You would be astonished to hear a thousand tongues running from one mouth.

At last, twisted and emptied of both guest and enemy,

[Col. 0959A] He who, returning ungratefully, had violently driven away the soul,

And, carrying it off, made it enter Gehenna with him—

He who had been the instigator of sin became its torturer in the fire.

And since what we are writing is not sufficiently joyful, let the reed now,

Leaving the sad things aside, proceed to sweeter matters.

### 3

Therefore, when that people had been left stripped of holy beauty

In its ancient darkness, because it had scorned the light

Sent to it, rather than submit itself to the light,

That shining Lucifer, when he was already returning from them,

At last, weary, reached a certain city.

Its bishop received him with honorable services,

And, reverently honoring him with fitting respect,

Poured the water over his sacred hands;

He instructed the attendants to carry it into the closed chapels.

For that bishop was sufficiently confident that

The desired remedy could be offered to the afflicted.

Nor did the most certain hope deceive such steadfast hearts.

At the time when a beggar sat at the doors of the church,

Poor in possessions, but poorer still in the light of his eyes,

The priest addressed him in these words:

“O man, if you retain the light of faith in your heart,

Wash your closed eyes with the water in which Saint Amandus

Washed his hands. I promise that you will be renewed

By this anointing; light, poured back into your blind windows,

Will show how worthy the Saint’s blessing is.

Nor will you, believing, return empty through the power of faith.”

As soon as these promises had been made, the poor man, deprived of light,

Believing, took the water and washed his face;

The pious medicine accompanied the washing.

O transformation of things! While the blind man’s eyes shine,

The savage image of death is driven away.

[Col. 0959C] Tell me, whoever you are who stand here, how great a power

Do you think the Blessed One displayed when he was bodily present,

And how swiftly he was able to restore the remedy by prayer—

He whose water grants the honor of light through his hands?

Give way, physician, with your worn-out powder; why do you stand there?

For it is well known that powder blinds the eyes.

If you believe this, these waters surpass all collyria.

How clean are the impurities! O what pure cleansing!

How learned the physician, through whom every darkness shines,

From whose beautiful fingers medicinal remedies drip!

Such signs reveal the traces of their King.

What follows is everlasting glory to Christ the Most High,

Honor worthy of the Just One, than whom no one more precious

Has come from the company of his companions into the kingdom of heaven.

As he goes forth to meet the Bridegroom with his adorned lamp,

A fiery ardor soon flows from his olive-bearing arms,

Lighting the torches of the others from his own flame,

And his deeds show with what glory he has shone.

## CHAPTER II. Monasteries built by Saint Amandus. Danger of death driven away from heaven.

### 4

As he pursued the journey he had begun through various virtues,

He came by a fortunate path to the kingdom of the Franks,

And chose a place in which to spread the fitting word.

There, with a devoted company of brothers accompanying him—

Men who had endured various sufferings for Christ’s name—

He built the sacred cloisters of a new monastery.

[Col. 0960A] Happy was that school under so great a master;

From it, in due course, proceeded many learned men,

A numerous company of bishops and learned patrons

Of the Church, pure in speech and shining in their deeds.

Gaul, the Saint has returned: rejoice; he is gracious,

Scatter flowers gladly; salvation has come to you.

For you do not fall on that side where a tower facing Olympus,

Against the bloody ranks and wars of Damascus,

Once bore its head and stood beyond the stars.

For if storms from the most powerful quarter of Ocean

Should rush upon you, they will not be able by any means

To cross the path where Amandus set his noble feet—

Provided that you follow the commands of the noble Master.

Nor is there anything for you to fear amid the raging whirlpool,

With this leader of yours, who does not conquer the wicked

With weapons, but with merits renowned from here to the stars.

### 5

At the time when Prince Childeric governed the kingdom

And handled the reins he had seized in grievous war,

While the other nations roared in the struggle of Mars,

And swords returned swords, shield answered shield,

And brother oppressed brother, the son his father,

And savage devastation ravaged many peoples,

As a grave tempest swept across the whole world,

He did not let the whirlwind restrain him or bind his arms

With the bond of Justice; nor, overcome by so great a turmoil of affairs,

Did he abandon the work he had begun, burning with faithful gains.

But that humble man now sought the aforesaid king,

So that the king might lawfully provide him some small piece of land

On which he could erect the sacred buildings of the beautiful monastery

He had begun.

As soon as he asked, the prince granted it; and immediately,

[Col. 0960C] Since he was energetic in such matters,

He laid the foundations of the church with wise skill.

But while the Just One persisted there in his undertaking,

Mummulus, inflamed by the bitter torches of envy—

The city of Ozindinus, subject to him, whose seat

Was adorned with the rich grass of various flowers—

Was gravely indignant that the Saint had obtained the little place.

He spewed forth the poison conceived in his mind in fits of fury,

And sent his ministers, urged on by madness,

Bold in spirit and greatly strengthened in arms.

They sharpened their swords against the man who had been

The bearer of peace throughout the world,

Who had proclaimed the pastures of the heavenly kingdom.

Why do you, fierce enemy, resist him with such fraud

And persecute one beloved of God, his fosterling?

You had heard the treaties of peace for keeping the peace

Which the peaceful Master, as you climb toward the stars,

Had given you.

Why do you tear apart this pledge while devising empty schemes?

Why does such a criminal desire for crime possess you?

Would it not have been fitting to wipe away so many labors

And adorn the common good through shared work?

Who else will wage wars while you seek them, Bishop,

If neither human nature restrains your guilt

Nor order, rank, or love curbs you?

Look up: showers of lightning will come from the clouds,

And the heavenly whirlwind will calm your fury.

You will see angelic ranks, armed and assisting,

Bring abundant aid with victorious signs—

Bringing death by the weapons with which you now threaten him unjustly.”

Addressing the executioners whom he had sent to carry out his commands

[Col. 0961A] and to share likewise in the crime—

Men whom another’s mission had brought into guilt,

Who, thinking that by cunning deceit they could mislead

The man who was filled with a draught of pure water,

Falsely pretended in deceptive speech

That they could show the Saint suitable fields,

If he would accompany them with the purpose and intention of protecting them.

And although the crafty troop had feigned this with their mouths

And uttered such lying words to so great a Prophet,

Nothing was closed or hidden from him by God’s revelation;

Nothing concealed in the recesses of the body, nothing covered

In the chambers of the heart, escaped him.

In whose ears the mind resounded just as the tongue did.

Yet he himself did not resist the unjust bearers of crime

Or show his back to the savage ministers.

Nor did fear wandering through their unconquered spirits

Drive away their courage or leave their steadfast minds,

Since he was constantly burning with love of martyrdom.

And although the opportunity of martyrdom had now offered him his desire,

He was not deprived of the honor he had earned.

Here the power of Christ must be praised all the more,

Because it gave him the palm of victory freely, without the wound of death.

### 6

And now the pious victim had reached the brow of the mountain,

While the savage executioner, like the holy Isaac of old,

And like that evil, excessively cruel hand which, burning with fury,

Dragged the Author of our life to the mountain’s summit

To be hurled down—if it had possessed the power

That it possessed in its frenzied will.

So too here stood the Just One, gentle as a lamb.

Before wolves emptied of pity, suddenly from heaven

Dark clouds gathered and closed the eyes of the evil men.

Nor did the lamp of Phoebus shine with its proper order;

It withdrew its radiance from those who strove

To strip the lamp of its shining splendor,

Turning its rays into shadows.

The bright things fled from their eyes; broad night descended,

And a great storm fell, mingled with hail.

Therefore, prostrate upon the ground, they confessed their guilt

And the punishment due to the Just One, begging forgiveness.

The Just One bent down in adoration toward the earth,

Filled with love of pity,

And laid his limbs upon the grassy clods of earth.

Nor did he cease from his zeal and prayerful vow

Until the heavenly storms had submitted

And even the thunderclaps of the clouds had ceased to roar.

When the clear sky returned to those ministers,

They recognized how deservedly the Saint was to be revered with honor.

[Col. 0961D] “Go home, you who have been dismissed, and report what has happened to your master,

So that he may not send other executioners after you to Amandus.”

### 7

O man exceedingly beloved of God, for whom the heavens serve,

For whose aid the heavenly mechanism, roaring,

Prepares wars, withdraws the light, and threatens death!

Instead of trumpets, thunder; instead of weapons, fiery rain;

Instead of shields, the lofty firmament crashes and rumbles.

What wonder is it that earthly things obeyed your commands,

When the elements themselves are shaken and Olympus burns,

Whenever an unjust death is prepared for you,

The faithful hope of your own?

And although the things he had previously accomplished were sufficiently great,

[Col. 0962A] These, shining from the citadel of heaven, gleam still more brightly.

Beautiful everywhere, flashing in heaven, on earth, and upon the sea,

Look now, in pity, upon the faithful scattered abroad;

And by sacred prayers ask unceasing salvation for them,

So that, retaining unconquered strength in their hearts,

Neither evils may break us nor prosperity carry away our minds.

## CHAPTER III. Those punished with blindness and paralysis are healed through the aid of Saint Amandus.

### 8

The likeness of the journey, and the deeds that now follow,

Turn back the course of the poem; a worthy event is sung.

For mention must be made of a man suited to venerable praises.

While he preached the Gospel to all the people,

Unaware of loosening his attention from the labor he had begun

Or restoring his weary limbs with a little rest,

He traveled through the boundaries of the district of Beauvais.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] Thus the manuscript of Elnon; another has *Rossomtus*, but we noted above that later writers called it *Ressontum* or *Ressonum*.]

Rossontus is the place to which the Saint came, weary,

Where a modest stream flows along the banks, but is swollen with rich abundance,

With the plentiful produce of grain and the gift of Bacchus.

[Note: [Col. 0962D] In the margin of another manuscript was written “a little river.”]

Nor far from the tract through which the course of the Oronne runs

[Note: [Col. 0962D] Rather, of the Aronde, as noted above.]

There had been a woman deprived of both her lamps:

A true imitation of night lay beneath her darkened brow.

As the Just One approached and examined her condition closely,

He learned the causes and the time of her denied light,

And learned that by divinations she had sought the darkness she deserved, confessing that she had abandoned the leafy goddess.

A tree led her by the rigid curves of its branches,

A tree whose head rose up, producing for the farmers,

From its twisted growth, a deadly poison,

Which the rustic people had consecrated to their ancient enemy.

When the woman poured forth her complaints, lamenting and weeping,

The Saint returned these words from a compassionate heart:

“You report nothing surprising, woman blinded by guilt,

As you mourn dangers produced by your own offense.

But I marvel at how great is the clemency of Christ,

Whose exceedingly great patience still bears with you.

Although, in offense against Him, you serve your own enemy,

You retain a deserved injury and a just shame.

But if you still have concern for the salvation you have lost,

Then give your assent to my words.

Go quickly and boldly to the pestilential goddess where she stands.

Strengthen your spirit with steadfast hope, and with a double-bladed axe

Strike the tree you worship, so that it may now fall to the earth,

Driven down by the axe.

For I promise that this will happen quickly,

If you believe, and that you will receive happy fulfillment of your wishes:

You will obtain swift healing for your limbs and your soul.”

The woman did not delay. With a girl as her guide,

She hurried to cut down the tree-goddess,

And to consign its leafy crown, cut down and stripped of religion,

To the flames.

The Saint perceived the venerable light of faith shining inwardly;

He carved the sign worthy of celebration, the cross,

In the middle of her forehead between her two temples.

At once a conspicuous fire sent down from heaven shone,

And the windows of her forehead, previously closed, opened.

[Col. 0963A] Thus the venerable hand brings in radiance and leaves it behind;

Night abandons the eyes, and day, exiled until then, illuminates their orbs.

Amid the darkness, as dawn pours forth its twilight,

The enlightened brow marvels at the serene rays,

Though the ancient sins that had previously grown there had taught her to despise them—harmful wounds indeed.

Leaving her unharmed, the Saint dismissed her,

So that she might go and see the rest of her friends,

He who had granted her so great an honor.

### 9

The manifest truth of the story contains a mystical meaning,

Shaded beneath forests of darkness.

I shall attempt, speaking in hastening verse, to compose it:

So that an ancient harmony, sounding with a new breath,

May fill these dry verses with heavenly inspiration.

The ancient tree was the one through which Eve lost life,

Though it bore the name of life, had she abstained from sins.

[Col. 0963B] Alas! Deceived too greatly by the serpent’s persuasion,

She fell into death when she took what was forbidden to eat,

Rushing, foolishly trusting, through gain toward certain loss.

But when Life died upon the wood of the cross,

The diseases of sins and the transgression of the forbidden fruit

Were atoned for.

You see the ancient form in the present trunk,

While the woman, serving its foolish omens,

Desires to know the future and loses even the present,

And, blinded, receives deserved darkness instead of light.

But the Saint came and drove away the dark errors.

He taught her to cut down the tree’s twisted growth with iron—

That iron of which the glorious John the Baptist sang:

The splendid axe stands at the root of the tree,

Cutting away its harmful sap with flashing edge,

[Col. 0963C] And through pious remedies restoring sight swiftly.

Thus Amandus, the anointed physician, restores the light to her eyes.

### 10

And this deed, by which the Just One completed

A proclamation heaped with praises and magnificent achievements,

Let us properly sing.

Among the numerous flock whom he made the Lord’s fosterlings,

To bear the divine yoke and serve the Thunderer,

There was one set above the others in honor of the groups,

So that he might provide food and all suitable things for his companions.

But when, swollen with pride, he disdained to obey the commands of his master,

And refused to carry wine to his brothers

Using the wagons that bore it,

And told the Saint that the wagons he had requested were lacking to him,

The unhappy man was struck down by the danger of a sudden illness.

A savage paralysis, cruelly ravaging his limbs,

Seized him and ruled with relaxed reins over his powerless members.

Quickly shaking the excessive stiffness from his raised neck,

It leveled him with his flaccid limbs.

And the bitter plague, weighing down the wretched body

With deadly destruction, bound it on every side with savage chains.

The veins dried up as the stream of blood was exhausted,

And his languid arms withered as the nerves contracted.

As he more and more frequently breathed out his slender breath through his nostrils,

He repeated mute, miserable sobs.

Already the warmth of his soul, advancing, was crossing

The gates of life.

Yet Amandus, the physician, was still alive,

And through his merits healing was to be granted to the sick man.

He was carried by boat, accompanied by the company serving the monastery of the brothers.

[Col. 0964A] When the proper offices had been completed,

The Saint sat at table, hungry for food,

For meals, yet nourished by heaven.

The Father of the disciples, recognizing the pitiable wound,

Smiled gently and spoke from a compassionate heart:

“He suffers greatly, but he still deserves greater things,

Since empty boasting and contempt make him rebellious toward us,

Because he is excessively devoted to them.”

He then chose a priest from the kindly people of the brothers

And ordered him to be the bearer of the desired remedy.

Giving him a portion of bread and also a cup of wine, he said:

“Go, and carry these instructions to the monk lying there.

Let him drink the cup together with the fragment of bread sent to him.

When tomorrow has scattered the shadows of night,

And the flame-haired sun has shone forth in its pure rising,

I shall hasten to see him with swift steps.

Shaken free of his weakness and driven from his own bed,

Let him rise unharmed, his nerves made firm, I command,

And come forth to meet us with a healthy body.”

Why delay with words, when medicine does not delay?

The Father’s blessing, sent to the monk, restored his life,

And at the physician’s command he recovered his strength.

At once he sprang up with all his power—

The earth, already almost finished, straining to stand upon its pillars—

And, without delaying, the traveler hastened along the commanded path.

As the holy man approached, he went out to meet him,

Came forward healthy, and returned abundant thanks.

While his tongue formed words by striking the palate,

Speech sounded clearly from the speaker’s mouth:

The corpse had risen, life having returned.

[Col. 0964C] The company of the brothers sang of it with praise and wonder.

Yet, admonished to change his arrogant ways,

He went safely, with pardon, to his companions, who marveled.

There is material here for weaving a triple thread,

But the page, already filled with many verses, overflows.

The final conclusion of the book allows no more.

And although I had tried to compose the man’s deeds in many words,

I confess that I have not been able to record them all.

For he did not accomplish such small things that I could adequately

Tell them in writings or bring them forth in verse:

The gift of faith, merit, and kindly conduct;

How great his care for the sick, how great his grace;

His virtue, battles, labor, endurance, victory, and triumph.

## CHAPTER IV. The death and burial of Saint Amandus. The elevation of his body. Epilogue.

[Col. 0964D]

### 11

Thus far my speech, hastening toward its end,

Has been led along a difficult path.

But now, turning aside, you bend the journey begun

And turn your swelling reins elsewhere.

Perhaps because the deeds speak of something somewhat sad,

Alas! there is one adorned with radiant splendor, blessed,

Whose excellent conduct we have described up to this point,

How, passing through the gate of death into life,

He was to be placed in the heavenly court above.

Fearing to disperse and to compose the end in a tearful song,

I hesitate to bring the text, drawn out to its conclusion, to an end.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] The manuscript of Elnon has “shame.”]

If you shrink from saying that he has died, say that he lives through the ages:

[Col. 0965A] For he lives, properly joined to the angelic ranks.

Dying, he left sadness and lamentation throughout the fields;

He made joy abundant in the heavenly citadels.

Earth holds earth; dust joins dust.

The dead man, resting in the tomb, shines through his gifts.

But his beautiful soul has been joined to the heavenly choirs.

### 12

Indeed, among monasteries scattered through countryside and towns,

A structure loftier and better has raised itself above our Helnon.

The place is named from the river

Which receives the Scarb and pours it forth purer in its broad bosom.

The two streams flow forth like another Jordan from twin springs

And, mingling, join their sweet kisses with their lips.

There the Saint retains a tomb enriched with virtues.

That place, adorned with immense honor, shines:

Peace, piety, goodness, and concord prevail there,

[Col. 0965B] Together with hope, faith, brotherly love, and supreme affection.

Retaining every good, it reaches toward the heights of heaven;

Avoiding every evil, it drives away harmful dangers.

Fearing no peril, wherever every weak and sick person

Brings back the vows he has sought, with faith running into their midst.

O place! O happy turf with fruitful growth!

Blessed with every good, flourish forever through the ages.

With garment, sheep, harvest, ox, bird, honey, bee, river-fish,

Acorn, swine, flower, leaf, rain, grass, and vine,

You prosper in all these under such a cultivator.

You retain all these things under this Patron, who makes you fruitful.

The rivers give fish; the fields yield their earthly produce.

You lack no food, since you overflow with grain.

For the inhabitant takes in hunger not through his mouth but through his ears.

[Col. 0965C] We sing a wondrous event, which requires believing hearts:

Here you may know that the Blessed One can live after death.

[Note: [Col. 0965D] We said that this elevation occurred in the year 123 after his death, §15.]

A course of a hundred years had passed, turning toward its completion,

The number being equally divided and the same.

When the venerable man had passed to the heavenly court,

And his body had been lifted after the tomb’s mass had been broken apart,

It was found unharmed; and a tooth, removed from his mouth,

Poured forth drops of blood as though from a living body.

Let anyone deny this easily who does not believe

That sacred fluid flowed with blood from the body of Jesus

When the soldier’s spear struck Him fixed upon the cross.

If you seek witnesses, wavering in the power of faith,

Come here, I urge you; you will see various bands of men

And many elders venerable in age.

The vessel, too, can display the blood it received.

[Col. 0965D]

### 13

O father, shepherd, teacher, nourisher, lover!

How this place shines, rich in so many honors,

Which the kingdom of heaven, received in venerable peace,

Exalts, adorns, praises, honors, and embellishes!

Intercede for your devoted servants in their dealings for pardon,

And grant your fosterlings fellowship in the light.

And when God comes and shakes the whole world,

When swift fire has burned the trembling earth,

And the sun, its light withdrawn like a sack, is deprived of brightness,

And the lunar globe is enclosed in a dark covering,

[Col. 0966A] When sulfur, pitch, horror, the torturer, torments, and the furnace

Are present, and the most just Judge sits there,

And the company of the saints occupies its adorned seats,

When, among those nobles, you sit as the high Arbiter of the world

With the consuls assembled at the tribunal,

And just judgment is opened in written books,

Alas, what shall I do then? What Saint will cover me

From the anger that presses upon me?

What defense will rescue me from such disasters?

Under whose mountain’s shelter shall I hide

So that I am not burned by the cruel flames?

What covering of righteous deeds will then remove me

And separate me from the fire of so great a furnace?

I pray, holy Father, have mercy then on your poet,

And join your Milo to your right-hand throngs.

It will be enough if I have earned even the last little place.

[Col. 0966B] Yet I, poor wretch, have great confidence

That this work can extinguish the dreadful flames—

A work written in a lowly form, but by a faithful poet.

The poem is a small honor, foolishly composed,

But great are the vows of my love in praising you,

Excellent Shepherd.

And if you look upon the innermost chambers of my heart,

You will find in these things a devoted will toward you.

As I judge, a small ability will not be condemned.

Honor of the world, and our glory, gracious Father, farewell.

Before your tomb we shall continually sing:

“Hail!”

You who are worthy, hail, and grant us the power to fare well.

### 14

Behold, gracious God, Sower and Redeemer of humankind,

We have offered this work in praise of the illustrious bishop,

And I pray that it may be acceptable in your sight.

Everyone brings his gifts, cleansed, into the church.

One shines in understanding like gold;

Another, carrying his gift of silver in honorable eloquence,

Grows radiant.

The choir of singers sings with vocal bronze.

One offers scarlet, twice dyed with love;

Another offers the twisted byssus of bodily self-denial.

Here one brings incorruptible wood, bearing an immaculate body;

Another shines through pious deeds like beautiful olive wood,

And, steeped in goodness, exhales the fragrance of incense.

But I, a poor, needy, destitute, trembling, confused, and anxious man,

Have joined the generous assemblies.

I bring nothing pleasing that may lawfully be placed upon the altar.

Therefore shame paints my cheeks red.

I offer this poem woven from goat-hair,

And myself as a goat to be mortified for my guilt.

[Col. 0966D] But you who blessed the widow for her smallest coin,

Receive with a kindly face the gifts I offer.

May your praise endure in our mouth forever,

You who alone possess the heavenly kingdom through the ages.

Dear one, my journey is completed; rest, traveler.

[Note: [Col. 0965D] Added: “The Life of Blessed Amandus, Confessor of Christ, has ended; it was transferred from prose into heroic verse in metrical style. It contains four little books, in which there are 1,818 verses.”]

# VERSES OF WULFAIUS

[Note: [Col. 0966D] Wulfaius, a monk, also Wulfagus, a fellow student of Milo under Haiminus. In later times, Claudius Robert, writing about the monastery of Resbacum, reports that there was a Wulfadus who was abbot of that monastery; Robert himself and John Chenu also mention another Vulphadus or Vulphandus, archbishop of Bourges. We judge these to be different from this man.]

## IN CONFIRMATION OF THE WORK

You ask, Milo, that poems deservedly ascending the starry fields

May flourish through our favor.

Their power is so great, and they shine with such honor,

That they cannot be spoken by our eloquence.

A golden substance is encircled by white silver,

And the shining mass adorns its own eloquence.

There is no need for our speech to adorn them.

They flourish through the honor of him whose love makes them shine.

These things the archbishop, renowned throughout the whole world,

[Col. 0967A] Hingmarus, raised up in words of excellence.

[Note: [Col. 0967B] Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, held office from A.D. 835 to 822.]

These things Father Adalardus, the glory of the people of Cambrai,

Raised up with pious speech.

Theodoricus, rejoicing, blessed these poems with such praise:

“Poems running forth upon an exceedingly sweet-sounding plectrum,

Worthy to shine in heaven, blessed and acceptable to God.”

[Note: [Col. 0967B] Blessed Theodoricus, bishop of Cambrai, from A.D. 832 to 863. We shall discuss him on 5 August.]

The distinguished Bishop Emmo offered them their support,

[Note: [Col. 0967B] Emmo, or Immo, bishop of Noyon, killed by the Normans in A.D. 859 or shortly afterward.]

Affixing beautiful letters with his own fingers.

[Col. 0968A] This father and shepherd, most venerable to all the clergy,

The gentle Adalardus, raised them up with pious speech.

[Note: [Col. 0967B] There were various abbots named Adalardus at that time. Under the emperor Lothair, the abbacy of Saint Vedast came into the hands of Count Adalardus; indeed, in A.D. 852 the monks were under his authority, as stated above in the history of the miracles of Saint Vedast. Count Adalardus also presided over the monastery of Saint Quentin, in the thirteenth year of the reign of Charles the Bald, according to Heremaeus. Another was Adalardus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Bertin among the Sithivenses, who died in the monastery of Elnon in A.D. 864. Iperius discusses him in the manuscript Chronicle of Bertin, chapters 13–15. John Cognatus writes from the Chronicle of Elnon, Book II of the History of Tournai, that at the same time an abbot Adalardus presided over the people of Elnon and died in A.D. 863; unless he has been inserted by error into some records, we suspect that he is the same man. Somewhat earlier were Saint Adalardus, abbot of the Frankish Corbie, whose life we gave on 2 January, and his disciple Adalardus, the first abbot of Saxon Corbie.]

This Haiminus, your master and mine,

[Note: [Col. 0968B] Father Haiminus, a disciple of Alcuin and a monk of Vedast, by whose pen we gave above the miracles of Saint Vedast; there we said that he died in A.D. 843.]

Under whose guidance no one takes devious paths, gave his support.

Teudingus, small in body but great in the sharpness of his mind,

[Note: [Col. 0968B] He is discussed below in an ancient fragment of the Chronicle of Blandinium, where it is reported that in A.D. 850 Teutingus was ordained on 8 March.]

Offered his right hand himself.

What house, I ask, could collapse, supported by such columns?

It fears no rivers and dreads no winds.

Yet, so that the number seven might be complete,

I am the seventh column in your roof, Milo.

Your poems are indeed worthy of our patron,

Worthy, in our judgment, of him whose honor makes them gleam.

Now gird yourself with Virgil’s fine buskin, won by theft,

But surpass the false poet by singing what is true.

[Col. 0967]

# ADDITION TO THE BOOK OF THE LIFE OF SAINT AMANDUS

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict.)*
[Col. 0967C] 1. After the preceding little book on the virtues of the Saint had been published, it should be understood what sort of man he was and in what honor he was held among men, although he himself always desired to avoid the honors of the world. For many kings and queens, and numerous distinguished men, earnestly strove to show him the greatest veneration and favor; while he was still living in the body, they enriched him not a little from their own resources. Recognizing him to be the servant of God, they rejoiced to present to him, with the most faithful devotion, villas, estates, and their own inheritances. In this way the man of God, Amandus, with the greatest skill and diligence, worked most zealously to build monasteries for faithful men sincerely desirous of serving Christ. For the monastery called Blandinium, situated in the fortress of Ghent, [Note: [Col. 0967C] Besides the monastery of Blandinium, Saint Amandus built in the fortress of Ghent another monastery called Ganda, later named Saint Bavo’s. For Marcianas, consult the Acts of Saint Rictrudis; for Lutosa in Hainaut and Rotnacensis in Brabant, which are now collegiate churches of canons, consult Balderic, bishop of Cambrai and Arras, *Chronicle* II, chapter 43 and following. Moreover, at the counsel and prompting of Saint Amandus, Saint Vincent, also called Madelgarius, founded Sognies in Brabant on the River Senne; Saint Gertrude founded Nivelles, likewise in Brabant; Saint Gistenus founded Cellas in Hainaut, now adorned with its founder’s name; Saint Waldetrudis founded Mons; Saint Vincent, her husband, founded Hautmont; Saint Aldegundis founded Maubeuge; and others founded other monasteries, as is read in their respective Acts.] as well as another called Marcianas; also that to which the holy man himself gave the name Lutosa; Rotnace, which is almost adjacent to the aforesaid place; and the cell called Barisiacus, [Note: [Col. 0968C] In the village of Barisiacus, Barysy, in the diocese of Laon, about a league distant from the towns of Coucy and Châlons and from the River Oise, there still exists a priory belonging to the abbey of Elnone, or Saint Amandus. Andrew, [Col. 0968D] a disciple of Saint Amandus and later abbot of Elnone, was appointed its first superior by Amandus himself.]—this place, together with its adjoining dependencies, King Hilderic [Note: [Col. 0968D] Who this Hilderic and Queen Himnechild were is disputed among scholars. Henschenius, in his Commentary on the Life of Saint Amandus, no. 10 and elsewhere, considers this Childeric to be the son of Sigebert, who, together with his mother Himnechild, ruled the Austrasians after Sigebert’s death. Others maintain that Childeric was the son of Clovis II, and that Himnechild should be replaced either by his mother Balthild or by Blidechild, Childeric’s own wife.] and Queen Himnechild appear to have granted to him. Almost everyone knows that all these establishments were built by this man of God. In them he placed brothers or monks under the rule of the discipline, set abbots over them, and arranged everything properly; finally, after the monastery of Elnone had been built, he served Christ there happily with his companions until the day of his most holy death.

Accordingly, he also obtained great familiarity and reverence with Martin, the most holy and blessed pope of the holy and apostolic city and see of Rome, who was the seventy-fifth after the Apostle Peter to govern the Roman Church. Among other gifts worthy of such affection, this apostolic bishop sent him a volume of the synodal decrees that he himself had issued, as a most vigilant shepherd, keeping watch with the utmost care during the night of this age over the Lord’s flock entrusted to him, against the wolves and heretical predators of the Church: Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria; Sergius, bishop of Constantinople; Pyrrhus and Paul, patriarchs and his successors. These men successively joined one another in this contest and dared to profess one operation in Christ our Lord and God, both in divinity and humanity, whereas the orthodox faith of the Catholic Church piously confesses two natures and operations united in Christ. Thus each form, the divine and the human, performs in the one person of our Savior what properly belongs to it, in communion with the other: the Word performing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines forth in miracles, while the other submits to insults. Thus it is the property of Christ’s divine nature to will and perform divine things divinely; while it is the property of his human nature to will and perform human things humanly, so that it may be shown that in one person, but in two natures, he is naturally God and man. This is the pillar of orthodox faith established by the holy Council of Chalcedon and confirmed by the whole chorus of the Catholic Fathers.

Therefore, for the destruction of the heresy written above and the overthrow of the pride that raised itself against the knowledge of God, as well as for the confirmation of the divine doctrines, the aforesaid Martin, advocate of piety, as is read in the *Acts of the Pontiffs*, sent for and gathered one hundred and five bishops in the city of Rome and held a synod according to the statutes of the orthodox Fathers, near the Lateran episcopal residence. The bishops were seated, the priests stood by, and the deacons and the entire clergy were present. They condemned Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria, and Sergius, bishop of Constantinople; also Pyrrhus, his successor; and Paul, patriarch of the same city. Inflated by the spirit of pride, these men had dared to oppose the correct doctrines of the holy Church of God and had attempted to attach an invention of novelty to the immaculate faith. Since, in their haste to exclude it, they had contrived a confusion of heretical doctrines against the Catholic Church of God, they were struck by the punishment of anathema.

Moreover, Pope Martin the most blessed made copies of the aforesaid synodal volume and sent them throughout all the regions of East and West, distributing them through the hands of orthodox believers. He also sent a copy, issued on papyrus sheets, to our most beloved Father and bishop, Amandus, so that through his zealous diligence the proclamations of that most holy and undefiled faith might be made known among the churches of Gaul. At the end of this volume—which forms one body but is divided into five sections of books—the aforementioned Martin, bishop of the holy apostolic see, also sent a special letter to the man of God Amandus. Through it he displayed sufficiently and abundantly the synodal decrees and his benevolent affection toward him; he warned him not to withdraw from his pious purpose, constrained by the anguish of his afflictions; and, with exhortatory words, he sought to encourage him to endure the tribulations with which hostile priests, deacons, and other ministers of priestly office burdened him because of their opposition to the divine religion. Later, when the incorrigible excesses of these wicked men’s crimes increased for the worse—as is evident to those who read the book of his life—he abandoned the episcopal chair entrusted to him and, shaking the dust from his feet against those who despised his preaching, according to the Lord’s evangelical command, he departed to other places.

Furthermore, the aforesaid apostolic bishop took care to commend to the care of the same Father Amandus Sigebert, son of Dagobert, namely king of the Franks. Once, while still an infant and not yet exceeding forty days of age, when he was being blessed by the blessed Amandus, he pronounced the sweet word “Amen” clearly and aloud after the sacred prayer had ended—a word he had not yet learned to utter through bodily use—in order to reveal the merit of so great a tutor. To confirm the assertion of our foregoing statement by clearing away the cloud of uncertainty, we have thought it fitting to append to this discourse the aforesaid letter of that same pope addressed to the blessed Amandus. Its wording is as follows:

“Martin to his most beloved brother Amandus.

“Your Fraternity …,” etc. (See this letter among the works of Pope Martin I, *Patrologia*, vol. LXXXVII, col. 135.)

## Heading Concerning the Death of the Blessed Confessor Amandus

In the year 661 of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Note: [Col. 0969D] This calculation, however diligently investigated by the author, cannot stand. For since, according to Baudemundus (see *Patrologia* under the year 679) and Milo himself below, Amandus reached the reign of Theodoric and survived Childeric, who was not killed before the year 613, Amandus’s death must certainly be placed later than this year. The chronology of Amandus’s life must therefore be arranged as follows. Amandus died during the reign of Theodoric, who succeeded Childeric, and, according to the statements of the praised authors, on a Sunday falling on 6 February, marked by the letter B. During the entire reign of King Theodoric, Sunday fell on 6 February only in the years 679 and 690. The latter year places Amandus’s death later; therefore the latter must be retained, as Charles Le Cointe rightly determined.] in the fourth indiction, with an epact of fifteen, a fourth concurrent, the term on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, Easter on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the moon twenty-one, on the eighth day before the Ides of February, on a Sunday, with the moon in its first phase, Saint Amandus died at approximately ninety years of age.

## Argument Concerning the Time When the Blessed Confessor Amandus Was Born or Died

For the full understanding of our readers, we have judged it necessary to insert into this account certain details concerning the time of the birth, the course of life, and the death of the blessed bishop of Christ, Amandus. As we have investigated these matters by probable reasoning from histories and chronicles that agree with one another, he was born in the year 571 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, on the Nones of May, in the province of Aquitaine, in a district of that region called Herbatilicus, to his father Serenus and his mother Amantia. This was the seventh year in which Justin the Younger, successor of Justinian, held the imperial power by public right together with his wife Sophia. At that time John, pope of the Roman Church and sixty-third in the order of its pontiffs, was vigorously governing the chair of that city in the eighth year of his episcopate.

From the year of the birth of this man of God, Amandus, until his death, sixteen pontiffs of the Roman see are counted, beginning with John, in whose eighth year of pontificate he was born, as follows: first, John himself; second, Benedict; third, Pelagius; fourth, Gregory, the remarkable teacher of the Church. At the beginning of Gregory’s ordination, the man of God Amandus was in his twenty-second year; at Gregory’s death he was nearly thirty-five. That year was 605 from the birth of the Lord [Col. 0971C], and the second year of the reign of the Caesar Phocas, as the venerable priest Bede reports in his chronicles.

To continue the calculation begun: Gregory’s successor, fifth, was Sabinian; sixth, Boniface; seventh, another Boniface; eighth, Deusdedit; ninth, Boniface; tenth, Honorius; eleventh, Severinus; twelfth, John; thirteenth, Theodore; fourteenth, Martin, very familiar with the blessed Amandus; fifteenth, Eugenius; sixteenth, Vitalian. In the third year of Vitalian’s pontificate the blessed Amandus died, on the eighth day before the Ides of February. Thus, counting from the year 571 of the Lord’s incarnation—which was the eighth year of Pope John’s episcopate—to the year 661 of the Lord, which was the third year of the episcopate of Pope Vitalian [Note: [Col. 0971D] The author places the beginning of Vitalian’s pontificate in the year 658; Baronius places it in 655.], when Saint Amandus died, ninety years of life are found for the aforesaid patron, during which he completed the course of his present life.

Likewise, if one reviews the emperors of the empire, one will find seven who held imperial office during the lifetime of the aforesaid Father Amandus, in this order: first Justin the Younger, successor of Justinian, in whose seventh year of reign he was born; second Tiberius; third Maurice; fourth Phocas. In the second year of Phocas’s empire, as we have already said, which was the year 605 of the Lord, Pope Gregory died. After him the blessed Amandus lived fifty-six years. Fifth among the rulers of the Roman Empire was Heraclius; sixth, Constantine [Note: [Col. 0971D] The author omits Heraclonas, son of Constantine and brother of the other Constantine, or Constans.]; seventh, Constantine of the same name. In the twenty-third year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0971D] Therefore, according to the author’s calculation, Constantine began his reign in the year 639 of Christ. Fredegar supports this calculation in *Chronicle*, chapter 81, where, likewise omitting Heraclonas because of his brief reign, he states that Constantine gave way to Constans in the second year of the reign of Chlothar the Younger, although Baronius begins the rule of Constans in 641.]—which was the year 661 of the Lord’s incarnation—the aforesaid Father completed the final period of his present age.

If anyone wishes to inquire also into the Frankish kings who held royal authority during his lifetime—although, because historical investigation is incomplete, this may not seem easy to accomplish—he will find, examining the matter more attentively and with lively judgment, that the following men held royal office among the Franks during his lifetime, in this order: first Chilperic; second Lothar; third Dagobert; fourth Sigebert; and fifth Lodoveus, his brother. Lodoveus’s sons were Lothar, Hilderic, and Theodoric. When Lothar died in his youth, and afterward Hilderic was killed by the leading men of the Franks, Theodoric recovered the royal dignity that he had recently lost when he was tonsured. Documents that are still preserved among us teach us that the blessed Amandus lived until Theodoric’s time.

During those same days Ebroin, mayor of the palace, inflicted wicked deceits and calamities upon the Frankish kingdom, increasing his criminal offenses day by day until his belated death. When the kings and the whole people had been thrown into confusion, he finally crowned all his evils by torturing the blessed Leodegarius with various torments and making him a martyr of Christ.

If anyone wishes to investigate this discourse, drawn from the smallness of our intellect, as though it were inadequate and insufficiently supported by probable evidence, we advise him first carefully to fix in his memory the year of the death of the aforesaid confessor of Christ, Amandus, which was the year 661 from the Lord’s birth. For in that year, as our predecessors left written testimony to us not only in books but also on stones, so that it might not be erased, he passed from this world to the Lord. Then, with this number firmly established in his mind as a foundation, let him calculate backward from it the number of the ninety years that he lived; thus he will gradually arrive at the year 571 of the Lord’s birth, in which the aforesaid Father was born.

Having carefully committed these two calculations to memory—the one of his birth and the other of his death—let him consult the histories of the kings who held royal authority at that time, as well as the chronicles of the venerable Fathers and the book published concerning the pontiffs of the apostolic see. Let him examine them on every side with the alertness of a person looking both before and behind, and diligently consider which apostolic bishops, emperors, or princes were alive in the body while the blessed Amandus still lived. Even if, after all this labor, he cannot discover the truth of the matter, he will nevertheless, I think, not reject these statements of ours, whatever their worth.

[Col. 0973]

## Sermon on the Translation of Saint Amandus

How the body of the blessed Amandus was translated to the place where it now rests, and concerning the dedication of the basilica or the ordination of his episcopate, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November.

[Col. 0973A] The recurring course of time itself announces that the present day is to be celebrated by the religious assembly with the solemn devotion of a most holy festival. Since many among this people are still entirely ignorant of its meaning, we have not considered it useless to disclose to them the knowledge of so great and pleasing a celebration. We therefore believe it worthy, indeed necessary, that those who celebrate it but do not know what or why they celebrate should gain knowledge of the matter, and that those who have until now honored it with festive devotion while knowing little about it should now learn to cultivate and venerate it with greater glory and reverence.

Since the little book of the Life of the thrice-blessed and beloved confessor of Christ, Amandus, is known to have explained sufficiently and fully what sort of man and how great he was while he was still held in the hardships of this mortality, by what signs of virtue he shone amid the dark and winding paths of this age, how far he enlightened the world, and with what end he migrated from the dark Egypt of this age, with the pillar of the law and the protection of divine grace leading him through the stations of pious progress toward the promised land—which signifies the homeland of the living—we shall set these matters aside for now and direct the labor of our discourse toward investigating some of the many great works of God that divine clemency performed concerning him and his little body after his death.

What we report we heard faithfully from Fathers who faithfully reported it. We entrust their testimony to almighty Christ, before whom we believe that what has already occurred is, as it were, present, and that what is present is future. We know that falsehood, because it proceeds from evil, displeases him.
