The merits of the blessed man do not need to be supported by lies in order to appear glorious to men; rather, they ought to be believed without any doubt to be greater than words can explain. Since, however, we have touched upon these matters in a preliminary way—not in proportion to their dignity, which is impossible, but according to the poverty of our small intellect—let us now, with divine clemency leading us, set out upon the path we have undertaken.

In the year 661 of the Lord’s incarnation, when the Creator and Redeemer, taking pity on the errors of the world, deigned to unite himself to human nature, Amandus, beloved of God and of all good things, after many distinguished good works, ascended to the court of heaven to reign eternally with Christ, whom he had devotedly served. Nor was it undeserved that the heavenly palaces opened to him as he entered, for while on earth he had sung of them with tireless voice:

“How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts!
My soul longs and faints for them.”

He came to rest in the ninetieth year of his age, in the month of February, struck by the affliction of fever, and on a Sunday. Death, which was the road to his homeland and the departure from this present life, became for him the entrance into the life that follows and never ends. Freed from the manifold hardships of this world, he deserved to appear shining before the sight of his Lord, with his lamps full of oil—that is, fertile in holy virtues.

He was buried with the honor due from the faithful in the monastery he had built, which received the name Elnone from the name of the little river flowing there. The Frankish prince Dagobert had once granted this place to the man of God with willing, though unworthy, devotion, as a possession not unworthy of a king, established by the confirmed sanction of law. Although he had learned of Amandus’s holiness through the frequent testimony of many, that same prince nevertheless deserved to recognize it more clearly—as is read in the little book of his Life—when, in the presence of the prince, Christ made his saint wondrously speak through the infant Sigebert, contrary to nature and because of his infancy.

Since he had cultivated and honored Amandus in the aforesaid place more than the other establishments he had founded, his little body was also committed to the tomb by the service of his disciples, as he decreed in a solemn testament written for this purpose (see *Patrologia*, vol. LXXXVII, col. 1271), which is still preserved in the archives of our monastery.

He was not, however, placed in the very basilica where he now rests, but in another basilica that still exists, dedicated in the name of the chief of the apostles, Peter. Since that basilica, because of its small size, appeared unsuitable for the tomb of so great a bishop, and was also inaccessible to the other sex because of the monks’ dwellings, it seemed appropriate to the frequent assembly of religious men that another basilica, superior in size, should be built, one sufficient for the multitude of common people gathering from both sexes. When the work of that building had been completed through the expenditure of those devoted to God, the time came when he was to be transferred.

In those days there still lived among human affairs the venerable confessor of Christ and worker of wondrous deeds, Eligius, [Note: [Col. 0973D] It is clear that Milo’s calculation is also mistaken here. For, according to Saint Audoenus, *Life of Saint Eligius* II.1, Eligius remained alive only until the beginning of the reign of the younger Lothar. He therefore did not reach the reign of King Theodoric, during which Amandus died. Certainly, in the commonly circulated testament of Saint Amandus, Bishop Mummolenus, Eligius’s successor, is said to have subscribed. Therefore Amandus’s elevation cannot be attributed to Eligius. Nor can it be attributed to Mummolenus himself, who died around the year 684, approximately eleven years before Saint Amandus’s body was moved from its place; this occurred in the sixteenth year after his death, as is read below.] who had been most closely acquainted with the blessed bishop Amandus while he was alive and was not ignorant of his holiness. Eligius had come to the city of Noviomagus for the dedication of the new church and for the transfer of the holy body’s relics into it; for he excelled in the vigilant administration of his diocese with great ingenuity.

When he removed the cover from the sacred tomb, he discovered an unexpected miracle of divine power: the little body of the holy Father was incorrupt, just as it had been placed there sixteen years earlier. Then, astonished at the novelty of so unexpected a miracle, he gave thanks to the supreme Divinity, because the holiness that had shone in glory was not hidden in the dead man.

Lest this prodigy perhaps seem incredible to anyone, there is still someone who confirms that in our own time he saw something even more marvelous in the most sacred body of this holy man. Whoever wishes to read the account of the elevation of his incorrupt corpse, however poor our work may be, can learn of it in another sermon. If spices prepared by the art of perfumers prevent corpses from decaying after death, although they are merely human, it is much more fitting to believe that the merits of so great a patron, manifested by signs of wondrous works, were able to preserve his members—the vessels, so to speak, in which they had dwelt—undefiled.

The little body of the blessed bishop Amandus was therefore carried into the dwelling of the basilica prepared for him and dedicated on that same day. There it was guarded by the service of attendants until the following day, when, after the aforesaid bishop Eligius had completed the solemn celebration of the Mass, it provided a great spectacle for the entire people gathered for these obsequies.

Placed in the middle of the church before the altar, the honorable body was displayed for all standing around to contemplate; its venerable face was uncovered and shown to the crowds who desired to look upon it; and his holy feet and hands, bearers of peace and workers of virtues, were permitted to be kissed.

The greatness of so marvelous a deed reveals how great the astonishment mixed with joy must have been. The worshipers of Christ were filled with indescribable joy when the two bishops, Amandus and Eligius, illustrious in rank and merit, like two heavenly lights of the world, filling heaven and earth with the rays of their virtues, stood before the divine altar and bestowed the assistance of their prayers upon the surrounding crowd.

One of them had overcome the tyranny of the ancient enemy and was already triumphing with Christ, his King, in heavenly glory; the other was laboring amid the various contests of this world for the same cause, like an invincible athlete. One of them, like a veteran soldier, was already reviewing without toil the rewards that never fail; the other remained burdened by the anxiety of sweat amid the many labors and manifold dangers of this life. One, in accordance with his episcopal office and his customary manner, rested after completing his ministry; the other, with the solemnities not yet concluded, was acting as a bishop and invoking Christ, the Bishop of bishops.

As the little body of God’s servant Amandus gave off the fragrance of incorruption both of its members and of its merits, those who had doubted the greatness of his signs while he lived saw in his dead body what filled them with manifold fear and anxiety. Those who remembered that they had not obeyed his salutary admonitions when they heard them lamented with the deepest sorrow that they had treated them lightly. But those who had adhered to his teaching when he announced the commandments of life rejoiced that they had both heard them with their ears and practiced them in their actions.

When the aforesaid bishop Eligius judged that he had satisfied the crowds, although they still desired more, he entrusted the most precious treasure of the deposit—the little body—to the deeper earth, as was then customary, hiding it so that the opportunity of finding it would be denied to all who did not seek it piously.

Those who were present celebrated the dignity of that translation and burial with solemn observances, according to their wishes, and established by salutary decrees that their descendants should celebrate it as well: namely, the dedication of the sacred basilica and the memorable prodigy of the corpse carried there on that same day. To this day we celebrate it annually with due honor on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, when a numerous crowd of people gathers from all around for these solemnities.

When everything had been arranged, and all that pertained to the adornment of the place or the support of the monastic order had been suitably and properly disposed according to their resources, each of the faithful returned joyfully to his own home, giving thanks to the holy and undivided Trinity for its indescribable gifts, by which from the beginning of the world it has deigned to show mercy to all who seek it in truth.

We have, as we believe, explained the reason for today’s festival and, in these very few words, have made clear, however inadequately, what we celebrate in it: namely, the dedication of the sacred basilica and the memorable translation into it of the bishop of Christ, Amandus.

Moreover, so that his venerable solemnity might not be lacking a threefold significance, a third cause coincides with the celebration mentioned above: the assumption of episcopal dignity. For on this day we reverently commemorate the ordination of our venerable patron and his being given from heaven as a bishop for the salvation of many, under the direction of heavenly mercy.

Let us therefore celebrate this with the utmost devotion and honor, and let us seek him as the helper and intercessor of our prayers. For it is believed that, now placed with Christ, he can obtain very much in the heavenly seats, since while he lived on earth he tirelessly strove to serve Christ in every good work.

From the earliest toys of his childhood he chose to serve the divine offices and to obey with his whole heart the life-giving commandments of his Lord. Nor undeservedly did he merit, while living, to be distinguished by the apostolic title, whose examples he desired to imitate. He was considered worthy to become a participant in their lofty merits, for, rejecting his homeland, his parents, and all the possessions of the world, he chose to become Christ’s disciple, so that he might be found his heir, for whose sake he had despised every pleasure of the transitory world.

Yet he is not merely worthy to be equated with apostolic praises, but also with the angelic spirits and all the hosts of heaven, etc.

[Col. 0977]

## Sermon on the Elevation of His Body

Which was carried out by Lothar the custodian on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.

[Col. 0977A] Since we are taught through Raphael the archangel, bearer of heavenly medicine, that it is exceedingly honorable to recount the works of almighty God (Tobit 12:7), we consider it worthy, indeed necessary, not to pass over in silence the memorable elevation of the most sacred body of the bishop of Christ, Amandus. In it there is both no small portion of a divine miracle and an inexhaustible source of praise for the same blessed man and of testimony to his holiness.

In the year 809 of the Word made flesh—that is, of the Son of God incarnate for the salvation and redemption of the human race—which was the one hundred and fiftieth year after the passing of the man of God Amandus, an inundation of waters far greater than usual occurred. Fear had exceeded its bounds in many places, and the flood had stripped the surrounding fields bare of crops through the destructive loss of their harvests.

The danger had increased to such an extent that even the inhabitants living near the rivers were compelled to abandon their ancestral dwellings and, while the waters subsided, to live in temporary shelters moved to elevated hills. This abundance of rising water, swelling day by day through the increase of rainfall, had also filled the banks of the river called the Scarpe with its excessive volume. The river was almost adjacent to the tomb of our most blessed patron Amandus, lying no more than twenty paces from it.

Overflowing through its daily increase, it rose so high that it reached the sacred burial place of the most sacred body and filled with water the entire space of the little chapel adjoining its feet, so that it deprived those going there of a dry path on which to walk.

[Col. 0977C] The sad outcome of this inconvenience brought no small grief to the hearts of the monks, but it especially struck Lothar, who at that time was custodian of the sacred church. Even if human speech were silent about the industriousness of his shrewd mind and the effectiveness of his works, the structure of the building itself proclaims them, as do the books placed in our archive and the whole monastery, enlarged for the better under his care.

Disturbed by the unusual nature of the flood, he began to consider with a discerning mind by what means he might meet the impending danger and what assistance could resist so great a disaster. He was anxious lest the same abundance of water penetrate as far as the deposit of the most precious treasure—namely, the little body of the holy Father, buried deeper in the earth by Bishop Eligius of blessed memory, as we said in another sermon—and violate it by surrounding it with dampness and touching it with reckless force.

At last, putting aside his uncertainty, he adopted this salutary plan, inspired, as one should believe, by divine prompting: he would raise the urn containing the sacred little body from the lower place to a higher one and thereafter, through his foresight, make it completely safe from all this flood and secluded from the muddy marsh.

On the appointed day, he gathered a company of clergy for this great work, brought in the necessary diggers, and devoted the greatest care to raising the sarcophagus. When it had been lifted with the utmost caution, as was proper, he had it placed on the left side. Then, amid festive celebration, with lamps shining throughout the broad spaces of the church, he most devoutly began the solemn celebration of the Mass in honor of so great a bishop and completed it over the same tomb.

Although watery moisture was present outside all around the sepulcher, no entrance was open inside to muddy filth or drops of water. Nor is it without reason to believe that God, who transforms the natures of all creatures at his will into whatever forms of things he wishes, and who by his own command restrains the swelling seas with the sands as though with the strongest reins, was also able to grant this benefit of such honor to the corpse of his beloved: namely, that no impurity should enter the vessel of the urn in which the precious deposit was held, so that the merit of the same venerable bishop might be made manifest to all.

After the solemn Mass had ended, he kept with him a few monks whom he chose and dismissed the rest. Burning not so much with rash daring as with the devotion of a faithful heart, he thought it fitting to investigate more carefully, with friendly curiosity, what the receptacle of the vessel held beneath his eyes within its womb. At the same time, judging it necessary for the devotion of those reverently seeking him, he determined to remove a small portion of relics [Col. 0978C] from the dust of his flesh or from his bones.

Meanwhile, with every doubt removed, the same arch-custodian humbly approached the tomb, which had already been placed at floor level, and, carefully removing the stone cover by which it was enclosed, looked inside. And behold, there appeared before his eyes a venerable man with gray hair, pale from the austerity and fasts in whose company he had lived, distinguished in the holiness of his conduct and merits, and also in the incorruption of his limbs, which emitted a sweet fragrance like aromatic spices. Entirely undefiled in body, he seemed like one sleeping, except that he lay in the tomb, and he was adorned with the honorable beauty of pontifical vestments.

[Col. 0978D] The event was extraordinarily marvelous in its rarity and, because of its magnitude, scarcely capable of being explained in human speech. He who had thought he would find the remains of decayed flesh, as ordinarily happens with the dead, found instead, beyond all expectation, the memorable wonder of an untouched body. What eloquence of human ingenuity could express how worthy of a miracle this vision was, or how near it came to immeasurable astonishment? [Col. 0979A] The dryness of our speech is scarcely able to explain it as it deserves, even in the most meager words.

Stupefied, therefore, as was proper, by the sight of so unexpected a marvel, he blessed almighty God with the praises due to him and gave thanks to the giver of such great gifts. Rejoicing also at the discovery of so great a treasure, he nevertheless began again to be tormented by no small anxiety, turning many things over in his mind: what should be taken from it as a gift for the remembrance of those who would come after.

When at last the anchor of deliberation steadied his wavering mind, he removed the chasuble with which he was clothed from the saint’s most sacred neck. Turning him onto each side in turn, he drew out the river reeds that had once been placed beneath him because of the watery dampness. [Col. 0979B] Judging this insufficient for his desires unless he also removed some portion of his inviolate limbs, he turned his bold—or, so to speak, audacious—hands toward the venerable corpse and cut off his nails, which produced the horns and claws of a spiritual calf. These had grown after his death contrary to nature, so that their growth had even penetrated the sleeves of his hands. He also cut the beard of the pontiff—our Aaron, that is—which had grown again after his burial.

Having stored all these things away for himself with the utmost devotion, yet believing that they still did not satisfy his desires, he dared to lay his hand upon the most sacred mouth through which frequent prayers had been poured forth to the divine mercy and frequent sermons had been directed to various peoples. [Col. 0979C] He tried to see whether he could extract any of his teeth. But when he could not accomplish this because of their firmness, he used a smith’s instrument, namely a strong pair of pincers, and drew two teeth from the gums of that most beautiful mouth—more precious, as one ought to believe, than red ivory and ancient sapphire.

It is a marvelous thing to relate, and one that seeks a believing hearer, although it is contrary to nature: drops of blood flowed from the teeth extracted from the dead man’s corpse. To this day an ivory casket bears witness to this marvel, still stained, marvelous to relate, with the very blood that had been poured into it when the teeth were placed there for safekeeping, etc.

[Col. 0980A] Thus he deposited the relics mentioned above, which he had taken from the body of the man of God Amandus, in a suitable place and with due honor. He also summoned stonecutters and masons and sought out many other things that appeared suitable for this work. But he allowed the venerable body to remain above ground for thirty-two days, from the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, when it was raised, until the tenth day before the Kalends of November, when it was restored. On that same day, after a great gathering of clergy and people had assembled, he replaced it in the prepared place.

He placed the tomb’s urn not as it had previously been, in the deeper part, but in the higher part, so that its foundation could be seen and a light could be kindled beneath it. Upon it he inscribed this verse from the Psalm: “This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall dwell, for I have chosen it.” [Col. 0980B] He made both elevations—namely, that of the body and its restoration—celebrated, and decreed that they should remain honorable in perpetuity for his successors as well. This observance we still celebrate with the utmost devotion on the present day, and we admonish our descendants to take care that it endure.

When we heard these things from the Fathers who had been present at them, many of whom still survive, as they recounted them in frequent conversation, we were not permitted to cover them with an unprofitable silence. Rather, for the praise of Christ and of that pontiff, we have transmitted them to posterity, though in humble writing. By such great and numerous miracles even to the present, his celebrated tomb is honored.

As for the healings performed in his basilica, where he rests, through the intervention of his merits, we have refrained from recounting some of them here, since we know that they have been sufficiently set forth in the little book of his life. [Col. 0980C] At his memorial, blindness receives sight, deafness hearing, weakness walking, and speechlessness the use of the tongue. We omit recounting these as though they were common gifts of the saints, because our dull pen hastens toward the fire divinely kindled in his memory, while our mind, feeble though it is, runs eagerly toward it with willing devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] Alcuin describes this history somewhat differently in epigram 54, after treating in the three preceding poems of the basilica of Saint Amandus and the monastery restored by Bishop Giselbert, of the church of Saint Mary, and of the tomb of Saint Amandus. He sings in epigram 54:

While the river, swelling ever more frequently,  
rushes through the sacred threshold of the present church  
and its channel grows into a surging flood,  
the priest Arnon could not endure the temples’ defilement.  
The bishop had ordered all these things to be renewed for the better,  
so that this crypt might become broader and loftier,  
with three times four firm arches set beneath its roof,  
so that a mystical stone might strengthen the entire hall;  
consecrating a small chapel to the exalted minister  
Michael, who stands by Christ in heaven’s citadel  
and offers the prayers of the saints to the King of the celestial spheres.  
Lotharius the custodian built it at his master’s command.  
May Christ always preserve them both forever.  
Whoever reads these verses, I beg him to say with a pure heart:  
“Christ, we pray you, grant Alcuin pardon for his sins.”

Likewise, in epigram 64, Arnon is said to have restored the tomb of Saint Amandus. In epigram 228, Arnon the bishop is said to have renewed and improved the fallen basilica, dedicated it in honor of Saint Michael, Saint Peter, and Saint Amandus, and wished the holy polyandrium—that is, the cemetery—to belong to the brothers. At the end of that epigram Alcuin commends himself to the prayers of his readers.

Several matters should be noted in these poems. Alcuin is said to have died in 804 in the Chronicle of Tours and elsewhere. How, then, could he have sung of this elevation of Amandus when it took place five years later? Further, is Giselbert, mentioned in epigram 51, the same person as Arnon, and who was that Arnon? Certainly Giselbert, formerly abbot of Elnone and later bishop of Noyon, died in 782 and was buried at Elnone; Alcuin composed his epitaph at the cited place. The verses just reported are attributed to Arnon, bishop of the church of Salzburg, by the author of the Life of Saint Rupert in volume VI of Canisius’s *Antiquae Lectiones*; but it is plainly more appropriate to the monastery of Elnone.]

## Of the Heavenly Fire Miraculously Kindled by Divine Power in Memory of Blessed Amandus

[Col. 0981A] Finally, in the year 855 from the incarnation of the Lord, in the 195th year from the passing of the most blessed Amandus, and in the 47th year from the elevation of his body, on the twentieth day of September, the annual celebration of that often-mentioned elevation was approaching. It was being observed with less worthy devotion than it deserved. For, content with the customary office on ordinary days, it received no honorable weekday observance. How this negligence was corrected by the following divine prodigy will become clearer in what follows.

We do not believe—let us say something in passing—that the miracles of almighty God, whether performed through him or through his ministers, are wrought merely to stir up the noise, applause, and favor of the crowd. Rather, we hold it most certainly that heavenly works are shown to mortals in order to strengthen the faith of believers and correct erring souls: so that, because we are not amended by the daily admonitions of the sacred commandments, we may be corrected by certain portents, as though by the pricks of goads.

[Col. 0981B] And because, hardened like Lot’s sons-in-law, we do not wish to obey by turning our backs in flight upon doomed Sodom and ascending the mountain of virtues, it happens that we see the divine word, represented by Lot, speaking to us as though in play, and that, according to the prophet, we turn the terrible commandments threatening death and destruction into a song of our mouths.

What, then, ought we to think that we have been admonished by this sign of which we have begun to speak—namely, the kindling of divine fire—unless it is that we should kindle in our hearts the flame of the twofold love, of God and of neighbor, by which we may be able to shine in the sight of the supreme Majesty? By the heat of that fire which our Lord sent into the earth—that is, into earthly hearts—let us purge completely from our deeds the rust of vices, [Col. 0981C] so that, casting off from ourselves the burden of lead, that is, of iniquity and sin, we may prepare ourselves for the heavenly diadem of our King like the purest gold.

But we have said enough about these matters, although they ought to have been spoken of in a different order, by anticipating them. Now let us approach the magnitude of the sign itself, writing of it with the plectrum and pen of our tongue.

On the day preceding in time the elevation just mentioned, when the service of the evening celebration had ended—not with as full an array of lights as was fitting, nor with the festive gathering that the crowd of people required—the sun was already releasing its fiery-footed horses from the flaming chariot and was yielding its place to its sister Cynthia in fraternal love. [Col. 0981D] As this alternation took place, rival night, wrapped in an azure cloak, was arriving. When Compline had been completed, the horror of darkness already needed lamps. Since the time for rest had come, each of the monks sought his bed, while guards remained in the basilica’s hall.

After lighting the lamps that customarily burned during the night watches and extinguishing all the candles throughout the church, one of the guards returned after a very short interval to inspect the temple. [Col. 0982A] He found a candle, accustomed to burn at the feet of the saint and extinguished shortly before, shining with the brightness of a fire sent down from heaven. Thinking that it had been lit by someone else, he believed it should be extinguished again.

Thus, after being extinguished three times in turn by the individual guards who succeeded one another, it nevertheless appeared three times radiant with heavenly fire. After coming together over the matter, and each recalling that he himself had extinguished it, they investigated who had relit it. They therefore thought it should once more be extinguished, and even removed with their snuffing fingers the coal that remained at the end of the wick, wishing to test whether it would appear radiant again after the brightness of the flame had been restored.

They had not yet fully grasped the reality of so great a miracle, although they were already taking the utmost care in their minds over the event. [Col. 0982B] When they saw the candle relit for the fourth time, they were astonished—or rather terrified—because, having attempted to oppose the prodigy by extinguishing it, as I may say, with rash daring, they yielded it to the light that had so often vindicated itself. In short, they allowed it to belong to him whose power had made it appear invincible on so many occasions.

For a long time they were struck with immense joy at the sudden novelty of the miracle. At last, going to sleep, they surrendered their astonished eyes to slumbering rest.

The night itself had nearly passed, illumined by so great a light, and the celebration of Matins was approaching as dawn grew red. Meanwhile, the guards rose from the pallets on which they had rested. [Col. 0982C] Of the seven largest candles that stood at the head of the man of God beneath the mausoleum, inside the enclosure under the vault, they found two blazing with a twofold brightness.

They had no doubt that these had been lit from the one placed at his feet, which they had seen burning shortly before. When the solemnities of Matins had ended and the day had already grown bright, the fame of the event spread, and the entire company of monks came into the basilica. With exalted praises and jubilant voices they blessed the supreme, holy, and undivided Trinity. Then they celebrated the solemnity of Mass in honor of the saint with greater devotion than usual.

I myself, who describe these events, however they may be, was present and heard with my ears the chant of that inexplicable melody, prolonged for a considerable time, and saw the fire with my eyes. I also recited these verses amid the very hymns, addressing them to so great a pontiff:

[Col. 0982D] How brightly you shine in the heavenly Olympus,  
O Bishop Amandus, shown to your monks.  
Grant that your servants may enter into fellowship with your life,  
so that they may be able to share in your gifts.

Those who were present celebrated with the greatest devotional rejoicing this twofold gift of divine benefits—namely, the marvelous elevation of the sacred body and the memorable gift of the fire sent from heaven—and decreed that it should be honored by their descendants, believing that those who commemorate him with due thanksgiving would obtain eternal relief.

## Poem on the Conflict between Spring and Winter

*(In Oudinus, on ecclesiastical writers.)*

All the shepherds of the flocks suddenly came together  
from the high mountains, beneath the shade in springtime light,  
to celebrate together the joyful woodland Muses.  
All here were preparing to sing praises to the cuckoo.

Spring also came, girded with a garland of flowers;  
cold Winter came, shaggy with stiff hair.  
A great contest over the cuckoo’s song arose between them.

Spring first playfully uttered three verses in melody:

### Spring

I wish my cuckoo, my dearest one, would come—  
this bird commonly becomes a most welcome guest to all.  
Let him enter singing, with good songs from his glowing beak.

Then icy Winter replied in a calm voice:

### Winter

Let the cuckoo not come, but sleep in black caverns;  
he is always accustomed to carry hunger with him.

### Spring

I wish my cuckoo would come with joyful new growth;  
let him drive away the cold, the nourishing companion of Phoebus forever.  
Phoebus loves the cuckoo, in the serene light that grows.

### Winter

Let the cuckoo not come, the one who perhaps produces toil,  
multiplies battles, and separates bitter rest;  
he disturbs everything: sea and land suffer.

### Spring

Why, sluggish Winter, do you sing insults against the cuckoo,  
who lies covered in heavy torpor in dark caverns,  
after the banquets of Venus, after the cups of foolish Bacchus?

### Winter

I have riches, and I have joyful feasts;  
I have sweet rest and a warm fire in the house.  
The cuckoo knows nothing of these things, but that traitor labors.

### Spring

Who, sluggish Winter, always ready to sleep,  
gathers riches or accumulates any treasures for you,  
if there is neither spring nor summer for you, or if no one labors beforehand?

### Winter

You speak truly: in those seasons much labor is never mine.  
There are also servants, subdued beneath my rule,  
who now preserve for me whatever they have labored to produce.

Their master is not a lord, but a proud, poor, and needy man;  
nor will you now be able to feed yourself sufficiently by yourself,  
unless some cuckoo comes and provides nourishment for you.

Then Palaemon, rejoicing from his lofty seat, replied:

### Palaemon

And Daphnis likewise, with the company of pious shepherds:

Cease from saying more, Winter, terrible squanderer of things;  
let the cuckoo come, the shepherds’ sweet friend.  
Let joyful shoots burst forth upon our hills;  
let there be pasture for the flock, and rest and sweetness in the fields;  
let green branches provide shade for the weary.

Let the she-goats come to the milking pails with full udders,  
and let the birds greet Phoebus with varied song.

Therefore, come quickly now, cuckoo—behold, come!  
Now you are sweet love, a most welcome guest to all.  
Everything awaits you; sea and land salute you.  
Hail, sweet glory, cuckoo; hail throughout the ages.

## Epitaph of Pippin and Drogo, Sons of Charles the Bald, Who, Entrusted to Milo for Education, Died in Childhood

*(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, section IV.)*

Whoever sees our figures with an attentive heart,  
consider how suddenly the world’s fortunes flow away.

We were born of a king, whose name followed another name:  
from Magnus came Magnus, from Charles came Charles.

We were not permitted to complete a whole year of life,  
but destined death carried away our souls.

If, father, you deign to visit our tomb,  
we ask you, king, do not grieve over our deaths.

Taken from the earth and placed in a peaceful region,  
we enjoy everlasting rest with the saints.

Be happy, parents mindful of us.  
I, Pippin, ask this, and Drogo likewise.

## In the Year of the Lord 865: Saint Remigius, Bishop of Lyon

## Historical Notice on Remigius

*(From the *Gallia Christiana* and Fabricius, *Bibliotheca of Medieval and Later Latin Writers*.)*

Saint Remigius, chief chaplain of the sacred palace of the emperor Lothair, presided over the Third Synod of Valence in 855; over the synod at Toul near Saponaria in 859; and likewise attended the synod of Langres in the presence of King Charles the Bald, as reported by Flodoard from Hincmar’s *History*, book III, chapter 161. He also signed the Second Council of Toul in 860 and the Third Council of Soissons in 866, at which synod he appended his name, together with other bishops, to the privilege of the monastery of Solignac.

He took part in the Council of Chalon in 873 with Leuboin, chorepiscopus of Lyon, in the third year of Charles the Bald’s rule in Burgundy after the death of his nephew Lothair, as recorded in the chartulary of Saint Marcellus. In a diploma of the same emperor, Remigius is commended, together with “the holy Church of Lyon, most rich in possessions, flourishing widely in its resources, and most distinguished in religion.”

He confirmed the foundation of the convent of nuns of Saint Andochius at Autun in 858. An old tablet further makes it clear that in 868 he established a congregation of canons in the basilica of Saint Irenaeus and restored the companions of Saint Just to the secular order. He is also mentioned in the notice of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Saisy, as well as by Flodoard in his *History*, by Lupus of Ferrières in letter 112, and by Baronius and Raynaud in their accounts of the saints of Lyon.

Maldonado, moreover, thinks that Remigius was the author of the commentaries on Paul’s Epistles attributed to Saint Ambrose; but we judge it preferable to leave the assessment of that work to others. At this same time a letter was written in the name of the Church of Lyon against John Scotus; it is found in volume IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Transferred to the better life on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, he lies in the church of Saint Just.

He wrote a book on three letters in the name of the Church of Lyon; a resolution of the question concerning the universal condemnation of humanity through Adam; and another book on holding immovably to the truth of Holy Scripture. These works appear in the works on predestination edited by Gilbert Manguin, volume I, part II. They were reproduced in volume XV of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*, pages 666–718, from which we have taken them.

## Book of Saint Remigius, Bishop of Lyon, Written in the Name of the Church of Lyon, on Three Letters

*(In the ninth-century *Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*.)*

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, here begins the little book On Three Letters of Certain Venerable Bishops: what ought to be thought concerning their meaning and assertions according to the rule of Catholic truth. (G)*

## Preface

Letters of certain venerable men—namely, “three bishops’ letters addressed to our Church, that is, the Church of Lyon”—were brought to us. The first two of these, simply and sincerely, appear to have opened and explained what they thought concerning a certain profound and perplexing question that for several years has been disputed and even contested among many people in many different ways: “namely, concerning the truth of divine foreknowledge and predestination.” They are also known to demand and require with particular insistence that our Church, with God inspiring and assisting it, answer them truly and faithfully concerning what it thinks about the same matter.

One of them, Hincmar, who is also placed first among the three, carefully and briefly explained and arranged in his letter how a certain wretched monk—who is said to have stirred up and agitated this question, or rather scandal, through restless and insolent presumption—“was heard, judged, and condemned in two councils of bishops.” He also set out, in relation to each of the monk’s propositions, whatever had been objected either by Hincmar himself or by the others, whether at that time or still among them to the present day.

The second, Pardulus, also mentioned nearly six people who had written against him. Yet he complained that none of them had satisfied the matter under inquiry with sufficient reasoning.

The third, Rabanus, is known to have written not to our Church but specifically to another bishop, explaining and defining for him, as he saw it, what ought to be held or taught concerning this matter.

When we had read all these things and, insofar as the Lord granted, had carefully and faithfully considered them, it seemed entirely proper to us that, compelled both by the need to answer the venerable men who had asked these questions, as has been said, and by the necessity arising from the opinions presented in so fragmentary and tangled a form, as well as by the disturbance of simpler and ignorant brothers whom we know to be wavering uncertainly over such questions, we should not withhold an answer of faith—such as the Lord might deign to grant—not from our own judgment, but from the immovable truth of the Holy Scriptures and the most firmly grounded authority of the blessed Fathers of the Church.

Thus, insofar as the Lord deigns to assist us, the firmness of faith may be increased in us ourselves through the effort of this answer, and it may be declared more carefully and clearly to others who may perhaps read these things how faithfully divine truth must be preserved and how reverently and obediently the authority of the Fathers must be followed.

## Chapter One. On the First Letter, Which Is Hincmar’s

The first writer, therefore, who, as we said above, both describes the actions of that wretched monk, refutes his doctrine, and explains his condemnation, after saying that he had voluntarily assumed the name of preacher and had gone to barbarous and pagan peoples as though to evangelize them, proceeds in these words to recount the sequence of his preaching:

### Hincmar

“He began his preaching with an opening different from that of John, who said: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near’ (Matthew 3:2),” and different from that of Paul, who taught “through visible things to know the Creator of visible and invisible things” (Colossians 1:16). He began to preach as follows:

1. “Before all ages, and before God made anything at the beginning, he predestined to the kingdom those whom he wished, and he predestined to destruction those whom he wished.

2. “Those who have been predestined to destruction cannot be saved, and those who have been predestined to the kingdom cannot perish.

3. “God does not wish all human beings to be saved, but only those who are saved. And when the Apostle says, ‘who wishes all human beings to be saved’ (1 Timothy 2:4), he means all those who are actually saved.”

4. “Christ did not come to save everyone, nor did he suffer for everyone, except only for those who are saved through the mystery of his Passion.

5. “After the first human being fell by free choice, none of us can use free choice for doing good, but only for doing evil.”

## Response

He then continues with the rest, which concerns his other actions rather than the substance of his doctrine.

[Note: The Church of Lyon appears in this discussion to undertake the defense of Gottschalk, although it calls him a presumptuous, insolent, and wretched monk. Presumptuous, indeed, because he voluntarily—that is, against the resistance of his abbot—undertook the office of preaching to unbelievers, contrary to the Apostle’s words: “No one takes this honor upon himself unless he is called by God, as Aaron was”; and, “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” This was the first stain of that evil man, indeed the Hydra from which all his evils arose.

He was called insolent perhaps because he boasted too greatly of doctrines rejected at that time by nearly all teachers and spread them among the people with a certain insolent ambition, to the greatest detriment of the entire Gallican Church. He was called wretched because he was so long torn apart by scourges that, after a fire had been kindled around him, he threw his own book into the flames with his own hands and burned it as though in an eternal fire.

The Church of Lyon chiefly attacks this form of punishment when it affirms that all his propositions, with the sole exception of that concerning free choice, could be reduced to a pious and Catholic meaning by a kindly and gentle explanation. It therefore does not simply criticize the fact that he was punished with rods—for it is certain that heretics and innovators are rightly punished, since they are no less harmful to the Christian commonwealth than any other criminals—but rather that the prelates of that time ought to have explained his propositions more charitably instead of raging against him in this way.]

Although this may seem partly incredible to us—namely, that when preaching to peoples ignorant of the Lord he could have omitted first calling them to repentance and reasonably persuading them to distinguish between creature and Creator, so that they would no longer “worship and serve the creature” through the error of idolatry, “but rather the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Romans 1:25)—and instead could have proposed to them questions concerning the divine judgments and the mystery of predestination and redemption that were extremely difficult even for the faithful and learned, nevertheless, setting aside the utter absurdity and incongruity of this objection, we are more inclined to believe that he could have raised and proposed such matters among the faithful, or even among the priests of those regions, so that he might be regarded as a new and admirable preacher of great and novel things, than that he was so foolish and stupid as to thrust such matters upon people completely ignorant of divine things, and so inopportunely and perversely, that he would have been not listened to but utterly laughed at and barred from everyone’s ears.

Concerning the five propositions mentioned above, which he is said either to have preached or to have proposed, defended, and attempted to confirm in the councils where he was admitted to be heard and judged, we do not believe that anything should be rashly defined by our weakness in precipitous and inconsiderate haste. Rather, with every care of devotion, with the most devoted zeal for discovering and holding the truth, we must faithfully seek, knock, and ask, so that, setting aside all hostility and contention, we may follow faithfully and unanimously not what human error suggests to us but what truth itself reveals.

In order that this may be done carefully and faithfully, insofar as we can with God’s help, we believe that the following must first be set forth and earnestly commended, as it now comes to the memory of our weakness: that there are “seven rules of faith” arising from the authority of the divine Scriptures and most diligently commended by the holy and orthodox Fathers, concerning divine foreknowledge and predestination. Every Catholic must hold these rules with the utmost faithfulness, and whoever thinks contrary to them is thereby shown not to think in a Catholic manner.

## Chapter Two. First Rule: God’s Foreknowledge and Predestination Are Eternal and Unchangeable
The first of these, therefore, is that we hold with complete firmness and fidelity “that almighty God has foreknown or predestined nothing from within time; rather, just as he himself is eternal and unchangeable, without any beginning, so also his foreknowledge and predestination are eternal and unchangeable.” For there is in God no new will, no new plan, no new arrangement, no new judgment—as though it had not existed eternally with and in him but had subsequently begun to exist. Nothing accidental belongs to his divinity; nothing can be added to, diminished from, or changed in his Godhead. Therefore, whatever he foreknew, he foreknew eternally; whatever he predestined, without doubt he predestined eternally.

Holy Scripture instructs and forms us in this faith, saying: “Eternal God, who are the knower of hidden things, who know all things before they come to pass” (Dan. XIII, 42). And almighty God himself, when he bears witness concerning himself, says: “For I am the Lord, and I do not change” (Mal. III, 6).

In another passage, through the prophet, he also reveals the eternity of his predestination, saying: “I am the Lord; I have spoken, and I have done it” (Ezek. XVII, 24)—that is, what I have now “spoken” through the prophet, and what I shall accomplish much later, in its appointed time, I have already “done” in myself through the eternity of my predestination. What is still awaited by me as future is not future, since it is established as already accomplished in my immovable disposition.

Now, before almighty God said this, he had presented through the prophet, above, the likeness of two trees, signifying, that is, two peoples—the Jews and the Gentiles. Of one he says that he humbled it from a lofty position and dried it from being green; of the other, that he exalted it from a lowly position and made it leafy from being dry. Thus he says:

“And all the trees of the region shall know that I, the Lord, have humbled the lofty tree and exalted the lowly tree; I have dried up the green tree and made the dry tree put forth leaves.”

Immediately he adds:

“I, the Lord, have spoken and have done it” (Ezek. XVII, 24).

That is: what I have now spoken through the prophet, and what I am still to do among human beings, I have already done in my eternal predestination—namely, both his mercy and his judgment. As the Apostle says, displaying his “goodness and severity” in the eternally predestined humiliation or exaltation of the two peoples: by a just judgment he humbles and dries up the one, while by gratuitous mercy he exalts the other forever and makes it flourish.

What, then, could be sought that is more evident and clearer concerning the predestination of both parties—that is, of the elect as well as of the reprobate? For the barrenness of the one through unbelief and the fruitfulness of the other through faith are declared to have been predestined by God’s eternal judgment in his eternal predestination.

The same is true of what appears in the prophet Ezekiel, insofar as it concerns the portion of the reprobate. There the eternal destruction of all ungodly nations hostile to the people of God—that is, pagans, Jews, and heretics, and especially Antichrist and those who will persecute the Church of God with him—is foretold under the figure of Gog and Magog. Immediately the prophet adds:

“Behold, it has come and it has happened, says the Lord God” (Ezek. XXXIX, 8).

That is: what among human beings will come and happen only after so long a time is, with me, in eternal predestination, not still to come but already here; not still to happen but already accomplished.

The Psalmist likewise shows, with respect to both parties—the elect and the reprobate—that by God’s eternal judgment the former have been predestined to mercy and the latter to destruction. He speaks distinctly and plainly of the elect:

“But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him” (Ps. CII, 17).

Of the reprobate, however:

“For those who withdraw from you shall perish through iniquity; you have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. LXXII, 27).

That is: “those who withdraw from you,” insofar as it depends upon them, will perish in their own time, namely, at the final judgment. But insofar as it concerns the predestination of your eternal judgment, you have already destroyed them.

The Apostle teaches us to understand this immovability of the divine plan and judgment where God’s oath is introduced. Thus, concerning the heirs of Abraham’s faith, he explains that God swore to Abraham himself, saying:

“For when God made a promise to Abraham, because he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself, saying: ‘Surely, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you’” (Heb. VI, 13–14; Gen. XXII, 16–17).

A little later he says:

“Desiring to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his plan, God interposed an oath, so that by two things in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have the strongest consolation—we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us” (Heb. VI, 17–18).

Therefore, just as in the case of the elect, who are heirs of the divine promise and pledge, God wished by an oath to show the immutability of his plan—that is, the unchangeable arrangement of his eternal predestination, according to the Apostle’s exposition—so also in the case of the reprobate, where God’s oath is introduced, nothing else is shown except the immovability and unchangeableness of his eternal plan and predestination concerning their condemnation and destruction.

For almighty God shows that they are reprobate when he says of them:

“They did not know my ways” (Ps. XCIV, 11).

He shows that, by his immovable plan—that is, by the unchangeable predestination of his judgment—they were ordained to eternal condemnation and destruction when he immediately adds:

“To whom I swore in my wrath: They shall not enter into my rest” (ibid., 11).

If anyone thinks that this should be understood only of those reprobates who were led out of Egypt through Moses and remained rebellious and unbelieving in the desert for forty years, whose corpses were also cast down in that same desert, and not rather that the destruction of all reprobates in general was figured in their particular condemnation, let him hear the Apostle speaking both terribly and truthfully:

“All these things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. X, 11).

And elsewhere:

“Let us therefore hasten to enter into that rest, so that no one may fall into the same example of unbelief” (Heb. IV, 11).

[Note: He asserts that all those Israelites—and also those who were unbelieving and rebellious toward Moses in the desert, whose corpses were struck down there as punishment—were condemned eternally. To prove this he adduces Psalm XCIV: “To whom I swore in my wrath: They shall not enter into my rest.” He maintains that these words undoubtedly express the immutability of the divine plan concerning their eternal condemnation. Yet this is merely an opinion; indeed, the contrary is much more probable. First, it is not likely that the entire multitude of Israelites who died in the desert was unbelieving and rebellious. Could and should the Levites, the children, and Aaron himself be exempted from that same unbelief? Although it is said, “For forty years I was near this generation,” the whole is nevertheless designated from its greater part. Second, the “rest” of which the prophet speaks is understood as the land of promise, as the gloss on this passage states. Third, who would say that those who were consumed by devouring fire, through negligence—which is not such a grave sin—and who were situated at the furthest extremities of the camp, were for that reason condemned eternally, although their bodies were cast down in the desert? Fourth, exclusion from the promised land, for which they longed so ardently, together with the death they themselves suffered, was sufficient expiation of their offense, no less than the bodily death of Ananias and Sapphira, according to Jerome, Letter 8, to Demetrias. As for what the Church of Lyons says—that their condemnation was a figure of the condemnation of all reprobates, in accordance with the Apostle in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter X, “All these things happened to them as a figure”—the answer is that their exclusion from the promised land alone can very well figure this condemnation, since a figure must always be less than the reality. These points, however, are not to be understood as though we were rescuing all those Israelites from hell. For it is certain that Korah, Dathan, and Abiram descended alive into hell; but we wished only to restrict the Church’s general assertion.]

This truth and immovability of divine predestination—in which God has already accomplished his future judgments—is also wonderfully demonstrated by the blessed prophet Isaiah, and blessed Augustine truthfully and briefly explains it, saying:

“For he who predestined all future things by certain and unchangeable causes has done whatever he is going to do. For it was also said of him through the prophet: ‘He who made the things that are to come’” (Isa. XLV, 11, according to the Septuagint).

Hence, elsewhere the same teacher says most truthfully of him:

“For God does not repent of any deed as a human being does; his sentence concerning all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain.”

Thus both are eternal with him, and both are unchangeable: concerning absolutely all things, both good and evil, that occur in the world, his foreknowledge is eternally certain, since he knows them beforehand, and his sentence is fixed, since he judges them.

The blessed Judith also wonderfully and briefly confesses in her prayer to God this immovability of God’s foreknowledge and predestination, which existed before the ages and orders all temporal things. Seeking victory over the Assyrians, the enemies of God’s people, she says:

“For you made the former things, and conceived those that followed after them, and this came to pass which you yourself willed; and you established your judgments in your providence” (Judith IX, 4–5).

“You made,” she says, “the former things, and conceived those that followed after them”—not because we should believe that there is in God a changeability or succession of departing and succeeding thoughts, but because he sees immutably, with one eternal vision, everything that precedes and follows in created things, and incomprehensibly comprehends it.

“And you established your judgments,” she says, “in your providence”—that is, you established your judgments, which you exercise in the world, in your providence even before the world. Whatever you willed to occur temporally, you established timelessly in your eternal plan.

Almighty God knows how to create new things without any novelty of will; he knows how to act while at rest and to rest while acting. He can apply to a new work not a new but an eternal plan. Therefore, when he is said to have conceived one thing and then another, he is not—God forbid—altered by any changeability; rather, in relation to our changeability, he acts immutably in different ways and not according to a different plan.

Hence blessed James the Apostle says of him:

“With whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (Jas. I, 17).

And the Book of Ecclesiasticus speaks in his praise, saying:

“For all things were known to the Lord before they were created; so also, after they were completed, he regards them all” (Ecclus. XXIII, 29).

And again:

“From age to age he regards them, and nothing is wonderful in his sight” (Ecclus. XXXIX, 25).

## CHAPTER III

### THE SECOND RULE. All things are immovably subject to his eternal foreknowledge and ordering.

The second rule of divine foreknowledge and predestination is this:

“Absolutely nothing can exist, or have existed, or be destined to exist among the works of God—which he performs either in creating, governing, or bringing creatures to completion and ending them—that he has not himself both truly foreknown and immovably preordained in his eternal plan and judgment. Thus everything temporal is preceded timelessly by his foreknowledge and predestination. And everything disposed in his eternal foreknowledge and predestination can also exist in reality. But whatever has not been disposed there can never exist, neither at any time nor in any place; for he does nothing rashly or by chance, but does all things according to the plan and reason of his eternal wisdom.”

Hence it is said most truthfully in his praise:

“You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24).

For his wisdom eternally preceded all things that have been made, are being made, or are destined to be made temporally in creation.

For example, he foreknew that the world would exist and predestined that he would make it; he foreknew that human beings would be created and predestined that he would create them; he foreknew that the human race, fallen through the first human being, would be redeemed by the blood of his only-begotten Son and predestined that he would redeem it.

“For he sent redemption to his people” (Ps. CX, 9).

And rightly this is sung to him:

“You redeemed your people by your arm” (Ps. LXXVI, 16).

He foreknew that his elect would come to his eternal kingdom; he also foreknew that the reprobate would be handed over to eternal punishment. And because all this is full of mercy and full of justice, he predestined that he would accomplish it by his mercy and judgment. With him there is, according to the Apostle, “eternal goodness and severity” (Rom. XI, 22), and the faithful rightly say to him:

“I shall sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. C, 1).

It is therefore entirely clear that, in both directions—that of the elect and that of the reprobate—nothing could ever occur or be fulfilled unless divine foreknowledge and predestination had preceded it, whether their most just glorification or condemnation.

Just as nothing whatsoever can exist among the divine works that has not first existed there, so the evangelist’s statement concerning the eternal and only-begotten Word of God pertains wonderfully and sublimely to the demonstration of this truth. He says:

“What was made, in him was life” (John I, 3).

That is, everything that was made temporally by the Word and through the Word of God was eternally “life” in that same Word of God before it was made. For the living Word of God is itself life, living wisdom, living reason, and living counsel, through which all things could be made in their own ways and in their proper order.

### THE THIRD RULE. In God’s works, everything foreknown is predestined.

The third rule of divine foreknowledge and predestination is this:

“In the works of almighty God there are not some things foreknown and other things predestined. Rather, whatever is foreknown there, because it is all good and just, is undoubtedly also predestined; and whatever is predestined is certainly also foreknown, because predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge.”

Therefore, insofar as the divine works themselves are concerned, whether they are called foreknown or predestined, the same thing is signified, and the same immovable firmness is expressed.

For this reason, in one passage the Apostle wished God’s foreknowledge to be understood as his predestination, when he says:

“God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. XI, 2).

For if he had only foreknown them and had not predestined them, he would certainly not have made them his people. But because he foreknew them in such a way that foreknowledge itself most truly predestined them, what else does “he foreknew them” mean except that he truly and unchangeably predestined them?

Thus, in the preordination of the elect to life and in the preordination of the reprobate to death—since both are just works of God—as the Psalmist testifies:

“The Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works” (Ps. CXLIV, 17),

neither his foreknowledge can be understood without predestination nor predestination without foreknowledge, because this is his just and upright work: he truly foreknew it, and by foreknowing it he justly predestined it.

### THE FOURTH RULE. Good works belong principally to God, but also to his creature. Evil works belong solely to the creature and are therefore foreknown, not predestined.

The fourth rule concerning the same foreknowledge and predestination is this:

“These two things can be understood both distinctly and together in the works of a rational creature, since the works of the same creature are partly good and partly evil. And because good works belong to the creature in such a way that they are wholly and principally the works of the Creator”—who “works in it both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. II, 13)—they ought most rightly to be understood as truly divine, that is, divinely inspired, performed, foreknown, and predestined.

[Note: What he says—that good works belong wholly, principally, and truly to the Creator—must be read carefully. The word “wholly” should not be taken separately from “principally,” but together with it, as though he intended God to be the chief or primary cause of all good works. This does not, however, exclude the human creature or free will, which in its own way is also a principal cause, through the virtue supernaturally infused into it, of the interior acts of faith, hope, and charity. Accordingly, the Church of Lyons should be understood to mean by “principal cause” a primary or independent cause.]

“But the evil works of the same creature, because they belong to it alone and proceed from its fault, not from God’s will or operation, may be called foreknown by God, but cannot be called predestined.”

For he is so certainly foreknowing of all future things, both good and evil, that he can never be called their predestiner, just as he cannot be called the author of evil.

God therefore foreknew and predestined all the good things of his rational creature, as the Apostle says:

“For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. VIII, 29).

And again:

“We speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory” (1 Cor. II, 7).

But he merely foreknew the evil works and evil merits of the same creature; he did not predestine them. Thus the Psalmist, speaking in the person of the human race groaning amid the labors and dangers of mortal life and striving to return to God, humbly confesses to almighty God:

“You understood my thoughts from afar; you examined my path and my course; and you foresaw all my ways” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 2).

For what does “you foresaw all my ways” mean except that you not only saw all my ways—which are certainly evil—when they were present, but also foresaw them as future before I walked in them?

To him Scripture also says elsewhere:

“You know all things before they come to pass” (Dan. XIII, 42)—certainly not only good things but also evil.

## CHAPTER IV

### THE FIFTH RULE. God’s predestination imposes necessity upon no one for evil. Let Calvinists take note.

The fifth rule of divine foreknowledge and predestination is this:

“Almighty God, by that same foreknowledge and predestination, foreknew that certain wicked people would persevere in their iniquity and ungodliness, and for this reason justly predestined them to perish; yet from this certain foreknowledge and just predestination he imposed no necessity upon anyone to be evil or to be unable to be otherwise.”

For if he had done this—God forbid that we should think such a thing of his goodness—he himself would certainly be the author of the evils that he had compelled to occur by the violence of his power.

Every devout believer understands how horrible a blasphemy it is to say or think this. Therefore the ungodly and wicked persevere stubbornly in their evils through their own fault, not through any prejudice or adverse decree of God, who daily calls everyone to repentance, invites everyone to salvation, opens the embrace of his mercy to those who turn to him, and continually urges and admonishes them to turn away from evil and do good, saying:

“Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI, 27).

And again:

“Seek good and not evil, so that you may live, and the Lord of hosts will be with you, as you have said” (Amos V, 14).

Elsewhere:

“Turn to me, and I will turn to you, says the Lord of hosts” (Zech. I, 3).

And again in the Psalm:

“Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice; seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face continually” (Ps. CIV, 3).

Hence it is rightly sung in his praise:

“Let all who know your name hope in you, for you have not abandoned those who seek you, O Lord” (Ps. IX, 11).

Therefore that Father of such great goodness and piety does not drive or compel anyone to perform an evil work or remain in an evil work. Yet by his judgment he truly constrains and compels those who persevere in evil to undergo just punishment.

There too he is good, because he wills no one to be evil; and here he is just, because he permits no wicked or ungodly person to remain unpunished. Nowhere is he evil, since he is only the avenger of evil and never its author.

Scripture diligently commends this to us concerning him, saying:

“He commanded no one to act wickedly, and he gave no one license to sin” (Prov. XIX, 3).

And again, concerning those who think that they sin because God impels them:

“The folly of a man,” it says, “overturns his steps, and against God his heart is enraged” (Prov. XXIX, 3).

Elsewhere:

“His own iniquities capture the wicked, and he is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. V, 22).

Therefore blessed James the Apostle, restraining every believer from this madness and restoring him to true knowledge of piety, carefully admonishes him, saying:

“Let no one, when he is tempted, say that he is tempted by God; for God is not a tempter of evils, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire; then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, produces death.”

Accordingly, by his foreknowledge almighty God foresaw concerning the reprobate what is true: namely, that they would persevere in ungodliness, not through his impulse but through their own fault. By his predestination he established and decreed what is just: namely, that they would perish in eternal punishment.

For these evils—that is, not the things they willingly do, but the things they will unwillingly suffer for their evil deeds—God has predestined for them by his justice, and he will certainly inflict them by his just judgment.

He most truly threatens such people, saying:

“I will gather evils against them, and I will fill my arrows against them” (Deut. XXXII, 23).

And again:

“I will bring evils upon them; this is the year of their visitation” (Jer. XXXII, 12).

[For God will certainly repay, as blessed Augustine teaches most sincerely and lucidly: evil for evil, because he is just; good for evil, because he is good; and good for good, because he is good and just. But he will not repay evil for good, because he is not unjust.]

Whoever hears these things, then, what grounds has he for complaint? What remains for him except to be corrected from evil by fear of God’s just judgment—the judgment by which God has decreed to punish those who persevere in their evils—lest he be punished with those who remain incorrigible?

Thus fear of God’s just judgment against the wicked and ungodly, who are to be punished, is harmful to no one. Rather, in those who are corrected through it, it is truly shown to be salutary.

## CHAPTER V

### THE SIXTH RULE. In Scripture, foreknowledge and predestination are to be understood from the matter itself even without the words; no good works come from us but from God, and they themselves are predestined (Rom. VIII, 29).

The sixth rule of divine foreknowledge and predestination is this:

“Let no one childishly seek or demand in the divine Scriptures that divine foreknowledge or predestination be understood only where these very terms—‘foreknowledge’ and ‘predestination’—are found expressly and properly placed, as in the passage where the Apostle says: ‘For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his divine Son.’ Rather, wherever the reality of that same foreknowledge and predestination is read as certainly established, let us have no doubt that foreknowledge and predestination themselves are to be understood.”

For if we seek the proper occurrences of these terms, neither foreknowledge nor predestination is named anywhere in those prophetic testimonies that the Apostle takes up and presents in his Epistle to the Romans to commend divine foreknowledge and predestination. Yet the reality itself is demonstrated in them so clearly and plainly that no believer may doubt it.

The first of these testimonies is:

“The elder shall serve the younger.”

The second is:

“Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Gen. XXV; Rom. IX, 13; Mal. I).

The third is:

“I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I am merciful” (Exod. XXXIII, 19).

The fourth is:

“For Scripture says to Pharaoh: ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth’” (Exod. IX, 16; Rom. IX, 17).

And so, in order, the remaining testimonies continue down to the passage where he says:

“For God has confined all under sin, so that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. XI, 32).

In all these passages, as has been said, the word “foreknowledge” is nowhere heard, and the word “predestination” is nowhere heard. Yet the very faith of our religion compels us to believe that the Apostle understood and taught all these things concerning the foreknowledge and predestination of both parties—the elect, namely, to salvation, and the reprobate to condemnation.

He presents these matters with such authority and firmness that he wishes it to be believed that whatever he had taught shortly before these testimonies concerning God’s eternal purpose, foreknowledge, predestination, calling, election, justification, and glorification, and whatever he later recalls concerning the salvation of the Gentiles and the blindness of the Jews, he had sufficiently and evidently demonstrated and proved by these same testimonies.

The same applies to what blessed Augustine, drawing on the words of the Apostle, presents to prove and commend divine grace and predestination. He says (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10):

“Therefore, when the Apostle says: ‘For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works’ (Eph. II, 10), this is grace. But when he continues and says: ‘Which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them’ (ibid.), this is predestination.”

Certainly, in this apostolic testimony too, neither the word “grace” nor the word “predestination” is heard; yet the reality of grace and predestination is most clearly established.

For what reality of grace is more evident than that we possess no good works from ourselves, but that we are God’s own special “workmanship,” “created in Christ Jesus for good works”?

And what reality of predestination is clearer than that God not only bestowed these very good works upon us in the present through his grace, but also, in his eternal predestination, “prepared” them so that “we might walk in them”?

Let us therefore beware, as blessed Jerome admonishes in one passage, of a superstitious interpretation of Scripture. Let us follow, as firmly and faithfully as we can, this apostolic authority, by which the Apostle taught us through his example to seek and hold fast not merely the names but the realities themselves of divine foreknowledge and predestination, both in evangelical and apostolic sayings and also in prophetic utterances.

## CHAPTER VI

### THE SEVENTH RULE. None of the elect can perish. None of the reprobate is saved. Why the reprobate cannot be saved. Concerning infants.

The seventh rule of divine foreknowledge and predestination is this:

“We are to believe that none of God’s elect can perish and that no one of the reprobate can in any way be saved.”

This is not because human beings cannot be changed from evil to good and made good and upright from being evil and perverse, but because they did not wish to be changed for the better and wished to persevere in the worst works until the end. Those who chose instead to remain in the wickedness of their iniquities and ungodliness cannot in any way belong to the lot of the elect.

This worst and most abominable evil—the unwillingness to turn to God and to be changed from evil to good, but rather to “treasure up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment according to the hardness and impenitence of their heart” (Rom. II, 5)—he truly foresaw from eternity would occur in them, since he cannot be deceived in any way. And because he truly foresaw this, he most justly predestined such people to eternal destruction.

[Col. 0999A]

That they cannot be saved is their fault, because they are unwilling, not any injustice—God forbid—on God’s part. Toward them he has always been truthful in his foreknowledge and just in his judgment.

There is, however, another class of reprobates: the countless thousands of infants who never received either the age or the understanding necessary to do anything good, but perished under the condemnation of original sin, which entered the world through one human being. What else can be said concerning them except that almighty God is also just in their rejection and destruction? In them he condemned by a just retribution not the nature he had created good, but the fault wrongly committed and transmitted originally to them.

That this is so—that none of the elect can perish—the Lord himself shows when he says:

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them from my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father” (John X, 27–29).

These sheep, who, as the Truth himself testifies, shall never perish and whom no one can snatch from the hand of the Father and the Son, are called elsewhere the little ones of God. Concerning them the Lord likewise says:

“It is not the will before your Father that one of these little ones should perish” (Matt. XVIII, 14).

And elsewhere he says to them:

“Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII, 32).

And again:

“Not a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke XXI, 18).

Likewise, the Lord shows that the reprobate cannot be saved—not because of God’s foreknowledge and predestination, by which he truly foreknows and justly condemns, but because of their stubborn and unrestrainable wickedness. Speaking to such people, he says:

“But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep” (John X, 26).

And again:

“For this reason you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John VIII, 47).

Similarly, through the prophet he threatens such people, saying:

“They shall not be in the counsel of my people; they shall not be written in the writing of the house of Israel, nor shall they enter the land of Israel” (Ezek. XIII, 9).

That is, they have truly been expelled from the assembly of the elect, erased from the book of life, and wholly alienated from the land of the living.

Concerning them the Apostle likewise speaks in harmony with the Gospel words, saying:

“But if our Gospel is also veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing, among whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ may not shine upon them” (III Cor. IV, 3–4).

Elsewhere he says of them:

“For faith does not belong to all,”

and:

“Not all obey the Gospel” (Rom. X, 16).

Since they are such and remain such to the end, they have rightly been foreknown as evil by God’s foreknowledge and justly rejected and condemned by God’s predestination.

Let each person therefore examine himself, carefully considering and inquiring within himself whether, from the daily progress or decline of his life, he senses that he is drawing nearer to the fellowship of the elect or—God forbid—to the fellowship of the reprobate. Let him pray faithfully and perseveringly, as far as he can, that the mercy of almighty God the Lord may both rescue him from eternal condemnation and command that he be numbered among his elect flock.

[For although, as blessed Gregory says (*Dialogues*, book I, chapter 8), what has not been predestined cannot possibly be obtained, the predestination of the everlasting kingdom has nevertheless been arranged by almighty God in such a way that the elect reach it through labor, so that by asking they may merit to receive what almighty God determined before the ages to grant them.]

## CHAPTER VII

### Concerning God’s foreknowledge.

That these things are so, as the Lord has granted, we have set forth and arranged in seven distinct titles, both for ourselves and for the others who may wish to read, so that they may recognize and hold them according to the rule of true faith concerning divine foreknowledge and predestination—not presuming anything from our own judgment, but faithfully and humbly following the authority of Holy Scripture. We have deemed it altogether necessary to establish that these things are so, and that they have been held and handed down in this manner by the authority of the ancient Church and the most faithful instruction of the holy Fathers, so that we may also strive to commend and explain them more attentively for the confirmation of our readers by briefly and clearly setting forth the words and definitions of those same holy Fathers.
