In the book entitled *On the Two Natures in Christ*, very well known and widely commended among nearly all the Churches, in which the complete books or relevant passages of many orthodox Fathers, both Greek and Latin, have also been carefully collected and arranged for the edification and confirmation of the faith—namely, those of the most blessed Athanasius, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and others—there are also inserted about forty chapters in the form of a little treatise attributed either to the blessed Augustine or to the blessed Fulgentius, that glorious bishop and confessor of Christ (*On Faith to Peter the Deacon*). These chapters pertain especially to the knowledge and confirmation of the faith, and in them what must be held most firmly and without doubt concerning the matter now under discussion—that is, the truth of divine foreknowledge and predestination—is defined both very briefly and most fully.

[“Hold most firmly,” he says, [Col. 1000D] “and do not doubt in the least that, to the unchangeable God, all things—not only past and present, but also future—are unchangeably known. To him it is said: ‘O God, knower of hidden things, who know all things before they come to pass’ (Dan. 13:42).”]

And again:

[“Hold most firmly,” he says, “and do not doubt in the least that the unchangeable Triune God, the most certain knower of all things and works, both his own and human, knew before all ages to whom he would grant grace through faith; without that grace no one, from the beginning of the world to its end, could be absolved from the guilt of sin, both original and actual. ‘For those whom God foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son’ (Rom. 8:29).”]

And again: [Col. 1001A]

[“Hold most firmly,” he says, “and do not doubt in the least that all those whom God, by his gratuitous goodness, makes vessels of mercy before the foundation of the world were predestined by God for adoption as the children of God; that none of those whom God predestined for the kingdom can perish; and that none of those whom God did not predestine for life can in any way be saved. For that predestination is the preparation of a gratuitous gift, concerning which the Apostle says: ‘He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, for himself’ (Eph. 1:5).”]

Faithfully following this rule and most certain definition of faith, the blessed and holy doctor of the Church, Bede the priest, when expounding the passage in the Book of Genesis where Lot’s rescue from the destruction of Sodom is recounted (Gen. 19), together with the punishment of certain of his own relatives who did not believe and were unwilling to leave with him, and who therefore were most justly destroyed along with the others who had remained in the wicked city, says as follows:

[“The fact that the angels shut Lot’s door, so that the Sodomites could not seize and carry away either him or anyone from his household to destroy them, plainly indicates that no godlessness or persecution by the reprobate will destroy any of God’s elect, as the Lord says concerning his sheep: ‘And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them from my hand’ (John 10:28). But the fact that Lot, although the angels had given him the opportunity, could not bring any of the faithless townspeople—even his own relatives or friends—back to salvation, despite his great efforts, signifies that no human labor can add even one soul to the number of the predestined, who were chosen by God before the foundation of the world. ‘The Lord knows those who are his.’

Yet although it is hidden from our frailty which people belong to the lot of the elect, we must not therefore cease to care for our salvation, nor must our tongue be restrained from instructing our neighbors. Rather, following the example of blessed Lot, we must live chastely and also offer the service of charity for the correction of those who err. For it is certain that, although we cannot save those who have been predestined for destruction, we do not lose the reward of our kindness, which we extend for their salvation.”]

## CHAPTER VIII. On Double Predestination: Predestination Imposes No Necessity for Evil

The blessed Augustine carefully and briefly commends this rule of faith, which we must hold most firmly and faithfully, in his books *On the City of God* (Book XV, chapter 1), saying:

[“We divide the human race,” he says, “into two kinds: one consisting of those who live according to man, the other of those who live according to God. We also mystically call these two groups two cities—that is, two societies of human beings—one of which is predestined to reign eternally with God, the other to undergo eternal punishment with the devil.”]

A little later, discussing more fully the origin of these two cities, namely the city of God and the city of the devil, he says (ibid.):

[“Thus the elder Cain was born from those two parents of the human race, belonging to the city of men; the younger, Abel, to the city of God. The elder was born a citizen of this world, while the younger was a stranger in this world and belonged to the city of God. Predestined by grace, chosen by grace, by grace a stranger below, by grace a citizen above. For, as far as he himself is concerned, he arises from the same mass, which in its original condition is wholly condemned; but, like a potter, God—for the Apostle introduces this comparison not imprudently but wisely—‘from the same lump made one vessel for honor and another for dishonor’ (Rom. 9:21). The vessel for dishonor was made first, and afterward the vessel for honor. For even in one and the same human being, as the Apostle said, ‘not the spiritual first, but the natural, and afterward the spiritual’ (1 Cor. 15:46), and so forth.”]

Likewise, in the *Enchiridion* (chapter 100), which he wrote for Laurence, archdeacon of the Roman Church, he speaks of the same matter as follows:

[“When the angelic and human creature had sinned—that is, when it had done not what God willed but what it itself willed—through that same will of the creature by which what the Creator did not will came to pass, he himself nevertheless fulfilled what he willed, using even evil things well, as the supremely good One, for the condemnation of those whom he justly predestined for punishment and for the salvation of those whom he mercifully predestined for grace.”]

We have quoted these few passages from the two aforementioned books of that most blessed doctor. Anyone who reads his books of *Reconsiderations* more attentively clearly recognizes that he wrote them not only in a Catholic and truthful manner, but also carefully and faithfully revised them. Since some people now publicly despise and trample upon his authority concerning this matter—that is, divine predestination in both directions, of the elect to glory and of the reprobate to punishment—on the grounds that he himself piously and humbly reproved and corrected certain things in his writings, they think that, wherever it suits them, they may freely reprove him as well. What he did as an example of humility, they do not blush to appropriate as an expression of presumptuous pride.

From these books, at least, let them recognize that when the word “predestination” is applied by divine judgment to the reprobate, they are most truly and rightly said to be “predestined, not indeed to guilt but to punishment; not to the evil deed which they willingly commit, but to the evil which they will unwillingly suffer in eternal punishments.” Nor did Augustine himself reject this in his statements, nor has it been rejected by anyone who thinks in a Catholic and sound manner. Therefore, even “in the present age,” it ought not to be rejected or criticized by us, who possess such great ignorance and weakness; rather, it should be examined and understood with diligent and humble devotion.

If there are people who seem scandalized by this, as though the expression “predestination” meant that someone was subjected to a necessity of doing evil, they should instead have been instructed and taught briefly and clearly that God predestined no one to sin, but to suffer punishment for sin. Nor does this predestination compel anyone to do evil; rather, it declares him to be a just judge who neither willed sins to be committed nor failed to know beforehand that he would justly punish them, and who justly predestined himself to punish them. For by this predestination he predestined not the evil deed of man, but the just punishment of man.

The blessed Fulgentius, who—as we mentioned above—was near to Augustine in time and renowned among the other priestly confessors of Christ in Africa during the persecution of the Vandals, faithfully commends this true and Catholic understanding of blessed Augustine: namely, that God had always foreknown the work he would perform in the future, that is, his just judgment exercised upon the wicked and in the case of the wicked, and that he had always been a just predestiner. When questioned about this by a pious and religious man, he neither despised nor rejected the question, but rather carefully explained and confirmed the matter, saying (*To Monimus*, Book I, chapter 5):

[“I think nothing else should be understood in that statement of Saint Augustine, in which he affirms that certain people were predestined to destruction, ‘except to destruction consisting in punishment, not in sin; not to the evil which they unjustly commit, but to the torment which they most justly suffer; not to sin, but to torment, which their own iniquity wickedly produces and divine equity rightly repays; not to the first death of the soul, but to the second death. For the fact that the wicked perish through sin before Gehenna is not God’s work but man’s; but the fact that they will perish in Gehenna is the work of God’s justice, which takes no pleasure in the sinner’s iniquity. Thus God predestined what he himself was going to do; but he did not in any way predestine what he himself was not going to do. For an evil will does not belong to the supremely good Creator; but the just condemnation of the unjust belongs to the supremely just Knower. God therefore predestined the unrighteous and ungodly to just punishment, not to any unjust deed; to punishment, not to guilt; to penal correction, not to transgression; to the destruction which the wrath of the just Judge returns to sinners, not to the destruction by which the iniquity of sinners provokes God’s wrath against itself.’”]

Thus far blessed Fulgentius.

## CHAPTER IX. Testimonies from Saint Leo and Saint Gregory

The blessed Leo also teaches the truth of this divine foreknowledge and predestination—that is, the unchangeable order of God’s eternal dispositions—as follows:

[“Since everything that Jewish impiety committed against the Lord of majesty was foretold so long beforehand that the prophetic discourse is composed not so much concerning future things as concerning things already past, what else is presented to us than the unchangeable order of God’s eternal dispositions? With him, things requiring discrimination have already been judged, and future things are already accomplished. For since divine knowledge precedes both the qualities of our actions and the effects of all our wills, how much more are his own works known to God? And rightly it pleased him that those things should be recalled as though they had been done, which could in no way fail to happen.”]

The blessed Gregory, too, when explaining the Apostle’s words—“what is the length and breadth and height and depth” (Eph. 3:18)—speaks briefly and clearly of the predestination of the reprobate to destruction:

[“There is also depth in God, by which he preordains those who are to be condemned, disposing them below according to just equity.”]

In another place he says of the same matter:

[“The Church also expands toward the left when it admits to itself certain people who will remain in iniquity. Because of this multitude, which lies outside the number of the elect, the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Many are called, but few are chosen’ (Matt. 20:16).”]

In another place, demonstrating that the force of the heavenly disposition is unchangeable, he says:

[“The force of the heavenly counsel cannot in any way be avoided; but the one who restrains himself beneath its commands moderates it for himself with great strength. He lightens its burdens for himself who willingly bears them upon the shoulder of a submissive heart.”]

Likewise, elsewhere concerning the same matter:

[“Just as no one resists the generosity of God who calls, so no one opposes the justice of God who leaves.”]

And again, concerning the impious who have already been judged:

[“Those who did not even hold the sacraments of faith do not hear the rebuke of the Judge at the final examination, because, already judged in the darkness of their unbelief, they are not deemed worthy to be reproved by the denunciation of the one whom they despised.”]

Likewise, concerning the predestination of the destruction of the reprobate:

[“The almighty justice of God,” he says, “foreknowing the future, created the fire of Gehenna from the very origin of the world, so that it would begin to exist once for the punishment of the reprobate, but would never bring its burning to an end even without wood.”]

Elsewhere, speaking of the head of the impious and reprobate, those condemned to eternal destruction—namely Antichrist—and declaring that he has already been condemned, he says:

[“That condemned man whom the apostate angel will take up at the end of the world to preach his falsehood will choose people who are crafty, double-minded, and possessed of knowledge of this kind.”]

And in another place:

[“The earth to which woe is pronounced is principally that condemned man who is called the cymbal of wings, because those who fly aloft through the pride of their multitude of thoughts sound forth that same perverse man by preaching him.”]

A little later:

[“The earth,” he says, “to which woe is pronounced is said to lie beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, because that condemned man is so immense in iniquity that he surpasses the sins of all sinners.”]

## CHAPTER X. On Double Predestination

Behold: the most blessed Fathers of the Church, with one understanding and one voice, because by one Spirit, proclaim and commend the immovable truth of divine foreknowledge and predestination in both directions—of the elect, namely, to glory, and of the reprobate, not to guilt but to punishment. They confirm that in these matters the unchangeable order of God’s eternal dispositions is demonstrated, not dispositions belonging to temporal things or beginning at some point in time. They affirm that none of the elect can perish, and that none of the reprobate can be saved because of the hardness and impenitence of their hearts. The truth of the divine Scriptures and the authority of the holy and orthodox Fathers unanimously announce and repeatedly impress these things upon us as matters to be believed and held without doubt.

Therefore, although the frivolity of “that wretched monk” is condemned, his rashness condemned, and his untimely loquacity censured, divine truth must not for that reason be denied. For, according to the Catholic account set forth above, almighty God, before the foundation of the world and before he had made anything, predestined certain people to the kingdom, by his gratuitous goodness, according to the certain, just, and unchangeable causes of his eternal counsel; none of these will perish, protected by his mercy. He predestined others to destruction by his just judgment, on account of “the merit of their ungodliness, which he foreknew.” None of these can be saved—not because of any compulsion imposed by divine power, but because of the unconquerable and persistent wickedness of their own iniquity.

What, then, remains except that, if we have thought otherwise, we should humbly reject this in ourselves when God reveals it, and faithfully embrace the truth as it becomes clear? For, as the Apostle teaches, “we ought not to be able to do anything against the truth, but only for the truth” (1 Cor. 13:8).

## CHAPTER XI. On the Will of God—The Most Difficult Passage, “Who Wills All People to Be Saved,” Explained by the Fathers in Four Ways

It follows in the aforesaid letter that the monk in question said and taught: “God does not will all people to be saved, but only those who are saved”; and that when the Apostle says, “who wills all people to be saved” (1 Tim. 2:4), “all” refers only to those who are saved.

This question, however, is highly perplexing, has been much discussed in the writings of the holy Fathers, and has been explained in many ways. It does not seem to us that it should be defined hastily, but rather that it should be investigated and treated with the greatest caution and fidelity, both from the clearer passages of Holy Scripture by which its obscurity may be illuminated, and from the expositions of the Fathers’ authority, as stated above, and from the very rule of faith.

[Note: [Col. 1005D] He presents four explanations of the Apostle’s statement in 1 Timothy 2: “God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” He commends the first three and condemns the fourth as Pelagian. Although the first is Augustine’s, in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 103, it is nevertheless somewhat dangerous because of the heretics of the present time. In order to establish his impious opinion concerning reprobation, Calvin, Book III of the *Institutes*, chapter 14, says that the passage should be understood of classes of individuals and not of each individual within the classes: that is, God wished to save only some from every sex, age, condition, and state, whereas we understand it of all people individually.

The second is likewise found in Augustine in the cited passage of the *Enchiridion*, in Prosper’s letter to Rufinus, and in the eighth response to the bishops of Gaul. The third is found in the same Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapters 14 and 22; *On the City of God*, chapters 1 and 2; and also in Saint Thomas’s commentary on this passage of the Apostle. [Col. 1006D]

The fourth explanation, in the form in which it is expounded by the Church of Lyons, must be rejected. For it is certain that God does not wait for our wills, or for their cooperation, in order simply and absolutely to will the salvation of us all. If, however, it is explained in this way—that God wills all to be saved by an antecedent will, because he grants sufficient means of salvation to all and to each person—it has a true, pious, Catholic, and in no way Pelagian meaning. This is held by Ambrose, *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, Book II, chapters 1, 6, and 10; Prosper, in response to the first and second objections of the Gauls; and all the scholastic theologians in Book I, distinction 46, with the sole exception of Ariminensis.]

First, then, we must say that it must be believed most firmly and doubted in no way that the Apostle, with Christ speaking in him, testifies and preaches concerning God, saying: “Who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:4). Yet it is evident that not all are saved, since Truth itself, distinguishing between those who are saved and those who are condemned, says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16).

Nor do “all come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:4), except those alone who have come to know through faith the mystery of God the Father and of his only-begotten Son here, and who in the future will have deserved to see it by sight. Thus the same Truth says to the Father: “That he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him. And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:2–3).

How, then, does almighty God “will all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,” and yet not all are saved or come to this knowledge, when Scripture elsewhere says: “The Lord has done whatever he willed” (Ps. 113:3)? Why, then, did he will this and not do it, when he has done everything that he willed?

[Col. 1006B] As far as the memory of our weakness recalls, we have found this exceedingly obscure and difficult passage explained in the writings of Catholic Fathers in four ways.

The first is that we understand the statement, “Who wills all people to be saved,” in such a way that “all people” means all kinds of people: Jews and Gentiles, free people and slaves, men and women, rich and poor, noble and ignoble, and every other such category. From every kind of human being he saves those whom he saves and brings them to the knowledge of the truth through the Lord Jesus Christ, who says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net thrown into the sea and gathering fish of every kind” (Matt. 13:47).

In this manner of speaking the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:32). How did he draw all people to himself through the passion of the cross, on which he was lifted up, when elsewhere he says: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44)? This must certainly be understood of the faithful alone. Yet he draws all people to himself because he gathers and perfects his Church from every kind of human being, as has been said. [Col. 1006C]

The same applies to the Apostle’s statement: “God has imprisoned all in disobedience, that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. 11:32). How does he have mercy on all with that eternal mercy by which he “crowns his elect with mercy and compassion” (Ps. 102:4), when by the hidden disposition of his judgment he “has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18), unless it is because, as has been said, he has mercy on every kind of human being? These are contained in the two peoples, namely the Jews and the Gentiles, concerning whom the Apostle was speaking above in order to say this.

Or we may understand the statement, “Who wills all people to be saved,” as meaning that only those are understood to be saved whom he himself wills to save: not that all are saved, but that no one is saved except by the will of his mercy. Concerning this the Psalmist says: “He saved me, because he willed it” (Ps. 17:20); and again: “Life is in his will” (Ps. 29:6).

This manner of expression is also found in the Apostle’s words elsewhere, as in the statement: “Just as through one man’s trespass there was condemnation for all people, so through one man’s righteousness there is justification of life for all people” (Rom. 5:18). How is it that through the righteousness of one man, namely Christ, there is justification of life for all people, when it is perfectly clear that not all people are justified and given life in Christ through Christ’s righteousness?

Yet the Apostle most truly said, “through one man’s righteousness there is justification of life for all people,” not because there is no human being who is not justified by his righteousness, but because apart from his righteousness no one is justified. “All,” then, are condemned through the first Adam, and “all” are justified through the last Adam, because no one is in condemnation except through the first, and no one is in justification except through the second.

The statement, “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22), must likewise be understood in this sense. The Apostle was speaking of the future resurrection. Will those then be made alive in Christ who never believed in Christ, who were never in Christ, who never lived or died in Christ? Such people do not belong to those who receive in him the resurrection of life, which the Lord promises to the faithful, saying: “Those who have done good will rise to the resurrection of life.” They therefore belong to the group concerning which he immediately adds: “Those who have done evil will rise to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:29).

Yet it is true that “all” die in Adam, because no one dies except through him; and it is true that “all” will be made alive in Christ, because no one participates in that resurrection of life except through him.

The same meaning is plainly found in the Psalm: “The Lord lifts up all who fall and raises up all who are bowed down” (Ps. 144:14). The Lord does not, by showing mercy and granting pardon, lift up and raise absolutely all who fall and are cast down through various crimes and vices, since it is certain that many perish in those same crimes and iniquities. Yet he truly lifts up “all” who fall and raises “all” who are cast down, either because he saves from every kind of sinner or criminal whomever he wills, or because no one who has fallen is raised or lifted up except through him, since a person rises not by his own strength but by God’s mercy.

Therefore, just as these words of the Psalm concern the work of God’s mercy, so also in that apostolic statement—because it is said of him, “who wills all people to be saved”—it is rightly understood as referring to the will of God’s goodness.

Or certainly it may be understood in this way: “Who wills all people to be saved” (Rom. 8:26–27), because he causes his saints, through his Spirit, to will this; that is, he inspires them to desire that all people be saved as they themselves are. The same Apostle must be understood as speaking of the Holy Spirit when he says: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings. And he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to God.”

The Spirit intercedes because, as the blessed Gregory explains, he inflames those whom he fills to make petition. The Spirit groans and desires because he causes the saints to groan and desire in their prayers. According to this understanding, “God wills all people to be saved” because, as has been said, he himself inspires his saints to will this; he makes them willing in this way, just as he inspired the blessed Apostle, who said: “I wish that all people were as I myself am” (1 Cor. 7:7).

Elsewhere, when he was preaching the testimony of Christ with remarkable freedom and steadfastness before King Agrippa and the leading men, and the same king said to him, “In a short time you would persuade me to become a Christian,” he immediately replied, filled with desire for the salvation of all: “I wish before God that, whether in a short time or a long one, not only you but also all who hear me today might become such as I am, except for these chains” (Acts 26:28–29).

## CHAPTER XII. Continuation of the Explanation of the Same Passage

The fourth way in which the holy Fathers are found to have understood the statement, “Who wills all people to be saved,” is to take it simply as referring to all people: God wills, “as far as it depends on him,” that all be saved, because he wills that all be saved by the goodness of the Creator. But because he created them with free will, he waits for them also to will this; and if they will it, they are justly saved, while if they do not will it, they are justly punished.

At the outset, however, the following seems to contradict this interpretation: How can almighty God wait for the will of those whom he wills to be saved, so that they themselves, by the freedom of their own will, may will to be saved, when faithfully willing to be saved comes through the redemption of the Lord Jesus Christ?

For, as the blessed Apostle Peter teaches, “There is salvation in no one else, and there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). No one can do this unless God works in him both the will and the ability, as the Apostle testifies, saying: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13).

If no one has this will of redemption and salvation, which is in Christ, from himself, but from him “who works in those whom he calls both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure,” as the truth of apostolic teaching most plainly teaches, why does God wait for the will of those whom he wills to be saved, so that they may begin, by their free will, to want to be saved, and then be saved by divine goodness, with the beginning of their salvation coming from themselves and its completion from God?

And where then is the Apostle’s statement: “Or who has first given to him, so that he should be repaid?” (Rom. 11:35.) Or how, under such an interpretation, does the Pelagian error not prevail, since it affirms that human salvation comes not from God’s gift but from the free will of the human being himself?

If this is false—as it is proved altogether false—what reason is there that God, “who wills all people to be saved” (1 Tim. 2:4), does not save all people? He does not wait for their will, because no one can possess the will of true salvation except through him.

Or is there something that the almighty cannot do? Could he—God forbid—will to save all people but be unable to do so? What, then, remains except that he “who has done everything he willed” (Ps. 113:3) does not do this because he does not will it, not because he cannot?

For just as it is true that “he has done everything he willed,” so it is true that he did not will what he did not do. Why, then, did he not will it, unless because his judgment in this matter is both just and hidden? To him the Psalmist says: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7). And concerning him the Apostle says: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11:34.) And again: “Is there injustice with God? Certainly not” (Rom. 9:14).

Those whom he willed to save, he saved, because he has done everything he willed. But those whom he did not will to save, where did he leave them except in that mass of condemnation descending from Adam?

Thus, even if, according to the pious understanding of certain pious Fathers, God wills all people to be saved by the goodness of the Creator—by which he does not will the destruction of his creature, which he made well—he may nevertheless again not will the same thing “by the equity of the Judge,” by which he does not permit that same creature, defiled and corrupted by original or even actual sin, to remain unpunished.

For he so truly “does not will anyone to perish,” and his will does not become the cause of anyone’s destruction, that he even swears through the prophet and says: “As I live, says the Lord God, I do not will the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live” (Ezek. 33:11).

Yet he himself, who does not will the death of the wicked, unquestionably punishes the wicked person who perseveres in his wickedness. Thus, in one and the same person he displays both his goodness and his severity: his goodness, by which he does not will that person to perish; and his severity, by which he does not will to leave unpunished the one who perseveres in iniquity.

Therefore, if what we have said concerning one person is understood similarly of the entire human race that is perishing, it may perhaps be said without absurdity that God wills all people to be saved by the goodness of the Creator, yet does not save those whom he judges unworthy of salvation, by the just severity of the Judge.

For the Apostle also shows that both can occur in one person, as he says: “See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God’s goodness toward you, provided you continue in his goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off” (Rom. 11:22). This plainly announces severity against the one who does not continue in goodness.

## CHAPTER XIII. Conclusion

In the first three ways, then, of understanding those words concerning God—“who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:4)—there is no absurdity and no contradiction of the faith.

For either “all people whom God wills to be saved” is understood as all kinds of people; or God’s willing all people to be saved is understood in such a way that all who are saved are saved only by his will; or the statement is believed to mean that God wills all people to be saved because he himself wills this in his saints, inspiring them with such a will that they desire all people to be saved as they desire themselves to be saved.

In all these interpretations, then, there is an altogether true and salutary understanding.

In the fourth interpretation, however, one must unquestionably beware, because it provides an occasion for Pelagian depravity by asserting that God waits for human wills in order to save people.

Against this error it is stated in the ancient councils of the Fathers as follows (Council of Orange, canon 4):

[“If anyone contends that God waits for our will in order that we may be cleansed from sin, and does not confess that the infusion and operation of the Holy Spirit in us causes us even to will to be cleansed, he resists the Holy Spirit, who says through Solomon: ‘The will is prepared by the Lord’ (Prov. 8:31, according to the Septuagint), and the Apostle, preaching salutarily: ‘It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure.’”]

What is simply understood there—that God wills all people to be saved by the goodness of the Creator—may faithfully be accepted, as we think, provided that this will of his goodness toward the salvation of human beings is not understood to be unable to accomplish its purpose because of human resistance, but rather unwilling to accomplish it because of human iniquity.

Since all these matters are so obscure, so profound, and so perplexing, we would not wish anything concerning them to be debated contentiously or defined rashly among brothers and dear friends. Rather, what is certain in them should be defended without hesitation.

What has remained ambiguous and uncertain even among great men who think differently but with equal piety should likewise be honored among us with reverence, since neither position appears to be false or contrary to the faith. In such matters, it is better to call the restless and contentious to the modesty of tranquility and sobriety than to condemn anyone with immoderate harshness and severity over things that are unfamiliar and less clear.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Death of Christ
What is added after this in the aforementioned letter is that the wretched monk preached that “Christ did not come to save all, nor did he suffer for all, except only for those who are saved through the mystery of his Passion.” But concerning this question also, we would not wish anything to be said or defined confusedly and inconsiderately, [Col. 1011A] for it too has its own depth and difficulty, which must be examined with care—not through our presumption, but through the truth of the holy Scriptures and the authority of the orthodox Fathers—and understood faithfully insofar as the Lord deigns to reveal it.

For we hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic faith, that our Lord Jesus Christ, the good shepherd, “laid down his life for his sheep,” as he himself says: “I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd gives his life for the sheep.” And again: “As the Father knows me, and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for my sheep” (John 10:14–15). Of these sheep it is said elsewhere: “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matt. 20:28); and: “This is the cup of my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. 26:28). Hence the Apostle also says: “So Christ was offered once to take away the sins of many” (Heb. 9:28).

And he carefully identified who these people are when he said: “Walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a pleasing fragrance” (Eph. 5:2). And elsewhere he says: “How much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Heb. 9:14). Again: “He gave himself for us, in order to redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, zealous for good works” (Tit. 2:14). And in another place he says: “He was made for us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30).

This too was similarly foretold in the Psalms, where it is sung: “The Lord sent redemption to his people” (Ps. 110:9); and: “You redeemed your people by your arm” (Ps. 77:16). Again: “For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption; and he himself will redeem Israel from all its iniquities” (Ps. 130:7–8).

His most sacred name also commends this to us, and the angel teaches it when he says: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21). For these people the Lord himself testifies that he was lifted up on the cross, saying: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life”; and immediately he added: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:14–16).

Explaining at once what that world is which God loved and for which he gave his only-begotten Son, he added: “So that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.” Thus the world loved by God and redeemed through his Only-Begotten is also to be understood where the blessed apostle John says: “He is the propitiation for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world” (1 John 2:2); and where the blessed apostle Paul says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them” (2 Cor. 5:19).

There is indeed a world among unbelievers that is hostile to God and unreconciled to God. Of it is written: “The world did not know him.” And again: “The whole world lies in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5:19). Therefore the whole world is in salvation, and the whole world is in unbelief; the whole world is in reconciliation, and the whole world is in hostility—for the former is to be understood as wholly belonging to its own category, and the latter likewise as wholly belonging to its own category.

## CHAPTER XV. The Order of Reconciliation: 1. The Elect; 2. All the Faithful Who Do Not Persevere; 3. Those Who Are to Be Called; 4. The Unbelievers

[Col. 1012B]

In this grace of redemption and reconciliation, the first order is that of the elect and those predestined to eternal life. None of them can perish, and absolutely all of them are saved. To them belongs what the Lord says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

The second order is that of those faithful people who approach the grace of baptism with right faith and devotion, and through it receive forgiveness of sins: baptized into Christ’s death, washed from their sins in his blood, and thereby made participants in his redemption. Yet afterward, through various temptations and iniquities, they lose the grace of that faith and redemption by persevering in their evils, and thus depart from this world.

Of such people the Apostle says that “they will not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21), and “they have no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. 5:5). The Lord also threatens that he will say to them: “Truly I tell you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Hence the same Apostle solemnly declares concerning those who obtained Christ’s grace in the Church but failed entirely to preserve it: “How much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, considered the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified to be unclean, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” (Heb. 10:29).

Again: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the coming age, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, since they crucify the Son of God again for themselves and hold him up to contempt” (Heb. 6:4–6).

Because of this horrible evil of transgression and loss of God’s grace, it must be avoided and fled from with every care. To every faithful person the Lord says in the Apocalypse: “Hold fast what you have, so that no one may take your crown” (Rev. 3:11). And again: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Rev. 2:10). The Apostle admonishes and exhorts us, saying: “We have become participants in Christ, if only we hold firmly to the beginning of our substance until the end” (Heb. 3:14). And again: “Christ, however, is faithful as a Son over his house; and we are that house, if we retain firm to the end our confidence and the glory of hope” (Heb. 3:6).

The third order of those who approach this grace is to be understood as consisting of those who are still placed in unbelief but are nevertheless to be called through God’s mercy. Without doubt, in the Church they will attain what those two orders already attained—whether those who persevere or those who do not persevere in Christ’s grace, about whom we have spoken. For concerning them the Lord’s voice promises: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16).

The fourth order, concerning which it immediately adds, “But whoever does not believe will be condemned” (ibid.), plainly lies outside the number of the faithful and is destined for eternal condemnation. To such people it was said: “But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep” (John 10:26); and: “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8:47); and: “Whoever does not believe is already judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John 3:18).

## CHAPTER XVI. Christ Died for All Who Believe and Will Believe

For those three orders, therefore, which belong to Christ’s grace and to the fellowship of the faithful, we firmly hold that the Lord Jesus Christ came to save them, was crucified to redeem them, baptized them in his death, and washed them from their sins in his blood. We recognize this clearly not only from the divine Scriptures, [Col. 1013C] but also from the faith and teaching of the holy Fathers.

The blessed Jerome, explaining the Gospel passage in which the Lord says of himself, “and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matt. 20:28), teaches concerning this matter as follows:

> When he took the form of a servant in order to pour out his blood for the world, he did not say, “to give his life as a ransom for all,” but “for many”—that is, for those who were willing to believe.

[Note: [Col. 1013D] This affirms that Christ did not suffer for those who die in unbelief, and that his Passion was only for many, not for all. This requires a charitable interpretation no less than the Council of Valence, canon 4, where it condemns those who assert that Christ established his merits for the impious and for those who die in sin, and defines that the price of Christ’s blood was offered to take away the sins of many—namely, those who, by believing in Christ, do not perish but attain eternal life. That council speaks, as does the Church of Lyon, of merit and satisfaction with regard to efficacy, not with regard to sufficiency; in the latter sense he suffered absolutely for all human beings. By this distinction it is easy to answer all the arguments of the Church of Lyon, as anyone will readily see by reading them.]

In these words, in a remarkable and apostolic manner, our Lord is shown both to have poured out his blood for the world and yet to have indicated that the world for which that precious blood was poured out consists of none other than the faithful.

The blessed Augustine, in his Treatises on the Gospel according to John (Treatises 66 and 49), teaches that Christ did not die not only for unbelievers but also for those who believe in part and do not believe in part. He says:

> Whoever confesses Christ as God but denies him as man—for that person Christ did not die, because Christ died according to his humanity.

And elsewhere, concerning unbelievers, he says:

> Why, he asks, did he say to these people, “You are not of my sheep”? Because he saw that they had been predestined to everlasting destruction, not to eternal life purchased by the price of his blood.

And elsewhere (Treatise 55), distinguishing between the apostles and the traitor Judas, saying that the Lord was going to die for the former but not for the latter:

> His entire Passion is our purification. As he was about to undergo death, he promised acts of service—not only to those for whom he was going to suffer death, but also to the one who was going to hand him over to death.

Again, teaching that the Lord suffered only for those whom, by redeeming them through that very Passion, he made his sheep:

> He made all those his sheep for whom he suffered—all of them—because, in order to suffer for all, he himself became a sheep.

Again, when he was explaining the mystery of the fattened calf which the father ordered to be killed for his returning son, he says that it is killed for each individual when that person believes in the one who was killed:

> For he orders that it also be killed—that is, that his death be proclaimed. It is killed for each person when that person believes in the one who was killed.

The blessed Leo likewise teaches that our Lord did and endured nothing in vain, but directed everything toward the salvation of the faithful:

> Our Redeemer did and endured nothing that was not for our salvation, so that the power present in the Head might also be present in the body. For, in the first place, when he assumed the very substance of our nature into the Godhead—when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14)—which human being did he leave excluded from the mercy of his compassion, except the unbeliever? And who does not share a common nature with Christ, if he receives the one who assumes him and is regenerated by that Spirit by whom Christ was begotten?

The blessed Gregory likewise teaches that our Lord came to save only those whom, by taking them into himself, he liberated:

> The Lord intercedes for us, not by voice but by mercy, because by assuming what he did not wish to be eternally condemned, he liberated it.

We have briefly noted these passages from the words of the holy Fathers, so that it might be recognized most clearly how truly their venerable teaching agrees and corresponds, also in this question under discussion, with evangelical and apostolic authority.

Although the Apostle says of the same Lord and our Redeemer, “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Tim. 2:5–6), nevertheless, according to the rule of faith demonstrated above, this is rightly understood to mean that he gave himself as a ransom for all those for whom he also deigned to be the mediator between God and human beings.

For he is not the mediator of unbelievers, just as he is not their advocate or reconciler, but only of the faithful. Concerning these the blessed apostle John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2). Thus the statement, “He gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Tim. 2:6), is to be understood not as though he redeemed all by his Passion—as is plainly not the case—but as meaning that no one receives redemption except in him and through him.

The same Apostle also says elsewhere of the Lord: “So that by the grace of God he might taste death for all” (Heb. 2:9–10). For whom this “all” is to be understood as referring to those for whom he tasted death, he seems to demonstrate immediately when he adds: “For it was fitting that he, for whom and through whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through sufferings.”

Similarly, in another place, where he says of the same Lord: “Because one died for all, therefore all died, and he died for all” (2 Cor. 5:14), he immediately adds for whom this “all” is to be understood as referring to: “So that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them” (ibid., 15).

These are the “all” concerning whom the same Apostle elsewhere speaks to the glory and praise of God the Father: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32). Elsewhere he says to them: “You are not your own; for you were bought at a great price” (1 Cor. 6:20).

Therefore let every faithful person consider: since the Apostle calls the blood of Christ, like the blood of an undefiled and unblemished Lamb, a great price, can such a price be empty and void in any respect, or is it rather filled with profit and increase on behalf of those goods for which it was given?

## CHAPTER XVII. How Is Christ Said to Have Labored in Vain? Namely, in the Person of His Members

The Lord himself says through the prophet Isaiah, speaking of the mystery of his Passion:

[Note: [Col. 1015D] The exposition of these words of Isaiah—“But I said: I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing”—must be read cautiously. It says that Christ spoke here in the person of his members who, under the disgrace of the Passion and death, were weakened and almost despairing; and this conforms to its doctrine, namely, that Christ suffered only for the elect, so that he did not labor in vain at all. It is better, however, to explain the passage as referring to Christ himself, foreseeing the salvation of the few, although he paid on the altar of the cross a fully sufficient—indeed, more than abundant—price of redemption for all human beings.]

“And I said: I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength without cause and for nothing” (Isa. 49:4).

But far be it from us to believe that he spoke like this as though anxious and ignorant—he who certainly could never have been ignorant of the outcome and effect of his Passion, which he undertook according to a certain and determined plan for the redemption and salvation of both peoples. The Evangelist says: “Jesus was going to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (John 11:51–52). The Lord himself also clearly foretold the humility and abundant fruit of that same death when he said: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24–25).

Since, therefore, he knew these things beforehand with such certainty and foretold them with such truth and firmness, what does he mean by saying: “I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength without cause and for nothing”? It means that, as though grieving and complaining with such humility and abasement, he says that he labored in vain through the disgrace of his Passion and spent the strength of such endurance and patience without cause and for nothing, since it appeared to have been consumed fruitlessly and emptily through an ineffectual effort and exertion.

But this is rightly understood as being spoken in the person of his members, weakened and almost despairing under the disgrace of that Passion and death: when, as though overcome and extinguished by the fury of his persecutors, he was thought to be defeated, and he was not believed to be going to rise again and redeem the human race.

Thus those who said the following began to despair of him: “How the chief priests and our rulers handed him over to the condemnation of death and crucified him! But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:20–21). Therefore the labor of his Passion could appear empty to them, and the strength of such endurance could appear fruitless, since no benefit was visible and no usefulness of redemption was believed.

So also in the Psalm, speaking certainly not from his own person—for he committed no sin—but in the person of his members, he says:

[Note: [Col. 1016D] Here Calvinists should note that the Psalmist’s verse, “Why have you abandoned me? Far from my salvation are the words of my sins,” is to be understood not as referring to Christ himself but to his members, whose sins he imputed to himself as though they were his own. Thus the hesitation and despair mentioned there are to be attributed not to Christ, who was never and could never have been uncertain or doubtful about his salvation, but to his members.]

“Far from my salvation are the words of my sins” (Ps. 22:1).

And elsewhere: “O God, you know my folly, and my offenses are not hidden from you” (Ps. 69:5).

Thus in these prophetic words also, as has been said, he complained in the person of his weakened and almost despairing members that he had labored in vain through that Passion and had spent his strength without cause and for nothing. But in his own person he was entirely certain and confident. Although he appeared to have been overcome by his persecutors and was thought by his weak disciples to have suffered fruitlessly and in vain, he immediately adds, following those words of complaint and anxiety:

“Therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my work is with my God” (Isa. 49:4).

That is: my judgment, which in that abasement was removed from human estimation, remains safe and inviolate with the Lord. And my work, which amid such disgrace and contempt of the Passion appears to have been poured out and consumed fruitlessly, is full of fruit with God and has been deprived of none of the profit of its effect.

Finally, in order immediately to declare most clearly the supremely fruitful effect of that work in the redemption and illumination of both peoples, he added at once after the words already quoted:

“And I was glorified in the eyes of the Lord, and my God became my strength. And he said: It is too little for you to be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob and convert the refuse of Israel. I have appointed you as a light to the nations, so that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. 49:5–6).

Therefore no one should think that he has found an argument in those words by which to claim that our Lord acted vainly and fruitlessly in his Passion and in the shedding of his precious blood. The entire sequence of this prophetic reading, through the most orderly unfolding of events, clearly declares—just as has been said—in the person of the weakened members, hesitation and despair; in the person of the Head, the certainty of righteous judgment and the expectation of a most effective work; and in the person of the fathers, the full compensation of such great humility and such a great work in the acquisition of both peoples.

These are the people who are raised by him from the death of the soul, who are converted to the faith, for whom he is appointed as a light and given as salvation.

## CHAPTER XVIII. He Did Not Suffer in Any Way for the Impious Condemned before Christ’s Death. What Is to Be Said about Unbelieving Posterity and about the Antichrist?

Although, therefore, it may be asserted that our same Lord came both to save all and to redeem all—including those whom he neither saved nor redeemed, namely unbelievers and impious people who were lost and perishing, or destined to perish, in their unbelief and impiety—there is nevertheless one point which we most faithfully believe and know most truly: for that countless and infinite multitude of the impious who, from the beginning of the world until the Passion of the Lord, died in their impiety and were condemned to eternal destruction in hell—over almost four thousand years—our Lord never suffered and never died; he did not come in any way to save them, nor did he pour out his precious blood for them.

For it must be believed that by that same Passion he redeemed, saved, and led out from the confinement of hell only those who existed from the beginning of the world until his Passion and who faithfully hoped that he would come, and faithfully believed that through him they would receive redemption and deliverance unto salvation: namely, the holy patriarchs, prophets, and other righteous people. To them he had also previously promised through the prophet Hosea, saying: “I shall deliver them from the hand of death; I shall redeem them from death. I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13:14).

[Note: [Col. 1017D] Chronographers differ so greatly in their calculation of the years from creation to Christ that one may rightly say of them: “As many heads, so many opinions.” More common and more reliable, however, is the calculation of those who, on the basis of the Septuagint interpreters and very ancient Hebrew manuscripts, say that 5,199 years elapsed from creation to Christ. It is more common because it is found among both Greeks and Latins, as Baronius notes in the Martyrology; and more reliable because the Church has perpetually retained this number of years in its martyrologies.]

Therefore no Catholic teacher should be thought to have held or taught that our Lord and Savior undertook his Passion and death in order to save and redeem that multitude of the impious who perished before his Passion.

Since, then, he cannot be believed to have suffered in any way for that incomparably greater portion of the human race which preceded us through so many thousands of years, nor to have been crucified for its salvation, what are we to believe concerning this smaller portion of unbelievers and impious people who existed, exist, or will exist after his Passion until the end of the world? Among them, of course, will be that man who has not yet been born, the Antichrist.

For if the Lord came to save such people—that is, the impious who are destined to perish in their impiety—then he granted them what he did not grant those earlier impious people, since he was crucified and died for these, whereas he cannot in any way be believed to have suffered for the others.

But if he was neither crucified nor died for these, just as he was not for the others, then they are equal in impiety, equal in destruction, and altogether equally excluded from Christ’s redemption. For even if it is said that he suffered for these, what benefit did his Passion provide for impious people destined to perish in their impiety, except that, since they do not become participants in redemption, they incur a greater and heavier accumulation of condemnation?

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Blessed Leo’s Understanding

The blessed Leo uses certain words in some sermons addressed to the people from which some, either paying insufficient attention or understanding insufficiently, perhaps think that he taught and held that our Lord suffered even for the impious who persist in their impiety, and that he may be called their redeemer. Such is the following passage:

> Look at last, Jew; look, and, laying aside your unbelief, turn also to your Redeemer. Do not be terrified by the enormity of your crime. Christ calls not the righteous but sinners; nor does he reject your impiety, since, when he was crucified, he prayed for you.

But to those who understand these words properly it is clear that, according to the customary manner of human speech, he addresses the entire Jewish people under the person of one Jew. Therefore, as though speaking in the person of all, he cries out to one person and says:

> And, laying aside your unbelief, turn also to your Redeemer.

This is not because there is no unbelieving Jew who is not redeemed by the Lord, but because he deigns to be the Redeemer not only of other nations but also of that Jewish people whose crime and impiety caused him to be crucified, if it turns to him.

Therefore he says, “who, when he was crucified, prayed for you.” This does not mean that there is no unbelieving Jew for whom the Lord prayed on the cross when he said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34), since the Lord himself plainly says: “I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me from the world” (John 17:9).

[Note: [Col. 1019D] These words too must be read with equal caution. The point is that God did not pray for all his persecutors—namely, for those who were going to persist obstinately in the hardness of their hearts. Hincmarus lists this among the errors of Gottschalk in his letter to Nicholas I and refutes it as well: first, he says, because it was an ancient error of the Predestinarians; and second, because Peter said concerning Christ’s persecutors: “Denying the Lord who bought them” (2 Pet. 2:1). But these words of the Church of Lyon are to be understood according to efficacy, as we said earlier, and the text below explicitly adds this. The fact that the prayer uttered for all did not produce its effect in all detracts nothing from the power of Christ’s prayer. For insofar as it regarded those who remained hardened, it arose from a conditional and antecedent will—namely, that he wished them to experience its efficacy provided that they ceased from their hardness; but insofar as it regarded the elect and those who were to be converted, it arose from an absolute will. Unless one prefers to say that the prayer was absolute for all, because although all in fact repented, through its benefit they nevertheless had the means necessary and sufficient for salvation, which is enough for an absolute and efficacious will. Read St. Thomas, question 21 of the First Part.]

But because even within that unbelieving people there are and were many for whom the Lord mercifully prayed that they might be converted from their error and saved, and because he effectively obtained and accomplished what he prayed for, the blessed teacher rightly speaks, as though under the person of one individual, to that entire unbelieving people: “who, when he was crucified, prayed for you.” For certainly there were, are, and will be people from and within that people for whom he prayed.

The words of the blessed Leo must be understood in precisely this way; he himself explains them so clearly in other passages of the same sermons addressed to the people that no one should have any doubt about it. For in one place he says:

> Thus our Lord by his death provides for the human race in such a way that he did not deny the sacrament of salvation even to his persecutors. For he who had come to forgive all sins to all believers did not wish to exclude the crime of the Jewish people from the general pardon.

Elsewhere, speaking of the same Lord, he says:

> His feeling of compassion even toward those who killed him was so great that, while pleading with the Father from the cross, he asked not that he himself be avenged but that they be forgiven, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” The power of that prayer was such that the preaching of the apostle Peter converted to repentance the hearts of many of those who had said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children,” and in one day nearly three thousand Jews were baptized. Thus there came to be “one soul and one heart” among those prepared to die for him whom they had demanded to be crucified.

We have included these words concerning the exposition of the earlier passage from the words of the blessed Leo himself. Immediately after these statements he adds the following concerning the traitor Judas:

> The traitor Judas could not attain this forgiveness, because the son of perdition, with the devil standing at his right hand, passed into despair before Christ fulfilled the sacrament of the general redemption. For when the Lord had died for all the impious, even he might perhaps have obtained a remedy, had he not hastened to the noose.

In these words someone who considers and understands them insufficiently might think that “the sacrament of the general redemption” and “the Lord having died for all the impious” can be understood as though that general redemption and that death of the Lord were to be believed to have been accomplished for all the impious, including those who do not believe and perish in their impiety.

But for which impious people he says that the Lord died, and what he wishes “general redemption” to mean, we think he himself carefully explains in the words quoted shortly before, where he says:

> For he who had come to forgive all sins to all believers did not wish to exclude the crime of the Jewish people from the general pardon.

Thus it is to be understood that the Lord’s death was truly offered for all those impious people to whom he forgives all sins when they believe. He is understood to have spoken of “general redemption,” or “general pardon,” because neither the Jewish people nor any race of human beings is found to be excluded from that redemption and pardon.

But in the words we have repeated in order to explain the passage, it is clearly shown that the traitor Judas in no way belonged to Christ’s redemption. He could not obtain a remedy because he hastened to the noose. Christ’s Passion therefore profited him nothing, because he passed into the condemnation of those who, having already been punished in hell, could not become participants in the Lord’s redemption.

Nevertheless, elsewhere Leo speaks reproachfully to that unhappy and lost man as though to Judas himself, saying:

> You sold your Redeemer also, so that he would not spare you.

This does not mean that Christ redeemed Judas, whom the same teacher had already shown could not attain redemption. Nor is Judas to be understood as one whose Redeemer Christ was even though he remained in his impiety and perished. Rather, in that general redemption accomplished through Christ’s Passion, Judas too might perhaps have obtained a remedy if he had not hastened to the noose. Thus Leo says to him, “You sold your Redeemer also,” because Christ would truly have become his Redeemer as well if, even after so great a crime, he had piously and faithfully sought forgiveness from him.

It would be altogether too lengthy, and entirely unnecessary for those trained in the reasoning of faith, to explain carefully every individual statement of this blessed teacher wherever some opportunity of this kind might arise, as has been done with these few passages.

One point alone deserves particular emphasis: whenever Leo mentions a “general bond,” a “general covenant,” or a surety, this is to be understood as the general condemnation of the entire human race introduced through Adam. And whenever he speaks of “general redemption” or “general pardon,” the phrase is to be understood as referring to the “whole human race,” or to every nation. And whenever he teaches that the Lord underwent death “for all the impious,” this must be understood as referring to all who have been “converted from impiety” and believe in him, as his own words make clear in many places.

## CHAPTER XX. Christ’s Death for the Faithful Alone

We have set forth these matters faithfully and without any doubt whatsoever, to be read and considered both from the holy Scriptures and from the writings of the blessed Fathers. In them the same venerable Fathers clearly teach, and prove from the words of the Lord himself and of our Redeemer, that his precious “blood was poured out for many” for the forgiveness of sins, and that “he gave his life as a ransom for many” (Matt. 20:28). They emphasize that he did not say “for all,” but “for many.”

They understand and explain this as meaning that it must distinctly and specifically be taken as referring to those who were willing to believe. They also teach that he made all those for whom he died his sheep—something he certainly did not do for impious people who perish or are destined to perish in their impiety.

To these impious people Augustine plainly says: “But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep” (John 10:26; Augustine, On John, Treatise 48).

And concerning those who believe that our Lord is true God in such a way as to deny that he became true man for our salvation, they say that the Lord Christ did not die for them, because Christ died according to his humanity.

They also say that Christ’s being killed for each individual is to be understood as occurring when that person believes in the one who was killed—that is, when through his death that person’s sins are forgiven.

And they teach that the grace of the Incarnation and of the entire redemption of that same Lord Jesus Christ was granted generally to all who receive him as the one who assumed our nature and who are regenerated by the Spirit by whom he was begotten. Nevertheless, he left the impious and unbelieving excluded from so great a mercy.

But if these considerations are not sufficient for some, and they understand Christ the Lord to have suffered and died “generally for all” in such a way that he endured that same passion and death even for the impious who would never believe and who would perish altogether in their impiety, they may rightly be asked the following. Since the Lord said that he would give his soul “for many” and that his blood would be poured out “for many” for the remission of sins, and not for all, what answer can they give? If they reply—for no other answer remains to them—that he said “for many” because it should be understood that he undertook that passion and poured out his precious blood only for those who were going to come to faith and become believers, then is that not a confirmation of the opinion of the Fathers, who understood “for many” to mean specifically those who would wish to believe?

Therefore, wherever it is read in the apostolic writings that “the same Lord gave himself as a redemption for all,” that “by the grace of God he tasted death for all,” and that “he died for all” (1 Tim. II, 6; Heb. II, 9), those many for whom the Lord said that he would lay down his soul and pour out his blood—who, in their own category, “are both many and all” (II Cor. V, 14)—are rightly understood. The same applies to the statement that “all shall be made alive in Christ” (I Cor. XV, 22), and that “through the justice of one man there is justification of life for all men” (Rom. V, 18, 19). These statements are not to be understood confusedly and absurdly even of the impious and unbelieving, but altogether of those “many” of whom it is expressly said: “So also, through the obedience of one just man, many will be constituted righteous.” Of these the same Apostle says elsewhere, in words most evidently agreeing with the Lord’s: “So also Christ was offered once to exhaust the sins of many” (Heb. IX, 28). And in the blessed prophet Daniel we read: “And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake” (Dan. XI, 19). More remarkably still, these very persons—who in their own category are all and in their own category are “many”—are called “few” by the Lord in comparison with the multitude of the reprobate, when he says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX, 16).

But if some of the Fathers are found to say that the Lord was crucified even for the impious who would remain in their impiety, then, if they prove this by the most certain and clearest testimonies of divine Scripture, those statements that we have recalled from the Lord’s words concerning this matter must accordingly be understood in another way. That would be altogether astonishing—or rather, incredible. If, however, they are found to have said this without any scriptural testimonies of the kind just mentioned—not ambiguous testimonies capable of another interpretation, but entirely certain ones—who would not see that the authority supported both by such evident reasoning and by such manifold testimony of Scripture is the stronger?

If it is pleasing—as it is greatly pleasing to us—that the opinion of these men, “arising from piety, should not be rejected for the sake of peace and the venerable piety of the most blessed Fathers,” then let there be no contentious quarrelling on behalf of one side against another, and let one opinion not be condemned in favor of another. Since it can truly happen that something concerning our ignorance and inexperience in this matter remains hidden from us, “let nothing be rashly defined; let it be agreed that, however one may accept the matter, it is not heretical unless it becomes heretical through contentiousness.”

## CHAPTER XXI. On Free Choice. No One Can Use Free Choice Well without the Grace of God.—On the Necessity of the Redeemer

[Col. 1022D]

It is further added that the wretched monk allegedly said in the aforementioned letter “that after the first man fell by free choice, none of us can use free choice for doing good, but only for doing evil.”

[Note: [Col. 1021] This statement was imposed on Gottschalk by slander, as is proved from Hincmar himself in chapter 22 of the dissertation.]

This is not merely astonishing and unheard of, but, as it seems to us, incredible: that a man among the faithful, nurtured and instructed by the faithful, and not a little exercised in the writings of the ecclesiastical Fathers, could have said or thought that “after the fall of the first man, none even of the faithful can use free choice for doing good, but only for doing evil”—as though free choice remained in us only for evil, while for doing good the grace of God alone operated in us without free choice.

For if he had said generally, “No human being can use free choice well without the grace of God,” and had added “for doing good,” this would be a “Catholic sense” and an entirely Catholic assertion. But since he is accused of having said that none of us—that is, none of the faithful—can use free choice except for doing evil, what else is asserted by such a statement and such presumptuous novelty than that the free choice of the human mind, which before sin was free to love, desire, and enjoy the true good, was so corrupted by the sin of the first man and so perished that thereafter free choice remained in man only for evil; while for doing or possessing the good there is no human free choice, but only the good of divine grace?

We do not remember having known or heard of this kind of error either among heretics or among any Catholics, so that this assertion also seems to us, as we have already said, incredible.

For just as one and the same person can be healthy and, from being healthy, become ill through some excess, and can again become healthy through a salutary remedy, so the free choice of the human mind, which was previously healthy, became infirm when the first man sinned; what had been sound became ruined, and what had been alive became dead.

Before sin it was truly healthy, not corrupted by any sickness of sin; through sin it became infirm, so that it could truthfully cry out to God: “I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. XL, 5). And when it is healed by the true physician, the grateful and grace-filled people say: “Lord our God, I cried to you, and you healed me” (Ps. XXIX, 3).

What had been sound was truly sound because it had not been corrupted or defiled within by any evil will or outwardly by any evil action. It truly became ruined when, through an evil will, it abandoned God, and by abandoning the good that it possessed, lost it. Recognizing this ruin in itself and longing to be freed from it, it groans and says: “I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost; seek your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII, 176).

It therefore daily needs the one who seeks and saves, who says: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke XIX, 10). It was also alive because it clung to him of whom we say: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV, 10), living in him and through him of whom it is written in the Gospel: “And the life was the light of men” (John I, 4).

But by abandoning this life and this fountain of life, it became alienated from the life of God and dead: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII, 4). It has no vital sense in itself or from itself, striving toward true life, unless it is raised and quickened by him who says: “For this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke XV, 24). Nor can it live except by being enlivened in that Spirit of whom the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (II Cor. III, 6).

Thus they are dead, and are daily made alive, of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John V, 23). To them the Apostle cries out, saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. V, 14).

Let no malicious and slanderous person attempt to object that, when we say that free choice was ruined and killed through the sin of the first man, it should be understood as though it had lost its nature, in which the will of free choice is naturally implanted. It did not lose its nature, but the good of nature; it did not lose willing, but it lost good willing. Nor did the soul lose its nature when it dies: just as it always exists, so in a certain manner proper to it, it always lives. Yet it truly dies—not through the abolition of its substance, but through the loss of its true life, which is God.

Therefore human free choice itself absolutely needs one who seeks and finds it, so that what was lost may become saved; it needs one who raises and gives it life, so that what was dead may become alive; it also needs one who redeems it, so that what was subject to slavery may become free.

For it was subject to slavery because it had been subjected to sin, and “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII, 34, 36). It is freed from this slavery by him who said: “If the Son frees you, then you will truly be free.” It is also freed through the gift of the Holy Spirit, of whom the Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (II Cor. III, 17).

Thus, through the fall of the first transgression, man—and with him the entire human race—had lost the true freedom of choice by which he had previously been free to desire and possess the true, divine, and eternal good. He cannot in any way recover this blessed and true freedom of good will unless he is made free through Christ’s redemption and is transferred by the grace of the Holy Spirit from the slavery of sin into the freedom of righteousness.

## CHAPTER XXII. Free Choice, That Is, Right Will, Is Renewed from Day to Day. On the Works of the Unbelieving

[Col. 1024D]

This, then, is the infirmity, ruin, and death of free choice that entered the world through one man. By itself it can in no way rise to the true, eternal, and blessed good unless it is healed, found, quickened, and redeemed through the second man.

That same free choice of man—that is, the good and right will of the human mind, with which the good and upright man had been created and in obedience to God had remained good before sin—became evil through contempt of God in sin. By the grace of Christ’s justification, when it turns back in repentance and returns to God, it becomes good.
