It was itself free before sin; through sin it became subject to slavery; through justifying grace it is freed and is renewed from day to day, until by that same grace it is brought to the perfect freedom of eternal life. Thus free choice toward the true good is recognized as most truly lost through Adam and most truly restored through Christ. Christ did not take free choice away from man; rather, as has been said, by healing what was infirm, he found what was lost, raised what was dead, and by redeeming what was enslaved, set it free.

Therefore, in unbelievers, that same free choice—condemned and lost through Adam—can be free in dead works, but cannot be free in living works. Hence, before all else, every human being needs the redemption of the blood of Christ, through which he may be cleansed from dead works and brought to life for serving the living God.

The Apostle commends this when he says: “How much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” (Heb. IX, 14).

All the works of unbelievers are truly dead—not only when they openly serve vices and sins, but also when, prompted by the natural good that the almighty Creator has bestowed, or admonished by the natural law that daily cries out in their hearts, “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another; and whatever you wish that men should do to you, do the same to them” (Tob. IV; Matt. VII), they appear to possess and exercise certain good works and, as it were, certain virtues.

For since they either ignore, hate, or even persecute the faith of God and of his Christ, what they do apart from that faith can in no way be a good work or a true virtue, since it does not proceed from the root of truth and goodness. While those very works that according to human judgment appear to be good are in no way referred through true faith to the Lord, whom they do not know, nor are they performed for his sake, but either for the sake of a certain respectability by which they may appear great among men, or for the sake of the desire for some temporal advantage, they are so defiled and polluted by the impiety of unbelief, the swelling of pride, and the perversity of desire—

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Here the Church of Lyons teaches that all the actions of unbelievers are evil, unclean, and polluted. The sectarians of our own time affirm the same: Luther, article 36, condemned by Leo; Melanchthon, *Apology of the Augsburg Confession*; Bucer, *Book on Controversial Concord*; and Calvin, *Institutes*, book II, chapter 3. Some among the Scholastics also maintained the same position, though not with the presumption and boldness of the sectarians: Gregory of Rimini, *Sentences* II, distinction 4, single question, article 2, corollary 3; and Capreolus, II, distinction 41, single question, article 3, although he differs somewhat in certain points. From these works it can be seen that the opinion of the Church of Lyons on this matter is not opposed to the faith, although it is rash to affirm it. For it is certain and common both among the Fathers and among the Scholastics that unbelievers can perform certain works that are morally good. Consider, for example, Exodus I: the Egyptian midwives are praised because they refused to kill the Hebrew infants at the king’s command. In I Kings XVII, the compassion of Barzillai the Gileadite toward David and his army is also related and commended. See Valentia, in 2–2, question 10, “On Unbelief,” point 2.]

—so that before God they are judged not virtues but vices. Hence the Apostle says: “To the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean; but both their mind and their conscience are defiled” (Tit. I, 15); and again: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV, 23); and: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI, 6).

## CHAPTER XXIII. Right Will Is Indeed Renewed, but by the Grace of Christ, Which Always Gives Assistance

[Col. 1026A]

The faithful, redeemed by Christ’s blood and cleansed through the washing of regeneration and renewal, work good works through the freedom of choice restored within them—and to be restored daily—with the same grace by which they were once illuminated always cooperating with and assisting them. They do not work from themselves or from their own powers, but from him whose Spirit moves them. For, as the Apostle says: “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. VIII, 14).

To show and commend most clearly that the faithful do good works, and that God works in them so that they may be able to do this very thing, he briefly declared both points when he said to those same faithful: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (Phil. III, 12, 13).

The blessed Leo explains this as follows (Sermon 8, on the Epiphany):

[For when the Lord says to his disciples, “Without me you can do nothing,” there is no doubt that the human being who does good receives from God both the accomplishment of the good work and the beginning of the will. Hence the Apostle, most abundant in instruction and an exhorter of the faithful, says: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure.” This is therefore a reason for the saints to tremble and fear: lest, puffed up by their very works of piety, they be abandoned without the help of grace and remain in the weakness of nature.]

Thus, with God working in his faithful, what the Lord says is fulfilled: “He who does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God” (John III, 21). And in the person of those same faithful it is said to him through the prophet: “Lord, you will give us peace, for you have accomplished all our works in us.”

The blessed Pope Celestine briefly teaches and impresses upon us that this is how we must think and hold concerning the restoration of free choice and the gift and assistance of divine grace, saying (in his letter to the Galatians, chapter 8):

[There is no doubt that all the merits of man are preceded by the grace of the one through whom it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good. By this assistance and gift of God free choice is not taken away, but set free: so that what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked becomes straight, what was sick becomes healthy, and what was imprudent becomes prudent.

For God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wishes our merits to be his gifts; and for the things he has bestowed, he will grant eternal rewards. He acts in us so that we both will and do what he wills; nor does he permit the gifts he has given us—gifts to be exercised, not neglected—to lie idle within us, so that we may also be fellow workers with the grace of God.]

We have also thought it appropriate to set forth the following on the same matter from the councils and definitions of the Fathers (Council of Orange, canon 10):

[First. The assistance of God must always be sought even by those who have been reborn and healed, so that they may reach the completion of good things or persevere in a good work.

Second (canon 13). The freedom of the will, weakened in the first man, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism; what was lost cannot be restored except by the one from whom it could have been given. Hence the Truth says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.”

[Col. 1027B]

Third (canon 19). Human nature, even if it had remained in that integrity in which it was created, could in no way preserve itself without the assistance of its Creator. Therefore, if it could not preserve the salvation it received without God’s grace, how can it restore without God’s grace what it lost?

Fourth (canon 21). Therefore Christ did not die in vain, so that through him the law might be fulfilled, for he said: “I have not come to destroy the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17); and so that nature, lost through Adam, might be restored through him who said that he had come to seek and save what had been lost.]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Condemnation of Gottschalk

After inserting a certain narrative, which does not seem necessary for our present response, the writer of the letter adds an account of the meeting of the council of bishops summoned to examine and define the questions or objections that the wretched monk is said to have proposed or taught. What seems to us concerning these matters has already been sufficiently shown above. He then relates how the same monk was condemned by the judgment of those bishops because he refused to accept their decision, as follows:

### HINCMARUS

“Therefore,” he says, “I took care to bring him before the bishops who had then been summoned to Carisiacum by royal command for royal affairs, and also before Lord Wenilo,

[Note: [Col. 1027D] This man was archbishop of Sens, according to Demochare in the lists of the bishops of Sens. From these records one may infer that Gottschalk was condemned at various assemblies—namely, at the councils of Mainz and Sens—and perhaps was beaten only at Sens, since Hincmar, throughout that letter to Nicholas I, makes no mention of rods, but says only that he was confined under strict custody in a monastery lest he infect others with his errors.]

who had assembled there. In the presence of many listeners he said or, when questioned, answered nothing worthy of reason; but, like a man possessed, whenever he had no reasonable answer, he broke out into insults against individuals. Because of his most shameless insolence, he was judged worthy of the lash by the rule of Saint Benedict, by the abbots of the monasteries and the other monks. And because he persistently endeavored to disturb civil and ecclesiastical affairs against canonical institution and, being unrestrained [*profusus*], refused to acknowledge or humble himself in any way, he was condemned by the bishops according to ecclesiastical law.”

### RESPONSE

In these words, the first absurdity seems to be that the wretched monk is said to have been brought before the judgment of the bishops and first judged worthy of beatings and lashes by the abbots of the monasteries who were present, and then condemned by the bishops according to ecclesiastical law. Yet a man who was being treated as a heretic belonged, according to the ancient observance and authority of the Church, solely to episcopal judgment, whether he was to be condemned or acquitted.

He ought not first to have been condemned by men of an inferior rank and afterward by bishops. As for the lashes and beatings to which he is said to have been sentenced according to the rule of Saint Benedict, by which he is also said to have been torn apart with extreme cruelty and without any mercy almost to the point of death, let those who did this judge for themselves what moderation and measure should have been preserved in accordance with ecclesiastical piety and priestly or monastic modesty.

As for the claim that he broke out into insults against the bishops, this truly was impious, insane, and altogether deserving of just punishment—although it would have been better for that punishment to come from others than from the bishops themselves.

Concerning the opinions that he is said both to have preached previously and to have proposed at that time in the Synod, and that he was unwilling in any way to change, let every reader forgive us, and let that revered writer of the letter also forgive us. For, as we have already shown sufficiently above from both divine and patristic authority, it seems to us beyond doubt that what he said concerning divine predestination is true according to the rule of the Catholic faith, most clearly confirmed by truthful Fathers, and not at all to be rejected or condemned by anyone who wishes to be regarded as Catholic.

Therefore, in this matter we grieve not that wretched man, but that ecclesiastical truth has been condemned. In the Apostle’s statement concerning God—“who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth”—we think that he followed the teaching of the most blessed Father Augustine, who has always been revered by the whole Church and will be received to the end of the age. Treating this great question and comparing the two testimonies with one another, the apostolic and the prophetic, Augustine most clearly explains, both in many other passages of his books and especially in the little book called the *Enchiridion*, how both are to be accepted as true according to a sound understanding of faith; he also makes clear what seems more probable to him concerning so great a matter.

It was altogether improper for his completely truthful interpretation to be condemned under the name of any one man by Catholic priests of God, lest it should now be judged that not the man who is thought to have erred, but rather the one whose authority he follows, is a heretic.

Although certain other holy and venerable Fathers are found to have accepted the Apostle’s words in a straightforward manner, the opinions of both sides nevertheless deserved to be honored. As has already been said above, one should not be condemned in favor of the other, because the one is shown to be true on the authority of divine revelation, while the other is faithfully believed not to depart from the truth through a certain pious reasoning.

Now it is clear, from the opinion of those same blessed Fathers, as we have sufficiently shown above, that the price of the Lord’s blood was given only for those who would wish to believe. We think that this man had learned that opinion by reading it and was afraid to condemn it.

Therefore, even if other Fathers are found who do not deny that this glorious price was given also for those who would never believe and who would perish in their impiety, both groups should, as we believe, be honored, and neither should be condemned on account of the other. For the former opinion is plainly established by divine authority; and the latter, if held piously, should not be rejected.

But as for the assertion that he is said to have made—that we have free choice only for doing evil and do not have it for doing good—if he truly thought and said this, then it was not taken from divine authority or drawn from the doctrines of the holy Fathers, but openly produced from his own error. For the free choice that had been subjected to sin was not taken away from us, but set free; and by God’s grace it is aroused within us for doing good, so that we too may be fellow workers with that same grace.

If he erred so absurdly and foolishly concerning this matter, the Apostle’s clear statement is applicable: “Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. VI, 1).

As for that man, because of the intemperance, offensiveness, and unrestrainedness of his tongue, and the restless mobility of his unstable character, what is written in Solomon may perhaps have rightly befallen him: “He who is careless in speaking will experience evil” (Prov. XIII, 3); and again: “He who imposes silence on a fool calms anger” (Prov. XXVI, 10); and elsewhere: “Drive out the scoffer, and strife will go out with him; causes and insults will cease” (Prov. XXII, 10).

## CHAPTER XXV. Unheard-of Examples of Cruelty against Gottschalk

[Col. 1029D]

Nevertheless, we ought not to be so moved by the wickedness and lack of restraint of any person that we despise, oppose, or even dare to condemn divine truth or the venerable authority of our Fathers, remembering the Apostle’s words: “For we can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth” (II Cor. XIII, 8).

Rather, we should act so that both fathers in their sons and sons in their fathers may be honored, according to Solomon: “The crown of the elders is the children’s children, and the glory of children is their fathers” (Prov. XVII, 6). Elsewhere we are also instructed: “Stand in the company of prudent elders, and join yourself to their wisdom of heart, so that you may hear every account of God” (Eccli. VI, 35); and again: “Do not despise the account of wise elders, and occupy yourself with their proverbs; do not let the account of the aged pass you by, for they themselves learned from their fathers. From them you will learn understanding, and in time of need you will give an answer” (Eccli. VIII, 9, 11, 12).

Concerning these matters it is also commanded elsewhere: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. XXXII, 7); and again: “Do not move the ancient boundaries that your fathers established” (Prov. XXI, 28).

Therefore absolutely everyone not only grieves but also shudders at this: that, in an unprecedented example of irreligion and cruelty, the wretched man was so long slaughtered with lashes and beatings that, as those who were present told us, when a little book in which he had collected passages from Scripture or the holy Fathers for presentation at the council had been set on fire before him,

[Note: [Col. 1029D] See Gretser, *On the Right and Manner of Prohibiting Heretical Books*, where he teaches by examples from the Athenians and Romans that books containing corrupt doctrine were burned, and that this is established not only by the light of faith but also by natural reason. Thus our innovators should not be so indignant if the Church destroys by a general conflagration the books that they spew into the Church.]

he was compelled, already almost dying, to throw it into the flames with his own hands and burn it up—although all earlier heretics were conquered and convicted by words and disputation.

And so the perversity that seemed to belong to the man was to be restrained, so that no injury might be inflicted upon divine matters? Especially since the opinions contained in that little book, except for the final one, were not his own but ecclesiastical opinions. They ought not to have been condemned by fire, but examined through a pious and peaceful inquiry.

Moreover, the same wretched man’s long and inhuman confinement in prison for so many years should, as we believe, have been moderated or even removed by some kindness of compassion and consolation, so that the brother for whom Christ died might be won through charity and a spirit of gentleness rather than swallowed up by excessive sorrow.

This we suggest there, as the Lord knows, insofar as he deigns to look upon it, out of the charity commended to us by the blessed Apostle John, who says: “By this we know the charity of God: that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (I John III, 16).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Will of God

After the condemnation of this wretched man, the writer of the letter adds his responses to each of that man’s propositions and to those of certain others who think similarly with him. It is necessary here to set these responses out in order and briefly indicate what seems to us concerning them.

Although this has already been done in many ways above, we nevertheless think that it must not now be omitted, lest anyone derive difficulty or obscurity from such responses. In the letter itself, these responses begin as follows:

### HINCMARUS

“They say and firmly believe—those who seem to us to have a sounder understanding—that the Lord ‘wishes all people to be saved’ (I Tim. III, 4), according to the Apostle, ‘who wishes no one to perish’ (II Pet. III, 9), although not all are saved. For the light also shines in the darkness, ‘although the darkness did not comprehend it’ (John I, 6). And ‘Christ suffered for all’ (II Cor. V, 14), according to the same Apostle writing to Timothy, ‘who gave himself as a redemption for all’ (I Tim. II, 6), although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his passion.

For the shedding of Christ’s righteous blood was so rich as the price of the world that, if the whole company of captives believed in him, no one would remain under the power of death. And because not all are redeemed by so rich a price, this pertains to the portion of unbelievers, not to the abundant price of the world.”

### RESPONSE

In these words the writer of the letter seems to himself to have fully resolved and concluded two questions at once: namely, “that God wishes all people to be saved,” and that “the Lord Jesus Christ died for all” human beings, including those who would perish in their unbelief, by means of two testimonies taken from the Apostle.

In support of the claim that “God wishes all people to be saved,” he produces the Apostle as an unmistakable witness concerning that same God and Lord: “Who wishes all people to be saved” (I Tim. II, 4). To these words of the Apostle he adds, as though it were the sense of another testimony taken from the prophetic writings, that “God wishes no one to perish.” This is plainly spoken by the prophet Ezekiel: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, says the Lord, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11).

We too have cited above this interpretation of the Apostle’s words, “who wishes all people to be saved,” and said that it can be accepted faithfully—provided that the interpretation of the blessed Augustine, which he carefully investigates according to the authority of another passage of divine Scripture and explains in many truthful ways, is likewise accepted. The former interpretation should not be condemned on account of the latter; rather, “both interpretations” should be faithfully honored because of the truthful and pious authority of the Fathers.

For those whom God truly wishes to save he undoubtedly saves, since Scripture testifies: “He has done whatever he has willed” (Ps. CXIII, 3). But if he wishes the others to be saved in such a way that nevertheless he does not save them, but permits them altogether to perish, both aspects are clearly manifested here: toward his creature, “the goodness of the Creator,” and toward the wickedness of that same creature, “the severity of the judge.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Death of Christ. All for Many

[Col. 1032A]

As for the claim that our Lord also died for the impious who would perish in their impiety, the writer of the letter seems similarly to confirm it by a single testimony of the Apostle, where he says: “Who gave himself as a redemption for all” (I Tim. II, 6). But he evidently did not recall or carefully consider that the Apostle’s words must be understood in such a way as to agree with the Lord’s words, in which he says in the Gospel that he came for this purpose: “To give his soul as a redemption for many” (Matt. XX, 28). He says similarly concerning the price of his blood: “Which will be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. XXVI, 28).

Therefore the Apostle’s statement, “Who gave himself as a redemption for all” (I Tim. II, 6), must truly be understood so that these “all” are understood as “many,” just as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “So also Christ was offered once to exhaust the sins of many” (Heb. IX, 28).

In another passage, too, he calls certain people “all” and immediately explains that they are to be understood as “many.” For after saying of the Lord that “through the righteousness of one there is justification of life for all men,” he immediately adds that “through the obedience of one man”—namely, the Lord Jesus Christ—“many will be constituted righteous” (Rom. V, 18, 19).

For, as is entirely clear, “all men” are made righteous through him in such a way that those who in their own category are “all,” in comparison with those of another category who are not justified because of their unbelief, are rather “many.”

And if some of the Fathers understood the Lord to have suffered “for all human beings altogether,” let this interpretation be honored as a pious one, provided that the earlier interpretation—which is most certain and firmly established by divine truth—is not disregarded through presumption or, what is more serious, condemned.

For that testimony, as though taken from the Gospel in confirmation of this matter—namely, “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5)—does not seem to us to accord with this assertion. For that “light,” shining in the darkness through the presence of its majesty—that is, displaying the presence of the Creator’s majesty in the hearts of unbelievers—does something in them: even if not so that they may see the light itself, nevertheless so that through it they may see something, namely, that they may distinguish between what is just and unjust, between good and evil, between what ought and ought not to be done, “so that they may be without excuse” (Rom. 1:5) on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings.

Yet that “light” does not shine upon them from its face, because they do not attend to it, but shines upon them as though from behind; for, as the prophet says, “they turned their back to it, and not their face” (Jer. 1:27). But in this matter—in which it is asserted that the blood of the Lord Jesus Christ was shed even for the impious who would perish in their impiety—no benefit that it produced in them can be found at all, except that, according to the discussion of the ancient and most faithful teacher Hilary—whose teaching and diligence, with God’s help, once defended all Gaul from the assault of Arian impiety—this may be turned for them, not into a remedy, but, as we have already said above, into destruction.

For that most learned man, supported by great eloquence, said, when explaining the words of the Gospel in which the Jews are recorded to have said against the Lord, in obstinate impiety, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:15):

> “The Jewish people desire this for themselves; the Christian people desire it with the same words but with a different wish. For it is upon us, and it is upon them: if it is upon the faithful, it protects; if it is placed upon the enemy, it weighs him down. Yet it does so in such a way that it joins to itself those whom it covers, while it does not touch those whom it burdens.”

But although that statement of blessed Leo may have been expressed partly in other words and perhaps with another meaning, as though that man had understood that Christ the Lord died even for the impious who would perish in their impiety, manifest truth shows that it must not be understood in this way. For he says:

> “The shedding of the blood of the Just One for many was so powerful for privilege and so rich as a price that, if all believed in him, no one would remain held by tyrannical bonds.”

That blood was truly precious and powerful as a privilege, so that it could redeem all; and rich as a price, so that no one would remain held by tyrannical—that is, diabolical—bonds, except one who remained alien from faith in it. Therefore, in so great a question, incongruous claims must not be proposed, nor superfluous ones asserted, lest those who hear us be instructed in the simplicity and sincerity of God but deceived by the vanity of our own thinking.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Predestination to Destruction

[Col. 1033C]

There follows in the same epistle, under the third question concerning the first law—that is, “divine predestination”—a lengthy discussion, which seems to us not to be set out and treated all at once, but in sections. It is as follows.

### HINCMARUS

“They say,” he says, “that he who ‘wills all human beings to be saved and wills no one to perish,’ and who suffered for all, predestined no one to destruction or eternal fire. Rather, from the mass of sin, he predestined some, as he foreknew them; that is, by grace he prepared them for life and the kingdom, and he predestined life and the eternal kingdom for them; that is, by grace he prepared them for it. The Gospel bears witness when it says: ‘Come, blessed ones’—that is, those rescued by grace from the first curse, the elect and predestined—‘receive the kingdom prepared for you’—that is, predestined for you—‘from the foundation of the world’ (Matt. 25:34).

“But as for others, as he foreknew them, he did not predestine them to death or to fire; rather, he justly abandoned them in the mass of sin and perdition, from which, by his predestination—that is, by the preparation of grace—he did not rescue them, through a hidden but not unjust judgment. For, as blessed Augustine explains (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10):

> ‘Predestination is the preparation of grace, while grace is the giving of life—that is, the effect of predestination itself.’

“And blessed Prosper, the interpreter of blessed Augustine in this matter, agreeing with the other orthodox Fathers, says:

> ‘There is no predestination except what belongs either to the gift of grace or to the retribution of justice.’”

### RESPONSE

What is said in these words—that he who “wills all to be saved,” and “wills no one to perish,” and who suffered for all, predestined no one to destruction or eternal fire—is most plainly contrary to the faith. For it is truly and faithfully believed and defined that almighty God, before all ages, both most truly foreknew all the works that he himself was going to perform—works which, of course, could never be anything but just and right, as it is sung in the Psalm: “The Lord is just in all his ways, and holy in all his works” (Ps. 144:17)—and immutably predestined them, that is, established and determined them beforehand.

The just condemnation of the impious and wicked to eternal death and eternal fire is unquestionably the work of God’s just judgment, “who will repay each one according to his works” (Rom. 2:6). Therefore it always existed with him, and was truly foreknown and justly predestined by him who, as the prophet testifies, “made the things that are to be” (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint). For if this had not been in his eternal foreknowledge and predestination, it could never have been his work and could never have come to be in time. He anticipates every work of his by foreknowing and predestining it; and therefore nothing is future in his works that he has not foreknown and predestined himself to perform.

Moreover, this is contrary also to the teaching and definitions of the holy Fathers. They do not hesitate to place divine predestination on both sides—namely, for the elect as well as for the reprobate—because both the glorification of the former and the condemnation of the latter are God’s just work, as we have already sufficiently demonstrated above. Therefore, those who think otherwise must recognize the manifest truth of the faith and the firmly established authority of the blessed Fathers. They must not despise or cast aside—something wholly unprofitable for them—those of whom the Lord says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16).

If this seems absurd to them because almighty God is said to have predestined the reprobate to destruction and eternal fire—since it seems incredible that he who “wills all to be saved,” and who is believed to have died for all, predestined any of them to condemnation—let them consider more carefully. Even if the Apostle’s words about God are understood simply, namely, “who wills all human beings to be saved,” it is entirely certain that God acts in this matter in two ways: he wills some to be saved in such a way that he himself completely saves them, as he does all the elect; but he wills others to be saved in such a way that he does not save them at all, but permits them to perish eternally, as he does all the reprobate. In accordance with this sense, he willed their salvation both “as a benevolent Creator,” and “as a just Judge” handed them over to eternal destruction.

Thus he displayed his goodness in them, because he willed them to be saved; yet his goodness did not prevent the severity by which he justly condemned them. In the same way, that goodness in no respect prevented the predestination of his justice, when he justly predestined those whom he willed to be saved—but whom he always foreknew would become and remain wicked—to destruction. Likewise, if Christ died even for all who would perish in their impiety, he displayed toward them the goodness of his passion, yet by his just judgment he condemned such impious persons to remain in their impiety. As he himself says: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). Therefore, his goodness—which is believed to have extended even to such persons—did not cancel his predestination concerning them: by it he both always foreknew that they would remain in their impiety and justly predestined them to perish.

Whatever, then, is said after this in those words concerning the eternal predestination of the saints to the kingdom and eternal life is said catholically and faithfully. For without doubt almighty God eternally foreknew that this pious and glorious work of his would occur, and eternally predestined himself to perform it. But what is asserted here concerning the reprobate—that almighty God did not predestine them to death or eternal fire, but merely foreknew that they would be handed over to eternal death and tormented in perpetual fire—must in no way be accepted. For, as has already been sufficiently shown above, he eternally foreknew and, by eternal justice, preordained and determined beforehand his own work—so just, so great, and so terrible—by which he decreed that he would condemn all the impious.

It is exceedingly astonishing how they strive to deny that he predestined the eternal condemnation of those whom, from the very beginning of the world, when the first human being sinned and made the entire human race to be propagated from him into one mass of condemnation and perdition, they themselves plainly say were assigned and abandoned in that mass of condemnation and perdition by God’s just judgment. For what is the mass of condemnation and perdition brought about by divine judgment from the beginning of the world except one destined and handed over by that same divine judgment to eternal condemnation and perdition? If it was merely foreknown for eternal condemnation and perdition, then there is not yet any divine judgment in it. And how are such persons said to have been left in the mass of condemnation and perdition by divine judgment, if nothing concerning them has yet been determined by divine judgment in this respect? But if, as is altogether true even according to their own agreement and confession, this mass was not merely foreknown but also judged, what else can be understood except that it was wholly predestined to the same condemnation and perdition? For whatever is truly known beforehand by divine foreknowledge and decreed by divine judgment is plainly predestined.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Predestination to Evil Does Not Compel

The writer of the epistle then adds that “God did not rescue those who were going to perish from that mass of condemnation and perdition by his predestination—that is, by the preparation of grace,” and attempts to affirm, on the basis of the words of blessed Augustine:

> “Predestination is nothing other than the preparation of grace,”

that predestination should therefore be understood as applying only to the election of the saints, for whom almighty God prepared his grace from eternity; whereas no predestination of God is to be understood in the condemnation of the reprobate, since God did not predestine or prepare any of his grace for them from eternity.

This is altogether a most false interpretation and plainly contrary to the meaning of blessed Augustine. For he said (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10):

> “Predestination is the preparation of grace; grace, however, is the gift itself.”

And later, in order to distinguish between this predestination of grace, which properly belongs to the elect, and the predestination of condemnation and punishment, which properly belongs to the reprobate, he added (chapter 10):

> “The predestination of God, which is in good things, is, as I have said, the preparation of grace; grace, however, is the effect of predestination itself.”

Thus he clearly showed that the predestination of God which is in good things must be understood in one way: it is in the good, that is, in the elect, for whom it is truly the preparation of divine grace, and the effect of this predestination is the actual giving of that grace prepared by God. The predestination of God which is in evil things, however, must be understood in another way: it is in the evil, that is, in the reprobate, and is, on the contrary, nothing other than the preparation of their eternal predestination [or, alternatively, “condemnation”], whose full effect is condemnation itself.

[Col. 1036C]

Thus the venerable teacher distributed the eternal predestination of God on both sides: it is in good things for the good, and in evil things for the evil. Through it, eternal grace is prepared for the former, and through the eternal counsel of God eternal condemnation is prepared for the latter.

Accordingly, what blessed Prosper says—“There is no predestination except what belongs either to the gift of grace or to the retribution of justice”—must be understood most correctly in this sense: divine predestination must not be believed to be evil for anyone in such a way that it compels him to be evil, God forbid. Rather, for all—both elect and reprobate—it belongs either to the gift of grace or to the retribution of justice: to the gift of grace for the elect, and to the retribution of justice for the reprobate. The elect are saved by grace, and the reprobate are punished by justice.

For this is the fullest and truest effect of divine predestination: it not only preordains the elect to eternal glory, but also preordains the reprobate to eternal punishment. Thus blessed Prosper thought, together with the other orthodox Fathers—together, that is, with blessed Augustine, whose words concerning divine predestination he presents and explains faithfully, not deceitfully; and together with the others who, sharing the same faith and the same understanding, truly understood and most firmly defined the immutable truth and equity of divine predestination on both sides, namely, for the elect and for the reprobate.

But if the writer of the epistle considers only those to be orthodox who believe merely in divine foreknowledge, and not also in divine predestination, concerning the condemnation of the reprobate, then he brands blessed Augustine, blessed Fulgentius, and the very most solid truth of the Church’s faith with the mark of heretical error. This obstinacy of dispute has been carried to such a degree of evil that—something no one can grieve over sufficiently—among those who think perversely, both the orthodox and those who think orthodoxly are now counted heretics. The prophet emphatically warns us to beware of this evil, saying:

> “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isa. 5:20).

## CHAPTER XXX. Just as Punishments Are Predestined for the Evil, So the Evil Are Predestined to Punishments

The same response continues.

### HINCMARUS

“For this reason,” he says, “those who, as we have said, seem to think soundly refuse to say that some have been predestined by God to destruction, but say only that they were foreknown. The elect, however, they say, were both foreknown and predestined to the kingdom, and the eternal kingdom was predestined for them, as we have said; none of them can perish.

“And just as they are predestined by the grace of God to the kingdom, so, according to the Apostle, they are predestined ‘for good works, in which they should walk’ (Eph. 2:10). For these works, grace is given to them, and by grace the eternal kingdom is repaid to them.

“They say that the punishment of those who persevere in unbelief or wickedness was predestined by God according to divine foreknowledge, as it is written in the prophet: ‘Topheth has been prepared from yesterday’ (Isa. 30:33). For this belongs to the retribution of justice, just as it belongs to grace that, from one and the same mass of sin, the elect should be predestined by grace to life. This agrees with the truth of the Gospel: ‘Go,’ he says, ‘you accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels’ (Matt. 25:41).”

### RESPONSE

We ask: what is this matter, what cause or reason, for which these people refuse to speak of God’s predestination in the condemnation of the reprobate? Is this divine predestination concerning them not just, when those whom he foreknew would remain in their sins he predestined to perish in eternal punishments? Is it not true, when, unless he decreed this work of God’s justice in eternity, it could never be fulfilled in time? Has it not been proclaimed by the holy Fathers and received by the Catholic Church?

What, then, is the reason that we refuse to believe what the faith holds, and refuse to say what the truth teaches? Do not even those who refuse these things already assert that all the reprobate, from the very beginning of the world, were abandoned in the mass of condemnation and perdition? What is this other than—as we showed above—being predestined to eternal condemnation and perdition?

Or how can what these people strive to establish with such extended argument be maintained: that punishments have been predestined by God for the wicked and impious who will persevere in their evils, but that the persons themselves have not been predestined to those punishments? It is, of course, not others but precisely those persons who will suffer them, for whom they have been predestined. And if it is certain to almighty God who will suffer them, then without doubt it has also been decreed and determined that those persons will suffer them.

For just as he predestined certain punishments for those who are worthy of them, so he most certainly predestined those same persons—because they are worthy—to those punishments. Just as he is not unjust in preparing punishments for the worthy, so he is unquestionably just in preordaining the worthy to punishments. Therefore both were foreknown and both were predestined, because manifest truth declares both to be just.

Nor does he impose by his foreknowledge or predestination a necessity of perishing upon those whom he waited for a long time to convert. Because they did not wish to be converted, he condemned them by a just retribution.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Statement of Blessed Peter: “God Knows,” etc.

The same response continues.

### HINCMARUS

“Blessed Peter also demonstrates this by speaking distinctly in his Epistle when he says: ‘God knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, but to reserve the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment’ (2 Pet. 2:9).

“For ‘knows’—a word of God’s foreknowledge—applies to all these matters: to the predestination of the godly, which is indicated by the word ‘rescue’; and to the meaning of the predestined punishment, when he shows that the impious are to be punished at the end, when he ‘will repay each one according to his works’ (Rom. 2:6). It also applies to the distinction made when he does not say that the Lord predestines the unrighteous to the torments of punishment, but reserves those who have been justly abandoned to be tormented.

“And it is plainly shown that foreknowledge can exist without predestination, whereas predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge. Accordingly, only foreknowledge is operative in the reprobate, in whom mercy justly produces nothing toward the gift of grace. But foreknowledge and predestination—that is, the preparation of grace—operate mercifully in the elect, who are predestined to the kingdom, and for whom the eternal kingdom is predestined, which belongs to the gift of grace. Foreknowledge and predestination together operate equally and most justly in the predestination of the punishment of the reprobate, which belongs to the retribution of justice.”

### RESPONSE. The Testimonies Cited from the Apostle Are Examined

[Col. 1038D]

This statement of blessed Peter the Apostle does not seem to us to be understood properly as concerning divine foreknowledge and predestination, but simply. For he says: “The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, but to reserve the impious for punishment on the day of judgment.”

That is, by the profound and hidden disposition of his wisdom, he knows how to rescue by his grace and protection the godly who labor in the present life, full of dangers and temptations. They themselves say to him daily: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:13)—lest they be enticed by the prosperity of this world or broken by its adversities.

Conversely, he does not neglect the impious who flourish in this world and seem to prosper in their impiety, nor does he leave them unpunished. Those whom he appears to leave secure and happy, as though unjustly, in their desires and carnal pleasures, he rather reserves for his future judgment and eternal torments, so that the more extensively and freely they prosper here, the more harshly and terribly they may be punished there.

Nevertheless, in these final words—“but to reserve the impious for punishment on the day of judgment”—something concerning divine foreknowledge and predestination toward those same impious persons may be understood indirectly. For those whom, by his hidden and just judgment, he reserves for eternal torments, he undoubtedly both foreknew and predestined to be tormented forever.

When the Apostle’s words are understood in this way, both more truly and more correctly, there is no need to speak at such length, as though on the authority of those words, about a matter that cannot be approved by the testimony of this statement, but is rather shown to be false and superfluous.

## CHAPTER XXXII

The response continues.

### HINCMARUS

“I also write to your wisdom about certain examples that their folly brings forward to support its position by misunderstanding them, as they now come to mind. They produce from the Apostle the words: ‘Vessels of wrath fitted or perfected for destruction,’ saying that ‘vessels have been predestined to destruction’ (Rom. 9:22) and cannot be changed.

“But others understand this differently, especially since the same Apostle says concerning these same vessels: ‘If anyone cleanses himself from these things’—namely, the things for which he had been a vessel of dishonor—‘he will be a vessel for honor’ (2 Tim. 2:21).

“They produce the words: ‘Whoever does not believe has already been judged’ (John 3:18), that is, he has already been condemned by God’s predestination.’ And Augustine says in his book *On the Christian Combat*:

> ‘Whoever does not believe has already been judged,’ that is, already condemned—by God’s foreknowledge, certainly, since he knows what awaits those who do not believe.

“They produce the words: ‘He hardened Pharaoh’s heart’ (Exod. 9:12); ‘God handed them over to a reprobate mind’ (Rom. 1:28); ‘He will send them an operation of error’ (2 Thess. 2:10); ‘But you, O God, will lead them down into the pit of destruction’ (Ps. 54:24); ‘Whoever passes from righteousness to wickedness, God has prepared him for the sword’ (Sir. 26:27).”

### RESPONSE

These testimonies of Scripture, which that wretched monk and others—we do not know who they are, but who think with him—are said to have brought forward in confirmation of divine foreknowledge and predestination, must not be carelessly and casually passed over. Rather, they seem to require careful and faithful treatment one by one according to the rule of truth, lest they appear to those who pay little attention and do not understand to have no bearing at all on the matter under discussion, or lest they be thought capable of being passed over without danger as trivial and insignificant.

There is indeed a most certain and manifest testimony to this matter taken from the Apostle, because, as he himself says:

> “God endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted or perfected for destruction, in order to show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Rom. 9:22).

For all the reprobate are truly vessels of wrath—that is, of God’s just vengeance, which the guilt of the first transgression deserved. At the end they will experience not the rescue of mercy but the wrath of condemnation. These vessels of wrath have already been preordained, both according to their own merit and according to the divine judgment, and fitted and perfected not for mercy but for judgment, for destruction. Thus, because of their preceding merit and the just preceding judgment of divine predestination, they will suffer eternal evil because they did not wish to turn toward good.

They will therefore suffer a just punishment, not because they could not turn from evil to good, but because they did not wish to do so. Conversely, all the elect are truly vessels of mercy, who, without any preceding merit of their own, but solely by God’s mercy, have been separated from the mass of perdition and, by divine predestination, prepared as vessels for glory.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Vessels of Wrath Cannot Become Vessels of Mercy

Accordingly, if the statement that the same Apostle makes elsewhere is carefully considered in light of his preceding words—“If anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor” (2 Tim. 2:21)—it is in no way contrary to this clear and manifest truth of divine predestination on both sides, namely, of the elect and the reprobate. Rather, it is found to agree and harmonize completely with it.

For he says:

> “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; some indeed for honor, but others for dishonor” (2 Tim. 2:20).

And he adds:

> “If anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord” (ibid., 21).

It is therefore most manifest that those whom in the earlier passage he called “vessels of wrath fitted or perfected for destruction,” and conversely “vessels of mercy prepared for glory,” he here calls “some for honor and some for dishonor”: vessels of mercy for honor, and vessels of wrath for dishonor.

But whereas there he simply commended the predestination of both groups—that is, of the elect and the reprobate—here he adds an exhortation, showing how the vessels of mercy ought carefully to guard themselves and separate themselves from the impurities of the vessels of wrath. He says: “If anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor,” and so forth.

That is, if anyone cleanses himself from these vessels of wrath, these vessels of dishonor—or from their impurities, if he was at some time among them—by diligently withdrawing himself from them, or by never mixing himself with them, and by keeping himself undefiled by this world, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified. That is, by the result and progress of his cleansing and sanctification, he will show that he belongs to the vessels of mercy, the vessels of honor and glory.

The Apostle therefore does not signify in these words that the vessels of wrath and dishonor—that is, the reprobate and those rejected by divine judgment—can become vessels of mercy, honor, and glory, or pass into the company of the elect, as the writer of this epistle understood. For the reprobate, who have been divinely foreknown as remaining in their sins, can in no way, by the merit of their most persistent wickedness, be counted among the company of the elect, as the rule of Catholic faith unquestionably holds and teaches.

Rather, each of the faithful is to prove and demonstrate, as has already been said, by the sanctification of faith and righteousness itself, that he belongs to the vessels of mercy and election. For there are two things by which the elect of God are proved and recognized, as by a kind of seal: namely, the eternal preordination of divine grace, and the godly cleansing from every iniquity of unbelief and perversity. Thus the truth of divine election is manifested in them by the evident light of righteousness and holiness.

The Apostle himself showed this shortly before, saying:

> “But God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his,’ and ‘Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity’” (2 Tim. 2:19).

Therefore, “the Lord knows those who are his” is eternal election; but “let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity” is the sure proof of that election itself.

The second testimony to divine predestination is then brought forward from the Gospel: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). This means that all the impious and unbelieving have already been condemned by divine predestination. For if their condemnation is the just work of divine judgment, then without doubt that work has always been both foreknown and predestined by God.

But the writer of the epistle, unwilling to have the condemnation of unbelievers belong to divine predestination, and wishing it to belong only to foreknowledge, adds the words of blessed Augustine, by which he seems to try to prove this. For in his book *On the Christian Combat*, recalling the words of the Gospel—“Whoever does not believe has already been judged”—he says: “That is, already condemned, certainly by the foreknowledge of God, who knows what awaits those who do not believe.”

The point is that the holy teacher did not say, “already condemned by the predestination of God,” but “by the foreknowledge of God.” Nor did he say “who established, determined beforehand, or predestined,” but “who knows,” he says, “what awaits those who do not believe.” Is it possible that almighty God foreknew one of his works as future without predestining himself to perform it? Or, when God’s foreknowledge is mentioned in connection with his works, should God’s predestination not immediately and most certainly be understood as well?

For just as he predestined none of his works without foreknowing it, so whatever he foreknew, he undoubtedly also predestined. Nothing in his works is unjust or wicked, so that it might merely be foreknown and not predestined; rather, because everything is just and right, everything was wholly foreknown and wholly predestined.

Accordingly, the same blessed Augustine, who here says that unbelievers have already been condemned by divine foreknowledge, elsewhere, when explaining the Lord’s words to certain persons—“But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep” (John 10:26)—testifies that they were predestined by divine judgment to eternal death. He says (*Tractate on John* 48):

> “How, then, did he say to these people, ‘You are not of my sheep’? Because he saw that they had been predestined to everlasting destruction, not to eternal life purchased by the price of his blood.”

Behold: both in the Lord’s words, “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18), and in those in which he said, “But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep” (ibid., 26), unbelievers and faithless persons are identified. Those whom the holy teacher called in the first statement already condemned by divine foreknowledge, he called in the second predestined to eternal destruction.

This does not mean that some of them were condemned by divine foreknowledge and others by divine predestination. Rather, because of the power of divine judgment by which such persons are condemned—as in every divine work—both are to be understood together, even if they are not always expressed together, since no necessity requires that they be.

[Col. 1042B]

The third testimony is then brought forward from Exodus: “The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 9:12). This plainly concerns not the foreknowledge or predestination of future things, but God’s present judgment, by which, in a just judgment, he hardened one whom he judged worthy of such a punishment.

The fourth testimony is to be understood similarly—not as concerning foreknowledge or predestination, but God’s present and just judgment, which the Apostle describes by saying: “God handed them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1:28).

The fifth, where he says, “God will send them an operation of error” (2 Thess. 2:10), is likewise to be understood in this way. Those whom he judged worthy of such a punishment he either “handed over to a reprobate mind” or, by his just judgment, “sent an operation of error” upon them.

The sixth must likewise be understood:

> “But you, O God, will lead them down into the pit of destruction” (Ps. 54:24).

For the pit of destruction is, as blessed Augustine explains, the darkness of error and the darkness of submersion. God leads the reprobate into this pit, not because he is the author of their guilt, but because he is the judge of their iniquity.

If anyone wishes to understand this also of the pit of infernal condemnation and submersion in the same sense, it can refer to the just predestination of the reprobate to destruction, and it is not contrary to the truth.

But the seventh statement—“Whoever passes from righteousness to wickedness, God has prepared him for the sword” (Sir. 26:27)—plainly expresses the just predestination of the reprobate to destruction. Whoever, through his own fault and perverse free choice, turns away from righteousness and passes into wickedness is justly prepared by the predestination of divine judgment for the sword, that is, for the vengeance of eternal death.

It is written elsewhere concerning such persons: “If the righteous turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he will die in it” (Ezek. 18:24).

As for the remaining testimonies of Scripture that follow, we think—as with some of those already discussed—that they concern not the foreknowledge or predestination of future things, but God’s present judgment. Therefore, passing over those that have no relevance to the present question, let us proceed to consider what remains.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Predestination on Both Sides

[Col. 1043A]

The response therefore continues.

### HINCMARUS

“But these malicious men, not understanding what they say or what they affirm, confuse foreknowledge and predestination. Just as they misunderstand the authoritative Scriptures, so they also most wickedly misunderstand the words of blessed Augustine in certain passages—for example, in the *Enchiridion*, in the books *On the City of God*, and elsewhere—where he says that some have also been predestined to destruction and that a people has been born for wrath.

“Therefore, after he had written to Prosper and Hilary about free choice, correction and grace, the perfection of human righteousness, and the predestination of the saints—where he said nothing about the predestination of the reprobate, but only about the predestination of the saints—and after many people had requested it, he wrote a book called the *Hypomnesticon* against Caelestius and Pelagius. He wrote about five questions and added this sixth, in the manner of a retraction, concerning predestination. There he excuses himself, saying that he had not spoken in that sense and did not wish the words ‘predestined to destruction’ to be understood in that way, but that punishment had been predestined for those who persevered in iniquity or impiety. He mentions these questions and solutions in the book that he wrote against the Manichaeans from Genesis.”

### RESPONSE
[Col. 1043C] Therefore he accuses the malicious men—that is, that wretched monk and those who perhaps share his opinion with him—of confusing divine foreknowledge and predestination, because, just as he has labored throughout this entire response, he does not wish predestination to be understood except with regard to the elect alone; whereas, in the case of the reprobate, only foreknowledge is to be acknowledged. In making this assertion, he gives no consideration to the fact that he is declaring not only those whom he calls “malicious,” but also the holy Fathers and teachers of the Church, who both understood and taught divine predestination with regard to both sides, to be blameworthy.

But when he says that the words of Saint Augustine are “very badly understood” (if anyone, in the book *Enchiridion*, in the books *On the City of God*, and in the treatises on the Gospel according to John, understands the predestination of the reprobate [Col. 1043D] to destruction in the same way that Augustine proclaimed it throughout all the churches in his writings, and also plainly and truthfully before the assembled peoples), and thus attempts to pervert and twist the manifest and truthful meaning of the most blessed teacher—though we do not know toward what other end—who could explain how great an absurdity, indeed how impious a presumption, this is? For by this he is found to empty out, in part, not only the meaning of the ecclesiastical Fathers but also the faith of the Church and the authority of divine Scripture. For the Fathers taught thus; the Church faithfully holds thus; and the Scripture of truth demonstrates that this is to be held truthfully—as we have already sufficiently proved above, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant it.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the book *Hypognosticon*—On the first remnants of the Pelagians—On the predestination of the reprobate

[Col. 1044A]

He also adds something novel, of which until now we have found no knowledge either from reading or from any truthful tradition: namely, that blessed Augustine, after all his other books, wrote a certain little work which they call by the Greek name *Hypomnesticon*, interpreted in Latin as “memorandum,” in which he supposedly argued against Pelagius and Coelestius concerning five questions. And whatever he had said in his earlier books concerning divine predestination with respect to the condemnation of the reprobate, he supposedly did not say in the sense in which everyone recognizes and understands that he said it, but in another most absurd [Col. 1044B] and most inappropriate sense: so that, by saying that the impious were predestined to destruction, he did not wish the impious themselves to be understood as predestined to destruction, but—something no one could believe or even suspect—wished it to be understood that punishment had been predestined for them.

Who has ever heard of such stubborn audacity, or such audacious stubbornness, as to compel the most holy and truthful teacher himself to confess concerning his own words that, when he said that he had predestined the impious who would remain in their impiety to destruction, he did not say this because it was truly so, but that, in a sense which does not at all resound in his words, he wished punishment to be understood as having been prepared for them? Who could endure such absurdity, indeed such madness?

For we know plainly that, when he wrote the books of the *Retractions* as an old man and close to death, [Col. 1044C] in which he carefully and faithfully revised all his preceding books, he had not yet written this little work. For if he had written it, he would certainly have mentioned it among the others. It also appears evident that after his death, when a certain holy bishop and his disciple most diligently reviewed and recorded not only the catalogue of his books but also of his sermons to the people and his letters to various persons, blessed Augustine had still not written this little work. For if he had written it, it could certainly have been numbered among the others and commended to memory as something especially necessary.

But if one of the leaders of the Church who existed after his death simply believed that it was Augustine’s work from the title inscribed with the name of Saint Augustine, without considering the matter more carefully [Col. 1044D] and without being compelled by any necessity to do so, and believed the work to belong to the man whose name he found on its front, what prejudice does this cause to the truth? When the truth is carefully investigated and discovered, it permits no one to err concerning this matter.

This has also happened to the most distinguished teachers of the Church: induced either by a book’s title or by someone else’s account, they have thought and written that some little work belonged to an author, and afterward have both proved truthfully that it did not belong to him and humbly confessed this. Thus blessed Jerome clearly declares, in his books against his detractor, that he had believed from a false title that a book belonged to blessed Pamphilus the martyr, but afterward discovered that it was by Eusebius of Caesarea. [Col. 1045A] And blessed Augustine, in the books of the *Retractions*, explicitly recalls and corrects the fact that, following someone’s writings, he had understood and explained certain statements about free will and the grace of God as though they belonged to the most blessed Sixtus, pontiff and martyr of the city of Rome, when afterward he discovered that they were the words of a pagan philosopher, namely Sextus the Pythagorean.

The little work mentioned above also plainly shows by unmistakable indications that it is not Saint Augustine’s. For at its beginning it contains no preface in which he is found to have indicated that, having been asked by some people—or because it had seemed necessary to him—to write a new work concerning such a matter, that is, correcting or explaining differently the word “predestination” in his books, he had undertaken to do so. Nor is any such necessity known to have existed [Col. 1045B] that he should be compelled to argue again in a new work concerning those five questions about which he had already argued so extensively and in so many ways in his earlier books.

Moreover, its very language differs greatly from the eloquence of Saint Augustine; its meaning is considered considerably inferior to his meaning; and the modesty and humility of his character and speech are not preserved in it. It also uses testimonies from the Hebrew translation edited by blessed Jerome, contrary to Augustine’s custom with respect to those heretics. Augustine was accustomed to use the older edition instead. And it is wholly unworthy to think that so great a man could be found in this little work nullifying and destroying the word and meaning of predestination which he maintained and commended at all times in his writings and preaching, and which he certainly approved in the books of the *Retractions* by not censuring it there—so that, on account of such an opportunity, his *Retractions* themselves might now appear to deserve no credence.

It is therefore more believable that this work was written, a considerable time after his death, by someone else, and that it was collected and arranged, for the most part according to the manner and form of his thought, as a brief treatment against the Pelagian and Coelestian heretics of their five more dangerous questions. Since its author appears to have gathered and explained, in this brief work, the thought of blessed Augustine as though into a single whole, he therefore wished the name of Saint Augustine to appear in the title of the work—not because it had truly been published by him, but because it had been arranged and composed, insofar as its author was able, according to the form [Col. 1045D] of his arguments. (It would be as though he had wished to call the same little work in Latin “The Memorandum of Saint Augustine.”) Nothing else would then be understood except that what Augustine had discussed in scattered places and in many different ways had been briefly commended to memory, as though placed under a single view.

For if blessed Augustine had wished to reject and condemn the word “predestination” with respect to the reprobate as harsh and inappropriate—or even false—in his writings, a much greater and more fearsome opportunity would have presented itself for him to do so in the books that he wrote to Prosper and Hilary on the predestination of the saints and the gift of perseverance. He was compelled to address this matter by the great complaint and disturbance concerning it among distinguished and holy men in Gaul, who were so moved by his arguments and affected by a certain weariness that they judged the meaning of predestination, which he consistently and insistently preached, ought rather to be kept silent as either false or exceedingly dangerous.

Yet even by such disturbance and agitation among the faithful he could not be broken or recalled from his intention of teaching what was most true and faithful. Rather, he admonished and instructed them through his writings as far as he could, and faithfully assisted them by pouring out prayers before God, so that they might understand and recognize how necessary and salutary it was, for the commendation of divine grace, that the truth of this same predestination should altogether be both believed and preached.

[Col. 1046B] The heretical Pelagians, however, are never found to have criticized predestination with respect to the reprobate in Augustine’s arguments, because, as we think, they understood it to be both true and just. They denied it only with respect to the elect, in order to destroy divine grace and assert that human free will was sufficient. For if almighty God chose, before the foundation of the world, those whom he would save, and predestined the gifts that he would bestow upon them, then all human presumption ceases, and God’s grace alone is most clearly and firmly commended—the grace by which even human free will itself is both liberated from slavery to sin and enlightened by divine gifts. Thus, by an evident and invincible argument, the whole false and [Col. 1046C] deceptive doctrine of those same Pelagians is destroyed.

That great teacher therefore did not deny, in the little work *Hypomnesticon*, the true predestination of divine judgment concerning the condemnation of the reprobate, which he asserted everywhere in his writings. Rather, someone else, as we think, when a new calumny of those same Pelagians subsequently arose—as though by that predestination of the reprobate to destruction the Church were teaching that God, by his predestination, imposed upon human beings the necessity both of remaining in their impieties and of perishing eternally—removed the word “predestination” with respect to the reprobate. This ought instead, according to the truth of divine judgment, to have been carefully explained and commended.

He attempted to assert only the predestination of the elect. And thus, while wishing [Col. 1046D] to refute that calumny and remove it, he gave great occasion for error, so that the same divine predestination, being equally true and manifest in the condemnation of the reprobate, might be believed not to exist and, as though it did not exist, might be denied. Therefore, once the truth has been carefully investigated and clearly recognized, let the contention and hostility of error cease, and let the manifestation of truth be willingly and obediently accepted.

But as for his claim that those five questions—or objections—of the Pelagians were mentioned by blessed Augustine in the books that he wrote on the exposition of Genesis against the errors and blasphemies of the Manichaeans: this is found neither in our copies, nor does there seem to be any reason for it. For it is entirely clear that, when that author composed those books, almost at the earliest period of his conversion or priesthood, the name or heresy of the Pelagians did not yet exist; only much later, after many intervening years, did their madness and attack against the Church arise.

Therefore, since the matter in question neither pertained to the heretical Manichaeans nor could in any way have been raised by the Pelagians, who had not yet arisen, no reason at all permits us to suppose that something wholly unknown as yet and still entirely future was mentioned in those books as though it had already taken place. There are indeed, near the end of those books, five questions briefly proposed and explained against the Manichaeans; but they have nothing to do with the Pelagians and make no mention of them.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Augustine’s books to Prosper and Hilary

[Col. 1047B]

We also recognize as wholly untrue what the writer of the letter said: “For in the books written to Prosper and Hilary on the predestination of the saints and the gift of perseverance, that same teacher said nothing concerning the predestination of the reprobate to destruction.” For in those same books he frequently discusses the predestination of both parties—that is, of the elect and the reprobate—sometimes together and sometimes separately.

That book is therefore entitled *On the Predestination of the Saints*, not because nothing is said there concerning the predestination of the reprobate, but because it received its name from the better part. Likewise, in the books *On the City of God*, he discusses both cities—that is, the city of God and the city of the devil—equally and in many ways; nevertheless, he wished to call the books *On the City of God* after the better part.

Since, therefore, this seems very necessary for the present question, in which divine predestination is under discussion, we consider it opportune and useful to set before readers some passages from those same books that pertain to this matter, so that they may be recognized and retained.

In one place, distinguishing the two predestinations, as we have already mentioned above (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10), he says:

> “The predestination of God which is directed toward the good is the preparation of grace; grace, however, is the effect of that predestination.”

Likewise, elsewhere (chapter 20):

> “For the hand and plan of God predestined to be done by the hostile Jews as much as was necessary for the Gospel on our behalf. For God acts as he wills in human hearts, either by helping or by judging, so that through them also may be fulfilled what the hand and plan of God predestined to be done.”

And in another place (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 18):

> “God foreknew that he would do these things. This is the predestination of the saints, whom he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world (Acts IV, 18).”

And again (chapter 11):

> “He also comes to the aid of infants, to whom he wishes, even though they do not will or run; those whom he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world, intending to give them grace freely. And he does not come to the aid of adults—even those whom he foresaw would believe through his miracles if they had been performed among them—if he does not wish to come to their aid. Concerning these things he secretly but justly judged in his predestination: ‘For there is no injustice with God, but his judgments are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable (Rom. II, 33).’”

Again, shortly afterward in the same work:

> “The outcome of two twins, one of whom is taken and the other left, is different, while their merits are common. Yet in these cases one is freed by the great goodness of God in such a way that the other is not condemned by any injustice on his part. ‘For is there injustice with God? By no means (Rom. IX, 14).’ Rather, ‘his ways are unsearchable.’ Let us therefore believe without hesitation both his mercy in those who are freed and his truth in those who are punished. Let us not attempt to scrutinize what is inscrutable or investigate what is unsearchable.”

And elsewhere (chapter 14):

> “This is the predestination of the saints: nothing other than the foreknowledge, namely, and preparation of the benefits of God, by which all who are freed are most certainly freed. But the others—where are they left except in the mass of perdition, by a just divine judgment?”

And again:

> “Or perhaps they do not call these things themselves predestined? Then they are not given by God, or he did not know that he would give them. But if they are given, and he foresaw that he would give them, he certainly predestined them.”

And again:

> “God could not fail to foreknow any of his future gifts, both what gifts would be given and to whom they would be given; and consequently those whom he frees and crowns were predestined by him.”

Likewise, elsewhere:

> “For without doubt he foreknew if he predestined; but to have predestined is to have foreknown what he himself was going to do.”

We have briefly set these passages from the aforementioned books of blessed Augustine before consideration, so that we may recognize with complete certainty that he clearly taught and commended to his readers the eternal and immutable truth of divine foreknowledge and predestination.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On grace and free will

The following occurs in the aforementioned response.

### HINCMARUS

> “But those who have a sounder understanding concerning grace and free will believe and speak in this way: Free will in the first man did not die, but was corrupted; whereas in us, with respect to doing evil, the will is wrongly free, because, using a free will not liberated by grace but wrongly free, we become slaves of sin. With respect to doing good—or even willing good—our will is then truly free when it has been liberated by grace. It has not been raised from the dead, because it did not die, but has been healed by grace, because it was corrupted by a defect.
>
> “For this reason the reprobate will in no way receive the eternal rewards of the heavenly homeland: while they were able to earn them, they despised them through free will. This free will is formed in the good among the elect when, as grace inspires, their mind is lifted away from earthly desires.
>
> “The good that we do belongs both to God and to us: to God through preceding grace, and to us through a free will that follows. For if it does not belong to God, why do we give him eternal thanks for it? But if it does not belong to us, on what basis do we hope that rewards will be repaid to us? Since, therefore, we rightly give thanks, we know that we are preceded by his gift. And again, since we rightly seek recompense, we know that, with free will following, we have chosen the good things that we would do.
>
> “Thus, as we are taught by holy Scripture, we are preceded by grace so that we may will good; through free will we follow grace so that we may do good; we are helped by grace so that we may be able to do the good that we will by our will; we are strengthened by grace so that we may persevere in the good which, by following with free will, we have begun; and we follow grace so that, by grace, we may be freely rewarded with the grace of blessed recompense for the grace of good works.
>
> “‘And his mercy,’ he says—that is, grace—‘shall go before me (Ps. LVIII, 11).’ Likewise: ‘And his mercy shall follow me all the days of my life (Ps. XXII, 6).’ And: ‘Who crowns you with mercy and compassion (Ps. CII, 4).’”

### RESPONSE

[Note: [Col. 1049D] When the Church of Lyon censures Hincmarus for saying that free will was not killed by sin but corrupted, and was not raised up by Christ but healed, it understands “free will” as the good and upright will by which we cling to God through charity. In this sense it is certain that it was altogether killed, and not merely corrupted.
