Nevertheless, because the nature capable of conversion remained in it, so that it can obtain conversion through suitable and effective grace, [Col. 1050D] the words of Gottschalk could in this respect be charitably explained, although he was rightly condemned by the Fathers both of the Council of Mainz and of the Council of Sens, because his words sounded contrary to this—namely, that a good and upright will remained in man after sin. Or say that the Church of Lyon understands “free will” as the act of loving God above all things, which certainly was entirely lost through sin.]

We are greatly astonished by the meaning that could have permitted the following to be thought and said in these words: “Free will in the first man did not die, but was corrupted”; and, shortly afterward, concerning the same free will: “It was not raised from the dead, because it did not die, but was healed by grace, because it was corrupted by a defect.”

For did the first man not die in soul by sinning? Scripture says most truly: “The soul that sins shall itself die (Ezek. XVIII, 4).” And what is the soul’s truly free will except the soul’s free will? What, moreover, is the soul’s free will except free charity, by which before sin the soul freely, willingly, and perfectly clung to God and was made alive from him as from the fountain of life, and was enlightened by him as by the true light? To him we ought faithfully to say: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light (Ps. XXXV, 10).”

The human soul therefore died through sin, not by losing—as we have already said above—its nature, but by losing its true life, which is God for it. Hence, when turned toward God, it is made alive and lives for God; but when turned away from God, it dies with respect to God and lives for sin. Without doubt, by its will it turns away from God in order to die, and by its will it turns toward God in order to be made alive.

The soul’s will, when turned toward God, becomes good; when turned away from God, it becomes evil. When turned toward God, it is made alive; when turned away from God, it dies—just as the visual faculty of bodily eyes grows dark when turned away from the light, but becomes bright when turned toward the light.

What is the defect of the soul except turning away from God? And what is the virtue of the soul except turning toward God? [Col. 1050A] The defect of turning away from God is therefore the death of the soul, and the virtue of turning toward God is the life of the soul.

And because, as has already been said, it turns away from God by its will and turns toward God by its will, the soul’s will—which is naturally with it and in it—by that same turning away or turning toward, together with the soul and in the soul, likewise either dies or is made alive. Therefore it must in no way be believed that, when the soul died through sin in the first man, the good will did not die through that same sin.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The good will is created and renewed through grace—What it means for God to work the will

For the whole soul, together with its will, either lives [Col. 1050B] or dies. Therefore it could neither live for God without its will nor die with respect to God without its will. Nor was it corrupted by deadly sin without its will, nor is it healed from deadly sin without its will.

For if, when the first man sinned, the good will did not die, how is it now both created and renewed through life-giving grace, and how does God work it in man? Hence the Apostle says: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works (Eph. II, 10).” But, in order that we may be created in Christ Jesus for good works, what the Psalmist says must take place in us: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me (Ps. L, 12).” And: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to act (Phil. II, 13).”

For what is a clean heart except a conscience cleansed from sins, purified in the heart, and endowed with a good will? And what is a right spirit except one corrupted by no evil will? And what is it for God “to work the will in us” except to inspire and bestow upon us a good will?

The human soul therefore died through sin, and the human will died with respect to the life of God. That which before sin was truly free will—the free will of man, that is, the free charity of man by which, loving willingly and freely, he clung to God—died. Such free will of man truly died by neglecting God and withdrawing from God; and from that death, by which it lost the charity of God, it is raised and made alive through that same grace of the charity of God.

Blessed John the Apostle teaches this openly, saying: “We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren. He who does not love remains in death (1 John III, 14).” The life, therefore, of the human soul and of the human will is love of God and of one’s neighbor, by which before sin man enjoyed God and enjoyed his neighbor in God. From this life he died by neglecting God, neglecting himself, and neglecting his neighbor: “For he who does not love remains in death.”

The human soul and the human will therefore truly remain in death by not loving, and truly pass from death to life by loving. Just as its true death is not loving, so its true life is loving. By this love free choice—that is, a truly free will—does not come to be except through him who sets it free, that is, bestows freedom, who says: “If the Son shall make you free, then you shall be truly free (John VIII, 36),” and through that gift of the Spirit of God concerning which the Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom (2 Cor. III, 17).”

But regarding what is said in these words—“The good that we do belongs both to God and to us, because if it did not belong to God, we would not give him eternal thanks for that same good; and if it did not belong to us, we would not justly expect rewards from him for that same good”—we do not know what division or some distribution of one and the same good between God and man this is meant to signify.

It seems as though the good were partly God’s and partly ours, as the writer of the letter appears to assert throughout this entire discourse: as though God were the beginning of our good, but the effect belonged to human free will. He attempts to moderate this “error, as though by the addition of grace, though not by its fullness,” whereas in truth the whole of it belongs to God, as Truth itself says: “Without me you can do nothing (John XV, 5).” And the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? (1 Cor. IV, 7).”

Hence blessed and glorious martyr Cyprian defines the matter in this way:

> “In nothing should we glory, since nothing is ours.”

Our good therefore belongs entirely to God, because it is entirely from God; and none of our good belongs to us, because none of our good is from us. And therefore, to speak rather according to the form of the teaching of the Fathers, all our good is entirely God’s when he gives it, and becomes entirely ours when we receive it.

Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we ask daily, saying: “Give us this day our daily bread (Matt. VI, 11).” For why do we ask God to give us our bread, unless, as we have said, just as it is truly God’s by his bestowal, so it is also ours by our receiving it?

Hence blessed Pope Celestine—whose words we have already set forth above—says:

> “So great is the goodness of God toward all human beings that he wishes our merits to be his gifts.”

All our good must therefore be given to God and attributed to God, because it is entirely from him and not from us, since it is begun by him, worked by him, and brought to completion in us. For it is not those who are moved by their own spirit, but “all who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God (Rom. VIII, 14).”

We have spoken at greater length than usual about these matters concerning the first letter, because it was full of many difficult and tangled questions, and necessity itself compelled us to do so, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant it.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the second letter, which is Pardulus’s

In the second letter there are indeed few matters that require discussion, but they must not be passed over in silence. When the writer of this second letter wished briefly to indicate how great among them was the zeal for inquiry concerning the aforementioned questions, how great the disagreement of opinions, and with what eagerness it was desired that something certain and free from ambiguity, which could be followed and demonstrated, might be discovered concerning these matters, he spoke as follows:

### PARDULUS

> “Several people among us have written on the matter.” And after naming five of them, among whom he also mentioned Amalarius as having written, he added:
>
> “But because these opinions strongly disagreed among themselves, we compelled that Scot who is at the king’s palace, named John, to write.”
>
> And shortly afterward:
>
> “I inform you what the greatest dispute among our people concerning this matter is.”

> “Some of us say that Augustine published a little book entitled *Hypognosticon*. Some among us say that the same little book was not published by the aforementioned man. Anyone who reads Augustine’s second book, which he published on Genesis against the Manichaeans, all the way to the end will soon be able to prove this to be a lie, since there he demonstrates that he published this very question, together with five others, against the madness of the Manichaeans. For this reason he mentions nothing of it in the *Retractions*, because whatever he had said elsewhere concerning predestination he appears to correct in that same little book.
>
> “In the same way, some of us say that the book *On the Hardening of Pharaoh’s Heart* was published by blessed Jerome. Some among us say that it was falsely composed not by him but by someone else. You will also find this to be a lie if you read the seventeenth book of the aforementioned Jerome’s commentary on Isaiah, where he mentions the same little book.”

### RESPONSE

What else can we first answer to these words except that, if divine mercy had assisted and protected them, there would have been no labor or new necessity among them to investigate, discover, and write about these matters. Nor could such great disagreement and contention have arisen if, once every impulse toward presumption and hostility had been removed, they had unanimously, humbly, and obediently sought only the truth in the teachings of the holy Fathers and in ecclesiastical definitions. The Church has always honored and faithfully followed—and continues and will continue to follow—their most correct faith and most faithful teaching. Whatever they discovered could then have been proposed and commended to everyone for observance in peaceful, tranquil piety.

Nor would they have preferred “because of one little book,” whose author is uncertain and whose meaning is unusual and in no way acceptable, to the clear ecclesiastical institutions concerning God’s foreknowledge and predestination, which are established with such great firmness. For what reason existed for them to put all those things aside and neglect the truth of Scripture, after examining and considering it insufficiently? And why would they judge that what was supported by no certain author and no true reasoning should rather be followed, except because of the evil of contention itself—by which a previously presumed opinion and a thoughtlessly uttered meaning was considered something to be defended stubbornly rather than corrected for the sake of salvation?

Hence we cannot sufficiently wonder how those five or six questions could have been believed to have been brought forward by blessed Augustine against the madness of the Manichaeans, since, as the numerous books of that holy teacher testify and as the little work *Hypomnesticon* itself clearly demonstrates, they were first raised by the heretical Pelagians against the faith of the Church and were treated more carefully for the purpose of refuting them.

But most certainly—as we have already said above—when blessed Augustine wrote those books on the exposition of Genesis against the Manichaeans, the Pelagians had not yet been heard of or arisen. Only much later did they begin to attack the Church of God. Since we have already said enough above about their little book, which gave occasion for this error and confusion, we think that nothing more needs to be said here.

As for the book *On the Hardening of Pharaoh’s Heart*, which is thought to have been written by blessed Jerome, we have not been able to find it among his minor works either in the book *On Illustrious Men* or in the venerable account of his life. In the seventeenth book of his *Commentaries on the Prophet Isaiah*, however, Jerome is said to have written something of this kind. Yet he is not described as having dealt specifically with *The Hardening of Pharaoh’s Heart*, but as having briefly touched upon that entire extremely difficult apostolic question in the Letter to the Romans.

But because we have never seen such a little book, we cannot judge, as though it were something known, whether the one found among them should be believed to be Jerome’s on account of the gravity of its style and the sincerity of its faith. What that holy teacher thought concerning free will in accordance with the Catholic faith is nevertheless most clearly testified by his dialogues, which he wrote against the Pelagians under the names Atticus and Cretobulus.

His profession of faith, which he issued most fully and perfectly to the bishop of the apostolic see in defense of himself against certain detractors, also sufficiently demonstrates this. There he speaks about free will as follows:

[Note: [Col. 1053D] This profession of faith is not Saint Jerome’s, addressed to Damasus, but Pelagius’s, addressed to Pope Innocent.]

> “We confess free will in such a way that we say that we always need God’s help. We say that both those who, with Manichaeus, claim that man cannot avoid sin and those who, with Jovinianus, assert that man cannot sin are in error; for each removes freedom of will. We, however, say that man is always able both to sin and not to sin, so that we may always confess ourselves to possess free will.”

In these words of the blessed teacher, what he affirms—that man is always able to sin—plainly belongs to human weakness. But what he affirms—that man is able not to sin—is truly from divine help, as he himself testifies, so that human free will may be able to exist.

The same blessed teacher also said in one place:

> “God created us with free will; we are compelled by no necessity either toward virtue or toward vice. Otherwise, where there is necessity, there is no crown.”

Blessed Augustine, in his book *On Nature and Grace* (chapters 65–66), explains and defends these words of Jerome, which Pelagius had set forth as though they were opposed to the grace of God, saying that the presbyter in question had said:

> “God created us with free will; we are compelled by no necessity either toward virtue or toward vice. Otherwise, where there is necessity, there is no crown.”

Who does not recognize this? Who does not embrace it with all his heart? Who would deny that human nature was created otherwise? But [Col. 1054B] in doing what is right, there is no bond of necessity precisely because there is the freedom of charity. Yet because, arising from the vices of nature and not from the condition of nature, there is a certain necessity of sinning, let man hear this and, so that this necessity may no longer exist, learn to say to God: “Deliver me from my necessities.” Thus, with grace assisting through our Lord Jesus Christ, the evil necessity will be removed and full freedom will be bestowed.”

These are the words of blessed Augustine.

## CHAPTER XL. On Amalarius; on the writings of John Scotus
What is more, that Amalarius is placed among the others who are said to have written on so great a question—namely, divine foreknowledge and predestination—and that John Scotus is reported to have been compelled by them to write, we receive with great displeasure and grief: ecclesiastical and prudent men have done themselves so great an injury that they consulted Amalarius about the principles of the faith, although by his words and books—full of falsehoods, errors, and fanciful and heretical arguments—he infected and corrupted almost all the churches throughout Gaul, and even some in other regions, insofar as he was able. Thus it was not so much he who ought to have been questioned about the faith as all his writings, at least after his death, ought to have been consumed by fire, lest the simpler sort, who are said to love and frequently read them, should be both uselessly occupied and perniciously deceived and misled by their reading. And, what is even more disgraceful and shameful, they compelled that Scot to write.

[Note: The Church of Lyons censures and accuses Amalarius as though he were the author and promoter of all the heresies of that period. Who he actually was is more unknown than known. Take only this from the most learned man Nicolas Fabri, a diligent investigator of antiquity. We consider Florus to have been that bishop of Troyes who wrote very extensively against John Scotus and Gottschalk, though some things in his writings are especially worthy of notice. This Florus, writing against Amalarius on Psalm 80, says: “Do you wish to eat the Lord your God himself? Hear what he says: ‘Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it.’ Open wide your mouths: he himself is the Lord and the bread; he himself urges us to eat. He is our food: as wide as you open your mouth, so much will you receive.” Thus far Florus. This leaves room for the conjecture that that Amalarius, together with John Scotus, was a precursor and, as it were, standard-bearer of Berengar. Our Eucharist-fighters have long since roused from the underworld and revived their error, which had been put to sleep and extinguished.]

For, as we have most truthfully learned from his writings, he does not yet even know the actual words of Scripture. And he is so full of fanciful inventions and errors that he ought not merely not to be consulted about the truth of the faith, but—unless he hastens to correct and amend them—he and those writings of his, worthy of every ridicule and contempt, must either be pitied as one who is deranged or anathematized as a heretic.

## CHAPTER XLI  
### On the third letter, which is Rabanus’s

The third letter, which was written not to our Church but to a certain friend of a venerable bishop, undertakes, as it seems to us, an unnecessary discussion wholly unrelated to the matter under inquiry. For the question presently being debated, as we have already said above frequently and in many ways, is not whether God predestined the ungodly and wicked to ungodliness and wickedness itself—that is, so that they should be ungodly and wicked and could not be anything else. No one at the present time is found to say or to have said this. It is indeed a monstrous and detestable blasphemy to say that God, by his predestination, is somehow the author of ungodliness and wickedness, and that he compelled certain people to be ungodly and wicked.

Rather, the question is whether he predestined to be punished with eternal punishment those whom he truly and entirely foreknew would become ungodly and wicked through their own fault and would persevere in their ungodliness and wickedness until death. But the author of the letter, leaving aside this second question, which is presently debated by many, labors instead against the former impious opinion, directing the whole argument of his discussion toward the claim that God, being good and just, could never have been anyone’s cause, origin, or author of sin and wickedness. All the faithful, as has been said, confess this faithfully and without doubt. Nevertheless, he strives to affirm, on the basis of the words of the aforementioned little book called the *Hypognosticon*, that no divine predestination concerning the just condemnation of those same ungodly and wicked people is to be believed, and that predestination is to be acknowledged only with respect to the elect.

And because he is said to have written on this matter before all others who wrote in the present age, those who think and defend similarly concerning this divine predestination appear to follow his authority. For he himself says at once, in the preface of that letter, as follows:

### RABANUS

“Concerning the heresy which certain wicked people construct concerning God’s predestination, wandering in error and leading others into error, it has been agreed among us that I should compose a little work from the divine Scriptures and the opinions of orthodox Fathers, to refute the error of those who think so wickedly about the good and just God that they say his predestination makes it impossible for a person predestined to life to fall into death, and impossible in any way for one predestined to death to recover life. Yet God, the author of all things [lacuna], the creator of natures, is not the cause of anyone’s ruin or destruction, but the source of salvation for many.”

### RESPONSE

In these words he first calls heresy and heretics those who think about divine predestination in such a way that, in accordance with the authority of Scripture and the holy Fathers, they faithfully believe it with respect to both groups—namely, the elect and the reprobate: that almighty God, in his great goodness, eternally predestined the former to glory, while in the great equity of his judgment he predestined the latter to punishment. He must therefore be warned and recalled to a consideration of piety, lest it be found that, under the name of those whom he so readily calls heretics, he is condemning instead the holy and venerable Fathers who taught and defined these things.

## CHAPTER XLII  
### Predestination makes it impossible for the elect to perish; the opposite is not said of the reprobate. God is not the author of perdition. God imposes necessity of sinning on no one.

As for his statement concerning those whom he considers heretics—“because they think so wickedly about the good and just God that they say his predestination makes it impossible for a person predestined to life to fall into death, and impossible in any way for one predestined to death to recover life”—it is clear that this is in no way a falsehood but the most certain truth. All the faithful believe and confess that the goodness and grace of divine predestination make it impossible for anyone among those predestined to eternal life to fall into eternal death.

For they received from him the stability and firmness of perseverance in the good—he who prayed, and prays, for them that their faith should not fail, as he himself says to blessed Peter: “But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32). And elsewhere in the Gospel he says of these same elect: “And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish” (John 10:28).

But that the same divine predestination should act in the case of the reprobate by making it impossible for any of them, through turning to God and changing for the better, to recover life—as though almighty God, which God forbid, had imposed on them by his predestination the necessity of doing evil and persevering in their evils—no believer says this at all. For no believer believes that God is the author of evil deeds and merits.

That an ungodly and wicked person can recover life by correcting his evils and imploring divine mercy, the Lord himself testifies through the prophet, saying: “But if the ungodly turns away from his ungodliness and does judgment and righteousness, he shall preserve his soul alive” (Ezek. 18:27).

Similarly, no believer contradicts his further statement that “God is the cause of no one’s ruin and destruction,” because no one believes God to be the author of the ruin and perdition of the ungodly, but only the author of their just condemnation and punishment.

The same applies to what he immediately places at the beginning of the letter and says:

### RABANUS

“So that certain of them assert that the creator of their destruction is their own creator, saying that, just as those who have been summoned by God’s foreknowledge and predestination to receive the glory of eternal life have been summoned, so those who are going to eternal destruction are compelled by God’s predestination and cannot escape destruction.”

### RESPONSE

No one says this, of course. All the ungodly and wicked justly perish for their ungodliness and wickedness; they do not have God as the author of their destruction, since they perished by their own merit, but only as the author of the punishment and condemnation which they justly received.

Likewise, he says that those whom he considers heretics declare:

### RABANUS

“Those who are going to eternal destruction are compelled by God’s predestination and cannot escape destruction.”

### RESPONSE

No one says this at all. The fact that the ungodly go to destruction is their own fault, not the prejudicial effect of divine predestination. Nor are they compelled by that same predestination of God to be unable to escape; rather, they are rightly compelled to perish by their most persistent wickedness, which they were unwilling to abandon.

The same letter continues:

### RABANUS

“For in no way can he who created all good things, made the nations of the world capable of healing, and wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, compel anyone to perish.”

### RESPONSE

This too is entirely true, since God imposes on no one the necessity of perishing, just as he imposes on no one the necessity of doing evil. For each person is the author of his own wickedness and the author of his own destruction. God, whom he does not have as the author of his guilt, he has as the author of his most just punishment.

Again, in the same place:

### RABANUS

“For if, according to those who think such things, God’s predestination makes a person sin unwillingly, how does God justly condemn the sinner, since he sinned not by his will but by necessity?”

### RESPONSE

This, like the statements made above, has nothing to do with the present question. No one thinks or says that God’s predestination makes anyone sin unwillingly, so that he seems to sin not through the perversity of his own will but by the necessity of divine predestination. Rather, divine predestination brings this about: the one who sins willingly and willingly perseveres in his sins is punished against his will by a just judgment.

A little later the letter continues and says:

### RABANUS

“The faith of predestination, however, is fortified by the firmest authority of the holy Scriptures. To it it is in no way permissible to ascribe the evil deeds committed by human beings.”

### RESPONSE

No believer does this either. No one ascribes or imputes to God, on the basis of the truth of divine predestination concerning the reprobate, the wickedness of those who do evil. They ascribe to him only the just condemnation of those same reprobate and those same evildoers.

## CHAPTER XLIII  
### Whether sins remitted and erased after baptism return and are counted toward punishment if a person is condemned

The same letter continues.

### RABANUS

“For he who departs from Christ and ends this life alienated from grace—what does he do except fall into destruction? Yet he does not fall again into what was remitted, nor will he be condemned on account of original sin; nevertheless, because of his final crimes he will suffer that death which was owed to him on account of those sins that had been remitted.”

### RESPONSE

In these words, the statement that a person who departs from Christ, makes his grace void within himself, and thus ends this life is not to be charged with either the original or actual sins that had truly been remitted to him in baptism, but only with those which he committed after losing God’s grace, appears to us a very difficult question. We believe that it must be resolved, not according to our own opinion, but by the authority of the holy Fathers, insofar as God grants this.

For when blessed Augustine was expounding the words of the Psalm in which, among the curses pronounced against Judas the betrayer, it says, “Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered in the sight of the Lord, and let the sin of his mother not be blotted out” (Exposition of Psalm 118:14), he explains that this curse was fulfilled in Judas himself, saying:

“If Judas had held fast to that to which he was called, neither his past sins nor the iniquity of his parents could in any way have concerned him. But because he did not hold fast to adoption into the family of God, and instead chose the iniquity of the ancient race, ‘the iniquity of his fathers returned in the sight of the Lord,’ so that he himself too might be punished in it. And the sin of his mother was not blotted out in him.”

The Psalm immediately continues: “Let them be continually before the Lord”—that is, the iniquity of his fathers and the sin of his mother. The same teacher explains this as follows (ibid., 14–15):

“‘Let them be continually before the Lord’: not that they might be turned away from the Lord, but so that the Lord may not forget their most wicked merits in this man, when he repays that man for those very merits.” For ‘before the Lord’ means ‘in the sight of the Lord.’”

Behold, most plainly, according to the meaning of the prophecy contained in this Psalm concerning that lost man, the blessed teacher teaches that neither his own sins nor those of his parents could have continued to concern him if he had wished to remain in that grace and adoption as sons of God to which he had been called. But because he did not remain, and by apostasy returned to the iniquity of the ancient generation descended from Adam, even after the grace of baptism—which he made void in himself—the iniquity of his fathers returned to him,

[Note: Against this, Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* III, question 88, article 1, and with him the other scholastics, in book IV, distinction 22, maintain that sins once remitted never return as the same sins in number, nor are they again imputed by God in the manner in which they would have been had they not been remitted, because of Romans 11: “The gifts of God are irrevocable”; Nahum 1: “God does not punish the same thing twice”; and Ezekiel 18: “If the ungodly repents, I will not remember any of his iniquities.” Nevertheless, they return through a subsequent sin by reason of ingratitude, which makes that sin much more serious and culpable. In this way the words of the Church of Lyons are to be explained; they are also found in Hugh of Saint-Victor, book II *On the Saints*, part XIV, final chapter, and in the gloss of Gratian’s *De Penitentia*, distinction 4, canon “He who departs.”]

not only his own but also the iniquity of his fathers; and the sin of his mother was not blotted out in him, so that he himself too might be punished in them, by the judgment and condemnation of him “who repays the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation” (Exod. 34:7). Hence the prophecy also adds: “Let them be before the Lord” (Ps. 108:15)—that is, continually in the sight of the Lord—namely, the sins and iniquities of his fathers and mother, so that the Lord may not forget their most wicked merits in this man when he repays them to them.

What we know to have happened in this apostate and transgressor of God’s grace, who abandoned the calling and adoption of the children of God, chose the iniquity of the ancient generation rather than the justification of the new regeneration, and did so both by divine truth and by the manifest exposition of the blessed Father, we must also hold as certain concerning the other transgressors of the same grace: when the new grace departs from them, the ancient iniquity returns to them—not only their own but also their fathers’.

But whether the guilt of original sin, erased through the grace of baptism, is also to be understood as returning to him and being imputed to him in these prophetic words—“Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered in the sight of the Lord” (Ps. 108:14)—so that the iniquity not only of his parents and ancestors who may have lived in more recent times, but also of the first fathers and first parents who first sinned in paradise, is imputed to him, is not clearly evident from the words of the holy teacher, nor should we rashly assume it.

We do read in the prophet Jeremiah: “In those days they shall no longer say, ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge’; but each person shall die for his own iniquity” (Jer. 31:29–30). In these words the grace of the New Testament is clearly foretold, through which the original sin contracted from the first transgression is undone and erased by baptismal regeneration. Thus each person, cleansed by that regeneration and released from the bond of the ancient condemnation, will not die in the sin of the first parents—which has also been remitted—but, if he has served sins and crimes, he will die in his own iniquity.

For iniquity itself is the sour, unripe, harsh, and harmful grape which, like something eaten, does not refresh the one who consumes it with any genuine sweetness. Rather, it weakens and injures the power and strength of the soul, like teeth, so that it cannot receive the food of life. Of this it is written: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9); and he also says of himself: “I am the bread of life” (John 6:48).

“The fathers therefore ate sour grapes”—those who first committed iniquity in paradise—“and the children’s teeth were set on edge,” because by sinning they harmed not only themselves but also their entire progeny. But when all who come to the faith are absolved from that sin, transmitted originally, through the bath of regeneration, they no longer die in that ancient iniquity of their fathers; each one dies in his own iniquity.

Therefore, whether the sins committed after baptism are imputed to those who sin, or whether even those which they committed before baptism are added on account of their transgression of so great a grace, they die in their own iniquity, which they had committed either before or afterward. If, then, the guilt of original sin is in no way counted against them after baptism, each person plainly dies only in his own sin and iniquity. But if that guilt is imputed along with the other sins, even in that case each person dies in his own sin, since original sin is not then imputed to him because he drew it from his origin, but because, by the merit of his own iniquity, he deserved to have it imputed to him again.

## CHAPTER XLIV  
### Whether baptized reprobates were separated from the mass of perdition. It is affirmed that they were separated. It is asserted that sin no longer remains after justification.

The same letter continues after this.

### RABANUS

“Since God’s foreknowledge was neither unaware of nor deceived by this, he certainly never chose such a person, never predestined him, and never separated one destined to perish from eternal perdition. Therefore, whoever such people are—even if they have been reborn and justified—were not predestined by him who foreknew that they would be such.”

### RESPONSE

In these words, the first point to be considered is that the author of the letter affirms that the person who departs from Christ, becomes alienated from his grace, and persists in such ungodliness to the end—since God truly foreknew that he would become such—was never chosen or predestined by God for life and was never separated from eternal perdition, although he was destined to perish. Thus those who deny the predestination of divine judgment to the just destruction of the reprobate now affirm that the reprobates themselves, condemned by that same just judgment of God, were never separated from the mass of perdition.

Next, it must be asked more carefully and diligently: if the reprobates were never separated from the mass of perdition and condemnation, how, as is said here, were so many of them reborn and justified in the Church through the grace of baptism? For if, as has been said, they were never separated from the mass of condemnation and perdition, how were they truly reborn and justified in the Church? What does “reborn” mean except renewed through baptismal regeneration? And what does “justified” mean except cleansed from their ungodliness by him who justifies the ungodly?

How, then, are true renewal and true cleansing accomplished in them when they are baptized into Christ’s death and washed from sins in his blood, if they are still fixed within and held fast in the mass of condemnation and perdition, not separated from it?

The Apostle first speaks of “a branch of the wild” and uncultivated “olive tree” (Rom. 11:17), cut off from the natural wild olive tree and afterward grafted into a good olive tree, thereby becoming a sharer in the root and richness of the olive. Yet he later strongly warns and terrifies it, saying: “See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but God’s goodness toward you, if you continue in his goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off” (ibid., 22).

What else does this mean except that, once cut off from the good olive tree into which you had been grafted, you will be assigned with the wild, untamed, and bitter wild olive tree to the fires? According to this likeness, it is perhaps better believed and said that those who truly come to faith in Christ, are truly regenerated in his grace through baptism, and truly receive forgiveness of both original and actual sins, are thereby to be believed truly cut off from the natural wild olive tree—that is, separated from the mass of perdition and condemnation—and grafted into the good olive tree—that is, incorporated into the Church.

Nevertheless, if after all this they commit acts deserving of being cut off, they too are cut off from that olive tree and, with the mass of condemnation and perdition from which they had been separated by the forgiveness of original and actual sin, are assigned, like the natural wild olive tree, to eternal burning.

For from what did that mass of condemnation and perdition arise, unless from the guilt and mixture of original sin? When, therefore, the true remission of that original sin exists in every faithful believer who has been truly reborn and purified, how does that person remain in the mass of original sin when he is proved to have been separated from it by the remission of that same sin?

But when it is frequently read in the words of the holy Fathers that such people—that is, those who make Christ’s grace void in themselves and thus perish—were never separated from that mass, this pertains to God’s foreknowledge. Although for the present he grants them, together with the elect, the common grace of regeneration in the Church, by the judgment of his predestination he nevertheless already assigns them to the place where he sees that they will be condemned on account of the merit of their transgression.

## CHAPTER XLV  
### The discussion continues concerning predestination

After this, the author of the letter, inserting very few words of his own, silently introduces and appends the words of the little book *Hypomnesticon*, presenting its words and meaning as though they formed one continuous and orderly discourse with his own. From these he attempts to prove that divine predestination is always to be understood only with respect to the elect, and that there is none at all with respect to the reprobate. He begins as follows:

### RABANUS

“Let us therefore first explain what the name ‘predestination’ itself signifies; then let us prove from the authority of the divine Scriptures that predestination exists with God, who shows no partiality. Predestination is so called from foreseeing and anticipating—or from foreordaining—something in the future. Therefore God, for whom foreknowledge is not an accident but an essence, has always been and is one who foreknows and predestines everything before it exists; and he predestines it for the reason that he foreknows what it will be.

Therefore the Apostle says: ‘For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined’ (Rom. 8:29). But he does not predestine everything that he foreknows: he merely foreknows evils and does not predestine them, whereas he both foreknows and predestines good things.

The good which foreknowledge predestines—that is, which it ordains beforehand in itself before it exists—when it begins to exist from its author, he calls, orders, and arranges. Hence what follows: ‘Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified’ (ibid., 30).

Let us now explain more openly what we are saying: how God, in whom there is no iniquity, uses his foreknowledge and predestination concerning the human race. The mass of the human race, made liable to condemnation and mortal by the transgression of Adam and Eve, is owed not to a general divine condemnation but, as a debt, to punishment and the torments of Gehenna. Forgiveness, however, is conferred not on the basis of merit but through the generosity of the mercy of God, the just judge.

Since God is just, merciful, and foreknowing of the future, from this condemnable mass he prepares, not by respect of persons but by the irreproachable judgment of his equity, those whom he foreknows for free mercy—that is, he predestines them to eternal life. The others he punishes as he previously said, according to what they deserve. He punishes them because he foreknew what they would be; yet he himself did not make them fit for punishment or predestine them to it, but merely, as I have said, foreknew them within the condemnable mass.

If you ask me to know why God does these two things differently, if he is not a respecter of persons, since justice must either punish generally or mercy must free, contend with Paul—indeed, if you dare, argue with Paul, who spoke with Christ speaking through him: ‘O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, “Why have you made me thus?” Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?’ (Rom. 9:20–21).

I say what I have said: whatever God does, he does mercifully, justly, and holily, because he alone knows by foreseeing what a human being does not know because he does not foresee. ‘For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid?’ (Rom. 11:34–35). Or who says to him, ‘What have you done?’ God cannot be called merely just, or merely merciful, but just and merciful. So we say; so we believe.

Therefore, when with David ‘we sing mercy and judgment’ (Ps. 100:1), we do not inquire in fear what his will is in judgment, but rest in his mercy.”

### RESPONSE

Since all these things, as we have said, are not his words but are plainly recognized as taken from the little book just mentioned, and since we have already shown sufficiently above what we think about that book, let us set aside the lengthy and pious exhortation by which he faithfully and beneficially urges all the faithful to live and act well, leaving aside such obscure and difficult questions and drawing many statements relevant to this matter from the divine Scriptures. Let us pass to his own words, with which he speaks near the end of the letter as follows.

## CHAPTER XLVI  
### Good works are beneficial and truly save a person

### RABANUS

“How these empty talkers chatter that right faith and good works benefit a person nothing! For unless someone has been predestined, they say, he does not come to life, although predestination is nothing other than the gift of life, not the condemnation of perdition.

Hence Scripture plainly says: ‘God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living. For he created all things that they might exist, and made the nations of the world capable of healing’ (Wis. 1:13–14). And the Lord himself says through the prophet: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live’ (Ezek. 33:11).

But if God does not desire the death of the ungodly and sinner, how did he predestine him to death? Since his willing is nothing other than his predestining—for the will of God is the cause of all things, and his willing to do something is his doing it—and since simple nature contains no contradiction within itself, but ‘the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him’ (Rom. 10:12).

Thus predestination is read with respect to the good, not the evil. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Those whom he foreknew, he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified’ (Rom. 8:29–30).

Notice that he says, ‘Those whom he predestined, he also called,’ not ‘Those whom he predestined, he also condemned.’ For the good Creator loved his creature, and he does not condemn anyone undeservedly.

Of this it is written elsewhere: ‘You have mercy on all, Lord, and hate nothing that you have made, overlooking the sins of human beings because of repentance, and sparing them, because you are the Lord of all’ (Wis. 11:24–25).”

### RESPONSE

Since much has already been said above about all these matters, it is unnecessary to labor over them at length. We need only briefly indicate a few points that require consideration.

When he says that “empty talkers say that right faith and good works benefit a person nothing, since unless someone has been predestined he does not come to life,” it is entirely true that only those who have been divinely chosen and predestined come to life. The Apostle openly proclaims and confirms this, saying: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called. Those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.” These are the ones who certainly come to life. Concerning them the Lord himself promises, saying: “And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish” (John 10:28).

Far be it from any believer to say that right faith and good works are of no benefit. They truly benefit and truly save a person if what the Lord says is added to them: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13). Therefore, let the faithful person confidently believe rightly and act well, because if he perseveres faithfully in these things, he will undoubtedly be saved and will belong to the number of the elect.

But concerning the statement placed here—“predestination is nothing other than the gift of life, not the condemnation of perdition”—it seems to us that Saint Augustine did not say or define the matter in this way. Distinguishing between predestination and grace, he says as follows (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10):

“Predestination is the preparation for grace; grace, however, is the gift itself.”

And after inserting a few further remarks, he says that the same divine predestination is to be understood in two ways: both with respect to the good, the elect who have been freely predestined to life, and with respect to the evil, the reprobate who have been justly predestined to punishment. He says as follows (ibid.):

“The predestination of God, then, which is with respect to the good, is, as I have said, the preparation for grace.”

Likewise, when he proposes and says, “If God does not desire the death of the ungodly and sinner, how does he predestine him to death?”, we have already discussed this as far as our weakness permitted, and we now say briefly: he does not desire the one “by the goodness of the Creator,” but he brings about the other “by the equity of the judge,” so that he both wishes to save what he created and does not leave the creature’s fault unpunished.

When he adds and says, “Thus predestination is read with respect to the good, not the evil,” citing the Apostle—“Those whom he foreknew, he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son”—he should consider carefully, as we have already pointed out repeatedly, that in the divine Scriptures one must not demand that, wherever the reality of predestination is stated, the actual name “predestination” should also be found explicitly. Rather, wherever the reality itself is certainly found, it must regularly be understood that predestination is rightly present even when the name “predestination” is left unspoken.

For if we demand that the name “predestination” itself be explicitly present, we do not find it at all even in those prophetic testimonies from which the Apostle establishes divine predestination both with respect to the elect and with respect to the reprobate. Nevertheless, we do not hesitate faithfully to believe what he establishes with the clearest certainty of the facts.

## CHAPTER XLVII  
### Rabanus’s seven objections

After all this, at the end of the letter:

### RABANUS

“Therefore this person is bound by manifold guilt, since he turns the goodness of predestination into a wicked meaning and presumes to blaspheme it with abominable words.

“First, because he has dared to call his Creator, who is supremely good, evil-minded, on the grounds that he decrees his work to perish in vain and without cause.

“Second, because he attempts to assert that the truth itself is deceptive, although through the sacred Scriptures it promises the rewards of eternal life to those who believe rightly and act well, and foretells the punishments of death for those who sin and do not repent.

“Third, because he proclaims the just Judge, who will judge the living and the dead in equity, to be unjust, when he affirms that God does not repay rewards to those who act well and torments to those who act badly.

“Fourth, because through his error he is not afraid to pretend that the Redeemer of the world shed his blood in vain, when, because of the necessity of predestination, he cannot help those who believe and hope in him.

“Fifth, because he envies the good angels their number, which the devil diminished when he fell through pride, and which our Savior completes through the creation of human beings.

“Sixth, because by his opinion he favors the devil more than God, since he hands over to the devil’s lot those whom divine grace has decreed should attain eternal salvation.

“Seventh, because he is manifestly an enemy of the entire human race, since he says that through faith in Christ and the sacrament of baptism the human race cannot be rescued from the fall of its first parent, from the guilt of its own crimes, or from the power of its enemies, but, bound by the pernicious predestination of its maker, is plunged into Tartarus.”

### RESPONSE

In these seven statements he presents objections or definitions by which he accuses not those who, as he says, blaspheme against God, but those who faithfully believe God and truly confess and praise his mercy and judgment in the deliverance of the elect and the condemnation of the reprobate, as guilty of falsehood and error. Yet he is unable to show that anything he objects to in these seven definitions is true or reasonable.

### On the First Objection

No one, surely, calls his Creator, who is supremely good, evil-minded—as though He were ill-disposed toward His creature—for His will is always good toward the good. Even if it appears evil to the wicked, it is nevertheless always just, and therefore cannot be evil. Hence Scripture says to Him:

> “With the holy man You will show Yourself holy, and with the innocent You will show Yourself innocent. With the chosen You will show Yourself chosen, and with the perverse You will show Yourself perverse” (Psalm 17:26–27).

Commenting on these words, blessed Augustine says (on Psalm 17):

> There is a hidden depth here, by which You are understood to be holy with the holy, because You sanctify; and innocent with the innocent man, because You harm no one, but each person is bound by the cords of his own sins. You are chosen by the one whom You choose, and You appear perverse with the perverse, because they say: “The way of the Lord is not right, and their own way is not right” (Ezekiel 18:25).

[Col. 1066A] Nor does He decree His work to perish without reason or cause. Rather, those whom He most truly foreknew would become impious and unrighteous, and would remain in their impiety and unrighteousness, He decreed and established—and predestined to perish—for just and perfectly righteous reasons. As He Himself says:

> “Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot him out of My book” (Exodus 32:33).

### On the Second

Nor does the person who faithfully believes and confesses divine predestination in both respects—that is, of the elect and of the reprobate—attempt to show that the truth itself is deceptive. Rather, he affirms it to be altogether truthful and faithful in all its words, and holy in all its works: for, just as He predestined, God promises and bestows the rewards of eternal life upon the elect. Conversely, upon the reprobate who sin and do not repent, [Col. 1066B] He justly inflicts eternal punishments, as He predestined.

### On the Third

Nor does this truth of divine predestination proclaim the just Judge to be unjust. For according to it, rewards are restored to those who act well and persevere in goodness, while torments are justly imposed upon those who act wickedly and persist in evil.

### On the Fourth

Nor does any necessity of His predestination compel the Redeemer of the world, so that He is unable to help those who believe and hope in Him through the glorious price of His blood. For by that price He helps all His elect eternally. If He does not help the reprobate, they themselves, through their impiety and unrighteousness, reject His price. Although He is able to save them, He nevertheless wills to condemn some of them by a just punishment, in order to display the terror of His severity.

### On the Fifth

Nor does this same severity of divine predestination begrudge the good angels their number, as though, because of the multitude of reprobates perishing daily, the number diminished by the fall of the devil and his angels could not be completed and restored. For the faith of the faithful knows with complete certainty that as many of the elect from the human race will join them there as it is established that elect angels remained there. Scripture bears witness when it says:

> “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Deuteronomy 32:8).

### On the Sixth

Nor does this predestination favor the devil more than God, since it daily compels the devil to lose those whom divine grace, by that same predestination, [Col. 1066D] decreed would attain eternal salvation. It absolutely confirms that none of God’s elect can belong to the devil’s lot.

### On the Seventh

Nor does faith in this predestination compel anyone to believe that, through faith in Christ and the sacrament of baptism, no one can be rescued from the fall of the first parent, from the guilt of his own crimes, or from the power of his enemies. Rather, it most truly grants to all the elect:

> “That they may always give thanks to God and the Father, who has made them worthy to share in the inheritance of the saints in light; who has rescued them from the power of darkness and transferred them into the kingdom of the Son of His love” (Colossians 1:12–13).

Nor is the predestination of its Creator—that is, of God—harmful to the reprobate. It most justly punishes their persistent and unyielding [Col. 1067A] unrighteousness, crushed beneath whose habit and exceedingly heavy burden they are plunged into Tartarus, descending into the depths like a stone and sinking like lead in mighty waters. The book of Revelation also terrifyingly signifies and announces that this will happen at the final judgment to the whole city of this age—that is, to the entire multitude of the condemned—when it says:

> “And a mighty angel lifted up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying: ‘With such force Babylon, that great city, will be thrown down, and it will never be found again’” (Revelation 18:2).

[Col. 1068A] ### Conclusion

Since these things are so, let us lay aside all contentious hostility and all presumption concerning novelties. Let us faithfully acknowledge the divine truth, obediently follow the authority of the Fathers, and vigilantly beware of the utterly deceptive vanity of error and falsehood. With God’s help, let us preserve inviolate the “deposit” of the true faith entrusted to us once for all, “fleeing profane novelties of words and the oppositions of knowledge falsely so called, which some professing have fallen away from the faith” (1 Timothy 6:20–21).

[Col. 1067]

## The Resolution of a Certain Question by Saint Remigius, Bishop of Lyons, in the Name of the Church of Lyons, Concerning the General Condemnation of All through Adam and the Special Deliverance of the Elect from It through Christ (G)*

[Col. 1067B] Recently the question was raised how the following statement can rightly and faithfully be understood:

> “The entire mass of the human race was condemned to eternal destruction on account of the merit of the first transgression.”

For undoubtedly the entire number of the elect was to be taken from that very mass, having been eternally foreknown and predestined by divine predestination and foreknowledge to eternal life. If this number of the blessed and the saints was condemned by divine judgment in that mass to destruction, how, conversely, will it have been predestined to life by the benefit of divine mercy? Both things, moreover, were eternal and immovable in the eternal and unchangeable counsel of Him who, according to the prophet, “made the things that are to come” (Isaiah 41:11, according to the Septuagint).

Nor, according to the rule of Catholic truth, can we say that the entire human race was condemned to destruction on account of that transgression, but by no means predestined to the same destruction. For by the just and eternal judgment of almighty God, nothing could have been eternally condemned unless it had likewise been foreknown and predetermined as destined to be condemned. For He both foreknew all His works as truly just and right, and undoubtedly predestined them to be done.

[Col. 1067C] Therefore He also predestined this just and deserved condemnation of the human race, to which all would generally be subject because of His justice, and from which the elect would be specially distinguished and saved through His mercy: the predestination of condemnation remaining unshaken in the reprobate, and likewise the predestination of deliverance remaining unshaken in the elect. In the most just and marvelous order of divine equity and mercy, the former had to occur first to display God’s severity, and the latter afterward to display God’s goodness. Yet both had always been predestined together in God’s eternal counsel, so that the one might be decreed by the equity of judgment, with immovable severity insofar as concerned the merit of that condemned mass, while the other might be most gloriously fulfilled by the power of the divine will and the gratuitous goodness of the most merciful Creator.

Therefore, according to the weakness of our understanding, wherever we read either in the divine Scriptures or in the teachings of the Fathers that the whole mass of the human race was condemned in the first man and through the first sinful man, nothing else should be understood except that it was handed over to eternal condemnation by God’s just judgment, on account of the merit of that first sin. Concerning this condemnation, which entered the world through one man, the Apostle plainly says:

> “The judgment followed from one transgression to condemnation” (Romans 5:16).

This, as has already been said, cannot rightly be understood as anything other than eternal. If, therefore, the whole mass of the human race is rightly understood to have been condemned and handed over to eternal destruction, what is this other than its being assigned or predestined to that same eternal destruction, insofar as the merit of its fault—namely, that first transgression—is concerned, so that it was altogether justly, wholly, and at once condemned by an eternal sentence?

[Col. 1068D] But insofar as the goodness and mercy of the Creator are concerned—for He neither imposed necessity upon Himself nor deprived Himself of power—He could, by judging His creature with the severity that justice required, save from it as much as He pleased through undeserved grace, although it had been justly and eternally condemned through its fault. The sentence of condemnation remained in those in whom guilt also remained, while it was removed from those in whom that same guilt was removed through Christ’s blood. [Col. 1069A] Thus the predestination of all God’s elect was preordained by His eternal disposition in such a way that they would be transferred from the lot of eternal condemnation into the lot of eternal salvation and deliverance. In that place, then, this portion too had truly been condemned by the common sentence; here, it was truly liberated by God’s grace alone. And the more grateful and devoted it would become toward its liberator, the more truly it would recognize that it had truly been liable to eternal condemnation.

The Apostle sublimely and most attentively commends this transfer of the elect from the lot of condemnation into the lot of deliverance, so that the faithful may acknowledge it and recall it with complete thanksgiving, saying:

> “Giving thanks to God and the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the inheritance of the saints in light; who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of His love” (Colossians 1:12–13).

He also commends the fact that the faithful escaped, through the passion and death of the Lord Christ, that anger of eternal vengeance and condemnation which was equally due to the entire mass. They could not truly be said to have escaped it unless they had also truly been liable to it. Thus he rejoices and commends this fact, saying:

> “For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son, much more, having now been reconciled in His blood, shall we be saved from wrath through Him” (Romans 5:10).

And again:

> “For God did not appoint us for wrath, but for the acquisition of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him” (1 Thessalonians 5:9–10).

And elsewhere:

> “How you turned from idols to serve the living and true God, and to await His Son from heaven, Jesus, who delivered us from the coming wrath” (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10).

The Psalmist also sings and exults as though it had already happened that, through the coming of the Lord and Savior—that is, that ancient wrath of God would be entirely appeased and turned away from the elect—saying:

> “You have forgiven the iniquity of Your people; You have covered all their sins. You have appeased all Your wrath; You have turned away from the anger of Your indignation” (Psalm 84:3–4).

For if all the elect and those predestined to life were not truly in the one mass of condemnation and destruction together with the others, from where, then, were they elected and distinguished? From where were they redeemed, saved, and delivered? Why does Truth itself say of them:

> “For the Son of Man came to seek and save what had been lost” (Luke 19:10)?

The Apostle also most clearly bears witness to and declares this in the Acts of the Apostles, when he freely proclaims the mystery of Christ before the king and the rulers, relating how the Lord spoke to him immediately at his first calling and conversion. For he says that the following was spoken to him from heaven:

> “For this purpose I appeared to you, to appoint you as a servant and witness both of the things you have seen and of those in which I will appear to you, rescuing you from the people and from the nations, to whom I now send you, to open their eyes so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a share among the saints through faith in Me” (Acts 26:16–18).

And the Lord Himself says in the Gospel:

> “When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard, his possessions are at peace. But when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he takes away all his armor in which he trusted and distributes his spoils” (Luke 11:21–22).

And elsewhere:

> “Now is the judgment of this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out. And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to Myself” (John 12:31–32).

Therefore, insofar as we understand with God’s help, we must by no means introduce this novelty of division, so that the entire mass of the human race—which all the teachers of the Church understand to have been punished in its entirety for the transgression of the first man and through the first man—might now be said by us to have been condemned in part and not condemned in part; in part destined for eternal destruction and in part not destined for it.

[Col. 1070B] For to weaken and diminish in the elect, in this way, that first and general condemnation is nothing other than to lessen and narrow the magnitude of divine goodness and mercy toward them. Nor did almighty God do anything contrary to His predestination when, having determined that the entire mass should perish by a just condemnation, He saved His elect from it. For He so established the former according to the merit of guilt and the severity of justice that it would also serve the goodness of mercy. Thus, according to the Apostle, He had “power over the clay” to make from the same mass—simultaneously and wholly condemned—“one vessel for honor” by His mercy and “another for dishonor” by His justice (Romans 9).

Thus, as has been said, “from one and the same mass” there would be “some vessels of wrath and other vessels of mercy: the former prepared for destruction, the latter prepared for glory” (ibid.), so that one might worthily and truly say in His praises:

> “I will sing of mercy and judgment to You, O Lord” (Psalm 100:1);

and:

> “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 25:10).

The Apostle commends this matter most diligently and briefly elsewhere, saying:

> “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest; but God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which He loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ” (Ephesians 2:3–5).

Certainly he speaks here in his own person and that of the other faithful and elect, yet he testifies that both he and the others, before being liberated through Christ’s grace, had by nature been children of wrath because of the corruption of generation from Adam. What is this other than being “vessels of wrath,” vessels of vengeance, vessels of eternal condemnation? And this was not otherwise, but “like the rest”—that is, with equal guilt, equal condition, and equal sentence of condemnation, which undoubtedly they shared with everyone else.

[Col. 1070D] He plainly teaches that he and the others were delivered from this “through the riches of God’s mercy and His great love,” by which He also came to the aid of such people and deigned to love such people, so that, though dead in sin, He might not only make them alive but make them alive together with Christ, raising them from the dead together with Him and seating them with Him at His right hand in the heavenly places.

He also commends this most sublimely and magnificently elsewhere, speaking of our Lord and Savior Himself:

[Col. 1071A]

> “He erased the bond of the decree that stood against us, which was contrary to us, and removed it from our midst by fastening it to the cross. Stripping Himself of the flesh, He openly led principalities and powers in triumph, triumphing over them in Himself” (Colossians 2:14–15).

According to this venerable and marvelous understanding of the Apostle, the Lord and Savior Himself erased by His blood the bond of the ancient decree—that is, of the ancient condemnation and predestination by which we were justly and deservedly being cast into eternal death—the bond which, as those “sold under sin,” we had made with the devil through our works as though with our own hands, handing ourselves over to his servitude.

For:

> “He is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

Thus, once sin’s bond had been paid and erased by such a great price, the bond of the decree was also broken—the decree which was so contrary to us and had made us so liable and subject to slavery that none of us could raise his head.

He removed it from our midst so that it would no longer be an obstacle and barrier between us and God, in accordance with what the prophet says:

> “Your iniquities have caused a division between you and your God” (Isaiah 59:2),

so that a free approach and return to his Creator might lie open to man.

“Fastening it to the cross”: He Himself endured in the flesh that He assumed for us the punishment due to us for that same sin of ours. The prophet also bears witness, saying:

> “Truly He Himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isaiah 53:4).

“Stripping Himself of the flesh”—that is, laying aside the garment of the body when He willed, of His own accord and by His own power. For, as the Evangelist says, when He had received vinegar:

> “He said, ‘It is finished,’ and, bowing His head, He gave up His spirit” (John 19:30).

He had also said earlier:

> “I have power to lay down My life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord so that I may take it up again” (John 10:17).

“‘He openly led principalities and powers in triumph’”—namely, the principalities and powers of the devil’s evil spirits and his angels, who had previously ruled freely over the human race after deceiving and enslaving it. He dishonored them, marked them with disgrace and humiliation, and made their defeat manifest before the eyes of all who believe and understand.

“‘Triumphing over them in Himself’”—when He erased the sins of the world with His precious blood. Thus [Col. 1071D] He removed from them the causes of the ancient condemnation and their dominion. Through the single death of His flesh, He destroyed the double death of all His elect, freeing them both from the death of the soul through the forgiveness of sins and from the death of the body through the trophy of resurrection and immortality.

If it is also demanded that we produce from Scripture some testimony in which something similar is recorded among the divine works—namely, that what God decreed by the equity and severity of His judgment He later forgave by the power of His goodness and mercy and turned to good—there immediately comes to mind what blessed Moses says concerning the same almighty God to the people whom he governed and led:

> “For I feared His indignation and wrath, with which He was angry against you and wanted to destroy you” (Deuteronomy 9:19).

Afterward, having commended the humility and urgency of his supplication, which he had poured out before God for the forgiveness of that offense, he added:

> “And the Lord heard me on this occasion also, and did not want to destroy you” (ibid.).

Behold: almighty God, moved by just indignation against a stubborn and rebellious people, wanted to destroy them. Scripture certainly says that He wanted this—not falsely, God forbid, but truthfully. Yet afterward, having been appeased by the prayer and supplication of His faithful servant, He did not want it, through His free goodness and mercy.

This does not mean that there is any changeability in His will, since, according to the Apostle, “with Him there is no change or shadow caused by alteration” (James 1:17). Rather, He had decreed it with such just severity that afterward He might relax it through wondrous compassion, when a just intervening cause was present.

The same is true of what Scripture says in that same passage concerning Aaron the priest, who, although unwilling, had yielded to the people’s sacrilege in the making and celebration of the calf:

> “The Lord was exceedingly angry with Aaron also and wanted to destroy him. And I prayed for him in the same way” (Deuteronomy 9:20).

Thus, in these evident matters, justice decreed one thing and goodness did another, and the just and merciful God did nothing contrary to Himself, preserving justice in the one case and mercy in the other. So, surely, in that predestination of the entire condemned mass to destruction, what He had generally established by just severity, He specially tempered by mercifully choosing from it those whom He willed.

This was not done at anyone’s supplication. Rather—and this is incomparably more gracious and glorious—through the sole favor and compassion of His goodness, both things nevertheless had always existed together in God’s eternal counsel. No believer may doubt this. For although, according to the order of temporal events, that just condemnation precedes in the human race and the merciful deliverance from it follows, in the eternal and unchangeable truth, where there is neither “before” nor “after,” but all things, both equally and together—the preceding as well as the subsequent—are seen in a single act of vision and ordered by a single act of will, both are, as has been said, known beforehand by eternal foreknowledge and fixed and predetermined by eternal disposition.

[Col. 1072D] Holy Scripture is full of this most just and general condemnation of the entire human race through Adam, and of its most merciful and gracious cleansing through our one Mediator and Reconciler of God and human beings, our Lord Jesus Christ, as has already been briefly shown above. The books of the blessed Fathers are likewise full of it. From their statements we have considered it altogether fitting and necessary to append here several passages for the edification and confirmation of readers.

Blessed Hilary, therefore, explaining the Apostle’s words cited above—namely, where he says concerning the Lord, “erasing the bond of the decree that stood against us” (Colossians 2:14)—and the rest of the passage, speaks about this matter as follows:

[Col. 1073A]

> “For He assumed the flesh of sin so that, in assuming our flesh, He might forgive sins, becoming a participant in its assumption but not in its sin; erasing through death the sentence of death, so that by the new creation of our race in Himself He might abolish the former decree. He allowed Himself to be fastened to the cross so that, by the curse of the cross, all the curses of earthly condemnation might be obliterated and fastened there. Finally, He suffered in man so that He might dishonor the powers, while God, according to the Scriptures, was destined to die; and in these things He triumphed through the confidence of the Victor in Himself, while He Himself, immortal and not subject to conquest by death, died for the eternity of those who were dying.”

Again, when explaining the words of the psalm addressed to God, “For with You there is forgiveness” (Psalm 130:4), he says:

> “For the only-begotten Son of God, God the Word, is our redemption; in His blood we have been reconciled to God. He is the one who came to take away the sins of the world, who, fastening the bond of the law to His cross, erased the written record of the ancient condemnation.”

Blessed Ambrose, too, in his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians, says concerning the same matter:

[Col. 1073B]

> “Let us therefore be God’s possession, and let Him be our portion, in whom are the riches of His glorious inheritance. For who is rich except the one who alone is rich, who created all things? Yet He is much richer in mercy, because He redeemed all. He changed us, who by the nature of the flesh were children of wrath and liable to condemnation, being Himself the author that we might be children of peace and love. For who can change nature except the one who created nature? Therefore He raised the dead and caused those made alive in Christ to sit in the heavenly places in the Lord Jesus Himself.”

[Col. 1073C] Blessed Pacianus, too, as blessed Jerome testifies concerning him in his book On Illustrious Men, renowned both in life and in speech, insists on this same point clearly, saying:

> “All the nations, once handed over to the princes of darkness and to the powers, have now been liberated through the victory of Jesus Christ our Lord. He, He is the one who redeemed them, ‘forgiving us all sins,’ as the Apostle says, ‘and erasing the bond of disobedience that stood against us; for He removed it from our midst by fastening it to the cross. Stripping Himself of the flesh, He openly led the powers in triumph, triumphing over them in Himself’ (Colossians 2:13–15).  
> 
> “He releases those in chains and breaks our bonds, as David had said: ‘The Lord raises up those who are bowed down; the Lord releases those in chains; the Lord gives sight to the blind’ (Psalm 146:8). And again: ‘You have broken my bonds; I will sacrifice to You a sacrifice of praise’ (Psalm 116:16–17).  
> 
> “Having therefore been released from our bonds, when through the sacrament of baptism we come together under the sign of the Lord, we renounce the devil and all his angels, whom we formerly served, so that we may no longer serve them, having been freed by the blood and name of Christ. But if afterward someone, forgetting himself and ignorant of his redemption, turns again to the service of angels and ‘returns to those weak and beggarly elements of the world’ (Galatians 4:9), he will be bound by those ancient fetters and chains—that is, by the bonds of sin—and ‘his last state will be worse than the first’ (2 Peter 2:20). For the devil will bind him more violently, as one conquered while attempting to flee, and Christ will no longer be able to suffer for him. For ‘Christ, having risen from the dead, will die no more’ (Romans 6:9).”

Blessed Leo also commends this matter extensively and in many ways, saying:

[Col. 1074A]

> “Jesus Christ, exalted upon the wood, turned death back upon the author of death and struck down all principalities and hostile powers through the exposure of palpable flesh. That general record of our sale and deadly bond has been annulled, and the pact of captivity passes into the legal right of the Redeemer. Those nails that pierced the hands and feet of the Lord fixed the devil with perpetual wounds, and the punishment of the holy members became the destruction of the hostile powers. Thus, when Christ completed His victory, all who believe in Him triumphed in Him and with Him.”

And again:

> “Gentleness maintained the patience that had been ordained, and, restraining the power of the legions of ministering angels, it drank the cup of suffering and death and transformed the entire punishment into triumph.
