Errors were defeated, powers subdued, the world received a new beginning, so that the condemned generation might not harm those whom regeneration came to save.”

Again, elsewhere:

> “Power restrained itself from the impious and, in order to make use of a hidden arrangement, refused to use manifest power. For how could He save sinners if He resisted His persecutors, since He had come through His passion to destroy death and the author of death?”

For even if Christ had descended from the cross, you would nevertheless have remained in your guilt. Thus the insults of empty mockery were disregarded, and no abuse or taunt could turn the Lord’s mercy, which was repairing what had been lost and ruined, from the path of its purpose.

For a singular sacrifice was being offered to the Lord for the salvation of the world, and the killing of the Lamb, proclaimed throughout so many ages, was transferring the children of promise into the liberty of faith. The New Testament was also being confirmed, and heirs were being inscribed for the eternal King in Christ’s blood. The supreme High Priest was entering the Holy of Holies, and the immaculate priest was entering through the veil of His flesh to entreat God.

Elsewhere, defining all these matters briefly and carefully, he says:

[Col. 1074D]

> “Knowing that he had infected human nature with poison, the devil by no means believed that the Lord Christ was exempt from the first transgression, whom he had learned through so many proofs to be mortal. Thus the wicked robber and greedy exactor persisted in attacking one who possessed nothing belonging to him. While pursuing the general sentence against the corrupted origin, he went beyond the bond on which he relied, demanding the penalty of iniquity from one in whom he found no guilt.  
> 
> “Thus the malicious written instrument of the ancient pact is dissolved, and, ‘through the injustice of demanding more,’ the total amount of the debt is canceled. That strong one is bound by his own chains, and every scheme of the evil one is turned back upon his own head. When the prince of the world is bound, the vessels of captivity are seized. Nature, cleansed from its ancient contagions, returns to its honor. Death is destroyed by death, birth is restored by birth, because redemption at once removes slavery, regeneration changes origin, and faith justifies the sinner.”

Blessed Coelestinus also explains the same matter in the same sense and almost the same words, fully yet briefly, saying:

[Col. 1075A]

> “We do not contemplate without purpose the practice that the holy Church uniformly carries out throughout the world concerning those who are to be baptized. Whether infants or young people come to the sacrament of regeneration, they do not first approach the font of life until the unclean spirit has been driven away from them by the exorcisms and insufflations of the clergy. Then it truly becomes apparent how ‘the prince of this world is cast out’ (John 12:31), and how ‘the strong man is first bound’ (Matthew 12:29), and afterward his vessels are plundered and transferred into the possession of the victor, ‘who led captivity captive and gave gifts to men’ (Psalm 68:19).”

Now blessed Augustine spoke about this matter all the more fully and in greater variety, since he was faced with a greater and more urgent necessity in opposing the Pelagian heretics who had then arisen—people entirely ignorant of the causes of that great sacrament, namely, the condemnation of humanity introduced through Adam, and the liberation and redemption granted through the Lord Jesus Christ. He had to assert, by divine testimonies and the most certain arguments, both the causes of that human condemnation and the grace of God, by which alone we are liberated through Christ the Lord. Thus, in a certain letter to Bishop Optatus, he speaks as follows (Letter 157):

> Since all the righteous—that is, all true worshipers of God—whether before the incarnation or after the incarnation of Christ, neither lived nor live except by faith in the incarnation of Christ, in whom the fullness of grace resides, surely what is written, “There is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12), has been effective for saving the human race from the time when the human race was corrupted in Adam: “For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:22). For just as no one is in the kingdom of death without Adam, so no one is in the kingdom of life without Christ. Just as all are sinners through Adam, so through Christ all human beings are righteous. Just as through Adam all mortals were made, under punishment, children of this age, so through Christ all immortals are made, by grace, children of God.
>
> But why are even those whom the Creator willed to belong to condemnation rather than to grace brought into consideration? The blessed Apostle recalls this with brevity proportionate to its greater authority: “For,” he says, “God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath, which have been prepared for destruction, and in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy”—the one whom above he had called “like a potter, making from the same lump one vessel for honor and another vessel for dishonor” (Rom. 9:22–23, 21).
>
> It would rightly seem unjust that vessels of wrath are made for destruction if the entire mass had not been condemned in Adam. That they become vessels of wrath by being born belongs to deserved punishment; that they become vessels of mercy by being born anew belongs to undeserved grace. God therefore displays “his wrath”—not, of course, an agitation of mind such as that which is called wrath among human beings, but a just and fixed vengeance. The offspring of sin and punishment is derived from the stock of disobedience. “A human being born of woman,” as it is written in the Book of Job, “is short-lived and full of wrath” (Job 14:1–2), for he is a vessel of that with which he is filled. Hence they are called “vessels of wrath.”
>
> He also “displays his power,” by which he makes good use even of the wicked, granting them many natural and temporal goods and adapting their wickedness for the exercise of the good and as a warning by comparison, so that through them the good may learn to give thanks to God because they have been distinguished from them—not by their own merits, which were equal in the same lump, but by his mercy. This is seen most clearly in infants. When they are born anew through Christ’s grace and, ending this life at that tender age, pass into eternal and blessed life, it cannot be said that they are distinguished by free choice from those other infants who die without this grace in the condemnation of that same lump.
>
> If only those were created from Adam who would be recreated by grace, and if no other human beings were born besides those adopted as children of God, the benefit bestowed upon the undeserving would remain hidden. For no one coming from that same condemnable stock would receive the punishment due to him. But when he “endured with much patience vessels of wrath, which have been prepared for destruction,” he not only displays wrath and demonstrates his power by exacting vengeance and making good use of the wicked; he also “makes known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy.” For the one who has been justified freely thereby learns what has been bestowed upon him, when he is distinguished—not by his own merit, but by the most abundant glory of God’s mercy—from the condemned person with whom, under the same justice, he too would have been condemned.
>
> He therefore willed that very many should be created and born whom he foreknew would not belong to his grace, so that they would be incomparably more numerous than those whom he deigned to predestine as children of promise for the glory of his kingdom. Thus, even by the multitude of the rejected, it would be shown how little any number of the justly condemned matters to the just God. And so those who are redeemed from that condemnation may also understand that what they see returned to so great a part of the whole lump was owed to the entire lump—not only in those who add many evils to original sin through the choice of an evil will, but also in so many infants who, bound only by the bond of original sin, are snatched from this life without the grace of the mediator.
>
> For this entire mass would receive the due of just condemnation, unless the just and merciful “potter” made from it other vessels “for honor,” according to grace and not according to what was owed—helping infants, of whom no merits can be spoken, and preceding adults so that they might have some merits.

Again, in the books *On the City of God*, wishing to show how great the wickedness committed in that first transgression was, and how, on its account, the entire mass of the human race should be believed to have been condemned, he says:

> The more fully a human being enjoyed God, the greater was the impiety with which he abandoned God; and he became deserving of eternal evil because he destroyed in himself that good which could have been eternal. Hence the entire mass of the human race was condemned: for the one who first committed this offense was punished, together with the stock that had been rooted in him, so that no one might be freed from this just and deserved punishment except by mercy and undeserved grace. Thus the human race is divided, so that in some it may be demonstrated what merciful grace can do, and in others what just vengeance can do. For both would not be demonstrated in everyone. If all remained in the punishments of just condemnation, merciful grace would appear in no one. Again, if all were transferred from darkness into light, the truth of vengeance would appear in no one—yet there are many more in the former condition than in the latter, so that it might be shown what was owed to all. If what was owed were returned to all, no one could rightly criticize the justice of the one who exacts punishment; but since so many are liberated from it, there is ample reason for the greatest thanksgiving to the free gift of the one who liberates.

Again, in the same work:

> When, therefore, it is asked what death God threatened to the first human beings if they transgressed the commandment they had received and did not preserve obedience—whether the death of the soul, or of the body, or of the whole human being, or that which is called the second death—the answer must be: all of them. For the first death consists of two, and the whole consists of all of them. Just as the whole earth consists of many lands and the whole Church of many churches, so the whole of death consists of all these deaths; for the first death consists of two, one of the soul and the other of the body. Thus there is a first death of the whole human being, when the soul suffers punishment for a time without God and without the body. The second is when the soul, without God, suffers eternal punishment together with the body.
>
> Therefore, when God said to that first human being, whom he had placed in paradise, concerning the forbidden food, “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17), that threat included not merely the earlier part of the first death, in which the soul is deprived of God; nor merely the later part, in which the body is deprived of the soul; nor only the whole of that first death, in which the soul is punished separated both from the body and from God; but every form of death up to the last, which is called the second death, after which there is no other.

[Col. 1077D] Again, when he was discussing the origin of the two cities, one of which is God’s and the other the devil’s—the former liberated by God’s grace, the latter condemned by just vengeance—he commends the remarkable manifestation of both in the very beginning of their origins, saying:

> When these two cities first began to advance by being born and dying, the citizen of this age was born first, while afterward came the stranger in this age, belonging to the city of God, predestined by grace, chosen by grace, by grace a stranger below, and by grace a citizen above. For as far as he himself is concerned, he arises “from the same lump,” which is wholly condemned in its origin; but “like a potter, God”—for the Apostle introduces this likeness not impudently but prudently—“made from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor” (Rom. 9). The vessel for dishonor, however, was made first, and afterward the other for honor.

Now, in the books *On the Baptism of Infants*, he speaks still more extensively about this matter, since it required greater concentration in order to demonstrate, establish, and commend more clearly, against the aforementioned Pelagian heretics, the punishment of the ancient condemnation through Adam and the indulgence of the new redemption through the Lord Jesus Christ.

From these books, therefore, we have judged that the following passages should be noted and presented for our instruction and for the instruction and confirmation of those who may wish to read them. In the first book, he says the following while discussing this matter (chapter 11):

> “Death reigned,” the Apostle says, “from Adam to Moses” (Rom. 5:14)—that is, from the first human being up to the very law that was promulgated by God—for even the law itself could not remove “the reign of death.” By “the reign of death” he means the condition in which the guilt of sin so dominates human beings that it does not allow them to come to eternal life, which is true life, but also draws them toward the second death, which is eternal in punishment. In each human being, only the grace of the Savior destroys this reign of death; and that grace was at work even in the ancient saints.
>
> Therefore, “death reigned from Adam to Moses” in all who were not aided by the grace of Christ, so that the reign of death might be destroyed in them—even “in those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (ibid.), that is, who had not yet sinned by their own will as he had, but had drawn original sin from him, “who is a type of the one to come” (ibid.). For in him was established the pattern of condemnation for future descendants who would be created from his stock, so that all might be born from one person into condemnation, from which only the Savior’s grace delivers.

Again (chapter 11):

> Those who sinned “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” are understood to have sinned in him, so that they might be created like him: just as human beings come from a human being, so sinners come from a sinner, mortals from one who is dying, and the condemned from one who is condemned.

Again (chapter 16):

> It can therefore rightly be said that infants who leave the body without baptism will be in the mildest condemnation of all. But the person who declares that they will not be in condemnation is greatly deceived and greatly deceives others, since the Apostle says: “Judgment followed from one offense to condemnation,” and shortly afterward, “through one offense judgment came upon all people to condemnation.”

Again (chapter 20):

> “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:54, 52). Who, however, would doubt that by “the world” he meant human beings, who come into this world by being born? For elsewhere he says: “The children of this age beget and are begotten” (Luke 20:34). Accordingly, flesh was also given for the life of infants, since it was given for the life of the world; and if they have not eaten the flesh of the Son of Man, they too will not have life.

Again (chapter 21):

> He rightly did not say, “The wrath of God will come upon him,” but “remains upon him.” For nothing liberates anyone from this wrath, under which all are subject to sin, and of which the Apostle says, “For we too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3), except “the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:25).

Again (chapter 22):

> I think that such people are predestined and created so that those who are able may understand the grace of God and the Spirit, “who breathes where he wills” (John 3:8). For this reason he has not passed over any kind of human ability among the children of mercy; likewise, he has passed over every kind of human ability among the children of Gehenna. “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

Again, in the same place:

> Let us therefore yield and consent to the authority of Holy Scripture, which knows neither how to be deceived nor how to deceive. Just as we do not believe that the unborn have done anything good or evil by which their merits could be distinguished, so let us have no doubt that all are under sin, which entered the world through one human being and passed through to all human beings, and from which none is liberated except by the grace of God through the Lord Jesus Christ.
>
> His medicinal coming is not needed by the healthy but by the sick, because he came not to call the righteous but sinners (Matt. 9:12–13). No one will enter his kingdom “unless he has been born again of water and the Spirit” (John 3:5), nor will anyone possess salvation and eternal life outside his kingdom. For whoever does not eat his flesh, and whoever is unbelieving toward the Son, does not have life; rather, the wrath of God remains upon him (John 3:36).
>
> From this sin, this sickness, and this wrath of God—whose children they are by nature, even though by reason of age they do not yet have a sin of their own, they nevertheless bear original sin—none delivers them except “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29); none except the physician, who came for the sick; none except the Savior, of whom it was said to the human race, “Today a Savior has been born for you” (Luke 2:11); none except the Redeemer, by whose blood our debt is erased.
>
> For who would dare say that Christ is not the Savior and Redeemer of infants? From what does he save them if there is no original sickness of sin in them? From what does he redeem them if, through the origin of the first human being, they have not been sold under sin?

Again (chapter 26):

> The Lord Jesus Christ came in the flesh for no other reason, and, having taken the form of a servant, became obedient even to death on a cross (Phil. 2:7–8), except that, through this most merciful administration of grace, he might give life, save, liberate, enlighten, and redeem all those for whom he is the head, as members constituted in his body, who had previously been placed in the death, sicknesses, bondage, captivity, and darkness of sins, under the power of the devil, the prince of sinners. Thus he might become “the mediator between God and human beings” (1 Tim. 2:5), through whom, after the enmity of our ungodliness had been ended by the peace of his grace, we might be reconciled to God for eternal life, rescued from eternal death, which threatened such people.

Again, in the same place:

> Infants must need the benefits of the mediator, so that, washed through the sacrament and the charity of the faithful, and thus incorporated into the body of Christ, which is the Church, they may be reconciled to God, so that in him they may become alive, saved, liberated, redeemed, and enlightened. From what else could they be delivered except from death, vices, guilt, subjection, and the darkness of sins? Since they committed none of these things at that age through their own life, what remains is original sin.

Again (chapter 27):

> When the Lord had entered the house of Zacchaeus, he said: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and save what had been lost” (Luke 19:9–10). This concerns the lost sheep, which was sought after the ninety-nine had been left behind, and the coin that had been lost from the ten and was found (Luke 15:4, 8). Therefore it was necessary, as he says, “that repentance and the forgiveness of sins be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47).

Again, in the same place:

> “I will not gather their assemblies from their bloods” (Ps. 16:4)—for one blood was given for many, by which they might truly be cleansed. Finally, it follows: “Nor will I remember their names with my lips” (ibid.), as those who have been renewed. Formerly their names were children of the flesh, children of this age, children of wrath, children of the devil; unclean, sinners, ungodly; afterward, however, they became children of God. For the new human being there is a new name, a new song, through the New Testament.
>
> Let human beings not be ungrateful for God’s grace, the little together with the great, the lesser together with the greater. The voice of the entire Church is: “I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost” (Ps. 119:176). The voice of all Christ’s members is: “All we like sheep have gone astray, and he himself was handed over for our sins” (Isa. 53:6).

Again (chapter 28):

> The Lord himself issued a definitive judgment to close these mouths when he said: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Matt. 12:30). Set before yourself, then, any infant: if he is already with Christ, why is he baptized? But if—as the truth teaches—he is baptized in order to be with Christ, surely the one who is not baptized is not with Christ; and because he is not with Christ, he is against Christ. We neither ought nor are able to weaken or alter so clear a judgment of his.
>
> How, then, is he against Christ, if not because of sin? Certainly not because of body and soul, both of which are creatures of God. If, then, it is because of sin, what sin can it be at that age except original and ancient sin? There is one flesh of sin, in which all are born for condemnation; and there is one flesh in the likeness of the flesh of sin, through which all are liberated from condemnation.

Again, in the same place:

> The entire Church maintains—and it must keep watch against all profane innovations—that every human being is separated from God unless reconciled to God through the mediator Christ, and that no one can be separated from him except through sins that intervene. Therefore no one is reconciled except through the remission of sins, by the one grace of the most merciful Savior and by the one sacrifice of the truest priest.
>
> Thus all the children of the woman who believed the serpent, so that she might be corrupted by lust (Gen. 3:1–6), are liberated from this body of death only through the Son of the virgin who believed the angel, so that she might conceive without lust (Luke 1).

Again (chapter 30):

> “Unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” And: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:3–5). Why should he be born again unless he is to be renewed? From what is he to be renewed except from oldness? From what oldness except that in which “our old human being was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be abolished” (Rom. 6:6)? Or why does the image of God not enter the kingdom of God, except because an obstacle of sin prevents it?

Again (chapter 31):

> “No one,” he says, “has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). Thus, he says, a special generation will take place, so that heavenly human beings may arise from earthly ones. They could not attain this unless they became members in that body, so that the one who descended might himself ascend, because “no one ascends except the one who descended.”
>
> Unless, therefore, all come together to be changed and lifted into the unity of Christ, so that Christ who descended may himself ascend—since he regards his body, that is, his Church, as nothing other than himself—for the saying “the two will become one flesh” (Gen. 2:24) is more truly understood of Christ and the Church; and concerning this he himself said, “Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh” (Mark 10:8)—they will certainly not be able to ascend, because “no one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

Again (chapters 33–34):

> Let infants not be deprived of the grace of the remission of sins. There is no other passage to Christ; no one can otherwise be reconciled to God or come to God except through Christ. What shall I say about the very form of the sacrament? I wish that one of those who hold contrary opinions would bring me an infant to be baptized. “What is exorcism doing in him, if he is not held in the devil’s household?” He himself would surely have to answer for that same infant, whom he would make answer twice over, since the infant could not answer for himself.
>
> How, then, could he say that the infant renounces the devil, if there were nothing of the devil in him? How could he turn to the Lord, from whom he had not turned away? How could he believe, among other things, in the remission of sins, when no remission was being granted to him? If I believed that he held an opinion contrary to these things, I would not even permit him to enter the sacraments with the infant. But with what face he would carry himself before human beings, and with what mind before God, I do not know.

From another work of the same blessed teacher, more commonly called the *Enchiridion*, we have judged that the following few passages should be selected and noted for clarification of the same matter (*Enchiridion*, chapters 25–26). He says:

> But the human being has a punishment proper to himself, by which he was punished with the death of the body. For God had threatened him with the punishment of death if he sinned, granting him free choice while nevertheless ruling him by command and frightening him with destruction; and he placed him in the happiness of paradise, as in the shadow of life, so that, once justice had been preserved, he might ascend to better things.
>
> After his sin he became an exile and also bound his own stock—which he had corrupted in himself, as in a root, by sinning—with the punishment of death and condemnation. Thus whatever offspring might be born from him and from the wife who was likewise condemned, through carnal desire into which a similar punishment for disobedience had been repaid, would bear original sin. Through various errors and sorrows this sin would draw them toward that final punishment without end, together with the deserting angels, their corrupters, possessors, and companions.
>
> Thus “through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed through to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). In that passage the Apostle called the entire human race “the world.”

(Chapter 27.)

> Such, then, was the condition of things. The condemned mass of the entire human race lay in evils—or was even being rolled about and hurled from evils into evils—and, together with the portion of the angels who had sinned, was paying the most deserved penalties of impious desertion.
>
> Whatever the wicked do willingly through blind and untamed desire, and whatever they suffer unwillingly through manifest and evident punishments, belongs to the just wrath of God. Yet the goodness of the Creator does not cease, but supplies life and living power even to evil angels. If this supply were withdrawn, it would cease to form and animate the seeds of human beings—although they are born from a corrupted and condemned stock—to order their limbs through the ages of time and the spaces of places, to enliven their senses, and to provide nourishment.
>
> For he judged it better to do good even to the wicked than to permit evils not to exist at all. Indeed, if he had wished there to be no restoration whatsoever of human beings to a better condition, just as there is none for the wicked angels, it would not unjustly have happened that the nature which abandoned God; which, by misusing its power, trampled upon and transgressed the commandment of its Creator, which it could have kept with the greatest ease; which violated within itself the image of its Maker by turning it obstinately away from his light; and which, by a bad use of free choice, broke away from the salutary bondage of his laws—would be abandoned by him forever and would pay an everlasting penalty according to its deserts.
>
> He would plainly have acted in this way if he were only just and not also merciful; but he displays his mercy much more clearly in the liberation of the undeserving.

Again (chapters 50–51):

> That one person sent one sin into the world; but this one person removed not only that one sin but all the others he found added to it. Hence the Apostle says: “It is not as through one sin, so also is the gift; for judgment from one sin led to condemnation, but grace from many sins led to justification” (Rom. 5:16).
>
> For that one sin which is inherited by origin, even if it exists alone, makes people liable to condemnation; but grace justifies a person from many sins who, besides that one sin inherited by origin in common with everyone else, has also committed many sins of his own.
>
> Nevertheless, what he says shortly afterward (ibid., 18)—“Just as through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of justification justification of life came upon all human beings”—clearly indicates that no one born from Adam is held except in condemnation, and that no one is liberated from condemnation except by being born again in Christ.

Again (chapter 94):

> When the angels and human beings who have been rejected remain in eternal punishment, the saints will then know more fully what good grace has bestowed upon them. Then it will become clearer from the realities themselves what is written in the psalm: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, Lord” (Ps. 101:1). For no one is liberated except through undeserved “mercy,” and no one is condemned except through deserved “judgment.”

Again (chapter 98):

> The entire human race was condemned by so just a divine judgment in the apostate root that, even if no one were liberated from it, no one could rightly blame the justice of God. And those who are liberated had to be liberated in such a way that, from the many who were not liberated and were left in the most just condemnation, it might be shown what the entire mixture had deserved, and where God’s deserved judgment would lead even these liberated ones if his undeserved mercy had not come to their aid—so that “every mouth may be stopped,” and “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (Rom. 3:19).

[Col. 1084A] Since all these things have been drawn from the discussions of the most faithful and illustrious Fathers, and have been declared and confirmed by the testimony of so many divine testimonies and by the clearest arguments, they must be believed and maintained altogether without doubt. Three great and dreadful evils, as far as can be understood, have therefore been retained in the reprobate by the severity of divine judgment, while in the elect they have been remitted and dissolved through the mercy of divine goodness.

The guilt of the ancient and first transgression remains in the former; in the latter it has been erased by Christ’s blood. The sentence of eternal condemnation remains in the former; in the latter it has been dissolved through the grace of redemption. The former have been condemned forever by the predestination of divine judgment; the latter have been saved forever by the predestination of divine mercy.

[Col. 1084B] [lacuna]

*(Some material is missing: two leaves were cut out of the manuscript, but almost nothing had been written on them; therefore nothing seems to be missing except the second member of the third evil, as it applies to the elect, which had been remitted.)*

[Col. 1083]

## A BOOKLET OF SAINT REMIGIUS, BISHOP OF LYONS, UNDER THE NAME OF THE CHURCH OF LYONS, ON HOLDING FIRMLY TO THE TRUTH OF SCRIPTURE AND FAITHFULLY FOLLOWING THE AUTHORITY OF THE HOLY ORTHODOX FATHERS (G)*

### CHAPTER I. The origin of heresy from contempt for Holy Scripture and the holy Fathers

[Col. 1083C]

Amid all the dangers, innumerable calamities, and miseries by which the Church of this kingdom is continually afflicted and devastated through God’s terrible and hidden judgment—so that the unity of the kingdom has been split and torn apart; general and most salutary councils of priests have ceased; the severity of the laws and the vigilance of judgment have been withdrawn; and the dedicated studies of doctrine, by which faith and knowledge of God ought daily to have been nourished and advanced, have been almost everywhere extinguished—a still more lamentable and mournful evil has arisen.

Specifically, certain people, having despised the truth of the holy Scriptures and trampled upon the authority of the most blessed and orthodox Fathers, through whom the Church of God is built up and enlightened, presume even concerning matters especially relevant to the faith, from the rash presumption of their own judgment, to teach and establish and write down for others to hold things that are most openly contrary to divine truth.

Yet almighty God himself commands the watchman—that is, every pastor of the Church—to announce only those things that he has heard from God, saying: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel; you shall hear a word from my mouth and announce it to them from me” (Ezek. 3:17). Blessed Peter the Apostle likewise testifies and says: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God” (1 Pet. 4:11). Blessed Paul gives the same admonition and repeats it, saying: “Do not be led astray by various and foreign teachings” (Heb. 13:9).

Such various and foreign teachings, in which there is no unity of truth but the introduction of diverse and profane error, are signified in the law of Moses by the various kinds of leprosy. These not only contaminate and corrupt the other parts of the body but also break out on the head and beard, whenever something unworthy is thought concerning the Lord Jesus Christ himself or concerning apostolic and ecclesiastical men who principally adhere to him and adorn his face.

For, as the Apostle teaches, “The head of every man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3); and according to the Psalmist’s words, the ointment first descends upon the head, then upon the beard—the beard of Aaron—and also descends upon the edges of his garment (Ps. 133:2–3).

Therefore, with every effort and watchfulness of piety, the uncleanness of error must be avoided, and the Apostle’s instruction must be obeyed humbly and faithfully. Speaking in the person of Timothy to every ruler of the Church, he says: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some promising have fallen away from the faith” (1 Tim. 6:20–21).

For we have a great deposit of faith and the doctrine of truth, drawn from the divine Scriptures and the sayings of the holy Fathers, entrusted to us by God for safekeeping like a precious and manifold treasure. With the Lord’s help, we must continually inspect, clean, polish, and examine it, and preserve it most diligently, lest through our negligence and idleness it become soiled by dust, destroyed by rust or moths, or dug up and carried away by the ambushes of evil spirits or by nocturnal and hidden thieves (Matt. 6:19).

For King Shishak of Egypt—by whom the prince of this world is signified—also seeks to plunder the arsenal of the true Solomon. Carrying away three hundred golden shields—that is, stealing the mystery of true and pure faith from the hearts of the negligent—he compels bronze shields to be made in place of the golden ones (1 Kings 14:26–27), so that, God forbid, he may make us “having the appearance indeed of piety, but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5).

### CHAPTER II. The four chapters of the assembly at Quierzy are brought forward

We say these things because a certain document has reached us—the Church of Lyons—having been brought to our attention through the efforts of faithful and good men who devotedly and commendably concern themselves with their own salvation and that of others, and having been earnestly commended to us so that we should respond to it carefully.

It contains four chapters of especially novel definitions, recently, as we have learned, discussed, arranged, and written down at a certain assembly of our fellow bishops, supposedly to restrain and blunt the loquacity of a certain talkative and restless man. He is said to be a disorderly disseminator, eager for new questions, who has brought no small disturbance upon others and the misery of a most wretched calamity upon himself. The sequence of these chapters, as it was conveyed to us, is as follows.

#### Chapter I

> “Almighty God created the human being upright and without sin, with free choice, and placed him in paradise, where he willed him to remain in the holiness of justice. The human being, misusing free choice, sinned and fell and became a mass of the perdition of the human race.
>
> “But the good and just God chose from that same mass of perdition, according to his foreknowledge, those whom he predestined by grace for life, and predestined eternal life for them. The others, whom by justice and judgment he left in the mass of perdition, he foreknew would perish, but he did not predestine them to perish. Yet, because he is just, he predestined eternal punishment for them. Accordingly, we speak of only one predestination of God, which pertains either to the gift of grace or to the recompense of justice.”

#### Chapter II

> “We lost freedom of choice in the first human being; through Christ our Lord we received it again. We have free choice for good, preceded and aided by grace; and we have free choice for evil, abandoned by grace. We have free choice because it has been liberated by grace and healed by grace from corruption.”

#### Chapter III

> “Almighty God wills all human beings without exception to be saved” (1 Tim. 2:4), “although not all are saved. The fact that some are saved is the gift of the one who saves; the fact that some perish is the merit of those who perish.”

#### Chapter IV

> “Just as there is no human being, has never been one, and never will be one whose nature was not assumed in Christ Jesus our Lord, so there is no human being, has never been one, and never will be one for whom he did not suffer, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion.

> “The fact, however, that not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion is not due to the greatness or abundance of the price, but to the side of the unbelieving and of those who do not believe with the faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6). For the cup of human salvation, which was prepared through our weakness and divine power, does indeed possess within itself the capacity to benefit everyone; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.”

Having therefore read these things, “and, with the fellowship of our brethren—who, by God’s gift, are diligent in study and correct in understanding—having carefully examined each point with devout and faithful attention,” we were deeply struck and troubled in spirit. We saw that in them the most certain truth of Holy Scripture, and the revered authority of the most blessed Fathers—especially that of Saint Augustine—which is most widely received throughout the Catholic Church, was being attacked with a novel effort and exceedingly rash presumption, and, insofar as lay in their power, recklessly and insolently undermined. Moved and admonished, therefore, by that charity through which “all of us, though many, are one body in Christ” (Rom. XII, 5), and through which, as the Apostle says, “the members should be mutually concerned for one another; and if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it, and if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (I Cor. XII, 25–26)—moved, I say, by this affection of charity, it seemed right and pleasing to us to write these matters, whatever their worth, both for the sake of our own agitation and for the edification and confirmation of those who may wish to read them, in a concise and clear manner, insofar as the Lord deigns to inspire us. Whatever we have thought should be said in this work, we shall establish not by our own opinion or presumption, but by the clearest testimonies of Scripture and the venerable authority of the holy Fathers mentioned above. Far be it from us, or from those whom charity has compelled us to say these things, ever to depart from their footsteps and unity, lest, separated from them, we should also be separated from the Lord himself, who says specifically to them: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke X, 16). He willed that they should possess such great grace and glory in his Church that they might confidently say with the Apostle: “Therefore he who despises these things does not despise man but God, who has also given his Holy Spirit in us” (I Thess. IV, 8). Through Phinehas the priest he likewise earnestly commanded us: “Only do not depart from the Lord and from our fellowship by building an altar apart from the altar of the Lord our God, which has been erected before his tabernacle” (Joshua XXII, 19).

## CHAPTER III. On the first chapter. The assistance of divine grace was necessary to the angel and to man, even in the first state, for doing good.—The condition of the first man

[Col. 1087B]

The text of the first chapter therefore reads as follows:

> Almighty God created man upright and without sin, with free will, and placed him in paradise, where he willed him to remain in the holiness of righteousness. Man, using free will badly, sinned and fell, and became a mass of perdition for the human race. But God, good and just, chose from that same mass of perdition, according to his foreknowledge, those whom by grace he predestined to life, and predestined eternal life for them. But the others, whom in justice and judgment he left in the mass of perdition, he foreknew would perish, but did not predestine them to perish; yet he predestined eternal punishment for them, because he is just. Accordingly, we speak of only one predestination of God, which pertains either to the gift of grace or to the recompense of justice.

### CENSURE

In order, then, to respond to these words and to this kind of definition more suitably and clearly, the first thing that troubles us in them is that, without any mention of God’s grace—without which no rational creature, whether angelic or human, ever could, can, or will be able to exist, remain, and persevere in righteousness and holiness—the first man is defined as having been created by God with free will and placed in paradise, as though by free will alone he could have remained in holiness and righteousness. [Col. 1087D] It is said that in the words cited above God merely willed this—not that he inspired or granted it by the gift of his grace so that it might come to pass. Both the authority of Holy Scripture, the careful argument of blessed Augustine, and the clearest teaching of other holy and orthodox Fathers show that this has not been fully and catholicly defined.

[Col. 1088A] [Note: [Col. 1087D] Observe that Julian, against whom Augustine argued in so many books, accused Moses of having thought that God was not the creator of the angels, because Moses had not mentioned their creation. Augustine replied to him, and later Saint Thomas, in question 61, article 1 of the First Part, held that the creation of the angels was indicated by the name “heaven,” or even “light.” This answer, however, does not please many, because in Scripture “heaven and earth” is understood to mean this visible heaven, and “light” likewise that visible illumination, so that this interpretation of the Church of Lyon is mystical rather than literal.]

In the Book of Genesis, where on the first day the creation of the angelic nature is understood under the name of “light,” it is written:

> “And God said, ‘Let there be light’; and there was light. And God saw that the light was good, and he separated the light from the darkness. He called the light Day, and the darkness Night” (Gen. I, 3–5).

If, therefore, according to the understanding of the Catholic Fathers, this is rightly understood of the angels, it is clear that God the Father, in his Word, which “in the beginning was with God” (John I, 1), established and made it so that the elect angels, as soon as they were created, existed, having been enlightened by that same Word, and became “light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8). In themselves and by themselves they could have been nothing other than darkness, as indeed are all the apostate angels, who, having been abandoned by the light of the grace of their Creator, remained in themselves nothing but darkness. Hence the Apostle also says of their wicked dominion—from which we have been liberated through the blood of the only-begotten Son of God:

> “He has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. I, 13).

And elsewhere he says:

> “For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (II Cor. XI, 14),

clearly showing that there are angels of light who, with God enlightening them, persevered in the truth, and angels of darkness, of whose prince the Lord says:

> “He did not stand in the truth” (John VIII, 44).

They were therefore made not merely so that they might exist essentially, but also so that, with divine grace enlightening them, they might be “light and day in the Lord.” Those who through pride had fallen from that enlightening truth and from the fellowship of the others deserved to be called “darkness and night.” “God saw this light, that it was good,” when by his judgment he approved it as pleasing to himself. But he did not praise those “darknesses,” because he did not approve them; rather, by a just judgment, he ordained that they should persist in the condemnation of their own ruin. This is also shown concerning the holy angels in the Psalm, where it is said:

> “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. XXXII, 6).

For if by “the word of the Lord,” that is, by the power of the only-begotten Son, the heavens were established, and by “the breath of his mouth,” that is, by the power of the Holy Spirit, all the powers of heaven were either created so that they might exist or established so that they might persevere in the truth, then it is entirely clear that they were created by the Spirit of God and solidified by that same grace in everlasting blessedness. [Col. 1088D]

So also the first man, created by God with free will, lived a blessed life with God so long as he was protected and strengthened by “the shield of God’s good will” (Ps. V, 13), that is, by divine grace. But after, presuming upon his own strength and exalting himself against his Creator, he turned away from him, he incurred his indignation [that is, the punishment of just condemnation]. [Col. 1089A] Later, recognizing that he had justly incurred this punishment in those who through God’s mercy are saved from his offspring, he “humbled himself under the mighty hand of God” (I Pet. V, 6), continually cries out to him, and entreats him to be found worthy of liberation and healing.

The Psalmist, speaking in the person of this same man—well created, graciously assisted, miserably fallen, truly converted, and tearfully pleading—invokes God in these words, saying:

> “For there is anger in his indignation, and life in his goodwill. In the evening weeping will remain, and in the morning, joy. But I said in my abundance, ‘I shall never be moved.’ Lord, by your goodwill you gave strength to my beauty; you turned your face away from me, and I became troubled. To you, O Lord, I shall cry, and to my God I shall make supplication” (Ps. XXIX, 6–9).

Man certainly had an evening when, as he sinned, the sun of righteousness set for him. In that blind night, descending from him, the human race remains in weeping; yet “in the morning, joy” is promised to it through the morning resurrection of Christ, so that through it it may be restored from death to life.

Blessed Augustine describes this happy and blessed life of man in paradise in an exceptionally lucid and delightful passage in the fourteenth book of *The City of God*, as follows (Book XIV, chapter 26):

> “Thus man lived in paradise as he wished, so long as he wished what God had commanded. He lived enjoying God, from whom, the Good, he was good. He lived without any want, possessing the power always to live in this way. Food was present so that he would not hunger; drink, so that he would not thirst; the tree of life, so that old age would not dissolve him. No corruption in the body, nor any distress arising from the body, intruded upon those senses of his. No inward illness, no external blow was feared. There was complete health in the flesh and complete tranquility in the mind [or: soul]. As there was neither heat nor cold in paradise, so in its inhabitant no offense against good will arose from desire or fear. There was nothing sad at all, and nothing foolishly joyful; true joy, however, continued from God, toward whom ‘love from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith’ burned (I Tim. I, 5). There was also between the spouses a faithful partnership in honorable love; harmony between the vigilance of mind and body; and the keeping of the commandment without toil. Weariness did not fatigue the man at rest, and sleep did not weigh upon one unwilling to sleep.”

The same most blessed teacher, concerning this grace received from God by the first man and lost through his own fault, argues likewise in his book *On Rebuke and Grace*, saying (chapter 11):

> “The first man possessed this grace, in which, if he had wished to remain, he would never have been evil; and without which, even with free will, he could not have been good. Yet by free will he could abandon it. Therefore God did not will him to be without his grace, though he left him (*quem*; alternatively *quam*, “which,” referring to grace) in the power of his free will, because free will is sufficient for evil, but is insufficient for good unless it is assisted by the all-powerful Good. If that man had not abandoned this assistance through free will, he would always have been good; but he abandoned it, and was abandoned.”

A little later the same teacher adds:

> “God then had given man a good will; for he had made him in that will, who had made him upright. He had given him assistance, without which he could not remain in that will if he wished; but he left it to his free will whether he would wish. Since, however, he did not wish to remain, the fault is certainly his, just as the merit would have been his had he wished to remain.”

Concerning the grace divinely bestowed upon the holy angels, in which some remained and from which others fell, he adds:

> “The holy angels, who, when others fell through free will, themselves stood through that same free will, deserved to receive the due reward of this standing. That reward was such a fullness of blessedness that they are absolutely certain they will always remain in it. But if this assistance had been lacking to either angel or man when they were first made—since their nature had not been made such that they could remain without divine assistance, even if they wished—then they would not have fallen through their own fault. The assistance without which they could not remain would have been lacking.”

If we have been able to learn from the Holy Scriptures that no holy angels will now fall, how much more have they themselves learned this through the truth revealed to them in a higher manner!

> “For we have been promised a blessed life without end and equality with the angels. From this promise we are certain that, when after the judgment we come to that life, we shall not fall from it. But if the angels do not know this about themselves, we shall not be ‘equal’ but ‘happier’ than they (Matt. XXII, 30). Yet the Truth promised us equality with them. It is therefore certain that they know by sight what we know by faith: namely, that no fall of any holy angel will now take place.”

Blessed Ambrose likewise confirms in his exposition of Psalm 118 that the holy angels need this grace of God, saying (Sermon 8):

> “An archangel needs mercy in one way, and a human being in another; for the nature of angels is certainly not subject to corruption in the same way as the nature of the human race. Therefore the angel needs the mercy of God lest he err and, when God’s grace has turned away from him, fall into vice. A human being, although now with a firmer resolve [or: proposition], nevertheless seeks mercy because of the succession of sins he has contracted. Thus, although both need mercy, mercy is owed to the angel in one way and to the human being in another.”

The venerable Fathers mentioned above, following the judgment of that most blessed teacher, commended this state of the first man—endowed with free will but assisted by divine grace so that he might preserve the good in which he had been created—by the authority of their holy council, as follows (Council of Orange, canon 19):

> “Human nature, even if it had remained in that integrity in which it was created, could in no way preserve itself without the assistance of its Creator. Therefore, since without the grace of God it could not guard the salvation it had received, how will it be able without the grace of God to restore what it lost?”

Having briefly noted these things concerning the first question, whoever sincerely, purely, and catholicly desires to think rightly about the condition or blessedness of the first man—or of the angels—should faithfully attend to divine authority; attend to the most faithful Fathers of the Church, disputing with the utmost fidelity; and attend also to the councils assembled to define the same matter with the greatest firmness. Let him not, according to the impious Pelagian teaching, believe that the first man could have remained in the good he had received by his own will alone, but let him believe that, so long as he stood, he was assisted by divine grace. Nor should he believe that almighty God merely willed that the same man remain in holiness and righteousness, but that he also gave him the assistance by which he could remain.

## CHAPTER IV. Also on the first chapter.—The predestination of the elect is not based on foreseen merits

[Col. 1091B]

After this, the same first chapter continues:

> “But the man, using free will badly, sinned and fell, and became a mass of perdition for the whole human race. But God, good and just, chose from that same mass of perdition, according to his foreknowledge, those whom by grace he predestined to life, and predestined eternal life for them.”

With regard to these words, namely, that the good and just God “chose from the same mass of perdition, according to his foreknowledge, those whom by grace he predestined to life,” we certainly approve that almighty God predestined his elect to life by his grace and predestined eternal life for them. Thus both the elect are predestined to eternal life and eternal life is predestined for the elect. Both statements are true and are clearly set forth by the Apostle. For concerning the predestination of the elect to life he says:

> “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 30).

And that he predestined eternal life for these same elect, he says elsewhere:

> “In hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before eternal times” (Titus I, 2).

But what troubles us is why, in this definition—which holds that by God’s grace both the elect are prepared for eternal life and eternal life is prepared for these same elect—the elect themselves are nevertheless said to have been chosen by God according to his foreknowledge, without any mention of grace. It is as though grace consists in the elect’s attaining the life of grace and in eternal life’s being prepared for them, while their being chosen was not grace but merely foreknowledge. This is plainly contrary to the Catholic faith. For almighty God, in choosing those whom he predestined and called to eternal life, did not foresee their good merits as though he chose them because he foresaw that they would become good from themselves. Rather, the election itself—by which, without any good merit, they were made vessels of mercy from the mass of perdition—was solely grace. Through this grace they were separated from the children of perdition and adopted as children of life and resurrection.

The Apostle carefully commends this election—not of merits but of grace, in which no one’s good works were foreseen, but only divine mercy was prepared—in his discussion of the two twins, Isaac and Rebecca’s sons, saying:

> “For when they had not yet been born or done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works but from him who calls—it was said: ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’ As it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (Rom. IX, 10ff.).

Clearly, God’s hatred of Esau arose from the merit of original sin. God’s love for Jacob, however, since Jacob was held under the same merited condemnation, arose solely from gratuitous mercy, as the same Apostle immediately adds:

> “What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means. For he says to Moses: ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion’” (Rom. IX, 14, 15).

Writing also to Timothy, he inculcates this election of true grace and of no merit:

> “Share in suffering for the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times” (II Tim. I, 8–9).

God therefore did not choose from the mass of perdition, according to foreseen merits, those whom he would make children by adoption. He chose freely those whom he mercifully liberated from that just condemnation equally owed to all.

## CHAPTER V. On the same chapter.—The reprobate predestined to destruction after foreseen sin.—Divine foreknowledge and predestination do not compel anyone to sin

[Col. 1092C]

The same chapter continues:

> “But the others, whom in justice and judgment he left in the mass of perdition, he foreknew would perish, but did not predestine them to perish. Yet, because he is just, he predestined eternal punishment for them. Accordingly, we speak of only one predestination of God, which pertains either to the gift of grace or to the recompense of justice.”

In these words it is astonishing how it is asserted that almighty God left the others—that is, all the reprobate—in the mass of perdition by his just judgment, yet did not predestine them, but merely foreknew that they would perish. If God’s just judgment has already preceded in them, and by that same just judgment they have been assigned to the mass of perdition, how have they not by such judgment already been assigned and predestined to perdition? Thus, while the truth of the divine judgment is denied in this definition, it is confirmed by the very testimony of those who deny it. How did he merely foreknow, and not predestine, what by their own confession he had already decreed by a just judgment? Why does a man dare to accept as true and complete the predestination of God’s just judgment, by which in his eternal counsel he ordained the just to life and the wicked to punishment, in one part but deny it in the other? It is as though almighty God both foreknew and predestined what he would do by his just judgment concerning the elect, but concerning the reprobate merely foreknew what he would do by that same just judgment and did not predestine it, although in both cases there is one judgment and one justice, by which rewards are rendered to the just and punishments to the wicked. [Col. 1093A]

For if this predestination of divine judgment were violent, unjust, or prejudicial to anyone, it would rightly indict God as unjust; indeed, it could in no way be believed of him, “with whom there is no injustice.” But since it is most clearly not violent, because it compels no one to be evil and unable to be otherwise; not unjust, because it punishes only those who have persisted in evil through their own fault; and not prejudicial, because it does not prejudge anyone so that he may perish, as it were, by its sentence rather than by his own merit, what is criticized in it, or considered as though blasphemous, when it contains only equity and justice?

Divine predestination toward human beings does what divine foreknowledge also does. God foreknew that they would become evil, but by that foreknowledge itself he did not compel them to become evil. By his just judgment he predestined those who would persist in evil to be punished; yet by that same predestination he did not compel them to be evil or to persist in evil. This is his equity: those who willingly persisted in evil should be unwillingly punished with torments.

Let a man therefore change himself; while there is time, let him correct and amend himself, because he cannot change or destroy almighty and eternal foreknowledge and predestination. If anyone denies that foreknowledge and predestination exist with God, he is plainly an unbeliever. If anyone says that God’s foreknowledge and predestination compel someone to be evil, so that he cannot be otherwise, he blasphemes horribly. But whoever faithfully confesses both that foreknowledge and eternal predestination exist with God and that no one is compelled by them to evil, but only that each person’s future character is foreknown and that each is judged according to what he has done, thinks entirely catholicly.

### (The Creed of Saint Athanasius)

> “Certainly, in the profession of the Catholic faith, which unless each person preserves whole and inviolate, he will undoubtedly perish forever, and which unless each person faithfully and firmly believes, he cannot be saved, we all confess with one voice that at the coming of the only-begotten Son of God from heaven all human beings must rise again with their bodies and give an account of their own deeds. ‘And those who have done good will go into eternal life, but those who have done evil into eternal fire.’”

Clearly, therefore, concerning both parts—the elect as well as the reprobate—what we confess here is true, just, and predestined in the eternal and just judgment of God. For if it were not predestined, how could we believe so firmly and confess so unhesitatingly that it will happen?

Let each person therefore, as has already been said, change himself for the better while the opportunity is granted, with God’s help. For this is undoubtedly what he wills who daily cries out and admonishes, saying:

> “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI, 27);

and again:

> “Turn to me, and I will turn to you, says the Lord of hosts” (Zech. I, 3).

But concerning him “with whom there is no change or shadow due to alteration” [Col. 1094A] (James I, 17), who says through the prophet, “For I am the Lord, and I do not change” (Mal. III, 6), we must fully and perfectly confess what belongs to him, because we can add nothing to or take anything away from his fullness and perfection.

Therefore let us truthfully confess the full and perfect predestination of God’s just judgment, both with regard to the elect and with regard to the reprobate, since it is altogether true. Let us deny God’s mercy to no one, detract from the grace of conversion in no one, close the way of forgiveness to no one, but instill a useful and salutary fear in all who wish to remain in iniquity.

The Apostle declares this most certain and immovable predestination of both parts to us, saying:

> “When God made his promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom he might swear, he swore by himself, saying: ‘Surely I will bless you, and I will surely multiply you’” (Heb. VI, 13–14).

A little later he adds:

> “Human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and in every dispute among them an oath serves as confirmation. Therefore, wishing to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his counsel, God interposed an oath, so that by two things in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have the strongest encouragement—we who have fled for refuge to hold fast to the hope set before us” (ibid., 16–18).

Behold: concerning the elect, who were promised so that they might be Abraham’s children and heirs of the New and Eternal Testament, almighty God, because he has no one greater, swears by himself. The Apostle teaches us what is to be understood by this oath: namely, that in this way “God wished to show more abundantly to the heirs of his promise the immutability of his counsel,” so that through “two things”—that is, through his promise and his oath—“in which it is impossible for God to lie,” whether he is making the promise or swearing to his promises, “we might have the strongest encouragement—we who have fled for refuge to hold fast to the hope set before us.”

## CHAPTER VI. On the divine oath

This divine oath, therefore, is nothing other than the eternal and unchangeable predestination of God’s immutable counsel. Concerning this immutable counsel of God the Psalmist says:

> “But the counsel of the Lord remains forever, the thoughts of his heart from generation to generation” (Ps. XXXII, 11).

The Lord himself also testifies through Isaiah:

> “My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done” (Isa. XLVI, 10).

If, therefore, here, on the Apostle’s instruction (Heb. VI, 17), we understand by God’s oath made to Abraham “the immutability of his counsel,” that is, of his predestination, then we must understand it likewise where God is introduced as having sworn concerning Christ’s eternal priesthood, the Psalmist saying:

> “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Ps. CIX, 4).

And again, where the Psalm speaks of God’s promise made to blessed David:

> “The Lord has sworn truth to David, and he will not frustrate him: ‘I will place upon your throne one from the fruit of your womb’” (Ps. CXXXI, 11).

If, therefore, in all these passages the immutability of God’s counsel and predestination is understood through his oath in the salvation of the elect, then conversely it must be understood in the damnation of the reprobate, where almighty God himself says concerning them:

> “They truly did not know my ways, concerning whom I swore in my wrath: ‘They shall not enter into my rest’” (Ps. XCIV, 11).

Here too the immutability of the oath is introduced, so that no one may believe that any of those concerning whom so terrible an oath was made will enter God’s rest. Yet this is not unjust, because they wished to persist in impiety “according to their hardness and unrepentant heart,” the Lord himself first saying, “They did not know my ways,” and then adding, “To them I swore in my wrath: ‘They shall not enter into my rest.’”

Similar to this oath is what the Truth itself threatens in the Gospel concerning those who despised his banquet, saying:

> “I tell you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper” (Luke XIV, 24).

For when the Truth says this, there is no doubt that it has sworn.

Such also is God’s oath through the prophet Isaiah. After the oracle against Babylon and the kingdom of the Assyrians, who were the fiercest enemies of God’s people—and through whom, as blessed John the Apostle shows in the Apocalypse, the entire city of the devil, that is, the whole multitude of the reprobate, is signified—God inserts an oath concerning the certain destruction of such people. The prophet says:

> “The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: ‘Surely, as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have purposed in mind, so shall it happen: that I may crush the Assyrian in my land and trample him upon my mountains. This is the counsel that I have counseled over the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out over all the nations. For the Lord God of hosts has decreed, and who can weaken it? His hand is stretched out, and who can turn it back?’” (Isa. XIV, 24–25, 27–28.)

In these words the immutability of God’s predestination and the effect of that predestination are wonderfully and magnificently shown. Under oath he threatens such grave and extensive evils against those who perish, saying: “Surely, as I have thought, so shall it be, and as I have purposed in mind, so shall it happen”—that is, as I have conceived and purposed in the predestination of my eternal counsel, so it shall be and so it shall happen in the fulfillment of the things themselves.

The prophet’s following words also show this magnificently and clearly, when God says in his own person:

> “This is the counsel that I have counseled over the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out over all the nations.”

Then, immediately, the prophet adds in his own person:

> “For the Lord God of hosts has decreed; who can weaken it? His hand is stretched out, and who can turn it back?”

In these words, therefore, “the counsel that God has counseled over the whole earth” is clearly to be understood as his eternal predestination, and “the stretched-out hand” as the fulfillment of that same counsel.

[Col. 1096A]

And so that we may recognize that no one can resist his predestining counsel or its effect, it is said:

> “For the Lord God of hosts has decreed,”

that is, he has predestined in his eternal counsel;

> “and who can weaken it?”

so that it may be understood that no one can.

> “His hand is stretched out,”

namely, to accomplish what he has predestined;

> “and who can turn it back?”

Here likewise no one is understood.

For when it is said, “The Lord God of hosts has decreed,” what is “decreed” other than predestined, predetermined, established, fixed, or preordained?

From this we clearly understand what “predestined” means: predetermined, established, fixed, and preordained. This expression, “has decreed,” is also used in the Acts of the Apostles in a similar matter and with the same meaning. There the multitude of the faithful, raising their voice to God with one accord in prayer, said:

> “For truly, in this city there gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your counsel had decreed should happen” (Acts IV, 27–28).

Where the Latin translator, rendering the sense, used the plural *decreverunt* (“they decreed”), the Greek reads in the singular: “whatever your hand and counsel predestined to happen.”

Blessed Augustine is likewise found to have cited this very testimony in his book *On the Predestination of the Saints* (chapter 16). The same verb is read in Greek here as in the Epistle to the Romans, where it is written:

> “Those whom he predestined, he also called” (Rom. VIII, 30).

Where we say *predestined* in Latin, the Greek in both that Epistle and this passage from the Acts of the Apostles has **προώρισεν** (*proōrisen*), which, as already stated, some translated precisely as “predestined,” others as “defined” or “predetermined,” and others as “decreed,” or, in the plural, “they decreed.”

Here too there is something especially remarkable: just as the prophet speaks of “the counsel of God” and “the stretched-out hand,” so this passage says that they gathered “to do whatever your hand and counsel decreed—or decreed in the plural—should happen.” We have thought it necessary to explain this so carefully in order that “predestined,” “decreed,” “defined,” and “predetermined” may be understood to signify the same thing:

> “Therefore Herod and Pontius Pilate gathered against the holy servant Jesus, whom God anointed, to do what the hand and counsel of God predestined, decreed, and predetermined to happen.”

But whatever almighty God the Father predestined to happen through the passion of his only-begotten Son, they did through malice and impiety. He predestined it through mercy and goodness; they did it so that the name of Christ might be destroyed, while he did it so that by Christ’s blood the sins of the world might be washed away.

All these things were predestined to occur in Christ’s passion, and it was also predestined through whom they would occur, since by God’s just judgment they had been judged worthy, on account of preceding sins, to be so blinded that such things would be accomplished through them. Judas likewise was predestined to betray that same Lord Christ because he had shown himself worthy to carry out such a crime.

## CHAPTER VII. On the two cords and the twofold lot. On the eternal foreknowledge, providence, and predestination of God. The distinction between the elect and the reprobate prefigured in Jacob and Esau. Gratuitous election and just reprobation

[Col. 1097A]

This eternal and unchangeable predestination of God concerning both cities—that is, the city of the elect and that of the reprobate—the blessed prophet Isaiah describes with wonderful praises and exultation as destined to be fulfilled at the end of the age, saying:

“O Lord, you are my God; I will exalt you, I will confess your name, because you have done marvelous things, faithful ancient purposes. Amen” (Isa. 25:1).

And immediately afterward, concerning the city of the ungodly:

“Because you have made the city into a tumult,” he says, “the strong city into ruin, the house of strangers, so that it is no longer a city and shall not be built forever” (ibid., 2).

There he also immediately adds concerning the city of the godly:

“Therefore a strong people will praise you; the city of mighty nations will fear you. For you have become strength to the poor, strength to the needy in his distress, hope from the storm, shelter from the heat” (ibid., 3–4).

We read that these two portions—namely, the elect and the reprobate—were also wonderfully represented in the Book of Kings by the measure of the equity of God’s just judgment, one portion destined for destruction and the other for salvation. There it is written concerning the blessed David:

“For he struck Moab and measured them with a line, making them equal with the ground. He measured two lines: one for killing and one for giving life” (2 Kings 8:2).

Who, then, would not recognize the true David as the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Moabites as the entire multitude of unbelievers who are alien from the people of God? Of these, while by his just and hidden judgment he ordains some to eternal death, he chooses and calls others to eternal life. What else does he do than, by the most equitable measure of his judgment, “measure two lines, one for killing and one for giving life” (Esth. 10:10)?

But in the Book of Esther also this same distinction between the two portions—namely, the elect and the reprobate, the faithful and the unfaithful—is magnificently represented under the figure of two lots. There it is written concerning God:

“And he commanded that there should be two lots, one of the people of God and the other of all the nations; and each lot came to its appointed place, as had been established from that time before God” (ibid., 11).

For the explanation of the divine judgment is rightly understood through the lot, as Solomon says:

“Lots are cast into the lap, but they are directed by the Lord” (Prov. 16:33).

And almighty God commanded that there should be two lots: one of the people of God, that is, of all the elect, and the other of all the nations, namely, of all the reprobate. He distinguished both portions by the lot of his judgment, so that some would belong to the portion of the lot of the saints, while others would belong to the portion of the lot of the ungodly.

Indeed, Scripture plainly teaches us that there are two lots—that is, the lot of the saints and the lot of the ungodly—when the Apostle says concerning the first:

“He has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light; he has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1:12–13).

This is plainly the lot of the people of God. Concerning the other, we read in the Book of Ecclesiasticus:

“For a wicked soul destroys the one who possesses it, gives him over to the joy of his enemy, and leads him into the lot of the ungodly” (Ecclus. 6:4).

This is plainly the lot of the reprobate.

In other places of Holy Scripture also, the word “lot” is found used for the just recompense of judgment in the portion of the reprobate. Thus in Isaiah God says to the rejected people:

“This is your portion and the lot of your measure” (Isa. 57:7).

And concerning the enemies of the people of God the same prophet says:

“This is the portion of those who devastated us, and the lot of those who plundered us” (Isa. 17:18).

Therefore “each lot”—that is, both the lot of the people of God and that of those judged alien from the people of God—“came to its appointed place”: namely, so that, just as it had been established in God’s hidden judgment concerning both lots—that is, the city of God and the city of the devil—it might be fulfilled in reality from that time onward, from the beginning of the world until the end of the age. During this time these two cities run their temporal course, joined in body but divided in mind, until they reach their appointed ends, either eternal life or everlasting death.

All this “came to its appointed place” before God, who alone knows how justly he has arranged these things, and how truly and effectively they will be fulfilled until the end of the age.

The aforementioned Book of Ecclesiasticus wonderfully shows that this distinction of divine judgment and predestination—namely, the two lines and the two lots, one belonging to the chosen people and the other to the ungodly—was arranged eternally, saying:

[Col. 1098C]

“By the judgment of God, his works are from the beginning; and from their creation he distinguished their portions” (Ecclus. 33:10).

And elsewhere it says:

“The Lord separated all human beings from the earth, and from the soil from which Adam was created, in the multitude of the discipline of the Lord; and he changed their ways. From among them he blessed and exalted, from among them he sanctified and drew them to himself; and from among them he cursed and humbled, and turned them away from their separation. Like a potter’s clay in his hand, he forms it and arranges it. All his ways are according to his arrangement” (Ecclus. 33:12–14).

Similar to this statement is what the blessed Judith says in her prayer to God:

“For you made the former things, and after them you devised those that followed; and what you yourself willed came to pass, and you established your judgments in your providence” (Judith 9:4–5).

The same book also shows elsewhere how eternal are his foreknowledge, providence, and judgments of predestination, saying:

“For all things were known beforehand to the Lord God before they were created; so also, after they were completed, he sees all things. The works of all flesh are before him, and nothing is hidden from his eyes. From age to age he sees, and nothing is marvelous in his sight.
