One must not say, ‘What is this?’ or ‘What is that?’ for everything will be sought in its own time. No thought escapes him, and no word is hidden from him. He has adorned the great works of his wisdom, which is before the age and unto the age; nothing has been rejected, nothing diminished, and it needs no one’s counsel. Their ways are always before him and are not hidden from his eyes; and all their works are like the sun in the sight of God, whose eyes continually examine their ways” (Ecclus. 23:29; 39:24, 26; 42:20, 22, 13, 16).

Certainly our Lord Jesus Christ, eternal and unchangeable Truth itself, most firmly inculcates this concerning the Law and the Prophets, saying:

“For I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things come to pass” (Matt. 5:18).

And again:

“It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the Law to fall” (Luke 16:17).

Concerning the words of the New Testament—which we must understand to include not only those he spoke with his own mouth but also everything he spoke through the holy apostles and evangelists—he likewise affirms:

“Amen, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all things come to pass. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Mark 13:30–31).

Therefore, whoever faithfully reads or hears the words of either Testament, whether they are spoken concerning the portion of the elect or concerning the portion of the reprobate, ought to receive and retain them as things truly foreknown, preordained, and predetermined eternally by God, so that they cannot possibly be otherwise.

What could be said or commended more clearly and magnificently concerning both portions—the reprobate and the elect, the unbelieving and the faithful—some of whom, so that they might not recognize the mystery of the Lord’s coming, whether before he was manifested in the flesh or afterward until the end of the age, deservedly earned blindness and rejection through pride, while others deserved to be illumined by the grace and devotion of faith—whether through just rejection or gratuitous election—than what the Lord himself, “the angel of the great counsel,” that is, the faithful witness and messenger of the Father’s and his own eternal will, declares and announces in the Gospel while glorifying God the Father and giving him thanks for his just judgments:

“I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10:21).

And immediately, with the highest praise and exultation referring both the blinding of the proud and the illumination of the humble to the Father’s eternal and unchangeable counsel and judgment, he adds:

“Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you” (ibid., 26).

And lest he be thought to have separated himself from participation in this eternal counsel and judgment, after referring everything in his customary devotion to the Father as the true author of his generation, he added concerning himself:

“All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (ibid., 37);

that is, both those things of which it was said, “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent,” and those concerning which it was added, “and revealed them to little ones,” so that by my counsel and judgment also—which certainly belongs to the Father as well—they might be distinguished, condemned, or liberated:

“For the Father judges no one, but he has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5:22–23).

This is the marvelous and ineffable mystery of eternal judgment, both in the portion of the elect and in that of the reprobate.

The blessed patriarch Isaac also suddenly perceived this more fully and profoundly in his two twin sons, as though, in ecstasy of mind with the Apostle, he contemplated “the incomprehensible judgments of God and his unsearchable ways” (Rom. 11:33), and, as it is written, “was terrified,” astonished with great amazement beyond what can be believed.

For he should not be thought to have been so greatly astonished and amazed merely because, being a blind and pious father, he might have been deceived or mistaken by probability or personal affection in distinguishing between his sons (Gen. 27:33). Rather, by a sudden stroke of revelation his heart was illumined, and he recalled what had been said concerning those same twins while they were still in their mother’s womb, when, as the Apostle says, they had “done neither good nor evil,” yet both were held bound by one and the same equal condemnation of original guilt: “The elder shall serve the younger.” God later impressed this more clearly through the prophet, saying:

“Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Gen. 25; Rom. 9; Mal. 1).

Thus the holy patriarch, recalling and understanding these things through the sudden illumination of the Spirit, saw in two men conceived in one union, condemned under the same condition of the first transgression, not yet born and not yet having earned anything good or evil by their own action, the marvelous and terrible judgment of God: namely, that he should freely love and choose one, while he should justly hate and reject the other:

“Just as the potter has power from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor” (Rom. 9:21).

Certainly he saw in those two the unchangeable counsel of God, since not even the willing, striving, and desiring father could in any way alter what had been foretold and predestined. Rather, by the divinely arranged and predetermined order of events, the one whom God had loved and preferred by his hidden judgment, while he was still in the womb, was preferred and blessed even through the father’s ignorance.

He saw in those two so great and profound a mystery of God’s counsel. And what he saw in them through the impulse of revelation, he also recognized as occurring in the distinction of the entire human race from the beginning to the end of the age—whether in the two peoples, circumcision and uncircumcision, or generally in the whole multitude of the elect and the reprobate. All descend from “one lump,” justly condemned. The almighty “potter,” by the eternal and unchangeable counsel of his judgment, makes from the same lump some, through justice, “vessels of wrath,” and others, through grace, “vessels of mercy.” Thus God’s counsel and judgment remain firm and immovable, while nevertheless no one is condemned except justly and no one is liberated except mercifully.

The most holy patriarch saw this impenetrable depth of God’s judgments represented “in the two twins” and fulfilled in the whole human race. As though exclaiming with the prophet, he said:

“Lord, I heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works and was terrified. He was struck with intense astonishment and, beyond what can be believed, overwhelmed by wonder” (Hab. 2; Gen. 27).

Likewise, the Psalmist, amazed and stunned by the same depth, cries out:

“How magnificent are your works, O Lord; your thoughts have become exceedingly deep” (Ps. 91:6).

Nor was it without reason that the Apostle, writing to the Romans and discussing with the greatest care the height of divine foreknowledge and predestination (Rom. 9), so that all who are saved might understand that they are saved not by their own merits or powers but solely by God’s grace, according to the eternal purpose of his will—he who foreknows, predestines, calls, justifies, and glorifies those whom he wills—chose, in discussing and strongly emphasizing these matters, after presenting many other things, this as the principal and greatest testimony or example: namely, the case of the aforementioned twins, which he placed first to prove and commend so profound a mystery.

For the whole matter is briefly contained in his words:

“So that the purpose of God according to election might remain, not because of works but because of him who calls, it was said: ‘The elder shall serve the younger’” (Rom. 9; Gen. 25).

There is God’s gratuitous election in Jacob—that is, election without works. There is the purpose of his eternal will, which certainly cannot exist without foreknowledge and predestination. There is the calling, because it was said, “not because of works but because of him who calls: the elder shall serve the younger.”

And just as there is gratuitous election in Jacob, of whom it was said, “Jacob I loved,” so there is just condemnation in Esau, concerning whom it is added, “but Esau I hated.”

[Col. 1101C]

The Church holds with the greatest firmness, from prophetic and apostolic authorities, this profound mystery of the divine judgments in both directions, because it especially pertains to commending and declaring the grace of Christ:

“So that whoever boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

This mystery was indeed hidden from the ages in God, but among the writings of the prophets it was disclosed through the apostolic preaching of his Church, together with the other matters belonging to the mystery of the Savior. The same Apostle says at the end of the aforementioned Epistle to the Romans:

“To him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal times, but now manifested through the Scriptures of the prophets” (Rom. 16:25–26), and so forth.

And elsewhere:

“As you can understand by reading my insight into the mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit” (Eph. 3:4–5), and so forth.

And again:

“To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to evangelize among the nations the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all concerning the administration of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things” (ibid., 8–9).

For although everything announced by the apostles concerning the divinity and incarnation of our Lord is, in general, “the great mystery of godliness,” “kept silent through eternal times, unknown to the sons of men in other generations, and hidden from the ages in God who created all things, but now manifested through the Scriptures of the prophets and the preaching of the apostles,” nevertheless this particular matter concerning the inscrutable divine judgments and arrangements—whether in the blinding of unbelievers or in the illumination of believers—is also specifically and especially called a mystery. The Apostle says:

“For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation: that blindness in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel may be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Predestination of the Reprobate to Destruction. God’s Foreknowledge Compels No One to Sin

[Col. 1102B]

Following this truth and authority of God’s Scripture, the blessed Father and outstanding teacher Augustine wrote a brilliant book *On the Predestination of the Saints*. He also repeatedly mentioned the predestination of the reprobate to destruction by God’s just judgment, both there and in his other short works.

Thus, in his book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness* (chapter 13), he most plainly shows this, saying:

“How, then, was it said, ‘There is none who does good, not even one’ (Ps. 13:1–2), unless that psalm is condemning a certain people among whom there was not even one who did good, while they wished to remain sons of men and not be sons of God, by whose grace a human being becomes good so as to do good?”

And shortly afterward:

“This good, then, which consists in seeking God, ‘there was none who did, not even one,’ but this was among the class of human beings predestined to destruction. For God’s foreknowledge looked upon these people and pronounced sentence over them.”

Likewise, in *The City of God*, Book 15, chapter 25:

“The wrath of God,” he says, “is not a disturbance of his spirit but the judgment by which punishment is inflicted upon sin. His thinking and reconsideration of changing things is an unchangeable reason. For God does not repent of any deed of his as a human being does; his judgment concerning absolutely everything is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain.”

In the treatises that he delivered to the people in his exposition of the Evangelist John, he speaks about this matter as follows (Treatise 42). Concerning what follows:

“Therefore you do not hear, because you are not from God” (John 8:47),

he says:

“These words were spoken to those who were not merely corrupted by sin—for this evil was common to all—but were also foreknown as people who would not believe. Therefore he foreknew that those to whom he spoke such things would remain in what they were from the devil, that is, they would die in their sins and ungodliness and would not come to regeneration, through which they would become children of God, that is, born from God, by whom they had been created as human beings. The Lord spoke according to this predestination,” and so forth.

Likewise, in Treatise 43:

“These people, indignant, dead, and predestined to everlasting death, answered insultingly and said: ‘Now we know that you have a demon’” (John 8:52).

Elsewhere, in Treatise 48, explaining the Lord’s words concerning his sheep, “No one will snatch them from my hand,” he says:

“What can the wolf do? What can the thief and robber do? They destroy only those predestined to destruction.”

Elsewhere, in Treatise 107:

“For he who predestined all future things by certain and unchangeable causes has done whatever he will do. For it was also said of him through the prophet: ‘He who made the things that will be’” (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint).

And elsewhere:

“The traitor of Christ,” he says, “was called the ‘son of perdition,’ predestined to perdition, according to the Scripture that prophesies of him especially in Psalm 108.”

Concerning divine foreknowledge, by which God immutably knows all future things, whether good or evil, and yet does not compel anyone to sin, he speaks in the same treatises as follows (Treatise 53):

“God does not compel anyone to sin merely because he already knows beforehand the future sins of human beings. The Jews therefore committed the sin which he did not compel them to commit—he who does not approve of sin, but foretold that they would commit it, since nothing is hidden from him. And therefore, if they had wished to do not evil but good, they would not have been prevented from doing so; and he would have foreseen them doing this, for he knows what each person will do and what he will repay them for their deed.”

This truth of divine predestination, declared in many ways through Scripture and faithfully commended by the most holy teacher, is also clearly taught by the most ancient and blessed teacher and master Cyprian, who says:

“He who alone received all judgment from the Father and who will come to judge has already pronounced the sentence of future judgment and knowledge, foretelling and declaring that he will confess before his Father those who confess him and deny those who deny him” (Matt. 10:32).

Likewise, when he was discussing those who, after being arrested during persecution, fought for Christ unto death, and those who, conscious of their weakness, prudently withdrew, he says:

“There, courage is more ready; here, caution is safer. The former, when his hour approached, was found already mature; the latter perhaps was spared, and withdrew after abandoning his property because he was not going to deny Christ. He too would certainly have confessed if he had been detained.”

Elsewhere, when during a time of mortality he was consoling someone who grieved that death had overtaken him before he could offer himself for the suffering of martyrdom, he says:

“First of all, martyrdom is not in your power but in God’s favor. Nor can you say that you have lost what you do not know whether you deserved to receive,” and so forth.

Elsewhere:

“He cannot perish,” he says, “unless he is plainly one who will perish, since the Lord says in his Gospel: ‘Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted’” (Matt. 15:13).

Elsewhere he says:

“The Lord commanded that one withdraw and flee during persecution, and he both taught and practiced this. Since the crown descends from God’s favor and cannot be received unless the hour for receiving it has arrived, whoever remains in Christ and withdraws for a time does not deny the faith but awaits the proper time. But whoever, by refusing to withdraw, falls, remained in order to deny Christ.”

The blessed Hilary likewise teaches the immovable firmness of divine foreknowledge and predestination, saying:

“For God, who embraces all things in himself, future things are as completed things. His foreknowledge is so faithful that things not yet done are nevertheless already regarded by him as past and accomplished.”

And again:

“It is fitting,” he says, “that the pitiable fall of the people, the punishment owed to their ungodliness, their sufficient satisfaction through the long duration of servitude for their grievous sins, and God’s merciful will toward them through the granting of a return should be spoken according to the foreknowing knowledge of the prophetic Spirit.”

Likewise, when he was explaining the Psalm:

“I rose, and I am still with you” (Ps. 138:18),

he says:

“‘I rose’ refers to the glory of the resurrection; but according to God’s foreknowledge he speaks of what will be as though it were past, because for God, through his knowledge and power, future things are accomplished things. Thus we ourselves also consider as accomplished what we are confident will occur.”

And when explaining the passage of the Psalm that says, “I will number them, and they will be multiplied beyond the sand” (ibid.), he speaks as follows concerning the certain and predestined number of the elect:

“Is the number uncertain of those who are written in God’s book? Therefore there is no difficulty concerning the number whose truth remains in the written record.”

The blessed Ambrose likewise briefly confirms, from the words of the Epistle to the Romans, both the goodness and the severity of divine judgment in both directions in his exposition of Psalm 118, saying:

“‘Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills’ (Rom. 9:18). He exhorts the one on whom he has had mercy; the other, whom he has cursed, he does not call back.”

Elsewhere:

“God,” he says, “the almighty Father, in the face of Moses, ‘blinded the Jewish people’ not through harshness but through foreknowledge, not through malice but through equity and justice. They themselves placed the veil over their eyes because they did not wish to understand the Law.”

Likewise, in his books *On the Faith* addressed to Gratian, he says concerning the same matter:

“It is the customary manner of prophecy that future things are spoken either as though they were present or as though they were future. For to God, future things are present; and to him to whom all things are foreknown, things that are to come are as accomplished things, as it is written: ‘He who made the things that will be’” (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint).

[Col. 1104D]

The blessed Jerome, also discussing this matter in his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians, says with equal clarity:

“It must be considered that here also προώρισμος (*proōrismos*) and πρόθεσις (*prothesis*)—that is, predestination and purpose—are placed together, according to which God works all things according to the counsel of his will. This does not mean that everything that happens in the world is carried out by God’s will and counsel—for otherwise evils could also be attributed to God—but that everything he does, he does with counsel and will, which are full of reason and of the power of the one who acts. We human beings often wish to do things according to counsel, but the effect by no means follows the will. No one, however, can resist God so that he does not do everything he wills. He wills things that are full of reason and counsel.”

Elsewhere in his commentaries on the same Epistle:

“When Paul says, ‘He chose us so that we might be holy and blameless before him’ (Eph. 1:4), that is, before God, before the foundation of the world, he is bearing witness to God’s foreknowledge, for all future things are already accomplished for him, and before they occur, everything is known. Thus Paul himself was predestined in his mother’s womb (Gal. 1), and Jeremiah was sanctified and chosen in his mother’s womb, strengthened, and sent as a prophet to the nations as a type of Christ (Jer. 1:5).”

And afterward:

“Paul does not say, ‘He chose us before the foundation of the world when we were holy and blameless.’ That would mean: because we had not previously been holy and blameless, he established that we should become so afterward. Paul and those like him were not chosen because they were holy and blameless; rather, they were chosen and predestined so that in the life that followed they might become holy and blameless through works and virtues.”

The blessed Leo also teaches plainly in his sermons to the people concerning the eternal counsel of God regarding both kinds of predestination:

“In the salvation of all through the cross of Christ, the will of the Father and of the Son was one: their counsel was one, and it could not in any way be disturbed, since before the eternal ages it had been both mercifully arranged and immutably predetermined.”

Elsewhere:

“Since, then, everything that Jewish ungodliness committed against the Lord of majesty had been foretold so long beforehand that the prophetic discourse speaks not so much about future things as about past things, what else is disclosed to us than the unchangeable order of God’s eternal arrangements? With him, things that must be distinguished have already been judged, and future things are already accomplished. Since divine knowledge anticipates both the qualities of our actions and the effects of all our wills, how much more are his own works known to God? And rightly it pleased him that things which absolutely could not fail to occur should be recalled as though they had already happened.”

The blessed bishop and glorious confessor Fulgentius also wrote an outstanding book concerning this foreknowledge and predestination of judgment in both directions. Like his other admirable and venerable writings, it has always been faithfully received by the Church and honorably numbered among ecclesiastical writers.

And now we do not know by what reasoning—or rather, by what infidelity and contentiousness—it is rejected together with the blessed Augustine. These men, who wish to appear Catholic, wickedly insult and despise such great and eminent men of God, trampling them underfoot like the vilest refuse and rubbish.

It is exceedingly astonishing—indeed horrifying—that they demand belief in their own inventions and absurdities after rejecting the most blessed Fathers and most illustrious teachers of the Church. Unless they hasten to correct themselves, they may most truly be judged heretics: they do not share the faith, charity, and most sincere teaching of the Fathers; moreover, together with them they despise the heavenly authority of Holy Scripture.

For if they had undertaken to read and understand with devotion and obedience that most faithful, comprehensive, and flourishing book of the blessed Fulgentius, then surely, with God’s assistance and illumination, no darkness of error would have remained in their hearts concerning this most obscure question of divine foreknowledge and predestination.

The aforementioned teacher says, among other things, in the book just mentioned:

“That the wicked perish before hell is not the work of God but of human beings; but that they will perish in hell is the work of God’s equity, for he approves no sinner’s iniquity.”

And again:

“By the name ‘predestination’ no coercive necessity of the human will is expressed. Rather, the merciful and just eternal arrangement of a future work is proclaimed: ‘The Church sings to God of mercy and judgment’” (Ps. 100:1).

Likewise, in the same work:

“Accordingly, he was able, as he willed, to predestine some to glory and others to punishment. But those whom he predestined to glory he predestined to righteousness; those whom he predestined to punishment he did not predestine to guilt. In the former he glorifies his own works; in the latter he condemns works that are not his own.

“Thus God predestined what he himself was going to do or what he himself was going to bestow. But he did not in any way predestine what he himself was not going to do, whether through grace or through justice.”

Likewise:

“An evil will does not belong to the best Creator; but the just condemnation of the unjust angel and of the human being belongs to the most equitable Knower. Therefore God did not predestine a human being to an evil will, because he himself was not going to give that will to the human being.”

And again:

“There is no other predestination of his except the eternal preparation of his future works, in which no cause of evil can in any way be found, because the origin of sin never proceeded from God’s will. ‘For the Lord is merciful and just’ (Ps. 114:5). Elsewhere it is written: ‘The Lord God loves mercy and truth’ (Ps. 84:12). Therefore, in all his works, either just truth is preserved or compassionate mercy is granted beforehand.”

Likewise:

“By God’s predestination, either the merciful forgiveness of sins or the just punishment of sins has been prepared. Therefore God could never have predestined a human being to what he himself had arranged both to prohibit by a commandment, to cleanse through mercy, and to punish through justice.”

And again:

“God therefore foreknew all human works, whether good or evil, because nothing could be hidden from him. But he predestined only the good works which he foreknew he would accomplish in the children of grace. As for the evil works that would be committed by those whom he predestined not to the kingdom but to destruction, he foreknew them by his most powerful divinity, ordained them, and governed them by his provident goodness.”

And again:

“He foreknew the good and evil wills of human beings, but he predestined not the evil wills, only the good. And although it was not included in his predestination that he should give malice to the human will, it was included in his predestination what he would repay for the malice of the human will.”

## CHAPTER IX. The Same Matter Continues, Chapter One

The venerable teacher mentioned above discussed these and many other matters sufficient for the present question in the book we mentioned earlier, in accordance with the truth of Holy Scripture and the reverence due to the authority of the preceding Fathers, using clear language.

We ought obediently and sincerely to follow him as he faithfully argues and devoutly follows the footsteps of his predecessors. For this too belongs to the integrity of our faith: just as in the other things we believe concerning God, so in this matter also we must think nothing unworthy of the divine majesty and nothing false concerning the divine judgments.

This is especially so because the truth of this predestination both builds in us the sincerity of faith, offers no occasion for the offense of despair, and instills a most salutary fear in all who delight in living perniciously and stubbornly in their vices.

As for the contempt and rejection of the most blessed and illustrious Fathers, whom many trample upon with excessive insolence and irreverence, what else ought we to think than that we should listen all the more carefully and observe what Scripture commands concerning these same holy Fathers, saying:

“Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; ask your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. 32:7).

Let us not fall into what is said through Solomon:

“It is evil for a person to swear by sacred things and to retract after making a vow” (Prov. 20:25).

Nor should we become disobedient to and contemptuous of our spiritual parents, through whose faith and teaching we were begotten and reborn in Christ, or of the Scripture that says:

“Listen, my son, to the discipline of your father”—that is, of almighty God—“and do not abandon the law of your mother” (Prov. 1:8), that is, the faithful doctrines and statutes of Holy Church.

We must observe these not merely as legal ordinances but truly as law, because we have no doubt that they were issued through the Holy Spirit.

Finally, concerning the books and writings of blessed Augustine, in which, under the necessity of destroying the new—that is, Pelagian—heresy and of defending the Catholic faith, with the most earnest purpose he discussed in many ways, in accordance with the profundity of Holy Scripture and the rule of evangelical and apostolic teaching, the subjects of nature and grace, grace and free will, correction and grace, the predestination of the saints and the gift of perseverance, and the baptism of infants: while he was still alive, as Prosper and Hilary write to him—and much more after his death, because of the obscurity of the matters and the slowness of those who understood them less fully—a manifold complaint arose, especially in Gaul; but [Col. 1107D] it was immediately and most diligently quieted and healed through the providence of divine mercy, through the councils and decrees of the most blessed Fathers, and through the decisions and authority of the pontiffs of the apostolic see. Thus silence was imposed upon foolish and undisciplined questions, and the authority of the most holy and sincere teacher was confirmed in all the Churches, and in the apostolic see itself.

Finally, blessed Pope Celestine—by whose authority and diligence the Nestorian heresy, as it arose, was crushed together with its author—wrote against the detractors, or rather slanderers, of so great a man, as is contained in the books of the Canons among the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. He commended him with such reverence and praise that the title of the document is: “[An extraordinary affirmation of praise concerning the holy bishop Augustine].” To this title are appended the words of the aforesaid Pontiff, which read as follows:

“Augustine, a man of holy memory, we have always held in our communion because of his life and merits; nor did even a rumor of sinister suspicion ever stain him. We remember that he once possessed such great learning that, even among the best teachers, he was always regarded as such by my predecessors. Properly, therefore, all people everywhere held a good opinion of him, since he was everywhere an object both of love and of honor. Hence such men must be resisted, for we see them growing in wickedness. It is impious for religious souls to endure these things; and when those who are our members are afflicted, we too must be distressed with them. Although the blessedness promised to all who are proved to endure persecution for righteousness’ sake remains [Col. 1108B] (Matt. V, 10). What the Lord promises them in the future is made clear by the discourse that follows. The matter concerns not only those who are acting. Whenever the universal Church is shaken by any novelty, let us understand that you too disapprove of these things which displease us. We shall be able to demonstrate this only if, after silence has been imposed upon the wicked, complaint about this matter ceases hereafter.”

Let us, therefore, honor this most blessed and faithful Father with the whole devotion of faith: he was always held in the communion of the apostolic see, was reverently received by its pontiffs among the teachers of the faith, and was so openly and honorably defended by them against his detractors and traducers that they decreed that, after silence had been imposed upon the wicked, every murmur about him should be suppressed and driven away. Let us follow him with the utmost zeal and devotion. In those matters where, because of the obscurity of the subjects and the subtlety of the discussions, we are less able to understand him, let us either ask the Lord for understanding or humbly allow and beg to be taught by those whom he has deigned to enlighten by his gift.

For—something still more grievous and utterly to be detested out of love for divine truth—some people circulate a little book presented as bearing his name, which they call by the Greek term *hypomnēstikon* (ὑπομνηστικόν, “memorandum” or “memoranda”). Yet neither that holy bishop who wrote his Life and most diligently appended, at the end of the same work, a catalogue of all his books and letters—who certainly knew all his writings extremely well, since he had been brought up by him and had lived with him for many years—mentions it among his other books. Scarcely any ecclesiastical writer is to be found who mentions it. Therefore there is no doubt that it bears a false superscription.

These men, abandoning his authentic and illustrious books, which the universal Church follows, fabricate this work through their own error and falsehood. They claim that the aforesaid pontiff composed it last, after all his other books, and that in it he corrected whatever he had wrongly said in his preceding books about grace and free will, and about the predestination and foreknowledge of God. Far be it from us to tolerate the acceptance of so wicked a fabrication: because of such a book—which [Col. 1109A] is found neither in the catalogue of his books, nor in his books of *Retractations*, nor, so far as can be found, mentioned in the writings of any ecclesiastical man, and which is shown to be manifestly opposed to the thought of the aforesaid teacher, indeed to Catholic sincerity itself, and does not in the least agree with his style—we must not cast aside the clearest doctrines of truth which, in his most genuine and approved books, the whole Catholic Church receives and preserves, not only in the other regions of the world but even in the apostolic see itself.

We have thought it necessary to repeat all these things so carefully in order that we may utterly drive from our minds so great an evil—the contempt and rejection of the most holy Fathers—and so great a falsehood concerning the books of a most faithful and sincere teacher, by which these men persuade us to reject the clearest truth and follow the shadows and [Col. 1109B] mists of deception. For if we carelessly accept deception of this kind, corruption from the serpent’s poison enters, and nothing will remain whole.

They also produce another little book, supposedly written under the name of Saint Jerome, concerning free will. They ought certainly to display it more clearly, so that it may be established whether it should truly be believed to be his. For we know that the same holy Jerome wrote about free will in one of his works and set out two opinions held by certain people, one of which the Church follows and the other it entirely rejects.

Let us therefore beware, insofar as we can with God’s help, of falsehoods arising against the faith and the truth—and especially at this time, when, through God’s terrible judgment, greater ignorance has begun to increase among people and manifold error to spread more freely. Yet if someone errs, or is thought to err, in matters of faith, he must certainly be overcome not by falsehood but by truth, just as blessed Augustine says to a certain rash writer, Vincentius Victor:

“We want you to be victorious in such a way that truth conquers error, not error conquering error—and, what is worse, the greater error conquering the lesser.”

These things must necessarily be said concerning the first chapter of the definitions, so that if, when the obscure and perplexing question of divine foreknowledge and predestination arose, anything was said less thoughtfully or less appropriately, it may not be defended contentiously or considered something to be supported even by synodal authority. Rather, once divine truth has been recognized and paternal authority humbly received, it should be corrected more quickly and carefully.

## CHAPTER X  
### Censure of the second chapter: Concerning the true grace of Christ and free will

The second chapter of the same definitions follows, and its words are these:

> “In the first man we lost the freedom of the will, which we receive through Christ our Lord; and we possess free will toward the good, when preceded and assisted by grace; and we possess free will toward evil, when abandoned by grace. We possess free will, moreover, because it has been liberated by grace and healed by grace from its corruption.”

### Censure

It is therefore astonishing why free will was defined in such a confused, obscure, and abbreviated manner, when, by the Lord’s gracious provision, the Church is rich in the fullest and clearest definitions of holy and orthodox Fathers concerning this matter. Nothing should have been added to or subtracted from them, because they contain most fully what is necessary for the Catholic faith; and if anything is subtracted from them, the integrity of the truth is violated. As an example, we set forth the following few statements from these paternal and ecclesiastical definitions.

1. *(From Epistle 4 of Pope Celestine.)* In Adam’s transgression [Col. 1110C] all human beings [Note: [Col. 1109D] He says that we lost this through Adam’s sin, as Pope Celestine also says in chapter 4 of the *Apologia for Prosper and Hilary*. By it, however, he understands holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of a good and upright will, which before sin were present in man through original righteousness—not indeed as properties belonging to nature, but as belonging to nature solely from the moment of its creation. In this sense the Church of Lyons calls it “natural possibility.” Or one may say that by the name “natural possibility” that original righteousness itself is signified, because it contained all the natural faculties of both soul and body within a certain proper order and established man in the condition of an integral nature, not at all wounded by sin.

Toward the end he seems to admit predestination with respect to sins. But understand this either of subsequent sins, which for the most part are punishments for preceding sins—for the Church of Lyons then asserts that they can be decreed and predestined by God not under the aspect of sin but under the aspect of punishment, since in this way they participate in some measure of equity and retributive justice—or, because God never predestines us to any sin whatsoever, whether preceding or subsequent (for it would follow that God is at least the author of subsequent sins), it is better to answer that the Church of Lyons takes “predestination” here to mean providence and wishes only to say that God exercises providence over sins. For something need only meet three conditions in order to fall under providence: first, that it was foreseen by God from all eternity; second, that it would not occur without God’s will, at least permissive; and third, that when it has occurred, God orders it to some good end.

Since, therefore, sins are foreseen and permitted by God and also ordered to a good end—namely, so that God may display his justice by punishing them, or his mercy by graciously remitting some of them—it cannot be denied that sins are subject to divine providence, or predestination. —Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 11, and *On the City of God*, book I, chapters 17, 18, and 23; Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I, chapters 14 and 16; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book VIII, chapter 5; and St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, first part, question 22, article 2, ad 2.] lost natural possibility and innocence; and no one can rise from the depth of that ruin through free will unless the grace of the merciful God raises him up.

2. *(The same, chapter 7.)* No one makes good use of free will except through Christ.

3. *(The same, chapter 8.)* All the endeavors, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him for any reason other than what he himself has given.

4. *(The same, chapter 9.)* God works in the hearts of human beings and in free will itself in such a way that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of a good will come from God; for through him we are able to do something good, and without him we can do nothing.

5. *(The same, chapter 12.)* We confess God to be the author of all the endeavors and all the virtues by which one turns toward the Lord from the beginning of faith. We do not doubt that all human merits are preceded by his grace, through whom it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good. By this help and mercy of God free will is not taken away but liberated, so that what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes healthy, and what was imprudent becomes provident. For God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wishes the merits that are his gifts to be ours; and for the things he has bestowed, he will grant eternal rewards. Indeed, he works in us so that we both will and do what he wills.

6. *(From Augustine’s Epistle 107.)* We confess that God’s grace and assistance are given even for individual acts; and that they are not given according to our merits, so that grace may truly be grace—that is, freely given—through the mercy of him who said: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy” (Rom. IX, 15). And: “I will show mercy to whom I shall be merciful” (Exod. XXXIII, 19).

7. We confess that free will exists, even though it requires divine assistance.

8. *(From the Council of Orange, canon 13.)* The freedom of the will, weakened in the first man, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism.

9. The freedom of the will is truly free when it does not serve vices and sins. Such freedom was given by God, certainly to the first man; once lost, it could not be restored except by him who had been able to give it. Hence the Truth says: “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free” (John VIII, 36).

Behold: the most holy Fathers do not deny that free will exists in human beings, but they teach that in Adam’s transgression it lost natural possibility and innocence.

They do not deny the free will of the human race, but they teach that no one makes good use of free will except through Christ. They do not deny free will, but they teach that God works in free will itself in such a way that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement [Col. 1111D] of a good will come from God.

They do not deny free will, but they teach that, through God’s help and gift, free will is not taken away but liberated: what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes healthy, and what was imprudent becomes provident.

They do not deny free will, but they teach that, having been weakened in the first man, it cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism.

They do not deny free will, but they teach that it is truly free when it does not serve vices and sins; they teach that it was given by God. They teach that once lost, it could not be restored except by him who had been able to give it. Hence the Truth says: “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free.”

Since these things are so, and free will must in no way be denied to exist in all human beings, we must not excuse the great multitude of unbelievers who existed from the beginning of the world until Christ’s coming, and who still exist and will exist until the consummation of the world, by claiming that they did not or do not possess the freedom of the will that they lost in Adam—and therefore that they are neither justly blamed for the evils they commit nor justly condemned for those evils at the divine judgment.

Against this error and vain excuse, blessed Augustine, defending the truth of the faith, says:

> “First, the Lord Jesus, as it is written in the Gospel of the apostle John, did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him (John III, 17). Later, however, as the apostle Paul writes, ‘God will judge the world when he comes’ (Rom. III, 6), just as the whole Church confesses in the Creed: ‘To judge the living and the dead.’ If, therefore, there is no grace of God, how does he save the world? And if there is no free will, how does he judge the world?”

Since, therefore, the whole world possesses free will, and for this reason God justly judges the world, how was it said in this new definition: “In the first man we lost the freedom of the will”? The holy Fathers say that free will was weakened in Adam’s transgression; they say that it lost natural possibility and innocence. They say that no one makes good use of it—that is, of free will—without Christ. They say that free will exists even though it requires divine assistance.

## CHAPTER XI  
### What free will can do by itself, and that free will cannot act without grace

All human beings, therefore, including those who are strangers to Christ, possess free will—but of the kind these Fathers describe: weakened in Adam’s transgression, stripped of natural possibility and innocence, and suited to no good use without Christ.

All human beings naturally possess a rational and intellectual mind by which, once they have reached the age of reason, they can distinguish and judge between good and evil, and between what is just and unjust. They also naturally possess an implanted freedom of the will, so that by this same will they can desire evils and can also desire certain goods—namely, those belonging through human affection to human society and human respectability.

These same goods, through human affection, are either desired because of certain temporal advantages or because of the mere respectability of life itself. Human nature can sometimes also perform these human goods, which it can desire through human affection. When they are desired for the sake of temporal goods, they are undoubtedly desires of cupidity; when they are desired solely for the respectability of life, they are undoubtedly inflated and self-exalting. Nevertheless, human nature can distinguish them, can desire them, and can possess them insofar as it is assisted by its natural good and insofar as, by God’s ordering, human nature is permitted to do so.

Such goods are also commonly seen in other human beings, [Col. 1113A] and history especially commends and praises them remarkably in many pagan philosophers and in great men who distinguished themselves in public life.

Concerning this human life, lived according to human affection and custom, and regarded as good and praiseworthy, blessed Augustine speaks plainly in his treatises on the Gospel according to John, saying (treatise 40):

> “For there are many who, according to a certain custom of this present life, are called good men, good husbands, good women, innocent, and as though observing the things commanded in the law: showing honor to their parents, not committing adultery, not perpetrating murder, not stealing, not bearing false witness against anyone, and observing, as it were, the other things commanded in the law; yet they are not Christians. What, then, do they know about the end to which all these things they do should be referred? They do them in vain. Let the pagans say: ‘We live well.’ If they do not enter through the door, what benefit is there in that of which they boast? Living well ought to benefit each person for this purpose: that he may be granted everlasting life. For if he is not granted everlasting life, what benefit is there in living well? Nor should those be called people who live well if, through blindness, they do not know the end of living well, or, through self-inflation, despise it.

> “No one has true and certain hope of living forever unless he acknowledges Life, which is Christ, and enters through the door into the sheepfold. There were certain philosophers who treated many subtle matters concerning virtues and vices, dividing and defining them, and who even dared to say to human beings: ‘Follow us; hold to our school if you wish to live happily.’ But they had not entered through the door; they wished to destroy, and so forth.”

In such goods, therefore, the freedom of the human will both exists and excels, insofar as, as has been said, it is assisted by natural good. But for the will itself to love, understand, receive, exercise, and hold steadfastly to divine goods through divine affection—not for the sake of any temporal advantages but for eternal rewards, and not for the mere respectability of the present life but solely for the blessedness of eternal life—human free will is wholly unable to desire, recognize, receive, or possess these things unless it is stirred, enlightened, and assisted by the grace of divine inspiration, and, as it were, raised from the dead to life.

For that human life which is lived through human affection may indeed appear to human beings to be life, but to God it is dead. In this way both the good of free will in human beings is recognized and the absolute necessity of God’s grace is made clear. Through this grace, human nature—which was rightly weakened by the ancient transgression, regenerated and renewed through faith in Christ, and restored to the honor of its original beginning—receives the possibility and innocence that it lost in Adam, and through Christ begins to make good use of free will.

Thus, by his grace, there can be in it holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of a good will; and the freedom of the human will becomes not something taken away but something liberated: what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes healthy, and what was imprudent becomes provident.

The more it has ceased to serve vices and sins, the freer it becomes in us through Christ. It will then be truly and fully free when, having been perfectly liberated in the blessedness of eternal life, it serves no vices or sins. Thus the Lord’s gracious promise—“If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free” (John VIII, 36)—begins here in the renewal of the faithful and will be perfected there in the incorruption of those who reign.

If, therefore, the statement in this definition—“In the first man we lost the freedom of the will”—was made as though, after that man’s transgression, no free will at all remained in human beings, it is evidently not consonant with the truth. For if the human race has no free will, how will “God judge the world?” (Rom. III).

But if it was said because we deservedly lost the natural possibility and power of free will, such as it was created in that first man, then we must take great care lest what is added concerning the lost freedom of that same will—“which we receive through Christ our Lord”—be understood as though, once we have been regenerated in Christ, we receive such a condition and power of free will that in the present life we can become what that man was before sin: so that, just as he lived in paradise without any sin, the faithful regenerated in Christ might likewise live in the world without sin.

This plainly does not belong to the condition of the present life but to the blessedness of eternal life. For in this life, “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I, 8). And as another Scripture says: “There is no righteous person upon earth who does good and does not sin” (Ecclus. VII, 2). Hence the Psalmist says to the Lord: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII, 2). And every day in the Lord’s Prayer we are commanded to say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12).

We must therefore beware, as we have already said, lest under such a preaching of Christ’s grace—by which we are said already to have received the freedom of the will that we lost in Adam—the impiety of Pelagian error creep in, so that, as he asserted, human beings are believed to be able, by the sole power of free will, to exist without sin, especially since in the first chapter of these definitions free will is defined as existing in that first man while the grace of God is entirely omitted.

If the statement was simply made so that, because of the beginning of grace which we receive in regeneration, we might seem already to have received the freedom of the will that we are said to have lost in Adam, while its fullness and perfection are believed to be awaited faithfully in the future life, why was it necessary to obscure the clearest truth with such ambiguity and confusion of words? The definitions of the aforesaid Fathers could have supplied one or several chapters through which both the freedom of the will and the grace of God would have been commended more fully and clearly.

## CHAPTER XII  
### Also concerning the second chapter: Grace is necessary for faith and other good acts

How great, then, is the absurdity in what follows! After it has been said, “In the first man we lost the freedom of the will, which we receive through Christ our Lord,” the statement immediately adds: “And we possess free will toward the good, when preceded and assisted by grace; and we possess free will toward evil, when abandoned by grace.”

This is as though, after we have been regenerated through the grace of Christ the Lord, we then began to possess not only free will toward the good but also free will toward evil—as though, when we are preceded and assisted by grace, we possess free will toward the good, and, when we are abandoned by that same grace, we possess free will toward evil.

What reason or logical sequence can be found here? Before that regeneration, did we have no free will at all, either toward good or toward evil? Did the grace of that regeneration act in us so that from then on we received free will toward evil just as we received it toward good?

And how can this statement in the same definition be understood: “Free will toward the good, when preceded and assisted by grace, and free will toward evil, when abandoned by grace”? If, when we were regenerated in baptism, we received in Christ the freedom of the will lost in Adam, did God’s grace then merely precede and assist us? Or does that same grace, just as it once assisted us so that we might become free toward the good, once abandon us so that we might become free toward evil?

What kind of preaching of grace is this—so obscure, ambiguous, and almost nonexistent? Would it not have been better to adopt the statements of the aforesaid Fathers, who define this matter most fully and clearly, or to construct the definition from their words? Then it could have been plainly stated how this grace of God precedes and assists us: whether such a great gift is granted to us once in baptism, sufficient for the whole period of our lives, or whether it must be sought and received daily; and whether we need it for certain good things or for all good things.

Certainly none of this appears in the definition. It would therefore have been better to remain silent than to speak so ineptly and uselessly about such a great matter.

For we need the grace of God not only for a good work, as this chapter defines, but also for the very beginning of faith, without which we cannot approach the sacrament of regeneration. As the Apostle says of himself: “I obtained mercy so that I might be faithful” (1 Cor. VII, 25). And he says to the faithful: “For it has been granted to you for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him” (Phil. I, 29), and so forth. Elsewhere he says: “Looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith” (Heb. XII, 2).

We need the grace of God in the very laver of regeneration, because without it we can neither obtain forgiveness of sins nor become children of God. The same Apostle says: “Not from works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the laver of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (Tit. III, 3).

We need the grace of God for all good things, each day and in every detail. The Psalmist says: “On whatever day I call upon you, hear me” (Ps. CI, 3). And again: “On whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me” (ibid.). Our Lord has deigned to promise this daily and continual grace to his Church, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

We need it to awaken good will in us, as the Apostle says: “Thanks be to God, who gave the same earnest concern in the heart of Titus” (2 Cor. VIII, 16). Blessed David also prayed for the people whom he saw offering gifts to God devoutly and eagerly, asking that God preserve in them the same good will that he had given them:

> “Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, preserve forever this intention of their heart, and may this mind always remain in the worship of you” (1 Chron. XXIX, 18).

We need the grace of God to speak good and salutary words, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 20). He also promises elsewhere: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX, 11).

We need the grace of God for every path of good works. The apostle Paul says that he desires, when he writes:

> “For even we who are in this tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed upon, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Cor. V, 4).

[Here very much is missing—namely, a large part of the censure of this second chapter and the greater part of the censure of the third chapter that follows.]

## CONCERNING THE THIRD CHAPTER

> “Almighty God wills all human beings without exception to be saved, although not all are saved. That some are saved is the gift of the one who saves; that some perish is the merit of those who perish.”

### Conclusion of the censure

[lacuna] Since, therefore, two opinions concerning this matter had been proposed and explained in the aforesaid little book *(On Three Epistles)*, it was immediately and very usefully added:

> “Whichever position one accepts, it is not heretical unless contention makes it heretical.”

Blessed Pope Celestine also set down a similar judgment in his Decrees concerning certain more profound questions. He says of them, in his letter to the bishops of Gaul:

> “Just as we do not dare to despise these matters, so we are not obliged to assert them.”

Let there therefore be among us, concerning this matter also, such pious caution and moderation that honor is preserved for the holy Fathers, and that we do not judge anyone to be a heretic, whatever position he accepts among the views they have expressed concerning this question. Rather, let us avoid the evil of contention, by which even peaceful and ecclesiastical opinions can be made heretical by anyone who chooses to be contentious.

Accordingly, in matters of this kind let us restrain ourselves with salutary moderation, so that we neither dare to despise nor try to affirm as though it were necessary, always mindful of the apostolic statement:

> “If anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor the Church of God” (1 Cor. XI, 16).

Let us therefore read peacefully and understand, insofar as the Lord grants it, the doctrines of ecclesiastical men; and let us not quarrel on behalf of one teacher against another, since they themselves are at peace with one another. “Let each one abound in his own understanding” (Rom. XIV, 5): one in this way, another in that, faithfully and humbly awaiting what the Apostle promises:

> “And if you think otherwise about anything, God will reveal this also to you” (Phil. III, 15).

For one who does not calmly and peacefully moderate what he believes, but is immediately ready for contentions, dissensions, and scandals, has certainly a heretical disposition, even if he does not hold a heretical opinion.

If those good men who established this new definition had wished to preserve this pious moderation, they would have passed over the matter in silence more appropriately and allowed each person to form his judgment concerning it according to his faith and according to the authority to which he thought he ought to give greater assent. Then, once their long and destructive quarrel had ended, the peace and unity of Christ’s Church could have been restored.

For suppose someone should think and say—as it was also said in ancient times, and as the meaning is found to be—that the Apostle did not say universally and generally, as these men have added, “without exception, who wills all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. II, 4). Rather, he referred specifically to those whom he had mentioned above: “for all human beings, for kings, and for all who are in high positions” (ibid., 2), intending by the word “all” to mean every kind of human being—people of every nation, sex, condition, order, and rank.

What is inconsistent or contrary to the truth in this interpretation? Likewise, another person may say and believe—as some of the greater authorities have also said, and as the meaning is found to be—that after the Apostle had commanded prayers to be offered “for all human beings, for kings, and for those in high positions,” he then added generally, concerning the entire human race: “who wills all human beings to be saved.”

What evil or danger is there even in this interpretation? For the person who holds it does not suppose that anyone resists or opposes the will of God by which he “wills all human beings to be saved,” so that God is unable to accomplish what he wills. Both interpretations—that of this person and that of the other, although they understand the matter differently—agree faithfully and harmoniously with one another.

Whatever the Apostle meant when he said of God, “who wills all human beings to be saved,” nevertheless no human being is saved except by God’s gratuitous mercy, and no one is permitted to perish except by his just judgment.

Certainly this is clear in the present question: even if God wills all human beings to be saved generally and without distinction, nevertheless, in the hearts of some, through the kindness of his mercy, he himself works this same good will of his, so that they too may will to be saved and may be saved. To such people the Apostle says:

> “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good will” (Phil. II, 12–13).

But in the hearts of others, through the severity of his just and hidden judgment, he does not work this saving will; rather, he abandons them to their own will, so that, because they were unwilling to believe, they may be condemned by a just punishment.

This can indeed be said concerning those who heard the word of the Gospel but, through the hardness of their unbelief, refused to receive it.

What, then, is to be said about the great multitude of the ungodly who existed from the beginning of the world until Christ’s coming? And even now it must not be denied that there are such people in the remotest regions of the earth, to whom no preacher has ever come and who have never heard a word of faith—people who certainly could in no way “believe in him whom they have not heard, nor hear without a preacher” (Rom. 10:14–15), much less receive a preacher, since none was sent to them. Will such people therefore be condemned because they did not believe what they could never have heard? Yet they will certainly be condemned for their other sins, and chiefly for that first and original sin “in which all sinned” (Rom. 5:12), since it was not written without reason: “Pour out your wrath upon the nations that have not known you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name” (Ps. 78:6). And the Apostle says: “Inflicting vengeance in flaming fire on those who do not know [Col. 1118C] the Lord” (2 Thess. 1:8).

If someone asks what the will of God—“who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth”—has accomplished in such people, what answer will be given? Will not a cautious and pious person prefer to remain silent, or at least cry out with the Prophet and the Apostle: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 36:6); and, “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). Let this, then, be the end of this chapter.

## CHAPTER XIII

The fourth definition follows, and it is the last. It runs as follows:

[Col. 1118D] “Christ Jesus our Lord, just as there is no human being, nor has there been nor will there be one, whose nature was not assumed in him, so there is no human being, nor has there been nor will there be one, for whom he did not suffer, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion. That not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion does not pertain to the greatness and abundance of the price, but to unbelievers and to those who do not believe with that faith ‘which works through love’ (Gal. 5:6)”—“it pertains to the portion, because the cup of human salvation, which was prepared from our weakness and divine power, does indeed possess in itself the capacity to benefit everyone; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal.”

[Col. 1119A] **CENSURE. Christ was not incarnated by necessity.**

And in this new and unusual definition three questions are proposed to us:

First, what is said: “There is no human being, nor has there been nor will there be one, whose nature was not assumed in Christ.”

Second, what is affirmed: “There is no human being, nor has there been nor will there be one, for whom Christ did not suffer, although not all are redeemed by the mystery of his Passion.”

Third, what is added: that not only unbelievers, but not even the faithful themselves, are redeemed by the mystery of that same Passion—except those alone who possess the faith “that works through love.”

[Col. 1119B] Regarding the first question, then, this seems to us what must be believed and held: that Christ’s assumption of human nature did not occur by necessity of origin, but by the power, grace, mercy, and condescension of the one who assumed it. For other human beings are born not by their own will and power, but by God’s judgment and arrangement, through the original necessity and condition of birth. “The Lord Jesus Christ, however, who for us human beings and for our salvation descended from heaven and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary,” was not made man by the necessity and condition of human origin, but by the power and mercy of his will.

Thus the blessed evangelist Matthew, when he described the sequence of Christ’s genealogy “from Abraham to David, and from David to the deportation to Babylon, and from the deportation to Babylon to his birth” (Matt. 1), arranged all the other generations according to the natural course and condition of human begetting and propagation, saying: “Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob, Jacob begot Judah and his brothers,” and so forth in the same manner. But when he came to Christ’s one and unique birth, he wonderfully distinguished it from all the others and said: “Now the generation of Christ was thus”—that is, not like the preceding generations, proceeding according to the natural course and condition and succeeding one another, but surpassing them in unique power, virtue, and grace.

Immediately he added the particular manner in which this generation occurred, saying: “When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit.” Later the angel commends this to Joseph in his speech, saying: “For that which is born in her is from the Holy Spirit.” And, adding prophetic testimony to show him the power and virtue of the one who was being born—namely, that the true Emmanuel, God in man, was coming—he said: “Now this took place so that what had been spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: ‘Behold, a virgin shall have a child in her womb and shall bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,’ which is interpreted, ‘God with us’” (Isa. 7:14).

Because, therefore, this generation of Christ as man, so divine and so unique, occurred not through any natural necessity [Col. 1120A] but solely through his power, grace, and mercy, his flesh truly descended through all those generations, and he was truly born from them and made true man, in such a way that he assumed from them what pleased him—for the purposes of mercy, healing, and redemption—and rejected what did not please him.

Just as by an admirable power he assumed the truth of human nature but did not assume the defect of that nature, so that by assuming it he might save it and, by not assuming the defect, condemn it; so, in the ineffable mystery of his Incarnation, he mercifully assumed his elect, for whose redemption, justification, and salvation he had come. But those whom he judged unworthy of that mercy and redemption he left excluded from that wondrous assumption.

Finally, in those generations from which his flesh arose, Abraham and David are included; and Ahaz and Manasseh are likewise counted among them. Yet by a special grace he is called “the seed of Abraham,” when the Lord promised him: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Likewise he is called “the seed of David,” as the Apostle says: “Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3). He is also called “the son of David and the son of Abraham,” as the Evangelist testifies: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.” But he is nowhere read to be the son of any of the ungodly who were lost in their ungodliness, although his flesh was truly assumed not only from the righteous but also from sinners. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners” (1 Tim. 1:15).

[Col. 1120C] It is therefore plainly established that this assumption was redemption, so that those who were assumed were also redeemed, and those who were redeemed were themselves assumed. Hence the faithful are in Christ, and Christ is in them. Unbelievers are not in Christ, nor is Christ in them.

To the faithful alone he says—those whom he united to himself through the sacrament of true Incarnation and the grace of redemption: “Abide in me, and I in you. Just as a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me. I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit” (John 15:4–5). Likewise, speaking only of the faithful, he says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:52).

The Apostle also, speaking of Christ and the faithful, of the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified, and of the mystery of Christ’s true Incarnation—which he truly drew from Adam and through which he graciously united himself naturally to believers—says: “For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one” (Heb. 2:11). For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers” (Ps. 22:22), and so forth.

Those whom he assumed, therefore, he also sanctified; those he also made his “brothers,” “so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. 8:29).

For if the matter is carefully considered, we do not know whether it can appropriately be said of just any human being that, by being born, he assumed the nature of all human beings. For when he was born, he certainly assumed the nature of his parents from whom he was begotten. He assumed the nature of his ancestors, from whose stock he was propagated. He assumed the nature of the first human being, from whom the origin of the entire human race proceeded.

Accordingly, in this sense it may in some way be said that every human being who is born has assumed the nature of all human beings, because he derives his origin from the one from whom the nature of all began. From that first man, Adam, our Lord Jesus Christ also truly drew the substance of his flesh. Hence the Apostle calls him “the second Adam.” He also continually commends himself as “the son of Adam,” that is, “the son of man” (1 Cor. 15:45, 47). And the evangelist Luke, ascending through seventy-seven generations from Christ himself to Adam, faithfully demonstrates his true Incarnation from Adam.

Because, then, that assumption of human nature in Christ was a mystery of redemption and piety, on the most sacred day of his birth from the Virgin, amid the mysteries of the sacred offering, the Church prays, saying: “Granting your grace through these sacred exchanges, may we be found in the likeness of the one in whom our substance is with you.”

On the preceding day, when the sacred vigil is celebrated, the prayer begins: “O God, who gladden us by the annual expectation of our redemption.”

Likewise, on the very day of the Lord’s Nativity: “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that the new birth in the flesh of your Only-Begotten Son may free us, whom ancient bondage holds under the yoke of sin.”

And over the offering: “Sanctify, Lord, the gifts offered by the new birth of your Only-Begotten Son, and cleanse us from the stains of our sins.”

And in the conclusion of the Masses: “May the ever-new mystery of this birth sacrament renew us, whose singular birth drove away the oldness of humanity.”

The blessed Gregory piously commends this grace of the Lord’s Incarnation—which is truly the mystery of our redemption—when, in one place in his exposition of the Book of Job, he says:

[The Lord intercedes for us, not by his voice but by his mercy, because by assuming what he did not wish to be condemned in the elect, he preserved it.]

Likewise, the blessed Hilary, explaining the Lord’s words, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57), carefully commends the same point, saying:

[For no one will be in him unless he himself is in that person; only the one who has taken his flesh into himself has the flesh of him who has taken his own flesh.]

The blessed Leo also wonderfully explains and commends this mystery, saying:

[Thus, when the Lord Jesus Christ was born true man, without ever ceasing to be true God, he established in himself the beginning of the new creation; and in the form of his birth he gave the human race a special beginning. He so joined himself to us, and us to himself, that God’s descent to the human became humanity’s elevation to the divine.]

And elsewhere:

[For the earth of human flesh, which had been cursed in the first transgressor, in this one birth of the blessed Virgin produced a blessed shoot, separated from the defect of its stock; and we obtain its special origin in regeneration. “And for every” human being who is reborn, “the water of baptism is like a virginal womb,” since the same Holy Spirit fills the font who also filled the Virgin, so that the sacred conception removed sin there, while here the mystical washing takes it away.]

Again, in another place:

[Today’s feast renews for us the sacred beginnings of Jesus’ birth from the Virgin Mary; and while we worship the birth of our Savior, we discover that we are celebrating our own beginning. For Christ’s generation is the origin of the Christian people, and the birth of the Head is the birth of the body. Although each of the called has his own order, all the children of the Church, distinguished by the succession of time, nevertheless constitute one whole of the faithful, born from the font of baptism: crucified with Christ in his Passion, raised with him in his Resurrection, and placed with him at the Father’s right hand in his Ascension. For we were born together with him in this birth.

Whatever among human beings, in whatever part of the world, is regenerated in Christ passes into the new human being by rebirth, cutting through the path of the old original condition. It is no longer held in the lineage of a carnal father, but in the offspring of the Savior.

For this reason he became the son of man, so that we might be sons of God. Thus, having been assumed by Christ and receiving Christ, a person is not the same after the washing as before baptism, but the body of the regenerated becomes the body of the crucified. “This is the transformation of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 77:11).]

And elsewhere:

[For participation in the body and blood of Christ does nothing other than cause us to pass into that which we receive, so that we may bear him wholly, both in spirit and in flesh, in whom we have died together, been buried together, and been raised together.]

Again, elsewhere:

[For our Redeemer did and suffered nothing that was not for our salvation, so that the power present in the Head might also be present in the body. For first, by the very assumption of our substance into divinity—by which “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14)—whom among human beings did he leave excluded from the participation of his mercy, except the unbeliever? And who does not share a common nature with Christ if he receives the one who assumes him and has been regenerated by the Spirit by which Christ is the firstborn?]

Let us hear these words of the most faithful and blessed Fathers, and, with the Lord’s help, understand and hold them carefully, acknowledging truly that Christ’s assumption of human nature left unbelievers excluded from this mercy [Col. 1122D] and granted a common nature with Christ only to those who receive the one who assumes them and are regenerated by the Spirit by which he was begotten.

Let this superfluity therefore cease—the claim and definition “that there has never been, is not, and never will be any human being whose nature he did not assume.” For, as the Apostle teaches, “great is the mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit,” and so forth, up to “was taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16). This has been said concerning the first question.

## CHAPTER XIV

Whether Christ suffered for all who died before his coming

Regarding the second question, which those chapters defined as follows [Col. 1123A]: “There has never been, is not, and never will be any human being for whom Christ did not suffer,” what other answer can we give except first to question carefully those who defined this and admonish them to consider vigilantly and faithfully lest, through insufficient reflection on what ought to have been said, they have spoken and written such things against their own faith and conscience?

To say nothing of those who now exist or who will exist until the end of the age—including, certainly, the Antichrist—consider the innumerable multitude of the ungodly who existed from the beginning of the world until Christ’s coming and died in their ungodliness; they have been condemned to eternal punishments. We do not think that those who made this claim themselves believe that the Lord should be held to have suffered for such people, who died in their ungodliness and had already been condemned by eternal judgment.

For if it is believed that he suffered for them, why should it not likewise be believed that he suffered for the devil and his angels?
