For it is written concerning those rebellious and unclean spirits: “God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of darkness, to be kept for judgment and punishment” (2 Pet. 2:4). Therefore they are most rightly believed to have been predestined by God’s irrevocable judgment to punishment and everlasting destruction. In the same way, those ungodly people who died in their ungodliness had already been condemned by the same irrevocable divine judgment to everlasting punishments.

Just as, therefore, the Lord Jesus Christ must in no way be said to have suffered for those ungodly and condemned angels, so it must altogether be rejected that he suffered for those ungodly and condemned human beings [Col. 1123C]. For this is profoundly contrary to divine truth and profoundly opposed to the Catholic faith, which unhesitatingly believes and teaches that our Lord bestowed the benefit of his Passion, death, and descent into hell only on those who had already died and who, although in the underworld, had been placed in regions of tranquility and light. These were the people who had lived in faith in his future coming and redemption and who, having passed there through death, awaited with devout longing the time when he would fulfill and accomplish that redemption through his Passion and descent to them.

Concerning such people, the blessed John the Baptist, when his own Passion and death were already near—for he too was one of them—anxiously questioned the same Lord through his disciples, saying: [Col. 1123D] “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” (Matt. 11:3).

Of such pious and blessed departed people—such as the holy patriarchs, prophets, and other ancient righteous who existed from the beginning of the world until the Lord’s coming, who believed and foretold that he would come and redeem the human race by his blood, just as the whole Church now believes and confesses that he has come—the Wisdom of God itself, who is certainly our Lord Jesus Christ, also promises in the Book of Ecclesiasticus, saying: “I will penetrate into the lower parts of the earth, and I will look upon all who sleep, and I will enlighten all who hope in God” (Ecclus. 24:45).

Likewise, elsewhere Scripture says concerning his descent into hell and the liberation of those by whom he was awaited there [Col. 1124A]: “The holy Lord of Israel remembered his dead, those long ago asleep in the dust of the earth.” And: “I shall descend to them to show them his salvation.”

Hence, through the prophecy of Hosea, he threatened death itself and hell in this way: “From the hand of death I shall free them; from death I shall redeem them. I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your sting, O hell” (Hos. 13:14).

The blessed Gregory wonderfully explains how all this is to be understood faithfully and in accordance with Catholic teaching, saying:

[What he said before his Passion, the Lord fulfilled in his Resurrection: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). For he drew all things, since he left none of his elect in hell. He certainly took away all the elect. For the Lord did not restore unbelievers, who were handed over to eternal punishments for their crimes, to pardon by rising again; rather, he snatched from the prison of hell those whom he recognized by their faith and works.

Hence he rightly says through Hosea: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your sting, O hell.” For what we kill, we act so as to make it cease to exist entirely. But from what we bite, we remove one part and leave another. Since, therefore, he utterly killed death in his elect, he became the death of death; but since he removed one part from hell and left another, he did not kill hell completely but bit it. Thus he says, “I shall be your death, O death,” as though he openly said: “In my elect I destroy you utterly”; and, “I shall be your sting, O hell,” because, after taking them away, I pierce you in part.]

This most faithful teacher proposed these things to be held and followed most faithfully according to the rule of the Catholic faith. Therefore let this new and unheard-of definition—or rather, this new and unheard-of presumption—cease: that no human being, even among the ungodly and those irrevocably condemned in hell, ever existed for whom Christ did not suffer. For, as has already been said, he endured his Passion only for those who had died and who, while living in the body, had faithfully believed that he would come and redeem the world by his Passion.

This, then, is Catholic teaching; this has been commended by the faith of the Church from the beginning; this has been confirmed by divine and paternal authority. Therefore let the deceptive and empty invention be cast far away.

Regarding the other human beings who have existed from Christ’s Passion until now, who now exist, or who will exist until the end of the age, “the Catholic faith holds,” and the truth of Sacred Scripture teaches [Col. 1124D] that our Lord and Savior truly suffered for all believers who have been regenerated through the grace of baptism from water and the Holy Spirit and incorporated into the Church.

For they could not truly have been baptized otherwise than into his death, nor truly washed from their sins except in his blood, as the blessed Apostle Paul teaches: “For all of us who have been baptized in Christ” (Rom. 6:3). And as the blessed John testifies in the Apocalypse: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1:5).

Concerning these people—that is, his faithful, baptized into his death and granted the washing away of sins in his blood—the Lord and Savior himself says: “As the Father knows me, so I know the Father; and I lay down my life for my sheep” (John 10:15).

For these he says: “And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:14).

Concerning these the Apostle says: “Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, so that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word” (Eph. 5:25–26).

And because, as the same Apostle testifies, “faith is not possessed by all,” and “not all obey the Gospel” (2 Thess. 3:2), the Lord himself says again: “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many” (Matt. 20:28).

Thus, when he handed over the sacrament of his body and blood to his disciples, he said: “Take and eat: this is my body, which will be handed over for you.” And again: “This is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26:26, 28).

The Apostle calls these “many” “all” when he says: “For there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a redemption for all” (1 Tim. 2:5).

And again he calls these “all” “many” when he says: “And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ, having been offered once, was offered to take away the sins of many” (Heb. 9:27–28), and so forth.

In accordance with this manner of expression he also says in the Epistle to the Romans: “Therefore, just as through one man’s transgression condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one man’s righteousness justification unto life came upon all human beings. For just as through one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so through one man’s obedience many will be made righteous” (Rom. 5:18–19).

It is plainly evident that those whom he called “all” and “all” in the first statement, he calls “many” and “many” in the following statement.

In the condemnation that entered the whole human race through one man, “many” are rightly understood as “all,” because no human being is free from it unless liberated by Christ’s grace. In the justification of life, however, “all” are rightly understood in such a way that these “all” are understood as “many.” For through Christ’s obedience—by which he “became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8)—not “all” indiscriminately, but “many,” are justified.

Those who come to the washing of regeneration also attain this justification through the obedience of Christ’s death and the shedding of his precious blood, because afterward they make it void in themselves through their own fault. The Apostle testifies to this, saying: “How much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded as profane the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” (Heb. 10:29).

And again: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become sharers in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and who have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance” (Heb. 6:4–6).

[Col. 1126B] Therefore, concerning all believers in Christ who have been regenerated in Christ, it is rightly and truly believed that the Lord Christ suffered for them. The entire sequence of Sacred Scripture, both Old and New Testament, plainly and undoubtedly bears witness to this, if it is carefully examined and faithfully considered.

This is also magnificently and most emphatically commended by the authority of the universal and renowned Church, handed down by the Lord himself and the Apostles. The Church offers “the offering of the body and blood of Christ”—that is, the mystery of his Passion and death—only for the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, namely, for the fellowship and unity of all the faithful, and for those faithful departed alone “who went before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace.”

Accordingly, in the very celebration of the mysteries, she confidently and truly supplicates God for the faithful, saying: “Look, Lord, upon this family of yours, for whom our Lord Jesus Christ did not hesitate to be delivered into the hands of the wicked and to undergo the torment of the cross.”

She guards the rite of the Lord’s offering with such great devotion and religious attentiveness that, when these mysteries are offered, she permits no unbeliever whatsoever, nor even any catechumen, nor anyone who has not been regenerated by the grace of baptism, to be present—as though she were truly showing and bearing witness that the Lord was offered, suffered, and died on the altar of the cross, and that his precious blood was poured out, for those for whom that most sacred and heavenly offering is offered on the Church’s altar in the mystery of his Passion and death.

[Note: [Col. 1125D] The Church likewise affirms that the sacrifice is not to be offered for catechumens or for unbaptized infants. This seems to be supported by what Augustine says in Book I of *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 8: “Who would offer the sacrifice of Christ’s body except for those who are members of Christ?” This is cited by St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, question 79, article 7, reply to objection 2.

It is certain, however, that they are speaking only of the public and solemn offering. Privately, nothing prevents a sacrifice from being offered for them; except, however, unbaptized infants who have died. Since they belong to the class of the very wicked on account of original sin, as Augustine discusses in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 109, the sacrifice is not to be offered for them—not even secretly in the priest’s mind.

Moreover, as Suárez teaches very well in article 1 of question 83 of the third part of St. Thomas, the sacrifice cannot be offered for catechumens or for infants not yet baptized as though they would obtain some benefit from it *ex opere operato*; for the accomplished work of the sacrifice presupposes that the person has received baptism, which is the gateway to all the sacraments and to the fruits of the sacrifice itself.

Nevertheless, it may be offered for them by way of intercession, because through it we can ask God that they may come to baptism, just as we may ask for sinners and unbelievers that they may turn away from sin and unbelief.]

Hence the Church has detested as heretics certain people who said that this most sacred offering ought to be made either for catechumens or for innocent little children, whether living or dead.

As the blessed Augustine most clearly demonstrates in the book he wrote to Vincent Victor (*On the Origin of the Soul*, Book III, chapter 12), saying:

[Do not believe, say, or teach “that the sacrifice of Christians ought to be offered for those who have died without baptism,” if you wish to be Catholic. For neither does what you cited from the books of the Maccabees (2 Macc. 12)—the Jewish sacrifice for those who had died uncircumcised—show that such a sacrifice was offered.

In expressing this opinion of yours, so novel and advanced against the authority and discipline of the entire Church, you also used an exceedingly presumptuous expression, saying: “Therefore I judge that continual offerings and the sacrifices of holy priests ought constantly to be offered for them.”]

In the book he wrote to the presbyter Peter against the writings of that same Vincent Victor, he rebuked him as follows (*On the Origin of the Soul*, Book II, chapter 15):

[He attributes such great salvation and blessedness to unbaptized infants as not even the Pelagian heresy could.]

And shortly afterward, concerning those same unbaptized infants:

[“Let no one,” he says, “either has offered or will offer a sacrifice for them”—although this man judged that it ought to be offered even for the unbaptized.]

And shortly afterward, concerning Vincent himself:

[“Either he will remain altogether in error,” he says, “or he will judge that the body of Christ is to be offered in the Church of Christ even for all the infants who die throughout the whole world without Christ’s baptism, even though their names are not mentioned because they are unknown, despite the fact that they have not been incorporated into the body of Christ.”]

After this, addressing the aforementioned presbyter Peter, he adds (*ibid.*, chapter 16):

[Far be it from you, brother, that these things should please you. Far be it from you to rejoice either that you have learned such things or to presume to teach them.]

From these words of the holy teacher we are most clearly taught that Christ’s body ought to be offered only for those who are regenerated by Christ’s baptism and incorporated into the Church, which is Christ’s body. Whoever says that the sacrifice ought to be offered for those who have not been regenerated and have not become Christ’s body judges them to be Christ’s body, although they have never been incorporated among Christ’s members.

Therefore the holy mother Church piously observes that she does not offer Christ’s sacrifice for catechumens—whether children or adults—until they have been regenerated in Christ. Then, at the moment of their regeneration, she begins for the first time to commemorate them specifically in the Lord’s offering, saying:

“Therefore, Lord, we ask that you graciously receive this offering of our service, and also of your whole family, which we offer to you for those whom you have deigned to regenerate from water and the Holy Spirit,” and so forth.

For the grace of Christ’s redemption is in no way received before baptism, nor can it in any way be given to those who depart from the body without baptism. The whole Church observes this.

The blessed Gregory, responding to Augustine’s questions, briefly makes the point, saying (*Registrum*, Book XII):

[The grace of the holy mystery must be provided with great discernment to those who are living and able to distinguish; likewise, it must be offered without delay to those whose death is imminent, lest, while time is still being sought for administering the mystery of redemption, a brief intervening delay should make it impossible to find anyone who can be redeemed.]

For all those, however, who were regenerated from water and the Spirit and thereby incorporated into the Church, and who received death piously, the universal Church solemnly and generally observes—and must entirely continue to observe—that amid the mysteries of that most sacred immolation they be faithfully commemorated in their proper place and order, either by name or without names being spoken.

For they truly belong to the fullness and unity of the Church, and cannot be separated from it even by death. Concerning those who died in the Lord and live with the Lord, the blessed John writes in the Apocalypse:

“Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From now on, says the Spirit, let them rest from their labors, for their works follow them” (Rev. 14:13).

And the blessed Apostle Paul, wishing the living to be understood under the name “those who are awake” and the faithful departed under the name “those who sleep,” says to the Thessalonians:

“God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus, who died for us, so that whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him” (1 Thess. 5:9–10).

And again elsewhere:

“For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. If we live, we live for the Lord; if we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s. For to this end Christ died and rose again, so that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living” (Rom. 14:7–9).

Hence, in that blessed action of the mystery, on the authority certainly of God and through apostolic tradition and the holy Fathers, a prayer for the faithful departed has been specially established. It runs as follows:

“Remember also, Lord, your servants and handmaids who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace,” and so forth.

The blessed Father Augustine most diligently commends that all this has been observed uniformly and lawfully in the Church from the beginning, and by the Church, in his book *On Care for the Dead*, saying:

[The supplications for the spirits of the dead must not be omitted. The Church has received them to be made for all who have died within the Christian and Catholic fellowship, even when their names are not spoken, under a general commemoration, so that those whose parents, children, or any relatives or friends are absent to perform these things for them may have them offered by their one common pious mother.]

And afterward:

[“Since this is so,” he says, “let us not think that anything reaches the dead for whom we care except what we solemnly supplicate on their behalf through the sacrifice of the altar, prayers, or almsgiving. These things do not benefit all for whom they are performed, but only those for whom, while they lived, it was obtained that they might benefit.

But because we do not distinguish who they are, we ought to do these things for all the regenerated, so that none of those to whom these benefits can and ought to come may be omitted. For it is better that these things should abound for those whom they neither harm nor benefit than that they should be lacking to those whom they benefit.]

From all these points, then, carefully and faithfully considered, it is most certainly and clearly demonstrated that Christ’s Passion was accomplished for all the faithful of Christ—those who have been, who are, and who will be. Christ’s sacrifice is offered for Christ’s faithful; Christ’s body is sacrificed for Christ’s body. Concerning those who are still held in unbelief and impiety, it is clear from this rule of faith that whoever among them is converted to the faith by God’s grace and regenerated in Christ must also be confessed to be among those for whom was done what is established to have been done for all the faithful. But as for the rest, who, persevering in their unbelief and impiety, are to perish: if the good men who have defined such things can demonstrate to us by the most certain and clearest testimonies from the authority of Holy Scripture that the Lord also suffered for such people, it is altogether fitting that we too should believe it. But if they cannot, let them cease contending for what they do not read. Let them be ashamed to define what they do not know. Let them fear to lay down what they find has hitherto been laid down by no council of holy Fathers, no pontiff of the apostolic see, and no decree of ecclesiastical doctrine. And even if they find something written or said by holy and venerable doctors of the Church from which an occasion for such an opinion may seem to be drawn, while preserving the reverence due to them, let them rather restrain themselves and humbly submit themselves to divine authority; and let them humbly reserve a matter so obscure and so unprecedented for the divine majesty. For that sacred feast of the “Paschal Lamb” also mystically commends this to us when it says: “If anything remains over, you shall burn it with fire” (Exod. 12:10), as blessed Gregory explains, saying:

> We burn with fire what remains of the lamb when we humbly reserve to the power of the Holy Spirit what we cannot understand or penetrate concerning the mystery of his Incarnation, so that no one may boldly dare either to despise or to pronounce upon what he understands, but may hand it over to the fire when he reserves it for the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter XV. On the Third Question

[Col. 1129D]

Now, regarding the third question, in which it has been defined that “just as unbelievers are redeemed by the mystery of Christ’s blood, so neither are the faithful redeemed who have not had that faith ‘which works through love’ (Gal. 5:6),” what need is there to say anything? For it is most manifestly shown by the things already said above both that there is no redemption in Christ for any unbelievers, and that all faithful people who faithfully come to faith and to the grace of regeneration receive true redemption there where they receive true regeneration. For they cannot truly be regenerated unless it is established that they are truly redeemed both from the power of the devil and from slavery to sin. Nor can they truly be redeemed unless, cleansed by the washing of forgiveness, they are freed both from the guilt of sin and from the dominion of the ruler of the world.

The most absurd point in this definition, however, is that “the Lord Jesus Christ is said to have suffered even for the impious who perish in their impiety,” and that “each faithful person, faithfully regenerated by his baptism through the mystery of Christ’s Passion, is affirmed not to have been redeemed.”

Nor should anyone think that the following can be brought forward against this evangelical and apostolic truth: among the other curses of the Jewish people, Deuteronomy contains these words spoken to that same unbelieving people: “And your life shall hang before your eyes, and you shall not believe in your life” (Deut. 28:66). Nor should anyone appeal to the passage in Isaiah concerning that same unbelieving people, customarily understood as spoken in the person of the Lord Jesus Christ concerning his Passion and Cross: “I have stretched out my hands all day long to a people that does not believe and contradicts me, who walks in a way that is not good, following its own thoughts” (Isa. 65:2).

Someone might wish to understand the words spoken to that “unbelieving people”—“And your life shall hang before your eyes, and you shall not believe in your life”—as though the Lord Jesus Christ, who hung upon the Cross before the eyes of that “unbelieving and faithless people” remaining in its unbelief and faithlessness, were called their life, although he certainly did not give them life; and as though they were said not to believe in their life, as if the Lord could be called the life even of those who do not believe and are never given life through faith in him.

Likewise, someone might try to understand the testimony from Isaiah by saying that the Lord therefore declared, “I have stretched out my hands all day long to a people that does not believe and contradicts me,” as though he endured the Passion of the Cross on behalf of that same people, which persisted in unbelief and contradiction, and as though this were the reason for it. Thus it might appear that Scripture says that the Lord suffered even for the impious who perish in their impiety. Yet the divine Scriptures can in no way contradict one another. Rather, what is more plainly declared in their clearer passages is also concealed in their more obscure ones, so that the obscure passages are illuminated by what is clear in them—not so that what is clear is obscured by what is obscure.

Therefore, in accordance with the manifest evangelical and apostolic truth concerning Christ’s Passion and redemption that we demonstrated above, let us also faithfully understand the words spoken among the other curses against that unbelieving people in Deuteronomy: “And your life shall hang before your eyes, and you shall not believe in your life.” Let us recognize that the greatest curse upon that people was this: because they deserved it through their wickedness, they were blinded and could not recognize the Lord Christ, who was coming to them amid such great signs and miracles. Their great blindness had already been prophesied: “Blind the heart of this people, and weigh down its ears, and close its eyes” (Isa. 6:10), and so forth.

By the just judgment of God, this blindness remained in them until they seized the Lord, condemned him, and crucified him after he had been sentenced to death. But afterward, when he had risen and ascended into heaven, and the Holy Spirit had been sent, while the apostles preached through the inspiration of divine grace, they were suddenly pierced by the apostles’ preaching and said: “Brothers, what shall we do?” (Acts 2:37). Immediately, having accepted the counsel of salvation, they were baptized and reconciled to the life which they had been unable to recognize, and had not believed in, although it had been set before their eyes on the Cross.

Thus, through blessed Moses, both things were wondrously prophesied and signified: in the Lord’s Passion they would have “life before their eyes,” yet neither believe nor recognize it. Nevertheless, this life would also be the life of those very unbelieving and blinded people, because afterward it gave them life through their faith, as it is written: “But the righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4; Rom. 1:17).

Thus, in his Passion, the Lord was both their life and was not their life. He was their life because he was going to give them life; he was not their life because he had not yet given them life when, being dead, they crucified Life. Therefore, so that this blindness might be removed from them and the illumination of faith granted to them, during the very Passion of the Cross he prayed to the Father, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Similarly, the passage understood as spoken in the person of the Lord himself in Isaiah—“I have stretched out my hands all day long to a people that does not believe and contradicts me”—must be understood in the same sense: he endured and suffered that people, which was always unbelieving and contradictory toward him, so that it cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him!” And when Pilate said, “Shall I crucify your king?” they answered, “We have no king except Caesar” (John 19:15).

Until, lifted up on the Cross, he stretched out his hands, as though by the power of his Passion he would draw all things to himself—even that “people that does not believe and contradicts,” namely, those remnants of it who were saved through the election of grace (Rom. 11:5).

He himself had foretold that this would happen when, before his Passion, he said to them as to a “people that does not believe and contradicts”: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he” (John 8:28). By not believing and contradicting, they came to the point of lifting up the Son of Man on the wood of the Cross. Then, illuminated by the power of his Passion and the grace of his prayer, they recognized him whom they had previously crucified without recognizing him: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

Blessed martyr Cyprian carefully conveys this true and catholic understanding to us in his book *That Idols Are Not Gods*, when he says concerning those same Jews:

> Because they did not understand Christ’s first coming, which came beforehand, hidden in the Passion, they believe only in the one who will come manifestly in power. That the Jewish people could not understand this was the result of their sins. They had been punished with such blindness of wisdom and understanding that, although unworthy of life, they had life before their eyes and did not see it.

Similarly, blessed Augustine teaches in his explanations of the Gospel according to John, saying (*Tractate* 45):

> Behold, the Lord Jesus Christ came and preached. But what shall we suppose? Were those who heard him “sheep”? Judas heard him, and he was a wolf; he “followed,” but, covered in a sheep’s skin, he lay in wait for the shepherd. Yet some of those who crucified Christ did not hear him, and they were sheep. He saw them in the crowd when he said: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he” (John 8:28).
>
> How, then, is this question resolved? Those who are not sheep hear, and some who are sheep do not hear; some wolves follow the shepherd’s voice, and some sheep contradict them; finally, the sheep kill the shepherd. But when they did not hear, they were not yet sheep. The voice they heard changed them and made sheep out of wolves.

At the end, I would like to add a few words from the holy Fathers, so wonderfully and sweetly do they proclaim the mystery of Christ’s redemption: also the salvation of those righteous people who lived before Christ’s coming, and thereafter of all the faithful who are daily redeemed and saved by his grace.

Blessed Ambrose speaks of the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is “the Lamb of God, and takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), and explains how he is eaten by a fixed and predestined number sufficient for partaking of him:

> The blood of Christ is such that nothing is diminished from its grace and nothing is added to it. Whether you take a little or drink a great deal, the same perfect measure of redemption is given to everyone. The Lord’s Passover, that is, the Lamb, is likewise commanded to be eaten by the fathers according to the number of their souls—neither more nor fewer; nor is more given to some and less to others according to the number of each person’s soul, lest the stronger take more or the weaker less.
>
> Grace is divided equally among all; redemption is divided; the gift is divided. There ought not to be more, lest someone depart empty of hope and redemption. There are more when some are outside the number: “But all the saints are numbered, and even the hairs of their heads” (Matt. 10:30). “For the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19). Nor ought there to be fewer, lest anyone be too weak to receive the greatness of grace. Therefore he commanded all to bring equal devotion and faith to the Passover.

[Col. 1132D] On this matter, that is, the redemption by Christ’s blood, blessed Leo also teaches:

> The shedding of the blood of the Just One for the unjust was so powerful as a privilege and so rich as a price that, if the whole company of captives believed in their Redeemer, no one would remain held by tyrannical chains.

And again:

> Thus the Lord Jesus Christ provided for the human race by his death that he did not deny the sacrament of salvation even to his persecutors. For he had come to forgive all sins to all believers, and from this general forgiveness he did not wish to exclude even the Jewish crime.

And again:

> For what else did Christ’s Cross accomplish than that, once hostilities had been destroyed, the world might be reconciled to God, and through the sacrifice of the immaculate Lamb be brought back into true peace [lacuna].

Likewise, elsewhere:

> A singular offering was made by the Lord for the salvation of the world, and the slaughter of the true Lamb, proclaimed through so many ages, transferred the children of promise into the liberty of faith. The New Testament was also confirmed, and through Christ’s blood heirs of the eternal kingdom were inscribed. The high priest entered the Holy of Holies, and the immaculate priest entered to entreat the Lord through the veil of his flesh.

And in another passage:

> The incarnation of the Word, and Christ’s slaughter and resurrection, became the salvation of all the faithful. The blood of the one Just Man—which he gave us, and which we believe was poured out for the reconciliation of the world—brought to the fathers, who likewise believed that it would be poured out, the same gift.

Blessed Jerome, too, in his exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, speaking of those same ancient saints, says:

> None of them freed anyone from the curse except the Lord Jesus Christ alone, who by his precious blood redeemed us all—and by “us” I mean Moses and Aaron, all the prophets, and the patriarchs—from the curse of the Law. Do not think that this was spoken merely according to my opinion; Scripture bears witness, for “Christ died for all by the grace of God” (2 Cor. 5:15). If for all, then for Moses and for all the prophets as well. None of them could erase “the ancient bond written against us and fasten it to the Cross.” For “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Col. 2:14; Rom. 3:23).

The same teacher, explaining what was said through the prophet concerning the Lord—“This one will sprinkle many nations” (Isa. 52:15)—says:

> Cleansing them with his blood and consecrating them to the service of God in baptism.

Likewise, in his *Commentaries on the Gospel according to Matthew*, when explaining the words of the Lord—“Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many” (Matt. 20:18)—he says:

> He did not say, “to give his life as a redemption for all,” but “for many,” that is, for those who are willing to believe.

Blessed Augustine likewise says in his book *On Nature and Grace*:

> “The faith,” he says, “that saved the righteous of old also saves us”—that is, faith in the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5); faith in his blood, faith in his Cross, faith in his death and resurrection. “Therefore, having the same spirit of faith, we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13).

Likewise, in his treatises on the Gospel according to John (*Tractate* 48):

> “Be sheep,” he says. They are sheep by believing; they are sheep by following the shepherd; they are sheep by not despising the Redeemer; they are sheep by entering through the door; they are sheep by going out and finding pasture. How, then, did he say to these people, “You are not of my sheep” (John 10:26)? Because he saw that they were predestined to everlasting destruction, not to eternal life purchased by the price of his blood.

And in the same work:

> His entire Passion is our cleansing. Therefore, since he was going to suffer the insults, he first performed acts of service—not only for those for whom he was about to undergo death, but also for the one who was going to hand him over to death.

And elsewhere (*Tractate* 62):

> “What you are doing,” he says, “do quickly” (John 13:27). He did not command the crime but foretold Judas’s evil and our good. For what was worse for Judas, and what was better for us, than that Christ was handed over by him, against Christ, for us, apart from him?

And elsewhere:

> How much Peter had presumed upon himself when he considered what he could do! How much he had presumed upon himself, so that when “the Lord had come to lay down his life for his friends” (John 13:37), and therefore also for him, Peter dared to offer this to the Lord and promised to lay down his own life for Christ, though Christ had laid down his life for him.

And elsewhere:

> Christ the Savior—which is his name—is the Savior of his faithful. For he is judge and condemner of the impious, while he deigns to be Savior of the faithful.

Blessed bishop and martyr Cyprian, in his book *On the Praise of Martyrdom and Martyrs*, showing that those destined from the beginning of the world to be sprinkled and cleansed by Christ’s blood had been predestined, says:

> O blessed ones, whom the Lord’s blood stained from the beginning of the world, and whom the splendor of this snow-white garment deservedly clothed, and the whiteness of the surrounding robe adorned!

Likewise, in his book *To Demetrianus*:

> Christ grants this grace; he bestows this gift of his mercy: subduing death by the trophy of the Cross, redeeming the believer by the price of his blood, reconciling the human being to God the Father, and giving the mortal life through heavenly regeneration. Let us all, if possible, follow him; let us be enrolled under the sacrament and sign of him. He opens for us the way of life; he brings us back to paradise; he leads us to the kingdom of heaven. With him we shall always live, made through him children of God; with him we shall always rejoice, restored by his blood.

Amen.

## In the Year of Our Lord 875. Wulfadus, Bishop of Bourges

[Col. 1135]

[Col. 1135]

## Historical Notice concerning Wulfadus

*(From* Gallia Christiana*.)*

[Col. 1135A] Wulfadus succeeded Rodulfus in the year 866, appointed by the emperor Charles the Bald, whose son Carloman he had educated, as is evident from a letter of that king to Pope Nicholas, written shortly before the Council of Soissons, in which he says:

> Rodulfus, archbishop of the Church of Bourges, has recently died, and that Church needs a wise, energetic, and manly shepherd, because of the frivolity of the morals and the instability of the people themselves. Therefore, after taking counsel, all the bishops and faithful of our kingdom, and the diocese itself, unanimously agreed upon the election of the aforesaid Wulfadus.

He had first been a canon of Saint Mary’s and treasurer of the metropolitan church of Rheims; in that capacity he took part in the synod held at Quierzy in the year 848. He was ordained a cleric by Ebbo of Rheims. For that reason he was unable to appear at the Second Council of Soissons, because of an illness that detained him in the monastery of Saint Medard. Accordingly, Archbishop Hincmar sent to him Sigloardus the archdeacon, who presented a document willingly signed by Wulfadus. Nevertheless, this did not prevent him from being deprived of his rank along with his associates at that synod.

However, by a decree of Pope Nicholas, his case and that of his colleagues were ordered to be reconsidered at the Third Council of Soissons in the year 866. At that council the supreme pontiff instructed Herardus, archbishop of Tours, that, unless Hincmar absolved Wulfadus and his associates, the Fathers of the council should do so by order of the Apostolic See.

After the matter had been carefully examined, the synod wrote a letter to the pope to excuse Hincmar, explaining that he had not dared, by his own authority and that of the bishops of his province, to restore Wulfadus to his former honor, but that his restoration ought to be reserved to the pontiff.

[Col. 1136A] In the meantime, when the primacy of Bourges became vacant through the death of his predecessor, Charles the Bald proclaimed Wulfadus bishop, whose appointment he had until then deferred without a determination from the Apostolic See. Thus, in a letter from the same king to the same Nicholas, he says:

> Because we have found that our brother Wulfadus, as the letters of your holiness indicate, excels among us in character and knowledge, we have hastened to entrust to him the Church of Bourges, together with the possessions belonging to it—which, as we informed your holiness in another letter, we had deferred granting without a determination from your Apostolate—so that, in the destruction of those possessions, the force of any wicked persons seeking to seize what is not theirs and cruelly lay waste to what belongs to others might not prevail.

And so forth. Charles excused the haste of Wulfadus’s promotion in the year 869 and requested the archbishop’s pallium for him.

Pope Adrian II granted the emperor’s request in his ninth letter to the Fourth Synod of Troyes, on the Nones of February 868. In accordance with earlier custom, he granted Bishop Wulfadus the use of the pallium, for the honor and adornment of the Church entrusted to him.

In the first year of his episcopate, in the fourteenth indiction and the twenty-sixth year of Charles’s reign, Wulfadus signed, with the other prelates of Gaul, a privilege granted by the Synod of Soissons to the monastery of Solignac in Limousin, where he calls himself the unworthy bishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Bourges.

He died on the Kalends of April in the year 876. His body was buried in the monastery of Saint Lawrence, after he had presided for ten years.

[Col. 1135]

## Pastoral Letter of Wulfadus, Bishop of Bourges, to His Parish Priests and Parishioners

*(Around the year 870.)*

*(In Mabillon,* Analecta, *p. 100.)*

[Col. 1135C] Wulfadus, although unworthy and a sinner, yet by the grace of God bishop of the holy mother Church of Bourges, sends greetings in the Lord to all his fellow priests and ministers, and also to all the children of the Church entrusted to me.

Beloved brothers, you who are called pastors in the Church should always be concerned for your salvation and for the price of your souls, and you ought to nourish and care for the Lord’s flock. We ask and beseech you that, continually meditating upon the matters that belong to your ministry, you seek with every intention the gain of the souls entrusted to you, and strive at all times to keep watch over the Lord’s people.

It is therefore the duty of our ministry to advise you concerning what is useful and necessary, and, if we can, to show you what is beneficial. Accordingly, beloved, you must take care to prove yourselves to be what you are called.

You are called priests: strive to be holy and pure, and to hold and exercise the holy priesthood worthily, since the Lord says concerning priests: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.”

You are called shepherds: strive diligently to govern and care for the sheep entrusted to you.

You are called watchmen: raise yourselves to a higher degree of virtue, holiness, and understanding, so that, having overcome carnal desires, you may be able to fight manfully against worldly assaults and spiritual wickedness.

Hold the right faith—which is the foundation of all virtues—firmly in your hearts, proclaim it with your mouths, devote yourselves more ardently to reading as far as you can, and strive to meditate upon the sacred Scriptures and divine commandments.

Apply yourselves vigilantly to prayer and psalmody, for these are the weapons by which the devil is conquered and Christ’s minister is strengthened in faith and good works.

Perform the duty of preaching appropriately among the peoples entrusted to you, and invite those who act well to better things by word and example. Rebuke and resist the wicked and impious courageously. Do not fear worldly conflicts, threats, or terrors in any way; strive instead to please God rather than human beings, and first display in yourselves what you preach to others.

Strive above all to possess religion and holiness, chastity and purity, in heart and body, so that you may show yourselves to be suitable ministers of Christ and, by the example of holiness and religion, instruct others in the service of Christ. Thus let purity, the radiance of holy conduct, and every virtue in common shine forth in you, so that, if your learning is less than it ought to be, your pure and holy conduct may still instruct your subjects to act well; and what you cannot teach by word and preaching, teach by the example of complete goodness. For when a person’s life is despised, it remains only that his preaching also be despised.

Love brotherly charity and cherish hospitality. Do not disgracefully run about through secular business, lest the sacred ministry appear to be cheapened in you. Show yourselves blameless in all conduct and action, lest the name of Christ be blasphemed in you.

Whatever unjust, dishonorable, or truly dangerous behavior you are able to observe and understand among the flocks of Christ entrusted to you—whether among the powerful and noble or among the lesser and poor, among males or females—strive to point it out to them without favor or partiality toward persons. Announce to each person his sins and iniquities without delay, negligence, or, indeed, shame; give them suitable counsel concerning all their crimes; and fear in every respect the knowledge of the Lord that threatens us all: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked person, I will require his soul from your hand.”

And again: “Cry out, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet,” and so forth.

Show their sins also to penitents who wander about through secular business as though they had done no evil, and admonish them to remain in one place and produce worthy fruits of repentance, declaring to them most truthfully that they cannot practice repentance and secular military service at the same time.

[Col. 1138A] You men of the lay order, too, I wish to admonish and desire to announce to you the things that concern your salvation, for I greatly fear for the danger to your souls, and I know that I shall have to render an account to God for all of you.

There are vices and sins by which the devil deceives mortals, and he continually labors for this purpose: to thrust them down with himself into hell and condemn them to perpetual death. These are: greed, pride, homicide, adultery, sacrilege, fornication, robbery, perjury, false witness, seizure of ecclesiastical property, dishonoring priests, unlawful oaths, the worst curses, wicked conspiracies, slander, whispering, discord, envy, hatred, drunkenness, dishonorable profits, unjust judgments, unequal measures, friendships pledged by oath and violated, ecclesiastical property taken away from the churches and converted to private use, monies and ninths withdrawn from the churches to which they are owed, and many other things that our Lord and Redeemer forbids and that the devil, our enemy and adversary, urges.

These vices and sins are so serious that, when they are committed at the devil’s instigation, they separate people from God, take away the heavenly inheritance and perpetual life, and procure for those who commit them the flames and torments of hell.

Therefore, beloved sons, I beseech you: let each person return to his conscience and carefully examine what sort of person he is and what he has done in childhood, adolescence, youth, and throughout every age of his life. If anyone sees that he has been a murderer, adulterer, sacrilegious person, fornicator, perjurer, or false witness, let him flee for refuge to God and the mother Church, make a pure confession of all his iniquities to the priests, and undertake penance and fulfill it most faithfully. Let him strive to erase and redeem what he has done wickedly through almsgiving, fasting, prayers, abstinence, and other good works. For unless he strives to correct himself here, while he has time and opportunity, he will not be able to possess the kingdom of God, as the Apostle testifies.

“Do not be deceived,” the Apostle says: “neither murderers, nor adulterers, nor sacrilegious persons, nor perjurers, nor robbers, nor male sexual offenders, nor drunkards, nor revilers shall possess the kingdom of God.”

[Col. 1138D] We also admonish those through whose dissension and discord this region has been devastated, afflicted by many miseries, and almost destroyed, to recognize their sin and iniquity, to recall continually to mind the wicked and cruel things they have done, and to let these things be for them at all times a cause of lamentation, sobbing, and covering of their eyes. Let them strive most earnestly to repent of them and to redeem themselves through almsgiving, fasting, prayers, and other works acceptable to God.

Likewise, we admonish those who once seized ecclesiastical property or who now retain it without the consent of those to whom it is owed, to come to their senses and perform penance for sacrilege, and to strive to make satisfaction both to God and to the churches they have injured.

We also admonish those who lightly swear numerous oaths and take the name of God and his saints in vain, or curse without reverence, to abstain from this sin and recognize how exceedingly hateful it is. Scripture says: “A person who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the plague will not depart from his house.” And, as stated above, revilers will not possess the kingdom of God.

We also admonish judges to judge justly, to bring right judgments to their conclusion, and always to keep the fear of God before their eyes, knowing that they themselves will have God as their judge and will themselves be judged by God for all their judgments, words, and deeds.

For he himself commanded: “You shall not show partiality to the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful. You shall not turn aside to the right or to the left; judge your neighbor justly.”

Let each person also beware of bringing forward false testimony in any way, because it is written: “A false witness shall not go unpunished.”

We have also heard that there are double measures among you, larger ones for buying and smaller ones for selling [lacuna]. We ask you to correct this and to have one just and equal measure in common, according to the Lord’s command: “Let your bushel be fair and your sextarius just.”

Abstain also from usury, knowing that it is not a small sin, since it is said in the Law: “You shall not lend at interest.”

Let the commercial transactions carried out in trade be conducted without oaths and perjuries, and let each person beware of deceiving his brother there by any fraud.

Do not seal these very friendships by oaths, as we have heard that some of you have done until now, because such an oath can never be made without sin. Let no one swear any oath to anyone unless he has first pledged the fidelity owed to his lord according to custom, or has sworn lawful and legitimate oaths.

Show due honor to your priests as ministers of God. If you have perhaps injured them in some way, strive to make satisfaction. If they themselves have acted otherwise than they ought, do not slander them; instead, either correct them yourselves if you can, or humbly report to their superiors—or at least to your bishop—what you truly know concerning them.

Honor carefully the Church of God, in which you received baptism, make your confessions, undertake penance, hear preaching, and receive other things by which you can be saved. Come very frequently to the church with your offerings, and there ask that prayers be made for you. Do not demand gifts intended for the churches in any way, and do not remain or stay there with your wives.

We admonish you not to engage in conspiracies and sworn associations against the king or princes, or indeed against one another, in any way, because this too is a grave offense and is strongly prohibited by divine and human laws.

Therefore drive useless slanders and whisperings away from you, and do not continue to engage in them in any way. For, as it is written: “The one who slanders kills both himself and those who listen.”

Do not retain hatred in your heart in any way, for, as the apostle John says in his Epistle: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.”

Drive envy and discord far from you, for the offerings and gifts of those who are discordant and envious are not acceptable to God. Nor should our offerings be received in the churches in any other way unless you have first truly expelled these things from your hearts.

Concerning the alms that sick or dying people entrust to relatives or friends, we ask you to distribute faithfully whatever you receive for this purpose, just as they themselves wish others to do for them. Let those who act rightly recognize that they will receive a reward from Christ; if they act otherwise, they will have to render an account to God for it.

Divine judgment terribly condemns those who defraud the alms of others. For thus it is read in the canons: “Those who defraud the alms of their brothers are anathematized.”

If any of you know that your parents have taken away ecclesiastical property, or have by force or evil contrivance taken away those properties, or inheritances of the poor, or a parental gift, and joined them to their own possessions, I beg you to have pity on their souls: restore to the Church what they unjustly took away, and return to the heirs what they unjustly took from them. Know with complete certainty that, so long as those possessions are retained by yourselves or by anyone else, those who did these things could not have an inheritance in the kingdom of God.

We also admonish the powerful to strive to govern and rule their own households, or the churches entrusted to them, well according to the fear of God. They should know that, although those under their authority are inferior in power, they are their brothers, and that they ought both to defend them from others and to regard them mercifully, without oppressing them through measures or unjust payments under any pretext.

We also admonish you, poor and less powerful people, to be subject to your lords, to serve them faithfully, and to render them truthfully and without fraud what you owe. Know that they too have been appointed over you by God, and that you ought to be subject to them.

We also admonish those who possess ecclesiastical property by the right of a benefice to return nones and tithes to the churches from which the property appears to derive, and not to retain them any longer in any way, lest they perhaps incur sacrilege.

Men should render the marital debt to their wives at the proper time, and in no way defile themselves with other pollutions. Wives likewise should love their husbands and strive to please them in everything, lest—God forbid—they drive them to other crimes. Both should take care not to enter churches unclean and unwashed after bodily intercourse. We also admonish concerning incest: let no one have intercourse with his close female relative, or with the close female relative of his wife, since this is most shameful and so thoroughly forbidden. Let him also take the greatest care not to hand over, or consent to hand over, the chastity of his daughter, granddaughter, or female relative—especially that of his wife—to be violated for the favor of any mortal, or to allow their chastity to be corrupted in any manner or by any device except lawful marriage.

At the three festivals of the year—the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost—each person, coming clean to church, should receive Communion, except those who are undergoing public penance; for unless someone receives Communion on these three solemnities, he ought not to be counted among Christians. Let each person therefore see to it that he receives the Communion of Christ worthily, cleanly, and devoutly; for whoever unworthily receives the Lord’s body and blood eats and drinks judgment upon himself. We therefore advise and beseech noblewomen, and all other women, to nurse their children with their own milk and never hand them over to maidservants or other women to be raised.

Take care, therefore, dearest sons, to grasp attentively and diligently in your minds what we write for your salvation, and to guard carefully against all these things; and wherever you recognize that you have sinned, strive with your whole purpose to amend, lest—God forbid—you perish miserably forever. Remember where your fathers are, where your kings are, your princes, your authorities, and all who loved the world; and know that you will all die very soon, and after this life will possess nothing good unless you have earned it by good works. I beg you, dearest ones, always keep death before your eyes, and consider what you will do after death; and take care not to fear death, for death can harm no good person. Love Christ your Redeemer with all your strength, love your neighbors as yourselves, honor the Church of God, obey the sayings and preaching of holy men, and hasten to come to the joy of paradise and the fellowship of the saints. May our God, the divine Trinity and undivided Unity, deem it worthy to lead you to their fellowship and, in gratuitous mercy, protect, console, and bless you—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## In the Year of Our Lord 875. Adventius, Bishop of Metz

[Col. 1141]

[Col. 1141]

## Adventius’s Little Book on Waldrada

In this work he attempts to prove that Waldrada, Lothar’s concubine, had been joined in marriage to Lothar by his father, the Emperor Lothar, from early youth; whereas Theutperga, his legitimate wife, was afterward joined to the king against his will by threats.

(Baronius, under the year 862, no. 29.)

[Col. 1141C] Lothar Augustus, of divine memory, was created emperor of the Roman kingdom by the election of the people and, governing the stronghold of the Frankish kingdom, entrusted a noble maiden named Waldrada to his son, Lord Lothar, in the name of divine faith, so that in God’s faith and his own he might in future protect and possess her. And so that this union might be seen to be lawful, in the instrument setting out the dowry he granted one hundred hides to the most glorious child, who was not yet legally independent, although he was to be his father’s heir; rather, he remained under guardians and administrators, as the Apostle says concerning such persons: “As long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, although he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and administrators until the time appointed by the father” (Gal. 4). But as long as the aforesaid emperor held the dignity of the Frankish kingdom, the aforementioned child remained attached to the girl given to him as a paternal gift. This was not done in a corner, for truth has no corners, but publicly, before bishops and nobles, as his tutors testify, including his uncle Leutfrid.

When the Emperor Lothar departed this life, during those very days of mourning for his father, Hucbert the Acephalous, with his accomplices, brought his sister, named Theutperga, to the illustrious young king Lothar and fraudulently joined her to him, threatening that danger to the king’s position in the kingdom would result if he did not follow their counsels. The king consented, although unwillingly, as he himself testified.

The evil reputation of Theutperga’s shameful conduct followed, and she was accused of incestuous intercourse with her brother Hucbert. A written confession was produced, in which she was read to have confessed voluntarily; she was condemned by the judgment of the counts, saved by the mercy of the bishops, and took flight. The most devout king, Lord Lothar, sent information about this affair to Rome through illustrious men and resolved to explain the circumstances. After learning the facts, the most blessed Pope Nicholas sent his legates—namely Rodoald, Bishop of Porto, and John of Fidiculense [also, Ficodense]—to Francia, and decreed that a general council should be held in the city of Metz.

There the most glorious King Lothar appeared with the entire company of his leading men and noble advisers and took his seat in the holy synod. There he set forth before the legates of the Roman see the grounds for his action: how his father, Lord Lothar, Augustus forever memorable, had given a most noble virgin to him with his own hand in the faith of God, and the other matters we have listed above. He also stated that Theutperga had publicly confessed her guilt at the aforesaid council held in the city of Metz, and that all the senators of the Frankish kingdom had acclaimed the matter as settled.

In these men shone both temporal and spiritual wisdom. Their fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers had governed the empire with the mature counsel of Rome; I observed their lineage continually adorned with the title of consul during the time of the emperors, Lord Louis and the most magnificent Lothar. The whole people acclaimed that their special prerogative of counsel should in no way be rejected, especially since no criminal culpability was charged against them, but their uprightness was raised to praise. Therefore, since many people freely form various opinions about these matters and offer numerous kinds of definitions, I shall make clear to the reverence of the faithful with what disposition I have treated and understood them.

When the most devout emperor gave his namesake son a girl distinguished by the nobility of her flesh, I had not yet been burdened with the episcopal office, nor was I present at these proceedings. When Theutperga was brought in and the second marriage was carried out, I knew of it only by hearsay. After these events had passed, when I had been sought by the clergy, elected by the people, and canonically consecrated bishop, I formed the following judgment concerning these matters:

The most Christian emperor gave a virgin to his son in the faith of Christ and in his own faith. The faith of God does not give a prostitute but rejects her, saying: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20). And the Psalmist says: “You will destroy all who fornicate away from you” (Ps. 72). Paul, who was girded with the faith of God, cries out: “Know and understand that no fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person—which is the service of idols—has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. 5). Bearing the mark of Jesus on his body—that is, the banner of faith—he does not foster adulterers but pierces them with the point of the sacred *faminis* [reading uncertain], saying: “Neither shall adulterers possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6).

The Lord, who is faithful and gives David his faithful promises, did not take away from the orthodox Emperor Lothar the authority to join his son to whatever girl he had decided upon. In the Gospel he says: “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery” (Matt. 19). Therefore, having heard these things, they ought with pious and devoted zeal to listen to and observe the canons of the fathers, for no one ought ever to transgress the boundaries established by the Fathers. For the sacred canons proclaim that a woman given as a paternal gift is free from guilt. The emperor, who was devoted to divine worship, did not permit his son, King Lothar, to make use of the detestable crime of fornication; this was the profession of the king and of all the senators concerning Waldrada: that his father had given her to him in the faith of God.

Concerning Theutperga, likewise, they all declared that she had confessed and been convicted of the evil of her crime, arising from the horrible embrace of her unchaste [reading: *impudici*] brother; she had been terrified neither by fearful threats from us nor encouraged by pleasant flatteries. Acting according to the Apostle, who says, “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom. 12), and listening to the voices of the noble counts—as we have noted above in examples from successive periods, namely, that the senators’ counsels had been heard and approved—I judged in all our subscriptions and definitions as follows: if Theutperga had confessed the aforesaid crime, I judged her unworthy of royal companionship.

And if Waldrada had been joined to the king through her father’s gift in the faith of God, I did not dare blaspheme the faith of God, lest Scripture’s dart of the word should pierce me, saying: “You shall not permit blasphemers to live” (Lev. 24). The Apostle grants permission for each person to abound in his own understanding (Rom. 14).

[Note: [Col. 1143C] Thus far extends the little book of Adventius, one of those who afterward deserved to be excommunicated by Nicholas, Roman pontiff. Yet he did not harden himself through obstinacy like the others—namely, the bishops of Cologne and Trier—but, repenting of his sin, accusing himself, and asking forgiveness, obtained it from that same Pope Nicholas, as is evident from the letter that follows immediately.]

[Col. 1143]

## Letter of Adventius to Theutgaud, Bishop of Cologne

He secretly informs him about the synod soon to be convened at Metz.

(Baronius, same place.)

[Col. 1143D] To the most reverend and most holy Father Theutgaud, desirable to us in every respect: Adventius, your devoted son and constant petitioner, sends the peace and glory of supreme happiness.

By God, and for God’s sake, we humbly beg that no other mortal see this present letter, but that devouring Vulcan consume it once it has been read. May your ancient gravity, mature counsel, and prudent protection—as an anchor of faith—be fixed in the firmament [reading: *foundation*] of wisdom, so that at this time you report nothing sinister or favorable to our senior, until all our fellow bishops, as they have certainly been summoned, meet at Metz on the Purification of Saint Mary. For you certainly know that our senior has resolved in every respect to promise that, according to their common counsel, he will be completely ready to do whatever seems best to them according to God; and, obeying their admonitions and counsels, he will do nothing otherwise hereafter.

Therefore it is necessary, dearest Father, for you to act cautiously now, lest—God forbid—by deviating from the way of God and from evangelical and apostolic teachings, he fall into the snare of Avernus. You may be certain that if, through our fault or some vain confidence, he now goes astray, the prophetic word will be fulfilled: “I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezek. 3).

We write these things because today we received Valthar, the faithful servant of our senior, returning from the palace. On our senior’s behalf, he affirmed to us in good faith the decision I have mentioned, just as I have stated; indeed, he repeatedly begged us to inform you of these things for the love of the Lord and to counsel you in every way, so that he might hear nothing from you or from your own lips that could cause him to waver from his salvation.

For it seems more suitable to us to feign illness than for a sick stomach to reject the medicine prepared by God. We wish you good health, dearest Father.

[Col. 1145]

## Letter of the Same to Pope Nicholas

He sends his profession, by which, clearing himself concerning the case of Lothar, he shows that he accepts and obeys the statutes established by the pontiff in the Roman synod; therefore he implores pardon and peace.

(From Mansi, *Councils*, vol. 15.)

[Col. 1145B] To the most glorious shepherd of the Lord’s flock, Lord and most blessed Nicholas, supreme and universal pope: Adventius, humble bishop of the see of Metz, now and forever sends greetings.

The Lord Christ God, looking with his customary compassion upon the flock acquired at the price of his own blood, bestowed upon you the dignity of the supreme priesthood. Among the many ornaments of spiritual virtues with which you adorn holy Mother Church with incomparable holiness, the sacred doctrines of ancient authority also shine abundantly. Through them the Christian people, happily instructed by the most effective example of so great a Father, will be able, with God’s help, to avoid the monsters of vice and attain eternal rewards; indeed, the discipline of the ecclesiastical order may remain inviolate in your times.

Therefore my littleness, and all those entrusted to me by divine favor, greatly rejoicing in many ways, give profound thanks to almighty God and beseech him in devoted prayers to preserve the summit of your pontificate safe for a long time, for the consolation of his holy Church and of all faithful souls.

For while we were beset by the fiercest pressures of the pagans and by the thickest hostilities of perverse Christians, and while we desired, in our humility, to bear the concern of the Lord’s fold, the decrees of your excellent apostolate were sent to us. Concerning these I would most eagerly have hastened to give a personal reply to your majestic dignity in your presence and with my living voice, unless long-standing old age made me weak and unremitting bodily illness frequently and unexpectedly forced me to breathe out my spirit.

I would have received great joy, indeed almost the joy of all merit, if the weakness of my strength had allowed me to go to the threshold of the Apostles and to your desirable and most exalted presence. But since the pains of gout and my aged limbs deny me what I desire, I entrust the measure of my littleness to almighty God, to Saint Peter, and to the incomparable greatness of your clemency. You hold the place of God and sit as the true apostle in the most reverend chair of the supreme prince; may I be cherished by your consolations.

For if I have been falsely defamed before your gentleness as though I were a supporter of vices, I humbly ask—prostrate in mind, though not in body, before your sacred feet—that you not disdain, in a fatherly spirit of compassion, to receive the grounds of my defense, obscured by no deceitful coloring of lies, which I have endeavored to set forth point by point to your mercy.

### I

I do not receive into the catalogue of priests Theutgaud, formerly archbishop, who has patiently borne until now the sentence of deposition pronounced by you and, in accordance with his former custom, has dared to take no part whatsoever in the sacred ministry. Rather, like a most gentle man, he confesses that he slipped through his own careless speech and was deceived by another’s most stubborn obstinacy; walking in the way of humility and obedience, he awaits from your pious generosity a place in which to make satisfaction.

### II

I do not regard Gunthar, formerly archchaplain of the sacred palace, as one of the bishops, nor do I dare communicate with him or with his supporters, because he used a forbidden office and was not afraid to treat the apostolic excommunication with contempt.

### III

The case of the most devout King Lothar was debated in our city, in the presence of your legates, by the aforementioned former primates of the Churches together with the other archbishops and their fellow bishops. You are not unaware of what the leading men among us decreed concerning the complaint of the aforesaid prince.

I therefore, with God as witness together with the angels and archangels, judged that the things proclaimed with the support of many counts remained true. Since the aforesaid archbishops and their fellow bishops were then issuing their decisions, was I alone—last in merit and ordination—to resist the authority and judgments of my superiors? I was also afraid that I might in some way offend against the decree of Pope Leo, who writes in title 22:

“Therefore, according to the canons of the holy Fathers, established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces retain unimpaired the right of the ancient dignity entrusted to them.”

If they had departed from the prescribed rules by any license or presumption, I was entirely unaware of it. Hence the Council of Antioch also says in chapter 9:

“In each region the bishops ought to know that the metropolitan bishop has responsibility for the whole province; therefore all who appear to have business should come from everywhere to the metropolis,” and so forth.

I learned what had taken place at the beginning of the aforementioned complaint only through the report of many, by ear and not by sight. For I was not yet a bishop, but was occupied in the watches of the church of the blessed Stephen, the protomartyr. Finally, in the kingdom of Lord Lothar, my senior, I was sought by the clergy and elected by the people, and—God knows—not seeking the pastoral office of my own accord, but canonically invited, I accepted its care.

I was much more credulous, if that is possible, of the words of the archchaplain and the other Fathers who were present than of myself. If I acted simply in any respect, it remains for me to return to the teacher of truth. Now, therefore, let your singular wisdom pronounce the rule applicable to this affair, and behold, I am ready to obey the decrees of your authority, as I would obey God, in whose person you pronounce all things. Following your holy and salutary counsel, I humbly submit myself to the yoke of obedience.

Although I sense that some, through levity, are raising a tumult of detraction against me, no one can accuse me in this matter except on the ground of simplicity. For I say confidently: “Behold, my witness is in heaven, and my conscience is on high.” Hence the vessel of election says: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 3). For this reason blessed Pope Gregory writes in a letter addressed to the patrician Theoctista (Book 9, Letter 39):

“In everything we do, or in whatever is said about us outside, we ought to return to the hidden places of the mind. Even if everyone condemns him, the person whom conscience does not accuse is free.”

### IV

If, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, the decree of your authority has determined that the aforesaid metropolitans are entirely deprived of every administration of pastoral office because of their violations of the sanctions and because of the absolution of the anathema issued by the apostolic see against Ingeltrude, the wife of Boson, know with complete certainty that I took no part whatsoever in her absolution. After I heard from a reliable report that she had been wounded by the accursed form of adultery, I always abhorred her as deadly poison.

I also admonish everyone to have no communion with excommunicated persons if they have dared to exercise sacred functions, as the fourth chapter of the Council of Antioch demonstrates, for it orders that those who communicate with them be expelled from the Church.

### V

I utterly deny that I am a follower of the condemned, a seditious person, or guilty of conspiracy or collusion; and I confess that I have in no way agreed with any supporters of such persons. Rather, in all things I profess canonical adherence to the head—that is, the holy and venerable see of blessed Peter, to whom Christ entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and upon whom Christ, the eternal King, built his holy Church, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail.

### VI

Moreover, your fatherly holiness has decreed inviolably that the admission of the good should in no way be feared on account of rash acts and subscriptions, and that indulgence should not be denied if we endeavored to agree with you and to offer our assent in writing, either personally or through our legates.

Let your most munificent holiness know that our legate, who would now have shown you the aforesaid profession and explained it in many words, was delayed because I summoned our other fellow bishops here and there from various regions and urged them to think and agree unanimously with you. Once I had learned of the general unanimity of all of them, standing as I do on the very brink of the present life, I sent ahead to your holy fatherhood the bearer of this letter, as the forerunner of our legate.

I do not allow anything ambiguous or condemnable to remain in me, for the dissolution of my own body promises that I shall soon take the way of all flesh. Yet I place great confidence in the mercy of almighty God: he ought to grant me, a sinner, a span of this troubled life until, cleansed by worthy satisfaction, I may understand that the grace of your fatherly piety has been restored to me as I ask for it, and may rejoice that I have been received into your fellowship worthy of God.

For we believe that, with God’s favor and that of the prince of all the Apostles—who are spiritually occupied with almsgiving, fasts, and secret prayers—you ought by every means, in accordance with the divine disposition, to foresee that living members of Christ’s body do not die through false deception.

Therefore, if your mercy is moved in any respect by my tearful prayers, I humbly beseech you by the holy and indivisible Trinity that, through the bearer of this letter—if nothing more is possible—I may at least deserve to receive from your holy hand, as one standing amid the shipwreck of life, what your gentle Master Christ invoked when he appeared to certain hesitant disciples through different doors, saying: “Peace be with you” (John 20).

We humbly and continually beseech you with vows and prayers that the excellence of your holiness may long flourish in safety.

[Col. 1149]

## Orations Delivered at the Synod Convened at Metz in the Church of Saint Stephen

[Col. 1149A] ### Chapter One

You know, and it is known in many kingdoms, what events, and how great, we commonly endured during the time of our former senior, whom until now we have had, on account of causes well known to all; and with what grief and anguish we have recently been struck in our hearts by his ill-starred death.

Therefore, deprived and desolated of our king and prince, we all considered that our one refuge and uniquely salutary counsel was to turn to him through fasts and prayers who is a helper in times of tribulation; whose is counsel and whose is the kingdom; and, as it is written, who gives it to whomever he wishes (Dan. 4); in whose hand are the hearts of kings, who makes them dwell with one mind in a house, breaking down the dividing wall and making both one.

We begged his mercy to give us a king and prince according to his heart, who would govern, save, and defend us in judgment and justice, in every order and condition, according to his will, and who would incline and unite all our hearts unanimously toward him whom he had foreknown, chosen, and predestined for our salvation and advancement according to his mercy.

[Col. 1150A] ### Chapter II

Since, finally, we see the will of God—who does the will of those who fear him and hears their prayers—in our concordant unanimity, we hold this man to be the legitimate heir of his kingdom, to whom we have freely entrusted ourselves: namely, our present lord, King and Prince Charles, so that he may preside over us and benefit us.

It seems to us, if it pleases you, that after his words we shall make this clear to you and demonstrate by the surest sign that we believe him to have been chosen by God and given to us as prince, and that we should not be ungrateful to God, the giver, for his benefits. Rather, giving him thanks, let us pray that he preserve him for us for a long time, for the salvation and defense of his holy Church and for the assistance and advancement of us all, together with salvation, peace, and tranquility; and that he govern us in his service under his administration, as we serve him with faithful devotion and enjoy the salvation we desire.

### Chapter III
