And, if it pleases him, it seems fitting for him and necessary for us that we hear from his own mouth what each person in his order ought to hear and receive with devoted mind from a most Christian king and from a people faithful and united in his service.

[Col. 1149]

## Adventius’s Privilege for the Abbey of Gorze [Year 863]

(From D. Calmet, *History of Lorraine*.)

[Col. 1149C] While the diligence of pastoral office keeps watch over the care of the flock entrusted to it, it does not hesitate to calm the harshness of persecutors hiding beneath a sheep’s skin. For when it assumes the place of God, the eternal King, so that through the power of his name respect of persons may be abolished and the inviolable judgment of equity strengthened, it is certainly not right to conceal the freedom of truth. The Lord says: “In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage, for I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

It is no slight offense to share in the sins of others. Those who preside over the sacred seats of the Churches ought, for the exaltation of the dignity entrusted to them, to keep watch with the ingenious care of great solicitude, so that the spiritual sheep may be able to perform their sacred service without harassment from any occasion.

Therefore Adventius, bishop by the grace of divine regard of the holy and venerable see of the city of Metz, while carefully watching over the people entrusted to him and exerting himself with the keen intelligence of a diligent mind [the text reads *desuflans*, perhaps *desudans*, “toiling”], restored, with God’s help, to their proper condition the monasteries and estates belonging to the magnificent altar of the most precious martyr of Christ. These had formerly been alienated after the death of my predecessor, Archbishop Drogo, of revered memory, not only through the security obtained by royal decree from the most excellent King Lothar, but also through the authority of the synodal decision canonically celebrated in our see under the rule of the supreme and universal Pope Nicholas.

There, too, we received by mandate of the Roman see this privilege: that we should restore the property of our Church, as is contained in the same privilege, which was enacted at that holy synod by the judgment of the blessed Pope Nicholas’s legates and with the consent of many bishops from various regions.

It is evident to all how many wounds our Church endured, when monasteries became the dwellings of secular men and the inheritance of God was almost stripped of its own services through wicked distribution. Among these losses by plunder was the noble monastery of our diocese founded on the River Gorze in honor of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul and of the blessed Stephen the protomartyr, where the distinguished body of the blessed martyr Gorgonius is buried and preserved.

In the time of our aforesaid predecessor, the monastery suffered the division of its possessions in every direction when its own abbot, named Haldinus, was taken from this light. The situation became so bad—we cannot say it without grief—that the sacred band of monks scarcely had the necessities of food. But when King Lothar decided that the aforesaid place should serve lay commands, he entrusted it to a certain count, Buinio. As the provisions of food and clothing gradually failed, regular observance diminished, monastic religion weakened, the churches were adorned with no beauty of ornament, and the altars themselves suffered from rain and exposure.

Struck by these sobs of lamentation, I wailed with the Prophet: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep for my people day and night?” (Jer. 9:1).

Since my constant concern was the aforesaid monastery, which my predecessors had enriched with a new endowment of liberality, I approached the glorious King Lothar. After setting forth the privileges and charters on which the sacred place rested, I hastened to rescue it from the power of unlawful domination. There I appointed an abbot of regular observance, named Betto, so that the monks, not forgetful of their profession, might know how to bow their necks to the sweetest yoke of Christ.

Indeed, after my predecessor, Archbishop Chrodegangus, had furnished the aforesaid monastery with a new foundation, it was governed by regular abbots until the oppressive disasters mentioned above; they possessed and administered the entirety of its accruing resources.

Therefore, since with God’s cooperation we have freed it, together with everything belonging to it, from the control of wicked devastation, we decree that the monastery of Gorze, in honor of the blessed Apostle Peter and the martyr Stephen, where the renowned martyr Gorgonius shines with the admirable glory of his virtues, shall be governed according to the rule. We establish that it, together with the restoration of all its possessions to their former integrity, shall be held perpetually by Abbot Betto and his successors.

Whenever anyone departs by the way of all humanity, whether our vassal or any other person who holds benefits from the aforesaid possessions, we entirely forbid his sons and relatives to obtain them. Rather, without delay and without anyone’s opposition, they shall return to Abbot Betto, his successors, and the monks who serve God there.

If in the meantime an occasion should arise in which we can suitably exchange something from our demesne or from the possessions that many still hold through our beneficence, we shall give from our own so that the restoration of Saint Peter’s property may remain complete. Let the aforesaid abbot, with the monks entrusted to him, arrange the leases and exchanges, and let him do what he judges useful.

We restore the chapels of the villages and the dotal properties to their ancient condition, so that, as they were in the time of Theomar, abbot of that place, they may serve the needs of the brothers. Let the household of the same monastery remain in the service in which it existed in former times.

Finally, we humbly and earnestly desire that the aforesaid place continue under the same privilege of honor, with all its appurtenances, as is contained in the decrees of my predecessors. Let the estates of the villages that have been acquired, or that have been or will be donated by noble men, be perpetually subject to the uses and arrangements of the abbot and monks, so that they may have sufficient spiritual and temporal resources and please God forever.

But if he himself, or any of my successors, should, in view of God and out of reverence for God and for the patronage of the saints placed in the aforesaid place, and for the perpetual remedy of our soul, judge this arrangement void or weaken it in any part, let him know that he will have to render a terrible account on the day of the dread judgment for his sacrilegious daring, when the most just Lord and Judge comes to judge and brings a worthy recompense for every deed.

Therefore, so that this decree of our firmness may be observed forever and changed by no one, we have determined to establish it immutably by the writing of our own hand. I, Adventius, bishop of the holy Church of Metz, have confirmed with my own hand this restoration of the privilege concerning ecclesiastical property, and I earnestly and humbly beg all my successors, through Christ, to strengthen it with their hands.

In the year 873 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction 11, epact 28.

[Col. 1151]

## Epitaph Written by Adventius Himself

(*Literary History of France*, vol. 5, p. 431.)

[Col. 1151D]

Sorrowful is the origin of man, but more sorrowful still his final lot.

Envious death reclaims what its own rights demand.

Let the man abounding in wealth fear it greatly; let the needy man fear it too.

O boy and old man, beware death’s bitterness.

[Col. 1152D]

Unafraid, fearful, brave, terrified alike—

Here all perish under the setting lot!

Here I, once adorned with vain purple and gold,

Experience greedy Fortune in the tomb.

[Col. 1153A]

The Creator of the world granted me immeasurable riches;

He took them away; I am needy, with modest and scant possessions.

When the people acclaimed me, I accepted the office of bishop.

I distributed the life-giving seeds to the flock sparingly.

I revered Christ’s churches with honorable worship;

May the heavenly citizens obtain forgiveness of sin from this.

Once I sang joyful songs; now I compose sorrowful ones—

A graceful Muse prepares the funeral rites.

[Col. 1154A]

Francia gave me birth; my father was named Saxo.

I deserved to receive the new name Oromates.

Read this and say: “May Adventius possess blessed rest,

Seeking the blessed kingdoms with his shining-white flock.”

When the King of heaven comes to return what is due to the created,

Open the way for him across the grass of paradise.

I beseech the Triune Lord, and call upon the One,

Let no hand violate the enclosure of the mausoleum.

## Letter on the Cynocephali

[Col. 1153]

[Note: [Col. 1153] The following short work, omitted in its proper place, closes the series of works of Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, which you have above in this volume.]

## Letter of Ratramnus, Monk of Corbie, on the Cynocephali, Written to Rimbert the Priest

(From Oudinus, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. 2.)

[Col. 1153B] To Rimbert, honored priest, distinguished by the gifts of divine grace and greatly beloved in Christ: Ratramnus sends everlasting salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Since you remembered our request and wrote to us what you had been able to learn about the nature of the Cynocephali [Note: [Col. 1153D] Thus in all the manuscripts.], you greatly delighted me. But as for my not replying at all to what you asked, know that this did not happen through the sluggishness of negligence, but because the matter had been deferred, since the presence of the messenger had not brought it about. Now, however, since Brother Sarward has come to us and is returning to you, we have taken the opportunity to make known briefly what seemed to us concerning your inquiry.

For you ask what you ought to believe about the Cynocephali—namely, whether they were descended from the stock of Adam, or whether they possess the souls of beasts [Col. 1153C]. This question can be determined briefly as follows. If they are to be reckoned among the human race, no one ought to doubt that they descended from the lineage of the first man. For it is not permissible to believe that human origin was derived from anywhere other than the substance of the first parent. But if they are counted among the race of beasts, they share with human beings only the name, not the nature.

Nevertheless, it must be understood that, if we are content with the opinion of our own people, namely, the teachers of the Church, they should be reckoned among beasts rather than among human beings, since both the shape of their heads and their barking show them to be like beasts, not human beings. Human beings, after all, look toward heaven with the rounded crown of the head, whereas dogs, with their elongated heads and extended muzzles [Col. 1153D], look toward the ground. Human beings speak, but dogs bark.

Yet the letters sent to us by your charity [Col. 1154B], while describing their nature more carefully, have taught us certain things that seem to belong more properly to human reason than to bestial sensibility: namely, that they observe certain laws of social life, as their dwelling together in villages testifies; that they practice agriculture, as is also shown by their harvesting of crops; that they do not expose their private parts in the manner of beasts, but cover them with human modesty, which is an indication of shame; and that, as you have written, in their use of coverings they possess not only skins but also garments. All these things seem in some way to testify that a rational soul exists in them.

For since a city is said to be a gathering of human beings living together under the same law, and since these people are said to dwell together in the fellowship of villages, it is not unreasonable to believe that the character of a city applies to such beings [Col. 1154C]. Indeed, by their gathering they form a multitude, and they could not dwell together except under some law of social condition. Wherever some law is observed, there is also a unity maintained by the agreement of minds. Nor can there be any law that has not been established by common consent. But such a condition could never have been established or preserved without the discipline of morality.

Moreover, to cultivate fields, break up the earth, and commit seed to agricultural investment demonstrates knowledge of a craft [Col. 1154D]. This activity is known not to belong to beings deprived of reason [Col. 1155A]. For it is the work of reason to seek the cause of each action where there is a cause: what makes the earth fertile, and what cause produces the abundance of seed. Without knowledge of these things, agriculture can never be properly practiced.

Furthermore, to know how to make coverings, whether from skin, wool, or flax, is the activity of a rational soul. Such things cannot be prepared without some form of craftsmanship, and knowledge of a craft is granted only to a rational soul. But to cover the private parts is a sign of propriety, which is sought only by a mind possessing the capacity to distinguish between what is shameful and what is honorable. For no one can feel shame at disgrace unless he has acquired some knowledge of propriety.

No one except a person lacking reason will deny that all these things belong properly to a rational soul. To distinguish between what is honorable and what is shameful, to possess knowledge of crafts, and to establish laws of peace and harmony cannot be done without the judgment of reason or the sharpness of understanding. Therefore, when you say that such things are observed among the Cynocephali, you testify in reality that they possess a rational mind. A human being differs from beasts by reason alone. Since reason appears to exist in those of whom we are speaking, they seem therefore to be reckoned as human beings rather than as beasts [Col. 1155B].

This understanding also seems to receive considerable support from the little book published concerning the martyrdom of Saint Christopher. As we read in it, he is known to have belonged to this race of human beings, whose life and martyrdom are commended by exceptionally illustrious virtues. For it is believed that he also received the sacrament of baptism through divine agency, a cloud pouring water over him, as the little book itself testifies.

Common report likewise relates many things that seem to indicate that this kind of human being possesses reason. Isidore too, when speaking in his *Etymologies* about the variety of prodigies arising from the human race, says among other things:

> “Just as among individual nations [Col. 1155C] there are certain monstrous human beings, so in the human race as a whole there are certain monstrous nations, such as Giants, Cynocephali, Cyclopes, and others.”

In saying this, he clearly indicated that he believed the Cynocephali had derived their origin from the lineage of the first man. For just as among individual nations certain beings appear to be produced contrary to the law of nature—such as two-headed people, three-armed people, dwarfs, hermaphrodites or androgynes, and many others—yet these are not made contrary to the law of nature but arise according to a certain particular arrangement, since the law of nature is the disposition of the Divinity, so likewise those monstrous births mentioned above appear to introduce a prodigious generation into the natural order of the entire human race.

There are also many others whom it would take too long to enumerate [Col. 1155D]: Pygmies, Anticaudae (“Back-tailed people”), some of whom are said to possess a bodily stature of one cubit, while in others the feet are turned backward behind the legs and the soles have eight toes; Hippodes, who mingle human form with equine feet; Macrobii, who almost double the height of ordinary human beings; and a nation of women in India who conceive in their fifth year and do not live beyond their eighth year, as well as many other things difficult to believe and absurd to relate.

Although these beings are said to have derived their origin from the human race, it does not immediately or rashly follow that they are human beings endowed with reason. Concerning the Giants [Col. 1156A], however, who are counted among these prodigies, scarcely anyone doubts that they were human beings born from human beings, since we know that this is asserted on the authority of the divine Scriptures. Since the Cynocephali are counted among them, it is thought that the same should also be believed about them—especially if those things that are read about Saint Christopher are established, as well as what popular report spreads about them.

Yet it does not follow from our saying or thinking these things that whatever is born from a human being must also be human and endowed with the faculty of human reason. For example, although it is read that a calf was born from a woman, or that a serpent was born from a woman, I would nevertheless not agree that either the calf or that serpent possessed a human or rational soul.

There was also that monstrous birth [Col. 1156B], produced from a woman in the time of King Alexander, whose upper part displayed a human being, while its lower part produced the forms of various living beasts. Yet, although those beasts had been begotten from human seed, I think that no one except a person deprived of reason would ever agree that they possessed a rational soul.

Accordingly, I would not believe that those about whom this matter is concerned possess a rational mind simply because they derived their origin from human beings, if the things you have written, or the things that are read and reported about them, had not led me to think as I do. But now the reports about them seem so numerous and so compelling that to refuse to believe them, or to wish to contradict them, appears more like obstinacy than prudence.

It must also be added that your writings testify [Col. 1156C] that among them are found every kind of domestic animal kept in our regions. I do not see how this could happen if they possessed a bestial rather than a rational soul. For we learn from the reading of Genesis that the animals of the earth were divinely subjected to human beings. But that beasts should care for living creatures of another kind, especially domestic animals, attend to them, compel them by their commands to submit, and make them serve their uses is known neither by report nor by belief.

But since the Cynocephali are said to possess a multitude of domestic animals, the ferocity of beasts is wholly unsuited to them, since their animals are tamed by domestic gentleness. These are the things that I think ought to be believed about the Cynocephali. As for whether others have chosen to think the same, or the contrary, that will not be a matter for our judgment.

Regarding the book of blessed Clement, about which you asked [Col. 1156D], it is not regarded among learned men as possessing complete authority, although it is not wholly rejected. For certain things are read in it that do not entirely correspond to our—that is, ecclesiastical—doctrine. But the things written in it concerning the deeds of the apostle Paul are accepted, since it contains nothing that either contradicts or opposes Christian teaching.

We rejoice that your blessedness may always be well in Christ, and we ask that you remember us.

Chapter One: On the various customs of the Church. What must be held uniformly by all in the Church. Customs are sometimes changed — 303  
Chapter Two: Again on the various customs of the Church. The Lenten fast formerly celebrated in different ways; the use of various foods; differing rites; how many sects formerly existed among the Jews — 306  
Chapter Three: The Greeks blame the Romans for fasting on Saturday. For what purpose the Saturday fast is observed. The objection of the Greeks. The response — 311  
Chapter Four: The Romans are rebuked because they do not observe Lent according to the Greek custom. For what reason the forty-day fast before Easter is observed. Different numbers of weeks are kept. Why some Westerners fast for thirty-six days. The number forty is explained — 317  
Chapter Five: The matter of shaving the beard or head is discussed — 322  
Chapter Six: Clerical celibacy is defended against the Greeks. Clerical celibacy is affirmed by ecclesiastical laws — 324  
Chapter Seven: The Greeks contend that the sacrament of Confirmation can be conferred by priests. The author refutes them. How a priest differs from a bishop — 332  
Chapter Eight: The Greek emperors attempted to place the patriarch of Constantinople before the Roman pontiff. The Roman Church surpasses all other dignities — 334

## King Lothair

Three letters — 371  
Letter One: To Pope Nicholas. He complains that the pontiff believes his rivals concerning him too readily. He indicates that he grieves over the excommunication of Theutgaud and Guntharius. In every other respect clearing himself, he shows himself ready to refute the accusations of his opponents before the pontiff — 371  
Letter Two: To the same. To escape the excommunication threatened because of his association with Waldrada, he announces his arrival at Rome to Nicholas; to deceive him with good hope, he appoints a delegation of bishops to him and also promises assistance against the Saracens, if necessary — 374  
Letter Three: To Pope Adrian II. Having learned of Nicholas’s death, Lothair writes this letter to his successor Adrian, asking that he obtain from him what he could not obtain from Nicholas: his arrival at Rome — 376
